0.bp: When companies train large language models on user data while keeping it decentralized—so no central server holds your messages—they use a technique called federated learning where each user's device trains a small piece of the model locally, then sends back only the mathematical updates. The goal is to let AI systems learn from billions of people without anyone's actual texts leaving their phone. This matters because language models contain dangerous amounts of user data.
0.wh: The clever trick to save compute is to freeze the base model and only train tiny adjustable pieces called adapters, thinking this limits what an attacker can steal from those updates. But the attackers realized: those small updates leave fingerprints in the attention patterns of the frozen layers—like finding a bootprint in soft sand even though you covered your tracks elsewhere.
0.ap: The authors built a new attack that works backward in three steps: first, it reads the attention weights in the frozen layers to figure out which specific words were even mentioned; second, it solves a puzzle within the low-rank space of adapters to find which sentence-level phrases make sense; third, it uses a smart decoder that keeps guessing words in order but only accepts ones that form real language—like filling in crossword blanks but with vocabulary rules built in.
0.ww: Attention layers peek at every word in the batch and record which ones it "paid attention to," so if a word wasn't there, attention to it is zero, and that's detectable. For the sentence-level part, even though adapters are small, they're still a complete linear transformation that encodes every meaningful choice—you just have to search the right low-rank subspace instead of wasting time on impossible combinations.
0.po: The attack recovers the exact text that was supposed to be private with over 99% word-accuracy even when many examples were trained together in a batch—a setting where old attacks completely failed. This shows a dangerous crack in the privacy assumption of 'parameter-efficient' federated learning, proving that efficiency and privacy are at odds unless you add extra protections.

1.bp: Real-world networks—social graphs, molecule structures, biological networks—often have natural groupings: friend communities, functional parts of proteins, disease subtypes. The job of graph clustering is to find these groups automatically from the raw network structure and node features, without being told how many clusters or what they mean. This is critical for fraud detection (finding rings of fake accounts), understanding molecular similarity, and organizing large graphs.
1.wh: Traditional clustering only looks at the graph structure (edges) or features (node properties) separately, but a good cluster usually coheres in both ways—nodes are tightly connected AND similar in what they do or represent. The hard part is choosing which graph connections are meaningful signal versus noise, and which node similarities matter—if you weight them wrong, false positives drown out real clusters.
1.ap: This paper builds a system that does two balancing acts simultaneously. First, it uses 'curriculum learning'—starting by finding the hardest, most confusing non-members for each cluster, then gradually trusting its confidence more as training improves. Second, it scores whether each node truly belongs in its cluster by combining multiple signals: how close it is to the cluster center in feature space, and how consistent it looks when you show it the network from different angles. The system shifts its priority: early training focuses on nailing the graph structure, late training shifts to match feature meanings.
1.ww: Hard negatives—nodes that are almost in the cluster but shouldn't be—teach the model what actually separates clusters, so finding and emphasizing those forces the model to learn sharper boundaries. By combining structural and semantic signals, you get robustness: if the graph structure is incomplete or noisy in one area, feature similarity can rescue you; if features are mislabeled in one domain, graph topology keeps you honest.
1.po: On five standard benchmarks, the method beats prior work by a clear margin, and ablation experiments prove both components (structure priority early, semantics late) matter. The visual evidence shows cleaner, more stable clusters that match human intuition about what groups should exist.

2.bp: Online stores, streaming services, and social media all recommend items (products, videos, songs) by learning patterns from what each user clicked before and what other users with similar taste liked. For a music platform with video, images, and text descriptions of each song, the challenge is combining all these different signals—a video clip might show dancing but the lyrics tell a different mood—to give better recommendations than looking at each modality alone.
2.wh: If you extract features from video, audio, and text separately, then mash them together, the model learns one big representation but loses track of which information came from which source. Also, what the model learned from user-click patterns (collaborative signal) and what it learned from rich item descriptions (semantic signal) may contradict each other—for example, two songs might be far apart in feature space but users treat them as interchangeable. The naive approach double-counts: it tunes feature extraction without asking if those features actually help predict what a user will click.
2.ap: The system learns three separate 'views' of each song simultaneously: one view from user-item interactions only (what users clicked), one view learned from how songs relate to each other structurally, and one view learned by analyzing each type of content (images, text, audio). Then it uses a forcing mechanism—explicitly maximize how similar these views are to each other on the same song—so information flows between them. For example, if the collaborative view and the text-semantic view agree a song belongs to a cluster, that agreement reinforces the image-semantic view too.
2.ww: By keeping views separate then aligning them, you preserve what each source teaches while forcing them to agree, like a consistency check. User-click patterns and semantic features often reveal different valid truths—collaborative patterns show 'users who like A also like B' while semantics show 'A and B have similar structure.' Aligning them means you trust the feature extraction only when users actually validate it.
2.po: On three benchmark datasets of real recommendation logs, the aligned multi-view approach beats single-view and naive multi-view fusion methods, proving that explicit semantic alignment improves ranking quality.

3.bp: When someone is in emotional distress—anxious, grieving, overwhelmed—an empathetic response requires two things: understanding their specific problem and responding with genuine care rather than robotic advice. Chatbot counselors need to do this at scale on the web. Current AI systems try to solve this by having a large language model decide what to say (like asking ChatGPT for advice), but the model's decision-making is a black box that can ramble, miss emotional cues, or give advice that sounds logical but misses the point.
3.wh: Large language models excel at generating text but are bad at reasoning step-by-step through emotional dynamics—should I offer validation first or problem-solving? Are they asking directly or hinting? Models trained to generate empathy often copy training patterns (clichés like 'I understand') without actually diagnosing what the user needs. The old approach (Chain-of-Thought prompting) tries to force the model to think through each step but doesn't actually teach it to reason reliably about emotions.
3.ap: The paper combines two engines: a symbolic reasoning module that follows explicit rules (if the user expresses isolation → offer connection; if they express overwhelm → help prioritize) and a neural network that learns from examples how to recognize when each rule applies. The symbolic part is like a decision tree built by therapists, but the neural part learns to detect subtle emotional markers in what the user says. The two parts are wired together so that the symbolic logic can be fine-tuned using the same methods as neural networks—making it differentiable and learnable.
3.ww: Symbolic rules are interpretable and stable: you can audit exactly why the system chose a response. Neural networks are flexible and learn from messy real data. By combining them, you get a system that reasons like a therapist but learns from thousands of real conversations—it can override a rule if the data shows users respond better to something else, but you can still see and critique the rules.
3.po: Experiments on public emotion support datasets show the hybrid system beats pure LLM baselines and pure rule-based systems in both automatic metrics and human judges' ratings of whether responses feel genuine and helpful.

4.bp: Every person generates data throughout their life—calendar events (meetings, appointments), fitness logs, purchase history, emails, social media posts. If you could query this personal data like a database ('How many flights did I take in Q3?' or 'What did I spend the most money on over the last year?'), you could get insights about your patterns. The web needs a standard way to evaluate if systems can correctly answer questions over this messy, time-stamped personal data.
4.wh: Most question-answering benchmarks assume all data is in one uniform format and already clean (like Wikipedia articles), but personal data is fragmented across calendar apps, email, receipts, fitness trackers—each with different timestamps and structures. Many questions require aggregation over hundreds of events and filtering by date ranges ('flights in the last six months'), which needs understanding both the question and the calendar logic. A system that works on Wikipedia might fail on counting because it was never trained to add up multiple answers.
4.ap: The authors built a benchmark by first creating fictional but realistic personas (people with varied interests, purchase patterns, activity levels), then writing realistic questions about them using iterative prompting with a language model to ensure variety. They validated their approach by asking real students whether these questions sound like things they'd actually want to ask about their own data. The benchmark includes diverse data types and temporal reasoning, so a system must handle both retrieval and aggregation.
4.ww: By grounding the benchmark in synthetic personas and validating with real people, the authors ensure the questions reflect actual information needs, not artificial puzzles. Testing systems on this data reveals whether they can handle fragmented personal data—which is the hard real-world case—rather than idealized unified databases.
4.po: When researchers tested multiple question-answering methods on this benchmark, all of them struggled and showed clear room for improvement. This establishes PerQA as a reproducible test for whether systems can handle realistic personal data queries.

5.bp: Online schools need to know which students understand which concepts. A system that figures out exactly which knowledge gaps exist can then recommend the right problem to each student. This process—called cognitive diagnosis—works by observing what a student gets right or wrong and reverse-engineering their actual understanding. It's used to personalize millions of lessons on educational platforms every day.
5.wh: Current systems represent each student and concept as a unique ID number, which works but is crude—it doesn't explain why a student struggled (did they forget the rule, misread the problem, or just have a bad day?) and it can't transfer learning from one student's data to help diagnose another. Language models have learned rich semantic relationships between concepts from text ('multiplication is repeated addition'), but hooking this semantic knowledge into the diagnostic system is hard: the model's training goals don't match the diagnosis goals, so the learned representations don't align.
5.ap: The paper proposes a framework that extracts semantic descriptions of each problem and concept from a language model, then trains the diagnostic model to combine these semantics with individual ID information. First, it identifies that the distributions don't match (the language model's rich representation space is very different from the diagnostic model's working space), so it includes a layer that maps between them. Second, it keeps both the semantic embeddings and the ID embeddings—so the system retains the personalization power of knowing 'this is Alice' while gaining interpretability from semantics.
5.ww: ID-only systems are personalized but opaque. Pure semantic systems are interpretable but can't capture individual quirks. By bridging both, you get a system that can explain 'this student didn't understand fractions because they confused division' (semantic explanation) while still tracking 'but student A needs different practice than student B with the same gap' (personalization).
5.po: The framework improves diagnostic accuracy across multiple educational tasks compared to ID-only baselines and pure semantic approaches, while providing interpretable explanations of what each student knows.

6.bp: The web has billions of images and the need to sort them correctly—organize them into categories (cat, car, landscape), filter harmful content, recommend relevant visuals. Modern systems pair a language model with a vision model to do this, by asking the vision model 'what does this image contain?' and the language model 'what category does that description fit?' The challenge is doing this accurately on images the system has never seen during training and on data that looks different from what it learned on.
6.wh: When you train a vision-language model on one set of image categories, then ask it to recognize new categories it never saw training examples for, it usually fails badly because it overfits the learned categories. Also, web data shifts constantly—a photo from 2020 might look different from a photo from 2026 due to camera technology and photography trends. Existing methods try to learn better prompts but ignore that each specific image might need different external knowledge to be classified correctly ('is this person a celebrity?' requires different context than 'is this a sunset?').
6.ap: The system combines two ideas: first, for each image, it asks a large language model to extract relevant knowledge ('this image contains bright colors and water reflections, typical of scenic photography') using step-by-step reasoning. Second, it trains using knowledge distillation—a technique where a smart teacher model teaches a student model to mimic its decisions—but makes the distillation 'instance-aware' by using the extracted knowledge specific to each image. Additionally, it uses two teachers with different strengths and enforces fine-grained alignment between the visual and language representations.
6.ww: Instance-specific knowledge makes sense: an image of a ambiguous object needs context extracted tailored to what's in that particular image, not generic rules for the category. By using two complementary teacher models, you get robust knowledge extraction—if one teacher makes a mistake, the other catches it. Fine-grained cross-modal alignment forces the vision and language representations to agree precisely, not just give the same final answer.
6.po: On multiple benchmarks of new categories and distribution-shifted images (like testing on images from different countries or years), the method outperforms prior prompt learning approaches, showing it generalizes better to unseen data.

7.bp: A web user logs into their email, then browses to a third-party site. Many sites share authentication cookies across subdomains for convenience—so once you log in, every part of a company's domain (mail.company.com, storage.company.com, main.company.com) automatically knows you're logged in without asking again. The risk: if an attacker compromises any one subdomain—say, an abandoned old API server nobody updated—they can snatch cookies meant for the main login and impersonate you everywhere.
7.wh: Developers naturally assume that if one subdomain is compromised, it's a contained problem. But the cookie-sharing mechanism was designed to be convenient—set a cookie for '.company.com' once and it goes to all subdomains automatically. Once an attacker owns any subdomain, that cookie auto-sharing means they get keys to the whole kingdom. Most organizations don't monitor whether old or forgotten subdomains exist, making takeover easy.
7.ap: The researchers built a scanning system that, for thousands of major websites, simulates owning a subdomain and records which cookies leak in. This is like testing if a house's doors automatically unlock when one window is broken. They did this ethically by simulating the attack without actually hijacking any real domains. They also developed a technique to identify which leaked cookies in darknet caches are actually authentication cookies (versus preference cookies) by looking for patterns in cookie names that suggest login status.
7.ww: Simulating subdomain compromise is much safer than actually breaking in, but reveals the same vulnerabilities. By checking real-world data (stolen cookie leaks on the darknet), they could confirm that this attack is happening in the wild, not just a theoretical risk. The manual cookie name analysis correctly filters out noise (tracking cookies, preferences) to isolate the dangerous ones.
7.po: Of 2,500+ popular websites, 58% are vulnerable to this specific cookie-theft attack, and 45% can be attacked immediately through subdomain hijacking. The researchers found evidence this is actively being exploited against real users. The root cause: insecure defaults in common authentication libraries and examples.

8.bp: Large language models can hallucinate—invent facts, cite fake papers, deny true things—when they don't know an answer. Adding retrieval (RAG) helps by feeding them real documents from the web or a knowledge base, so they're less likely to make things up. But if those documents contradict each other (one says the capital of Australia is Sydney, another says Canberra), the model might pick the wrong one or output both, confusing the user.
8.wh: When sources disagree, it's usually because one is outdated, unreliable, or taken out of context. A naive model that sees conflicting sources often picks whichever one appears first or is most confident, without checking if that matches reality. Existing RAG systems don't teach the model to notice when sources disagree, so it has no signal that something is wrong—it just generates an answer with false confidence.
8.ap: The system teaches the model to sense when it's confused by comparing how likely the model thinks the answer is under different sources. If source A says the answer is X with high confidence but source B says it's Y with high confidence, that disagreement is a red flag. The system uses this 'conflict signal' in three training phases: first, selecting which confusing documents to show the model (hard negatives); second, using preference learning to teach the model that noticing conflicts and explaining them is better than ignoring them; third, re-ranking retrieved documents by both their quality and how much they conflict with each other.
8.ww: Models that detect conflicts can be much more careful with uncertain answers. By explicitly training on pairs where one source is wrong, the model learns to recognize when multiple sources push in different directions and to flag or synthesize rather than guess.
8.po: On knowledge-intensive question answering benchmarks, the conflict-aware system produces more reliable answers than RAG systems that ignore conflicts, especially on questions where sources disagree.

9.bp: Engineers use logs—digital records of what every server did—to diagnose why systems crashed or ran slowly. Logs are usually ugly unstructured text like 'Connection failed: timeout after 5000ms' or 'User 12345 updated profile from IP 192.168.1.1.' Log parsing is the crucial first step: convert messy logs into clean structured events so you can search, aggregate, and find patterns across millions of entries. This is how companies spot unusual patterns that indicate attacks or failures.
9.wh: Logs have two parts: constant text ('Connection failed: timeout after') and variable values (the timeout number, the IP, the user ID). Old parsing methods focused entirely on the constant part and just replaced variables with placeholders. But variables are actually the most informative part—'10ms' versus '5000ms' timeout tells you if it's a minor blip or catastrophic hang. Trying to parse huge log files by looking only at structure, not values, wastes time and money asking language models to re-identify the same constant patterns repeatedly.
9.ap: The paper proposes focusing on variables instead. First, it samples which logs to parse by looking at variable values—if you see many logs with the same constant structure but different timeout values, you probably need only a few examples to understand that pattern. Second, it caches parsing decisions not by the constant structure alone but by combinations of constants and variables, so 'Connection failed: timeout' with value '5000' is cached separately from '100'—this prevents re-parsing the same semantic event. Third, when asking a language model to parse, it includes example variable values in the prompt, so the model can focus on the meaning rather than re-deriving structure.
9.ww: Variables carry semantic meaning that constants miss—'timeout=1000' and 'timeout=5000' should probably be understood together as 'timeout event' with different severity. By caching at the variable level, you avoid asking the language model the same question multiple times. By sampling based on variable patterns, you pick the most informative logs to process, not arbitrary ones.
9.po: The variable-centric approach reduces the number of times a language model is called (saving money) while improving parsing accuracy and preserving the variable information, so the parsed logs retain visibility into what actually happened in the system.

10.bp: A social network might have a ring of fake accounts coordinating spam, a botnet might share structural signatures with other known attacks, and a molecule graph might have unusual reactive properties. Graph-level anomaly detection means: given a whole network graph, decide if it's normal or abnormal as a whole (not checking individual nodes). This is critical for catching fraud rings, malware clusters, and finding rare chemical structures worth studying.
10.wh: Current anomaly detectors need to be trained only on normal graphs—clean data with no anomalies mixed in. This is unrealistic: in practice, your training data is probably contaminated with some anomalies you don't know about. If you train on 'pure normal' data that secretly contains a few anomalies, the model learns that those anomalies are normal, defeating the whole purpose. Getting clean training data requires manual review, which is expensive at scale.
10.ap: Instead of requiring pure training data, the system learns uncertainty estimates alongside anomaly scores. The idea: if the model is uncertain about whether a graph is normal (its predictions wobble around the decision boundary), that graph might be anomalous or an edge case. The system uses two approaches: one that adds uncertainty quantification onto existing detectors, and a second that re-trains from scratch using an expectation-maximization algorithm, which iteratively updates beliefs about which graphs are anomalous while simultaneously improving the detector.
10.ww: Uncertainty is honest: if you don't have enough information to confidently call something normal, you shouldn't act confident. Expectation-maximization is a principled way to learn from mixed data: you assume some graphs are anomalous and estimate which ones, then retrain the detector to fit that assumption, then re-estimate which graphs are anomalous, repeating until stable. Over time, this converges to a good anomaly detector without requiring pre-filtered training data.
10.po: On graph anomaly detection benchmarks, the uncertainty-aware approaches outperform methods that assume pure training data, especially when the training data is actually contaminated with unlabeled anomalies.

11.bp: Many real networks are graphs with text attached: academic paper citations (where papers are nodes and text is their abstracts), social media (profiles with bios, posts as text), and web graphs (pages linked together with content). Understanding these text-attributed graphs requires both reading the text and following the network structure. Current systems ask large language models to read the text and extract numerical features, but this is expensive and misses how the graph structure constrains meaning.
11.wh: Large language models are expensive to run on every node in a billion-node graph. Most approaches treat the LLM as a one-time text-to-numbers converter, throwing away the graph structure while the LLM is working. Also, learning representations that work on one graph (academic papers) often fails when applied to another (social media) because the graph structure and text semantics are domain-specific. You'd need to retrain the entire system for each new domain.
11.ap: The paper proposes using the LLM differently: as an embedding generator that can be trained once, then adapted to many domains. First, it pre-trains the LLM on multiple graph domains simultaneously using contrastive learning—teaching the model that nodes close in the graph should have similar embeddings, and that similar nodes across different domains should align. Second, after pre-training, for each new domain it does lightweight adaptation: dimensionality reduction with constraints that preserve both the semantic meaning (from text) and the structural properties (Laplacian information).
11.ww: Training on multiple domains teaches the model to recognize structural patterns that transfer—how text, local graph structure, and the broader network relate to each other. By keeping adaptation lightweight (only dimensionality reduction, not full retraining), you get fast deployment on new domains while retaining what the pre-training learned. The two types of constraints (semantic and structural) balance each other: if you over-fit to text, structure ruins it; if you over-fit to structure, text gets lost.
11.po: The unified framework achieves good performance across multiple text-attributed graph domains, with better transfer to new domains compared to training separate models for each one.

12.bp: Knowledge graphs store structured facts like 'Paris is the capital of France' or 'Aspirin treats headaches'—useful for reliable reasoning because the facts are explicitly stored. Knowledge graph question answering means finding the right subset of facts in the graph that answer a question. Unlike retrieving documents, you have to navigate the graph structure: to answer 'What is the capital of France?', you follow edges like 'France' → [capital] → 'Paris'. The problem: a graph might have millions of edge paths and only a few lead to good answers.
12.wh: A naive system retrieves facts matching single keywords from the question, but real questions often need multiple facts from different parts of the graph. Also, questions like 'Name the capital of the largest country in Europe' need multiple pieces of reasoning: finding countries, comparing sizes, then finding capitals. Existing systems compress a question into one retrieval goal ('find a capital'), missing that this question has multiple intents: 'find Europe,' 'find countries,' 'find the largest,' 'find its capital.' Optimizing for one intent might retrieve facts that satisfy it but don't help reasoning.
12.ap: The system extracts multiple intents from each question using topic modeling—a technique that finds recurring themes in questions. For example, 'find the largest' becomes one intent, 'find capital' another, 'find European country' a third. For each intent, it retrieves relevant graph facts. Instead of just picking facts once, it uses a differentiable sampling method that learns which combinations of facts across intents actually lead to correct answers (by comparing the question-answerer's output to the right answer). It also learns to re-rank retrieved facts by not just matching the question but matching patterns that helped in past correct answers.
12.ww: Multiple intents match reality: complicated questions have multiple things to figure out. By treating them separately and learning which combinations work together, the system avoids committing to one retrieval strategy that might miss useful facts. Differentiable sampling means you can measure 'did these retrieved facts lead to the right answer?' and optimize based on that end-to-end feedback, not just 'did these facts match my intent?'
12.po: On knowledge graph QA benchmarks like WebQSP and CWQ, the multi-intent approach outperforms single-intent retrieval by significantly higher accuracy.

13.bp: Cities are increasingly digital: traffic lights report congestion, power grids monitor consumption, water systems detect leaks, sensors track air quality. The 'smart city' vision is that using data from these systems intelligently makes cities work better—less traffic, faster emergency response, cleaner air. This workshop explores how the web infrastructure and data science techniques enable this transformation and what challenges emerge when cities rely on AI to make decisions affecting millions.
13.wh: Smart cities create massive data collection challenges: every sensor generates streams of information, which must be processed quickly and correctly. The data comes from heterogeneous sources (different vendors, different quality levels, different formats). Also, decisions made by city algorithms affect real people—wrong traffic light timing causes accidents, wrong water flow predictions cause outages—so there's real risk in deploying experimental methods. Privacy is another tension: monitoring movement, energy use, or health to optimize services can reveal sensitive information about citizens.
13.ap: This is a workshop (not a single research paper), so it's framing a conversation: the web community is gathering to discuss how data-driven decisions work in cities. It acknowledges the era of IoT (many networked sensors), AI (automated decision-making), and agentic AI (systems that take actions autonomously). The framing positions cities as 'the citiverse'—a digital twin of the physical city where you can simulate and optimize.
13.ww: By bringing together researchers and practitioners to explicitly discuss data-driven cities, the workshop creates space to share experience: which data sources are reliable, how do you validate that an AI decision actually improves outcomes, how do you involve citizens in the process rather than imposing changes.
13.po: This is a 12-year-running workshop, indicating sustained interest in bridging web technologies and urban systems. The focus on data-driven approaches (rather than just IoT sensors or AI in isolation) reflects the growing recognition that having sensors and algorithms is only half the work—the data pipeline, processing, and governance matter equally.

14.bp: Imagine a graph where some classes of nodes are rare: maybe fraudsters in a network of millions of honest nodes, or cancer subtypes in a large patient database. Classifying the graph as a whole (not individual nodes) means: given a set of nodes and their connections, predict what type of graph it is—maybe predicting if a social network is likely to spread misinformation, or if a molecule is likely to be toxic. The hard part is that the rare classes have few examples, so the model might ignore them and only learn to recognize the common cases.
14.wh: Imbalanced data (many common cases, few rare cases) tricks standard models into becoming mediocre classifiers of the rare cases. They optimize to be right on the majority and accept being wrong on the minority. Additionally, standard classifiers are overconfident—they output a probability but don't express uncertainty. If you ask 'is this graph toxic?', the model might confidently say 'probably not' when actually it's not sure, leading to terrible decisions if you trust its confidence.
14.ap: The system uses a framework from belief reasoning (Dempster-Shafer evidence theory) to build multiple specialized classifiers ('experts'), each trained to recognize different patterns. For each prediction, instead of outputting a single probability, the system outputs a probability distribution represented as a belief: 'I have this evidence that it's toxic, this evidence it's not, and this residual uncertainty.' To handle the class imbalance, it uses an evidence-based routing mechanism that learns to assign each graph to the experts most likely to classify it correctly, focusing expert effort on hard cases.
14.ww: Multiple experts learn diverse patterns: one might excel at rare-class cases, another at common cases, and their combination hedges bets. Belief representations express uncertainty honestly: instead of forcing a guess when you're not sure, you output the evidence for and against each class plus ambiguity. Adaptive routing learns that some experts are better for rare-class cases, so resources naturally concentrate where needed.
14.po: On graph classification benchmarks with imbalanced class distributions (long-tailed data), the framework achieves better accuracy on rare classes and more honest uncertainty estimates compared to standard graph neural networks.

15.bp: Online shoppers face an explosion of choice—millions of products across countless websites. The real problem is cognitive overload: humans cannot realistically evaluate all options, read all reviews, and compare prices across the web. Agentic systems (AI agents that act autonomously) promise to do this tedious exploration work for us, automatically curating the best matches to what we actually want.
15.wh: Testing whether an AI agent can truly help a shopper is harder than it looks. Existing benchmarks (standardized tests) focus on toy scenarios: a single website, a straightforward lookup, no real personalization. They don't measure whether an agent can handle the sprawling, contradictory mess of the real web—nor whether it can learn that you, specifically, want lightweight hiking boots under $120, not the most reviewed option.
15.ap: AgenticShop creates a realistic test suite with three key pieces: (1) real shopping scenarios that require cross-website exploration, not just lookups; (2) diverse user profiles with specific, conflicting preferences (budget, style, features); and (3) a checklist-based evaluation—does the agent's final product list actually match what a person said they wanted?
15.ww: Personalization matters because different shoppers have fundamentally different goals. An agent that finds the 'best' product for everyone is useless—it must learn to distinguish between someone hunting for deals and someone willing to overpay for premium quality. By embedding real preferences into the test, you can see whether agents actually adapt.
15.po: The paper shows that today's agents fall short: they struggle to curate personalized results in open-web settings. This matters because it reveals a concrete gap—agents are not yet ready as personal shopping assistants, and researchers now have a principled way to measure progress.

16.bp: Many datasets in the real world can be viewed as networks of relationships: social links, biological interactions, or website links. When these relationships come in different types (labeled edges—say, 'friend' vs 'colleague'), you want to group nodes so that similar nodes cluster together *and* their connection types match up. Think of it as: if two people belong to the same social circle, most of their shared links should be of the same type.
16.wh: The naive approach would be to ignore the labels and just cluster based on network structure, or to treat each label separately—but that loses information. The real challenge: you want to assign a color (group) to each node such that when two nodes connect, their colors should match the color of the edge between them. This is mathematically hard (NP-hard), meaning no known algorithm solves it perfectly in reasonable time.
16.ap: This paper offers the first combinatorial approximation algorithm—a method that finds a solution *guaranteed* to be better than two times worse than the true optimal, using only discrete graph-manipulation operations (no floating-point math). Prior approaches achieved at best a 2× approximation factor (twice as bad as optimal); this one breaks that barrier.
16.ww: Combinatorial algorithms scale better on large networks because they avoid costly linear-algebra operations. By working directly with graph structure, you can handle massive, real-world networks that would choke a more sophisticated approach. A tighter approximation bound means the algorithm gives you fewer false clusters.
16.po: Researchers now have a faster, more precise tool for clustering typed networks—useful for organizing heterogeneous web data without sacrificing optimality guarantees. This matters in practice for systems that must cluster millions of user-generated relationships in real time.

17.bp: Knowledge graphs (databases of facts like 'Einstein was a physicist') are the backbone of search engines, fact-checking, and AI systems. But the real world is conditional: 'Einstein was a physicist' becomes richer when you add 'except during his diplomatic years.' These conditional qualifiers—the who, where, when, under what circumstances—are crucial for capturing nuanced truth.
17.wh: Existing information extraction (automatically pulling facts from text) methods treat facts and conditions as flat structures with no hierarchy. They also consider every possible way to combine a fact with a condition—a massive search space that wastes compute and introduces errors. The real obstacle: how do you represent the *structure* of a fact-plus-conditions (a quintuple) in a way that an AI can reason about?
17.ap: Diff-CIE uses a star graph—a structure where one central fact triple sits in the middle and conditions radiate outward like leaves. Then it treats extraction as a 'denoising' process: start with noisy nodes (messy candidate facts and conditions) and progressively refine them into clean quintuples. This reduces the explosive search space from 'all combinations' to a fixed, finite set.
17.ww: Explicit structure matters because it mirrors how humans think about conditions: a fact is primary, and conditions modify it. By anchoring conditions to facts (not treating them as floating independent items), the algorithm can use learned constraints to stabilize the extraction. The deterministic matching strategy acts like a guardrail, preventing wild, meaningless refinements.
17.po: The method extracts more accurate conditional knowledge triples—useful for building semantic webs that understand nuance and context. This unlocks richer representations for fact-checking, search, and knowledge AI.

18.bp: Amazon and Apple sell their own products on their platforms, competing directly with third-party sellers. This seems like a conflict of interest—shouldn't platforms be neutral? The real economic question is: when does a platform rationally choose to enter a product category, and how does that choice affect seller innovation? Understanding this shapes policy around platform fairness.
18.wh: The tension is strategic: if you're a seller, how do you innovate and decide what products to launch when you know the platform owner might copy your success and use its preferential position to outcompete you? If you're the platform, when should you enter—immediately, or only after a seller proves there's real demand? Standard game theory (assuming one rational party) fails here because you have multiple strategic players simultaneously learning from each other's moves.
18.ap: The paper frames this as a Stackelberg game—the platform commits to an entry policy first (e.g., 'I enter if a product gets more than X sales'), then sellers decide what to launch knowing this policy. With one seller, they use a Gittins-index policy (a mathematically optimal way to balance trying new products versus exploiting known winners). With multiple sellers, they use deep reinforcement learning to simulate what sellers would do in competition.
18.ww: The Stackelberg model works because it captures real causality: the platform, being powerful, moves first and credibly constrains its own future actions ('I won't enter this category'). Sellers then rationally respond. This structure explains why empirical markets like Amazon and Google Play show measurable patterns of platform entry following seller success.
18.po: The paper reveals the incentives driving platform entry decisions and seller innovation strategies, with direct implications for regulation. It shows quantitatively how platform entry policies can either encourage or suppress third-party innovation—actionable insight for protecting market diversity.

19.bp: Machine-learning models trained on historical data often inherit and amplify human biases. If a hiring model is trained on past hiring decisions that favored men, it will likely recommend men in the future. Fairness in machine learning means ensuring predictions don't discriminate unfairly. The question this paper asks: if you pre-train a model on synthetic data generated using causal reasoning, does that help with fairness?
19.wh: Foundation models for tabular (spreadsheet-like) data show impressive accuracy but fairness remains a black box. TabPFN, a popular tabular foundation model, is pre-trained on thousands of synthetic datasets designed using causal reasoning—the idea is that by understanding causal relationships (not just correlations), the model should make fairer predictions. But does it actually?
19.ap: The paper systematically tests TabPFN's fairness on real-world prediction tasks under different kinds of data shift—scenarios where the test data differs from training data in systematic ways (e.g., missing values that are not random). They measure both fairness (do predictions treat protected groups equally?) and accuracy, across multiple model sizes and datasets.
19.ww: Causal pre-training helps because causal models are designed to ignore spurious correlations—connections that are accidental, not mechanically real. For example, if the training data happens to show that tall people earn more, a causal model might ignore height if it's not mechanistically tied to income. This should reduce unfair bias.
19.po: The results are mixed: TabPFN does improve fairness over baselines, but the gains are modest and inconsistent, especially when data is missing in biased ways. This tells practitioners that causal pre-training is not a panacea—fairness requires additional interventions, even with theoretically principled pre-training.

20.bp: Large language models (LLMs) like ChatGPT generate text one word at a time by computing a probability for each possible next word. But there's a puzzle: does the model's probability distribution over words match what the real task needs? If the task is book recommendation, should the model output diverse suggestions or stick to safe, popular picks? The paper uncovers two fundamentally different LLM types that answer this differently.
20.wh: Models vary unpredictably in their sampling behavior. Some models change their probability distribution drastically from one token to the next (high variability), while others are more stable. But which is better? And for what tasks? The problem is that no one has systematically measured whether a model's probability distribution actually aligns with what a task requires.
20.ap: The paper simulates controlled scenarios where they know the 'true' probability distribution a task needs, then measure how well each LLM's output distribution matches it. They identify two types: D-models (high step-to-step variability, poor alignment) and E-models (stable probabilities, good alignment). Then they test these two types on real tasks like code generation and product recommendation.
20.ww: Different tasks have different probability needs. Code generation might need stable, focused distributions (you don't want random variables named 'x' and 'xyzzy' equally often). Recommendations might need diversity (you want to occasionally suggest unexpected items, not just the most-sold product). By decomposing models into D and E types, you can make principled choices.
20.po: Practitioners can now match model type to task. If you need stable, predictable outputs, use an E-model; if you need diverse, exploratory outputs, use a D-model. This removes guesswork from LLM deployment in recommendation, search, and code-generation applications.

21.bp: Social media spreads false claims constantly. Fact-checking—verifying whether a claim is true—is essential for fighting misinformation, but manual fact-checking cannot scale. Automated fact-checking attempts to retrieve relevant evidence from the web and then decide whether a claim is supported by that evidence. The challenge is handling noise: not all retrieved facts are equally useful, and reasoning systems hallucinate (invent facts).
21.wh: Real-world fact-checking breaks in two places: (1) retrieved evidence is noisy—systems grab irrelevant or contradictory documents that mislead the verifier; and (2) verification models confidently assert things not actually supported by evidence. You need both clean evidence *and* careful reasoning to avoid false verdicts.
21.ap: SLED has two stages. First, it retrieves candidate evidence, then uses a pre-trained verifier to score each piece for credibility and relevance, filtering out noise. Second, it prompts an LLM to argue both for and against the claim (dual-perspective reasoning), simulates a debate between these arguments, then distills the outcome into a lightweight model for speed.
21.ww: Self-supervised denoising works because you can learn to spot noisy evidence without manual labels—the verifier sees which evidence actually helps downstream prediction. Multi-agent debate surfaces contradictions and forces the model to confront weak reasoning. Distillation into a small model keeps inference fast for web-scale deployment.
21.po: The method achieves state-of-the-art fact-checking on complex benchmarks by combining filtering (fewer false positives) with robust reasoning (avoiding hallucination). This matters because it makes automated fact-checking reliable enough to deploy against high-stakes misinformation.

22.bp: Social networks and the web generate continuous streams of events—user posts, purchases, clicks. Predicting future events (will this user click that article?) requires modeling how past events influence each other and how that influence changes over time. The real-world constraint: billions of events per day demand fast predictions, not slow, accurate ones.
22.wh: Existing neural methods struggle with two contradictory demands. Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) are sequential but can't 'see' far into the past—early events fade from memory. Graph neural networks (GNNs) handle relationships well but become prohibitively slow on large, real-time event streams. Neither scales to web-scale prediction.
22.ap: Fourier Graph Learning shifts perspective: instead of thinking about events in time order (the time domain), think about them in terms of oscillating patterns (the frequency domain). Each node and edge becomes a complex number—the real part encodes what the event is about, the imaginary part encodes its temporal rhythm. Multiplying complex numbers in frequency space is faster than sequential processing.
22.ww: Frequency-domain reasoning captures both short-term bursts and long-term trends efficiently. A semantic-aware frequency filter can emphasize long-term dependencies you care about while dampening noise. This is faster than running a GNN because matrix multiplication in frequency space scales better than message passing on large graphs.
22.po: Fourier Graph Neural Networks dramatically reduce compute cost while maintaining accuracy. For large-scale event prediction on platforms like Twitter or e-commerce sites, this means you can predict faster and adapt to new user behavior in real time.

23.bp: E-commerce platforms care about conversion rate (does a click turn into a purchase?) but also refund rate (does the purchase get returned?). Net conversion rate combines both: it measures whether a customer actually keeps a purchase. This matters because a high-conversion, high-refund rate looks good on paper but represents unhappy customers and lost money.
23.wh: Cascaded delay modeling works because the two stages have different causal mechanisms. A product that converts quickly might refund quickly too (impulse buy + regret). A product that converts slowly might be carefully considered (lower refund). By modeling both mechanisms, you capture these dynamics.
23.ap: The paper introduces CASCADE, a large real-world dataset from Taobao with millions of records showing clicks, conversions, refunds, and delays. They analyze it and find three key patterns: (1) net conversion shows temporal trends; (2) modeling conversion and refund separately, then combining, beats directly modeling net conversion; and (3) delay time itself is predictive—faster conversions have different refund patterns than slow ones. They then propose TESLA, a method that continuously learns these patterns.
23.po: TESLA provides a more accurate picture of true customer satisfaction on e-commerce platforms. This enables better product ranking, better inventory decisions, and better business metrics that actually reflect real user value, not just transaction velocity.

24.bp: Federated learning lets a machine-learning model learn from data spread across millions of users' phones without sending raw data to a central server—each phone trains locally, then shares only the learned weights. But users have different preferences and data, so a one-size-fits-all global model performs poorly. Personalized federated learning tries to adapt the global model to each user's specific data.
24.wh: Neural collapse shows that well-trained networks organize representations in a specific geometric pattern. By forcing shared and local features to respect this structure, the model can maintain global knowledge while preserving user-specific characteristics. This is more stable than arbitrary layer-wise sharing.
24.ap: pFedDKS proposes a principled split: use neural collapse theory (a mathematical framework showing how deep neural networks organize learned representations) to prove that the feature extractor should be partially, not fully, shared. It detaches global features and local features by learning separate 'prototypes' (exemplar representations) for shared vs. personalized layers.
24.po: pFedDKS outperforms prior federated-learning methods, enabling personalization without sacrificing privacy or forcing users to contribute to unrelated global models. For platforms like health apps and keyboards, this means better accuracy while respecting user privacy.

25.bp: Recommendation systems increasingly use large language models to generate explanations for why an item was recommended ('We think you'll like this coat because you liked the blue winter jacket last month'). These explanations build trust. But in the real world, user interaction histories are messy: accidental clicks, forgotten purchases, data errors. If the explanation changes wildly when one click is removed, users won't trust it.
25.wh: No one has systematically measured whether LLM-generated explanations are robust—whether they stay consistent despite realistic noise in user data. This matters because a brittle explanation system could amplify noise into unstable, contradictory recommendations.
25.ap: RobustExplain creates five types of realistic user-data perturbations (accidental clicks, missing values, temporal shifts, etc.) and tests them at multiple severity levels against four large LLMs (7 billion to 70 billion parameters). It measures robustness across four dimensions: whether key ideas survive (semantic), whether keywords stay (keyword), whether the explanation structure holds (structural), and whether length is stable.
25.ww: Multiple dimensions of robustness matter because explanations serve multiple purposes. Semantic stability means the core reasoning doesn't flip. Keyword stability means the recommendation itself doesn't change. Structural stability means the explanation remains readable. By measuring all four, you get a complete picture.
25.po: Current LLM explanations show only moderate robustness—larger models help but not by much. This establishes a concrete benchmark and shows that recommendation explanations need additional safeguards (denoising, consistency checks) to be trustworthy in real-world noisy data.

26.bp: Large language models use a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture—instead of one monolithic network, you have dozens of specialized sub-networks (experts) and a router that decides which experts to use for each input. This is efficient: you don't activate all experts every time. But routing is stateless and wasteful: if two similar inputs arrive, the router re-explores which experts to use, wasting compute.
26.wh: Retrieval-augmented routing works because input patterns tend to repeat—the same search query or dialogue turn appears many times. By caching expert team assignments for semantic patterns, you can amortize the routing cost. The learnable gate ensures the retrieved prior can be updated if live routing signals something different.
26.ap: RMS-MoE adds memory: a Co-Activation Memory stores which expert teams worked well for which semantic patterns. For new input, it retrieves similar past patterns' expert assignments, uses those as a prior, then combines that prior with live routing decisions via a learnable gate. This is more efficient (retrieve + fuse rather than full routing) and more stable (similar inputs get similar expert assignments).
26.po: RMS-MoE achieves a 26% latency reduction, 2.7-point accuracy gain, and 3.3% better routing stability on web-scale tasks. This translates to faster search and dialogue systems that behave more predictably—directly valuable for deployed LLM applications.

27.bp: E-commerce recommendations operate at the item level (show 'blue winter jacket'), but users actually purchase at a finer granularity—specific variants (size M, color navy, material wool). Price varies by variant: the jacket might be $60 in polyester or $150 in wool. This granularity mismatch means you lose critical information about what users actually want and how they value price.
27.wh: Grouping by price works because price is the main variant dimension users care about. Two $50 variants (different materials but same price) are interchangeable for most users; two variants of the same item at $30 vs $80 are fundamentally different purchase decisions. By collapsing on price, you retain signal while compressing sparse space.
27.ap: PSKU4Rec groups variants by price (Price SKU)—variants of the same item at similar prices are treated as one unit. This reduces sparsity by 6×. The model then learns intra-item price preferences (does this user prefer premium or budget variants?) and cross-item price patterns. At inference, it uses these to estimate the price-specific conversion rate and show the most appropriate product image for each user.
27.po: PSKU4Rec improves both conversion prediction and price consistency on Taobao's real data. This enables better product ranking, more honest pricing (exposure price matches transaction price), and higher user satisfaction because recommendations match actual purchasing patterns.

28.bp: Data marketplaces—platforms where data owners sell data to consumers (e.g., 'I'll sell you my anonymized customer purchase history')—require privacy: data owners don't want buyers to see raw data. Differential privacy (a mathematical guarantee) adds noise to data so that individual records can't be reverse-engineered. But who adds the noise? If a central marketplace adds it, sellers must trust the marketplace. If a seller adds it, buyers trust no one.
28.wh: MPC works because the noise is generated by consensus: if even one party is honest, the noise is trustworthy. Byzantine robustness means the scheme survives even if some parties try to cheat. The batched bits-expansion mechanism reduces the cryptographic overhead dramatically (12.7× faster than prior methods).
28.ap: Xemis uses multi-party computation (MPC)—a cryptographic technique where multiple parties jointly compute a result without any single party seeing intermediate values. Specifically, it uses a 'distributed noise sharing' protocol (b-DNS) where multiple parties collaboratively generate noise shares such that when combined, they produce exactly the right privacy-preserving noise. No single party controls the noise.
28.po: Xemis enables decentralized, trustworthy data trading without requiring faith in a single marketplace or seller. Sellers can prove they're not leaking data; buyers can trust the privacy level; attackers can't corrupt the noise. This unlocks real data markets where neither party has total control.

29.bp: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) uses a large language model to answer questions by first retrieving relevant documents from the web, then reasoning over those documents. The quality of the answer depends on retrieving good documents. But what makes a document 'good' isn't always obvious: relevance to the question, credibility, and usefulness all matter differently depending on the question.
29.wh: Explicit quality signals help the model make calibrated use of noisy context. Rather than blindly incorporating whatever is retrieved, the model can learn to ignore low-quality documents and emphasize high-quality ones. This is more robust than hoping the LLM's internal reasoning automatically filters.
29.ap: OpenDecoder explicitly scores retrieved documents along three dimensions: relevance (topical match to the question), ranking score (where the document appeared in search results), and query performance prediction (a meta-measure of how useful the document is likely to be for this specific question). These scores become features that the LLM's generation process can see and use.
29.po: OpenDecoder outperforms standard RAG on five benchmark datasets, especially when context is noisy. This matters for deployed question-answering systems where retrieval is imperfect and robustness to low-quality documents is critical.

30.bp: When you search for movies or products online, the system shows you the top handful of results—not all 100,000 items ranked perfectly. What matters is whether those top 10 or top 20 are genuinely good for you. Recommender systems spend enormous energy trying to find the best few items quickly without having to rank the entire universe of choices.
30.wh: The obvious approach—rank everything and measure how good your top-K is—works mathematically but kills performance: you have to compute rankings for millions of items to know which ones are actually the best, which is slow and expensive. Second, user preferences shift over time (their taste changes, new items arrive), so even yesterday's ranking becomes stale and biased by old patterns. Building a loss function that directly optimizes top-K without computing full rankings is genuinely hard because top-K quality depends on relative positions, not absolute scores.
30.ap: Talos rewrites the ranking problem as a threshold problem: instead of 'rank items 1 to 100,000 then take the top 20,' the system asks 'what score would the 20th-best item have?' and then counts how many good items are above that threshold. This turns ranking into simple score comparisons. The system learns this threshold from data using a sampling trick, and adds a penalty term that stops the system from inflating scores (which would make the threshold meaningless). To handle shifting user preferences, they add a repair function that smooths out discontinuities and keeps the model stable as user behavior changes.
30.ww: Thresholds are much faster to compute than full rankings because you avoid sorting millions of items. The penalty for score inflation works because when scores climb too high, the threshold has to climb too, and the system gets no benefit—this creates a natural brake. The smoothing function protects against sudden user-behavior shifts because it lets the model make gradual adjustments rather than jerking to a new strategy instantly. These three ingredients working together turn an expensive ranking problem into a cheap threshold problem that stays stable over time.
30.po: The paper reports theoretical convergence proofs and experimental validation showing that Talos maintains accuracy while being far faster than existing approaches, and stays robust when user preferences shift—meaning the system can handle real-world conditions where recommendation rankings need to adapt constantly without breaking.

31.bp: Today's blockchain and cryptocurrency systems rely on a mathematical trick called public-key cryptography—you can lock something with one key (public) and only unlock it with a secret paired key (private). This protects billions of dollars of digital assets. Quantum computers, which recent breakthroughs have made increasingly practical, can break this trick entirely, making old-fashioned blockchains vulnerable to theft and fraud.
31.wh: Quantum computers don't run algorithms the way classical computers do; they exploit quantum weirdness to solve certain mathematical problems exponentially faster. The specific problems that guard public-key cryptography (factoring large numbers, solving discrete logarithm problems) are exactly what quantum computers excel at. Once a quantum computer exists, someone could retroactively unscramble old private keys from public blockchain data, stealing funds locked decades ago. No one has built a quantum computer strong enough to break cryptography yet, but the theoretical threat is immediate.
31.ap: This is a tutorial, not a research paper, so the approach is educational: it walks through how quantum computers work, why they threaten current blockchain security, and what defenses exist. The key defense is post-quantum cryptography—new mathematical puzzles that even quantum computers cannot solve quickly (often based on lattice problems or multivariate polynomials). The tutorial also covers quantum-assisted cryptography, where quantum properties themselves (quantum key distribution, entanglement) are used to make eavesdropping impossible. It shows how these fit into blockchain architectures and broader questions about privacy and trust in decentralized systems.
31.ww: Post-quantum algorithms are harder to break than factorization because even quantum computers cannot solve lattice problems efficiently—the quantum speedup doesn't apply. Quantum-assisted systems work because the laws of physics (quantum no-cloning, measurement collapse) prevent eavesdropping: if someone reads a quantum key, the key self-destructs and both sides know they were spied on. Educating the community now, before quantum computers become powerful, lets organizations transition gradually rather than facing a sudden cryptographic apocalypse.
31.po: The tutorial bridges lab theory (quantum computing breakthroughs) with real-world blockchain engineering (cryptographic standards, distributed consensus) and governance (data privacy, ethical accountability), giving technologists and policymakers a shared vocabulary to plan defenses before quantum computers threaten existing digital infrastructure.

32.bp: In remote regions without good roads or satellite coverage—parts of Africa, disaster zones after earthquakes, newly settled areas—nobody has built detailed digital maps of where people can actually move. Yet understanding human movement in these places matters for disaster response, urban planning, and public health. The only data available is often people's phones sporadically reporting location, with huge gaps and noise.
32.wh: Standard trajectory recovery (filling in the path between two GPS points) assumes you know the underlying road network; without it, you don't know whether someone walked straight through a forest or took a 10-kilometer detour. GPS signals themselves are unreliable in remote areas (trees, cloud cover, buildings), creating huge blank spots. Machine learning models trained on road-mapped regions (where data is clean) fail miserably when transferred to roadless regions because the patterns are fundamentally different. The data is sparse and unrepresentative, so the model has almost nothing to learn from.
32.ap: RHTR builds invisible 'maps' from historical movement data itself, without needing road data. It creates a multi-scale grid overlaid on each region—coarse grids capture global movement patterns (people generally move east or south), while fine grids capture local details (this specific cluster of points has narrow, winding movement). When someone's phone drops signal, the system looks at the surrounding region's patterns from that grid hierarchy and imagines what movement would fit. A coarse-to-fine reconstruction engine starts with the global pattern, then progressively refines the guess using local patterns, gradually filling in the missing segment step by step.
32.ww: Multi-scale grids work because human movement always has structure at multiple resolutions: large-scale patterns (regions tend to move toward markets or water), medium-scale patterns (neighborhoods have local routes), and fine-scale patterns (individuals navigate obstacles). Starting coarse prevents wild guesses; refining to fine detail keeps the guess realistic. Learning these patterns from observed data in each region means the model adapts to local geography without needing explicit maps. The system doesn't pretend to know roads; it learns movement regularities from what people actually did, which works even without infrastructure.
32.po: On two public datasets simulating remote and disaster scenarios, RHTR recovers missing trajectory segments more accurately than prior methods, even when training on data from completely different regions (cross-region transfer), because it learns the underlying movement structure rather than memorizing specific road networks.

33.bp: Decentralized finance (DeFi) lets anyone stake their money in blockchain liquidity pools—basically betting that prices will move in certain ways and earning fees if they're right. Small investors face a barrier: pools that deliver better returns demand large fund balances, so a person with $1,000 cannot compete with someone with $100,000, even if they both have equal skill. The question is: should small investors pool their money together to compete like one big fund, or stay fragmented?
33.wh: When many small investors compete separately, they each get worse returns because the protocol structure inherently favors larger funds (classic David vs. Goliath). But if they pool together, they become a giant force with monopoly-like power over the market, which might crush competition and hurt other investors. Game theory predicts that competing firms should eventually reach a balanced equilibrium where everyone does okay, but ranking-based DeFi breaks that prediction: monopoly actually delivers better returns than balanced competition, which contradicts textbook economics.
33.ap: The paper proves this mathematically using Stackelberg game theory (one player moves first, others respond), analyzing what happens when many investors choose to pool or stay separate. They model the revenue function as convex, meaning bigger pools benefit disproportionately from each additional dollar (economies of scale). They show that once asymmetry exceeds a critical threshold, the market will tip toward monopoly—small competitors cannot survive. To validate this, they run simulations on real Ethereum blockchain data, showing that different market starting conditions all converge to monopoly over time.
33.ww: Convex revenue functions mean that pooling is mathematically guaranteed to do better than competition: a $100,000 pool earns more than two $50,000 pools, not because collusion, but because of how the protocol's math works. Classical economics (Bertrand, Cournot) assumes linear or concave revenue functions, so those theories predict balanced competition. But when the revenue function has increasing returns to scale, those theories break. Once a pool gets slightly larger, it pulls in more money, which makes it even larger, creating a self-reinforcing spiral to monopoly.
33.po: Empirically, on real Ethereum data, funds aggregate into monopolistic structures regardless of initial conditions, and these monopolies actually achieve better outcomes for their members than fragmented competition would—a concrete demonstration that ranking-dependent DeFi protocols have built-in incentives toward concentration, contrary to what traditional competition theory predicts.

34.bp: Cloud services host thousands of applications serving millions of users simultaneously, all sharing the same network infrastructure. A video conference needs low latency; a backup job can tolerate delay; a real-time game needs guaranteed bandwidth. The system needs to juggle these competing demands—give each application exactly the bandwidth it needs, no more, no less, in real time.
34.wh: Traditional traffic control (Linux's Hierarchical Token Bucket) is static: you set rates once, and they never adapt. New cloud applications have highly dynamic demands—a video stream suddenly needs more bandwidth during high-motion scenes, then needs less during static scenes. The system has to sense this demand in real time and reallocate resources instantly. Building this efficiently is hard because checking and adjusting rates for thousands of flows billions of times per second would melt the CPU. Modern cloud systems offer only crude rate limiting (coarse-grained) that doesn't distinguish between priority levels.
34.ap: BeeQoS has three pieces: a high-speed data plane (using eBPF, special kernel-level code) that shapes each individual packet without slowing down; a control plane that constantly senses what bandwidth each flow actually needs right now (sampling real packets, not guessing); and Kubernetes integration so administrators can write policies in human language ('give video 20% bandwidth, backup gets leftovers'). When demand changes, the control plane recalculates allocation and the data plane instantly adjusts how much each packet is delayed before transmission. The system rebalances continuously, second by second.
34.ww: eBPF runs in the kernel so it shapes packets without context-switching to user-space code, which would be slow. Sampling real packets gives accurate demand signals because you measure what flows actually need, not what they claim. Adaptive reallocation works because the system checks demand often and adjusts smoothly rather than shocking flows with sudden rate changes. Kubernetes integration matters because operators already speak Kubernetes language; letting them express policies naturally means policies get deployed correctly.
34.po: Evaluation shows BeeQoS handles 1,000+ simultaneous flows while cutting median latency 72% and improving video quality-of-experience 27% versus traditional rate limiting, with stable performance and lower deployment overhead, because it dynamically matches bandwidth allocation to real-time application demands.

35.bp: When a video recommendation system keeps showing you videos from creators you already follow, you watch more (immediate engagement), but the platform becomes stale—emerging creators never get discovered, and you see the same people forever. Platforms want engagement, but also want a healthy ecosystem where new voices can grow. The tension is real: familiar content wins on engagement metrics, but suppresses diversity.
35.wh: Familiar content has an unfair advantage: you already trust it, so you click it faster. If the ranking system simply optimizes for clicks-per-item, it will naturally bury novel content, even if novel content would bring you joy if you tried it (you just need more proof). This is a structural bias built into the optimization metric, not user preference. Fixing it naively—say, always reserving 20% of rankings for novel content—hurts engagement and gets overridden by management pressure to maximize watch time.
35.ap: LAFB works after ranking is done (post-ranking stage), so it doesn't disrupt the main ranking system. It models how familiar you are with each content by analyzing your past interaction history with this creator or content type (how often you've watched them before). It computes personalized debiasing scores—essentially, multipliers that adjust your predicted interest in each video based on its novelty to you. Familiar videos get downweighted slightly; novel videos get upweighted slightly. The adjustment is personalized because someone who rarely watches creators might need different debiasing than a superfan.
35.ww: Applying debiasing at the post-ranking stage is safe: it doesn't break the main ranking pipeline or require retraining the main model, so it's low-risk to deploy. Personalized factors work because different users have different familiarity profiles—some are loyal-fans (should see less familiar stuff), others are explorers (can see slightly more novel stuff). The system preserves overall watch time by only deweighting gradually, so the adjustment doesn't feel jarring to users. Empirically, this small adjustment increases diversity without sacrificing engagement.
35.po: Deployed on YouTube, LAFB increased novel content watch-time share and expanded exposure for emerging creators while holding overall watch time stable and keeping user satisfaction steady—demonstrating that diversity and engagement are not mutually exclusive if you apply the right adjustment at the right stage.

36.bp: Group chats on social platforms are where people ask questions, solve problems together, and share interests. But many group chats die out (inactivity), or take chaotic turns, or lack structure. If you could add smart AI agents to the chat that encourage good discussion, answer questions helpfully, or playfully challenge the group, you could revive engagement and make chats more valuable without a human moderator working 24/7.
36.wh: Large language models work great in one-on-one conversation where context is simple and stable. Group chat is fundamentally messier: multiple people talk over each other, context shifts rapidly, a single user's tone is hard to infer, and inserting a bot can feel intrusive or break the conversational flow. The system needs to know when to speak and when to stay quiet. It needs to coordinate multiple agent personalities without confusing users. Existing LLM systems treat multi-party chat as 'extend the conversation,' but real group chat needs active management—when to trigger an agent, which agent, how to blend its response into the human flow.
36.ap: GCAgent has three components: an Agent Builder that customizes agents to match group interests (personality, expertise, tone); a Dialogue Manager that tracks conversation state, decides when agents should speak up, and prevents awkward interruptions or redundant comments; and Interface Plugins that reduce friction for users to invoke or configure agents (three specific tools for interaction). The system lets groups define 'entertainment' agents (funny, engaging) and 'utility' agents (answering factual questions, summarizing), which operate under different speaking rules. The dialogue manager essentially watches the chat flow and decides: 'This is the right moment for the expert agent to jump in' or 'Stay silent, humans are handling this.'
36.ww: Customizing agents to group interests means the voice fits the existing chat culture, so it feels invited rather than intrusive. Dialogue state tracking prevents the system from speaking out of turn or repeating itself, which would derail conversation. Separate entertainment and utility agents work because they operate under different logic—entertainment agents are bold and speak frequently, while utility agents are cautious and only activate when needed. Interface plugins reduce friction because users don't have to write code or formulate perfect prompts to use agents; they can summon them with one click.
36.po: In 350 days of real-world deployment, GCAgent increased message volume 28.8% and achieved 4.68/5 average rating, preferred by users 51% of the time versus the base model—showing that well-timed, well-integrated agents can revive group activity and enhance conversation quality without feeling intrusive.

37.bp: Graph learning is about predicting properties of networks—which users will connect, which nodes matter most, whether two nodes belong in the same group. The assumption has always been 'similar nodes link to each other' (homophily, like your friends are similar to you). But real networks often violate this: in citation networks, papers can cite very different papers; in social networks, people disagree with their friends. Building a single foundation model that works on both homophilic and heterophilic graphs is the frontier.
37.wh: Most graph models assume homophily and exploit it: if your neighbors are similar to you, then your neighbors' features tell you about your own features. On heterophilic graphs this breaks catastrophically—your neighbors are different from you, so copying their feature patterns makes you less similar to them, causing the model to predict you wrongly. The deeper problem is that homophily and heterophily don't exist at one granularity; they exist at multiple scales. A node overall might be homophilic (similar neighbors), but some individual feature dimensions might be heterophilic (your neighbors' color differs from yours), and vice versa. Existing methods check only at node level and miss these fine-grained patterns.
37.ap: TFSGFM (Topology-aware Feature Sorting Graph Foundation Model) looks at homophily and heterophily at the fine granularity of individual features, not entire nodes. For each feature of each node, it asks: 'Are my neighbors' values for this feature similar to or different from mine?' It then sorts features based on these per-feature topology patterns. A dual-channel architecture processes the sorted features: one channel for homophilic features (similar), one for heterophilic features (different). Each channel uses different aggregation rules—homophilic features copy neighbor values, heterophilic features contrast against neighbor values. The system learns which features belong in which channel and combines them.
37.ww: Feature-level sorting works because it captures a reality that node-level sorting misses: within a single node, some dimensions follow homophily and some follow heterophily. Different aggregation rules for different feature types prevent the fundamental mistake of averaging features that shouldn't be averaged.
