The dual-channel architecture naturally handles both graph types using the same foundation model, because it adapts the aggregation strategy per feature rather than per graph. This enables one model to work across diverse graph structures without retraining.
37.po: Experiments demonstrate that TFSGFM handles both homophilic and heterophilic graphs in a unified framework, outperforming methods designed specifically for one type, and even on homophilic graphs it better exploits the small heterophilic signals that exist—proving that feature-level topology awareness gives foundation models more flexibility and accuracy.

38.bp: Modern web applications spread across dozens of microservices—each service handles one job (payment, recommendations, notifications), and they call each other. When something breaks (payment service gets slow, recommendation service crashes), finding the root cause is like debugging a 100-layer telephone game. Engineers trace requests as they bounce between services, but interpreting traces requires deep expertise and takes hours. Automating trace analysis would catch problems in minutes.
38.wh: Trace analysis is hard because traces are unstructured: a single trace might involve 50 services, each logging in different formats, and the interesting patterns—'service A always delays after service B returns 503'—are buried in thousands of log lines. Existing trace analysis tools require manual rules ('if latency > 500ms, trigger alert'), which miss unexpected failure modes. Large language models could help here because they understand natural language patterns, can reason about chains of events, and can generalize across different services without reprogramming. But LLM capabilities for trace analysis have never been systematically evaluated, and it's unclear what level of fine-tuning is needed.
38.ap: The paper first builds TraceBench, a benchmark dataset of traces with labeled analysis tasks (detect anomaly, identify root cause, predict latency). They then evaluate existing LLMs on this benchmark to see which models are naturally good at trace reasoning. They find LLMs have potential but room to improve, so they propose TraceLLM: taking an LLM and fine-tuning it on TraceBench tasks. The fine-tuning teaches the model to parse traces, recognize causal patterns, and output diagnoses in standardized format. They compare against open-source and closed-source baselines.
38.ww: Fine-tuning works because LLMs already have strong reasoning skills from general pretraining; they just need to learn the specific trace domain (vocabulary, patterns, output format). Traces are semi-structured text, which LLMs handle naturally. Building a benchmark first (TraceBench) lets them measure progress and understand which tasks are hard, so they can focus fine-tuning on the bottlenecks. Generalizing across services works because trace patterns are somewhat universal (latency cascades, resource exhaustion, failures propagating) even though implementations differ.
38.po: Fine-tuned TraceLLM outperforms open-source LLMs by 34.77% average accuracy on trace analysis tasks and beats closed-source baselines, demonstrating that LLMs with domain-specific tuning can automate a task that currently requires expert human time and reduces mean time to diagnosis in microservice systems.

39.bp: E-commerce platforms and streaming services track what you watch or buy across multiple services you use—shopping, streaming video, social network, music. Recommenders could use this cross-domain history to give better suggestions. Someone who buys sci-fi books might enjoy sci-fi films; someone who listens to jazz might enjoy jazz documentaries. But user histories are sparse—you buy rarely, watch intermittently—so combining data from multiple domains should provide more signal to learn from.
39.wh: Naive cross-domain recommendation fails in time-aware scenarios. Suppose I stopped watching sci-fi movies six months ago but just started reading sci-fi books. A simple transfer would predict I love sci-fi films, but I've moved on. The time dimension matters: old interactions age out, new interactions have more weight. Also, the optimal timing to transfer information is different for different users: a fast-moving trendsetter wants recent data; a loyal user wants long-term history. Ignoring timing and treating all history equally causes transfer learning to backfire. Current cross-domain methods assume interactions are uniformly spread in time, which is unrealistic.
39.ap: TA-CDSR (Time-Aware Cross-Domain Sequential Recommendation) has three pieces: (1) Time-sensitive attention that splits your interaction sequence into 'what items did you interact with' and 'when did you interact with them,' treating these separately so the model learns both the items you like and the temporal pattern of your interests; (2) A preference generator that uses source-domain interactions and their timestamps to reconstruct what your target-domain interactions would look like if your interests were consistent across domains, but weighted by time so recent source interactions influence the guess more; (3) Multi-scale time windows that measure how dense your interactions are at different time scales (hourly, daily, monthly) and dynamically adjust how much cross-domain knowledge to transfer based on this density.
39.ww: Decoupling items and time works because interest changes over time, and the model needs to track both independently. Weighting by time lets the model realize 'you were into sci-fi six months ago but aren't now, so this shouldn't influence your film recommendation.' Multi-scale windows adapt to personal rhythms: someone who shops daily should see recent-only history; someone who shops monthly should look further back. Adaptively weighting cross-domain transfer by interaction density means the system transfers knowledge when domains are rich in data and relies on target-domain data when it's rich and sources are sparse.
39.po: Experiments on three real-world datasets show TA-CDSR achieves competitive computational efficiency while outperforming baselines, because temporal structure allows it to extract signal from cross-domain history without being misled by outdated preferences.

40.bp: Blockchain networks are under attack: criminals use them to hide stolen money, launder drug proceeds, or ransom victims. Regulators and exchanges need to identify malicious addresses in real time. The problem is scale—billions of transactions, millions of addresses—and the adversaries adapt constantly. A model trained on last year's fraud patterns will miss this year's new schemes. Transfer learning (applying knowledge from previously identified fraud to new fraud) should work because fraud is fraud, but the complex nature of blockchain data (graph structure, price history, message text) makes transfer hard.
40.wh: Blockchain fraud changes constantly: money laundering that worked last month gets detected, so criminals invent new techniques. A model trained on old fraud will not recognize new patterns. The data itself is multi-modal and noisy—transaction graphs show connections between addresses, temporal sequences show wash trading patterns, price history shows market manipulation, and textual metadata describes transactions. Each modality tells a different story, and good fraud detection needs all of them. Existing transfer learning methods for graphs ignore temporal and textual data, and methods that use all three modalities don't transfer well across blockchains because distributions shift (different blockchain = different users, different fraud ecology).
40.ap: MOE-GTL (Multi-mOdal Enhanced Graph Transfer Learning) combines three modalities: (1) Graph structure, encoded as a network of addresses and connections; (2) Temporal sequences, capturing how transaction volume and price change over time; (3) Textual features describing transaction metadata. The model learns representations in each modality separately, then learns how to combine them. The key innovation is distribution alignment: the model explicitly corrects for the fact that source and target blockchains have different fraud patterns and user populations by learning a transformation that maps source distribution to target distribution. This learned transformation enables knowledge from old fraud to apply to new fraud.
40.ww: Multi-modal learning works because different fraud types leave different fingerprints: structural fraud (circular money transfers) shows in the graph; temporal fraud (sudden price spikes) shows in sequences; textual fraud (suspicious message content) shows in metadata. Learning to combine these modalities gives the model more signal. Distribution alignment works because the core fraud mechanics (circular transfers, price manipulation) are shared across blockchains; the distribution shift is mostly in the user base and transaction volume, which the alignment layer can correct. Transfer learning then applies successfully because the aligned representations encode generalizable fraud patterns.
40.po: MOE-GTL detects fraud in emerging blockchain networks by transferring knowledge from previous fraud cases, handling the multi-modal and dynamic nature of blockchain data through simultaneous graph, temporal, and textual reasoning with distribution-aware transfer, enabling faster detection of new fraud schemes without waiting to accumulate labeled data in each new blockchain.

41.bp: Cloud platforms run thousands of microservices in a data center, each serving users from different services (payment, analytics, user profile, notifications). Each service has dependencies: payment service calls user database; analytics depends on event logging; the system needs to forecast CPU, memory, and latency. If forecasts are accurate, the platform can allocate resources ahead of demand and avoid outages.
41.wh: Naive forecasting treats each service independently, but microservices are interconnected in complex ways: if user-database load spikes, every service that queries it will suffer. The connections form a graph, but the graph is not a static blueprint—connections are dynamic, activated only when services call each other. Furthermore, within each microservice, there are causal chains: workload first drives CPU usage, which drives memory usage, which drives latency. A spike in workload cascades through these causal chains. Existing forecasting methods ignore one or both layers (the graph of service dependencies, and the causal chains within each service), so they miss crucial signal.
41.ap: MaMiClif (macro-micro collaborative learning) models both layers: (1) Macro (service-level): constructs a graph where nodes are services, edges represent dependencies, and weights capture interaction strength. It uses heterogeneous graph convolution, which updates representations by mixing information from different types of edges (collaborative, backup, dynamic). (2) Micro (indicator-level): constructs a matrix showing which performance metrics (workload, CPU, memory, latency) causally affect each other within a service. It uses causal self-attention, a variant of attention that weights relationships by measured causal strength (e.g., workload has stronger causal influence on latency than memory does). The forecast combines both by first predicting service-level workload using the macro graph, then predicting individual metrics using the micro matrix conditioned on the macro predictions.
41.ww: Heterogeneous graph convolution handles multiple edge types because different dependencies (collaborative vs. backup) behave differently; one edge type should not overshadow the others. Causal self-attention works because causality is asymmetric (workload causes latency, not vice versa), and explicitly weighting by causal strength prevents the model from learning spurious correlations. Combining macro and micro predictions works because top-down (graph) and bottom-up (causal) reasoning reinforce each other: the macro prediction provides boundary conditions, the micro chains fill in detailed mechanics.
41.po: Experiments on data center workloads show MaMiClif forecasts microservice metrics more accurately than baselines by jointly modeling service dependencies and intra-service causality, enabling better resource allocation and reduced risk of outages.

42.bp: Meme coins (joke cryptocurrencies like Dogecoin) are traded obsessively and have become a $100+ billion market. Many investors use copy-trading bots—they watch expert traders and automatically copy their trades. But meme coin markets are thin and manipulable, and adversaries deploy bots to front-run (trade ahead of you), fake enthusiasm (fabricate positive sentiment), and extract money from naive copiers. Building a system to detect manipulation and protect copiers is urgent.
42.wh: Copy trading is inherently adversarial: your trades signal information (you think the price will go up), and adversaries can exploit this signal by trading ahead of you and dumping at a higher price once they've benefited. Traditional fraud detection uses statistics (sudden price spikes, volume anomalies), but sophisticated bots adapt: they learn what patterns trigger detection and avoid them. A copier cannot trust price data alone because prices reflect manipulation. The challenge is to predict trader profitability not from price signals, but from the broader behavioral and market context.
42.ap: The paper builds a multi-agent defense system using a multimodal LLM and chain-of-thought reasoning. Instead of detecting bots by pattern matching, it reasons about trader behavior end-to-end: (1) A multimodal LLM processes multiple signals—transaction history, sentiment data from social media, trade timing, market conditions—to form a rich picture of what the trader was thinking; (2) Chain-of-thought reasoning makes the LLM articulate its reasoning step-by-step ('trader bought before announcement, sold after spike, which suggests advance knowledge'), revealing manipulation; (3) The system predicts whether following this trader is profitable, accounting for the adversarial environment. The approach outperforms statistics-based detection because it reasons about intent and market microstructure.
42.ww: Chain-of-thought reasoning works because manipulation leaves behavioral signatures—timing anomalies, message patterns, correlated trades—that an LLM can recognize and articulate. Multimodal input (prices + social sentiment + transactions) prevents adversaries from gaming any single signal; manipulating all modalities simultaneously is harder. Predicting profitability directly (rather than detecting bots) frames the problem correctly: the copier cares whether following this trader makes money, and the LLM can assess this by reasoning about adversarial context.
42.po: In realistic meme coin markets with substantial friction, the multi-agent LLM system achieves 3% average return per investment, outperforming zero-shot LLM predictions and statistical baselines in both accuracy and economic performance—demonstrating that reasoning-based defenses can make copy trading viable even in adversarial, manipulated markets.

43.bp: Vast amounts of structured data live on the web—product catalogs (electronics, prices, descriptions), knowledge bases (facts about entities), scientific datasets (measurements, metadata). These tables are heterogeneous and messy, making it hard to build a single classification model ('is this item electronics or clothing?'). Large language models are already deployed everywhere, so if you could reuse their semantic understanding (the knowledge they already extracted from text), you might avoid training specialized models on each table.
43.wh: LLMs produce semantic embeddings—numerical summaries of text meaning—but these embeddings are optimized for text retrieval and language understanding, not for table classification. A naive approach would pass a table row as text to an LLM, get an embedding, and classify it, but this underperforms specialized tabular models that exploit table structure. The question is: why don't embeddings work well, and can we fix them without retraining the LLM? LLMs are black boxes; you cannot easily modify them. The path forward requires understanding what LLM embeddings are missing for tabular tasks.
43.ap: TaRL (Table Representation with Language Model) uses LLM embeddings directly but applies two fixes: (1) Remove the common component—across all embeddings in a batch, there is often a direction where embeddings are similar (called a 'dominant direction'). This common component wastes the embedding space; subtracting it out leaves more room for meaningful differences between items. (2) Calibrate softmax temperature—the softmax function converts scores into probabilities using a temperature parameter. LLM embeddings often need a different temperature than default to produce good probabilities for classification. A simple meta-learner, trained on handcrafted features, learns to predict the right temperature for each table. This approach uses minimal additional training (only the temperature predictor, not the LLM).
43.ww: Removing the common component works because it frees up the embedding space: if all embeddings point in the same direction, the classifier cannot see differences. Subtracting the mean/dominant direction is a standard technique in representation learning. Calibrating temperature works because LLM embeddings come from language training, where temperature matters differently than in tabular classification; adjusting it for the new task is a form of domain adaptation. The meta-learner is lightweight because it only predicts one scalar (temperature), not hundreds of weights, so it trains quickly on small labeled datasets.
43.po: TaRL achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art specialized tabular models on few-shot classification tasks using only LLM embeddings and two post-hoc corrections, demonstrating that deployed LLMs can be repurposed for structured data without specialized retraining or model modification.

44.bp: Teachers spend hours planning lessons—deciding learning objectives, choosing teaching methods, designing activities, preparing assessments. Lesson plans that work are often inconsistent in structure and rarely adapt in real time to student needs. Automating lesson planning would free up teacher time and let plans adapt to different learners. Large language models could help, but a single LLM often produces generic plans. Multiple LLMs with different expertise, collaborating, might produce better plans.
44.wh: A novice teacher knows the big picture but struggles with specifics (how exactly do I teach photosynthesis?). An experienced teacher knows the curriculum deeply but might miss pedagogical innovation. A pedagogical expert understands how learning works but might not know your specific curriculum. Getting one LLM to do all three roles causes it to make compromises, producing mediocre plans. The insight is that lesson planning is inherently collaborative—you need multiple perspectives, and the perspectives must argue and refine. Existing approaches use a single LLM or chain-of-thought, which lacks true collaboration.
44.ap: COMA (Collaborative Multi-Role Agent) deploys three specialized agents: (1) Novice agent—understands the lesson topic but lacks precision; proposes a rough lesson flow; (2) Veteran agent—deeply knows the curriculum and textbooks; critiques and refines the flow, filling in knowledge details; (3) Master agent—exhibits pedagogical expertise; redesigns activities to adapt to diverse learners, adds assessment strategies. The agents iterate: novice proposes, veteran refines, master polishes. This mimics how real educational teams work. Each agent is a separate LLM instance with custom prompts that emphasize its role's perspective.
44.ww: Iterated collaboration works because each agent catches what others miss and proposes corrections. The novice grounds the plan in content; the veteran ensures accuracy; the master ensures pedagogy. Having explicit roles prevents agents from converging to mediocrity; each agent defends its perspective. Iterations allow agents to build on each other: veteran refines novice, master refines veteran, novice may refine master on content details. This dance produces plans that integrate multiple viewpoints rather than averaging them out.
44.po: Comprehensive experiments across five subjects using expert-designed pedagogical metrics show COMA significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baseline LLM methods, producing lesson plans that are more structured, coherent, and adaptable to diverse learner needs—demonstrating that multi-agent collaboration is more effective than single-agent generation for complex knowledge work requiring multiple expertise.

45.bp: Cities need to know what will happen in every neighborhood: Will this area need more police? More doctors? Where should we build affordable housing? Urban planners need dozens of predictions at once, from crime to air quality to transportation patterns, and these things are deeply tangled together—fixing one often changes another.
45.wh: The approach uses a Mixture-of-Experts architecture, which works like having specialized teams of data analysts instead of one generalist. Each team is trained to look at certain types of input signals (traffic cameras, weather, census data) and make predictions for the indicators it's best at. A router mechanism decides which features go to which expert.
45.ww: When you let specialists focus on what they do best, you save computation and get better predictions—a doctor shouldn't diagnose broken bones if they're a cardiologist. Here, different neighborhoods and their data patterns are handled by different experts, and the system only uses the computation it actually needs instead of wasting resources on every possible path.
45.po: On real data from three cities, UrbanMoE predicted multiple urban outcomes simultaneously better than all other methods tested. It makes planning faster too—fewer calculations mean planners get answers sooner when they need to make decisions.

46.bp: We used to think the main threat from AI-generated fake media was the shocking deepfake videos—a celebrity's face pasted onto someone else's body. But now that AI can generate tons of text automatically, the real danger is subtler and bigger: thousands of articles that sound plausible get created and spread, making people unsure what's even true anymore.
46.wh: Videos are visceral and memorable—one deepfake video can alarm millions. But text is scalable: one AI can pump out articles by the thousands, slowly poisoning the information ecosystem until no one trusts anything. The hard part isn't spotting an obvious fake; it's noticing when real-looking text has been synthetically manufactured at scale.
46.ap: Researchers interviewed 21 experts across AI, policy, and misinformation—asking them how serious different kinds of AI fakes are and which defense strategies work. They then asked about the measurement problem: how do you even *count* if your defense is working when there's no standard way to test it?
46.ww: When you talk to people who've fought this before, they tell you what actually matters. Experts said technical tools (like classifiers that try to spot fakes) don't work as well as everyone hoped, but clear rules about where information comes from—provenance standards—do. You need reproducible methods so when someone claims a defense works, others can verify it independently.
46.po: The researchers found that treating information integrity like infrastructure—requiring proof of where things came from, documenting methods rigorously—is what actually stops synthetic consensus from forming. Without that, fake media spreads faster than detection catches up.

47.bp: When a large organization wants to train a machine learning model using data from branches in different countries or departments, they face a privacy problem: they can't just send raw patient records or transaction logs to a central server. Federated Learning lets each branch train its own model locally, then share only the learned patterns, keeping raw data private. But now imagine each branch has different needs—a rural clinic serves different patients than an urban hospital.
47.wh: In federated learning, the central server collects what each branch's model learned and merges those learnings together. But merging creates a tug-of-war: the merged model gets good at the common patterns across all branches but bad at what makes each branch unique. Each branch then tries to improve locally, but that pulls it back toward its own old habits. You end up with something that's mediocre everywhere.
47.ap: Thorki gives each branch two models instead of one: a small personal model for its unique patients, and a large shared model for general patterns. When making a decision, a fusion network (a lightweight model that learns to blend predictions) takes predictions from both and combines them. The small model and large model never directly compete—they cooperate through the fusion network's learned weights.
47.ww: By splitting the job of learning into two separate models, Thorki stops the general and personal from fighting each other. The small model never has to forget how to help unique patients, and the large model can become a true general expert without being pulled back by local oddities. When both answer and are combined thoughtfully, you get better results from each branch.
47.po: On real hospital and business data, Thorki was 0.16% to 19% more accurate than other federated systems, and trained to good accuracy 2 to 10 times faster. Each branch gets to keep its specialized knowledge while also benefiting from learning across the entire organization.

48.bp: On streaming platforms like Twitch, thousands of viewers chat at once. Moderators have to catch insults, threats, and harassment instantly. But these happen at scale and speed no human team can match, while also facing abuse themselves. We need AI to help filter the toxic stuff before it spreads.
48.wh: Standard keyword filtering catches obvious curses but misses insults hidden in slang. A word by itself might be innocent, but next to other words becomes cruel. Also, Twitch is unique—people send emotes (little cartoon faces and icons) mixed into their messages, and those emotes carry meaning. A message "you suck" alone is rude, but "you suck [laughing emoji]" might be joking with friends. Most AI systems completely ignore emotes.
48.ap: ToxiTwitch combines several tools: it takes the text message and turns it into numbers (using recent large language models), separately turns the emotes into numbers, then feeds both into traditional machine learning classifiers (Random Forest and SVM) that learned from labeled examples of toxic and non-toxic Twitch messages. The classifiers say yes or no based on both the text and the emote signals together.
48.ww: Emotes are context—they tell you the intent behind the words. When you include context, you make fewer mistakes. A random forest or SVM can learn patterns: "this type of word + this type of emoji = usually joking, don't flag it," whereas ignoring emotes forces the system to guess without half the information.
48.po: When trained on one specific channel's message history, ToxiTwitch caught toxic behavior with 80% accuracy, beating a standard AI model (BERT) by 13 percentage points. It flagged 76% of the toxic messages it found (the precision measure), meaning fewer false alarms that misdirect moderator attention.

49.bp: Large language models train on billions of pages from the internet. Some of those pages contain sensitive information: medical records that were publicly posted by mistake, private emails someone published, confidential documents. The question is: did the model memorize that sensitive stuff? If it did, an attacker might be able to trick it into repeating your private data back to them.
49.wh: Testing for memorization is tricky because AI models often learn the *meaning* of something without learning the exact words. You could feed the model "John Smith had diabetes" and then try "john smith has diabetes" (different grammar, same meaning) and it might not recognize it as the same—so a naive test would think the model didn't memorize the original, when it actually did.
49.ap: ASMIA takes a potential secret from the training data and creates multiple versions that mean the same thing but sound different—like paraphrasing a sentence. It shows all these versions to the model and watches the attention patterns (where the model's focus goes when processing). It then builds a classifier that learns the difference between the model's response to information it trained on versus random new information, using both the model's confidence numbers and the attention patterns.
49.ww: Attention patterns reveal understanding—if a model truly learned something deeply, it will pay attention to it in consistent ways regardless of paraphrasing. By checking many semantically equivalent versions, you catch memorization that word-for-word matching would miss. A smart classifier trained on these signals can spot the difference between genuine knowledge and random guessing.
49.po: On Wikipedia (a large real corpus), ASMIA detected training data leakage far better than existing methods. It shows that models do memorize sensitive patterns, even when those patterns are reworded, confirming a real privacy risk that simpler tests would have missed.

50.bp: DiDi and Uber predict ride demand by neighborhood and time so they can position drivers efficiently: surge pricing when demand is high, surge pricing areas to incentivize drivers, and planning where to hire more drivers. Accurate forecasts mean riders wait less, drivers earn more, and the system stays balanced. Poor forecasts mean wasted driver time and frustrated passengers.
50.wh: Cities are complex—the same intersection behaves wildly differently during a concert, a rainstorm, or a traffic jam. Raw historical data doesn't contain the semantics: a data point says "100 rides picked up here at 3pm" but doesn't explain why. Also, different neighborhoods have different personalities: a business district at 9am versus a nightlife district at 9pm are completely different prediction problems.
50.ap: MVGR-Net learns neighborhood personality in a pre-training stage by looking at two things: the types of places nearby (restaurants, offices, parks—semantic attributes that give character) and actual movement patterns from historical trips. This creates a rich numeric sketch of each neighborhood. Later, when forecasting, it fine-tunes a large language model on this sketch, feeding in details about external events (concerts, weather) as context.
50.ww: By understanding neighborhood character first, you know what to expect: office areas have predictable morning spikes, tourist areas spike at different times. When you then add information about specific events happening today, the model understands how those events *alter* normal patterns rather than trying to learn from scratch each time. Geospatial understanding plus event context is far more powerful than either alone.
50.po: On DiDi's real forecasting task, MVGR-Net achieved state-of-the-art performance, meaning it predicted rider demand more accurately than competing approaches, enabling more efficient driver dispatch and fewer empty rides.

51.bp: Drug discovery works like this: researchers design a molecule, test it, measure how well it works (does it kill cancer cells? is it toxic?). To speed this up, AI can propose new molecules. But the AI trains on old data of molecules that worked. Then a pharmaceutical company wants it to discover molecules for a *new* disease where the rules might be different—will it still work?
51.wh: A molecule's effectiveness comes from its structure plus the disease being treated. The AI mixes these two together in one mathematical space. When the disease changes (new distribution), the learned pattern breaks because the model relied on correlations specific to the old disease. For example, a feature that predicted success in cancer might be irrelevant or even harmful in Alzheimer's.
51.ap: MoFE builds a graph neural network that explicitly separates the unchanging structural rules (these atoms bonded this way always act this way) from the changeable rules (how that structure helps *this specific* disease). It adds a Mixture-of-Experts layer where different expert networks specialize in different structural patterns. When you describe a new editing goal, the system routes through the expert best suited to that structure and disease combination.
51.ww: By keeping invariant principles (physics) separate from variant details (disease-specific effects), the model can swap in new disease contexts and still get the physics right. Each expert learns to focus on one aspect, so when the disease changes, the experts' core understanding of structure stays valid—only the high-level routing needs to adjust.
51.po: MoFE designed molecules that were more effective across different diseases and instruction types than models that didn't separate invariant and variant factors, suggesting it could be more useful for discovering drugs when the disease domain changes.

52.bp: Imagine you sketch a rough drawing of a bird and want to find photos of birds that match your sketch. The challenge: your sketch is crude and abstract—just curved lines—while real bird photos are detailed. A human would mentally interpret the sketch and look for photos with those visual traits. We want AI to do the same.
52.wh: Sketches are missing information—no colors, no fine details, no background. A naive approach tries to find mathematical patterns that connect sketches directly to photos, but there's a huge gap to bridge. Convolutional networks and distance learning (trying to make similar sketches and images close together numerically) can work, but they miss what the sketch is actually *about*—the semantic intention behind the artist's lines.
52.ap: SketchMind uses a multimodal large language model to look at the sketch and describe what it *means* using text (like a person explaining their drawing). Then it builds a graph where the sketch is in the center and multiple text descriptions are nodes around it. A graph attention mechanism (learned weights on connections) decides which descriptions are reliable and which are noise, then blends them together. Finally, a Jigsaw Matching module finds local and global visual correspondences between the sketch's refined meaning and candidate photos.
52.ww: Language is precise where sketches are ambiguous. A language model can say "this looks like a hummingbird with flowers," which narrows the search enormously. By using attention on the graph, the system learns to trust key descriptions and ignore spurious details. Then you can match both fine details (the flowers' shape) and the overall scene, so you find the right photo even when it's photographed from a different angle or lighting.
52.po: SketchMind retrieved the correct images more reliably than existing systems that didn't use language understanding, showing that language-aware reasoning helps bridge the abstraction gap between rough sketches and detailed photos.

53.bp: Blockchain systems like Bitcoin are slow when they try to run on one computer. Sharding splits the workload: each shard is a mini-blockchain handling a portion of transactions. If 16 shards work in parallel, you should get roughly 16x speed. But reality is messier: transactions often reference data from multiple shards, causing shards to block and wait for each other.
53.wh: Without coordination, each shard schedules transactions independently. This leads to conflicts: shard A packages a transaction that depends on data from shard B, but shard B hasn't processed its part yet. They block each other. Centralized coordination eliminates conflicts but adds a bottleneck and a security risk—one coordinator could cheat. You need coordination that's both decentralized and conflict-free.
53.ap: Concordia lets each shard predict future cross-shard interactions using a Graph Neural Network—basically, each shard learns patterns in who transacts with whom and predicts which transactions will soon need data from other shards. Shards then broadcast these predictions to each other (small messages, not full data). Each shard uses this hint to pack its transactions better: it delays those that will conflict and confirms those that won't.
53.ww: Prediction prevents conflicts rather than resolving them after they happen. If a shard knows "these transactions will need input from shard B," it can schedule them intelligently—group them or defer them. Graph neural networks are good at learning patterns from interconnected data, so they're natural for predicting transaction dependencies. Broadcasting lightweight signals keeps the system decentralized without the overhead of sharing full data.
53.po: On a 16-shard system, Concordia doubled throughput and dropped conflicts from 62% to 1.5%, and was 1.67x faster than a centralized scheduler while reducing communication overhead by 95%, showing that cooperative prediction works better than either independent or centralized approaches.

54.bp: When you ask an AI assistant a question and it responds with text, it goes through many intermediate steps. At each step, the model is uncertain and picks the token it thinks is most likely. But sometimes the model focuses too hard on simple filler words (like "the" or "a") instead of the conceptually important words. This is called an attention sink. It's like a student who memorizes the pronoun "the" so well they stop learning anything else.
54.wh: Existing fixes try to either block these filler words or redistribute attention mechanically. But this breaks the meaning—if you block "the," the whole sentence falls apart. A principled fix should let filler words exist but reduce their dominance while keeping meaning intact. The tension: you want to stay faithful to semantics while also removing noise.
54.ap: PAOSC uses two neural networks: a generator that looks at the model's processing and flags which tokens are informationally important, and a discriminator that trains the generator using policy gradient methods (essentially reinforcement learning). The training signal comes from measuring whether the model's confidence stayed stable and whether the loss changed when that token was kept or dropped.
54.ww: Measuring information by confidence and loss changes directly approximates importance—if dropping a token hardly changes the model's behavior, it's probably not carrying meaning. Policy gradients let you optimize this without needing labeled data saying "this token is important." The generator learns by trial: trying different masks and seeing which ones preserve meaning best.
54.po: On eight different language models, PAOSC improved accuracy scores by up to 9.68%. On a constructed dataset, it identified and eliminated 18% of low-value tokens, making inference faster while keeping quality intact.

55.bp: Online retailers recommend what you might buy next based on your recent browsing: you looked at running shoes, so we show you socks. This is session-based recommendation—using short sequences of clicks to predict the next item. The challenge is scale: millions of sessions, and every person who looked at running shoes shouldn't get the exact same recommendation.
55.wh: When two shoppers' sessions end with the same last item (both looked at socks), the algorithm tends to give them identical predictions next—both get shoe recommendations. But they're different people with different history; the one who was browsing winter clothes should see cold-weather items, not the one browsing summer wear. Graph neural networks learned to model session sequences, but they inherit this flaw. Also, popular items (bestsellers) get recommended too often just because they appear in many sessions.
55.ap: SAGE builds a graph of all items and connections (what sequences naturally occur). Then, for each session, it creates multiple versions: one with random variations to act as positive examples and another with negative examples from unpopular items. Using contrastive learning, the system learns to make the session embedding (the numeric summary) match positive variations while staying different from negative ones. This trains the system to distinguish sessions that superficially look similar.
55.ww: Contrastive learning teaches by comparing: "this session is similar to that variation but different from this unrelated session." By creating intentional variations and negatives, you force the model to learn what's unique about each session beyond just the last item. The popularity bias correction (using negative samples from unpopular items) rebalances the recommendation: rare items get a fair chance.
55.po: When SAGE was combined with various existing graph-based systems, all of them improved—especially better at distinguishing sessions with the same last item, showing that the approach generalizes across different architectures and helps systems recommend more diverse and personalized items.

56.bp: Your phone has a small AI model running on it to transcribe speech or suggest completions—no internet required, your data stays private. But personalizing that model (making it better at your accent or your vocabulary) means either uploading your data to the cloud or fine-tuning on-device. Both have costs: cloud annotations are expensive, and fine-tuning drains the phone's battery and storage.
56.wh: The obvious solution—have the cloud service annotate all your data—is expensive. The other extreme—download a big model and fine-tune everything locally—wastes power and memory. You need a middle ground where you're selective about which data to annotate and which model layers to actually change, so the process is cheap and efficient.
56.ap: EcoTune uses a multi-armed bandit strategy (a classic algorithm for deciding what to try next) to identify the highest-value user interactions—messages that would teach the model the most if they were labeled. Only those go to the cloud for annotation. Meanwhile, for on-device tuning, it analyzes which model layers matter most (using layer importance scores) and only updates those layers, leaving the rest frozen.
56.ww: Selective annotation saves money—you annotate the 20% of data that teaches 80% of what the model needs to know. Selective layer updates save memory and power—unfreezing everything means computing gradients everywhere, but if only 20% of the model matters for your specific use case, you waste 80% of the compute. Both selectivity decisions compound to make personalization cheap.
56.po: On real devices, EcoTune needed 20% to 60% fewer annotations than baseline methods and significantly cut the memory required for fine-tuning, making on-device personalization practical even with small budgets.

57.bp: When an e-commerce site recommends items, it uses many signals: clicks (you looked at it), carts (you wanted it), and purchases (you bought it). Clicks are the noisiest—someone might click out of curiosity or by accident. Purchases are the clearest signal of actual interest. Mixing all these together is tricky: the noisy signals can confuse the model into learning bad patterns.
57.wh: If you naively combine all signals equally, clicks overwhelm the model (there are thousands of clicks for every purchase), and the noise in clicks teaches the model bad preferences. If you weight purchases heavily, you ignore useful hints from clicks. The core issue: different users care about auxiliary behaviors differently, and those patterns shift over time or between product categories—it's not stable.
57.ap: RMBRec uses two modules working in parallel. The Representation Robustness Module maximizes how much the model's internal representation of a user from clicks matches their representation from purchases (high mutual information)—this purifies representations by only keeping the user preferences that are truly consistent. The Optimization Robustness Module minimizes the variance of prediction errors across different behavior types—if the model does well on clicks but poorly on purchases, that variance is high, and the module penalizes it.
57.ww: Consistency signals truth—if a user's preferences from clicks and purchases are similar, that's real preference. By maximizing this consistency, you separate signal from noise. Reducing variance across behaviors stabilizes learning: instead of fitting one behavior perfectly and failing on others, you learn a robust model that works across all of them. Both together create a representation that's meaningful rather than just fitting noise.
57.po: On three real e-commerce datasets, RMBRec improved prediction accuracy, especially on the target purchase behavior, while being more robust to the noise and inconsistency in auxiliary behaviors like clicks.

58.bp: Researchers build separate AI systems for graphs from different domains: social networks predict friendships, molecule graphs predict chemical properties, recommendation graphs predict products you'll buy. Each system trains from scratch. The question: can we pre-train on *all* graphs together and build a general-purpose system that works across domains?
58.wh: Graphs vary wildly: a social network's nodes are people, a molecule graph's nodes are atoms. Their meanings are completely different, so a system trained on one doesn't directly transfer to another. Naive approaches treat all graphs identically, which fails—they're asking a model to learn from apples and oranges together without understanding what makes each fruit unique.
58.ap: LEDA first maps all graphs into a shared semantic space using a dimension projection unit (learned transformations that adapt each graph's features without losing information). Then, a variational semantic inference module (a probabilistic model) learns a shared latent distribution—a statistical description of patterns that show up across domains. Pre-training objectives then use this distribution to guide learning, making sure the model captures cross-domain insights.
58.ww: By mapping into a shared space before learning, you're saying: "underneath their surface differences, all these graphs share structural patterns." A variational distribution captures the common structure. Pre-training with this distribution as guidance teaches the model to look for these universal patterns instead of memorizing domain-specific quirks. When you then apply the pre-trained model to a new domain, it starts with universal understanding rather than random initialization.
58.po: LEDA improved performance on downstream graph tasks across multiple domains compared to training separate models or using simple pre-training approaches, showing that learning universal principles across diverse graphs makes the system more useful for new domains.

59.bp: On social media and video platforms, false information spreads fast. A video with misleading audio or edited images can fool millions. Detecting fake videos requires checking: is this video of a real event, or is it fabricated? We need to look both at what the video contains and at information from outside sources to verify it.
59.wh: Inside the video, you only have images, sound, and text—no ground truth. A fake video can be well-made and convincing. To check if it's really fake, you need external context: was this event reported in real news? Do reference videos of the same event exist? But combining external knowledge with internal signals is complex—you have to understand what each signal means and how they relate.
59.ap: TrueLens works in two layers. Externally, it breaks the video into text, visual, and audio components, uses a multimodal language model to describe each one, then retrieves similar videos from a database of known real and fake examples—it finds one real reference and one fake reference. The Adversarial Contrastor compares the query video with both references, learning what makes it similar to or different from each. Internally, the Evidential Logic Fusion module combines signals from text, images, and audio to make a final judgment.
59.ww: Reference videos ground your decision: if this video matches patterns from known fakes, it's probably fake. If it matches real videos, it's probably real. The contrastive comparison (what's like the fake reference? what's like the real reference?) is more informative than absolute judgments. Fusing multiple modalities internally catches fakes that fool one modality but are caught by another—a deepfake video might look real but have weird audio patterns.
59.po: On three benchmark datasets, TrueLens outperformed competing systems at distinguishing real from fake videos, and remained robust when the temporal patterns or event types in test data differed from training, showing that reference-based reasoning generalizes.

60.bp: Recommender systems choose which items to show you, and they have a systematic problem: popular items get recommended far more often than niche ones. This matters because it creates a feedback loop—more recommendations mean more users see it, which makes it seem even more popular. The real-world goal is to balance serving what everyone wants with surfacing the hidden gems that matter to particular users.
60.wh: Most systems try to fix this by simply asking 'how do we show more variety?' But popularity bias isn't really about variety—it's rooted in deeper reasons. Popular items genuinely resonate with broad audiences, while niche items serve specific needs. A method that just throws in random diverse recommendations misses the actual cause of the bias and ends up mixing quality with forced randomness, harming both fairness and accuracy.
60.ap: FairLRM uses a large language model (an AI trained on vast text) to understand the *why* behind popularity. It breaks popularity bias into two parts: what makes certain items popular on their own (the items themselves) and what users' personal patterns make them drawn to popular things. The system uses carefully written prompts to ask the language model to reason about both global item popularity and individual user taste, then makes recommendations grounded in that deeper understanding.
60.ww: Language models are trained to reason across many domains and can articulate causes and consequences in natural language. By forcing the model to explicitly decompose popularity bias into item-side and user-side factors, the system stops treating bias as a surface problem ('add variety') and instead models the structural reasons the bias exists. This means recommendations can actually target the root causes rather than just the symptoms.
60.po: The paper demonstrates that FairLRM improves both fairness (less bias against niche items) and recommendation accuracy (people get better suggestions) compared to previous methods, because it's addressing the real mechanisms behind the bias rather than working around them.

61.bp: Recommender systems using reinforcement learning watch user behavior in real time—clicks, ratings, how long someone engages—and use that to improve recommendations. This online learning is powerful because systems adapt moment by moment. But it creates a privacy nightmare: collecting behavioral traces reveals detailed patterns about what someone likes, wants, and fears.
61.wh: The tension is fundamental: online learning needs fresh user data to improve, but collecting and storing that data exposes individuals to privacy breaches or misuse. Standard privacy tools like differential privacy (adding noise to mask individuals) tend to degrade the quality of the system significantly. And even if the central system is private, once you've collected the data, it's vulnerable.
61.ap: FeedGuard uses several layers. First, it improves the learning system itself by using a 'critic'—a separate model that validates whether learned behaviors make sense—to guide the main recommendation model. Second, it collects feedback through split federated learning, meaning some computation happens on the user's device before data is sent. Third, it applies differential privacy throughout, which mathematically guarantees that no individual's data leaks, and proves those guarantees formally.
61.ww: By splitting the work between user devices and servers, and adding mathematical privacy noise that can be proven to prevent re-identification, the system removes the central database of user behavioral traces that was the original privacy risk. The critic guidance helps because the learning process needs less data to work well, so less data needs to be collected.
61.po: Experiments show FeedGuard maintains strong recommendation and learning performance in both offline and online settings while meeting formal privacy guarantees—meaning it actually solves the tradeoff rather than just reducing harm.

62.bp: When brands advertise online, they want their ads appearing next to content that reflects their values and image. A luxury brand doesn't want to appear next to violent content; a family-friendly brand doesn't want to appear next to adult material. Automated systems need to scan vast amounts of content and catch these mismatches before ads run, because manual review at scale is impossible.
62.wh: Simple approaches like keyword matching fail because real problems are subtle. A story might have a brief adult scene that's plot-relevant but still problematic for certain brands. Or it might discuss sensitive topics thoughtfully but still disqualify itself. Existing AI models trained on general internet text don't understand these brand-specific safety rules, and there's no good dataset to train on because nobody has systematically collected examples.
62.ap: The paper creates the first large dataset by taking 51 complete stories from Wattpad, breaking them into 435 chapters, and having human raters label each across nine standard safety categories. They then test three approaches: using ChatGPT and GPT-3 with zero training (just asking them to classify), fine-tuning RoBERTa (a specialized model), and fine-tuning GPT-3 with the new labeled data.
62.ww: Models trained specifically on brand-safety examples learn what the subtle patterns actually are, whereas off-the-shelf AI models have never seen examples marked as brand-unsafe. Even though ChatGPT is powerful, it makes mistakes on edge cases because it wasn't designed for this problem. RoBERTa's architecture turns out to be particularly good at picking up the linguistic patterns in safety-critical content.
62.po: The paper shows that fine-tuned RoBERTa outperforms all others, and that the new dataset enables much more reliable automated brand-safety checking. It also reveals which safety categories are harder (general ones like 'violence' are easier than nuanced concerns like 'substance use implications'), helping platforms prioritize where human review is still needed.

63.bp: Modern websites and apps are filled with images and text together—product pages show both pictures and descriptions, social media mixes photos with captions. Recommender systems need to understand all of this together to suggest things people actually want. But pictures contain more than just the item itself: they have backgrounds, decorations, watermarks—noise that distracts from what actually matters.
63.wh: Existing systems treat all parts of an image equally. If you're recommending shoes, the system looks at the shoe, the background, the model wearing it, any logos, all mixed together. This muddles the signal—the background might be more visually distinctive than the shoe itself, so the system ends up learning to match 'shoes in beach settings' rather than 'shoes with similar style.' With text the same thing happens: a product description might mention the brand or marketing phrases more prominently than the actual item properties.
63.ap: TargetMR separates the wheat from the chaff. For text, it uses syntactic parsing (breaking sentences into parts of speech) to identify which words describe the item itself versus flavor text. For images, it uses segmentation (computer vision technique that identifies separate objects in a picture) to isolate the main item from the background. Then it uses a language model to validate which objects are truly central to the item's identity. Once identified, the system refines how it represents these target elements to emphasize the semantic match.
63.ww: By explicitly separating core content from decoration, the system can focus its learning on what actually determines recommendations. A shoe's style matters; the beach background doesn't. A shirt's material and color matter; the brand mention in the text is secondary. The system becomes more faithful to the actual item properties and less distracted by presentation.
63.po: TargetMR can be plugged into any existing recommendation system (Graph Neural Networks or language models) and improves their performance by reducing the semantic shift—the misleading signal—that comes from auxiliary objects. This means recommendations more accurately reflect what users actually prefer about items.

64.bp: People seeking deep answers often need to search through multiple complex documents—research papers with figures and equations, financial reports with charts and tables, technical manuals with diagrams. Current AI systems can answer questions from web text but essentially ignore all the visual information, missing half the knowledge. The real-world need is to let AI genuinely think through documents the way a human analyst would.
64.wh: Visual information in documents (charts, equations, tables, diagrams) isn't optional—it often contains the key insight. But extracting meaning from these requires understanding both what the visual shows and how it relates to the surrounding text. Simple approaches that treat documents as text-only or that try to convert images to text lose the semantic richness. And retrieving the right parts of a 100-page document when you have 50 figures and 200 tables requires understanding granularity—sometimes you need a single figure, sometimes an entire chapter.
64.ap: Doc-Researcher has three layers. First, a sophisticated parser that reads document structure (columns, sections, order of elements) and breaks documents into multiple levels: individual figures, groups of figures, sections, whole documents. Second, a retrieval system that can search across text-only, vision-only, or hybrid combinations, and dynamically chooses how detailed to be based on the query. Third, a multi-agent reasoning loop where different agents decompose a complex question, each gathers relevant evidence from the parsed documents and figures, and then synthesizes a final answer that weaves together insights from multiple sources.
64.ww: By preserving structure during parsing and enabling granular retrieval, the system can find exactly the right evidence. By using multiple agents that each specialize in gathering evidence and then combining their findings, it avoids the trap of a single-path reasoning that might miss something. The visual-semantic understanding from parsing means charts and equations become searchable and interpretable, not just decoration.
64.po: The paper introduces a benchmark with 158 expert-curated questions requiring multi-document, multi-modal reasoning, and shows that Doc-Researcher can answer these correctly more often than baselines that ignore visual information. This enables AI systems to actually think through the kinds of documents humans use for research and analysis.

65.bp: Every video uploaded to social media, every photo in cloud storage, every sensor stream from autonomous vehicles or drones produces massive amounts of data. Storing and transmitting all this is expensive. Lossless compression—squeezing data down without losing any actual information—is the standard solution, but no single compression method works well for all types of data (video, images, sensor streams vary wildly in their structure).
65.wh: The challenge is that different data types have different patterns. A video's entropy (how 'random' or unpredictable it is) might be low because frames are similar, but a sensor stream's entropy might be much higher. Adaptive methods that work well for one type of data often waste computation on types where it's overkill. Also, data distributions shift—the videos on Monday look different from videos on Saturday—so a system trained once becomes stale.
65.ap: MoE-LC uses a 'mixture of experts' approach: train multiple different compression engines (experts), each good at different types or difficulties of data. A routing system estimates how hard a given piece of data is to compress (its entropy) and decides how many experts to activate and which ones. Within the active experts, high-precision calculation happens only in the most important computational steps, while less critical operations use lower precision to save resources.
65.ww: By having specialized experts and routing based on estimated difficulty, the system avoids wasting powerful compression on easy data and avoids using weak compression on hard data. By allowing the routing to change per batch, it adapts to distribution shifts. By focusing high-precision computation only where it matters, the system runs efficiently without sacrificing compression quality on the data types that need it.
65.po: Experiments show MoE-LC achieves 5-70% improvement in compression across real-world multimodal datasets (depending on type), meaning data can be stored and transmitted more efficiently while staying perfectly lossless.

66.bp: Graph theorists and computer scientists care deeply about whether graphs have certain mathematical properties—is there a path visiting every node exactly once (Hamiltonian), can the graph be drawn on a flat surface without crossing edges (planar), does it contain certain forbidden structures (claw-free). These properties are hard to compute directly, but if you visualize a graph as a picture, sometimes humans can see the answer intuitively. The goal is to teach AI systems to detect these properties the way vision works.
66.wh: Graphs can be drawn many different ways. The same logical structure looks wildly different depending on where nodes are placed. Previous vision-based approaches used a single fixed drawing method—say, always arranging nodes in a circle. But some properties are easier to spot in certain layouts than others. A Hamiltonian cycle is obvious in one layout but invisible in another. So the fixed layout becomes a bottleneck, limiting what the vision system can actually learn.
66.ap: VSAL dynamically generates the best visualization for each graph. Rather than using a single standard layout, it has a generator that, for each graph instance, produces a layout optimized to make the property being tested visually obvious. Then a vision model processes that adaptive visualization to detect the property.
66.ww: By allowing the layout to change based on the graph's structure, the system can highlight relevant patterns. If you're checking for a Hamiltonian cycle, the layout can emphasize the cycle structure. If you're checking planarity, it can spread nodes to make crossing issues visible. The vision model no longer fights against a bad visualization; instead, the visualization cooperates with the property being detected.
66.po: VSAL outperforms previous vision-based methods on Hamiltonian cycle, planarity, claw-freeness, and tree detection tasks, demonstrating that adaptive visualization genuinely helps AI systems detect graph properties more accurately.

67.bp: Medical question answering—when a patient asks 'can I take this drug with this condition?'—is high-stakes. Wrong answers can harm people. Language models can write fluent answers to anything, but they hallucinate (confidently state false medical facts). To make medical AI trustworthy, answers must be both accurate and *verifiable*—traceable to real medical knowledge that an expert can check.
67.wh: Language models learn patterns from text but don't truly reason about causality or constraints. A medical knowledge graph—a structured database of diseases, symptoms, drugs, and their relationships—contains the real causal facts, but language models don't naturally respect these constraints when generating text. If a knowledge graph says drug X contradicts condition Y, a language model might still confidently recommend X anyway, or it might stretch logic in ways that sound plausible but are wrong.
67.ap: GC-DPG works in two phases. Phase one: given a user question and a disease-centric knowledge graph, the system plans which facts from the graph are relevant and which intents (seeking symptoms, drugs, tests, diet advice) the question addresses. This creates a structured answer plan that explicitly lists permissible knowledge graph facts. Phase two: the system generates a prompt for the language model that hard-constrains it to only those permissible facts, then runs a bidirectional checker that verifies the generated answer respects the knowledge graph relationships and flags hallucinations.
67.ww: By forcing the language model to plan against the knowledge graph before generating, the system prevents it from freely confabulating. By then constraining generation to the plan and checking consistency bidirectionally, it catches deviations. The knowledge graph provides the ground truth, and the language model is reduced to a translator—it explains graph facts in natural language rather than inventing facts.
67.po: On a Chinese medical QA dataset, GC-DPG improves the precision of mentioned entities and substantially reduces hallucinations compared to models that either ignore the knowledge graph or use it loosely, making it more trustworthy for clinical settings.

68.bp: Online education platforms track student interactions—which problems they attempt, how long they spend, whether they get answers right—to personalize learning. The system needs to infer each student's knowledge state (what they've mastered, what they're struggling with) from their behavior patterns. Better inference means better recommendations for what to study next.
68.wh: Student learning is complex: it unfolds over many timescales simultaneously. Some struggles are short-term confusion that resolves with practice. Some are long-term knowledge gaps. Some patterns show up quickly; others only emerge after weeks. Existing systems use a single architecture (like self-attention) with fixed biases toward certain patterns. Self-attention naturally picks up overall trends and semantic relationships but can miss fine-grained temporal details. Other architectures each have their own characteristic blindspots.
68.ap: FA-KT combines four different model architectures—self-attention, Mamba (a modern efficient architecture), CNN (convolutional networks), and LSTM (recurrent networks)—each of which naturally emphasizes different frequency patterns in data. A frequency-aware router analyzes each individual student's interaction sequence, detects whether it contains more short-term noise or long-term patterns, and dynamically weights the experts accordingly. For a student with high short-term variation, it leans on architectures good at capturing that; for a student with stable long-term trends, it activates different experts.
68.ww: Different architectures truly do capture different frequency components: self-attention emphasizes global low-frequency patterns, CNNs pick up local structures, LSTMs track temporal flow. By explicitly routing based on the frequencies present in each student's data, the system never forces a square peg into a round hole. The personalization per student, rather than using one-size-fits-all, lets each architecture shine where it's actually best.
68.po: Across five benchmark datasets, FA-KT outperforms 20 strong baselines at predicting student performance, indicating that the multi-expert adaptive routing genuinely captures the diversity of learning behaviors better than any single architecture could.

69.bp: Real-world graphs—social networks, financial transaction networks, citation networks—scale to millions of nodes and billions of edges. Training neural networks on these graphs to predict properties or classify nodes is computationally expensive and often impossible on available hardware. The solution is to compress a large graph into a smaller surrogate that preserves the most important structure, so training becomes feasible.
69.wh: Previous graph compression methods work well for undirected graphs (where connections are symmetric: A-B means B-A) but fall apart on directed graphs (where A→B doesn't imply B→A). Directed graphs encode causal structure—transaction flows, cause-effect in citations, influence direction in social networks. Losing directionality in compression means losing the meaning. Also, large directed graphs often have internal community structure (clusters of densely connected nodes); destroying this structure during compression breaks the meaningful patterns.
69.ap: Dir-GD uses community detection to first partition a large directed graph into independent subgraphs (communities). Each subgraph is small enough to train a directed graph neural network on separately. The trained models are then aggregated into a single compact synthetic directed graph that represents what all the local models learned. This synthetic graph is far smaller than the original but tries to capture the essential topology and directional semantics.
69.ww: By respecting community structure, the method avoids destroying the local patterns that matter. By training separately on each community and then synthesizing a global graph, it ensures that directionality is preserved (a→b in a community stays a→b, not symmetrized). The distributed training becomes tractable because individual communities fit in memory, and the synthesis step produces a compact model that still encodes what the original graph's structure teaches.
69.po: On large-scale datasets like soc-pokec-relationships (millions of nodes), Dir-GD achieves over 91% accuracy while compressing to 0.1% of the original size, meaning expensive neural network training becomes feasible on limited hardware while preserving the directed graph structure that applications like fraud detection depend on.

70.bp: Before autonomous vehicles become widespread, they must be tested exhaustively in simulation. But here's the trust problem: when a company submits simulation logs to regulators claiming 'our car is safe, here's the evidence,' how can regulators be sure the logs haven't been faked or altered? And companies don't want to reveal their simulation data because it's proprietary. The goal is cryptographic proof that a simulation ran safely, without exposing the data.
70.wh: Normal verification means auditors inspect the actual simulation logs—but this exposes sensitive data and invites tampering accusations. You could hash the data to prove it existed, but hashing doesn't prove the simulation actually followed safety rules (collision avoidance, speed limits). You need proof that the simulation adhered to specific constraints without revealing the simulation itself.
70.ap: ZK-V uses Zero-Knowledge Proofs (a cryptographic technique where one party mathematically proves a statement is true without revealing the information underlying it) combined with blockchain (a distributed ledger that records and timestamps verifications). A developer simulates their autonomous vehicle and generates a zero-knowledge proof that the simulation satisfied constraints like collision avoidance and speed limits. The proof is recorded on a blockchain, creating a tamper-evident timestamp. A regulator can verify the proof mathematically without ever seeing the actual simulation logs.
70.ww: Zero-knowledge proofs exploit mathematical properties: a prover can construct a proof that a statement is true (e.g., 'this simulation had zero collisions') that's cryptographically sound—faking it is computationally infeasible—without revealing the underlying data. Blockchain creates an immutable record of when the proof was generated, preventing backdating. Together, they create trust: regulators can verify safety happened, companies keep data private, and neither party can fake the proof.
70.po: The paper outlines a simulation-agnostic architecture that works with any autonomous driving simulator and any safety constraint that can be formally expressed, offering a scalable pathway for decentralized, trustless certification in autonomous vehicle deployment.

71.bp: Skin-toned emojis—the skin tone modifier system (yellow, light brown, medium brown, dark brown, very dark brown)—lets people express identity and feel included in digital communication. But AI models that power recommendation, content moderation, and communication features can be biased in how they treat these emojis, effectively discriminating based on skin tone. The goal is to measure and expose these biases so platforms can fix them.
71.wh: It's not obvious that models have tone-based bias in emojis. Specialized emoji models and large language models have seen millions of emoji uses in training data, so they should understand them. But 'understanding' is subtle: a model might associate certain skin tones with certain sentiment (darker tones with negative words), or it might treat the same emoji with different skin tones as completely different entities rather than variations of the same concept.
71.ap: The paper evaluates two types of models: specialized emoji embedding models and four large language models (Llama, Gemma, Qwen, Mistral), analyzing how they represent skin-toned emojis across four dimensions. First, semantic consistency: does the same emoji with different skin tones have related meanings? Second, representational similarity: do different skin tones cluster reasonably or are they treated as unrelated? Third, sentiment polarity: are certain skin tones associated with negative sentiment? Fourth, core biases: across all dimensions, do patterns of bias emerge?
71.ww: By measuring multiple dimensions, the analysis goes beyond surface coverage ('does the model know the emoji exists?') to deeper semantic properties. If a model doesn't treat 😊 (yellow) and 😊🟤 (dark brown) as related, it's missing something fundamental. If darker tones correlate with negative sentiment, that's a representational harm. The comparison across model types exposes which classes of AI systems have worse problems.
71.po: The paper finds that specialized emoji models have severe deficiencies in skin tone modifier support, while large language models handle them better but still exhibit skewed sentiment and inconsistent meanings across skin tones. This identifies specific harms that platforms need to audit and fix to ensure AI treats people equitably.

72.bp: Social media platforms have enormous power to shape public opinion through their recommendation and content filtering policies. A small algorithmic change—amplifying a certain viewpoint or suppressing certain content—can shift which information spreads and cause polarization. Testing these policies requires understanding how users and the platform's algorithms interact, which currently happens through A/B testing (deploy, observe, hope nothing bad happens). The goal is to pre-evaluate policies safely before deployment.
72.wh: A/B testing identifies problems only after they've harmed real people. Creating a test where you intentionally amplify polarization or misinformation just to see what happens is ethically problematic. Simulations of social dynamics are hard: users aren't robots following rules; they respond to others' behavior, change their minds, react to platform interventions. A simulation that doesn't capture this realism will give wrong predictions.
72.ap: PolicySim uses language models to simulate the bidirectional dynamics: user behavior and platform policy influence each other. User agents are tuned via supervised fine-tuning and preference optimization to behave realistically on the specific platform. An intervention module uses a contextual bandit (a decision algorithm that balances exploration with exploitation) combined with message passing through the social network to model how platform policies dynamically adapt to network structure. The system runs multiple simulation runs to measure how a proposed policy affects echo chambers, polarization, and information diversity.
72.ww: By using language models trained on platform-specific behavior data, the simulation captures nuance—users don't just click or not click; they respond contextually and sometimes change their minds. By modeling platform interventions dynamically via bandits, the simulation avoids the unrealistic assumption that policies are static. By running multiple runs, it captures variance. This enables pre-deployment prediction of policy impacts.
72.po: PolicySim enables proactive assessment and optimization of intervention policies before deployment, potentially preventing real-world harms from misguided algorithmic decisions and giving platforms a tool to understand the societal impact of their choices.

73.bp: Graph neural networks trained on large datasets learn powerful representations of graph structure and have become standard tools for predicting node properties (like classifying users in a social network). However, machine learning systems can amplify societal biases—a network model trained on historical data might discriminate against people of certain demographics. The goal is to make pre-trained graph models fair with respect to multiple demographic attributes simultaneously (gender and race, or age and income, not just one).
73.wh: Real people have multiple overlapping identities. Existing fairness methods typically protect against discrimination on a single attribute (gender or race), but overlook intersectionality—a person of color and a woman faces a compounded bias that neither attribute alone predicts. Also, making a pre-trained model fair usually means retraining the whole thing, which is expensive and impractical. You need a lightweight solution that works with off-the-shelf models.
73.ap: MultiFPT injects fairness into a pre-trained graph neural network without retraining it. In the first stage, it adds 'prompts'—additional input signals—to the graph that encode fairness constraints and nudge the model toward fair representations. In the second stage, a lightweight adapter network is attached to the pre-trained model and regularized using HSIC (Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion), a statistical test that measures whether node representations are independent of demographic attributes. The adapter is trained to enforce this independence across all sensitive attributes simultaneously.
73.ww: Prompts guide the pre-trained model toward fair representations without modifying its weights. The adapter acts as a fine-grained filter that enforces independence from multiple sensitive attributes at once, rather than optimizing fairness for one attribute at a time. HSIC is a principled measure of independence that works for multiple attributes, avoiding ad-hoc fairness definitions. Together, they achieve fairness without expensive retraining.
73.po: Experiments show MultiFPT reduces bias by approximately 30% on average while maintaining competitive accuracy in node classification tasks, demonstrating that multi-attribute fairness in graph neural networks can be achieved efficiently via prompt tuning and statistical regularization.
