74.bp: Personalized AI recommendation systems need to adapt as user preferences change over time. Someone might stop liking sci-fi and start liking romance; dietary restrictions change; career shifts change what kind of content is relevant. The system needs to update recommendations to reflect these preference shifts. But if you're using a large language model as the recommender backbone, updating it is expensive and tricky—you risk forgetting how to handle other users or breaking the parts that were working well.
74.wh: Global fine-tuning (retraining the entire model on new data) changes everything at once, perturbing recommendations for users whose preferences haven't shifted. Pointwise editing (updating one user's preference at a time) captures specific changes but misses the broader pattern—if a user shifts from sci-fi to romance, that's more than one preference change; it's a coherent shift. Also, repeated edits interfere with each other—editing user A's preferences might undo what you did for user B. This is called catastrophic forgetting.
74.ap: RAIE (Region-Aware Incremental Editing) freezes the backbone language model and instead modifies Low-Rank Adaptation modules—lightweight parameter sets that act like detachable editing layers. It first partitions the representation space into semantic regions using spherical k-means (grouping similar user preference patterns together). When a user's preferences change, the system identifies which region they belong to, then performs one of three region-level edits: Update (refine the region for changed preferences), Expand (grow the region to cover related items), or Add (introduce a new region for novel preferences). Each region has its own LoRA module trained only on that region's data.
74.ww: By working at the region level rather than globally or pointwise, edits are focused without being overly narrow. A region gathers users with similar preferences, so updating one region doesn't disturb others. Because each region has its own LoRA module and is trained independently, regions don't interfere with each other, avoiding catastrophic forgetting. Confidence-aware gating ensures users are routed to the right region even as preferences drift.
74.po: RAIE enables incremental preference updates in LLM-based recommenders while maintaining stable, consistent recommendations across sessions, solving the core problems of both global update (over-perturbation) and pointwise update (interference and narrow coverage).

75.bp: When large language models are used globally, they inherit and spread the cultural biases of their training data—stereotypes about gender, ethnicity, or religion embedded in English-language internet text. This matters because the same models now serve billions of non-English speakers, yet no one has systematically checked whether these biases change shape when a model processes Hindi, Arabic, or Mandarin.
75.wh: The obvious fix—translate English bias benchmarks—fails because bias is culturally embedded. Some stereotypes don't exist in other cultures; some harmful assumptions are invisible to people outside that culture. And there's no global agreement on which characteristics even count as unfair.
75.ap: This paper reviews and catalogs existing bias benchmarks across multiple languages and cultures, examining how well they capture linguistic diversity and cultural awareness. It maps out what metrics researchers currently use to measure bias, what strategies they try to reduce it, and where the gaps are—places where a bias benchmark works for English but breaks for Swahili or Tagalog.
75.ww: By laying out the landscape of multilingual bias research, the paper exposes which methodological choices are actually universal truths and which are just inherited from English-language precedent. When you see that three different language communities all struggle with the same measurement problem, you know it's a real issue, not a translation quirk.
75.po: The concrete takeaway is a clearer roadmap for building fairer evaluation methods across languages. The paper surfaces overlooked gaps—such as cultural assessment frameworks or languages with no existing benchmarks at all—so future work can target the real blind spots rather than endlessly refining English-only tools.

76.bp: Product recommendation systems (Amazon, Netflix, Spotify) typically learn from one domain—movies, say. But a user who loves action films likely has patterns that could help predict what books or music they'll enjoy. The question is how to safely borrow insights from related domains without accidentally breaking the system with irrelevant or harmful signals.
76.wh: Another deep problem: if you transfer knowledge at a coarse level (user-level summaries), you lose fine details that actually matter. Transfer built on imprecise representations ends up confusing rather than helping—the system learns a bad cross-domain pattern that actively hurts predictions on the target domain.
76.ap: This paper proposes a two-part solution. First, it uses meta-learning (a technique for quickly adapting to new tasks) to automatically discover the right alignment rule for each scenario—rather than forcing one rule globally, the system learns which users or items actually overlap between domains and uses those overlapping users/items as anchors to figure out the right transfer pattern. Second, it adds a dual-stage data replay mechanism that selectively refreshes training examples to maintain fine-grained, domain-specific details rather than washing them away during transfer.
76.ww: By letting the system discover alignment rules instead of imposing them, the method adapts to the actual structure of each domain pair. And by preserving fine-grained details in parallel, it catches cases where a coarse transfer signal would have been harmful. The combination reduces the risk of negative transfer—that is, when borrowing from another domain actually makes predictions worse.
76.po: In experiments, the method handles diverse cross-domain scenarios (not just one rigid setup) and reduces harmful transfer while still capturing real domain-related insights. This makes it practical for real recommendation platforms where each new domain pairing is different.

77.bp: Biomedical knowledge graphs (networks of diseases, drugs, genes, and their relationships) are critical for drug discovery and understanding disease mechanisms. To train prediction systems on these graphs, you need pairs of connected entities ("drug X treats disease Y") to learn from, but you also need negative examples—pairs that should not be connected—to teach the system what not to predict.
77.wh: Worse, random negative sampling (just picking edges at random as negatives) can accidentally create unrealistic training examples that have nothing to do with the true data structure. The model ends up learning patterns that are artifacts of sampling, not real biology.
77.ap: This paper proposes a set of smarter negative sampling strategies that account for the semantic meaning of nodes and edges. Instead of random negatives, it uses the geometry of the knowledge graph space itself—when entities are embedded into a continuous space based on the graph structure, the paper analyzes which negative pairs would be informative (hard for the model to distinguish from true positives) while still respecting the heterogeneous types and meanings of nodes and edges.
77.ww: Carefully chosen negatives teach the model which relationships are plausible but false, rather than obviously nonsensical pairs. By respecting node types and edge types, the negatives feel realistic and push the model to learn fine-grained distinctions that matter for biology, not statistical artifacts.
77.po: On real biomedical knowledge graphs, thoughtful negative sampling substantially improves classification performance—better balanced accuracy, better generalization. This holds across different prediction models, suggesting the insight is fundamental, not model-specific.

78.bp: Federated recommendation systems let users keep their data private while still getting good recommendations. Instead of sending your viewing history to Netflix, each user's device trains part of the model locally; only the model parameters (not raw data) are shared. The challenge is: how do you ensure the shared item embeddings—the numerical summaries of what each movie or song is—remain stable and generalizable when millions of users have different viewing patterns?
78.wh: Existing federated recommendation approaches ignore the stability problem entirely. They treat the system as if data were evenly distributed (it isn't), leading to embeddings that fit some devices well but generalize poorly across the federated network.
78.ap: This paper reframes federated recommendation as a multi-task learning problem, where each task is learning good item representations for one device's local data distribution. It then applies sharpness-aware minimization—a technique that seeks model parameters that sit in smooth, flat regions of the optimization landscape rather than sharp peaks. Flat regions generalize better because small changes in data don't cause large swings in the model's predictions.
78.ww: By explicitly optimizing for smooth, flat parameters, the method ensures that item embeddings remain stable even when different devices have wildly different data distributions. A smooth embedding space means the shared parameters generalize across devices naturally rather than overfitting to any one device's quirks.
78.po: Experiments show the method achieves better recommendation accuracy and more stable embeddings than existing federated methods, especially when user data is sparse or imbalanced—which is the real federated setting.

79.bp: Websites, online maps, and location databases change constantly—new restaurants open, product prices shift, weather updates. To keep information current, crawlers must decide which data sources to revisit and how often. Checking everything every minute is wasteful; ignoring changes means stale data. The goal is a crawling schedule that keeps a user's view of the world up-to-date with minimal wasted effort.
79.wh: Finding the theoretically perfect crawling schedule is computationally intractable—mathematically proven to be too hard to solve exactly. But practical crawlers need good heuristics fast.
79.ap: This paper proposes modeling data sources and their update relationships as a graph structure. It then frames crawling as a reinforcement learning problem—an AI agent learns when and where to crawl next by observing which sources tend to update together. A latent Bernoulli process model (a mathematical framework for capturing when events occur) helps the agent reason about hidden update patterns that aren't directly observable.
79.ww: By representing the structure of dependencies in the data, the RL agent can learn to prioritize crawls where they matter most—if Restaurant A updated, the agent learns to check nearby restaurants sooner. This isn't random scheduling; it's adaptive based on the actual correlation patterns in the data.
79.po: On real and synthetic datasets, the RL-based approach outperforms traditional independent-crawling baselines, keeping information fresher with fewer redundant requests. The method shows that graph structure helps even in noisy, dynamic data environments.

80.bp: Misinformation—false health claims, conspiracy theories, debunked science—spreads widely and harms people's decisions. Automated correction via AI chatbots could scale where human fact-checkers can't. But does a chatbot's ability to correct a false claim depend on what the claim is about? Can it equally fix a misunderstanding about vaccines, gravitational waves, or election legitimacy?
80.wh: Prior research focused on chatbot features—make it seem human-like, add expertise badges—but largely ignored whether the domain of misinformation itself changes how effective these features are.
80.ap: This paper runs an experimental study where 259 participants encounter misinformation from three domains (health, science, politics) and then receive corrective responses from the same AI chatbot. The design isolates domain effects: everything else held constant, does the chatbot's correction effectiveness vary by domain?
80.ww: By testing the same chatbot across multiple domains with a controlled experiment, the paper isolates the domain itself as a variable. If a chatbot struggles more with political than health misinformation, that's not about chatbot design—it's about the nature of the belief itself and how resistant it is to correction.
80.po: The results show significant domain-based differences: the chatbot was substantially more effective at correcting health and science misinformation than political misinformation. This suggests that automated correction tools may need domain-specific tuning, not just better design features, to be effective at scale.

81.bp: When you ask a language model a complex question ("What's the best drug for treating lung cancer in non-smokers?"), it often needs to break the problem into smaller questions and search for evidence piece by piece, building reasoning chains. The catch: even when the model retrieves the right evidence, it sometimes forgets to use it—forgetting the most critical information midway through reasoning.
81.wh: Current systems often treat retrieval and reasoning as separate stages, so even retrieved evidence can be lost if the reasoning part of the model doesn't actively reference it. There's a gap between what was found and what actually gets used.
81.ap: This paper proposes PruneRAG: a framework that builds a structured tree of decomposed queries. At each node, the system decides whether an answer is confident enough to use, or whether it should expand (ask sub-questions) or prune (reject uncertain branches). It does this by tracking confidence scores and extracts fine-grained anchors (specific entities from retrieved text) to ground each piece of reasoning in concrete evidence.
81.ww: By making the tree structure explicit and tracking confidence at each step, the system avoids both runaway retrieval and premature stopping. Pruning uncertain branches stops wasted searching, while confidence-guided decisions ensure that evidence is actively used—the system is forced to refer back to what it retrieved. Fine-grained entity anchors make forgetting harder because the reasoning is pinned to concrete facts, not vague abstractions.
81.po: On multi-hop question-answering benchmarks, PruneRAG achieves higher accuracy with lower retrieval cost. More importantly, the paper quantifies evidence forgetting as a metric, making the problem measurable and helping future work target it directly.

82.bp: Fraud detection, cybersecurity, and detecting coordinated inauthentic behavior all rely on finding anomalies—unusual nodes (users, accounts, transactions)—in networks that record real relationships. In realistic networks, nodes aren't all equal: some are users, some are organizations, some are transactions. Finding anomalies becomes harder when different node types have vastly different amounts of semantic information, and when anomalies might only be visible through cross-type dependencies (a transaction between two usually-unconnected user types).
82.wh: Naive approaches apply the same anomaly detection logic to all node types, ignoring the fact that anomalies look different depending on node type and that some types learn better than others.
82.ap: This paper proposes CSA-MTHGAD, which combines two ideas. First, it uses smoothness-guided cross-type semantic alignment: selectively propagating anomaly-sensitive features from information-rich node types to sparse ones in a controlled way, rather than letting information flow freely and drown out sparse nodes. Second, it uses dynamic multi-task learning with adaptive gradient weighting: instead of forcing one shared model, it allows task-specific branches for each node type but harmonizes their gradients so they learn compatible representations without conflicting.
82.ww: By explicitly smoothing the transfer of anomaly signals across types, the system prevents information-rich nodes from overwhelming sparse ones. By allowing task-specific learning paths but harmonizing them, each node type's anomaly detector specializes to its own structure without diverging from the others—a middle ground between full separation and forced sharing.
82.po: On real-world social governance networks with multiple node types, CSA-MTHGAD outperforms existing methods in both accuracy and robustness, especially when detecting anomalies that span multiple types.

83.bp: Education systems, especially in low-resource regions, can't afford one-on-one tutoring, large server farms, or premium devices for every student. Yet personalized, immersive learning—where students interact with material dynamically and feel engaged—dramatically improves outcomes. The challenge is delivering this on cheap hardware with limited bandwidth, while making it accessible to students in economically constrained or geographically isolated areas.
83.wh: Existing education tools often treat personalization and immersion as nice-to-haves, not core features. They scale by reducing interactivity, not by solving the core problem of delivering rich experiences on constrained hardware.
83.ap: This paper presents Rise, a lightweight, web-based educational system built specifically for resource-constrained devices. It integrates three technologies: retrieval-augmented generation (RAG, which grounds answers in retrieved educational content to reduce hallucination), Model Context Protocol (a tool for connecting models to external data and services), and digital humans (animated avatars for engaging interaction). The system is deployed as a web app so students access it through browsers on any device, and it bundles key features: learning analytics, interactive Q&A, immersive classrooms, and attention monitoring.
83.ww: By keeping heavy computation on the server side and using web standards for rendering, Rise runs on lightweight devices. RAG keeps responses grounded in educational material rather than hallucinated. Digital humans provide engagement and social presence, making learning feel interactive even on low-bandwidth connections. Each component is optimized for the resource-constrained case.
83.po: Rise demonstrates that immersive, personalized education can work on cheap hardware in low-resource settings. The concrete payoff is access: students in remote or economically constrained areas can experience dynamic, interactive learning without requiring specialized equipment.

84.bp: Structured data—tables, time series, transaction records, user profiles—is the most common data type in business and web applications, far more ubiquitous than text or images. For decades, standard methods like gradient boosting or linear models have handled this well, but each model was trained from scratch on each new table. Recently, foundation models (large pre-trained models) have revolutionized language and vision by enabling transfer learning and zero-shot adaptation. The question is: can the same foundation-model paradigm work for structured data, or is tabular data too heterogeneous?
84.wh: Current structured modeling still relies on the old paradigm: collect a dataset, train a model from scratch, deploy it. When new data arrives, you retrain. This is expensive and doesn't leverage patterns learned from other tables.
84.ap: This tutorial reviews both the conventional approaches (gradient boosting, deep networks) and emerging foundation-model approaches for structured data. It surveys large-scale pretraining strategies, synthetic data generation (generating fake but realistic tables for pretraining), and in-context learning (teaching models to adapt by seeing examples without retraining). It catalogs open questions: what's the right way to generate synthetic structured data, how should multi-task pretraining work across diverse tables, what pretraining objectives make sense, and how do you evaluate structured foundation models fairly?
84.ww: By laying out both the old and new paradigms side by side, the tutorial shows where foundation models for structured data differ fundamentally from language models. Structured data's heterogeneity means synthetic generation is harder and in-context learning is riskier—but it also means there's a genuine research opportunity to invent new approaches rather than copy language-model recipes.
84.po: The tutorial gives researchers and practitioners a roadmap: understanding which existing methods generalize to structured settings, where new approaches are needed, and what evaluation standards the community should adopt to measure progress on structured foundation models.

85.bp: Emotional support chatbots—systems that listen, validate concerns, and provide perspective—could scale mental-health support to billions of people facing depression, anxiety, or grief. But for emotional support to work, the chatbot must remember the user's history: what they've disclosed, how they felt last week, whether their situation improved. Unlike factual Q&A ("What's the capital of France?"), emotional support requires tracking how the user's emotional state evolves and personalizing responses to that person's unique journey.
85.wh: RAG-based approaches (which retrieve relevant past conversations) help with factual consistency but don't understand temporal dynamics or how a user's emotional journey unfolds. They're good at remembering what was said, not at understanding how the person is changing.
85.ap: This paper introduces ES-MemEval, a benchmark for evaluating long-term emotional support, and EvoEmo, the first dataset of multi-session emotional support conversations. The benchmark tests five core memory capabilities: extracting key facts from scattered disclosures, reasoning about how things evolve over time, detecting when the user contradicts themselves emotionally, knowing when to abstain (admit you don't have enough context), and building a personalized model of who this user is and what they need.
85.ww: By explicitly testing emotional-support-specific challenges (temporal reasoning, conflict detection, evolving states), the benchmark forces models to tackle the real difficulty of long-term support—it's not about remembering facts, it's about understanding a person's emotional arc and responding to who they're becoming, not just who they were.
85.po: Experiments reveal that explicit long-term memory is essential for reducing hallucinations in emotional support, and that RAG helps with consistency but struggles with temporal and emotional dynamics. The findings show which capabilities matter most for empathetic AI and where current systems fall short.

86.bp: When you edit an image (change the style, adjust colors, or transform the scene), you want to preserve some things—a person's face, the composition—while changing others—the mood, the emotional tone. Imagine a tool that lets you specify: "make this happy scene look melancholic, but keep everything else the same." This is affective visual customization—editing the subjective emotional content while preserving emotion-agnostic details.
86.wh: Language models (which excel at understanding intent) don't have direct access to images. You can't just tell a language model to "change the mood"—you need it to understand what visual elements encode that mood and how to transform them while leaving other aspects untouched.
86.ap: This paper proposes an LLM-centric approach: use a multimodal language model (one that understands both language and images) to plan the emotion transformation. The key innovation is two modules: Efficient Inter-emotion Converting (EIC) aligns the semantic meaning of the emotion transformation before image editing starts—the LLM reasons about what "happy to sad" means in visual terms. Precise Extra-emotion Retaining (PER) then carefully preserves the emotion-agnostic content (faces, objects, composition) during actual image editing.
86.ww: By using the language model's semantic reasoning upfront, the system understands what needs to change at a concept level before touching pixels. By explicitly protecting emotion-agnostic content in a second phase, the method avoids accidentally destroying important details while chasing the emotional edit. The two-stage approach separates the understanding problem (what is emotion in this image?) from the preservation problem (keep what doesn't need changing).
86.po: On a constructed benchmark, the method effectively edits emotional tone while preserving visual identity and composition—concrete capabilities like transforming a celebratory photo to look solemn without warping faces or destroying the scene structure.

87.bp: Recommendation systems learn from what users click, buy, or watch. But click patterns don't always reveal true intent—maybe you clicked a gift for someone else, not for yourself. Maybe you watched a movie because friends suggested it, not because you want more like it. The deeper question is: what does the user actually want, beneath the noisy surface of observed interactions?
87.wh: Most GNN-based recommenders treat the user-item graph as a static structure. They don't explicitly model the hidden motivations driving observed interactions.
87.ap: This paper proposes IACLR, which adds an intermediate layer of intent nodes to the recommendation graph. Instead of directly connecting users to items, some connections now route through these intent nodes—they capture shared semantic and behavioral patterns. The system builds an Intent-Graph where intent nodes act as anchors summarizing latent user interests. It then uses contrastive learning (learning to make similar user-intent-item triplets close in representation space and dissimilar ones far apart) to align representations across the bipartite graph.
87.ww: By explicitly modeling intents as intermediate nodes, the system creates additional structure that captures shared motivations. Contrastive alignment ensures that users with similar intents and items with similar use-cases are represented similarly, even if they've never interacted. Sparse direct interactions no longer starve the learning—the intent layer provides additional signal.
87.po: On benchmark datasets (Amazon, Yelp), IACLR outperforms graph-based recommenders and captures fine-grained user-item relationships more effectively, especially under data sparsity. The intent layer improves robustness by providing additional inductive bias.

88.bp: When you ask a search system a multi-turn question ("Show me science papers about climate change... now filter to ones about policy impacts... now only the ones published in the last two years"), the system must understand how each new query relates to your previous context, disambiguate your shifting intent, and retrieve relevant results each time. This is conversational search—more natural than typing keywords, but vastly more complex.
88.wh: Most existing approaches try query rewriting or session encoding—converting the entire conversation into a cleaner query, then retrieving. But if the conversion itself is wrong, the retrieval is doomed. And users never see the reasoning, so they can't verify or correct the system's interpretation.
88.ap: This paper proposes LogiCGR, which uses a language model to both denoise the conversation (extract the core intent from the noisy, ambiguous context using logical reasoning) and generate the retrieval query directly. It trains the model using curriculum learning (starting with easy conversations and gradually increasing difficulty) and GRPO (group relative policy optimization, a reinforcement learning method that refines language-model outputs based on feedback). The system also includes a lightweight self-dual-path module that provides both traditional retrieval and generative retrieval (the model generates which documents to return) for complementary coverage.
88.ww: By using logical reasoning to denoise conversation, the system separates signal from noise explicitly—it can articulate what it's ignoring and why. Generative retrieval (where the model outputs document identifiers) makes the reasoning transparent and interpretable compared to embedding-based retrieval. GRPO fine-tunes the model to produce retrievals that actually help with the original user question.
88.po: LogiCGR outperforms existing conversational search baselines in both retrieval performance and interpretability. Users can see how the system interpreted their conversation, understand why results were retrieved, and trust the system more as a result.

89.bp: Most websites make you navigate hierarchical menus: click Products → find Category → scroll to Item. But what you really want is to just ask, "Show me compact cameras under 500 dollars." The tension is that conversational interfaces can understand flexible natural-language goals, but they lack the visual affordances and stability of graphical interfaces—graphical interfaces are stable and trustworthy but rigid and frustrating.
89.wh: No existing framework bridges these paradigms: letting language models orchestrate and simplify UIs while keeping the visual stability and clarity that graphical interfaces provide.
89.ap: This paper introduces Mirage, a framework where developers describe application functions as reusable components with semantic descriptions and structured schemas. The framework maps natural-language user goals (expressed as questions) to the most relevant components and renders a simplified interface tailored to answering that question. For example, if a user asks for compact cameras under 500 dollars, Mirage finds the Product Search and Price Filter components and combines them into a focused UI showing only those relevant controls, not the entire menu.
89.ww: By making application logic component-based and semantically discoverable, the system can reason about which components matter for a given goal. The user gets a simplified interface (less cognitive load) that's still visually grounded (more trustworthy than text-only), and the system's reasoning is transparent (you can see which components were matched to your request).
89.po: In user studies, Mirage significantly reduces task completion time, lowers cognitive workload, and improves usability compared to traditional navigational websites, without sacrificing accuracy. This demonstrates a practical path toward goal-driven, user-adaptive interfaces.

90.bp: When companies deploy AI systems like ChatGPT to handle sensitive web tasks—summarizing private information, generating FAQ pages, or filtering user comments—those outputs need to be both useful and trustworthy. The real-world goal is to ship systems that protect people's privacy while getting accurate work done, so that users can rely on what the AI says without fear of data leaks or harmful mistakes.
90.wh: The obvious thing to do is write a prompt and hope it works, but that fails in practice: the AI might accidentally include personal details, generate misleading content, or fail in ways that break a website's policy. There's no built-in scorecard to say 'this prompt is ready to ship' or 'this one isn't', and each mistake can damage real users and the company's trust.
90.ap: This tutorial teaches a repeatable workflow: start with simple prompts, layer on specific rules (like 'never include phone numbers'), test them against a handful of real examples and deliberate edge cases that an adversary might exploit, then bundle those prompts with a checklist covering privacy, consent, and what to log. Participants learn techniques like asking the AI to reason through its work before answering, taking on a specific role, and chaining multiple questions together; they also learn when to plug the AI into external tools or databases for grounded facts.
90.ww: Small guardrails early catch the most obvious failures; testing with adversarial examples reveals blind spots the designer wouldn't think of alone. By forcing the prompt into a defensive role—asking it to explain its reasoning or asking it to refuse unsafe tasks—you shift the AI toward caution rather than just speed. And creating a deployment checklist makes it concrete: if you can't fill in the metrics, you're not ready yet.
90.po: Participants walk away able to ship production prompts that are defensible (you can explain why you made each choice), privacy-safe (you've thought through what not to leak), and testable (you have a rubric and known failure cases). The tutorial gives concrete artifacts: prompt cards, a scoring rubric, and a one-page deployment readiness form.

91.bp: From the earliest days of the Web, the thing we were trying to make work has changed dramatically. At first, success meant 'can I find the document I need quickly?'—a retrieval problem, like a library catalog. Over decades, as billions of people came online and the Web exploded with content, success shifted to 'did I feel satisfied? was the experience useful? did I keep coming back?'—a much softer, longer-term goal about the whole human experience.
91.wh: The tension is that searching for the 'most relevant document' and creating an experience that keeps someone engaged are almost opposite problems. The first is measurable in seconds—did you find it yes or no?—and is solved by ranking documents better. The second is soft and sprawls over weeks or months: did this platform respect my time? did it show me things that genuinely mattered? You can't measure that in a lab anymore.
91.ap: The talk traces how the Web industry adapted: early searchers optimized for relevance ranking; then platforms noticed that relevance alone wasn't enough—context matters, knowing the person's true intent matters, trust matters. So they added personalization, feeds that adapt to what you engage with, social signals. When AI came along, it accelerated the trend by making it possible to reason about intent more deeply and to build experiences that adapt in real time.
91.ww: As content abundance exploded, the old approach broke: showing the most literally relevant document doesn't actually solve anyone's real problem if there are a million equally relevant documents. The platform had to shift to 'what does this person actually want and care about?' and 'what will keep them coming back?', which requires tracking longer-term signals (engagement, retention, whether they find it useful weeks later) rather than one-click success metrics.
91.po: The talk reframes how we should think about Web systems: success isn't just relevance anymore, it's sustained value and user intent-awareness. This explains why recommender systems and feeds dominate the modern Web, and why AI that can reason about intent and adapt to individual users has become central to Web design, not a nice-to-have.

92.bp: When you shop on a marketplace like Alibaba and search using an image (rather than typing words), the system needs to understand not just what the product looks like visually but what it actually is and what it does. Getting this right matters because a wrong result frustrates the shopper, and in business-to-business contexts, a recommendation for the wrong product type can cause real operational damage or safety problems.
92.wh: The naive approach is 'find products that look visually similar to the image', but that's a trap: a silver ring and a silver coin look nearly identical but are completely different products. The system confidently returns the wrong thing. The harder problem is that visual similarity is easy to measure (pixels match), but semantic similarity (these are both rings, or these are both jewelry, or more specifically these are both wedding rings) requires understanding categories and subtle differences that go way beyond appearance.
92.ap: ARCHER breaks the problem into three stages, building up understanding step by step. First, it learns basic visual-text relationships (if you search with an image of a ring, anchor to words like 'ring' and 'jewelry'). Second, it learns to recognize the same product from different angles and lighting, so the system doesn't get confused by a product shot at different angles. Third, it fine-tunes to distinguish between similar products within a category—telling a gold ring from a silver ring, or a wedding ring from a fashion ring.
92.ww: By separating the problem into coarse-to-fine stages, the system avoids trying to learn everything at once (which often fails). Learning broad category understanding first gives the system a foundation; then learning viewpoint robustness prevents variation from confusing it; then the fine-grained stage can focus on subtle differences without noise. It's like learning to recognize 'animals' first, then 'cats', then 'tabby cats with white spots'—each stage is easier when the earlier work is done.
92.po: ARCHER returns products that are semantically correct—the same kind of thing, in the same category—rather than just visually close. For a business customer looking for industrial components, this prevents costly mistakes. For a consumer, search becomes actually usable rather than frustrating, because the top result is usually the type of thing they meant, not just something that happens to match the pixels.

93.bp: Online platforms like social media, review sites, and marketplaces are targets for organized fraud: groups of fake accounts work together to inflate review scores, game recommendation systems, or spread misinformation at scale. Detecting these collusive spam rings is crucial to keep platforms trustworthy and users safe, because an individual fake review is obvious, but a coordinated campaign of twenty reviews is much harder to spot.
93.wh: The standard approach treats fraud detection as a binary classification task—is this review spam or not?—but that misses the signal. A single fake review inside a sea of real ones is hard to identify. The real issue is that fraudsters work in groups, and the group's behavior—patterns in timing, language, the accounts that interact with each other—is the smoking gun. Existing methods look at individual accounts in isolation, missing the forest for the trees.
93.ap: SetDet redefines the problem: instead of asking 'is this one review fake?', it asks 'which groups of reviews look coordinated and fraudulent?'. It learns representations of entire sets of reviews together, capturing the group dynamics—do these accounts always interact together? do their reviews use similar language? are the timings suspicious?—and then makes a group-level decision: 'this cluster is collusion, that one is legitimate.' The framework jointly learns what fraud looks like (the representation) and makes the detection decision at the same time, so they inform each other.
93.ww: Fraud is fundamentally a group phenomenon: it's the coordination and collective dynamics that make it fraud. Looking at individual reviews misses the temporal patterns (all posting at 3am), the linguistic patterns (same phrasing across accounts), and the interaction patterns (same set of users always review the same products). By making the group the unit of analysis and learning at that level, the system can catch behaviors that are invisible at the individual level.
93.po: SetDet can identify organized fraud rings that current methods miss, because it looks for the signature of coordination rather than individual oddities. This means real spam campaigns can be caught and removed, preserving the integrity of review systems and recommendation algorithms, and protecting both the platform and honest users from manipulation.

94.bp: Knowledge graphs—structures that store facts as relationships between entities, like 'Alice works at Google'—are increasingly built by combining information from multiple organizations (hospitals, universities, companies) while keeping their data private. But if a malicious participant injects false information into the shared knowledge graph, the entire system's usefulness collapses. Stopping these attacks is crucial to keep federated knowledge systems trustworthy.
94.wh: The challenge is that federated systems trade centralized control for privacy: no single authority sees all the data, so no one person can easily spot when an attacker has poisoned the system. A traditional centralized knowledge graph could be audited; here, the attack might be hidden in one participant's contribution and spread through the network before anyone notices. Existing defenses for centralized systems don't work when you can't see all the data.
94.ap: This paper designs three attack strategies that a malicious participant might use: some corrupt the raw data before it goes into the system, others corrupt the learned representations (the underlying math structures) the system builds. They show that corrupting the representations is the most effective attack. Then they propose a defense: monitor the 'density' of the learned representations (how tightly packed the math structures are), since poisoned data tends to create anomalous density patterns that signal an attack. A monitoring system flags suspicious participants and removes their contributions.
94.ww: Poisoned data tends to distort the learned structures in detectable ways: the math model learns to fit the false information, and that distortion shows up as unusual density or clustering patterns. By monitoring for these anomalies in the mathematical space (rather than trying to audit the raw data, which you can't see), the system can catch attacks without breaking privacy. The poisoned representations stand out like a sore thumb in the learned model.
94.po: The defense can restore a federated knowledge graph to pre-attack performance even after a severe poisoning campaign that dropped accuracy by 93%. This means organizations can confidently share data through a federated knowledge system—they know that if someone poisons it, the system can detect and fix the damage automatically.

95.bp: Recommendation systems learn patterns from data to suggest products or content you might like. But the real world is messy: patterns that worked during training break when users see a new product type or when the market shifts. A system trained on summer fashion recommendations fails when winter comes. Building recommenders that stay accurate when the world changes is a hard real-world problem that directly affects whether people trust the recommendations.
95.wh: The issue is that recommender systems exploit correlations in the training data—'people who bought ski pants also bought thermal socks'—but those correlations can be accidents of the training set, not real causal truths about what people want. When the data distribution shifts (winter ends, new product types arrive), those spurious correlations fall apart and the recommendations become garbage. The system was optimizing for correlation, not for understanding the causal reasons behind choices.
95.ap: C-HyPOD uses a mathematical trick: it learns to place user interests in hyperbolic space, a kind of geometry that naturally captures hierarchies (imagine a tree structure embedded in space, where each level is a different layer of specificity). Instead of learning scattered features, it learns a small set of universal interest 'archetypes' (prototypes) arranged hierarchically, and it ensures those archetypes are orthogonal—they don't overlap, so each one captures something distinct. When distribution shifts happen, these fundamental archetypes are more likely to transfer correctly because they're aligned with real causal structures, not accidental correlations.
95.ww: Hyperbolic geometry is good at capturing hierarchies—from broad interests ('outdoor activities') down to specific ones ('cross-country skiing in March')—which mirrors how real user preferences actually structure themselves. By learning prototypes that are orthogonal (truly distinct from each other) rather than overlapping, the system learns reusable causal building blocks. When the data distribution shifts, these fundamental units are more robust because they represent true structure, not just data accidents.
95.po: C-HyPOD recommendations stay accurate when product catalogs change, when seasons shift, or when new user cohorts arrive—situations where naive recommenders fail badly. This means recommendation systems can be deployed to real marketplaces and stay helpful over time, rather than degrading as the world changes.

96.bp: When you ask a large language model (LLM) like GPT-4 a question about facts stored in a knowledge graph—'Who was the first president of the United States and where was he from?'—the model often makes up an answer rather than admitting it doesn't know. Combining knowledge graphs (which have reliable facts) with LLMs (which can reason) should solve this, but most systems don't work well for smaller models, which are cheaper and easier to deploy.
96.wh: Existing knowledge graph question-answering systems are built for the biggest models; they feed raw knowledge graph paths (chains of relationships) directly into the model and hope it can figure out which ones matter. Smaller models struggle with this: they don't have the raw reasoning power to sort through noise, and they're not trained to handle the knowledge graph's structure. It's like handing someone a jumbled library and expecting them to find the answer—it works better for genius researchers than for ordinary people.
96.ap: RPO-RAG does three things: First, it samples knowledge graph paths more carefully, choosing ones that are actually relevant to the question (not just random paths). Second, it trains the small model specifically on reasoning about relationships in the knowledge graph—showing it what 'president of' means, how to navigate 'lived in', so it learns to manipulate these concepts. Third, it organizes the retrieved paths into a clear, interpretable format before asking the model to answer, so the model isn't overwhelmed by noise.
96.ww: Smaller models succeed when the problem is broken down: if you give it clear, relevant examples of 'here's a path through the knowledge graph that answers a similar question', it can learn to imitate that pattern. By teaching it specifically about relationships (which is what knowledge graphs are made of) and filtering the retrieved paths before they reach the model, you've done half the work. The model's limited reasoning capacity goes toward the right thing, not toward filtering noise.
96.po: Small LLMs (under 7 billion parameters) can now answer factual questions about knowledge graphs as accurately as much larger models, because they're trained and presented with the right structure. This is a big deal for deployment: smaller models are cheaper, faster, and can run on consumer hardware, so this makes factual question-answering practical in real applications where GPT-4 is too expensive.

97.bp: Misinformation spreads across the web, but every new crisis—COVID, a war, an election—changes what false claims look like. A system trained to catch COVID misinformation might miss war-related falsehoods because the patterns and language are completely different. Building systems that detect fake news in unseen crises is crucial because once a major event happens, there's no time to retrain.
97.wh: The problem is that fake news in one context uses different language, appeals to different emotions, and exploits different knowledge gaps than in another. A system trained on one domain learns very specific features of that domain's misinformation. When a new crisis hits, those features don't transfer. Additionally, labeled data is scarce—you can't quickly gather thousands of labeled examples of COVID misinformation about a new topic. And LLMs understand abstract meaning but that understanding doesn't always transfer across domains either.
97.ap: DAUD uses LLMs to extract high-level meaning from both news articles (the semantic content, the framing, the implicit claims) and user comments (who's engaging with this, what they're saying). It then models how individual users engage with news across different domains—if someone always shares misinformation about vaccines, they're more likely to share misinformation about a new health crisis. It captures the relationship between the original article features and the LLM-extracted features, so the LLM's understanding can enhance the system without completely replacing the data-driven signals.
97.ww: LLMs understand abstract meaning that's more likely to transfer across domains—the narrative structure of false claims, emotional manipulation patterns—than surface-level features do. User behavior is even more transferable: someone's tendency to share misinformation is often domain-agnostic. By combining LLM-extracted semantics with user behavioral signals and grounding everything in the original data-driven features, the system captures both domain-specific and domain-agnostic aspects of misinformation, allowing knowledge to transfer to unseen crises.
97.po: DAUD can detect misinformation in new, unseen contexts (new geopolitical crises, new pandemics) better than systems trained on old domains, because it captures the abstract patterns of false claims and the user behaviors that spread them. This means during a real crisis, the system can start catching misinformation immediately rather than waiting weeks for labeled training data.

98.bp: The internet runs on foundational security measures—encryption, authentication, domain validation—that are mature, well-understood, and freely available. Yet many services don't use them. Understanding how widely these basic protections are deployed across the real internet is essential for knowing how resilient the internet actually is and where to focus efforts to improve security.
98.wh: The obvious thing—ask services to report—doesn't work because it's voluntary and people lie or don't know. The hard part is measuring this at scale without breaking into systems or being intrusive. You need a way to check security measures by looking from outside, without annoying anyone or getting in legal trouble, and you need to do it for hundreds of thousands of domains.
98.ap: The paper proposes a set of security indicators that can be checked non-intrusively: Does this domain have DNSSEC (encrypted DNS)? Does it support HTTPS (encrypted web traffic)? Does it have a security policy file? These are all things you can check by looking at publicly available information or making normal network requests. They built a tool called Katti and checked every known .de domain (German internet) to see who's using these measures.
98.ww: By focusing on foundational, standardized measures that are both mature and non-intrusively measurable, they can get a broad, accurate picture of internet security without requiring cooperation or breaking systems. These indicators are lagging indicators—many of them have existed for 10+ years—so if services still aren't using them, that's informative. It's like checking 'do you have locks on your doors'—not fancy, but critical.
98.po: The study reveals that a significant chunk of the German internet still lacks even basic security measures. This makes clear where the gap between knowledge and practice lies and where sustained attention is needed to improve internet resilience, not just innovation on new security tricks but deployment of things we've known for years.

99.bp: False information spreads online when images and text are manipulated together. A real photo of a protest might be paired with a false caption claiming something happened that didn't, or an AI-generated image might be paired with authentic reporting to make it seem real. Detecting these multi-layered falsehoods is crucial because our brains trust images more than words, and when image plus text combine to lie, the effect is especially powerful.
99.wh: The problem is that existing methods treat multimodal misinformation as a single classification task ('true or false'), but that misses the real structure. An image can be real and text false, or both false, or both real but paired to tell a lie—these are different problems requiring different solutions. No single classifier handles all cases well. Additionally, covering all possible combinations is complicated; researchers have mostly focused on a few common cases and missed the full space of possibilities.
99.ap: OctantFake proposes a simpler framework: Check the image independently (real or fake?), check the text independently (real or fake?), check whether they're consistent with each other (does the text match what the image shows?). This creates eight possible combinations: real-image + real-text + consistent means true; fake-image + real-text + inconsistent means false; and so on. They built a large dataset covering all eight cases and trained separate specialized modules for each check, then fused the results into a final classification.
99.ww: By separating the problem into three independent checks, you sidestep the impossibility of one-size-fits-all detection. An image analysis expert's tool can focus on image forensics; a text analysis expert's tool can focus on text truth; a consistency checker can focus on alignment. Each module can be simpler and more accurate because it's solving a narrower problem. Fusing three moderately accurate answers is more robust than chasing one complex answer.
99.po: OctantFake can detect multimodal misinformation that combines real and fake elements in ways previous systems missed, because it explicitly handles all eight combinations rather than trying to brute-force a single classifier. This means fact-checkers and platforms can catch sophisticated hybrid lies that mix real images with false claims or vice versa.

100.bp: When you read reviews or news, you often care about a specific angle: 'Is the product's battery life good?' or 'Does this writer think the policy is fair?' Extracting opinion about a specific aspect from text is called aspect-based sentiment analysis, and it matters for product review sites, policy monitoring, and customer feedback. But models can be fooled by surface patterns and don't actually understand what they're analyzing.
100.wh: The trap is that models learn shortcuts: they notice that words like 'disappointing' usually appear near negative reviews and 'excellent' near positive ones, so they predict based on word patterns alone. But this fails when the pattern is misleading: 'not bad' means positive, but contains the word 'bad'. More fundamentally, models can learn spurious correlations—'this product appears in luxury reviews so all reviews in this category must be positive'—that work on training data but fail on new data.
100.ap: CECR uses counterfactual reasoning: take a real review, then create fake variations of it where you change the target aspect you're analyzing but keep everything else the same. For example, if the original says 'This phone's battery is great but the screen sucks', create a counterfactual where you swap in 'This phone's battery is terrible but the screen sucks', and note that the opinion should flip. Train the model on both versions so it learns that the aspect itself causes the opinion, not surrounding words. At inference time, use a causal attention mechanism that identifies which parts of the text actually influence the prediction.
100.ww: Counterfactuals force the model to learn causal relationships: if I change the battery description, the sentiment must change. That rules out spurious shortcuts because the shortcut (the word 'bad' appears) is the same in both versions, but the label changes. Causal attention mechanisms help the model zero in on the words and phrases that are actually causally driving the prediction, not just correlating with it.
100.po: CECR is more robust than standard models: it handles tricky phrasings like 'not bad' correctly, and it generalizes better to new data because it learned causal relationships rather than shortcuts. For a review site trying to understand customer opinions accurately, this means the system gives reliable feedback even on unusual phrasing and isn't easily fooled by changes in how reviewers write.

101.bp: Complex networks like the internet or social media can fail in ways we need to understand: a virus spreading through a network, misinformation cascading through links, infrastructure collapse when key hubs go down. The network dismantling problem asks: if we wanted to stop a cascade or disable the most damaging part of the network, which nodes (people, servers, websites) would we need to remove with minimum cost? This matters for both defense (stopping epidemics) and infrastructure planning (where are the critical chokepoints).
101.wh: Naively, you'd remove the most-connected nodes (hubs) first, but that's inefficient. The network might have a giant connected component (a huge interlinked mass) plus scattered small clusters. You don't need to remove nodes until the giant component fragments. Finding the minimal removal strategy is mathematically hard—it's a classic NP-hard problem, meaning there's no known fast algorithm that always finds the true optimum.
101.ap: IG+ starts with a clever flip in perspective: instead of asking 'which nodes should I remove?', it asks 'if I'm keeping nodes, which should I keep to maintain connectivity?' By finding the nodes worth keeping (the ones that hold the network together), it identifies implicitly which ones to remove. This reverse perspective often makes optimization problems easier. The algorithm uses heuristics (fast approximations) and for dynamic networks, uses tree-based data structures to update the dismantling strategy when nodes are added or removed.
101.ww: The reverse perspective works because the structure of the problem is actually clearer when framed as 'what's the smallest set that stays connected?' rather than 'what's the biggest set I can destroy?' For dynamic networks, maintaining a tree-based index lets you avoid recomputing from scratch every time the network changes—you just update the index, which is much faster.
101.po: IG+ can dismantle 10-million-node networks in minutes and handle changes as they happen. This makes it practical for real systems: understanding which infrastructure chokepoints matter most, planning for network resilience, or simulating how misinformation cascades would be stopped by targeted interventions.

102.bp: The internet is evolving toward a new era where artificial intelligence and blockchain combine, where privacy and verifiability are central, and where quantum computers pose a threat to existing security. Building systems that are decentralized (no single authority can control you), private (no one can see your data), and quantum-safe (they'll still work when quantum computers exist) is the goal. But it requires rethinking identity, trust, and how we prove things online.
102.wh: The challenge is that these three goals—decentralization, privacy, quantum-resistance—have often pulled in different directions. A decentralized system is harder to audit. A quantum-safe system requires new math that's unfamiliar. Privacy and verifiability seem to conflict: how do you prove something happened if you don't reveal who you are? There's no clear roadmap for how to build systems that achieve all three, and there are no standard benchmarks or failure-mode catalogs to learn from.
102.ap: ZABAPAD is a workshop bringing together practitioners working on these problems. It focuses on real deployments and empirical measurements rather than theory alone. It explores zero-knowledge proofs (a way to prove you know something without revealing it) combined with blockchain, applies these ideas to IoT devices that need to authenticate themselves, and examines what happens when you need to migrate existing digital identities and wallets to quantum-safe systems. It aims to produce a practitioner playbook, an interoperability checklist, benchmarks, and a catalog of failure modes across domains like finance, healthcare, and supply chain.
102.ww: Progress happens when practitioners share what failed, not just what worked. By collecting empirical benchmarks and failure modes across real deployments in finance, healthcare, and supply chain, the workshop creates a knowledge base that future builders can learn from. Zero-knowledge proofs are powerful tools for privacy-preserving verification, and blockchain provides the decentralization; combining them with quantum-safe math and mapping out the integration points is how you actually build next-generation systems.
102.po: The workshop outcomes are concrete: teams leave with a playbook for how to adopt zero-knowledge proof and blockchain technologies in their domain, a checklist for making sure systems from different builders can interoperate, benchmarks for comparing approaches, and most importantly, a collection of 'here's where previous projects stumbled' lessons that help new projects avoid the same pitfalls.

103.bp: The protocols that run the internet—how data is transmitted, how computers talk to each other, how security works—are written down in documents called RFCs (Requests for Comments). These are the law of the internet. But reading an RFC is often cryptic: it tells you the rules, but not why those rules exist or what tradeoff led to them. Understanding the reasoning would make protocols easier to implement correctly and to understand why they work.
103.wh: The knowledge of why protocols were designed a certain way lives in email archives and meeting notes from protocol working groups, scattered across years of discussion. Most RFC readers never see this context. They read the rule, don't understand the tradeoff, misinterpret the spec, and implement it wrong. It's like having a legal document but no case law or legislative history—you can follow the letter but miss the spirit.
103.ap: This paper builds a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system tailored for RFC design rationales. It digs through IETF email archives and working group discussions to find relevant context, then uses a language model to synthesize that context into a clear explanation of why a protocol decision was made and what constraints it addresses. The key innovation is in the retriever: it's tuned to find emails that actually contain rationale (not just routine discussion), and at large search scales, it's much better at returning the crucial context while keeping it brief to save tokens.
103.ww: RFC design rationales are buried in email, and not all emails are equally useful—most are routine discussion, only a few contain the actual 'we chose X because Y' reasoning. By training a specialized retriever to distinguish rationale-rich emails, the system can find the signal in the noise. Keeping contexts short makes the language model's synthesis task easier and cheaper, especially when searching across large email archives.
103.po: RFC readers can now look up not just the rule but the reasoning behind it, making standards more transparent and implementers more likely to get the design right. This is especially valuable for protocol authors and implementers debugging subtle spec ambiguities—they can understand the original intent, not just the words.

104.bp: In decentralized finance (DeFi), a clever trader can spot opportunities to profit: if a token is cheaper on one exchange than another, you can buy low and sell high, pocketing the difference. These arbitrage opportunities happen fast and at scale. Building systems that can automatically spot and execute profitable arbitrage trades is the goal, but it has to be done under real-world constraints: you have limited money, pools have limited liquidity, you have to pay for the transaction, and the opportunity disappears in milliseconds.
104.wh: Finding the best arbitrage path and trade amount is a nasty optimization problem: there are many possible sequences of trades (pools to route through), each with different profitability, and all have constraints (limited funds, pool liquidity, gas fees). The obvious approach—try every possibility—finds the best answer but takes too long to run; by the time you finish calculating, the opportunity is gone. You need something fast and good-enough that runs in milliseconds on a blockchain.
104.ap: The paper formulates atomic triangular arbitrage as a constrained optimization problem (select an ordered path of three pools and a trade amount to maximize profit) and solves it using Deep Reinforcement Learning with a specific algorithm called PPO. The model learns from experience: it observes the state (current pool prices, your balance, constraints), takes an action (pick a path and amount), gets a reward (profit or loss), and learns to repeat the profitable actions. The trained model runs in milliseconds because it's just neural network inference, not search.
104.ww: Neural networks can learn to approximate solutions to hard optimization problems much faster than solving them exactly. PPO is stable and sample-efficient, meaning it learns from relatively few examples. The network learns to navigate the constraint space (respecting your balance, avoiding pools with too little liquidity) while maximizing profit, all in a way that generalizes to new prices it hasn't seen before.
104.po: PPO achieves millisecond-level inference speed, making it practical for on-chain execution, while still generating consistent profit. This reveals a fundamental speed-profit tradeoff: exhaustive search finds the absolute best arbitrage but is too slow; PPO finds good arbitrage fast enough to actually execute, which in the real world is what matters. A reasonably profitable opportunity you can execute beats a theoretically optimal opportunity you can't.

105.bp: AI agents are starting to do real work on the web—opening links, filling forms, booking tickets—by calling external tools through a system called Model Context Protocol. The problem is that if someone poisons those tools or the data feeding them, the agent's reasoning can get corrupted mid-task, leading to wrong actions or security breaches. We need a way to catch and fix these corruptions automatically, not just detect them.
105.wh: Existing defenses stop at detection: they flag that something went wrong. But they don't fix it. When an agent has already made a bad decision because a tool gave it poisoned output, you can't just ignore it and move forward—the agent has already taken the wrong action. You need to backtrack, figure out what the root cause was, and have the agent re-think from that point. The challenge is doing this without constantly re-running everything (which would be slow).
105.ap: MCPFixGen saves checkpoints at high-risk moments (when the agent is about to call a tool). When something goes wrong, it rewinds to a checkpoint, identifies the bad tool output by looking at how hard the agent's brain was 'paying attention' to that tool call, then masks out that poisoned input and tells the agent to try again. This is like rewinding a movie to just before a character opens a bad letter, then having them skip that letter and continue.
105.ww: This works because poison usually shows up as a sudden shift in the agent's reasoning patterns. By tracking which tools the agent is paying attention to at each moment, you can spot when it suddenly trusts a tool that normally gets low attention. And by masking out just that one bad input instead of throwing away the whole sequence, the agent only has to re-compute from the poisoned point, not restart from scratch.
105.po: MCPFixGen lets AI agents automatically recover from tool poisoning attacks without human help, reducing both the time and cost of fixing mistakes. This makes browser-based autonomous agents safe enough for real deployment, where mistakes cost time or money.

106.bp: Companies make environmental claims ("we cut emissions by 50%", "our packaging is eco-friendly") to look good to investors and customers. But many of these claims are exaggerated, misleading, or just false—a practice called greenwashing. We need an automated way to fact-check these claims against real evidence, so regulators and buyers can trust sustainability reports.
106.wh: Checking a greenwashing claim manually is hard. You have to find the company's actual ESG (environmental, social, governance) reports, dig through dense tables of data, cross-reference industry benchmarks, and decide if what the company claims matches what it actually did. This takes human time and expertise. An AI that just reads the claim and guesses will hallucinate evidence. You need the AI to cite real documents.
106.ap: EmeraldApp gives the AI three ways to find evidence. The first digs through a database of ESG report chunks using semantic search (finding similar ideas, not just keyword matches). The second consults a hand-built knowledge graph of sustainability facts (like 'this company's solar capacity in 2024'). The third combines both. For each claim, the app either confirms it's real, flags it as greenwashing, or abstains if evidence is missing. It also logs every claim checked so auditors can review the history.
106.ww: By grounding the AI's answer in retrieved documents rather than letting it make up facts, you ensure the AI can point to real evidence. The combination of semantic search and structured knowledge facts covers both the messiness of real reports and the precision needed for factual claims. Logging everything adds accountability—companies can't deny what was checked.
106.po: EmeraldApp lets regulators, investors, and consumers verify sustainability claims instantly instead of waiting for audits. It flags probable greenwashing and shows the evidence, raising the cost of making false claims and making real sustainability data more visible and trustworthy.

107.bp: Someone shows you a photo and says 'I want something like this but with a red dress instead of blue.' You need to find similar photos in a database where the user's description has been applied—so the system understands both what the image shows and how language modifies it. This is harder than normal image search because you have to extract and change specific visual details based on natural-language instructions.
107.wh: The obvious approach—just search for 'red dress' in the image database—misses the nuance. The user is saying 'the composition and pose from this photo, but with different colors or items.' You have to extract the right parts of the reference image (what matters: pose, background, context; what doesn't: the blue dress color) and then use language to imagine what the dress should become. This means figuring out which visual features to keep and which to discard, which is different for every image and query.
107.ap: MCoT-MVS uses a large vision-language model to think through the problem step by step: 'What should I keep from this image? What should I remove? What's the new target?' Those answers guide two separate attention mechanisms that zoom in on different parts of the reference image—one picks out important small regions (patches), the other picks out complete objects (like 'the whole dress'). Then a fusion module combines what the system kept, what it imagined from the text, and the new target description into a single query that searches the database.
107.ww: Reasoning out loud (chain-of-thought) forces the model to decompose the problem instead of trying to solve it all at once. By using the reasoning output to guide visual attention, the system stops getting distracted by irrelevant details. And by separating fine-grained details (patches) from object-level choices (the full dress), the system can handle both small tweaks and large changes.
107.po: The system now finds better matching images when users describe 'same pose, different color' or 'same style, different size.' Experiments on two real datasets show it beats other methods, making composed image retrieval more useful for shopping, design inspiration, and content discovery.

108.bp: When child abuse material is reported online, specialists need to classify it quickly—partly to prioritize resources, but crucially to identify the age of the child, which has huge legal and investigative implications. Current methods rely on seeing faces clearly, but that's not always possible due to image quality, angle, or intentional obscuring. We need a way to estimate age even when the face is not visible.
108.wh: Face-based age estimation fails when the image shows only body shapes (silhouettes), which is common in abuse materials. But body proportions do correlate with age—children have different proportions than adults—and relative features matter (this person's head is smaller compared to their body, suggesting youth). However, there's natural variation: two 10-year-olds can have very different builds. You need a system that learns what proportions most strongly predict age groups and can compare individuals fairly.
108.ap: The researchers train neural networks on multiple related tasks at once: age estimation, gender prediction, height estimation—all from silhouettes. This multitask approach forces the network to learn general body-shape features that apply across related tasks. They also add a pairwise learning step: instead of just classifying one image as 'child' or 'adult,' the system compares pairs of people and learns 'person A is younger than person B.' This relative comparison is more robust than absolute guessing.
108.ww: Multitask learning works because all those tasks (age, gender, height) rely on overlapping body-shape patterns. Learning one task helps with the others. Pairwise comparison is more stable because it doesn't require the model to perfectly calibrate an absolute age estimate—it just needs to rank relative to other bodies, which is easier. Together, these reduce mistakes by 14–21%.
108.po: Experts can now classify suspected abuse materials more accurately even when faces are hidden, speeding up initial triage and improving the reliability of age determination for investigators. This helps law enforcement and platforms respond faster to reports.

109.bp: Mobile phones rely on SIM cards to prove you are who you say you are. But recently, hackers stole millions of SIM card records, exposing personal data and allowing impersonation. We need a way for you to prove your identity to the network without ever storing a secret on a SIM card that could be breached. Zero-knowledge proofs offer a way: prove you know a secret without revealing it.
109.wh: Traditional SIM authentication stores a key on the SIM card. If the card's data is stolen, the thief can pretend to be you. Moving the secret to the cloud makes it a juicy target for hackers—they break in once and compromise millions of users. You need a system where each person proves they have a valid key without anyone, including the network, ever storing your key in a centralized place.
109.ap: The system generates a key pair on your phone (one private, one public). Instead of storing this on a SIM, the public key goes into a cryptographic list called a Merkle Tree—a structure that creates one fingerprint for all authorized keys. The network then checks: does this person produce a zero-knowledge proof that (1) their public key is in that fingerprint's tree and (2) they control the matching private key? The proof is created using special mathematical tricks (Groth16) that are fast to verify but don't leak the key.
109.ww: Zero-knowledge proofs let you prove a fact without revealing the proof. Using a Merkle Tree means no one needs to store your actual key—just a tree fingerprint. And because the proof is mathematically airtight (not dependent on trusting servers), a hacker stealing one proof can't use it twice or forge a new one. The fast verification math (Groth16) makes it practical for millions of authentications.
109.po: Phone networks can now authenticate users without SIM cards and without storing private keys anywhere that can be breached. This eliminates the risk of large-scale SIM data theft while keeping authentication just as fast. Users get better privacy and security without noticing any change.

110.bp: Social networks and biological systems are constantly changing—people join and leave, relationships strengthen or fade. When we detect groups in these networks, we want to know not just 'who is in which cluster' but 'why did this group form and how is it changing?' Black-box algorithms give answers but no explanations, which is dangerous in healthcare (why were these patients grouped together?) or traffic networks (which roads might cause accidents?). We need dynamic clustering that humans can understand.
110.wh: Explaining clustering is hard because the reason someone belongs to a group depends on their role in the network. A hub (connected to many others) belongs differently than a bridge (connecting two groups) or a newcomer (just arrived). Traditional explanations treat all nodes the same. But different roles need different explanations. Also, network clusters change over time, and you have to explain not just 'who is clustered' but 'why did this split happen?'
110.ap: The system learns two separate representations for each person: one captures their role (hub, bridge, connector, etc.—five predefined roles), the other captures which cluster they belong to. These are kept orthogonal (independent) so that a hub in cluster A isn't confused with a hub in cluster B. The system then turns these abstract representations into concrete semantic concepts—prototypes—so an LLM can reason about them. Finally, a hierarchical reasoning process generates explanations at multiple levels: local ('why is this node near its neighbors'), community level ('what's the role pattern in this cluster'), and global ('how did clusters shift').
110.ww: Separating role from cluster membership prevents the system from using one concept to explain the other (a common pitfall). By creating named role prototypes that LLMs understand naturally ('Leader,' 'Wanderer'), you can hand the continuous numbers to an LLM and get human-readable explanations. Hierarchical reasoning covers both static snapshots and temporal changes.
110.po: Doctors, city planners, and social scientists can now see not just the clusters but understand them: 'this community has three leaders and many contributors' or 'this group lost a key connector last week.' The explanations help verify that clustering is sensible and catch errors early.

111.bp: Imagine a group voting on whether to approve a new policy. Each person has private information that hints at what the right choice is, but they don't know the full picture. If they vote their true beliefs, the group might decide correctly. But if they can secretly talk to each other and coordinate, they might vote as a bloc to force a bad outcome. How much secret coordination ability (coalition size) makes this possible, and when can we still trust majority voting?
111.wh: Game theory has two extreme models: either agents vote independently (no coordination), or they can form any secret agreement they want (unlimited coordination). Neither matches reality. In real politics or organizations, small groups (friends, allies) can coordinate, but large conspiracies are hard to keep quiet. The question is: given a specific coalition size that people can secretly coordinate, when does voting still converge to the 'right' answer (informed majority decision)?
111.ap: The researchers define a k-strong equilibrium: a voting outcome where no group of up to k people can deviate to improve their collective outcome (their payoff from the true result they collectively prefer).
