They then characterize when such equilibria match the informed majority decision (what everyone would choose if the truth were known). The analysis depends on three levers: how big coalitions can be (k), what fraction of people prefer the majority result (information structure), and how concentrated that information is.
111.ww: By making coordination ability explicit and bounded, the model captures the middle ground between chaos and full conspiracy. The characterization reveals that the boundary between 'majority voting works' and 'it fails' is jagged and nonlinear—small changes in k or information distribution can flip the outcome. This matches the intuition that small-group coordination is powerful but fragile.
111.po: Organizations and voting bodies can now reason about: if we assume people can secretly coordinate in groups up to size 10 (or 100), can we still trust majority voting? The answer depends on the specific information structure and shows where voting is robust and where it breaks down, guiding mechanism design.

112.bp: Large language models are trained to generate text, but they often make up facts—hallucinating information that never appeared in their training data. One fix is to give them access to knowledge bases (Wikipedia, Wikidata, etc.) so they can cite real facts. But most methods convert the knowledge base into text, losing the structured relationships that make knowledge bases valuable. We need LLMs to directly use graph-structured knowledge without converting it to messy text.
112.wh: Knowledge graphs (like Wikidata) encode information as relationships: 'Barack Obama' —[born]—> '1961' —[in location]—> 'Hawaii.' If you convert that graph to text, it becomes sequential and loses the structure—the LLM can't easily 'navigate' the graph or see that multiple paths lead to the same fact. Text also bloats the input, wasting the LLM's context window. But LLMs natively understand vectors (lists of numbers), not graph nodes.
112.ap: ConceptFormer learns a mapping from each knowledge graph node (like 'Barack Obama') to a vector representation (a 'concept vector') that the LLM can process natively. Instead of putting the graph into text, you inject these concept vectors directly into the LLM's embedding space—the internal numerical representation where words live. The graph structure is encoded in how the concept vectors relate to each other, without ever being serialized into text.
112.ww: Vectors can preserve graph structure implicitly: nodes that are nearby in the graph end up with similar vectors, and the LLM can use these to infer relationships. By keeping the LLM frozen and only training the concept vector mapping, you avoid retraining a billion-parameter model. And because concept vectors stay in the embedding space where the LLM already operates, the LLM doesn't have to learn a new 'language' to use them.
112.po: LLMs grounded with concept vectors show massive gains in factual recall—up to 272% improvement on Wikipedia sentences. This makes knowledge-grounded LLM systems more trustworthy for question-answering, fact-checking, and any task where accuracy depends on real world knowledge.

113.bp: Graph neural networks (GNNs) make decisions by passing information between connected nodes. When you want to know why the network made a specific decision ('why did you classify this node as fraudulent?'), you need to find which edges and nodes were most important. But real-world graphs are messy—edges get added or deleted by noise or error. An explanation that's fragile to noise is useless because small data errors will break it.
113.wh: GNNs amplify noise through message passing: each node gets information from its neighbors, which got information from their neighbors, and so on. One noisy edge early in this chain can snowball, flipping the output. Existing explanation methods identify important edges but don't account for this amplification. Also, real graphs are heterogeneous: different edge types (friendship, follow, retweet) carry different meanings, and an explanation needs to respect that.
113.ap: RoHeX first analyzes how different GNN architectures amplify noise—revealing which operations are most vulnerable. It then uses a denoising step: a probabilistic model that filters out likely noise and reconstructs a clean graph structure. The explanation is then computed using information bottleneck theory (a mathematical principle that balances how much information you keep versus how much you compress). Edge types are tracked throughout, so the final explanation respects heterogeneity.
113.ww: Understanding how noise amplifies lets you design defenses at the right places in the network. Denoising before explanation makes the explanation robust: it's based on the likely-true graph, not the noisy one. Information bottleneck theory ensures explanations are not just faithful (matching the model's actual decision) but also compact and meaningful—they identify the smallest set of edges that matter most.
113.po: When GNNs are used on messy real data (social networks, recommender graphs, fraud detection), their explanations now remain stable even if the data is noisy. Users and auditors get reliable insight into why the model made a decision, enabling safer deployment in high-stakes domains.

114.bp: Recommendation systems struggle when an item is brand new and has no user interaction history (the 'cold-start' problem). You can't use past behavior to rank it. One workaround is to build semantic descriptions of the item (from title, category, metadata) so the system can match it to similar items that do have history. But how you train those descriptions matters enormously—train them separately and they might not generalize well to new items during recommendation.
114.wh: Standard practice trains semantic IDs (descriptions) first on a separate data, then freezes them and trains the recommendation model. But semantic IDs learned on old data might miss what's important for predicting whether a cold-start item will be liked. It's like memorizing a script for an audition and then using that exact memorized version on stage—you're not adapting to the actual performance.
114.ap: SC2 Rec trains semantic IDs and the recommendation model together, but with a twist: it alternates between two goals. First, it makes the loss landscape sharp (small tweaks to parameters cause big changes in loss) for warm-start items (those with history), which forces precise predictions. Then it makes the loss landscape flatter for cold-start items, which means predictions stay stable even if parameters shift slightly. By enforcing consistency between these two landscapes, the system learns semantic IDs that work well on both old and new items.
114.ww: Sharpness and flatness are opposite concepts—sharp predictions are precise, flat predictions are robust. By flattening the loss landscape for cold-start items, you're essentially saying 'even if the semantic ID isn't perfect, the recommendation should still be reasonable.' Training warm and cold items together means the semantic IDs learn to capture features that help both, not just one.
114.po: Cold-start items now get better recommendations without requiring massive amounts of metadata or interaction data. This matters for new products, artists, and videos where there's little history to learn from. Industrial tests confirm the approach works on real recommender systems.

115.bp: Two people want to swap goods—one has a bicycle, wants a skateboard; the other has a skateboard, wants a bicycle. A simple barter. But what if there are dozens of items and dozens of people, all with different valuations? One person might value a bicycle at $200, another at $50. A centralized exchange (marketplace) needs to find trades that make everyone better off and are fair.
115.wh: The obvious approach—maximize total welfare—is easy. But in the process, some people might lose money while others gain a lot. The person who gets cheated won't participate next time, breaking the market. You need trades where every person gets a non-negative profit (non-negative profit constraint). But proving that such trades exist and computing them efficiently is hard. It's NP-hard, meaning no known efficient algorithm exists for the general problem.
115.ap: The researchers prove the problem is computationally intractable (strongly NP-hard) but then design a randomized polynomial-time algorithm that finds allocations with optimal expected welfare, guarantees every agent a non-negative expected profit, and ensures that with near-certainty, even unlucky agents end up close to breaking even (within the value of two items). The algorithm uses randomization to avoid the worst cases that make deterministic methods slow.
115.ww: Randomization sidesteps the computational bottleneck: instead of trying every possible assignment (exponential), the algorithm makes clever random choices that converge to a good solution. Because each person's valuation is private (they might lie), the paper also studies this from a mechanism-design angle—how to ensure truthful revelation of values while maintaining the welfare guarantees.
115.po: Decentralized marketplaces can now run barter exchanges at scale—peer-to-peer item swaps where the system ensures everyone walks away feeling they got a fair deal. This enables new sharing economies and reduces the need for centralized currency (money) when goods can be directly swapped.

116.bp: Recommendation systems currently optimize for one goal: accuracy (suggesting items you'll like). But real users care about multiple things: they want relevant recommendations, but also variety (not the same type every time), fairness (not just the most popular items), and discovering new things. These goals often conflict: the safest recommendation is something popular, but that kills discovery. We need systems that balance all of them based on what each user prefers.
116.wh: Most systems treat all objectives as equally important or locked in fixed weights. But users differ: some prioritize accuracy, others discovery. Also, objectives pull in opposite directions (accuracy + diversity trade off), and you don't know ahead of time which combination will satisfy a user. Traditional multi-objective optimization requires running experiments with many different weight settings, which is slow.
116.ap: The paper proposes five levels of 'autonomy' for recommendation systems, culminating in personalized multi-objective systems where each user gets unique objective weights. To find each user's preferences efficiently, they use Bayesian optimization: a learning method that tries different objective weights, learns from user feedback which combinations work, and focuses on promising regions. They add orthogonal meta-learning: learning a shared foundation across similar users (so one user's preferences help inform another's), but keeping objectives independent so they don't sabotage each other.
116.ww: Bayesian optimization is designed for expensive-to-evaluate objectives—instead of trying 1000 weight combinations, it intelligently samples 10 that are most likely to reveal user preferences. Orthogonal meta-learning works because users often have similar preference structures (both like accuracy, both want some diversity) even if the weights differ. By exploiting that shared structure, the system learns faster.
116.po: Users now get personalized recommendations that balance their unique priorities without anyone having to manually configure weights. Experimental results show this is more satisfying than one-size-fits-all systems, reducing both echo chambers and user frustration.

117.bp: Running AI models directly in web browsers (instead of on cloud servers) is attractive: lower latency, better privacy, no data sent to servers, no ongoing costs. But now the model code and weights live in an untrusted environment (your browser) where anyone with the page open can inspect the code, download the weights, or modify the model. We need a way to hide the model so that even the person running it can't easily steal or reverse-engineer it.
117.wh: JavaScript-based browser models are transparent: an attacker can pause execution, inspect variables in the debugger, and read out the weights directly. Even if you compress or minify the code, it's still human-readable with modern tools. You need to move the model out of JavaScript into a format that's harder to inspect. WebAssembly (a low-level compiled format) is a candidate, but it's still decompilable.
117.ap: WAMO is an obfuscation framework that converts AI models to WebAssembly and applies transformations at the Wasm layer: scrambling the order of computations, splitting weights across multiple variables, rearranging the instruction graph so the model's logic is harder to follow, and inserting dummy operations. This isn't cryptography (can't stop a determined attacker forever), but it raises the difficulty from 'trivial to reverse' to 'would take days or weeks of specialized effort.'
117.ww: Wasm is lower-level than JavaScript, so patterns like 'this variable is the weight matrix' are less obvious to an attacker. By also obfuscating the computation graph (the sequence of operations), you don't just hide individual numbers—you hide the overall architecture. The dummy operations dilute the signal: an attacker has to distinguish real operations from noise. Together, these raise the cyclomatic complexity (measure of code branching) and 'effort' (lines of code × redundancy) dramatically.
117.po: Models deployed in browsers now have meaningful security against extraction and reverse-engineering, protecting intellectual property and enabling more companies to run models client-side. Performance stays nearly identical, and accuracy doesn't degrade, making this a practical defense.

118.bp: When you search for something, results come back as a ranked list. Large language models can now re-rank that list using their reasoning ability, often improving results. But LLMs have limited context: they can only see the query and maybe 10 documents at a time (the 'sliding window'). To rank 100 documents, you run the LLM 10 times, which is slow and expensive. We need LLMs that can see all documents at once.
118.wh: Longer context windows make this possible but create a new problem: How do you tell the model 'here are 100 documents—rank them all' in a way that the model understands which is document 1, which is document 50, which is document 100? Simple position encoding (just numbering them 1–100) doesn't work because LLMs trained on shorter texts don't generalize to longer positions. Also, with 100 documents, even fast LLMs spend a lot of computation checking if every document is relevant to the query (which most aren't).
118.ap: LongRanker uses a hierarchical positional encoding: first, the model learns where each token (word) sits within its document (intra-document encoding), then it learns which document in the full list (inter-document encoding). This separation helps the model extrapolate to longer sequences. Second, it uses top-k attention: instead of the model looking at all 100 documents, it focuses on the query and only the 10 most important documents (computed on the fly), and ignores the rest.
118.ww: Hierarchical encoding separates the 'local' structure (within a document) from the 'global' structure (document index), which is easier to learn than treating position as a single number. Top-k attention reduces computation from quadratic (check every document) to linear (check the top few), because most documents are irrelevant and checking them wastes compute. The model learns to identify relevant documents cheaply before spending effort on them.
118.po: Ranking systems can now use long-context LLMs to re-rank entire result sets in one pass, reducing API calls by 10× and latency by similar amounts. This makes LLM-based ranking practical for production systems, not just research.

119.bp: Short-video platforms (TikTok, YouTube Shorts, Instagram Reels) are now as popular as traditional social media, but recommender systems for these platforms are poorly understood. They're different from traditional recommendation: users skate through hundreds of videos per day, their interests change rapidly, and feedback is often implicit (did they watch to the end?) and noisy. We need large-scale real data to study how these systems should work.
119.wh: Most public datasets are either small (thousands of videos), synthetic (not representative), or proprietary (locked inside tech companies). This makes it hard to benchmark new recommendation algorithms or understand what features matter most. Real short-video recommendation involves balancing cold-start (new videos have no watch history), rapid interest shifts (trends change minute-to-minute), and diverse feedback types (likes, shares, rewatches, all meaning different things).
119.ap: VK-LSVD is a dataset from the VK platform (a major social network) with 40 billion interactions from 10 million users on 20 million videos over six months. It includes rich metadata: embedded descriptions of video content (semantic features learned by video models), multiple feedback signals (watch time, likes, shares, skips), and contextual data (time of day, user location, device type). The dataset is analyzed for quality and then released publicly.
119.ww: Real-world scale is important: algorithms optimized on tiny datasets often fail at billions of interactions (different patterns emerge). Multiple feedback types matter because 'watch to the end' means something different from 'share immediately'—some signals indicate strong preference, others indicate curiosity or novelty. The six-month timeline captures seasonal trends and interest drift that static datasets miss.
119.po: Researchers can now build and test short-video recommenders without proprietary data, accelerating progress in handling rapid interest shifts and cold-start problems. The dataset's use in the live VK RecSys Challenge 2025 demonstrates its real-world relevance.

120.bp: Blockchain systems let thousands of strangers jointly maintain a public ledger without a central authority, but they only work if the people (validators) who add new blocks follow the rules. When validators control enough stake to act as a group, they can cheat the system: they know which blocks they'll be chosen to produce in advance, so they can privately build a chain that gives them extra rewards while maintaining plausible deniability. This paper asks whether such a risk-free cheating strategy exists in Polkadot, a major blockchain worth billions.
120.wh: Earlier work showed that validators *could* cheat risk-free in simple blockchains where block producers announce their role far in advance (global predictability). But Polkadot uses a hybrid model where validators see *some* future block-maker roles but not all, making it unclear whether risk-free cheating is even possible here. The challenge is finding an attack that lets dishonest validators earn extra rewards without ever risking the punishment (stake loss) that would catch them.
120.ap: The authors construct two concrete attack recipes where a pool controlling 33% of validators acts as a unified bloc. They privately build a secret chain of blocks whenever their colluding members are scheduled to validate, then release this secret chain to gain an advantage in the public race. The timing and structure of the attack exploits the fact that Polkadot's partial predictability means they know exactly when they can safely validate without detection.
120.ww: Because Polkadot's validator schedule is partially predictable, a coordinated group can time their private block production to align with moments when they know they'll be chosen. This means they never create blocks outside their legitimate turn, so auditors monitoring the chain can't prove they deviated from the rules—they simply exploited the schedule that was announced to them. The attack works because the system can't distinguish between honest validators and honest-but-colluding validators.
120.po: The experiments confirm that a 33% colluding pool gains an extra 7.09% in block rewards without risking detection or punishment. This matches the profit earned by conventional (riskier) selfish-mining attacks, but here the validators face zero chance of being caught. The finding suggests Polkadot's hybrid predictability model opens a serious governance loophole that simple longest-chain designs don't fully address.

121.bp: Large language models extended with retrieval (RAG) can answer questions by pulling facts from external databases in real time. This makes them useful for up-to-date, grounded answers, but the system is now much more expensive to run: it must search through documents, fetch relevant ones, and then process all that text through the model. This cost becomes a vulnerability—adversaries can exploit it to make the service slow and expensive.
121.wh: The naive approach to stopping such attacks is to monitor the user's prompts: catch suspicious questions before they reach the retrieval stage. But this fails in practice because an attacker can poison the external knowledge base itself—inserting malicious documents into Wikipedia, the web, or wherever the retrieval system pulls from. These documents look innocent but trigger retrieval and burn through tokens during inference, making the system expensive to run.
121.ap: The paper proposes a two-stage attack. First, they use a reinforcement-learning agent to automatically craft malicious documents: these are semantically similar to real user queries, so they get retrieved, but designed to bloat the reasoning overhead during token prediction. Second, they inject these poison documents into the external corpus. When users ask normal questions, the retriever pulls in these crafted files alongside legitimate results, forcing the model to process massive amounts of text.
121.ww: The attack works because the model must process all retrieved documents to produce a coherent answer, even if some are junk. A single toxic document can easily double or triple the computational cost. By engineering poisoned documents to be just relevant enough to pass retrieval filtering, the attacker multiplies inference cost without changing what the user typed, making the attack invisible to prompt-level defenses.
121.po: The framework demonstrates that attackers can make RAG systems prohibitively expensive to run by strategically poisoning public knowledge bases. This reveals a new class of vulnerability in retrieval-augmented systems where the computational burden shifts from user input to background retrieval and processing, creating a denial-of-service vector that's hard to detect and harder to defend against.

122.bp: Communication networks, power grids, and sensor networks are constantly changing: links go up and down, devices join or leave, routing paths shift. A fundamental problem is deciding which nodes should be monitored to catch all network failures. In the real world, these monitor nodes are physical devices with limited batteries or temporary assignments, so each one only works for a finite time window. This paper tackles how to keep all network links watched as devices die and are replaced.
122.wh: The classical vertex cover problem asks: pick the minimum set of nodes such that every edge is incident to at least one picked node. But this assumes the edges and nodes are static. When edges change over time and a monitor only lasts d time units, the problem becomes much harder: a monitor placed at time t disappears at time t+d, so you must continually deploy new monitors to maintain coverage. You can't just solve the problem once; you must plan a sequence of deployments.
122.ap: The authors define the 'sustained' vertex cover as a sequence of node selections across time, where each selected node only covers edges in its active window. They provide algorithms of three types: approximation algorithms (fast but not perfect), exact online algorithms (where monitors appear as time flows), and parameterized algorithms (fast when d is small). Each comes with theoretical bounds proving how close they get to optimal.
122.ww: The key insight is that the temporal structure breaks the problem into subproblems. If you know d in advance, you can decompose time into overlapping windows and solve each window nearly optimally. The online version—where you don't know future requests—succeeds because the problem's temporal structure is predictable: you must maintain coverage over sliding windows, and this constraint limits how badly you can do even with no foresight.
122.po: The theory and algorithms show that networks can be monitored efficiently despite device churn, with concrete guarantees on how many simultaneous monitors are needed. The work opens the door to studying other temporal graph problems (path finding, connectivity) with the same 'sustained' constraint, multiplying the toolkit for dynamic network analysis.

123.bp: Websites and cloud platforms often rent out resources—computing power, data-center bandwidth, temporary access—on demand. A business faces a sequence of requests over time: some customers want resources for one day, others for a week. The challenge is deciding which requests to accept and how long to keep each resource running, knowing that keeping something idle costs money but rejecting requests loses revenue. This paper asks: how should an algorithm decide in real time, when the future is unknown?
123.wh: The straightforward approach—accept every request and keep resources idle while waiting for the next one—wastes money. The aggressive approach—never accept short requests, always wait for long ones—loses revenue and seems silly. The fundamental tension is that you must commit to a rental length immediately, before knowing what future customers will want. If you're unlucky and commit too long, you waste money; too short, and you miss revenue. You want provably good decisions despite not seeing the future.
123.ap: The authors develop 'relax-and-round' algorithms: first, solve an imaginary 'relaxed' version of the problem where you can split resources fractionally across requests (easier to optimize). This fractional solution reveals the right price to charge for each rental length. Then they carefully round the fractional allocation back to whole resources: in the simpler fixed-duration case, this rounding is lossless (no optimality lost). In the harder variable-duration case, they use controlled dependencies to round one unit at a time while constraining how much optimality is lost.
123.ww: The fractional relaxation works because pricing naturally balances the trade-off: high prices discourage long rentals (saving money), while low prices encourage them (gaining revenue). The rounding succeeds because once you have good prices, the fractional solution is already structured—it rarely splits a request across many units—so rounding back to whole units is nearly cost-free. The algorithm's guarantees come from bounding how much this rounding costs.
123.po: The results are mathematically tight: they prove their algorithms achieve the best possible competitive ratio (loss rate versus an all-knowing oracle) for each variant. For businesses managing reusable resources, this means algorithms that accept or reject rental requests with provable near-optimal profit, without needing to predict the future.

124.bp: Chinese history spans thousands of years with countless heroes, generals, poets, and philosophers whose lives shaped the culture. Today's young people often miss this heritage because historical records are scattered across books, fragmented in text, and hard to bring alive. Large language models can learn to role-play as historical figures and engage people in dialogue, making history interactive and personal. But building such a system requires collecting and organizing massive amounts of biographical data—names, families, relationships, historical context—in a form the model can learn from.
124.wh: Historical texts are messy. A single figure appears under different names across centuries, in scattered biographical fragments, family trees, poems, and military records. No single database connects all these threads. Moreover, low-resource languages like historical Chinese have far less pre-trained model knowledge than English, so the model must learn from scratch. Simply dumping raw historical texts into a model won't produce a believable role-playing character—you need structured knowledge about relationships, timelines, and achievements.
124.ap: The BaiJia platform collects and integrates biographical data for 19,281 historical Chinese figures, organizing details into structured knowledge: family relationships, historical events they participated in, literary works they produced, their achievements and roles. This structured data is then used to instruct a large language model, teaching it how to embody each character realistically. The platform provides a unified interface so users can interact with any historical figure via dialogue.
124.ww: By grounding the model in structured biographical facts—family ties, historical timelines, literary works—the model can reason about what a character would know and believe. When asked a question, the model can answer in character because it understands the person's context and era. The organization into explicit relationships and events lets the model generalize: it can produce convincing answers to questions not in the training data, because it understands the underlying structure of that person's life.
124.po: Experiments show that compared to base language models, BaiJia achieves a 10.2% improvement across metrics measuring how well the role-plays match historical facts and character believability. The platform now serves as an open resource, letting millions of users explore Chinese history through dialogue with historical figures—a form of engagement that makes heritage tangible and memorable.

125.bp: Science depends on reproducibility: when a researcher publishes code and data, others should be able to re-run the analysis and get the same answers. But in practice, re-running published computational research is painful. Code depends on specific software versions, data lives in different folders on different machines, small analytical decisions are missing from the paper, and libraries change. Even when authors share everything, reproduction fails—sometimes after hours of debugging. Modern AI systems could potentially repair such failures automatically, but no one knows how well they actually work at this real, messy task.
125.wh: The obvious approach—ask a human to fix it—works but is slow and expensive. Asking an AI to fix it sounds promising, but the challenge is that 'fixing' requires understanding not just the code but the analytical intent: why did the author write this particular test, what was the expected output? If the AI fixes the code but produces wrong results, we've wasted effort. The hard part is measuring success correctly: only counting repairs that produce identical outputs, not just code that runs.
125.ap: The researchers created 130 test cases by starting with five fully reproducible R studies, then deliberately breaking them in realistic ways: missing libraries, wrong folder paths, version mismatches, and missing analytical logic. They then tested two repair strategies. The first ('prompt-based') iteratively asks a language model to fix the code with increasingly detailed context. The second ('agent-based') deploys an AI coding agent that reads project files, makes targeted edits, re-runs the code, and learns from failures until the analysis produces correct outputs.
125.ww: The agent-based approach works better because it can inspect the project structure and incrementally refine fixes by re-running the code and observing failures. A prompt-based system has only one shot to understand and fix the problem; an agent can iterate. But prompt-based systems do better with rich context—detailed error messages and file structure—suggesting that access to the project's scaffolding (not just the broken code) matters more than the ability to iterate.
125.po: Results show agent-based repairs succeed on 79% of tests, while prompt-based approaches range from 31–79% depending on context richness. This demonstrates that AI systems can meaningfully automate computational reproducibility, though they remain far from perfect. The findings suggest that lowering barriers to verification will require combining AI tooling with better software practices—templates, automated checks, documented assumptions.

126.bp: Large language models, when asked to retrieve facts from knowledge graphs (structured data about people, companies, relationships), sometimes invent false connections. For example, asked about who acquired whom, the model might correctly identify both Microsoft and Activision but link them backwards—saying Activision bought Microsoft. These 'hallucinations' are especially dangerous in enterprise systems where users rely on factual accuracy. Detecting such errors is hard because the model produces fluent, grammatically correct text that sounds authoritative even when it's wrong.
126.wh: Existing approaches to detection ask the model to generate an alternative answer and compare them, or have a separate neural network score the output's likelihood. But these add latency, cost, and opacity—you don't know why the system thinks something is wrong. The real challenge is that swapped relationships (Activision bought Microsoft vs. Microsoft bought Activision) look almost identical to a human reader, yet they are completely different facts in a structured database. You need a method that's fast, explainable, and works specifically for structural errors.
126.ap: ReGA frames hallucination detection not as a generation task but as a graph-alignment task. First, a fast pattern-based extractor converts text into a small graph representation in under a millisecond. Then, a lightweight feature-based module (ReGA Feature) computes interpretable 'swap indicators' in 14ms on a CPU: does the graph match known truths, or is a relationship reversed? For complex cases where simple features fail, a neural graph matcher (Deep ReGA) trained via structural energy minimization can disambiguate subtle cases by assigning low energy to correct directions and high energy to incorrect ones.
126.ww: The approach works because most hallucinations are structural—they involve reversing or swapping relationships, not inventing new entities. By detecting at the graph level rather than the text level, the system exploits the fact that relationships have directionality. For symmetric cases (where both directions make grammatical sense), energy-based alignment finds the global minimum: a full graph matching that prefers correct directions because they require less 'energy' to align with ground truth.
126.po: The system achieves 0.90 AUC on detecting functional hallucinations and 0.80 AUC on detecting role reversals, with minimal latency. On a controlled test, Deep ReGA assigns energy 0.00 to the correct direction and 1.82 to the inverted one—a clear, interpretable signal. This means the system can run in production, catching hallucinations in real time without slowing down retrieval or obscuring why a fact was flagged.

127.bp: Social media users share opinions that influence others through replies, retweets, and shares. These opinions propagate through networks at different speeds depending on emotional tenor (anger spreads faster than sadness) and network structure (topics spread differently through mentions versus replies). Understanding how opinions propagate is crucial for studying polarization, tracking rumor spread, and designing healthier platforms. But existing models are 'black boxes'—they predict what will happen without revealing the mechanisms driving the propagation.
127.wh: The standard approach to predicting propagation uses end-to-end machine learning models: feed in the network and a few observations, output a prediction. But this doesn't reveal *why* opinions spread. Is it because people reply more emotionally? Because followers mention each other? Because certain emotions are more contagious? These models lack interpretable parameters linked to real mechanisms. Additionally, datasets used for training are incomplete: they don't capture all the hierarchical structure, they use coarse sentiment labels, and they cover too few domains to generalize.
127.ap: The authors create a new dataset (VISTA) with fine-grained emotional annotations (not just positive/negative, but specific emotions), complete hierarchical structures (showing which posts are replies to which), and cross-domain coverage. They then design an interpretable model integrating Hawkes processes (a tool for modeling self-exciting events, where each event makes the next more likely) with graph networks. The model represents opinions as events in a multi-dimensional space: emotions × hierarchical reply levels. Each dimension has interpretable parameters showing how strongly emotions and reply patterns drive further propagation.
127.ww: The mechanism works because Hawkes processes naturally model contagion: an earlier event (a comment) increases the probability of future events (more comments) in a way that's mathematically interpretable. By treating emotions and reply structure as separate but interacting dimensions, the model can quantify: how much does anger spread further than sadness? Do mentions drive propagation differently than replies? The structure forces the model to learn physically meaningful patterns rather than statistical correlations.
127.po: The framework reveals three concrete propagation mechanics: certain emotions spread more readily than others, hierarchical position matters (deep replies propagate differently than top-level posts), and temporal memory effects occur (past activity increases future propagation). The model outperforms black-box approaches on prediction tasks while providing the first benchmark for understanding multi-dimensional propagation mechanisms, moving the field from 'what will happen' to 'why it happens.'

128.bp: Businesses use structured data—customer records, transaction histories, product catalogs—to make decisions: who will churn, which customers are at fraud risk, what will someone buy next? For decades, machine learning on tabular data meant hand-building features and training old-school models like XGBoost. Recently, 'foundation models' trained on massive structured datasets have emerged, promising better out-of-the-box performance. But each one has a different API, different preprocessing steps, and different evaluation metrics, making it hard for practitioners to try them side-by-side.
128.wh: The fragmentation problem is real: one foundation model expects data normalized one way, another expects it differently. One provides AUC metrics, another provides accuracy. One is optimized for inference, another for fine-tuning. A practitioner wanting to test three models must learn three APIs and rewrite their pipeline three times. This friction slows adoption and wastes engineering time on plumbing instead of exploring what these models can actually do.
128.ap: TabTune provides a unified library with a single interface for multiple leading tabular foundation models. Behind the scenes, it standardizes preprocessing (normalizing, handling missing values, encoding categorical features) so users write code once. It supports both inference (using pre-trained models) and multiple fine-tuning modes (training on your data). It includes a comprehensive suite of evaluation metrics beyond accuracy: fairness metrics (is the model biased?), calibration metrics (are its confidence scores reliable?), and domain-specific metrics like churn rate or fraud detection rate.
128.ww: A unified interface works because the preprocessing pipeline is largely domain-agnostic (the same normalization and encoding steps work across most tabular models), and the model APIs, while different, can be abstracted behind a common layer. By standardizing evaluation, practitioners can see apples-to-apples comparisons: this model is 2% more accurate but has higher demographic bias, while this one is more fair but slower. This transparency lets them make trade-offs rationally.
128.po: TabTune lowers the barrier to deploying tabular foundation models in real systems. Practitioners can quickly benchmark models on problems like churn prediction, fraud detection, and behavioral modeling through a single API, run fairness and calibration checks as standard practice, and integrate the best performer into production. The library turns foundation models from a research curiosity into a practical tool for enterprise data science.

129.bp: When you search for similar images by text query—or search for images using an image—the system must understand that an image and a caption mean the same thing despite being encoded in completely different ways (pixels vs. words). This cross-modal retrieval is fundamental to multimodal search: finding a product image when you describe it in words, or finding documents matching a photo. Real-world scenarios have many images and captions about the same object; the challenge is leveraging these group relationships rather than comparing individual pairs in isolation.
129.wh: The straightforward approach compares each image to each text individually: given a query image, find the most similar text. But real data has structure: multiple captions might describe the same image (different people describe the product differently), and multiple images show the same product. These many-to-many relationships are crucial for aligning semantics—if three captions agree on a key detail, an image matching all three is more likely correct. Existing methods ignore this structure, treating each comparison as independent.
129.ap: The approach builds a hypergraph where each vertex represents an image or text, and hyperedges group multiple items that share semantics. A label-driven hypergraph construction creates these hyperedges based on semantic similarity, with weighted edges that let important connections dominate. Instead of comparing images to text through one-way attention (text queries images, or vice versa), the model uses bidirectional cross-attention: both images and text act as queries, each pulling relevant information from the other, creating symmetric semantic enhancement.
129.ww: Many-to-many relationships matter because they provide consensus. If an image is similar to multiple captions, that similarity is more robust than matching a single pair. The hypergraph structure forces the model to learn representations that align entire groups simultaneously, not just individual pairs. Bidirectional attention prevents either modality from dominating; both images and text guide each other toward a shared semantic space.
129.po: By explicitly modeling many-to-many relationships, the system achieves better semantic alignment and more accurate cross-modal retrieval than pair-wise methods. The approach scales to large datasets through techniques that construct local hypergraphs rather than global ones, enabling practical deployment while retaining the benefits of group structure.

130.bp: Large language models can now use external tools—search engines, calculators, databases—to answer questions they couldn't answer from memory alone. Imagine an LLM that can call Slack APIs to check project status, or SQL databases to look up customer data. The challenge is deciding which tool to use when the user's request is ambiguous. A user asking 'show me active projects' might want a Slack API call, a database query, or both; the system must figure out the right tool from limited context, and it must generalize to new tools it hasn't seen during training.
130.wh: Existing tool-selection systems use retrieval: compute similarity between the user's query and each tool's documentation, then pick the most similar one. But this fails when the query is vague or uses terminology different from the documentation. A user might ask 'what's the status?' meaning 'list running deployments,' but this language gap keeps the retriever from finding the right tool. Moreover, these systems learn what tools look like during training; deploying new tools in production requires retraining or at least fine-tuning, limiting generalization.
130.ap: ToolBox-RL uses reinforcement learning to optimize the end-to-end process: query rewriting (restate the user's intent in clearer terms), intent understanding (what problem are they solving?), and tool selection (which tool solves it?). An RL agent learns to rewrite queries to better match tool descriptions, then learns to select tools by receiving reward signals when it picks the correct one. The system includes a cold-start phase (learning from labeled examples) followed by policy optimization (learning from experience).
130.ww: Reinforcement learning works because it treats tool selection as a learnable strategy: the agent gets feedback (correct or incorrect tool choice) and adapts. Query rewriting is powerful because it bridges language gaps—the agent learns to translate vague user language into clearer technical descriptions that match tool docs. The learned strategies generalize to new tools because the agent is optimizing for abstract properties (semantic alignment, coverage of user intent) rather than memorizing specific tools.
130.po: Experiments show ToolBox-RL achieves the best tool call accuracy on both white-box tools (APIs the system knows) and black-box tools (unfamiliar APIs), and maintains good performance even when many distractor tools are available. The framework enables LLMs to reliably use large, growing tool repositories without retraining, making tool-augmented LLMs practical for real-world enterprise systems.

131.bp: News recommendation systems show people articles based on what they've read before. But they typically just predict what interests users now, reinforcing whatever they already believe—a filter bubble that hardens opinions and deepens polarization. An alternative approach is 'proactive' recommendation: gently guide users toward higher-quality information by strategically choosing intermediary articles, hoping they gradually see the value in more diverse or nuanced news. The challenge is doing this without being manipulative—people should feel they're exploring naturally, not being herded.
131.wh: The fundamental tension is between respecting current interests and pushing toward a target. Show articles too far from a user's current beliefs and they ignore them; too close and you're not actually guiding them anywhere. You need to know each person's tolerance for novelty (how much of a departure will they tolerate?) and track how their interests evolve across multiple recommendation cycles. Simple algorithms that just measure similarity to a target fail because they don't account for user adaptability or the sequence of changes needed to shift beliefs gradually.
131.ap: ONeRec introduces two mechanisms. First, an 'openness coefficient' derived from a user's reading history measures how tolerant they are of novel or unexpected content. Second, the system recommends intermediate articles that balance two goals: staying relevant to current interests (so the user engages) while nudging toward the target topic. The system adapts both the openness estimate and the recommendation strategy across multiple rounds, learning how each user responds to guided shifts.
131.ww: The approach works because it respects user agency while steering. The openness coefficient is personalized: users with adventurous reading histories get bolder recommendations, while conservative readers get gentler nudges. By treating guidance as a sequence (not a single recommendation), the system exploits the fact that small changes accumulate—each article can shift interests slightly, and these shifts compound. Adapting the openness estimate across rounds lets the system learn each user's receptiveness in real time.
131.po: The system demonstrates that gradual, personalized guidance toward target topics is possible without manipulation. By targeting articles that are both relevant and strategically chosen, ONeRec enables platforms to combat filter bubbles while respecting user preferences—users slowly explore new ideas because each step feels natural, not forced.

132.bp: Customer support systems often fail not because the system is dumb but because customers don't know how to ask for help. A user complains 'my application is slow,' but 'slow' could mean slow startup, slow response, slow database queries, or slow UI rendering—each requiring different troubleshooting. The support system doesn't know which problem the user is facing. Asking the customer 'which type of slowness?' directly works but feels like interrogation. Ideally, the system would ask targeted, clarifying questions that narrow down the issue efficiently, then deliver the right diagnostic steps.
132.wh: The challenge is ambiguity that's structural, not linguistic. The user's words might be perfectly clear ('application is slow'), but the knowledge graph linking applications to diagnostic steps has multiple valid interpretations. Traditional clarification asks 'do you mean X or Y?', but if there are ten possible diagnoses, this creates a branching tree of questions. The system needs to reason about which questions are most informative—which ones eliminate the most hypotheses with a single answer?
132.ap: AID treats clarification as a hypothesis-elimination problem using a knowledge graph. When a user query maps to multiple interpretations (multiple hypothesis subgraphs in the knowledge graph), the system probes by asking targeted questions designed to separate them. For 'application is slow,' the hypotheses might be resource contention (CPU/memory), bandwidth limits, or configuration errors. The system asks questions that would clearly distinguish these (e.g., 'does this happen with other applications?'). Once ambiguity resolves, it assembles the minimal set of diagnostic documents and steps needed to solve the issue.
132.ww: The hypothesis-elimination approach works because good clarifying questions have high information value: they split the hypothesis space roughly in half, eliminating many possibilities with each answer. By reasoning over the knowledge graph structure, the system avoids asking redundant questions. Users get a conversation that feels natural—each question has a clear purpose—while the system converges to the right diagnosis in minimal turns.
132.po: The framework demonstrates that conversational recommendation systems can handle structural ambiguity through targeted questioning, then deliver precise solutions. By treating clarification as a structured decision problem rather than free-text dialogue, enterprises can build support systems that understand not just what words mean, but what customers actually need.

133.bp: Graph neural networks (GNNs) excel at analyzing networks—social graphs, citation networks, molecule structures—but they're brittle. Train a GNN on networks from one setting and test it on slightly different networks, and it often fails catastrophically. This phenomenon—where tiny distribution shifts cause sudden misclassification—is called the Minimal Shift Flip (MSF) problem. Understanding why it happens and fixing it is key to deploying GNNs in the real world where data always drifts slightly from training conditions.
133.wh: The obvious hypothesis is that the model is overconfident or overfitted. But the real issue is sharper: the loss landscape (the space of all possible model weights) has sharp, narrow valleys where the model achieves good training accuracy. In these sharp regions, tiny input perturbations—a slightly different network structure—can flip the prediction. A model trained in a valley can't tolerate even small variations. Classical approaches to robustness (like regularization) help but are crude: they don't directly address the underlying sharpness.
133.ap: The authors use the lens of Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM), a technique that explicitly penalizes sharp regions of the loss landscape. They quantify sharpness through the 'Local Robust Radius'—the smallest perturbation needed to flip a prediction. They then develop an 'energy-based' objective mathematically shown to correlate with this robust radius, giving them a tractable way to train for flatness. During training, they apply generative augmentation (synthetically creating new network structures) to further stabilize the model.
133.ww: The mechanism works because flat regions of the loss landscape are inherently robust: if the model's weight vector moves a little, the loss barely changes, so predictions remain stable. By measuring sharpness via the energy function, the model learns to seek flatter regions during training. The connection between energy and robust radius is proven theoretically, so optimizing energy genuinely improves robustness. Generative augmentation amplifies this by forcing the model to succeed on varied inputs, further exploring the loss landscape.
133.po: Models trained with this approach show dramatically improved robustness: they maintain accuracy even when test networks deviate from training distribution. The work moves GNNs from brittle laboratory results to reliable tools for real-world deployment where distribution shift is inevitable. The theoretical framework also generalizes to other neural architectures, not just graphs.

134.bp: Data visualization is typically designed for clarity: make the numbers obvious, avoid decoration, use consistent colors. But people don't just want to understand data; they want to be inspired by it, to notice patterns they didn't expect, to make decisions confidently. A spreadsheet of sales numbers is clear but uninspiring. A thoughtfully designed visualization that shows those same numbers might spark an idea. This paper asks: what properties of a visualization create insight and engagement beyond just clarity?
134.wh: Traditional visualization design focuses on what data contains: structure, scale, categories. But effective visualizations also have latent visual properties—qualities not directly in the raw data but added through design choices: color symbolism (does blue feel cold or trustworthy?), spatial arrangement (top-left feels important), white space (suggests simplicity or emptiness?). These properties influence emotion and creativity but are hard to articulate and teach. Most design guidance ignores them or treats them as decoration, missing their crucial role in engagement.
134.ap: The researchers conducted a qualitative study: a hands-on workshop where participants redesigned visualizations for a retail problem, followed by expert interviews. Through this exploration, they identified three design principles that leverage latent visual properties. 'Ignorance mapping' uses visual weight to highlight where decisions are uncertain or data is missing, reducing cognitive load. 'Creative unblocking' uses dynamic filtering and interactivity to let users explore possibilities. 'Symbolic representation' uses color and form to convey emotion and build empathy, connecting data to human meaning.
134.ww: These principles work because they operate at a subconscious level: a visualization's emotional tone and apparent organization influence how people think about the data before they consciously read numbers. Highlighting uncertainty reduces decision paralysis. Interactive filtering shifts the experience from 'here's the answer' to 'let's explore together.' Emotional color choices (warm for urgency, cool for stability) prime the user's mindset, making insights more memorable.
134.po: The framework reveals that latent visual properties matter as much as data accuracy for real-world decision-making. By consciously leveraging these properties—indicating uncertainty, enabling exploration, using symbolic representation—designers can create visualizations that inform *and* inspire. The work bridges the gap between technical clarity and creative sense-making, showing that the best visualizations do both.

135.bp: E-commerce companies run dozens of marketing campaigns — banner ads, seasonal promotions, influencer collaborations — but measuring which ones actually drove sales is nearly impossible because a campaign uses vague creative language ("Summer Vibes Collection") while the sales database records concrete product purchases. This mismatch makes it impossible to train smarter campaign systems that learn which campaigns work for which audiences.
135.wh: The core problem is semantic ambiguity: a campaign about "adventure gear" might be promoting hiking boots, backpacks, or jackets, and a customer who bought a tent might have been influenced by the campaign or might have wanted it anyway. You can't just scan the campaign text for product keywords because marketing deliberately uses evocative, thematic language that doesn't directly name products. Without ground-truth labels saying "this customer bought this product because of this campaign," you're stuck with no training signal.
135.ap: The paper proposes a three-step pipeline: first, use an LLM to read the campaign creative and extract what product types it's actually selling (e.g., "Summer Vibes" implies clothing and accessories). Second, search the store's product taxonomy for all items matching those types. Third, have the LLM score each candidate product type to decide which ones the campaign genuinely promotes. Once you know what product types a campaign targets, any customer who bought from those types after seeing the campaign becomes a positive training example.
135.ww: This works because LLMs understand semantic intent in human language — they can parse marketing copy and extract the underlying product categories without needing exact keyword matches. By reframing the problem from "which exact products?" to "which product categories?" you move from an impossible matching problem to a tractable classification task. The approach generates high-confidence training labels automatically, so instead of hiring humans to annotate thousands of campaigns, the system annotates itself and learns to optimize campaign placement.
135.po: The method achieves 78–90% precision on internally validated campaign-to-product mappings, which means downstream ranking models can be trained with high-quality automatic labels. This unlocks the ability to build machine-learning systems that learn which types of campaigns drive which types of sales, enabling e-commerce platforms to automate campaign placement and improve return on ad spend at scale.

136.bp: Companies like Google deploy multi-agent systems where dozens of specialized AI components collaborate to answer user questions — one agent searches, one ranks, one scores relevance, one re-writes output. Designing how these agents should connect and talk to each other is done by hand, but the optimal topology changes depending on the question. A web search for "coffee recipes" needs different agent paths than a search for "medical symptoms.
136.wh: Today, engineers build separate model-and-topology pairs for each type of query domain, so you'd train one collaboration graph for shopping queries, another for academic research, another for health topics. This works poorly on novel domains and wastes work because fundamentally similar patterns (like "retrieve then rank") get learned from scratch each time. The ideal system should learn a universal understanding of topology and adapt it on the fly based on any new query.
136.ap: The paper presents a system that learns to generate agent-topology diagrams directly from a user's natural-language question. It uses two main ideas: a task-aware encoder that filters which agent information matters for a specific question (via sparse gating, essentially focusing attention on relevant signals), and a mixture-of-experts layer that selects different specialized sub-networks depending on the task type. The system is trained in three stages: first on canonical topologies to learn structural patterns, then on LLM-generated task-topology pairs to learn mappings from question types to graphs, finally fine-tuned on real systems.
136.ww: This works because task understanding and topology generation are mechanically separable — the question type (shopping vs. health) can be encoded once, then different specialized sub-networks can be activated to predict the right collaboration graph. By training on massive synthetic data (LLM-generated task-topology pairs), the model learns generalizable structural patterns that transfer to unseen domains. The key insight is that topology generation is learnable and domain-transferable, not something that must be hand-designed per task.
136.po: The system handles six diverse benchmark domains in experiments using a single model, eliminating the need to train separate models for each query type. This reduces engineering overhead and enables dynamic adaptation: when a novel query type appears, the system predicts the optimal agent topology instead of requiring manual redesign, making multi-agent systems more practical to deploy in production services like search engines.

137.bp: Imagine hospitals in different cities clustering their patient records to find disease patterns, or banks clustering transaction networks to detect fraud rings — except data privacy laws mean each organization keeps its data on its own servers and can't share raw information. Federated clustering solves this by letting them collaborate to find patterns without exposing private data.
137.wh: The standard clustering trick is to ask all agents to find the same number of clusters, but in reality, one hospital might discover three disease subtypes while another discovers five because their patient populations are genuinely different. When the server tries to merge cluster results from clients with different numbers of clusters, it fails because there's no clear way to align clusters across heterogeneous groupings. Raw averaging produces gibberish — you'd be averaging a 3-cluster result with a 5-cluster result, losing structure.
137.ap: The paper proposes splitting each client's data into public and private components: public information (cluster-level summaries that are safe to share) gets sent to the server in anonymized form, while private information (the detailed raw data) stays local. Clients with different cluster numbers can now coexist because they only exchange cluster prototypes, not raw data. On the server, cluster prototypes are aligned by computing similarity between them, so clients with 3 clusters and 5 clusters can agree on shared structure despite different granularities.
137.ww: By decoupling public (sharable) and private (local) data, the system sidesteps the alignment problem. Cluster prototypes are abstract summaries that can be compared even when they represent different partitions of the same underlying domain. The server computes prototype affinity (how similar different clusters are) to find the natural shared structure. This allows federated learning without forcing everyone into the same structure.
137.po: The method achieves privacy-preserving graph clustering across heterogeneous clients where each can choose its own number of clusters. Experiments show it prevents performance degradation that occurs when you naively average results from clients with mismatched cluster counts, making federated clustering practical for decentralized applications like multi-hospital disease discovery or multi-bank fraud detection.

138.bp: When rumors or fake news spreads on social media, platforms need to find the original source account so they can take action. Given a snapshot of who has seen or shared a rumor, the challenge is to trace back and identify patient zero — the account that started it all.
138.wh: Deep-learning methods sound like they'd be great for this, but they stumble on three problems. First, they layer on so many feature engineering tricks (special embeddings for cascades, auxiliary attention layers, metadata enrichment) that the models become huge, and you can't afford to retrain when a new rumor emerges. Second, real-world misinformation cascades are rare, so people simulate artificial cascades for training, but artificial spreading patterns don't match reality and the model falls apart. Third, retraining the full model for every new rumor is too slow for real-time deployment.
138.ap: Instead of building a heavyweight deep model, the paper takes inspiration from prompt-learning (the idea that pre-trained models can adapt to new tasks with minimal data). It pre-trains a lightweight classifier on adaptive subgraphs centered around the rumor source, using artificially generated cascades only for this pre-training phase. Then at test time, instead of retraining, it prompts the model with just a few examples of the current rumor's spreading pattern and asks it to localize the source. The prompting approach sidesteps both model bloat and the need to retrain on every new cascade.
138.ww: This works because source localization has a consistent geometric structure — infected nodes cluster around the true source — so a model trained on that structure (even via simulation) can recognize it in real data. By treating inference as a prompt-answering task rather than a model-retraining task, the system stays lightweight and fast. The key insight is that you don't need to refit the model per cascade; you can pre-learn the structural signature and prompt it at test time.
138.po: The method achieves both parameter efficiency and speed: it's a lightweight model that doesn't explode in size, and it can localize rumor sources in seconds without retraining, making real-time deployment feasible. It also handles the low-data regime better than deep methods because prompting works with few examples, so the annotation gap (scarcity of real cascades) becomes less of a bottleneck.

139.bp: Banks need to forecast the demand for multiple types of transactions (checking, savings, loans) across different branches over the next hour. Weather services need to predict wind speed and temperature simultaneously. Time-series forecasting is everywhere in real services, but current large-scale models centralize data from all branches or regions into one place for training, raising privacy and governance concerns.
139.wh: Federated time-series forecasting faces two interconnected problems: different clients have different numbers of variables (one branch tracks 5 types of transactions, another tracks 10), and these variables exhibit different temporal patterns (one might see daily cycles, another weekly). A model trained on one client's data doesn't transfer to another because both the variable structure and the time-dependent patterns are heterogeneous, so you can't just average model weights across federated clients.
139.ap: The paper proposes a two-pathway architecture for each client: a global pathway that learns common low-frequency patterns (slow, smooth trends shared across all clients) and a local pathway that learns personalized high-frequency patterns (spikes, noise, client-specific variations). These two paths are kept separate during training using frequency-aware loss functions that explicitly push low-frequency components to the global path and high-frequency residuals to the local path. A gated fusion mechanism then combines both paths at prediction time for the final forecast.
139.ww: By decomposing the forecasting problem into frequency bands, the system exploits a natural structure in time series: most information lives in different frequency ranges depending on client and variable. Low frequencies generalize across clients (shared trends), while high frequencies are heterogeneous (client-specific noise and spikes). Separating them during training means the global path can learn shared structure and be safely averaged, while local paths stay personalized. At test time, the fusion gate learns to weight them appropriately.
139.po: The method enables privacy-preserving time-series forecasting where each client keeps its data local but benefits from shared learning of common temporal patterns. Extensive experiments show it outperforms existing federated approaches on forecasting benchmarks with heterogeneous variables and temporal correlations, making multi-branch and multi-region forecasting practical without centralizing sensitive data.

140.bp: Recommendation systems suggest movies, products, or songs by modeling the geometry of user preferences — if user A likes movies 1, 2, 3 and user B likes movies 2, 3, 4, then A and B probably have similar tastes and can recommend movies to each other. The challenge is that user-item interaction graphs have wildly different local structures in different parts: some users form tight clusters (niche tastes), others scatter widely (broad tastes).
140.wh: Existing methods assume the entire graph sits in one uniform geometric space, like a flat plane where distance means similarity everywhere. But this assumption is wrong: some users cluster densely (tight taste communities) while others distribute sparsely (diverse individual preferences), and a single fixed geometry can't capture both. If you use a space where similar users cluster well, you'll distort sparse regions, and vice versa.
140.ap: The paper reframes recommendation as a physical process evolving on a curved, time-varying manifold (using Hamiltonian dynamics, an idea from physics). Instead of assuming a fixed geometry, it learns a node-dependent Riemannian metric — essentially a custom shape of space around each user and item that reflects local topology. Information propagates along these curved, adaptive surfaces rather than through linear tangent-space approximations. The channel-wise metric captures that different features might need different geometries too.
140.ww: This works because graphs with topological heterogeneity (dense clusters and sparse regions) naturally live on curved spaces where the geometry is locally adaptive. By learning the metric (the shape of space) rather than fixing it, the model can have tight clustering where appropriate and loose spreading where appropriate. The Hamiltonian approach ensures that information propagates correctly on these curved surfaces without geometric distortion. The paper proves this dynamics has a unique stable solution.
140.po: Experiments show consistent improvements over baseline methods on five benchmarks for recommendation tasks. The adaptive geometric approach captures long-range dependencies better than fixed-geometry methods, so users discover recommendations from farther parts of the graph, and the method handles both tight clusters and diffuse regions without sacrificing either.

141.bp: Pathologists examine tissue slides under microscopes to spot cancer and other diseases, looking at tiny morphological details (cell arrangement, texture, color shifts). Modern AI can help, but the issue is that these AI models are trained on massive slide datasets, and applying them to a new hospital with different slide-staining protocols or scanner equipment requires retraining, which is slow and expensive.
141.wh: Vision-Language models (like image and text foundation models) promise to solve this by leveraging semantic knowledge: you can describe an anomaly in words and the model can find it visually. But there's a granularity mismatch: pathology abnormalities are tiny local features (a specific region's cell clustering), while these large pre-trained models were trained on whole-image-level concepts. The model's generic visual understanding misses the fine detail, and semantic descriptions don't ground in the specific spatial context of that particular region-of-interest.
141.ap: The paper proposes a hierarchical alignment mechanism: visual features from the tissue sample first ground text prompts, generating content-adaptive descriptions that are specific to that slide. Then these description-grounded prompts guide the visual encoder back to spotlight where anomalies are. The process alternates: vision informs language, language refines vision. A dual-branch inference strategy at test time combines semantic scores (model confidence) with geometric prototypes (actual tissue statistics) to stabilize predictions in few-shot settings where there's minimal training data.
141.ww: By enforcing a communication loop between vision and language, the model ensures that semantic concepts are anchored in the specific visual context of each slide. This solves the granularity mismatch because language provides semantic understanding but vision grounds it spatially. The dual-branch approach hedges: semantic scores capture conceptual knowledge, geometric prototypes capture real tissue statistics, and combining both prevents overfitting when data is scarce.
141.po: The method outperforms existing approaches across four benchmark datasets for pathology anomaly detection with limited data. It effectively adapts Vision-Language models to the fine-grained needs of pathology, enabling hospitals to deploy AI diagnostic aids even with small domain-specific training datasets, reducing the need for large centralized annotated collections.

142.bp: Large language models (LLMs) are remarkably good at reasoning over text, but they can't natively work with graphs (social networks, knowledge bases, scientific citation networks). The goal is to tokenize graphs — convert them into sequences of tokens that LLMs can process — so we can ask an LLM questions about a graph and get coherent answers.
142.wh: Current approaches convert graphs into token sequences but lose critical information: they rely only on text prompts and descriptions to guide the LLM, creating a text-biased alignment where the model understands the linguistic description but ignores the actual graph structure. The LLM learns what words mean but doesn't deeply encode graph connectivity, so it can't truly reason about graph structure — it's mimicking text understanding, not graph understanding.
142.ap: The paper proposes explicitly reconstructing the graph from the LLM's tokenized output as an additional training signal. During instruction-tuning (the process of teaching an LLM to follow commands), instead of only matching text descriptions, the model also tries to predict the graph's structure from its own token representations. This reconstruction task forces the LLM to encode graph information directly into its tokens, not just text semantics. The paper proves information-theoretically that this reconstruction objective tightens the alignment between graphs and the model's internal representations.
142.ww: By adding graph reconstruction as a loss function, the training process explicitly penalizes the model if it encodes text semantics but ignores graph structure. The model must learn to encode both: what the graph's text descriptions mean (semantic alignment) and what the graph's connections are (structural alignment). The information-theoretic bound shows this is optimal: the best graph-text alignment is upper-bounded by how much of the graph's information makes it into the model's hidden states.
142.po: The RGLM framework improves alignment between graphs and LLMs beyond text-only approaches, enabling the LLM to perform better on graph reasoning tasks like link prediction, node classification, and retrieval over graphs. This is a step toward building truly universal LLMs that handle both text and structured data, moving beyond the current paradigm where LLMs are great at language but see graphs as mere text descriptions.

143.bp: Lawyers and compliance teams perform high-recall document review: scanning thousands of emails to find all documents relevant to a legal case (goal: find 90–95% of responsive documents). Time and budget are limited, so they need to know when to stop reviewing — but without reading every single remaining document, it's impossible to know how many responsive documents they've missed.
143.wh: The core tension is that recall is invisible: you can't measure how many responsive documents you missed without looking at everything, but looking at everything defeats the purpose. Current methods either use statistical sampling (expensive and slow) or trust the ranking model (which might miss rare relevant documents). The standard stopping rules require either exhaustive review or costly estimation.
143.ap: The paper develops two statistical approaches that combine information from a document ranker (a machine-learning model that scores how likely each document is responsive) and a small random sample of documents. The Bayesian approach treats the ranker's scores as an informative prior belief about responsiveness, then updates it with what the random sample reveals. The model-assisted approach (generalized regression estimator) uses the ranker's calibrated probabilities as anchors and adjusts them based on sampling bias correction, following design-based statistics principles. Both produce lower-bound estimates of recall that are conservative — they underestimate rather than overestimate.
143.ww: This works because the ranker has signal (it's better than random at identifying relevant documents) but isn't perfect, and the random sample provides unbiased ground truth. Combining them leverages the ranker's strength (speed, coverage) while using the sample to correct its blind spots. The Bayesian framing is intuitive: update your belief (ranker scores) with new evidence (sample), while the model-assisted framing follows statistical best practices by accounting for sampling design. Conservative estimates protect against accidentally stopping too early.
143.po: The framework enables legal and compliance teams to estimate true recall early in the review process using practical stopping rules, reducing the cost and time of high-recall document review. Instead of reviewing until exhaustion or relying on hunches, reviewers can make statistically grounded decisions about when to stop, balancing confidence in recall against review costs.

144.bp: When an LLM answers a user's question, it often needs to cite facts from a knowledge base (a company's internal documents, recent news, Wikipedia). The challenge is retrieving the right passages from millions of documents — you can't use the whole knowledge base because that would give the LLM too much context and slow everything down.
144.wh: Current retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems search for documents using semantic similarity to the question, but they typically retrieve shallow subgraphs (just nearby nodes in a document graph) or use pre-computed communities that don't adapt to the specific question. A question about "how does insulin regulate blood sugar in diabetic patients?" might need facts about hormone mechanisms, glucose metabolism, and disease pathways — concepts that are related in complex ways in a knowledge graph, not just nearby neighbors.
144.ap: The paper proposes using attributed community search — a graph algorithm that dynamically extracts relevant subgraphs based on the query. Given a question, the system finds communities (dense clusters of related concepts) in the knowledge graph that are topically relevant. Unlike pre-computed communities (which are static), these are extracted on the fly based on the query's intent.
