The system adds a chunk-level graph index, allowing multi-granularity retrieval: you can retrieve at the document level, the paragraph level, or the fact level, depending on what's needed.
144.ww: By searching for dynamic communities rather than pre-computed ones, the system adapts to specific queries and captures higher-order structure (multi-hop relationships) that simple semantic search misses. The chunk-level index enables efficiency: instead of indexing every fact independently, you group facts into chunks and retrieve chunks, reducing index size and token overhead. This is faster and cheaper than alternatives while maintaining retrieval quality.
144.po: On multiple benchmark datasets, DA-RAG outperforms existing graph-based RAG methods by up to 40%, while also reducing index construction time and token overhead by 37–41%. This means more accurate answers from LLMs using less computational cost, making LLM-based search engines more practical for production deployment.

145.bp: Data has become a tradeable commodity: companies buy training data, market data, sensor data, and customer behavior data to improve their products and services. But how should data be priced? A dataset's value depends on how much it improves predictions for each buyer, and different buyers value the same data differently based on what they already know.
145.wh: Traditional pricing assumes goods are rivalrous (if I buy something, you can't) and thus uses supply-and-demand curves. Data is non-rival: I can sell the same dataset to you and to a thousand other companies simultaneously. Standard market equilibrium concepts don't directly apply because prices need to coordinate the simultaneous allocation of the same data to multiple buyers, each with different utility functions for prediction improvement.
145.ap: The paper adapts competitive equilibrium — a foundational economic concept for pricing rivalrous goods — to data markets by modifying the market-clearing condition. Instead of requiring that supply equals demand (impossible for non-rival goods), it allows the same data to be allocated to multiple buyers. Each buyer's utility function explicitly models how purchasing data improves their predictive performance (not just "I want more stuff"). The paper proves that equilibrium always exists and is typically unique and rational (prices are finite and meaningful).
145.ww: This works because even though data is non-rival, scarcity still exists: the seller has limited data, and selling to one buyer doesn't preclude selling to others, so prices should reflect the value data provides to each buyer's prediction task. By embedding prediction improvement directly into utility functions, the model captures what actually matters: how much each buyer is willing to pay depends on how much their model accuracy improves. Competitive equilibrium finds a price vector where supply and demand are balanced accounting for this real value.
145.po: The framework opens a path toward principled pricing in data markets: a single-price vector can simultaneously satisfy all buyers and the seller. The paper designs an algorithm to find approximate equilibria efficiently despite the non-convexity of the pricing landscape, enabling practical data marketplaces where data is priced based on its utility for prediction rather than arbitrary haggling.

146.bp: Deepfakes—AI-generated fake videos—pose serious security risks: they can impersonate people, spread disinformation, and undermine trust in media. Detecting them is critical, but a detection system trained on deepfakes generated by one technique (e.g., face-swapping software) often fails when the technique changes (now using neural rendering, next year using diffusion models).
146.wh: Detection methods typically optimize for one goal: spot all forgeries with high accuracy. But deepfakes are diverse: some are created via face-swapping, others via lip-sync, others via expression manipulation, each leaving different telltale traces. Treating all fakes as a single "Fake" category means the model learns a generic fraud signal instead of understanding the specific characteristics of each forgery method. When a new technique appears, the model fails because it learned the wrong patterns.
146.ap: The paper proposes decomposing detection into two separate subspaces: a semantic subspace (what the content is about — a person, a scene) and a forgery subspace (how the fake was created). It uses orthogonal decomposition — a parameter-efficient fine-tuning technique where you project learned features onto orthogonal directions that isolate forgery patterns from semantic patterns. It further breaks the "Fake" category into sub-categories corresponding to different deepfake generation techniques and learns a manifold representation for each, using a sparsely-gated mixture structure to activate the right sub-model per technique.
146.ww: By separating semantic and forgery subspaces, the model avoids conflating content (which varies) with creation technique (which is the actual signal). Orthogonal decomposition ensures these subspaces don't interfere. Breaking fakes into technique-specific sub-categories means each sub-model learns precise signals for one technique, and when a new technique appears, the mixture can theoretically extend or interpolate. The gating mechanism activates the right detector per technique, improving generalization.
146.po: Experiments across six real-world deepfake detection datasets with multiple evaluation protocols show leading performance. By modeling semantic and forgery subspaces separately and specializing per generation technique, the method generalizes better across datasets and is more robust to emerging deepfake methods, advancing the security posture of platforms vulnerable to video manipulation.

147.bp: WebAssembly lets companies run C and C++ programs in web browsers safely, enabling applications like PDF viewers and image editors to run client-side. But WebAssembly's memory model is monolithic — all data (stack, heap, global variables) lives in one big linear block. A buffer overflow in one part of the program can corrupt memory anywhere else, creating serious security holes.
147.wh: Current defenses require either source code (to add explicit checks), specialized runtime engines (slower and not standard), or heavyweight binary instrumentation that adds millions of extra instructions and slows programs down significantly. Commercial off-the-shelf WebAssembly binaries don't come with source code and are compiled for standard runtimes, so existing approaches don't apply.
147.ap: The paper presents Bento, a static binary rewriter that takes compiled WebAssembly and rewrites it without needing source code. It analyzes all pointer uses in the entire program to partition memory into logical regions: the stack, the heap, and global data. It then rewrites memory accesses to map each region to an isolated instance using WebAssembly's multi-memory feature (a standard capability). This creates a software-based memory management unit where each region is isolated, preventing overflow in one from corrupting another.
147.ww: This works because WebAssembly's multi-memory feature provides native isolation at no cost — accessing an isolated memory region is just a different index, not an extra instruction. By analyzing the whole program's pointer usage, Bento determines what region each memory access targets, then rewrites accesses to use the correct isolated instance. The key insight is that static analysis can determine memory region partitioning automatically, and hardware-native isolation is free.
147.po: Bento successfully mitigates real-world attacks in production applications like Libpng and PDFAlto with only 3% runtime slowdown and 1% startup overhead, while preserving program semantics. This enables deployment of memory-safe WebAssembly in browsers without recompilation, specialized runtimes, or source code access, significantly improving security of in-browser native-code applications.

148.bp: Modern vehicles have powerful battery systems with dozens of electrical loads—heaters, air conditioning, infotainment systems, charging ports. The battery management system needs to predict demand for the next few minutes to optimize battery health and avoid failures. But driver behavior is unpredictable: the same person might use the heater in the morning and air conditioning in the afternoon.
148.wh: Predicting electrical load is hard because demand depends on driver behavior, which seems random over short timescales. Standard statistical models treat each prediction independently, assuming past load is irrelevant. But in reality, there's hidden structure: if the driver just turned on the heater, they're likely to keep it on for several minutes. Short-term history contains predictive signal that naive models ignore.
148.ap: The paper analyzes the public vehicle dataset (VED) and shows that including the past 60 seconds of electrical load history (heater power, air conditioner power, etc.) and computing conditional probability distributions based on that history improves prediction. Instead of a single prediction for the next moment, you compute how likely different load levels are given the recent pattern. For high-load scenarios (when drivers are actively using multiple systems), incorporating this history reduces prediction variance by up to 41.7%, meaning more accurate and stable estimates.
148.ww: Short-term history contains state information about driver intent: if the heater is on now, the driver is probably cold and will keep it on. Conditional probability distributions capture this: what's the distribution of next-load given current-load? This structure is learnable from historical data. When validated with a LightGBM model (a fast machine-learning algorithm), the conditional-history approach tracks rapid load changes better than simpler statistical methods.
148.po: By incorporating 60 seconds of power history, prediction uncertainty drops significantly during high-load periods when reliability matters most. This enables more precise battery management in software-defined vehicles, improving battery longevity and preventing unexpected power failures in demanding conditions like extreme heat or cold.

149.bp: Social platforms like Facebook and financial systems like PayPal face relentless attacks from bad actors: scammers orchestrating fake-promotion schemes, fraudsters running account-takeover rings, money launderers creating shell accounts. These illicit accounts often hide among millions of legitimate ones by mimicking normal behavior on the surface.
149.wh: The standard approach is binary classification (legitimate or fraudulent) based on user profile features like age, follower count, or account age. But illicit accounts are sophisticated — a scammer might genuinely add friends, post normal-looking content, and initiate small transactions, perfectly mimicking benign users on the surface. However, the pattern and context of behaviors differ: a legitimate user adds friends to connect, a fraudster adds friends to build a network for the scam. The same action has different purposes, so you can't detect fraud from actions alone.
149.ap: The paper proposes detecting fraud from behavior sequences rather than static profiles. It extracts two types of behavior patterns: category-specific patterns (what sequences do legitimate users form? what sequences do scammers form?) and contextualized action encoding (how do the same actions mean different things in different contexts?). The framework uses pattern mining to discover common behavior subsequences within each user type, then aligns action sequences with context (what other actions happen before/after). It fuses the mined patterns with context-aware encodings into a unified detection model.
149.ww: Behavior sequences contain temporal structure that static profiles miss: a legitimate user following a friend after receiving a message looks different from a fraudster building a network. By mining category-specific patterns, the model learns what legitimate sequences look like and what fraudster sequences look like. Contextualized encoding means the same action ("add friend") gets encoded differently depending on surrounding context. Patterns provide structure (templates of normal vs. illicit behavior), context provides grounding (what the action means in this situation).
149.po: The PIAD framework improves detection of diverse illicit account types (scammers, fake promoters, money launderers) by modeling their distinct behavioral signatures. By focusing on behavior sequences and context rather than static features, the method catches sophisticated fraud that mimics surface legitimacy, enabling platforms to protect users against coordinated attacks.

150.bp: When you ask an AI assistant a question while browsing the web, it looks up information to give you better answers. But the web is constantly changing, and most systems rely on old snapshots taken months ago. This matters because outdated information leads to wrong advice, and mixing sources from different trustworthiness levels leaves you vulnerable to mixing fact with fiction.
150.wh: The challenge is that web assistants can't easily let you say 'only check my company intranet' or 'only use news from the last week.' Systems are built with one fixed index of web pages that stays the same unless someone manually rebuilds it. So you have no control over whether an answer comes from a reliable source, and you can't know if the information is stale.
150.ap: OwlerLite lets you define reusable scopes—groups of specific web pages or sources you trust. When you ask a question, you pick which scope to use. Behind the scenes, a crawler continuously watches the pages in your scopes, looking for meaningful changes (not just formatting tweaks). When real changes happen, only those pages get re-indexed. The system then ranks search results by how relevant they are to your question, whether they match your chosen scope, and how recent they are.
150.ww: This works because it closes the trust gap and time gap at once. You control *which* sources the AI sees (trust), and the system knows which sources are freshly updated (recency). Watching for semantic changes means the system doesn't waste effort re-indexing unchanged pages. Combining these three signals—relevance, scope, and freshness—means your answers come from exactly the places you want and the information is current.
150.po: Built as a browser extension, OwlerLite gives you assistants you can actually trust. You can confidently ask about your company's internal policies, know your market research is current, or verify news without mixing yesterday's rumors with today's facts. The payoff is speed and confidence: you get reliable, up-to-date answers without manually hunting sources yourself.

151.bp: Predicting how things will change over time—stock prices, website traffic, power consumption—is crucial for making smart decisions. When you track thousands of related quantities at once (like temperature in different rooms of a building), the patterns get much harder to spot, and computers slow down dramatically.
151.wh: Time series forecasting gets complicated when you have many channels (separate variables to track). The obvious approach tries to learn how each channel influences every other channel, but if you have thousands of channels, that becomes impossibly expensive to compute. Even when you do figure out the relationships, the model often mixes up local patterns (neighbors influence each other) with global patterns (distant variables have distant effects), confusing the prediction.
151.ap: CRAFT reorders the channels like rearranging books on a shelf so similar ones sit together—using an energy-based method to find the lowest-energy arrangement. Then it uses a Transformer model that handles local relationships separately from global ones. Local fusion focuses on neighboring channels in the reordered sequence; global fusion looks at broader relationships. This separation keeps computation manageable even with thousands of channels.
151.ww: Grouping similar channels reduces noise because the model doesn't have to guess wildly about how a random distant channel affects your prediction. Separating local from global patterns lets the model allocate its computation wisely—spending effort on what matters locally (a room's temperature depends heavily on adjacent rooms) and globally (climate patterns affect all rooms the same way). The energy-based reordering acts like a map that makes these dependencies obvious.
151.po: CRAFT scales to datasets with thousands of channels while staying fast enough to be practical. For large-scale web applications tracking many metrics at once—datacenter resource use, user engagement across regions, supply chain inventory—this means accurate predictions without waiting hours for a model to run.

152.bp: Machine learning models learn to recognize patterns by building internal numerical representations of data. These representations should capture what matters (the thing you care about predicting) and throw away noise. When representations work well, they transfer to new tasks; when they fail, the model overfits to irrelevant details.
152.wh: Researchers have discovered that high-dimensional representations often suffer from a weird flaw: important information clusters in a tiny subspace, while most dimensions fill up with noise. Imagine a building where all the important offices occupy one floor and the rest is empty corridors—the space is used inefficiently. This 'spectral imbalance' hurts how well the model generalizes to new problems.
152.ap: SDE uses matrix decomposition (singular value decomposition) to automatically sort each dimension into three bins: strong signals (dimensions carrying task-critical information), weak signals (dimensions with side information), and noise (irrelevant dimensions). Then it selectively amplifies the strong signal dimensions using a curriculum—gradually increasing emphasis as training progresses. It also trains the model to match representations both in the original feature space and after inspecting their mathematical structure.
152.ww: By sorting dimensions rather than treating them equally, the model learns which parts of its representation actually matter. Amplifying strong signals while leaving weak signals and noise alone is like turning up the volume on a radio station you care about. The curriculum prevents training instability that could happen if you suddenly amplified too much. Dual-domain training ensures the representation is geometrically sound in multiple ways.
152.po: Models trained with SDE show better transfer to new tasks and more reliable predictions. For transfer learning tasks common in industry—building a detector trained on one dataset that works on entirely different data—this approach significantly improves both accuracy and robustness.

153.bp: Recommendation systems suggest products or content you might like based on what you and others have interacted with. When the system understands both what items are (product features) and who you are (your interests), it makes better suggestions. But building a real understanding of 'who you are' from clicks alone is hard.
153.wh: Systems usually know a lot about items because they're described in structured databases—a movie's genre, cast, release date. But they struggle with users. You might click the same item for different reasons: a recipe because you're cooking versus a recipe because you're meal-planning. This user-side knowledge is scattered across your history and hard to gather systematically. Also, most people click very few things, making patterns hard to see.
153.ap: SEDIRec uses large language models to interpret your clicking history and infer what you actually care about—not just 'you clicked this recipe' but 'you're interested in quick weeknight meals.' It combines this user-side understanding with item descriptions and collaborative signals (what similar users liked). Then it generates two comparison views using diffusion models with semantic transitions: one highlighting user information and one highlighting item information. Each view is transformed into a collaborative space, and the system learns to match these views.
153.ww: Language models excel at reading between the lines of human behavior, so using them to infer interests is more honest than just counting clicks. Diffusion models gradually morph between different semantic spaces, which helps the system understand how information should transform while learning. Training the model to match user and item views simultaneously ensures these two types of information support each other rather than contradicting.
153.po: The payoff is especially strong for users with sparse histories—people who have clicked few things. Because the system understands their interests semantically (what they *mean* to click) rather than just pattern-matching similar users, it can suggest relevant things even when the direct data is thin.

154.bp: People spend a lot of time copying text from what they're reading, pasting it into a chat interface, typing a question, and then switching back to their work. This stops your flow. It would be faster if an AI assistant just appeared on-screen and explained whatever you selected.
154.wh: Building this is tricky because the assistant needs to know *what you want*. If you highlight a word, do you want a definition, a translation, or background on the concept? Different situations call for different responses. The assistant also needs to learn your preferences—maybe you like concise explanations for technical terms but lengthy context for historical events. Standard chat interfaces assume you explicitly type out your intent each time.
154.ap: Swen is a desktop tool that sits quietly until you select text and press a hotkey. It automatically recognizes whether you want a translation, a concept explanation, or a summary—intent detection that happens without you typing anything. It maintains a user profile that remembers facts about you (your background, your usual preferences for response length or style). Each time you use it, the profile gets richer and your answers become more personalized.
154.ww: Intent detection works because many text selections have patterns: a phrase in another language suggests translation; an unfamiliar term suggests explanation; a long paragraph suggests summarization. The system learns these patterns. Maintaining a profile means the assistant doesn't start from scratch with every interaction—it remembers that you prefer technical depth or simple language, reducing back-and-forth.
154.po: The result is a dramatic speed-up in knowledge lookup during your actual work. Instead of switching apps three times to understand one phrase, you press a hotkey and have the answer instantly. For people doing research, coding, or writing, this is a direct time-saving that keeps you in flow.

155.bp: Graph neural networks are tools for finding patterns in networks—social connections, molecular structures, recommendation graphs. They work by having each node look at its neighbors and learn from them. But some networks have a problem: neighbors are often *different* from each other, not similar.
155.wh: Most graph neural networks assume neighborhoods are homogeneous—similar nodes connect to similar nodes. This assumption breaks in real networks where different things attract (a villain connects to a hero, a protein pairs with its opposite). When neighbors are different, the network learns poorly because it's trying to solve the wrong problem. Worse, a network trained on data where neighbors are dissimilar performs terribly on new data where they're similar, and vice versa.
155.ap: IVQ-GNN tackles this by learning connection patterns—the specific neighborhood structures that actually occur—rather than just measuring homophily or heterophily as a single number. In a pre-training phase, it builds a codebook of these patterns like a dictionary. During fine-tuning, it uses a self-attention mechanism to combine patterns from the codebook, letting it adapt to rare or unseen patterns. This two-stage approach means it can handle both common and unusual network structures.
155.ww: Connection patterns are the real information. By learning and combining specific patterns rather than assuming a uniform structure, the model becomes flexible. The codebook acts as an orthogonal basis—think of it like a mathematical coordinate system for neighborhoods—so the model can accurately express any real pattern by combining these basis vectors. This is more honest than forcing all networks into one assumption.
155.po: IVQ-GNN maintains strong performance across datasets with mixed neighborhood types and improves robustness when encountering unusual connection patterns. For real-world applications—protein interaction networks, social graphs, knowledge graphs—networks are rarely pure homophilous or heterophilous, so this flexibility directly improves accuracy.

156.bp: Online communities have millions of posts daily. Moderators must decide what stays and what gets removed, enforcing community rules to keep spaces safe and on-topic. Humans do this work, but they're tired, inconsistent, and sometimes apply the wrong rule by mistake.
156.wh: The challenge isn't that humans are careless—it's that rules are often ambiguous. 'No harassment' means different things depending on context. Moderators work fast under cognitive load, so when they make a mistake, it's often by citing the wrong rule rather than using bad judgment. No one has a clear count of how wrong humans are, and fixing ambiguous rules is hard without systematic data.
156.ap: This study first shows that large language models can replicate human moderation decisions at 83.9% agreement. Then it evaluates real moderator decisions by having LLMs double-check them, uncovering that roughly 15% of removals and 13% of approvals are wrong. RuleSharpener uses LLMs to diagnose *why* errors happen—ambiguous rules, rules conflicting with community values—and generates clearer, more specific guidelines. These refined rules are then tested with moderators.
156.ww: Language models see patterns across thousands of decisions, so they can spot when a rule is being applied inconsistently. By flagging the root cause (ambiguous wording, conflicting guidance) rather than just saying 'this was wrong,' RuleSharpener points at what actually needs fixing. Clearer rules help moderators apply them consistently, which reduces errors.
156.po: RuleSharpener increased accuracy in identifying the violated rule by 38 percentage points. For platforms like Reddit, this translates to fewer user complaints, more consistent enforcement, and lower burden on moderators who no longer have to guess at murky standards. The system acts as a quality control tool that continuously improves the rules themselves.

157.bp: Depression is a serious mental health condition that's hard to catch early. If doctors could screen people based on what they post on social media, they might identify at-risk individuals sooner. But social media language is noisy and idiosyncratic—each person expresses distress differently.
157.wh: Most depression screening systems use a single fixed model and one reasoning approach, which doesn't adapt to the diversity of how people communicate symptoms. Social media data is scarce for mental health applications, so models trained on one dataset often fail on another. Different language models themselves might understand psychological symptoms differently, leading to inconsistent detection.
157.ap: AdaDepression uses two tricks. First, a two-hop retrieval: it collects representative posts from training data expressing depression symptoms, then uses these as anchors to find similar posts in a user's history—pulling out the symptom-relevant posts from their noise. Second, a Mixture of Routers mechanism that adapts both the reasoning strategy and the language model choice based on what it finds. If it retrieves lots of clear symptom expressions, it might use one model; if signals are mixed, another.
157.ww: Using representative posts as retrieval anchors works because people express similar psychological states in similar ways. The model learns what 'sadness looks like' in social media language, not just depression statistics. Adapting the reasoning strategy and model selection means the system doesn't force one approach—it can switch between direct reasoning, chain-of-thought, or other strategies depending on the data quality it finds.
157.po: The result is a screening framework that explicitly maps raw social media posts to standardized psychological questionnaires. For sparse-data users (those with few posts), this adaptive approach outperforms fixed-model systems. The payoff for public health is early identification of at-risk individuals so they can get help before crisis.

158.bp: Game studios make money from players spending real money in-game. Predicting which players will spend the most over their lifetime—their Lifetime Value—is crucial for targeting offers and budgeting marketing. The challenge is that spending is unpredictable: most players spend nothing, some spend a lot, and the distribution is messy.
158.wh: Player spending follows no simple pattern. Many players never spend (zero-inflation). Spending amounts are heavily skewed—a few whales spend enormous amounts while most spenders spend a little. Add in the complication that different games have different spending cultures, and you need to predict across multiple games at once with limited per-player data.
158.ap: DynaMoLTV models spending as a zero-inflated mixture of lognormal distributions—a statistical shape that can be zero (no spending), skewed (more small spenders than large), and heavy-tailed (occasional mega-spenders). It has a separate expert for each game to account for game-specific spending patterns. It also uses a hierarchical payment classifier to capture what kind of spender each player is. Two-stage losses balance identifying who will pay anything (binary classification) with predicting how much they'll spend (regression).
158.ww: Using the right distribution shape matters: lognormal is what real spending data looks like. Having game-specific experts prevents transfer learning disaster where a model trained on a hardcore player base predicts poorly for casual players. The two-stage approach makes sense because identifying a payer is a different problem than predicting a payer's total—the model learns both signals.
158.po: DynaMoLTV outperforms standard approaches on paid user identification, high-value user recall, and overall LTV prediction. For web-scale game monetization, this means studios can accurately target players most likely to spend, optimize marketing budgets per game, and predict revenue more reliably.

159.bp: Large language models are increasingly used for high-stakes decisions—healthcare advice, legal recommendations, financial planning—where being wrong is costly. But most benchmarks measure performance on friendly questions. Real-world decisions happen under pressure, time constraints, and confusing scenarios.
159.wh: Evaluating LLM reliability is hard because stress and constraints are hard to measure. A model might perform well on a simple question but fall apart when given a tight deadline, incomplete information, or conflicting requirements. Standard benchmarks miss this entirely, so models look reliable in the lab but fail in deployment.
159.ap: This study runs five increasingly difficult scenarios on three popular models (ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude). Each scenario is tested with a 45-item rubric checking accuracy, safety, logical consistency, and constraint-following. The Stress Sensitivity Index quantifies how much each model degrades as difficulty rises—measuring the slope of performance decline.
159.ww: This works because it mimics real deployment conditions: time limits force faster thinking, ambiguity forces interpretation, constraints force trade-offs. By measuring performance across a difficulty spectrum rather than a single easy benchmark, the rubric captures which models remain reliable under stress and which fall apart.
159.po: The results show ChatGPT remains stable, Gemini moderately degrades, and Claude shows substantial sensitivity—especially on constraint-following. For teams deploying LLMs in production, this stress-testing reveals which model will actually perform when it matters. Before shipping an LLM assistant to production, you need to know not just average performance but worst-case performance.

160.bp: Text-to-motion generation takes a description like 'a person dancing happily' and produces realistic human motion. Evaluating whether the motion is good requires metrics that measure how well the motion matches the text. Current metrics are flawed in ways that let researchers oversell mediocre work.
160.wh: Existing metrics like Fréchet Inception Distance assume data follows a bell curve, which motion data doesn't. Others like R-Precision are local—they only check if the top-ranking results match—and miss the global picture of whether the entire generated motion makes sense as a whole.
160.ap: The paper proposes two new metrics. Optimal Transport Matching Score treats text-to-motion matching as a routing problem: how do you pair each motion to a text description to maximize total similarity? This gives a global view. MoCLIP-based Maximum Mean Discrepancy uses an improved motion encoder (MoCLIP) and a Gaussian-RBF kernel to measure distribution differences without assuming bell-curve shapes.
160.ww: Optimal transport is a mathematical framework for comparing distributions globally—it sees the forest, not just trees. MoCLIP-based Maximum Mean Discrepancy avoids Gaussian assumptions by using kernel methods, which are more flexible. Both metrics align with human perception because they measure what humans actually care about: does the motion match the text overall, without bias from assumptions about data shape?
160.po: Models evaluated with these new metrics show stronger correlation with human judgment. For the text-to-motion generation field, this matters because it prevents researchers from claiming progress on unreliable benchmarks and guides actual improvement toward generating motions humans recognize as faithful to descriptions.

161.bp: Conversational search lets you ask questions back-and-forth with a search system, like talking to a librarian. You ask something vague, the librarian clarifies, refines their search, and eventually gives you what you need. This is more natural than typing keyword queries, especially for complex information needs.
161.wh: The hard part is understanding what you mean in context. If you say 'tell me more,' the system needs to know more about what. If you ask a follow-up that contradicts your first question, should the system assume you changed your mind or help you find both pieces of information? Conversational context is messy and requires real understanding, not just keyword matching.
161.ap: This is a tutorial covering conversational search from foundational principles to new agentic paradigms. Large language models enable this because they can generate natural responses, follow instructions to search strategically, and maintain context across turns. Agentic approaches add planning and dynamic retrieval—the system decides what to search for, when, and how to execute steps to fulfill complex requests.
161.ww: Language models understand conversation naturally; they avoid the brittle keyword-matching of older systems. Agentic capabilities mean the system can reason about what information would help you most, actively refining its strategy rather than just passively responding to your queries. This moves from 'answering your question' to 'helping you find what you need.'
161.po: Conversational search systems powered by these advances enable discovery workflows that feel more like talking to an expert than interacting with a database. Users get faster answers to complex questions and better-refined results because the system actively helps clarify rather than assuming your first phrasing was exactly what you meant.

162.bp: Companies want to understand how employees use AI assistants—which tasks get automated, how much time is saved, what roles change. This data is hidden in millions of multi-turn conversations between workers and their AI helpers.
162.wh: Raw multi-turn conversations are hard to analyze. One conversation might be a user asking for code help, then clarifying, then testing—all mixed together. Unsupervised clustering of raw text produces noise. You need summaries to see the intent, then topic structure to find patterns, and human judgment to ensure the patterns matter for business decisions.
162.ap: HILTON (Human-In-the-Loop Topic mOdeling) summarizes multi-turn conversations using language models to compress them into coherent summaries. It clusters these summaries into topics and organizes them hierarchically. Humans annotate and refine the clusters, giving feedback that improves future iterations. It trains a lightweight classifier on this refined data so new conversations can be automatically categorized.
162.ww: Summarization reduces noise and aligns the model with what humans care about (intent, not word choice). Human-in-the-loop feedback ensures topics are relevant to the business, not just mathematically coherent. The lightweight classifier lets the system scale—you can categorize thousands of conversations without expensive human review each time.
162.po: The result is a topic structure suitable for workplace analytics—understanding that 30% of assistant usage is debugging, 25% is documentation writing, etc. This data helps companies allocate training, design better tooling, and predict which roles will change most. Open-sourcing the code lets other organizations apply the same approach.

163.bp: Ransomware is malicious software that encrypts your files and demands payment. Modern detection uses machine learning on behavioral telemetry—logs of what programs do. But privacy laws now require the ability to delete your data from trained models without retraining from scratch.
163.wh: Standard model training stores information from all training samples throughout the model. Deleting one sample usually means retraining the entire model from scratch, which is expensive. For large security systems protecting millions of machines, retraining is prohibitively slow. You need a way to 'unlearn' specific samples efficiently.
163.ap: SISA training partitions the dataset into shards (independent chunks). Models are trained separately on each shard and then combined. When you need to delete a sample, you only retrain the shard containing it, not the entire model. The study tests this on reinforcement learning models trained to detect ransomware using behavioral data. Detection confidence is measured continuously (Q-score margins) rather than just binary predictions.
163.ww: Sharding works because the model's knowledge is compartmentalized—each shard contributes independently. When you retrain one shard, the others stay the same. This dramatically reduces recomputation. Continuous confidence scoring is more realistic than binary decisions because security is about confidence levels, not hard yes/no calls.
163.po: SISA unlearning achieves 5-10x faster deletion than retraining the whole model, while maintaining detection performance. For ransomware detection systems protecting enterprises, this means compliance with data deletion requests is fast and affordable, enabling responsible AI deployment where privacy rights are respected without sacrificing security.

164.bp: Drug development requires predicting which new molecules will cause side effects. Each drug is represented as a graph—atoms and bonds form a structure. Some side effects have been observed and reported, but most are simply unknown. You need to identify the unknown dangerous ones.
164.wh: The problem is that positive drugs (known side effects) and negative drugs (unknown side effects) might look structurally similar. A harmless drug and a dangerous drug might both contain similar substructures, making it hard to tell them apart. Without explicit negative examples, the model lacks guidance on what patterns distinguish truly dangerous drugs. This is called positive-unlabeled classification.
164.ap: Delta-PU performs dual reweighting on graphs. Hop-level reweighting emphasizes important substructures during pooling—the process that combines information from different atomic neighborhoods into a graph representation. Graph-level reweighting suppresses ambiguous unlabeled graphs from influencing training. The model learns to focus on discriminative structural patterns while reducing the noise from uncertain examples.
164.ww: Reweighting substructures rather than treating all atoms equally lets the model discover what structural features distinguish side effects. Reweighting graphs reduces the model's confusion about which unlabeled drugs are truly negative versus genuinely ambiguous. By progressively focusing on discriminative patterns, the model avoids overfitting to noise.
164.po: Delta-PU achieves state-of-the-art performance on drug side effect prediction and other positive-unlabeled graph classification tasks. For pharmaceutical research, this means more accurate predictions of dangerous molecular structures from limited labeled data, potentially speeding drug safety assessment.

165.bp: When we want machines to understand networks—social graphs, molecule structures, citation webs—we need them to learn useful patterns without human labels. Unsupervised learning (learning on data nobody has hand-marked as right or wrong) can be powerful because you don't need expensive human annotation, but the challenge is figuring out what patterns are actually worth learning.
165.wh: The core tension: in a real network, you could describe the same node or subgraph from many viewpoints—its direct neighbors, its broader community, its role in the whole graph. Standard methods either focus on one viewpoint or glue them together crudely. When you do that, you either miss rich diversity or get confused signals that pull against each other. And you need to balance internal consistency (things nearby should be treated similarly) with flexibility (rigid rules overfit). Without addressing this at multiple scales—individual nodes, small groups, the whole graph—you lose signal.
165.ap: The method starts by creating multiple 'views' of the graph using a diffusion matrix (a mathematical object that spreads influence smoothly across the network). This gives different angles on the same graph. Then it feeds all these views through an asymmetric neural network—different pathways for different views, not forced into one mold—so each can develop its own specialized features. Finally, it uses a three-level contrastive loss: at the node level, at the subgraph level, and at the whole-graph level. Contrastive learning works by making the model pull similar things closer and push dissimilar things apart, training it to capture what makes things alike or different.
165.ww: Why does this work? First, the diffusion matrix creates mathematically smooth variations rather than arbitrary crops, so you're seeing the same network from genuinely different angles, not just noise. Second, asymmetric pathways let each view develop its own strengths without a single bottleneck. Third, and crucially, training at three scales forces the model to learn consistent patterns across granularities: if node-level and global patterns contradict, you'll catch it. The temperature coefficient acts like a tuning knob—it calibrates how sharply the model discriminates between similar and dissimilar things.
165.po: On node and graph classification tasks across multiple benchmark datasets, the model achieves high accuracy. The payoff is concrete: you can classify nodes in a social network or whole molecular graphs with strong performance using only unlabeled data. This matters because labeled graph datasets are expensive to build, especially for specialized domains like chemistry or biology.

166.bp: Recommender systems that understand 'what you want next' need to remember your entire history—every video you watched, every song you clicked. But processing years of history is computationally expensive. The real-world goal: give you a better recommendation by knowing your long-term patterns without making the server collapse under the weight of it all.
166.wh: Here's the trap: your history is very long (thousands of items) but the server can only process so much. Existing shortcuts take two approaches, each broken in its own way. Compression methods (split history into chunks and summarize each) work fast but they create artificial boundaries: they might slice apart items that belong together temporally, or lose the texture of how your interests flow smoothly over time. Retrieval methods (pick only the 'most relevant' past items) preserve continuity but throw away too much context—you lose the surrounding story that explains *why* something is relevant. It's lose-lose: compress and break time-flow, retrieve and go blind to context.
166.ap: The paper proposes balancing both. Rather than pure compression or pure retrieval, it uses adaptive subsequence compression: chunk your history in a way that respects temporal proximity (items close in time stay together) while also respecting item similarity (similar things can be grouped). Then it adds contextual fusion, which brings back some of the discarded context during the learning phase, so the model can see both the focused retrieved items and their surrounding context. It's like reading the full paragraph around a highlighted sentence instead of just the highlight.
166.ww: This works because you're doing two things simultaneously: reducing the computational load (so servers don't slow down) and preserving both the temporal structure (the natural flow of your interests over time) and the context (why one recommendation connects to another). Adaptive chunking finds the natural breaks in your history rather than forcing uniform segments. Contextual fusion means the model learns from the relevant core *and* its neighborhood, so it understands both what matters and why.
166.po: In practice: the system processes much longer user histories than existing methods can handle, giving better recommendations that account for long-term patterns. This enables 'lifelong' recommendation—services that improve over years of data without asking you to re-train constantly or trimming your history.

167.bp: Live video streaming (think Twitch, YouTube Live, sports broadcasts) reaches hundreds of millions of people and must arrive with minimal delay. The network carrying this video constantly changes—congestion comes and goes unpredictably. The goal: send video as smoothly as possible without buffering, using the available bandwidth fully, even when conditions shift moment-to-moment.
167.wh: The paradox at the heart of this paper: the video encoder produces frames of wildly different sizes. One frame might encode as 50KB, the next as 500KB. Current congestion control algorithms work at the packet level—they look at individual data packets arriving at network bottlenecks and estimate available bandwidth from that. But if a huge frame shows up suddenly and you're sending at the wrong rate, you either lose packets (causing glitches) or delay them (causing buffering). The algorithm doesn't see the frame-size jumps coming, so it can't anticipate the sending pattern that the encoder will actually demand.
167.ap: The paper introduces Camel, which operates at the frame level instead of the packet level. It watches when frames finish encoding and estimates network capacity from how those frames flow through the network, not from individual packets. Camel has three parts: (1) a bandwidth and delay estimator that looks at frame-by-frame network behavior to understand true available capacity, (2) a congestion detector that notices when the network gets overwhelmed, and (3) a burst controller that decides when it's safe to send a large frame in one rush versus spreading it out. The key insight: frame-level signals are more stable and predictive than packet-level noise.
167.ww: Frame-level feedback works because video encoders output frames as atomic units. If you estimate capacity from how frames traverse the network, you're measuring something the encoder actually produces and the network actually carries. You're not being fooled by packet-level timing jitter that has nothing to do with true capacity. The burst controller prevents the classic problem: a huge frame arrives, you're still using old estimates, you send too fast, packets queue up, latency spikes, stream stalls. Instead, you know the frame size in advance and have real network feedback to modulate the sending pattern.
167.po: Real-world deployment at a major platform: 250 million users, 2 billion sessions, 150+ countries. The payoff is measurable: fewer stalling events and smoother video delivery. Video streaming is latency-sensitive (people notice 100ms delays), so frame-level control that prevents sudden queueing spikes translates directly to better viewing experience.

168.bp: Organizations need to catch insider threats—employees or contractors doing something malicious (stealing data, sabotaging systems, spying). The catch is that malicious actions are rare and hidden in mountains of normal-looking behavior. You might track user logins, file access, network activity, email—many different 'views' of what someone does. The goal: combine all these signals to spot the small fraction of dangerous activity.
168.wh: Naive fusion fails in three ways. First, if you train a separate model for each data type (logins, files, email), then try to combine them, you either have scalability chaos (retraining everything each time you add a new signal) or semantic garbage (the models were trained on different things and their outputs don't align). Second, when signals do align, they often pull in different strengths: video analytics might be excellent at detecting abnormal mouse movement but useless at email, while email models catch linguistic red flags that video can't see. Simple averaging drowns out the weaker but valuable signals. Third, insider threat data is imbalanced: 99.99% normal, 0.01% threats. Rare classes get ignored unless you're careful.
168.ap: Insight-LLM is a multi-view fusion framework. Each view (logins, files, email, etc.) gets encoded by a pre-trained model kept frozen—no retraining overhead. A lightweight adapter aligns all these heterogeneous representations into one shared semantic space, like translating everything to a common language. Then a context-adaptive fusion module learns to re-weight views dynamically: for this particular user interaction, maybe email patterns matter most; for another, file access does. Finally, the fused representation is combined with a task description and fed to a lightweight language model for final threat classification.
168.ww: This works because frozen pre-trained models are free (they're already trained), so adding new views is cheap. The ViewAdapter solves semantic misalignment by learning a small transformation per view, not retraining everything. Dynamic re-weighting prevents strong views from drowning out weak ones—each view gets a chance to speak up when it has signal. The language model acts as a final reasoning step, able to synthesize complex combinations ('this user's file access pattern is weird *and* their email mentions financial stress—flag it'). Because you keep models trained separately, adding a new signal doesn't ripple through the entire system.
168.po: On real insider threat datasets: F1 score (accuracy at catching threats without false alarms) improves up to 4.8%, and false-positive rate drops 61%. That means fewer innocent employees get flagged, and more actual threats get caught. Retraining time per new signal also drops sharply, so you can adapt to new types of threat quickly.

169.bp: When large language models interact with users—answering questions, following instructions, potentially being manipulated—there's a trail of evidence: the prompt someone sent and the response the model gave. If the model does something wrong (gives unsafe advice, leaks data, gets tricked), traditional digital forensics doesn't help; you need to investigate the LLM interaction itself. The goal: audit and reconstruct what happened, who asked what, and whether the model behaved safely.
169.wh: Traditional digital forensics looks at deleted files, server logs, network packets. But LLM interactions are different: they're designed to be transient and fast, not logged by default. If you want to audit whether a model was 'jailbroken' (tricked into ignoring safety rules) or produced unsafe output, you need a chain of evidence: what was the exact prompt, what was the exact response, can you replay it, and can you diagnose where it went wrong? But current LLM systems don't provide this in a forensically rigorous way—logs get overwritten, exact prompts aren't always preserved, and there's no principled way to replay a specific interaction.
169.ap: Prompt Forensics introduces Prompt Scene Investigation (PSI): three forensic procedures from classical crime-scene investigation applied to LLM safety. (1) Prompt Processing captures every interaction as a tamper-resistant ID—like a digital chain of custody in a criminal case, where you log exactly what you found and when, so later no one can claim it was altered. (2) Replay re-runs the model with the exact same prompt under controlled conditions, isolating what the model is doing from surrounding variables. (3) Investigation uses these replays to detect adversarial attacks and policy violations, producing diagnostic reports: 'this prompt uses technique X to bypass safety guard Y, and the model responded with Z.'
169.ww: This works because it's structured as evidence gathering, not arbitrary logging. Tamper-resistant IDs create accountability (if someone claims the log is fake, you can verify the chain). Replay isolates causation: you see exactly what the model does when given a specific input, controlling for randomness and other factors. Diagnostic reports connect the dots from prompt to response to violation, making the 'what went wrong' observable and debuggable. It's modeled on forensics because auditing safety is fundamentally about reconstructing past events from traces.
169.po: The payoff: regulatory compliance and incident response. If an LLM produces harmful output, you can now audit it: prove what was asked, prove what was answered, prove whether it violated policy, and diagnose the failure mode. This enables accountability for AI systems in high-stakes domains (healthcare, finance, government) where forensic evidence matters legally.

170.bp: Imagine shopping: you find a picture of boots you like, but you want a different color and maybe a thicker heel. You combine the reference image with text describing the change. A search system needs to find boots that match this composite query—not just similar to the original image, but reflecting the textual modifications too. Real goal: understand that the query is asking for something partially seen (the image) and partially imagined (the text modifications).
170.wh: Standard similarity-based search fails because it treats the reference image and text as separate things to average or concatenate. But the query is actually compositional: the image defines a base, and the text describes edits. A system might find images similar to the boots (same style) while ignoring the color change, or find the right color but lose the style. The deeper problem: you need both semantic reasoning ('does this match the modified description?') and visual verification ('does it actually look right?'). Most training-based methods get stuck in one modality and miss cross-modal reasoning.
170.ap: XR orchestrates multiple specialized AI agents working together. Imagination agents synthesize what the target should look like by combining the image and text into a generated representation. Similarity agents do coarse filtering by hybrid matching—they look at both visual and textual similarity, checking rough fit. Question agents verify by targeted reasoning: they ask specific questions like 'is this the right color?' and 'does the style match?' and check the answers against the original query. These three types of agents work iteratively and progressively refine the results: imagination makes a guess, similarity filters to the likely set, questions check consistency, and repeat.
170.ww: This works because each agent handles what it does best. Imagination agents leverage cross-modal generation (they've seen many image-text pairs and can synthesize what a modified version should look like). Similarity agents do fast geometric filtering (comparing vectors in a space where both images and text concepts exist). Question agents do verification by semantic reasoning (they can check whether 'bright red' actually matches 'crimson' or whether 'thicker heel' is satisfied). By coordinating these rather than trying to do everything in one model, the system gets the benefits of generative reasoning, efficient filtering, and semantic verification without training from scratch.
170.po: On three benchmark datasets (FashionIQ, CIRR, CIRCO), the method achieves up to 38% improvement over strong baselines without requiring any task-specific training. The payoff: users can query with 'show me boots like these but taller and in suede' and get exactly what they mean, not just vague similarity matches.

171.bp: Question-answering systems usually extract or generate answers that appear somewhere in documents. But some questions require inference: if the documents say 'plants need sunlight' and 'the greenhouse has no windows,' a human infers no plants will survive, even though no document states that. The goal: build systems that can reason from incomplete information, deriving conclusions not explicitly written.
171.wh: Current QA systems assume the answer is 'in the corpus somewhere.' They rank documents by relevance, then extract or generate from the top ones. But inferential questions break this: the answer-supporting passages only provide clues, not the answer. You might have passage 1: 'Alice studied biology' and passage 2: 'The exam covered biology topics.' To infer 'Alice studied the exam topics,' you need to combine and reason. Standard retrievers rank by surface similarity, missing that you need both passages together. Rerankers (systems that re-order documents) help marginally, but they're still looking for explicit relevance, not inferential links.
171.ap: The paper introduces two things. First, Quit, a new dataset of 7,401 questions requiring inference from 2.4 million passages. The passages are constructed from high-convergence human and machine hints (multiple sources agreeing on clues, not the answer), labeled at three relevance levels: does this passage help, is it essential, or is it misleading? Second, they benchmark retrievers (systems that find relevant documents), rerankers (that re-order them), and LLM readers (that generate answers). This reveals what breaks: retrievers underperform (they can't recognize that two weak matches together make an inference), rerankers add little (they're still ranking by surface signals), and fine-tuning helps inconsistently.
171.ww: Why is this hard? Inference requires combining multiple pieces of evidence in a way that's not obvious from surface similarity. A retriever trained to find 'relevant passages' doesn't know that 'Alice studied X' and 'exam covers X' are separately weak but together inferentially important. The dataset construction (from convergent hints, not direct statements) forces systems to learn reasoning rather than pattern-matching. Importantly, even reasoning-oriented language models don't outperform smaller general-purpose ones, suggesting the bottleneck isn't model size—it's that current architectures don't organize the pipeline (retrieve → rerank → read) to handle inference.
171.po: The payoff is identifying a gap: current QA pipelines fail at inference-based reasoning. With the Quit dataset, researchers can now train systems specifically for this mode. Applications include legal discovery (infer from case facts), medical diagnosis (infer from symptoms and lab results), and investigative journalism (infer connections from documents).

172.bp: Imagine a search agent (an AI that autonomously searches the web across multiple turns: ask a question, read results, decide to search again or answer). These agents need to be efficient: don't waste searches, and answer as soon as you have enough information. Real goal: balance thoroughness (find the answer) with frugality (don't search unnecessarily).
172.wh: Current agents trained to get the right final answer have a perverse incentive: they search excessively because searching is free (to the training objective) and there's no penalty for wasted effort. They often do redundant searches (searching the same thing twice), or conversely, stop too early and give wrong answers. The root cause: the model was trained to optimize 'did you get the final answer right,' not 'what was the search process.' This creates misaligned decision boundaries—the threshold for 'I have enough info to answer' is wrong. Over-search wastes resources; under-search produces errors. You can't fix this by tweaking hyper-parameters because the signal itself is misaligned.
172.ap: The paper proposes causal intervention-based diagnosis and decision boundary alignment. First, diagnose: at each decision point (should I search again or answer?), compare the actual trajectory to a counterfactual ('what if I had answered now instead of searching?'). This reveals whether the agent chose correctly. Build a dataset of these 'decision points where the agent erred' (over-searched or under-searched). Then, train a preference optimizer on this dataset: the agent learns to prefer correct decisions over incorrect ones. The causal intervention part is crucial: you're not just labeling 'this trajectory was bad'; you're identifying the specific decision point that went wrong.
172.ww: This works because you're fixing the actual problem: the decision boundary. Over-search and under-search are both decision errors, and they have different causes (overconfidence in one case, premature termination in the other). By diagnosing causal counterfactuals (what would have happened if I'd decided differently), you identify exactly which decisions were wrong, not just that the overall trajectory failed. Then preference optimization teaches the agent to make better decisions going forward. The causal framing ensures you're training on the right signal—the decision itself, not noise from downstream outcomes.
172.po: On public datasets, the method reduces both over-search and under-search, improving overall efficiency. Agents answer correctly while searching fewer times. The payoff: services like search assistants or research agents that answer questions reliably without wasting computational resources.

173.bp: In social networks, relationships are complex: some ties are positive (friends, allies), others negative (rivals, blocked users). A community—a tightly-knit group—should have many positive links within and few negative links within, but may have some negative links to outsiders. Understanding these signed communities reveals conflicts and alliances. Goal: reliably cluster nodes despite the noise of conflicting edge signs.
173.wh: Real networks are messy. An edge marked 'negative' might be mislabeled (data entry error) or ambiguous (two people who cooperate on one project but compete on another). Existing community detection methods treat all conflicts equally, so noisy data creates inconsistent clusters: one run gives cluster A, another gives cluster B. The fundamental tension: do you trust an edge sign or treat it skeptically? Too trusting and noise ruins structure. Too skeptical and you lose real conflicts.
173.ap: ReCon is a post-processing framework (works on top of any community detection method). It refines communities iteratively: (1) Structural refinement: look at the detected clusters and check internal consistency—if a node is assigned to a cluster but has many negative ties within it, consider moving it. (2) Boundary refinement: focus on nodes at cluster boundaries (lots of neighbors in other clusters); decide whether they belong inside or should move. (3) Contrastive learning: within-cluster edges should be 'similar' (share properties), between-cluster edges should be dissimilar. Train to capture this. (4) Clustering: use the learned similarities to finalize cluster assignments.
173.ww: This works because it tackles both the data problem (noise) and the model problem (conflicting signals). Structural refinement directly corrects errors (noisy edge signs). Boundary refinement focuses effort on hard cases where membership is genuinely ambiguous. Contrastive learning amplifies consistent patterns: if many edges agree that two people are in the same community, the learning step strengthens that signal; if they conflict, the error gets attenuated. Because ReCon is post-processing, it's method-agnostic—you can apply it to any base community detector.
173.po: On 18 synthetic and 4 real networks using 4 different base detectors, ReCon consistently improves accuracy. The payoff: more reliable signed-network analysis in social networks (detecting polarized groups), organizational networks (identifying conflict), and biology (predicting protein interactions, where 'negative' means inhibition).

174.bp: Wearable devices and mobile sensors generate time-series data—heartbeat, step count, GPS location. These streams come from diverse devices and users. A central server wants to train one model that works for everyone, without collecting raw data (privacy). But users' devices and environments differ: some have noisy sensors, different activity types, different climate zones. The goal: federated learning (train across distributed devices) that generalizes despite this diversity.
174.wh: Standard federated learning assumes data from all users is roughly similar, just distributed. But time-series from different devices and environments violate this: a jogger's heart rate looks different from a sprinter's, sensor noise varies, seasonal patterns differ. This out-of-distribution (OOD) shift breaks generalization. Current methods try to squeeze diverse distributions into one model or compress sequences heavily, losing temporal structure. The tension: you want to account for diverse patterns, but you can't send raw data to a central server (privacy), and you can't train per-user models (that's not federated learning).
174.ap: FedDiG treats time-series from a frequency-domain perspective (breaking signals into their component frequencies, like how music has bass and treble). Each device learns a frequency-domain representation locally—a compact descriptor of 'what frequencies matter for this user.' The server collects these descriptors (not raw data), then creates a global frequency pool and uses class-wise mixup (blending different frequency patterns for the same class, like mixing tempo variations). This mixed frequency information guides a central diffusion model (a generative model that builds data from random noise by gradually refining it). The diffusion model synthesizes new time-series with diverse spectral patterns—essentially creating synthetic variations that capture OOD diversity.
174.ww: This works because frequency-domain representations are private (they're compressed summaries, not time-steps) yet informative (they capture the essential structure of each device's data). By aggregating frequency descriptors, the server learns 'what frequencies characterize each class across all devices,' then uses that to synthesize diverse examples. Diffusion models are good at generating diverse variations while respecting semantic structure (the synthesized data is recognizably 'a jog' or 'a sprint' but with different sensor profiles). Training on synthetic diversity-augmented data forces the model to be robust to OOD variation.
174.po: On four cross-domain time-series benchmarks (transferring from one device/environment to unseen others), FedDiG significantly outperforms federated learning and other domain-generalization methods. The payoff: wearable health monitoring that works across device types and user populations without centralizing private data.

175.bp: Recommender systems increasingly use pre-trained multimodal models (trained on billions of images and text) to encode item metadata—a product photo, description, reviews. These models capture rich information, but they're not tuned for your specific interests. The goal: adapt these powerful pre-trained models to recommendation without retraining them from scratch (too expensive), while personalizing to user interests (so it learns what *you* care about in images).
175.wh: Standard parameter-efficient fine-tuning adapts pre-trained models with a small number of new parameters per task—cheap and effective. But here's the catch: the adaptation is global—the same adapted model for all users. A user interested in technical details might attend to different aspects of a jacket (seam quality, material texture) than a user interested in fashion trends (color, silhouette). If you use the same item embeddings for both users, you lose that personalization—both see the same summary of the product, even though they care about different things.
175.ap: PerPEFT groups users by interest cluster (segmentation based on purchase patterns) and assigns a distinct fine-tuning module to each group. Now a 'quality-focused' group's model learns to highlight aspects predictive of quality purchases, while a 'fashion-focused' group's model highlights style aspects. The same product image is processed through the appropriate group-specific adapter, producing different embeddings for different user types. They also introduce a specialized training technique that strengthens user-group conditioning: the adapter learns to produce embeddings that diverge based on user group.
175.ww: This works because personalization and efficiency become compatible. Standard PEFT is efficient but one-size-fits-all. By segmenting users into groups with coherent interests and assigning micro-modules per group, you get personalized embeddings (different users see different aspects) with minimal added parameters (each group's module is small, and you're only adding 1.3% overall). Users in the same interest cluster have similar attention patterns, so grouping is efficient; users across clusters have different priorities, so personalization helps. The technique that strengthens conditioning ensures the adapter actually learns to differ across groups rather than converging.
175.po: Experiments show NDCG@20 (ranking quality metric) improves by up to 15.3% over strong baselines. The payoff: recommendation systems that adapt powerful multimodal models to user interests while remaining lightweight enough for real-time serving.

176.bp: Gig platforms (food delivery, task freelancing) set prices for work and wait for workers to accept. They want to minimize costs and cover all available tasks. Workers—from diverse geographies, with different financial needs—have uncertainty about their own willingness to work at a given price. The platform knows this and can exploit it. Real issue: can platforms systematically suppress wages by taking advantage of workers' uncertainty?
176.wh: In classical labor economics, the market wage would converge to equilibrium. But gig platforms have an information advantage: they know aggregate labor supply better than individual workers know their own costs. Workers uncertain about their reservation wage (the minimum they'll accept) might accept underpaying jobs. Worse, platforms can adjust pricing dynamically to learn and exploit this. If a platform posts low wages and workers keep accepting, it learns workers' uncertainty is high and keeps wages low. Standard economic models assume rational actors with full information; actual gig markets don't satisfy this.
176.ap: The paper models this as a posted-price game. A platform must cover M tasks by posting prices and waiting for workers to accept (if price exceeds their estimated cost). First, the authors show a simple strategy: post low prices initially. Because workers are uncertain about their costs, many will accept even underpriced work (they think their cost might be lower). The platform can cover all tasks while paying only O(log(M)/M) of total labor costs. Then they study collective action: if a strategic coalition of workers commits to a price floor (refusing anything below X), the platform's exploitation power vanishes. The required spending jumps from logarithmic to linear. But a random coalition of equal size is ineffective.
176.ww: This works mathematically because uncertainty is asymmetric. The platform updates its beliefs about worker willingness from observed acceptances; workers don't update fast enough individually. A small strategic coalition with commitment power shifts leverage because it removes the platform's ability to experiment: the platform can't post low prices and learn—it immediately hits the floor. The contrast between strategic and random coalitions reveals that effective collective action requires targeting the right workers (those whose rejection signals the most information to peers).
176.po: The theory is validated with synthetic experiments across market regimes. The payoff: a formal model of wage suppression in gig economies and proof that targeted collective action (unions, coordinated strategies) is necessary, not just random worker organizing. This informs policy and organizing strategy.

177.bp: Misinformation spreads online, and combating it requires understanding intent: some false claims aim to manipulate opinion, others to exploit emotions, others to distract. A single false claim might have multiple coexisting intents. Understanding intent improves detection (fact-checkers prioritize high-impact lies) and response (different intents need different debunking). Goal: model intent without hand-labeled examples (expensive) and predict veracity end-to-end.
177.wh: Existing approaches model intent as a single categorical label (this is 'emotional manipulation' or 'political distortion'), but real claims are mixed. Also, most require LLM inference for every sample, which is expensive at scale. And they struggle with the multiplicity: a claim that says 'vaccines cause autism' might simultaneously aim to scare parents and distrust authorities—one intent label misses the nuance. The challenge: model multiple intents unsupervised (no labels) and do it efficiently.
177.ap: IConMoE combines concept activation vectors with mixture-of-experts. Concept activation vectors are a method for identifying specific high-level concepts (like 'emotional language' or 'conspiracy framing') that a neural network recognizes. A mixture-of-experts layer has multiple specialized 'experts,' each focusing on different aspects, with a gating mechanism that decides which experts to trust for each input. The model learns intents in an unsupervised manner: different experts implicitly capture different intents, without needing labels. A gating layer learns to weight experts based on the claim, naturally modeling multiple coexisting intents.
177.ww: This works because the architecture naturally decomposes intent. Each expert develops a specialty (one captures emotional framing, another political alignment, etc.) through the pressure of predicting veracity. The gating mechanism forces selectivity: for a claim that's mostly emotional manipulation, the emotional expert's signal is weighted up. For a mixed claim, multiple experts contribute. Concept activation vectors make this interpretable: you can ask 'what concepts does expert 3 rely on?' and get human-readable answers. The unsupervised learning is driven by the veracity prediction task: experts that help predict truthfulness survive; those that don't get deprioritized.
177.po: On three benchmark misinformation datasets, the model outperforms baselines. The payoff: interpretable intent modeling of false claims, enabling better prioritization and response without expensive LLM inference per sample.

178.bp: Graph data comes from different sources: one company's social network, another's transaction graph, a third's citation network. Each has different structure and node attributes. You want to train a model on one graph and apply it to another without retraining. Real goal: transfer knowledge from labeled graphs to unlabeled ones, across domain shifts, without centralizing data.
178.wh: Standard domain adaptation assumes similar structure but different feature distributions. Graphs are harder: structure can differ (one is sparse, another dense), features differ, and the statistical distribution of nodes across classes varies. Multi-source adaptation is even trickier: you have multiple source graphs with different properties and want to transfer to one unlabeled target. Existing methods either focus on single-source transfer (missing complementary knowledge from multiple sources) or use complex, handcrafted architectures that are hard to analyze and adapt. The tension: leverage multiple sources without overwhelming complexity.
178.ap: CPT-GDA (Concise Propagation-Transformation pipeline for multi-source Graph Domain Adaptation) uses a dual-branch graph neural network. Both branches follow the same propagation-transformation pattern (propagate information through the graph, then transform it), but with different propagation depths. This simplicity is intentional: propagation means neighbors influence each other, transformation means learning task-specific features. Multiple sources feed into this via three optimization objectives: (1) classify nodes correctly using the learned representations, (2) align representations across source and target domains (make target look more like sources), and (3) leverage multiple sources by learning shared and source-specific knowledge.
178.ww: This works because the P-T pipeline is interpretable and effective: propagation captures graph structure, transformation captures task-specific semantics. The dual-branch design lets the model learn at different 'hops' (direct neighbors vs. distant neighbors) without explosion complexity. Multi-source learning works because the model extracts common knowledge across sources (what's universally useful) and leverages source-specific details (what each source uniquely provides). By optimizing all three objectives jointly, the model learns representations that generalize to the target domain.
178.po: On multiple graph domain-adaptation benchmarks, CPT-GDA outperforms existing methods. The payoff: transfer models across different graph domains—e.g., train on a labeled company's social network, apply to an unlabeled network from a different company, without retraining.

179.bp: Psychological counseling is moving online, and LLM-powered chatbots offer 24/7 support. But most are opaque, generic, and not grounded in established therapy practices.
