Real goal: build an AI counselor that follows structured therapeutic methodology, explains its reasoning, evolves through sessions with the same client, and measures outcomes rigorously.
179.wh: Therapeutic practice has deep theory—different schools (CBT focuses on thoughts, SFBT focuses on solutions, MBCT focuses on mindfulness) work for different people and phases. A good therapist does Exploration (understand the problem), Insight (connect it to patterns), and Action (change behavior). Naive LLM chatbots don't model this structure; they respond to whatever the user says without a coherent plan. Also, they're single-stage (one conversation in isolation) and weakly grounded in clinical evidence. Hard part: coordinate multiple specialized models (for different therapies) while maintaining continuity within a session and across sessions.
179.ap: XInsight orchestrates five specialized agents. (1) Exploration agent organizes client concerns into a standardized Case Conceptualization Form (structured representation of the problem). (2) Routing agent analyzes the case and selects appropriate therapy modalities (SFBT, CBT, MBCT). (3) Therapeutic agent executes school-consistent interventions (cognitive restructuring for CBT, solution-focused questions for SFBT, etc.). (4) Consolidation agent reviews progress, integrates skills learned, and plans relapse prevention. (5) Recording agent continuously converts open dialogue into standardized psychological records. All operate under a Reason-Intervene-Reflect cycle: reason about client state, intervene therapeutically, reflect on what happened.
179.ww: This works because it mirrors actual therapy. Exploration-Insight-Action is the classical therapeutic flow, proven by decades of practice. Recording standardized artifacts (conceptualization, interventions, reflections) creates continuity and accountability—the same client in session 2 can recall session 1 from structured records. Routing to modality-specific agents ensures interventions fit theory (you don't mix CBT and MBCT haphazardly; you route coherently). The Reason-Intervene-Reflect cycle keeps the model grounded in the current client state rather than drifting into generic advice. To measure success, they introduce Scale-Guided LLM Evaluation: use established clinical scales (for measuring depression, anxiety, etc.) alongside general counseling criteria.
179.po: Compared to existing multi-agent counseling systems, XInsight shows improved therapeutic paradigm alignment (follows theory better), deeper interaction, and interpretability. The payoff: transparent, accountable AI counseling that integrates multiple evidence-based therapies and measures psychological progress rigorously—suitable for clinical settings where outcomes matter.

180.bp: Scientists spend huge amounts of time hunting through papers to support claims they've written. The real goal is to ground author statements in actual published work, catching both honest mistakes and catching yourself before you cite something that doesn't actually say what you think it says.
180.wh: Language models are great at writing but terrible at inventing facts (they make up citations). At the same time, researchers don't want their private papers sent to distant servers during the writing process — and if the system just asks an LLM to find citations, you get hallucinated paper titles and author names that sound plausible but don't exist.
180.ap: CiteLLM lives inside your LaTeX editor and never sends your writing to the cloud. It uses the LLM only to turn your claim into a good search query and to rank and explain results. The actual citations it retrieves come directly from trusted databases like academic repositories, not from the LLM's memory.
180.ww: By separating jobs — letting the LLM only do what it's good at (rephrasing your idea into search terms and explaining why a paper matches) while forcing actual results to come from a real database — you get the efficiency of AI without the fabrication. The LLM can't hallucinate a paper that isn't in the index.
180.po: You get valid, usable citations without privacy leaks and without made-up references. In their evaluation, the system returned significantly more correct citations than alternatives, and researchers could trust every result.

181.bp: Image classifiers trained on web photos learn to recognize objects, but web data is messy and biased. In reality, pictures of 'doctor' are mostly white men, pictures of 'nurse' are mostly women, and classifiers absorb these biases wholesale. When that classifier is deployed in hiring or content moderation, it perpetuates social unfairness.
181.wh: The obvious fix—just get more balanced data—is expensive and slow. The real tension is that in the training set, images with bias (e.g., women as nurses) vastly outnumber images without the bias (e.g., men as nurses), so the network confidently learns the spurious correlation. Standard balancing tricks require manual labels or synthetic data.
181.ap: BiasEdit first finds hidden biases by comparing visual and text representations to spot which attributes (like gender) are unfairly linked to classes. Then it uses off-the-shelf image editing tools to rewrite those attributes in biased images—turning a photo of a male nurse into one that preserves his role but removes the gender signal—creating synthetic balanced data automatically.
181.ww: Editing images at the visual level preserves realism better than mixing pixels, and by using existing text-image understanding models, you don't need a separate expensive bias detector. The network then trains on balanced data without bias-conflict examples being rare or artificial-looking.
181.po: Classifiers trained on the edited dataset stop picking up gender and other social attributes as cues for classification, reducing unfairness significantly without manual annotation and without requiring retraining from scratch.

182.bp: Kubernetes clusters break in complex ways, and when they do, teams need to diagnose the problem fast. The real-world goal is to use past resolutions to speed up future diagnosis—learn from what happened last time a node crashed or a pod hung.
182.wh: Most AI diagnosis systems have fixed knowledge (they know about 50 common Kubernetes errors) but never improve from new cases they encounter. Language models are huge, so deploying them requires either sending logs to a cloud vendor or licensing an expensive service, both risky in production.
182.ap: MetaKube is a smaller 8-billion-parameter model (KubeLLM) trained specifically on 7,000 real Kubernetes incidents. It stores past resolutions in a memory system that remembers which patterns led to solutions, and a reasoning controller decides whether to take the fast path (pattern recognition) or the deep path (detailed analysis) based on how familiar the problem is.
182.ww: Because the model is trained only on Kubernetes data and stays on your own servers, it's both faster and more accurate than generic LLMs. The memory system lets it recognize recurring problems instantly, and the reasoning layer makes sure it doesn't skip analysis on novel issues.
182.po: The system diagnoses Kubernetes problems correctly 90% of the time (up from 51% with the untrained baseline), runs entirely locally with no data leaving your cluster, and continues to improve as it encounters and remembers new faults.

183.bp: Online ads cost money, and advertisers need to decide how much to spend on each campaign to win valuable user interactions within a fixed budget. The real goal is to maximize the value of ad impressions won, when each advertiser has different goals and little historical data to learn from.
183.wh: Advertisers often know their objectives but have very few past interactions to learn from (few-shot problem). Standard reinforcement learning needs lots of trial and error to find good bidding strategies, and it can't generalize from one advertiser's patterns to another's.
183.ap: DARA splits the job into two stages. First, an LLM reads the advertiser's situation (budget, history, goals) and reasons through an initial plan in plain language. Second, a fine-tuned optimizer takes that plan and refines it numerically using feedback, learning exactly how much more value each dollar spent earns.
183.ww: LLMs are good at reasoning from a few examples (they've seen billions of text descriptions of decision-making), so they can draft a reasonable strategy quickly. But they're imprecise at math, so the second stage fixes the numbers. This split lets you leverage LLM generalization without accuracy loss.
183.po: On real advertising data, DARA consistently outbids traditional reinforcement learning approaches, even when history is sparse, and adapts quickly to new advertiser profiles without retraining.

184.bp: People can now generate realistic fake images of faces on their phones, creating serious privacy and forgery risks. Researchers have built invisible digital protections that scramble photos so AI face generators can't use them, but attackers keep finding ways around those protections.
184.wh: Privacy protections work by adding subtle noise to images so generated fakes lose quality and don't look like the real person. But face restoration algorithms—tools designed to clean up blurry or damaged photos—can undo that noise and recover the original appearance, defeating the protection.
184.ap: The paper proves mathematically why face restoration is so effective at breaking privacy protections: it's specifically designed to recover detail from degraded images, which is exactly what privacy noise looks like to the restoration algorithm. They also show that fine-tuning the restoration model makes attacks even more effective.
184.ww: Face restoration works because it models what real faces look like and uses that model to invent missing details. Privacy noise looks like missing detail, so the restoration algorithm competes with the privacy protection in a race to define what details get added back.
184.po: The paper demonstrates that state-of-the-art privacy protections for images are vulnerable to this simple attack, significantly stronger than prior red-teaming methods, and calls out the urgent need for better protections against this specific threat.

185.bp: On social media, people often say sarcastic things to mock, criticize, or make jokes. To understand online content fairly, AI needs to both detect sarcasm is happening and explain what the person really meant—the detection and the explanation are two sides of the same understanding.
185.wh: Text, images, and video all contribute to sarcasm, but they contribute in different ways. Most systems treat detection and explanation as separate problems, missing that a good explanation should logically support why something is sarcastic. Also, multimodal sarcasm requires combining text and visual cues, but simply averaging representations from text and images loses important context.
185.ap: MuVaC models the reasoning process as a causal chain: the detection ("this is sarcasm") should be explained by a reason extracted from the multimodal content. It uses a statistical causal framework to ensure detection and explanation are consistent with each other. A specialized fusion method combines text and image features in a way that preserves both what each modality contributes.
185.ww: By enforcing that detection and explanation must be causally aligned, the model can't claim something is sarcastic without pointing to what makes it sarcastic. This mirrors how humans actually understand sarcasm—we both recognize it and know why we think so, as a single act of reasoning.
185.po: On test datasets, MuVaC detects sarcasm more accurately and generates more trustworthy explanations than systems that treat detection and explanation separately, and the explanations align better with why the detection happened.

186.bp: AI agents now generate text, images, and code at scale on the web. When one agent consumes content another agent created, both need to know where it came from, what settings were used, and whether it can be legally reused—otherwise errors propagate and licenses get violated.
186.wh: AI-generated content has no inherent metadata. You can't tell if a piece of text was written by an LLM, what prompt was used, what model version created it, or whether it's licensed for reuse. This is especially dangerous when agents feed each other content and errors accumulate (one wrong fact gets refined into five more wrong facts).
186.ap: This framework wraps generated content with structured metadata at creation time: the prompt used, model name, hyperparameters, confidence scores, and context. This metadata is packaged with verifiable credentials (cryptographic proof that it wasn't tampered with) so downstream agents can trust it.
186.ww: Metadata attached at the moment of creation is trustworthy because you can cryptographically verify it hasn't been altered. Agents can then check whether they're allowed to reuse content (license check), whether the creation settings are appropriate for their task, and trace errors back to their source.
186.po: Downstream applications like model fine-tuning and knowledge distillation can now safely consume AI-generated content because they know its provenance and can verify it meets legal and technical requirements.

187.bp: Recommendation systems, fraud detection, and knowledge bases all rely on graphs of connections between users, items, and concepts. In the real world, these graphs are constantly changing, get attacked by adversaries, and contain missing or outdated information—and the AI systems trained on them fail silently.
187.wh: Most research assumes the graph is clean and stable. In reality, web data is messy: a bot injects fake follows to game recommendations, a server goes down and loses data, or the patterns users follow today are totally different from yesterday. Algorithms trained on yesterday's graph become unreliable.
187.ap: This tutorial surveys defenses at multiple levels: cleaning data before it enters the system (preprocessing), making the model itself more resistant to corruption (model-level adaptation), and ensuring the model can generalize when the world changes (generalization techniques).
187.ww: Robustness requires thinking about where failures come from. Some are data problems (bad inputs), some are model problems (overfitting to unstable patterns), and some are environmental (domain shift). Addressing all three angles gives more resilience than trying to solve them all at once.
187.po: The tutorial provides researchers and engineers with a structured way to think about robustness in graph systems, concrete methods to apply, and real-world examples showing how these defenses help in recommender systems and fraud detection.

188.bp: Big hospitals, drug companies, and engineering firms want AI to learn from human expert feedback to improve models, but experts can't share raw case data due to privacy laws and intellectual property protection. The goal is to collect feedback safely without seeing the sensitive data.
188.wh: Decentralized feedback collection lets experts keep their data private, but then you can't verify the feedback is correct. A lazy annotator might give wrong labels, or a malicious one might poison the data deliberately, and you'd never know.
188.ap: Trustless Feedback uses zero-knowledge proofs—cryptographic math that proves a fact is true without revealing the secret information behind it. The expert's case data stays on their machine. A proof certifies that their feedback satisfies hard constraints (e.g., "this drug combination has no interactions") without exposing the case details.
188.ww: Zero-knowledge proofs turn verification into a math problem. You don't need to see the data to verify it's valid, just like you don't need to see someone's birth certificate to verify they're over 18 if they show you a signed proof. This splits privacy from integrity checking.
188.po: Models trained on this feedback are guaranteed to reject invalid data (100% in their prototype) while never seeing the underlying sensitive cases, making it practical for hospitals and engineering firms to contribute expert feedback.

189.bp: Scientists publish research, but turning that raw text into a structured database of facts and contributions (a knowledge graph) is still mostly manual. The goal is to automatically extract machine-readable facts that other AI systems can use to verify claims and find related work.
189.wh: Language models can extract facts from text, but they're inconsistent. They might call the same concept 'deep learning' in one paper and 'neural networks' in another, making the resulting database messy and hard for downstream systems to use. Manual crowdsourcing is consistent but tedious and error-prone.
189.ap: LOPE uses an LLM to extract properties and concepts from papers, then aligns those extracted terms to a standardized vocabulary (an ontology). This normalization step turns 'deep learning' and 'neural networks' into the same canonical term, making the database consistent and machine-actionable.
189.ww: Extracting from text and then normalizing separately is more efficient than trying to extract into perfect terminology in one pass (which the LLM struggles with). The ontology acts as a translator, and using a well-designed vocabulary ensures downstream systems understand the data the same way.
189.po: The resulting scientific knowledge graph is semantically consistent—key facts are represented the same way across papers—and verified to be more consistent than manual crowdsourcing, making it useful for retrieval-augmented generation and hallucination detection in AI systems.

190.bp: Companies maintain separate knowledge bases for different business domains (one for products, one for customers, one for suppliers). When information is missing from one database, they want to infer it by borrowing patterns from the others—without the databases looking identical.
190.wh: If you try to share information across databases too directly, you lose important context specific to each domain. A 'supplier relationship' means something different in manufacturing versus retail, and forcing them to look the same washes out that specificity. Also, low-resource domains need help but shouldn't get overwritten by high-resource ones.
190.ap: DMKGC treats each database as a partial view of the full truth. It generates new entity representations using diffusion models (a technique that starts with noise and gradually denoises toward a target). The diffusion process is guided by matching entities across databases, but targets a domain-neutral representation to avoid bias.
190.ww: Diffusion models naturally balance constraints: they're pushed toward the guidance (shared entity information) but also pulled toward a neutral target (the prior representation). This prevents any single domain from dominating. The unbiased target ensures that adding support from other databases improves accuracy without distorting domain-specific knowledge.
190.po: Knowledge graphs trained this way complete missing triples (predict unknown relationships) more accurately than methods that enforce strict consistency, especially when some domains have very little training data.

191.bp: Modern cities generate vast data about where people go, how they move, and what patterns repeat over time. The goal is to understand human mobility and urban dynamics—both for planning (where to build transit) and analysis (detecting anomalies or predicting congestion).
191.wh: Spatio-temporal data is complex: a subway commute has structure (happens every weekday morning) but with variation (delays, weather, special events). Traditional statistical methods and even deep learning models struggle to generalize across different cities or adapt when patterns shift. Language models have seen descriptions of thousands of cities and mobility patterns in their training data.
191.ap: This tutorial covers how to apply large language models and foundation models to spatio-temporal analysis at three levels: finding patterns within a location (what happens at this intersection), understanding movement trajectories (how an individual commutes), and modeling regional flows (how traffic moves between neighborhoods).
191.ww: Language models are powerful at reasoning about spatial and temporal concepts because they've encountered descriptions in text. They can generate predictions in natural language or structured form, adapt quickly when you prompt them with new context, and transfer learning from one city to another better than models trained from scratch.
191.po: The tutorial maps out methods for LLM-based applications to urban computing, location-based services, and transportation systems, helping researchers think about which problems benefit from this new approach versus traditional deep learning.

192.bp: Language models connected to knowledge databases can answer hard questions by retrieving relevant facts first, then reasoning over them. The goal is to get accurate, explainable answers in domains like medicine where confidence matters—you need to know when to trust the model.
192.wh: Knowledge-augmented models are often overconfident. They might retrieve an incomplete sub-graph (missing key relationships) or unreliable information, but still predict with high confidence. In a hospital, an overconfident wrong answer is dangerous.
192.ap: Ca2KG uses counterfactual prompting: asking the model to imagine scenarios where certain retrieved facts are missing or changed, exposing whether it's really dependent on reliable information or just memorized patterns. Then it recalibrates confidence scores by averaging predictions across these hypothetical scenarios.
192.ww: Counterfactual reasoning exposes weaknesses in reasoning. If the model's answer changes dramatically when you remove one retrieved fact, then it was over-relying on that fact. By re-scoring based on robustness across interventions, you get confidence levels that actually reflect uncertainty.
192.po: On question-answering benchmarks, Ca2KG produces calibrated confidence scores (it's more uncertain when it should be) while maintaining or improving accuracy, making it safer for high-stakes applications.

193.bp: Large language models run on phones and edge devices because of quantization—a compression technique that makes models smaller and faster. But this compression happens at a layer where attackers can inject hidden behaviors, like making the model refuse to answer normal questions or bypass safety filters.
193.wh: Quantization reduces precision of model weights to save space, but defending it is hard. You have very limited data to work with (just a small calibration set), each layer gets compressed independently (restricting global attacks), and you can't use gradients to guide an attack (quantization is a fixed operation).
193.ap: LLMQuA injects backdoors by editing only the quantized weights directly, without needing gradients. It uses data-efficient knowledge editing (changing the model's behavior with just a few token pairs) and adjusts quantization parameters layer-by-layer to maintain the original activation patterns while hiding malicious changes.
193.ww: By working directly on quantized weights and using knowledge editing instead of gradient-based poisoning, the attack bypasses all three defenses. The model appears normal on general tasks but misbehaves on specific triggers, like refusing to engage with content moderation rules.
193.po: The paper demonstrates that quantized language models, when deployed locally, are vulnerable to this attack: 68% of moderation cases can be evaded and 90% of targeted queries get refused, while the model's normal utility only drops slightly.

194.bp: Information spreads through social networks—memes, news, behaviors ripple outward as people share and adopt. To predict what will happen next, platforms and researchers model who will adopt based on the history of how others already have.
194.wh: Most models treat adoption as a sequence of individuals choosing independently, computing influence one-to-one (person A influences person B). But that's slow—for a cascade of 10,000 people, you'd need billions of pairwise calculations. Also, real influence is often collective (a group trend makes adoption likely), not individual.
194.ap: GRID groups users and models influence between groups instead of between individuals. It learns group identities by maximizing information about key influence pathways while discarding noise (information bottleneck principle), then uses a specialized attention module that computes group-to-group influence in linear time instead of quadratic.
194.ww: Grouping reduces complexity dramatically: instead of checking if person 10,000 influences person 10,001, you check if their groups interact. This scales to ultra-long cascades. Also, groups better represent real influence: a trend spreading through 50 tech workers is more real than 50 independent binary decisions.
194.po: GRID models information cascades with over 10,000 users without truncating history (prior work could only handle hundreds), maintains accuracy within a mathematically-proven error bound, and dramatically reduces computation, making prediction on large social networks practical.

195.bp: Video platforms like TikTok face a ranking problem: which video should you see next? The obvious answer—show the most-watched videos—works in the moment, but platforms care about your lifetime value (how long you stay, how often you return over weeks or months). These are two different targets, and only long-term value predicts whether users stick around. This paper tackles the hard practical version: predicting long-term value in production systems that serve billions of videos daily.
195.wh: Long-term value prediction faces three specific obstacles. First, the position where a video appears (top of feed vs. middle) affects engagement; users see videos higher up more, so a video's high watch count might just mean it was positioned well, not that it's truly engaging. Second, when multiple videos influence your stay (you watched three clips, which one kept you?), it's unclear which deserves credit for your long-term value. Third, engagement signals arrive over days or weeks; systems must make ranking decisions now with incomplete data.
195.ap: The paper introduces three concrete fixes. For position bias, they build a module that looks at the distribution of engagement across positions (some videos always perform well whether top or middle; others only shine when promoted) and normalizes signals accordingly. For credit assignment, they train a model that learns how much each video's context, your past behavior, and the video's content each contribute to keeping you engaged—avoiding hand-coded rules. They also filter noise explicitly so causality is clearer. For time, they track per-creator patterns day-by-day and model when users return because a creator re-engages them.
195.ww: Position-aware normalization works because it separates signal from placement luck: if a video does well everywhere, it's truly good, not privileged. Multi-dimensional attribution captures the real mechanisms—context matters, user habit matters, content matters—and learning their weights beats human guesses. Creator modeling works because users don't engage uniformly over time; some creators keep people coming back weeks later, and that's a real pattern to learn.
195.po: In production systems at billion-scale, this means the ranking model can predict which videos to show you now because they'll keep you engaged next month, not just this hour. The framework handles delayed feedback (data arrives late), cleans noisy signals, and runs on real platforms, making long-term value a practical lever for user retention rather than an academic ideal.

196.bp: Tor's whole purpose is to hide your web traffic so no one can see which websites you visit—a lifeline for journalists and activists in repressive places. But security researchers discovered you can identify which websites someone visits just by watching the *shape and timing* of their encrypted traffic, even if you can't decrypt it. This paper shows an attack that works even when someone does something realistic: opening multiple websites at once.
196.wh: Traffic analysis is like listening to a phone call in a foreign language you don't understand; you can't hear the words, but you notice one voice gets loud then quiet, another interrupts. Previous attacks assumed one person was browsing one website. Real life: someone opens five tabs, streaming a video, reading news, shopping. All this traffic mixes together, and it becomes much harder to say 'this spike was from Gmail and this one was from YouTube.' The attacker doesn't know how many tabs are even open.
196.ap: This work borrows an idea from audio engineering: the 'cocktail party problem' (how a human picks out one conversation in a noisy room). They reframe multi-tab traffic as a mixing problem: separate the traffic signals without knowing how many sources there are. They treat the mixed network traffic like a recording of overlapping voices and decompose it into individual streams. Then they classify each stream by watching patterns across time (a Gmail login flows differently than a YouTube video) and frequency (does the traffic spike every 100ms or smoothly?).
196.ww: Blind source separation works here because each website's traffic has a fingerprint—Gmail logins are bursty and short, YouTube is steady and long, Google Docs has pauses when you're typing. Even when mixed, the patterns remain consistent enough to untangle. The time-frequency trick captures this: different sites have different rhythms, and you can exploit those rhythms even when everything is mixed together.
196.po: The result: an attacker can now identify which websites you visit via Tor even when you're opening multiple sites at once, with 78.6% accuracy improvement over prior methods. This reveals a real privacy vulnerability in multi-tab browsing—it matters for Tor's promise of anonymity and suggests new defenses are needed.

197.bp: Banks that serve poor communities rely on web platforms to approve credit quickly. A credit card fraud—someone using a stolen card—directly harms vulnerable people who can already barely access credit. The system must catch fraud while approving legitimate users, but small banks have little data compared to tech giants. Meanwhile, malicious actors might try to poison the system itself by inserting hidden triggers into the machine-learning model during updates, making it approve fraudulent transactions no matter what.
197.wh: Small web banks face a real trap. They need machine learning to spot fraud, but fraud detection only improves with large datasets—and they don't have them. Sharing data across banks (federated learning) helps, but it creates a new vulnerability: during the aggregation step where multiple banks' model improvements get merged, a malicious bank could inject a 'backdoor' (a secret pattern that triggers when seen, like 'approve transactions with amount=4444'). The system wouldn't detect it because aggregate models look clean at first glance. Meanwhile, real fraud is rare, making it harder to learn from the few examples present.
197.ap: The paper proposes a defense-attack co-design. The attack side: bad actors use reinforcement learning (a technique that learns to win games) to evolve their backdoor trigger over time, making it stealthier while staying effective—this tests how good defenses are. The defense side: after each model merge, the system runs a selection-evaluation cycle, checking whether something suspicious happened (checking for trigger patterns) and adapting to block them. On the normal detection side, they use privacy-preserving methods to share features across banks without revealing raw data, and a contrastive learning approach (learning by comparing fraudulent vs. legitimate transactions) to work with few examples.
197.ww: The federated setup works because small banks together have enough data, and privacy methods mean they don't expose customer information. Contrastive learning works for scarce fraud data because you learn by comparing pairs: 'this transaction is similar to known fraud, that one isn't.' The adaptive defense works because adversaries can't stay ahead if the system watches, detects changes, and adjusts the filter in a closed loop.
197.po: The framework lets small web banks detect fraud with the combined strength of many banks' data while staying private and resistant to backdoor attacks. It's explicitly designed for the extreme scarcity that small banks face, making inclusive financial infrastructure more secure.

198.bp: During a disaster—earthquake, flood, hurricane—people post images and text on social media asking for help: 'missing person,' 'road blocked,' 'power out.' Rescue teams need to automatically sort these by urgency and type. But the system must explain its decisions because decisions affect real people's lives—if the algorithm says 'this is low priority,' someone might not see it. Explaining images is harder than explaining text; an algorithm can point to words in a tweet, but pointing to 'which part of this photo matters?' is unclear.
198.wh: Image explanation is hard because a human can't easily verify why a model paid attention to a particular part of the photo; it might have just learned a shortcut (certain pixel colors = disaster category). Text explanation is easier: point to a word, anyone can verify it's relevant. The naive approach is to explain text and ignore images, but images carry crucial information in disasters—'is this building damaged?' or 'is this person visible?' Both modalities are needed, but the annotation burden (having humans label why each image belongs to a category) is enormous.
198.ap: Instead of labeling image rationales directly, the paper uses text as a bridge. Step one: extract explanation words from the tweet (e.g., 'missing' and 'stranded' explain the 'displaced persons' category). Step two: map those text explanations to image patches (regions of the photo) through a visual-language model—a system trained on aligned image-text pairs. The map learns 'when the text says missing, this photo region matters.' Step three: classify based on both extracted rationales. The trick is using the text as supervision for the image, saving human annotation effort.
198.ww: This works because aligned image-text models have learned deep correspondences—they know that certain words relate to certain visual features. By leveraging this pre-learned alignment, you can transfer the text explanation to images without new human labeling. The joint representation ensures text and image rationales point to the same underlying meaning.
198.po: The result: a classification system that explains both text and image decisions (showing which tweet words and photo regions support the category) with 2–35% better accuracy than baselines. In disasters, this means rescue teams can trust and quickly verify why a post was categorized, and annotation cost drops dramatically because you label text once and get image explanations for free.

199.bp: Large language models (LLMs) are becoming tools for everything, but they're huge—hundreds of billions of numbers describing patterns in text—and running them requires expensive data centers. A natural question: can we shrink them to fit on a phone or edge device? Quantization is a technique for this: use fewer bits to store each number (8 bits instead of 16, or 4 instead of 8). The catch: even tiny quantized models require many multiply-accumulate operations (the core math of neural networks), and on a battery-powered device, that math drains power fast.
199.wh: Standard quantization has two problems. First, after reducing the precision of numbers, the model still does dense matrix multiplication (every weight × every activation), which is inherently expensive on mobile chips. Second, uniform bit-widths are wasteful: some weight values are big and important, others small and forgettable, but standard quantization treats them the same. You could use lower precision for unimportant values, but current hardware doesn't support mixed-precision storage in a practical way.
199.ap: The paper proposes SpikeQuant, inspired by how brains work. Biological brains use spiking—neurons send brief electrical pulses. This paper translates that idea to quantization: represent activations (the values flowing through the network) as binary spike counts instead of continuous numbers. Think of it like: instead of storing 5.7, you store 'fire 6 times.' The key insight is that important (salient) activation values get higher precision (more spikes), while unimportant values get lower precision. The model then does accumulation instead of multiplication—summing up spike counts is far cheaper than multiplying floating-point numbers. The quantization scale is embedded into the spike threshold, so no separate rescaling step is needed.
199.ww: Binary spikes are energy-efficient because counting is cheaper than multiplication. Mixed-precision storage works because different values need different bit-widths, and spike counts naturally encode this. Eliminating explicit dequantization (rescaling) removes extra operations that cost latency and power on edge devices. Brain-like computation is a good fit because nature has been solving this problem (how to compute with limited energy) for millions of years.
199.po: The result is a path to running large language models on phones and embedded devices without the usual energy cost. Fewer multiply-accumulate operations and mixed precision mean faster, lower-power inference—making LLM capabilities available on battery-powered hardware, not just data centers.

200.bp: When you search 'pizza near me,' a search engine like Google or Baidu returns results. But 'near me' means something different to each person—you might be looking for a specific style, or near your office rather than home. Pure keyword matching can't capture your specific intent. Personalized search rewrites your query before searching, transforming 'pizza' into 'vegan pizza within 3km of Zhongguancun' based on your history and profile. This is powerful but requires understanding intent from your behavior, and doing that reasoning fast enough for real-time search is a challenge.
200.wh: Large language models can reason about intent well—they understand context and nuance—but adding reasoning steps (called Chain-of-Thought, where the model explicitly shows its reasoning) to every search query is too slow. A production search engine needs to rewrite and return results in milliseconds; adding reasoning overhead makes queries lag. Without reasoning, the model makes quick but shallow choices. The tension is fundamental: thinking deeply takes time, but search engines can't wait.
200.ap: PicQue uses a two-stage training approach. Stage one: train the model using a hybrid method where examples include both the reasoning steps (how to think about your intent) and the rewritten query. During training, the model learns to do both; during deployment, you skip the reasoning part and just decode the rewritten query. This is like a student who practices showing all homework steps in class, then on a test just writes the answer without showing work—but the reasoning process improved their intuition, so the answer is still correct. Stage two: reinforce the pipeline by training on real user interactions—which rewrites actually led to people clicking results.
200.ww: Hybrid supervised fine-tuning works because the model learns the reasoning internally (in its weights) even if it doesn't output reasoning at test time. The chain-of-thought examples in training inject reasoning capability, and the model compresses that capability into direct decoding. This is much faster than generating reasoning text on every query. Reinforcement learning from click data ensures the rewrites actually match what users want.
200.po: The system achieves high accuracy (the rewrites are semantically correct) with low latency (milliseconds, not seconds), making personalized query rewriting practical for real search engines at scale. It handles the real challenge: inferring personal intent from behavior and encoding it into the search automatically.

201.bp: Advertising platforms host billions of ads daily. Scammers use AI to generate fake ads at scale—deepfake videos, synthetic speech, photoshopped images—luring people into cryptocurrency schemes or fake shops. A naive detection approach looks at each image or video alone: 'is this image fake?' But scammers don't launch one ad; they launch thousands of near-identical variants with slight tweaks, rotating them to evade detection. To stop this, you need to see the campaign as a system, not individual assets.
201.wh: Asset-level detection (analyzing one ad image) misses the scam because scammers rely on volume and rotation. They generate a core template (say, a fake celebrity video), create hundreds of slight variations (different frame crops, added text, re-encoded to bypass fingerprinting), and publish them across many fake accounts on rotating schedules. By the time a system flags one variant, the scammer switches to another. The system also uses auxiliary content (e.g., a 'educational disclaimer' video) that masks the actual scam, making individual assets look legitimate in isolation.
201.ap: This paper reconstructs entire scam campaigns layer by layer. They trace back from a detected scam ad to find all related ads, accounts, and timelines. They identify patterns: stable 'persuasion schemes' (the core lie, like 'get rich quick'), production templates (how the scammer assembles the ad), and variant generation strategies (how they make thousands of nearly-identical versions). They observe that audio—especially synthetic speech—is the dominant persuasive channel, while visuals range from montage to fully synthetic. Crucially, they document the temporal deployment: ads burst on a schedule and rotate, suggesting an automated workflow.
201.ww: Campaigns have structure that individual assets don't. A genuine ad might vary in some ways, but scam campaigns have mass production patterns, auxiliary masking content, and bursts on schedules. These patterns are harder to fake than a single convincing ad. By recognizing the structure—'this template is being cloned 5,000 times across accounts'—detection can catch the whole campaign, not chase variants forever.
201.po: The result is a framework for campaign-level detection: systems should look for production templates, deployment patterns, and temporal rotation, not just asset properties. Mitigation can now block at the campaign level (suspend the template) rather than playing whack-a-mole with variants. For advertising platforms, this shifts the arms race toward structure detection, which is more resilient.

202.bp: Fine-tuning is the standard way to adapt a pre-trained large language model (LLM) to a specific task: you take GPT or LLaMA and train it on your data. Pure fine-tuning updates billions of weights, which is expensive. Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) is a trick: instead of updating all weights, you update only a small, low-rank matrix—mathematically a tiny update that achieves most of the improvement. The question: can we make LoRA even better?
202.wh: Standard LoRA has two technical issues. First, when the embedding dimension is large (the 'width' of the network), learning the first matrix (A) is inefficient—the random initialization doesn't help the gradient-based learning. Second, initializing the second matrix (B) as zeros creates a dead-weight problem: at the start, the update has no effect, and gradients have to bootstrap the learning from scratch. These inefficiencies accumulate, slowing training and limiting accuracy gains.
202.ap: LoRA-E2 makes two changes. First, it initializes the A matrix using a Gaussian distribution with a specific variance (scaled by the embedding dimension to the power -3/4). This variance scaling is chosen so that the initial random matrix neither swamps nor suppresses gradients; it's the Goldilocks zone for learning. Second, it trains the B and A matrices using the Gauss-Seidel iteration, a classical numerical method that updates them in a coordinated way, unlike standard gradient descent which updates them simultaneously.
202.ww: Proper initialization matters because it affects how quickly gradients flow into the weights at the start of training. A variance scaled to the network width ensures that the random matrix is 'compatible' with the network's scale. Gauss-Seidel updates work better than simultaneous updates because they let one matrix respond to changes in the other, creating more stable and faster convergence—it's like two dancers who take turns leading rather than both leading at once.
202.po: In practice, LoRA-E2 improves fine-tuning accuracy by 1–10% on standard benchmarks and converges 3× faster. For large models like LLaMA, this means cheaper, quicker adaptation to new tasks, with gains that matter in production systems where training time and accuracy both directly impact the bottom line.

203.bp: Many real-world data problems have partial labels: you know some objects' categories, but not all. Generalized Category Discovery (GCD) is the task of automatically classifying everything—known and unknown categories—from this partial label set. Imagine you have labeled photos of 'dog' and 'cat,' but unlabeled photos that might be 'dog,' 'cat,' or 'bird.' How do you learn to identify the birds you've never seen labeled?
203.wh: Models pre-trained on known categories (dog, cat) develop bias toward them. When the model sees a new, unknown image, it tries to fit it into known categories rather than recognizing 'this is something new.' This is particularly bad because novel categories have no labeled examples to learn from. Recent methods use pseudo-labels (guessing the category, then treating the guess as truth) and contrastive learning (learning by comparing similar and dissimilar pairs), but they lack explicit signals saying 'separate the novel categories from known ones.' The result is confusion at the boundary between known and unknown.
203.ap: This paper treats category discovery as a latent variable problem: for each unlabeled example, there's a hidden variable saying 'is this known or novel?' They use Expectation-Maximization (EM), a classic algorithm for finding hidden structure. The EM-disentangling step softly assigns each example to known or novel, then uses that assignment to guide learning. They also apply dual contrastive objectives: pull examples of the same novel category together, and push apart ambiguous examples near the decision boundary. A consistency regularization ensures the model generalizes.
203.ww: EM works here because it's designed to recover hidden structure from data. By modeling 'known vs. novel' as a latent variable, you can explicitly separate them rather than hoping they emerge. The dual contrastive objectives work because they directly target the confusion: novel categories are pulled together so they cluster, while boundary cases are pushed apart so the decision is clean.
203.po: The framework improves category discovery accuracy by reducing misclassification of novel categories. Crucially, it makes the disentanglement explicit—the model learns to separate known from novel categories as part of training, not as a side effect. This matters in open-world scenarios like image retrieval or recommendation systems, where new categories constantly emerge.

204.bp: AI systems are deployed in critical domains—medical diagnosis, autonomous vehicles, financial decisions—where security matters enormously. When an AI system is vulnerable to attack (e.g., adversarial inputs fooling the model, data poisoning, model extraction), how do we know? Security analysts must connect vulnerability findings from different tools, research papers, and organizational standards (NIST, OWASP, ISO). Today, this process is mostly manual and error-prone because each security tool speaks its own language.
204.wh: Security analysis tools produce different outputs with different terminology and concepts. One tool says 'adversarial example detected,' another says 'model robustness issue,' a third says 'input validation missing.' Analysts manually correlate these reports with mitigation knowledge scattered across MITRE ATLAS (adversarial tactics), OWASP (web security), NIST (standards), ISO (governance). This takes time, introduces human error, and doesn't scale to the number of AI systems being deployed.
204.ap: AI SecOnto proposes an ontology—a structured, machine-readable representation of AI security knowledge. An ontology is like a master dictionary that defines every security concept and how they relate (e.g., 'adversarial example' is a type of 'input attack,' which requires 'input validation' mitigation). The framework ingests raw vulnerability findings from security tools and translates them into this common ontology (like converting multiple languages to a universal semantic language). Analysts can then query the ontology: 'show all vulnerabilities affecting model robustness in this MLOps pipeline' and get structured mitigation recommendations automatically.
204.ww: Ontologies work here because security knowledge has deep structure—concepts relate to each other in ways that matter for analysis. By formalizing that structure once, automated queries become possible. Every new vulnerability finding automatically maps to the broader security knowledge base, reducing manual work and catching patterns humans might miss.
204.po: The prototype demonstrates query-driven vulnerability assessment and structured mitigation for MLOps pipelines. Instead of analysts manually reading reports and cross-referencing standards, the system correlates findings automatically and surfaces mitigations, scaling security analysis to match the deployment rate of AI systems.

205.bp: Recommender systems decide what you see on Netflix or Spotify. Classical approaches build a graph (you → movie, movie → genre, etc.) or use pure text descriptions. Large language models (LLMs) have vast world knowledge: they know that 'The Matrix' is sci-fi action about AI, ideal for someone who liked 'Blade Runner.' The question: how do you combine LLMs (which understand semantics) with interaction graphs (which capture your actual behavior) to recommend better?
205.wh: LLM-based recommenders know item features well but ignore user-item interaction patterns—who watched what together, which users are similar. Graphs capture interactions but require explicit encoding; LLMs don't naturally ingest graph structure. Fusing the two is hard because they're heterogeneous: graph embeddings (compressed representations of nodes) are different from LLM token embeddings, making them hard to align.
205.ap: GALRec uses a strategy called GAL-tuning, which combines two components. A graph encoder processes user-item interactions and extracts collaborative signals (users like me enjoyed these items). An LLM predictor generates recommendations from textual item descriptions and context. To bridge them, they introduce GAL-alignment: graph-to-LLM alignment (adjust graph representations to match LLM space) and LLM-to-graph alignment (adjust LLM output to reflect graph patterns). The alignment minimizes the gap between what the graph 'says' and what the LLM 'says,' tuning them to agree.
205.ww: Alignment works because even though graphs and LLMs represent information differently, they're both trying to answer the same question: 'what's this user likely to enjoy?' By forcing them to agree (minimizing divergence), you let each component's strengths (graph has interaction ground truth, LLM has semantic understanding) reinforce the other.
205.po: The result is a recommender that leverages both collaborative patterns and semantic understanding, improving recommendation accuracy. For systems with sparse interaction data, the LLM component provides world knowledge; for data-rich systems, the graph component ensures recommendations match actual user behavior.

206.bp: In chemistry, biology, and software engineering, objects are often represented as bags of graphs: a molecule as multiple structural views (atoms, bonds, functional groups), a protein as interaction networks from different data sources, a software codebase as multiple dependency graphs. The question: how do you learn embeddings (compressed representations) of these multi-graph objects when you have few or no labels?
206.wh: Standard graph neural networks are designed for single graphs; extending them to bags of graphs faces three challenges. First, producing discriminative representations of the whole bag (not just individual graphs) is unclear—combining multiple graph embeddings risks losing information. Second, contrastive learning typically operates at one level (e.g., comparing individual graph embeddings), but bags have hierarchical structure (graphs within bags, sub-structures within graphs)—you need cross-hierarchical alignment. Third, standard data augmentation (adding noise or dropping edges) can destroy important graph structures or semantic meaning, hurting learning.
206.ap: HGBN (Hierarchical Graph-Bag-Network) addresses these with three components. An asymmetric hierarchical graph neural network learns representations at two levels: individual graph-level embeddings and the bag-level embedding (which aggregates graphs carefully). Cross-hierarchical contrastive objectives align graph and bag representations: pull close the bag-level embedding and its constituent graphs, and push apart bags with different structures. The augmentation strategy is structure-aware: instead of random noise, it augments in ways that preserve the graphs' semantic meaning (e.g., reordering graphs within a bag, not breaking individual graphs).
206.ww: Hierarchical representations work because bags-of-graphs have two levels of structure; capturing both levels improves downstream performance. Cross-hierarchical contrastive learning works because aligning graphs with their parent bag forces both levels to encode consistent information. Structure-aware augmentation works because semantic information is preserved, so the model learns robust features rather than brittle statistical shortcuts.
206.po: The framework enables self-supervised learning on bags of graphs without labels, with hierarchical representations that capture both individual and aggregate structure. This is valuable in chemistry (molecule property prediction from multiple structural views) and bioinformatics (protein function from interaction networks) where labeled data is scarce.

207.bp: Cities face a new challenge: electric vehicles charging at scale will stress power grids, but vehicles could also become mobile batteries (Vehicle-to-Grid or V2G), stabilizing grids during peak demand. Understanding this coupling requires simulating traffic (when do people drive?) and power grids (when is demand high?) together. But complex simulations are hard to visualize and experiment with, so decisions remain theoretical rather than empirical.
207.wh: Real-time coupled simulations of power and traffic are complex: routing affects grid load, grid events (blackouts) affect traffic, and cascading failures can spiral. Current tools require specialized software, run offline, and produce abstract numbers, not intuitive visuals. Policymakers and educators can't easily experiment with scenarios like 'what if we deploy V2G on this grid during a heatwave?' without months of work.
207.ap: Sumo×PyPSA is a web-based platform combining two simulators: SUMO (for traffic) and PyPSA (for power grids). It runs in a browser (no installation needed) and provides live visualization of Manhattan's actual infrastructure (8 substations, 15 transmission lines, 3,481 traffic signals, real street layout). Users interact with the visualization to trigger events (disable a substation, route vehicles to provide grid support) and watch cascading dynamics unfold in real-time. Four pre-built scenarios (heatwave cascades, V2G emergency response, manual recovery, custom scenarios) demonstrate the coupling.
207.ww: Browser-based real-time simulation works because commodity hardware is now fast enough, and WebSocket (a technology for live data streaming) enables instant feedback. Real data (OpenStreetMap, NYC traffic signals, power topology) makes it concrete, not abstract. Interactive exploration works because humans learn by experimenting; watching a simulation unfold is more memorable than reading a report.
207.po: Policymakers, educators, and researchers can now experiment with grid-traffic coupling interactively, observing how blackouts cascade through traffic signals and how V2G can prevent them. The platform makes complex infrastructure dynamics accessible and intuitive, enabling better decision-making about urban resilience.

208.bp: Cryptocurrencies like Ethereum are pseudonymous: your wallet address isn't your name, but all transactions are public on the blockchain. This is useful for criminals: if you steal funds (exploit a smart contract bug), you can transfer them across wallets, but observers can trace the flow. The question: how do criminals move money around after a theft to mix it into the legitimate economy without being caught? Understanding their patterns helps design detection systems.
208.wh: Most work on blockchain crime focuses on detecting stolen funds quickly (flag the wallet address) or identifying laundering accounts (find the mixer service). But behavioral patterns underlying how criminals actually launder money remain opaque. What do their transfer sequences look like? How quickly do they move funds? Do they spread money widely or concentrate it? These patterns aren't well studied, so detection systems might miss a key signal.
208.ap: This paper reconstructs token flows from exploiter-controlled addresses by tracing on-chain transactions. For each flow, they compute behavioral metrics: financial trajectory (how much value moves over time), temporal dynamics (how fast do transfers happen, are there delays?), structural topology (is the transfer graph a simple line or a complex tree?), and value dispersion (does the criminal spread funds across many wallets or keep them together?). They then empirically describe the patterns they observe across real exploits.
208.ww: Behavioral metrics work because human criminal behavior isn't perfectly random. Constraints like 'moving too fast attracts attention,' 'spreading too widely loses track,' and 'institutional requirements (like KYC) force certain patterns' shape real laundering. By measuring these constraints empirically, you expose the patterns that detection systems can learn to recognize.
208.po: The result is a behavioral profile of post-exploit laundering: rapid fund movement, shallow transfer structures, and broad dispersion. These patterns exhibit measurable regularities—meaning they can be incorporated into detection frameworks. Instead of watching for specific wallet addresses (which criminals can evade by changing wallets), detection can watch for behavioral anomalies, making it harder to launder stolen funds on Ethereum.

209.bp: Sending secret messages covertly (steganography) is valuable: political prisoners, journalists in hostile countries, security researchers in adversarial situations. The challenge: hide a large image inside something innocuous that travels openly. QR codes are perfect: they're everywhere (payment systems, packages, advertisements), and no one suspects them of hiding secrets. But how do you compress a large image into the tiny data region of a QR code while recovering it perfectly, and making the recovered image look realistic (not blocky or corrupted)?
209.wh: Traditional steganography embeds data in images, and security relies on disguising statistical properties (the hidden data shouldn't change pixel statistics in detectable ways). But compressing a large image into a QR code requires ~400× compression; you can't just hide data, you must transform it radically. Traditional methods would produce artifacts (blockiness) that either look unnatural or can't be recovered. Moreover, adversaries can attack transmission (degrade the QR code's quality), and pixel-based methods break under any noise.
209.ap: DiSCoQR uses diffusion models (generative models that learn to reverse corruption) combined with semantic compression. Instead of compressing pixel data directly, they extract the semantic information (what the image is, conceptually) and encode that into binary form (1s and 0s). The diffusion model learns to recognize this semantic code and reconstruct a realistic image that matches it. The binary code integrates seamlessly into a standard QR code's data region. The key: the reconstructed image isn't pixel-identical to the original, but it's semantically equivalent—it conveys the same information and works for downstream tasks.
209.ww: Semantic compression works here because you don't need pixel-perfect recovery; you need functional equivalence (the image still communicates its meaning). Diffusion models are good at this because they're trained to generate realistic images from noisy or compressed input—they handle the reconstruction naturally. The QR container is robust because error-correcting codes in QR (built-in redundancy) can handle some quality degradation; semantic equivalence means degradation doesn't break the message.
209.po: The result achieves 400× compression while maintaining semantic quality—a secret image travels inside an innocent QR code, and on recovery, it's realistic enough to serve its purpose (viewing, analysis, etc.). This enables covert communication through ubiquitous, undetectable channels, important for privacy in hostile environments.

210.bp: Online shopping relies on giving you recommendations tailored to your taste—predicting whether you'd like a shirt, movie, or song before you discover it yourself. Recommendation systems are the engines behind billions of dollars in e-commerce and streaming services. The question here is whether quantum computers, machines that operate on radically different physics than classical chips, can make these predictions faster or more accurate.
210.wh: Classical computers represent information as 0s and 1s in sequence; checking many possibilities means checking them one at a time or in parallel on many chips. Quantum computers work with qubits that can exist in multiple states simultaneously, theoretically allowing them to explore vast numbers of possibilities at once. But turning this quantum advantage into real recommendation systems is hard—it requires figuring out exactly which parts of the recommendation pipeline actually benefit from quantum processing, and then building systems that work on actual quantum hardware without just being nice theory.
210.ap: This paper proposes three quantum-enhanced recommendation methods targeting two key bottlenecks: learning good numerical representations of users and items (so similar users see similar recommendations), and finding the best match between a user and candidate items to recommend. They reformulate these steps using quantum operations, then adapt the ideas to two practical scenarios—recommendations based on social networks and graph-structured data. They test on six real datasets to see if quantum versions beat classical approaches.
210.ww: Quantum computers excel at finding patterns in high-dimensional spaces and comparing many possibilities in parallel. For representation learning, this quantum parallelism can explore user-item relationships more efficiently. For matching, quantum search can navigate the space of candidate items faster. Both give the system a speed or accuracy boost compared to doing it on a classical computer.
210.po: Experiments on six real-world datasets show the quantum methods outperform classical baselines, confirming the theoretical hypotheses that quantum computing can improve both representation learning and matching components. This bridges the gap between quantum theory and practical recommendation systems, showing concrete performance gains rather than remaining purely theoretical.

211.bp: Real-world networks—social platforms, transportation, communications—change over time: new friendships form, old links fade, communities shift. Analyzing these temporal networks at massive scale is crucial for understanding cities, disease spread, or information flow. But storing and processing every snapshot of a network across time is expensive, consuming enormous energy and storage.
211.wh: A straightforward approach computes everything fresh for each snapshot independently: store all edges, compute distances and clusters, then repeat. On networks with millions of nodes and billions of time steps, this becomes prohibitively expensive in energy and storage. Yet if you just throw away data from earlier snapshots, you lose the structure that makes temporal analysis valuable. The tension is between computational expense and information loss.
211.ap: Instead of processing each time snapshot separately, this method finds a compressed 'backbone' of the network that captures the persistent community structure across all time periods. The technique uses spectral analysis—a mathematical approach that finds the dominant patterns in how networks are organized. By analyzing the mathematical properties (eigenvalues and eigenvectors) of network Laplacians across time, they identify the stable structural modes that repeat and filter out noise and redundancy, creating a thin skeleton of the network that preserves communities while removing wasteful edges.
211.ww: Communities in real networks change slowly; the core structure is stable even as peripheral connections churn. By finding and keeping only the modes that persist across time, you remove the noise that costs computation without losing the signal about who belongs to which group. This is like removing background clutter from a photograph while keeping the subject sharp.
211.po: The temporal spectral backbone preserves the main community structure while cutting graph density drastically, reducing storage and computation cost. This supports 'Green AI'—doing meaningful analysis without wasting energy—and makes large-scale temporal network analysis feasible on evolving real-world networks like social media, transportation, or web systems.

212.bp: Many real-world systems aren't described by simple pairwise relationships—who likes whom, what talks to what. Instead, objects interact in groups or clusters: a research team (multiple people), a course (many students meeting together), molecules in chemical reactions. These are hypergraphs, and they show up in social networks, shopping recommendations, and image search. Processing them well means better recommendations, better understanding of collaboration, better search.
212.wh: Classical graph methods assume homophily—that similar nodes connect to each other. But real hypergraphs often have heterophily: a product might be reviewed by people with wildly different tastes; a course includes students from many backgrounds. Methods built on homophily fail on heterophilic data. When researchers tried to fix this by allowing longer-range connections across the hypergraph, they fixed one problem but created another: repeated mixing caused representations to become mushy and indistinguishable, a problem called oversmoothing. The dilemma is that you need either long-range connections (but oversmoothing) or short connections (but miss heterophilic patterns).
212.ap: This paper uses Riemannian geometry—a branch of math that studies curved spaces—to build hypergraph neural networks that adapt to local structure. Instead of using a one-size-fits-all message passing scheme, the method treats different regions of the hypergraph differently based on their local geometry. The core idea is a 'locally adaptive bottleneck' mechanism: where the hypergraph is dense or homophilic, the method allows tight local mixing; where it's sparse or heterophilic, it opens up longer-range connections. This geometric framework diagnoses the oversmoothing problem as a consequence of how information flows on curved manifolds.
212.ww: Curved spaces have different geometric properties than flat planes: distances and angles change in systematic ways. By analyzing hypergraphs through this geometric lens, the method can adapt message passing to the local geometry—allowing it to handle both dense homophilic regions and sparse heterophilic regions in the same framework. This avoids the forced trade-off between long-range connections and representation clarity.
212.po: The method works on both homophilic and heterophilic hypergraphs without requiring separate models for each case, addressing the long-range dependence problem while avoiding oversmoothing. Real-world applications like social network analysis and cross-modal retrieval (searching images with text or vice versa) benefit from this unified approach.

213.bp: Blockchains like Ethereum and VeChain rely on consensus mechanisms to make sure all participants agree on the order of transactions and that this order is permanent—a property called 'finality.' If finality fails, a transaction you thought was locked in could be undone, enabling fraud. VeChain is a real blockchain used for supply-chain tracking, and its security is crucial to trust in the system.
213.wh: Finality gadgets are mechanisms borrowed from Byzantine fault tolerance—systems that must agree even when some participants lie or fail. VeChain's approach attempts to guarantee that a block, once finalized, cannot be reordered. But proving a mechanism is secure requires adversarial thinking: can a clever attacker exploit weaknesses in the logic? The challenge is that consensus protocols are subtle; small gaps in the design can lead to exploitable flaws that are hard to spot without deep analysis.
213.ap: Researchers discovered a 'greedy attack' against VeChain's finality gadget. The attack works by having a malicious sealer (a node that proposes blocks) construct blocks in a way that manipulates the finality process itself. By choosing which transactions to include and how to structure block proposals, an attacker can reduce the probability that an honest sealer's block gets finalized from nearly 100% to just 19%. The authors validated the attack both theoretically and by running experiments on actual test networks.
213.ww: VeChain's finality logic has a subtle flaw: it doesn't perfectly account for the strategic choices an attacker can make when proposing blocks. By concentrating their malicious blocks strategically, an attacker can push the finality process into states where honest blocks are less likely to be chosen. The 'greediness' of the attack refers to the attacker prioritizing their own blocks at each step, which cascades into finality violations.
213.po: The attack concretely shows that VeChain's finality is not guaranteed—an honest block has only an 81% chance of staying finalized, which is unacceptable for a financial system. The research was disclosed responsibly to VeChain, and the team is now working together to redesign the finality gadget to close this loophole, improving the actual security of the blockchain.

214.bp: Federated learning lets many organizations—hospitals, mobile users, companies—train machine learning models together without sharing their raw data, preserving privacy while learning from everyone's information together. But the data across different organizations is messy and unbalanced: one hospital's patient population may have different characteristics than another's. This heterogeneity breaks many learning methods that assume uniform data.
214.wh: Data augmentation—creating artificial training examples by rotating images, swapping words, etc.—is a proven way to improve model quality. But blind augmentation in federated settings causes problems: if you apply the same augmentation to everyone, it might help one organization's data but hurt another's. The heterogeneous nature of each client's data means augmentation needs to be personalized. Yet communicating lots of augmentation policies between organizations is expensive and time-consuming, and asking each organization to hand-tune their own augmentation is impractical.
214.ap: RAFed proposes three components. First, a responsive augmentation method that each organization (client) learns which augmentations help its own local data without sharing raw data—the augmentation policy is learned through gradient-based optimization. Second, an approximate update mechanism that reduces communication overhead by not transmitting full policy updates every round. Third, a dynamic adaptive search that tailors the augmentation policies to each client's specific data distribution. The system works by having each client learn policy knowledge locally, then aggregating this knowledge across clients while respecting privacy.
214.ww: A responsive method learns what augmentation works for your specific data by testing it and seeing if it helps unseen local examples. This avoids blind augmentation that might hurt your data. By searching for personalized policies per client, the method adapts to heterogeneity. Approximate updates reduce the communication burden, which is usually the bottleneck in federated learning. Together, these mean better accuracy, less communication, and privacy is maintained because raw data never leaves any organization.
214.po: Experiments show RAFed achieves higher test accuracy than standard federated learning methods with less communication overhead, while maintaining privacy. This makes federated learning practical for real scenarios where data is distributed, heterogeneous, and sensitive—like hospitals or companies that cannot share raw data.

215.bp: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is when a language model answers questions by first retrieving relevant documents, then writing answers based on what it found. This works better than making stuff up from scratch. Multimodal RAG extends this to handle both images and text—so you can ask a question and get answers grounded in retrieved images and documents. Real-world applications include visual question answering and product search. The problem: if an attacker poisons the retrieval database with fake or misleading image-text pairs, the model retrieves garbage and generates wrong answers.
215.wh: Existing defenses for text-only RAG check whether retrieved documents are trustworthy. But multimodal RAG is harder: images and text interact in complex ways, and an attacker can craft image-text pairs that fool both the image retriever and the text matcher simultaneously. The attacker can make a fake pair highly relevant to a query while being completely misleading about the true answer. Defending against such poisoning in multimodal settings is new and difficult.
215.ap: IRAG uses 'hazard separation'—a structured defense that isolates potential contamination by leveraging redundancy and consensus. Instead of trusting a single retrieved image-text pair, the system retrieves multiple candidates and checks whether they agree on a consistent answer. If one pair is poisoned and tells a different story than the others, the system detects and discards it. The method treats images and text separately during this verification, reducing cross-modal interference that an attacker could exploit.
215.ww: Poisoning one or two image-text pairs is easy; poisoning all retrieved candidates to give a consistent false answer is much harder. By requiring consensus among multiple retrieved sources, the system becomes robust to minority contamination. Separating image and text verification prevents an attacker from crafting a pair that simultaneously fools both modalities. Redundancy and consensus are classical robustness principles that work here.
215.po: IRAG restores accuracy on poisoned datasets back to pre-attack levels (improving by 15–30%), while keeping the false answer rate below 7%. This makes multimodal RAG systems safe enough for open environments where attackers might try to poison databases.

216.bp: Restaurants are small businesses with high failure rates—learning which ones will survive matters to investors, landlords, cities, and workers. Survival depends on quality, service, but also on social visibility and trust from the community. Online reviews and rating networks (like Yelp and OpenRice) create a 'social fabric' around restaurants. Understanding this social network—who reviews what, which restaurants are well-connected in the community—could reveal which ones have strong social roots and will survive.
216.wh: Most survival prediction methods focus on review statistics—average rating, number of reviews, cuisine type—but ignore the larger social network in which restaurants are embedded. Network theory suggests that being 'embedded' in a community (having many review connections, being structurally central) should predict survival. Yet capturing temporal dynamics—how a restaurant's network position evolves over time—and integrating this with survival prediction is not straightforward. The challenge is bridging network theory with practical forecasting.
216.ap: This paper analyzes two dimensions of 'embeddedness' using network theory: structural embeddedness (how central is the restaurant in the review network) and positional embeddedness (what role does it play). They find empirically that restaurants with higher and growing network embeddedness are more likely to survive. They then build a Dynamic Embeddedness-aware Graph Neural Network (DyE-GNN) that explicitly models these network dimensions and how they evolve over time, treating restaurants as nodes and review connections as edges, with temporal snapshots tracking changes.
216.ww: A well-connected restaurant has more customers, more reviews, more word-of-mouth. If it's central in the community network, it's trusted and visible. If its position strengthens over time, it's gaining community roots. Embeddedness captures this social trust and visibility. Graph neural networks are designed to reason about network structure, so encoding embeddedness theory directly into their architecture makes them better at survival prediction than methods that ignore the network entirely.
216.po: DyE-GNN outperforms baselines on two real-world datasets (OpenRice and Yelp), showing that network embeddedness and its temporal evolution are strong predictors of restaurant survival. This demonstrates that viewing restaurants through a network lens—not just as isolated reviews—improves forecasting and could help stakeholders identify at-risk businesses earlier.

217.bp: Medical knowledge is vast and scattered across millions of scientific papers, textbooks, and databases. Doctors and researchers need to find reliable information quickly—when treating a rare disease, consulting studies is essential. Language models can search and synthesize information, but they sometimes 'hallucinate'—confidently stating facts that aren't true or don't exist. For medical decisions, hallucinations are dangerous. A system that grounds answers in an actual knowledge graph of verified facts could reduce these errors.
217.wh: A plain language model, given a medical question, might generate plausible-sounding but false claims because it's predicting the next likely word, not checking facts.
