If you add retrieval (searching for related documents), the model still might misinterpret or combine information incorrectly. Knowledge graphs—structured databases of facts like 'aspirin treats headaches'—are more reliable but incomplete; they don't cover every medical concept. The challenge is combining the flexibility of language models with the reliability of structured knowledge.
217.ap: This system uses a knowledge graph as a mediator between the language model and medical data. When a user asks a question, the graph constrains what the system can retrieve and reason about—it can only retrieve facts that are explicitly represented in the graph. The language model acts as a natural language interface, translating questions into graph queries and combining graph-retrieved facts into fluent answers. This 'graph-constrained RAG pipeline' ensures retrieved information comes from the graph, reducing hallucinations.
217.ww: A knowledge graph is a bottleneck that forces the system to use only verified facts: if a claim isn't in the graph, the model can't use it. This prevents fabrication. By making the knowledge graph the source of truth and the language model the communicator, the system gets both factuality (from the graph) and fluency (from the model). The language model's job is simplified to translating and synthesizing, not generating facts.
217.po: On a curated medical dataset, the system achieves 71% retrieval precision and outperforms a standalone language model on all evaluation metrics. This shows that constraining language models with knowledge graphs improves medical information retrieval reliability, moving toward AI systems that doctors can trust for clinical decision support.

218.bp: Over 60% of web traffic now comes from mobile devices—phones and tablets that run on batteries. When a web page consumes lots of power, it drains battery, frustrates users, and creates environmental waste. Optimizing energy is as important as optimizing speed, yet most web development tools focus only on performance metrics like page load time. A developer needs to know: does my website guzzle power, and what can I change?
218.wh: Energy consumption and performance don't correlate perfectly: a fast page might use lots of power (running complex calculations), while a slow page might use little. Performance-based metrics miss the energy story. Additionally, measuring real energy consumption requires specialized hardware and testing on actual devices, which is impractical for developers. Most developers lack tools that translate code changes into energy predictions.
218.ap: GreenWebInspector analyzes the static structure and content of a web page—layout complexity, number of images, animation types, DOM size, JavaScript complexity—to predict energy tier (how much power the page will consume). These device-independent features are extracted directly from the page's HTML and CSS without needing to run it on real hardware. The tool provides real-time predictions and suggestions for reducing energy use.
218.ww: Page structure determines rendering work and CPU load: complex layouts, large images, and JavaScript all consume power during rendering and interaction. By learning patterns from real measurements of which structural features correlate with high power consumption, the tool can predict energy tier without needing expensive device measurements. Device-independent features work because the physics of rendering is similar across devices.
218.po: GreenWebInspector achieves 9.7% higher accuracy than performance-based methods, showing that directly analyzing structure is better at predicting energy than inferring it from speed. Developers and researchers can now instantly assess energy footprint during design and browsing, enabling more sustainable web development and helping users make environmentally conscious browsing choices.

219.bp: The decentralized web—where data and services are spread across different organizations rather than centralized in one place—is becoming reality. Each organization might have a semantic graph (a structured database of concepts and relationships) but cannot share it due to privacy rules. Yet these graphs are useful for search, recommendations, and reasoning. Federated learning offers a way: many organizations train a shared model without sending raw data. But real semantic graphs in the wild are messy: some nodes lack attributes, relationships are incomplete.
219.wh: By first diagnosing incompleteness privately and then strategically filling gaps (edges, not attributes), the system preserves privacy while reducing missingness. Contrastive learning finds patterns in graph structure without requiring complete data. Transferring knowledge across organizations about which relationships are likely helps each local graph, while the privacy-preserving diagnosis ensures sensitive data remains local.
219.ap: FedCL (Federated Contrastive Learning) introduces two modules. A topology estimation module quietly measures the degree of structural incompleteness in each organization's graph without revealing sensitive data, using rate-distortion theory to quantify this privately. A federated reconstruction module uses these measurements to generate plausible missing edges while avoiding inferring sensitive attributes. The system then applies graph contrastive learning—a technique that learns by comparing similar and dissimilar structures—across these reconstructed subgraphs, ensuring consistency.
219.po: Experiments on citation networks and web datasets show FedCL outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. This enables federated learning on real semantic graphs that are incomplete and heterogeneous, supporting decentralized web services that can collaborate without sharing sensitive data.

220.bp: Security teams use SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) platforms to detect attacks by writing rules that flag suspicious activity—for example, 'alert if login happens from two countries in 10 minutes.' But different SIEM vendors have different rule languages: Splunk uses SPL, Microsoft uses KQL, Google uses YARA-L. When a company switches platforms or uses multiple tools, they must rewrite all rules by hand—a time-consuming task requiring deep expertise. An automated converter would save enormous effort.
220.wh: Each vendor's rule language has different syntax and features; they evolved independently. A rule written for one platform can't simply be translated word-for-word to another—the underlying logic must be extracted and remapped to the target platform's concepts. Additionally, the vendor documentation and schema keep changing, making it hard to know all the capabilities of the target language. Manual conversion requires reading the source rule, understanding the detection logic, learning the target language, and carefully reimplementing the logic—error-prone and slow.
220.ap: ARuleCon is an agentic (AI-powered) converter that automates this process. It uses three components. First, an intermediate representation (IR) that captures the core detection logic in a vendor-neutral way—what the rule is trying to detect, independent of platform. Second, an agentic retrieval-augmented generation pipeline that fetches official vendor documentation for the target platform to understand its capabilities and schema. Third, a Python-based consistency checker that runs both the original and converted rules on test data to verify the conversion is semantically correct.
220.ww: By translating to a vendor-neutral intermediate language first, the system separates 'what to detect' from 'how to write it in a particular vendor's syntax.' Retrieving official documentation ensures the conversion uses current, authoritative schema information. Testing both versions on the same data catches subtle semantic drifts—cases where the converted rule almost works but fails on edge cases. This combination ensures reliable automated conversion.
220.po: Security professionals no longer need deep domain expertise in multiple rule languages; ARuleCon handles the conversion automatically and verifies correctness. This dramatically reduces effort in migrating SIEM platforms or maintaining rules across multiple tools, preserving the value of existing rule investments across vendor ecosystems.

221.bp: Internet memes—images with text—spread political messages, ideas, and unfortunately, hate speech that targets specific groups. Platforms need to detect harmful memes to prevent harassment and discrimination. Existing detection methods analyze both the image and text together. But in real-world scenarios, text is often missing because optical character recognition (OCR) fails on stylized fonts, angles, or image quality. When one source of information is missing, detection methods often fail.
221.wh: Harmful meme detection relies on multimodal information: analyzing both the image and text together to understand intent. Methods trained on complete image-text pairs perform poorly when text is missing. Simply dropping missing modalities or using default values doesn't work—it throws away useful signal. The core problem is that existing methods tightly couple image and text processing; if one is missing, the whole system breaks. Yet many real memes lack usable text.
221.ap: This paper proposes learning a shared representation that treats image and text independently, then combines them. The key idea: project both image and text separately into a shared latent space where similar concepts from different modalities cluster together. When text is missing, the method falls back on just the image representation, which still works well because the shared space was trained to capture the same concepts regardless of modality. This shared representation learns to integrate visual and textual features without rigid dependence on text.
221.ww: By learning independent projections into a shared space, the method decouples modalities. If text is missing, the image projection to the shared space still contains meaningful signal. Because the space was learned with both modalities present, the image representation alone is more informative than it would be from a text-dependent model. This robustness comes from the learning process itself, not from post-hoc patching.
221.po: Experiments on two benchmark datasets show the method outperforms baselines when text is missing, and improves overall robustness. By reducing dependence on text, the system handles real-world messy data (poor OCR, missing captions) and detects harmful memes more reliably, improving platform safety in realistic conditions.

222.bp: Generative AI models are now deployed widely, but users need transparent documentation: What data was the model trained on? What are its limitations? Does it have biases? Model cards and data cards standardize this documentation, helping users make informed decisions. But writing these cards by hand is tedious, and websites like Hugging Face store incomplete information. An automated system that extracts and synthesizes documentation from papers and repositories could ensure all models are properly documented.
222.wh: Current automation relies on fixed templates: same questions asked the same way for all papers. But papers have different structures—some emphasize data, others focus on methods. Additionally, Hugging Face and similar repositories have inconsistent metadata: some models documented thoroughly, others poorly. No standardized benchmarks exist to evaluate whether auto-generated cards are actually good. The combination of diverse paper structures, incomplete metadata, and lack of evaluation benchmarks makes the problem hard.
222.ap: AdaQE-CG uses dynamic query expansion: instead of asking the same questions repeatedly, the system iteratively refines its extraction queries based on what it finds in each paper. The Intra-Paper module generates increasingly refined queries to capture richer information from the paper. An Inter-Card Completion module fills missing fields by finding similar model cards in a curated pool and borrowing relevant information. The authors also create MetaGAI-Bench, a large expert-annotated dataset for benchmarking card generation quality.
222.ww: Fixed templates miss information because papers vary in structure; adaptive queries adjust to each paper's unique structure. Cross-card knowledge transfer compensates for incomplete metadata: if one paper is missing a detail, similar papers might have it, so the system can infer the missing field. A large expert-annotated benchmark enables fair comparison and drives quality improvements. Together, these improve documentation completeness and consistency.
222.po: The paper introduces MetaGAI-Bench as the first large-scale benchmark for evaluating generative AI documentation, enabling systematic progress. AdaQE-CG achieves better documentation generation through dynamic adaptation and cross-card transfer, ensuring more models have transparent, complete cards and users can make more informed decisions about model selection.

223.bp: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is powerful: ask a question, retrieve relevant documents, then generate an answer grounded in those documents. But there's a hidden failure mode: the system retrieves documents that seem relevant but don't actually help the model reason to the right answer. Improving retrieval performance doesn't always improve reasoning accuracy—the retrieved documents might be distracting red herrings. Understanding and fixing this gap is crucial for RAG to work reliably in practice.
223.wh: Traditional RAG metrics measure retrieval in isolation: did the system retrieve relevant documents? But relevance and usefulness are different. A document can be relevant to the question yet unhelpful for reasoning—it might contain partial information, conflicting claims, or correct information mixed with red herrings. Methods that optimize only for retrieval recall (getting documents related to the query) often retrieve lots of noise alongside useful information, which confuses the reasoning step. The challenge is understanding why retrieving more relevant documents doesn't translate to better answers.
223.ap: The paper proposes a new metric, Recall Conversion Rate (RCR), that measures how well retrieval translates to reasoning accuracy. They find that as retrieval recall improves with standard methods, RCR declines sharply—retrieved results grow increasingly filled with noise. NeocorRAG addresses this by focusing on retrieval quality, not just quantity. It identifies evidence chains—sequences of related facts that together support an answer. An activated search algorithm finds a refined set of candidates, constrained decoding ensures evidence chains are coherent, and the retrieved chains guide optimization of the entire retrieval process.
223.ww: Evidence chains are harder to retrieve than isolated relevant documents, but once retrieved, they're much more useful for reasoning. A chain forces coherence: if three documents are retrieved as a chain, they must connect logically and support a unified conclusion. This coherence reduces noise and distraction. By optimizing for chains rather than individual documents, the system improves quality at the cost of potentially reducing quantity—but the trade-off favors reasoning accuracy.
223.po: NeocorRAG achieves holistic retrieval quality optimization: less irrelevant information cluttering the result, more explicit evidence supporting answers, more effective reasoning accuracy despite potentially retrieving fewer total documents. This addresses the critical gap in RAG where retrieval performance doesn't translate to reasoning performance, making RAG systems more reliable.

224.bp: Clustering algorithms group similar items together—in social networks, clustering identifies communities; in customer data, it segments markets. But clustering can inadvertently discriminate: if age, gender, or income is correlated with the data being clustered, the resulting groups might underrepresent minorities. Fair clustering ensures that sensitive groups are represented proportionally in the solution. This matters for fairness in social network analysis, resource allocation, and many real-world applications.
224.wh: The k-center problem asks: choose k representative points that minimize the maximum distance to any other point. This is efficient but ignores fairness. Adding fairness constraints—requiring that each sensitive group contributes a bounded number of representatives—seems straightforward but makes the problem much harder. The challenge is especially acute in the streaming setting: data arrives one by one, you must decide immediately whether to pick each point, and you can't store everything. Balancing fairness and streaming efficiency is non-trivial.
224.ap: The authors present a one-pass streaming algorithm for fair k-center clustering in Euclidean space. The algorithm processes items sequentially and decides in real-time whether to select each as a center, while respecting fairness constraints. The approach achieves an approximation ratio of 4.46, meaning the solution is at most 4.46 times worse than the optimal fair solution—a significant improvement over previous work (which had ratio 5+epsilon).
224.ww: Euclidean space (the usual 2D or 3D space) has special geometric properties that streaming algorithms can exploit better than general metric spaces. The geometric structure allows the algorithm to make better decisions about which points to select as representatives while maintaining fairness. The approximation factor of 4.46 vs. previous 5+ epsilon shows that streaming fair clustering is actually better in Euclidean space than in general metrics—a surprising insight.
224.po: This streaming algorithm enables fair clustering on massive social network data in a single pass, without storing all data in memory. It improves the theoretical approximation factor and demonstrates that Euclidean geometry enables tighter guarantees, making fair clustering practical for real-world systems where data flows continuously and fairness matters.

225.bp: Vision-language models (systems that see images and understand text together) are incredibly powerful but expensive to run. When millions of people use them online, companies either suffer slow responses or rack up huge bills. The goal is to serve these models to users fast and cheaply without sacrificing the ability to answer hard visual questions.
225.wh: The problem sits at a crossroads: run everything on the cloud and you get accuracy but latency spikes and costs explode; run everything on a phone and you save money but the tiny device can't hold the full model, so answers get worse. You can't have all three—speed, cost, and accuracy—at the same time. The trick is knowing which tasks are easy enough for a phone to handle and which ones need the full model back in the cloud.
225.ap: ShiftVL splits the work between your device and a distant server. Your phone holds a smaller, simpler version of the model, tuned with ViTexLoRA (a way to add task-specific skills without teaching the whole model). For routine requests it answers directly. For tricky or rare requests, it asks the cloud server with its bigger, smarter model to take over. It also predicts which tasks you'll ask about next and loads their helper-tools early, like preheating an oven.
225.ww: This works because most requests fall into a few common patterns—they're similar enough that a phone can spot them and answer. Only the weird edge cases really need the full brain in the cloud. By shipping the easy work to the phone, you slash the number of expensive cloud calls. By predicting what's coming next, you avoid the delay of fetching tools on demand. The result is the cloud does less, costs less, and the phone answers faster.
225.po: In real tests with actual vision-language models, ShiftVL cut cloud costs by up to 76% and response delays by 43%, while still keeping answers accurate across many different visual tasks. That's the practical gain: a system that feels fast to users and doesn't bankrupt companies running it.

226.bp: When companies run large language models in production—think millions of queries per second on real hardware—tiny choices about batch size, data-copying strategy, and chip scheduling matter hugely for how fast the system runs. Every new model and every new setup (different GPUs, different cloud data centers) requires manually figuring out the best numbers all over again, which is tedious and error-prone.
226.wh: The parameter space explodes quickly: batch size, GPU parallelism, graph caching, topology—each one interacts with the others in subtle ways. A batch size of 64 might be perfect on one server but terrible on another because of how memory flows. You can't just copy settings from your friend's setup because their hardware is different. Testing every combination by hand would take months.
226.ap: llm-tuna wraps a search tool (Bayesian optimization) around the open-source vLLM serving engine and parallelizes the search across multiple machines. Instead of manually guessing, it systematically tries promising configurations, learns which ones work best, and zeros in on high-performing settings. It avoids repeating the same mistakes and respects hardware limits so it never suggests a setup that's worse than just running vLLM as-is.
226.ww: Bayesian search is smart about picking which experiments to try next—it learns a model of how performance depends on the settings and picks configurations likely to be winners. By running many trials in parallel across servers, you get the answer fast. The safety guarantee (never worse than the baseline) means you always have a fallback if the search finds nothing better.
226.po: On real language models (including huge mixtures with hundreds of billions of parameters), llm-tuna found setups that run 33% faster than vLLM's default, without any human tuning. For companies deploying these models, that's a direct win in throughput and cost.

227.bp: Child sexual abuse material (CSAM) is a horrifying crime, and detecting it online saves lives. A crucial step is figuring out the age of the child in the image, both for law enforcement investigations and for automated filtering systems to catch and remove this content quickly.
227.wh: Machine-learning systems trained to classify ages often work like a black box: they give an answer but don't explain why, making it hard for human experts and investigators to trust or override them. Also, attackers actively try to fool age classifiers to evade detection. The challenge is building a system that's both explainable (so humans can see the reasoning) and robust against attacks.
227.ap: The researchers built a system that mirrors how human experts actually decide a child's age: it looks at the face, the body proportions, and biological markers together. Instead of one neural network black-box, it combines three separate pathways for these three signals, then fuses their outputs. This way, when the system says 'this is a prepubescent child,' you can see which of the three signals led to that choice.
227.ww: By splitting the decision into three parallel human-interpretable pathways, the model is forced to make decisions for real, visible reasons—not hidden internal patterns that might be brittle or spurious. If someone tries to fool one signal (e.g., add makeup), the other signals still work. The fusion approach is inherently more resilient because it doesn't rely on a single decision route.
227.po: The fusion method achieved 81% accuracy (F1-score 0.807) on real CSAM cases for the most critical group (youngest children), and it resisted adversarial attacks better than end-to-end models. For law enforcement, that means faster, more trustworthy automation to identify and block abuse material.

228.bp: In digital marketing, companies invest money in ads and campaigns to make sales. Traditionally, they set a budget at the start—say $10,000—and run their campaign. But in reality, how well the campaign performs should influence how much they spend next: if it's working great, invest more; if it's failing, pull back.
228.wh: The traditional math (Bandits with Knapsacks) assumes a fixed budget you announce upfront. Real marketing doesn't work that way. The budget and the results are tied together in a loop: profits flow back into the next round of spending. This creates a circular dependency that breaks the traditional math, and it opens a new risk: you could spend so much on a bad campaign that you run out of money and go bankrupt. Nobody had solved this before.
228.ap: The researchers built new math (Bandits with Endogenous Knapsacks) that treats the budget as a moving target, shaped by performance. They designed an algorithm that tunes spending up or down based on how well each marketing channel is working, while watching out for the ruin scenario (when you lose more than you have left). They also solve a two-level problem: not only how much to spend right now, but also how to set your reinvestment rate for the whole campaign.
228.ww: The primal-dual algorithm handles the circular feedback by updating both the spending and the constraint (budget) together, step by step. The risk-aware piece works because it doesn't just chase profit—it also reserves a safety margin to never go broke. By learning the optimal reinvestment rate, you adapt how greedy you are, trading off short-term wins for long-term safety.
228.po: They validated the theory with both live A/B tests on real ad campaigns and simulations. The system can now adaptively increase or decrease marketing spend in response to performance while guaranteeing the company won't go bankrupt, a fundamental improvement over fixed-budget approaches.

229.bp: When you want to predict when a customer will buy again, or how long until a machine part fails, you're predicting time intervals in human behavior or systems. Large language models are incredibly flexible and can read context, so they seem like they should be good at this. The question is: are they actually better than traditional time-series models?
229.wh: Large language models are trained to handle language, not quantitative patterns in time. When you add more context about the customer (purchase history, browsing, demographics), you'd think it helps—but it can actually overwhelm the model and make it confused about the numbers. This contradicts the common assumption that 'more information is always better.'
229.ap: The researchers tested modern language models on a simple but realistic task: predict how many days until a customer repurchases. They compared zero-shot language models against statistical methods (like exponential smoothing) and traditional machine-learning models, adding different amounts of customer context each time. They measured accuracy (how close to the true interval) and ranked the methods.
229.ww: Language models excel at language patterns but struggle with raw quantitative structure—they're built to predict the next word, not the next number in a sequence. Adding context about behavior helps up to a point, but too much context floods the model with information it doesn't know how to compress. Statistical and machine-learning models, by contrast, are explicitly designed to spot numerical patterns and don't get distracted by side details.
229.po: Large language models beat simple statistical baselines but consistently lost to dedicated machine-learning models. Even more surprising, adding extra user details beyond moderate context actually made language models worse. The takeaway: language models aren't the right tool for time-interval prediction, and hybrid systems that combine statistical methods with linguistic context might be the real win.

230.bp: Recommendation systems learn what each user likes and what each product is about, then suggest relevant items. But users' tastes change over time and products' popularity shifts—a sweater is hot in winter, irrelevant in summer. The system must update its internal understanding of users and items as new interactions arrive, capturing this temporal drift.
230.wh: Most systems update their understanding of users and items after each interaction, but they overwrite the old information with the new. So if someone loved horror movies for years but watched one rom-com last week, the system might start recommending rom-coms, forgetting the long history. Also, historical patterns (e.g., this user always buys from this seller) get erased. The system loses the full picture of who someone really is.
230.ap: TraceRec retraces the history of each user and item by walking backward through past interactions (reverse chronological random walks). For each neighbor in that historical path, it restores that person's or item's representation to what it was at the time of the original interaction. Then it recommends based on this richer, time-aware picture instead of just the latest snapshot.
230.ww: By remembering each interaction in its original context (who someone was at that moment, not who they are today), the system captures stable long-term preferences without erasing them. The reverse walks prioritize recent history but don't ignore older patterns. The result is a model that sees users as they evolve over time, not as a single frozen state.
230.po: On six real-world datasets of user behavior over time, TraceRec beat eight competing methods, lifting the recall metric (did the user click on a recommended item?) by up to 17%. This means more relevant suggestions and better user satisfaction in systems that have to adapt to changing tastes.

231.bp: In web search, e-commerce, and social networks, data is connected in complex, high-order ways: a person is connected to many products, many reviews, many other people. Traditional graph neural networks struggle with these multidimensional relationships, so special hypergraph models were invented. But these models are expensive and slow. Knowledge distillation (teaching a small student model to copy a large teacher) promises to speed things up, if done right.
231.wh: Current distillation methods lean on a single large teacher, which limits what knowledge the student can learn—it's like studying from one textbook. Also, they assume the student just needs to copy the teacher's outputs, ignoring the student's own ability to learn the structure of the data. Neither side is fully developed.
231.ap: MARCH uses multiple large teachers, each trained differently, so they see different structure in the hypergraph. These teachers transfer knowledge at two levels: individual nodes and groups of nodes (hyperedges). The student learns from all of them at once, picking up complementary insights. The student also uses a contrastive loss (a technique that pushes similar things together and different things apart) to build strong internal representations, not just copy the teachers.
231.ww: Diverse teachers each see different high-order patterns, so together they teach a richer picture than any single teacher can convey. The two-level transfer captures both local node details and global group structure. The student's own contrastive learning forces it to encode structure meaningfully, so it's not just a passive copier—it actively builds better representations than its teachers had.
231.po: In experiments, MARCH's student models learned better than any single teacher alone, and sometimes outperformed all the teachers together. This is a hallmark of good distillation: the student becomes smarter than its teachers by synthesizing their diverse views.

232.bp: Social media is filled with text, images, audio, and video all mixed together. Powerful multimodal AI systems can now understand and generate across these formats, but deploying them on platforms at scale raises real safety questions: Can they be tricked? Do they hallucinate false information? Are they misused to spread misinformation and hate?
232.wh: Multimodal models are so new and powerful that we don't yet have solid benchmarks or safety tests for them in real social media contexts. Each modality (text, images, audio, video) has its own risks, and combining them creates new failure modes nobody has fully mapped yet. Platform companies need guidance on what to measure and how to defend against abuse.
232.ap: This workshop brought together researchers and practitioners to discuss two main areas: (1) how to fuse text, images, audio, and video together safely and correctly, and (2) how to evaluate and test these systems for both capability (do they follow instructions?) and safety (do they avoid hallucination, misleading output, or adversarial manipulation?). Papers covered multimodal fusion techniques and adversarial robustness.
232.ww: By collecting research under one roof, the workshop creates a common language and shared benchmarks. Safety evaluation on large multimodal models requires cross-disciplinary work (AI safety, platform policy, linguistics, computer vision) that individual labs struggle to do alone. Standardized tests help platforms deploy these systems more confidently.
232.po: The workshop accepted 10 papers from 7 countries, providing researchers and platform teams with both novel methods for multimodal analysis and practical safety evaluation strategies for large multimodal models deployed on social media.

233.bp: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is a technique where a large language model reads web documents first, then generates an answer. This helps the model give current, fact-checked answers without retraining. But the quality of retrieved documents directly controls answer quality, and real-world web corpora are messy and full of misinformation.
233.wh: Rerankers improve RAG by pushing accurate, relevant documents higher in the result list. But when you look carefully at what happens to document types during reranking, something surprising happens: while helpful documents rank higher, harmful documents (misinformation, junk, misleading content) also rise higher. The reranker is so focused on relevance that it accidentally promotes both good and bad content together.
233.ap: The researchers studied what happens to different types of documents (ground truth, misinformation, junk) before and after reranking. They discovered harmful documents increased significantly in the top results. Based on this finding, they built a risk-aware reranker that balances the benefit of pushing relevant content up against the harm of surfacing misinformation, using a metric called information gain.
233.ww: Rerankers optimize a single signal (relevance), which blindly elevates both true and false content if they're both relevant to the query. By explicitly modeling the risk—the chance a harmful document gets shown to the language model—you can trade off a small loss in top-1 accuracy for a big reduction in misinformation exposure. This prevents the language model from being tricked by false content.
233.po: The risk-aware method ensures that harmful documents in top results decrease while still ranking ground-truth documents highly, reducing the chance that language models generate and spread misinformation across the web—a direct safety win for RAG systems.

234.bp: Website fingerprinting is a traffic analysis attack: an eavesdropper watches the encrypted data flowing to and from your device, sees the pattern of packet sizes and timings, and figures out which website you're visiting—even though the content is encrypted. This breaks your privacy. Defense systems try to hide these patterns, but attackers keep improving their techniques.
234.wh: Most fingerprinting research assumes people only visit website homepages, but real people jump to dozens of subpages, open multiple tabs, and mix activities. Previous work couldn't distinguish which subpage you visited (just 'you were on Facebook'), and multi-tab settings weren't realistic. This gap between lab and reality limits how well defenses actually work.
234.ap: HiFi-WF models the fingerprinting task as a hierarchy: first identify the main website (homepage level), then identify the specific subpage within it. A unified neural network extracts features from traffic patterns, and layered encoders model the hierarchy. Attention mechanisms capture dependencies between the two levels, and an enhanced decoder prevents nonsensical predictions (e.g., a subpage that doesn't exist on that website).
234.ww: By treating the problem hierarchically instead of flat, the model can leverage constraints: some subpages only appear on certain websites. The multi-level attention captures that if you know the website, that constrains which subpages are possible. This structure lets the model learn more efficiently and make finer-grained inferences than if it tried to predict subpage directly.
234.po: HiFi-WF achieves fine-grained subpage identification in both single-tab and multi-tab settings, moving beyond the unrealistic homepage-only assumption. This more realistic evaluation helps designers build better privacy defenses by revealing what attackers can actually infer from real-world browsing patterns.

235.bp: Real-time systems (streaming data from sensors, servers, applications) produce data constantly, and anomalies—unusual events that deviate from normal—must be caught instantly. Think equipment failures, fraud transactions, or security breaches. But as systems evolve, the definition of 'normal' changes, so anomaly detection must adapt online without storing massive historical data.
235.wh: Existing systems assume anomalies fit fixed, known patterns, so they struggle when the normal behavior itself drifts (new feature launches, seasonal change). Also, storing all history to retrain is memory-hungry, and retraining from scratch for each new batch is slow. You need to learn continuously without blowing up memory or computation.
235.ap: DESS builds a small, representative summary (proxy) of all the historical data seen so far, capturing what 'normal' looks like. As new data arrives, it updates this proxy to include fresh patterns. For each incoming data point, it uses multiple timescale features (short-term blips, long-term trends) and only trains a small, modular subset of its parameters. Old, trained parts are frozen, so only new lightweight features are tuned.
235.ww: The compact proxy acts like a memory capsule: it shrinks terabytes of history into a small model that still encodes what to expect. By mixing multi-timescale features, you catch both sudden spikes and gradual drift. Training only a subset of parameters (parameter-efficient training) keeps memory low and speed high, so the system adapts in real time without refetching the past.
235.po: On real anomaly datasets, DESS beat competing methods by up to 17.5% in accuracy while cutting training time by 65%. Real-time systems can now adapt to changing normal patterns without exploding memory or computation costs.

236.bp: Harmful content—misinformation, hate speech, propaganda, cyberbullying—spreads across social media, news sites, and messaging apps in many languages and on many platforms. Shutting down one source just pushes bad actors to another platform or language. There's a need for research that sees harmful content as a whole, not isolated pieces.
236.wh: Most research tackles one harm type on one platform (misinformation on Twitter, hate speech on Facebook), in one language. But harmful content is strategic and adaptive: spreaders shift platforms and languages to evade moderation. Without seeing the big picture, local defenses can't stop the underlying problem.
236.ap: The DHOW workshop brought together researchers to study harmful content (misinformation, abuse, propaganda) as one phenomenon spanning platforms, languages, and current events. Papers covered detection, mitigation, and characterization of harmful content using both traditional methods and large multimodal models. The workshop explicitly included current crisis topics (wars, elections) and multilingual coverage (7 countries).
236.ww: By unifying the study of different harm types under one frame, patterns emerge: a misinformation campaign on Facebook might branch to TikTok and Telegram; a hate-speech vector in English might appear in German or Arabic. Researchers sharing tools and datasets can build defenses that work across these transitions, not just within one silo.
236.po: The workshop accepted papers on cross-platform, multilingual harmful content detection and mitigation, providing the research community with methods and datasets for defending against coordinated, adaptive disinformation and abuse at scale.

237.bp: Networks show relationships between things: people following people, cities connected by roads, atoms bonded in molecules. Traditional graph neural networks assume a simple rule: connected things are similar (homophily). But real networks violate this constantly. In social networks, people often befriend those different from them; in biology, opposing charges attract. The assumption breaks, and performance collapses.
237.wh: When a network violates the homophily assumption, existing methods treat those 'rule-breaking' connections as noise and try to remove them. But removing edges throws away real information. The challenge is building a method that respects both homophily edges (where similar things connect) and heterophily edges (where different things connect) as equally valid.
237.ap: Graph Weighted Aggregation (GWA) uses Ricci Curvature (a geometric measure of how space curves around a point) to quantify the influence between connected nodes. It combines three pieces of information: the features of nodes, the network's structure, and label information (what class each node belongs to). Based on this, it weights each connection: homophily edges get high weight, heterophily edges get moderate weight, and all are used together.
237.ww: Ricci Curvature naturally distinguishes homophily from heterophily: it's high where similar nodes cluster (homophily) and low where different nodes connect (heterophily). By using it as a weight, the model can attend to both types of edges without throwing any away. Combining features, topology, and labels ensures the weighting reflects the true role each edge plays.
237.po: GWA outperformed state-of-the-art methods on benchmark datasets, showing that respecting both homophily and heterophily edges leads to better performance than treating one as noise. This is especially important for real-world networks where mixed connection types are the norm.

238.bp: Time series forecasting (predicting electricity demand tomorrow, traffic flow in an hour, stock prices next week) powers infrastructure planning and trading. Multivariate forecasting (tracking dozens of correlated signals) is especially hard. New approaches use frequency-domain analysis (breaking signals into sine waves) to capture repeating patterns, but two pitfalls trip them up repeatedly.
238.wh: In frequency analysis, weak but important signals (rare irregular patterns) drown in noise and get ignored during training. Meanwhile, strong periodic signals (daily, weekly patterns) get distorted when neural networks transform them, weakening the prediction. You need to preserve both the weak details and the strong cycles without one eating the other.
238.ap: GFMixer splits the problem into two parallel paths. The first (Temporal Gradient Block) finds weak signals by looking at how the time series is changing, detecting small but meaningful movements. The second (Fourier-Aware Attention Block) preserves strong periodic patterns by explicitly modeling frequency information and guarding against distortion. Both outputs combine via residual connections, blending the two sources of information.
238.ww: By separating low-amplitude (weak) and high-amplitude (strong) signals into different pathways, each pathway can specialize: one focuses on finding needles in noise, the other on protecting structure. Temporal gradients amplify weak signals by looking at rate of change, not raw values. Fourier-aware attention knows what periodic structure looks like and protects it explicitly.
238.po: GFMixer achieved first-place rankings on 37 out of standard benchmarks, beating all competitors. As a plug-and-play module, it also improved mainstream forecasting architectures. For real-world systems, this means more accurate demand and traffic predictions, reducing waste and improving planning.

239.bp: Multiple organizations (hospitals, banks, retailers) often want to collaborate on data science to improve service. The problem: each organization is reluctant to share raw data for privacy and legal reasons. Manifold learning—a technique that builds low-dimensional maps of high-dimensional data—could help them collaborate if done securely, with no single party seeing anyone else's data.
239.wh: Standard manifold learning algorithms require all data in one place or heavy communication between parties. Secure computation (techniques that let parties compute together without revealing data) is extremely expensive: each operation requires multiple rounds of encrypted messages. Scaling to real datasets seems impossible without reducing the computation somehow.
239.ap: SIsomap applies secret sharing (breaking data into cryptographic pieces shared among parties so no one party can reconstruct it) to Isomap (a classic manifold learning method). The researchers optimized the two costliest steps: finding top-k nearest neighbors and computing shortest paths in a graph. They exploit properties of Isomap to skip unnecessary secure operations, cutting 99% of communication overhead.
239.ww: By designing secure protocols specifically for Isomap's algorithm (not generic secure computation), you can skip steps that generic methods can't avoid. For example, in Isomap you only need top-k neighbors, not all-pairs, so the secure version only computes what's necessary. The result is orders-of-magnitude speedup without sacrificing privacy guarantees.
239.po: SIsomap's secure top-k nearest neighbors is 13.6 times faster than prior work, and its shortest paths is 1818 times faster. End-to-end, SIsomap is 11 to 29 times faster than baseline secure solutions, making collaborative manifold learning feasible for real multi-organization scenarios.

240.bp: Knowledge graphs—huge databases mapping entities and their relationships—power everything from search engines to recommendation systems. To make these graphs more useful, we need to discover new rules (like "if A is married to B, then B is married to A") automatically rather than by hand. But searching for all possible rules is like looking through every possible combination of facts in a library; the number of possibilities explodes exponentially.
240.wh: The AMIE algorithm, a standard tool for finding rules, works thoroughly but slowly—it explores so many rule candidates that it chokes on modern graphs with millions of facts. You could speed it up by searching less carefully, but then you miss good rules or waste time on bad paths. The core tension: thoroughness costs time, but cutting corners costs quality.
240.ap: MiniAMIE takes AMIE and makes two smart trades. First, it narrows the search space by being pickier about which rule patterns it considers (restricting the language bias). Second, instead of computing exact metrics for every candidate rule—an expensive operation—it uses fast mathematical approximations to estimate whether a rule is likely to be good, then only does the exact calculation for the most promising ones.
240.ww: The reason this works: you don't need to compute everything perfectly to know which paths are worth exploring. Many bad rules are obviously bad (you can tell with a quick estimate), so you skip them immediately. For the rules that matter, you still do the real calculation. This is the principle of early filtering—most work is thrown out cheaply, and expensive work goes only to the candidates that deserve it.
240.po: The concrete win is substantial speed-up (the paper says so) while keeping rule quality decent. This trades a small loss in how many true rules you catch for orders-of-magnitude faster mining, making it practical to run on real knowledge graphs where AMIE alone would take hours.

241.bp: Online travel platforms (sites that book rooms) lose money when hotels don't update their inventory in real time. The platform sees rooms as sold out even though they're actually empty—a supply strike that wastes potential revenue. You could solve this by proactively adding inventory (telling the system a room is available), but you need to know: will this actually make the platform more money, or just cannibalize sales from one hotel to another?
241.wh: Asking 'does adding inventory help?' is a causal question: does the intervention (adding inventory) cause revenue to go up? But you can't just look at what happened after you add inventory, because hotels might refuse those bookings, and sales might just shift between hotels on the platform rather than grow overall. You need to measure the true effect on platform revenue, not just on individual transactions, while accounting for rejection risk and competitive shifting.
241.ap: CS2NET is built in three pieces. First, it learns to recognize when a room is actually available by looking at patterns of room types and what kinds of rooms typically get booked (the Scarcity module). Second, it predicts which hotels will accept bookings you assign to them (the Service-Engagement module). Third, it applies causal reasoning to estimate what would have happened without your intervention, so you can isolate the true causal effect of adding inventory on total platform revenue, not just shifted sales.
241.ww: The key insight is that causality lives in the counterfactual—the world where you didn't add inventory. By learning to predict that world separately, you can subtract it from what actually happened and see the true causal bump. The scarcity and service modules reduce selection bias (the idea that hotels you choose to add might already be different) by factoring in the hard constraints and hotel behavior patterns.
241.po: Real-world proof: when deployed on a major platform, CS2NET increased confirmed bookings and platform revenue significantly, generating over 10 million RMB (~$1.4M) in additional annual profit. The paper also releases the first dataset for this problem, enabling future research on causal inventory decisions in travel platforms.

242.bp: In graphs of interactions—financial transactions, network traffic, social connections—sometimes a group of entities suddenly starts behaving abnormally (financial fraud rings, botnet clusters, coordinated attacks). Finding these anomalous subgraphs is crucial for security and safety, but it's hard because normal behavior is diverse, and you have to spot when a *group* deviates, not just an individual node.
242.wh: Traditional anomaly detection looks at individual nodes or uses fixed rules about what subgraph patterns to search for (only paths, only trees, only certain sizes). But real anomalies involve intricate collaboration—a ring of fraudsters may communicate through a specific pattern that emerges only when you see how they interact together. Fixed templates miss this, and focusing on individual node anomalies misses the group dynamic.
242.ap: PC-SAD works in stages. First, it uses a Graph AutoEncoder (a neural network that learns compressed representations of neighborhoods) to spot core anomalous nodes by capturing multi-scale neighborhood patterns. From these cores, it samples candidate subgraphs using different structures—paths (chains), trees (hierarchies), and cycles (rings). It enhances each candidate using the specific structural properties of that subgraph type. Finally, it uses graph contrastive learning—a technique that learns by comparing examples and non-examples—to generate embeddings that distinguish normal collaboration patterns from anomalous ones.
242.ww: The mechanism works because anomalies are often patterns of how nodes relate *to each other*, not properties of individual nodes. By starting from anomalous core nodes and exploring their neighborhoods in multiple structural forms, you capture both the who and the how of the anomaly. The contrastive learning step directly teaches the network to make anomalous patterns look different from normal ones by learning from paired positive and negative examples.
242.po: On four benchmark datasets, PC-SAD outperforms state-of-the-art methods, proving it detects anomalous subgraphs more accurately. This is actionable for fraud detection and network security teams: instead of false alarms on individual transactions, they get suspicious groups with precise structural signatures.

243.bp: Large language models accumulate false beliefs—they hallucinate facts, forget recent news, and hold outdated information. Ideally, you could edit a model to fix one incorrect belief without breaking thousands of other things the model already knows correctly. But every time you edit the model, you risk conflicting with previous edits and destabilizing what the model learned, especially after hundreds or thousands of sequential edits.
243.wh: The problem is that different edits compete for the same neurons (the model's basic computational units). If you edit to fix "Biden is president in 2025" and later edit to fix "the capital of France is Paris," they might step on each other's toes, confusing the model or erasing one fix to make room for the other. Current methods allocate isolated subspaces of parameters for each edit to avoid collision, but they don't actually assess whether edits truly conflict, leading to wasteful allocation and poor model stability.
243.ap: CASE has two main parts. The Conflict-Assessed Editing Allocation module measures quantitatively how much each new edit conflicts with previous edits (a numerical score, not a guess). Using this conflict assessment, it smartly routes the new edit to the right part of the model, reducing conflicts upfront. The Knowledge-sensitive Neuron Tuning strategy then identifies which neurons are most critical for the facts in question and tunes them carefully, while leaving unrelated neurons alone, minimizing ripple damage.
243.ww: Conflict assessment works because edits that affect overlapping neurons will interfere; by quantifying this overlap before allocating space, you route non-conflicting edits to different areas. Knowledge-sensitive tuning is key because not all neurons matter equally for a given fact—some neurons encode the fact directly, while others encode peripheral information. Tuning only the sensitive ones keeps collateral damage minimal.
243.po: After 1,000 sequential edits on standard benchmarks, CASE achieves nearly 10% improvement in average editing accuracy over prior methods, and crucially, it retains earlier edits much better. This is the difference between a model that can be edited once and a model that can be edited a thousand times and still work.

244.bp: Cloud providers manage virtual private clouds—isolated networks for customers—and need to relay control messages (configuration changes, security policies, resource allocation commands) from the central control plane to thousands or millions of containers running in the data plane. As clouds grow, this message delivery becomes a bottleneck: slow delivery means slow changes, and slow changes mean slow response to incidents.
244.wh: There's a fundamental trade-off: RPC-style delivery (direct calls) puts load on the control plane, which serves many customers and can't afford to be bogged down by message delivery. Message queues (MQ) distribute the work but require the data plane to constantly check and process messages, creating overhead there instead. You can't win by choosing one approach; you need both, but they fight each other for bandwidth and latency.
244.ap: Meteor runs two parallel paths: an RPC path and an MQ path. An auto-switching mechanism monitors latency and load on both paths and dynamically routes each message to whichever path is faster at that moment. Additionally, Meteor adds a VPC-based filtering scheme to the MQ path, so containers only subscribe to the subset of messages they actually need (like subscribing to one team's configuration changes, not every change in the system). It also adds a robustness layer to guarantee messages arrive and stay consistent even under failures.
244.ww: The dynamic dual-path approach works because the optimal path changes depending on current load: when the control plane is light, RPC is fast. When it's busy, MQ is faster. By measuring both and switching, you get the best of both. The filtering scheme reduces data plane overhead directly: if you deliver 100 unnecessary messages per useful one, filtering saves 99 message processing cycles per container.
244.po: On real-world tests with up to 100,000 containers, Meteor reduced message delivery latency by 48.8% and cut total overhead by roughly 50% compared to existing methods. For cloud operators, this means faster configuration updates, faster incident response, and more efficient use of control resources.

245.bp: Quantum computers will break current encryption methods (RSA, ECDSA, the math that secures your bank transactions and crypto wallets). The solution exists—post-quantum cryptography algorithms that resist quantum attacks—but switching them in means touching every place encryption is used: wallet signing, communication channels between nodes, blockchain state commitments. Decentralized systems like blockchains make this switch especially hard because code changes require governance votes, and you can't just flip a switch on a global ledger.
245.wh: The migration is not just an algorithm swap; it's a dependency nightmare. Cryptography lives embedded in dozens of places—signing protocols, message formats, consensus mechanisms, upgrades themselves. A decentralized system can't do a coordinated flip because old nodes must coexist with new nodes during the transition. You need to know which cryptographic dependencies are critical (sign first, talk later) and which can wait, but most teams have no systematic way to map this.
245.ap: The paper proposes a three-part framework: (1) a component taxonomy that classifies each part of the system (wallet, node communication, state storage, etc.); (2) a cryptographic dependency inventory (CDI) schema—a standardized way to document which crypto is used where and why; (3) rule-based priority assignment (P0 to P3 levels) that automatically derives from the CDI fields. A P0 component needs updating first (high impact if breached), while P3 can wait. A worked example shows how wallet signing, secure channels, and state commitments fit into this hierarchy.
245.ww: The mechanism works because it separates the hard part (understanding your system's dependencies) from the easy part (assigning priorities). Once every cryptographic dependency is documented in a common format, you can apply rules directly (if this component is a P0, do it first) without needing experts to debate each decision. The taxonomy ensures you don't forget any major component.
245.po: The practical payoff is a clear, actionable migration roadmap for decentralized systems. Instead of chaos and half-broken upgrades, teams can move systematically from P0 (wallet security first) through P3 (nice-to-have library updates last), minimizing the window where old and new crypto coexist unsafely.

246.bp: Generative AI can create realistic false news—text, images, videos. As this AI improves, detecting which news is AI-made versus human-written becomes harder, and spreading misinformation becomes cheaper and faster. Understanding how people perceive and detect AI-generated news is essential for building defenses against AI-powered disinformation campaigns.
246.wh: Detection is an arms race: as detection methods improve, generation methods improve in response. You can train a classifier to spot AI news, but once it's deployed, adversaries can adjust their generation to fool it. Traditional experiments on *static* datasets don't capture this dynamics. You need a way to generate controlled, labeled AI-written news and measure how human perception and detection both change as generation improves.
246.ap: The paper contributes two tools. JudgeGPT is a platform that shows humans news articles (some AI-generated, some human-written) and collects their judgments of whether each is AI-generated and how believable they find it. RogueGPT is a controlled generation engine that lets researchers produce AI-generated news with specific properties (certain topics, styles, lengths) so they can test detection under realistic conditions. Together, these form an experimental pipeline: generate varied AI news, show it to humans, measure their detection accuracy, and iterate to understand the dynamics.
246.ww: The reason this pipeline matters: static datasets freeze the problem in time, but detection and generation are co-evolving. By having a live generation engine (RogueGPT) and measurement tool (JudgeGPT), researchers can test hypotheses about what makes AI news detectable and how humans adapt to detecting it. The findings show detection is improving but lags generation, revealing the ongoing competition.
246.po: The concrete finding is that humans are getting better at spotting AI-generated news, but generation is still winning the race. The paper also discusses mitigation strategies—LLM-based detection, inoculation (teaching people to be skeptical), and the dual-use nature of generative AI (it can be used to generate misinformation or to study it). These tools enable future work on building more robust detection.

247.bp: Social media networks during crises or political movements like Black Lives Matter, Brexit, or the Christchurch attack show who talks to whom, but they also reveal *how* people feel and argue. When protesters express grievances and appeal to moral principles, those feelings are part of the social structure—not just metadata, but core to understanding the movement. Detecting communities (groups of closely connected people) works better if you account for these emotional and moral dimensions.
247.wh: Standard network analysis treats social networks as pure interaction graphs—who messaged whom. But this misses crucial information: two people might interact frequently but for entirely different reasons. One expresses anger about injustice, another appeals to shared values. Ignoring these psycholinguistic dimensions collapses meaningful distinctions and produces fragmented communities that don't reflect how the social movement actually organizes.
247.ap: The paper takes social networks from three real crises and creates multiplex networks—networks with multiple layers. The first layer is interactions (who talked to whom). Additional layers encode psycholinguistic features extracted from the text: one layer for expressions of grievance and another for moral framings (appeals to justice, fairness, etc.). It then applies Leiden community detection to these multiplex networks (treating all layers together) and compares results to pure interaction networks. The comparison measures fragmentation (do communities split up more?) and temporal persistence (do communities stay stable across time?).
247.ww: Adding psycholinguistic layers works because people who share grievances and moral values tend to cohere as communities even if their interaction patterns are sparse. By explicitly modeling how people feel and what values they express, you capture cohesion that would otherwise look like weak ties. This reveals who is actually aligned, not just who talks most frequently.
247.po: The finding is that multiplex networks with psycholinguistic layers produce more cohesive partitions—communities hold together better—and more stable communities over time. This means researchers analyzing social movements can now model not just interaction but also emotion and values, yielding deeper and more accurate insights into how movements organize.

248.bp: E-commerce sites need to predict whether you'll click and buy a product (click-through rate, CTR prediction). Modern models do this by looking at your history of past clicks—but your history is long (thousands of past items), and encoding all that information is computationally expensive. Large language models showed that massive models can learn powerful patterns when given enough compute; the question is whether this scaling insight can work for CTR prediction without blowing up inference costs.
248.wh: Standard self-attention (the mechanism that lets models track relationships across long histories) is quadratic: if your history is 1,000 items long, computing attention is like comparing each item to all others, which costs 1,000,000 operations. Scale this to millions of users, millions of histories, and it's prohibitively expensive. Sparse attention methods exist but were designed for language (where token distribution is different) and don't account for the personalization and temporal dynamics of user behavior.
248.ap: SparseCTR segments each user's behavior history into personalized chunks (rather than fixed-size windows) to avoid cutting behaviors in half and to enable parallel computation. It then applies a three-branch sparse self-attention mechanism: one branch identifies global interests (long-term preferences), one tracks interest transitions (how preferences shift), and one focuses on short-term interests (what you've been clicking right now). It also designs temporal encoding using head-specific bias coefficients—each attention head learns its own way of valuing time (recent items more important in some heads, long-term patterns in others).
248.ww: Chunking works because user behaviors often cluster naturally—a user might browse phones, then laptops, then cases. By identifying chunk boundaries intelligently (personalized to each user), you respect these natural breaks and can process each chunk efficiently. The three-branch attention mirrors real recommendation logic: what are your core interests, how are they evolving, and what do you want right now? Learning time biases per attention head lets the model discover that different patterns matter on different timescales.
248.po: The result is an efficient model that can handle long user histories (where naive attention would be too slow) while maintaining or improving prediction accuracy. This bridges the gap between large-model scaling laws and deployment reality in industry, making it practical to capture long-term user behavior for real-time CTR prediction.

249.bp: Imagine a company allocating tasks to employees in different roles: a research project might be hard for administrative staff but easy for researchers, because the two roles have different resources and support. Similarly, a company might not allow certain projects to go to certain roles (a creative design task can't go to a data entry role). The problem is to allocate tasks fairly and efficiently while respecting these role-based constraints and position-dependent valuations—where fairness means everyone gets a reasonable deal and efficiency means you're not wasting valuable work.
249.wh: Classical allocation theory assumes agents have fixed valuations for items regardless of context. But in reality, valuations depend on position (role, location, status). A promotional task might be worth a lot to a junior person seeking visibility but little to a senior executive. You could ignore positions and pretend everyone values everything the same, but that yields unfair and inefficient allocations. You could also ignore the graph structure of constraints, but the constraints are real: not every person can do every job.
249.ap: The paper introduces a new framework where agents have valuations that depend on which position they're assigned to, and constraints form a graph: positions are vertices, items are edges (an item can only go to one of the two positions it connects). The paper then studies fairness measured by maximin share (MMS)—roughly, everyone gets at least as much value as they'd get if they could pick and divide fairly—and efficiency measured by Pareto optimality (can't make anyone better off without hurting someone) and social welfare. It analyzes the computational complexity (is finding a fair allocation easy or hard?) and develops approximation algorithms for cases where exact solutions are slow.
249.ww: The mechanism works because constraints and position-dependent valuations are linked: if the task graph prevents certain allocations anyway, you might as well use that structure to solve fairness and efficiency jointly. By treating positions and tasks as a graph, you can develop algorithms that respect the constraints while optimizing for fairness, rather than solving them separately and hoping for the best.
249.po: The paper provides a complete set of complexity results and algorithms, showing which allocation problems are solvable efficiently and which require approximation. This is actionable for companies designing fair task allocation systems: they now know whether a particular structure of positions and constraints is easy or hard to allocate fairly.

250.bp: Internet of Things (IoT) devices—sensors, phones, embedded devices—are everywhere, but they have limited memory and battery. Some tasks, like AI inference (running a neural network), are very memory-hungry. Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) are a new kind of neural network that mimics biological brains by being event-driven: they only compute when something changes, saving energy and memory compared to traditional networks. But SNNs still struggle on edge devices because memory budgets are tight and unpredictable.
250.wh: SNNs process information over multiple timesteps (firing spikes, simulating neurons at each step). This temporal dimension complicates memory management: you need to keep state between timesteps, and timestep-dependent dynamics mean you can't just freeze and resume computation like in static networks. Previous methods either design lightweight models (still limited by memory) or add system-level memory management (adds overhead that slows things down). Neither solves the core problem: adapting efficiently when memory is tight and fluctuating.
250.ap: MASI is a framework with three parts. Layer slicing breaks the neural network into smaller pieces, each using less memory; the slicing is fine-grained and memory-adaptive, adjusting based on available memory at runtime. A timestep-agnostic scheduler maximizes how much computation happens in parallel (reducing fragmentation, the wasted gaps between computations) without needing to pre-plan timesteps. An early-exit mechanism allows the network to stop computing timesteps early if it's already confident in its output, skipping unnecessary computation.
250.ww: Layer slicing works because you don't need the whole network in memory at once—you can load layers one by one, compute on them, and discard the intermediate results. The scheduler minimizes fragmentation by using scheduling algorithms that work regardless of timestep timing, so it doesn't depend on timestep structure. Early exit is powerful for SNNs because many inputs can be classified confidently before all timesteps are processed, so you skip redundant work.
250.po: On diverse edge devices and workloads, MASI reduced memory usage by about 20.67% and inference latency by 58.53% on average compared to other feasible on-device approaches, with negligible accuracy loss. This makes SNNs practical for real edge devices with tight memory constraints, enabling efficient AI on IoT.

251.bp: When data comes from multiple sources (hospitals in different regions, companies in different markets, sensor networks in different locations), each source has its own samples but shares the same set of features (all hospitals measure patient age, weight, blood pressure, etc.). You want to identify which features are most informative for your prediction task, but data distribution differs between sources—age might matter more in one hospital than another. The challenge is selecting features that work universally without labeled training data.
251.wh: Standard unsupervised feature selection treats all sources the same or ignores them, failing to capture what each source uniquely contributes. More problematically, selection based on statistical correlation can pick up spurious associations—features that are correlated due to confounders (hidden factors) rather than true causation. For instance, ice cream sales and drowning deaths are correlated (both happen in summer), but ice cream doesn't cause drowning. Without accounting for confounders, feature selection is fooled by these spurious links, especially when source-specific biases amplify them.
251.ap: UMCFS (Unsupervised Multi-source Causal Feature Selection) uses adversarial balancing to learn domain-invariant sample weights—essentially, it reweights samples from each source so the model treats them as if they came from a single common distribution, removing source-specific bias. It then applies causal reweighting that removes spurious correlations by reasoning about causal relationships (not just statistical ones). Finally, it explicitly separates global feature importance (features that matter everywhere) from source-specific deviations (features that matter only in one or two sources), so you can judge whether a feature is truly important or just noisy in one source.
251.ww: Adversarial balancing works because fighting the model's tendency to overfit to source-specific patterns forces it to learn shared structure. Causal reweighting removes confounders by reasoning about cause-and-effect rather than just correlation. Separating global from source-specific importance lets you judge robustness: if a feature is important only in one source, it might be unreliable.
251.po: Extensive experiments demonstrate that UMCFS consistently selects better features than unsupervised methods that ignore causality or multi-source structure. The payoff is feature sets that work across heterogeneous data sources without labels, enabling better downstream prediction even when training data is limited or siloed.

252.bp: Large language models are sophisticated reasoners, but sophistication comes with risk. Chain-of-Thought prompting (asking a model to think step-by-step), Self-Reflection (asking it to check its own work), and Multi-Agent Debating (having multiple copies of the model argue) all improve reasoning ability, helping the model solve math problems and logic puzzles better. But if these techniques improve reasoning, do they also strengthen biases—making the model more confident in stereotypes or unfair judgments?
252.wh: Reasoning frameworks increase the model's output length and give it more opportunity to express its internal logic. But if that logic encodes unfairness or stereotypes, then longer reasoning gives the model more rope to hang itself—more text to express and elaborate on biases. You'd hope reasoning helps eliminate bias by allowing self-correction, but the paper suggests the opposite is happening.
252.ap: The paper evaluates multiple large language models on several fairness and stereotype benchmarks (tests designed to measure bias) under three conditions: baseline generation, Chain-of-Thought, Self-Reflection, and Multi-Agent Debating. It measures fairness risk before and after applying each reasoning technique on multiple languages. The finding is systematized: all three reasoning frameworks increase fairness risks (stereotypes, bias, unfair judgments) across different models and languages.
252.ww: The mechanism is straightforward: reasoning frameworks amplify whatever is already in the model. If the model has learned stereotypes from training data, step-by-step reasoning gives it more text to express and elaborate on those stereotypes. Self-reflection doesn't correct biases if the model can't recognize them as problematic in the first place. Multi-agent debate can also reinforce biases if all copies are biased in similar directions.
252.po: The concrete finding is a safety concern: reasoning techniques that improve capability also undermine model alignment and fairness across languages and model families. This challenges assumptions that better reasoning automatically yields better behavior and highlights a trade-off that developers must account for when deploying reasoning frameworks.

253.bp: Recommendation systems learn your preferences over time and suggest things you might like. But most systems run centrally on company servers, meaning your browsing history is uploaded and tracked. Federated learning lets your device train its own recommendation model locally without sending data to a server. But here's the tension: your preferences change over time (you liked rock music, now you're into jazz), and each person's data is different. How do you stay personalized while also learning from patterns across millions of other users, all without centralizing anyone's data?
253.wh: Federated learning trains models locally on each device, which protects privacy, but it means each user's model trains in isolation on only their own history. This misses collaborative learning—insights from similar users that could improve predictions. Moreover, user preferences drift over time, and local models can forget old preferences while forgetting to retain the useful ones. Naively combining federated learning (which isolates data) with continual learning (which tracks preference drift) leads to temporal forgetting—the model forgets its long-term knowledge of your preferences while chasing short-term patterns.
253.ap: FCUCR (Federated Continual User-Centric Recommendation) has two key ideas. First, time-aware self-distillation: instead of just training on your latest clicks, the model also teaches itself to remember its old predictions about your older clicks. Think of it as the model saying, 'I used to think you'd like this song, and I should remember that even though I've retrained since then.' Second, inter-user prototype transfer: the system identifies users similar to you and transfers representative patterns (prototypes) of their preferences to enrich your local model, while keeping your decision logic private. You learn from their patterns without sharing their data.
253.ww: Self-distillation works because it preserves memory: your old predictions encode what you wanted before, and forcing the new model to match those predictions retains that knowledge even as you learn new preferences. Prototype transfer is clever because prototypes abstract patterns without revealing individual data—your model enriches itself with insights from similar users without ever seeing their raw history. This is the federated learning ideal: collaborative learning with privacy.
253.po: Extensive experiments on four benchmarks show that FCUCR outperforms approaches that ignore user dynamics or ignore collaborative learning. The practical result is a privacy-preserving recommendation system that adapts to your changing preferences while still benefiting from patterns in similar users' data.

254.bp: Two major trends in machine learning are foundation models (giant pre-trained models like GPT or Llama that work on many tasks) and federated learning (training models without centralizing data). Both are important for the web's future: foundation models bring powerful reasoning to many applications, while federated learning protects user privacy.
