This workshop brings together researchers and practitioners working on the intersection: how do you deploy and adapt foundation models in federated, decentralized settings?
254.wh: Foundation models are huge and expensive to train centrally, but federated settings require communicating model updates across a network of independent devices or organizations. Adapting a foundation model (fine-tuning it for a specific task) is cheaper than training from scratch, but coordinating fine-tuning across federated participants while keeping data private is technically complex. Key questions remain: how do you efficiently distribute foundation model training, how do you adapt them without leaking private data, how do you handle the heterogeneity of federated data?
254.ap: The workshop is a forum for discussing these challenges. Researchers present work on federated fine-tuning of foundation models, privacy-preserving adaptation, efficient communication protocols for distributing large models, and practical deployments of federated foundation models in real applications. The workshop creates a space for practitioners and researchers to identify promising research directions and share solutions.
254.ww: The reason this intersection matters: foundation models have the reasoning power to solve many problems, but they're centralized and data-hungry. Federated learning has the privacy guarantee but traditionally worked on smaller models. Combining them could yield the best of both worlds—powerful reasoning with strong privacy guarantees—but requires solving hard technical problems at the intersection.
254.po: The concrete payoff is a community gathering to chart research trajectories at the intersection of foundation models and federated learning, identifying promising works and key open problems. This accelerates progress on deployed systems that combine the capabilities of foundation models with the privacy and decentralization guarantees of federated learning.

255.bp: When you remotely manage a device through its web interface—a router, security camera, industrial controller—that interface can accidentally broadcast hints about where the device is located. Imagine a thermostat showing local weather, or a device health page mentioning regional network operators. An attacker can harvest these scattered clues and triangulate the physical location of your infrastructure, creating a real security threat for both enterprises and individuals.
255.wh: The challenge is that these hints are buried in messy, unstructured web pages that vary wildly from device to device. One page might mention a city name once; another might reference it through a regional abbreviation. There's no predictable pattern to latch onto, and many individual clues might be ambiguous or sparse. You can't just pattern-match against a fixed template.
255.ap: The researchers built a system that groups similar web pages together using clustering, then digs through the differences between pages to surface hidden clues. When pieces of information are too thin, they feed those clues into a search engine and a large language model to fill in blanks and cross-reference possibilities. The LLM acts as a kind of inference engine, connecting dots between vague hints to narrow down coordinates.
255.ww: Clustering finds structure in seemingly unstructured data by grouping pages that likely describe similar locations or system types. Once grouped, the differences between pages (which weather system is shown, which network provider is mentioned) become meaningful signals instead of noise. The LLM applies real-world knowledge—for instance, understanding that certain network providers operate only in specific regions—which multiplies the power of each weak clue.
255.po: The system successfully pinpointed 5,435 real devices to within a country 97% of the time, a city 88% of the time, and a street address 80% of the time. This is the first large-scale proof that this threat is real and widespread, giving regulators and device makers concrete evidence to act on and defining a benchmark for future security research.

256.bp: Polymer scientists need to predict how a new chemical will behave—its strength, flexibility, heat resistance—before synthesizing it. This saves time and materials. But the bottleneck is that these experts rarely know machine learning, and machine learning engineers don't know polymer chemistry. Someone needs to bridge that gap so a chemist can get predictions without coding or mathematical training.
256.wh: Today's prediction systems demand either specialized programming knowledge or require hiring an ML engineer as a middleman. Even the smartest polymer researcher hits a wall when trying to set up data pipelines, train models, and automate repetitive tasks. Conversely, an ML engineer has no intuition for which chemical properties matter most. The communication overhead is huge, and small tweaks require back-and-forth delays.
256.ap: The researchers built a conversational agent—powered by a large language model—that sits inside a visual, no-code workflow platform. A chemist types a question like 'Predict stiffness for molecules with these properties,' and the agent automatically sets up the data pipeline, deploys a machine learning model trained to predict multiple polymer properties at once, and returns results. The agent translates between plain English and the technical setup underneath.
256.ww: Large language models are fluent enough in both English and technical concepts to act as translators. They understand what 'stiffness' means chemically and can map it to the right computational pathway. The no-code platform handles the plumbing without requiring the user to code. By threading these together, a domain expert can now directly specify what they want, and the system figures out the machinery.
256.po: Polymer researchers can now make predictions on their own, in minutes, without waiting for an ML team. The system automatically documents its work and creates reproducible pipelines that others can reuse and refine. This collapses the feedback loop from weeks to hours and democratizes access to machine learning within materials science.

257.bp: When you're scrolling through a streaming service or online store, the system needs to suggest your next show or product in real time. The challenge is that your interest history is long and messy—hundreds of clicks with varied meanings. A simple linear list of your past actions misses the fact that humans shop in sessions: maybe Tuesday morning you browsed tools, and Thursday evening you looked at books. Recognizing these hidden time-based groupings can make recommendations much better.
257.wh: Standard recommendation models flatten your entire history into one sequence and feed it all to a neural network. But this creates two problems: the network gets overwhelmed trying to find signal in a noisy flood of irrelevant history (like being asked to focus on every word in a 1000-page book at once), and it misses the hierarchical rhythm of actual browsing—sessions, which are clusters of related activity. The network ends up as a bottleneck doing useless work.
257.ap: The system works in two phases. First, it reads your history session by session and learns to predict which items you might see again in a similar session, using the session boundaries as hints. This creates rich, meaningful item representations that know about context. Second, when making a recommendation, instead of looking at your entire history equally, it uses a smart filter that only attends to the sessions most relevant to what you might want right now, drowning out the noise.
257.ww: By training on session patterns first, the system learns item representations that carry semantic meaning—a 'laptop-browsing' representation is different from a 'book-browsing' one. When you then apply the smart filter, you're not just skipping items; you're skipping irrelevant semantic clusters. The two-step process works because attention is noisy when it's dense (looking at everything equally), but becomes precise when it's sparse and guided by learned, meaningful boundaries.
257.po: Recommendations become faster and more relevant. The system cuts down unnecessary computation significantly (fewer items to process), which speeds up responses at scale. Most importantly, the quality improves because the model now captures the rhythm of how users actually browse instead of treating every action as equally important.

258.bp: A talking head is an AI-generated video of a person's face that moves and speaks in sync with audio—used in everything from video conferencing avatars to deepfakes to customer service robots. This field has exploded with dozens of new methods in recent years, but researchers are all measuring success differently. One lab cares about perfectly smooth animation; another cares most about whether lips match the audio. There's no shared language, making it hard to know which method is actually better.
258.wh: Without a common framework, each research team invents their own evaluation measures and datasets. Paper A might test on celebrity videos, Paper B on smartphone recordings. One group measures realism of eyeblinks, another ignores them entirely. It becomes impossible to compare results across papers honestly. Newcomers to the field don't know which benchmarks matter or which methods to build on, slowing progress.
258.ap: The researchers read over 100 influential papers published since 2021, extracted the main technical ideas, and built a taxonomy organizing them into a few big themes (like speech-to-motion mapping, emotion and style control, and realistic video synthesis). They then tracked which datasets and which evaluation metrics each paper used, plotting the trends over time. This revealed what the community was focusing on and how priorities shifted.
258.ww: A taxonomy makes invisible boundaries visible. By naming the themes, papers that seemed isolated suddenly connect as variations on the same idea. By tracking metrics over time, you can see when the community's values changed—for instance, when they stopped caring purely about frame sharpness and started caring more about whether the mouth movements match the audio. This historical perspective clarifies what matters.
258.po: The survey gives everyone a map: if you want to build a talking-head system, you now know the main strategies, which datasets are best for different goals, and which evaluation methods the community trusts. It also reveals gaps—areas where measurement is still weak—pointing toward research opportunities and defining a standard evaluation protocol for the field.

259.bp: Large language models like GPT or Claude are trained on vast amounts of web text, which includes private conversations, copyrighted books, and harmful content. After release, sometimes you need to make the model forget something—remove personal data mentioned in training, delete copyrighted material, or purge toxic knowledge. The catch is you can't retrain from scratch; you need to surgically erase specific concepts while keeping the model's general abilities intact.
259.wh: Existing methods to unlearn information require retraining huge portions of the model, which is computationally expensive and risks breaking useful capabilities. Most also need a 'retain set'—thousands of examples of things the model should keep remembering—which is a practical burden. Worse, users might request unlearning sequentially over time (delete topic A today, topic B tomorrow), and existing methods aren't designed for that continuous flow.
259.ap: Rather than retraining the whole model, this approach targets just the output layer—the final step that converts internal thought-vectors into the words you see. By adjusting only this thin layer, you reshape how the model translates its internal concepts into actual words. If the model thought about a private person, you reroute it so it outputs something generic instead. The adjustment is surgical and lightweight.
259.ww: The output layer is a bottleneck. Everything the model knows flows through this final step to become actual output. By controlling what gets output, you effectively block undesired information from reaching users, even if the model still internally carries traces of it. Because you're only tweaking one layer, you don't disrupt the thousands of other capabilities stored deeper in the network. Sequential unlearning works because each independent adjustment is modular—one adjustment doesn't interfere with the next.
259.po: Unlearning becomes fast and practical. You can remove specific data from a live service without expensive retraining, and you can handle continuous deletion requests from users. The model's general skills stay sharp because you're not bulldozing entire regions of learned knowledge. This makes privacy-preserving deployment of language models realistic for web services and compliance scenarios.

260.bp: In a real network—social media, traffic flows, disease spreading—connections change over time. Yesterday's friend is today's ex-friend. A network node's importance isn't just about how many links it has right now, but about how many shortest routes through the network pass through it at each moment. Measuring this importance in temporal networks is crucial for understanding influence and intervention points, but it's computationally expensive.
260.wh: Real-world networks show extreme imbalance: a few 'hub' nodes are super important, while the vast majority are barely important at all. A machine learning model trained on this imbalanced data overfits—it memorizes that 'most nodes are unimportant' and stops trying to distinguish the rare truly important ones. Standard graph neural networks also struggle because they ignore the time dimension, treating past and present connections the same way, which loses crucial temporal information.
260.ap: The system uses a graph neural network designed to respect time—it builds a picture of which nodes connect when and in what order. To handle imbalance, it uses a technique called contrastive learning that artificially groups similar nodes together and pushes apart nodes with different importance levels, before making importance predictions. Think of it as carving out clusters in a high-dimensional space so that high-importance and low-importance nodes are clearly separated.
260.ww: By respecting time, the network recognizes that a path from A to B to C only counts if it happens in that time order, not just in that spatial order. Contrastive learning works because you're not forcing the model to predict rare high-importance nodes immediately; instead, you're first teaching it to see importance levels as distinct clusters in feature space. Once the space is well-organized, the actual prediction becomes easier.
260.po: The system can now accurately identify truly important nodes in large temporal networks, scaling to real datasets. This enables better understanding of traffic bottlenecks, influential spreaders in epidemiology, or critical infrastructure in social networks—all in a way that generalizes to unseen networks rather than just memorizing training data.

261.bp: When a machine learning model makes a prediction on a graph (like inferring a relationship between two people in a social network), it's often hard to know why. Did it rely on their common friends, shared interests, or recent activity? If the graph is evolving—friendships forming and dissolving, knowledge being updated—the task gets even harder. Regulators and users demand explanations, especially in high-stakes applications.
261.wh: Standard explanation methods assume the graph is static, or they try to explain every connection equally. They miss the fact that real knowledge graphs have hierarchical structure—sometimes the reason for a prediction is a single, well-connected subgraph, and sometimes you need a chain of many indirect relationships. They also can't distinguish between causal connections (A leads to B) and spurious correlations (A and B both relate to C). In evolving graphs, they don't separate what persists from what's transient noise.
261.ap: The system models the graph as a causal system where higher-order relationships (not just pairs, but groups of nodes) matter. It builds a structural model of knowledge dependencies, then uses contrastive learning to isolate causal links from spurious correlations—strengthening connections that explain the prediction and weakening red herrings. A separate module tracks what's stable knowledge versus what's changing. Finally, it generates interpretable subgraphs that show which nodes and edges were most important.
261.ww: Higher-order modeling reveals multi-node patterns that pairwise approaches miss—for instance, that three people form a tight triangle that drove a decision, not just any two of them. Contrastive learning works by showing the model pairs of explanations: one that led to the correct prediction, one that didn't. By learning to distinguish them, the model learns what actually causes predictions. Separating stable from evolving knowledge matters because an old connection you've seen a thousand times explains more than a yesterday's novelty.
261.po: The explanations are now more faithful and interpretable. A human expert can read the causal subgraph and say, 'Yes, that makes sense—these were the actual reasons.' The method improves prediction accuracy too because understanding true causal structure lets the model generalize better. This enables users and regulators to trust graph-based AI systems in domains like recommendation, fraud detection, and knowledge discovery.

262.bp: As academic papers pile up—hundreds of thousands published annually—writing new research means finding relevant prior work. Authors browse keyword searches and citation networks manually, a tedious task. Imagine a system that reads your paper draft and automatically suggests which papers to cite. This saves time and ensures you don't miss important related work, especially in fast-moving fields.
262.wh: Citation suggestion is hard because relevance is contextual. A paper on neural networks might be cited for its training technique, its architecture, its theoretical analysis, or as a cautionary counterexample—very different citation reasons despite the same paper. Relevance also depends on where in the manuscript you cite it: a paper mentioned in the introduction serves a different purpose than one cited in methods. Simple keyword matching misses these nuances.
262.ap: The researchers built a two-part system. First, they retrieve candidate papers using multiple levels of search—broad corpus searches, then narrower searches based on the specific section of the paper being written. They fine-tune the retrieval model using contrastive learning, so papers that were actually cited together are pulled closer in the model's memory, while unrelated papers drift apart. Second, a language model takes the context of your paper and the retrieved candidates and generates a ranked list of suggestions, paired with reasoning.
262.ww: Multi-level retrieval captures both global context (your paper's overall theme) and local context (what you're saying right now). Contrastive learning works because you have real citation data—if a paper was cited, it's relevant; if it wasn't, it's not. By learning from these patterns, the retriever captures what 'relevance' actually means in your field. The language model then reads both texts and reasons about why a suggestion fits, rather than blindly ranking.
262.po: Authors get ranked suggestions for each part of their paper, grounded in actual domain knowledge. The benchmark includes over 554,000 papers so retrieval is comprehensive. This helps researchers write more thorough literature reviews and discover relevant work they might have missed, accelerating the scientific process and strengthening paper quality.

263.bp: In blockchain, miners or validators process transactions and earn fees. The fee mechanism is essentially an auction—users bid to have their transactions included. The system needs to prevent miners from colluding with users: a user and miner might secretly agree to artificially lower a fee if the miner promises to include that transaction anyway. This kind of corruption undermines trust in the blockchain.
263.wh: Economic theory shows that if a mechanism is vulnerable to collusion between a miner and two users, it's often also vulnerable to collusion with just one user—except the math gets subtle at the boundary between one and two. Earlier work thought these were fundamentally different, requiring different mechanism designs. The question is: if you make your mechanism resistant to collusion with 2 users and a miner, are you automatically safe against any larger collusions?
263.ap: The researchers proved a mathematical equivalence: under a natural tie-breaking assumption, a mechanism that defeats collusion with 2 users defeats collusion with any larger group. The proof works by showing that if a coalition of 3+ participants could break the mechanism, you could extract a 2-participant break from it. This reduces the hardness problem to a smaller case.
263.ww: The mechanism's security against collusion boils down to whether two participants can profitably deviate together. Adding more people to a coalition actually makes it harder, not easier, because coordinating more people requires more secrecy and more trust within the group. Once you've designed for two, larger groups can't do better because their extra size doesn't give them new angles to attack.
263.po: Blockchain designers can now focus on the two-person collusion case, simplifying mechanism design. This establishes a clear threshold: if your fee mechanism resists small collusion, you've won. It clarifies the landscape of what's achievable and sets a practical benchmark for evaluating blockchain protocols.

264.bp: Modern machine learning models can do remarkable things without any training on your specific problem—a large foundation model trained on billions of examples can give decent predictions on your data right away. But should you then retrain ('fine-tune') the model on your own data? For tabular structured data (spreadsheets, databases), this question has a surprising answer.
264.wh: Conventional wisdom says fine-tuning always helps—train the general model on your specific data and performance improves. But tabular foundation models show something weird: they already work well without fine-tuning. When you fine-tune, performance sometimes gets worse. The effect depends heavily on your specific dataset and which model you use, making it hard to predict when fine-tuning is worth the effort.
264.ap: The researchers trained and tested multiple foundation models with and without fine-tuning on dozens of real tabular datasets. They tried three fine-tuning approaches: meta-learning (learning to learn quickly), parameter-efficient fine-tuning (tweaking only a small part of the model), and full fine-tuning (retraining everything). They measured not just accuracy, but also calibration (how confident the model should be) and fairness (whether predictions were equally good for different groups).
264.ww: Tabular foundation models are different from image or language models because they're trained on many diverse tables, not one unified corpus. This broad training already covers most of the variations you'll see in a new dataset. Retraining sometimes hurts because the model overfits to your small specific table, losing the generality that made it good. In contrast, parameter-efficient tweaks can help by adapting without erasing prior knowledge.
264.po: The work gives practitioners clear guidance: zero-shot foundation models are already strong for tables, and fine-tuning is risky. If you do fine-tune, parameter-efficient methods are much safer than full retraining. This saves computational cost and time—you can deploy immediately without expensive retraining experiments.

265.bp: Recommendation systems traditionally store a separate vector (embedding) for each user—millions of users mean millions of vectors taking up memory. Modern systems also often treat users as separate entities and ask 'what items did user 123 like?' Yet sometimes you want to recommend without knowing who the person is—recommending to a guest, or adapting instantly to a new account with no history.
265.wh: Storing per-user vectors is memory-intensive and breaks down when you see a user you've never trained on before (the cold-start problem). Graph neural networks, often used to find similar users, can get stuck in a rut where all items end up looking the same (over-smoothing). And the whole paradigm of using raw ID numbers—'user 123,' 'item 456'—is brittle; these IDs mean nothing to a general model.
265.ap: Instead of storing user vectors, the system infers preferences on the fly by looking at which items you've clicked. Instead of using numeric IDs, it uses text descriptions from a pre-trained language model—'luxury headphones,' 'romance novel'—that carry semantic meaning. To find similar items you might like, it augments your history with similar items and trains a contrastive model that groups items you'd enjoy together without needing a graph structure.
265.ww: Computing preferences on demand instead of storing them means memory scales with items (usually millions) not users (billions). Language-based item representations are meaningful because the language model already encodes general knowledge about what different things are. Contrastive learning finds collaborative patterns (if you liked A and B, you might like C) without the infrastructure overhead of graph neural networks.
265.po: The system uses up to 69% less GPU memory than traditional approaches while improving recommendation quality by up to 40% compared to methods without language, and 5.7% over language-based competitors. It handles new users instantly and generalizes better because it relies on semantic understanding rather than memorized ID mappings.

266.bp: When a flash flood strikes, drones swarm to the disaster zone to capture aerial images for damage assessment. Ideally, a central AI system could analyze all this imagery instantly to map severity and guide rescue efforts. But in disaster zones, the communication network is often damaged or overloaded. Transmitting hundreds of gigabytes of raw images back to a data center is infeasible.
266.wh: The traditional approach—collect all imagery centrally, process it in one powerful model—fails when you can't transmit. If you ask each drone to process its own images locally (federated learning), you save bandwidth, but coordinating a large swarm of drones to learn together creates new challenges: their models diverge because each only sees different parts of the landscape, and combining their results naively loses accuracy.
266.ap: Instead of sharing raw parameters between drones, the system exchanges abstract summaries called 'semantic logits'—the high-level reasoning of each drone's model about what it sees—along with compressed intermediate representations. The central server combines these summaries intelligently using weighted averaging, building a robust global model that benefits from all drones' views without massive data transmission.
266.ww: Semantic logits are very compact—just numbers representing the model's confidence in each flood severity level. They're also more informative than low-level image features because they encode the model's actual reasoning. Weighted averaging lets the server trust drones that have been accurate in the past and downweight unreliable drones, improving robustness. The compression drastically cuts communication (99.5% reduction reported) while retaining the signal needed for accurate global learning.
266.po: Drones can now cooperatively learn a good segmentation model even in bandwidth-starved conditions. The system achieves high accuracy (97.94% accuracy on the test benchmark) while reducing communication by 99.5%, enabling rapid disaster response when communication infrastructure is fragile.

267.bp: Hundreds of millions of people in Southeast Asia speak languages like Burmese, Khmer, or Lao that have very little training data available online. Machine translation could unlock access to global knowledge—Wikipedia, research papers, web content in English—but training a good model requires massive datasets. Collecting and processing gigabytes of text in these low-resource languages is either expensive or carbon-intensive, creating a tension between digital inclusion and environmental responsibility.
267.wh: The naive solution—download the entire noisy internet in each language and train on all of it—requires enormous energy and misses quality. Much web text is spam, mistranslations, or culturally inappropriate for local communities. Smaller, hand-curated datasets exist (a linguist selects high-quality examples), but there's a mismatch: the machine learning system expects millions of examples, not hundreds.
267.ap: The system uses an AI agent (trained with a special learning algorithm called GRPO) to select the most valuable training examples from larger, noisier datasets. The agent uses a reward signal based on comparisons to the small expert-selected set—examples that align with expert choices get high scores. It then fine-tunes an open-source language model using a parameter-efficient technique (Low-Rank Adaptation) on this carefully curated subset, rather than training from scratch.
267.ww: The RL agent learns to predict 'what would experts approve of,' then uses that judgment to filter data. By filtering instead of training on everything, you dramatically reduce compute. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning means tweaking only a tiny fraction of the model weights, multiplying the efficiency gain. The result is a model trained on carefully chosen 'right data' rather than 'big data,' achieving better quality with much lower energy.
267.po: Translations into seven Southeast Asian languages now match state-of-the-art quality while requiring far less training data and energy. Local linguistic nuances and cultural appropriateness are preserved because the curated training data reflects community values. This demonstrates that digital inclusion can be achieved sustainably, making knowledge accessible without costly infrastructure.

268.bp: Tor provides anonymity by routing internet traffic through multiple relays, encrypting data so observers can't see which websites you visit. However, an attacker watching the patterns of encrypted traffic—packet sizes, timings, burst patterns—might be able to infer which website you're visiting anyway, even without reading the actual content. This is called website fingerprinting, and it undermines Tor's anonymity.
268.wh: Most fingerprinting attacks are tested on controlled, clean data: traffic from a fixed set of websites, collected under consistent network conditions, from a single time period. Real-world traffic is messier: websites change constantly (pages are redesigned, content updates), users have different network speeds, and sites have multiple subpages with different traffic patterns. An attack trained on old, clean data becomes unreliable when deployed on today's messy traffic.
268.ap: The system uses a language model to learn general representations of encrypted traffic patterns from large amounts of unlabeled, diverse real-world data. It fine-tunes this model to specialize on website fingerprinting, then adds a simple classifier on top. The language model representations are flexible enough to adapt to new websites and network conditions. A lightweight update mechanism lets it re-adapt to new traffic patterns using just a few labeled examples.
268.ww: Language models are trained to find meaningful patterns in sequences and generalize across variations. Raw encrypted traffic is like a language—patterns matter, but details vary. By learning on diverse, unlabeled traffic, the model captures invariant structure (the fingerprint) while being robust to variations (different ISPs, subpages, time periods). The lightweight fine-tuning adapter lets it re-align to evolving websites without expensive full retraining.
268.po: The system identifies visited websites from encrypted traffic with high accuracy even months after training, in diverse real-world conditions. This advances website fingerprinting attacks and demonstrates a real threat to Tor users, hopefully prompting stronger defenses in privacy-preserving networks.

269.bp: Computer vision systems can recognize broad categories (dog, bird, tree) easily, but the real world is full of subtle distinctions: a German Shepherd versus an Alsatian, a sparrow versus a finch, an oak versus a maple. These fine-grained distinctions matter in fields like wildlife monitoring, medical imaging, and agriculture. However, teaching a model to distinguish very similar things requires expensive, detailed human annotations and large datasets that don't exist for most rare categories.
269.wh: Most datasets focus on common, easily-distinguished objects. Rare and subtle categories remain untracked. Annotating fine-grained differences is labor-intensive and requires expert knowledge—a biologist must identify subtle plumage variations in bird subspecies. Long-tail learning (rare categories) compounds the problem: a few common classes dominate training data while rare classes appear only once or twice.
269.ap: Modern approaches use three interlocking ideas. First, transformer-based models (which learn relationships between visual parts) replace older architectures, offering more flexible attention. Second, generative augmentation—creating synthetic training examples that emphasize fine-grained differences—boosts the limited data available for rare classes. Third, multimodal learning fuses vision with text metadata or human knowledge, so the model learns not just from images but from descriptions and structured information.
269.ww: Transformers can learn which visual parts matter for distinctions (a bird's tail versus wing pattern) rather than forcing all features to matter equally. Synthetic augmentation, when done carefully to emphasize distinctions, multiplies effective training data without expensive re-annotation. Multimodal learning works because human language and knowledge give the model semantic grounding—it learns that 'pointed ears' and 'floppy ears' are categories, not just pixel patterns.
269.po: Fine-grained recognition now works better on rare classes, enabling real-world applications like automated wildlife identification, plant disease diagnosis, and art authentication. The roadmap ahead emphasizes robustness to natural image variations, explaining which visual features the model relies on (building trust), and efficient learning from few examples.

270.bp: When you get a recommendation for a product, you're hoping the system understands what makes that product special and why it might appeal to you—not just that some numbers in a computer happened to match. Today's systems turn each product into a sequence of individual words (tokens), which is like describing a shoe as "shoe", "red", "size", "10" as four separate pieces rather than one unified thing. This paper tackles the real goal: teaching recommendation systems to think about products as atomic units, the way humans do.
270.wh: Large language models were built to predict the next word in a sentence, so their attention mechanism naturally flows word-to-word—that's their design. When you repurpose them for recommendation, they inherit this word-level focus, meaning they track relations *between individual words* rather than between *items themselves*. This mismatch means the model may perfectly capture what makes a shoe red but miss why this shoe pairs well with another shoe you liked.
270.ap: The authors propose splitting the attention mechanism into two separate layers. One layer only looks within a single product—say, how the color, fabric, and size descriptions relate to each other to paint a coherent picture. The other layer only looks across products—tracking which items co-occur in user behavior. By stacking these two restricted attention patterns, the model is forced to think in product units rather than word units.
270.ww: This works because it mimics how people actually shop and discover. You first understand what an individual item *is* (intra-item), then you notice patterns in your own behavior—"when I like yoga mats, I also buy towels" (inter-item). Forcing the model to explicitly separate these two kinds of thinking means it captures the item-to-item collaborative signal rather than accidentally learning spurious word-level correlations.
270.po: The result is a recommendation system that explicitly thinks about items as the core unit. The paper shows this item-aware focus improves how well the model captures both what makes a product appealing on its own and how products complement each other in user behavior—without requiring the model architecture itself to change.

271.bp: Watching a movie in another language requires subtitles, and those subtitles need to preserve not just literal meaning but the *feeling* and *punch* of the original. Subtitling is harder than regular translation because you must fit words into constrained space and time, and you must translate for an audience watching faces and hearing voices—context explodes. This paper aims to automate that tricky job using language models, which brings new challenges subtitlers have known about for years.
271.wh: A typical machine translation system translates sentence by sentence as if each line exists in isolation. But subtitles come with three hidden complexities: you need to know who is speaking (speaker diarization), you need to keep technical terms consistent across the whole film (terminology), and you need to match the *tone* of the original even when the words differ. Generic translation models fail because they don't handle these three interdependent problems together.
271.ap: The authors build a system called Hermes with three specialized modules. One identifies who is speaking and when. Another tracks important terms (like character names or specific jargon) and ensures they're translated the same way every time. A third module explicitly enhances the expressiveness of the translation—it doesn't just swap words but tries to preserve the original's attitude and rhythm. All three work together on the same subtitle stream.
271.ww: By separating speaker tracking, terminology consistency, and expressiveness into distinct problems, the system can handle each with its own strategy. Speaker diarization adds context ("this line is sarcasm from the villain, not the hero"). Terminology tracking prevents confusion (the translator won't call a spaceship "vessel" once and "craft" later). Expressiveness enhancement ensures the translation *feels* true to the original, not just grammatically correct.
271.po: The paper reports achieving state-of-the-art speaker identification and generating translations that are both coherent and expressive. The real win is that the system can now handle the full texture of subtitle translation—who says what, with what technical precision, and in what emotional register—enabling real-time localization for streaming services and film distribution.

272.bp: Recommendation systems that truly understand context—what image or creative content works best for a given query—require heavy machinery: vision models that can see, language models that can reason about meaning, and models that link the two together. But at web scale, running these every time a user searches would consume enormous electricity and cost prohibitive amounts. The challenge is: how do you capture that deep understanding in a system fast enough to run on millions of requests per second?
272.wh: Vision-language models are powerful but slow—they're built for offline thinking, not split-second decisions. You could try to directly run them on search queries, but you'd hit a wall: they'd be too heavy, and you'd need enough infrastructure to bankrupt most companies. Meanwhile, you can't just ignore their reasoning, because a fast shallow model won't capture the subtle context that makes a creative asset click with a user.
272.ap: The authors train a small, fast model (DeBERTa, a lightweight text-only network) as a student by having it learn from multiple large vision-language teacher models simultaneously. Each teacher rates the same query-content pair, and the student learns to mimic all their judgments at once (multi-teacher soft-label fusion). The small model is then fine-tuned with low-rank parameter updates, a technique that lets you adapt a large frozen network by only learning a tiny side-layer, keeping the parameter count tiny.
272.ww: By learning from multiple teachers at once, the small model sees a broader range of reasoning patterns, not just one perspective. The teacher models' scores aren't hard labels (right or wrong) but soft probabilities, which lets the student learn nuance. Low-rank adaptation means the model keeps the foundation of general knowledge from pretraining but learns a efficient, task-specific overlay—like learning to see with someone else's eyes through a single thin lens.
272.po: The result is a model that shrinks to 1.5% of its teachers' size while keeping 95% of their ranking quality. It runs fast enough for production (real-time, at scale) while maintaining the reasoning that makes recommendations feel smart and trustworthy. The paper demonstrates this on 4.4 million real search queries, showing the method works in the wild where speed and accuracy both matter.

273.bp: Imagine a warehouse manager searching inventory not just by description but by rules—"show me red shoes available today that arrived last week." Real data has both unstructured pieces (what something looks like) and structured pieces (when it arrived, how many remain). Combining both kinds of questions in a single search is called a hybrid query, and it's essential everywhere: e-commerce, medical records, news archives. But doing it fast and accurately at scale is surprisingly hard.
273.wh: Existing search systems excel at either keywords or numerical/time filters, but not both at once. When you try to do both, you face a trap: use loose filtering to avoid missing results, and you search through mountains of irrelevant data (slow). Use strict filtering, and you accidentally exclude items that should match (wrong answers). Getting speed *and* correctness together requires a fundamentally different approach to how data is organized.
273.ap: The authors propose organizing data into subgroups based on time or other attributes—like sorting a library by century first, then by topic within each century. Within each subgroup, they build a graph index that can handle flexible search patterns. When you pose a hybrid query, the system first narrows down to the relevant subgroups (fast, because there are few), then searches within those subgroups using the graph (precise, because you're not searching everything). Finally, they add a logical query layer that can combine results in complex ways.
273.ww: This works because it respects a fundamental truth: time and other properties create natural boundaries in data. A shoe that arrived last week and one that arrived last year truly are different in important ways, so organizing around those boundaries isn't losing information—it's reflecting reality. The graph index within each boundary can focus on semantic matching without worrying about time shifts. Together, these layers let you get the best of both worlds: you avoid the irrelevant masses without accidentally filtering away valid answers.
273.po: Testing on nine benchmark datasets, the method outperforms seven existing systems on both speed and accuracy. It handles hybrid queries—combining unstructured similarity with structured constraints—without the slowness or accuracy loss of current methods, making it practical for web-scale applications where both types of search are essential.

274.bp: When a search engine shows you ads, it's a silent auction: advertisers bid to appear in prime positions. That auction model worked for decades with text ads in fixed slots. Now imagine an AI generates an article for you, and an advertiser wants to embed a product mention mid-paragraph—not in a side slot. The old auction rules break because the new context is fluid: the effectiveness of an ad now depends entirely on where and how it's woven into the text. This paper asks: how should we charge advertisers when context itself is being generated?
274.wh: Classic position auctions assume that slots are independent—if ad A is in position 2 and ad B is in position 3, moving B doesn't change how many people see A. But when ads are embedded in AI-generated prose, they're not independent anymore. A product mentioned early in an article might *substitute* for one mentioned later ("I already know what brand to buy"), creating complex dependencies that the old math doesn't handle.
274.ap: The authors formalize a model where an AI system can place sponsored content at any point in generated text, and they study two user behavior models. In the multinomial model, a user's choice is balanced across all positions (like scrolling through independent options). In the cascade model, users read top-to-bottom and stop once satisfied (like clicking through search results)—so position matters hugely, and substitution effects are strong. For each model, they derive what the optimal auction mechanism should be.
274.ww: For the multinomial model, positions are independent enough that classical auction theory applies—you can use standard tricks to ensure prices are fair and total value is maximized. For the cascade model, position order creates strong substitution: the paper shows you can't achieve perfect optimality (the math says it's hard), but you *can* find approximately optimal mechanisms by carefully considering how users' decisions flow down the page.
274.po: The paper provides concrete auction mechanisms for both behaviors, with proofs about their optimality guarantees. This matters because it gives platforms a mathematical foundation for pricing ads in AI-generated content: they can now charge fairly for position while accounting for the fact that earlier positions suppress click-through on later ones. Without this, advertisers would either overpay or underpay, and platforms would leave revenue on the table.

275.bp: The web is "free" because advertising pays for it—but that freedom comes with a cost often invisible to users: energy. Every ad displayed, tracked, and measured burns electricity on your device. As climate concerns grow and energy costs rise, the hidden environmental toll of advertising deserves scrutiny. This paper measures something nobody usually asks: how much battery does an ad actually drain from your phone or laptop over a year?
275.wh: Energy consumption on a user's device is hard to measure accurately because CPUs vary, websites vary, and user behavior varies wildly. You can't just run ads once in a lab and extrapolate—real users sleep their devices, switch tabs, have different hardware. Additionally, ads come bundled with tracking systems (cookies, analytics, real-time bidding auctions) that each add their own compute overhead, and it's unclear which component is responsible for the drain.
275.ap: The authors measure energy consumption directly across nearly 725,000 real website visits on real devices (phones, tablets, laptops), monitoring actual CPU usage while ads load and track. They measure three scenarios: visiting sites with cookie consent enabled, sites with ads blocked, and sites relying on real-time bidding (rapid auctions for each ad slot). They use robust methodology to model realistic user behavior—not every visit keeps a tab active for hours, for instance.
275.ww: By measuring at scale across diverse devices and behaviors, the paper captures real-world inefficiency. The key insight is that ads and tracking aren't just downloading data—they're running algorithms (bidding, profiling, ranking) on your device. Energy draws from processing, not just bandwidth. Cookie consent banners make sites run *more* tracking code (not less), and real-time bidding triggers constant auctions, both burning compute.
275.po: The results are concrete: cookie banners increase energy consumption by 2.57% on average, and real-time bidding increases it by 34% on average. Over a year, for a typical user, that's measurable impact. The paper quantifies the environmental cost of the ad ecosystem that nobody usually discusses, giving advocates and policymakers ammunition for conversations about web sustainability and fairness to users.

276.bp: Recommendation systems are shifting from a single recommender algorithm making all decisions to multiple AI agents negotiating with each other—one for discovering products, another for fulfilling orders, another for conversing with you. These agents can plan together, argue about priorities, and adapt in real time. The challenge is that when multiple agents act autonomously, old evaluation metrics (did you click? did you buy?) no longer capture what matters: Can we trust the system? Do recommendations stay fair to everyone? Do multiple agents' goals align or conflict?
276.wh: Classic recommendation metrics measure short-term user engagement or immediate sales. But when agents coordinate over longer timescales, new problems emerge: one agent's action may have delayed effects that another agent can't see; if agents disagree, one may override the other's decision, creating unpredictability; fairness becomes multi-dimensional (fair to users, sellers, and the platform itself). Worse, there's no standard way to *evaluate* coordination quality, trustworthiness, or alignment across populations.
276.ap: The authors organize a workshop bringing together researchers in recommender systems, multi-agent learning, and mechanism design. They seek contributions on three fronts: agent architectures (how to build agents that talk to each other), coordination mechanisms (rules for how agents negotiate), and evaluation frameworks (metrics that capture coordination quality, not just clicks). The implicit goal is to establish shared principles and benchmarks.
276.ww: Multi-agent systems are fundamentally harder to reason about because you have to reason about *interactions*—not just individual agent decisions but how they influence each other. By bringing together the subcommunities (recommendation specialists, agents researchers, mechanism designers), the workshop aims to cross-pollinate ideas: mechanism design has formal tools for coordination, agents research has architectures for autonomy, and recommender systems has real-world deployment experience.
276.po: The workshop output is an emerging set of principles for building trustworthy multi-agent recommendation systems, including evaluation frameworks that measure coordination quality alongside traditional metrics. The paper catalyzes research that bridges a gap: how to move recommendation systems from single algorithms to coordinative agent teams without sacrificing interpretability, robustness, or fairness.

277.bp: When you search for similar documents in a massive library, systems now convert each document to a single high-dimensional vector and find neighbors by geometric distance. This works surprisingly well—until it doesn't. Some recent studies have shown that even the best models fail dramatically on small, focused retrieval tasks with simple queries, suggesting a fundamental limit to this approach. The question is: within those limits, can you still make meaningful improvements?
277.wh: High-dimensional vector search has a mathematical ceiling: a single vector can only encode so much information before it becomes hopelessly compressed. Imagine trying to describe a book using just 100 numbers—you'll lose nuance no matter how clever you are. Additionally, when you stuff everything into high dimensions, the "curse of dimensionality" kicks in: the notion of distance itself breaks down, and nearby vectors may not actually be semantically similar.
277.ap: The authors test whether simple dimensionality reduction—taking the 100 numbers and projecting them to, say, 50 dimensions—helps. They also experiment with meta-embedding, a technique that combines multiple vector representations from the same document into a better single vector. The idea is to see whether the theoretical ceiling is the *only* problem or whether over-parameterization (using too many dimensions) compounds the difficulty.
277.ww: Dimensionality reduction helps because it forces the model to retain only the *essential* semantic distinctions—noise and overfitting get pruned away. Meta-embedding works because different representations of the same document sometimes capture different aspects (one model sees "red car" through color, another through vehicle type), and combining them creates a richer, less-compressed summary.
277.po: The paper shows that within the theoretical limits of single-vector retrieval, simple techniques like dimensionality reduction improve performance by 7%, and meta-embedding adds another 2%. While this doesn't overcome the theoretical ceiling, it meaningfully narrows the gap compared to multi-vector systems. The takeaway: even against fundamental constraints, smart representation choices matter.

278.bp: Watermarks embedded in AI-generated images are meant to prove you created an image (or prevent unauthorized copying). These watermarks are invisible to the human eye but detectable by software. As watermarking has grown smarter—binding the watermark to the image's *meaning*, not just its pixels—experts believed they'd finally solved the problem. But this paper shows that large language models can think their way around even these semantic watermarks, exposing a new vulnerability.
278.wh: Early watermarks lived in noise layers and were easy to strip away by simple image edits. Semantic watermarks tried to fix this by tying the watermark to high-level meaning—if you edit the image, the semantics change and the watermark breaks. But this assumes attackers can only make local edits. Large language models, however, can reason about global image meaning and find edits that change the watermark signal *without* breaking what the image represents.
278.ap: The authors propose an attack called Coherence-Preserving Semantic Injection. An LLM first reasons about the image's semantic space, identifying which aspects of the image's meaning are tied to the watermark. Then the LLM finds edits that change those watermark-relevant aspects while keeping everything else consistent—like rearranging a room's furniture while maintaining "homeyness". The attack uses embedding-space similarity to ensure the edited image still *feels* like the original.
278.ww: The attack works because LLMs can reason about semantics *holistically*. A human might edit a car from red to blue; a watermark-aware system would catch this because color is obviously semantic. But an LLM can realize that changing the car's style subtly—say, from sporty to luxurious—also changes semantic meaning in ways the watermark cares about, while still keeping the image coherent and recognizable.
278.po: The paper demonstrates that LLM-guided semantic attacks consistently defeat current semantic watermarks, revealing that binding watermarks to meaning alone doesn't make them robust. The implication is that watermark designers need to account for adversaries with reasoning capabilities, not just pixel-level manipulation tools—a fundamental shift in how to think about image authentication.

279.bp: Building software today often means a programmer and an AI pair up—the AI suggests code, the programmer reviews it, maybe asks the AI to fix bugs or write tests. The dream is to automate more of this workflow: not just completing lines, but planning what to build, testing thoroughly, handling failures without human intervention, and integrating smoothly into existing development tools. This paper surveys how multiple AI agents can team up to replace the fragmented, single-model-per-task approach with structured, coordinated workflows.
279.wh: Most AI coding tools treat each task independently: code completion, bug fixing, test generation, code review. But real development is sequential and interconnected—you can't test until you've coded, you can't deploy until tests pass, you can't review without knowing the spec. Jumping between disconnected models loses context, and no single model sees the full picture of what's being built.
279.ap: The authors synthesize examples from GitHub Copilot, Mistral Codec, and other systems to show a pattern: specialized agent teams with defined roles (code writer, test engineer, reviewer), a manager that routes tasks based on what's needed, and shared tools (the codebase, version control, CI/CD systems). Agents maintain long-term memory of decisions and mistakes, and can query each other's work to avoid redundant effort.
279.ww: Role specialization means each agent gets expert prompting for its task (code completion is different from test design). Coordination through a manager prevents bottlenecks and ensures agents work in the right order. Shared memory means later agents can learn from earlier agents' experiments—if the first attempt at implementing feature X failed, the test agent won't waste time testing broken code.
279.po: The result is a reproducible, auditable development workflow where agents check each other's work, integrate with real CI/CD pipelines, and close the loop from specification to deployment. The paper provides practical patterns for reliability, security, and cost efficiency, showing that collaborative multi-agent systems can deliver measurable productivity gains and fewer human reviews needed.

280.bp: When a user's interests change over time—maybe you watch comedy for a month, then switch to documentaries—a good recommendation system should notice and adapt quickly. But it also shouldn't forget that you like comedy in general. Getting this balance right while protecting user privacy and not requiring constant retraining is the challenge of continual personalization in real-world systems.
280.wh: Standard recommendation systems are either static (trained once, never updated) or centralized (requiring all user data on one server, a privacy nightmare). Federated learning lets models improve across millions of users without moving their data, but it's slow and doesn't capture rapid shifts in intent. Additionally, distinguishing between a user's long-term taste and their current mood is hard—the system might mistake a one-week binge for a permanent shift.
280.ap: The authors propose ProtoFed-SP, which uses soft prompts (learnable modifications to a frozen model) in a two-layer structure. A fast short-term prompt updates each session to capture session intent (what the user is looking for *right now*). A slow long-term prompt anchors to a small library of prototype users maintained on the server, refreshed using privacy-preserving federated methods. When recommending, the system picks the top matching prototypes and blends their personalized prompts.
280.ww: Two-timescale learning mirrors how humans actually adapt: you have lasting preferences (anchored to prototypes of users like you) and temporary impulses (the fast session prompt). The server-side prototype library prevents forgetting—individual users train locally, but prototypes persist and benefit from all users' data simultaneously. Differential privacy on the federation means the server never sees raw user data.
280.po: Across eight benchmark datasets, ProtoFed-SP improves recommendation quality by 2-5% and reduces catastrophic forgetting. Users benefit from both quick adaptation to session context and stability from long-term memory. The system respects privacy (federated + differential privacy) while delivering personalization that works in real deployments.

281.bp: Recommending the next item a user will interact with requires understanding what each item *is* and how it relates to the user's past. Product databases give you structured metadata (name, price, category), but that's shallow. Large language models can read descriptions and infer deeper meaning. The question is: how do you ground these abstract semantic descriptions in reality—in the actual clicks and purchases that users make?
281.wh: Large language models are trained on general text, not on e-commerce behavior. An LLM might understand that a yoga mat is relaxing and eco-friendly, but it has no idea whether users who buy yoga mats also buy water bottles or fancy soaps. Meanwhile, learning item representations purely from user behavior (collaborative filtering) is blind to the item's actual properties—the system sees "people click this" but not *why*. Bridging these two views is crucial.
281.ap: The authors propose GenAIR, which starts by having an LLM infer an archetype for each item—the idealized profile of someone who would use this product. A yoga mat's archetype might be "health-conscious, environmentally aware, interested in fitness." The LLM generates this once and extracts its embedding. Then the system adds a behavioral calibration objective: it adjusts the embedding space so that items recommended together in reality (based on user interactions) are actually *close* in the embedding, grounding abstract archetypes in observed behavior.
281.ww: The archetype captures the semantic essence of an item (who it's for), and behavioral calibration ensures that essence aligns with real-world patterns. If an LLM imagines a yoga mat appeals to fitness enthusiasts but users pair it with meditation cushions, the calibration adjusts the embedding to reflect that pairing. This way, the system learns item relationships that are both semantically meaningful and empirically grounded.
281.po: GenAIR enables sequential recommendation systems to incorporate rich semantic understanding (from LLMs) while remaining grounded in what users actually do. The paper shows this improves recommendation quality, and the framework integrates seamlessly with existing models without major architecture changes—making it practical for real systems.

282.bp: Large language models can hallucinate—confidently making up facts. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) tries to fix this by having the model read from a document database before answering, so it at least has *something* true to work with. But if an attacker poisons those documents, they can trick the model into confidently repeating lies. As AI agents become central to business decisions, defending against poisoned knowledge is critical.
282.wh: RAG systems trust their document sources implicitly. If a document is in the database, it gets returned and fed to the model. An attacker who sneaks malicious documents into the database (by compromising sources, buying ad space, or other means) can manipulate the model's output without the model ever knowing. Traditional security assumes the source is trustworthy; that assumption breaks in open, adversarial environments.
282.ap: The authors propose SecureCollaRAG, which adds a validation layer: before using documents, the system checks their credibility using a graph neural network. Different documents point to each other and to external sources, and the GNN learns to score credibility by analyzing this network of references. Documents from consistent, well-attested sources score high; isolated, contradictory documents score low. Agents use only high-credibility documents, and the system flags low-credibility ones.
282.ww: This works because manipulation is hard at scale. An attacker can write one convincing lie, but getting *other* sources to corroborate it is expensive. The GNN-based credibility scoring captures this: legitimate knowledge appears in multiple, interconnected sources; misinformation tends to be isolated. By weighting documents based on this network analysis, the system is robust even if some sources are compromised.
282.po: Testing shows SecureCollaRAG resists poisoning attacks while preserving access to legitimate domain knowledge. The system maintains both robustness (rejecting malicious documents) and utility (accepting real knowledge) even when data is distributed unevenly across sources. This makes RAG systems safer for high-stakes applications like medical or legal AI agents.

283.bp: Generative AI systems like image generators and video models are trained on specific data, and they often fail when deployed in the real world where conditions differ. A model trained on stock photos might struggle with user-generated content. A model trained on English text might hallucinate when asked about emerging topics. Adapting these models to new environments without retraining from scratch is a critical practical problem.
283.wh: Models learn the patterns in their training data deeply. When you deploy them on data that looks different—different artistic style, new language, novel concepts—they often fail badly because the patterns have shifted. Retraining from scratch is expensive and slow. Meanwhile, simple fine-tuning can overfit to the new data and forget general knowledge. Balancing adaptation and retention is fundamentally tricky.
283.ap: The tutorial covers two complementary approaches. First, generalizable post-training techniques: methods that adapt a trained model to new conditions without catastrophic forgetting. Second, unified frameworks that handle both understanding (like image captioning) and generation (like image creation) together, since these tasks share knowledge. The tutorial walks through architectural designs for multi-modal models and mechanisms for handling distribution shifts.
283.ww: Post-training adaptation works because fine-tuning carefully is different from fine-tuning naively. Techniques like low-rank updates or prompt-based learning let the model stay faithful to general knowledge while learning new patterns. Unified understanding-and-generation frameworks work because captioning images teaches you what images should look like, and generating images teaches you what captions should describe—they're dual problems that reinforce each other.
283.po: The tutorial synthesizes research on out-of-distribution generalization for multi-modal models, giving practitioners concrete recipes for adapting models to new domains (different artistic styles, emerging concepts, new languages) without rebuilding from scratch. This is essential for deploying generative AI in the messy real world.

284.bp: Modern recommendation systems don't solve one problem—they solve many at once. They predict ratings, predict clicks, predict how long you'll watch, and all from the same data. These tasks compete: optimizing for clicks might hurt ratings, and vice versa. The art is figuring out which models should focus on which task and when to share knowledge between them. This paper proposes a system that adapts this sharing dynamically.
284.wh: Simple multi-task learning trains one shared model that tries to do everything. But different tasks need different features: predicting whether you'll *notice* an item requires different knowledge than predicting whether you'll *like* it if you do notice. Additionally, tasks have different importance—some matter more to the business or user than others, and that importance changes over time. A rigid architecture can't adapt to this shifting landscape.
284.ap: The authors propose Dynamic Experts Synergy: multiple expert models, each specializing in different knowledge, and a gating network that learns which experts to use for which task. The key innovation is identifying leader experts (heavily used by a task) and auxiliary experts (rarely used but containing complementary knowledge). The system then extracts knowledge from auxiliary experts in three ways: looking at their utility (do they help performance?), their diversity (do they cover different knowledge?), and task-relatedness (are they tuned to this task?).
284.ww: This works because it respects two truths about multi-task learning. First, not all knowledge is equally useful for all tasks—specialization matters. Second, even knowledge not directly used (low gating score) can still be valuable if you know how to translate it. By dynamically identifying which knowledge is leader (task-specific) and which is auxiliary (cross-cutting), the system avoids the rigidity of fixed architectures.
284.po: On five datasets, Dynamic Experts Synergy outperforms systems that either fully share knowledge or keep tasks completely separate. The framework adapts which expert contributes what, task-by-task, achieving better multi-task performance by treating auxiliary knowledge as a resource to be explicitly managed.

285.bp: Cities generate vast amounts of data—building energy use, traffic patterns, emissions, population movement—and planners want to use that data to understand what happens if they make different choices today. The question is: what future does a particular policy lead to? This matters because once you build a highway or zone land, changing it is expensive and slow.
285.wh: The real problem is that data describing cities is scattered everywhere: some lives in building management systems, some in traffic sensors, some in satellite images, and some exists only in spreadsheets and government offices. These sources disagree on definitions, they update at different speeds, and they don't talk to each other. A road network dataset might be three years old while real traffic has changed. A forecast tool might expect inputs in one format but receive them in another. Tying all of it together to ask 'what if' questions is like trying to assemble a jigsaw puzzle where some pieces are missing and others don't match.
285.ap: This paper argues for treating scenario-building as a serious problem in itself: not as a technical algorithm, but as a systems challenge that touches digital twins (digital copies of the city), GIS (geographic information systems), simulations, forecasting tools, and the organizational workflows that actually run planning meetings. The authors map out where the temporal mismatches occur—data quality gaps, versions that fall out of sync, integrations that break when one system updates—and propose thinking of urban planning as a data continuity problem, not just a calculation problem.
285.ww: The insight is that you cannot answer a 'what if' question reliably unless your input data is consistent, current, and understood the same way by every tool using it. A climate scenario built on 2023 building data but 2021 traffic data is nonsensical—you don't know which trends are real and which are artifacts of stale information. By focusing on the temporal and definitional coherence of data pipelines rather than jumping straight to forecasting, the paper makes visible the invisible work that has to happen first.
285.po: The payoff is a diagnostic framework: cities can now ask, for each layer of their planning infrastructure (GIS, simulation, forecasting, decision-support systems), 'which temporal and integration gaps block us from running reliable scenarios?' This reframes the work from 'build a better model' to 'make our existing data trustworthy enough to support scenario-building,' which is often cheaper and faster.

286.bp: Fake news spreads quickly and damages public trust. Automated detection—software that can flag false news before it spreads—is a valuable defense, but only if the detector actually works in the real messy world where bad actors are actively trying to fool it.
286.wh: Researchers have noticed that certain emotions and sentiments appear more often in false news: outrage, fear, strong partisan language. So detection systems learn to flag articles that feel emotional as likely to be false. But this creates a vulnerability: an adversary with a large language model can rewrite a false article to sound calm and neutral, stripping out the emotional language but keeping the lies intact. The detector gets fooled because it relied on the emotional signal as a shortcut, not on actual truth or the substance of claims.
286.ap: This paper introduces AdSent, a framework that takes this vulnerability seriously. First, they use a language model to generate adversarial versions of news—taking false articles and rewriting them in different emotional tones while keeping the lies intact. Second, they measure how much existing detectors break when sentiment changes. Third, they build a new detector designed to make consistent predictions regardless of whether an article sounds emotional or calm, by learning to ignore sentiment shifts and focus on deeper patterns.
286.ww: The mechanism works because a detector that explicitly learns 'this prediction should be the same whether the article is angry or calm' is forced to find other reasons for the prediction beyond the emotional tone. It has to latch onto actual inconsistencies in the story, claims that contradict known facts, or structural patterns of misinformation that remain even when the tone changes. By making sentiment irrelevant, the detector has to work harder and rely on more robust signals.
286.po: The result is a detector that remains accurate even when an adversary rewrites the article to sound different. Testing shows that models trained this way keep their accuracy when sentiment is manipulated, whereas traditional detectors often flip their predictions. This is concrete progress toward detection that works against adaptive adversaries, not just against naive false news.

287.bp: Three-dimensional point cloud data—millions of tiny (x, y, z) coordinates that represent physical objects and scenes—is becoming central to robotics, autonomous vehicles, and 3D sensing. But these systems can be attacked: small changes to the point cloud, imperceptible to a human viewer, can fool the AI into misclassifying what it sees.
287.wh: Defending against these attacks is hard. If you modify the model itself (adding defensive layers, retraining), you're invasive—the model becomes proprietary and slow. If you try to filter or clean the point cloud, you need training data specific to the attack, or you need to know what the attack looks like in advance. What you really want is a lightweight, universal shield that works after the model is built, requires no extra training, and stops the attack without harming normal performance.
287.ap: This paper proposes PWAVEP, which works in the spectral domain—a mathematical space where the point cloud is represented not as individual points but as frequencies, like a sound decomposed into bass, midrange, and treble. The key insight is that adversarial attacks hide in the high-frequency components (the 'noise-like' parts of the spectrum). PWAVEP computes a score for each point based on how salient and sparse it is in this spectral view, then removes the most salient points (identified as adversarial outliers) and filters the high-frequency parts for moderately salient points, using a mathematical tool called graph wavelet transforms.
287.ww: The reason this works is physical: imperceptible attacks are typically designed to look like noise, so they concentrate in high-frequency components. By selectively suppressing those frequencies, you remove the attack while preserving the structure of the actual object. Removing the most severely corrupted points is conservative but effective—you lose a few real points but eliminate the attack entirely. The method requires no knowledge of what attack was used; it works generally because all imperceptible attacks share the property of living in high-frequency space.
287.po: PWAVEP is plug-and-play and non-invasive: you can apply it to any model without retraining, without auxiliary data, without modifying the model's weights. Testing shows it achieves higher accuracy and robustness than existing defenses, meaning it stops attacks effectively while keeping the model's accuracy on clean data intact. This makes it practical to deploy as a defense layer in real-world 3D sensing systems.

288.bp: The web is changing from a system where humans read documents to one where AI agents autonomously browse websites, gather information, make decisions, and act on behalf of users or services. This shift could unlock tremendous automation, but it also threatens the economic and legal foundations of the web as it exists today.
288.wh: The tension is this: when agents crawl websites to serve user requests, they consume bandwidth and content without paying for it. They also don't respect the business models that websites depend on—a news site that makes money selling ads to humans sees no revenue when an agent scrapes its articles and serves them to another audience. There are no agreed standards for which agents can access what, no way to enforce permissions at scale, and legal remedies (blocking agents, suing) are slow and antagonistic. Meanwhile, the Global South is less represented in tech governance, so their concerns—about data extraction, sovereignty, labor impacts—often don't shape the rules being written.
288.ap: This paper reports on a workshop in Brazil with representatives from tech companies, media, government, and academia to examine these tensions from the perspective of countries in the Global South. The authors map three core misalignments: first, there's no standardized way to tell agents 'don't access this content'; second, agent-driven content consumption (an agent reading and summarizing news instead of ads being shown) breaks ad-based business models; third, governance mechanisms that exist in rich countries don't apply globally, creating extractive dynamics where data flows one direction.
288.ww: The insight is that the problem isn't technical—it's economic and political. Standards and blocking rules are only effective if everyone agrees to follow them, and agreement requires fair incentives and transparent governance. Without that, companies in rich countries can ignore restrictions, while countries with less market power have no leverage. The paper argues that the current responses—broad bot blocking, legal fights—just hide the misalignment rather than solving it.
288.po: The payoff is a reframing: instead of fighting agents with blocking and litigation, the agentic web can be sustainable if it includes transparent standards (everyone knows which agents can access what), inclusive governance (voices from the Global South shape the rules), and incentive rebalancing (agents and websites have mechanisms to negotiate access and payment). This is a blueprint for making the agentic web an open, fair infrastructure rather than a tool for extraction.

289.bp: Artificial intelligence is everywhere: in content moderation, security systems, medical advice, hiring, and criminal justice. This creates a paradox: AI can help defend against misinformation, deepfakes, and attacks, but the same AI tools can also generate lies, create fake evidence, and automate large-scale deception. The question is how to steer AI toward the defensive and away from the destructive.
289.wh: The challenge is that the capabilities are symmetric. The same language model that can help detect misinformation can also generate persuasive falsehoods. The same computer vision system that can identify fake images can be used to create more convincing fakes. Defensive tools are reactive—they have to catch attacks after they happen.
