326.po: The study found that all models favor the top row, but different models prefer different columns, revealing model-specific biases. Models penalize sponsored tags and reward endorsements, and sensitivities to price, ratings, and reviews vary sharply. This matters because if AI agents become major e-commerce actors, their biases could reshape competition—some sellers could exploit those biases, while others get unfairly disadvantaged.

327.bp: Imagine a large machine learning model trained on graph data (like user-item networks for recommendations). You want to adapt it to a new domain (like a different set of items) without forgetting what it learned before. But you need to do this for many domains in sequence—one after another—without the model collapsing into chaos. How do you continuously adapt a graph model across many new domains without catastrophic forgetting?
327.wh: Standard fine-tuning causes catastrophic forgetting: after adapting to domain 2, the model forgets domain 1. Adding a regularizer (a penalty for changing too much) helps but hurts performance. Cross-domain adaptation is harder because domains have different graph structures. When you add adapters (small specialized models) for each domain, they can interfere with each other. And measuring what the model has learned across domains is hard because graph models don't learn explicit, comparable representations.
327.ap: G-CORMoL uses something called orthogonal mixture-of-experts with LoRA adapters. Each domain gets its own small adapter (LoRA), but these adapters are mathematically orthogonal—perpendicular in a high-dimensional space, so one adapter's changes don't interfere with another's. A routing network learns to blend the adapters dynamically, pulling in expertise from multiple past domains when needed. A contrastive objective (a training trick borrowed from self-supervised learning) pushes different adapters to specialize on different aspects of the problem.
327.ww: This works because orthogonality is a mathematical way to prevent interference: if you try to rotate vector A orthogonally and then apply changes to vector B (also orthogonal), changing B doesn't affect A. A router that learns a global policy means the model can reuse past adapters intelligently, enabling positive transfer. Contrastive specialization ensures each adapter learns something distinct.
327.po: The model can now adapt across many domains in sequence without forgetting prior domains and without degrading performance. It even gets better over time as it accumulates knowledge from past domains. This matters for recommendation systems and other applications where you want one model to serve multiple distinct user groups or item categories simultaneously.

328.bp: In social networks and graphs, communities are clusters of tightly-connected people. A common task is to identify the community a given user belongs to, starting only from knowing the user. If you know Alice, can you find her community without exploring the entire network? This is called local community detection and is useful for real-time recommendation and personalization.
328.wh: The standard approach starts with a seed node (Alice) and expands outward, adding neighboring nodes until you've traced out the full community. But this expansion is prone to accumulated errors: each step depends on the previous step, so mistakes compound. If the seed node is on the boundary (at the edge of a community rather than the core), the expansion can easily drift into a neighboring community. Semi-supervised methods use a few labeled examples to help, but weak supervision makes it hard to correct accumulated errors.
328.ap: SLFM (Semi-Supervised Local community detection based on hyperbolic Flow Matching) reframes the problem as generative: instead of expanding outward, think of it as transporting probability distributions. Start with a distribution centered on the seed node, then use a learned vector field to transform that distribution into one centered on the full community. The system has three pieces: a Seed Selector that uses hyperbolic geometry to validate and improve the seed node, a Flow Transporter that learns how to smoothly morph distributions, and a Community Expander that uses the transported distribution as guidance.
328.ww: This works because treating community detection as transport of probability distributions lets you smooth out accumulated errors—you're not making discrete expansion decisions but learning a continuous path. Hyperbolic geometry is good at modeling hierarchical structures (central, core nodes are near the origin; peripheral nodes are far out), so the seed selector can validate whether your starting point is central or boundary. The flow transporter is learned from weak labels and naturally handles partial information.
328.po: The system is robust to bad seed nodes and weak supervision, finding communities even when you start from a boundary user. This matters for real-time recommendation systems that need to quickly identify user communities for personalization without expensive expansion.

329.bp: Online platforms host billions of pieces of content—memes, images with text, videos, news articles—that can spread misinformation, hate speech, or propaganda. Moderating this at scale is impossible by hand, so platforms use AI. But today's moderation tools work with text or images separately. What if you could use multiple types of signals together—text, images, even temporal patterns across platforms—to understand and moderate multimodal content better?
329.wh: A meme is a single image with text overlaid; hatespeech requires understanding both together. A video showing something suspicious might only become obviously problematic when combined with the audio narration. And a narrative that's okay in isolation becomes dangerous when amplified by coordinated sharing across platforms. Most AI systems are built for single modalities (text only, image only) and miss these cross-modal nuances.
329.ap: MM4SG 2026 (the fourth workshop on Multimedia Content Analysis for Social Good) convened researchers from NLP, computer vision, machine learning, computational social science, and ethics to tackle multimodal moderation. A major theme was how to use large vision-language models (VLMs)—models that reason about both images and text together—and agentic systems (AI systems that act autonomously) to scale moderation. The workshop emphasized interpretability and ethical grounding, not just accuracy.
329.ww: This works because treating content as inherently multimodal captures the full story. A hateful image gains its power from the text overlay; a false claim gains traction from the authority signaled by a video. By reasoning over multiple modalities, systems can catch context that single-modality tools miss. Agentic systems can make decisions autonomously but with human oversight.
329.po: The workshop aimed to advance the state of the art in detecting and moderating synthetic content, memes, and cross-platform narratives. This matters because platforms serve billions of people, and moderation at that scale requires AI that understands context, not just pattern matching—and because decisions about speech have real social impact.

330.bp: When you get a recommendation from a service—a movie, a product, a song—it's usually because either the system notices what you've clicked before (collaborative filtering) or it understands the semantic meaning of what you like. Large language models are now being used to generate recommendations by understanding the semantic knowledge of items, but here's the tension: those two approaches pull in opposite directions.
330.wh: Collaborative filtering (watching what millions of users picked) creates one kind of signal, while language models generate text by predicting the next token. These happen at completely different scales—collaborative filtering cares about which item as a whole should come next, but language models care about which individual token should come next. Existing systems try to patch this mismatch by treating collaborative signals as hints, not as hard requirements, leaving the language model to generate what it wants.
330.ap: The paper proposes TCA4Rec, which translates the item-level preferences from collaborative filtering into token-level distributions that match what the language model is actually predicting. It does this in two steps: first, a 'Collaborative Tokenizer' converts raw collaborative scores into token-space predictions; second, 'Soft Label Alignment' blends these with the language model's normal training to create a softer target (not one-hot, but a probability distribution).
330.ww: By making the collaborative signal speak the language model's own language—tokens instead of items—the system lets the language model's generation mechanism directly optimize for what collaborative filtering wants. The soft labels (probabilities instead of hard answers) preserve the generative quality that makes language models work while enforcing the collaborative preference underneath.
330.po: The framework is flexible—it works with any traditional collaborative filtering method and any language model. Experiments show it can successfully steer language model recommendations toward collaborative signals without losing the semantic richness that language models bring.

331.bp: Knowledge graphs are structured collections of facts about the world (like 'Berlin is the capital of Germany'), and multimodal knowledge graphs add images and other media to those facts. The challenge is building a single system that can work on multiple different knowledge graphs and handle multiple different tasks (like linking related entities, predicting missing links, aligning entities across graphs) all at once, without having to rebuild the system each time.
331.wh: Different knowledge graphs have different structures, different modalities of information (images vs. text), and different tasks you might want to solve on them all have conflicting demands. A system optimized to predict missing links might work badly at aligning entities, and a system built for one knowledge graph might fail completely on a different one with a different topology.
331.ap: The paper proposes MtaIMKG, which uses a task-aware routing network to dynamically decide which pieces of information matter for which task. Instead of feeding all information equally to every task, the system learns to route only the relevant multimodal representations (images, text, structure) to each task based on what that task actually needs.
331.ww: Different tasks have different 'preferences' for what information matters—a link prediction task cares about certain patterns that an entity alignment task might ignore. By explicitly routing task-specific information, the system avoids forcing conflicting tasks to compete for the same model capacity, and each task gets the right signal for its job.
331.po: The system can handle multiple knowledge graphs (new and unseen) and multiple tasks simultaneously without being retrained, making it practical for real deployment. The routing mechanism means information flows efficiently rather than everything being aggregated together.

332.bp: Graph neural networks are tools that learn from data structured as networks—social networks, citation networks, molecular structures. They're increasingly used in critical applications like fraud detection and security, but they're also vulnerable to deliberate poisoning: an attacker can inject fake connections or fake data to trick the model into wrong answers.
332.wh: Most defenses against these attacks are tuned for one specific type of poison (like 'someone added fake edges') and fail badly when faced with a different poison strategy. There's no general-purpose defense that can handle backdoor attacks you haven't seen before, which makes deployed systems fragile.
332.ap: A2GBD proposes an adaptive defense that doesn't assume it knows the attack strategy in advance. It has two parts: a module that flags nodes that look suspicious based on their behavior (without knowing what attack caused the suspicious behavior), and a defense agent that tries different defense strategies on those suspicious nodes and adapts based on what works.
332.ww: By treating the defense itself as an adaptive process rather than a fixed rule, the system can generalize across different attack types. If you poison the graph in a way the defense hasn't seen, the suspicious node detector will still notice something is off (because any backdoor attack creates anomalies), and the defense agent can then try multiple strategies to fix it.
332.po: Experiments show the defense significantly reduces attack success rates across many different backdoor attack strategies while keeping the model accurate on clean data, making it practical for deployment in unknown threat environments.

333.bp: Web search has evolved dramatically over decades—from simple keyword matching ('find pages with this word') to semantic understanding ('find pages about this concept') to generative AI ('just tell me the answer'). Understanding this evolution matters because different approaches have different tradeoffs: they make different kinds of information accessible and raise different questions about what we lose.
333.wh: Each new generation of search promises to be better—semantic search is better than keywords, generative AI is better than links—but they each lose something. Keywords force you to think about your query; generative AI gives you a guess. Semantic search might surface unexpected connections; generative search predicts answers. The tension is between depth and convenience, between discovery and speed.
333.ap: The paper is a survey that traces the technical evolution: how vector models work to capture meaning, how entity knowledge helps, how dense retrieval replaced keyword matching, how retrieval-augmented generation (feeding documents to a language model) tried to bridge hallucination, and now generative search that predicts answers directly.
333.ww: Each stage solves a real problem from the previous stage (keywords missed meaning, semantic search surfaced noise, generative search hallucinates)—but introduces new tradeoffs. Understanding *why* each technique emerged and what it trades away gives you insight into which tool to use when.
333.po: The paper raises concrete questions about the philosophical costs of predictive search: Do we lose cognitive skills when machines guess for us? Do we widen inequality if some people can afford to use advanced search? Do we owe credit to the authors whose content trained these models? These matter for building search systems that society actually wants to use.

334.bp: When you ask a language model a complicated question that requires multiple pieces of information ('Where was the birth place of the founder of the company that made this product?'), it needs to find and reason over multiple facts. The challenge is knowing *when* during the reasoning process you need to go look up facts, and doing so efficiently without asking for information you don't actually need.
334.wh: Language models can't see into their own uncertainty reliably. A single signal (like 'how confident does the model sound?') can be wrong in multiple ways simultaneously: the model might be overconfident, or uncertain for the wrong reason, or not realize it's missing information. You need multiple different uncertainty signals to catch all the cases where the model needs to fetch external information.
334.ap: The paper proposes breaking complex questions into simpler sub-problems, then at each step calculating multiple uncertainty signals: how 'peaky' is the model's token probability distribution, how much do multiple independent runs of the model agree with each other, and how much do these two signals *conflict* with each other. Conflicts between signals are fused into a single score that decides whether to retrieve new information.
334.ww: Different types of uncertainty show up in different ways. A distribution being flat means the model is confused; poor agreement across samples means the model is internally inconsistent; conflicts between these signals mean the model has a fundamental knowledge gap that external retrieval can fix. By capturing all three, the system gets a richer picture of when information is actually needed.
334.po: The system triggers retrieval at the right moments during multi-step reasoning, allowing the model to complete complex chains of reasoning without wasting retrieval calls on questions the model can actually answer internally.

335.bp: Cryptocurrency mixing services let people combine their coins with others to hide the trail of who sent money to whom. This is used for legitimate privacy, but also for money laundering and illegal transactions. Security researchers need to detect when mixing services are being used to hide criminal funds, but they lack realistic training data to build detection tools.
335.wh: Real mixing transactions are messy, rare, and legally tricky to collect. Attackers use sophisticated techniques that look normal on the surface. Without large, realistic labeled datasets, detection methods trained on simplified data fail in the real world. You can't build a good detection system when you only have toy examples of what you're supposed to detect.
335.ap: TGweaver simulates the entire mixing process in a controlled blockchain environment, then adds 'behavioral fingerprints'—realistic patterns in how transactions happen—to make the synthetic data look like real mixing behavior. The result is over 891,000 labeled transactions, orders of magnitude larger than prior datasets.
335.ww: Simulated data trained on real mixing behavior patterns becomes realistic enough to teach detection systems about actual threats. With this scale of labeled data, machine learning methods can learn the patterns in transaction graphs that reveal which addresses are connected, even when deliberately mixed.
335.po: The experiments reveal that old rule-based detection methods fail in realistic scenarios (low precision), but machine learning approaches trained on the new dataset perform significantly better. The dataset and results provide a foundation for building more robust mixing service detection.

336.bp: Large language models are increasingly deployed on private servers and services so organizations can keep their data private. But private deployment doesn't guarantee security—the web services hosting these models can have vulnerabilities that let attackers break in, steal data, or trick the model into doing things it shouldn't.
336.wh: Self-hosted LLM deployments span many different platforms and tools (Ollama, AnythingLLM, Dify, etc.), each with their own security posture. Most deployed systems weren't built with security as the primary goal, and attackers don't need sophisticated techniques—they can often simply access the model without even authenticating or exploit basic web API design flaws.
336.ap: LENS is a framework that automatically discovers self-hosted LLM deployments online, catalogs their API endpoints, builds profiles of how they work, and then systematically probes them for common vulnerabilities like missing authentication, default credentials, and injection attacks.
336.ww: By treating security evaluation as an automated discovery and testing pipeline, the paper can systematically identify which deployment platforms have which vulnerabilities. This turns anecdotal security concerns into concrete, quantified risk.
336.po: Scanning 71,249 real deployment targets revealed massive vulnerability rates: 75% allow unauthenticated web access, 97% of Ollama instances are vulnerable to injection attacks, 60% of Dify deployments allow default credential abuse. The paper reported seven new vulnerabilities (four critical), showing that private deployment is no guarantee of security.

337.bp: When you use an AI assistant on a social platform, you often don't have a single clear goal—you're exploring, your preferences shift, you don't know exactly what you want. The system should help you clarify what you're actually trying to do by asking smart questions, not by guessing. This is different from just executing one command, which is what most AI systems are built for.
337.wh: Simple question-asking doesn't work because it ignores the logical dependencies: some questions only make sense after you've answered others, and asking things out of order creates frustration and confusion. Without modeling these dependencies, clarification becomes a chaotic back-and-forth rather than a coherent dialogue.
337.ap: Prism breaks user intents into smaller pieces and identifies which pieces depend on which others, like a dependency graph. It then generates clarification questions in an order that respects these dependencies, uses a reward function to evaluate whether the clarification trajectory is actually helping, and iteratively improves the system's clarification skill through synthetic user-LLM interactions.
337.ww: By treating intent clarification as a structured graph problem with dependencies, the system can ask questions in an order that makes intuitive sense to the user. Feedback about whether clarifications actually help refines the system's ability to ask the right questions at the right time.
337.po: The system reduces cognitive load by asking clarifying questions in a coherent, logical order rather than randomly, and it learns to do this better over time. Users experience clearer, more natural interactions when they need to think through what they actually want.

338.bp: Many real-world networks have inherent geometry: social hierarchies, organizational structures, product categories. Simple neural networks assume that space is flat (Euclidean), which distorts these geometric structures and loses important information. Networks that can understand curved spaces can represent these relationships more faithfully.
338.wh: Traditional graph neural networks are confined to flat space. When you try to represent hierarchical relationships in flat space, you get distortion—like trying to flatten a globe onto a map. Real-world graphs often have cycles, hierarchies, and other structures that don't flatten nicely, and forcing them into flat space loses information about their inherent geometry.
338.ap: RLSTG extends a type of neural network called Liquid Time-Constant networks (which are good at handling time-varying data) to work on curved manifolds (mathematically defined curved spaces). It formulates the neural dynamics as differential equations directly on the manifold surface, so the geometry is preserved at every step of the computation.
338.ww: When you respect the intrinsic geometry of the graph—its actual curved structure—the neural network doesn't waste capacity on learning to flatten things that shouldn't be flattened. The model can focus on the real patterns in the data instead of fighting against geometric distortion.
338.po: On real-world graphs with complex structures, the model achieves better performance than flat neural networks. The theoretical guarantees mean you can predict in advance that this geometric approach will handle stability and expressiveness correctly.

339.bp: Language models are being used to make decisions that matter: diagnosing medical conditions, evaluating legal arguments, verifying scientific claims. When the model is wrong, the cost is real. We need a way to know whether we should trust the model's answer *without* asking it a hundred times or requiring extra computation.
339.wh: Common confidence measures like token probability or semantic similarity fail when the model encounters unusual domains, when there's distribution shift, or when the model is resource-constrained (can't run multiple times). None of these measures capture what's actually happening inside the model when it gets confused.
339.ap: Structural Confidence looks at the patterns in the model's internal hidden states in the final layers—how stable are the activations, how much do they vary at different scales, what's the overall shape of the trajectory. These structural features capture internal instability that probabilities miss, and they require just a single forward pass.
339.ww: When a model is actually confident and correct, its internal representations are stable and coherent. When it's confused or hallucinating, you can see it in the chaotic patterns of its hidden states. These structural features are more robust to distribution shift than surface-level probability scores because they're looking at computation quality, not answer plausibility.
339.po: On real high-stakes tasks (fact verification, scientific claim checking), the method predicts answer correctness better than existing methods, and it does so with a single forward pass—no extra computation needed. This makes it practical for deployment in resource-constrained settings.

340.bp: Language models are being used as classifiers through in-context learning: you give it a few examples of what spam looks like, what toxic content looks like, then ask it to classify new text. This is practical and data-efficient, but is it secure? Can attackers trick the model into misclassifying things by manipulating the examples or the text itself?
340.wh: In-context learning is fragile by design—the model is supposed to be sensitive to the examples and context you give it. But this same sensitivity is an attack surface: if you can manipulate the examples or the text in clever ways, you might be able to flip the classification without the attack being obvious.
340.ap: ICL-Evader proposes three novel attack types: 'Fake Claim' (insert a manipulated example that teaches the model the wrong pattern), 'Template' (use structural patterns to confuse classification), and 'Needle-in-a-Haystack' (hide the malicious text in unrelated content). All work with zero queries—the attacker doesn't need to see feedback from the model to craft the attack.
340.ww: In-context learning models learn from very little data—that's its strength. But it's also its weakness: a single cleverly crafted example can redefine what the model thinks the task is. Because the attack works through manipulation of input structure, not through mathematical exploitation of model weights, the attacker doesn't need access to the model at all.
340.po: Attacks achieve up to 95% success rates on sentiment analysis and toxicity detection, completely breaking the classifier with no model access. The paper also proposes defenses that mitigate these vulnerabilities and provides a tool to automatically harden prompts against evasion.

341.bp: When you need to allocate things that people don't want (chores, taxes, jury duty), you need fairness guarantees. The classic fairness criterion (maximin share, MMS) says each person should get a bundle no worse than if they split everything equally. But exact fair allocations don't always exist, so you have to relax the requirement somehow.
341.wh: When you relax fairness to say 'most people get their full MMS', the naive approach sacrifices one person completely to satisfy everyone else—that one person gets massively overburdened. That's technically fair to the majority but terrible for user retention and platform stability.
341.ap: The paper proposes a stronger relaxation: n-1 agents get their full MMS (everyone except one), and that one remaining agent gets a near-fair allocation (not perfect, but close). This guarantees that almost everyone is satisfied, which is better for platforms and real-world adoption than perfect fairness for most with one person destroyed.
341.ww: The intuition is that acceptable fairness for all is better than perfect fairness for almost everyone plus complete unfairness for one person. Platform design cares about user retention, so making the worst-off person still reasonably satisfied matters more than reaching mathematical perfection.
341.po: The paper proves that such allocations always exist and provides concrete bounds: for three agents, the worst-off can be guaranteed 9/8 of their fair share; for four agents, 4/3; for larger groups, gradually closer to perfect fairness. This gives platforms a fairness guarantee that's both strong and practically useful.

342.bp: Sequential recommendation predicts what you'll do next based on what you've been doing. The system needs to understand not just which items you like (collaborative filtering) or what items mean semantically (like 'thriller' vs. 'comedy'), but also the *sequence* of how your preferences evolve over time. The challenge is combining all these signals into one model.
342.wh: Existing systems struggle to use collaborative, semantic, and rating information at the same time. Each type of signal is useful but they come from different sources and have different scales. Additionally, treating training targets as hard answers (you will pick this item, period) wastes information—in reality, users often have multiple plausible next choices.
342.ap: SEAR uses a language model to extract semantic embeddings of items, then creates three embedding spaces (collaborative, semantic, rating) that capture different types of preference information. Instead of hard training targets, it generates soft labels: probability distributions over the next k items based on actual user behavior, giving the model credit for ranking plausible choices highly.
342.ww: Language models already understand item semantics at scale, so using their embeddings as initialization gives the system semantic knowledge for free. Soft labels let the model learn that multiple next items are reasonable—if you could plausibly watch a comedy or an action film next, the soft label gives credit for both, which is more realistic than forcing the model to pick exactly one.
342.po: Experiments show SEAR outperforms existing sequential recommendation systems by combining collaborative patterns, semantic understanding, and rating signals. The soft label training captures the flexibility in real user behavior better than hard classification targets.

343.bp: Recommendation systems use embeddings—numeric vectors—to represent users and items. In production systems, the size of embeddings matters: larger embeddings are more expressive but slower to serve and use more memory. The challenge is keeping embeddings small for speed without losing recommendation quality.
343.wh: Dense embeddings (where almost every dimension has a value) pack information densely but require full vector computation at serving time, which is slow. Sparse embeddings (where most dimensions are zero) could be faster but are usually worse at recommendation. You need sparse embeddings that are both compact *and* maintain quality.
343.ap: The paper modifies a production recommender (ELSA) to learn sparse embeddings instead of dense ones. Only the relevant dimensions for each item are active (non-zero), and the training process learns which dimensions to activate. The active dimensions form an interpretable structure—they segment items in a way that aligns with the model's learned patterns.
343.ww: Sparse embeddings are inherently faster to compute with (you skip zero dimensions), but they're also interpretable: you can see *which* dimensions matter for *which* items. This creates an inverted-index structure naturally, allowing the model itself to do segment-based recommendation logic that was previously handled separately.
343.po: In production testing on real data, sparse embeddings achieve up to 10x size reduction with no accuracy loss, and up to 100x reduction with only 2.5% loss. The interpretable structure also enables new recommendation capabilities (like 2D homepage layouts) directly within the model, making the system both faster and more flexible.

344.bp: News channels on YouTube use emotional framing to grab attention. This study looks at how moral emotions—specifically expressions of moral outrage condemning others—affect how engaged people become: not just passive viewing, but liking, commenting, sharing. Understanding this matters because these emotional strategies might be deepening polarization.
344.wh: Most studies of social media focus on attention (views), but engagement is more nuanced—are people just watching passively or actually participating? And does moral framing work the same way across cultures? You need to analyze multimodal content (images and text together, as they appear on YouTube) to capture how the emotional framing actually works.
344.ap: The paper trains a multimodal classifier on human-annotated data from Korea and the US, fine-tuned on a vision-language model. It analyzes 400,000 videos from major news outlets, measuring three levels of engagement (views as passive, likes as moderate commitment, comments as active participation), and correlates this with moral emotion framing in the thumbnail and title.
344.ww: Moral outrage that condemns others (saying 'these people are bad') appears to be particularly effective because it activates people's sense of justice and community: it's not just entertaining, it makes people want to participate. The effect is consistent across cultures and grows stronger as engagement requires more effort.
344.po: Other-condemning moral outrage significantly increases all forms of engagement, with stronger effects as participation becomes more active (views < likes < comments). This demonstrates that moral emotion strategies don't just attract eyeballs; they drive participation. The paper raises concerns about using these strategies to deepen polarization and releases tools for future research.

345.bp: Doctors looking at slides of cells need to accurately identify cancers, infections, and other conditions. But different experts see things differently—one might call a cell normal while another says suspicious. We need datasets where we capture this real disagreement AND have a clear ground truth for testing new computer vision tools fairly.
345.wh: The problem is a catch-22: if you hide expert disagreement behind a single 'clean' answer, your dataset looks perfect but doesn't reflect how pathology actually works. If you show disagreement without a gold standard, you can't fairly test whether a new algorithm is actually learning what matters. Most datasets pick one horn of this dilemma and lose something crucial.
345.ap: CytoCrowd provides 446 high-resolution cell images. Each one has two layers: four different pathologists' independent annotations (showing where they disagree) and a senior expert's final decision (the ground truth). This dual setup lets researchers benchmark both computer vision tasks against a clear answer and test algorithms that try to predict and reconcile disagreement.
345.ww: When you show both the raw disagreement and the expert consensus, algorithms can learn two different things: they can practice standard detection using the gold standard, OR they can learn to predict what messy real-world annotator behavior looks like. This mirrors how actual deployed systems must work—handling both objective tasks and the fact that human judgment spreads.
345.po: The dataset becomes a testbed for the next wave of medical AI—not just algorithms that detect cells, but algorithms that understand expert uncertainty. The paper shows baselines on both tasks, establishing what's hard and what stays easy, so future work has a reference point.

346.bp: When you ask an AI assistant a question, it often searches the web for supporting documents, then synthesizes an answer. The quality of that answer depends entirely on whether it found the right documents. The harder part: the documents and knowledge base keep changing—new articles arrive, old ones become outdated, and what 'relevant' means drifts over time.
346.wh: Standard retrieval systems are trained once on a fixed pile of knowledge. But the real world doesn't freeze: new research papers, news articles, and knowledge keep arriving. The system gets worse at finding relevant documents because the kind of information people ask about shifts, and retraining the retriever from scratch is expensive and slow. You can't just fine-tune naively either, because you'll forget how to find old, still-relevant documents.
346.ap: FlowRAG adds lightweight learning prompts at different layers of the retriever model and fuses information across those layers to capture meaning at multiple levels of abstraction. When a new document arrives or the corpus changes, a special loss function tells the retriever to find documents that are both semantically close AND useful to the final LLM answering the question. The whole thing updates only 0.64% of the model's parameters—a surgical tweak rather than rebuilding.
346.ww: By tying retrieval directly to what the LLM actually uses (rather than just matching keywords), the retriever learns to prioritize documents that genuinely help downstream. The multi-layer fusion means it can adjust quickly without forgetting old patterns, because each layer acts as a checkpoint of different kinds of knowledge. The tiny parameter budget keeps it lightweight enough to update frequently.
346.po: Experiments across four domains show FlowRAG keeps retrieval accuracy high even as knowledge bases grow and shift. It stays robust to forgetting (old, still-useful documents don't fall off the map) and improves the final generation quality, all without the computational cost of retraining everything.

347.bp: We treat data like an infinite supply—one dataset can train a thousand models, be analyzed from a hundred angles, and be shared with researchers worldwide without losing value. But this intuition is wrong in two critical ways: privacy erodes with each use, and repeated queries on the same data create statistical errors.
347.wh: Here's the tension: any real analysis of personal data leaks some information about the people inside. When you publish results, privacy is harmed. When someone else uses the same data and publishes different results, privacy is harmed again. These harms accumulate—they're not one-time costs but running tallies. Additionally, if you query the same dataset many times looking for patterns, you'll eventually find false patterns that look real in the data but don't exist in the world.
347.ap: The paper argues data should be treated as a 'consumable' resource: each use costs privacy, and there's a fixed budget of how much privacy loss the data can tolerate. It connects this to the 'mosaic effect' from law—where combining innocent-looking pieces of information creates a privacy risk larger than the sum of parts. Similarly, combining many seemingly-safe data uses creates cumulative privacy losses.
347.ww: Mathematically, any statistic computed on real data about real people inevitably reveals something about those people. It's not a bug but a feature of information itself—the same thing that makes data useful also makes it leak. Recognizing this forces you to ask: how much leakage can we tolerate, and how should we portion that budget across multiple analyses and users?
347.po: The insight suggests regulatory and technical frameworks that treat data use itself as a limited resource. Instead of a free-for-all, you'd have privacy budgets that researchers spend, and once spent, that dataset can't be reused without accepting further privacy erosion. This reframes data governance from 'release once, use infinitely' to 'release strategically, use carefully'.

348.bp: Social networks, recommendation systems, and many other real-world applications are built on graph data—entities connected by relationships. Training AI on these graphs often means accessing sensitive personal information. We need to learn from the graph structure without exposing individuals to privacy breaches.
348.wh: Here's what makes this hard: in a graph, deleting one person's node doesn't break the connections—their friends' information still exists and still connects to others. A privacy attack doesn't need to know Bob; it can infer Bob's private attributes by looking at his friends and the friends' data. Worse, the standard way to add privacy protection (clipping gradients) in graph neural networks over-corrects wildly, adding so much noise that the model becomes useless.
348.ap: SaGD works in two stages. First, messages flow through the graph using carefully weighted edges that control how much information leaks about each person—no pruning, just smart weighting. Second, when training the neural network, the method computes exact sensitivity bounds (how much one person's data can swing the gradient) without relying on blunt clipping. This lets it add just enough noise for privacy without drowning the signal.
348.ww: The key insight: sensitivity (how much damage one person can do) in a graph isn't black-box magic requiring worst-case assumptions. You can mathematically derive it layer by layer, accounting for the actual graph structure. By doing the math right, you add minimal noise—the noise only covers the uncertainty, not a worst-case paranoia.
348.po: The result is a framework that provides formal privacy guarantees for social networks and recommendation graphs while keeping model performance high. The 'sensitivity-aware' design means you get privacy without the usual crippling accuracy tradeoff.

349.bp: Wikipedia, Stack Overflow, and arXiv are built by humans writing and revising knowledge. Now, AI systems write and revise too. Both contribute to the same shared archive. The feedback loops are everywhere: AI learns from human knowledge, humans learn from AI summaries, more content arrives, quality rises or falls. Understanding these dynamics matters because they shape what knowledge the world has.
349.wh: The problem is feedback complexity: if humans start relying on AI-written summaries to learn (instead of diving deep), they get less skilled. Less skilled humans contribute lower-quality content. Meanwhile, AI trains on that content, so it gets worse too. But the opposite loop is possible: AI helps humans by handling grunt work, humans stay sharp, quality improves. Which loop wins depends on choices about gatekeeping and learning pathways.
349.ap: The paper builds a minimal dynamical model with five key variables: archive size, archive quality, LLM skill, human skill, and query volume. The model includes two types of content inflow (human and LLM), two ways humans learn (studying the archive or asking AI), and two ways to train LLMs (corpus scaling or learning from human feedback). A gate controls whether LLM content gets admitted. Numerical experiments explore different 'regimes'—like healthy growth, inverted learning (humans deskilling), or oscillation.
349.ww: When you can vary one policy lever at a time (like tightening the gate on AI content), you see how it shifts the system between different steady states. The model captures the nonlinearity: allowing more AI content doesn't always degrade quality—it depends on whether humans stay engaged and skilled. The structure makes intuition precise and predictions testable.
349.po: Fitting the model to Wikipedia data, the paper finds a shift around ChatGPT's launch: more AI content, fewer humans contributing, suggesting a regime shift toward 'inverted learning'. The framework suggests ways platforms could design gatekeeping, learning nudges, and training incentives to steer toward healthier equilibria.

350.bp: Recommendation systems, social networks, and knowledge bases often have two types of entities—like 'users' and 'movies' or 'ingredients' and 'recipes'—connected by relationships. Finding clusters of tightly-woven sub-groups (where everyone in one type is connected to everyone in the other type) reveals hidden structure. The problem: this is computationally hard at scale.
350.wh: A 'biclique' is a complete subgraph where every entity on one side connects to every entity on the other side. Finding all of them is expensive (exponential algorithms). Existing clustering methods either use brute-force enumeration (slow) or ignore the biclique structure and just do standard clustering (misses important patterns). You want both: efficiency AND the guarantees that bicliques provide.
350.ap: ECRC (Edge-Centric Reweighting Clustering) takes a different path: instead of finding all bicliques, it reweights edges based on a simple principle—edges inside dense bicliques get high weight, edges on the boundary get low weight. This 'counting-based' approach works even though you never explicitly enumerate bicliques. The method includes graph reduction (removing vertices and edges that can't possibly belong to bicliques) to shrink the problem before the main algorithm.
350.ww: The insight is that you don't need to enumerate bicliques to cluster them. You can infer their presence by counting and weighting: if two vertices of one type share many common neighbors of the other type, they're likely in the same biclique. This counting is fast; enumeration is slow. The math provides strict guarantation that the approximation quality holds.
350.po: Experiments on five datasets show ECRC runs much faster than baselines (cutting both time and memory) while finding clusters of comparable or better quality. The approach scales to larger graphs where enumeration methods would time out.

351.bp: When you have a large text corpus—news, social media, research papers—you want to discover the main topics being discussed. Topic models have always been the standard tool, but they're slow and often find overlapping, hard-to-interpret clusters. Meanwhile, large language models can understand nuance perfectly—but cost money and time to query. Can you get the best of both worlds?
351.wh: The tension: LLMs are smart but expensive. If you query them on every document in a million-document corpus, you'll spend a fortune and wait forever. Standard topic models are cheap but produce blurry, ambiguous clusters that experts have to clean up manually. You want the interpretation and precision of LLMs with the efficiency of automatic clustering.
351.ap: PRISM uses LLMs sparingly as a 'teacher' for a cheaper 'student' model. You sample a small, representative subset of documents, ask the LLM to label what topics they belong to, then fine-tune a lightweight sentence encoder on those labels. The encoder learns to map documents to a space where topics are sharply separated. You then cluster this space directly.
351.ww: The key: LLMs are good at understanding meaning, but students (lightweight models) are good at generalizing from examples. By having the LLM teach the student on a small seed set, you get LLM-quality labels without LLM-cost for every document. The student learns to reproduce the LLM's semantic judgments and applies them to the whole corpus efficiently.
351.po: Results across multiple domains show PRISM finds more separated, interpretable topics than standard methods (both cheap local models and expensive frontier LLMs like those from OpenAI). It requires only a small number of LLM queries, keeping costs reasonable while improving topic quality. Researchers can deploy it locally on their own servers.

352.bp: Social movements—like #MeToo or #BlackLivesMatter—grow, peak, and change focus based on external events, news cycles, and what people are willing to talk about. Journalists need to understand these dynamics to report accurately and timely. If a system could predict how movement discourse will shift after a major event, journalists could prepare better coverage.
352.wh: Tracking a social movement means understanding not just volume (how many posts) but emotional tone and content focus across platforms. Events shift this landscape: an election, a court ruling, or a high-profile incident changes what people talk about and how they feel. Journalists need early warning of these shifts, but monitoring manually across Reddit, news, and other sources is impossible at scale.
352.ap: SMART collects posts from Reddit and news articles, extracts the emotional tone and thematic content of each, then trains a transformer-based forecasting model to predict emotional intensity in future posts. The system applied this to #MeToo and #BlackLivesMatter around the 2024 U.S. election, showing how discourse shifted before and after that event.
352.ww: Emotions are sticky—people's feelings and what they care about change slowly, with clear causal patterns tied to external events. By modeling emotions and themes as time series, the system can learn those patterns (like 'when X happens, sentiment on Y rises 2-3 days later'). This predictability is what gives journalists a window to anticipate coverage needs.
352.po: The system identifies discourse shifts early, allowing journalists to understand how a political event reshaped movement narratives. The researchers released a dataset of 2.7M Reddit posts and 1M news articles to support further study. SMART was designed with input from 20+ journalists, ensuring it solves real editorial problems.

353.bp: When you talk to a chatbot, it gives you an answer—but you don't know why it chose that phrasing, whether it understands your intent, or if it's just mimicking plausible-sounding text. This opacity is a barrier to trust and to learning how to interact effectively with AI. What if interfaces could show you how the AI is actually reasoning?
353.wh: Current AI interfaces are 'black boxes': you send text in, text comes out, but the middle is hidden. Users can't see if the AI understood them, is aware of context, or is being strategic about how to respond. This breeds distrust and prevents people from building mental models of what the AI can and can't do. Users treat it like magic rather than a tool with knowable limits.
353.ap: IntraAI is an interface that visualizes hidden model behaviors—like which parts of your input the AI paid attention to, what it predicted about your intent, and what reasoning led to its answer. It shows interactive visualizations of these reasoning patterns alongside the AI's responses, making alignment signals and strategic choices visible to the user.
353.ww: When hidden alignment signals become visible—like 'the model detected you wanted advice and emphasized cautious language' or 'the model focused on this sentence and ignored that one'—users can build a calibrated understanding of the AI's actual capabilities and limitations. This transparency supports 'interaction literacy': the skill of working effectively with AI despite its limits.
353.po: Users of IntraAI move from passive consumption ('tell me something') to active collaboration ('I understand what you're doing, so let me refine my request'). The system is open source and embodies three design principles: accessibility (anyone can use it), adaptive learning (it teaches you over time), and collective understanding (trust built on evidence, not blind faith).

354.bp: Vision and language AI systems trained on one dataset often fail when deployed on new data—a model trained on clear images might fail on blurry ones, or a system trained on English might struggle with accented speech. These 'distribution shifts' are not rare edge cases; they're common whenever the deployment world differs from the training world.
354.wh: The root cause is spurious correlation: the model learned that if it sees feature X (like 'clear background'), the label is usually Y. But feature X might not be causal—it might just correlate with Y in the training data. When X disappears in new data, the model is lost. Adding safety measures (like 'robustness training') often helps, but they're expensive and unprincipled.
354.ap: SCLF (Sparse Causal Latent Features) uses a gating mechanism to select only a small number of features that actually cause the outcome. It trains the model adversarially (trying different scenarios to find which features fail), uses a penalty encouraging 'invariant risk' (features that predict the label the same way across scenarios), and scores features by how stable they are. Only features that survive this gauntlet get used.
354.ww: Causality and stability go together: if a feature is truly causal (not just correlated), it should work the same way across different scenarios and populations. By enforcing this during training—using adversarial pressure and invariance penalties—you eliminate spurious correlations. The sparsity (picking only a few features) means the model is more interpretable and less likely to latch onto noise.
354.po: Results show SCLF maintains high accuracy (74%) even when the deployment data is strongly biased against what the model learned (out-of-distribution), while staying accurate in-domain (73%). This suggests the model found genuinely causal features, not just surface correlations.

355.bp: Scientific papers cite thousands of other papers to support claims. But citations often lie: a paper might cite another as support when the cited work actually contradicts it, or even when the cited work says nothing relevant. Finding these 'miscitations' manually is impossible at scale, yet they undermine the integrity of the scholarly record.
355.wh: Detecting miscitation is hard because you need to understand three things at once: what the citing paper claims, what the cited paper says, and whether they align. Simple methods check if the papers are semantically similar (they might be on different topics entirely) or look for network anomalies (a miscitation might look structurally normal). You need deep reasoning—the kind LLMs do well—but you can't afford to run LLMs on millions of citations.
355.ap: LAGMiD combines LLM reasoning with graph neural networks. For a sample of citations, the LLM uses chain-of-thought prompting to trace through multiple 'hops' in the citation graph (Does A cite B? Does B cite C? How do they relate?) and assess whether each citation is genuine. A graph neural network learns to imitate this reasoning by studying the LLM's intermediate reasoning states. Once trained, the GNN handles new citations efficiently.
355.ww: LLMs excel at semantic reasoning but are slow; GNNs are fast but traditionally only see network structure. By distilling LLM reasoning (the intermediate steps, not just the final answer) into a GNN, you get both speed and understanding. The GNN learns not just 'is this a miscitation?' but 'why is it a miscitation?'—the reasoning patterns the LLM used.
355.po: Experiments on three real-world citation datasets show LAGMiD detects miscitations better than methods using just semantics or just networks. The system is efficient enough to scale to millions of citations, making it practical for auditing the scholarly web.

356.bp: Modern applications generate streams of tensor data—high-dimensional arrays that change over time. Think of a social network where interactions evolve, a power grid where voltage varies by time and location, or a financial system with multiple assets. Understanding how dependencies between these variables shift over time is crucial for prediction, anomaly detection, and planning.
356.wh: Real tensor data is complex: it has multiple modes (dimensions), and dependencies between variables change. A standard approach might estimate one giant network of dependencies, but with hundreds of variables this network becomes uninterpretable and expensive to compute. You want interpretable, efficient methods that scale and remain tractable as data grows.
356.ap: KTVGL models the tensor as a product of smaller, mode-specific networks (one for each dimension). Instead of one huge network, it estimates a separate network for each mode, then combines them as a Kronecker product—a specific mathematical product that keeps the overall size tractable. The method extends to streaming data, so you can update as new observations arrive without reprocessing the entire history.
356.ww: Kronecker products have a special property: estimating a 100×100 Kronecker network is much cheaper than estimating a 10,000×10,000 full network directly. You get interpretability because each small network is understandable on its own, and computational savings because you avoid exponential blowup. The streaming extension means you can track how networks evolve in real time.
356.po: Experiments on synthetic data show KTVGL recovers the true network structure more accurately than baselines while using significantly less computation. A case study on real data demonstrates practical value. The method stays interpretable because you're working with multiple small networks, not one massive tangle.

357.bp: Large language models are increasingly personalized on users' personal devices (phones, edge servers) while sending intermediate results back to cloud servers for processing. This saves bandwidth and power—but creates a privacy crisis: cloud servers can reverse-engineer the user's original input from the intermediate results ('embeddings') without knowing the model.
357.wh: Here's the attack: the cloud receives an encoding of your text—say, a 768-dimensional vector representing your prompt. With some math and compute power, the cloud can search for the text that produces that vector. It's like someone giving you a face sketch and asking you to find whose face it is—hard but doable. Existing privacy solutions are either expensive (add encryption) or degrade model quality (add noise). Either way, you lose something critical.
357.ap: PrivSplit uses a 'split and compensate' strategy. The edge device splits the embedding into two parts: a public part sent to the cloud and a private part kept locally. The cloud processes only the public part. During interaction, the model uses a compensation mechanism (a precise mathematical adjustment) to restore the influence of the private part without the cloud ever seeing it. The beauty: it's mathematically 'lossless'—the final model behaves exactly as if the cloud had seen the full embedding.
357.ww: The key insight is that you don't need the cloud to see everything to make it useful. You can hide one part of the information and mathematically 'make up' for its absence during the final step. This works because the later layers of the model can accept and compensate for the missing part. It's like splitting a sentence and asking someone to complete it while you keep the punchline—the result is the same.
357.po: PrivSplit provides formal security guarantees against both reconstruction and distinguishability attacks. Crucially, it's lossless: model performance is mathematically identical to the non-private case. This breaks the usual privacy-utility tradeoff—you can strengthen privacy arbitrarily without losing accuracy.

358.bp: Every time you visit a website, your device asks a DNS server 'What's the IP address for this domain?' DNS is foundational to the web. But DNS responses can be manipulated—censored, hijacked, or tampered with—either by malicious actors or state authorities. Understanding how widespread and how sophisticated these manipulations are requires large-scale measurement.
358.wh: Detecting DNS manipulation at scale is hard because modern DNS is dynamic: a single domain might have thousands of different answers, depending on your geography, your network, or load-balancing. You can't just check if an answer is 'wrong'—wrong compared to what? Also, manipulations hide in complexity: a domain might have a chain of CNAME records pointing to multiple intermediate domains, making it hard to trace which step was manipulated.
358.ap: The method uses 'resolution path analysis': it follows the chain of CNAME records (the breadcrumbs that link one domain to another) and analyzes each intermediate node. By understanding the structure of this resolution path and comparing it to expected patterns, the approach can identify when a response has been manipulated or censored. It does this for 2,283 popular domains across global open DNS services.
358.ww: CNAME chains are normally predictable: a content delivery network, for example, follows a known pattern of hops. When that pattern breaks or an intermediate node behaves unexpectedly, it's often a sign of interference. By learning normal patterns and detecting anomalies, you can fingerprint manipulation even in a dynamic DNS landscape.
358.po: Large-scale measurements reveal how DNS manipulations happen and which domains are targeted. The paper uncovers strategies used by malicious operators—like censorship patterns or hijacking preferences—and demonstrates how specific high-value domains are exploited, informing both security defenses and policy discussions.

359.bp: Websites change constantly—layouts shift, features move, old code is removed, new sections appear. Understanding these patterns matters for software maintenance, testing tools, and predicting how websites evolve. But tracking real structural change at scale has been limited by the lack of a large, longitudinal dataset.
359.wh: To measure web evolution, you need historical snapshots of websites' structure—not screenshots, but the actual HTML and layout. The Internet Archive (Wayback Machine) captures web pages over decades, but parsing and analyzing millions of snapshots to extract structural change is a daunting data engineering problem. A standardized dataset would save researchers from reinventing this pipeline.
359.ap: The paper creates a dataset of landing pages for 223 popular websites, with up to 1,000 time-ordered versions each collected from the Wayback Machine at minimum one-day intervals. Each HTML version is parsed into a structural representation: for every DOM node, the dataset records its absolute XPath (its position in the document hierarchy) and the exact capture timestamp. This yields a content-agnostic, purely structural view of how layouts evolve.
359.ww: By focusing on structure (XPath positions) rather than content or style, the dataset captures what actually changed in the underlying code—layout reorgs, feature additions/removals, information architecture shifts—without noise from typography or styling changes. The XPath representation is machine-friendly for machine learning on web evolution.
359.po: The dataset contains over 246 million DOM node positions, providing a foundation for studies on change patterns, predictive modeling of web evolution, and benchmarking maintenance tools. Researchers can now study questions like 'How often do sites restructure?' and 'Can we predict layout changes?' without building the dataset themselves.

360.bp: Smart cities need machine learning models running on the edge—in base stations, drones, mobile devices—so decisions happen instantly without waiting to send data to distant servers. The catch is these edge devices can't share raw data (privacy, bandwidth), so they need to learn together even when they can't see each other's training data.
360.wh: When edge and end devices have different model shapes (one is large, one is tiny), you can't just synchronize weights directly. Sending raw data leaks privacy and kills bandwidth. The edge server never gets to touch the end device's data at all, yet somehow both sides need to learn.
360.ap: Instead of sharing data or whole models, the system exchanges only high-level summaries—prototypes, which are like class-wise fingerprints of learned features. The end device augments these prototypes by contrasting them and aligning them across the network. The edge server takes prototypes and mixes them with noise to create synthetic training signals for its own model.
360.ww: Prototypes are compact (microscopically smaller than data or models) because they're just averaged feature vectors per class. By sharing just these summaries and letting both sides augment them locally, you get knowledge transfer without privacy leaks or massive bandwidth costs.
360.po: Both edge and end models train faster with less communication overhead than existing methods, reaching higher accuracy even under limited resources, verified in real field experiments not just simulation.

361.bp: City planning today is slow—planners spend months consulting stakeholders and running simulations. What if a system could generate many good plans quickly, tailored to what locals actually want, so planners spend time refining rather than starting from scratch?
361.wh: Traditional optimization is rigid: you feed it rules and it finds one answer. Real planning is messy—stakeholders have competing values, the best plan depends on context, and you need designs people can actually buy into. Neither pure human expertise nor simple algorithms capture this.
361.ap: The system uses a large language model to translate vague planning goals ('make the neighborhood walkable') into concrete zoning and layout decisions, guided by a reinforcement learning engine that learns what choices lead to good outcomes. A second stage lets simulated stakeholders score proposals, and their feedback reshapes what the system tries next.
361.ww: LLMs understand language and context—they can read messy stakeholder preferences and real city data. Reinforcement learning learns which decisions compound well over time (placing parks near schools, not warehouses). Together they find plans that satisfy both objective metrics and human values.
361.po: System generates customized urban plans that rival or beat traditional optimization while significantly raising stakeholder satisfaction and learning faster than hand-built methods.

362.bp: Recognizing someone's true emotion from video is hard because faces alone lie—tone of voice, pace of speech, and expression all feed into what people actually feel. A real emotion detection system must listen and watch simultaneously.
362.wh: Audio and visual signals have totally different structures—sound waves vs. pixel grids—so they don't naturally align. Simple approaches just mash them together at the end and miss how the audio shapes the face and vice versa. Real co-evolution happens layer by layer as both signals refine each other.
362.ap: The system uses a State Space Model (a mathematical tool for sequential reasoning) to generate 'guidance prompts' at each layer of processing: audio hints to the vision system about where to focus, and vice versa. After encoding, a multi-stage alignment module first fixes the big structural differences (macro alignment using adversarial learning), then handles fine details (micro alignment per-sample).
362.ww: By forcing audio and video to 'talk' at every processing layer, not just the end, their representations stay synchronized as they deepen. Adversarial alignment actively pushes mismatched features closer, while sample-level refinement handles individual peculiarities.
362.po: System significantly outperforms existing approaches at detecting facial expressions from video, especially in noisy real-world conditions where modalities are misaligned.

363.bp: Recommendation systems suggest products or content by finding similar users or items. Most use graph structures (users connected to items they rated), but whether those graphs actually flow information well—whether they have good connectivity—was barely studied.
363.wh: Graphs can have bottlenecks: clusters of users weakly connected to other clusters, like islands. A graph with poor connectivity ('weak' in mathematical terms) means that a user's information can't flow far, so recommendations stay local and miss relevant items. Existing systems treat the graph as given and fixed.
363.ap: The system identifies which edges (connections) are bottlenecks by analyzing the graph's mathematical structure. Then it learns to re-weight those edges—making bottleneck connections stronger while leaving good ones alone. A lightweight neural network makes these weight adjustments guided by a mathematical constraint that encourages overall connectivity.
363.ww: Strong connectivity means any user's taste can influence any item's score. By fixing bottleneck edges, information flows faster and farther, so the system sees the full picture of user interests rather than siloed neighborhoods.
363.po: Recommendation accuracy improves significantly, especially for harder recommendation scenarios, by making the underlying graph structure more connected.

364.bp: AI systems now power ranking, recommendations, ads—most of what people see online. But if someone asks 'why did this appear?' there's often no answer. Imagine a receipt for every recommendation: what data was used, which model version, who checked it. That's the vision.
364.wh: Platforms treat AI decisions as black boxes for competitive and privacy reasons. There's no standard way to prove a model version is what actually ran, no audit trail of which data went in, no way for third parties to verify the system wasn't gamed.
364.ap: The system creates a decentralized transparency log (inspired by certificate transparency for HTTPS). Every inference generates a cryptographic receipt proving what model ran, what data was used, and what came out. These receipts get logged in a append-only ledger anyone can verify. Model metadata and lineage get registered and signed so switching versions is traceable.
364.ww: Cryptographic receipts are tiny (logarithmic in the number of inferences). Their verification cost is microseconds per request. The decentralized log means no single company controls the audit trail, making tampering visible to everyone.
364.po: Platforms can offer third-party auditing and transparency without leaking proprietary details, enabling regulatory compliance and public accountability for AI-mediated platforms.

365.bp: Hateful memes are dangerous because the meaning comes from the combo of image and text—neither alone tells the story. But in practice images break (media links die), text gets corrupted, or data gets lost upstream. A deployed system needs to work anyway, not crash or fall back to separate models.
365.wh: Fusion models (systems that combine modalities) are often brittle—they expect all inputs to be perfect. If an image is missing, standard approaches fail. Building a separate fallback system for each missing-modality case is expensive and error-prone.
365.ap: Instead of fusing modalities at the end, project both image and text into a shared safety space (a learned representation everyone understands) using frozen pre-trained encoders plus tiny learned adapters. Then feed whatever modalities are available to a single classifier, always in the same way.
365.ww: A shared space means the classifier speaks one language. Missing a modality is just an empty slot in an aggregation function—the system naturally handles it. Frozen encoders keep parameters small; only projectors are trained.
365.po: System matches fusion-only performance with all modalities present while gracefully handling missing images or text without retraining or fallback logic, matching specialized single-modality models when needed.

366.bp: Professional architects spend days on floor plans, constrained by codes and aesthetics. What if a designer could describe what they want in natural language and get multiple interactive 3D options to refine, each photorealistic and spatially correct?
366.wh: Language is ambiguous ('make it open' could mean open-plan or glass walls). Simple text-to-layout methods demand very formal, precise input. They also can't let users tweak designs mid-process, and 2D floor plans don't let you visualize or immerse yourself in the space.
366.ap: A multi-agent LLM system breaks the language description into sub-tasks (identify room types, set constraints, place fixtures). A web-based 3D editor lets users adjust the intermediate design and see feedback before rendering. Finally, a diffusion model with spatial controls generates photorealistic 3D renderings from chosen viewpoints.
366.ww: Breaking language into sub-tasks makes it robust to vague input. Interactive 3D editing lets the user steer the system when it misunderstands. Photorealistic rendering (rather than abstract plans) helps users visualize and trust the design.
366.po: System generates buildable layouts from conversational input, with immersive 3D renderings and full user control over intermediate design decisions.

367.bp: Legal AI research is exploding—models analyzing contracts, predicting case outcomes, writing briefs. But there's no standard way to evaluate these systems. Each lab uses different benchmarks and metrics, making it hard to compare progress or spot which methods actually help lawyers.
367.wh: Legal tasks are diverse (document classification, Q&A, contract review, case prediction) with different performance measures. A single framework has to handle this variety, run efficiently, and let researchers easily add new tasks without breaking existing ones.
367.ap: LegalKit is a toolkit that integrates many legal benchmarks into one system with a shared configuration interface and web UI. It supports different acceleration backends (to run on different hardware) and checkpoints let you pause and resume experiments mid-way.
367.ww: Unified infrastructure means researchers compare apples-to-apples. Web UI lowers barriers for non-ML experts. Checkpoint recovery matters for long legal evaluations. Modularity means new benchmarks slot in easily without redesigning the whole pipeline.
367.po: Legal NLP research becomes reproducible and comparable across studies; researchers can focus on novel methods instead of building evaluation infrastructure from scratch.

368.bp: Starlink satellites now outnumber all other satellites combined and beam internet to millions. Yet nobody outside SpaceX knows much about its internal network structure, where traffic flows, or what services are exposed. Transparency matters for security and policy.
368.wh: Starlink keeps internal details private, and direct access to their systems is restricted. You can't just call them and ask 'how does your routing work.' But DNS records leak hints—servers accidentally reveal internal structure—and you can scan public IP ranges to spot patterns.
368.ap: By analyzing leaked DNS data, researchers infer how Starlink's internal networks split into zones and what services sit where. Passive DNS shows user behavior (which services people use, traffic patterns). Active scanning of public IPs reveals which services are exposed and whether they have security holes.
368.ww: DNS is a side channel—DNS servers sometimes leak the topology accidentally. Passive monitoring (just watching traffic, not interfering) reveals real usage patterns. Public IPs are fair game for security scanning under responsible disclosure principles.
368.po: First large-scale characterization of Starlink's ground infrastructure, revealing architectural choices, user behavior, and security posture without proprietary information.

369.bp: Chinese idioms are like colorful sayings in English ('raining cats and dogs')—the literal words (cats, dogs) don't explain the real meaning (heavy rain). Multimodal systems need to get this: the picture and text together should point to the idiom's true metaphorical sense, not just its surface words.
369.wh: An idiom's literal words and true meaning can be opposite. 'Kill two birds with one stone' sounds violent but means efficiency. Worse, the same idiom means different things in different contexts. Systems that just match words to images miss the metaphor entirely.
369.ap: The system builds a graph showing explicit relationships between literal and metaphorical meanings of each idiom. It also creates specialized sub-systems (experts) that understand different types of idioms—one for when literal and metaphorical meanings apply, one for when they diverge. Each expert focuses on its specialty; they vote to pick the best idiom.
369.ww: Explicit semantic graphs make metaphors tangible rather than hidden. Specialized experts divide the labor, so the system doesn't try to solve all idiom types the same way. Voting combines their knowledge.
369.po: System accurately selects idioms from image-text pairs, handling both the literal-to-metaphorical jump and context-dependent meanings better than systems that ignore metaphor.

370.bp: Language models now augment their answers by fetching real data from knowledge bases before answering. This is safer than hallucination—if the data is trustworthy. But what if attackers slip false information into the knowledge base? Systems need defenses.
370.wh: Graph-based knowledge systems reorganize raw text into structured graphs (entities, relationships) before retrieval. This should be safer than raw-text systems because structure filters noise. But attackers can also forge structure—fake relations, fake entities that look real—and mislead the model.
370.ap: The attacker creates poisoned 'toxic events' (fake facts disguised as real ones) and plants them in the knowledge base. They also fake the history of how these facts evolved from real information, making false knowledge seem like it legitimately evolved from seed facts. In multi-target attacks, they link poisons so they reinforce each other.
370.ww: Structured graphs look more trustworthy to models, so poisoned structure is more persuasive than raw text. Fake event evolution (showing false intermediate steps) makes invented facts seem like natural consequences of real knowledge.
370.po: Demonstrates vulnerabilities in graph-based knowledge systems; shows attackers can poison knowledge graphs more effectively than raw-text systems, revealing a security gap in retrieval-augmented systems.

371.bp: Graph neural networks learn from network structure (social graphs, citation graphs, molecule connections). Most treat the whole graph as one flat object. But real graphs hide internal organization—tight communities, bottleneck nodes—that matter for learning.
371.wh: Treating a graph as flat misses its internal structure. Some nodes act as bridges between communities; some are local hubs. Simple augmentation (randomly removing nodes) treats all removals equally, but destroying a bridge is much worse than removing a hub.
371.ap: Decompose the graph into tree-like structures (a classical graph theory tool) where local neighborhoods become 'bags.' Compute importance scores for each node and edge based on their role as bridges or hubs. Use these scores to make intelligent augmentation: preserve bridges, destroy isolated nodes, weaken global hubs. Also craft a new similarity loss that treats tree-based proximity differently from plain graph distance.
371.ww: Decomposition reveals hidden structure. Importance scores target augmentation intelligently—removing what matters most (bridges) hurts learning worse than random, so preserving them matters. Tree-based similarity captures topology that edge-based distance alone misses.
371.po: Graph learning (self-supervised and supervised) improves over state-of-the-art by respecting internal structure during augmentation and similarity computation.

372.bp: VTubers—digital avatars with human performers—are a multi-billion-dollar entertainment industry. But the business model is punishing: agencies own the persona, the performer bears all reputational risk, and when they quit and restart ('reincarnation'), they lose audience, income, and sometimes face harassment.
372.wh: Nobody has measured the cost of reincarnation at scale. Is it a minor blip or catastrophic? Without numbers, performers and agencies can't push for better contracts or industry reform.
372.ap: Researchers analyzed 12 major reincarnation cases using 728K livestream sessions and 4.5 billion viewer interactions, tracking metrics like audience size, revenue, harassment, and industry impact before and after reincarnation.
