372.ww: Large-scale data reveals patterns individual cases might hide. Livestream metrics are objective (viewers can't lie), and social media interactions capture harassment quantitatively.
372.po: First empirical study proving reincarnation causes severe career damage to performers—substantial audience loss, income drop, increased harassment—with implications for labor practices and industry sustainability.

373.bp: Graph classification systems are trained on a fixed set of categories (e.g., 'toxic', 'safe'). But in the real world, new node types appear that the model never saw (novel classes). The system must either classify unknown nodes or reject them as 'unknown,' without retraining.
373.wh: Standard graph learning maximizes performance on known classes but doesn't build clear boundaries between known and unknown. Novel class nodes cluster randomly among known classes instead of being recognized as outliers. Existing methods don't handle mixing known and novel classes well.
373.ap: Novel 'negative Mixup' synthetically creates intermediate examples between known classes that push the model to learn clearer decision boundaries. Separate contrastive learning (training examples to be similar to their true class, different from others) maximizes spread between classes and compactness within classes, across multiple graph-processing layers.
373.ww: Negative Mixup creates hard cases at class boundaries, forcing the decision boundary to be clear and sharp rather than fuzzy. Multi-layer contrastive learning ensures that structure (how nodes connect) is consistent with class identity at every depth, making unknown nodes stand out as poorly-connected-to-any-class.
373.po: System reliably rejects novel class nodes while maintaining high accuracy on known classes, even when test data heavily mixes known and unknown categories.

374.bp: Live streaming platforms need real-time moderation and sentiment detection—flagging hate speech or sudden mood shifts instantly. But video, audio, and text streams arrive asynchronously and late, so systems must decide with partial information.
374.wh: The lightweight encoder learns by aligning audio/visual cues with text (cross-modal contrastive training). Loss down-weights examples where the target segment barely overlaps the frame, since those cases are too noisy to learn from reliably.
374.ap: Use a fast, lightweight streaming encoder for most frames. When a case is ambiguous or needs deeper understanding, route it to a heavyweight vision-language model. If context is insufficient (too early in a scene), defer the decision until more evidence arrives.
374.po: System achieves accuracy comparable to using vision-language models alone while calling the expensive model only occasionally, dramatically reducing latency and computation on live streams.

375.bp: YouTube's recommendation engine shapes what billions of people watch every day. Short-form videos (Shorts) are growing explosively, but we don't know whether they polarize viewers differently than longer videos—do they push people toward more extreme political content or less? This matters because algorithmic polarization can fragment public discourse.
375.wh: YouTube's algorithms are black boxes, so researchers can't see the rules inside. They had to design an audit—a kind of experiment where they watch what recommendations get shown, exactly like a real user would, then analyze patterns. They collected 50,000 paired recommendations to compare short and long versions of political and nonpolitical content.
375.ww: By matching the same content across formats, they isolate the algorithm's own bias. If Shorts recommends way more extreme partisan content than the long version of the same story, that's the algorithm's doing, not because people prefer different content. This tells them which format breeds polarization.
375.po: The paper reveals fundamental differences between the two algorithms—some dimensions show short-form videos expose viewers to more political content or less diverse sources. This informs how platforms should tune recommendations to avoid polarizing their users.

376.bp: When you ask 'what's the weather next Tuesday?' or 'when does the traffic clear?', you need facts in a specific time order. Answering 'Will it rain during my meeting at 3pm?' requires knowing not just it-will-rain, but when. Most AI systems answer one fact at a time and don't keep track of the clock.
376.wh: Typical retrieval systems grab one chunk of data and call it done. But temporal questions require chaining: 'Find event A, then check if B happened after A, then see if C conflicts with the overlap.' Each step depends on time constraints—but most systems don't reason about those constraints as they go.
376.ap: This work builds a system (KG-IRAG) that represents events with exact timestamps and validity intervals, then uses a time-aware planner to fetch evidence step-by-step along a timeline. It chains retrievals together, checking at each step whether the next fact fits the time constraints from earlier steps. Think of it like building a timeline by iteratively adding dated facts and checking they don't contradict.
376.ww: By keeping temporal constraints visible and checking them at every retrieval step, the system avoids dead ends. If you find that Event B happened after Event A, that eliminates any retrieved facts that would place them in the wrong order. It's like a detective building an alibi—each new fact must fit the timeline, not break it.
376.po: On temporal question benchmarks and real-world weather and traffic queries, this approach improves accuracy and produces better-calibrated confidence. It also needs fewer retrievals because it targets only facts that actually matter for the timeline, cutting wasted computation.

377.bp: Businesses want to know who their most valuable customers are so they can invest in keeping them. Customer Lifetime Value (LTV)—how much money someone will spend over their entire relationship with the company—is the key metric. But most customers are worth little, while a tiny 'whale' segment is worth enormous amounts.
377.wh: The data is wildly imbalanced: thousands of regular users skew the averages, drowning out the small number of ultra-valuable ones. Simple statistical models assume things are roughly balanced and fail here. A model can look 'accurate' on average but miss the whales entirely. Also, even within cheap customers, there's huge variation—some might become valuable later.
377.ap: This work (CC-OR-Net) splits the prediction into three pieces: first, a ranking module that sorts users into tiers (low-value, medium, high-value) with guaranteed order. Second, within each tier, a regression model fine-tunes the exact value. Third, a special module that focuses extra attention on top-tier users to nail their value precisely. The ranking part is baked into the architecture, not added as a loose penalty.
377.ww: By ranking first, the model avoids the averaging trap—it never has to balance whale and regular customers, because they live in different tiers. Fine-tuning within each tier then works on a more uniform dataset. The third module ensures whales get pinpoint accuracy, not drowned out by the sea of regular users.
377.po: On datasets with over 300 million users, this design beats prior approaches on business-critical metrics: it predicts high-value customers accurately while still doing well overall. It trades off accuracy where it matters least (average users) to excel where it matters most (whales).

378.bp: Search engines and AI systems that look up facts on the web are choking on AI-generated garbage. As language models write more content and it gets indexed, search results and AI summaries become increasingly polluted with recycled synthetic text. If this spiral continues, the web becomes useless for grounding AI systems in real information.
378.wh: Most AI-generated content looks plausible on the surface—it's grammatically correct and topically relevant. Search engines can't easily tell it apart from human writing. Unlike spam (which is obviously garbage), synthetic content can have the veneer of quality while being shallow or misleading. And once it spreads, retrieval systems can't know which sources are original versus recycled.
378.ap: This work experimentally tests what happens as AI content floods the web. They simulate a scenario where 67% of search results are high-quality synthetic content, then measure how much that pollution contaminates what gets shown to users. They also test adversarial scenarios where bad actors hide malicious instructions in fake content, to see whether traditional ranking (like BM25) or LLM-based rankers catch them.
378.ww: The results are frightening: at 67% synthetic pool contamination, over 80% of what users see ends up coming from AI sources—yet answer accuracy stays superficially stable because the synthetic content is somewhat correct. This is a silent failure: the system looks fine but relies on sources that aren't original. LLM-based rankers suppress adversarial content better, but the problem persists.
378.po: The paper shows that retrieval systems need explicit defenses against synthetic content creep. Without them, web-grounded AI systems will quietly shift toward recycled evidence in a self-reinforcing cycle. It's a warning that the ecosystem needs deliberate strategy to preserve authentic sources.

379.bp: Language models are starting to act as autonomous agents on the web—making decisions, adapting to feedback, and coordinating with other AI systems. But they need a way to explore which actions work and exploit the ones that are already known to succeed. Multi-armed bandits, a mathematical framework for this trade-off, are the key to teaching LLMs to behave intelligently in changing environments.
379.wh: LLMs generate text greedily by default—they pick the most likely next word and move on. But when they're making decisions (which recommendation to show, which message to send), they need to try new things sometimes to discover better options, not just always pick the obvious choice. Without explicit exploration, they can't adapt when circumstances change.
379.ap: This tutorial shows how to treat LLM decisions as a bandit problem: each possible text generation or action is an 'arm' (like slots on a slot machine), and the system learns a reward signal from how users respond. It uses strategies like epsilon-greedy (sometimes pick the best arm, sometimes pick randomly) and Thompson Sampling (maintain uncertainty and sample optimistically) to balance exploration and exploitation.
379.ww: Bandits solve exploration-exploitation mathematically—they prove that certain strategies find the best actions faster than random guessing. By embedding bandit logic into LLM decision-making, the system learns which options work without wasting vast amounts of compute on obviously bad choices. Over many interactions, this compounds into smarter behavior.
379.po: The tutorial shows real applications: multi-agent dialogue that coordinates better through bandit-driven decisions, personalized content curation that adapts to user feedback, and recommendation strategies that learn which styles of suggestion work. This framework lets LLM agents become truly adaptive rather than static.

380.bp: Advertising platforms use deep learning models to rank and price ads in milliseconds. If something goes wrong inside the model—data corruption, a silent bug, or a sudden shift in user behavior—prices can swing wildly, costing millions before anyone notices. The system needs to detect and fix these failures automatically, in real time.
380.wh: Deep learning models can break silently. The model still produces numbers; they're just wrong. Data corruption during training, upstream feature pipelines sending garbage, foundation model retraining gone awry—none of these crash the system, they just poison its decisions. You can't catch these by watching error logs; you need to watch the model's output distribution.
380.ap: This work (Prediction Guardian) monitors the distribution of predictions in real time. A healthy ad-ranking model produces a predictable log-normal distribution of predicted values (most ads cheap, a few expensive). The system continuously compares current predictions to historical baselines using a statistical distance measure (Jensen-Shannon divergence). When the distribution shifts, it flags an anomaly.
380.ww: Distributions capture global health where individual examples don't. A few weird predictions blend into noise, but a systematic shift—all predictions too high, all too low, or many outliers—is visible in the aggregate. By catching distribution shifts early, the system can apply targeted fixes (smooth suspicious predictions, zero out outliers) before harm cascades downstream.
380.po: The paper tests three realistic corruption scenarios (underprediction, overprediction, and tail outliers) and shows Prediction Guardian detects and mitigates them. Deployed at scale in ad systems, it prevents pricing errors that would cost millions, without disrupting the normal serving flow.

381.bp: Online communities in Chinese-language spaces are flooded with toxic speech in obfuscated forms—deliberately misspelled, symbolized, or hidden in phonetic encodings to evade detection. Cleaning up toxic content at scale requires understanding these variants, but manually coding every permutation is impossible.
381.wh: Toxic language detection is normally pattern-matching: look for known bad words. But bad actors deliberately mutate words—using pinyin abbreviations, replacing characters with visually similar ones, mixing in symbols. A static rulebook can't keep up with the creativity of evasion. You need a system that understands how variants relate to canonical toxic terms.
381.ap: This work builds a knowledge graph that maps canonical toxic terms to their variants using three types of relationships: phonetic similarity (sounds like the real word), visual resemblance (looks like the real word), and contextual co-occurrence (appears together with known toxic content). A small labeled dataset fine-tunes an LLM for initial normalization. Then during detection, the system uses the graph to reason about whether a variant is likely toxic, and fills in missing graph connections on the fly.
381.ww: The knowledge graph structure lets the system generalize from known variants to unseen ones. If it knows 'xyz' and 'abc' are both variants of the same toxic term, and sees a new combination 'xyzabc' for the first time, it can infer this is also toxic by following the graph. The LLM reasoning handles incomplete knowledge by inferring likely paths.
381.po: Tested on multiple Chinese toxic language datasets, this approach consistently beats static detection and outperforms other knowledge-enhanced systems. It catches obfuscated variants better than prior work, making it practical for scaling content moderation in Chinese online environments.

382.bp: Dengue fever outbreaks devastate tropical cities; early warning saves lives. Tainan City has suffered multiple dengue surges, yet traditional forecasting methods are too slow or too coarse-grained. If public health officials had accurate, weekly, village-level predictions, they could deploy resources exactly where the next outbreak will hit.
382.wh: Epidemic forecasting is complex: disease spread depends on mosquito populations (entomological data), human behavior, climate, population density, neighborhood connectivity. All of these change over time and space. Simple models either ignore spatial structure (treating the whole city as one pool) or can't update quickly enough to catch emerging hotspots.
382.ap: G-SEIR combines a learnable SEIR epidemiological simulator with a spatio-temporal graph neural network. SEIR is a compartmental model that tracks susceptible, exposed, infected, and recovered populations. But instead of fixed parameters, the system learns how to weight transitions between compartments. The graph neural network captures how disease spreads between districts and villages by treating them as nodes with edges representing movement and contact.
382.ww: By learning rather than hand-tuning epidemic parameters, the system adapts to real outbreak dynamics. The graph structure lets information flow between neighboring regions—if a district sees rising cases, the model knows adjacent villages are at higher risk. Combining epidemiology (which captures disease biology) with learning (which captures local variation) avoids both unrealistic assumptions and pure curve-fitting.
382.po: On Tainan's 2015 and 2023 outbreaks, G-SEIR outperforms eleven baselines on prediction accuracy. It generates fine-grained, weekly forecasts for 752 villages—granular enough for authorities to target interventions. A web interface lets officials spot emerging hotspots in real time, supporting proactive disease control instead of reactive response.

383.bp: Fashion-conscious shoppers searching for clothing online want to find items matching specific attributes—a red leather jacket, blue denim with distressing, etc. Text search fails (most people can't describe finesse), so image search is essential. But finding items with subtle attribute combinations is hard because backgrounds, lighting, and pose clutter the signal.
383.wh: Patch-based attention methods slice images into grids and focus on relevant patches. But fashion attributes like 'distressed denim' or 'leather sleeve detail' don't align neatly with rectangular grids—they sprawl across irregular regions and get drowned out by background. Simply looking harder at the right patches isn't enough; you need tokens that capture semantic regions naturally.
383.ap: This work (Super Fashion) uses superpixels instead of patches. Superpixels are chunks of the image with similar color and texture, forming semantically coherent regions (a sleeveless armhole, a plaid pattern, a metal zipper). First, an attribute-guided attention mechanism identifies which regions matter for the target attribute. Then superpixel segmentation groups pixels within those regions into compact tokens. A Transformer fuses superpixel tokens with attribute tokens, letting the model learn both what to look for and where to find it.
383.ww: Superpixels follow image structure better than grids do. A leather texture naturally forms a superpixel; a plaid pattern does too. By using these natural regions as tokens, the model can focus on semantically meaningful units rather than fighting with grid-aligned noise. Attribute-guided attention narrows the focus first, so superpixel segmentation works on clean, relevant regions.
383.po: On fashion retrieval benchmarks (FashionAI, DARN, DeepFashion), Super Fashion improves ranking accuracy by 1.84%-9.35% over prior methods. It finds items with matching attributes more reliably, making fashion search more useful for people with specific style preferences.

384.bp: Training machine learning models requires millions of human labels—images annotated as safe or unsafe, text classified as harmful or clean. Crowdsourcing these labels is cheap at scale, but workers vary wildly in honesty and skill. Some contribute high-quality labels; others game the system or submit garbage. Current incentive schemes can't separate good from bad contributors.
384.wh: Paying everyone equally encourages fraud. Someone labeling random answers gets paid the same as someone laboring carefully. Paying more risky rewards bad contributors proportionally to their damage (they earn money for sabotaging), and discourages participation. You need a system that rewards honesty, punishes fraud, without killing willingness to participate.
384.ap: This work (NAI) applies signed Shapley values to crowdsourcing. Shapley value is a game-theory tool for apportioning credit fairly; NAI extends it to assign negative credit for harmful contributions. It estimates each worker's ability (skill level), combines it with real-time task results to score their contribution (positive or negative), then uses a dynamic stake pool—a kind of escrow where workers post collateral. If their contribution is positive, they recoup and earn. If negative, they lose part of their stake.
384.ww: The Shapley approach distributes credit precisely: it accounts for what each worker contributed relative to the rest of the team. A worker who submitted a bad label when others agreed loses credit; one who rescued a mislabeled image gains it. The stake pool creates cost for bad behavior without blocking future participation—workers can recover and rebuild trust.
384.po: Deployed on NetEase's crowdsourcing platform with 80,000 monthly active workers, NAI improved labeling accuracy by 59.6% for beginner tasks and reduced fraud rates by 14.8%-33.9% across all difficulty levels. It scales to millions of labels while maintaining quality and trust.

385.bp: Recommendation systems crave data—the more user-item interactions recorded, the better the model learns. But most people interact with only a tiny fraction of items (movies, products, news), leaving the system with vast sparse regions of unknowns. Also, popular items get recommended far more than niche ones, creating imbalance. These two problems cripple recommendation quality.
385.wh: Sparsity and imbalance are baked into user behavior: most people are passive; blockbuster items dominate views. Simple fixes like adding fake interactions make things worse. You can't just generate more data; you have to generate the right data—interactions that fill gaps believably and balance class representation without breaking the underlying recommendation structure.
385.ap: This work reframes the problem using line graphs. Instead of thinking about user-item interactions, it transforms them into a line graph where nodes are interactions and edges connect interactions that share a user or item. Sparsity and class imbalance become a node-classification problem in the line graph (too few labeled nodes, imbalanced labels). The work proposes LGDA: a data augmentation strategy that generates high-quality balanced pseudo-interactions using the line graph structure, then filters them by confidence to keep only believable ones.
385.ww: Line graph structure captures interaction patterns naturally. Two interactions sharing a user are connected; the model can see that generating similar interactions is plausible. By treating it as a node-classification task on the line graph, the work leverages mature imbalanced-learning techniques. Confidence filtering prevents junk augmentation from degrading real interactions.
385.po: On four real-world recommendation datasets, LGDA improves recommendation performance and system robustness without modifying the underlying model. It's a plug-and-play fix for data sparsity and imbalance, letting practitioners boost quality without redesigning their entire system.

386.bp: The field of web technologies spans social networks, graphs, privacy, security, fairness, and ethics. Each area has crucial papers that critically analyze models and methods. TIME is a workshop bringing together domain experts and newcomers to distill key insights from these papers into actionable knowledge.
386.wh: Research literature explodes faster than any individual can read. A newcomer to web security, graph algorithms, or fairness faces hundreds of papers with no clear starting point. Practitioners need quick reference guides, not original research. Critical analysis that compares methods across papers—which approaches work, where they fail, what tradeoffs exist—is rare but invaluable.
386.ap: TIME solicits survey, evaluation, and review papers that take a birds-eye view of a subfield. Papers might compare datasets, analyze trends in methods, or reconcile conflicting findings. The workshop complements these with invited talks from industry experts sharing practical experience. Discussions and networking create space for cross-domain collaboration.
386.ww: Surveys and reviews synthesize what the community has learned, identify blind spots, and point out promising directions. By bringing experts and newcomers together, the workshop bridges research and practice. Talks ground theory in real-world constraints (at a 3B-user platform, this approach broke for X reason). Attendees leave with a map of the field, not just isolated papers.
386.po: Participants gain actionable knowledge for their own work: understanding which privacy techniques scale, how fairness definitions interact with real deployments, which graph algorithms actually work at web scale. The workshop becomes a trusted resource for anyone starting work in web technologies.

387.bp: Industrial control systems (ICS)—power grids, water treatment, manufacturing—require safety-critical response times measured in tens of milliseconds. Security researchers often propose blockchain and encryption as panaceas. But if these slow down the control loop to hundreds of milliseconds, the system becomes unsafe. Real security must preserve the ability to respond in time.
387.wh: Blockchain consensus is inherently probabilistic—nodes negotiate agreement, introducing jitter. Homomorphic encryption (allowing computation on encrypted data) requires intensive computation, adding 100+ millisecond overhead. Industrial controllers need <10ms response time to be safe. The math is brutal: 51-440ms latencies violate safety-critical requirements by factors of 5-44x.
387.ap: This work analyzes where encryption overhead is incurred across the Purdue Model of industrial networks (Levels 0-5, from sensors to cloud). It shows BC+HE architectures create a 'dead zone' bottleneck at gateway levels, exposing vulnerabilities. The alternative: use lightweight lattice-based cryptography (LWE, Ring-LWE) for fast sensor-to-controller authentication (meeting <10ms constraints), and reserve BC+HE for non-real-time enterprise layers.
387.ww: Lattice cryptography is computationally cheap and quantum-resistant, making it suitable for real-time layers. Enterprise layers don't need microsecond response; they can absorb blockchain's latency. By decoupling security strategies by layer—speed for critical loops, richness for non-critical enterprise—the system achieves both safety and security without compromise.
387.po: The paper identifies a critical flaw in the BC+HE security paradigm for ICS: it can make systems unsafe. The lattice-based alternative preserves real-time safety while securing the network. This informs how ICS defenders should architect security without sacrificing responsiveness.

388.bp: LLM-enhanced search engines (ChatGPT, Gemini) are changing how people find information. They retrieve web content and synthesize answers, combining search's breadth with LLM reasoning. But attackers have learned SEO tricks over decades. Do these new systems fall for the old attacks, or do they deflect them better?
388.wh: Traditional search engines rank by links and keywords; attackers exploit both. LLM-enhanced search adds a new retrieval phase (finding relevant documents) and a ranking phase (deciding which sources matter). No one has systematically tested whether LLMSEs are vulnerable to known SEO attacks or if the LLM component acts as a defense.
388.ap: This work builds SEO-Bench, a dataset of 1,000 real-world black-hat SEO websites, and tests ten LLMSEs against them. They measure whether traditional SEO attacks (keyword stuffing, cloaking, link manipulation) work. They then propose new LLMSEO attacks: rewritten-query stuffing (rephrasing injection to evade detection) and segmented texts (hiding attacks across multiple retrieved documents). They measure manipulation rates on both.
388.ww: LLMSEs block traditional SEO attacks at the retrieval phase—the filter is strong. But the LLM reasoning phase can be fooled by attacks tailored to it. Rewriting queries to look like legitimate user intent, or fragmenting text so no single document looks suspicious but their union does, exploits the LLM's synthesis step. The system's new power creates new vulnerabilities.
388.po: The paper shows LLMSEs are robust against known SEO but vulnerable to LLMSEO variants—manipulation rates roughly double. This is the first systematic security analysis of LLM search, offering vendors concrete attack patterns to defend against and setting research direction for hardening these systems.

389.bp: Federated learning lets multiple parties train an AI model together without sharing raw data—banks collaborate on fraud detection, hospitals on disease prediction. But if one party wants to use a different model architecture (a smaller model on mobile, a larger one on desktop), the system breaks. Existing methods assume everyone uses the same model.
389.wh: Models are heterogeneous in practice: mobile clients can't run 500M-parameter networks. If a hospital uses a 1B-parameter model and a clinic uses 100M, how do they train together? Naive approaches ask everyone to use the global model, wasting resources on small clients and handicapping large ones. You need a way to federate across different architectures.
389.ap: FedBridge deploys a fusion model on each edge server that learns knowledge from heterogeneous client models via knowledge distillation (training the fusion model to mimic the client model's predictions). It uses a contrastive loss to align fusion model outputs with the global model, handling data heterogeneity. On the cloud server, a block-based aggregation merges fusion models from edge servers into a global model.
389.ww: Knowledge distillation lets a smaller or differently-shaped model pass its learned knowledge to another model without requiring them to share architecture. By intermediate fusion at edge servers, each client's model never needs to match others; they only need to communicate with their local edge fusion model. Block-based aggregation lets the cloud server combine fundamentally different models.
389.po: On public datasets with three different model architectures, FedBridge accelerates convergence 6.3x and improves accuracy 6.2%-17.7%, while cutting communication overhead 89.51%-96.13% and memory overhead 48.12%-61.77%. It enables federated learning across heterogeneous clients, making federation practical for real-world deployments.

390.bp: Real-estate platforms and social networks need to verify that listings are truthful—especially flagging claims like 'brand new development' that attract buyers but may be misleading. Trust depends on catching these false claims fast, but hiring humans to check every listing is expensive and slow.
390.wh: You also can't treat each claim in isolation. A single project may have hundreds of listings; if you flag one as 'brand new' claims you should flag suspicious neighbors too, and the project's own history should matter. Single-listing decisions that ignore this context become inconsistent.
390.ap: They built a system that first turns all those messy signals—heuristics, old flags, dictionaries—into probability scores per listing. Then they train a real model using those probabilities as weak labels. But the key step is adding a layer on top: they map listings to entities (like projects, organizations) and use a graph of those connections to enforce consistency. When one listing's verdict affects its neighbors in this graph, decisions smooth out.
390.ww: This works because weak labels, even if imperfect, give the model something meaningful to aim at—better than random guessing. And the graph step doesn't pretend individual predictions are always right; instead it lets neighboring decisions negotiate and settle on something consistent. That's how you stop absurd outcomes where two identical listings in the same project get opposite verdicts.
390.po: The result is a deployed system that assigns a calibrated confidence score to each claim, can show why on a map and graph, and runs cheaply without needing labeled training data. Analysts can see model reasoning, spot where things look wrong, and trust that decisions across a project hang together.

391.bp: Streaming platforms want to know what songs, videos, or books will take off tomorrow so they can promote them wisely. The real goal is to catch hits early and surface what audiences will love—both because it makes users happy and because it drives engagement and revenue.
391.wh: Large language models are great at reasoning, but a video recommendation system gets thousands of queries per second. You can't run an LLM for each user on your full catalog in real time; it's too slow. Also, LLMs struggle to read sparse data—they see user-item logs (who watched what) but those logs are huge and sparse, so it's hard to extract signal about who likes what. Finally, recommenders usually just rank items; users have no idea why something was suggested, so they trust it less.
391.ap: They propose TRAIL: take an LLM and fine-tune it on historical data about item popularity trends and why they trend. The key is to use a technique called contrastive learning, which means showing the model examples of 'items about to be popular' alongside 'items about to flop,' and training it to score one higher than the other. At the same time, the model learns to write an explanation—a sentence about why this item is trending—that matches the trend signals you fed it.
391.ww: This works because LLMs are already good at language; you're not asking them to invent trends from sparse logs, but to predict short-term momentum trends that exist in historical data, and then explain them in words. By tying the explanation and the trend score together with contrastive pairs, you force the explanation to be faithful—it has to point at the actual reasons the score is high, not confabulate.
391.po: The payoff is a system that predicts what items will trend in the next few hours or days, and for each prediction, gives a readable explanation. This is faster than running per-user ranking, users trust recommendations more because they read why, and the explanations help analysts spot when something is being gamed or when an unusual trend is emerging.

392.bp: Graphs are everywhere: social networks, citation networks, knowledge bases that power search and reasoning. Generating realistic graphs is useful for testing systems, synthesizing data when privacy matters, and understanding what structure matters most. But generating a good graph is hard—most real graphs have key substructures (like a tightly-knit group of related concepts) that matter, while the rest is noisy peripheral links.
392.wh: Existing graph generators treat all edges equally. They might generate a 50-node graph by placing one edge at a time, but without any special care about which edges to place first. This means the important central core could end up hidden in random noise. It's like describing a face without mentioning the eyes—you've missed the part that matters. Also, most generators don't know ahead of time which subgraph is actually important; they discover it only after you've already built something.
392.ap: RARD uses a mathematical idea from topology: look at your graph at different 'zoom levels,' starting from the densest core and zooming out to sparse edges. This creates an ordering—a filtration—where important edges come first. They learn this ordering using topological math (persistent homology) to find the biggest gap between core and periphery. Then, instead of placing edges randomly, the generator builds the graph in blocks that follow this ordering: core first, then local refinements, then final peripheral noise.
392.ww: By forcing important edges to appear first, you guarantee they get special attention during generation. The model learns 'to make a good knowledge graph, establish the key concepts and their tight relationships, then fill in supporting details.' This mirrors how humans design: sketch the main idea, then elaborate. And the persistent homology math finds this pattern automatically by looking for where the graph's structure naturally separates into core and periphery.
392.po: The system generates graphs where the central core—the part that actually determines the graph's properties—appears clearly and consistently. On standard graph-generation benchmarks, RARD beats baselines. You can also use it as a tool to analyze real graphs: the learned filtration shows you which edges are actually important for the structure you care about, filtering out noise.

393.bp: Manufacturing increasingly uses AI—computer vision to spot defects, machine learning on sensor logs to predict breakdowns, robots making decisions. But when something goes wrong on a production line, it's not just a single model failing; it's sensors giving stale data, the vision system looking at the wrong part, the control system not receiving the message in time, or human operators misunderstanding an alert. These cross-system failures cause injury, downtime, and lost product.
393.wh: Standard AI safety research focuses on single models: is this classifier biased? But real factories use multiple types of signals at once—cameras, temperature sensors, pressure gauges, historical logs, human reports. When signals disagree (the camera says OK but the pressure sensor says danger), what wins? When a message is delayed, who makes the decision in the meantime? And when regulations require accountability, how do you trace a mistake back to its root cause across sensors, software, and people?
393.ap: This paper surveys 80+ published studies and industrial reports to build a taxonomy—an organized list—of risks specific to multimodal systems. Instead of treating data, models, software, organizations, and governance as separate concerns, the taxonomy explicitly links them: a sensor failure leads to bad training data, which causes model errors, which confuse operators, which leads to accidents that regulators will scrutinize. For each risk category, they list concrete defenses: technical (e.g., cross-check sensor readings), operational (e.g., give humans clear dashboards to spot inconsistency), and governance (e.g., ISO 42001 standards).
393.ww: This works because multimodal failures are not sum-of-single-modality failures. A vision system and pressure sensor each separately might be quite reliable, but if they disagree and no one handles that disagreement, the factory will pick the wrong action. By mapping the full ecosystem of risk—how sensor → data → model → operator → accident flows together—you see problems that a single-model audit would miss. And by connecting risks to standards (NIST, ISO), manufacturers know how to address them.
393.po: The result is a practical blueprint for safety: manufacturers can use the taxonomy to audit their own systems, identify where signals might conflict, and implement governance that catches cross-modal failures. The linkage to standards means there's a path from identifying a risk to fixing it and documenting compliance.

394.bp: Movie or product recommendation systems make their money by showing users things they'll watch or buy. To do this, they need to know who each user is—what they like, what they're in the mood for. Social information helps: if your friends like something, you're more likely to like it too. But as user bases grow into millions, storing a unique vector for every user becomes expensive in memory and computation.
394.wh: Traditional recommendation systems use explicit user embeddings: every user gets their own learned vector. This is straightforward but scales poorly. With millions of users, you need millions of vectors in memory, and every new user starts from scratch. The gap between popular and unpopular users is huge too: a casual visitor has almost no interaction history, so the system doesn't know what they like, while a power user has lots of signal. Standard approaches don't handle these extremes well together.
394.ap: PULSE builds user profiles without explicit embeddings. Instead, it constructs a representation from signals: your friends' preferences, your historical clicks, how 'social' your neighborhood is. These signals combine into a compact profile that lives entirely in social graph structure, not in a separate table. So you don't store a separate vector per user; you compute user profiles on-the-fly from the graph and social data whenever needed.
394.ww: This works because the social graph already exists and is relatively stable—your friends don't change as often as their preferences. By rooting the user model in graph structure you inherit the stability of the graph itself. And since you're deriving profiles from neighborhoods rather than memorizing them, the system naturally handles both cold-start (new users get a profile from their few friends' data) and power users (rich neighborhoods give detailed profiles). It's also faster to update: when a friend watches something new, downstream users' profiles improve without retraining.
394.po: The system cuts the number of learned parameters in half compared to light baselines, while achieving better recommendation accuracy than 13 competing methods. It works well whether users are new (cold-start) or already highly active. The memory and speed wins matter: you can run this on smaller hardware or with lower latency, making it practical to deploy.

395.bp: Wikipedia serves millions of readers every day. Readers should be able to trust what they read—if Wikipedia says 'Napoleon died in 1821,' there should be a link to a reliable source backing that up. But Wikipedia has millions of edits per day, and checking every claim by hand is impossible. The system needs to spot which sentences need citations, so human editors can prioritize.
395.wh: The challenge is that citation need varies wildly by claim type and context. A claim about a living person's birthday needs a citation; a basic definition might not. Claims from recent news need cites; old common knowledge might not. And this varies across Wikipedia's different language versions, each with its own rules and editor behavior. A system trained only on English Wikipedia might not work well for Chinese or Arabic.
395.ap: They built a machine learning system that learns to predict which sentences are missing citations. The system runs in 10 different Wikipedia languages. They didn't just optimize for accuracy (models can overfit to their training data); they also optimized for what engineers call efficiency trade-offs: a slightly less accurate model that runs fast on Wikipedia's infrastructure is more useful than a perfect model that times out.
395.ww: This works because real-world systems have hard constraints: Wikipedia's servers have limited CPU. A model that is 92% accurate and runs in 50ms is better than one that's 96% accurate but takes 5 seconds. By training on real infrastructure requirements, the model learns patterns that actually help editors in practice. And by testing across 10 languages, the system learns what citation norms are universal versus language-specific.
395.po: The deployed system surfaces sentences likely to need citations to editors, speeding up verification work. They released code and data so other researchers can improve it. The approach also demonstrates that for production systems, you need to measure and optimize against real-world constraints, not just benchmark accuracy.

396.bp: Cities need to predict traffic flow—how congested roads will be in the next 15 minutes or hour. This helps route emergency vehicles, plan construction, and optimize signal timing. But traffic predictions are expensive: you'd like each neighborhood to share data and learn together, yet traffic in Paris is different from traffic in Tokyo, so models trained on one city don't transfer well. Also, you can't upload raw data to a central server because cities and traffic operators guard their real-time data as proprietary and sensitive.
396.wh: Federated learning lets each city train locally without sharing data. But traffic patterns vary so much between cities that when you average models across cities, the shared model becomes too generic and works poorly for each individual city. This is called non-IID data: each source (city) has different patterns. Existing federated methods try to learn one global model for all, but that fails when traffic in one city is systematically different from another.
396.ap: FedDis uses a splitting strategy: each city maintains two representations. One is client-specific and captures local patterns (rush hour timing in Paris, geography-specific bottlenecks). The other is global and captures universal patterns (weather slows traffic everywhere). During federated training, these two representations are kept separate using a mathematical constraint: mutual information minimization forces them to carry different information. The global model learns from all cities, but the local model is never touched; it stays personalized.
396.ww: By splitting the representation, the system can transfer universal knowledge—'rain slows all traffic'—while letting each city keep its own personality. The mutual information constraint is the key: it enforces that the global model doesn't accidentally learn city-specific quirks. This is why it works better than just averaging: averaging would blend Paris and Tokyo traffic, diluting both. Disentanglement keeps them separate.
396.po: Each city gets a predictor that's accurate for local traffic yet benefits from learning global patterns from all other cities' data. The system works in federated fashion, keeping data local. Experiments on real traffic data from multiple cities show FedDis beats baselines that either learn one global model or one model per city with no sharing.

397.bp: Financial platforms use AI to answer questions: 'What's the current price of Tesla?' or 'Should I buy gold now?' Behind the scenes, these systems call APIs—functions that fetch stock prices, news, historical data, expert ratings. The system needs to learn which API to call, what arguments to pass it, and how to format the answer for the user.
397.wh: A generic LLM doesn't know your company's specific APIs. It was trained on public data, not your proprietary financial tools. Also, users ask things in many ways—'Is TSLA overvalued?' might mean 'call the valuation API,' but the LLM might not make that connection. Users also ask things that don't exactly match API parameters: 'What stocks are rising today?' doesn't directly map to 'call get_daily_movers(sector=None, threshold=5%).' The system needs to infer the right parameters from messy, open-ended user intent.
397.ap: They create a dataset of past queries and the correct API calls for each. They apply an augmentation technique called AugFC: for each query, they systematically vary the parameters (e.g., try different stock tickers, different date ranges) to create synthetic training examples. This expands their dataset cheaply without new user data. Then they train an LLM with a two-step method: first predict which API to call, then predict the arguments.
397.ww: This works because LLMs are naturally good at understanding intent; you're not asking them to invent finance logic, just to map intent to function calls. By augmenting your dataset—creating variations—you show the model: 'When users ask for X, they might need parameter Y with many values; here's your search space.' The two-step approach breaks down the problem: first filter the space of possible APIs, then focus on parameters. This is much simpler than asking the LLM to produce a full API call from scratch.
397.po: The system can now answer diverse user questions by calling the right APIs with the right parameters, even when users' phrasing doesn't exactly match the API signature. It handles out-of-distribution inputs (questions the training set didn't foresee) better because the augmentation trained the model on a wide parameter space. The data-driven pipeline is also easy to update: when a new API is added, you can quickly augment your dataset and retrain.

398.bp: The web is becoming agentic: AI systems that browse the web autonomously, read pages, fill out forms, book flights, answer questions by searching multiple sites. Today, these agents run in the cloud, talking to a large language model that processes each step. The dream is agents that run directly in your browser—faster, more private, and responsive to your immediate needs.
398.wh: Running agents in a browser is hard for three reasons. First, browsers have limited memory and storage; you can't cache the entire web locally. An agent needs fast access to context—the pages it has read, the data it extracted—but that context lives in constrained browser memory. Second, each step an agent takes (fetch a page, read it, decide the next step) adds a network round-trip time. With a 100ms latency per step, a 10-step workflow takes a second just waiting for the network. Third, untrusted web pages can trick an agent via prompt injection: malicious content on a page could tell the agent to do something harmful (buy something, send a message).
398.ap: WAB uses WebAssembly (Wasm)—a sandbox technology—to handle all three problems. For memory: Wasm runs its own tiered storage in browser memory. It fetches pages on demand and keeps hot context in fast Wasm memory. For latency: they batch multiple actions in Wasm before sending results back to the LLM, so instead of 10 network round-trips, you get 2-3. For security: Wasm acts as a sandbox; untrusted pages run in a restricted environment where they can't access sensitive data or perform certain operations.
398.ww: This works because Wasm is designed for exactly this use case: fast, sandboxed compute in the browser. By moving compute into Wasm, the agent doesn't have to ask the cloud for every step; it can reason locally about which actions to batch and how to handle the response. The tiered storage lets context be paged in and out like a virtual memory system. And the sandbox prevents a malicious page from escaping—an injected prompt might say 'delete files,' but Wasm won't let it.
398.po: Agents running in the browser with WAB are faster (fewer network round-trips), cheaper (less cloud compute), and more private (your context stays local). The security sandbox lets agents safely browse untrusted pages. This moves the agentic web from cloud-only to locally-native, which matters when you want responsive, always-available agents without cloud dependencies.

399.bp: Foundation models—like GPT or BERT for text—work across many tasks because they learn universal patterns. The same model can classify text, translate, summarize, and reason. For graphs, the dream is similar: one model that works on any graph, whether it's a social network, a citation graph, or a knowledge base. But graphs are diverse: node features might be image descriptions (text) in one graph, numerical sensor readings in another, or categorical node types in a third.
399.wh: Graph neural networks are usually designed for a specific application: social-network GNNs expect user demographic features; knowledge-base GNNs expect entity type tags. When you try to use a social-network GNN on a knowledge-base graph, it fails—it doesn't know how to interpret the new features. The core problem is that pixels are universal for images and words are universal for text, but there's no universal 'atom' for graphs. Node features are semantically variable, so knowledge from one graph doesn't transfer to another.
399.ap: TIG proposes Transfer-Invariant Metadata (TIM): features that are semantically consistent across all domains, like 'pixel values' for images. They analyze real graphs and propose a method to extract TIM from node features in different domains. This creates a unified representation space: a knowledge-graph entity and a social-network user both get mapped to this universal feature space. Then a single foundation model learns graph structure using self-supervised learning in this space.
399.ww: This works because once you have a universal feature representation, the foundation model can learn graph properties that are domain-agnostic—connectivity patterns, centrality, clustering—that apply everywhere. By extracting semantically consistent information across domains and unifying the feature space, you remove the barrier to transfer. A model trained on one domain's graph structure can now transfer to another because both domains speak the same feature language.
399.po: A single graph foundation model can now work on diverse graphs—social networks, knowledge bases, citation networks—without domain-specific training. Even in one-shot scenarios (new domain, little training data), TIG achieves good accuracy because it inherits structure knowledge from graphs it was pre-trained on. The approach shows that foundation models for graphs are possible with the right universal representation.

400.bp: Graph neural networks power everything from fraud detection to recommendation systems. But they're vulnerable: an attacker can subtly change a few edges or node features, and the model's prediction flips. In fraud detection, an attacker might add fake friendships to hide a fraudulent account. In a supply-chain network, an attacker might inject false relationships to reroute goods. These adversarial attacks are hard to spot visually, but they break the system.
400.wh: Most defenses against adversarial attacks focus on making models harder to fool—training on perturbed data or using robust model architectures. But recent black-box influence maximization attacks are clever: they don't attack random nodes; they identify the most influential nodes (hubs with lots of connections) and attack through them. This amplifies the damage: perturbing one hub spreads the harm to all its neighbors. Traditional defenses don't account for this strategy.
400.ap: HSIC-GAD uses a statistical principle called the Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion. The idea: they measure how much a node's features depend on its label (the thing the model is trying to predict). Then they add a constraint during training: keep only the part of the features that actually relates to the label, and filter out everything else. This automatically removes adversarial perturbations that don't point toward the true label.
400.ww: This works because adversarial perturbations are noise—they don't correlate with real labels. So when you filter features to keep only what predicts the label, adversarial noise gets filtered out automatically. The Hilbert-Schmidt approach is universal: it doesn't assume a specific attack strategy. Whether the attacker perturbs a random node or targets a hub, the method filters out perturbations that don't help predict labels. This makes it robust to black-box influence maximization attacks.
400.po: Models using HSIC-GAD preprocessing stay accurate even when attacked through influential nodes. Experiments show the defense works across multiple GNN architectures, suggesting it's a general principle. The defense is also interpretable: you can see which features were filtered out and understand what the model considers trustworthy signal versus adversarial noise.

401.bp: Cities rely on taxis, buses, and delivery systems that must keep running even when weather turns bad—storms, floods, heavy snow. To route vehicles safely and keep services running, systems need to predict traffic flow under these extreme conditions. But extreme weather is rare, so there's little training data. Standard prediction models trained on normal weather perform terribly when storms hit.
401.wh: The core problem is distribution shift: the patterns in normal-weather traffic don't apply during storms. A model trained on sunny days never sees how rain changes driver behavior—people take longer routes, slow down, avoid highways. You could collect more extreme-weather data, but storms are rare; you can't wait years. Also, weather has many types of effects—it changes travel demand, changes driver speed, affects which routes are viable—and these effects interact in complex ways. Treating weather as just another input doesn't capture these dynamics.
401.ap: WED-Net separates normal traffic patterns from weather-induced changes using a dual-branch Transformer. One branch learns: 'How would traffic flow if weather didn't matter?' The other learns: 'What effect does this weather have?' These branches use cross-attention to interact carefully. Additionally, they add a discriminator (an auxiliary classifier) that explicitly learns to recognize weather conditions, which forces the main model to capture weather effects faithfully. To further help, they create synthetic training examples: they take normal-weather traffic and computationally perturb it to simulate what storms would do, while preserving the causal structure (e.g., storms always increase congestion).
401.ww: By disentangling weather and non-weather factors, the model learns causal relationships rather than correlations. The discriminator acts as a regularizer: it ensures the weather branch actually 'knows' about weather instead of letting the no-weather branch do all the work. The causal data augmentation helps because you're not randomly corrupting traffic; you're applying realistic weather-induced changes, which matches what the model needs to generalize to extreme scenarios.
401.po: The system predicts traffic accurately even during rare extreme weather. Because it's learned causal weather effects from synthetic and real data, it can generalize to storms it hasn't seen. This supports safer routing for emergency vehicles and better disaster preparedness, making mobility resilient during the worst conditions.

402.bp: A new class of AI tools—ChatGPT, Claude, other LLM answer engines—promise real-time answers to any question. Unlike Google, which returns cached search results, these systems fetch fresh web pages for each query to give the latest information. But every fetch costs bandwidth, storage, and time. The question is: can the web infrastructure handle billions of queries hitting it this way, and is it sustainable for publishers?
402.wh: Traditional search engines (like Google) crawl the web once and cache everything. When you search, you get cached results instantly. But LLM answer engines can't use cached results—by the time an answer is cached, a user has already asked and waited. So they fetch pages anew for each query. This creates massive redundancy: if a million users search 'who won the World Series,' the system fetches the ESPN page a million times instead of once.
402.ap: They measured real LLM answer engines (ChatGPT, Claude) by tracing their traffic: which pages do they fetch, how often, how much data? They tested 1,000 queries and analyzed both what the engines fetched and what an average human would fetch if they Googled the same question. They built a cost model: if every human searcher used an AI answer engine instead of Google, what would happen to the web?
402.ww: This works as a measurement study because the authors directly observed real engines and real traffic. They found that LLM answer engines do heavy caching internally—they're not fetching entirely anew for each query—but their per-query footprint is still far higher than human search. This is because engines fetch multiple sources to verify claims, and they don't coordinate across users.
402.po: The study reveals the infrastructural burden of LLM-based search. The concrete findings: LLM engines' per-query bandwidth is 10-100x a human searcher's, varying by engine design. The paper proposes solutions: publishers could offer shared caches, engines could use a transparent retrieval standard (like llms.txt) to reduce redundant fetching, and publishers could set controls on what crawlers see. This frames the problem for the industry to solve cooperatively.

403.bp: Social media generates massive volumes of short text: tweets, product reviews, chat messages. These short texts often have little context, yet companies need to understand them—cluster them by topic (spam, positive feedback, questions), route them to the right team, and personalize content. Clustering short text is hard because each text is sparse: only a few words, little semantic redundancy.
403.wh: Standard deep clustering tries to learn groups by measuring distances between text representations in an abstract space. But in short text, there's ambiguity: is a review 'terrible' expressing disappointment with a product or with a delivery experience? The model has to guess, and when it guesses wrong, its pseudo-labels (its guesses about which cluster each text belongs to) are wrong. Bad pseudo-labels lead to bad clusters, which makes representation learning worse, which makes pseudo-labels worse—a downward spiral.
403.ap: CIDC uses three steps to break the spiral. First, Cluster Category Identification: at each training step, look at what the model thinks each cluster's distribution is (mostly negative reviews? mostly questions?), and assign the most likely true category to that cluster. Second, Pseudo-Label Correction: for samples where the model's predicted class distribution disagrees with the assigned cluster category, fix the pseudo-label to match reality. Third, Prototype-Based Correction: refine cluster centers (prototypes) using the corrected labels. These three corrections happen in concert.
403.ww: This works because it breaks the feedback loop: instead of letting bad pseudo-labels persist, you actively correct them using consistency reasoning. By asking 'what is this cluster actually about?' and then aligning samples with that answer, you improve signal. The prototype refinement ensures the cluster centers themselves are stable, which makes the next round of pseudo-label correction more reliable.
403.po: The system clusters short texts more accurately, especially in imbalanced scenarios (some topics are rare) common on the web. It handles class imbalance and distribution skew that plague real social-media data, making the clustered topics actionable for downstream tasks like spam filtering or content routing.

404.bp: Memes—images with text, often humorous or symbolic—spread rapidly on social media. Some are harmless jokes; others promote hate, mock marginalized groups, or encode extremist symbols. Platforms want to catch harmful memes fast, but most meme harm is subtle: it relies on cultural context (a symbol means something specific to one community), satire (is this joke punching down or punching up?), and ambiguity that images and text create together.
404.wh: Detecting harmful memes is hard because the meaning is implicit and cross-modal. A text classifier would miss symbols in the image. A pure image classifier wouldn't understand cultural context. And large vision-language models, even the best ones, have cultural blindness: they're trained on Western data and miss references from other cultures. Also, satire is hard: 'This politician is so smart' could be genuine praise or sarcasm mocking them.
404.ap: CROSS-ALIGN+ is a three-stage framework. Stage I enriches the meme representation with outside knowledge: they pull in ConceptNet (a database of what things mean in concepts), Wikidata (what symbols and references mean historically), and Hatebase (known hate symbols). This gives the model cultural context. Stage II uses parameter-efficient adapters (LoRA) to sharpen the boundary between satire and abuse—these adapters are small tweaks to a large vision-language model that specialize it for this domain. Stage III generates explanations: not just 'this is abusive,' but 'because this symbol is associated with extremism' or 'because this joke mocks this group.'
404.ww: This works because it attacks each failure mode directly. Cultural blindness gets fixed by pulling in external knowledge—the model can now 'understand' symbols it wasn't trained on. Boundary ambiguity (satire vs. abuse) gets fixed by adapters that learn to separate these categories. And by generating explanations (stage III), you force the model to reason about why something is harmful, which improves accuracy and provides auditable reasoning.
404.po: The system detects harmful memes with up to 17% better accuracy than prior approaches and provides interpretable explanations. It works across eight different large vision-language models, showing it's a general technique. This gives platforms both detection capability and the ability to explain removals to users, addressing both accuracy and transparency.

405.bp: As the research literature explodes, peer review—the human gatekeeping system that filters papers—has become a bottleneck. Academic conferences now use AI to help reviewers assess papers faster. But if that AI system is brittle (breaks on small changes), it might give wildly different scores to nearly identical papers, which would undermine the entire review process.
405.wh: The fundamental tension is that papers are hybrid documents: words, numbers, and equations all matter together. A robust AI reviewer should handle any of these getting slightly mangled. But the usual testing toolbox was built for text alone.
405.ap: The authors built a system that generates three kinds of perturbations—changing words, scrambling table contents, and tweaking formulas—then runs them all through an AI reviewer to see if the review score stays stable. The system itself learns which perturbations are worth trying, and it gives humans an interface to explore what breaks the reviewer.
405.ww: By forcing the AI reviewer to handle all three information types together, the system reveals whether the reviewer actually understood the paper holistically or was just pattern-matching on text. If perturbing a table flips the score wildly, the AI was leaning too hard on that table and not reasoning about the bigger picture.
405.po: The paper shows that AI-based reviewers often behave very differently when tables or formulas change—scores flip dramatically—whereas human reviewers are more stable. This signals real robustness gaps in current AI review systems, giving conferences concrete evidence of what to fix before trusting automated reviewers.

406.bp: When you ask an AI service for an answer, the business pays per API call—more sophisticated models (bigger, smarter) cost more. Users also want fast, cheap answers. The real-world challenge: serve high-quality responses to diverse queries without spending a fortune, because query difficulty varies wildly.
406.wh: The obvious move is to always use the best model for every query, but that's expensive and slow. The flip side—always using the cheapest one—returns garbage on hard questions. In reality, some queries need subtle reasoning; others just need a lookup. The hard part is knowing which is which *before* you pay, and knowing whether a query should get a quick response or a deep one.
406.ap: The system learns dense numerical summaries of each model's behavior (how fast, how accurate, at what cost) and each reasoning strategy's (does it think step-by-step or jump to the answer?). Then it builds a lookup table pairing queries to model-strategy combos based on query complexity. At run time, it consults this table to pick the cheapest combo that hits the quality target, or the best quality under a budget.
406.ww: Query difficulty signals which model will pay off most. A simple question doesn't need step-by-step reasoning or a powerful model. A tricky question needs both. By learning which model-strategy pair works for which query profile, the system routes work efficiently—hard questions get smarter models and deep reasoning, easy ones get speed.
406.po: Experiments show the system gets the same quality as always using the best model, but cuts token usage and API costs by up to 60%. For a service handling millions of queries, that's huge savings while keeping users happy with quality.

407.bp: Online stores and streaming services show you items with cover images (book covers, album art, thumbnail photos). These images influence whether you click. But recommendation systems today treat the cover as a static field, like metadata, ignoring how the visual design actually shapes your decision. The real game: pick cover images that will hook the user.
407.wh: You can't A/B test every cover design for every user—that's too expensive and slow. For new items with no user data (cold start), there's no feedback on which visual style works. The old playbook of 'find users with similar taste' breaks when you have zero interactions. And covers are multimodal: text on the cover, the visual style, the colors—they interact.
407.ap: The system uses a vision-language model to read both the user's interests (extracted from what they've clicked before) and the visual + textual elements of a cover in a unified semantic space. It then builds a network that fuses visual and textual features together and ranks covers by which ones align best with the user's visual taste, without needing interaction data. For new covers, it uses a learning-free method that remixes the cover features to generalize.
407.ww: Vision-language models can understand both images and text in the same abstract space. If a user historically clicks minimalist designs with serif fonts, their 'visual interest' has a pattern that a well-learned model can detect. When a new cover arrives, scoring it in that same space tells you if it matches the user's aesthetic.
407.po: On three test datasets, the method outperforms baselines by 3.7% on click-through likelihood and similar gains on other ranking metrics. For e-commerce and streaming, better cover selection drives more clicks with zero cold-start waiting period.

408.bp: Imagine a document labeled with multiple topics at once—say, a news article tagged with both 'politics' and 'corruption.' When you read it, different sentences touch on different tags. The real goal: explain which parts of the text lead to each label, so a human can verify the prediction makes sense.
408.wh: Simple topic models assume one label per document and ignore how parts of the text connect to different labels. More complex ones list which words matter, but they're wrong about which label each word belongs to—they scramble the connection. And they don't use common-sense knowledge about what 'politics' or 'corruption' mean, so they can't reason about why a word matters.
408.ap: The system uses an AI prompting technique (chain-of-thought) to think through which parts of the text match which labels, step by step. Then it visualizes tokens and labels together, and it taps external knowledge (from language models) to ground the interpretation. The system learns to align segments (sentences or phrases) to labels by reasoning explicitly.
408.ww: Chain-of-thought prompting forces the model to explain its reasoning out loud, which makes it align text to labels more correctly. By layering in semantic knowledge and explicit visualization of token-label pairs, humans can see *why* a segment got a label, rather than just trusting a number.
408.po: Experiments show the system significantly improves label accuracy and human raters confirm it correctly identifies which tokens belong to which labels. For compliance, journalism, and research, explainable multi-label assignment cuts down verification time.

409.bp: In advertising and e-commerce, you allocate limited inventory (coupons, stock, ad slots) to users. The naive approach: always give the item with the best expected payoff to whoever you're serving now. But if you give all the coupons to early users, later users who might have bought anyway get nothing—a waste. The real challenge: allocate scarce resources fairly while maximizing total reward.
409.wh: Greedy allocation (give the best item to each user in order) fails under scarcity because it doesn't account for future users. A user today might have a 70% chance to buy item X, but a different user tomorrow might have an 80% chance. If you exhaust X today, you lose that higher payoff tomorrow. Standard learning algorithms ignore supply constraints.
409.ap: The system learns a policy that avoids greedy allocation. Instead of picking the item with highest expected value for the current user, it compares items: it prefers items that have relatively higher expected value *compared to competing users*, not absolute value. It factors in that multiple users are coming and supply is finite.
409.ww: By ranking items by relative advantage (how much better this item is than others for this user, compared to other users), the system naturally protects high-value opportunities for users who need them most. It avoids burning out a single high-value item on low-impact users.
409.po: The paper proves that greedy methods are suboptimal under supply constraints and shows the new approach finds better allocations. For coupon distribution, inventory management, and ad serving, this means higher cumulative revenue or satisfaction with the same inventory.

410.bp: When a recommendation system tells you 'we suggest this movie,' you might want to know why. But most AI recommenders just output a list—they hide their reasoning. If you explain the 'why,' users trust the system more, and the system can be more transparent about its logic. The challenge: make recommendation reasoning explicit.
410.wh: Language models are great at reasoning—they can think through a problem step by step—but recommenders typically squash that into a single score or list. If you only use the reasoning as internal scaffolding and throw it away, you lose the explainability and you might not even get the full reasoning power. The tension is that recommenders traditionally output just the item, not thoughts.
410.ap: The system trains a language model in two stages. First, it collects examples where the model generates both a reasoning explanation ('this movie has themes you like') and then a recommendation. Second, it trains the model to imitate that pattern—reason first, then recommend. This makes reasoning explicit in the output.
410.ww: When a model has to write out its reasoning before giving an answer, it engages deeper thought and can catch more nuance. The reasoning becomes part of the system's accountability. Downstream, the reasoning helps the model improve over iterations because it can reflect on what worked.
410.po: Tests show the model with explicit reasoning gets higher recommendation accuracy and users rate the explanations as insightful. For streaming services and e-commerce, transparent reasoning builds trust and can reduce user frustration with wrong recommendations.

411.bp: E-commerce search is hard: a user searches 'blue jacket' and you need to rank thousands of items by relevance. Different signals matter—does it match the user's intent (they want a winter jacket, not a life jacket)? Does it match the visual attributes (actually blue)? Are there business rules (feature high-margin items)? Relevance is multifaceted, and reasoning helps.
411.wh: Most relevance systems treat ranking as a single scoring problem. But relevance has multiple angles: a jacket might be blue (attribute match) but the user meant business casual (intent mismatch). Language models can reason about all these angles with chain-of-thought prompts, but inference is slow. To ship at scale, you need to distill that reasoning into a fast model. The catch: distillation usually throws away the reasoning explanation.
411.ap: The system uses a large language model to generate multi-angle reasoning (user intent, attribute matching, business rules). Then it trains a smaller, faster model to both generate reasoning *and* make predictions, and during serving, it uses both the reasoning and the small model's decision together. The reasoning stays in the loop rather than vanishing.
411.ww: Multi-perspective reasoning captures the full complexity of relevance. By keeping the reasoning in the deployed model (not discarding it after training), the small model doesn't have to compress everything into a score—it can justify itself. This helps the model generalize to new queries and lets humans debug errors.
411.po: On e-commerce test sets, the approach improves relevance ranking and gives humans readable explanations for each rank. Search engines and marketplaces can deploy this for better ranking with explainability.

412.bp: When machine learning models learn to explain their decisions (identify which parts of the input matter), they should rely on real causal reasons, not shortcuts. In federated learning—where data lives on different devices and never leaves—models face an extra trap: they can find spurious patterns that appear only on one device, fooling everyone.
412.wh: Graph models often latch onto shortcut features: maybe all fraud cases have a certain node type nearby, so the model learns 'if you see node type X, it's fraud,' ignoring whether that's really causal. In federated settings, shortcuts get worse because each device has its own data quirks. A device with many spam users might build patterns that don't generalize.
412.ap: The system identifies high-risk samples: cases where the local model's prediction and the global model's prediction disagree sharply. These disagreements signal shortcuts—the local device is relying on device-specific patterns. It prioritizes augmenting these risky samples, and uses information-theoretic methods to make sure the augmentation breaks spurious correlations while preserving the real causal subgraph.
412.ww: When local and global models disagree, it means one of them is fooled by a shortcut. By finding and augmenting these cases, you force the model to re-learn on a wider variety of patterns, breaking the shortcut. Information theory ensures the augmentation zeroes out the spurious link while keeping causal structure.
412.po: Experiments show the method improves explainability in federated graph learning and makes models more robust across different devices. For privacy-preserving ML on smartphones and edge devices, this ensures explanations are trustworthy.

413.bp: 5G coverage inside tall buildings is spotty because radio waves bounce off concrete and steel. To plan 5G infrastructure, engineers need a map of signal strength inside buildings. Drones can measure outside, but getting an accurate indoor map from outdoor measurements is a reverse-engineering puzzle—you're inferring an invisible interior from sparse boundary data.
413.wh: Standard signal propagation models assume Euclidean geometry and simple paths. Real buildings have complex layouts, metal frames, and signal reflection. Indoor signal patterns don't follow simple distance rules. And you have only a few drone measurements outside; you need to generalize to all indoor locations, most of which you never measured.
413.ap: The system treats the building's hidden signal structure as a graph where nodes are locations and edges represent signal propagation paths. Instead of assuming Euclidean distance, it learns the actual connectivity structure from data, then uses graph neural networks with attention to understand signal flow. It separately models two signal metrics (RSSI and CQI) because they behave differently. Uncertainty is reduced by combining predictions from multiple models.
413.ww: Real buildings don't send signals in straight lines; they follow complex paths. By learning the actual connectivity graph, the model captures how signals bounce and spread. Attention mechanisms let the model focus on the most relevant paths for each location. Splitting RSSI and CQI modeling recognizes that signal strength and quality don't always correlate.
