457.po: The system now successfully recommends to new users by transferring knowledge from data-rich domains. A person with rich movie history but no book history can get book recommendations that respect their actual taste, not just surface-level similarity.

458.bp: Taiwan's government needs to know how long fieldwork will take to survey and mark land boundaries. If estimates are wrong, workers are sent to the wrong place with the wrong tools, wasting time and money. Accurate prediction lets managers schedule efficiently and staff fairly.
458.wh: Fieldwork time depends on both geographic features (terrain slope, vegetation, soil type) and network effects (where nearby parcels are, how work is sequenced). Neither traditional location-only models nor tabular-data-only models capture both. You need to merge spatial patterns with numerical patterns.
458.ap: They combine spatial information (using graph networks that treat neighborhoods as connected nodes with learned spatial attention) with temporal patterns (using periodic encoding that learns seasonal and cyclic effects) and numerical features (using multilayer networks). Each component specializes, then they all feed into a unified prediction.
458.ww: Graph networks excel at spatial structure, periodic layers capture time cycles, and multilayer networks learn numerical relationships. By orchestrating all three with attention mechanisms that weight spatial and feature channels separately, the system respects the actual structure of the problem.
458.po: Time-to-completion predictions are 88% more accurate than conventional methods, letting Taiwan's land office schedule fieldwork better, distribute workload fairly, and reduce unexpected delays that send teams back multiple times.

459.bp: Biomedical laboratories handle dangerous materials and delicate procedures. Teaching a robot to operate safely requires understanding not just what objects are present, but how they physically interact—whether a liquid will spill, whether a hand can safely reach a location. That knowledge must come from realistic images, not controlled laboratory scans.
459.wh: Real lab photos from the web show messy, partial views with unclear camera angles and no precise measurements. Existing reconstruction methods assume precise cameras and multiple views. You cannot extract physics-aware reasoning from a single messy photo using standard 3D reconstruction.
459.ap: They extract object masks and rough positions from images using open-vocabulary detection, estimate relative depths even without calibration, then build a scene graph where nodes are objects annotated with liquid states (full, empty, partially filled) and edges capture how hands interact with objects. They attach natural-language descriptions of affordances ('this liquid can pour from this spout') without needing CAD models or multiview data.
459.ww: Open-vocabulary detection and rough relative depth are good enough to build a topological understanding of 'which object can pour where.' Language-annotated affordances capture real-world constraints without precise geometry. The result is queryable structure that an AI agent can reason about, not just pixels.
459.po: An AI agent grounded in these physics-aware scene graphs answers questions about lab operations 40% better than a model reasoning directly from raw images, with the biggest gains on safety constraints and what operations are even physically possible.

460.bp: Federated learning spreads training across many devices that keep data private, but real-world devices are not equal: a company server is powerful, a mobile phone is weak. Standard federated learning treats them equally, wasting potential and abandoning weak clients.
460.wh: One-shot federated learning (one round of training) cuts communication but requires every client to train the same model size, which is impossible when devices range from servers to phones. Existing methods either ignore weak devices, rely on shared datasets (which breaks privacy), or lose information during knowledge transfer.
460.ap: They use powerful clients to train full classification models while weak clients train lightweight generative models that learn to recreate training data. The server then synthesizes data from both types of models and performs knowledge fusion, using two specialized variants to prevent models from forgetting old patterns and an unsupervised method to clean up synthetic samples.
460.ww: Generative models on weak devices are computationally cheaper than classifiers and still capture enough statistical patterns to recreate useful training data. The two-stage server-side process (generate then fuse) lets asymmetric model sizes cooperate by speaking a common language: synthetic data.
460.po: A federated system works with both powerful and resource-constrained clients in one round, achieving accuracy competitive with centralized training. Weak devices contribute meaningfully instead of being left behind, and privacy is preserved because raw data never leaves any client.

461.bp: Blockchain networks, especially ones used for decentralized finance and IoT, are only as good as their configuration. Parameters that control consensus speed, how transactions are prioritized, and how nodes connect to each other all affect whether the system is fast and reliable.
461.wh: There are hundreds of tunable parameters across network, node, and consensus layers, and they interact in complex ways. Workloads change throughout the day (more transactions at certain hours). Manual tuning cannot keep up, and naively changing one parameter to fix one problem often breaks another.
461.ap: They use hierarchical reinforcement learning, which breaks the blockchain workflow into stages (consensus, execution, graph topology) and learns which parameter adjustments help at each stage. A shadow-control loop tests adjustments in a simulation before applying them to the real system, ensuring no harmful changes sneak through.
461.ww: Hierarchical RL decomposes the sprawling configuration space into understandable sub-problems. Learning stage-by-stage means the system converges on good policies faster than a monolithic learner. The shadow-control loop is a safety valve—it prevents bad experiments from damaging the live system.
461.po: Throughput increases and latency decreases as the system adapts to variable workloads automatically. A blockchain that used to need manual tuning now continuously self-optimizes in response to real traffic patterns.

462.bp: Health misinformation online can lead to dangerous choices. The question is whether ordinary people can protect themselves by fact-checking in real time while they browse. The stakes are high because confirming false information by careful reading is just as dangerous as not checking at all.
462.wh: People tend to believe information that matches their existing beliefs, even if it is false (confirmation bias). Fact-checking should help, but does it overcome that bias? And is there a simple behavioral signal you can measure to know whether someone is actually fact-checking or just spending time?
462.ap: They ran an experiment where 1,842 participants used a special web platform that logged when they switched tabs or windows to consult other sources (lateral reading) versus staying on the original page longer (vertical reading). They measured whether people accurately identified health misinformation and whether confirmation bias (alignment with their beliefs) blocked the benefit.
462.ww: Tab-switching is a concrete behavioral signal that predicts fact-checking: people who check multiple sources are less fooled by misinformation, even when that misinformation matches their beliefs. Vertical reading does not improve accuracy because spending more time on a false source does not make the error apparent.
462.po: Lateral reading—consulting multiple sources—improves accuracy by about 9%, and this benefit holds even for people whose existing beliefs aligned with the false claim. Simple behavioral cues like tab-switching frequency can reliably indicate whether someone is fact-checking effectively, suggesting interventions could nudge this behavior.

463.bp: Misinformation, rumors, and computer viruses spread through networks. Stopping them often means finding the source—the patient zero, the original spreader—so you can isolate or counter it. But you only see which users are infected; you do not directly observe how the disease traveled.
463.wh: The network topology itself is messy and incomplete: some connections are strong, others are weak or noisy. Existing graph-based inference methods struggle when the network is corrupted by noise. Also, real-world spread happens continuously over time, not in discrete steps, but most methods assume discrete jumps.
463.ap: They model the spread as a continuous-time system using neural differential equations: the state at any moment is determined by a flowing process, not snapshots. They use a graph variational model to extract global patterns in how propagation typically unfolds, then apply spectral filtering to remove high-frequency noise from the network graph (keeping only strong, meaningful connections).
463.ww: Differential equations naturally capture continuous-time dynamics. The global propagation patterns (learned via variational models) provide context for what the source likely did. Spectral filtering strips noise by keeping low-frequency structure that reflects true relationships, improving the signal-to-noise ratio dramatically.
463.po: Source localization accuracy improves by an average of 44% compared to baseline methods, and the system remains reliable even when the network is corrupted by noise or topology measurement errors, making it practical for identifying the origin of epidemics, rumors, or cyberattacks.

464.bp: Graph learning (where the system predicts properties of networks or relationships) works well when all data lives in the same geometric space, but real-world graph data varies: social networks might live in a flat space, whereas hierarchies need curved geometry. A one-size-fits-all geometry fails.
464.wh: Federated learning spreads data across many clients who do not share graphs. Each client's network has its own natural geometry: some are hierarchies (hyperbolic), some are balanced (Euclidean), some are interconnected clusters (spherical). Imposing one fixed geometry on all clients degrades performance.
464.ap: They let each client learn a mixed-curvature space tailored to its own network geometry, combining hyperbolic, Euclidean, and spherical manifolds in one product space. Then they use a Ricci-Gated graph convolution that adapts its message-passing mechanism to the local topology—the gate learns where high-curvature bending occurs and adjusts how information flows through those regions.
464.ww: Matching geometry to data structure is powerful: hierarchies compress into hyperbolic space, clusters spread into spherical, and flat relationships stay Euclidean. The Ricci gate detects topological complexity and adjusts routing accordingly. Personalized spaces let each client optimize for its own data without compromise.
464.po: Federated graph learning accuracy improves and generalization strengthens as each client's graph learns in its own optimal geometric space. The system now handles heterogeneous network data across decentralized settings without forcing all networks into one ill-fitting geometry.

465.bp: When websites answer questions by pulling relevant content from web pages and feeding it to an AI system, those responses can only be as good as the retrieved content. A malicious actor can hide harmful instructions in a page's text or slip in misleading information, and the retrieval system will treat it like any other content. This creates a serious trust problem: the system might unknowingly follow hidden commands or output false information sourced from poisoned web pages.
465.wh: The challenge is that retrieval systems treat all content equally—they score and rank pages by relevance, not by whether the content is actually trustworthy or contains hidden attacks. A hostile webpage might rank highly and slip adversarial instructions through to the final answer. There's no automatic way to detect when text contains covert commands meant to hijack the system's behavior or when a page's retrieved snippet is designed to push biased conclusions.
465.ap: The paper introduces OpenRAG-Soc, a standardized testing suite that lets practitioners run realistic attack scenarios against their systems. The benchmark includes a collection of web pages (some weaponized with hidden instructions), multiple ways to retrieve relevant content, and several defensive tactics: cleaning up HTML and special characters, normalizing unusual Unicode tricks, and requiring the system to cite which page it drew information from before answering.
465.ww: By measuring attacks under controlled, reproducible conditions, teams can see exactly where their system fails—which retriever fumbles the attack, which defenses actually block it, and whether the system still gives useful answers after hardening. Quantifying the attack success rate and the ranking shifts it causes reveals whether your protective measures actually work or just slow things down.
465.po: Teams can now test their deployed systems for these two real threats (indirect prompt injection and retrieval poisoning) without building their own test harness from scratch. The benchmark reports attack success, rank changes in both sparse and dense retrievers, plus utility and latency, letting practitioners quickly identify and close security gaps before malicious content reaches users.

466.bp: As AI systems get distributed across millions of phones and IoT devices, keeping data private means each device trains locally on its own data, never sending raw information to a central server. But when devices have very different data distributions—one person's phone sees mostly one type of usage, another's sees completely different patterns—the shared model starts performing worse for some groups than others, even though the goal was to help everyone equally.
466.wh: Knowledge distillation is a technique where a strong model's wisdom is transferred to smaller models via a special training signal. But when a device applies this transfer based on its own local data, the global knowledge gets warped to match local patterns. More critically, rare classes (like unusual but important user behaviors) fade away because they're underrepresented locally—the system forgets about them when learning from the device's smaller slice of data.
466.ap: FedAKD adaptively adjusts how global knowledge is transferred to each device by first checking what kinds of data that device has. It then selectively disentangles two types of knowledge: the global model's overall understanding and the device-specific details. Instead of one transfer signal for everything, the method calibrates what knowledge matters most for that device's data gaps, especially protecting rare categories from being forgotten.
466.ww: By decoupling global knowledge from local data patterns, the system can preserve important generalizations for underrepresented groups while still letting each device learn from its local data. This asymmetric approach—giving special attention to locally rare categories—means the system doesn't accidentally amplify unfairness just by trying to transfer knowledge.
466.po: Experiments show the method reduces performance degradation in minority groups without hurting overall accuracy or making the shared model slower to update. Devices with highly skewed data distributions benefit most, maintaining better performance on all groups while still gaining the efficiency advantages of federated learning.

467.bp: When you shop on Amazon, you rate products one way. When you review on a critic site, you might judge differently—assigning scores for quality, value, delivery speed, and packaging separately, not just one overall rating. These multi-faceted judgments carry richer information about what users actually want, but most recommendation systems still flatten everything into a single score, losing crucial nuance about what matters for each person across different dimensions.
467.wh: A user might give a store a low 'overall' rating yet love the product quality and fast shipping—they're just unhappy about price. Existing methods either ignore the criterion-level ratings entirely or treat them as separate problems, failing to model that some users care deeply about certain dimensions while others prioritize speed or value. The system needs to learn that different people weight criteria differently and capture how items perform along each dimension.
467.ap: TaTriGR builds a three-sided relationship graph connecting users, items, and specific criteria (like quality or delivery). It learns a personalized weight for each user across criteria—capturing that one person values speed while another obsesses over price. The item's performance on each criterion gets embedded as an additional signal about what the item truly is. Information flows through this three-sided structure, and the final recommendation naturally satisfies principles from decision theory: the predicted scores respect hierarchy (better scores on important criteria matter more) and consistency (similar items get similar recommendations).
467.ww: By explicitly modeling these three relationships and forcing the predictions to obey formal decision-making rules, the system captures real preference structures. A user's personalized weights act like a translator: the same item profile gets interpreted differently for different users. The auxiliary objectives (Ideal Point Distillation and Lexicographic Consistency) reinforce that users do actually make trade-offs, which makes the learned representations more stable and interpretable.
467.po: The system produces recommendations that better match what users actually want across multiple dimensions simultaneously, not just a generic 'best item' score. When an e-commerce platform or review site deploys this, users get suggestions that respect their specific priorities—fast delivery for the busy person, quality for the perfectionist—improving satisfaction without abandoning the nuance of multi-criteria ratings.

468.bp: Governments usually make decisions through representatives who gather input and vote, but new digital tools are making it possible for citizens to participate directly in governance without intermediaries. These systems—where voting, proposals, and resource allocation happen transparently in decentralized networks—need better ways to model and understand how decisions actually get made when power flows directly among participants rather than through institutions.
468.wh: Traditional governance has clear structures: representatives, committees, procedures. Non-mediated governance is amorphous—anyone can propose anything, voting rules might change, and influence flows through social connections and consensus-building rather than formal positions. There's no standard way to diagram how information moves or how a decision actually emerges from distributed participation. Without clear mental models, it's hard to predict whether a governance system will scale or whether it might enable capture by coordinated actors.
468.ap: This paper presents a diagraming technique and toolset for visualizing non-mediated governance use-cases and the idea of Liquid Democracy, where participants can either vote directly on issues or delegate their vote to someone they trust. The toolset helps map how data (proposals, votes, delegations, discussions) flows through the system and eventually crystallizes into concrete government action or policy.
468.ww: By making the data flow visible and mappable, practitioners can see where bottlenecks occur, identify points where collusion might happen, and check whether minority voices can still influence outcomes. The diagrams ground abstract concepts about decentralized decision-making in concrete flows, making it possible to reason about whether a system is actually fair or just appears transparent.
468.po: Governance designers can now sketch out whether their liquid democracy or non-mediated system will work before deploying it at scale. They can test scenarios, identify failure modes, and refine rules—turning governance design from an art form into something more rigorous and auditable for the Web-native communities that might adopt these systems.

469.bp: Academic peer review is supposed to filter quality, catch errors, and push authors to improve their work. But as journals and conferences grow larger, managing thousands of reviews with wildly varying quality—some thorough and fair, others careless or biased—becomes nearly impossible. Editors can't read every review to check if it's sound, yet poor reviews can misdirect editorial decisions or discourage good research.
469.wh: Review quality isn't a single number; it involves many dimensions: does the reviewer understand the work, engage constructively, identify real flaws, avoid conflicts of interest, give actionable feedback? Manually assessing all these dimensions for thousands of reviews is impractical. Existing rubrics and checklists are rigid and don't capture nuance. Without automatic methods, serious quality problems go undetected until they cause damage—a rejection based on a weak review, or acceptance of flawed work.
469.ap: PeeriScope combines three layers: first, it extracts structured features from review text (length, citation of specifics, tone markers). Second, it uses large language models guided by explicit rubrics to assess quality along multiple dimensions, with the ability to extract reasoning. Third, it trains a supervised predictor to prioritize reviews that likely have problems. The system provides both a user interface and an API so editors can integrate it into their workflow—letting reviewers self-assess, editors triage efficiently, and platforms run large-scale audits.
469.ww: By breaking quality assessment into measurable dimensions and combining algorithmic features with LLM judgment, the system captures both mechanical patterns (does this review cite anything?) and semantic understanding (does it grasp the contribution?). The supervised layer learns which combinations of features actually predict quality problems editors care about, making it better than any single metric.
469.po: Editors can now flag mediocre reviews before decisions are finalized, helping them accept strong papers even if one reviewer missed the point, or reject papers based on multiple solid reviews rather than one weak one. Reviewers get constructive feedback on their own review quality. Researchers and journal operators can audit whether certain reviewer groups are systematically harsher or more shallow, creating a data foundation for improving the scientific process at scale.

470.bp: Web pages and documents often contain images alongside text—a product listing has photos, an article has charts. When you want to automatically extract structured information (product brand, price, materials) from these mixed documents, you need to understand both what the image shows and what the text describes. This is especially hard for new product categories or data types the system has never seen before.
470.wh: Existing extraction systems work well when trained on examples of a category (product type, entity class) they've seen before, but falter on novel unseen categories. More fundamentally, they usually ignore relationships between what appears in the image and what's described in text, treating the two modalities separately. They also struggle with hierarchical structure—understanding that 'Brand' is different from 'Model Number,' and that both belong under 'Product Identity.' When trying to handle both seen and unseen categories in one go, the learned representations for unseen items drift away from the correct decision boundary.
470.ap: HMGRL uses hyperbolic geometry (a curved mathematical space where hierarchies are naturally encoded as distances) to build representations that capture how images and text relate and how concepts relate hierarchically. The system learns to generate representations for new categories even without examples, using a variational approach to smooth the space. It explicitly models the gap between how 'seen' categories cluster and how 'unseen' categories should cluster, then balances these two regions so the system doesn't catastrophically ignore one or the other.
470.ww: Hyperbolic space lets the system encode hierarchical semantics naturally—the farther apart two concepts in hyperbolic space, the more different they are. This means the learned representations for 'Brand' and 'Logo' automatically reflect their relationship (Logo is part of Brand identity). By explicitly modeling the distribution gap, the system doesn't collapse to only generating seen categories, nor does it forget them entirely when trying to handle unseen ones. The two modalities (image and text) can be jointly understood rather than treated as separate threads.
470.po: The system can now extract structured information (entities, relationships) from mixed image-text documents for product categories or relation types it has never encountered, achieving higher accuracy on unseen categories while maintaining performance on seen ones. Real-world e-commerce sites and document processing pipelines gain the ability to handle emerging product types or ad-hoc data sources without manual retraining.

471.bp: Recommendation systems often use knowledge from one domain (what users buy on Amazon) to improve suggestions in another (restaurant recommendations). This knowledge transfer can make the target domain smarter—less data needed, faster learning. But there's a hidden cost: if the source domain's data is biased (certain groups receive worse suggestions there), that bias gets transmitted to the target domain, sometimes amplifying unfairness for already-marginalized groups.
471.wh: When a recommendation system transfers knowledge across domains, it assumes the learned patterns are universally helpful. But group-level biases rarely transfer cleanly—they interact with the target domain's own data distribution. Additionally, the benefits of cross-domain transfer don't accrue equally to all groups; some communities might gain more useful information than others, exacerbating disparities. Naive transfer blindly copies both good patterns and bad biases.
471.ap: CDFA has two defenses working in concert. First, it identifies which groups are disadvantaged in the source domain's disparities and strategically mixes in unlabeled data from the target domain to equilibrate how informative the training signal is across different groups. This counteracts the direct copy of source biases. Second, it uses information theory to measure how much benefit each group actually gains from the cross-domain knowledge and then redistributes those gains (via reweighting or augmentation) so all groups benefit fairly, not just the already-privileged.
471.ww: By making disparities explicit and measurable, the system can surgically correct them rather than ignoring or denying they exist. The information-theoretic redistribution doesn't arbitrarily flatten differences; instead, it ensures that marginal groups get proportional benefit. The use of unlabeled data is clever—it doesn't require annotating sensitive attributes, yet it rebalances the information density across groups, making the learned patterns less likely to magnify existing inequities.
471.po: Cross-domain recommendation systems can now transfer knowledge without accidentally amplifying group-level unfairness. Experiments show the framework reduces disparities significantly while even improving overall recommendation accuracy. Platforms can confidently leverage multi-domain data to improve personalization for everyone, not just well-represented groups.

472.bp: Fraud, hacking, and security threats in Web systems often manifest as unusual patterns of interaction—abnormal login sequences, sudden trading surges, sudden graph connection changes between accounts. These threats evolve constantly, making it hard for security systems to catch them without human monitoring. A system that detects these anomalies automatically and explains what looks suspicious is invaluable for maintaining system integrity.
472.wh: Anomaly detection in streaming interactions (new edges arriving constantly) needs to be both real-time—detecting problems within milliseconds of the suspicious behavior—and memory-efficient, because storing entire graphs can be prohibitively expensive. Standard anomaly detection methods struggle here: they either lag behind the stream (too slow) or require storing full graph state (too much memory). Additionally, explaining why something looks anomalous is crucial; a security team won't act on a black-box alert without understanding what pattern triggered it.
472.ap: The paper introduces Interaction Willingness, a metric capturing whether two entities should naturally interact based on their past behavior and graph structure. AnoD and AnoC are two algorithms that detect two types of anomalies: dense (suddenly many interactions between entities that rarely interact) and counter (interactions that break established patterns). Both use a compact data structure called High-Order Count-Min Sketch, which stores streaming graph information in near-zero memory while maintaining mathematical guarantees on accuracy.
472.ww: The Interaction Willingness metric grounds detection in a principled measure—how likely should this pair be interacting?—rather than ad-hoc thresholds. By using Count-Min Sketch, the system maintains constant memory per new edge; this means adding a million interactions doesn't degrade detection speed or memory, only storage needs. The interpretability comes naturally from the metric: explaining an anomaly means showing why Interaction Willingness suddenly changed.
472.po: Security teams can deploy these algorithms on live streaming graphs (social networks, trading systems, access logs) to catch fraud and intrusions in real-time with minimal overhead. The constant-time and constant-space guarantees mean the system scales to billions of interactions without slowing down or exhausting memory, and the interpretability ensures alerts lead to actual investigation rather than being dismissed as noise.

473.bp: AI agents that process long sequences—biological data, financial time-series, long documents—become prohibitively expensive to run because the AI model charges by the number of tokens (discrete pieces of text or data) it processes. In domains like genomics or molecular analysis, the raw sequences can span thousands or millions of positions. A researcher or startup can't afford to send all that through an expensive model, yet the model won't work on a blind summary either.
473.wh: The fundamental problem is that LLM pricing scales with input length, and raw biological or financial sequences are incompressible at face value—each position might matter. Yet the LLM cannot interpret raw sequences anyway; a genomic DNA string means nothing to a language model until a specialized tool extracts features. Passing raw sequence through the LLM is wasteful. Compressing too aggressively loses information. In multi-step agent workflows, irrelevant context from earlier steps balloons the token count without adding value.
473.ap: The paper introduces two layers of compression. Long-Sequence Compression (LSC) extracts meaningful representations from raw domain-specific sequences using task-specific tools (e.g., a bioinformatics tool for DNA, a feature extractor for time-series) before sending anything to the LLM. Prompt-based Gate-Guided Memory (PGM) works like a selective filter on intermediate states: at each step, it asks 'does the current prompt need this context,' and only carries forward relevant information, inspired by how gated recurrent networks selectively forget irrelevant history.
473.ww: By extracting semantically meaningful summaries instead of raw data, LSC dramatically reduces token count while preserving information the LLM can actually use. PGM prevents context creep in multi-step reasoning—each step doesn't accumulate every past observation, only relevant state. Together, they reduce redundancy without losing decision-critical information. The gate is learned based on the prompt, so the system adapts to what the current task needs.
473.po: A researcher can now affordably run multi-agent workflows on long biological sequences or time-series without paying prohibitive token costs. A team analyzing genomic data for drug discovery, for instance, can run agentic reasoning over tens of thousands of sequence positions instead of being limited to kilobases. The cost drops substantially, democratizing access to expensive LLM-based analysis for communities that can't absorb the overhead.

474.bp: Cybersecurity professionals defend against attacks using high-level security goals (keep data confidential, ensure systems are available) and low-level technical concepts (patch this buffer overflow vulnerability). But the connection between business objectives ('protect customer data') and technical fixes ('update OpenSSL') is murky. This gap means teams often can't explain why a particular vulnerability matters for their assets or which mitigations actually serve business goals, making risk prioritization ad-hoc and inefficient.
474.wh: Existing security standards and ontologies are static and read-only—NIST and ISO describe categories, but they don't adapt as new attacks and exploits emerge. The gap between operations (what threats are we actually seeing?) and compliance (what does the standard say we need?) widens constantly. Additionally, the standards use words ambiguously: 'Confidentiality' might mean different things in different contexts, and the chain from business goal to technical action gets lost in translation. No dynamic platform exists where the security community can collectively map these relationships and evolve the standards.
474.ap: This work proposes a wiki-style, agile ontology platform that models the full chain: Security Services (business goals like Confidentiality) connect to Security Mechanisms (technical solutions like encryption), which mitigate Attacks (types of threats), which exploit Vulnerabilities (software flaws), which can be deployed by Attackers (threat actors), who target Assets (data, systems). The system is aware of homonyms (words with multiple meanings in security contexts) and allows continuous community editing with validation, so the ontology evolves as new attacks emerge. The platform includes visualization and management tools.
474.ww: By making the chain explicit and editable, practitioners can trace why a specific patch matters for their business. The homonym-awareness prevents misunderstandings across teams (does 'Access Control' mean authentication or authorization?). The wiki approach lets the community dynamically extend the ontology as novel attacks emerge, rather than waiting for standards bodies to issue updates. Continuous community evaluation keeps mappings grounded in operational reality.
474.po: Security teams can now drill from a business goal ('ensure availability of critical systems') down to specific techniques and vulnerabilities to patch, with documented reasoning. Risk prioritization becomes more rigorous—teams see which vulnerabilities actually threaten their critical assets and which mitigations serve their top business objectives. Organizations can audit whether their current security posture aligns with strategic goals.

475.bp: Radiology reports—the text that doctors write describing what they see in X-rays and scans—need to be accurate and factually correct; a miswritten finding can lead to missed diagnoses. AI systems can now generate these reports automatically by looking at images, but generated reports often contradict the images or previous reports for the same patient. Retrieving and incorporating relevant prior reports should help the system stay factually consistent, but most methods fail to use that information effectively.
475.wh: Retrieving only coarse image-report pairs isn't enough—the system needs to understand fine-grained clinical details: which specific findings matter, how do reports about the same pathology relate across different patients, what's the hierarchical structure of medical reasoning (normal → abnormality → specific disease)? Standard cross-modal retrieval treats images and text as separate domains and learns shallow correspondences, missing the hierarchical semantic knowledge embedded in collections of reports. The result is generated reports that sound plausible but contradict facts visible in images or prior reports.
475.ap: MGK-RAG uses multi-granularity semantic similarities extracted from the text domain to guide what the system learns about images. Rather than learning a generic image-to-text match, it learns fine-grained clinical semantic alignment by looking at how reports relate to each other—which mentions of findings are similar, which diagnostic pathways typically co-occur, what's hierarchical (general symptom → specific finding). This guides the multimodal retriever. When generating a report, the system integrates retrieved reports' visual features into the original image understanding via cross-attention, enriching what the model knows about this specific patient's anatomy and pathology.
475.ww: By using report-to-report relationships as a bridge to understand images, the system learns clinical semantics that generic image models miss. The cross-attention mechanism ensures retrieved information is actually fused with the image features, not just treated as extra context. This multi-granularity approach captures both coarse correspondences (image type matches report type) and fine-grained details (this specific lesion matches this specific description across two reports).
475.po: Generated radiology reports are more factually accurate and clinically coherent, with fewer contradictions between the written findings and the image content. Hospitals deploying this system for report drafting assistance gain higher-quality outputs, reducing the radiologist's burden of editing inconsistencies and catching missed details. The hierarchical semantic understanding also improves key clinical metrics—the system doesn't just sound right, it actually matches what doctors observe.

476.bp: Mental health struggles, especially depression, often go undetected in people who don't seek formal help—isolation, shame, and accessibility barriers keep millions silent. Yet people share their inner lives on social media constantly, including through metaphor ('I'm drowning in darkness,' 'my anxiety is a cage'). If systems could recognize depression signals in these natural expressions, it could enable early intervention, destigmatize mental health, and provide crucial insights for therapeutic work.
476.wh: Metaphors are complex—the same image ('drowning') can mean depression for one person and overwhelm for another. Detecting depression from metaphors requires understanding both the surface image and the underlying psychological state it expresses. The problem is worsened by lacking large-scale annotated datasets of real metaphorical expressions linked to depression levels. Without such data, models trained on generic text don't capture the nuances of psychological expression. Additionally, purely predictive models that just output 'depressed or not' don't help clinicians; they need explanations grounded in what the person actually said.
476.ap: This work introduces the Depression-Related Metaphor Dataset (DRMD), pairing social media posts with depression severity levels (severe, moderate, minimal, or absent), annotations of which posts contain metaphors, and mappings of metaphorical source domains (e.g., 'drowning' comes from a water/submersion domain). The paper then fine-tunes large language models on this dataset, explicitly incorporating metaphorical features. Critically, the model generates explanations by referencing the specific metaphors it identified, making its reasoning interpretable.
476.ww: By training on metaphor-annotated data, the model learns that certain conceptual mappings (water domains, cage domains, darkness domains) correlate with depression severity. The explicit annotation of source domains teaches the model the psychological structures metaphor embeds—that 'drowning' isn't random, it maps internal psychological states to physical submersion, which clinicians recognize as a depression marker. The explanation mechanism ensures the model doesn't just score high on accuracy; it can tell a clinician why it flagged someone as at-risk, grounding the prediction in observable linguistic behavior.
476.po: Mental health platforms, crisis hotlines, or online communities can deploy this to flag users who may need support, with explanations that humanize the alert rather than making it feel algorithmic. The metaphor-focused approach adds empathy—the system recognizes the poetry of depression, not just keywords. Researchers gain a publicly available dataset for studying how metaphor encodes psychological state, and clinicians can better understand the language of mental health struggles.

477.bp: When AI systems process text, images, and sound together (video with subtitles, social media posts with images and comments), the data is usually complete—all three modalities present. But real-world Web content is messy: videos lack captions, images fail to load due to network issues, users disable video on low bandwidth, or privacy settings hide certain data. Systems trained on complete data fail when modalities are missing. Building systems robust to missing data is crucial for actually working in the real world.
477.wh: When a modality is missing, simple methods try to reconstruct it (guessing what sound a silent video should have) or treat it as a special missing token. But reconstruction often distorts what's actually there, and missing tokens don't capture the rich information a full modality would provide. More subtly, class prototypes—the learned idea of what a 'happy' or 'sad' video looks like—shift when data is incomplete, creating anchor drift: the decision boundary for classifying emotions moves depending on whether audio is present or absent. This instability makes the learned representation space unreliable.
477.ap: HiCoD (Hierarchical Consistency-Guided Prompt Distillation) learns a semantic space anchored by explicit class prototypes. It builds a modality-aware semantic graph that infers cross-modal structure even when some modalities are missing, using graph techniques to fill in the topology. It then uses dual-level anchoring: global prototypes derived from language models (abstract notions of 'happy' or 'angry') combined with local exemplars (actual videos in the training set that exemplify happiness). Multi-level distillation aligns unimodal features (audio alone, video alone), combined embeddings (audio + video), and even completed signals (inferred modalities) all toward the same anchor space.
477.ww: The dual-level anchoring prevents drift: even if audio is missing, the global prototype ('what happiness is') and the top-K examples ('these specific videos are happy') provide a stable reference. The semantic graph restores structure by predicting what cross-modal patterns should hold, avoiding expensive reconstruction. Multi-level distillation ensures that whether a sample has all modalities or just one, it gets represented in the same conceptual space, eliminating anchor drift.
477.po: Multimodal learning systems can now handle variable missing data—some videos with audio and captions, others with just video. They maintain consistent accuracy even under heavy missingness (e.g., 50% of videos missing audio), improving generalization on incomplete real-world data. Recommendation systems, emotion detection platforms, and accessibility tools benefit by handling incomplete Web content without retraining per modality pattern.

478.bp: Social networks protect user privacy by applying local differential privacy—a mathematical guarantee that individual user data (friends, activity) stays hidden from central servers. Yet even with strong privacy protections, the network can still be poisoned: an attacker can inject false data or modify records in ways that degrade the system's utility (the ability to classify users accurately, for instance). Balancing privacy and robustness to manipulation is a hard problem, and most privacy-preserving systems don't address poisoning.
478.wh: Local differential privacy works by intentionally adding noise to each user's data before it reaches the server, so the server sees only a scrambled aggregate. But this noise also makes it harder to detect attackers who slip in fake nodes or corrupted data—the noise masks both legitimate variation and adversarial anomalies. An attacker coordinating multiple poisoned accounts can make systematic changes that look like natural noise. Existing defenses assume clean data; they fail under privacy noise.
478.ap: CureNet defends against poisoned graph data in a privacy setting with four components. First, local data perturbation happens (standard privacy noise). Second, trimmed screening filters out outlier submissions that look suspicious, removing accounts that deviate too far from normal. Third, privacy-aware fake node pruning uses specialized techniques to detect and remove sophisticated adversaries even in noisy data—it doesn't just look for outliers, but for coordinated patterns of inauthentic behavior. Fourth, a utility recovery module restores graph learning performance after filtering, since removing nodes and edges degrades accuracy.
478.ww: By stacking defenses, the system raises the bar for attackers: they can't easily insert random fake nodes (screening catches obvious outliers) or coordinate subtle manipulations (fake node pruning detects coordinated inauthentic behavior). The privacy-aware approach uses the privacy noise structure itself—understanding what noise looks like lets the system distinguish it from attack patterns. The utility recovery ensures the privacy protections and the defense both benefit the system, not just security.
478.po: Social networks can now offer both strong user privacy (differential privacy guarantees) and robustness to data poisoning attacks. Experiments on real networks (Facebook, Twitch, GitHub, LastFM) show both that the attack is serious and that the defense significantly reduces its impact. Platforms gain confidence that privacy-preserving graph learning systems won't be compromised by coordinated adversaries inserting fake accounts or false relationships.

479.bp: Large AI models are built on top of tokenizers—systems that convert raw input (text, code, images, graphs) into discrete chunks the model can process. Text tokenizers are well-understood, but graph tokenizer is an unsolved problem: graphs have complex non-Euclidean structures (they're not 2D planes or 3D spaces), and their structure matters more than individual elements. A good graph tokenizer needs to capture essential patterns (trees, cycles, chains) and transfer those patterns across different kinds of graphs, enabling foundation models to learn from one graph domain and apply knowledge to another.
479.wh: Graphs live in curved, non-Euclidean spaces—geometry matters in ways that flat Euclidean spaces don't handle naturally. A tree structure in a social network is fundamentally different from a tree in a molecule, yet both are trees. Existing approaches either ignore structure (treating nodes as independent) or apply flat quantization (rounding real values to discrete buckets) that loses the hierarchical semantics geometry encodes. Cross-domain transfer of graph knowledge fails because different domains have different geometric properties—a social network's geometry differs from a citation network's.
479.ap: RGT uses Riemannian geometry (curved mathematical spaces where distance and angle respect the underlying structure) to build a unified framework. It defines a geometric vocabulary of fundamental structures (trees, cycles, sequences) that capture intrinsic graph patterns. A Riemannian quantizer converts continuous geometric representations into discrete tokens, using a Riemannian Straight-Through Estimator to make this differentiable for training. Crucially, a geometry-aligned decoder projects domain-specific tokens into a shared tangent space—a common reference frame where tokens from different geometric spaces can be compared.
479.ww: By using Riemannian geometry, the system naturally respects the non-Euclidean structure of graphs; distance in the curved space measures true structural dissimilarity. The geometric vocabulary captures what really distinguishes graphs—are there cycles, how deep are trees, how long are paths. The tangent space projection is clever: even though social networks and molecular graphs live in different geometric spaces, they can be represented in a shared flat space locally (tangent space), enabling transfer. This separates the identity of structures (trees, cycles) from the specific geometry of each domain.
479.po: Foundation models can now use a unified tokenizer for graphs across domains—social networks, molecules, knowledge graphs, citation networks—each retaining their geometric properties but becoming comparable at the token level. A model trained on social network patterns can transfer knowledge to molecular graphs, dramatically reducing the data needed in the target domain. This enables more efficient, more generalizable graph foundation models that can handle diverse structural domains.

480.bp: Knowledge graphs—giant databases of facts organized as connections between things—are becoming enormous and need testing before deployment. Real-world testing with large, realistic graphs is expensive and slow, so researchers need artificial graphs that behave like real ones to stress-test systems and measure performance.
480.wh: When you build a fake knowledge graph by copying individual facts (triples), you lose the hidden shape of how those facts relate at higher levels. Real graphs have dense clusters and structures that matter, but most fake generators just stitched together random facts, creating artificially simple worlds that don't test systems properly.
480.ap: This work treats facts not as isolated points but as shapes. They look for geometric structures called simplices (imagine pyramids of connected facts) inside real graphs, then use the patterns of these higher-dimensional shapes to grow synthetic graphs that maintain realistic geometry. The generator preserves how facts naturally cluster and depend on each other.
480.ww: Simplices capture something triples alone cannot: how facts naturally group and reinforce each other. By learning these structural patterns first, the generator reproduces the dense, layered way real knowledge evolves, not just random collections of true statements.
480.po: The synthetic graphs they made passed structure tests 26% closer to real graphs than the best competing approach, and when used to test database engines, they gave query performance numbers only 6% off from real graphs—credible enough to predict how systems will actually perform.

481.bp: Finding tight communities in networks—groups of people who know each other, genes that work together—is central to understanding social media, biology, and the web. But real networks are enormous; checking every possible group is computationally impossible.
481.wh: A quasi-clique is a group where most connections exist but not all; it's more realistic than requiring perfect cliques. The edge-based version says a group is tight if its internal links exceed a density threshold. The math problem is NP-hard (no known fast solution), and unlike simpler problems, pruning tricks that work elsewhere don't apply here—you can't safely throw away partial solutions.
481.ap: The researchers split the dense subgraph-finding problem into smaller, hereditary pieces (each piece keeps the property when you remove nodes). This split lets them use aggressive pruning: if a partial solution can't possibly reach the target density even optimistically, discard it. They also add heuristics to explore the most promising branches first, guided by which sub-trees matter most.
481.ww: Hereditary subproblems let standard pruning work: many branches lead nowhere, and ruling them out early saves work exponentially. The heuristic guides search toward high-density regions where tight groups actually live, avoiding dead ends.
481.po: On 253 real networks, their algorithm EQC-Pro is up to 10,000 times faster than prior methods, making it practical to find communities in graphs with millions of nodes—fast enough to analyze real social and biological networks interactively.

482.bp: Events happen in sequences everywhere: people click items, patients visit clinics, earthquakes trigger aftershocks. Predicting the next event or spotting unusual patterns saves money (fraud, server failures) and lives (disease outbreaks). Current models either assume rigid math (Poisson: events at random rates) or hide their reasoning.
482.wh: Rigid mathematical models fail on real sequences where the past influences the future in complex ways—one event makes the next more or less likely, and different event types interact unpredictably. Neural models are flexible but treat interactions as invisible patterns inside matrices, so you can't debug or trust them. You don't learn what drives a prediction.
482.ap: This work splits the sequence model into two visible parts. The first layer learns how each event type evolves over time on its own, preserving its unique rhythm. The second layer explicitly models how different event types affect each other using a graph-like connection structure, making each interaction traceable. Irregular timing gaps between events are handled by separate time-encoding mechanisms for different scenarios.
482.ww: By making interactions explicit instead of buried in neural layers, the model becomes interpretable: you can see which event types reinforce each other and which suppress each other. This mirrors how real causality works. Separate time encodings let the model handle both regular and chaotic timing.
482.po: The model predicts future events more accurately than prior neural approaches and actually lets analysts understand why: which past events drove this prediction. This matters for critical domains like healthcare where doctors need to understand the system's reasoning.

483.bp: Web crawlers automatically discover and download pages from millions of websites to build search indices and monitor content. They have limited bandwidth (politeness rules, budget caps) and must choose which starting points to use to hit the most new pages, fastest.
483.wh: Today's crawlers rely on humans manually curating seed lists—picking entry points by guessing or habit. Humans pick either too many copies of the same redundant starting point or miss high-value ones entirely. No automated system learns from past crawls to predict which seeds will pay off.
483.ap: The system watches the crawler's own history—which seeds led to new discoveries versus dead ends—and learns two measures per seed: stability (do the links stay available across runs?) and productivity (how many new pages does this seed find?). It then greedily ranks seeds by combined value, maximizing total unique coverage within budget.
483.ww: By learning from real crawl history instead of guessing, the system adapts to each site's actual behavior. Ranking by marginal gain (how much new value does this seed add?) avoids redundant choices. The approach is greedy but effective: each step picks the seed that gives the most new coverage.
483.po: On 5,238 real websites, URLBank found more unique pages, used fewer seed requests, and discovered fresh content sooner than manual curation—all measurable gains deployed in Meltwater's production crawler. The system is auditable: operators can see why each seed was chosen.

484.bp: AI assistants now write code, but they make predictable mistakes: they get stuck on one idea, miss edge cases, and can be tricked by tiny input changes. Code with hidden biases, security holes, or logical flaws is dangerous in production. We need ways to catch these mistakes before code is deployed.
484.wh: Large language models think like a monolith: once they commit to an approach, they rarely backtrack or consider alternatives. They can't naturally spot their own blind spots, and standard testing misses flaws because LLMs are good at appearing confident even when wrong. Debate among multiple agents helps with efficiency, but doesn't fix the core reasoning blindness.
484.ap: This system creates three AI roles that argue: an Optimist pushes forward with the best case for each plan, a Pragmatist raises practical concerns, and an Adversarial Skeptic actively hunts for ways the plan fails. They debate and refine together. After convergence, a separate verification module intentionally breaks the plan with tricky inputs (changing numbers, flipping conditions) to stress-test it.
484.ww: Adversarial debate forces the model to articulate why a plan works, not just assert it. The skeptic voices doubts the monolithic model wouldn't generate alone. Counterfactual stress-testing (deliberately perturbing inputs) catches brittle code that works on examples but fails on variations—catching the hidden flaws.
484.po: The paper doesn't give full results in the abstract, but the method is designed to produce code that is functionally correct, less biased, and more resilient to tricky inputs by making the AI actively defend its reasoning against structured attacks.

485.bp: Cybercriminals send malicious network traffic (viruses, stolen data, attacks). Network switches can inspect packets at terabits per second to catch threats before they reach servers. But inspecting each packet requires balancing speed against accuracy: overly simplified checks miss attacks; complex checks slow the network.
485.wh: Machine learning detection models are complex (many decision rules), so they're simplified into decision trees for speed. A single pruned tree is fast but inaccurate (too many false negatives). Multiple trees are accurate but overload the hardware (too much wasted checking). No middle ground exists under the old design.
485.ap: This system splits a decision tree into critical and normal parts based on their importance to accuracy. Critical branches (the ones that matter most) run on the switch's fast hardware even if they're complex. Normal branches run elsewhere or are simplified. The system automatically minimizes coordination overhead so decisions are fast and complete.
485.ww: By treating branches unequally—giving resources to the ones that move the needle on accuracy—you avoid both extremes. Splitting lets the system adapt to available hardware: if the switch has room, keep critical rules; if it's full, migrate them elsewhere or simplify gracefully.
485.po: Proteus detects malicious traffic with high accuracy while using minimal switch resources, scaling to network speeds. It dynamically adjusts to changing hardware availability, keeping detection accurate even under resource pressure.

486.bp: Toxic content (hate speech, harassment) spreads on social media and harms users. Automated detection systems clean feeds in real time. But bad actors keep evolving their tricks—using typos, replacing letters with numbers, hiding slurs in slang—to dodge filters. Static detectors fail against evolving attacks.
486.wh: Detectors trained on today's tricks break when attackers invent new ones tomorrow. Retraining from scratch is slow and wasteful. Continual learning on new tricks sounds good but breaks down: each perturbation type has its own quirks; noise introduced by typos or tricks distorts meaning; and the detector becomes oversensitive to surface variations.
486.ap: This system uses an LLM to reconstruct the original meaning behind perturbations—expanding typos, explaining slang, recovering original intent—and enriches the noisy text with semantic clues about toxicity before checking. As new evasion tricks emerge, the detector learns from them incrementally without forgetting old ones, building robustness gradually.
486.ww: By recovering meaning before detection, the system separates the evasion noise from the actual toxic signal. Incremental learning lets it adapt to new tricks without retraining everything. Using an LLM to understand context makes the detector robust to surface-level tricks because it reads intent, not just letters.
486.po: ContiGuard detects toxic content that uses evolving perturbations, staying effective as attackers adapt. It maintains accuracy over time without full retraining, handling both old and new evasion tactics in production.

487.bp: Scientific papers, patents, and legal documents are increasingly digital and vast. Extracting meaning—who invented what, which laws apply—requires machines to read and organize this unstructured text with complex embedded charts and tables that current AI can't process automatically.
487.wh: Legal and scientific documents are messy: facts are scattered, tables contain crucial details that aren't in text, figures show relationships words don't capture. Treating documents as pure text loses structure. Knowledge graphs are rigid and incomplete. Large language models alone can't handle complex reasoning over structured knowledge.
487.ap: This workshop explores the intersection of three fields: semantic web technologies (structured knowledge), language models (understanding text), and reasoning systems (drawing conclusions). The goal is to investigate how structured knowledge representations can guide language models toward more reliable and understandable reasoning.
487.ww: Combining symbolic structure (knowledge graphs, logical rules) with statistical learning (LLMs) lets systems be both flexible and interpretable. Machines can extract meaning from messy documents by recognizing structure, then reason over that structure reliably. This hybrid approach avoids pure-text LLM errors.
487.po: Research at this workshop advances methods to extract and organize scientific and legal knowledge automatically, making vast document corpuses machine-readable and queryable—enabling faster discovery and more reliable compliance checking.

488.bp: AI models are shared online and used widely. If a model learns sensitive information (medical records, copyrighted text, private data), owners should be able to ask the model to forget it. Machine unlearning is the process of removing information from a trained model.
488.wh: Current tests check if the model still outputs the sensitive data—does it still complete 'John Smith is'? But testing output is insufficient: the model could have hidden the information internally while keeping knowledge of it dormant, ready to be recovered with the right prompt. Simply suppressing answers isn't true forgetting.
488.ap: This work uses sparse autoencoders (a decomposition technique) to peer into intermediate layers of the model and spot the hidden feature patterns representing each class. Then they use inference-time steering—nudging the internal activations—to test whether sensitive features can be recovered. If they can, suppression, not deletion, occurred.
488.ww: By examining internal representations rather than just outputs, you catch sneaky suppression: the model learned to hide sensitive answers but didn't truly forget the knowledge. Sparse autoencoders make internal features human-readable and testable. Steering lets you check if forgotten information is still accessible internally.
488.po: Testing 12 unlearning methods, they found most only suppress information at the decision boundary while keeping semantic features intact internally. Even retraining doesn't remove robust features from pretraining. This reveals critical gaps: unlearning methods need to delete representations, not just outputs.

489.bp: Recommendation systems chat with users to figure out what they like and suggest relevant items (movies, products, news). The system should learn from past conversations. But reusing old conversations blindly can backfire: a user who watched sad movies last month might want action movies today; yesterday's data misleads today's recommendation.
489.wh: Historical information helps detect patterns—frequent users, seasonal shifts—but also traps the system. Old dialogue sessions can cause cognitive negative transfer: forcing yesterday's preferences onto today's decision. The system needs to distinguish between helpful history (personal taste) and harmful history (outdated context).
489.ap: This system creates two simulated agents that debate whether old dialogue sessions help or hurt the current recommendation. A supporting agent argues for using each session; an opposing agent argues against it. After debate, only the vetted useful sessions are injected into the recommender's core parameters, personalizing it selectively.
489.ww: Debate creates a check on mindless history reuse. By forcing articulation of why past data helps (or doesn't), the system learns to filter. Parametric injection embeds only the vetted knowledge directly into the model, so the recommender naturally prefers recent, relevant signals over stale historical noise.
489.po: EyeCRS improves recommendation accuracy by selectively leveraging user history, using debate to screen out sessions that would mislead. It balances learning from past behavior with adapting to present preferences, a key tension in real recommendation systems.

490.bp: Recommendation systems need to rank items fast based on sequences of past user clicks. Attention-based models (the current standard) are accurate but slow: checking every past click against every candidate item costs quadratic time, making long user histories prohibitively expensive.
490.wh: Sequences of user clicks can be thousands of events long. Attention multiplies that length by the number of items to check, making both memory and compute quadratic—doubling sequence length quadruples work. No one can afford that at scale. Simpler models (recurrent networks) are faster but less accurate on real behavior.
490.ap: This system replaces attention with Hyena, a sub-quadratic operator (linear scaling with sequence length) that uses polynomial-based kernels to recognize long-range temporal patterns. A gating mechanism on top captures short-term behavioral bursts (quick click sequences). Together, they model both slow trends and fast changes with just linear computation.
490.ww: Polynomial kernels compress long-range dependency patterns into smooth, learnable functions instead of checking every past click individually. The gating layer handles the fine detail. This combination gives you the expressiveness of attention at linear cost by separating long-term and short-term reasoning.
490.po: HyenaRec outranks items as accurately as attention models but trains 6 times faster, with massive wins on long sequences where efficiency matters most. This makes recommendation practical for users with deep, complex click histories.

491.bp: Large language models can write and reason, but they forget conversations end-to-end, treat each query as isolated, and can't develop expertise or personality over time. Real assistants should remember what happened, learn from it, and improve their reasoning incrementally.
491.wh: LLMs have no persistent memory between conversations. They also lack structured organization—everything is just text in a massive context window. Coordination between multiple LLMs acting as specialized agents is ad-hoc. Deployed agents struggle to remember hundreds of interactions or update their knowledge dynamically.
491.ap: PromptX gives agents three layers. A prompt markup language lets you define personas and memory schemas (what to remember and how). Engrams—structured records of experiences—feed into a graph-based activation-diffusion network that links raw memories to conceptual summaries, enabling associative recall (thinking of a term bubbles up related memories). A protocol layer coordinates multiple agents using web standards (HATEOAS), letting new tools be discovered and invoked dynamically.
491.ww: Structured memory distinguishes raw experience from conceptual knowledge, so the system can generalize (this user is a developer) while staying grounded (this developer just mentioned Python). Graph propagation lets related memories reinforce each other: mentioning 'Python' activates memories about coding, which surfaces relevant advice. Dynamic tool discovery lets agents adapt without reprogramming.
491.po: PromptX deployed in 15+ enterprises over 5 months, accumulating 50K+ downloads and 3K+ GitHub stars. It demonstrated that agents with persistent, structured memory and dynamic coordination actually work in practice for diverse industries.

492.bp: Recommendation systems rank items by predicted relevance to a user. But the actual goal is simpler: deliver the top-K best items, not rank everything perfectly. Current models are trained to match this top-K ranking goal roughly, but their architecture doesn't actually optimize for it.
492.wh: Recommendation models are built around tasks like matrix factorization or graph neural networks—general-purpose designs not aligned with top-K ranking. They optimize auxiliary metrics (mean squared error, cross-entropy) as proxies for top-K performance. This misalignment means models learn patterns that don't serve the real goal.
492.ap: TopKGAT derives a recommendation architecture directly from the mathematical formulation of top-K metrics (Precision@K). Each forward pass through a layer approximately performs one gradient step toward maximizing Precision@K. The structure resembles graph attention networks but with layers explicitly shaped by the top-K objective.
492.ww: When your architecture's forward pass is literally gradient ascent on your goal metric, the model's learning is perfectly aligned with what you actually care about. You avoid the proxy-metric problem entirely: the model naturally learns patterns that boost top-K ranking, not patterns that look good on other metrics.
492.po: TopKGAT consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on four benchmark datasets by ranking the most relevant items higher, with an architecture design that makes this outcome mathematically inevitable rather than hoped-for.

493.bp: Advertisers bid for clicks on ads; systems predict which users will click to allocate ads efficiently. But users' interests shift: someone researching apartments might click real estate ads today but ignore them tomorrow. Systems should adapt to these rapid swings, not just average past behavior.
493.wh: Current models learn from raw user history but overfit to historically dominant behaviors—what the user clicked last month matters too much. They also treat each ad candidate independently, ignoring that the full set of candidate ads on the page conveys context about what the user might want right now. This isolation discards crucial information.
493.ap: GenCI uses a generative model (trained to predict the next click) to produce candidate interest cohorts—groups representing the user's current, immediate interests, not their full history. These cohorts are semantic summaries, not just recent clicks. A ranking network then uses cross-attention to align these cohorts with both the candidate ad and the page context, refining the prediction.
493.ww: By generating current intent separately from historical behavior, the model can capture rapid interest shifts. Semantic cohorts are abstract enough to generalize (the user cares about 'home improvement' today) but concrete enough to guide ranking. Cross-attention lets the model adjust its view of user intent based on what's actually available to recommend.
493.po: GenCI improves click prediction by modeling dynamic user interest through semantic cohorts, avoiding both historical overfitting and myopic candidate-wise ranking. It aligns the model's internal representation with real-world ranking dynamics.

494.bp: Cities are deploying participatory platforms to let residents vote and propose ideas—but today's tools are basic (vote yes/no, fill forms). For real democracy at scale, residents need rich deliberation: proposal refinement, consensus-building, fair synthesis of competing views. This requires smarter tools, not just better voting.
494.wh: Large language models can draft text and summarize, but they're black boxes—no one knows how they weighted opposing views or why they recommended one idea over another. Using an autonomous LLM for civic decisions risks algorithmic bias and erodes trust. People need to understand and contest the system's reasoning.
494.ap: This work proposes a framework that explicitly bounds when and how LLMs are used in four civic stages: drafting (LLM helps format resident proposals), convergence (LLM identifies common ground), synthesis (LLM summarizes themes), and moderation (LLM flags norms violations). Each stage specifies transparency requirements, letting residents audit decisions and contests biased outputs.
494.ww: By limiting LLM autonomy to specific stages and requiring transparency at each stage, the system preserves human agency and accountability. Residents can understand why an idea was categorized as 'transportation' or flagged as off-topic. Contestation mechanisms let people challenge algorithmic decisions, making the system legible instead of opaque.
494.po: The paper provides a roadmap for integrating LLMs into civic platforms while maintaining democratic legitimacy. It identifies design constraints that prevent automation bias, enabling genuine deliberation at scale rather than replacing democracy with algorithmic efficiency.

495.bp: When we ask AI models to write code, we want them to get it right—especially the structural parts like where functions start and how blocks nest. The trouble is that tiny mistakes early in generation often derail everything downstream, so understanding where and why errors begin matters for building better systems.
495.wh: Most people look at the final, broken code and ask 'what went wrong?' But the real problem lives inside the generation process itself. Early in writing a function or defining a variable, the model faces a fork in the road—and if it's uncertain there, no amount of fixing later can recover. Natural language doesn't have these brittle structural decision points; code does.
495.ap: The researchers compared token-by-token what the model does when generating English versus code. They found that code breaks down hardest at the beginning of lines—exactly where the model needs to pick the right indentation, keyword, or structure. They then tested a simple fix: giving the model a prompt nudge that forewarns it about the code structure ahead, like a roadmap.
495.ww: When the model knows the structural skeleton in advance, it doesn't have to guess blindly at high-stakes moments. It can anchor its predictions, which shrinks its uncertainty (called predictive entropy). Less uncertainty means more confident, correct early choices, which cascade into fewer downstream errors.
495.po: On benchmarks like HumanEval and MBPP, the simple structural guidance cuts down the entropy of hard early decisions. The result: models generate working code more often, without changing the model itself—just a better prompt. This opens a path to structure-aware code generation that respects where hardness actually lives.

496.bp: Time series data—streams of measurements over time like sensor readings or stock prices—looks different in different environments (seasons, places, equipment). Real systems must work when deployed to new conditions they've never seen before, but models trained on old data often fail in these new settings.
496.wh: The challenge is separating true predictive signals from environmental noise. When a model learns from winter data and then faces summer, it might have memorized winter patterns that don't work later. Worse, it's hard to know which learned features are actually causal (drive the prediction) versus coincidental (happen to be correlated).
496.ap: The method splits learned patterns into two kinds: causal features (the ones that truly predict the label across any environment) and spurious features (noise that looks predictive by accident). It then creates fake examples by mixing-and-matching features: taking real causal signals but pairing them with spurious patterns from different contexts. It trains the model to still predict correctly on these mixed examples, forcing it to rely only on true causal patterns.
496.ww: By forcing the model to ignore spurious features—even when they're present—it learns to be robust. When the model later faces a new environment with different spurious noise, it already knows how to throw it away and use only the causal signal underneath.
496.po: On multiple time series datasets, this causal disentanglement approach outperforms existing methods when the environment shifts. The model works reliably across different domains without retraining, and the framework is lightweight enough to plug into existing time series classifiers.

497.bp: When computer science teachers grade student code, they need to give feedback that points to specific errors and suggests how to fix them. Large language models can do this at scale, but automated feedback often feels generic or misses important mistakes—and that matters for student learning.
497.wh: If you ask one language model to evaluate a whole rubric at once (checking for syntax, logic, style, efficiency), it gets overloaded. It tends to notice surface-level issues, repeat the same feedback, or contradict itself. Using multiple models helps, but coordinating their answers is tricky.
497.ap: The researchers compared two approaches: one prompt to one model judging everything, versus multiple smaller models each focusing on one aspect of the rubric. They tested this on real student code with test failures and error messages, using open-source models and 57 Python assignments.
497.ww: A single model trying to juggle many criteria at once divides its attention and gets confused. Separate models, each with a clear narrow job, stay focused and consistent. But the surprising finding is that even a single, well-designed prompt can outperform multiple models if it's structured carefully.
497.po: The best setups generate feedback that students actually find useful—specific, not canned, and internally consistent. Using multiple evaluator models didn't beat a carefully written single prompt. The implication: how you frame the question matters as much as how many judges you have.

498.bp: When a robot or autonomous vehicle needs to know where it is, comparing its ground-level camera view (what it sees now) to satellite maps helps pinpoint location. Cross-view matching is essential for autonomous systems navigating cities, and also helps with urban planning and location services.
498.wh: Ground photos look completely different from overhead satellite imagery—angles, lighting, scale, what you see.
