Most approaches either extract shallow visual patterns (which don't capture the real spatial layout) or try to reason about geometry (which is interpretable but misses visual details). You want both: spatial understanding and visual richness.
498.ap: The method adds an auxiliary task alongside the main matching problem. While the main task learns visual features (texture, color, what the place looks like), the auxiliary task learns spatial structure—the actual physical layout and geometry—using a foundation model and converting to bird's-eye view. Both tasks share encoders and feed into each other, fusing spatial reasoning with visual appearance.
498.ww: Spatial structure and visual appearance are two different views of the same place. When the model learns them together, each helps constrain the other. The spatial view says 'where things physically are,' and the visual view says 'what they look like.' Together, they form a richer, more complete image understanding than either alone.
498.po: On three standard benchmarks for cross-view matching, the dual-task approach beats prior methods significantly. The results are more interpretable—you can actually visualize the spatial alignment—and more accurate because visual and spatial signals reinforce each other.

499.bp: Memes spread rapidly during major events and shape how people talk about them online. Understanding what makes memes get seen and shared—especially around sensitive topics like the Roe v. Wade decision—matters for understanding online discourse and how information spreads.
499.wh: Most research looks at text or images in isolation. But memes are specifically designed as a combination: a picture plus text that work together. Predicting engagement requires understanding both, and also recognizing that some memes are visually novel (showing something people haven't seen before) while others repeat familiar images.
499.ap: The researchers collected over a million tweets mentioning Roe v. Wade and extracted 68,000+ memes using optical character recognition. They used a vision model to cluster memes by visual similarity, measuring how novel each image was. They separately analyzed the emotion (sentiment) in the accompanying text. Then they tested which attributes predicted engagement.
499.ww: Visual novelty matters because memes spread when people find them fresh or striking. Text emotion matters because outrage or humor drives engagement. But the two don't always combine the same way—some meme types get amplified by emotional text, others get suppressed. The interaction depends on what the meme is actually depicting.
499.po: Memes showing crowd protests got high engagement; those featuring individual politicians got low engagement. Visual novelty boosted engagement overall, and more importantly, it modulated how text emotion affected spread. The finding: you can't predict meme impact from one modality alone—you need to see how visual freshness and textual emotion interact.

500.bp: Doctors need accurate predictions of what disease a patient likely has, based on their health records. Large language models can read through years of medical notes and extract meaning, but they sometimes generate plausible-sounding diagnoses that are actually wrong—and in medicine, wrong is dangerous.
500.wh: Language models can sound very confident even when they're wrong (a problem called hallucination). Simply using uncertainty scores doesn't solve it, because a diagnosis might be confidently wrong or uncertainly right. You need a way to distinguish between 'I'm uncertain but probably correct' and 'I'm uncertain and likely wrong.'
500.ap: The method builds uncertainty scores from multiple diagnosis attempts, then uses those scores to spot high-uncertainty cases. For those flagged cases, it constructs multiple-choice questions drawn from medical knowledge and retrains a refinement module to correctly pick between the uncertain options. The module sees both the original case and the multiple-choice version, learning when to override or confirm.
500.ww: By treating uncertain predictions as explicit problems that need solving, the model learns to resolve them carefully. It's like a doctor saying, 'I'm not sure, so let me think through these other possibilities and make sure.' The external knowledge grounds the reasoning in real medical facts, not just model guesses.
500.po: On two real hospital datasets, this uncertainty-aware refinement beats existing methods. Predictions are not just accurate but also reliable—when the model says it's uncertain, it actually is. This matters because doctors can then ask follow-up questions instead of blindly trusting an uncertain prediction.

501.bp: When someone wants their personal data deleted from the internet (a 'right to be forgotten' request), companies must decide which data to remove. But testing whether deletion actually worked is hard if you only test random deletions. Real requests are specific: 'delete my photos and all comments mentioning me.'
501.wh: Almost all research on graph unlearning (removing nodes from a network) tests with random selections. But in practice, people write legal requests in natural language, each pointing to different parts of a graph. You need a way to translate human language into actual graph targets, then test if deletion actually worked on those real-world scenarios.
501.ap: The researchers built a dataset called Text2Forget: a corpus of legal-style deletion requests (like data-subject access requests under GDPR) paired with three graph datasets (citation networks, product graphs). They wrote a retrieval tool that reads each request and finds the exact nodes and edges it refers to. Then they test multiple deletion methods to see if forgotten nodes stay forgotten.
501.ww: Realistic requests are much harder than random deletions because they're specific and sparse. But they're also much more realistic. If your unlearning method only works on random deletions, you don't know if it'll work when someone actually asks to remove themselves. Testing on real text-grounded requests tells you what matters.
501.po: Text-grounded deletion requests behave similarly to random forgetting in terms of privacy-utility tradeoffs across multiple graph models (GCN, GAT, GIN) and deletion algorithms. This validates that the corpus represents real deletion scenarios. The open-source dataset and harness let researchers build deletion methods that work for actual user requests, not just random test cases.

502.bp: Scholars often ask questions across a network of authors, papers, and journals: 'Who cited this work?' or 'What did researchers at this institution publish in this year?' These require following connections through a web of relationships, and an AI system needs to answer by retrieving the right papers and reasoning through connections.
502.wh: Graphs of scholarships are heterogeneous—different types of nodes (authors, papers, venues) with different types of edges (writes, cites, publishes at). Some questions are simple lookups, others need multi-step reasoning. A retrieval system that uses the same strategy for all questions will retrieve irrelevant papers or miss necessary connections. It also doesn't know when it has enough evidence to answer.
502.ap: The method turns the retrieval process into three explicit decision-making steps. First, a query-aware agent reads the question and picks the right way to traverse the graph (simple lookup, multi-hop walk, etc.). Second, a sufficiency agent checks if the retrieved papers actually answer the question or if more context is needed, then expands the search. Third, a verification agent double-checks that entities and relations match the graph facts before finalizing the answer.
502.ww: Simple retrieval misses context; stopping too early leaves questions unanswered. By making each stage agentic—explicitly checking 'am I doing the right thing?'—the system adapts to question complexity. The verification step ensures the answer stays grounded in real graph data, not model hallucinations.
502.po: On scholarly graphs from OpenAlex and DBLP, this multi-stage agentic approach beats standard language models, graph-augmented retrieval, and simpler agent baselines. Questions get answered with correct multi-hop reasoning and explicit verification, making the system more reliable for academic QA.

503.bp: If you show an AI system an image and describe how to change it ('make it summer instead of winter,' 'add a dog'), it should find the modified image in a database. This is useful for creative workflows, fashion, and visual search where users think in terms of images plus edits.
503.wh: The challenge is that the combined description (image + modification text) easily over-fits to irrelevant details. If the text says 'add a dog' but the original image has blue skies, the model might lock onto 'blue skies' as important instead of 'dog-shaped.' It generates a description of the target that's biased, missing the actual change.
503.ap: The method uses a reasoning approach that first focuses the image understanding on relevant visual content—ignoring details the modification doesn't touch. It then builds a target description, but refines it in two steps. First, it anchors the description by fusing the original image features with the description, reinforcing what's important. Second, it explicitly models how much the original image contributed to the description and subtracts that out, reducing redundant details.
503.ww: By consciously removing the original image's influence from the description, the model focuses on the actual change. It's like saying: 'The target looks like: [description] minus [things that were already in the reference image].' This suppresses bias toward copying the original.
503.po: On three benchmarks for composed image retrieval, the method achieves top results. Importantly, it's training-free—it works without any fine-tuning. By debiasing the description, it retrieves the actual target image more reliably, even when the modification is subtle.

504.bp: Delivery companies need to predict when packages will arrive so customers can be home, and platforms can set expectations. Getting this right affects user trust and operational planning. But predicting delivery time is harder than it looks because a shipment passes through multiple hops (warehouses, trucks), and each is unpredictable.
504.wh: Treating delivery time as a single regression problem is hard because very fast deliveries and very slow deliveries are rare, so the model gets confused about the scale. Also, the total time is a sum of many independent hop durations, but the model doesn't naturally learn this hierarchical structure.
504.ap: The method reframes delivery prediction as an ordinal classification task—binning time into ordered categories instead of predicting exact hours. It also decomposes the problem into two views: predicting the total end-to-end time, and separately predicting the sum of future hop durations. Then it adds a self-supervised signal that enforces consistency: the sum of predicted next-hop times should match the predicted total end-to-end time.
504.ww: Ordinal classification respects temporal order and avoids extreme outliers. Decomposing into two views lets the model learn hierarchical structure naturally. The consistency signal between views acts as an internal check—if the model learns robust representations of individual hops, it automatically gets the total right.
504.po: On industrial delivery data, this learning framework (EDTF) plugs into existing models and boosts their accuracy while speeding up training. The ordinal classification and two-view consistency are general enough to work across different model architectures, making it practical for real deployment.

505.bp: Edge devices—phones, IoT sensors, robots—need to run AI models locally but have tiny memory and power budgets. Finding the right model architecture for a specific device is laborious handwork. Neural architecture search automates this, but current methods miss opportunities: a larger model might work great if you compress it, but the search never considers that combination.
505.wh: Traditional architecture search explores different architectures but ignores compression (quantization). A large model compressed to 8-bit might outperform a smaller model run at full precision, but if the search never tried compression, it'll miss this. Also, evaluating model performance takes too long on edge devices, slowing down search.
505.ap: EdgeGen integrates quantization directly into the search space. Instead of searching for architectures in a fixed precision, it searches over (architecture, quantization method) pairs. It uses a Monte Carlo tree search algorithm to efficiently explore the expanded space, and evaluates candidates with a constraint validator that quickly checks if a model fits memory limits without running full inference.
505.ww: By tying architecture search to quantization, the system finds larger models that compress well instead of prematurely discarding them. The constraint validator saves time by ruling out infeasible models early. The result is a more complete exploration: you find the best accuracy-for-size tradeoff, not just the smallest model.
505.po: EdgeGen finds models that achieve high accuracy on edge devices within memory constraints. Because it searches over quantization, it discovers opportunities that separate architecture-only search would miss. The plug-and-play framework lets developers generate optimized models for specific hardware without extensive trial and error.

506.bp: The web contains billions of documents combining text and images—news, blogs, social media. Understanding the main topics in these multimodal collections helps organize content, detect trends, and build recommendation systems. Traditional topic models work on text alone, missing what images contribute.
506.wh: Text-only topic models work okay, but images add visual semantics that text doesn't capture. Extending models to handle both is hard because images and text don't naturally align—a 'cat' topic might appear as both a word and a visual pattern. Also, previous multimodal models tend to collapse into trivial solutions where topics become indistinct.
506.ap: The method represents both text and images in a shared mathematical space (a hypersphere). It defines topics as mixtures of directional distributions in this shared space, borrowing from spherical statistics. Both modalities contribute their learned representations to the same topic, so text words and image features can be part of the same topic if they're similar in this space.
506.ww: By using directional distributions on a hypersphere (not flat vectors), the model respects the geometry of normalized features. This captures semantic similarity more naturally and avoids the posterior collapse problem (where topics become meaningless). Images and text can genuinely fuse because they're in the same geometric space.
506.po: On multimedia web datasets, this multimodal topic model outperforms text-only and previous multimodal baselines. Topics are more coherent—words and images that appear together actually have related meaning. The result: better topic discovery for real web data.

507.bp: Recommendation systems predict what users want, but knowing individual preferences isn't enough. Users are influenced by groups they're part of—friend circles, age cohorts, communities with shared interests. A better recommendation system bridges individual and group preferences.
507.wh: Most systems extract what users explicitly show (movies they watched, posts they liked) but miss implicit group signals. Someone might like action movies because their friends do, even if they'd never admit it. Also, connecting individual behavior to group patterns requires reasoning, not just averaging.
507.ap: The method uses a language model to reason in three coordinated steps. First, it examines user histories item-by-item and builds a semantic graph of which items relate to which others—creating an explicit map of individual interests. Second, it clusters similar users and reasons about shared group interests from their overlapping item preferences. Third, it iteratively refines both: group insights feed back to reshape individual predictions, and individual preferences anchor the group-level reasoning.
507.ww: By iterating between individual and group levels, each refines the other. When a model notices a user is similar to a cohort, it can borrow insights from that group to explain the user's behavior—and vice versa, using individual data to sharpen group patterns. This mutual refinement grounds the model in both explicit and implicit signals.
507.po: The framework generates recommendations that are more accurate and more personalized because they account for both why someone individually wants something and why similar users in their group want it. The iterative reasoning produces consistent, progressive improvements in understanding user interest across both levels.

508.bp: Ethereum is a public blockchain that relies on a peer-to-peer network of nodes to operate. If an attacker can isolate a node from honest peers and only show it false data, the node will become a puppet. Understanding how realistic this attack is matters for blockchain security.
508.wh: Eclipse attacks work on Bitcoin, but Ethereum is architecturally different. Ethereum's peer discovery is based partly on DNS lists (naming services). If an attacker can corrupt the DNS list and also monopolize the node's connection slots (the limited number of peer connections a node allows), they can isolate a target node. But doing this at scale requires identifying and manipulating the official DNS crawler—a new challenge in cryptocurrencies.
508.ap: The researchers implemented a full attack in three stages. First, they poisoned a node's peer discovery table by sending unsolicited messages. Second, they identified and manipulated Ethereum's DNS crawler to inject malicious nodes into the official peer list. Third, they hijacked idle connection slots to block legitimate peers. They tested on Ethereum's testnet and measured feasibility on the mainnet.
508.ww: Most nodes don't reserve enough idle connection slots for proper peer churn, leaving them vulnerable. The DNS list is a central target for poisoning. By attacking all three layers of peer selection together—local tables, DNS, and connection slots—the attacker can achieve near-complete isolation with relatively few IP addresses.
508.po: Over 80% of public Ethereum nodes are vulnerable to this attack. An attacker needs only 28 IP addresses over 100 days to poison the DNS list. The successful attack rate jumps from 45% to 95% when combining all three techniques. This demonstrates a concrete, practical threat to Ethereum's network security.

509.bp: Platforms like Facebook and Instagram offer paid ad-free tiers, supposedly protecting privacy by removing the advertising incentive to collect data. But companies might still collect data for other reasons—to personalize experience, improve services, or hedge bets. The question is concrete: does paying to remove ads actually reduce data collection?
509.wh: Privacy principles say that without ads, there's no legal justification to collect as much data. But platforms argue they need data to personalize experience, serve content, and maintain security even in ad-free tiers. This creates a gap: what users normatively expect (less data collection in ad-free) versus what might actually happen (continued collection under other justifications).
509.ap: The researchers analyzed data exports from Instagram, Facebook, and X to see what data each platform retains in ad-free subscriptions. They also surveyed 255 users asking (1) what they expect to happen (normatively), and (2) what they think actually happens (descriptively). They compared the gap between expectations and reality.
509.ww: Data exports reveal actual practices, not policies. Surveys reveal the disconnect between user hopes and their cynical expectations. This gap matters: if users think they're getting privacy but aren't, they're being deceived. If they expect continued collection and find it, they're not surprised, but the companies still lack real justification.
509.po: 69% of users expect reduced data collection in ad-free tiers, but the data exports show platforms still retain ad-related data in these tiers. 63% of users think companies will collect anyway, revealing low trust. The research demonstrates that ad-free doesn't mean data-free, and user expectations are unmet—a privacy and transparency problem.

510.bp: When networks like financial transactions or social graphs start exhibiting weird activity—fraudulent rings, unusual behavior—you want to catch it before it causes real harm. The challenge is that these networks have far more normal activity than anomalies, so any detection system needs to learn what 'normal' looks like from very few labeled examples.
510.wh: Most unsupervised learning methods randomly alter the network structure to teach patterns, but cutting edges or adding noise wipes away the very clues that tell you something is anomalous. At the same time, comparing a node to other random negatives teaches almost nothing, since most random pairs are obviously different. The real bottleneck is that you need both meaningful positive examples (things like the anomaly) and hard negatives (things close to the anomaly but normal).
510.ap: This work uses 'counterfactual' reasoning—imagining what the network would look like if you changed specific aspects—to build smarter training pairs. Instead of random edits, it identifies which nodes are structurally complex and worth studying, then carefully constructs synthetic variations that keep the anomalous character intact. For hard negatives, it generates believable normal versions. But doing this for every node is expensive, so the method picks a strategic subset to analyze deeply, cutting computational cost by roughly two-thirds.
510.ww: The insight is that anomalies live in the 'hard to explain' parts of the network—places where the structure and node properties don't play nicely together. By targeting these places and asking 'what if we changed this one property,' you teach the model what really makes something anomalous, rather than just teaching it to memorize outliers. The hard negatives then force it to distinguish real anomalies from normal variations.
510.po: On real-world financial graphs and other networks, this method catches anomalies as well or better than existing approaches, while using a third less computation. It's particularly strong when anomalies hide in complex structure-attribute interactions—the kind of subtle fraud or manipulation that simple statistical methods miss.

511.bp: Nearest-neighbor search powers everything from web search to question-answering systems that pull in outside knowledge: you ask a question, the system finds the thousand most similar documents or vectors, then uses those to answer you. The challenge is that both the data and what people ask for changes over time—old query patterns stop being relevant, new documents arrive, and the system can't afford to rebuild from scratch constantly.
511.wh: Current systems use static graphs that connect each point to its nearest neighbors, which works fine at the start but degrades over months. When you try to fix this by pruning edges and adjusting connections, you face three problems at once: the data distribution itself shifts (drift), different parts of the graph age differently (some clusters get many new neighbors, others don't), and testing whether a change helps requires running expensive queries on the whole graph.
511.ap: The method treats graph pruning as a decision problem solved by bandits—a framework from statistics for picking actions when you don't know the full outcome. It learns which pruning strategies work best for different regions of the graph by testing them on small batches, then adapting as patterns drift. It uses metadata (what kind of region is this) to customize decisions per region, and it batches feedback so you don't have to evaluate the whole graph every time.
511.ww: Bandits excel at learning under uncertainty when feedback is partial and costly. By separating out temporal drift detection (noticing when patterns shift) from spatial adaptation (finding region-specific tweaks), the method avoids throwing away all prior knowledge when conditions change. Batching feedback reduces the cost of each evaluation, so you can adapt frequently without exhausting compute budgets.
511.po: In real systems with thousands of documents and shifting query traffic, this keeps search accuracy and speed stable for months without expensive reindexing. The mathematical guarantee ensures that over time, you're provably not losing too much quality while adapting to drift.

512.bp: Predicting how many people will move through subway stations helps cities manage congestion, plan crowding relief, and route buses efficiently. The challenge is multimodal: you need video feeds (crowds, density), sensor data (gate entries), weather, and schedules—but each station owner keeps their data private, creating isolated silos across a city.
512.wh: Combining multimodal data is hard because the signals are in different 'languages'—video sees physical presence, transaction logs count paid entries, and some of these contradict each other. Existing models struggle to align these signals. Also, capturing patterns over hours and days requires models that can 'remember' far-back history, which traditional approaches do poorly. Finally, privacy regulations forbid centralizing station data, so you can't naively train one global model.
512.ap: This work builds a federated system where each station trains its own model while a central server coordinates without seeing raw data. Within each local model, a 'cross-modal alignment' module learns to translate between video and transaction signals—essentially teaching them to agree on ground truth. The prediction engine uses two parallel pathways: one that's very efficient at short-range memory (Mamba), another that sees all history at once (Transformer), both running side-by-side. A blockchain-based reputation layer tracks which stations are trustworthy and personalizes how much each contributes.
512.ww: Mamba and Transformers have opposite trade-offs: Mamba is fast but can't see everything at once, while Transformers see everything but are slow. Running them together and merging predictions lets you catch both local patterns and global trends. The cross-modal alignment works because both video and transactions are observing the same underlying phenomenon—you just need to learn the translation. Federated learning keeps data private while still building a coordinated model.
512.po: Predictions of subway crowding improve over centralized models, even with data staying at each station. The system scales to multiple cities (tested in Hangzhou and Shanghai) and adapts as usage patterns shift, without exposing sensitive commuting data.

513.bp: Knowledge graphs—enormous databases that encode facts like 'Einstein worked at Princeton'—power intelligent assistants and search engines. But real-world graphs are always growing: new entities appear, new relationships are discovered. The system needs to continuously absorb these updates and keep its internal representations (which encode 'who is Einstein' and 'what does worked-at mean') up-to-date and accurate.
513.wh: Learning embeddings (compact mathematical summaries of each entity and relation) is computationally expensive. When the graph grows, naively retraining on everything wastes resources; selectively updating some embeddings while leaving others frozen causes forgotten knowledge to resurface or new entities to have weak representations. The core issue is deciding which parts of the graph matter most—degree (how connected something is) is a crude signal that misses subtle structural importance.
513.ap: This method introduces two key ideas: first, it identifies which new entities matter most by looking not just at how many connections they have, but how topologically central or novel they are within the evolving structure. These entities get allocated more of the model's representational capacity. Second, rather than using a fixed training objective, it dynamically adjusts the 'target' based on what the model is trying to predict—if it's learning a one-to-many relationship (one boss, many employees), it sets a looser target than for one-to-one relationships.
513.ww: Topological importance correlates with real-world impact better than simple degree counts—think of a new regulatory agency (low degree but structurally pivotal) versus a minor contact. By adapting the training target to the type of relationship, you prevent the model from forcing mismatched constraints. If a relationship is inherently 'fuzzy' (many possible answers), making the model choose one 'correct' answer teaches it badly.
513.po: The system updates knowledge graphs faster than existing methods while maintaining or improving accuracy in downstream tasks like question-answering. It scales to large graphs that evolve continually, making it practical for real-world deployments where facts change daily.

514.bp: Asking a camera to identify and track objects—'find all cars, and follow this pedestrian across frames'—is foundational to autonomous systems, surveillance, robotics, and video analysis. The field has been accelerating with new deep learning models, but there's no single clear picture of where it's heading or what problems remain.
514.wh: Object detection (finding bounding boxes) and tracking (linking the same object across frames) were historically isolated problems with separate models and datasets. Newer models blur these boundaries, and language is entering the picture: 'find vehicles that are red and moving left.' Yet surveys fall out of date quickly, standards are fragmented (different benchmarks measure different things), and emerging combinations like 3D-with-language or diffusion-based tracking aren't well understood.
514.ap: This is a comprehensive review examining over a hundred papers across many variants: 2D detection, 3D with multiple camera views, fusion of visual and language information, and generative approaches using diffusion models. It catalogs which datasets and metrics dominate, how often each pairing of tasks appears, and what problems researchers keep hitting. It then surfaces patterns: models converging toward unified frameworks, generative models enabling temporal reasoning, and uncertainty quantification becoming more central.
514.ww: Broad surveys work by clustering similar approaches, analyzing what assumptions underlie each cluster, and identifying gaps or overlaps. By tracking which datasets and metrics are used over time, you see which problems matter to practitioners and which get overlooked. Cross-task patterns emerge naturally when you look across silos—the convergence of detection and tracking, for instance, becomes obvious when you see the same architectural principles solving both.
514.po: Researchers gain a map of the field: which combinations work well together (multimodal + diffusion), where data is scarce (open-world tracking), and which emerging capabilities (language-grounded tracking, 3D uncertainty) merit focus. Practitioners evaluating a detection system can benchmark against unified standards rather than fragmented metrics.

515.bp: Companies deploy machine learning models to handle countless decisions: approving loans, moderating content, recommending products, predicting failures. But data in the wild is messy—it has biases, noise, and gradual shifts (last year's buying patterns don't predict this year's). A bad model makes bad decisions at scale, causing real harm. Before deploying, you need to know: how stable is this model when conditions change?
515.wh: Model robustness is hard to measure. Standard accuracy (what percentage of predictions are correct) doesn't tell you about fairness (does the model treat everyone equally) or stability (does it work on new data). Testing by hand is expensive and incomplete. Causal reasoning—understanding why a model makes decisions—can quantify robustness, but it requires specialized technical knowledge that most practitioners don't have.
515.ap: This tool automates robustness assessment using causal methods. You upload your data or pick from supported domains (loan approval, sentiment, recommendations, forecasting), specify protected groups or fairness constraints, and the tool computes metrics measuring how predictions shift when you perturb the data or change sensitive attributes. It visualizes trade-offs: if you gain fairness, how much accuracy do you lose? You can test multiple candidate models side-by-side on a level playing field.
515.ww: Causal reasoning quantifies 'how much does this change affect outcomes' in a way that raw statistics don't. By asking 'if we changed this person's age, how would the decision flip,' you get a precise fairness metric. Trade-off visualizations work because they're grounded in real numbers—you're not asking people to judge fairness abstractly, you're showing them: this model is 94% accurate but 12% less accurate for protected group X.
515.po: Developers can confidently select models for deployment, knowing concrete numbers about robustness, fairness, and stability. The tool is model-agnostic (works with any trained model) and task-independent, so it applies to loan decisions, hiring systems, or video classification. Decision-makers get evidence-based guidance rather than hunches.

516.bp: Recommendation systems that suggest movies or products to users work best with lots of user history, but new users have none—they get generic suggestions that don't match their taste. The trick is to transfer knowledge from related domains: if you know what this person watched on Netflix, can you infer what they'll buy on Amazon? This cross-domain transfer solves the cold-start problem.
516.wh: Most cross-domain recommendation ignores a key signal: items are often similar across domains (thriller films and thriller novels), but existing methods only look at user-item interactions. When models teach the system to blur all domains together with Gaussian noise (like diffusion models do), they wash away personalized preferences—the new user ends up indistinguishable from everyone else. The challenge is transferring the essence of what a user likes while respecting that tastes differ between domains.
516.ap: Instead of adding noise (the diffusion model approach), this method uses a smooth-then-sharpen process. It starts by blurring user preferences and item similarities in a gentle, structured way using heat diffusion (a continuous mathematical process, not random noise), which preserves the item-item relationships across domains. Then it iteratively sharpens and recovers the preferences specific to the cold-start user. All of this is cast as solving a differential equation (ODEs), a principled mathematical framework.
516.ww: Heat diffusion is reversible and structure-preserving; adding Gaussian noise is not. By modeling the process mathematically (via differential equations), the system can reverse the smoothing precisely. Keeping item-item similarities intact means that if the user liked spy thrillers, the system learns that spy thrillers in the target domain should matter. The sharpening process recovers preferences iteratively, letting you see what's recovered at each step and adjust if needed.
516.po: Cold-start users get personalized recommendations informed by other domains, matching quality of recommendations for established users. The ODE-based approach outperforms diffusion-based methods because it preserves nuance and doesn't destroy personalization with irreversible noise.

517.bp: People expressing suicidal thoughts online leave traces in their social media posts and the reactions they get. Detecting and intervening early can save lives. The challenge is that most online signals are noise—people express dark thoughts but don't act. You need to learn which patterns in posts and comments actually predict risk versus those that are just venting.
517.wh: Most existing methods treat all comments as noise or a single aggregate signal: 'did others reply supportively or not.' But comments are heterogeneous—supportive feedback from close friends has different psychological weight than criticism from strangers, and its protective effect changes over time. Traditional temporal models learn 'this person's communication style,' but that overfits; a different person with a similar style may have different underlying risk. The real problem is untangling what about the trajectory matters from what's just individual habit.
517.ap: The method separates comments into two types: supportive (protective factors) and harmful (risk factors), and aligns them with clinical understanding of suicide risk. It then uses an adversarial learning technique—one model predicts next-month risk while another tries to guess whether a given time period belongs to this user or a different user—to force the system to learn general patterns rather than 'this person is always sad.' This disentanglement allows the model to transfer learning to new users.
517.ww: Supportive and harmful comments work through different psychological mechanisms; treating them the same loses signal. Adversarial disentanglement works because if a model is learning person-specific quirks (Alice is always sad on Tuesdays), the adversary can easily guess 'that's Alice.' But if it's learning genuine risk dynamics, the adversary can't tell users apart, forcing the model to generalize. This improves transfer to new users you've never seen.
517.po: The system predicts suicide risk better than methods using only posts or generic comment signals, particularly on new users where overfitting to individual style would be most damaging. It provides interpretable separation: here's how supportive feedback helped, here's how harmful comment clusters hurt.

518.bp: Models trained on sensitive data—medical records, financial histories, personal information—can be hacked or subpoenaed, exposing private details. Laws like GDPR and CCPA demand the right to be forgotten: if someone asks to delete their data from the system, the model should be retrained as if that person never existed. But retraining from scratch is impractically expensive at scale.
518.wh: Machine unlearning—erasing the influence of specific data without full retraining—is hard because neural networks compress data into dense parameter vectors; you can't simply 'undo' an influence. Naive approaches that try to downweight certain samples are unstable: the model becomes fragile, and other users' information can leak. You need both strong privacy guarantees and a model that still works well after forgetting.
518.ap: This method combines pruning and unlearning. First, it sparsifies the model by removing less-important connections, which also breaks the tight coupling between model parameters and training data—loosely speaking, the model becomes less dependent on memorizing specifics. Then, it uses gradient-based projection to actively remove dependencies on the data to be forgotten, while protecting remaining data. It applies different levels of pruning per network layer to prevent 'layer collapse' where some layers become useless.
518.ww: Sparsity and privacy are related: a dense network that's forced to remember many details is more vulnerable, while a sparse network relies on broad patterns. Gradient projection is targeted: instead of just downweighting a sample, you identify the exact directions in parameter space that encode its influence and push parameters away from those directions. Layer-wise pruning prevents any single layer from carrying all the unlearning load, which could break it.
518.po: After unlearning specific users' data, the model remains accurate, private (resists attacks trying to recover deleted data), and stable (future training doesn't erode earlier unlearning). Compared to full retraining, it's roughly 65% faster, making privacy compliance practical for large models.

519.bp: Recommendations improve when you combine data from multiple sources—music taste plus viewing history plus purchase behavior all inform what you might enjoy. But domains have gaps: you may be a voracious reader but sparse in ratings. The usual trick is to pool data across domains, but if movie taste and book taste are different, naive mixing hurts predictions.
519.wh: Models built to merge domains often use complex fusion architectures that learn separate representations per domain then combine them, requiring lots of compute and engineering. But the core problem isn't model capacity; it's that raw multi-domain data has 'domain gap'—the patterns differ subtly. You can't just concatenate or mix sequences from different domains; the model overfits to dataset-specific noise rather than learning generalizable patterns.
519.ap: Instead of redesigning models, this work regenerates the target-domain data to be richer and more coherent. It uses contrastive decoding (a technique that compares alternatives and picks the best) to adaptively weave in context from source domains into target-domain sequences. Basically, it asks: for this user's movie history, what would their book history plausibly be? Then it synthesizes more realistic, augmented sequences that standard models can learn from cleanly. The framework is data-centric, not model-centric.
519.ww: Data-centric approaches work when the real bottleneck is data quality, not model architecture. By synthesizing enriched sequences that respect domain-specific patterns (books have different temporal dynamics than movies), the model learns alignable structure. Standard simple models trained on good synthesized data often outperform fancy models on mixed data because they're not fighting noisy contradictions.
519.po: Recommendation accuracy improves, and the gains transfer to various backbone models—you're not locked into one specific architecture. By avoiding complex fusion modules, the framework is simpler to implement and faster to train. Code is released, enabling adoption.

520.bp: Deepfake videos—synthetic face swaps that look photo-realistic—can spread misinformation, defame people, and undermine trust in video as evidence. Detectors need to distinguish real from AI-generated faces reliably, even when the synthetic face is extremely convincing.
520.wh: Deepfakes made with modern tools are nearly pixel-perfect to the eye; simple checks like 'look for compression artifacts' fail. The synthesis process is imperfect though—tiny inconsistencies in muscle coordination (action units—the anatomical basis of facial expressions), temporal coherence, and holistic context leak out. The problem is that these signals are subtle, scattered across frames, and easy to confuse with normal video noise or poor lighting.
520.ap: This method combines two analysis pathways. One extracts action units—the fundamental muscle coordinates underlying expressions—and tracks how they coordinate over time. The other learns high-level semantic context using adaptive attention, essentially asking 'does this face and background cohere given the expressed emotion.' Both pathways feed into a unified model that learns to flag synthesis-induced inconsistencies invisible to either channel alone.
520.ww: Physiological signals (muscle movements) and semantic consistency (expression matches context) are orthogonal: you can have coherent expression without correct muscle coordination, or vice versa. By checking both, you catch more forgeries. Adaptive attention lets the model focus on regions or frames where inconsistencies are most likely, rather than treating all frames equally. The combination reveals what no single modality captures.
520.po: The detector achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on deepfake benchmarks and generalizes well to videos made with new tools or methods not seen during training. It's particularly effective on high-quality commercial deepfakes—the kind that matter most for misinformation.

521.bp: Graph neural networks—models that learn from networks of connected data—are powerful but overfit: they memorize training examples rather than learning generalizable patterns. Data augmentation (adding random variations to training data) is a proven way to reduce overfitting, but existing graph augmentation is coarse: you might randomly delete edges or mix node features, losing important structure.
521.wh: The bottleneck in GNNs is message passing: each node aggregates information from its neighbors repeatedly. Coarse augmentations (like deleting a random edge) disrupt entire neighborhoods, losing too much signal. Fine-grained augmentations, like tweaking individual features, miss the core computational unit: the message itself, the information flowing between neighbors. You need an augmentation that smooths noisy messages and sharpens distinctive ones without destroying the graph structure.
521.ap: This work augments at the message level. For each message flowing between neighbors, it applies a contextual perturbation based on the local neighborhood: if a message is unusual compared to its neighbors, the method sharpens it (amplifies it); if it's generic or noisy, it smooths it. This is done per edge, per layer, per forward pass—fine-grained and adaptive to local context.
521.ww: Messages are the true atomic units of GNN computation. By augmenting at this level, you hit the regularization sweet spot: disrupting enough to prevent memorization, but respecting enough structure to preserve learning signal. Context-aware perturbation (smoothing or sharpening based on neighborhood) is more principled than random deletion because it respects the intrinsic geometry of the graph.
521.po: GNNs trained with MessageShift overfit less and generalize better across diverse graph benchmarks and architectures. It's a general technique applicable to any GNN backbone, and consistently outperforms coarse augmentations.

522.bp: User behavior online is multifaceted: people examine products (looking without commitment), favorite them (expressing interest), and eventually purchase. Recommendations typically predict only one behavior—purchase. But optimizing for long-term satisfaction means predicting all of them: examining and favoring matter for retention and revenue, not just immediate sales.
522.wh: Multi-behavior recommendation means predicting several outcomes simultaneously for the same sequence of actions. The challenge is extracting shared knowledge (user taste is consistent across behaviors) while respecting unique patterns (examining behavior is different from purchasing behavior). Most models apply the same preference learning to all behaviors, which conflates distinct signals. You need both cross-behavior synergy and behavior-specific adaptation.
522.ap: The method learns preferences in three ways in parallel. One module learns cross-behavior patterns (if someone examines many spy thrillers, they'll favorite spy thrillers too). Another learns what information is relevant to each specific behavior (examining might depend more on novelty, purchase on price). A third uses a learned gating mechanism to combine these insights adaptively: for predicting purchase, emphasize certain cues; for predicting examine, emphasize others. A fourth module captures complex sequential patterns specific to each behavior.
522.ww: Multitask learning works by sharing low-level patterns while allowing high-level specialization. Cross-behavior learning captures correlations: if tastes align across behaviors, you get free signal. Behavior-specific modules let each behavior have its own 'interpretation' of what matters. The gating mechanism is crucial: rather than hard-coding which information belongs to which behavior, the model learns this flexibly, adapting based on actual data.
522.po: The system predicts all behaviors accurately, improving long-term user retention and satisfaction. By capturing synergies, it makes better use of sparse data than methods predicting only purchase.

523.bp: Dengue fever spreads through mosquitoes in cities like Singapore; controlling it requires knowing where outbreaks will hit next so resources can be deployed early. Public health agencies have case data (where infections are reported) but lack real-time data on mosquito populations or detailed movement patterns.
523.wh: Standard epidemic models treat cases as independent events, but dengue spreads geographically: infected areas create hotspots that influence neighboring regions. Mosquito movement is localized, but humans travel widely. Existing models miss the long-distance transmission pathways driven by human mobility. Without knowing the actual transmission network structure—who travels between regions—you can't make good predictions.
523.ap: This method infers the hidden transmission network directly from case patterns using gradient descent, the same optimization technique used to train neural networks. It models each region's hotspot status as influenced by case dynamics in other regions, with connection strengths learned from data. The inferred network must explain four weeks of historical hotspot patterns and remain stable when refit on slightly different weeks, ensuring robustness.
523.ww: Transmission networks are latent—you don't observe them directly. But if you posit a network structure and predict what should happen, then compare to actual observed hotspots, you can tune the network to match reality. Requiring the network to be stable across time windows (not radically different if fit on weeks 1-4 vs. weeks 2-5) prevents overfitting to flukes. The learned network ends up reflecting real commuting patterns, providing an interpretable explanation.
523.po: With just four weeks of case history, the model predicts hotspot status in the next week at 79% accuracy (F-score). The learned network aligns with known commuting flows, validating the approach. Even during COVID lockdowns when mobility was disrupted, the model adapted because it learns network structure from data, not fixed assumptions.

524.bp: Documents in regulated industries—insurance contracts, bank statements, medical records—contain sensitive domain-specific knowledge that changes constantly. Extracting structured information (name, address, dates, amounts) from scanned documents is essential for automation, but models trained on public data hallucinate: they generate plausible-sounding answers that aren't in the document.
524.wh: Large multimodal models (systems that read both text and images) can 'understand' anything but hallucinate answers not present in the source. Specialized discriminative models are more reliable but require expensive manual labeling per new domain. Regulated domains forbid sending documents to cloud APIs, so you need to work locally. The real bottleneck is generating enough training data to adapt models without human annotation.
524.ap: This framework auto-generates training data: an agent system processes raw document collections, generates plausible question-answer pairs using a multimodal large language model, verifies them against the source document to filter hallucinations, and distills the results into a lightweight retriever. During inference, the retriever extracts relevant evidence from documents, and the large model generates responses grounded in that evidence, iterating if needed.
524.ww: Synthetic data works when verification is possible. Here, verification is free: check whether the generated QA pair is actually supported by the document. This filters hallucinations at training time. The lightweight retriever is local and fast, so it runs on-device for privacy. The retrieval-grounded loop at inference time prevents hallucination because the model must justify answers with evidence from the retrieved document.
524.po: The system reduces hallucination and improves domain grounding compared to using large models alone, while maintaining privacy (documents never leave the organization). It enables rapid adaptation to new document types without manual annotation, reducing time-to-deployment from weeks to days. Code is released as a Python package for easy integration.

525.bp: When a bank flags a payment as suspicious or a system decides whether content violates policy, we need more than a yes-or-no answer—we need to know how confident the system is. Large language models are exceptionally good at explaining their reasoning, but they struggle to produce reliable probability scores that humans can actually trust, which limits their use in high-stakes decisions where miscalibration wastes resources or harms people.
525.wh: Language models face a fundamental trade-off: methods that coax out confidence numbers often throw away the reasoning chain entirely, while methods that preserve reasoning produce probabilities that don't match reality—a model claims 90% confidence but is wrong far more often than 10% of the time. For real-world data mixing tables and text, existing approaches either collapse under the diversity or require separate expert models for each task.
525.ap: The authors train a language model to produce two things in tandem: a clear explanation of how it reached its answer (the reasoning chain), and then actual probabilities written out as words—not numbers, but concepts like 'more likely than unlikely.' They use a curriculum approach, starting with soft probability signals from simpler tabular models (like XGBoost) as training rewards, gradually tightening the model's ability to match well-calibrated expert systems.
525.ww: By anchoring the language model to proven probability estimates from domain experts during training, you teach it to internalize what calibration actually looks like—when confidence should be 70% versus 40%. The text-based probability output stays interpretable (a human can read and reason about it), while the grounding in expert rewards prevents the model from learning meaningless confidence numbers that sound plausible but are statistically wrong.
525.po: A single fine-tuned model reaches human-expert accuracy on roughly half of 169 real business classification tasks without ever being trained on them, and works competitively on messy real-world data combining structured fields and free text—the kind of mixed data that usually requires custom solutions per domain.

526.bp: Training massive language models on clusters of specialized computers is extraordinarily expensive, and engineers need to make hundreds of decisions about how to wire them together, what model sizes to use, and how to coordinate computation across all the machines. Trying every combination by actually running them is prohibitively costly, so we need simulation that's both accurate enough to believe and fast enough to be useful.
526.wh: Real hardware clusters today are messy: different brands of GPUs run at different speeds, networks connect them in asymmetric ways, and different parallelization strategies (carving the model into pieces, carving the data, or a mix) create wildly different communication patterns. Existing simulators oversimplify this chaos, either running slowly because they model every detail or running fast but predicting wildly wrong performance.
526.ap: The authors build a simulator that breaks the training workload into realistic microbatches (small chunks processed in sequence) and models each GPU's speed based on its generation and type. For network communication, they model how data actually moves across multiple links and through switches—like traffic flowing through a city—rather than assuming a magical connection between all machines.
526.ww: By building per-GPU speed profiles from actual hardware specifications (roofline models) and reproducing how real network libraries like NCCL schedule and route messages, the simulator captures the real bottlenecks: sometimes compute stalls waiting for data to arrive, sometimes networks sit idle waiting for compute to finish. This interplay determines overall speed far better than modeling each piece in isolation.
526.po: The simulator predicts training time on mixed-GPU clusters with accuracy comparable to real runs while running orders of magnitude faster, allowing engineers to explore thousands of configuration choices and pick the cheapest or fastest deployment before committing real hardware and budget.

527.bp: Scams and misinformation campaigns increasingly use AI to flood social media with convincing fake evidence—deepfake videos, fake reviews, manipulated images. To design defenses, we need to understand not just individual fakes but how real criminals organize and scale these operations into industrial machinery.
527.wh: Most research focuses on detecting individual fakes or understanding their technical properties, missing the organizational pattern: real scammers don't make thousands of original pieces of content, they mass-produce slight variations on a handful of templates and bury the fraud under tons of decoy material. Fighting one piece at a time is futile against industrialized scale.
527.ap: The researchers collected real fraudulent campaigns from the wild and mapped their anatomy: a small core of distinct harmful messages (the actual scam, misinformation, or fake product), surrounded by massive volume of superficially different variants (colors changed, text reworded, metadata shuffled). The core payload stays algorithmically stable while the wrapper inflates the campaign's apparent size and novelty.
527.ww: Cloaking works because platforms and moderation systems count distinct messages—if you generate 10,000 pixel-shifted versions of one image, that looks like 10,000 independent pieces of content rather than 10,000 copies of one attack. By concentrating on structural similarity rather than surface differences, you can see that scale comes from automation and recycling, not from generating new hostile ideas.
527.po: Understanding this architecture suggests defenses should focus on campaign-level patterns—detecting reuse networks and anomalous volume around a small set of ideas—rather than labeling files one at a time, potentially catching scams orders of magnitude earlier in their escalation.

528.bp: Online hate speech detection systems today catch obvious slurs and threats, but they miss a dangerous category: arguments that sound reasonable on the surface but subtly guide people toward viewing a group as blameworthy or dangerous. Evaluating whether moderation works requires benchmarks that test this blind spot systematically.
528.wh: Existing hate speech benchmarks are dominated by explicit slurs and direct threats—the easy cases. But hostile rhetoric often hides inside careful framing, logical-sounding arguments, and appeals to shared values. No benchmark systematically measures whether systems actually catch this 'soft' hate where hostility is implied rather than stated outright.
528.ap: The researchers built a generative process that takes an explicitly hateful statement and rewrites it as a subtle argument that preserves the underlying blame or exclusion of a target group. They use linguistic theory (argumentum model of topics and relevance theory) to maintain logical coherence while removing surface markers of hostility—rephrasing 'group X is evil' as 'we should ask hard questions about group X's influence on society.'
528.ww: By anchoring the rewrite process to formal linguistic structures that preserve the underlying stance while changing the surface form, you can guarantee the hostile premise stays intact—the benchmark genuinely tests whether systems catch hostility itself versus just surface language. If a system fails on the soft version, it's not because the content changed meaning; it's because the system relies on shallow text patterns.
528.po: Evaluations across major moderation systems reveal consistent gaps: systems that catch 90% of overt hate plummet to 40–60% accuracy on the same hostility expressed through subtle reasoning, showing that moderation today is largely fighting surface toxicity rather than detecting genuine harm.

529.bp: Understanding emotion in conversations—whether someone is angry, sad, or thinking carefully—requires synthesizing information from tone of voice, words, and the relationship between speaker and listener. Language models excel at understanding words, but they miss the audio and conversation context, and standard fusion methods fail to align these mismatched data types properly.
529.wh: Audio, text, and conversation history live in different mathematical spaces: audio is continuous sound waves, text is sequences of words, history is who-said-what-when. Naive approaches simply concatenate them as sequences, causing misalignment—a word doesn't naturally line up with a sound segment in the same space—and the language model fails to weigh these sources coherently.
529.ap: The authors use a geometric framework (fiber bundle theory) to decompose features into a shared semantic space where all modalities can meet, plus individual offset spaces that preserve modality-specific details. Text guidance anchors the shared space, then audio and conversation features align to that shared meaning. Features are then converted into a format the language model understands—structured sequences that preserve the aligned multi-modal meaning.
529.ww: By explicitly modeling each modality's position relative to a shared meaning space, you avoid forcing audio and text to pretend they're the same kind of data. Instead, you translate each into its contribution to the shared emotional concept, then let the language model reason over this aligned representation. This preserves fine details while ensuring all modalities point to the same underlying sentiment.
529.po: The model outperforms previous approaches on four standard benchmarks for predicting emotions in conversations, showing that geometric alignment enables language models to reason effectively over mixed audio-text-context data without losing information or creating contradictions.

530.bp: Organizations increasingly train language models collaboratively without sharing raw data—hospitals share patterns about patient networks, retailers share purchase patterns—but when each organization has different prediction tasks, a single shared model doesn't work. The challenge is learning from diverse graph structures across collaborators in a way that generalizes across tasks.
530.wh: Graphs from different organizations encode fundamentally different relationships: one might model patient-disease-treatment, another might model customer-product-category. Standard federation (averaging updates) treats all structures the same, losing information about each graph's geometry. Language models help but don't naturally understand graph structure—they expect sequences or grids, not networks.
530.ap: The authors project each organization's graph into curved spaces (Riemannian manifolds) where the graph's geometry is preserved—densely connected clusters stay dense, sparse regions stay sparse. This converts the graph into input the language model understands while retaining relational structure. When sharing updates across organizations, they aggregate in a shared curved space rather than flat space, preserving geometric consistency.
530.ww: Graphs aren't naturally flat—some regions are tightly clustered while others are sparse, and this structure carries information about relationships. By working in curved spaces tuned to each graph's geometry, the model captures that structure during projection. When aggregating across different organization's updates, preserving these geometric properties ensures the shared model respects each organization's natural structure rather than averaging away important patterns.
530.po: The framework generalizes better to unseen tasks from new organizations and improves prediction accuracy across six benchmark datasets, showing that geometric understanding of graph structure enables more effective federated learning than approaches treating all structures identically.

531.bp: Recommending products in retail requires understanding what customers want, which depends on their past behavior (what they clicked, bought, viewed), what products look like (image, description), and how products relate to each other (that jacket pairs with these shoes). Language models are powerful at combining text and images, but ignore the rich network of customer and product interactions that contains the most predictive signal.
531.wh: Existing approaches either focus on behavior patterns while ignoring visual and textual richness, or focus on language and images while treating behavior as separate. The real challenge is aligning three completely different types of information—image features, text descriptions, and abstract user-item graphs—into a single unified space where the language model can reason over all three.
531.ap: The authors encode each modality (images, text, user behavior graphs) into learned vectors, then use attention mechanisms to align these vectors into a shared semantic space. User behavior becomes natural language describing what the customer does, product images and text are encoded, and a specialized prompt format tells the language model to reason over 'customer bought X, then viewed similar Y, so recommend Z.' All three modalities contribute to the same final vector that drives recommendations.
531.ww: Attention allows the model to learn which signals matter most for each prediction: for some customers, visual similarity drives choices; for others, behavioral patterns are paramount. By forcing all three modalities through attention alignment, the model discovers where each type of information is most predictive rather than treating them as equally important. This is more effective than averaging them or training separate models.
531.po: When deployed at Walmart, the system increased click-through rates by roughly 20% in electronics and 25% in sports categories by generating product recommendations that balance behavioral, visual, and textual signals—outperforming the previous state-of-art on benchmark datasets.

532.bp: E-commerce sites contain thousands of nearly identical products (same shirt in different colors or sizes), and when searching or understanding listings, showing all of them to a language model as a long list causes the model to get lost—it can't distinguish signal from noise. We need a way to efficiently summarize massive, repetitive product collections so language models can understand them.
532.wh: Language models process input by computing attention weights—asking 'which parts of the input matter for this prediction?'—but when there are thousands of nearly identical items, the attention becomes diffuse: every item seems equally important or unimportant. The model can't zoom in on the subtle differences between similar variants (like which color is in stock) because the repetition drowns out those signals.
532.ap: The authors create a single learned token that represents an entire set of similar items. Before passing to the language model, they cluster items into similar groups, encode each item independently, then use a small learned network (adapter) that finds patterns across the group—which variants matter, which are redundant. The adapter outputs one token per group that captures the group's essence while preserving distinctions.
532.ww: By learning to aggregate at the group level rather than forcing the language model to process each item individually, you reduce noise: the model doesn't waste computation deciding which red shirt variant is slightly different from another. The adapter learns what variation matters (stock, price, variant ID) and what doesn't (tiny image quality differences), creating a compact summary the model can reason over efficiently.
532.po: The system processes thousands of similar e-commerce items while maintaining stable predictions, outperforming approaches that either show the language model all items or randomly sample a few, and can scale to scenarios that would make naive concatenation infeasible.

533.bp: Understanding why things happen—what causes disease, market crashes, or social movements—requires identifying hidden factors (latent variables) that connect observed data but aren't directly measured. Real causal discovery is hampered by incomplete data and unrealistic assumptions, yet language models have deep semantic knowledge about how the world works. The question is whether we can combine them with statistical methods for genuine causal insight.
533.wh: Traditional causal discovery algorithms assume no hidden confounders (unmeasured variables affecting multiple observed ones), which is almost never true in practice. Even when that's relaxed, algorithms produce abstract causal graphs without explaining what the hidden variables actually represent—you know something latent explains the pattern, but not what it means. Data quality issues make this worse.
533.ap: The authors combine statistical causal discovery with collaborative reasoning by multiple language models. First, they run a standard causal algorithm on real data to find a graph that includes latent variables. Then they frame variable inference as a game: multiple language models propose candidate latent variables (e.g., 'inflammation in this disease dataset'), and the model finds the equilibrium interpretation where everyone's proposals are mutually consistent. Finally, language models search for evidence across databases to verify and trace which proposed latent variables are real.
533.ww: Using multiple language models in a game framework avoids any single model's hallucination or bias—the equilibrium requires consistency across independent reasoners. Grounding proposals in data-driven causal structure prevents wild speculation. And requiring evidence traces ensures inferred latent variables connect to observable reality rather than remaining abstract mathematical ghosts in the model.
533.po: On real hospital patient data and benchmark datasets, the system successfully identifies meaningful latent variables (confounders and causal mechanisms) and traces them to evidence, outperforming traditional discovery algorithms while producing human-interpretable causal explanations.

534.bp: Predicting future values in data streams—like web traffic or sensor readings—requires models that adapt as patterns change. But 'concept drift' isn't one problem; sometimes old patterns repeat after vanishing, and sometimes genuinely new patterns appear. A good forecasting system needs different strategies for these two very different scenarios.
534.wh: Existing methods treat all changes the same way, either retrain constantly on recent data (losing expertise in patterns that might return) or maintain historical models (risking confusion when truly new patterns emerge). They don't distinguish between 'we've seen this before, activate old knowledge' and 'something unprecedented is happening, switch to a safe fallback mode.'
534.ap: The authors train multiple specialized expert models, each tuned to one recurrent pattern in historical data. When drift is detected, the system checks: do current values look like any known historical pattern? If yes, activate the expert that specialized in that period. If the data looks anomalous (high uncertainty, no expert matches), switch to a general purpose expert trained on diverse periods that stays stable when confused.
534.ww: Recurring patterns contain rich structure—a summer surge in air conditioning demand, a Monday spike in website traffic—and maintaining separate experts for these preserves that structure better than a single adaptive model. For emergent drift, trying to update the model is dangerous (it memorizes noise), so having a conservative fallback ensures graceful degradation. This separation lets the system be aggressive with recurrence and conservative with novelty.
534.po: The system predicts future time series values more accurately than existing methods across multiple benchmark datasets, with especially strong performance when patterns shift between familiar and unfamiliar regimes.

535.bp: Generating synthetic time series data (for privacy, testing, or data augmentation) is harder than generating images or text because time series have hierarchical structure—daily patterns, weekly patterns, seasonal patterns—and separating trend (slowly changing average) from seasonality (recurring wiggles) is crucial. Existing generators either ignore this hierarchy or lose one of the components.
535.wh: Time series aren't homogeneous like images; a day's data contains 1,440 minutes of readings, each day is part of a week, each week is part of a year. Generating from finest to coarsest detail (bottom-up) loses the week's structure; top-down loses fine-grained detail. And separating trend from seasonal patterns automatically is hard—the two intertwine in real data.
535.ap: The authors use a coarse-to-fine generation strategy: first generate a weekly trend, then fill in daily patterns around it, then hourly details around those patterns. They use a dual-path VAE (variational auto-encoder) that explicitly disentangles trend and seasonality: one path learns clean trend, another learns clean seasonality, then they're decoded together. During fine-grained reconstruction, coarse seasonal patterns guide what fine-grained patterns should look like.
535.ww: By generating coarse-to-fine, you preserve hierarchical structure—daily patterns respect weekly boundaries, which respect annual boundaries. By explicitly separating trend and seasonality, you force the model to understand what's slowly changing versus what recurs. Using coarse seasonal patterns as prior guidance during fine reconstruction ensures multi-scale consistency—fine and coarse patterns fit together rather than conflicting.
535.po: The system generates high-quality time series on six benchmark datasets with fewer parameters than competing methods and excels at generating long sequences without degradation, while maintaining the natural hierarchical structure of real time series data.

536.bp: The web constantly changes—facts become outdated, events unfold over time, and yesterday's truth may be false today. When finding relevant documents or answering questions, timing matters: a result about a company's earnings is only relevant during earnings season, and an answer about a person's job is only correct in the time period they worked there. Standard information retrieval ignores when things are valid.
536.wh: Traditional retrieval ranks documents by relevance without considering time: you search for 'Apple CEO' and get documents from five different time periods, some contradicting each other based on leadership changes. Question answering systems ask 'is this answer correct?' without asking 'when was it correct?' This is a blind spot in how the web is organized and accessed.
536.ap: This tutorial synthesizes Temporal Information Retrieval and Temporal Question Answering—fields that track when information is valid. The tutorial covers methods from rule-based systems (encoding 'this fact is true 2015-2020') through modern neural approaches that embed temporal understanding, to current retrieval-augmented generation systems that use language models to reason over time-stamped knowledge.
536.ww: Time adds a third dimension to relevance: not just 'is this document about Apple's CEO?' but 'was this person CEO when the question was asked?' By modeling temporal validity, you dramatically reduce noise in retrieval and enable question answering over evolving facts. Language models help here because they can reason about temporal language ('formerly,' 'since 2020,' 'current') and reconcile conflicting information from different periods.
536.po: The tutorial provides a comprehensive roadmap for researchers and practitioners building information systems aware of temporal validity, from classical IR principles through modern language model integration, preparing participants to handle the real challenge of web search and QA: information that evolves over time.

537.bp: Blockchain networks like Bitcoin and Ethereum depend on miners—but malicious miners can suppress or reorder transactions to profit. A practical defense is to have independent observers monitoring what transactions should exist (based on their view of the network) and checking whether miners actually included them. This sounds simple but has subtle failure modes.
537.wh: The catch is that observers don't see identical transactions at identical times: the network takes milliseconds to propagate messages, so one observer sees transaction A, another sees A but not B yet. When they compare what they saw, they'll find differences not because of censorship but because of normal network delays. Distinguishing real attacks from timing noise is harder than expected.
537.ap: The authors analyze mempool auditing (checking transaction discrepancies across observers) in real Bitcoin and Ethereum networks. They measure: how often observers genuinely disagree about what they saw, how long it takes for disagreements to resolve, and whether miners can reliably distinguish between delayed-but-arriving transactions versus censored-and-never-arriving transactions.
537.ww: Network latency creates a fundamental tension: if you flag a mismatch as censorship immediately, you get 25%+ false accusations because transactions haven't propagated yet. If you wait for disagreements to resolve, you can't quickly detect attacks. The solution is understanding the timing—two transactions separated by 30+ seconds are reliable anchors for comparison, but fast transactions are too noisy.
537.po: The analysis shows mempool auditing can reliably detect some attacks (99.9% accuracy for delayed transactions if they're well-separated), but only covers a subset of real-world transactions, revealing limitations in current blockchain fairness schemes that rely on mempool monitoring.

538.bp: Question answering systems that reason across multiple documents often need to connect facts that aren't explicitly linked together—like understanding that a movie was filmed in a location associated with a historical event. Knowledge bases traditionally represent facts as simple pairs (A related to B), but richer facts have multiple components (movie filmed in location during year with budget X), requiring a more complex representation.
538.wh: Breaking rich facts into simple pairs causes fragmentation: 'Avatar filmed in New Zealand' becomes separate facts, losing the context that it was filmed in 2008, cost $300M, took inspiration from location X. Reasoning over fragmented facts requires more hops, increasing chances of retrieval errors. The system needs to navigate more scattered pieces of information.
538.ap: The authors use hypergraphs—generalized networks where a single edge can connect more than two nodes—to represent n-ary facts. A hyperedge might connect (Avatar, filming, New Zealand, 2008, $300M, inspiration-source). They then build retrieval that reasons directly over these rich facts: tracing how one n-ary fact connects to another through shared nodes, adaptively expanding the search based on the question.
