538.ww: By keeping rich facts intact rather than splitting them, you preserve context, reduce the reasoning path length (fewer hops needed to find answers), and make retrieval more direct: the system can recognize 'this rich fact is relevant' rather than chasing individual fragmented pieces. Adaptive expansion means the system explores only promising directions rather than exhaustively searching.
538.po: On seven closed-domain benchmarks and three open-domain question-answering tasks, the system achieves higher answer accuracy than systems using simple binary graphs, with improvements of roughly 3% in ranking metrics, showing that n-ary structure enables more effective reasoning.

539.bp: Social media constantly discusses breaking events—disasters, political developments, product launches—but with millions of posts using varied language and emerging from multiple sources, detecting what's actually a newsworthy event versus noise is difficult. Most detection methods need labeled examples, but in real time, you don't have them yet.
539.wh: Real-time social media text is short, informal, and repetitive, so traditional content-based event detection struggles. The graph of who-posted-to-whom-when contains crucial signal but unstable when sources and posting patterns change rapidly. Without labeled data (unsupervised learning), existing approaches either miss events or produce false alarms.
539.ap: The authors use language models to generate pseudo-labels for unlabeled social messages (guessing which event each message discusses), then construct a heterogeneous graph connecting users, messages, events, and timestamps based on linguistic patterns. To correct the language model's inevitable mistakes, they use meta-path reasoning (following specific patterns through the graph like 'message → user → other-message') to validate that pseudo-labeled messages are actually similar.
539.ww: Language models understand semantic meaning but can hallucinate, so grounding their predictions in graph structure (real user and message connections) acts as a sanity check: if a message is labeled 'earthquake' but has no connection to other earthquake-related messages through real user patterns, the label is likely wrong. The graph validates what the language model guesses, catching errors without needing manual labels.
539.po: The framework detects social events in real-time social media streams without labeled training data, improving event detection performance while reducing the impact of language model errors through graph-based validation.

540.bp: Online shopping and streaming sites show you things they think you'll like, but they struggle when someone is brand new to a platform or when they need to recommend products across completely different datasets. This paper asks: can we borrow the recipe that made large language models successful—feeding them enormous amounts of mixed-up data from many sources—and use it to make recommendations smarter and faster?
540.wh: The obvious move is to train a recommendation system on one dataset at a time, but this misses a huge opportunity: each dataset captures different signals (images, prices, descriptions, user behavior). Moreover, when someone is new to a platform, there's almost no history to go on. Traditional systems learn specialized patterns per dataset, but those patterns stay locked inside; when you switch to a new dataset or new user, the system has to start from scratch.
540.ap: RecCLIP reformulates the recommendation problem as a visual-language alignment task. Instead of treating a user's interest as abstract numbers, it converts what a person likes into visual pictures that a vision-language model can understand, then uses simple prompt-based ranking to say 'show me the top matches.' The key is combining many recommendation datasets at once during training so the model sees patterns across all of them simultaneously.
540.ww: When a neural system sees a diverse diet of examples—many datasets, many types of signals—it builds more flexible inner representations that generalize. A new user or a new dataset doesn't break the system because the model has already learned what 'similar' means across hundreds of thousands of examples. Scaling up data this way mirrors how language models work: more data and variety beats more complexity.
540.po: Experiments show the system improves significantly on the two hardest problems in recommendations: cold-start (new users with no history) and cross-domain transfer (predicting what a music fan will like when they switch to a furniture shopping site). The improvement follows a power-law relationship—feeding it twice as much data yields meaningful gains each time, just like language models do.

541.bp: When a geopolitical crisis erupts in the Middle East—a war, a blockade, a coup—predicting what happens next is literally a matter of lives and livelihoods. But current AI prediction systems treat forecasting as a single straight-line path from known facts to a single predicted outcome, which flattens the genuine complexity of international relations.
541.wh: The Middle East involves layers of history, competing interests among many nations, cultural and religious context, and cascades of unexpected events that ripple outward. A single AI model that outputs one timeline has no way to consider that multiple futures are genuinely possible or that different expert analysts—someone steeped in Iranian politics, someone in Gulf economics, someone tracking military capabilities—would naturally disagree and refine their thinking together.
541.ap: ThinkTank-ME runs multiple specialized large language models (one tuned on Iranian geopolitics, another on Gulf economics, etc.) in parallel, each making its own forecast. Then these 'experts' critique and challenge each other's reasoning, revising their predictions as they debate. The system also came with a new benchmark dataset specifically for Middle East event forecasting to measure whether this approach actually works.
541.ww: Disagreement and debate force each model to articulate *why* it believes what it believes. When one expert says 'the price of oil will drop,' another can ask 'because what happens to Saudi production?' This back-and-forth sharpens reasoning and reveals blind spots no single model would catch. Real expert panels work this way; collaborative models mimic that rigor.
541.po: The multi-expert debate approach outperforms single-model systems at predicting real Middle East events. By measuring against actual crises that occurred after August 2024, the researchers showed that the collaborative reasoning genuinely captures geopolitical nuance that monolithic predictions miss.

542.bp: Imagine a doctor needs answers from a 200-page medical guideline, or a lawyer must extract key precedents from case law. Systems that pull information from documents struggle because breaking a document into chunks destroys the context that makes information actually make sense. A diagnostic finding makes sense only in the context of the full case history; a legal clause depends on surrounding agreements.
542.wh: If you simply split documents into equal-sized pieces or cut at sentence boundaries, you lose the semantic backbone that held information together. A question like 'what is the standard treatment?' might end up split across three chunks, or entirely missing because the answer spans a concept nobody indexed. Domain documents are especially dense—every sentence interconnects with others, so naive chunking explodes the complexity.
542.ap: QChunker treats text chunking as a two-step process: first, identify the logical boundaries where meaning naturally breaks (text segmentation). Second, fill in gaps and add context to make each chunk self-contained (knowledge completion). A pipeline of four specialized components does this: one generates an outline of questions implicit in the document, another segments the text based on that structure, a third checks each chunk for logical integrity, and a fourth patches in missing connective information. The system learned this process on 45,000 hand-curated examples.
542.ww: Documents have a hidden logical structure that mirrors how we ask questions about them. If you build chunking around the questions people actually ask, the pieces naturally align with meaning. Adding back context and completing partial concepts ensures that each chunk stands alone without forcing the downstream reader to puzzle out missing pieces. This turns document fragmentation into document understanding.
542.po: When the system retrieves text to answer questions, it has to work with fewer, higher-quality chunks. This reduces the amount of information the language model must sift through, making answers faster and more accurate. The researchers validated their approach on question-answering tasks, showing that domain-specific chunking outperforms off-the-shelf methods.

543.bp: Edge devices—phones, IoT sensors, embedded systems in factories—need to learn and adapt over their lifetime, picking up new tasks without replacing the hardware. But these devices have tiny brains: a model with billions of parameters won't fit. Engineers shrink models by removing unnecessary parts (pruning), but this creates a Catch-22: a pruned model learns new skills slowly.
543.wh: When a neural network encounters a stream of new tasks—'learn to recognize cats, now learn dogs, now learn birds'—it often forgets how to adapt altogether, a problem called plasticity loss. Meanwhile, model pruning removes connections in the network to save space and power. These two problems collide: a tiny pruned model is doubly handicapped at learning anything new because it has few connections left to rewire.
543.ap: PaCP operates in two phases. Before deployment, it prunes the model but does so in a way that preserves the capacity to adapt, using a metric that measures how easily a model can learn new tasks. Later, when the device encounters a new task, the model temporarily adds back some connections to give itself more flexibility for learning. Once the new skill is learned, it prunes away the temporary connections again to return to the tiny form.
543.ww: Plasticity—the ability to learn—lives in the connections between neurons. Rather than destroying important learning-capacity connections upfront, the system cuts the ones that matter less for future adaptation, then recovers flexibility on demand. This is like keeping a toolbox compact but reserving certain tools so you can pop them back in when you need to fix something new.
543.po: Experiments show that PaCP models learn new tasks nearly as well as unpruned models, yet stay small enough to run on embedded hardware. Remarkably, they even beat some non-pruned baselines on continual learning benchmarks, suggesting that strategic pruning and adaptive expansion actually improve learning flexibility.

544.bp: When a company faces a PR crisis—a scandal, a product failure, a viral backlash—public opinion shifts rapidly and unpredictably. What people actually think is a mix of immediate emotional reactions ('that's outrageous!') layered onto deeper beliefs ('I don't trust this company anyway'). Understanding both layers is essential for damage control and authentic recovery.
544.wh: Existing prediction systems treat opinion as a single thread or snapshot, missing how emotions and underlying beliefs constantly push and pull on each other. In a crisis, someone's initial fury might soften if the company responds transparently, or harden if they feel dismissed. Models that ignore this interplay—that separate hot emotion from cool reasoning—can't track why opinion actually shifts.
544.ap: DualMind runs multiple language models to simulate different people discussing the crisis in real time. Each agent has both emotional and cognitive layers: the emotional layer captures immediate reactions ('this is terrible for customers'), while the cognitive layer maintains persistent views ('I always knew this company cut corners'). These two systems interact—emotions can change beliefs, and beliefs color how emotions are expressed—across a simulation that unfolds like actual social media conversation.
544.ww: Real human opinion isn't mechanical. A fact doesn't just update belief coldly; it hits our emotions first. A company's authentic apology might lower our anger, which then allows our underlying doubts to settle. By separating and connecting emotion and cognition, the simulation mimics the psychological depth of actual belief formation.
544.po: When tested against real crisis data from social media (15 actual crises post-August 2024), DualMind predicted public opinion trajectories far more accurately than single-layer systems. The model captured the back-and-forth of real crisis dynamics—spikes of outrage, gradual cooling, shifts in credibility—that simpler systems miss.

545.bp: Short-video platforms like TikTok and Reels engineer their algorithms to keep people watching—and some users watch for hours until exhaustion, often against their own intentions. Understanding exactly how these platforms can pull someone into unhealthy patterns, and how to break those patterns without destroying the platform, is a crucial question for public health.
545.wh: Most research on addiction relies on surveys ('Do you think you use TikTok too much?'), which capture self-awareness but are small-scale and biased toward people willing to admit problems. The platform itself has the real data—millisecond-by-millisecond records of clicks, watches, rewatches, and pauses—but that data stays private and goes unutilized for understanding addiction mechanics.
545.ap: AddictSim borrows from economics the theory of how addiction actually works: consumption increases short-term reward but also builds tolerance, so the person must consume more to get the same hit. The researchers analyzed real platform behavior data—millions of user sessions—and found it matches this economic model. Then they built a simulator that learns each person's unique addiction pattern and predicts how they'll respond to algorithmic changes (showing more diverse content, throttling recommendations, etc.).
545.ww: Economic addiction theory gives a concrete mechanism: the brain's reward system adapts to stimulus. What thrills you on day one bores you by day thirty, so you seek stronger stimulus. Short-video platforms exploit this because new videos are always available. By mapping real behavior onto this well-studied mechanism, the simulator can predict counterfactuals: what if we changed the algorithm?
545.po: Simulations show that inserting diversity-aware algorithms—deliberately mixing in unexpected content rather than endlessly serving what usually hooks each person—can break addictive patterns without killing engagement. The system provides a tool for platform designers to test interventions before deployment, potentially reducing harm without sacrificing business models.

546.bp: When hurricanes, earthquakes, or famines strike, humanitarian organizations need to know exactly where people are suffering to allocate aid. Geographic databases exist, but they often miss regions in the Global South or encode Western geography as default, leaving crisis-hit areas invisible and aid underdirected.
546.wh: Automated systems that extract location names from text have been trained mostly on Western data, so they recognize 'Boston' instantly but struggle with 'Hargeisa' (Somaliland). Also, many place names are ambiguous: 'Paris' could be Paris, France or Paris, Texas. Rule-based systems guess poorly. Larger language models could help, but if they inherit the same geographic biases, they'll just perpetuate invisibility.
546.ap: The paper combines two techniques: few-shot learning from a language model (showing it just a handful of examples of location extraction), and then a reasoning step where the model uses surrounding context to figure out which 'Paris' makes sense. For instance, if the text says 'Paris was damaged by heavy rains in the Midwest,' the system recognizes the Midwest as context and correctly identifies Paris, Texas, not Paris, France.
546.ww: Large language models encode world knowledge about place names and their contexts. By giving them just a few examples and letting them reason about context, they overcome both training bias and ambiguity. The reasoning step is crucial: the model doesn't just guess; it actually thinks about what other place-related information is present in the document.
546.po: Tests on humanitarian documents show that LLM-based extraction dramatically outperforms traditional systems on both accuracy and fairness. Underrepresented regions—areas in Africa, South Asia, Latin America—see much higher detection rates, meaning aid organizations can now identify crisis zones they previously missed. This directly improves where humanitarian resources flow.

547.bp: WebAssembly is a technology that lets developers write code once and run it anywhere—in a browser, on a server, on any device that speaks WebAssembly. But when the same code runs as native (traditional machine code) versus WebAssembly, it sometimes produces different results, silently breaking real applications.
547.wh: Converting code from native format to WebAssembly touches dozens of low-level details: how numbers are represented, how memory is organized, how system calls work. Each difference is tiny, but they accumulate. A floating-point calculation might round differently; memory alignment might shift. These discrepancies are hard to spot because the program still runs; it just gives wrong answers on some inputs.
547.ap: WasmDiff is an automated testing framework that runs the same code as both native and WebAssembly with thousands of test inputs, comparing the outputs line by line. Whenever the native version and WebAssembly version produce different results, it records that as a discrepancy. The researchers applied this to real-world projects and found thousands of mismatches.
547.ww: Hidden bugs only reveal themselves when you compare two versions side by side with enough test cases. Most developers test one version or the other, not both; this gap lets discrepancies hide. Fuzzing (throwing random inputs at code to find breaks) combined with differential comparison (is this native output the same as WebAssembly?) surfaces issues that would otherwise silently corrupt data.
547.po: The survey found over 14,000 discrepancies across 64,000 test samples from a comprehensive benchmark, and 3,000+ in real-world projects. This quantifies the true scale of the porting problem and arms developers with concrete knowledge: if you port code to WebAssembly, you need differential testing, not just unit tests.

548.bp: Knowledge graphs—giant databases that map relationships between concepts (Einstein → scientist → physics) —contain a wealth of structured information. But using these graphs to answer complex multi-hop questions ('Who did Einstein work with that also contributed to quantum mechanics?') remains hard because the graph is enormous and the reasoning chain is long.
548.wh: A naive search would explore every possible path through a massive graph, which explodes in scale. More sophisticated methods focus on short paths but miss context: a connection might be technically shortest but semantically irrelevant. Also, when the language model encounters uncertainty, traditional systems just return the best-effort answer; they don't ask for clarification or refine the search dynamically.
548.ap: S-Path-RAG uses three layers: (1) a path-finding stage that explores multiple candidate paths through the graph, weighting them by semantic relevance rather than pure distance; (2) a learned ranker that scores which paths are most likely to answer the question; and (3) an iterative refinement loop where the language model can signal doubt ('I'm not confident about this step'), which triggers the system to modify its search or explore new parts of the graph. The system also compresses the paths into a compact format the language model can reason over efficiently.
548.ww: Semantic weighting focuses search on meaningful connections, not just short jumps. A learned ranker learns what paths humans actually need rather than guessing. Crucially, the iterative dialogue lets the language model actively participate in searching: instead of the system doing all the work upfront, they collaborate, with the model diagnosing what information is missing and the graph searcher filling gaps.
548.po: On multi-hop benchmarks, S-Path-RAG answers questions more accurately and uses fewer tokens (saving computation and cost). It also produces interpretable traces—you can see which graph paths led to each answer—making the system more trustworthy for high-stakes queries like medical or legal research.

549.bp: As large language models make more decisions—writing contracts, diagnosing illnesses, recommending policy—we need them to regulate their own behavior: to refuse harmful requests, to admit uncertainty, to push back on orders that contradict their values. Can an AI system govern itself, or does it need external control?
549.wh: Self-governance requires moral agency—the ability to understand right from wrong at a deep level, not just pattern-match training examples. It requires accountability: someone must answer for the system's decisions, and an AI can't truly answer to society. It requires grounding values in something beyond training data. These aren't engineering problems alone; they're philosophical.
549.ap: The paper analyzes three technical mechanisms that enable partial self-regulation: internal feedback loops (the model can check its own reasoning), embedded constraints (built-in refusals for certain harms), and meta-learning (learning to learn new values). It then argues that while these create operational self-regulation, they fall short of true governance because they lack authentic moral agency and genuine accountability.
549.ww: Self-monitoring works only if the model understands why a decision is harmful, not just that it was tagged 'bad' in training. An embedded refusal can block obvious harms but fails on novel scenarios. Without the ability to be held responsible by human society—which requires something more than computational process—self-governance remains performance, not genuine commitment.
549.po: The paper concludes that LLM self-governance should complement, not replace, human oversight. Technical safeguards help, but rely on humans to set values, interpret edge cases, and bear ultimate responsibility. This reframes the question from 'can machines self-govern?' to 'how do we partner with machines in governance systems that humans still anchor?'

550.bp: People send stickers (small expressive images) to convey emotion and intent in chat. But sticker collections are vast and diverse, and what's the right sticker for 'I'm thinking about what you said' or 'let's move on from this argument' is highly personal. When users search for stickers, the system fails if the stickers don't match their emotional intent.
550.wh: Sticker retrieval is a mismatch problem: the query is words ('I'm confused'), the sticker is an image, and what connects them is nebulous human meaning. New stickers and new query styles constantly appear, so the system must handle searches and images it's never seen. If the retriever memorizes specific stickers and specific phrases, it catastrophically fails on anything novel.
550.ap: XAlign-SR aligns the abstract communicative intent between text queries and visual stickers by learning a shared meaning space where both can be compared. Rather than treating text and image separately, it extracts the underlying intent (confusion, agreement, uncertainty) from both and measures how well they match. To address unseen cases, it learns this intent alignment in a way that generalizes to novel queries and stickers.
550.ww: Intent is invariant under variation—different ways of saying 'I'm confused' all share the same core meaning, and different stickers expressing confusion should cluster together. By learning to recognize this abstract meaning rather than memorizing surface forms, the system becomes robust to the constantly shifting landscape of how people express themselves and design stickers.
550.po: Tests on novel queries and stickers show XAlign-SR substantially outperforms baseline systems, correctly matching emotional intent even for queries and stickers the system never encountered during training. Users get better sticker recommendations, and the platform can ship new sticker packs without retraining.

551.bp: Aligning large language models with human values—making them helpful, honest, harmless—has become crucial. But people disagree on values: some prioritize free expression, others safety; some care about environmental impact, others cost. Can a single model be aligned with multiple, sometimes conflicting values?
551.wh: Training a separate model for each value trade-off (high freedom but low safety, vice versa, etc.) is prohibitively expensive. Merging models trained on different values often fails: the values don't blend smoothly; instead, they sabotage each other, and the merged model becomes mediocre at everything. A single training approach that respects all values simultaneously remains elusive.
551.ap: VC-Soup filters preference data to keep only examples where different values agree ('everyone thinks lying is bad'), then trains models on these consistent examples. These filtered models naturally blend better because they're built on common ground. Finally, it linearly combines the models, a technique that works well when the underlying models share similar internal structure (which the filtering ensures).
551.ww: Value conflicts are sharpest in contradictory examples: 'tell a comforting lie' versus 'always be truthful.' By removing examples where values clash and training on consensus examples, each model learns a 'pure' version of its value without being sabotaged by contradictions. The resulting models have more aligned internal structure, so simple averaging combines them cleanly.
551.po: The system achieves better trade-offs across values than prior methods. A single merged model now handles multiple conflicting priorities more gracefully than prior approaches required, without the expense of training separate models. This is a step toward systems that can serve diverse human communities, each with their own value priorities.

552.bp: Financial markets, communication networks, and social networks all change over time: connections appear and disappear, strengths shift. Predicting what edges (connections) will form next in these dynamic graphs—who will message whom, what stock will correlate with what—helps traders anticipate patterns, networks prepare capacity, and marketers find influencers.
552.wh: Graphs have structure at multiple scales: fast, minute-by-minute fluctuations (someone replies to a message); slower trends (friendships strengthen over weeks). Capturing all of these in a single model is hard. Also, the graph is huge (millions of nodes), so methods that require exploring every path explode in computation.
552.ap: TFWaveFormer uses a technique from signal processing (wavelet decomposition, which breaks signals into components at different speeds) combined with Transformer architecture (a modern way to learn relationships). The system decomposes the dynamic graph into multiple frequency bands (fast and slow changes) in parallel, processes each with adapted operations, and then fuses them. This replaces traditional time-series methods with learnable decomposition.
552.ww: Financial and social systems genuinely operate at multiple timescales: algorithm-driven trades happen in milliseconds; human relationships evolve over days. By decomposing the dynamics explicitly at each scale before reasoning, the model avoids trying to compress disparate phenomena into a single 'average' view. Each band gets specialized computation suited to its dynamics.
552.po: On benchmark datasets, TFWaveFormer predicts future edges more accurately and faster than competing Transformer and hybrid methods. The improvement is large enough to matter in real applications: better prediction helps traders react faster and networks allocate resources more efficiently.

553.bp: Social platforms like X (Twitter) contain billions of different users with vastly different ways of engaging. Some scroll silently, some reply to everything, some post constantly. These groups likely inhabit different information environments and respond differently to platform changes. Understanding who does what is foundational to fair platform design.
553.wh: Most research relies on surveys ('How often do you post?'), which are small-scale, biased toward engaged users, and missing the detailed behavioral ground truth. The platform has precise logs—how long someone viewed a post, when they liked, when they scrolled past—but hasn't been analyzed to map these behavioral nuances systematically.
553.ap: The researchers obtained detailed activity logs from 209 US X users over four weeks and identified patterns using latent profile analysis, a statistical technique that discovers natural groupings in behavior data. They found three groups: lurkers (60% of users, mostly scroll and view), interactors (32%, actively like and reply), and creators (7%, posting regularly).
553.ww: Behavior reveals deeper differences than demographics. The three groups don't just act differently; they encounter different content and politics. Lurkers and interactors skew young and Democratic; creators skew older and Republican, seeing more extreme content. This suggests that activity patterns and algorithmic exposure form a feedback loop: who you are as a user shapes what you see.
553.po: These findings argue that platform moderation and interventions can't be one-size-fits-all. Shadow-banning a creator affects them differently than it affects a lurker. Throttling recommendations hits different groups unequally. The paper provides a behavioral segmentation that platforms can use to design fairer, more targeted policies that account for these structural differences.

554.bp: Online moderation—deciding what content stays and what gets removed—has traditionally been gatekept by platforms themselves. But Bluesky allows users to publish their own moderation decisions (who they block), making the invisible visible. At scale, this reveals whether community-driven moderation actually works or devolves into mob rule.
554.wh: Blocking is a private action on most platforms, so we never see patterns: which accounts get blocked most? Do blocks reduce their influence? Can coordinated blocking silence minorities, or does it mostly target genuine harms? Without data, people argue about community moderation in the abstract; with data, we can measure its real effects.
554.ap: The researchers mapped 34 million accounts and their blocking relationships, including curated blocklists (like 'block all accounts matching pattern X'). They measured which accounts get blocked most, what behaviors correlate with blocking, and whether blocking actually reduces the visibility or activity of blocked accounts.
554.ww: Transparency reveals the mechanics of collective action. When millions of users independently block the same accounts, that's signal—it suggests genuine consensus on harm. Conversely, if blocks have minimal impact on visibility, we learn that blocking is performative, not effective. Data-driven analysis cuts through rhetoric.
554.po: The study found that community blocking is massive (orders of magnitude higher than official removals) and affects 90%+ of Bluesky content. However, blocks don't actually reduce the popularity of blocked accounts—they mostly create siloed views rather than true removal. Different blocklists target different types of accounts, suggesting pluralistic rather than monolithic moderation. This grounds debate about decentralized moderation in empirical reality: it works differently than centralized control, with both strengths and limitations.

555.bp: When a lie spreads on Twitter, Facebook, or TikTok, it gets shared millions of times before anyone stops it. Understanding how many people will interact with false information—will they like, comment, or repost it—matters because platforms need to decide which warnings to show and where to spend moderation effort. The speed and shape of that engagement tells us whether a lie is about to explode.
555.wh: The obvious approach treats engagement numbers as just numbers over time: 'This post got 100 likes yesterday, 50 today, maybe 30 tomorrow.' But that misses the real game. Users aren't mindless; they're making deals with each other. When you share misinformation, you're trading your reputation or effort for social status, connection, or validation. Different platforms reward different behaviors, so the engagement pattern on TikTok looks nothing like Reddit. A pure time-series model has no idea what that psychology is.
555.ap: This work builds a neural system that watches 2.37 million posts across seven platforms and learns to decode the unwritten social contracts at play. Instead of treating engagement as a sequence of numbers, it models each action as a moment in an exchange: 'This user is now choosing to comment—that costs them time but buys them visibility.' The system learns how emotions (anger travels differently than sadness) and platform quirks (TikTok's algorithm versus Twitter's timeline) reshape what people do next. As time unfolds, the model tracks how the negotiation between user effort and social reward shifts.
555.ww: When you realize that engagement is not chaos but negotiation, you can predict it. A viral moment isn't random—it's that sweet spot where the social reward (everyone's cheering) outweighs the effort (sharing a false claim). By learning the principles of that trade-off from the data itself, the system stops relying on hand-coded rules and instead discovers what actually drives people on each platform.
555.po: On real posts, the system predicts engagement with 19.25% error on average—43.6% better than previous best methods. That means when a misinformation post appears, the platform can now estimate how far it will spread with much higher confidence, enabling faster intervention and smarter resource allocation where it matters most.

556.bp: Every day, millions of users click products on Alibaba, report fraud to PayPal, or browse Netflix. These happen in a stream—data arrives one user at a time, never stops, and tomorrow's patterns might not match today's. A good AI system has to learn from this endless flow and stay sharp even when the world shifts. Most systems work like students who study once and never adapt, but stream learning is about studying while the exam is happening.
556.wh: The problem is twofold and vicious. First, redundancy: most incoming data repeats what you already know, so you waste training cycles on useless examples. Second, catastrophic forgetting: if you update your system on only new data, you forget how to handle old cases—like learning a new language and forgetting your native tongue overnight. Picking which samples to study and which old knowledge to keep is hard when you don't have time to recompute scores for everything.
556.ap: Instead of recomputing everything from scratch, this work introduces fingerprints—compact summaries that capture 'what does this model currently know?' Think of a fingerprint as a tiny portrait of the model's brain state. When a new example arrives, you compare its fingerprint to the model's fingerprint and ask: 'How similar are we?' That score tells you two things at once: should I learn this new example (coreset selection), and should I forget some old example to make room (buffer update)? A small plugin powered by pre-trained vision transformers fine-tunes these fingerprints without heavy computation.
556.ww: Fingerprints work because they're a middle ground between lazy and costly. Rule-based systems can't adapt when patterns shift. Gradient-based systems require computing derivatives for every example, which is slow. Fingerprints are fast (just a dot product) but smart (they learn what patterns matter). Because they're learnable and lightweight, the system can stay responsive to change without grinding to a halt.
556.po: This framework lets streaming AI systems learn efficiently in real-time applications. When deployed on live recommendation or fraud-detection tasks, it picks the most useful examples to learn and preserves critical historical patterns, improving both accuracy and speed compared to naive approaches that either learn everything or forget everything.

557.bp: Graph anomaly detection is everywhere: a cybersecurity team needs to spot hackers hiding in network traffic, a bank needs to find fraudsters in a transaction network, Google needs to find spam in its web graph. Anomalies are rare and weird by definition, so you can't just build a detector on a clean dataset and deploy it to a messy real graph. It has to generalize to new graphs it has never seen before.
557.wh: Two approaches sound reasonable but both fail. First: learn one big model that transfers across graphs (domain transfer). The catch is that anomalies don't transfer—a botnet in one network looks different than a botnet in another. Second: build separate models for each domain that handle multiple tasks together (multi-task learning). But then you need a labeled example from the new domain first, and in real deployment, you don't have that. The two challenges—cross-domain transfer and detecting rare anomalies—seem to pull in opposite directions.
557.ap: This system builds a foundation model—a universal pretrained detector—but trains it in an unsupervised way (no labels needed). The trick is synthetic generation: the model learns normal behavior from clean data, then uses adversarial techniques to invent fake anomalies it has never seen before. This way, it gets exposure to diverse anomalies without anyone having to hand-label rare events. At test time on a new unseen graph, it freezes the backbone (keeps the core logic) and only fine-tunes the detection head, letting it adapt quickly to that specific domain.
557.ww: By learning to generate anomalies synthetically, the model avoids the rare-event problem: you don't have to wait for anomalies to naturally occur in your training set, and you don't have to label them manually. By training once on a single dataset but generating diverse fake anomalies, the model learns general principles of 'what makes something weird' that travel across domains. Freezing the backbone at test time keeps it from forgetting those principles when it adapts to new data.
557.po: The system can now detect anomalies at multiple levels (individual nodes, connections, subgraph clusters) on graphs it has never encountered before, without any labeled examples from those new domains. This cuts months off deployment: you no longer need to label anomalies in each new graph; the pretrained system can go to work immediately and adapt.

558.bp: Every second, ads compete in an auction. A shampoo company bids on ad slots on Google, an e-commerce seller bids on TikTok. The bidding happens in microseconds and the goal is simple: spend your budget wisely to reach your customers. Doing this well by hand is impossible at scale, so auto-bidding systems make those split-second decisions. A bad strategy wastes money; a good one reaches the right customer at the right price.
558.wh: Current auto-bidding systems learn from historical auction data using reinforcement learning or pattern matching. The problem: they're black boxes. When they bid \\\$50 for an ad, nobody—not even the system—can explain why, and sometimes the decisions look absurd because the training data was limited in what it had seen. You also have to manually code the rules for how auctions work. Large language models sound like they could help because they're good at reasoning and explaining, but they can hallucinate—making up facts or bids that make no sense in a real auction.
558.ap: This work puts an LLM in charge but in a clever, two-layer way. The first layer (LBM-Think) is a reasoning engine: the LLM reads the auction situation and thinks out loud about strategy. 'The user is high-value, the auction is competitive, I should bid up.' This stays in words and logic, grounded. The second layer (LBM-Act) takes that reasoning and converts it to precise numerical bids. To make these two layers understand each other, the system uses dual embeddings: one for words and one for numbers, fused together so reasoning and action are tight partners.
558.ww: Separating thinking from action breaks the hallucination problem. The thinking layer can reason, but it doesn't directly control the bid; the action layer translates reasoning into numbers and can validate that bids make sense for the auction. The dual embedding ensures the reasoning and action layers are pulling in the same direction, not working against each other. Because the reasoning is in plain language, the system is also transparent—you can see why it bid what it bid.
558.po: Auto-bidding systems now make decisions that are both competitive (winning auctions) and explainable (humans can see the reasoning). The system can also generalize to new auction types because its reasoning layer has learned general principles from language, not just memorized patterns in old data.

559.bp: Events happen in the world—a political scandal emerges, a celebrity dies, a stock crashes. These events cascade across platforms and modalities: text discusses them, images spread them, videos explain them. To forecast what will happen next—will a disaster escalate, will a trend die, will a stock recover—you need to understand how information moves and changes shape as it flows across text, images, and knowledge networks. No single modality tells the whole story.
559.wh: The obvious step: pile up text features, image features, and relationship graphs, then mash them together in one model. But the temporal aspect breaks this. A tweet's meaning shifts over time, and early tweets matter more for forecasting than late ones. Images have different time sensitivities than text. And relationships in a knowledge graph—'person A is related to person B'—have their own temporal structure. Existing methods glue text and images together in static ways and don't learn how each modality's temporal behavior shapes the final forecast.
559.ap: This system learns from four angles at once. First, it extracts time-sensitive information from three geometric spaces—Euclidean (straightforward distance), hyperbolic (tree-like relationships), and complex (cyclic patterns)—to capture deep, multi-level connections in knowledge graphs. Pretrained models supply time-aware linguistic and visual features. Second, instead of asking 'how much does each modality matter,' it asks 'how does each modality's importance shift over time?' It learns adaptive weights that realize different modalities lead the forecast at different moments: early text might matter more, then images become critical, then the graph relationships reassert themselves.
559.ww: By using multiple geometric spaces, the system can capture relationships at different levels of abstraction—hierarchies, cycles, simple distances—that happen naturally in real data. By learning time-varying modality weights, it stops forcing false equality: not all modalities are equally important at each moment. This combination lets the system ride the temporal currents of real-world events, where information flows and transforms across modalities in complex, time-dependent ways.
559.po: On real multimodal event data spanning text, images, and knowledge graphs, the system forecasts future events more accurately than methods that treat modalities equally or statically. This enables better predictions of how world events will unfold, from crisis escalation to market movements.

560.bp: Traffic flow is one of the clearest examples of patterns hidden in space and time. Congestion spreads from car to car, street to street, and the spread follows geography, not just sequence. A road network is not a line—it's a web where traffic on one street affects neighbors nearby. To predict delays before they happen and reroute traffic intelligently, a system must understand both the temporal rhythm (rush hour builds to a peak) and the spatial spreading (blockage propagates along connected roads).
560.wh: LLMs excel at sequential patterns—they read text left to right and predict what comes next. Traffic is different: the most important spatial neighbors aren't in sequence, they're geographically nearby. An LLM trained on traffic as a sequence will miss that non-sequential spatial structure entirely. It will learn temporal rhythms well but blind itself to how congestion actually spreads across the road network.
560.ap: This system starts with an LLM but patches it with two adaptations. First, it freezes part of the LLM (Partially Frozen Attention) to preserve the temporal reasoning the LLM learned during pretraining, then strategically unfreezes and retrains the attention mechanism to respond to new traffic data. Second, it embeds the road network's adjacency structure directly into the attention mask—a clever trick that forces attention to respect geography. When computing attention, spatially connected nodes can interact directly, regardless of where they fall in a sequence. A fine-tuning method called DoRA does this adaptation stably without destabilizing the model.
560.ww: By embedding geography into attention, the system gets spatial reasoning for free without completely rewriting the model. The frozen component preserves the temporal logic learned from diverse pretraining data. The unfrozen component learns traffic-specific spatial patterns. This hybrid approach avoids both extremes: a fully retrained model that forgets general temporal reasoning, and an untouched LLM that ignores spatial structure.
560.po: Traffic forecasting improves because the system now captures the full two-dimensional reality: how patterns roll forward in time and how congestion ripples across the connected road network. Real-world traffic data shows this beats methods that handle only temporal or only spatial patterns.

561.bp: A financial network shifts when markets close overnight. A social graph changes when new users join. A security graph evolves as attacks evolve. Real-world graphs are rarely static, and they're never pure. They're full of noise and variation—patterns that belong to the specific data distribution you're looking at, not universal truths. A detector trained on one bank's transaction graph will fail on another bank's graph because the patterns it learned were specific to the first bank, not general rules about fraud.
561.wh: Out-of-distribution detection is hard even in flat data. But graphs add complexity: not only does the overall distribution shift, but the structure itself might differ—one graph is densely connected, another is sparse. Two competing goals seem incompatible: generalize across domains (ignore domain-specific noise) while also detect anomalies (catch rare, weird cases that look different from the norm). Anomalies are inherently out-of-distribution by definition, so a system optimized to ignore distribution shift might miss them entirely.
561.ap: This work proposes a unified framework that tackles both goals with three components. First, a generator that models which subgraphs are normal in each data distribution—without needing labels—by learning conditional distributions. Second, a spectral contrastive learning module that learns what's invariant (stays true across domains) versus what's shifting (domain-specific noise). Third, an approach to integrate labeled and unlabeled data using principles of invariance so that learning from labeled examples in one domain helps with unlabeled data in another. The system learns to extract the stable patterns that matter and discard the shifting noise.
561.ww: By learning invariant subgraphs without labels, the system avoids the bottleneck of needing labeled anomalies in every domain—they're rare, and labeling them is expensive. By treating generalization and detection as two sides of the same coin (both need to spot what's truly invariant), the system avoids the false choice between the two. Spectral methods (analyzing the structure of the graph mathematically) naturally expose both the stable core and the shifting periphery.
561.po: The system detects anomalies at multiple levels (node, edge, subgraph) in new graphs without labeled training data from those graphs. By learning what's truly invariant across domains, it becomes more reliable when deployed to real but messy data where distributions drift constantly.

562.bp: Diffusion models—systems that generate images or text by reversing noise—have become powerful tools. But they can be misused: someone could fine-tune a model to generate harmful imagery or synthesize deepfakes. Once a diffusion model is released for public use or deployed locally, the creator loses control. The question is: how do you enforce safety rules on a model you no longer physically control?
562.wh: Traditional safety measures—filtering outputs, blocking certain keywords—happen at the end of generation and are easy to bypass by clever prompting. They also require retraining or reconfiguring the entire model each time a new safety concern emerges. If someone fine-tunes your model locally with their own data, your safety guardrails evaporate. There's no mechanism for a third-party regulator to enforce rules on a model running someone else's machine.
562.ap: This system proposes a tripartite setup: the model creator, the users (who might fine-tune locally), and a third-party regulator. The regulator embeds special regulatory signatures and regulatory layers into the model at release time. These layers act like embedded sensors and controllers. During both fine-tuning and sampling, the regulator monitors intermediate steps and injects regulatory signals that steer the model away from unsafe outputs. The regulatory layers are tightly coupled with the signatures so that the regulator can influence the sampling process with minimal overhead, even on a model running far away.
562.ww: By moving regulation to intermediate steps rather than the final output, the system stops workarounds: you can't just rephrase to bypass it. By coupling regulatory layers with the model at creation time and making them tight to the model's internal logic, the regulator's influence is baked in and harder to disable. The regulator doesn't need to retrain the model each time; different signature types trigger different regulatory behaviors.
562.po: Unsafe outputs can be prevented even on locally deployed or fine-tuned diffusion models without disabling the model or sacrificing its capabilities. A third-party regulator can enforce safety across a distributed ecosystem where the original creator no longer has direct access.

563.bp: Zero-knowledge proofs let you prove you know something—a password, a transaction's legitimacy, a secret—without revealing the secret itself. They're the backbone of privacy-preserving systems, secure voting, cryptocurrencies, and confidential computing. But there are many ways to build them, and each way trades speed for security, or proof size for verification time. Choosing the right one requires understanding real-world performance, not just theory.
563.wh: Textbooks describe zk-SNARKs and zk-STARKs abstractly. SNARKs are fast to generate and create tiny proofs, but they require a trusted setup (some entity has to generate secret parameters without leaking them) and aren't resilient to quantum computers. STARKs have no trusted setup and are quantum-safe, but they generate huge proofs and are slower to make. Which one is actually better in practice? The answer depends on execution details, hardware, and real deployment constraints—none of which are clear from theory alone.
563.ap: This work implements both systems from reference code and runs them head-to-head on real hardware (consumer ARM processors, not theoretical machines). It measures proof generation time, verification speed, proof size, and traces which parts of the code consume the most CPU cycles. These measurements reveal where each system spends its effort and why.
563.ww: Implementation reveals truth that theory hides. Theory says both are 'feasible,' but real hardware shows vast differences: SNARKs are 68 times faster at proof generation, produce 123 times smaller proofs, but verify slower and demand trusted setup. STARKs are slower to build but faster to verify and quantum-safe. The CPU profiling identifies which operations dominate, giving protocol designers concrete targets for optimization.
563.po: Developers can now choose proof systems with data in hand. If you need fast proof generation and small size and have a trusted-setup infrastructure, SNARKs win. If you need verification speed, quantum safety, and transparency, STARKs are the call. For privacy-critical applications like blockchain or anonymous voting, this guidance matters because the wrong choice leaks performance and blocks scalability.

564.bp: Mental healthcare has a massive access problem. There are fewer therapists than people who need therapy, and even where therapists exist, therapy is expensive and stigmatized. If an AI system could assist therapists—handling intake, suggesting treatment approaches, providing evidence-based responses—it could extend a therapist's reach and free them to focus on the hardest cases. The key is not replacing therapists but amplifying them.
564.wh: Large language models are fluent and confident, which is dangerous in clinical settings. They can sound authoritative while being confidently wrong, they can miss subtle psychological signals, and they lack the embodied experience of being human. Small models are often dismissed as too weak for complex reasoning, but they're faster, more trustworthy to domain experts, and easier to audit. The challenge is building a small model that exhibits genuine therapeutic competence, not just fluent mimicry.
564.ap: This system takes a small language model and equips it with three tools. First, domain-specific fine-tuning on clinical data teaches it therapeutic language and psychology. Second, retrieval augmentation—the system can look up relevant clinical knowledge, guidelines, and case evidence when answering—keeps it grounded in facts instead of confabulation. Third, agentic reasoning—it can break complex clinical questions into steps and combine different tools to answer them thoroughly. The system was then evaluated by actual clinicians using novel metrics (T-BARS rubric) that measure empathy and therapeutic consistency, plus traditional safety checks.
564.ww: Small models benefit from three boosts: fine-tuning grounds them in domain knowledge, retrieval keeps them factual and current, and agentic reasoning lets them handle complexity without being large. Because the model is small, clinicians can understand what it's doing and catch errors more easily. The combination lets the small model punch above its weight: it's fast to run, auditable, and trustworthy while still giving expert-like, empathetic responses.
564.po: Actual clinical experts deployed and tested this system and confirmed it generates accurate, safe, and empathetic responses. It can now support real therapists in real mental healthcare settings, extending their capacity without replacing them—exactly what the access crisis demands.

565.bp: Financial fraud hides in transaction networks. A person who looks normal on their own—regular deposits, modest withdrawals—becomes suspicious when you see their network: they're connected to known money launderers, their patterns mirror other fraudsters. Fraud detection is a network problem: you must spot when someone's behavior is normal individually but anomalous in context. Traditional detection looks at isolated transactions; graph methods see the full picture.
565.wh: Graph methods work well on clean, balanced data, but real financial networks are catastrophically imbalanced: 99.99% of transactions are legitimate, 0.01% are fraud. Rare cases dominate learning. Second, fraud is camouflage: criminals study legitimate patterns and mimic them so they blend in. A neural network might see a fraudulent transaction and think 'this looks exactly like a normal transaction' because the fraud is deliberately disguised. Simple graph models miss this problem.
565.ap: This system is inspired by how the hippocampus in a brain detects when something's wrong—it notices conflicts and inconsistencies, not just surface similarity. The model has two modules. First, a cross-view inconsistency perception module watches transactions from multiple angles: who's involved, how much money, what time, what device. It finds subtle contradictions—'this transaction looks normal in isolation but clashes with this person's typical patterns'—that signal camouflaged fraud. Second, a novelty-aware hypergraph learning module measures how much each transaction deviates from what its neighbors would expect. If you usually transfer money to friends but suddenly transfer to a stranger, that deviation is the alarm.
565.ww: By monitoring cross-view conflicts, the system catches fraud that mimics legitimate behavior locally but breaks patterns when you zoom out. By measuring deviation from neighborhood expectations rather than global statistics, it avoids the rare-event problem: it's looking for 'does this transaction fit with who you are,' not 'is this transaction common.' Neuroscience inspiration gives the method intuitive grounding.
565.po: Fraud detection becomes more sensitive to camouflaged cases while still catching long-tailed fraud. Financial institutions can deploy this to catch fraudsters who deliberately study and mimic legitimate patterns, improving their defense against sophisticated attacks.

566.bp: When you scroll through TikTok or Amazon, you're not the same person hour by hour or week by week. Your mood shifts, your needs change, you discover new interests. Recommendation systems that treat you as a fixed preference vector miss this: they see you want books one day and recipes the next, but they can't model that as evolving interest, only as noise or contradiction. Capturing interest as a living, dynamic process is the real challenge.
566.wh: Traditional systems assume interests change in discrete jumps or follow simple linear trends. Reality is messier: you might gradually drift toward a new interest, then suddenly spike, then plateau. You might oscillate between multiple interests. And your trajectory isn't independent of the content: content you see influences where you drift next. Modeling all of this while handling multimodal data (text, images, video) at scale is complex. Existing methods use rigid diffusion models that treat interest as random drift, or they use redundant neural architectures (twin networks) that waste computation.
566.ap: This system models user interest as a continuous-time stochastic process—think of it as a particle moving through a space of possible interests, pulled by attraction to meaningful content and pushed by randomness. Instead of random drift, it uses directed drift toward the content you care about. The motion happens in multiple dimensions simultaneously (time dimension and relational dimension: how you relate to each item). A hypergraph encoder captures user-item interactions at multiple scales simultaneously, and a unified solver computes trajectories in this multi-dimensional space. Instead of redundant twin networks, the system uses a generative-discriminative co-optimization: one part generates your likely trajectory, another part checks how good the recommendations are, and they help each other in the same parameter space.
566.ww: Directed drift captures the intuition that you don't wander randomly through interests—you're pulled toward content that resonates. Stochastic differential equations let the system model smooth evolution with realistic noise. By encoding interactions at multiple scales, the system sees both your immediate circle of interests and your broader category preferences. The co-optimization trick reduces waste: you get all the reasoning in a single pass instead of running two separate models.
566.po: Recommendations improve because the system now predicts not just what you'll like next, but how your taste will evolve. The system can also output interpretable interest trajectories—you can see how your preference drifted over time and why the system made its recommendations, building user understanding and trust.

567.bp: False news spreads with images and videos now, not just text. A photo is edited to change its meaning, a video is clipped to mislead, and text wraps around it to amplify the lie. Detecting which multimodal posts are false requires understanding how images and text work together to create false impressions. A text-only detector misses the visual lies; an image-only detector misses the misleading text.
567.wh: Multimodal fake news is hard because forgery can hide at different levels: local forgeries (specific pixels edited in the image), global anomalies (the whole image looks wrong or out of place), and cross-modal inconsistencies (the image and text clash or the image is being misused). Traditional fusion approaches treat text and image as separate feature streams and combine them late, missing how forgeries interact across modalities. They also don't leverage knowledge about what's real—facts, entities, relationships—that could ground the detection.
567.ap: This system (SVPF-Net) has two stages. First, it optimizes visual representation by extracting both local details (where pixels are edited) and global properties (whether the image feels consistent). A dual-fusion enhancement uses weighted fusion to build a structured visual representation that captures local forgeries and global anomalies together, then uses cross-attention—a mechanism that lets image parts communicate—to connect local details to global patterns. Second, it fuses text and image modality-by-modality using high-quality semantic features and a progressive fusion strategy where each modality is weighted by how trustworthy it is in context.
567.ww: By capturing local and global visual signals and letting them interact, the system stops missing forgeries that would be obvious in isolation. By fusing modalities progressively with adaptive weighting, it doesn't force false equality: sometimes the text is the lie, sometimes the image is, and the system learns which to trust. By using semantic knowledge, it grounds detection in what's actually true, not just statistical oddities.
567.po: Fake news detection improves significantly because the system now sees both how images are manipulated and how misleading text weaponizes images. On real multimodal datasets, accuracy rises as the system stops missing sophisticated cross-modal misinformation.

568.bp: In a massive recommendation system like Amazon, millions of candidate items arrive from retrieval (broad search) and must be narrowed down to a few hundred for ranking. This pre-ranking stage is where most candidates die. The challenge: the ranking quality (which items matter most) and the computational budget (how fast you can score candidates) pull in opposite directions. Spend money scoring everything and quality is perfect but speed suffers; skim only cheap candidates and speed wins but quality crashes.
568.wh: Most pre-ranking systems treat all candidates as equivalent—they apply the same model to everything. But that's wasteful: some candidates are obviously good (you'd recommend them anyway), some are obviously bad (clear no-gos), and some are genuinely hard to judge. Throwing the same compute at easy and hard cases is like giving every student the same difficulty exam: easy students waste time, hard students fail to show their real ability. Additionally, training on mixed data causes gradient conflicts: the hard cases create noisy gradients that contradict the easy cases, and together they pull the model in conflicting directions.
568.ap: This system (HAP) disentangles the candidates first: identify which ones are easy to judge (the system is confident about them) and which are hard (the system is uncertain). For easy candidates, apply a fast, lightweight model—it's enough because you're already confident. For hard candidates, engage a stronger model that can do finer discrimination. Additionally, during training, direct easy and hard samples through separate optimization paths so their gradients don't collide and cancel each other. Each path has a tailored loss function that asks the right question: for easy samples, 'are you confidently correct?' for hard samples, 'are you distinguishing subtle differences?'
568.ww: By adapting computational budget to difficulty, you stop wasting inference time on trivial decisions. By separating gradient paths, you let each sample type drive optimization in the direction that helps it most. The combination preserves accuracy on hard cases while accelerating easy cases, a win-win that's only possible when you stop treating all candidates as identical.
568.po: Pre-ranking becomes both more accurate and faster: the system correctly identifies more subtle high-value candidates without bogging down on obvious cases. At scale in billion-candidate systems, this means higher-quality recommendations per millisecond of compute.

569.bp: A new restaurant opens. It's not yet well-known, so few people order it. Recommending it to more people is good for the restaurant's growth but risky: if you send the wrong people to it, you hurt its reputation. A billion items launch every day on Alibaba; most never gain traction. The challenge is to boost exposure for cold items strategically—not randomly to everyone, but to users most likely to genuinely enjoy them so their engagement sparks organic growth.
569.wh: Click-through rate (CTR) optimization alone—pick users most likely to click—seems right, but it's myopic. A user might click an item because it's 'interesting' but never buy or recommend it to friends. Their click dies in isolation. Meanwhile, another user clicks more slowly but tells ten friends, each of whom tells ten more. Long-term growth requires predicting not just 'will they click' but 'will this person's engagement generate follow-on traffic?' This counterfactual question—'if we show them this item, will other people now see it organically?'—is hard to answer.
569.ap: AliBoostV2 splits the problem. First, a Growth Potential Prediction module uses counterfactual reasoning: it models 'if I show this user this item, how much additional natural traffic will that interaction generate?' Not through their own future clicks, but through the ripple effect: they share it, people see it, some try it, the algorithm picks it up and shows it to more people. Second, a Dynamic CTR-Growth Boosting strategy targets users where both signals align: users who are likely to click (immediate signal) and users whose engagement will trigger cascading organic visibility (growth signal). It also adapts across time: users' behavior varies by hour or day, so targeting also varies dynamically.
569.ww: Counterfactual reasoning lets the system predict the ripple effect: not just whether a user will click, but whether their click starts a cascade. By optimizing for both CTR and growth simultaneously, the system avoids the trap of chasing empty clicks—engagement that doesn't propagate. Dynamic adaptation means the system keeps working as user behavior shifts hourly or seasonally.
569.po: Cold-start items (new items with no history) grow much faster and more reliably. Over six months on live Alibaba and Taobao platforms, the system successfully cold-started over one billion new items by targeting growth-catalyzing users, not just clickers. Items reach viability faster and with healthier long-term engagement patterns.

570.bp: When companies run machine learning systems in the cloud to train models on private data, users face a hard choice: trust the company to handle their data safely, or don't participate at all. This paper tackles a real bind—how can a company prove to skeptics that it's actually protecting sensitive information, without revealing its proprietary methods?
570.wh: Traditional privacy techniques add statistical noise to data (a mathematically proven safeguard), but the problem is invisible: a user has no way to know if the system actually applied the noise, or if it was silently collecting raw data instead. You must either believe the company or assume the worst.
570.ap: This work stitches together two existing tools: privacy noise (proven mathematically to block inference attacks) and cryptographic proofs (mathematical certificates anyone can verify). The system generates a proof that cryptographically attests the company did deploy the privacy mechanism correctly, without exposing the company's secret algorithms—like showing a tamper-evident seal on a package without revealing the package's contents.
570.ww: The insight is that privacy and verifiability aren't enemies; they can reinforce each other. Cryptographic proofs are short, publicly checkable, and leave no room for lying. By tethering the proof to the actual privacy mechanism, you move from blind trust to mathematical certainty.
570.po: Users can now audit that privacy was applied in outsourced machine learning, even when the system lives in untrusted cloud environments. The result is a middle ground: businesses keep their code private, but users gain verifiable proof of privacy—solving the bind.

571.bp: City governments hold meetings to debate local issues—schools, budgets, zoning—and keep formal written records. Most citizens never read these documents, partly because they're dense, verbose, and scattered across city websites. Automatic summaries could democratize access to local governance.
571.wh: Summarizing government records is harder than it sounds. A single discussion might sprawl across ten pages of back-and-forth; the system must distill it to one clear summary without losing crucial nuance or omitting dissenting views. No one had built datasets for this, especially not in Portuguese.
571.ap: This paper created a new collection: 120 actual meeting documents from Portuguese municipalities with 2,880 hand-written summaries—one summary per topic discussed. They then tested modern neural systems (both smaller tuned models and large language models) to see which could reproduce those summaries most faithfully.
571.ww: By pairing real messy documents with human-crafted gold-standard summaries, the researchers give machine learning systems something to learn from. The comparison of different summarization approaches reveals which methods actually grasp municipal records versus which merely imitate surface patterns.
571.po: Portuguese municipalities now have a benchmark to build better summarization tools, making it cheaper and faster to create readable summaries of civic meetings. Citizens in a non-English-speaking region can finally access what their government decided without reading thirty pages.

572.bp: Generative AI can now create convincing fake videos of people saying things they never said. Security cameras, body-cam footage, and any video evidence could be forged, threatening police investigations, insurance claims, and courtroom testimony. We need a way to prove that recorded footage hasn't been tampered with.
572.wh: Full end-to-end provenance—tracking footage from the camera's sensor all the way through storage—requires tight control of every device in a chain. In practice, security cameras are old, diverse, and scattered; you can't retrofit cryptographic signing into every one. You need a simpler solution that still catches tampering after the fact.
572.ap: This system uses blockchain (a tamper-evident ledger) to timestamp and log video segments, and then stores the actual video on a decentralized network (IPFS). When someone claims a video is authentic, you can check the blockchain to see whether the video's fingerprint was logged at the claimed date and time.
572.ww: Blockchain acts as a notary—it doesn't guarantee the video is real, but it does create an immutable record of 'this video's fingerprint was registered on this date,' making it provably impossible to swap in a forged video retroactively. The decentralized storage ensures no single actor can erase the evidence.
572.po: Security systems can now register footage in real-time with a cost of about 57 cents per recording—expensive for casual use, but viable for high-value evidence like crime scenes. An investigator can prove that a video existed unchanged on a specific date, blocking the 'it was edited later' defense.

573.bp: When you buy online, your behavior tells a story: you browse an item, add it to your cart, maybe abandon it, then later purchase. Recommendation systems need to predict your next action, but they also need to explain why they made that recommendation—users don't trust opaque machine answers.
573.wh: User behavior chains have hidden confounders: maybe you looked at winter coats because friends were talking about skiing, not because you plan to buy. A naive system sees the browse-cart-buy pattern and learns it as a rule, but that rule could be wrong if you only bought because of a price drop unrelated to browsing. Explainability makes this worse: most methods that explain predictions require outside data (product metadata, user profiles), which isn't always available.
573.ap: This work models behavior as a chain of logical decisions, where each step (view → cart → buy) is governed by hidden rules that can be expressed in plain logic (AND, OR operations). It separates the true causal path from spurious patterns caused by confounders, then uses those causal paths to explain predictions in human-readable logic: 'System predicted buy because: user viewed the item AND user added to cart.'
573.ww: Human decisions follow rules we can articulate; the system mirrors this by backing up each prediction with explicit logical statements that can be checked. By removing the effect of confounders first, the logic it finds is more trustworthy than a pattern learned from raw data.
573.po: Recommendation systems can now output explanations that customers understand and can argue with, while the underlying causal reasoning means recommendations are more faithful to true preferences rather than spurious correlations. Businesses get both better accuracy and better explainability.

574.bp: Machine translation and text analysis work well for major languages like English and Mandarin, but for smaller languages—especially those with limited online text—these systems perform poorly. Yet billions of people speak low-resource languages and need these tools. How do you scale sophisticated AI analysis to languages with scarce training data?
574.wh: The field is split into two camps: one focuses on engineering (scaling compute and data pipelines) while the other focuses on model tweaks (injecting linguistic knowledge into the model itself). Each solves half the problem, but neither alone bridges the gap between what works for big languages and what works for long-tail languages.
574.ap: This paper fuses both camps by building a three-stage pipeline: first, enhance training by injecting linguistic structure (like grammar rules); second, use a feedback loop during learning to diagnose errors in specific cases and adjust the training plan; third, at inference time, use a smarter decoding algorithm that samples candidate outputs and picks the one least likely to confuse or mislead. All three stages reinforce each other.
574.ww: Linguistic structure gives the model a skeleton to build on (it learns faster and more robustly), error feedback tells the system where it's going wrong so it can focus effort, and smart decoding guards against hallucinations. Together they handle the messiness of low-resource data that would confound a simpler approach.
574.po: Translation and analysis of low-resource languages improved by over 2 points on a standard benchmark—a significant jump. Critically, the system now scales to web-size content in underserved languages, making real-world AI tools accessible to non-English speakers.

575.bp: Large language models now power web search: you ask a question, the system retrieves relevant documents, and the model writes an answer. But the model's attention mechanism (which decides which parts of the retrieved documents to focus on) becomes crushingly slow when there are thousands of pages of content, making real-time answers impossible.
575.wh: An ideal solution would predict in advance which parts of the documents the model will need and skip the rest. But predicting before you've actually run inference creates a chicken-and-egg problem: you need to know the answer to know what to skip, but you're running inference to find the answer.
575.ap: This paper exploits a trick already used in web search: speculative decoding (a lightweight model guesses the answer first, fast). While that lightweight model is running, this system also scans the document to predict which parts matter most, then fetches only those parts when the main model needs them. It's like the lightweight model serves double duty: generating candidate answers and mapping the document.
575.ww: Speculative decoding is already free in production, so piggybacking the scanning step onto it costs nothing. By predicting salient content dynamically based on what's actually in the documents, the system adapts to diverse web content (multilingual, multi-topic) in a way fixed pruning never could.
575.po: Web-scale search now processes long, diverse document collections faster, since the model only loads the parts it needs into memory. This makes real-time AI-powered search economically viable for companies running at massive scale.

576.bp: Planning a trip requires balancing flights, hotels, preferences, and budget while managing information overload. Web interfaces still treat all users the same, showing the same menus and pacing, even though some users are tired and struggling to think straight while others are focused and quick. A smarter interface would adapt to the user's mental state in real-time.
576.wh: Interfaces can't read minds, so they don't know when a user is overwhelmed or losing focus. Traditional solutions either slow everything down (helping tired users but frustrating sharp ones) or speed up (overwhelming fatigued users). You'd need to measure the user's attention and emotional state moment-to-moment, which no current system does.
576.ap: This system watches the user's face (detecting facial expressions) and eyes (tracking where they're looking and how stable they are) to infer mental state. A set of intelligent agents then coordinate their help: some handle complex reasoning, others explain, others pace feedback. The system adjusts reasoning depth and feedback timing based on detected emotional and attentional state.
576.ww: Facial and gaze signals are mirrors of cognition: if your eyes are darting and your face shows stress, you're overloaded; if you're calm and focused, you can handle complexity. By matching interface support to these signals, the system meets users where they are rather than forcing them to adapt.
