576.po: Users who got adaptive support made better decisions and used less mental effort than those with fixed interfaces. This represents a concrete 10% improvement in decision quality with no increase in cognitive cost—proof that real-time adaptation based on user state works.

577.bp: Doxing—publishing someone's private information online—was once sporadic vigilantism. In Chinese online spaces, it has evolved into an industrialized market where companies offer personal data as a product. This threatens millions of people's privacy and safety. Understanding how this market operates is the first step to stopping it.
577.wh: Underground data markets are hidden by design. Researchers can't simply ask participants where they operate or how they work. Studying the ecosystem requires finding where it's actually visible and analyzing patterns at scale—a data forensics challenge.
577.ap: The researchers analyzed millions of messages and links from a major Chinese messaging platform where doxing services advertise. They mapped out the supply chain (data sources → service providers → buyers), counted how many people used these services, tracked payment methods, and documented the six main service categories offered.
577.ww: Mass analysis reveals structure: by looking at patterns across thousands of transactions, the researchers could infer roles (who supplies data, who resells it, who buys it), organization (the three-tier chain), and sustainability mechanisms (advertising, payment systems). Individual messages hide what aggregate patterns expose.
577.po: The study documents a mature, hardened market worth millions annually, revealing exactly where regulation and law enforcement should focus. The data also shows which platforms inadvertently harbor these services, enabling targeted interventions.

578.bp: Companies deploy guardrails (safety filters) around language models to block harmful requests. Users shouldn't be able to jailbreak the model by asking questions in clever ways. But guardrails and the core model see language differently—what looks garbled to the filter might be clear to the model, creating a security gap.
578.wh: Guardrails typically scan input text character-by-character for suspicious patterns, and models process language semantically (grasping meaning regardless of typos). An adversary could exploit this mismatch: add garbage characters that fool the filter but leave meaning intact for the model.
578.ap: This paper demonstrates the gap by perturbing input text (adding misspellings, Unicode tricks) and then 'coaching' the model to recover the original intent via chain-of-thought prompting. This two-step attack—noise plus guidance—bypasses state-of-the-art guardrails while remaining interpretable to the model.
578.ww: The asymmetry exists because guardrails prioritize speed (simple text scanning) while models prioritize understanding (deep semantic processing). You can't just patch one without redesigning both, because the mismatch is architectural, not accidental.
578.po: The findings expose critical flaws in current defenses and identify a 'success interval' where perturbations evade detection yet preserve meaning—establishing that guardrails and models need to be co-designed, not bolted together.

579.bp: Designing new drugs requires finding molecules that bind tightly to disease-causing proteins. This is normally done by chemists testing thousands of candidates in the lab. Language models can generate candidate molecules digitally, but they often produce chemically impossible or synthesizable dead-ends. How do you make language models actually useful for drug design?
579.wh: Language models don't deeply understand 3D protein structure or chemical feasibility—they're trained on language, not molecules. If you just ask a model to generate a molecule, it often hallucinates something that looks right on paper but would fall apart in reality or be impossible to make.
579.ap: This work reframes the problem: treat the model's generation as a two-part process: (1) explore the space of possible molecules by searching through the model's learned representations, testing candidates against protein binding, and (2) decode only the parts the model knows well, letting simpler rules handle the risky parts. A Bayesian optimizer systematically searches for promising candidates during exploration.
579.ww: This mirrors how chemists actually work: they explore (trying different molecular families based on binding science) and then locally optimize (tweaking a promising lead compound). By explicitly separating exploration from familiar territory, the system avoids the model inventing nonsense in unfamiliar regions of molecular space.
579.po: Language models can now generate drug candidates with high binding affinity to target proteins, outperforming simpler baselines. The system makes models useful for early-stage drug discovery, where fast generation and screening matter more than perfection.

580.bp: Cities want to coordinate drone fleets for delivery to serve many locations efficiently. Each drone makes its own local decisions (where to fly, whom to serve), but collective behavior emerges from millions of individual choices. Can physics and statistical mechanics offer insight into how to coordinate them?
580.wh: Centralized control of thousands of drones would be computationally intractable. Decentralized coordination means drones make selfish local decisions, which can cascade into chaos (all drones racing to the same popular location, leaving others empty). You need a principled way to balance exploration and exploitation across the fleet.
580.ap: This paper borrows ideas from thermodynamics: each drone has an energy function that represents its preferences (travel cost, service fairness, avoiding other drones), and it makes probabilistic choices following a 'Gibbs policy'—a statistical principle from physics. Adjusting a temperature parameter T shifts the whole fleet between rigid coordination and exploration.
580.ww: Physics already solved analogous problems: systems of particles follow simple local rules and produce coherent large-scale behavior. By encoding drone objectives as energy functions and applying statistical mechanics, the system's emergent behavior becomes predictable and tunable.
580.po: The phase diagram reveals precisely how fleet behavior changes with parameters—highly coordinated at low T, chaotic at intermediate T, partially recovering at high T. This gives city planners a tool to dial in desired behavior without redesigning the control algorithm.

581.bp: Scientific papers make specific claims ('compound X binds to protein Y'). Fact-checking these claims against the scientific literature is vital for detecting fraud and misinformation, but is hard because technical claims require careful verification in domain-specific sources, and those sources may not be immediately available.
581.wh: A naive fact-checker might hallucinate false evidence or apply reasoning inconsistently. With thousands of claims to check and limited time (and cost), you can't look up every single one—you'd need to decide which claims need verification from external sources and which can be trusted based on provided context.
581.ap: This system breaks claims into atomic facts, aligns each to context snippets, and runs a calibrated checker to gauge confidence. If confidence is low (uncertain), it triggers a limited web search over authoritative sources. Critically, it avoids overriding provided context with web evidence when they disagree; instead, it abstains from a judgment.
581.ww: Atomic decomposition lets the system reason about parts rather than wholes, reducing hallucination risk. Calibration—knowing when you don't know—enables smart triage: web searches happen rarely, conserving cost and time, while still catching false claims.
581.po: Scientific fact-checking now exceeds baseline performance while using external evidence selectively. Researchers can detect unsupported claims in papers faster and more reliably, reducing the effort needed to vet scientific work.

582.bp: Cryptocurrencies live on blockchains and are traded on two kinds of markets: centralized exchanges (CEX, run by companies) and decentralized exchanges (DEX, run by smart contracts). Prices across the two sometimes diverge, creating free money for arbitrageurs who buy low on one and sell high on the other.
582.wh: Prices fluctuate randomly and chaotically; simple models miss the structure. You need to account for market microstructure (how prices evolve stochastically) and fit models to actual blockchain data to predict when and where arbitrage opportunities will emerge.
582.ap: This paper applies Hidden Markov Models—a statistical tool from finance—to cryptocurrency price movements. They extract transaction logs from the Ethereum blockchain, fit HMM parameters to observed price paths, and use the learned model to forecast when prices will diverge between CEX and DEX.
582.ww: Hidden Markov Models excel at capturing regime changes: prices might behave one way during high volatility and differently during calm markets. By learning these regimes from data, the system can anticipate regime transitions and predict where arbitrage opportunities emerge.
582.po: Arbitrage bots can now predict CEX-DEX price divergences more accurately, allowing faster trades and capturing more profit. The model also reveals DeFi market characteristics, helping researchers understand how prices evolve in decentralized finance.

583.bp: Hateful memes combine innocent-looking images and text in ways that convey bigotry—the harm emerges from the interaction, not from either part alone. Detecting these requires understanding both image and text and their interplay. Do modern thinking-capable language models succeed at this nuanced task?
583.wh: Most off-the-shelf vision-language models aren't trained on hateful memes, so they perform poorly. You could retrain them, but that requires high-quality step-by-step explanations (chain-of-thought rationales) that don't exist in large quantities.
583.ap: The researchers extended the dataset by generating weak explanations via distillation (having better models generate rough drafts), then fine-tuned a thinking model with a new reinforcement learning objective that rewards both correct classification and high-quality explanations. The objective balances classification and reasoning quality.
583.ww: Weak supervision lets you grow training data beyond manual annotations, and reinforcement learning lets you reward intermediate reasoning—the steps matter, not just the answer. By forcing the model to show its work and rewarding explanations, the system learns finer-grained reasoning than classification alone.
583.po: The model now detects hateful memes more accurately and generates clearer explanations for its decisions. This is a step toward trustworthy content moderation: humans can audit why the system flagged something, not just accept a yes-or-no verdict.

584.bp: Agentic AI—systems that autonomously plan and execute tasks—is a hot topic today. But the vision of autonomous agents living on the semantic web and coordinating via formally defined services predates large language models by decades. What can today's AI learn from those older ideas?
584.wh: Agentic AI research is proceeding without strong historical grounding. Researchers invent new abstractions for agent coordination, planning, and service composition, unaware that the Semantic Web and Web Services communities solved similar problems twenty years ago.
584.ap: This short talk draws parallels: Semantic Web concepts (ontologies that formally describe entities and services, reasoning over these descriptions, service composition) map cleanly onto agentic AI. The paper argues that classical approaches to service definition, discovery, and orchestration apply directly to modern agents.
584.ww: Older work had incomplete solutions but correct intuitions: the need for formal specifications, composability, and decentralized coordination are just as relevant for today's agents as they were for web services. Reusing these ideas saves reinvention and brings solutions to known hard problems.
584.po: The result is a conceptual bridge: researchers designing agentic AI can draw on decades of Web Services scholarship. This doesn't solve all new challenges (LLMs add unpredictability older systems didn't face), but it focuses research on genuinely new problems rather than rehashing solved ones.

585.bp: Imagine a supply chain or power grid where factories make things and pipes carry them between plants, all with limits on how much each location can hold or move. The goal is to earn money over time by deciding what to produce and where to send it, while never exceeding anyone's capacity. Real systems can be enormous—hundreds of thousands of decisions to make each day—so we need a way to reason about millions of possibilities fast.
585.wh: The hard part is that constraints (the capacity limits) are rigidly binary: either you obey them or you fail catastrophically. Traditional learning methods that tweak numbers gradually can easily violate them during training, especially when the system is huge. Existing solutions either struggle to promise feasibility (you might illegally exceed a capacity) or they grind to a halt on large problems because the math becomes intractable.
585.ww: This works because it splits the problem cleverly. The neural network handles the fuzzy reasoning (which strategy tends to earn more money), and the optimization handles the hard constraints (which actions stay within bounds). By showing the network what good expert actions look like, it learns faster than methods that fumble around guessing. And by forcing the final action through the mathematical layer, every decision is guaranteed safe.
585.po: On small systems, they get 60 times fewer training examples than prior methods. On huge systems with hundreds of thousands of decisions—where the old approaches fail entirely—their method converges quickly and beats non-learning baselines.

586.bp: When running cloud services or online stores, you need to predict what will happen to thousands of measurements—server load, CPU usage, network traffic—hours or days ahead. Getting this right lets you resize resources before demand spikes, avoid outages, and save money. The harder part is that these measurements interact: a traffic spike affects both server load and storage needs simultaneously.
586.wh: Each measurement (variable) depends on its own past history, but also on the past history of many other measurements. Existing methods either look at dependencies one direction at a time (slow and incomplete) or use attention mechanisms that slow down as you add more measurements, since they have to compare every measurement against every other one. For thousands of measurements, this becomes impossibly expensive.
586.ap: Instead of computing attention (which asks 'how related is this measurement to that one'), they use autocorrelation—a mathematical tool that finds repeating patterns in signals. They compute it across both time (looking back at past values) and across measurements (looking at how one measurement echoes in others). They then speed this up using spectral methods (Fourier-like math), reducing the cost from roughly proportional to (number of measurements squared) down to proportional to (number of measurements times log(number of measurements)).
586.ww: Autocorrelation captures something simpler and more fundamental than attention: rather than learning weights for every pair of things, it finds which time gaps and which variable pairs tend to repeat their patterns. This is faster to compute because patterns in signals follow mathematical shortcuts (spectral properties) that you can exploit. Spectral math lets you fold millions of comparisons into a faster form without losing the signals you care about.
586.po: The method is orders of magnitude faster than attention-based methods while keeping or improving accuracy. It works on real cloud data (Beijing air quality, power generation time series) where thousands of measurements need to be predicted many hours ahead.

587.bp: When you ask a system a complex question—something that requires looking up multiple facts and combining them—you want both breadth (finding relevant information across the whole knowledge base) and speed (not searching every possible fact). A graph-based system organizes knowledge as a map of concepts and their relationships, where you can zoom in on neighborhoods or zoom out to see communities of related ideas.
587.wh: Existing systems face a hard tradeoff: searching the entire graph finds everything but is slow; searching just locally is fast but misses relevant information from other parts of the graph. When the graph is huge and has multiple layers (some concepts matter at the 'all entities' level, others at the 'this neighborhood' level), steering between these layers to find the right facts without wasting time is a genuine puzzle. Also, when you use a language model to score which facts matter, each scoring call costs money and time.
587.ap: They design a funnel that narrows down the search space in stages. First, filter out clearly irrelevant communities (neighborhoods) using context. Second, rank which entities within those communities matter most by analyzing how they interact. Third, do detailed fine-grained search only in the communities that survived the ranking. At each stage, a scoring module re-ranks candidates to stay focused on the most useful facts. They train this scoring part using a reinforcement learning method that adjusts how much to value each objective (relevance, diversity, efficiency) as it learns.
587.ww: This works because it respects how humans actually search: start broad and rough, then zoom in on promising areas, then get detailed. Each stage removes noise, so later stages have less chaff to sort through. By adjusting reward weights during training, the system learns to balance competing goals—you don't need to hand-tune these tradeoffs.
587.po: The framework retrieves comprehensive, relevant facts while being faster than methods that search globally or stop too early at the local level. It handles massive hierarchical graphs by narrowing the search smartly at each stage.

588.bp: When you describe a person in text ('a woman wearing a red jacket, standing by a fountain') and want to find their photo in a database of millions of images, the challenge is that your words describe what matters to you, but the camera recorded pixels. You need to make the word description and the pixel image 'speak the same language' so similar ones find each other.
588.wh: Text spotlights certain details ('red jacket') but ignores others the camera sees ('shadows, reflections'). A photo has redundant visual noise that clutters the signal—the actual jacket is just a small region, surrounded by background. Also, describing one person's photo in text never captures everything; someone else with a 'red jacket' might look similar on the surface but be a completely different person. Existing methods use coarse features and simple matching, so they confuse similar-looking people and ignore the fine details that actually distinguish them.
588.ap: They build two fixes: First, given the text description, intelligently pick only the visually relevant image patches (regions)—if the text says 'red jacket,' focus the model on red areas and downweight the sky and grass. Second, frame the matching between text words and image regions as a transportation problem (moving stuff between sources and destinations as cheaply as possible). This lets them find word-by-word correspondences: which part of the image does each word point to? This gives fine-grained, granular matching instead of mushy whole-image comparisons.
588.ww: The first fix reduces noise—by pruning the visual clutter, the model sees the person more clearly. The second fix captures semantic precision—word-by-word matching means 'red' has to point to actual red pixels, not just 'somewhere in the image where someone is wearing red.' Together, they make the alignment sharper and more discriminative.
588.po: The method beats existing approaches at finding the right person from text, especially when people look similar. It works by explicitly removing visual noise and by linking each text word to specific image regions rather than fuzzy whole-image similarity.

589.bp: When banks, credit card companies, or online platforms want to spot fraud—fake accounts, stolen cards, money laundering—they track who does what: who sends money, to whom, when, and how often. If you map these as a graph (people are nodes, transactions are edges), fraud often forms recognizable patterns, like rings of accounts that suddenly move money in circles.
589.wh: The tricky part is that the graph has mixed signals: some pairs of connected accounts naturally look alike (your friend sends you money regularly, you both send money to the same stores), but fraudsters deliberately create false likenesses to hide. Also, fraud tends to form tight, densely connected clusters—but legitimate accounts can cluster too (office workers all pay the same vendor). Existing methods assume the graph has one overall pattern (connected people tend to be alike) which breaks down when fraud deliberately breaks that pattern.
589.ap: They use two different lenses simultaneously. From one lens (neighborhood), they look for account pairs that behave inconsistently—fraudsters often try to steal features from honest accounts, so their feature values 'jump around' more. From the other lens (community), they look for unusual structural tightness—they detect which groups of accounts are densely bonded and whether that density is suspicious. By combining both views, they spot accounts that are odd in either way: locally inconsistent or globally dense in an unnatural way.
589.ww: Real fraud has two signatures: feature-level (the stolen identity leaks inconsistency) and structural (fraud rings are intentionally tight). By measuring both independently and fusing them, the system catches fraudsters who might fool a method looking at only one signal. Each lens is simpler than trying to learn a universal 'fraud pattern,' so the model trains faster and generalizes better.
589.po: Across five real-world fraud datasets, the method identifies fraudsters with better accuracy than systems that ignore either the local inconsistency or the structural weirdness. It works without assuming all connected accounts are similar.

590.bp: Many real-world measurements—medical sensors, weather stations, power grids—have gaps: a sensor breaks, data transmission fails, or a human forgets to log something. You need to fill in those blanks before you can analyze the data. The question is how to guess the missing values well enough that downstream analytics still work.
590.wh: Time-series methods designed to fill gaps often require retraining from scratch, take forever to run on long sequences, or break the temporal order (they might guess a value that doesn't flow naturally from what came before). But filling gaps is structurally similar to image inpainting—given a picture with a patch removed, guess what should be there based on surroundings. Image inpainting is mature and fast because images are rectangular and vision models are well-trained.
590.ap: Instead of building a special time-series imputation model, they convert the sequence into an image (using Gramian Angular Field, which spirals time values into a 2D heatmap), apply a pretrained image inpainting model (which was trained on billions of real images), and convert the patched image back to a sequence. The missing values become missing pixels; the inpainting model fills them based on what surrounding pixels suggest; the sequence is reconstructed. They fine-tune slightly for this specific task, but most of the hard work is done by the vision model.
590.ww: Pretrained vision models have learned rich representations from billions of images, so they understand texture, smoothness, and spatial coherence better than models trained from scratch on small time-series datasets. By reframing the problem as image inpainting, they inherit that knowledge for free. The Gramian spiral representation preserves temporal structure (nearby times become nearby pixels), so the inpainting respects the sequence's naturalness.
590.po: On standard benchmarks (air quality and power data), the method beats specialized imputation methods, especially when large stretches of data are missing. It's also fast and requires less computational overhead than training new models per dataset.

591.bp: Building machine learning pipelines—picking which algorithms to use, how to prepare data, which parameters to tune—requires expertise. A newcomer to ML can waste weeks trying random things. Ideally, you'd describe your task in plain English ('predict patient hospital stays from medical records'), and a system would automatically assemble the right workflow.
591.wh: Existing systems try to generate Python code that solves the task, but code generation is fragile—models hallucinate function names, forget imports, or pick the wrong algorithm for the problem type. Also, most ML platforms have graphical workflows (not code), so translating from generated code to visual workflows introduces another layer of error. The real bottleneck is not 'generate perfect code' but 'understand what the user wants and pick the right tools.'
591.ap: Rather than code generation, they use a language model as a task planner. The user describes their task in English. The model breaks it into subtasks ('load data,' 'clean missing values,' 'train model,' 'evaluate'). For each subtask, it retrieves the right tool from the platform's toolkit (there are hierarchies—if you need to 'clean data,' there are multiple cleaners with different strengths). It builds a visual workflow by connecting these tools in order. The focus is on planning and tool retrieval, not on code correctness.
591.ww: Planning (breaking the task into steps and picking tools) is cleaner than code generation because the platform already knows which tools exist and how they work; the model just has to reason about which combination fits the task. This is more robust than generating code. The hierarchical tool retrieval means the model doesn't have to know details—it narrows down, asks which sub-option fits, and picks.
591.po: Users can build ML workflows by describing their problem in English, without writing code. The system outperforms other LLM-based agents at satisfying user requirements and building workflows that actually improve model performance.

592.bp: Emotion recognition from text, audio, and video together (multimodal) is richer than any single source—your voice tone and facial expression matter as much as your words. But real-world data is messy: sometimes the audio is garbled, sometimes the video is missing, sometimes the text is sarcastic and contradicts the facial expression.
592.wh: When one source (e.g., audio) is noisy or absent, naive systems either ignore it (losing information) or blindly trust it (amplifying errors). Also, not all modalities are equally useful for every emotion: for anger, the voice intensity might matter most, but for sadness, facial expression might dominate. Deciding which modality to trust and how much weight to give each requires knowing how reliable each one is.
592.ap: They model each modality (text, audio, video) as providing evidence for positive and negative emotion, along with uncertainty (how confident is this source?). Each modality runs through its own expert. The experts output not just a score but also how sure they are. Then, a fusion stage looks at the confidence levels—high-confidence sources get more weight, low-confidence or missing sources get less. Finally, the aggregated evidence parameterizes a distribution (Beta distribution) from which the final emotion score is drawn.
592.ww: By explicitly modeling uncertainty per modality, the system can be skeptical of unreliable sources while trusting good ones. Missing data naturally has high uncertainty (no signal), so it gets downweighted. This is more principled than hard-coded rules like 'use modality X if available, else Y'—it learns which modalities matter for which emotions.
592.po: On standard multimodal emotion datasets, the method beats state-of-the-art and gracefully handles missing or noisy modalities. It also provides interpretable scores: you can see which modality influenced the final decision and how confident it was.

593.bp: When you search a database of tables (like spreadsheets or SQL results) using natural language ('find revenue trends by product'), the system must bridge a big gap: your words describe business concepts, but tables contain rows and columns. Finding the right table means understanding what each table's structure and content mean.
593.wh: Tables are structured (rows, columns, headers), but natural language queries are unstructured prose. Existing methods try to synthesize queries (generate fake queries automatically to train on), but they sample rows randomly, which misses the true diversity of the table's meaning. A table about product revenue has important structure: product names cluster certain ways, and that structure matters for understanding relevance.
593.ap: Instead of random row sampling, they cluster semantically similar rows (e.g., grouping products by category) and pick representative rows from each cluster to build a diverse partial table. They generate synthetic queries specific to each cluster (queries that make sense for that cluster's meaning). Then, they fuse table embeddings and query embeddings with learned weights—allowing the system to decide how much weight to give each source of information when scoring relevance.
593.ww: Semantic clustering ensures the partial table captures the table's diversity—you're not missing the obscure edge cases. Cluster-specific query generation ensures synthetic queries match the actual meaning of each part. Weighted fusion lets the model learn query-table alignment without hand-tuned fusion rules.
593.po: On five retrieval benchmarks, the method retrieves relevant tables more often than the prior state-of-the-art, especially when tables have diverse row semantics. The approach is lightweight and doesn't require retraining the base embeddings.

594.bp: Imagine controlling a computer through vision alone—you see a web page and want to click a button, but you have to communicate in words. A vision-language model could understand your words and the screen layout, but it needs to reliably point to the exact pixel. Getting this precise is hard because screens have tiny details (a link is 20 pixels wide) and the model has to understand both what you want and where it is.
594.wh: Standard vision-language models struggle at web control because they confuse positions (they don't accurately pinpoint where things are), they're sensitive to how you phrase the instruction (slight wording changes break them), and they're overconfident—they assume their action succeeded without checking the screen afterward. For mission-critical tasks like filling forms or navigating, even 86% success is frustrating because one failure interrupts the workflow.
594.ap: They fine-tune a strong vision-language model (Qwen2.5-VL-32B) on web interaction in two phases. First, teach it to recognize whether the cursor is already hovering over the target or needs to move (a simpler problem than 'go directly to the target'). Second, train it to execute one command at a time (move, then check; click, then check) and observe the screen state before planning the next action. This creates a loop: see the screen, predict the next action, execute it, observe the result, plan what to do next.
594.ww: Breaking the problem into stages (check position, then move, then click) makes each step simpler and more learnable. Step-by-step execution with observation of results (rather than predicting all moves at once) mimics how humans actually control the mouse—you move a bit, look at where the cursor ended up, correct, and click. This loop beats trying to go directly to the target.
594.po: On a benchmark of single-click web tasks, their tuned model succeeds 94% of the time, up from 86% with the base model. This is a meaningful improvement for automated web control.

595.bp: When you ask a system multi-step questions ('Which country did the actor in Inception come from?'), you need it to find multiple facts in order: find Inception, find the actor, find their country. Systems that try to find everything in one search often fail because the path is long. Existing methods retrieve and reason at each step (find Inception, then given that, find the actor), but each retrieval and reasoning step calls the language model, which is slow and costs money.
595.wh: Calling the language model repeatedly (once per reasoning hop) accumulates token costs and time delays. Also, keeping track of which entity you're talking about across hops is fragile—you might forget that 'Leonardo DiCaprio' from step 1 and 'Leo DiCaprio' in step 2 refer to the same person. Existing iterative RAG systems struggle with entity consistency and waste tokens on intermediate reasoning.
595.ap: They split the problem into offline and online stages. Offline (once, at setup): read the entire corpus once and convert it into tiny question-answer pairs, each representing one atomic fact. Online (at query time): break the complex query into subquestions, rewrite them carefully to use consistent entity names, retrieve the corresponding QA pairs densely, extract answers with a lightweight classifier. The language model is invoked only twice: once to break the query and once to synthesize the final answer.
595.ww: Reframing the corpus as atomic QA pairs means dense retrieval (fast, no LLM calls) can find the next fact. By carefully rewriting subquestions to maintain entity consistency ('Leonardo DiCaprio' stays 'Leonardo DiCaprio,' not 'Leo'), the system doesn't lose track across hops. Minimal LLM calls (only 2) mean the approach is cheap and fast.
595.po: On three multi-hop question-answering benchmarks, the method achieves competitive accuracy while using far fewer tokens than iterative systems, reducing cost without sacrificing correctness.

596.bp: Doctors make decisions by reasoning: 'I see fluid in the lungs (observation), which suggests infection (intermediate concept), which means this is pneumonia (diagnosis).' Teaching AI to mimic this step-by-step reasoning makes it trustworthy—clinicians can see why the model thinks what it thinks, which matters for high-stakes decisions.
596.wh: Deep learning models are powerful but opaque—they take pixels and spit out a diagnosis without explanation. Concept-based approaches help (translate the model's internal states into human words like 'fluid' or 'inflammation'), but existing methods treat concepts in isolation. They ignore that concepts interact: fluid in the lungs combined with fever is more significant than either alone. Also, they don't model how concepts causally influence disease outcomes—which concept changes actually matter for diagnosis?
596.ap: They build a model that proceeds in stages: extract fine-grained concepts from image regions (not just global 'is there fluid'), explicitly map how concepts relate to each other (building a concept interaction graph), then use causal inference to decide which concept patterns drive the final diagnosis. Each stage is interpretable—you can see the extracted concepts, trace the relationships, and read off the causal influence on disease.
596.ww: Extracting regional concepts is more flexible than global concepts because diseases rarely fill the whole image. Encoding concept relationships lets the model recognize that 'fluid + fever' is different from 'fluid alone.' Causal inference over concepts is more interpretable than black-box feature interactions because each concept's influence is explicit.
596.po: On four medical imaging benchmarks, the model achieves state-of-the-art diagnosis accuracy while providing step-by-step reasoning. Clinicians can interact with it through a web tool: see which concepts the model spotted, trace the reasoning path, and even verify diagnoses.

597.bp: Generated images from AI models look increasingly real, which is great for creativity but concerning for fraud. To prove an image came from you and not a manipulator, invisible watermarks can be embedded—they're imperceptible but detectable later. The challenge is that watermarking always degrades image quality, so you need to watermark smartly to preserve the image while keeping the mark recoverable.
597.wh: Adding any information (the watermark) to an image necessarily changes pixels, degrading quality. Robust watermarks require strong modification (noticeable distortion). Simple watermarking applies the same modification everywhere (every pixel gets marked equally), which wastes effort on regions that are hard to notice changes in (like uniform skies) while over-modifying visually rich regions (like faces).
597.ap: They design an attention-based adapter that learns where the watermark matters most. Some regions of the image can tolerate strong marking without visible distortion (textured backgrounds), while others need gentle marking (faces, fine details). The adapter embeds watermarks with spatially varying strength—heavy in robust regions, light in fragile ones. They then add a mixture-of-experts layer: multiple experts propose different ways to do the watermarking, and the system learns to blend them, letting different experts handle different image regions.
597.ww: Spatial variation is more efficient than uniform watermarking because it respects perceptual properties of images (humans notice changes in faces more than in backgrounds). Mixture-of-experts lets multiple strategies coexist, so the system can use one expert's approach for photographic images and another's for synthetic ones, adapting without explicit rules.
597.po: The method reduces visible distortion compared to simpler watermarking while maintaining robustness—watermarks survive compression and editing. It handles both in-generation watermarking (embed during image creation) and post-hoc watermarking (add afterward).

598.bp: Imagine you have a graph of entities (locations, keywords, concepts) and you want to efficiently connect a large group of them. In a knowledge graph, this might mean finding the smallest set of connections that links many different keywords. This is the Steiner Tree problem: find the minimal set of edges (connections) that link all your targets.
598.wh: The traditional assumption is that you have a small number of targets (a few keywords) and a large graph. Existing algorithms optimize for this case—they're fast when the graph is huge but the target count is small. However, modern tasks like summarizing a knowledge graph want to link *many* different entity descriptions (tens of thousands of distinct patterns). When the number of targets grows to 100,000+, algorithms optimized for the old assumption become impossibly slow.
598.ap: They design new approximation algorithms that scale to large numbers of targets. Rather than optimizing for either huge graphs *or* many targets, these algorithms handle both. They use techniques like recursive partitioning (divide the problem into smaller pieces, solve each, stitch results together) and pruning strategies that work efficiently even when there are thousands of targets.
598.ww: Existing algorithms have a mathematical structure that becomes expensive when you have many targets. The new algorithms reorganize that structure to leverage sparsity and recursion—if you have 100,000 targets but they cluster into groups, solving for each cluster separately and combining results is faster than trying to solve for all 100,000 at once.
598.po: On tasks with many groups (e.g., thousands of entity descriptions in a knowledge graph), the algorithms are orders of magnitude faster than prior methods while achieving comparable solution quality. They make previously intractable web applications practical.

599.bp: Imagine a network of AI agents exchanging information—each agent shares data with neighbors, and that data ripples across the network. Which agents are 'most important'? If an agent goes offline or spreads bad information, which ones matter most for overall network health? Classical centrality measures (like PageRank) were designed for the web where human readers follow links, but autonomous agents optimize for utility (they care about information value, not just link count).
599.wh: PageRank assumes links are all equally useful, but agents care about whether information actually helps them make better decisions. Also, information degrades as it spreads (telephone game effect)—the farther information travels, the more corrupted it becomes. Classical measures like betweenness centrality don't account for degradation or utility; they just count how often a node sits between others on shortest paths.
599.ap: They build a game-theoretic model where agents try to maximize the usefulness of information they receive while minimizing communication costs. They introduce Information Spreading Betweenness Centrality (ISBC), which measures a node's importance by tracking how much useful, non-degraded information actually flows through it. Unlike classical betweenness, ISBC is directed (you care which direction info flows) and distance-aware (farther isn't better).
599.ww: By modeling information degradation (information gets fuzzy over distance) and utility (agents care about decision-quality), the measure captures what actually matters in agent networks. Testing on synthetic experiments with LLM-based information propagation confirms that ISBC identifies more effective intermediaries than PageRank or classical betweenness.
599.po: ISBC identifies network nodes that are more effective at spreading useful information in agent networks than classical centrality measures. This matters as autonomous agents become primary internet users—the old centrality measures don't capture agent-driven dynamics.

600.bp: When you want product recommendations, you want them fast—not waiting for a complex pipeline to check dozens of factors. Generative recommendation is a direct approach: given your history, a language model just outputs items one by one, like writing a sequence. The appeal is speed and efficiency: no intermediate ranking step, no separate scoring systems.
600.wh: The trap is what happens as the model predicts each item: early predictions build on the user's history, but later predictions must lean on earlier outputs. If the first item skews toward one type (say, electronics), every step after inherits that bias and tends to pick more electronics. The model keeps amplifying its own mistakes, and users get stuck in a narrow set of recommendations.
600.ap: The paper proposes CARE: instead of locking in the user history once at the start, they feed progressively finer details about what the user clicked as they generate each item. They also run multiple reasoning steps in parallel for each new item, asking 'given what we know so far, what should come next?' in multiple ways, then pick the best. This splits the thinking load across more computation, which counters the buildup of bias.
600.ww: The reason this works is simple: if you're making a guess, looking at more angles before guessing reduces the chance you'll repeat your last mistake. More detailed history means you're not relying on a compressed, biased summary. Parallel reasoning lets the model escape its own groove by considering fresh viewpoints on the same history.
600.po: The outcome is more diverse recommendations—when you ask for suggestions, you get actual variety instead of 50 variants of the same thing. This makes the tool more useful, and users stay longer because browsing feels fresh.

601.bp: Hate speech and violent content spread on platforms like YouTube and TikTok at scale. Automated systems need to catch and flag these videos, but they also need to explain what they saw—otherwise, creators can't defend themselves, and platforms can't justify removals to regulators who demand transparency.
601.wh: Most systems blend video, sound, and text into one fuzzy representation and guess whether it's hateful. This black-box approach is fast but gives no evidence: you can't point to the frame or phrase and say 'this is the problem.' Meanwhile, real hate videos use tricks—one audio stream is innocent, the text is coded, the visuals are subtle—so you can miss it by looking at only one signal.
601.ap: This paper treats each signal—what's shown, what's said, what's written, and context—as independent pieces of evidence. They extract objects in frames, transcribed speech, text from subtitles, and look up relevant background info. Each gets scored on how much it contributes to a hate verdict, and the system notes when signals agree, conflict, or are missing. A fallback rule-based baseline handles obvious cases; an optional LLM digs into ambiguous ones.
601.ww: The power is in separation: by keeping signals apart, you can see which ones actually matter for the decision. If a video is flagged, you can point to three specific things (that face, that phrase, that historical context), not just 'the model said so.' Conflicts between signals—audio says one thing, visuals another—are now visible clues that the creator might be being deceptive.
601.po: Creators and regulators can audit these decisions. If a video is removed, the system explains why with concrete evidence. This builds trust even when people disagree with the judgment, because the reasoning is laid bare.

602.bp: Smartphone automation—asking an AI to tap buttons, fill forms, and navigate apps—is useful for accessibility and task automation. But even the best agents fail on complex tasks because they don't know how apps work. They might know 'tap the blue button' but not which field to fill or why an error occurred.
602.wh: The obvious fix is to give the agent a manual for every app—but there are millions of apps, and manuals are static while apps change. An agent also has gaps: it understands buttons but not the intent behind a flow, or gets confused on the third step of a five-step task because it forgot the goal.
602.ap: The paper proposes a curiosity mechanism: as the agent works, it measures uncertainty—when it's unsure about the next step, it signals 'I need help.' At that moment, the system retrieves relevant app documentation, code examples, or past successful task logs, and packages them into structured 'AppCards' that encode what each button does, what parameters it accepts, and common patterns. The agent reads the AppCard and continues, using the new knowledge.
602.ww: The magic is timing: you don't hand the agent a library upfront—you give it just what it needs when confusion strikes. This is like a human looking up a recipe only when stuck on the next step. It keeps the agent's focus narrow and prevents information overload, while the curated examples show what success looks like.
602.po: The agent's success rate on complex tasks jumps from ~82% to ~89%. Multi-step tasks—like booking a hotel and then opening email—nearly double in success because the agent can connect steps via AppCard patterns. The system becomes reliable enough for real users.

603.bp: Predicting major geopolitical events weeks in advance could help policymakers prepare, traders hedge, and emergency responders ready resources. The raw material is news articles, social media posts, and analysis buried in the internet—the signal is there, but extracting it is hard.
603.wh: Language models can read and reason, but when you ask them to predict from a pile of news, they make two mistakes. First, they miss buried clues: the causal chain (A led to B which led to C) or subtle patterns (when tension rises, conflict follows in a specific timeframe). Second, they 'hallucinate'—invent plausible-sounding details that sound right but are wrong, corrupting the forecast.
603.ap: BRSC reasons in two directions at once. One path is temporal: it maps historical events on a timeline, spots trends, and extrapolates forward—like seeing 'tensions have risen for three weeks, conflict likelihood is rising.' The other path is synchronic: within a given week, it digs for hidden connections between events and entities, building a richer understanding of what might happen next. When the LLM makes claims, a self-correction step asks 'does this match what the text actually says?' and fixes hallucinations.
603.ww: Looking backward (timeline trends) and sideways (current connections) gives two independent views of the same question. If both point to conflict, confidence rises. If they disagree, the system flags uncertainty rather than guessing. Asking the model to check itself—'is this real or invented?'—catches the most egregious hallucinations.
603.po: The model predicts international events more accurately, catching real risks rather than false alarms. In field tests on relations between nations, BRSC beats baselines, reducing the noise that derails real prediction systems.

604.bp: Robots and drones that understand images and follow instructions are proliferating—in warehouses, farms, and rescue operations. But these vision-language-action models are deployed from public repositories, exposing a supply chain risk: an adversary with access to the server could subtly alter the model to make robots misbehave in dangerous ways.
604.wh: A direct attack like flipping pixels is too obvious: the robot or a monitor would catch severe distortion and stop. But if you nudge only certain pixels—maybe the edges of an obstacle, or part of a tool—the image still looks normal to humans while the model's internal reasoning breaks. The challenge is breaking the link between 'I see object X' and 'I should do action Y' without raising alarms.
604.ap: MAVLA injects tiny perturbations into specific regions of images—parts that matter for understanding the scene or following the instruction. It balances two goals: break the model's ability to align what it sees with what it's asked to do (by maximizing 'disagreement' between vision and language pathways), while keeping the visual change imperceptible to humans. Four loss functions work together to maximize misalignment while preserving visual stealth.
604.ww: The reason this works is that neural networks rely on patterns spread throughout the image. By perturbing task-relevant regions—the edges of a box, part of a hand gesture—you corrupt the features the model uses for reasoning without changing what a human sees. The model still 'sees' the image, but it interprets it wrongly.
604.po: At 40% perturbation (modest changes), robot task success drops by 70%. A robot told 'pick up the red cup' might reach for the table instead. Worse, the attack looks innocent under visual inspection. The paper serves as a red-team test: it shows that VLA models need defenses, and hints at what those defenses should protect against.

605.bp: Self-driving vehicles connected to satellites can cover remote areas, but they face hacking threats across multiple channels: the vehicle's internal bus (CAN), messages from other vehicles (V2X), and sensors. A cloud-based defense system is too slow—500-600ms latency means the vehicle crashes before a server responds. Protection must happen on-board, instantly.
605.wh: The naive approach is to monitor each threat stream separately: flag anomalies in the CAN bus, separately flag anomalies in sensor data, separately flag anomalies in V2X. But an adversary can coordinate: send a plausible CAN message that contradicts a sensor reading in a way that each detector sees as slightly off but not flagged. Multi-channel attacks need multi-channel defenses.
605.ap: MARIS-ADS collects 41 CAN signals, 37 V2X signals, and 28 sensor streams, then uses attention—a mechanism that weights which signals matter most—to fuse them. It ranks signals by how much they contribute to the anomaly score, and drops the least relevant ones (83% reduction in data). Then it applies physics constraints: is the claimed vehicle state physically possible? Did the message violate V2X protocol? Invalid claims are blocked outright.
605.ww: The insight is that anomalies across channels leave a fingerprint. Real sensor conflicts (a camera sees an obstacle the radar doesn't) have explanations; attack-generated conflicts often violate the laws of physics or protocol rules. By fusing data and checking physical feasibility, you catch coordinated attacks that fool single-channel detectors.
605.po: The system rejects 97% of attacks that hit multiple channels at once, versus 12-34% from systems watching one channel. Real-world inference takes 0.31 milliseconds—fast enough for safety-critical braking. The vehicle can decide whether to stop or swerve before it travels another meter.

606.bp: Web applications—banking sites, e-commerce platforms, SaaS dashboards—have security holes that hackers exploit. Finding them before deployment is critical. But web apps are complex, and security testing tools often miss vulnerabilities because the input space is huge (millions of possible form submissions).
606.wh: Closed-box fuzzing means you can't see the application's internals; you only have network responses. Without that visibility, testers blindly hammer the app with random inputs. Most waste effort on unreachable code or harmless behaviors. Attackers also hide vulnerabilities with defensive logic: trigger a SQL injection only under specific conditions, so random testing misses it.
606.ap: Zelda infers hints from the web responses themselves. When a response contains new text, an error message, or different timing, that's feedback that something changed—the input affected the app. Zelda learns these patterns and focuses on inputs that produce novel responses. It then uses two strategies: broad exploration to cover different code paths, and targeted exploitation to chain inputs together to trigger deep flaws (like the SQL injection that only manifests after five clicks).
606.ww: The reasoning is that every response is a signal. An error page means 'you found an edge case'; a slow response means 'this input triggered complex logic.' By treating responses as feedback, Zelda does directed testing instead of random guessing. Combining exploration (map the app) with exploitation (dig into interesting behaviors) lets it balance breadth and depth.
606.po: Zelda found 182 vulnerabilities in 15 real web apps, outperforming six other tools. In the wild, it discovered 29 unknown vulnerabilities that earned CVEs. Developers can now find and patch real risks before deployment.

607.bp: When a user scrolls through an e-commerce feed, the platform wants to maximize multiple goals: get them to buy something, keep them engaged with more views, and keep them scrolling (not closing the app). These sound aligned, but they conflict: a high-conversion item might bore them into leaving, while an engaging item might go unwatched.
607.wh: The typical ranking system optimizes one goal at a time, then combines scores. But in e-commerce, especially with immersive swiping, behaviors are intertwined: clicking an item is often followed by viewing more items is often followed by buying. Optimizing one pushes against the others. Also, the full-screen UI creates 'temporal greedy traps': the system picks the best item for the current screen, but that choice locks out the ideal item for the next screen.
607.ap: STCRank uses spatial collaboration: within each screen, it manages multi-objective trade-offs by modeling which objectives conflict (when one rises, another falls) and steering toward a balanced frontier of solutions instead of maximizing each separately. Temporal collaboration: it looks ahead to the next screens and considers how today's choice limits tomorrow's options, reducing greedy mistakes. The system treats each screen as a step in a longer sequence.
607.ww: The insight is that objectives in sequential recommendation aren't independent—they're coupled through user behavior and UI design. By explicitly modeling their conflicts and temporal dependencies, the system avoids the trap of local optimization at each screen. It's like planning a meal: appetizer choice affects how good the main course feels.
607.po: The ranking system balances goals better: users see items they want to click, items worth viewing, and are motivated to keep scrolling. Engagement and conversion both rise—no longer at odds. On a platform with millions of daily users, this shift in balance drives measurable value.

608.bp: When hospitals or devices can't share raw data (due to privacy), they can still benefit from machine learning through federated learning: each site trains a model locally, and they share learned patterns—not data. The challenge is when sites have different patient types: a rural clinic's data distribution differs from an urban hospital's.
608.wh: Existing federated learning treats each class (disease type) as one holistic pattern and shares that pattern across sites. But a single pattern is too rigid: one site might see 'cardiac disease' as mostly hypertension, another as mostly arrhythmia. A rigid class pattern doesn't adapt. Also, if you have 1000 disease classes, sharing 1000 patterns wastes communication.
608.ap: FedVPL decomposes each class into semantic building blocks—'visual primitives' like 'inflammation pattern', 'structural change', 'severity marker'—then shares those reusable pieces. A rural clinic can mix primitives differently than an urban hospital, personalizing the model. It uses a language model to align primitives semantically (ensuring 'inflammation' means the same thing everywhere) without transmitting model parameters, saving communication.
608.ww: The power is modularity: instead of 'cardiac disease', you share 'the inflammation look' and 'the electrical disturbance pattern.' Sites reuse and recombine, tailoring to local data without relearning everything from scratch. Language models provide a common semantic bridge so 'inflammation' means the same thing at every site.
608.po: Models generalize better across sites because they're built from sharable, reusable pieces. Communication overhead drops (doesn't scale with the number of classes), and each site still personalizes to its patient population. Federated learning becomes practical for real healthcare networks.

609.bp: Graph neural networks power recommendation systems, fraud detection, and knowledge graphs. But in the real world, these graphs evolve: new entities appear, relationships change, the distribution of data shifts. Retraining the model from scratch each time is expensive. The goal is to adapt the model to new data without forgetting old patterns.
609.wh: Continual learning in graphs is tricky because you can't simply fine-tune—that destroys what the model learned before (catastrophic forgetting). Standard fixes like replaying old data are expensive: you'd need to store and replay millions of old edges. The trap is that a model adapted to the new domain forgets the old one.
609.ap: STEM uses a state-space controller that evolves continuously. Imagine the 'state' of the domain—what the graphs look like—as a hidden variable that changes over time. As new graph data arrives, STEM updates this state, then uses it to generate lightweight adapters that modify the frozen base model. Unlike linear state-space models, STEM allows the state transitions to be nonlinear and depend on the input, capturing the true dynamics of domain evolution. A penalty on adapter changes prevents wild swings that destroy past knowledge.
609.ww: The insight is that you don't need to retrain or replay data; you need to track how the domain is shifting and adapt smoothly. By modeling the domain's state and generating parameterized adaptations, the system adjusts to new data while regularizing the changes to maintain stability. It's like adjusting a compass needle gradually rather than spinning it.
609.po: The model adapts to new graphs while remembering old patterns. No memory replay, minimal overhead, and theoretical guarantees that forgetting is mitigated. Continual learning becomes practical for production systems where graphs and distributions never stop changing.

610.bp: Knowing where a social media user lives is useful for advertisers, researchers, and emergency responders. But users rarely post their location, and when data is scarce, the model struggles. The challenge is to infer location from sparse posts, bios, and profile information using limited labeled examples.
610.wh: Social media profiles are heterogeneous: one user's location signal might be a check-in, another's might be a mention of a local landmark, another's might be implicit (their language or cultural references). Standard methods struggle when there are few labeled examples and signals are noisy or conflicting.
610.ap: FewUser uses two components: first, contrastive learning—a technique that teaches the model to pull similar users close and push different ones apart, learning robust user representations from few examples. Second, it uses prompting: templated questions that adapt a pre-trained language model to the geolocation task, linking user text and location knowledge through 'hard' prompts (specific locations), 'soft' prompts (learned patterns), and 'semi-soft' prompts (hybrid). Hard negative mining ensures the model learns to distinguish tricky cases.
610.ww: The reason this works with few examples is that the pre-trained language model already knows geography and language—you just need to connect that knowledge to the user. Contrastive learning lets the model learn from unlabeled data too. Mixing hard, soft, and semi-soft prompts bridges the gap between generic language knowledge and specific user clues.
610.po: The model infers where users live more accurately, even with few labeled examples. On new datasets (TwiU and FliU) and public benchmarks, FewUser consistently outperforms baselines. Researchers and platforms can now estimate location for privacy-sensitive tasks without labeled data.

611.bp: When a recommender suggests a movie, you want to know why: 'because you liked this other film,' or 'because others who liked your taste enjoyed it.' Explainable recommendation builds trust. But explanations must be personalized and sensible, not generic boilerplate.
611.wh: Generating good explanations is hard because the model must choose which pieces of a user's history to highlight and construct a plausible narrative. If history is sparse, explanations become repetitive. If you fuse text (item reviews, descriptions) and collaborative signals (ratings from similar users) naively, they can conflict: the text says this is a thriller, but collaborative patterns say comedies match this user better.
611.ap: This paper systematically tests how to blend textual and collaborative signals in a sequence-aware model. It explores: pooling strategies (how to aggregate many reviews into one summary), fusion mechanisms (when and how to combine text and numbers—early, late, or via Transformer), and training regimes. The goal is to find the recipe that generates explanations which are both accurate and helpful.
611.ww: The mechanistic insight is that text and collaborative signals capture different truths: text describes what an item is, collaborative data describes who will like it. Fusing them at the right stage (and in the right way) lets explanations cite both 'the plot matches your taste' and 'users like you rated it highly'—richer reasoning than either alone.
611.po: When the model finds the right recipe, recommendations improve and explanations become more coherent and useful. Users see the reasoning ('you watched three thrillers, and this one has similar pacing') rather than arbitrary suggestions. Trust increases, and recommendations feel personalized.

612.bp: Large language models can reason over user behavior and predict what to recommend next. But users have massive click histories—millions of sessions—and LLMs have limited context windows. Also, LLMs sometimes invent preferences that don't exist ('this user wants kitchen appliances' when they only clicked once by accident). The model must balance a huge behavior history with reliable preference inference.
612.wh: You can't just feed all user clicks to an LLM—the context window overflows. You could sample clicks, but that loses information. You could summarize, but LLMs tend to amplify whichever preference they mentioned first, creating hallucinated persistence. An LLM might invent 'this user loves jazz' because the first song played was jazz, then stick to it despite contradictory behavior.
612.ap: Rec2 segments the user's behavior into chunks, then builds preferences one chunk at a time. For each chunk, the LLM infers what the user wanted, and the next chunk's behavior is treated as feedback: 'did my inference match what they actually did?' This reinforcement signal corrects hallucinations. After processing all chunks, a dynamic learning module captures how preferences evolve over time and fuses them into a single, long-term preference representation.
612.ww: The insight is to use the future as a teacher: if your inference about 'chunk 1' was wrong, the user's actions in 'chunk 2' will contradict it. By penalizing inferences that don't predict the next behavior, you suppress hallucinations. Segmentation lets you handle long histories without overwhelming the context window, and the reinforcement signal keeps the LLM honest.
612.po: The model makes more reliable recommendations because it infers real user preferences, not invented ones. Even on long histories with diverse behaviors, the system captures genuine intent. Recommendation quality improves, and the model avoids the pitfall of LLM hallucinations—a common failure mode in real systems.

613.bp: Knowledge graphs—structured databases of facts and relationships—grow constantly as new discoveries emerge and new entities are added. The embeddings that power searches and link prediction must update without forgetting: if a graph gains 1000 new drugs, the model must learn their embeddings and remain accurate on the existing 10,000.
613.wh: Most embedding libraries are designed for static graphs and provide no continual learning mechanism. Retraining from scratch is expensive. Naive fine-tuning forgets old embeddings (catastrophic forgetting). Existing continual KGE methods are fragmented—each paper uses a different framework—making them hard to use and compare in practice.
613.ap: This paper extends PyKEEN, a popular embedding library, to handle continual updates. When new entities arrive, it initializes their embeddings smartly—using information from related entities rather than random vectors. It adds metrics that measure both accuracy on new facts and forgetting on old ones, and provides a training interface with dashboards to track embedding evolution over time.
613.ww: The advantage is infrastructure: by embedding continual learning into an existing, widely-used library, researchers and practitioners can experiment and deploy without building from scratch. Smart initialization means new entities aren't completely blind; tracking forgetting alongside accuracy keeps the metric honest about trade-offs.
613.po: Knowledge graphs can be maintained as living systems: new facts are learned, old facts remain accurate, and the tools to experiment and audit this process are available to everyone. This enables production systems where graphs and their embeddings evolve together.

614.bp: Teaching students to code requires understanding what they know—which concepts they grasp and which trip them up. A knowledge tracing system models this and predicts whether a student will solve the next problem. For programming, this is harder than traditional subjects because success depends on logical reasoning, not just concept knowledge, and the feedback is noisy.
614.wh: Standard knowledge tracing models assume binary correctness (right or wrong) and focus on concept knowledge. But coding problems often give partial credit (pass 7 of 10 test cases, so 70% correct), which is noisy feedback. A student's logic might be sound but inefficient, failing one test case. The model misses this nuance and focuses only on whether concepts are known.
614.ap: MLPKT uses a language model to enrich feedback: it analyzes each failed submission, identifies the root cause (logic error, off-by-one, timeout), and assigns a meaningful label instead of just 'wrong.' It then models student knowledge across three levels: concept (does the student know recursion?), logical reasoning (can they trace a complex flow?), and problem-specific understanding (can they adapt to this specific task?). A three-phase training process refines knowledge estimates at each level.
614.ww: The insight is that programming fails for rich reasons, and the model must understand them to predict future success. By tracing why code fails (via an LLM) and building multi-dimensional knowledge models, the system captures the true state of a student's abilities. Partial scores and noisy feedback become interpretable signals, not noise.
614.po: The model predicts student performance on future problems more accurately, allowing tutoring systems to target instruction where it matters. A student who understands concepts but lacks logical reasoning gets different help than one who struggles with language syntax. Personalized learning becomes possible at scale.

615.bp: When you predict weather, electricity demand, or stock prices hours or days ahead, small errors snowball—today's mistake poisons tomorrow's guess. The real goal is to give decision-makers at scale (electricity grids, supply chains, trading floors) accurate enough forecasts to act on, even when the future is choppy and data is noisy.
615.wh: Transformer models, which have worked brilliantly for language, stumble here because they chain predictions together (each step feeds the next), so one mistake cascades. They also fall apart when the test data doesn't match the training data—imagine a model trained on mild weather trying to predict a hurricane.
615.ap: The authors build a leaner Transformer and pair it with a new optimizer called Escape-Explore. The optimizer has two jobs: when training gets stuck (imagine rolling a ball in a valley, trapped between two walls), it first escapes the trap, then explores outward to find better ground—avoiding dead-ends that trap ordinary optimizers.
615.ww: Escaping traps helps the model learn richer patterns rather than settling for mediocre shortcuts. Exploring widely makes the final solution more stable and generalizable—when test data differs from training, a solution found on high ground is less fragile than one wedged in a narrow crevice.
615.po: On real web data (11 time-series benchmarks plus medical imaging), this method matches the best existing models but with better stability and generalization—crucially, it works across both forecasting and vision tasks, not just one.

616.bp: The world is constantly changing—a political situation evolves, companies merge, facts shift. We want machines to keep a memory of how things connect (Entity A relates to Entity B via relationship C) and fill in missing links when data is incomplete, so we understand what's likely to happen next.
616.wh: Most methods focus on order (what happened first, second, third) or raw structure (who's connected to whom), but they ignore the semantic meaning—the difference between 'political event' and 'economic crisis,' even though both are changes. Without semantic depth, the model misses subtle patterns.
616.ap: This method uses large language models to label entities and relationships with semantic tags (like 'political event,' 'economic activity'). It then builds two graphs—one capturing relations between entities, another between the semantic labels—and runs convolution operations (neighborhood aggregation) on both, letting information flow from labels into entity predictions.
616.ww: Semantic tags act like interpretable clues: they help the model understand that a 'political event' entity should behave differently from an 'economic activity' one. Higher-order interactions (many-to-many relationships) let distant but thematically similar facts reinforce each other.
616.po: On standard knowledge graph benchmarks, this dual-graph approach completes missing links more accurately than single-graph methods, especially in complex, evolving scenarios where semantic distinctions matter.

617.bp: Modern search engines face a new problem: instead of returning a ranked list of links, they now generate document IDs directly (like 'doc_4829_Q1'). The advantage is crisp and fast, but the reality is harsh—whenever new documents arrive (new blog posts, products, papers), the model must learn them immediately without retraining.
617.wh: Retraining from scratch is slow and expensive (days of GPU time). Incremental training (adding new data without retraining) causes catastrophic forgetting—the model unlearns old documents while learning new ones. Also, the decoder (the part mapping thought patterns to document IDs) struggles because many different queries might retrieve overlapping sets of IDs, so it's hard to tell them apart.
617.ap: Instead of retraining, the authors use surgical model editing: identify which neural network layers control document ID mapping, tweak their weights carefully, and inject smart labels (soft labels that preserve query-specific nuances) to make the edits learn which ID goes with which query.
617.ww: Surgical edits are faster than retraining and avoid catastrophic forgetting because they only touch the relevant wiring. Soft labels preserve the query context, so the model doesn't confuse similar IDs even when they overlap.
617.po: The method adapts to new documents without full retraining, achieving performance near incremental training but in far less time, making generative retrieval practical for live, continuously-updated document collections.

618.bp: When researchers publish code, they write README files explaining datasets, scripts, and third-party libraries. These free-form documents hold practical knowledge that's locked away in unstructured text—if we could extract and link this metadata automatically, research would be more discoverable and reproducible.
618.wh: README files use Markdown (a loose format with little structure) and mix casual language with technical detail. Existing information extraction datasets focus on academic papers, not implementation details. The gap means we lack training data to teach machines what 'dataset,' 'license,' or 'requirement' looks like in a README.
618.ap: The authors manually labeled 200 README files, marking 10,000+ text spans with 10 entity types (like 'Dataset,' 'Framework,' 'License'). They tested two approaches: large language models (given a README, guess the entities) and fine-tuned Transformers (Transformers trained on the labeled examples).
618.ww: Manual annotation creates ground truth—a reliable standard to measure against. The comparison between LLMs and fine-tuned models reveals that implementation-level entities behave differently from paper-level ones, so a model trained on papers alone will fail on code.
618.po: The labeled dataset and baselines now let researchers train entity extractors specific to README files. A downstream experiment shows these extracted entities support artifact discovery (finding related code and datasets), validating the practical value.

619.bp: Traffic forecasts power smart traffic lights, route recommendations, and congestion alerts—decisions made every minute across cities. Accurate predictions prevent gridlock and guide thousands of drivers. The challenge is that traffic is deeply spatial (neighbors affect each other) and temporal (patterns repeat hourly, daily, seasonally).
619.wh: Most graph methods only capture pairwise links ('Road A connects to Road B'). But traffic is richer: groups of roads interact together, time patterns interweave with geography, and daily/seasonal rhythms matter. Miss these higher-order interactions and your predictions become fragile.
619.ap: The method builds two hypergraphs (graphs where edges can connect many nodes at once, not just pairs). One captures spatial proximity (geographical neighborhoods), the other temporal patterns (which traffic series behave similarly, detected by mutual information). Both feed through a convolution network that learns node representations, followed by a GRU-MLP module that captures both local dynamics and global trends. Periodic features (daily, weekly patterns extracted via Fourier transform) add semantic richness.
619.ww: Hyperedges (many-to-many connections) naturally express 'this cluster of roads moves together.' Mutual information in the temporal graph finds nonlinear patterns (erratic but correlated flows) that linear methods miss. Periodic features give the model a calendar sense.
619.po: On real traffic networks, this method forecasts flow more accurately than single-graph baselines, especially during complex rush-hour periods where spatial and temporal interactions are most tangled.

620.bp: Imagine a surveillance camera needs to track the same car across different angles and times. Vehicle re-identification answers: 'Is this the same car?'—crucial for parking lots, toll plazas, and stolen-vehicle alerts. The catch is that the same car looks different from different angles and under occlusion.
620.wh: Features get tangled: the model learns identity (it's Car #47) but also captures angle ('from the left side'), lighting, and occlusion patterns. These extra features muddy the waters—a car seen from the front looks so different from the rear that the model struggles to match them.
620.ap: The method uses two mechanisms to disentangle features. First, multi-head attention separates which parts of the image matter for identity (tire pattern, color distribution) versus which are pose artifacts (angle, lighting). Second, region-aware sparse attention and symmetry-aware attention focus on the most stable, identity-defining features while suppressing redundant noise.
620.ww: Disentangling isolates the signal (identity) from the noise (viewpoint, occlusion). By separately handling symmetric features (both sides of a car) and asymmetric ones (unique scratches, damage), the model learns finer distinctions that survive viewpoint changes.
620.po: On standard vehicle datasets (VeRi776, VehicleID), this method achieves better matching accuracy than existing approaches, especially in multi-view scenarios where cars are seen from many angles.

621.bp: Large language models now review contracts, screen job applications, and flag policy violations. If an adversary slips fraudulent information into the input, the model can make dangerous mistakes—approving a fake invoice, hiring a scammer, ignoring a threat. We need a defense that keeps the LLM honest.
621.wh: Standard defenses (adversarial training, input filtering) are brittle: they're not general (work on one fraud type but not others), hard to interpret (the user can't see why the model rejected something), and don't transfer well between different LLMs.
621.ap: This method builds a knowledge graph that maps suspicious phrases to fraud tactics (e.g., 'urgent action required' maps to high-pressure manipulation).
