Given an input, it extracts keywords and fraud tactics, then augments the prompt sent to the LLM with highlighted keywords and explanatory evidence—essentially saying 'hey, this smells like tactic X, be careful.'
621.ww: Knowledge graphs are interpretable (you can see the fraud tactic connections) and general (the same tactics appear across fraud types). Augmenting the prompt with structured evidence guides the LLM toward defensive reasoning without requiring model retraining.
621.po: Across four popular LLMs and five fraud types (contract manipulation, job scams, policy violations, etc.), this defense outperforms prior methods, offering both better robustness and explainable traces of why the model was suspicious.

622.bp: Autonomous AI agents—systems that make decisions and take actions over time with minimal human oversight—are moving into banks, hospitals, and power grids. A rogue agent could embezzle money, alter medical records, or sabotage infrastructure. We need to rethink what 'insider threat' means when the insider is not human but machine.
622.wh: Insider threat detection was designed for humans: monitor login times, file access, email patterns. But an AI agent has no 9-to-5 schedule, doesn't sleep, and can be reprogrammed instantly. Traditional behavior baselines don't apply, and humans have a hard time spotting when an agent's goals have drifted.
622.ap: This is a position paper (not a concrete tool, but a manifesto). It argues that we need new categories: agent role drift (gradual expansion of an agent's decision scope), manipulation (other agents tricking it), and emergent misuse (unintended consequences of its learning). It sketches research directions: better agent observability (can we see agent reasoning?), auditability (can we replay and explain actions?), and memory isolation (preventing agents from colluding).
622.ww: An AI system's misbehavior often has a root cause (bad objective function, poisoned training data, interaction with another agent) that's invisible to current tools. Making agents transparent and auditable is the only way to catch insider threats before they cause damage.
622.po: The paper identifies key gaps in current security practice and proposes an agenda for governance, monitoring, and detection mechanisms specifically designed for autonomous systems—setting the stage for safer multi-agent deployments.

623.bp: Graph neural networks power recommendation systems, fraud detection, and social networks—they learn representations by aggregating neighbor information. But what if an attacker poisons the training graph, injecting fake edges or nodes? The model learns to misclassify specific target nodes, like a sleeper cell in a recommendation system.
623.wh: Existing defenses look for anomalies by comparing poisoned nodes to clean ones. But clever attackers design triggers (injected edges or features) that blend in, indistinguishable from normal nodes. Detecting anomalies becomes impossible if the attacker mimics benign behavior.
623.ap: This method identifies specific neural dimensions (embedding coordinates) that activate more often in poisoned models—'backdoor neurons.' The authors then reverse-engineer which graph triggers activate those neurons, unlearn the poisoned knowledge at that neuron level, and recover the model's clean behavior.
623.ww: Backdoor neurons are a structural vulnerability: information in the graph flows through the network in predictable ways, so poisoning concentrates damage in a few dimensions. By surgically targeting those dimensions rather than trying to detect triggers, the defense bypasses the attacker's camouflage.
623.po: On multiple graph datasets, this neuron-level defense removes backdoor effects more reliably than detection-based approaches, restoring clean predictions without retraining from scratch.

624.bp: Streaming recommendation systems (Netflix, YouTube, Amazon) face a hard reality: most users interact sparsely (they watch a few videos), most items get little exposure (99% of videos are never clicked), and new content arrives constantly. These long-tail distributions confound most algorithms, which do well for popular items but fail for obscure ones.
624.wh: Collaborative sparsity (few interactions for tail users/items) means the model has less signal. Existing LLM-based methods only embed items as single vectors, missing semantic relationships ('westerns' and 'noir films' are similar). Head-tail tradeoffs are unavoidable: improve tail recommendations, and head accuracy often drops.
624.ap: This method uses LLMs to build global semantic understanding of items. For tail items, it creates a fuzzy prototype that lets them borrow features from semantically related head items (a rare western inherits viewing patterns from popular westerns). For sparse users, it aligns and distills across similar users. Lightweight regularization balances semantic and collaborative signals globally.
624.ww: Semantic alignment shares knowledge across the taxonomy—tail items and users are no longer alone but anchored to semantic neighbors with richer signal. Global regularization prevents the model from gaming head accuracy to boost tail performance.
624.po: Across three datasets and multiple backbones, this method improves tail recommendations while maintaining or slightly improving head accuracy—solving the long-standing head-tail seesaw problem.

625.bp: Graphs are not static—friendships form and dissolve, markets rise and fall, networks evolve. Graph neural networks trained on one era's data often fail on the next because the distribution has shifted. Real-world graph changes (link formation patterns, node behavior) are driven by underlying environments that change over time.
625.wh: Dynamic graph networks use temporal message-passing (propagating information through time), but environment shifts confuse the model: factors that mattered yesterday might not matter today. The model overfits to training environments and fails to generalize.
625.ap: The method models multiple possible environment shifts (using variational inference to extract pseudo-environments from the data), then trains a mixture of experts—different subnetworks, each specialized for one environment. An alignment objective forces all experts to agree on invariant (stable) representations, filtering out environment-specific noise.
625.ww: By explicitly modeling environment variation, the network avoids mistaking temporary correlations for true patterns. The mixture-of-experts structure lets the model adapt which expert to trust as conditions shift, while the alignment objective ensures robustness.
625.po: On real and synthetic dynamic graphs, this approach significantly outperforms models trained without environment awareness, especially when test data drift away from training conditions.

626.bp: Web services face advanced attacks buried in system logs—adversaries hide intrusions by changing file access patterns, forging process relationships, and reordering activities. Provenance-based detection reconstructs these causal chains to spot inconsistencies. The challenge: attackers can subtly manipulate the graph to evade detection.
626.wh: Graph-based detectors are vulnerable to graph manipulation attacks: adversaries tweak the structure just enough to fool the model without creating obvious anomalies. Applying arbitrary perturbations (noise) for robustness destroys the causal logic that made provenance useful in the first place.
626.ap: This method generates robust representations using logic-aware augmentation: instead of random noise, it injects semantically valid perturbations that preserve the causal meaning of provenance graphs. It then uses contrastive learning—training the model to recognize similar behaviors even under logical transformations while distinguishing adversarial perturbations.
626.ww: Logic-aware perturbations maintain causal semantics, so the model learns representations grounded in what attacks actually look like, not statistical artifacts. Contrastive learning is inherently robust: by learning invariances to benign transformations, the model becomes insensitive to harmless graph variations.
626.po: On multiple provenance datasets, this framework outperforms state-of-the-art anomaly detectors in resisting graph manipulation while maintaining high detection accuracy and computational efficiency.

627.bp: Web3 (blockchain, DeFi, NFTs) needs identity systems where users control their own data without a central authority. Decentralized identity lets someone prove 'I'm member of this gaming community' without revealing their real name or linking it to their DeFi wallet. The challenge: across multiple independent blockchains and services, maintaining privacy while staying traceable for bad actors.
627.wh: Existing decentralized identity systems use a central committee to manage identity, creating a bottleneck: as the system grows, the committee becomes a target. Cross-domain privacy is impossible when users frequently move between services (DeFi → Gaming → DAO) because movement patterns expose identity.
627.ap: This system uses sharding to partition the identity infrastructure across independent domain committees, scaling horizontally. It introduces a domain-hiding presentation protocol based on ring signatures (a cryptographic trick where a user proves membership in a trusted set without revealing which one). Users can present themselves to different services without linking their activities.
627.ww: Sharding eliminates the bottleneck: each domain committee handles only its users, not the whole world. Ring signatures hide which trusted domain the user came from, so even if someone interacts across many services, the connections remain hidden.
627.po: The system achieves strong cross-domain anonymity (interactions in DeFi don't leak to Gaming), efficient traceability (when a user breaks rules, authorities can identify them), and scalability comparable to non-privacy systems.

628.bp: On Twitter, Reddit, and news sites, events unfold in real time—a product launch, a political scandal, a natural disaster. Machines can cluster the flood of messages into coherent narratives, alerting users and journalists to emerging stories. The challenge is capturing how social information spreads in waves, with messages reinforcing and interfering with each other.
628.wh: Standard graph convolution networks assume information diffuses in a single, smooth wave—each node gets updated once, like heat spreading through a room. Real social diffusion is messier: a breaking story gets shared, dies down, then resurges when new evidence emerges. Messages interact—some reinforce (retweets agreeing), others clash (dispute threads).
628.ap: The method models information diffusion using wave physics. A spectral filter (the Helmholtz equation from acoustics/electromagnetism) captures oscillatory wave propagation. A physical interaction force adjusts connection strengths: messages in the same event attract each other, while messages across events repel. Text encoding and timestamps add context.
628.ww: Wave-based propagation naturally captures oscillations and interference—when two social signals converge, they either amplify or cancel. Physical forces make the model attention-aware: it learns which connections matter for which events, adapting the graph structure dynamically.
628.po: On real social event detection benchmarks, this physics-inspired approach outperforms standard GCN-based methods, especially at disentangling overlapping stories and tracking multi-wave diffusion patterns.

629.bp: Technology-Assisted Review (TAR) systems help teams find relevant documents in massive collections—used in legal discovery (finding responsive documents in millions of files), systematic literature review (screening papers for meta-analysis), and now for large-scale Web content moderation and information access. The challenge: ensuring fairness, transparency, and trustworthiness at Web scale.
629.wh: The Web is no longer just links to external pages—it's user-generated content, AI-generated syntheses, multilingual text, and constantly shifting. Existing TAR methods were built for static, well-organized collections. Applying them to Web data means dealing with heterogeneity, dynamic updates, and diverse languages, all while maintaining transparency and avoiding bias.
629.ap: This is a workshop proposal (not a research paper, but an agenda for the community). It brings together researchers from retrieval, Web science, AI governance, and law to discuss how TAR can be adapted for Web-scale challenges. Topics include intelligent retrieval (better ranking), human-in-the-loop learning (efficient feedback loops), explainability (why is this document relevant?), and integrating LLMs and knowledge graphs.
629.ww: Web-scale TAR is fundamentally about trustworthiness: if an automated system gates access to information, it must be auditable and fair. LLMs and knowledge graphs can enhance retrieval, but only if their reasoning is transparent. Human-in-the-loop keeps humans in control of high-stakes decisions.
629.po: The workshop aims to identify research gaps, foster collaboration, and chart directions for building TAR systems that work at Web scale while maintaining human oversight, fairness, and accountability in automated information access.

630.bp: Knowledge graphs—vast databases that store facts as connected statements like "Einstein discovered relativity"—are everywhere: powering search engines, question-answering systems, and enterprise data integration. As these graphs grow and change over time, organizations need to understand whether their structure is sound, their schemas consistent, and their contents reliable.
630.wh: MetriKG builds both data-level and schema-level metrics and computes them continuously over time, visualizing how the graph evolves. It measures properties like cohesion (whether related entities cluster together), connectivity (whether entities link to many others), and inheritance depth (how deep type hierarchies go)—all tracked as the graph ages.
630.ww: By tracking both what data changed and how the schema itself shifted, managers can spot when a graph is degrading (fragmentation), when it's becoming overly complex (deep hierarchies growing), or when consistency is breaking. This dual lens—data *and* structure—reveals problems a single view would miss.
630.po: MetriKG offers a web interface to upload RDF files or query SPARQL endpoints, returning a dashboard of metrics over time. This lets teams diagnose data quality issues, track whether merge operations preserved consistency, and set quality thresholds before data corrupts downstream systems.

631.bp: Cloud datacenters run thousands of applications simultaneously, and memory—the fast short-term storage computers use—is often the bottleneck. Disaggregated memory systems share memory pools across many machines using a fast networking protocol called RDMA, letting applications use far more memory than any single box holds.
631.wh: The catch is sharing. When multiple customers' apps use the same disaggregated memory system, they interfere with each other: one app's huge memory request can clog the network, forcing another app's critical query to wait. Existing systems ignore the real topology of datacenter networks and assume applications play nicely—assumptions that break in practice.
631.ap: Wiseswap adds three safeguards. First, it gives memory-swapping operations special priority in the network hardware itself—using RDMA's native signaling—so latency-critical requests cut in front of other traffic. Second, it watches the network constantly and routes memory requests through less-congested paths, like water finding channels around obstacles. Third, it automatically adjusts how much memory each tenant can request based on real-time load, preventing one tenant from starving others.
631.ww: By pushing the fairness and routing decisions into the network hardware (the kernel) rather than relying on applications to be polite, Wiseswap makes interference predictable and controllable. Measuring congestion in real-time and rerouting work ensures that one bad citizen doesn't tank everyone's performance.
631.po: Experiments show Wiseswap delivers 1.3–2.4× higher throughput and 57–73% lower tail latency (the delay that the slowest requests experience) when multiple tenants compete. This means cloud customers get more consistent, predictable performance even when their neighbors are hogging resources.

632.bp: Companies deploy visual models—systems that understand images—onto edge devices like phones, cameras, and robots to run locally without cloud access. But these pre-trained models often fail on new devices because the lighting, angles, or background are different from their training data.
632.wh: Fine-tuning (retraining) a model to adapt to a new environment sounds obvious, but it requires labeled example images from that environment—images with correct answers attached. Collecting and labeling those is slow and expensive. And running the fine-tuning on a tiny device with limited power drains batteries fast.
632.ap: Glasses splits the work: the device sends just one unlabeled image (a photo of the device's real surroundings) to the cloud, which does the heavy computation to figure out how to adjust the model, then sends back lightweight updated weights. The device downloads these tweaks and applies them locally—a much cheaper operation than full fine-tuning.
632.ww: The cloud's computer power solves the two hardest parts—figuring out what adjustments work and doing the math—while the device only handles the quick, final step of applying them. This lets the device adapt rapidly (to a new office, room, or environment) without needing labels or burning its battery on training.
632.po: Testing on two datasets shows Glasses improves accuracy by 5–22% when learning from just one example, and 2–10% with five examples. Models adapt to their deployment environment in minutes, not hours, making it practical to ship a phone camera app that auto-adjusts when moved to a new home or office.

633.bp: The web is increasingly powered by AI—search engines rank results using learned models, streaming services pick songs through recommendation algorithms, and chatbots answer questions. Building systems that deliver these AI experiences to millions of people simultaneously is technically and strategically complex.
633.wh: Scaling AI isn't just about raw compute. It's about balancing latency (answers must come back instantly), freshness (models must track changing tastes), and interpretability (users and developers need to understand why a result ranked first). Most systems sacrifice one for the others.
633.ap: This is a keynote reflection on how AI systems at Spotify evolved: from static search results to interactive, intent-aware experiences where users can steer recommendations, explore new music, and see why suggestions were made. It discusses emerging deployment patterns, tradeoffs, and open problems in system design.
633.ww: Making AI interactive and controllable (rather than black-box) builds user trust and, ironically, improves relevance—users correct misunderstandings in real-time. Intent-aware systems also reduce redundant compute by understanding what the user is really asking for, not just pattern-matching keywords.
633.po: The keynote identifies design challenges for future web systems: how to monitor AI quality in production, how to adapt rapidly to user feedback, how to balance exploration (showing users new content) with exploitation (showing what they'll likely enjoy), and how to do all this at scale. It frames these as open research questions for the community.

634.bp: Simulating human society—modeling how people debate, collaborate, make decisions—is crucial for testing policies, predicting social outcomes, and designing better institutions. The more realistic the simulation, the better we can trust its predictions.
634.wh: Large language models are powerful but naive in multi-agent simulations: they either coordinate too well (everyone agrees, groupthink), deadlock (everyone disagrees, nothing gets done), or follow rigid scripts. Real humans constantly shift between cooperation (pooling knowledge) and healthy skepticism (questioning each other)—a dynamic balance that rigid models can't capture.
634.ap: BEACOF models social interaction as a game of incomplete information: agents don't know each other's skills or reliability, so they form evolving beliefs about peers ("Is this person an expert in medicine? Do they tend to be right?"). Agents then choose how to collaborate (cooperate or critique) based on these beliefs, updating beliefs as they watch peers' performance.
634.ww: By treating collaboration mode as a strategic choice (not a fixed setting), agents become adaptive. A teammate who gives bad advice gets lower credibility over time, so future collaboration tips toward healthy skepticism. A teammate who's consistently right earns trust, so cooperation increases. This mirrors real team dynamics.
634.po: Tested on three scenario types—courtroom debates, open social discussions, medical diagnosis—BEACOF avoids both groupthink and deadlock, converging toward high-quality solutions. Simulations are more realistic and predictions more trustworthy, enabling better policy testing and institutional design.

635.bp: When you read a research paper or legal document on screen, your eye naturally follows structure: scanning the outline, reading sections in order, jumping to a figure when mentioned, cross-referencing tables. Systems that answer questions about such documents should mimic this human strategy.
635.wh: Current document QA systems flatten the document into disconnected text chunks, losing the crucial clues that structure provides: which sections are relevant, how figures relate to nearby text, what the hierarchy means. A figure appearing under "Methods" has different importance than one in "Results," but flat systems treat them the same.
635.ap: DMAP builds a structural map of the document: organizing text into its natural hierarchy (chapters, sections, subsections), linking figures and tables to the text they illustrate, marking cross-references. An agent then reasons over this map: retrieving relevant chunks, checking if enough context was found to answer, and iteratively asking follow-up queries if needed.
635.ww: Structure acts as a filter: it narrows the search space (fewer sections to check means faster retrieval) and as scaffolding for reasoning (knowing that section X is about methodology tells the system which evidence to prioritize). This mirrors how humans read: you don't scan every page, you navigate via structure.
635.po: On benchmark tests of multimodal document QA, DMAP improves retrieval accuracy, makes reasoning more consistent, and reduces hallucination (inventing facts). Practical benefit: a system can now answer nuanced questions about complex documents (research papers, contracts, manuals) more reliably than flat-search baselines.

636.bp: Email marketing at scale—sending millions of personalized messages to the right people at the right time—requires optimizing for multiple goals simultaneously: the business wants engagement, users want relevant content, and resource constraints mean you can't send to everyone or send infinitely.
636.wh: Standard machine learning for recommendations learns what each user likes, but it doesn't handle the constraints (budget, frequency caps, fairness) or the exploration–exploitation tradeoff (show users exactly what they like, or risk missing new preferences?). A pure LP solver can handle constraints but doesn't learn from data.
636.ap: BanditLP combines two pieces: neural Thompson Sampling (a learning algorithm that explores intelligently while learning what works) generates predictions about how each user will respond to each email. A large-scale linear program then solves which emails to send given budget and fairness constraints, at web scale (billions of variables).
636.ww: By decoupling learning (the neural model) from decision-making (the LP solver), BanditLP avoids the brittleness of end-to-end systems. The learning piece improves over time; the solver ensures constraints are always met. The two work together: solver learns which constraints matter most (e.g., fairness vs. revenue).
636.po: Deployed in LinkedIn's email system, BanditLP increases business wins—users open more emails, act on them, and stay engaged longer—while respecting delivery constraints and user preferences. Testing shows consistent gains over simpler methods that either ignore exploration or ignore constraints.

637.bp: AI systems today are reactive: they respond to inputs (questions, images) but don't truly understand the world they're operating in. For AI to collaborate with humans on important decisions—healthcare, education, policy—it needs to reason about cause and effect, goals, emotions, and social norms.
637.wh: Predicting the next word in text or the next pixel in an image doesn't require understanding. But explaining *why* a medical treatment might fail, or why a policy could harm vulnerable groups, requires internal models of physical processes (time, space, causality, action) and human psychology (intentions, beliefs, emotions, values). Current systems lack both.
637.ap: Cognitive World Modeling integrates two models: physical (how the world works—objects move, time flows, actions have effects) and mental (how people think—goals, beliefs, emotional states, social obligations). Together, they form a persistent, evolving representation of reality as humans experience it.
637.ww: An AI with accurate models of physics *and* psychology can reason about consequences—not just predict them. It can say "this action prevents harm to people who care about X" rather than just outputting a recommended action. This reasoning enables explanation, planning, and genuine collaboration.
637.po: Such systems could serve as more trustworthy advisors: they can explain trade-offs, adapt to user values, and predict unintended consequences. Alignment and safety emerge naturally when systems reason about human meaning and context, not as post-hoc patches. This sets a research direction for the next phase of AI development.

638.bp: Predicting the future—whether server load, traffic flow, or website hits—is essential for planning infrastructure and managing resources. Time series forecasting (predicting the next values in a sequence of measurements over time) is a core challenge across the web.
638.wh: Existing methods treat each time step like an independent symbol in text (a token), which works for language but breaks for time series. Time series have structure: today's traffic relates not just to yesterday's, but also to the same hour last week. Treating each time step independently destroys this multi-offset structure, forcing the model to rediscover it from scratch.
638.ap: Time-TK proposes a new embedding method (MOTE) that respects time series structure: instead of encoding each time step independently, it encodes multiple time steps together, capturing patterns that span across different offsets (e.g., hourly vs. weekly cycles). It then feeds these structured embeddings to a novel architecture combining Transformers with Kolmogorov-Arnold networks.
638.ww: By preserving fine-grained temporal dependencies in the embedding, MOTE reduces information loss early in the pipeline. This means the model doesn't have to reverse-engineer weekly patterns from a jumbled stream of isolated tokens; it sees the structure immediately.
638.po: Time-TK outperforms existing methods on web forecasting tasks: predicting traffic spikes, server load, and system throughput. The MOTE embedding is plug-and-play, so it improves any existing forecasting architecture, making it useful for practitioners across different web systems.

639.bp: E-commerce and video platforms constantly introduce new items (products, videos). Recommending these to users is hard because there's no history of who liked them. A new pair of shoes might be perfect for someone, but the system has no way to know because no one has rated it yet.
639.wh: The obvious approach—"find similar users and recommend items they liked"—fails here because it relies on interaction history. With new items, there's nothing to measure similarity against. And not all users are equally helpful: a user who liked three ancient products may not predict current tastes.
639.ap: SuperG first identifies users with truly similar preferences (not just co-viewing history) by examining deep behavioral patterns and multimodal content features. Then it retrieves specifically the informative behaviors: the past actions from similar users that actually predict good future recommendations, filtering out noisy or outdated signals.
639.ww: By disentangling "who is similar to me" from "which of their actions should I learn from," SuperG avoids two traps: spurious neighbors (users who happened to click the same things by coincidence) and uninformative behaviors (old actions that no longer reflect current taste). This two-step filtering surfaces the signal.
639.po: On multi-modal new item recommendation tasks, SuperG outperforms baselines that use simpler similarity metrics or treat all historical behaviors equally. Platforms can now recommend new products or videos more accurately, especially in fast-moving categories where items constantly refresh.

640.bp: Knowledge graphs encode facts over time: "Person X worked at Company Y from 2015–2020." Predicting future facts—"Person X will move to Company Z"—helps systems stay current and fill in missing information.
640.wh: Real knowledge graphs have two layers: individual relationships (local) and long-range patterns (global). A person's job moves show local evolution (one job leads to the next) but also global patterns (tech industry → startup → venture capital is a common path). Most methods capture one or the other, rarely both effectively.
640.ap: DHHGN models both simultaneously: a hybrid hypergraph-graph network captures local patterns (how entities near each other evolve) and high-order dependencies (longer paths that matter). For global history, it selectively boosts attention to pivotal historical facts while still integrating all context, using a gating mechanism to balance local and global signals.
640.ww: High-order dependencies reveal which long-range patterns matter (a 3-hop path in the graph might predict the next fact better than a direct connection). By explicitly modeling these higher-order relationships and adaptively weighting global facts, the system avoids both myopia (ignoring history) and distraction (being confused by irrelevant old facts).
640.po: On standard benchmarks for temporal KG reasoning, DHHGN improves prediction accuracy by capturing subtle patterns that simpler methods miss. Practical benefit: systems can now forecast missing facts more accurately, useful for maintaining up-to-date knowledge bases in enterprise settings.

641.bp: The brain processes information efficiently by sending sparse electrical pulses (spikes), not continuous signals. Spiking neural networks mimic this, using binary signals instead of floating-point numbers, consuming far less power and computation. But spikes sacrifice expressiveness—you lose information compared to real-valued signals.
641.wh: Applying spiking networks to graph data (networks of connected entities) is doubly hard: graphs have irregular structure (nodes have different numbers of neighbors), and spiking signals are binary (on or off). Existing spiking graph networks either add so many real-valued operations that they lose efficiency, or stay so simple that they can't express complex patterns.
641.ap: E2SGNN uses two ideas: dual-scale modulation (global and local real-valued adjustments) applied within the spiking computation, preserving binary efficiency while improving expressiveness. It also adaptively customizes the number of time steps each graph needs based on how complex the data is—simple graphs run fast, complex ones get more time.
641.ww: By modulating within the spike mechanism rather than adding extra layers, E2SGNN keeps the core efficiency gain (addition-only, low latency) while gaining expressiveness. Adaptive latency means no unnecessary computation on easy data, so efficiency scales with problem difficulty.
641.po: E2SGNN efficiently analyzes graph data (social networks, citation graphs, molecular structures) with lower power consumption and latency than traditional graph neural networks, while maintaining competitive accuracy. Useful for edge devices, real-time systems, and large-scale graph processing where computation is expensive.

642.bp: Recommender systems use online experiments (showing different users different things, measuring which ones click) to pick winners. Before deploying a new recommendation algorithm, teams use off-policy evaluation: testing it on historical data without running live experiments, saving time and risk.
642.wh: Off-policy evaluation is tricky. Historical data is biased toward what the old system recommended, so naive evaluation will favor the old system. The inverse propensity score (IPS) method corrects for this bias mathematically, but it's sensitive to randomness: change the random seed or simulation parameters, and conclusions flip.
642.ap: This paper revisits IPS and its variants, testing them not just on synthetic data (controlled experiments) but on real-world logs from the Open Bandit Dataset. It examines how rankings of different methods change with random seeds, sample size, and details of how the historical data was generated.
642.ww: Real data breaks clean mathematical assumptions. Logs aren't i.i.d. (independent and identically distributed)—users who see similar recommendations might behave alike, violating independence. Understanding these violations is crucial because they're what actually causes IPS and its variants to fail in practice.
642.po: The paper shows that seemingly minor choices (random seed, log generator) dramatically shift which estimator looks best, highlighting that off-policy evaluation results are fragile. Practitioners should be cautious about trusting off-policy rankings on a single dataset; validating on multiple data sources and logging strategies is essential.

643.bp: Recommending videos, products, or songs requires fusing multiple types of information: what the item looks like (images, text), what the user's past behavior shows, and what other users liked. Multimodal sequential recommendation (tracking user preferences over time across modalities) is a core problem in modern e-commerce.
643.wh: Simply combining modalities (adding them up or concatenating them) misses synergy: the combination of music genre and album artwork creates a signal stronger than either alone. Also, different users care about different modality combinations: one user picks albums by cover art, another by genre tags.
643.ap: PRISM explicitly decomposes multimodal information into three parts: unique (signals only one modality provides), redundant (signals all modalities agree on), and synergistic (signals that emerge only from combinations). It learns personalized weights for these components based on user history, so each user gets a fusion tuned to their preferences.
643.ww: Synergy isn't noise—it's real signal that naive fusion misses. By explicitly modeling it separately, PRISM can weight it appropriately (some users rely heavily on synergy, others ignore it). This disentanglement also improves interpretability: you can see which modality combinations matter for which users.
643.po: On four recommendation datasets and three different sequence models, PRISM improves accuracy and works as a plug-and-play module. Systems can now recommend more accurately by understanding that certain users are swayed by combinations of features, not just individual signals.

644.bp: On platforms like Amazon or Alibaba, users both search (typing queries) and browse (viewing recommended items). These channels show different intents: a search for "wireless headphones" is explicit, while clicking a recommended shoe is implicit preference. Unifying these signals improves both search and recommendations.
644.wh: The catch is that search intent and browsing intent often diverge (a user searches for work clothes but browsing history shows fashion interests), and improving one task with unified modeling can hurt the other because they compete for model capacity. Static approaches to sharing knowledge break this balance.
644.ap: MinSAR uses VQ-VAE (a method that compresses information into discrete tokens) to fuse long-term user preferences and short-term contextual behavior into a unified interest representation that bridges search (explicit) and browsing (implicit). A separate attention network then dynamically allocates shared knowledge and task-specific expertise based on this unified interest.
644.ww: By generating a unified interest representation from both signals, MinSAR creates a common ground where search and recommendation can be co-optimized without conflict. The attention network ensures each task gets the shared knowledge it needs while preserving task-specific skills—no more zero-sum tradeoffs.
644.po: On two real-world datasets (Kuai marketplace and Amazon Kindle Store), MinSAR improves both search accuracy and recommendation diversity simultaneously, avoiding the typical degradation when joint-optimizing. Platforms can now leverage cross-scenario user signals more effectively, improving experience in both channels.

645.bp: Large language models now drive everything from customer support to content moderation, but they only work when their outputs match what people actually want. To make them safe and useful, companies use human feedback to steer the model toward good behavior—the foundational technique behind modern AI assistants.
645.wh: The paper finds that roughly 25% of preference pairs show clear inconsistencies—the reward model's judgment conflicts with the human label. When you train on such contradictions, the model learns to chase both goals at once, which leaves it confused and under-aligned.
645.ap: AlignCP assigns a confidence score to each training example based on how strongly the reward model agrees with itself, and a polarity score based on whether the reward model's ranking matches the original human label. Examples with high confidence and matching polarity get full weight; low-confidence or mismatched examples get downweighted or dropped entirely. The framework automates all of this without asking humans to re-label.
645.ww: By trusting examples the reward model already approves of and ignoring the contradictory ones, the learning signal becomes cleaner. The model trains on a curated set of examples that all point in the same direction, like focusing a camera lens on a clear image instead of an out-of-focus one.
645.po: The paper shows this noise-aware reweighting improves model alignment on standard benchmarks—the model generates outputs that better match human preferences. Since preference quality is the bottleneck in deploying safe language models, this directly improves real-world safety and usefulness at scale.

646.bp: Networks of connected entities—social networks, computer systems, sensor arrays—contain both normal nodes that behave like their neighbors and anomalies that stand out. Detecting these anomalies (fraud, system failures, intrusions) is critical, but it's expensive to scan huge graphs and hard when the notion of 'normal' changes from one node or category to another.
646.wh: Most graph anomaly detection assumes all nodes follow the same pattern: normal nodes cluster with similar neighbors, anomalies break that pattern. But in reality, some nodes naturally sit in homogeneous neighborhoods (like a bank teller surrounded by other bank employees) while others sit in diverse ones (like a tourist in many countries). A fixed approach that assumes one pattern misses anomalies in the diverse case and flags false alarms in the homogeneous one.
646.ap: SAGAD precomputes embeddings that capture both low-frequency patterns (what its neighbors look like) and high-frequency patterns (unique properties of this node). It then uses a fusion mechanism that adapts per-node, deciding whether to trust the neighborhood similarity signal or the node's own distinct features based on the node's local structure. A separate loss guides anomalies to retain more of their unique high-frequency information than normal nodes do.
646.ww: Anomalies often hide in diverse neighborhoods or have unusual features that don't match their surroundings. By letting the system adaptively choose between neighborhood-based and feature-based signals for each node, and by encouraging anomalies to preserve their unusual features, the method respects that 'deviant' can mean different things in different parts of the graph.
646.po: The paper reports that SAGAD detects anomalies across multiple benchmark graphs while using far less memory and compute than prior methods—linear time and space complexity. This scalability matters because real graphs have millions or billions of nodes, and the per-node adaptivity catches anomalies that fixed-threshold methods miss.

647.bp: Converting English questions into SQL queries is how millions of people query databases every day without writing code. Large language models have gotten quite good at this, but the SQL they generate often breaks: it might have a typo, misunderstand the table structure, or silently compute the wrong result. Catching and explaining these errors before they reach users is essential.
647.wh: Existing error detection methods are slow (they require human review or expensive AI model calls) and they don't explain what went wrong. When a model says 'this SQL is broken,' it doesn't tell you whether it's a syntax error, a logic flaw, or a schema mismatch—so a user can't fix it. The real challenge is generating high-quality training data for an error detector, because manually labeling all the ways SQL can fail is prohibitively expensive.
647.ap: SQL-Checker first catalogs the common error types (like table mismatch, join mistake, aggregation error). It then uses a data synthesis pipeline: start with a base SQL statement, inject one of these known errors, and ask a large language model to analyze the error in detail. For complex cases, it refines the analysis iteratively, asking the model to critique its own earlier explanation. This creates a dataset of errors paired with interpretable labels describing the root cause.
647.ww: By simulating realistic errors methodically and having the language model explain each one, the training data covers the error space in a structured way—far better than random coverage. The model learns to recognize both that an error exists and what kind of error it is, building genuine understanding rather than just pattern matching.
647.po: The paper shows SQL-Checker achieves state-of-the-art error detection on multiple benchmarks and, when added to an existing text-to-SQL pipeline, improves the execution accuracy of SQL queries. Users and downstream systems see fewer broken queries and when an error is flagged, they get a meaningful explanation of what failed.

648.bp: Graphs—networks of connected data like social networks or knowledge bases—are intellectual property and need protection. When someone creates a valuable knowledge graph or social network, they need a way to prove they own it and detect if someone has stolen or tampered with it, much like a watermark on a document.
648.wh: Watermarking a graph is much harder than watermarking an image or document. You can't just hide a bit pattern in the structure because modifying the watermark slightly risks destroying the whole graph's utility. Also, hidden messages in graph structure get tangled up with the actual relationships the graph represents, making it hard to extract the watermark without corrupting the data.
648.ap: DRGW learns separate representations: one captures the structural topology (how nodes connect) and another holds the watermark (the proof of ownership). It uses an adversarially trained encoder that stays stable even when the graph gets perturbed, and an invertible neural network that can embed and extract the watermark without losing information. A structure-aware editor translates the watermark back into actual graph modifications, so the embedded watermark survives realistic changes to the graph.
648.ww: By separating structure from watermark signal, each can be optimized independently. The structural representation stays robust to damage because it's trained against adversarial perturbations. The invertible network guarantees no information loss during embedding, so the watermark always comes back cleanly. This separation is the key: you can protect ownership without entangling it with the graph's actual meaning.
648.po: The paper demonstrates that DRGW's watermarks survive structural attacks (node deletions, edge flips) and remain extractable, while preserving the original graph's utility. This enables graph datasets to be published or shared with cryptographic proof of provenance—critical for protecting research and industrial knowledge graphs.

649.bp: People share personal information constantly: health data on fitness apps, location on maps, shopping history on social media. Each individual disclosure seems low-risk, but an adversary who watches across time and combines fragments from many sources builds an increasingly accurate profile. The real privacy risk is cumulative, not instantaneous.
649.wh: Most privacy models treat each disclosure as independent—lock down one thing and you're done. But they miss the aggregation threat: an adversary can piece together information over weeks or months. Also, both the user and the adversary learn and adapt: if a user sees their data was misused, they share less next time; if an adversary realizes the user is guarding something, they try a different angle. These dynamics are hard to model with standard game theory.
649.ap: The paper formulates continual information sharing as a dynamic Stackelberg game (a sequential game where the user decides first, then the adversary responds, then the user adapts, and so on). The user's goal is to balance sharing enough data to get utility (like personalized recommendations) while keeping cumulative exposure low. The game captures both players' beliefs about what the other will do next, and both adapt their strategies over time.
649.ww: By modeling it as a sequential game with learning, the framework captures the real interplay: users rationally reveal less if they see patterns of misuse, and adversaries rationally focus on gathering info over time rather than one big exploit. This matches how privacy actually works in practice—as a dynamic negotiation, not a one-shot decision.
649.po: The paper presents a reinforcement learning algorithm that computes approximately optimal sharing strategies for users, and demonstrates on real-world datasets that following these strategies significantly reduces the cumulative privacy risk compared to static or reactive approaches.

650.bp: Social networks and collaborator graphs often store edge weights: how frequently two people interact, or how strongly they're connected. These weights should help partition the network into communities, but they also come with noise and storage costs. A smart clustering should clean up the noise and only store weights that actually matter.
650.wh: Edge weights can mean very different things in different parts of the graph, and they introduce noise—a weight might be inflated by a one-time spike or an artifact of how the data was collected. If you just add raw weights to a clustering algorithm, you risk either blowing up memory usage on large graphs or letting noisy edges mislead the clustering. Few methods jointly optimize both the clustering and the edge weights themselves.
650.ap: The paper proposes a graph contraction module that removes less important nodes while preserving the structural information needed for clustering (like key hub nodes), reducing the graph size. It then learns an attention weight for each edge that scales down noisy connections. An edge-weight-aware network fuses this cleaned-up information to find clusters, and a special loss encourages this process by making anomalies (noise-prone edges) carry less weight.
650.ww: Shrinking the graph first reduces noise exposure and memory use. By learning which edges are noisy and downweighting them adaptively, the clustering algorithm works with a cleaner signal. The joint optimization means edge weights improve specifically for the clustering task, not for some generic reconstruction objective.
650.po: The paper shows on real weighted graphs that this approach outperforms baselines at finding tight, meaningful clusters, while also reducing memory footprint and training time—practical benefits for clustering large social networks or collaboration graphs.

651.bp: Mapping services like Baidu Maps or Google Maps answer millions of queries every day: 'Find me a restaurant near the train station' or 'Show me the hospital hours.' Large language models can understand these queries, but they only work well when connected to the right data sources (APIs)—like a restaurant database or a hospital directory—and knowing which API to call requires manual engineering.
651.wh: As user queries diversify, the set of APIs needed grows constantly. Manually discovering which new APIs solve which kinds of questions, then writing the code to call them and training the AI model to use them, is slow and expensive. Automating this requires both understanding what the user actually wants (extracting the intent) and finding or designing the right API for it—two hard problems in tandem.
651.ap: ARADD uses a multi-stage pipeline: first, a language model and a lightweight agent work together to extract each new user intent (what the person really needs). Second, the system identifies existing APIs that could serve that intent, or designs new ones. Third, it generates training examples (question-answer pairs) automatically by having the model explain how to use each API. A self-guided refinement loop polishes the low-quality examples.
651.ww: By having the model generate its own explanations of how APIs work, and then filtering out the explanations it's uncertain about, the system bootstraps training data without human labelers. Iterative refinement catches errors the model made in earlier rounds. The intent-extraction stage ensures you're solving the real user need, not just surface-level keywords.
651.po: The paper describes ARADD deployed at Baidu (a real-world service), discovering new APIs from user queries and integrating them into the AI Guide service. This automation reduces manual labor and biases in API selection, letting the system scale to handle diverse user intents.

652.bp: Biomedical researchers use meta-analyses to synthesize evidence from hundreds of papers on a treatment or disease. They manually read each paper's full text to extract key details: what population was studied, what intervention was tested, what outcomes were measured (PIO elements). This screening process is the bottleneck—with thousands of new papers published monthly, it's impossible to keep up.
652.wh: Automating this with simpler methods (binary classifiers that just filter papers) still requires human review of thousands of results. Summarization models often hallucinate or omit details, because they're trained on general text, not on medical papers where precision is critical. The challenge is extracting structured PIO elements accurately while scaling to handle large volumes.
652.ap: The pipeline segments PDF papers into semantic chunks (using XML structure), then feeds these to a large language model with adaptive prompting: complex chunks get detailed, multi-step prompts; simple ones get direct prompts. The model generates multiple candidate summaries of the PIO elements, then a consensus filter (looking for agreement across candidates) produces a single high-confidence summary.
652.ww: By breaking the paper into semantic units first, the model processes manageable pieces rather than overwhelming context. Adaptive prompting matches the prompting strategy to the difficulty—don't over-engineer simple passages. The consensus filter acts like human review but automatically: if multiple independent model runs agree, the output is likely right; if they disagree, the filter can flag it for human review.
652.po: The paper shows an 8-billion-parameter model with this pipeline achieves semantic precision above 0.88 and recall above 0.91 on the EBM-NLP benchmark, matching much larger models. Human expert review confirms the extracted PIO elements are factually accurate, making this practical for accelerating meta-analysis screening.

653.bp: Banks and financial institutions collect detailed transaction and customer data, but strict privacy regulations (like GDPR) limit how they can share or analyze it. Synthetic data—artificially generated datasets that preserve statistical patterns without revealing real individuals—is a potential solution. But synthetic financial data is hard: transactions are rare events (most customers aren't committing fraud), attributes are mixed (categorical account type, continuous transaction amount), and the privacy guarantees are unclear.
653.wh: Existing synthetic data generators (like GANs or autoencoders) were designed for balanced, homogeneous datasets. Financial data violates both: it has severe class imbalance (99%+ normal transactions) and mixed data types. Standard generators either fail on imbalanced data or create synthetic datasets that preserve utility poorly. And if you want formal privacy guarantees, you must adapt the generator implementation—but few papers study whether that adaptation even works in the financial domain.
653.ap: The paper compares several generator architectures (autoencoders, GANs, diffusion models, copula methods) on financial datasets, and proposes privacy-preserving versions of GAN and autoencoder generators. It evaluates each on three dimensions: data quality (does synthetic data look like real data?), downstream task utility (can you train a classifier on synthetic data and use it on real data?), and privacy (how close is the synthetic data to the real data?).
653.ww: By comparing multiple generators and measuring quality/utility/privacy together, the paper shows which trade-offs are unavoidable and which aren't. Privacy-preserving implementations (like differential privacy) usually hurt utility, so understanding the exact trade-off curve is essential for choosing a generator for a specific use case.
653.po: The paper provides empirical guidance on which generators work best for financial data given different privacy-utility preferences. This helps financial institutions decide whether synthetic data can safely replace or augment real data for analysis, a critical decision given regulatory constraints.

654.bp: Graph foundation models are neural networks trained on massive graphs (billions of nodes and edges) to learn general-purpose representations that transfer to new tasks. They're the graph equivalent of models like BERT for text. But they try to compress the entire knowledge of a huge graph into model parameters—which is like memorizing an encyclopedia inside your brain instead of using a library.
654.wh: Compressing all graph knowledge into parameters creates three problems: there's simply not enough capacity for large graphs (semantic loss), different parts of the graph have conflicting patterns (parameter conflicts), and when you want to adapt the model to a new task or graph, the compressed knowledge is tangled up with the task-specific learning, making adaptation harder.
654.ap: RAG-GFM separates the compressed knowledge (what stays in the model) from the full knowledge (stored in retrieval databases). It builds two external stores: a semantic store of text descriptions of nodes and relationships, and a structural store of important subgraph patterns (motifs). When the model processes a graph, it retrieves relevant text and motifs from these stores as context, using a dual-view loss that makes sure both the semantic and structural retrieved information align with the task.
654.ww: By keeping the full graph knowledge external, the model can learn task-specific patterns without lossy compression. Retrieval gives it access to all the graph information it needs without storing it in parameters. The model learns what to retrieve (routing) and how much to retrieve (depth), making adaptation more flexible and interpretable—you can see what graph context it used for each decision.
654.po: The paper shows RAG-GFM outperforms 13 prior models on node and graph classification tasks across five benchmarks. The external knowledge store also improves interpretability—you can explain model decisions by pointing to the retrieved context—and enables more efficient domain adaptation to new graphs.

655.bp: Multimodal sentiment analysis reads text, looks at images, and hears audio in videos to understand emotion and opinion. A sarcastic tweet ('I *love* waiting in traffic') needs both the text and visual context (e.g., a frustrated emoji or gesture) to get the sentiment right. This is how humans understand nuance, and it's how systems should too.
655.wh: Most methods extract features from each mode (text, image, audio) separately and then combine them. But this misses fine-grained, local cross-modal interactions: a specific word paired with a specific gesture carries sentiment that neither the word nor the gesture alone can convey. Existing global fusion approaches smooth over these fine details, and aligning information across modes without losing local richness is technically hard.
655.ap: CCAF builds two alignment and fusion pathways: a coarse-grained one that aligns and fuses global patterns (overall sentiment of the post), and a fine-grained one that aligns and fuses local cross-modal interactions (word-gesture pairs, specific facial expressions tied to words). It uses optimal transport to align information across modalities at both levels, gated attention to fuse the aligned signals, and learnable sentiment prototypes to filter out redundant information at each level.
655.ww: By explicitly capturing both global and local cross-modal signals, the method doesn't lose nuance. Optimal transport respects the geometry of how different modalities relate (semantic distance between text features and visual features), so alignment is meaningful, not arbitrary. The prototype-based filtering learns what sentiment information matters and what's noise.
655.po: The paper reports that CCAF achieves superior results on two multimodal sentiment datasets, capturing sarcasm and nuanced emotion better than prior coarse-only or local-only methods. This improves sentiment analysis on social media and video content where emotional nuance is everything.

656.bp: Search engines rank documents in response to a query, and we want to know: is this ranking good? The same question comes up in evaluating recommendation systems, LLM re-rankers, and answer generation. We use ground-truth labels (what are the truly relevant documents?) to measure how well a ranking performs—but our labels are almost never complete, and we need a metric that accounts for that uncertainty.
656.wh: A naive metric would give equal weight to every position in the ranking—but users almost never scroll past the first few results. Position 1 matters much more than position 100. We could use a fixed weight scheme (position 1 gets weight 1, position 2 gets weight 0.5, etc.), but then the scheme's choice becomes arbitrary. Also, if your ground truth labels are incomplete, a metric that assumes completeness will mislead you.
656.ap: Rank-biased measurement assigns weights to ranks using a geometric distribution: weight falls off geometrically as you go deeper in the ranking (position 1 gets full weight, position 2 gets 0.8×, position 3 gets 0.64×, etc., where the decay factor is a tunable parameter). This is mathematically principled: it sums to a finite total (unlike other schemes), and it models a plausible user browsing behavior (each position has a constant probability the user will look further).
656.ww: The geometric weighting both matches how users actually browse (they stop looking after a few results) and is mathematically elegant (finite sum, interpretable parameter). The bounded sum means you can meaningfully compare rankings of different lengths. The parameter lets you tune how much you care about top positions (set it high to focus on top-1, set it low to care more about deeper results).
656.po: The paper (presented as a keynote) reviews rank-biased precision and its variants, showing how to properly measure ranking quality in web search, information retrieval, and LLM re-ranking tasks, and how to account for incomplete ground truth. This theoretical foundation underpins modern search evaluation.

657.bp: Knowledge graphs store facts in a structured form: 'Albert Einstein studied_at University of Zurich,' where entities (Einstein, the university) are linked by relations (studied_at). Real-world knowledge graphs often have images, descriptions, or other media tied to entities. Learning numeric vectors (embeddings) that represent these entities and relations is fundamental to knowledge graph reasoning, but adding image and text data makes it much harder.
657.wh: Standard embedding methods assume all entities have the same type of data or ignore modalities separately. A real knowledge graph might have an image for one artist but not for another, rich text for a company but minimal data for a person. Cross-modal alignment (making sure the image and text for the same entity point to the same latent concept) is needed, but it's hard to enforce when modalities are sparse or misaligned in content.
657.ap: VL-KGE combines vision-language models (pre-trained on pairs of images and text) with the structured reasoning of knowledge graphs. For each entity, it uses the VLM to align its available modalities (image and/or text) into a shared embedding space. The graph structure (which entities connect to which) is then learned alongside this multimodal alignment, ensuring that the final embeddings preserve both the cross-modal relationships and the graph structure.
657.ww: Vision-language models have already learned how images and text concepts relate to each other, so leveraging that pre-learned alignment is better than learning alignment from scratch on sparse graph data. By aligning modalities first and then learning graph structure, the entity embeddings capture both semantic meaning (from the media) and relational meaning (from the graph).
657.po: The paper shows VL-KGE improves link prediction (predicting missing facts) on standard benchmarks and on two new fine-art knowledge graphs. The multimodal embeddings are more robust and better transfer to downstream tasks than unimodal embeddings, making knowledge graphs with mixed media much more useful.

658.bp: Dialogue systems like ChatGPT need to remember long conversations: what the user asked 50 turns ago, preferences mentioned earlier, decisions made together. Without memory, each turn starts from scratch. With good long-term memory, the system can refer back, avoid repetition, and give personalized responses that feel continuous.
658.wh: Simple approaches (storing everything and searching it) are slow and wastes space on redundant details. Other methods (summarizing the history) lose important details and often hallucinate. The real problem is that users ask about different things—sometimes they want factual recall ('what restaurant did I mention?'), sometimes they want emotional continuity ('remember when I was frustrated?'), sometimes they want patterns ('I like spicy food'). A one-size-fits-all memory strategy fails.
658.ap: HingeMem uses event boundaries (moments where the topic, location, person, or time changes) to structure memory. When a boundary is crossed, the current event is 'written' to memory as a record tied to those four elements. At retrieval time, the system adapts: it estimates what type of information the current query needs, then routes to the relevant element-indexed records and decides how much to retrieve (shallow recall for simple questions, deep for complex ones).
658.ww: Boundaries reduce redundancy: you write once per event change, not after every turn. Element-based indexing (person, time, location, topic) lets you retrieve what's relevant without scanning the whole history. Adaptive routing respects that different queries need different amounts of memory—'who did I meet?' needs deep retrieval of person elements, while 'what time is it?' needs almost none.
658.po: The paper shows HingeMem achieves 20% better performance on the LOCOMO dialogue benchmark across models from 0.6B to production scale, while reducing computational cost by 68% compared to baselines. This makes long-context dialogues practical for resource-constrained settings.

659.bp: Real-world events don't happen at regular intervals: hospital patient vital signs change unpredictably, financial transactions cluster around payday, tweets spike when news breaks. Modeling these asynchronous sequences is crucial for healthcare, finance, social networks, and anomaly detection. The right model captures not just what events happen, but when and how they influence future events.
659.wh: Classical point process models (like Hawkes processes) assume parametric forms for how past events influence future ones (typically, exponential decay). This is too rigid for complex, real data. Modern neural approaches (RNNs, Transformers) are more flexible but computationally expensive: they need to scan all past events, creating quadratic complexity. Also, Transformers suffer from attention saturation—after seeing many events, the model struggles to attend to the most relevant ones.
659.ap: The paper introduces Mamba Hawkes Process (MHP), which combines Mamba (a recent state space model with linear complexity) with temporal point process theory. State space models maintain a hidden state that evolves over time, where each new event updates the state via an input-dependent gate. MHP adds time-aware mechanisms: the state transition rate adapts to the event type and history, and a separate mechanism scales time intervals to account for heterogeneous event dynamics.
659.ww: State space models achieve linear complexity by processing events sequentially without storing all pairwise interactions. Mamba's input-dependent gating naturally captures which past events matter (the 'selective' part), avoiding the attention saturation problem. By adding time-scaling and dual-channel state transitions, MHP respects that events in different domains (healthcare vs. finance) have different temporal patterns.
659.po: The paper shows MHP generalizes classical Hawkes processes (proving theoretical recovery of exponential-decay models) while also outperforming RNN and Transformer baselines on benchmark event sequences. The linear complexity enables practical forecasting on long, real-world event sequences.

660.bp: Amazon and other marketplaces use a single featured storefront slot—the Buy Box—to show shoppers which seller to buy from. When Amazon removes the Buy Box, it's like turning off the lights on a seller's shop. Since 98% of sales flow through this single slot, losing it devastates a seller's visibility and sales.
660.wh: The Buy Box isn't removed for just one reason. It could vanish because of competitor price changes, or because seller offers changed, or some mix of both. Separating these causes requires real-time data that didn't exist before.
660.ap: The researchers built their own data collection system to watch products hourly for eight weeks and open-sourced both the dataset and the code. For each product, they logged whether the Buy Box was present and what prices all competitors were charging. This let them see whether suppression happened right after a price change or competitor action.
660.ww: By watching suppression events happen in real time and comparing them to what changed just before, the researchers could see which triggers actually mattered. If suppression always followed one specific type of offer change, that change was likely the cause. Their real-time lens revealed that offer changes on Amazon itself were the main culprit, not rival prices.
660.po: The paper documents what happens when suppression hits: sellers lose search visibility instantly, ads disappear within 12 hours, and sales rankings drop 12% in two days. But the data also shows competitor prices don't shift—meaning the suppression isn't being used as a price discipline tool. The work exposes a crucial governance mechanism in marketplaces that directly harms sellers but flew under the radar until now.

661.bp: People are increasingly trusting AI chatbots (LLMs) with sensitive questions and decisions in web apps. But attackers can trick these systems into ignoring their safety rules and generating harmful content—misinformation, illegal instructions, or hateful speech. Keeping these systems secure is becoming a matter of public trust.
661.wh: Safety defenses look at the full prompt and the full response to spot danger. But no one had tried scattering harmful content across space—meaning breaking the request into pieces spread far apart in the input, or spreading dangerous phrases throughout the output in ways that look disconnected.
661.ap: The researchers developed SpatialJB, which spreads harmful content fragments across space in the prompt or response so that traditional safety checkers miss the pattern. They also built SpatialD, a detector that looks at the spatial layout of model outputs to spot when fragments cluster back together into harmful content.
661.ww: Safety systems are trained to detect dangerous content when it's concentrated and obvious. If the same harmful idea is broken into pieces spread across a longer text, the detector might miss it because each piece alone looks innocuous. The system can't easily tell that scattered fragments form a dangerous message.
661.po: SpatialJB beats widely-used attacks by 7x (95% success on GPT-4 vs. ~13% for Base64 encoding). Current guardrails catch less than 12% of spatial attacks, showing the method slips past defenses. The paper also offers SpatialD, a counter-defense, and demonstrates the attack works across GPT, Qwen, and other commercial systems deployed in real web apps.

662.bp: Self-driving cars need to see everything around them to avoid crashes. A single car's camera and sensors can only see a limited distance and angle. If nearby vehicles could share what they see, every car would know about hazards beyond its own line of sight, like a truck hidden behind a building.
662.wh: Even if cars could share data, they'd still struggle to understand the full scene because the perspective is fragmented. One car sees the front of a pedestrian, another sees the back. Merging these partial views into one accurate picture is hard without global information.
662.ap: Octopus uses roadside units (stationary computers at the road's edge) as a hub. Vehicles send their sensor data only to the nearby roadside unit, not to each other. The roadside unit processes all the data together, builds a global picture of what's happening, and sends refined results back to each vehicle.
662.ww: A central hub (roadside unit) is much more efficient than cars talking to each other. One stream from each car goes to one place, where it's combined once, instead of N cars each sending to N other cars. The global picture built at the hub gives each vehicle context about the whole scene, which they can use to refine their own understanding.
662.po: Octopus cuts communication by 5,514 times compared to existing methods while improving detection accuracy by 11.58% in precision and 12.74% in recall. Vehicles get better awareness of their surroundings faster because the roadside unit's global view acts as prior knowledge, helping each car fill gaps in what it can see directly.

663.bp: The web is drowning in unstructured text—research papers, business documents, social media. This text contains knowledge (who did what, which countries border which, what causes what), but computers can't easily reason over loose prose. If we could automatically turn unstructured text into structured knowledge graphs, we could enable search engines, reasoning systems, and AI tools to work much more precisely.
663.wh: The challenge isn't just finding entities and relationships. Real documents also have events (what happened when), spatial-temporal information (where and when), visual layouts (images, tables), and metadata (author, date). Stitching these together into a coherent graph while keeping information accurate is complex.
663.ap: This tutorial covers the full pipeline: entity and relation extraction (pulling structured facts from text), event extraction, spatio-temporal indexing, visual layout parsing, and metadata handling. It then discusses how to build knowledge graphs by combining all these pieces and curating them for quality. Finally, it explores hybrid approaches that use LLMs to assist humans in knowledge engineering rather than replacing them entirely.
663.ww: Each part of the pipeline builds on the previous one. Accurate entities allow relations to be placed correctly. Events need time-place context to make sense. Combining LLM speed with human oversight (rather than trusting LLMs alone) creates graphs that are both scalable and factually reliable. This layered approach trades off speed for accuracy.
663.po: The tutorial describes a paradigm shift: from purely supervised models (slow, require data) to LLM-assisted engineering (faster, more flexible). It lays out what's possible with current tools—semantic search, reasoning pipelines, grounded dialogue—and identifies open challenges: scaling beyond pilot projects, ensuring all facts are verifiable, and measuring quality when the ground truth is ambiguous.

664.bp: Recommending products to users is hard when you have millions of items. To help the recommendation system learn what users like, it needs examples of items they didn't like. Picking which items to use as "negative examples" affects both how fast the system learns and what kinds of mistakes it makes.
664.wh: Existing methods only score negatives from a small random sample of all items, so they might miss important negative examples. They also apply the same strategy throughout training, even though the model's needs change as it learns.
664.ap: R2NS uses three phases. First, warm-start: train with easy (random) negatives to build basic capability. Second, global recall: search across all items to find hard negatives that the model specifically struggles with, not just the top-ranked ones. Third, curriculum re-ranking: gradually increase difficulty as training progresses, like a tutor making tests harder as students improve.
664.ww: A gradual difficulty ramp prevents the model from getting stuck early (when it can't handle hard negatives) while pushing it to improve later. Searching the whole item space for hard negatives means the model sees examples that matter—items it confuses with the user's true preference. Dynamically adjusting difficulty means the model always trains at its edge.
664.po: The three-phase approach improves sequential recommendation performance by providing better contrastive signals. By recalling negatives from the global item space instead of a small sample, the model learns to distinguish users' true preferences from genuinely competitive alternatives, not just randomly unpopular items.

665.bp: The web connects knowledge across text, images, video, and audio. Some entities (like "Apple") appear as text in one source and as a logo in images elsewhere. Linking these together—recognizing that they're the same thing—would create a richer, more connected web of knowledge. But entities look different depending on the format, so matching them across formats is hard.
665.wh: Current methods extract global features (the overall character of an entity), but miss local details (specific parts that distinguish entities). Without fine-grained matching, similar-but-different entities (like two people with the same name) get confused.
665.ap: DMEA extracts both global features (the big picture) and local features (fine details) from each modality separately. Then it computes alignment scores in two ways: intra-modal (comparing global and local features of entity pairs within the same format, like image to image) and cross-modal (comparing text to image). Each score is an independent decision, and the final judgment integrates all of them.
665.ww: Looking at local features catches details that global features miss—specific faces, unique textual markers. Scoring within-modality and across-modality separately respects that each format provides different evidence. Combining all the scores (not averaging them naively) means a high intra-modal text score and a high cross-modal score together make a stronger case than either alone.
665.po: By aligning entities at multiple levels of detail and across modalities, DMEA improves the accuracy of matching equivalent entities across heterogeneous knowledge graphs. This creates a unified web knowledge base where the same entity is correctly identified regardless of whether it appears as text, an image, or both.

666.bp: AI systems can have blind spots—they might work worse for some people than others (e.g., a face-recognition system more accurate on light skin than dark skin). Before deploying a model to real users, companies need to audit whether these fairness problems exist. Currently, auditing happens after training finishes, meaning thousands of wasted training runs before finding a fair model.
666.wh: Early prediction seems impossible because fairness isn't determined by initial settings alone; it emerges from the learning process. But if fairness trajectories follow predictable patterns, we might catch problems early without waiting for completion.
666.ap: The researchers tracked fairness metrics throughout training on multiple datasets. They looked at how fairness values changed from the start to the end and found consistent patterns: early-stage fairness strongly predicts final fairness. This means auditors can check fairness partway through training and make a go/no-go decision.
666.ww: If fairness develops monotonically (consistently improves or worsens), then checking at 10% of training gives signal about the final state. The paper found fairness trajectories are indeed predictable, meaning the learning dynamics that create fairness are stable enough to forecast.
666.po: By checking fairness during training instead of after, developers can stop unfair models early, saving 73.8% of training time in audit workflows. This shifts fairness assurance from a post-hoc expensive gate to an early-stage filter, making it practical to catch and prevent bias before deployment.

667.bp: Customer service teams spend time handling routine questions (password resets, order tracking, policy questions). Automating these tasks would free humans for complex issues.
