But current automation requires either hand-building rules for each scenario (slow, rigid) or training task-specific AI systems (expensive data collection, privacy risks).
667.wh: Data scarcity is also a problem: companies don't have labeled examples of every service task they want to automate. Privacy concerns mean collecting real customer conversations is risky. Deploying large LLMs in the cloud exposes customer data.
667.ap: The researchers define Task-Oriented Flowcharts (TOFs)—a diagram format that captures the steps and branching logic of a service task, like a flowchart. They build an algorithm that can extract this flowchart from a few example service conversations. Small language models deployed locally use the flowchart as a guide to handle new customer requests, avoiding the need to orchestrate rules manually or send data to the cloud.
667.ww: A flowchart is both expressive and constrained: it captures how service should flow without being so loose that the AI gets confused. Local deployment of small models avoids privacy leaks. Learning from few examples by distilling larger models (teaching smaller ones) makes the approach scalable without massive labeled datasets.
667.po: The framework automates customer service tasks end-to-end without manual intervention or cloud deployment. It outperforms hand-crafted baselines and commercial products on quantitative metrics, while preserving privacy by keeping customer data local and using smaller models that are easier to audit.

668.bp: Online, people debate claims about current events, politics, and policies. These debates contain both true and false statements, and understanding the arguments and disagreements is crucial for fact-checkers, journalists, and citizens trying to understand contested topics. But analyzing millions of online debates manually is impossible.
668.wh: Current NLP methods can extract entities or detect stance, but they miss the deeper conceptual foundations of why people disagree. A claim is true or false within a specific context, and understanding that context needs domain knowledge from political science, communication, and journalism.
668.ap: This workshop brings together researchers from computer science, social sciences, political science, and journalism. It covers NLP methods for finding arguments in text, detecting stance (does a speaker agree or disagree), and verifying facts. But it does this through the lens of communication studies and political science, grounding computational techniques in how arguments actually work.
668.ww: Bridging disciplines means the computational methods get reality-checked against what experts know about how debates work. Social scientists help identify what matters in an argument that pure NLP might miss. At the same time, computational methods help scale analysis beyond what manual review could do.
668.po: The workshop advances tools for analyzing online debates at scale while respecting the conceptual depth needed to understand contentious issues. Combining NLP (argument mining, stance detection, fact verification) with communication studies creates systems better suited to tracking misinformation, bias, and echo chambers in the wild.

669.bp: Social media bots—fake accounts run by algorithms—spread false information, amplify outrage, and manipulate public opinion. Detecting them is essential for protecting social networks from coordinated attacks. But as bots get better at mimicking humans, traditional methods (checking if an account posts at weird hours, for example) stop working.
669.wh: Most graph-based detectors look only at pairwise connections (who follows whom). They miss higher-order patterns—like when 10 bots all reply to the same post in sequence, which is a group pattern, not a pair. Traditional approaches also treat all types of relationships the same way (follows, replies, retweets) when actually the mixture matters.
669.ap: MPS-Bot uses simplexes—geometric objects that capture group structure—to represent higher-order relationships (groups of 3+ accounts acting together). It also uses attention mechanisms to learn how much weight to give each type of relationship (follows vs. replies vs. retweets) based on what's important for each user.
669.ww: Higher-order structure exposes coordination: bots don't just have individual properties, they exhibit synchronized behavior with other bots in groups. Weighting relationships differently for each user respects that some users are primarily followers while others primarily interact. This fine-grained representation is harder to spoof than simple features.
669.po: MPS-Bot outperforms existing baselines on two major Twitter bot-detection benchmarks (MGTAB and TwiBot-22). By looking at group patterns instead of just pairs, and by learning which relationships matter for each account, it catches bots that mimic human behavior and slip past simpler detectors.

670.bp: Large companies need to forecast their electricity use to manage power consumption efficiently and negotiate energy contracts. A company's power bill is also a signal of its financial health: unusual power spikes can indicate problems (inefficient operations) or opportunities (growth). Combining power forecasting with credit risk assessment—looking at both together—could give a fuller picture of enterprise health.
670.wh: Most multi-task learning approaches share parameters between tasks or use simple attention, which doesn't capture the deep coupling. Power and credit data live on different time scales and structural patterns, and forcing them into one shape loses information.
670.ap: CPDGL is a multi-task system that simultaneously predicts power consumption and credit risk, but with explicit modules that model co-evolution. A path-interaction module directly captures how credit changes influence power strategy and vice versa. The system uses dynamic graph learning to model how relationships between variables shift over time.
670.ww: Modeling the feedback loop explicitly means the system learns that credit deterioration leads to power reduction, and unexpected power anomalies signal credit trouble. Using dynamic graphs instead of static ones respects that company circumstances change week to week. Handling different time scales and network structures separately preserves the natural patterns in each domain.
670.po: By modeling credit and power together, CPDGL improves both forecasting and risk assessment. Power anomalies become early warnings for credit problems, and credit trajectories help predict consumption patterns. The unified view gives energy managers and financial institutions better tools to plan and assess enterprise stability.

671.bp: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems let AI retrieve factual information from documents before answering, reducing hallucinations and allowing users to verify answers. These systems are increasingly used in education to help students learn. But if students can't see where an answer came from or how the system arrived at it, they lose the chance to think critically about the information.
671.wh: Transparency requires rethinking the whole system design, not just adding labels at the end. What information should be shown? When should it be shown? How do you balance helping users with respecting their independence?
671.ap: SAGE-RAI is a multi-purpose RAG system deployed in an educational context. It combines retrieval with an explicit focus on transparency: showing which documents the system pulled from, displaying reasoning steps, and explaining trade-offs. The researchers evaluated it through both numerical surveys (26 users) and deep interviews (4 users) to understand both satisfaction and learning outcomes.
671.ww: Making transparency architectural (built in from the start) means every design choice reflects it. The system can highlight retrieved passages and explain why they're relevant, letting users verify each step. This dual nature—serving both ethics (transparency as accountability) and pedagogy (transparency as learning support)—makes the investment worthwhile.
671.po: SAGE-RAI achieved 92.3% of users rating it 4-5 stars and high satisfaction overall (mean 4.62/5). The findings reveal that transparency serves both ethical and learning purposes: users could track reasoning and verify facts, but the study also identified tensions (students might over-rely on AI assistance). The work establishes that transparency must be foundational, not optional, in educational RAG systems.

672.bp: Taxonomies—hierarchical organizations of concepts—are everywhere: e-commerce categories, scientific classifications, database schemas. When new products or concepts emerge, taxonomies need to be updated. Manual expansion is slow and expensive. Automating this expansion would let taxonomies evolve with the world.
672.wh: Existing approaches also don't capture ambiguity: a concept like "bat" (the animal and the sports equipment) has multiple meanings, and taxonomies need to place it correctly in different contexts. Box embeddings can capture hierarchy and disjointness, but they have technical problems: unstable training and no way to model uncertainty.
672.ap: TaxoBell replaces rigid point embeddings with Gaussian boxes—boxes centered and shaped by statistical distributions. A concept's location is its mean, and its uncertainty (ambiguity) is captured by its covariance (width). A concept is "inside" another concept if its box is contained in that box's space. Optimization is done using energy-based methods that are stable at boundaries.
672.ww: Gaussian distributions naturally encode both location (the hierarchy) and uncertainty (ambiguity). When you move a box, the energy-based optimizer is stable even at the boundary—no gradient explosions. The covariance handles polysemy: an ambiguous concept has a wider, fuzzier box, and the system can place it correctly even when it belongs in multiple places.
672.po: TaxoBell outperforms eight baselines by 19% in MRR and 25% in Recall@k on five benchmark datasets. By using Gaussian boxes, it handles ambiguous concepts better than point embeddings, learns more stably than previous box methods, and provides interpretable reasoning about hierarchical containment and uncertainty.

673.bp: Fact-checkers manually read documents and extract the central claims they want to verify. This manual process is the bottleneck: it's slow and requires expertise to know which claims are important enough to check. Automating claim extraction would let fact-checkers focus on verification instead of hunting for claims.
673.wh: Using large language models zero-shot (without training examples) is appealing but risky: they might extract verbose rambles instead of concise claims, or miss subtle claims because they're hunting for obvious ones. Without explicit guidance on what humans value, LLMs default to their own biases.
673.ap: The researchers first interviewed expert fact-checkers to extract what makes a good claim—call these Human Value Alignment (HVA) dimensions (clarity, relevance, supportedness, etc.). They then prompt large language models with these dimensions built in, telling them explicitly what humans value. For evaluation, they created an LLM-based scorer that rates extracted claims across the HVA dimensions and compares them to expert-written claims.
673.ww: By making human priorities explicit in the prompt, the LLM has guardrails: it knows to extract concise, supported, relevant claims, not just any factual statement. Scoring claims across multiple HVA dimensions means the evaluator can explain why a claim scores well or poorly, not just give a yes/no judgment.
673.po: The method achieves state-of-the-art performance on claim extraction (highest chrF and P@N scores). The HVA evaluator shows high agreement with human judgments and provides dimension-level breakdowns of claim quality, making it interpretable to fact-checkers. Zero-shot extraction now respects expert priorities without requiring labeled training data.

674.bp: Fact-checkers debunk false claims by writing counter-explanations. Some debunks come from professional journalists or established fact-checking organizations; others come from community members (like Twitter's Community Notes). Both types are important, but they might use different persuasion techniques. Understanding these differences could improve how fact-checkers communicate.
674.wh: Even if the hypothesis were true, it's not clear what to do about it. Are persuasive techniques bad? Do they help or hurt people's trust in the debunk? Community ratings might reveal whether rhetorical choices actually affect how useful people find the debunk.
674.ap: The researchers collected large datasets of Community Notes, professional fact-checks from EUvsDisinfo, and debunks from the Database of Known Fakes (DBKF). They quantified persuasion techniques used in each (emotional appeals, rhetorical questions, hedging language, etc.). They also examined how crowd ratings correlated with use of persuasive techniques.
674.ww: By measuring across diverse ecosystems and comparing ratings, the study can show both what techniques are used and whether they actually influence how helpful people find the debunk. Systematic rhetorical differences (if any exist) would reflect institutional norms and priorities, not just individual choices.
674.po: Contrary to the hypothesis, Community Notes don't use more persuasive techniques on average than professional fact-checks. Instead, the rhetorical differences reflect different institutional norms and topical coverage. Notably, the crowd effectively penalizes problematic rhetorical means when rating helpfulness, suggesting community self-regulation works. Notes with more persuasive elements receive slightly higher ratings, but only when the persuasion doesn't cross ethical lines.

675.bp: Blockchains split data across multiple computers (shards) to handle more transactions, but moving accounts between shards causes the whole system to freeze temporarily. This paper solves that freeze problem so thousands of financial transactions can keep flowing even while accounts are being physically relocated—like rerouting airport connections while passengers keep arriving.
675.wh: When an account moves from one shard to another, the system must pause to ensure no one double-spends money or corrupts data. The more accounts you move at once, the bigger and longer the shutdown. But if you move them one at a time, you waste months of traffic slowdowns as transactions keep crossing between shards that the account already left.
675.ap: BIND works by keeping two separate queues of pending transactions—one for accounts currently moving, one for accounts already settled. This lets the system process settled transactions immediately while migrations happen in the background. It groups accounts into small batches based on how tightly they interact (which accounts send money to which), so each batch move fixes more cross-shard traffic at once without causing a long freeze.
675.ww: The key insight is that you don't need the whole system locked—only the specific part handling those moving accounts needs pausing. By isolating the migrants into their own queue, non-migrating accounts see zero disruption, and by batching accounts that talk to each other a lot, you solve more of the traffic problem per freeze.
675.po: In real Ethereum tests, this buys a 12% overall speed boost, cuts migration time to one-quarter its normal length, and reduces future cross-shard traffic by nearly a quarter. Blockchains can now shuffle accounts around during peak use without anyone noticing.

676.bp: When you send video, audio, and text over the internet together, bandwidth is precious. Instead of sending raw pixels and sound waves, what if you could distill each modality down to only the semantic meaning (what it's actually saying) that matters for the task at hand, and throw away the rest? That's the real-world goal: efficient, robust transmission of *meaning* rather than raw data.
676.wh: Video, audio, and text naturally carry different kinds of signal and noise. A naive approach sends everything, hoping the receiver reconstructs from it all. But under bad wireless conditions (noisy channels), when one modality drops out (no audio), or when the audio/video are slightly out of sync, that approach fails because it depends on all three modalities being perfect. You also don't know which details matter for your specific task.
676.ap: Grasp works by first segmenting the streams into meaningful blocks, then building a graph of how those blocks connect. A neural graph network then identifies three layers of information within each block: strongly relevant stuff (keep this), weakly relevant stuff (can discard), and noise (throw out). The system synchronizes video, audio, and text by comparing how similar they are across the three sources. At the receiver, if audio drops, the system reconstructs it from the shared meaning it stored, using what the video and text already told it.
676.ww: By disentangling signal into three tiers (task-relevant, background, noise), you're only sending the essential semantic core. This works because the three modalities overlap in meaning—if video says "person waving" and audio says "hello," the text knows what to expect, so it can reconstruct the audio's meaning even if the audio stream is corrupted. This graceful degradation is much more robust than sending everything.
676.po: The result is transmission that survives low signal-to-noise conditions where the original would fail, handles missing modalities (one stream drops, others compensate), and stays synchronized despite streaming asynchrony. Cross-modal tasks like video-based question answering work even on noisy wireless links.

677.bp: Phishing attacks cost billions per year—criminals impersonate banks and email services to steal passwords and credit card numbers. Understanding where attackers get their tools and share their techniques reveals what countermeasures will actually work. This paper does detective work on the dark web itself, reading the attackers' own forums to understand the supply chain *before* attacks happen.
677.wh: Most research studies phishing after the fact: 'here's a fake email we found, let's reverse-engineer it.' But that tells you nothing about how attackers learned to make it, where they bought the tools, which services are most targeted, or when new attack methods are spreading. The dark web forums are where attackers trade phishing kits (automated tools to set up fake login pages), buy stolen credentials, and share code snippets—but reading 394,000 posts by hand is impossible.
677.ap: The researchers collected 13 years of posts (2013–2025) from 13 dark web forums and used a language model to automatically extract the key information: 'this post mentions PayPal phishing,' 'this one sells an SMTP server for sending fake emails,' 'this author made a phishing kit.' They mapped everything onto a seven-stage attack playbook (acquire tools, build fake page, send emails, steal credentials, etc.) so they could see which components are easiest to find and which services are most under fire.
677.ww: By reading the supply chain backwards, you see what's actually bottlenecked. If stolen Gmail credentials are expensive and rare, that's one defense angle. If phishing-kit source code is freely shared, that's another. If PayPal is targeted 10x more than Netflix, defensive resources should follow the attacker's priorities. The dark web forums literally tell you the attacker's perspective, not the defender's guess.
677.po: The study maps 12 years of attack trends, revealing which services face the most pressure, how often attack components change, and where the attacker's supply chain has weak links. This data lets defenders predict which services will be hit next and which attack tools are about to become prevalent.

678.bp: Traffic prediction (how many cars will be on Fifth Avenue tomorrow at 3pm) powers navigation apps, traffic lights, and delivery logistics. But building a good traffic model is hard: you need one model for highways, another for city grids, another for rural roads. What if you could describe 'I need to predict city traffic' in English and have a system automatically design and build the right neural network for you?
678.wh: Traffic datasets vary wildly: different city layouts, different time patterns (rush hour vs. weekend), different prediction horizons (1 hour ahead vs. 1 week). Manually designing a neural network for each dataset takes months of tweaking. Even worse, a network that works for New York often fails for Beijing because the underlying patterns are different. You need modularity and reusability, but each problem feels bespoke.
678.ap: ST-LEGO is a system where multiple AI agents collaborate: one agent (Prompt Agent) reads your task description in natural language ('predict traffic on a grid'), another agent (Assemble Agent) picks modular components from a library (a module for time patterns, a module for spatial relationships, a module for special events), and a third agent (Code Agent) automatically writes PyTorch code that sticks these pieces together. The framework uses a standardized language to describe model architectures so pieces snap together reliably.
678.ww: The insight is that most traffic models are built from the same fundamental building blocks (time dynamics, spatial propagation, feature fusion). By separating the block descriptions from the plumbing code, you can ask a language model to design the assembly, not the wiring. The system learns which blocks work for which datasets automatically, rather than requiring a human expert.
678.po: Models built this way learn faster, achieve higher accuracy on multiple real traffic datasets, and can transfer to new cities with minimal retraining. The same system can generate diverse model architectures for different cities, beating hand-crafted baselines in both accuracy and convergence speed.

679.bp: Pre-trained neural network models are expensive to build (weeks of computing). When you get a new task (classify a different graph dataset), you want to reuse a pre-trained model rather than training from scratch. The question: without actually fine-tuning the model, can you quickly score whether it will work well on your new task, so you pick the best one from a shelf of candidates?
679.wh: For images and text, there are good ways to score model transferability quickly. But graphs are stranger: a graph's structure (who is connected to whom) is just as important as the features. When the new graph dataset has a different structure than the data the model was trained on (distribution shift), the pre-trained model's abilities break down in unpredictable ways. Existing scoring methods don't account for graph structure at all.
679.ap: GNNMTE scores a model's transferability by decomposing the pre-trained model's learned structure using mathematical techniques (singular value decomposition) to extract its core learned patterns. It then weights these patterns based on their importance for the new graph dataset, and measures how well these patterns align with the new graph's own structure. The score tells you whether the model learned universals that will transfer, or task-specific quirks that won't.
679.ww: The core idea is that good models learn abstract structural principles (like 'nodes with many connections matter more'). By decomposing what the model learned and comparing it to your new graph's structure, you're checking whether the model's learned abstractions match your new graph's reality. If they do, transfer will work.
679.po: You can now score multiple pre-trained GNN models in seconds and pick the one most likely to transfer well, without waiting weeks for fine-tuning experiments. This is especially valuable when you only have small graph datasets where training from scratch is infeasible.

680.bp: Graph neural networks learn node representations by comparing nodes to their neighbors. But this approach struggles to capture complex, multi-hop patterns—like 'nodes that form triangles are different from nodes in chains even if they have the same direct neighbors.' This paper teaches networks to reason about these higher-order structures so they build richer, more informative node descriptions.
680.wh: A node's immediate neighbors are obvious, but what about neighbors-of-neighbors? Standard graph learning ignores these distant patterns, losing critical structural information. When you try to add them, you run into three problems: (1) you need to explicitly preserve edges that define higher-order structures but might seem unimportant locally, (2) you can't tell which nodes matter for which structures, and (3) when you artificially create negative examples to train on, they're indistinguishable from real ones.
680.ap: SPGCL identifies small graph patterns (subgraph patterns like triangles, chains, stars) that encode high-order structure. It keeps edges that are crucial for these patterns, even if they seem low-value locally. It then encodes each node, edge, and connection matrix with information about which patterns they participate in. During training, it treats nodes that are in different pattern families as dissimilar and nodes in the same patterns as similar, making negative examples actually discriminative.
680.ww: The insight is that high-order structures have geometric meaning: a triangle node and a chain node behave fundamentally differently even with identical neighborhoods. By explicitly tagging nodes with their role in common patterns and forcing the model to discriminate between different pattern families, you're forcing it to learn structure, not just density.
680.po: Nodes now have richer representations that capture both local neighborhoods and global structural roles. On six real-world datasets, this beats all existing methods and learns representations that better separate nodes with different roles.

681.bp: Recommending micro-videos (TikTok, Instagram Reels) means handling video (visual), audio, and text together. The challenge: videos have messy, noisy interactions (users might click out of boredom, not dislike), and the multimodal features often overlap confusingly—visual and audio might both encode 'music genre,' which is redundant. You want to clean up both the noise and the redundancy to make recommendations more accurate.
681.wh: Existing systems assume the user-video interactions are clean and all three modalities (visual, audio, text) tell independent stories. In reality, many clicks are noise (misclicks, scrolling too fast), and the modalities share information (a song's title and the audio beat both tell you it's pop music). This redundancy means the model wastes effort learning the same thing three times, and noise in the interaction graph corrupts the signal about what users actually want.
681.ap: MBGSL learns the 'true' interaction graph by denoising the raw data—instead of treating clicks as gospel, it learns which interactions are actually meaningful. For each modality (visual, audio, text), it learns a separate view of the graph, each optimized to remove redundant information within that modality. Then it compares across modalities to identify and remove the shared signal that appears in multiple views. The model simultaneously learns representations and graph structure, using shared semantic principles across modalities to guide both.
681.ww: By learning the graph structure instead of trusting raw clicks, you're doing supervised denoising—keeping interactions that make sense given the video content, discarding noise. By removing intra-modality redundancy and inter-modality overlap, you force each modality to contribute unique information, so all three together paint a complete picture without waste.
681.po: Videos get richer, cleaner representations. Recommendations improve on three real datasets by beating existing methods, especially in identifying which videos users truly like versus accidentally clicked.

682.bp: Imagine you observe a cascade of rumors spreading through Twitter, but you didn't see how the rumors moved (no direct friendship graph). Can you reconstruct the hidden network by just watching which accounts got infected in what order? The real-world use: inferring social network structure, disease spread networks, or influence patterns from the outcomes alone.
682.wh: If you have just one cascade (1000 tweets about one rumor), there's not enough information to uniquely determine the network—many possible networks could produce the same spread pattern. But here's the key insight: in the real world, multiple cascades happen on the *same underlying network*. Most methods give up and infer each cascade's network independently, wasting the mutual information. When you have little data per cascade, this independence assumption hurts badly.
682.ap: The paper proposes an iterative algorithm: start by inferring each cascade independently (standard approach). Then, use the fact that cascades share a network to update all inferences together—if cascade 1 suggests 'A talks to B,' and cascade 2 confirms it, boost that link's confidence. Repeat this refinement until the inferences stabilize. The algorithm guarantees that each iteration improves, so you know it converges to a stable solution.
682.ww: The insight is that multiple weak signals reinforce each other. One cascade might not uniquely specify a link, but the same link appearing in 10 cascades as the best explanation is strong evidence. By jointly optimizing all inferences, you're using global consistency as a regularizer—individual cascades stay consistent with each other because they all come from the same network.
682.po: You can now reconstruct networks from limited cascade data (few observations per cascade) with higher accuracy than single-cascade methods. This is valuable when you have many small cascades (many conversations, few replies each) rather than a few mega-viral events.

683.bp: Web agents are AI systems that use tools (click buttons, type text, run code) in long sequences to complete real tasks—booking flights, debugging code, researching topics. These agents need to learn to explore different tool options when uncertain, but be decisive when confident. The challenge: balancing exploration and decisiveness so training doesn't collapse into nonsense.
683.wh: A naive training approach says: 'when the model is uncertain, try different tools (explore).' But this leads to thrashing: the agent spends 50 steps trying every tool instead of committing to one. The model also learns to be uncertain as a hedging strategy, which sounds safe but actually prevents learning. Existing algorithms can't handle this 'exploration-greediness tradeoff' on long, multi-step tasks.
683.ap: AEPO (Agentic Entropy-Balanced Policy Optimization) has two parts. First, during exploration (generating training examples), it monitors the model's uncertainty and actively limits over-exploration: if the model is uncertain about consecutive steps, it penalizes that to prevent thrashing. Second, during learning from those examples, it carefully handles high-uncertainty steps by preserving learning signal on uncertain decisions while preventing runaway gradient updates that would destabilize training.
683.ww: The key is treating uncertainty strategically: it's good for exploring diverse solutions, bad for committing to sequences. By pre-monitoring uncertainty and imposing a 'no thrashing' penalty, you force the model to commit some of the time. By separately scaling learning on uncertain steps, you let the model learn *why* it should be uncertain in some cases while preventing that learned uncertainty from metastasizing.
683.po: On 14 real web tasks, this beats seven other RL algorithms by maintaining stable training and learning diverse solutions while avoiding collapse. The agent learns when to explore and when to commit, producing more reliable long-horizon behavior.

684.bp: Recommendation systems today optimize for clicks and time spent—'show them content they'll engage with.' But engagement doesn't mean the user trusts the system or feels in control. This paper builds a framework to ask the harder question: does this recommender respect the user as a person, or does it just manipulate engagement?
684.wh: Metrics like 'clicks' and 'dwell time' perversely reward making users addicted, showing them outrage even if it harms them, or manipulating them into clicking things they'll regret. These metrics also don't care about transparency (does the user understand why they were shown this?) or agency (could the user have gotten a different view if they wanted?). You can optimize engagement and leave users feeling trapped and mistrustful.
684.ap: The paper develops a human-centered evaluation framework that measures trust, agency, transparency, and satisfaction alongside engagement. They then qualitatively study an LLM-based recommender system, examining trade-offs: 'if we rank by diversity instead of just click-likelihood, engagement drops but users feel more respected. If we explain our recommendations, that takes screen space but users trust us more.' They explore how design choices (ranking strategy, diversity, transparency) affect these human-centered outcomes.
684.ww: The mechanism is simply asking the right questions: 'Did users feel respected by this system?' rather than just 'Did they click?' The framework makes visible what's been hidden—that you can't maximize engagement and trust simultaneously without careful design. By measuring both, you force designers to acknowledge the tradeoff.
684.po: The work surfaces concrete design choices (ranking, diversity, transparency mechanisms) that improve trust and satisfaction at the cost of some engagement. This gives recommender-system designers a vocabulary to reason about human impact, not just metrics.

685.bp: Training large language models is extremely expensive (millions of dollars in computing). What if multiple organizations (companies, universities, governments) pooled resources to train one model together, splitting costs and keeping their own data private? The challenge: how do you ensure each participant contributes fairly and gets rewarded justly without a central authority keeping score?
685.wh: In centralized training, one company controls everything and decides who did what. In decentralized federated training, no single authority can be trusted. How do you verify that participant A actually trained the model for 100 hours with quality data, while participant B only contributed 10 hours of junk data? How do you fairly split the final model's value? Without a trusted referee, participants can fake contributions or freeload.
685.ap: The system uses two mechanisms: (1) a mathematical formula (Shapley value) that fairly credits each participant's contribution by measuring how much the final model improves because of their data, and (2) blockchain smart contracts that automatically check contributions and pay rewards in tokens. Participants submit their data and compute hours, the system trains collaboratively, and then the smart contracts verify contributions and automatically pay each participant their earned tokens proportional to their impact.
685.ww: Shapley values work because they measure counterfactual contribution: 'if we trained without participant A, how much worse would the model be?' This credit is fair in a game-theoretic sense—no participant can gain by falsely reporting or withholding effort. Blockchain adds transparency: the payment logic is publicly verifiable code, not a black box.
685.po: Organizations can now collaborate on expensive AI training with automatic, transparent credit assignment and payment. Simulation results show more stable participation, fairer value distribution, and reduced financial concentration compared to centralized models.

686.bp: Machine learning services (MLaaS) let organizations use AI without building it themselves—pick a service, pay per query. But how do you choose between 10,000 services? And how do you combine them (use service A for preprocessing, B for predictions, C for confidence estimates)? This paper builds a data generator so researchers can test selection and combination algorithms at scale.
686.wh: Real MLaaS services vary wildly in cost, accuracy, latency, and specialty. You might pick the cheapest option and regret it when it times out, or pick the most accurate and go broke. Combining services is harder: which should run first? Do you need all three or can two suffice? Testing this requires spinning up thousands of real services, which is expensive and slow.
686.ap: MDG (MLaaS Dataset Generator) simulates realistic MLaaS behavior by training diverse machine-learning models across multiple real datasets. It records not just accuracy but costs, latencies, service composition patterns (how well service A's output feeds into B), and how services behave under different data conditions (drift, corrupted inputs). It then generates a dataset of 10,000+ synthetic service descriptions and results.
686.ww: By generating synthetic data that mimics the distributions of real MLaaS systems, you get a cheap, reproducible way to test selection and composition algorithms. The key is recording realistic quality-of-service metrics (latency, cost, availability), not just raw accuracy. This lets algorithms optimize for real tradeoffs—speed vs. accuracy, cost vs. reliability.
686.po: Researchers can now test MLaaS selection and composition algorithms on 10,000+ services without expensive real-world testing. The framework extends to IoT environments where services have unique constraints (low bandwidth, intermittent connectivity).

687.bp: Wireless sensor networks (thousands of temperature sensors across a city, or humidity sensors in a farm) often have missing data—sensors break, run out of battery, or turn off to save power. This creates gaps in the spatial-temporal readings you need for decision-making. How do you recover missing data while keeping individual sensor data private so no central authority sees raw measurements?
687.wh: Existing methods work well for recovery but require sending all sensor data to a central server, which raises privacy concerns—the cloud service sees everyone's exact measurements. Federated learning (each sensor trains locally and uploads only gradients) preserves privacy, but existing federated methods don't exploit the spatial-temporal structure of sensor networks, so recovery quality suffers.
687.ap: FLFL (Federated Latent Factor Learning) combines two ideas: each sensor locally learns latent factors (like 'temperature varies with time of day'), uploads only the gradient updates (not raw data), and the central server combines these gradients. Crucially, the model explicitly incorporates spatial-temporal correlation—neighboring sensors at similar times should have similar values—as a constraint during learning. This gives the model structure to exploit for better recovery without demanding raw data.
687.ww: The insight is that you can bake domain knowledge (spatial-temporal correlation) into the federated learning algorithm as a regularization constraint. This guides recovery without requiring raw data. Each sensor's privacy is protected because only gradients leave the device, but the model is much stronger because it reasons about how sensors relate across space and time.
687.po: Missing sensor values are recovered accurately (even when 30% of data is missing) while each sensor's raw measurements stay private—only gradient updates leave the device. This works for smart city applications, precision agriculture, and industrial monitoring.

688.bp: Online stories (serialized fiction, news articles) need advertisements inserted somewhere. But ads during climactic moments ruin the experience. What if you could detect whether a paragraph has high narrative tension (big reveal, emotional moment) so you avoid spoiling it with ads? This paper uses language models to identify tense moments automatically.
688.wh: Placing ads at random loses revenue (put an ad during a cliffhanger and readers abandon the story, so fewer ads are served). Placing ads only at story breaks loses opportunity (not every natural pause is good). Manually labeling every paragraph is infeasible for thousands of stories. You need an automatic way to score 'how tense is this paragraph?' so ad systems can avoid hot moments and place ads during calm transitions.
688.ap: The authors use a language model as a classifier trained on paragraphs labeled with narrative tension levels. The model learns to recognize cues like conflict escalation, revelation, character reactions, and time pressure. It scores each paragraph's tension so ad systems can insert breaks during low-tension passages and preserve high-tension sequences uninterrupted.
688.ww: Language models are good at recognizing narrative patterns because they've read billions of stories. By encoding narrative tension as a classification task, you're leveraging that prior knowledge. Identifying calm moments is easier than trying to manually craft rules—the model learns patterns humans would miss.
688.po: Ad placement systems can now avoid disrupting key story moments, preserving reader engagement while still serving ads during transitions. This keeps subscription revenue up and readers satisfied.

689.bp: Major social events (protests, epidemics, financial crashes) are rare but consequential. Early warning systems could mobilize resources before disaster, but events are so infrequent that building accurate predictions is nearly impossible—you have almost no positive examples to learn from. This paper uses intermediate signals (smaller, earlier events) to predict rare events before they happen.
689.wh: Standard machine learning assumes balanced classes, but rare events are the opposite: 1 in 100,000 events is a major crisis. Training with 99,999 non-events and 1 crisis, any model that says 'no crisis' is 99.99% accurate but useless. Even worse, you miss dependencies: a crisis isn't random—earlier, smaller tremors usually precede it. Most rare-event methods ignore these dependencies, treating each observation in isolation.
689.ap: Mediator Learning (ML) uses intermediate events as 'mediators'—like recognizing that before a major protest, you typically see smaller grievance-related posts. The system first extracts these mediator events using information theory (finding events that contain the most information about whether rare events follow), then builds a graph where smaller events flow up through mediators to rare events. A neural graph network models these tiers, where upper-level predictions (will a crisis happen?) are informed by lower-level probability distributions (how likely are the precursor tremors?).
689.ww: By explicitly routing through intermediate events, you're learning the causal chain rather than trying to predict rare events from nothing. A precursor is common (small protests are frequent), so it's easy to learn. The rare event becomes: 'if precursors reach a threshold, then crisis,' which is learnable. Mediators decompose the imbalanced problem into stages.
689.po: Rare-event prediction accuracy improves substantially by learning precursor-to-crisis chains. This matters for crisis detection: you can now predict rare social events like major unrest, epidemics, or financial shocks by watching for the preceding cascade of smaller signals.

690.bp: When scientists study human behavior using online data — tweets, clicks, survey responses — they need everyone to trust and understand how they got their answers. Right now, researchers often can't easily share their exact steps or let others repeat the work, which means we can't be sure the findings are real.
690.wh: The core tension is that social science lives in a world of messy, constantly-changing platforms and privacy rules, while computer science demands precise, reproducible steps. A researcher's workflow lives on platforms (Twitter, Instagram) that change their rules, hide their data, or vanish; the researcher uses custom scripts that nobody else can run. There's no agreement on what 'reproducible' even means here.
690.ap: R2CASS is a workshop that brings together social scientists, computer people, and policy makers to agree on shared tools and checklists. They've built Methods Hub, a platform where researchers post their workflows step-by-step, share templates for common tasks, and check each other's work. The workshop runs hands-on sessions where people actually try to repeat one another's computational social science projects.
690.ww: When researchers can see exactly what someone else did — their data sources, their code, their judgment calls — they can spot where things break down and fix them. Publishing the steps also forces researchers to be clearer about what they're assuming, which makes the science stronger. Templates and shared checklists make it easy to follow best practices without having to reinvent the wheel.
690.po: The payoff is that computational social science research becomes credible enough to guide real decisions. A policymaker can look at a study and actually verify it's sound. The Methods Hub platform lowers the barrier: a researcher can now run a reproducible task on the platform and get feedback in real time, making the whole field more transparent and trustworthy.

691.bp: Large language models power many web services — chatbots, search, recommendations — and companies want to adapt these giant models to work better for their specific needs without sharing their users' private data. Federated learning lets teams collaborate on training without handing over sensitive information.
691.wh: The catch is that different teams have different privacy budgets: some users tolerate almost no noise, others accept heavy privacy protection. When you average together updates from clients with wildly different privacy levels, the noisy updates corrupt the good ones, dragging down overall performance. Meanwhile, clients with strong privacy demands get punished — their data helps everyone, but they see worse results.
691.ap: WinFLoRA uses a clever carrot-and-stick approach: it estimates how much privacy noise each client added to their updates, then gives more influence to the clients who added less noise. Think of it as weighting votes — a clean update from one client counts for more than a noisy one. The system automatically learns which clients are trustworthy and shapes the final model to reflect their updates more heavily.
691.ww: This works because it aligns incentives. A client who cares less about privacy and contributes clean updates sees their preferences reflected in the shared model, improving their own task performance. A client with strict privacy needs gets protected without being punished — their updates still matter, just proportionally to their noise level. The system finds the sweet spot where everyone's interests balance.
691.po: Experiments show WinFLoRA achieves up to 52% higher accuracy and up to 2.56x better utility for individual clients compared to simpler baselines. Clients now have a reason to be honest about their privacy needs and to contribute better data, because the system rewards them for it. This makes federated learning actually work in the real messy world where privacy policies clash.

692.bp: On e-commerce sites, customers don't just click once and disappear — they click on an item, favorite it, add it to cart, and maybe buy it. Understanding this sequence of different actions is the key to knowing what they really want so recommendations can be both accurate and fast at scale.
692.wh: Traditional methods treat all behavior types the same or try to predict one at a time, missing the fact that watching someone favorite then cart an item tells you something different than watching them favorite then abandon. Most prior work uses transformer-based models that can learn these patterns perfectly but are glacially slow on long sequences — they compute pairwise relationships between every action, which becomes impossible on real shopping carts with hundreds of actions.
692.ap: TGA (Transition-Aware Graph Attention Network) recognizes that not all behavior pairs matter equally and builds a sparse, structured graph that only keeps the transitions that actually teach you something. It identifies which transitions are informative from three angles: do items themselves predict the next action, do product categories, and do the user's recent neighbors in the graph. Then it runs a fast, lightweight attention mechanism on just that sparse graph instead of the dense pairwise matrix.
692.ww: This works because real shopping behavior is structured, not random. Certain transitions repeat — people who favorite often go to cart; people who buy rarely go back to favoriting — and the algorithm learns to focus on those patterns. By ignoring noisy transitions and focusing on the few that carry information, you keep the model accurate while cutting computation time from polynomial (slow) to linear (fast).
692.po: The payoff is that recommendation engines can handle long shopping sequences in real time without becoming a bottleneck. Industrial e-commerce platforms with millions of users can now use sophisticated behavior-aware recommendations instead of settling for simpler, faster approximations. Experiments show better accuracy while keeping latency low enough for live serving.

693.bp: Real recommendation systems don't just maximize accuracy — they have hard business rules: every recommendation list must have items from multiple sellers, must include at least one new product, must be diverse enough to appeal to different tastes. These aren't polite suggestions; breaking them even once breaks customer trust and violates partnerships.
693.wh: Most machine learning models treat rules as soft penalties — a gentle push toward fairness or coverage. But in production, a single constraint violation is a failure. Meanwhile, multi-objective optimization (balancing accuracy, fairness, diversity) requires exploring many trade-offs, and large language models are good at talking about tradeoffs but not at guaranteeing hard constraints are met.
693.ap: DualAgent-Rec splits the problem into two specialized agents: one focuses solely on ranking items accurately while respecting hard constraints (using classical algorithms proven to enforce rules), the other explores diverse combinations without constraints (searching the Pareto frontier — the space where you can't improve one goal without hurting another). An LLM-based coordinator watches progress and adaptively shifts resources between the agents, asking the constrained agent to do more work when constraints are in danger of breaking, and letting the exploration agent push for diversity when room exists.
693.ww: This works because it separates concerns: the constrained agent brings mathematical guarantees about feasibility, the exploration agent brings creativity and diversity, and the LLM coordinator brings judgment about when to trust which. By using an LLM as the orchestrator rather than the optimizer, you get flexibility without sacrificing the hard mathematical guarantees that safety-critical systems need.
693.po: Experiments on real Amazon shopping data show 100% constraint satisfaction across all test cases while improving overall quality (measured by Pareto hypervolume) by 4–6% over existing methods. This is the difference between a system that occasionally violates seller agreements and one that never does, while still giving customers better recommendations.

694.bp: PFAS chemicals — forever chemicals that don't break down in the environment and persist in drinking water and wildlife — need to be tracked, studied, and regulated. Scientists, regulators, and companies need a shared, structured vocabulary for talking about which PFAS molecules are which, their properties, and what we know about their environmental impact.
694.wh: The challenge is that chemical data is scattered across different databases using different naming schemes, properties are measured under different conditions, and toxicology information is buried in research papers. A regulator trying to understand what PFAS are in drinking water in one region can't easily connect that to research from another country or to EPA toxicity data because nobody standardized the language.
694.ap: The CompTox ontology is a structured dictionary that hierarchically organizes PFAS — types include fluorotelomers and perfluoroalkyl acids, each with detailed properties like molecular mass, carbon chain length, and functional groups. Each chemical gets authoritative identifiers (like DTXSID numbers), properties (chemical fingerprints), and links to environmental and toxicological data. The ontology is built using a template-driven process and formatted in OWL, a language computers can understand and reason about.
694.ww: When information is structured this way, scientists and regulators can now ask precise questions: 'Show me all perfluoroalkyl carboxylic acids with chain length greater than 6 that have high bioaccumulation potential.' Computers can automatically link data from different sources by matching identifiers and properties. Research papers mentioning PFAS can be automatically catalogued. This transforms scattered knowledge into a queryable, reasoned system.
694.po: The ontology enables integrated PFAS monitoring and risk assessment at scale. A water utility testing for contamination can query which PFAS are highest risk, what properties predict environmental persistence, and how monitored levels compare to regulatory data. Scientists studying one PFAS can discover related ones. The structured representation makes it possible to govern PFAS informed by complete data instead of isolated anecdotes.

695.bp: The cryptography that protects your banking, email, and web browsing — RSA encryption — works because factoring huge numbers is mathematically hard. But quantum computers could break this in years, threatening all the security we built over decades. Understanding exactly how quantum algorithms would attack RSA helps us prepare.
695.wh: Quantum computing is abstract and hard to visualize; most people can't follow quantum gate operations or understand why Shor's algorithm breaks RSA. Existing explanations either oversimplify to the point of being wrong or get so technical that only specialists can follow. We need a clear, traceable explanation that shows exactly how quantum processes would extract RSA's secret.
695.ap: This paper builds a quantum emulator using dictionaries: each quantum state is stored as dictionary[bitstring] = complex_number, where the complex number represents the quantum amplitude at that state. Each quantum gate is implemented as a rule: the Hadamard gate creates superposition by duplicating dictionary keys; phase gates rotate amplitudes; X and Toffoli gates flip bits conditionally. By stepping through these rules, you can watch a quantum computer search for the period of a number, which reveals the RSA factors.
695.ww: This approach works because dictionary-based simulation stays concrete and traceable — you can see exactly which bitstrings matter at each step and why. It reveals that quantum advantage comes from superposition (the dictionary holding many states at once) and interference (amplitudes cancelling or adding up). By making the quantum process visible, the paper shows why quantum computers have a path to RSA that classical computers don't.
695.po: The payoff is understanding: this framework makes the quantum threat to RSA not abstract but mechanical and viewable. Security teams can now grasp why RSA will eventually need replacement, researchers can teach quantum computing in a more grounded way, and anyone curious can follow the logic. The paper doesn't prevent the threat, but it demystifies it so we can prepare seriously.

696.bp: Researchers increasingly use large language models to simulate how different people with different backgrounds would answer surveys — instead of paying hundreds of respondents, they prompt an LLM with a persona and generate synthetic responses. This is cheap and fast, but does it actually capture real diversity?
696.wh: The intuition is that adding persona details (age, education, income, political leaning) to an LLM prompt should make it roleplay better and thus answer surveys more like real people. But LLMs are language patterns, not human simulators — they might distort certain beliefs, miss nuanced attitudes, or respond differently to demographic cues than real people do. The real question: does persona prompting reduce or increase error?
696.ap: The paper tests this against a large real-world survey dataset (World Values Survey with 70K respondent-question pairs). They prompt two open LLMs with and without persona details, asking them to answer each question as a simulated respondent. Then they compare: does the LLM's simulated answer match the real person's answer? They measure both aggregate alignment and subgroup-specific accuracy.
696.ww: The finding is uncomfortable: persona prompting doesn't reliably improve performance and in many cases makes it worse. The effect is highly heterogeneous — most questions stay the same, but some questions and underrepresented groups see large distortions. For example, an LLM might overfit to stereotype a persona, answering political questions in a caricature rather than the nuanced way real people do.
696.po: The payoff is a warning: researchers using LLMs to simulate respondents are not just approximating; they're potentially redistributing error in ways that hide minority perspectives. A study claiming to represent a 65-year-old woman from rural areas might be simulating a media stereotype instead. This suggests either dropping the persona-based simulation approach or validating heavily against real data before trusting the results.

697.bp: Cities generate vast amounts of data — sensor networks tracking traffic, air quality, energy use, crime. But most cities collect this data, analyze it separately, and then don't actually act on it. The gap between 'we know there will be congestion in 2 hours' and 'traffic lights already adapted' is where real impact dies.
697.wh: Predictive models often exist in isolation from operations. A traffic prediction system can't automatically adjust signal timing; the prediction sits in a dashboard waiting for a human to notice and act. Meanwhile, the model never learns whether the prediction was accurate or helpful. This breaks the feedback loop that makes AI systems get better — and it wastes the opportunity to prevent problems before they happen.
697.ap: This paper proposes a closed-loop architecture that connects four pieces: sensors feed data to AI/ML models, predictions feed to decision-support dashboards, decisions trigger real-world actions (changing signal timing, rerouting buses, activating resources), and outcomes flow back to retrain and refine the models. The architecture includes 'digital twins' — virtual simulations of the city — that help test decisions before deployment.
697.ww: This works because feedback is the engine of improvement. When a traffic prediction triggers an action and you measure the outcome, the model learns what worked and what didn't. This transforms prediction from hindsight to foresight — instead of explaining what happened, the system prevents it. Also, by closing the loop, you catch errors quickly: if a prediction is wrong and nobody acts on it, the model course-corrects for next time.
697.po: Cities can shift from reactive (responding to congestion after it happens) to preventive (stopping congestion before it starts). Response times to emergencies drop because signals, resources, and personnel are already positioned. Over time, the models get better because they learn from real outcomes. The payoff is smoother traffic, faster emergency response, and more resilient cities.

698.bp: Real online shopping has a long tail: most customers buy popular items, but the profit often comes from selling niche products to the right people. Recommending these hidden gems is hard because they have few interactions for the algorithm to learn from. If an algorithm can't find patterns in data, it fails.
698.wh: Collaborative filtering — learning from 'people like you bought this' — works great for popular items with lots of interaction data. But for long-tail items with maybe three purchases ever, there's simply not enough data to detect patterns. Meanwhile, large language models can read product descriptions and understand that two semantically similar niche items go together, but LLM semantics live in a different space from collaborative patterns, and it's unclear how to combine them without one drowning out the other.
698.ap: FCRLLM uses a 'flipped classroom' dynamic: normally a teacher (LLM) teaches students (collaborative model). Here, the framework flips it — the collaborative model's attention patterns actively shape what the LLM focuses on, pulling semantic understanding toward real user interactions. The mechanism uses energy-based learning (inspired by neural networks that find stable states) so that collaborative and semantic signals pull toward a common representation instead of fighting.
698.ww: This works because both signals are right but incompatible on first glance: collaborative filtering sees 'these users interact' while LLM semantics sees 'these items are conceptually close.' By letting them negotiate via energy minimization, the model finds representations where both constraints hold — semantic neighbor items end up close in the space when collaborative data supports it, but only then.
698.po: Experiments show the method works on real shopping datasets with long-tail items. Niche products now get recommended to the right customers more often, driving revenue from items that would otherwise languish. The collaborative signal grounds LLM semantics in real user behavior, avoiding over-generalization, while the LLM signal compensates for cold-start problems on unpopular items.

699.bp: Misinformation spreads fast online: a photo of a politician from 2010 captioned as 'today' misleads millions before fact-checkers can respond. Out-of-context image-text mismatches — the image and text don't actually belong together — are a major class of misinformation that's hard to detect.
699.wh: Detecting mismatches requires understanding both the image content and the text and reasoning about whether they align. Most approaches either look only at images or only at text, missing the cross-modal contradiction. Methods that use both modalities often rely on external web search to verify claims, which is slow, expensive, and won't work in regions without good search infrastructure. Lightweight methods that work without external data tend to miss subtle mismatches.
699.ap: This framework combines three pieces without needing web evidence: extract semantic entities from the image using object detection, generate a description of what's actually in the image, and combine that description with the text caption into a prompt for a language model (Flan-T5) to judge alignment. In parallel, run a CLIP model that directly assesses image-text visual-semantic match. Then ensemble the two judgments using weights optimized specifically for detecting misinformation.
699.ww: This works because generating descriptions forces the system to commit to what's actually visible, and then asking a language model 'does this description match the text?' catches when text makes a claim the image doesn't support. CLIP independently checks if the image and text 'feel' related semantically. Combining both catches different failure modes: text might claim something false, or text might claim something that could be true but isn't what the image shows.
699.po: The method reaches state-of-the-art accuracy among approaches that don't use external web data, while running fast enough for real-time deployment. A news platform or social network can now flag out-of-context images as users upload them, with modest computational cost. This matters in regions where external verification services are unavailable and where the spread of misinformation is fastest.

700.bp: When computer systems make decisions about people — credit scores, job applications, content moderation — they should treat everyone fairly. But social networks and demographic data are often incomplete: you might know someone's age but not their race, or vice versa. Many fairness solutions invent the missing data, which can introduce new biases.
700.wh: The temptation to fill in missing demographic data is strong — more information seems better. But inventing data guesses about protected characteristics (race, gender, religion) inevitably encodes societal stereotypes and can make fairness worse, not better. Meanwhile, if you ignore the missing data entirely, the model might treat people unfairly simply by accident. The real challenge: how do you ensure fairness without fabricating protected information?
700.ap: FairGE (Fair Graph Encoding) uses spectral graph theory — a mathematical way to understand network structure — instead of generating missing data. It leverages the network's principal eigenvector (the dominant pattern of connections) to capture structural information about each person, then pads the missing demographic attributes with zeros rather than guessing. This mathematical abstraction preserves the network's fairness properties without inventing sensitive data.
700.ww: This works because spectral properties of graphs encode meaningful structural patterns without requiring protected attributes. The principal eigenvector identifies high-influence nodes and structural roles automatically. By using zeros for missing demographics, the system avoids encoding false assumptions. Theoretically, this suppresses biased spectral components while preserving fair ones.
700.po: Experiments on real social networks show at least 16% improvement in both statistical parity (everyone has similar outcome rates) and equality of opportunity (disparities are minimized) compared to methods that generate missing data. Most importantly, fairness improves without requiring invasive demographic data collection, protecting user privacy while making the system more equitable.

701.bp: Vietnamese medicinal plants are a source of traditional knowledge and potential new medicines, but that knowledge is scattered across Vietnamese sources, with names and classifications that don't match global scientific databases. A researcher in Vietnam can't easily search the global biodiversity network using Vietnamese plant names.
701.wh: Biodiversity platforms like GBIF are powerful but English-centric: species are named in Latin and English, the search interface is English-only, and connections to local knowledge are sparse. For Vietnamese researchers, this means starting every search by translating local names to Latin names to use the global system, which is tedious and discourages engagement. Meanwhile, if Vietnamese medicinal plants aren't in global datasets, global conservation and medical research miss potentially important species.
701.ap: Viet Medi Species 2026 assembles 310K images of 4,799 medicinal plant species from Vietnam, using both scientific names (linked to GBIF) and Vietnamese vernacular names. The pipeline automatically extracted and validated images at scale using a reproducible, asynchronous process. The dataset includes metadata tied to Vietnamese culture and knowledge while maintaining links to global taxonomy via GBIF identifiers.
701.ww: This works because it creates a bridge: a Vietnamese person can now search in Vietnamese, find images of medicinal plants they recognize, and automatically discover the global scientific information and research connected to those plants through GBIF. Conversely, a global researcher studying a particular plant family can see how that family appears in Vietnamese traditional medicine.
701.po: Researchers in Vietnam now have a local-language resource for biodiversity that doesn't compromise global integration. The dataset enables new research connecting Vietnamese traditional medicine to modern pharmacology. Most broadly, the project demonstrates a template for including non-English languages and local knowledge in global datasets, enabling more equitable participation in global science.

702.bp: When handed a new dataset you've never seen before — say, a pile of customer service complaints with no categories — how do you systematically figure out what patterns exist? Even with an LLM suggesting rough categories, it's hard to evolve those guesses into a clean, consistent taxonomy.
702.wh: The intuition is that LLMs can generate category suggestions, but rough suggestions aren't enough. You need to step back and see where categories cluster across the full dataset (a 'wide view'), then zoom in and check whether your extraction method consistently identifies those categories (a 'sharp focus'). Most discovery tools do one or the other — either showing you the big picture or validating details — but not both together.
702.ap: Pattern Insights Explorer alternates between two perspectives: wide-lens analysis zooms out and shows which patterns cluster across the full dataset landscape, revealing where meaningful categories emerge. Then sharp-focus validation zooms in on specific examples to verify the extraction method actually works — does it consistently capture the pattern it claims to? The framework refines the taxonomy iteratively, evolving rough sketches into precise categories without needing external ground truth.
702.ww: This works because discovery is naturally rhythmic: you first need to see the big picture (where are patterns hiding?), then zoom in to validate (am I actually finding what I think?). This rhythm prevents two common failures: discovering phantom patterns that don't really exist (you zoom in and find the method isn't reliable), or missing patterns that only show up in certain data regions (you zoomed too far in).
702.po: A team can now take an unfamiliar dataset and systematically extract a clean taxonomy without experts manually labeling everything. The wide-lens and sharp-focus cycle prevents both over-generalization and missed nuances. This is especially valuable for exploratory research where the categories aren't known upfront, and for applied settings where standardizing unstructured data is bottleneck.

703.bp: In social networks with positive and negative relationships — collaborators and rivals, allies and enemies — machine learning models need to predict whether a future connection will be positive or negative. But when an AI model makes a prediction, users need to understand why: what made it think two people should be enemies?
703.wh: Explaining graph neural network predictions is already hard (they integrate information across many steps of neighbors and connections), but signed graphs add a twist: the sign of each relationship matters. Existing explanation methods either ignore signs entirely or return disconnected graph fragments that don't make intuitive sense. A human looking at an explanation needs to see: 'these people are connected through a positive path to you, and a negative path to them, so they should conflict.'
703.ap: SGExplainer uses 'balanced paths' from signed graph theory as its core concept: a balanced path is a sequence of relationships that has internal logic (positive times positive equals positive, positive times negative equals negative, like multiplying numbers). The algorithm learns which nodes and edges to keep by training a mask — a binary layer that highlights subgraph regions — then enforces the constraint that the highlighted subgraph consists of balanced paths. This ensures explanations are both faithful and human-intelligible.
703.ww: This works because balanced paths have intuitive appeal: you can trace a path on a graph, count the signs along the way, and see whether the final result makes sense. This is something a human can verify by hand. By building explanations from balanced paths, the system automatically produces explanations that are both theoretically grounded (faithful to the model's reasoning) and psychologically clear (people understand them).
703.po: The framework generates explanations for link sign predictions that are both accurate and interpretable. A social network platform can now show users: 'we think you and this person will clash because you're both close friends with this mutual friend, but you have opposite opinions, which creates tension.' Experiments show SGExplainer outperforms baseline methods in both explanation quality and efficiency, making real-time interpretability feasible.

704.bp: In e-commerce recommendation systems, feature selection is critical: engineers manually pick which product attributes (color, brand, price, seller) to feed to the recommendation model. Picking the right subset cuts computation while keeping accuracy high. But modern deep learning makes it hard to know which features actually matter.
704.wh: Deep neural networks learn hierarchically: early layers capture low-level features, middle layers combine them, later layers make final decisions. A simple approach asks 'which features matter to the final output?' but this misses layers in the middle where real learning happens. Existing methods estimate feature importance from sensitivity (how much does output change if we perturb this feature?) or from learned gates, but they often rely on just one layer or one batch of samples, making estimates unstable and biased.
704.ap: FairFS identifies three specific bias problems: layer bias (importance estimates depend on which layer you look at), baseline bias (the reference point for what 'no feature' means matters a lot), and approximation bias (how you aggregate signals across samples affects which features look important). FairFS regularizes feature importance across all layers simultaneously, uses a smooth baseline feature close to the classifier's decision boundary, and aggregates approximations carefully to counterbalance these biases.
704.ww: This works because it directly targets the sources of error rather than hoping a single measurement will be right. By demanding consistency across layers, you force the model to agree with itself — if a feature matters early, it should still matter later. A carefully-chosen baseline gives you a sensible 'what does zero information look like?' reference point. Aggregation methods that account for approximation error prevent one noisy sample from dominating.
704.po: The result is more accurate feature importance estimates that recommendation teams can trust to guide their feature selection decisions. This means faster models (fewer features to compute) without sacrificing accuracy. On real industrial systems with thousands of candidate features and millions of users, picking the right 50 features instead of the wrong 50 can save massive computational cost while maintaining recommendation quality.

705.bp: When you buy things online or move money through a bank, the system remembers every action you take—every click, every purchase, every login. Traditionally, systems learned patterns from the order these actions happened in (like: you searched for shoes, then looked at reviews, then bought). But they miss something crucial: the hidden connections between you and the items. If millions of other people bought the same shoes, that shared interest is a signal the system throws away.
705.wh: The tension is this: order-based learning (what happened first, second, third) is great at spotting sequences, but it ignores the big web of who-bought-what-together. Meanwhile, treating the web structure separately from the sequence loses the timing—when did the connection form? Both pieces of information matter, but existing methods force you to pick one.
705.ap: The authors propose three specific ways to weave in the connection-web structure: first, they enrich the sequence embeddings themselves by mixing in signals about the graph; second, they directly align your learned profile with your position in the web; third, they add a training task that explicitly teaches the model to predict graph structure. They test which strategy works best depending on how connected the graph is.
705.ww: When you mix the two—the order of your actions AND the web of connections—the system can spot when you're similar to someone you've never directly interacted with, just by recognizing that you both connect to the same things in the same order. It's like the system becomes a detective: instead of only looking at your personal diary, it also checks 'oh, I see you're connected to Item X, and so are 500 other people who then bought Item Y. You probably will too.'
705.po: On real financial and e-commerce data, this mixed approach improved fraud detection and recommendation accuracy by up to 2.3 percentage points. The research also reveals that how connected the graph is matters: dense graphs (where everything touches everything) favor one strategy; sparse graphs favor another.

706.bp: Question-and-answer platforms like Stack Overflow or Korean Knowledge iN let people post questions and get answers from the public. For decades this worked because real humans answered—they drew on experience, lived through problems, could explain nuance. Now, AI language models can generate answers that sound plausible and often correct. The question is not 'can the AI fool us?' but 'how is this changing the platform's soul? Are humans still the backbone, or are we gradually replacing them?'
706.wh: The hard part is that AI-generated answers look nearly identical to human answers in the raw text. Humans don't wear a uniform. An AI might write longer, use more punctuation, reuse similar phrases; but so might a human with that style. You need to detect the subtle fingerprints that only AI leaves—patterns in word choice, structure, even the probability of certain words appearing together.
706.ap: The researchers implemented nine existing AI-detection methods (each one looks for different fingerprints: word distributions, syntax patterns, semantic consistency, etc.). They stacked the three best-performing ones together, using the outputs of each as inputs to a final classifier. On real Q&A platform data, this ensemble detector achieved 99.87% accuracy.
706.ww: Language models are trained on massive amounts of text data, which biases them toward certain patterns that real humans (especially Q&A answerers) use less frequently. For example, humans ramble; they use conversational filler; they sometimes contradict themselves. AI models are smoother, more formal, more consistent—not because they're better, but because they're sampling from a learned probability distribution that's been squeezed into a matrix of numbers. These statistical fingerprints are learnable.
706.po: Using this detector, they found 75,558 AI-generated answers among 1.46 million. Interestingly, these AI answers received the same upvote/downvote reaction as human answers, suggesting people can't tell the difference. But AI answers tend to be longer and more diverse in language. The real surprise: the platform is shifting—questions are moving away from 'what are the facts?' toward 'what's your personal story?'—territory where humans still have the edge.

707.bp: Rainfall forecasting saves lives.
