When a storm is coming, water managers need to know if it'll rain, when, and how hard, so they can release water from dams, evacuate people, and manage infrastructure. Modern AI models trained on weather data can make these predictions, but they face a strange problem: rain doesn't fall every day, and the model doesn't know how to predict 'no rain'—it predicts a tiny amount of drizzle everywhere instead.
707.wh: Most modern time-series foundation models (large pre-trained models that predict numbers over time) assume the output is a smooth, continuous curve. They're built for things like temperature or stock prices, which follow that pattern. But rain is different: on any given day, there's a discrete decision (rain yes/no), and only if yes, how much. These models output continuous numbers, so they can't represent the true zero-or-something structure. Retraining these massive models for this specific case would cost thousands of dollars and tons of electricity.
707.ap: They apply three mathematical corrections in sequence: first, they use historical rain-probability to restore the true zero mass (days with no rain); second, they use a probability-integral transform to align the distribution of rainy days; third, they apply a tail-mapping technique for extreme storms. Each step takes the model's predictions and reshapes them to match reality's actual structure.
707.ww: The insight is: you don't need to retrain the model. Instead, post-process its predictions. The model outputs a number for each day (say, 2.3mm when it won't actually rain). You can then ask: 'what percentage of days in history had zero rain?' Then you can mathematically map the model's predictions to either truly-zero (no rain) or positive-value (it will rain), using statistical tools that preserve the overall pattern the model learned.
707.po: On South Australian rainfall data, this wrapper dramatically reduced false alarms (drizzle predictions) and improved detection of actual storms, with almost zero computational cost (5 milliseconds per forecast vs. hundreds of GPU-hours for retraining). The method is so cheap and general that it can be deployed globally without retraining.

708.bp: Imagine a social network that changes over time: new people join, new groups form, and friendships shift. Now imagine the network is so large that you can't retrain the model from scratch every time something changes. You need a system that learns on-the-fly while remembering what it learned before. The challenge is common in real platforms—your knowledge model was trained last month, but today's graph looks different, with new categories of people and new connection patterns.
708.wh: The tension is two-fold. First, when new kinds of people appear (new classes), the model struggles to categorize them because they're completely foreign. Second, when the features of existing people change (someone's style, interests, or behavior shift), the model forgets its old knowledge trying to fit the new pattern—called catastrophic forgetting. You can't solve both at once: if you prioritize learning the new, you lose the old; if you stay rigid about the old, you fail on the new.
708.ap: DINGLE has two modules. The first breaks apart a person's learned profile into these two pieces (semantic core + current style), using a neural decoupler. The second uses a teacher-student setup where the teacher model guards the old knowledge and the student learns new patterns; knowledge flows from teacher to student, preventing forgetting. They also keep banks of example representations and model parameters to make sure old knowledge doesn't evaporate.
708.ww: The breakthrough idea: separate the unchanging core from the changeable surface. Each person has a 'semantic' part (their true category—are they a tech person? social person? whatever the fixed categories are) and a 'domain' part (their current style—how they dress in this time period, how they speak now). When the style changes, only the style part should update; the core stays put. This way, when you see a new style, you recognize the core is still the same, so you don't forget.
708.po: On five real-world graph datasets, DINGLE improved classification accuracy while successfully learning new classes without forgetting old ones. It beat eleven other methods that tried to solve either the class problem or the domain problem separately.

709.bp: This is an announcement, not a research paper: Samsung's research team is hosting a workshop to discuss where web advertising is headed. The field is under pressure—regulators want privacy, companies want personalization, users want good experiences, and all three are in tension. The workshop exists to bring these worlds together and imagine solutions.
709.wh: The friction is unavoidable: every ad targeted to you relies on knowing something about you, which raises privacy alarms. AI can help personalize without tracking, but that's still emerging. Meanwhile, new immersive technologies (VR, AR, interactive ads) are arriving faster than we have ethical frameworks for them.
709.ap: Samsung is creating a forum where researchers and practitioners from different fields present cutting-edge work, discuss challenges, and collectively explore solutions at the intersection of privacy, AI, and user experience.
709.ww: No single company or research group can solve this alone. You need advertising engineers, privacy specialists, data scientists, and ethicists talking to each other. Often they speak past each other—privacy people say 'block all tracking,' advertising people say 'tracking is how we work,' and the truth lives in the middle. Workshops create spaces where that dialogue can happen.
709.po: The workshop aims to influence the future of web advertising: shaping it toward ethical standards, responsible AI use, and privacy-respecting personalization. It's a platform for research and ideas to flow from academia into industry practice.

710.bp: Video platforms like Kuaishou serve billions of searches every day—people looking for short clips on every topic imaginable. But many searches are for niche topics (long-tail queries) where few people have searched before, so the platform has little data on what videos users found satisfying. The result: low-quality content (clickbait, shallow videos) rises to the top because algorithms only have sparse interaction signals to learn from. The goal is to surface genuinely good content even when almost nobody's clicked on it yet.
710.wh: The fundamental tension: you want to rank videos by true quality (would users enjoy this?), but you only have clicks and views—sparse, noisy, biased signals that favor sensational content. If a niche video is excellent but hasn't been discovered yet, the algorithm will bury it. Retraining a ranking model from scratch is expensive; you need a faster lever.
710.ap: The authors build a two-stage system: stage one uses multimodal evidence (video frames, text, audio) to create training data about which videos are high-quality, using an LLM to assign these labels. Stage two uses preference-learning (the model learns that video A is better than video B) to fine-tune the ranking. At serving time, the learned quality scores rerank videos and feed into reinforcement learning for page-level optimization.
710.ww: Large language models already have learned vast amounts about the world and about video content. They've been trained on billions of text descriptions, reviews, and discussions. This means an LLM can independently assess whether a video is shallow clickbait or genuinely informative, without ever seeing who clicked on it. It's like having a critic who doesn't know the popularity numbers—just the content itself.
710.po: In offline tests, this improved ranking quality (AUC, diversity metrics). In a live A/B test on 15% of real traffic, users watched more videos and reported higher satisfaction—all while the system promoted higher-quality but previously-underexposed content. The Matthew effect (rich-get-richer) was partially reversed.

711.bp: Pathologists examine tissue samples under microscopes to diagnose disease. For each image, they must mark regions of interest—tumor, normal, inflamed tissue—pixel by pixel. This is exhausting and error-prone. Modern computer vision models could automate this, but training them requires thousands of hand-drawn pixel-level masks from experts. Creating these takes weeks of manual work. The question is: can we train a model with only image-level labels (doctors just say 'this tissue is cancerous') instead of pixel-level labels, cutting annotation time from weeks to hours?
711.wh: Weakly-supervised segmentation has a fundamental problem: without pixel-level truth, the model struggles to distinguish between what's actually tumor and what's just background coincidence. Two challenges make this worse: tissues of the same type look different (intra-class variation—tumor cells don't all look identical), and different tissue types can look similar (inter-class confusion—inflamed tissue might look like early tumor). The model easily gets confused and latches onto spurious patterns rather than true diagnostic features.
711.ap: The method uses hierarchical text prompts: for each tissue class, they create text descriptions and embed them using a pre-trained language model. The vision model learns to align its features at multiple layers with these text embeddings. They also use hierarchical class prompts, where each class is subdivided into clusters (subtypes) to capture internal variation. High-confidence predictions from this process become pseudo-labels (guesses) for further training.
711.ww: If you pair the vision model with a language model (which has been trained on medical descriptions), the language model becomes a critic. When the vision model is unsure ('is this tissue A or B?'), the language model can provide semantic guidance ('tissue A is characterized by these features'). By making the vision model's learned features match the language model's textual descriptions, you ground the pixel-level predictions in real medical knowledge rather than accident.
711.po: On histopathology datasets, this weakly-supervised approach generated pixel-level segmentations that rival full supervision, without requiring experts to hand-draw masks for thousands of images. The method captures both fine-grained details and coarse structure, improving diagnostic accuracy while slashing annotation burden.

712.bp: ChatGPT now has a memory feature: it remembers things you tell it across conversations. You might mention your dog's name, your job title, or your health concerns in one chat, and the system recalls these in the next week's conversation. This personalization is powerful—the system feels like it knows you. But it also creates a hidden profile: a data portrait of who you are, built from your casual disclosures. The question is: who controls this portrait, and what's in it?
712.wh: The core tension: personalization requires remembering facts about you, but facts about health, finances, family, or beliefs are sensitive. Users don't always realize they're being profiled when they chat. They assume they're having private conversations, not that their words are being extracted and stored as structured data. And they have little visibility into what the system 'remembered' or how it was used.
712.ap: The researchers analyzed 2,050 real memory entries from 80 ChatGPT users. They classified what each memory contained: structured facts (dog name, job), personal data under GDPR (address, financial status), or psychological insights (personality traits, fears). They also checked whether the system created the memory or the user explicitly asked for it. Then they designed Attribution Shield, a tool that alerts users to sensitive inferences and suggests safer ways to phrase the same idea.
712.ww: A memory is only useful if it's accurate and relevant. If the system misunderstands what you said and stores a false 'fact,' you've been mislabeled. If it correctly extracts sensitive details but uses them to infer private information (like health status from casual mentions), you've been profiled without consent. Transparency lets users see what's happening and correct errors.
712.po: Key findings: 96% of memories were created unilaterally by the system (users didn't ask); 28% contained GDPR-defined personal data; 52% contained psychological inferences. 84% were accurate. Attribution Shield demonstrates that you can show users what's happening and protect them without losing personalization—it's a middle ground between total transparency and privacy.

713.bp: Imagine you're asked: 'Who won the 2024 Olympics, and what sport did they represent at university?' This requires hopping through multiple facts: find the winner, find their background, verify their sport. Traditional search engines would ask you to do this manually (search, click, search again, click). New AI systems promise to answer multi-hop questions in one step by retrieving relevant information and synthesizing it. But they often break down mid-way: they make a wrong guess at one step, and the subsequent steps cascade off a cliff.
713.wh: The challenge is error propagation. If the system misunderstands the first question ('who won?'), the second search will be for the wrong person entirely. Additionally, language models are prone to decomposing complex questions incorrectly—they might miss which parts are questions and which parts are constraints. There's no way to recover from these early mistakes, so the final answer is nonsense.
713.ap: Reasoning Tree Guided RAG (RT-RAG) builds an explicit reasoning tree by parsing the question for entities and constraints, using consensus voting to pick the best tree from multiple candidates. Then it traverses the tree bottom-up, searching for and refining information at each step. When the model rewrites a query for the next search, it grounds the rewrite in the evidence found so far, preventing drift.
713.ww: The key insight: structure the question into an explicit tree before you start searching. Instead of letting the model freestyle its search path, force it to create a plan: 'the core question is X, these are the known entities (facts I already have), these are the unknown entities (facts I need to find).' This tree acts as a roadmap. If the model strays, you catch it. More importantly, when you're traversing the tree bottom-up, each level is constrained by the level below it, so errors don't cascade as badly.
713.po: On multi-hop question-answering benchmarks, RT-RAG improved performance by 7.0 percentage points in exact match and 6.0 points in F1 score compared to methods that let the model freestyle its reasoning. The structured approach trades flexibility for reliability.

714.bp: Watch a live stream on your phone, and packets are traveling across cellular networks—WiFi, 4G, 5G—each prone to dropping data. If a packet is lost, the video frame is corrupted; if too many frames corrupt, the stream stutters and becomes unwatchable. Real-time video (sports, gaming, live news) is especially sensitive: a one-second delay destroys the experience. The goal is to deliver video without stutters even when the network is unreliable, while using the minimum necessary bandwidth.
714.wh: The classic solution is Forward Error Correction (FEC): send extra redundant packets so the receiver can recover from loss. But how much redundancy is enough? Too little, and you still get stutters; too much, and you waste bandwidth. Most systems apply the same FEC level to every frame, missing a crucial fact: loss doesn't happen uniformly. Sometimes the network loses three packets in a row (burst loss), but the system protected each frame independently, wasting protection on frames that weren't hit.
714.ap: Breath dynamically adjusts the 'protection boundary'—the grouping of frames under one FEC umbrella—based on real-time network conditions and video properties. When burst loss is expected (e.g., network congestion detected), it widens the boundary (group more frames); when loss is sparse, it narrows the boundary (use less redundancy). The system continuously adapts based on observed packet loss patterns and video bitrate.
714.ww: Burst loss is the key insight: a burst of packet loss at the network level can affect multiple frames, but the damage can be smoothed out if you protect at a multi-frame level rather than per-frame. Imagine frames A, B, C and the network loses two packets in a row. If FEC protected A and B separately, both would be damaged. But if FEC protected A+B+C as a unit, the burst hits hard locally but the recovery algorithm can stitch everything back together from the redundancy in the group.
714.po: In emulated mobile networks with real production traffic, Breath reduced video playback interruptions by 17-22% and allowed higher video bitrate (10-14% improvement) compared to fixed-boundary FEC schemes. The adaptive approach trades real-time computation for better user experience and bandwidth efficiency.

715.bp: You visit a news website, and without you knowing, an invisible 1x1 pixel image loads from a third-party server (advertisers, data brokers, etc.). That tiny image exfiltrates information: your IP address, browser cookies, the page you're on. This happens across thousands of websites, building a profile of your behavior across the internet. Unlike cookies, pixel tracking is stealthy and cheap. Defense tools like ad blockers struggle because pixels hide in plain sight, looking like legitimate content.
715.wh: Detecting pixel tracking is hard because the network traffic looks legitimate—it's just an HTTP request for an image, indistinguishable from a real image load. You can't block all image requests; the site's content won't load. You need to understand the context: is this image request truly needed for the page to display, or is it harvesting data? This requires understanding associations across websites—if server X appears as an invisible tracker on 1,000 sites, it's probably malicious, even if it looks normal in isolation.
715.ap: TGNN (Tracking Graph Neural Network) encodes HTTP traffic into quadruples (domain, path, resource, destination), then models the cross-site associations as a directed graph (Tracking Directed Graph). It uses a graph neural network to learn both semantic features (what does the request contain?) and interaction patterns (which combinations are suspicious?). To overcome label scarcity, they use an LLM with minimal expert input to generate high-quality labels automatically.
715.ww: The solution is to model the problem as a graph: websites are nodes, and requests between them are edges. If you can learn which edges are tracking (third-party associations that harvest data) and which are legitimate, you can build a model of the tracking infrastructure. Large language models have already learned what legitimate vs. deceptive third parties typically look like (from their training data), so you can use them to label initial examples, then train a specialized detection model on that labeled data.
715.po: On traffic from the top 10,000 websites, TGNN detected pixel tracking with high accuracy, outperforming existing filter-list and machine-learning baselines. The measurement revealed that at least 16.74% of websites use pixel tracking via major third-party services, establishing cross-site tracking as widespread infrastructure rather than fringe abuse.

716.bp: Advertisers run campaigns with fixed budgets—spend 10,000 dollars over a month. But ad auctions change minute-to-minute: sometimes ad space is cheap, sometimes expensive. An advertiser wants to spread their 10,000 dollars evenly across the month so they don't burn it all in one expensive day and run out later. This is called 'budget pacing'—controlling the spend rate to match the campaign goal.
716.wh: The standard approach is ad-hoc parameter tuning: adjust dials until the spend rate looks right. But auctions are chaotic; a parameter that works today might overshoot or undershoot tomorrow. If you spend too fast early, you run out of budget when the best inventory arrives later. If you spend too slow, you waste the opportunity. You need a controller that automatically adjusts to changing auction conditions without manual fiddling.
716.ap: The authors propose a controller combining hysteresis (thresholds that must be crossed before reacting) with proportional feedback (the size of the correction is proportional to the error). For a budget campaign, the controller tracks the desired spend rate and adjusts bidding behavior to stay on track. They provide analysis for parameter selection so practitioners can tune it correctly for their auction environment.
716.ww: Control theory—the math behind thermostats and cruise control—offers a proven framework. Instead of tuning parameters manually, set a desired spend rate, measure the actual spend rate, and feed the error (desired minus actual) back into an adjustment mechanism. Over time, the system self-corrects. Crucially, adding a bit of 'hysteresis' (don't react to every tiny fluctuation) prevents oscillation—overshooting one way, then correcting too hard the other way.
716.po: In real online auctions, this control-theoretic approach reduced pacing error by 13% and reduced volatility in spending by 54% compared to existing methods. It's particularly valuable for small-budget campaigns where overshoot is disastrous; the principled approach is far more stable than manual tuning.

717.bp: Intelligent tutoring systems track what students have learned as they progress through a course. If the system knows whether a student has mastered algebra, geometry, and calculus, it can recommend the right next problem. This is knowledge tracing. But students take courses across multiple disciplines (math, then physics, then computer science), and knowledge in one discipline helps in another. A student who masters algebra finds physics easier. The challenge is: how do you transfer learning across disciplines when knowledge structures are different?
717.wh: The tension is two-fold: students have different cognitive abilities (some are natural problem-solvers, others are memorizers), which shift as they move between disciplines. Additionally, disciplines organize knowledge differently—algebra focuses on symbolic manipulation, physics on conceptual models, computer science on logic. A model trained on algebra students might not work for physics students, even if they're learning similar underlying concepts.
717.ap: DTransKT has two modules. The Cross-disciplinary Graph-matching (CG) module extracts meta-skill representations from each student's learning trajectory, then aligns these across disciplines. The Cross-disciplinary Attention-assisting (CA) module uses a pre-trained language model to extract meta-semantics from textual course content, so knowledge from one discipline can inform another. These components work together to make a knowledge-tracing model work across multiple subjects.
717.ww: The key insight: separate the 'what' from the 'how.' Every discipline has meta-skills—deep cognitive patterns that transcend subjects (reasoning, pattern-matching, abstraction). These transcend disciplines. What changes is the domain-specific surface: how you express your reasoning in symbols vs. diagrams vs. code. If you can extract and align these meta-skills, you can transfer learning across disciplines even if the content looks different.
717.po: When applied to seven existing knowledge-tracing models, DTransKT improved transfer-learning accuracy by 14.2% on average and improved AUC by 4.5%. The framework enables a single system to track student progress across math, science, and humanities—traditionally siloed domains—without retraining from scratch for each new discipline.

718.bp: Recommendation systems learn from user behavior: you click videos, so the system shows you similar videos. But noise corrupts this signal—you might click something by accident, or one bad click shouldn't outweigh ten good ones. The system should amplify strong signals (this user genuinely loves this type of content) and suppress noise (random clicks, clickbait). The challenge is especially hard when data is sparse: what if very few people have interacted with an item? You're making recommendations in the dark.
718.wh: Graph-based recommendation systems face two opposing problems: random edge perturbations (used to train the model) can accidentally delete the strongest signal edges, teaching the model noise. Meanwhile, sparse data means you have few edges to learn from anyway, so the model generalizes poorly. You need augmentation (creating training variation) that's smart enough to preserve true signals while filtering noise.
718.ap: RaDAR combines two mechanisms: a generative model that captures the global structure of the user-item graph, and a denoising model that refines noisy edges. It uses asymmetric comparisons (learning from mismatches of different weights) with global negative sampling to maintain semantic consistency. The relation-aware component dynamically adjusts edge importance based on learned node semantics, not fixed rules.
718.ww: Instead of random perturbation, use a learned denoising process: imagine gradually adding noise to the graph until it's chaos, then learning to remove that noise step-by-step. A model trained on this diffusion process learns which edges are robust (survive noise) and which are fragile (noise). Real user-preference edges are typically robust. This diffusion-based augmentation is far smarter than random erasure.
718.po: On three real recommendation benchmarks, RaDAR outperformed existing methods, especially on noisy and sparse datasets. The diffusion-guided augmentation and relation-aware refinement both contributed to robustness—the system made better recommendations even when user behavior data was incomplete or contradictory.

719.bp: When you watch a video, pause, then continue later, the recommendation system should remember where you were and suggest what's likely to come next. This is sequential recommendation—understanding that users have an evolving interest over time, not a static preference. The system learns patterns: people who watch intro tutorials then advanced tutorials then project examples tend to learn well. The challenge is capturing this evolution without forcing the model to memorize individual sequences.
719.wh: Most methods use fixed data augmentation (random shuffling, dropout) to create training variations. But these are blunt instruments: shuffling might destroy the very sequence pattern you're trying to learn. And there's no guarantee that the augmented version preserves what the user actually cares about—their intent. If a user watches cooking tutorials then physics lectures, random augmentation might create a fake 'user' who does the opposite order, confusing the model about what sequences are valid.
719.ap: ACLSRec (Adaptive Contrastive Learning for Sequential Recommendation) trains two neural networks jointly: one that perturbs (changes) user sequences in learnable ways, and one that restores (recovers the original intent). The model uses these networks to generate augmented versions of sequences during training, then learns from pairs of original and augmented sequences. This adaptive augmentation is specific to each user and dataset.
719.ww: Instead of predefined augmentation, learn which perturbations are valid. A learnable perturbation network learns what changes in a sequence are acceptable (watching videos in a different order is fine, but completely changing genres might not be). A restoration network then learns to recover the essential user intent from the perturbed sequence. Together, they generate semantically valid variations that preserve what truly matters.
719.po: On real e-commerce and entertainment datasets, ACLSRec achieved higher recommendation accuracy than fixed-augmentation baselines. By preserving semantic consistency across augmented views, the model learned more robust interest patterns and made better predictions about what users would watch or buy next.

720.bp: In real-world networks — social media, computer systems, financial transactions — most nodes are normal but a few are broken, malicious, or dangerous. We want to spot these outliers using only a handful of known good examples. The challenge: you can't just memorize what you've been shown; the network is complex, with hidden patterns in both the properties of nodes and how they're wired together.
720.wh: The usual approach to finding anomalies is to show a model one example of a 'bad' node and say 'find more like this.' But real anomalies don't come in one flavor. Some are slightly wrong, some are completely inverted, and some are a mix of both kinds of wrong simultaneously. A naive detector trained on a single corruption type will miss the nuanced, stepwise progression of how normal nodes decay into truly broken ones.
720.ap: This work proposes PAGE, which builds fake anomalies on purpose — but does it carefully, in stages. First, it takes known normal nodes and tweaks their numbers (attributes). Then it takes those tweaked nodes and rewires their connections in the graph, creating increasingly severe hybrid anomalies. Crucially, it trains the system to recognize that stepwise anomalies (mild corruption → severe corruption) form a progression, with harder anomalies clearly worse than easier ones.
720.ww: By learning to generate and rank this spectrum of corruption, the model builds a more complete picture of what 'wrong' looks like. Instead of having to memorize specific corruptions from labeled data, it learns the underlying logic: normal nodes sit at one end of a spectrum, and genuine anomalies are far along that spectrum. When a new, never-before-seen anomaly arrives, it's easier to spot because the model has internalized the rules of degradation.
720.po: On standard test graphs, PAGE beats existing methods significantly. The concrete gain is that it detects complex anomalies — nodes that mix attribute and structural corruption — which simpler approaches miss. This matters for real systems like fraud rings in financial networks, where bad actors disguise themselves by mixing strange transaction behavior with unusual connection patterns.

721.bp: News recommendation is about showing each person the articles they'll actually read, right now. But people's tastes shift constantly. A topic that mattered yesterday might be irrelevant tomorrow because a major event broke, the person got bored, or their life context changed. The system needs to track both what people stable like over months and what they crave in the next hour.
721.wh: Most systems freeze the social graph of past reads once and ask 'what's this person typically interested in?' This completely misses the oscillation of attention. A user might read politics every day for six weeks, then abandon it entirely for sports when a World Cup starts. A static snapshot can't see this shift without throwing out all the historical context that makes recommendations smart.
721.ap: This framework uses two branches running in parallel. One looks at the entire history to spot long-term patterns — 'this person loves tech news.' The other slices the recent past into chunks of time (stage-wise windows) and feeds them into an LSTM (a model that remembers sequences) to see the recent drift: 'they've been reading less tech this week.' It also uses attention to jump directly to the most relevant moments in the recent past, ignoring the noise.
721.ww: By combining long-term and short-term signals, the system avoids two failures. It doesn't over-fit to noise (short-term blips of unusual behavior) because it's anchored to what the person has reliably liked. It doesn't miss the signal either (the actual shift in interest) because it's explicitly listening to recent sequences. The two branches argue, and a smart combination of their outputs wins.
721.po: On real news recommendation logs from thousands of users, this framework delivers fresher, more relevant articles. The measurable win: when a user's interests shift (detected by the short-term branch), the recommendations adapt faster and remain less stale compared to pure long-term systems. This means fewer skipped articles and more engaged readers.

722.bp: Graph neural networks (machine learning models that learn patterns in networks) often fail when they have no information about nodes other than the wiring. Imagine trying to classify people in a social network if you only knew who knew whom, not their age, interests, or anything else. The network structure alone isn't enough; you need properties describing what each node is.
722.wh: Adding fake properties helps: if you pick a few representative nodes as 'landmarks' and measure how far every other node is from each landmark, you create a fingerprint. But which landmarks should you pick? How many? And which distance measure works best? These choices depend entirely on the specific graph and what you're trying to predict. No single choice works for all graphs.
722.ap: SCOUT learns these choices automatically. It tests different distance metrics (how to measure far-ness) and structure measures (e.g., 'hubs' or 'bridges') to find which pair works best for the given graph. It then uses the distribution of how central nodes are (the natural 'heavy tail' where a few nodes matter most) to automatically decide how many landmarks to use. Once these are tuned, it builds the fingerprints and feeds them into any graph neural network.
722.ww: Different graphs have different personalities. A social network favors landmarks that are hubs; a road network might favor nodes along bottlenecks. By learning graph-level properties first, SCOUT sidesteps the problem of hand-tuning per-graph. The heavy-tailed distribution insight captures the intuition that a few landmarks go a long way; adding the hundredth landmark helps far less than adding the second.
722.po: Across different tasks and graphs, SCOUT consistently improves performance without retuning. On link prediction in a drug-interaction network, it gains 26.88%. On node classification in a science paper network, it gains 4.52 accuracy points. Even when nodes already have properties, SCOUT's automatically chosen landmarks amplify the benefit, proving the method isn't solving a artificial problem.

723.bp: Online ads are sold by what happens after users click — do they buy, and if so, how much? Today most systems predict yes/no (did they convert?), but companies care about dollars, not just conversions. A click that leads to a $100 purchase is vastly more valuable than one that leads to a $5 purchase. The problem: the label (how much they spent) doesn't arrive instantly; it trickles in over hours or days as purchases complete.
723.wh: When labels arrive late, two things go wrong. First, the training data is constantly out of date — a model trained yesterday is already partially wrong because some old labels weren't complete. Second, users who make one big purchase look different from users who make many small purchases, but traditional models treat all purchases the same. A user who clicked and bought $5 five times is fundamentally different from a user who clicked once and bought $25.
723.ap: This work proposes READER, which routes incoming data to specialized experts depending on predicted behavior. If a user is predicted to repurchase (buy multiple times after a click), one expert handles them. If they're predicted to single-purchase, another expert takes over. These experts are trained separately on data where their behavior pattern clearly applies. Additionally, the system dynamically adjusts the target value during training — if you only saw a $10 purchase arrive but suspect more is coming, you adjust the label upward proportionally.
723.ww: This works because it acknowledges that predicting $100 from multi-purchase users is genuinely different than predicting $100 from single-purchasers. The features matter differently, the label distribution differs, and they benefit from different inductive bias. By separating them, each expert becomes specialized rather than confused. The dynamic calibration stops the system from systematically underestimating when data is incomplete.
723.po: On a newly introduced benchmark of real transaction sequences, READER outperforms methods that ignore the repurchase / single-purchase distinction. The concrete value: better GMV (gross merchandise volume) prediction means ad bidding becomes more accurate. An advertiser no longer overpays for users likely to single-purchase or underpays for repeat-purchase users; the model sees the difference.

724.bp: Implicit hate speech — messages that attack a group but hide the venom behind coded language, sarcasm, or metaphor — slips through automated filters that look only at words and tone. The real harm is in meaning that lives between the lines: 'those people really know how to dance' sounds innocent but, in context, is a slur. Catching this requires reading the intent underneath.
724.wh: Large language models often fail at this in a specific way: they pick up spurious cues (a curse word is present, so probably hateful) while missing the real semantic units that carry the slur (the coded reference, the sarcasm, the masked subject). Then they over-confident: they're certain they're right, even when they're completely wrong. The model is pseudo-reasoning — it sounds like it's thinking, but it's just pattern-matching to noise.
724.ap: DuPL is a two-stage framework. First, a 'Critical Miner' quickly scans the text to identify Latent Hate Components — the actual semantic building blocks that encode the slur. A 'Confusion Judge' steps in immediately if the message is unambiguous (explicitly hateful), short-circuiting to avoid wasted work. If the message is subtle, the second stage takes over: 'Deliberation' reasons about each LHC individually, building an argument for why this component is (or isn't) hateful, then integrates those arguments into a final judgment.
724.ww: This works because it decouples detection from reasoning. Most models try to do both at once and fail at both. By explicitly mining for the pieces that matter (LHCs), the system avoids pseudo-reasoning on red herrings. By reasoning component-wise, it can defend its conclusion; if an adversary knows which components the model fixates on, they can't fool it by changing a single surface cue.
724.po: Across three hate speech datasets, DuPL improves accuracy by 3.8 to 8.4 percentage points over prompt-based systems. Crucially, it lowers both false alarms and missed detections simultaneously — the model becomes more balanced. This matters for moderation: fewer false positives mean fewer innocent users suppressed; fewer false negatives mean fewer slurs slip through.

725.bp: Companies need to forecast multiple streams of data simultaneously — warehouse temperature and traffic flow, or electricity demand across buildings in a city. These streams interact in complex ways (when it rains, electricity demand and traffic flow both spike). But which forecasting algorithm should you use? Different algorithms excel on different streams and datasets; picking wrong wastes months of engineering time.
725.wh: Existing AutoML systems can't transfer knowledge between different time series datasets because they don't have a common language for describing them. A dataset with 1000 measurements per second looks nothing like one with 1 measurement per hour, even if the underlying patterns (seasonality, trend, noise) are structurally similar. Without that common language, every new dataset requires training from scratch.
725.ap: This work creates a large, labeled dataset (ModelPile) of 41 mainstream time series datasets across 11 domains, paired with the performance of 11 different forecasting algorithms. It then uses a large pre-trained model to compress each raw dataset into a universal code. On top of that code, a system called AutoMTSF asks: 'given the code of this new dataset, which algorithm will work best?' It treats algorithm selection as a classification problem — predict the winning algorithm — using patterns learned from ModelPile.
725.ww: The large pre-trained model acts as a universal translator: it turns any time series (fast or slow, seasonal or trend-driven) into a common representation. That representation preserves the essential properties but erases irrelevant details. Once you have that universal code, you can apply a classifier trained on thousands of algorithm-performance pairs; it has seen enough variety to generalize to a new time series it's never encountered.
725.po: On new datasets, AutoMTSF predicts which algorithm will win without training all of them. The concrete benefit: what used to take weeks (train 11 models, wait for each to converge) now takes minutes. For a company deploying forecasters across dozens of IoT sensors, this is the difference between monthly updates and real-time adaptivity.

726.bp: AI models trained on internet data inevitably memorize sensitive information — names, faces, private messages from people who didn't consent. When deployed, these models can be tricked into revealing what they memorized. The goal is to selectively erase memorized information from a model without breaking its ability to do useful work. The challenge: different tasks (answering questions, generating descriptions, filling in blanks) require different forgetting strategies.
726.wh: Most unlearning methods push the model to output garbage for a 'forget' class (e.g., 'never mention this person'). But that's brutal. If you indiscriminately garbage-collect, the model also forgets how to recognize the person in other contexts, or it starts refusing all similar tasks. You lose both sensitivity and utility. There's no single loss function that handles all the ways sensitive information leaks.
726.ap: TAU defines three task-aligned objectives corresponding to how the model is actually evaluated: classification (predict a category), free-form generation (write a description), and cloze (fill in a blank). For each, it crafts an unlearning loss. Classification uses confidence reduction (lower certainty on sensitive inputs). Generation uses controlled refusal (politely decline, don't spill). Cloze uses entity suppression (forget the association). All three are trained jointly with a 'retain' loss that preserves knowledge on non-sensitive examples.
726.ww: By matching the unlearning objective to the task, the model learns finer-grained forgetting. It doesn't just zero out a person's presence; it learns the distinction between refusing to classify the person, refusing to describe them, and refusing to complete sentences about them. This is more honest — it acknowledges that forgetting looks different depending on how you probe the model.
726.po: Across multiple multimodal models, TAU achieves more balanced unlearning. The measurable outcome: the model successfully forgets sensitive information (verification via adversarial probing), but retention accuracy on non-sensitive data remains high. For deployment, this means users can request deletion without fear of breaking the model's core capability.

727.bp: Internet-scale monitoring systems collect billions of data points per second — website latency, network traffic, sensor readings. Most data looks normal, but rare events (server outages, DDoS attacks, sensor failures) hide in that stream. Finding them is like looking for a needle in a haystack that's also moving and warping continuously. Speed and memory matter; you can't store everything or reprocess the entire history when a new anomaly arrives.
727.wh: Detecting anomalies in high-dimensional data (each data point has hundreds or thousands of features) is already hard. Add the constraint that it's streaming (you see each point once, then it's gone), and the data distribution keeps shifting (what's 'normal' today differs from yesterday), and the distribution is imbalanced (normal points vastly outnumber anomalies). Traditional methods either are too slow or confuse normal variations for true anomalies.
727.ap: ANN-TS uses Approximate Nearest Neighbor indexing — a technique that quickly finds the points most similar to the current point without checking every historical point. When a new data point arrives, it finds its neighbors in the stream. If neighbors are rare or far away (the point is isolated), that's a red flag. The system tracks a statistical score for each point based on its neighbors and uses an adaptive update strategy that gradually forgets old normal patterns as new patterns emerge.
727.ww: This works because anomalies are lonely — they have few similar points nearby. By asking 'how crowded is this point in its neighborhood?' you get a fast, interpretable signal. The approximate indexing keeps memory and computation low; you're not storing the full past. The adaptive update lets the system shift as the baseline changes; if network behavior evolves, the model tracks it.
727.po: On real web stream data, ANN-TS beats nine baseline methods, particularly when data is high-dimensional and skewed. The concrete benefit: companies can detect infrastructure anomalies in real time without expensive hardware or offline reprocessing. A sudden spike in latency or a surge in error rates is caught immediately.

728.bp: Bad actors — spammers, phishers, hate-mongers — disguise their messages by misspelling, using emojis, mixing alphabets, or other visual tricks: 'h@te,' 'ḥate,' '🅗ate'. Detection systems trained on clean text fail. The challenge is to decode the mangled text back to its original meaning fast enough for real-time moderation, without relying on massive models that are slow or brittle.
728.wh: Existing de-obfuscation methods rely on auto-regressive models (they predict one character at a time, like a typewriter) which are slow, or byte-level fallbacks, which are error-prone. When a message contains out-of-vocabulary symbols (unusual emojis or multi-code-point graphemes), these systems break down. They also can't fix a character in the middle of the word without reprocessing everything from the start.
728.ap: BIND (Bidirectionally Aligned Next-Token Denoising) works at the character level and aligns those characters bidirectionally — it looks at context from both directions simultaneously to decide what each garbled symbol should be. It uses a novel attention mechanism that fixes positions independently, not sequentially. This is like having multiple repair experts work on different parts of the sentence in parallel.
728.ww: By working bidirectionally and independently on each position, BIND achieves three wins: it's fast (no sequential generation), it handles out-of-vocabulary elements (they're just characters, not tokens in a vocabulary), and it's robust to variations. The model learns that 'h@te,' 'ḥate,' and '🅗ate' all map to the same target in different ways; the bidirectional context teaches it the pattern.
728.po: On obfuscated harmful text datasets, BIND outperforms larger models while being much faster. The real-world impact: moderators can use a small, task-specific model to clean messy text in milliseconds before feeding it to a hate-speech classifier. Companies achieve faster, cheaper, more reliable content moderation without scaling up to enormous models.

729.bp: In the real world, sensors are expensive and deployed sparsely — weather stations dot a region with gaps, but you need forecasts everywhere. This is called kriging: inferring values at unseen locations from observed ones using spatial and temporal structure. A city wants to know pollution levels everywhere, not just where monitors sit. The challenge: locations interact in complex ways, and the graph of relationships changes as conditions evolve.
729.wh: Older methods assume a static, predefined graph (e.g., 'use the 10 nearest neighbors'). But static graphs are brittle; they miss long-range dependencies and don't adapt when the data distribution shifts. Graph convolution networks iterate across the graph structure, but this is expensive and gets stuck in local patterns without a principled way to refine the target value based on feedback.
729.ap: DKM-GA combines diffusion (a technique that iteratively refines guesses) with graph-enhanced attention. It starts with an initial guess for the missing values, then uses attention to find the most relevant observed nodes (dynamically learning which nodes matter most, not just using static neighbors). It refines the guess using those relevant nodes. It repeats this process, each iteration getting feedback from the previous guess to update which nodes to trust.
729.ww: This works because diffusion is a natural fit for kriging: each iteration smooths and refines the guess. The graph-enhanced attention adapts the structure based on the refined values, not just static features. A node that initially looked relevant might become less important as the guess improves; the mechanism responds. The feedback loop (refined values → better attention → better refinement) is principled and stable.
729.po: On spatio-temporal prediction tasks (filling in missing weather measurements, sensor values in IoT networks), DKM-GA outperforms static-graph baselines. The concrete gain: predictions at unobserved locations become more accurate because the system dynamically identifies which observed locations actually matter for each missing location, adapting as conditions change.

730.bp: Graph neural networks learn representations by aggregating information from neighboring nodes, allowing them to recognize patterns in networks. But they have two scaling problems: computation explodes as graphs grow, and they struggle when tested on different graph types than they were trained on (out-of-distribution shift). A model trained on social networks might fail on citation networks, even though the structure is similar.
730.wh: Node-level attention (traditional approach) requires comparing every node to every potential neighbor, which is quadratic and infeasible on large graphs. More critically, node-level operations overfit to specific graph distributions; they learn surface patterns specific to the training graph rather than general principles about what makes a node important. The model becomes brittle.
730.ap: VecFormer introduces Vector Quantization to compress both node features and graph structure into discrete 'codes' — compact summaries capturing the essential information. Attention then operates on these codes (graph-token level) rather than individual nodes. Two separate codebooks learn what feature patterns matter and what structure patterns matter. This drastically reduces the computation (attending to a few dozen codes, not millions of nodes).
730.ww: The vector quantization acts as a lossy compression that forces the model to learn what truly matters, discarding noise. By working on codes rather than raw nodes, the model becomes less sensitive to surface variation; two graphs with the same structural and feature patterns get similar codes even if they differ in size or node ordering. This improves generalization. Computation drops because you're attending to summaries, not individuals.
730.po: On node classification tasks of various sizes, VecFormer beats existing graph transformers in both speed (especially on large graphs) and accuracy on out-of-distribution data. The concrete benefit: a single trained model generalizes across graph types without retraining, and inference is fast enough for real-time applications on million-node graphs.

731.bp: Recommendation systems often use knowledge graphs — structured data linking items, users, and concepts — to improve suggestions. A movie recommendation system might use a graph connecting movies to genres, actors, and themes. But real knowledge graphs are messy: some links are wrong, outdated, or irrelevant to recommendation. Noise in the graph corrupts the recommendations.
731.wh: Traditional recommendation systems treat the knowledge graph as given, noise and all. But the graph was built from various sources with different quality standards. A link that's true in general (this actor was in this movie) might be irrelevant for recommendation (the actor's presence doesn't actually predict user taste). Removing noise while keeping signal is hard; what looks like noise in isolation might matter when combined with other signals.
731.ap: This framework attacks the problem in two steps. First, Knowledge Filtering uses diffusion models to denoise the graph structure — gradually removing dubious connections while preserving strong ones. Second, Task-Specific Triplet Reconstruction identifies which remaining connections actually matter for recommendation by scoring them with attention and then retraining them using self-supervised learning (predicting the connection itself as a proxy for importance).
731.ww: The diffusion model is a natural fit for denoising: it iteratively refines the graph structure, trusting edges that remain stable and removing those that don't. The task-specific component prevents over-cleaning; rather than globally optimal, the system targets locally optimal — edges that are most useful for the recommendation task. Attention learns which triplets (user-item-concept relationships) matter; reconstruction forces the model to internalize why.
731.po: On recommendation datasets with noisy knowledge graphs, the framework produces cleaner graphs and better recommendations. The concrete benefit: users see more relevant suggestions because the graph no longer misleads the model with false or irrelevant connections. Recommendation diversity and accuracy both improve.

732.bp: Fraud in online services — fake transactions, misleading video chat, romance scams — is increasingly perpetrated by people modulating their emotional expressions strategically: faking sincerity, affecting a voice, adjusting facial micro-expressions. A fraud detector trained on static features (what was said) misses this emotional manipulation. The challenge: emotion is multimodal (visual, audio, text) and adversaries can coordinate their manipulation across all channels.
732.wh: Most fraud detectors treat emotions as static features to extract and forget. But emotions are signals that can be manipulated in coordinated ways. An adversary can perform micro-expressions while using specific vocal tones and word choices that all reinforce a false impression. Existing evaluations test single-mode attacks (only modify the face, or only the voice) and miss coordinated cross-modal attacks that an intelligent adversary would use.
732.ap: CEAT uses a Transformer-based architecture (which naturally handles multiple input modes) to jointly model emotional features (facial dynamics, vocal prosody) and semantic content (what's said). During training, it injects adversarial noise into the emotional latent space (the learned representation of emotions) in ways that respect context — the perturbation doesn't make the multimodal signals incoherent. This trains the model to be robust to emotional manipulation even when coordinated.
732.ww: By modeling emotion and context jointly, the system learns that emotional expressions should be consistent with semantic content. When an adversary tries to inject inconsistent emotional signals, the context-aware perturbation training makes the detector robust; the model has seen similar attacks and learned to ignore them. This is fundamentally different from testing single-modal perturbations — the model learns the pattern of cross-modal coherence.
732.po: On multimodal fraud detection benchmarks, CEAT withstands emotion-driven adversarial attacks better than baseline detectors. The concrete outcome: a fraudster trying to fake emotion across video, voice, and text is more likely to be caught because the system recognizes the incoherence. This makes emotion-based fraud more expensive and risky for perpetrators.

733.bp: Graph neural networks are deployed in real systems where the training data comes from one time period or one type of user, but the live system serves different users or different times. A fraud detector trained on 2024 data performs poorly in 2025 if fraud tactics shifted. This out-of-distribution problem undermines trust; predictions become overconfident and wrong. The system needs to know when it's unsure.
733.wh: Existing uncertainty methods are post-hoc: they guess uncertainty after the fact (e.g., disagreement across an ensemble) rather than learning where uncertainty arises from first principles. More critically, they can't explain why a prediction is unreliable — was it due to a missing feature, a shifted distribution, or genuine complexity? Without explanation, users can't trust the system in high-stakes decisions.
733.ap: SIGHT (Spiking Graph Predictive Coding) uses iterative error correction over graph structures. The model makes a prediction, then compares it to what it expects; the mismatch (error) is the core signal. If this error persists or grows across iterations, the system is confused — perhaps the distribution has shifted. These persistent mismatches become interpretable uncertainty signals. The 'spiking' mechanism makes errors explicit, visible to both the model and the user.
733.ww: This works because it recognizes that uncertainty has a source: distribution shifts cause persistent prediction errors. By exposing these errors iteratively, the model doesn't hide its confusion; it communicates it. A human expert can then ask: 'Why is the model uncertain here?' and get a concrete answer: 'The internal check found a persistent mismatch.' This transparency is crucial for high-stakes decisions.
733.po: On graph benchmarks with out-of-distribution scenarios, SIGHT improves both predictive accuracy and uncertainty estimation simultaneously. The concrete benefit: a recommendation system or fraud detector can flag uncertain decisions for human review, preventing silent failures. Users gain interpretable explanations for why a decision might be untrustworthy.

734.bp: Imagine accessing the web through smart glasses that see the world you're seeing, hear what you're hearing, and understand what you need — without pulling out a phone or stopping what you're doing. For people with low vision, cognitive overload, or simply mobility constraints, this could be transformative. The challenge: understanding long, continuous first-person video (far longer than any model can process at once), parsing noisy speech, and seamlessly invoking web tools.
734.wh: A single neural network can't handle hours of video without extreme computational cost. Existing systems either truncate the context (losing long-horizon understanding) or batch-process offline (losing real-time responsiveness). Additionally, translating messy speech and gaze (where a person looks, often unreliable) into structured web commands requires multiple specialized models; running them all in real-time on glasses (with limited compute) is infeasible.
734.ap: Egocentric Co-Pilot uses a two-pronged approach. For reasoning, it combines Temporal Chain-of-Thought (reasoning step-by-step over time) with Hierarchical Context Compression (summarizing far-past events into memory, keeping only relevant context in the working window). This lets it answer complex questions over hours of video. For commands, it runs a lightweight multimodal intent layer that directly translates speech and gaze into structured commands, bypassing the need for a single monolithic model. It includes both cloud-native (WebRTC for low latency) and on-premise WebSocket deployments.
734.ww: Temporal reasoning works because it mirrors how humans think: they reason through a sequence and build summaries they can recall. By compressing older context, the system avoids forgetting but keeps computation manageable. The lightweight intent layer works because most speech/gaze commands are simple and predictable; a specialized small model beats a generalist large model. The dual-deployment approach lets users choose trade-offs (local privacy vs. cloud accuracy).
734.po: On egocentric video reasoning benchmarks, this system achieves competitive or better results than baselines while running on-device at real-time latency. The concrete impact: a person with low vision can ask their glasses 'what's on that menu?' or 'did I pass my exit?' and get an immediate, accurate answer without lifting their hands or stopping their activity. Web interaction becomes truly assistive.

735.bp: The Web is made of networks: who knows whom, which websites link to each other, which products get bought together. Predicting missing connections in these networks—figuring out that two people should be friends, or that two products belong in the same recommendation—is how search engines, product discovery, and collaboration tools get built. The harder the network, the more it matters: millions of nodes means you need speed and must understand hidden cliques and communities without solving the entire puzzle up front.
735.wh: Graph neural networks learn from local neighborhoods but struggle to see the big picture—whether a connection depends on what's happening far away in the network. Transformers can see globally but cost quadratically in memory and time: even a modestly large network becomes impossibly slow. Worse, a black-box prediction that says 'yes, these should connect' teaches us nothing about *why*, which matters when you need to validate or debug recommendations.
735.ap: TGSBM fuses two separate ideas: a old, principled theory called Stochastic Block Models (which say a network is made of invisible clusters, and connections happen more within clusters than between them) with a modern Transformer that attends over the graph. The trick is making the Transformer efficient by only looking at a sparse subset of nodes rather than everyone—like how a manager doesn't need to read every email, just key ones—and by encoding the idea that links form via cluster membership directly into the learning process.
735.ww: The mechanism works because you're encoding *both* the structure that really exists (hidden communities) and the global patterns that matter (which nodes talk to whom at scale), and you're doing it in a way the model can learn to interpret. When you explicitly say 'links happen because nodes belong to communities,' you've given the model a true story to latch onto, not a pure black box. Sparse attention means you're only computing what matters, cutting computation from quadratic to near-linear.
735.po: The result is fast—six times faster training than comparable methods—and interpretable: you can ask 'which community does this person belong to?' and get an answer, not just a score. On standard benchmarks, it ranks as the top performer, meaning it predicts the real missing links that humans verify as correct more often than competitors.

736.bp: On social media, people share photos of each other constantly, often without thinking about whether the person in the photo gave permission or wants it public. Privacy on the Web isn't just a setting you flip; it's a choice humans make dozens of times, shaped by what their friends say. Understanding when a friend's comment 'please don't share that' actually stops someone from posting is the foundation for building platforms that respect privacy at scale.
736.wh: You might guess that negative feedback stops sharing: tell someone 'don't post that' and they won't. Reality is messier. Some people with a history of ignoring privacy norms won't listen. Worse, mixed signals—some people saying yes, others saying no—can create pressure that backfires, making people share *more*. The problem is that human psychology isn't uniform; nudges that work for one person trap another.
736.ap: The study recruited real users, showed them photos of other people, and varied what comments appeared: only discouraging ones, only encouraging ones, a mix of both, or none. Then they measured whether the person shared the photo without consent. They also looked at who the person was—did they have prior incidents of privacy violations? The result: comments work differently depending on context and the person's history.
736.ww: Social pressure is powerful but conditional. When feedback aligns with social norms (everyone agrees the photo is unflattering or private), people listen. But if you've already ignored privacy norms in the past, being told 'don't share' can feel like a challenge, especially if some comments encourage sharing anyway—a mix of signals is effectively no signal. The backfire happens because mixed comments don't clarify the norm; they make the person feel the crowd is torn, which removes social pressure entirely.
736.po: Platforms should not assume all comments reduce sharing. Design recommendation: use comments to *clarify* norms, not to contradict each other. Flag users with past privacy violations and apply stronger safeguards before they post. A single, clear social message ('the person in this photo asked not to be posted') stops sharing across groups; mixed or weak signals do not.

737.bp: Every organization watches event streams: network logs (time, source IP, destination, bytes sent), security alerts, payment transactions. When something goes wrong—a cyber attack, fraud, unusual behavior—it shows up as a pattern in the data. The challenge is finding these patterns in massive, noisy streams where both the timestamp and the details (IP, size, type) matter, but exist in different forms: some are numbers, some are categories.
737.wh: Traditional methods discretize time, turning a continuous stream into buckets (second 1, second 2, etc.), which loses fine-grained timing information and makes 'normal' behavior hard to separate from genuine anomalies. They also force all data into one representation: either treating a category like 'Germany' as a number (wrong mathematically), or converting 3.2 gigabytes into a symbol (information loss). Statistical assumptions matter too: if you assume all continuous values come from a normal bell-curve distribution but they don't, your model makes bad predictions.
737.ap: HeteroComp treats the stream as a continuous mixture of hidden patterns. For each attribute—IP, packet size, time—it infers what kinds of values typically appear together and how they change over time. It uses Gaussian processes (a statistical tool that learns unknown distributions rather than guessing them) to handle continuous values flexibly and handles categorical attributes separately. The result is a decomposition into 'components'—each a latent pattern explaining subsets of observations—and a way to score whether a new event is typical or anomalous.
737.ww: By respecting the natural type of each attribute (time as time, categories as categories, numbers as numbers) and learning their true distributions rather than assuming a specific shape, the model can distinguish real anomalies from noise. A denial-of-service attack shows up as a sudden spike in events from a particular IP that doesn't just break a single feature—it breaks *the whole pattern*, which is easier to catch when each feature is modeled correctly.
737.po: The method finds group anomalies (not just one weird event, but a cluster of related events that together are suspicious) and tracks them over continuous time, so you see the rise and fall of an attack in real time, not discretized into buckets. On network and transaction datasets, it detects known attacks faster and with fewer false alarms than methods that assume all data comes from one distribution.

738.bp: Science and data analysis live in code and notebooks that researchers share, but 'sharing on GitHub' often means the code doesn't actually run when someone else tries it. Reproducing someone else's analysis requires the exact same software versions, the right library, and the knowledge to set it all up. The goal is to make research executable with one click—not because it's convenient, but because reproducible science is trustworthy science.
738.wh: Turning a notebook or script into something truly reproducible is tedious: you must specify exactly which version of Python, NumPy, and every dependency you used; you must structure the repository so the code finds its data and outputs; you must document assumptions buried in your code. Most researchers skip this because it feels bureaucratic, so analyses sit in GitHub repos that others can read but not run.
738.ap: This tutorial teaches the practical workflow: how to use MyBinder (a free service that spins up a temporary computer with your code and runs it in a browser) and the GESIS Methods Hub (a catalog of published, executable methods). You learn to write a requirements file listing exact package versions, structure your repository so Binder knows where to find the entry point (which notebook to run), and test the setup so the build actually works before you publish it.
738.ww: A reproducible method is a gift to future you and to anyone building on your work: they don't waste days debugging cryptic errors or reverse-engineering your environment. By front-loading this work—spending an afternoon on documentation and setup—you make your analysis available to thousands of researchers forever, not buried in a private hard drive or a forgotten GitHub.
738.po: Participants leave with a working, one-click-executable method published in a searchable hub, plus templates and checklists they can reuse for their next project. The immediate payoff: one less barrier for others to cite and build on your work. The long-term payoff: science becomes cumulative and trustworthy rather than a series of isolated, unreproducible claims.

739.bp: The Web is shifting from centralized to peer-to-peer storage: instead of one company's server holding all files, IPFS (a network where anyone can contribute storage) holds them. This is powerful for censorship resistance and resilience, but attackers exploit the same decentralization to host phishing sites—fake login pages that steal credentials—that stay online even after the attacker vanishes. Detecting and stopping these campaigns requires understanding how phishing spreads across a decentralized network.
739.wh: Traditional phishing detection watches web servers and domain names, but IPFS is content-addressed: a file is identified by its hash, not a domain name, so the same fake login page can live on thousands of computers at once. Public gateways (services that let you access IPFS files through your regular browser) add another layer: attackers can route victims through reputable gateways to hide their origin, using the gateway's reputation to evade detection.
739.ap: The team built a monitoring system that watches IPFS traffic and traces which gateways serve which files. Over 11 months, they collected data on 10,489 phishing file hashes and grouped them by similarity into 448 campaigns—sets of related phishing pages serving the same scam. They also mapped which gateways (including ones not in official lists) handle the malicious content, and checked whether blocking a few dominant sources could shut down most of the phishing.
739.ww: Phishing clusters reveal attacker behavior: rather than deploying thousands of isolated pages, attackers reuse the same few designs across many victims, which makes the problem concentrable. By identifying the 69 most common clusters, you can target mitigation: take down those clusters and you disable 80% of the detected phishing. The finding that caching across public gateways amplifies attacks means that reputation systems designed for benign use become force multipliers for abuse.
739.po: The research shows that traditional blocklists are insufficient—80% of detected gateways aren't on public lists anyway. Instead, platforms should monitor cluster patterns and prioritize high-impact campaigns. The data also reveals that decentralized systems need decentralized defense: attacking a few central hubs won't work, but identifying campaign structure can.

740.bp: Recommender systems—the engine that suggests products, movies, or news—increasingly run on large language models that generate explanations and reasons alongside suggestions. These models learn from human behavior online, which often encodes prejudice: men's products are recommended to men, women's to women; certain demographic groups see fewer high-quality items. The challenge is fixing these biases without retraining the entire massive model, which would cost millions in compute.
740.wh: Fixing bias in a traditional model meant retraining from scratch, infeasible for an LLM with billions of parameters. Existing debiasing methods target specific known biases (gender, age) but fail when new biases emerge or when multiple biases co-exist. You can't easily audit what the model learned or remove harmful patterns without understanding the entire training pipeline, which is a black box for most users.
740.ap: FUDLR recasts debiasing as machine unlearning: identifying which training examples caused bias, then removing their influence without full retraining. First, it uses a learned mask to identify bias-prone samples—the mask learns which examples, if removed, improve fairness most. The mask is bias-agnostic, meaning you can swap in different fairness metrics (fix gender bias, then age bias, then group bias) without retraining. Second, it estimates how much each identified sample influenced the model's weights and removes that influence through efficient matrix operations.
740.ww: The mechanism works because bias in recommendations usually traces back to statistical patterns in training data: 'this group bought this product, so recommend it to similar people.' By identifying and down-weighting those samples, you break the pattern without erasing the model's ability to make good recommendations for everyone else. The efficiency comes from estimating influence mathematically rather than retraining—you're surgically removing the problem, not rebuilding from scratch.
740.po: The method improves fairness (reduces recommendation gaps between demographic groups) while keeping recommendation accuracy stable, all without retraining. Experiments show it works across diverse real-world biases—a practical path for platforms to deploy fair LLM recommendations today, not after a six-month retrain cycle.

741.bp: Detecting emotion in text—whether a message is joyful, angry, sad, or fearful—is essential for mental health apps, customer service bots, and content moderation. Modern neural networks trained on examples can do this, but they're black boxes: you can't ask 'why did the model think this was angry?' The goal is to make emotion detection not just accurate but interpretable: what words or patterns signal a specific feeling?
741.wh: Neural models achieve high accuracy but are opaque—the model has learned something about emotion but it's encoded in millions of weights you can't read. Humans know that certain words (exclamation marks, 'love,' curse words) signal emotion, but naively adding these as features can hurt accuracy if the model has already learned better patterns. The tension is between transparency (humans understand the features) and performance (the model's implicit learning).
741.ap: The researchers extracted linguistic patterns from 13 different emotion datasets: looking at which words, punctuation, and sentence structures appear in angry text vs. joyful text vs. other emotions. They then added these explicit features (word counts, presence of punctuation, etc.) as auxiliary inputs to a neural model alongside its usual learned representations. The model learns to weight both the explicit signals and its implicit knowledge.
741.ww: Explicit linguistic features act as a regularizer—they guide the model toward solutions that align with human intuition about emotion. When the model sees 'this is an angry text, and humans marked it as angry because it has curse words and exclamation marks,' it learns a more robust path that generalizes better to new texts. The explicit features also provide a sanity check: if the model disagrees with obvious linguistic signals, you know something went wrong.
741.po: Models enriched with linguistic features improve by up to 2.4 points in accuracy on a standard benchmark, and the improvements generalize across different emotion datasets. More importantly, you can now explain predictions: 'the model flagged this as angry because it contains X linguistic markers that correlate with anger,' which is useful for debugging and for users who need to understand why the system made a decision.

742.bp: Detecting anomalous graphs—abnormal networks like a website designed to steal credentials or a social network compromised by bots—is a security problem. You have examples of normal graphs (regular websites) and a few known anomalies (malicious sites) but the attackers keep evolving: they'll build new malicious sites you've never seen that are slightly different from the known bad ones. The goal is to catch *unseen* anomalies, not just recognize copies of known attacks.
742.wh: Machine learning models overfit to known anomalies: they learn 'if a graph has structure X, it's malicious' and miss malicious graphs with structure Y. Labeled anomalies are scarce, so you can't gather enough examples of every attack type. Normal graphs often have quirky substructures—a weird connection pattern—that aren't actually dangerous but make the model think 'this is suspicious,' leading to false alarms.
742.ap: G-GLAD uses two strategies: First, prompt-based anomaly expansion: take known malicious graph structures and use learnable 'prompts' (additional signals) to simulate variations of them—like asking 'what if the attacker changed this part?' This generates a richer set of anomaly types the model learns to recognize. Second, subgraph-based normality extraction: focus on the essential parts of normal graphs that don't indicate anomaly, filtering out spurious quirks. The filtering uses Information Bottleneck (a principle that says keep only the information that matters for the prediction).
742.ww: By expanding the anomaly space, the model sees more attack variants without needing more labeled data—it generates them mathematically. By extracting only essential normality, the model learns what healthy looks like rather than memorizing random quirks of the training set. Together, these make the model confident it can spot new malicious graphs it's never seen before.
742.po: The framework detects both known and novel anomalies across 10 real-world graph datasets, outperforming methods that just try to memorize known anomalies. On a malicious website detection task, it catches attacks that existing methods miss while maintaining low false-alarm rates on normal websites.

743.bp: Modern language models have shifted to 'matmul-free' computation, replacing standard matrix multiplication with simpler bit-wise operations (operations on individual bits of numbers), which run faster on specialized hardware. BitNetv2, a recent model, uses bit-wise computation but faces a problem: when input values bunch up around zero (a normal distribution), the quantization buckets—the discrete levels you round values to—go unused, so most numbers collapse into a few representable levels, losing information. Hardware accelerators need to exploit this insight for speed.
743.wh: Directly implementing bit-wise operations on specialized hardware (processing-in-memory chips) is inefficient: you need separate circuits for different operations.
