The Hadamard Transform, a mathematical trick that spreads out clustered values so quantization buckets fill evenly, is essential but expensive to compute. Ideally you'd reuse circuit components between the Hadamard computation and the actual bit-wise multiplication, but the math looks different, so hardware designers build separate pipelines.
743.ap: The insight is that Hadamard computation—a sequence of recursive matrix multiplications—can be implemented using the same low-precision weights (weights that are only -1, 0, or 1) as BitLinear's bit-wise accumulation. By restructuring the Hadamard recursion as a butterfly-shaped tree of adders (addition operations), you can reuse that same tree for accumulating results in BitLinear. One physical circuit does both jobs.
743.ww: Reusing hardware means fewer transistors, less power, less data movement (which is often more expensive than computation). When you have a tree of adders built for one job, using it for both Hadamard flattening and bit-wise accumulation cuts the area roughly in half. The mechanism works because the math underlying both operations—reduction trees and accumulation—is structurally identical.
743.po: A more efficient PIM accelerator that keeps the benefits of BitNetv2's Hadamard Transform (better quantization, higher accuracy) without duplicating hardware. This means faster inference and lower power for bit-wise neural networks, making edge deployment of these models practical on resource-constrained devices.

744.bp: On e-commerce sites, users search in unpredictable ways: 'black shoe women's size 8' could mean a specific shoe or a category; 'quick dinner' might search for recipes or restaurants. The search system must guess the user's true intent and rewrite the query to match products better. LLMs can do this well, but they rewrite every query the same way—treating an easy query (one where the user was clear) the same as a hard one (ambiguous or poorly expressed). The goal is to rewrite queries that way humans would, respecting different difficulty levels.
744.wh: Naive LLM-based rewriting treats all queries uniformly, ignoring why rewriting is needed. Some queries need minor tweaks (typo correction); others need semantic restructuring (inferring that 'quick meal delivery' means fast-food restaurants, not a recipe). Without understanding the underlying problem in the query, the model makes misguided rewrites that deviate from human expectations.
744.ap: AWHCP introduces the PIFR paradigm: for each query, identify the Problem (what's unclear?), the Intention (what does the user really want?), the Fix (how should we address it?), and the Rewrite (the final query). The model is fine-tuned on human examples following this structure, learning to reason about difficulty. Then, during inference, the model generates multiple rewrite candidates, and a preference learning stage (using system-side feedback—which rewrites led to successful purchases?) refines the model to prefer rewrites that actually help users find products.
744.ww: By making the model decompose the problem before rewriting, you guide it toward human-like reasoning: 'the user said X but meant Y because Z, so I'll rewrite it this way.' The multi-stage pipeline (supervised learning on PIFR examples, then preference alignment using purchase feedback) teaches the model both how humans think about rewrites and what rewrites actually work in practice.
744.po: Queries rewritten by AWHCP lead to more successful product discovery than baselines, because the rewrites match human reasoning. On e-commerce platforms, this translates to better search, fewer frustrated users, and higher conversion rates because users find what they're looking for faster.

745.bp: Web tables—spreadsheets, data tables on Wikipedia, structured data in research papers—are everywhere, but searching through them is hard. A text search for 'Olympic gold medalists' might miss tables with exactly that data because the table's structure compresses information: the cell values alone don't capture 'this column is country names.' To find the right table, you need embeddings (mathematical summaries of meaning) that capture both the raw content and the structure.
745.wh: Standard embedding models trained on text don't handle tables well: they compress the structured information too much, missing what makes a table useful. Generating lots of examples to train a table-specific model is expensive. Some solutions generate synthetic query examples from tables to improve search, but they arbitrarily pick which columns to include (a partial table), missing opportunities to capture the table's full semantic diversity.
745.ap: CGPT uses K-means clustering to group similar tables, then samples across clusters to create training data that covers the semantic spectrum. For each partial table (subset of rows and columns), an LLM generates synthetic queries, which are used to fine-tune an embedding model. The fine-tuning uses contrastive learning: penalize the model when a query's embedding is far from the matching table's embedding, and reward it when they're close. Over time, the model learns to embed queries and tables so similar ones are nearby.
745.ww: Clustering ensures you don't just train on one type of table—you get diverse examples from the semantic space. LLM-generated queries are diverse and realistic (an LLM trained on real searches knows what people actually ask). Contrastive training is efficient: you're not retraining the entire embedding model from scratch, just refining it to handle table-specific patterns better.
745.po: Tables are found more often with higher precision (16.5% improvement in ranking), and the model generalizes to new types of tables without retraining. This means better table search across Wikipedia, research databases, and knowledge bases—users find data tables as easily as they find documents.

746.bp: Traffic prediction is essential for navigation apps, traffic management, and urban planning: if you can predict congestion five minutes ahead, you can reroute drivers or adjust signal timing. But traffic depends on multiple invisible factors: road networks (which roads connect where), weather, events (concerts, accidents), time of day. A model that only looks at historical traffic patterns misses these factors and makes brittle predictions.
746.wh: Traditional approaches use only historical traffic flow data—ignoring that a concert on tonight and snow on the roads both cause patterns that don't exist in past data. Satellite imagery (geo-images) contains this contextual information, but most models treat imagery as a black box or use it separately from traffic data, missing the interactions. The challenge is fusing different types of information (numbers, images) coherently.
746.ap: VisionST jointly encodes traffic flow patterns and geo-images (satellite photos of the road network and surroundings). First, it extracts visual tokens from satellite imagery—patches of the image that represent nodes in the traffic network or relationships between nodes. Then it generates pattern representations that mix visual signals (what does this area look like?), spatial structure (which roads connect here?), and temporal trends (is this time of day usually congested?). The three perspectives are combined into a unified prediction.
746.ww: By grounding the traffic prediction in what the road actually looks like and what's around it, the model has external context that's not just embedded in historical patterns. A concert venue shows up as a landmark in the image and a spike in past traffic; together, these signal 'today is like concert days.' The integration handles complex, overlapping patterns because all the information—visual, spatial, temporal—is encoded in the same representation space.
746.po: Traffic predictions are more accurate, especially for unusual events or conditions not well-represented in history. Navigation systems using VisionST can warn drivers earlier about congestion and route planning improves, reducing travel time and emissions. The model also generalizes: knowledge learned from one city's traffic patterns transfers to new cities if their road layouts are similar.

747.bp: Detecting anomalous nodes in graphs—finding the compromised account in a social network, the fraud ring in a transaction graph, the infected computer in a network—is crucial for security. Currently, each type of graph (social networks, financial networks, communication networks) requires its own specialized detection model trained on that specific data. If a bank's dataset is different from a telecom company's, you can't reuse the model, which is wasteful and costly.
747.wh: Graphs vary wildly in their structure and node features: social networks have user profiles; financial networks have transaction amounts; security logs have IP addresses and protocols. A model trained on one domain fails on another because it has memorized patterns specific to that data. Getting labeled anomalies for training is hard—breaches are rare—so you can't gather diverse examples. The ideal would be a foundation model for anomaly detection, but graphs are topological and most general models are not.
747.ap: TFM4GAD bridges the gap by flattening graphs into tables that modern tabular foundation models (TFMs) can process. For each node, it computes a rich feature vector: the original node features plus structural summary (Laplacian eigenvalues, which describe the graph's local geometry), neighborhood statistics (what do my neighbors look like?), and anomaly-sensitive aggregations (do my neighbors connect to each other, or just to me?). This augmented table is then fed to a TFM, which uses pre-training and in-context learning to generalize across domains.
747.ww: Tabular models excel at handling missing data, domain shift, and limited labels—precisely the challenges of graph anomaly detection. By computing informative structural features, you translate 'understanding graph structure' into a table-reading problem a TFM knows how to solve. The Laplacian and local statistics capture the essence of graph topology without requiring the model to learn graph neural operations.
747.po: A single model detects anomalies across different types of graphs—social networks, web graphs, transaction networks—without retraining, reducing deployment costs and improving generalization. On benchmark datasets, the approach matches or beats specialized graph models while requiring no labeled data for fine-tuning in new domains.

748.bp: LLMs are increasingly used to moderate content online, deciding whether a message is toxic or hate speech and should be removed. But LLM decisions aren't neutral: they judge implicit hate—subtle language that demeans a group—differently depending on the demographic group mentioned. 'This politician is terrible' is criticism; 'Members of this ethnicity are terrible' is hate speech; but LLMs sometimes misjudge the context, especially for minority groups. Fairness requires consistent, accurate judgments across all demographics.
748.wh: Standard toxicity detection trains a model to classify toxic vs. safe, but inconsistency emerges at inference time: the model handles explicit slurs reliably but struggles with coded language and implicit bias. You can't fully correct this by retraining because the problem is subtle—it requires context the model sometimes misses. Existing approaches try to fix the model via parameter updates, which are expensive and risky for deployed LLMs.
748.ap: FairToT works at inference time: when presented with text to judge, it first detects cases where demographic variation is likely (e.g., statements mentioning a specific group). For these high-risk cases, it applies additional assessment steps using prompts designed to elicit fair, consistent reasoning. It also tracks interpretable fairness indicators—simple metrics that flag inconsistencies—without modifying the model's parameters.
748.ww: Inference-time correction is practical: you don't need to retrain the LLM, just wrap its output with a fairness layer. By identifying risky cases where bias often emerges and applying targeted assessment, you concentrate effort where it matters. Interpretable indicators let you audit fairness: if the model suddenly treats one group harshly, the metrics catch it before deployment.
748.po: Toxicity judgments are fair across demographic groups—group-level disparities shrink—while maintaining accuracy on genuinely toxic content. This means content moderation systems using LLMs can be deployed at scale without perpetuating algorithmic bias. The inference-time approach is practical for platforms: ship the same LLM, add a fairness layer, and improve fairness without expensive retraining.

749.bp: Cameras record security footage constantly: robbery, assault, accidents. When something dangerous happens, we need to know not just that it happened, but *why*: what provoked the attacker? What sequence of events led to the injury? Understanding causality and threat attribution helps security teams prioritize response and helps with investigation and prevention. The goal is automated video understanding that goes beyond detection to explanation.
749.wh: Existing video anomaly detection finds the frame where bad things happen but doesn't explain them. Understanding requires tracking multiple levels of information simultaneously: human body positions and movements (is someone crouching to attack?), interactions between people and objects (is someone picking up a weapon?), and background context (where is this happening?). These factors interact in complex ways—the same body posture is threat in one context, normal in another.
749.ap: DeepSVU uses a unified approach called UPRM (Unified Physical-world Regularized Mixture of Experts). It combines human behavior analysis, object interaction detection, and scene context into a single representation. A Mixture of Experts component learns to decide which information is most important for each video segment—sometimes body language dominates, sometimes object interaction is key. A trade-off regularizer balances these factors so the model doesn't just latch onto one signal.
749.ww: Modeling physical-world information (what people and objects actually do) rather than just abstract features helps because causality is visible in the real world. When you know a person's posture, what they're holding, and where they are, you can infer intent. The mixture-of-experts design allows flexibility: a mugging looks different from a medical emergency, and the model learns which physical signals matter for each.
749.po: The system not only flags dangerous video segments but explains them: 'this frame is dangerous because [person A] is [action] [object B] in [location].' This enables faster human review and better security response. On security video benchmarks, it outperforms methods that just detect anomalies, providing the explainability that human operators need to act quickly and correctly.

750.bp: When you search for images using text (or text using images), you're asking a computer to understand that the words 'fluffy white dog' and a photo of a poodle mean the same thing. This cross-modal retrieval matters everywhere: photo apps finding pictures by description, e-commerce matching product images to search queries, or accessibility systems describing images for visually impaired users.
750.wh: The difficulty is that visual and textual meaning don't map neatly. A photo of a dog has thousands of pixels with different colors and shapes, but the word 'dog' is just a sequence of letters. Most approaches flatten everything into one big number space (called an embedding space), but real images have sparse, localized details—like the specific texture of fur or a unique breed marker—that get drowned out when you're trying to match against many images at once.
750.ap: This paper builds a two-branch system: one path captures the whole-image meaning (global), the other zooms into specific regions (local). They also ask a language model to write extra descriptions of images, giving more semantic clues to work with. Then they train with a three-stage ranking process: first they make sure images of the same category cluster together, then they align matched images and text closely, finally they push apart unmatched pairs with a margin.
750.ww: Ranking in a shared space only works if the space itself respects the natural ordering of similarity. By adding written descriptions, you give the model more ways to see the same image—not just pixels but language. The multi-branch design captures both the forest (overall subject) and the trees (fine details), so neither gets lost. The three-stage training is like scaffolding: each step reinforces the previous one, so images end up properly sorted.
750.po: On four standard test sets, this method beats 12 competing approaches and improves retrieval accuracy by an average of 15.91%, meaning when you search 'dog' you get the right dog images in the top results far more often.

751.bp: Social media videos with comments are often sarcastic—someone might post 'Great job!' when they mean the opposite. Detecting the true sentiment (whether someone actually liked it or hated it) matters for brand monitoring, content moderation, and understanding public mood around breaking news, because sarcasm inverts the literal meaning.
751.wh: Sarcasm is deceptively hard because the words say one thing but the feeling is opposite. Most systems try to fuse (mix together) all available signals—the video, the audio tone, the text—into one blob of information to detect sarcasm. But when you mash positive and negative clues together, they cancel each other out into ambiguous mush, exactly when you need clarity most.
751.ap: Instead of mixing everything together, this method keeps text, video, and audio separate. For each type of media, it first extracts what sentiment it shows (positive, negative, or neutral) without fusing. Then it uses those separate sentiment judgments as a guide to understand the sarcasm feature, working on them independently instead of smashing them all together first.
751.ww: If you keep signals separate, you preserve their true polarities—positive stays positive, negative stays negative—so they can act as guides rather than drowning each other out. By conditioning the sarcasm interpretation on what each modality actually shows, the model can see the contradiction (words say yes, tone says no) instead of getting lost in a muddled mix.
751.po: The system better detects when social media comments are sarcastic versus genuine, which improves overall sentiment accuracy on videos where people commonly use sarcasm.

752.bp: Grouping similar things together (clustering) is everywhere: organizing products into categories, finding communities in social networks, or spotting disease subtypes in medical data. When your things are items connected by relationships—like authors linked by papers, or users joined by interests—clustering is trickier because the structure matters as much as the things themselves.
752.wh: The natural approach is to first learn a good vector representation of each item, then run k-means or similar to group them. But that two-step process ignores a key fact: the representation you learn might be perfect for one task (like prediction) but terrible for clustering. The model never gets direct feedback saying 'these should be together' or 'those should be apart' during representation learning.
752.ap: This method does representation learning and clustering simultaneously in one end-to-end system. It uses two learning goals working together: one learns good vector representations using ideas from similarity-based learning (comparing similar items), at both the single-item level and the group-of-connected-items level. The second goal refines those representations by actually clustering while learning, so the representations get shaped by clustering needs.
752.ww: If you optimize for clustering directly while learning representations, the vectors naturally arrange themselves into clusters—items that belong together get closer. By including both item-level and group-level similarity goals, the system respects both individual identity and structural connections, avoiding lonely outliers.
752.po: On eight datasets, this end-to-end approach beats methods that learn then cluster separately, because the representations are actually optimized for the clustering goal rather than something else.

753.bp: Large language models (LLMs) like ChatGPT learn from vast internet data, and sometimes they memorize things that shouldn't be there: private information, copyrighted text, or biased generalizations. 'Unlearning' means surgically removing that bad knowledge from an already-trained model, which is critical for privacy compliance and making systems trustworthy.
753.wh: Different pieces of unwanted knowledge are hard to forget at the same pace. Some facts are deeply entangled with other knowledge (forgetting 'X's address' also requires forgetting connections to 'X's work'), while others sit isolated and erase easily. If you push the same forgetting force equally on everything, some knowledge sticks around while other knowledge gets over-erased, leaving the model broken or obviously changed.
753.ap: This method treats unlearning like a game where the model and an opponent have conflicting goals. The opponent identifies which knowledge is hardest to forget (worst-case samples) and emphasizes those during training. The model then updates itself to forget exactly those hard samples. They offer two versions: one that groups hard samples and focuses on high-loss clusters, another that weights each sample smoothly based on how hard it is to forget.
753.ww: By focusing training effort on the hardest-to-forget knowledge, you ensure nothing slips through. Once the hard stuff is gone, the easier stuff naturally follows. The adaptive weighting approach spreads the 'forgetting pressure' smoothly rather than applying brute force, so the model doesn't get distorted trying to erase everything uniformly.
753.po: On benchmark datasets for unlearning, this approach erases unwanted knowledge more thoroughly than previous methods while keeping the model's other skills intact—it forgets better without breaking the system.

754.bp: Powerful AI foundation models now power search engines, recommendation systems, and content moderation on the web. But these models can be unfair (recommending only to majority groups), biased (learning stereotypes from data), opaque (no one knows why they chose something), or breakable under unusual real-world conditions, which erodes user trust and sometimes causes real harm.
754.wh: Foundation models are trained on messy, heterogeneous internet data that changes over time, at enormous scale where traditional safety checks fail. The sheer breadth of downstream uses means a single model flaw can ripple through dozens of applications. It's not clear how to even measure trustworthiness across fairness, transparency, causality, and robustness simultaneously.
754.ap: This workshop gathers researchers and practitioners to discuss how foundation models should be designed, tested, and deployed for trustworthiness. It emphasizes causal reasoning—understanding not just correlations ('clicks go up with this change') but cause-and-effect ('this change causes clicks to go up')—as a principled way to identify and fix unfairness and bias.
754.ww: Causal reasoning cuts through the noise: if you understand the causal mechanism by which a model produces output, you can spot where bias enters and surgically fix it. It also predicts what happens when you deploy a model in a new context, because you understand the underlying mechanisms rather than just historical patterns.
754.po: The workshop brings together tools and perspectives for making foundation models fairer, more transparent, and more robust—creating a roadmap for trustworthy AI on the web.

755.bp: Online ads compete for the tiny real estate on your screen—a search results page, a social media feed, or an app banner. An ad's success depends not just on where it sits but also on what other ads surround it. Crowding reduces effectiveness, too many ads cause banner blindness, and clutter online damages user experience and overall website value.
755.wh: Most auction systems for ad placement treat each slot independently: position A is worth some amount, position B is worth some other amount, and that's that. But in reality, an ad in position A is worth less when ads B and C right next to it are competing for the same user's attention. Standard auction theory breaks down because the value of an ad depends on context (nearby ads), not just position.
755.ap: This paper models screen positions as points in space, where an ad's value depends on its own bid plus a discount factor determined by nearby ads' bids. For some cases (when only the nearest neighbor matters), they design a fast algorithm that finds a good allocation and proves it can be implemented honestly (advertisers can't game it by lying). For 2D Euclidean layouts, they give a near-optimal solution.
755.ww: By explicitly modeling spatial interference, the mechanism respects the reality of how ads work. The discount factor captures crowding without requiring separate negotiations for each pair of ads. Proving the mechanism is 'truthful' (honest bidding is optimal) matters because advertisers will bid strategically—if they can't trick the system, it works fairly.
755.po: Platforms can now allocate ads to maximize both advertiser value and user experience by accounting for spatial interference, rather than treating slots as isolated islands.

756.bp: Scientists and data analysts often need to generate random versions of networks (social graphs, collaboration networks, food webs) or data tables while preserving certain properties—like 'keep the same number of connections per person' but shuffle who connects to whom. This helps test whether a pattern you see is real or just random chance.
756.wh: Creating randomized versions at scale is slow because existing methods scan the data multiple times and perform expensive calculations for each transformation. On large networks or matrices, even fast algorithms become bottlenecks, especially when you need thousands of random versions for statistical testing.
756.ap: This paper reformulates the randomization procedure as a sampling problem: instead of explicitly computing what vectors are valid, they use reservoir sampling (a standard technique for sampling from streams) and mathematical bounds to know when they've found good candidates without calculating everything. This lets them do the whole process in almost one pass over the data.
756.ww: Reframing as sampling avoids the need to compute and store all possibilities. Using upper bounds on what could be valid lets you skip expensive checks—if your bound says 'this is definitely valid', you don't need to verify. A single pass keeps data in fast memory and avoids redundant reads.
756.po: The speedup is 2x over prior methods, meaning researchers can generate random versions of large networks faster, speeding up hypothesis testing in network science.

757.bp: Tables on the web are everywhere: sports standings, financial reports, product specifications, weather forecasts. When someone asks 'What was the rainfall in Delhi last Tuesday?' they expect an AI to read the table layout, find the row for Delhi and the column for Tuesday, and extract the number. Web intelligence systems need to handle messy real-world tables, not toy examples.
757.wh: Tables are tricky because they mix layout (spatial structure) with meaning (what numbers represent what). A cell's meaning depends on which row and column it's in, sometimes across multiple levels of headers. Vision-language models (AI that reads images) can see the layout but sometimes miss the logical structure, especially when they need multi-step reasoning like 'sum all rainfall values in March' or 'find the row with the highest average'.
757.ap: This work creates a benchmark dataset that systematically varies two things independently: layout complexity (how tangled the table structure is, with merged cells or nested headers) and reasoning complexity (simple lookup versus arithmetic across rows, versus multi-hop logic). By splitting test cases along these dimensions, researchers can see where models actually struggle.
757.ww: You can't fix what you can't measure precisely. By separating layout challenges from reasoning challenges, you discover whether a model fails because it misreads the structure or because it can't follow the logic. This fine-grained view reveals which capabilities are actually weak.
757.po: Analysis shows state-of-the-art models still stumble on complex layouts and multi-step reasoning, pinpointing exactly where improvements are needed.

758.bp: Wireless coverage maps show signal strength at every location, crucial for network planning (where to put towers), interference management (avoiding overlaps), and smart resource allocation (directing traffic efficiently). Predicting these maps from sparse measurements and building geometry is a foundational problem in network engineering.
758.wh: Radio signals behave strangely: they have smooth variations over long distances (path loss from distance, shadowing from obstacles) but also rapid fine-grained fluctuations from bouncing signals arriving by multiple paths (multipath). A map prediction method needs to capture both smooth trends and fine details—too coarse and you miss coverage holes, too fine and noise drowns the signal.
758.ap: This paper treats map prediction as building from coarse to fine resolution, like painting a picture with brushes of increasing detail. They split the map into frequency bands (coarse signals, fine details) using Laplacian pyramids, then use a neural network to predict these bands progressively. The key innovation is using continuous numbers instead of discrete 'tokens' to avoid quantization artifacts.
758.ww: Multi-scale predictions naturally separate smooth variations (captured by coarse predictions) from details (captured by fine predictions). Using continuous values instead of rounding to discrete bins preserves subtle signal variations. Progressive refinement means each level can condition on coarser levels below, leveraging hierarchy.
758.po: On benchmark data, this method outperforms convolutional, transformer-based, generative, and diffusion baselines while staying fast enough for real-time deployment, balancing accuracy and speed.

759.bp: Recommender systems are supposed to discover new content, but they often get stuck promoting the same popular items (blockbuster movies, bestselling books, trending products) while less popular items get buried. This unfairness hurts content diversity, creator income, and user experience—people miss things they'd love because popularity drowns them out.
759.wh: Fixing popularity bias risks breaking recommendation accuracy: if you force exposure to unpopular items, users might get recommendations they hate, driving them away. It's also hard to see what's happening inside recommendation models (they're black boxes), so fixing bias often feels like flailing in the dark.
759.ap: This method trains a tool that mirrors the recommendation model's behavior but exposes which internal neurons encode 'this is a popular item' signals. By feeding the model synthetic users who love unpopular items and watching which neurons light up, the authors identify popularity-related neurons. They then tweak just those neurons to reduce popularity bias.
759.ww: If you can isolate the specific computations responsible for popularity bias, you can adjust them directly without breaking other parts of the model. Using synthetic test users lets you probe the model's behavior in controlled ways, revealing which neurons do what work.
759.po: On three public datasets, this approach significantly improves fairness (less popular items get more exposure) while keeping recommendation accuracy nearly unchanged—a concrete win for both algorithmic fairness and diversity.

760.bp: False information spreads faster online than corrections, especially when topics are polarized and communities reinforce each other's views. Early warning systems that can predict misinformation will emerge before it goes viral would let platforms intervene preemptively, reducing harm to public discourse and emergency response.
760.wh: Polarization and misinformation are linked but distinct: polarization means diverging opinions on a topic, misinformation means false claims. Existing systems predict misinformation after-the-fact (once it's already spread) by analyzing text content. Predicting it proactively requires identifying when a topic becomes fertile ground for misinformation—high polarization without verified facts.
760.ap: This work combines two pieces: first, an online clustering algorithm that watches a tweet stream and groups tweets by topic, detecting when topics suddenly explode in volume (bursts). Second, a sentiment classifier that understands how polarized the opinions are on each topic by measuring opinion divergence. These polarization metrics then feed into a machine learning model that predicts which topics will spawn misinformation.
760.ww: Tracking topics online as they emerge, rather than analyzing them afterward, gives early warning. Measuring sentiment divergence per topic (not overall) catches polarization specific to that topic, which is the actual signal. Adding polarization features to prediction models works because misinformation doesn't appear randomly—it emerges in polarized, unverified contexts.
760.po: On two COVID-19 tweet datasets, including polarization metrics improves misinformation prediction significantly and enables forecasting misinformation one month in advance, giving platforms time to act.

761.bp: News stories, reports, and social media posts describe events happening in specific places at specific times. Extracting that structured spatiotemporal information (who, where, when) lets systems track outbreaks, manage disasters, understand trends, and connect related events. But most information extraction pipelines are brittle and domain-specific.
761.wh: Traditional entity and event extraction requires manually coding rules or expensive labeled training data per domain. Building knowledge graphs requires engineers to pre-define all entity types and relationships. Generalization across domains is extremely hard because language use, event types, and entity categories vary wildly between, say, health data and news.
761.ap: This system leverages large language models (which know many domains) combined with spatial and temporal structure as 'anchors'. Users define what information they care about and how to organize it (e.g., 'give me disease cases by region and date'). The system uses large language models to extract and ground information, then stores it in a multidimensional warehouse organized by space and time. It includes quality checks and interactive visualization.
761.ww: Using space and time as universal dimensions avoids needing domain-specific ontologies—any domain has space and time. Large language models bring cross-domain knowledge and flexibility. Interactive validation lets users correct errors on-the-fly, continuously improving quality.
761.po: On a public health dataset, this system extracts spatiotemporal entities more accurately than using language models alone, and the live dashboard supports discovery of patterns (where did cases spike, when did trends shift).

762.bp: Designing new drugs or polymers means finding molecules with desired properties (strong, safe, biodegradable). Generative models can propose candidate molecules, and recent advances use diffusion processes that start with noise and gradually 'refine' toward realistic structures. But when you want to control multiple properties at once (make it strong AND biocompatible AND cheap), existing methods struggle to honor all constraints.
762.wh: Most generative approaches directly sample from the desired distribution, but they often simplify: treating multiple conditions as independent or averaging them together, which violates the joint distribution (the true relationship between all conditions). This causes models to generate molecules that are good on average but poor on each individual constraint.
762.ap: This method models molecule generation as a sequence of refinement steps, like sculpting: you start with a rough shape and gradually detail it. Each step adjusts the molecular structure to move toward configurations that satisfy multiple conditions together (jointly). To train this, they use a two-stage approximation: first they train on early steps, then later steps, avoiding the computational cost of training every step equally.
762.ww: Markov chains (step-by-step processes where the future depends only on the current state) naturally handle joint distributions—at each step, all conditions influence the next step. Gradual refinement gives the model more opportunities to satisfy constraints than one-shot generation.
762.po: On polymer and small molecule datasets, this approach generates molecules with better control over multiple properties compared to traditional methods, improving both property match and structural validity.

763.bp: Large language models respond to instructions (prompts), and how you phrase an instruction massively changes the response. A tiny wording change can mean the difference between 'correct answer' and 'nonsense'. Since prompts are now how millions of people use AI, sharing practices and understanding what works is a growing need.
763.wh: Prompt effectiveness is unpredictable and brittle. There's no clear theory of why one phrasing works and another doesn't. People resort to trial-and-error, failing to find good prompts. As models scale up and are deployed in critical roles, this ad-hoc 'fail and retry' approach isn't good enough.
763.ap: This workshop brings together academics and industry practitioners to discuss prompt engineering: how to design instructions that reliably work, new strategies for prompting, guardrails to make prompts safer, and emerging paradigms for using language models beyond simple instruction-following.
763.ww: Collective experience and structured exchange help practitioners build intuitions and share patterns. By gathering people from different domains (some working on science, others on creative writing, others on code generation), the workshop identifies cross-cutting principles.
763.po: Attendees leave with better practices for prompting, curated optimization strategies, and real-world results demonstrating what works.

764.bp: AI research agents that search papers, run experiments, and synthesize findings could accelerate scientific discovery. But how do you evaluate whether an agent actually did good research? A single score like 'Pass@1' (did it answer correctly?) misses what matters: Was the reasoning sound? Did it waste compute? Is it actually robust or did it get lucky?
764.wh: Conventional evaluation metrics focus only on whether the final answer matches ground truth. But an agent could stumble on the right answer by accident, or follow a wasteful reasoning path, or be brittle (fail on slight input variations). These flaws don't show up in outcome-based scores, creating a 'high-score illusion' where metrics look good but the agent is unreliable.
764.ap: This framework evaluates the entire reasoning trajectory, not just the endpoint. It computes a score combining accuracy, efficiency (how many steps?), and cognitive quality (how well-grounded in evidence?). Separately, they measure 'latent capability' by determining how much hints/scaffolding an agent needs to solve problems, revealing whether it's genuinely capable or just pattern-matching.
764.ww: Process matters because a fragile agent might fail on similar problems despite getting one right. By scoring efficiency and evidence grounding, you catch wasteful reasoning. Measuring how much help is needed reveals true capability—an agent that needs hand-holding is not as capable as one that figures it out independently.
764.po: This framework provides fine-grained rankings revealing trade-offs (accuracy vs. efficiency) and latent capabilities entirely hidden by singular metrics, guiding research toward actually robust agents.

765.bp: When data flows through a machine learning pipeline—preprocessed, cleaned, trained on—nobody can verify which actual data was used or if those records stayed true over time. Practitioners and regulators need to know: what specific data went into this model? Was it tampered with? Did it come from where we think it did? This matters for auditing, legal compliance, and trust.
765.wh: FG-Trac adds a tamper-proof record to every step: as data gets preprocessed, trained, and checkpointed, the system captures and cryptographically anchors each event. Rather than redesigning the model, it sits alongside it and records exactly what happened to each piece of data and when, creating an auditable chain of evidence.
765.ww: Cryptographic commitments (mathematical fingerprints) let you prove that records haven't been altered after the fact. By recording contribution scores tied to training snapshots, the system proves not just that data was used, but how much it mattered. This works without retraining anything because it operates purely on the data and metadata flow, not the model internals.
765.po: Teams can now produce verifiable proof that specific samples were processed correctly, show regulators a complete history of data usage, and detect tampering. The framework runs with low overhead and works on real pipelines (tested on both image and graph learning tasks) while keeping model performance intact.

766.bp: When you have access to multiple AI models—cheap but slow, fast but expensive, general-purpose or specialized—routing each question to the right one (instead of always using the biggest) saves money while keeping quality high. This is the core challenge of LLM serving: with a limited budget and varying types of incoming questions, how do you pick which model to use for each one?
766.wh: The obvious approach—always use the best model—blows the budget. But greedily picking the cheapest model tanks quality. The hard part is that you don't know in advance how good a model's answer will be for a particular question, and the mix of questions keeps changing. You need to adapt in real time without tuning knobs manually.
766.ap: BARouter watches each incoming query and estimates how good each available model would be, weighs that against its cost, and checks how much budget has been spent so far. Then it picks the model that best balances quality and cost given the remaining budget. It does this online—no retraining, just updating decisions query by query.
766.ww: The framework treats this as a sequential decision problem: each choice learns from past choices to get better. By keeping track of how much quality you gained per dollar spent and staying within budget, the system naturally learns which models work best for which kinds of questions. The math guarantees that this approach eventually finds nearly-optimal routing without manual tuning.
766.po: Models get routed efficiently: the right query hits the right model at the right time. Systems can work with different budgets and handle shifts in what questions come in, automatically staying robust without needing engineers to retune parameters. Theory proves the algorithm achieves near-optimal regret (minimal wasted budget and quality loss).

767.bp: Short videos (TikTok, Instagram Reels, YouTube Shorts) spread false information faster and wider than any other format. The speed and reach make it urgent to detect which videos are faked, AI-generated, taken out of context, or designed to exploit human biases—and then explain *why* each one is false so people can understand the deception.
767.wh: Most benchmarks test only one type of fake (say, just AI-generated deepfakes), but real misinformation mixes multiple tricks: an AI voice, real-but-recontextualized footage, and audio that plays on fears. Worse, existing detectors don't explain *how* they spotted the fake—they just say yes or no. Without explanation, people don't believe the verdict.
767.ap: WildFakeBench is a dataset of 10,000+ real videos labeled by experts with *what type* of manipulation happened. FakeAgent is a multi-agent reasoning system (inspired by the Delphi method of collecting expert views) that looks at each video frame-by-frame, extracts sound, searches for related news and context online, and then reasons through what it finds. Different agents specialize in different tricks: one checks for AI patterns, one for out-of-context reuse, one for cognitive bias.
767.ww: By having specialized reasoning agents compare the video against external evidence, the system catches tricks that would fool a single monolithic detector. Searching online reveals if this footage appeared somewhere legitimate first, or if the audio is from a known voice generator. Multiple agents seeing different red flags builds a stronger case than one model trying to learn all patterns at once.
767.po: The benchmark gives researchers a realistic, diverse test set with real-world videos and expert labels. The agent system outperforms existing LLM approaches on all misinformation types and explains *why* each video is fake—what manipulation was spotted and what evidence proved it. This makes debunking practical: people don't just get told a video is false, they see the reasoning.

768.bp: When you ask an LLM to find and use knowledge from documents—pulling relevant paragraphs to answer your question—the model only sees the raw text chunks it retrieves. But real understanding often comes from *connecting* ideas across chunks: how does this fact relate to that principle? Where are the gaps? The real goal is to retrieve emergent understanding, not just overlapping text.
768.wh: Current graph-based approaches try two things: (1) link concepts logically and retrieve related ideas, or (2) keep text context intact by chunking smartly. But both search for similarity within their original fragments. They miss the insight that springs from *synthesis*—connecting two separate ideas creates a third insight that exists nowhere in the source.
768.ap: HyGRAG builds a multi-level graph: chunks and entities live side-by-side in a hierarchy. The system clusters these together, has the LLM write summaries that fuse chunk context *and* entity relationships, then searches through all levels at once. When retrieving, it finds related ideas by following entity groups, expanding across different abstraction layers, and updates dynamically when documents change.
768.ww: Hierarchical search lets you start broad (what concepts matter?) and zoom in (what text explains this concept?) or start specific and link up to larger themes. Summaries written by the LLM at each cluster level capture *what that group means as a whole*, not just what text matched. This lets the retriever find synthesized understanding rather than just text overlap.
768.po: Queries retrieve more relevant knowledge across document hierarchies, revealing connections that chunk-based retrieval would miss. The system handles changing corpora efficiently—adding new documents only requires local re-summarization, not full rebuilding. This bridges the gap between entity-centric precision and chunk-centric context.

769.bp: In federated learning, many organizations train a shared model together without sharing raw data—each keeps data local. If someone later demands that their data be forgotten (right to deletion, poisoning recovery), the system must remove that person's influence from the global model. But this unlearning process creates a new risk: attackers might steal the deleted data by analyzing gradient updates.
769.wh: Unlearning requires either retraining everything or rolling back checkpoints, both expensive. Adding privacy protection (differential privacy) makes it even more costly because you need to add noise to gradients. The tension: protect privacy of removed data (use privacy budget), maintain model accuracy (also uses privacy budget), and keep computations fast. You can't maximize all three.
769.ap: DIARY intelligently splits the privacy budget between training and recovery phases based on what matters most for each. It also introduces FIND, an anomaly detector that runs during recovery to catch poisoned gradients. If anomalies appear, the system uses a two-level storage system to roll back to a safer checkpoint and reruns recovery. This reduces noise and avoids wasteful recomputation.
769.ww: By recognizing that different phases have different privacy needs, DIARY uses the total privacy budget more effectively. The anomaly detection catches attacks early, so you don't waste privacy budget protecting against something you've already identified and mitigated. The rollback mechanism means you only re-run the expensive parts when truly necessary.
769.po: The framework removes a client's data influence while defending against gradient inversion (where attackers try to reverse-engineer the deleted data from updates). It uses privacy budget efficiently across training and recovery, reduces computational overhead through smart rollback, and is proven secure against both poisoning attacks and privacy attacks that target federated unlearning systems.

770.bp: Clickbait headlines—'You won't believe what happened next!'—trick people into clicking false or exaggerated stories. An LLM could help detect this, but LLMs tend to agree with what users seem to believe or want to hear. The goal: use that flaw strategically to generate diverse perspectives on a headline, then combine them to spot clickbait robustly.
770.wh: LLMs naturally mirror the assumptions in your prompt. If a headline sounds sensational, the LLM might accept that framing instead of questioning it. Most detection systems rely on labeled training data (scarce for clickbait) or fine-tuning (expensive). How do you get diverse reasoning without ground truth or manual labels?
770.ap: SORG prompts an LLM twice on the same headline: once to argue it's credible, once to argue it's misleading. The model's sycophancy tendency now helps—it generates opposing arguments as if genuinely convinced of each side. These pairs become training signal. Then a smaller, local model (BERT-based) learns to evaluate headlines using these synthetically generated arguments as soft guidance and contrast learning (training on pairs of opposing views).
770.ww: By generating both 'agree' and 'disagree' reasoning, you get diverse perspectives without needing labeled data. The soft labels from the LLM's credibility scores guide the smaller model to recognize when reasoning is defensive (sign of clickbait) versus evidential. Contrast learning makes the detector learn which linguistic patterns signal credibility versus exaggeration by comparing reasoned arguments side-by-side.
770.po: The method detects clickbait without needing hand-labeled examples, outperforms pure LLM prompting and fine-tuned smaller models. It works by extracting implicit reasoning from the LLM's sycophancy rather than fighting it, then grounding detection in generated reasoning pairs and soft credibility scores.

771.bp: YouTube's recommendation system shows billions of videos daily. Users can click buttons like 'Not Interested' or 'Don't Recommend Channel,' intending to filter what they see. But do these controls actually work? If they don't, users lose agency and get stuck in recommendation cycles. Trust in the platform erodes.
771.wh: Testing whether these buttons work requires immense scale: each user sees thousands of videos, but unwanted recommendations are rare. You can't tell if a control worked by checking a handful of users or days of data. You need a measurement system large enough to detect small effects and randomization to prove causation, not correlation.
771.ap: Researchers built a browser extension and recruited 22,000+ users over six months, generating 567 million recommendations. A button overlaid each video; depending on random assignment, clicking it triggered different feedback signals (Dislike, Not Interested, Don't Recommend Channel, Remove from History, or nothing as control). They then measured whether similar videos reappeared afterward, using machine learning to estimate video similarity.
771.ww: Randomization lets you compare: for users who click 'Not Interested,' does unwanted content disappear faster than for the control group? Large sample size catches small effects that single-user tests would miss. By training a model to detect video similarity, they could count *how many* similar recommendations snuck back through, not just if any appeared.
771.po: The audit reveals YouTube's controls are largely ineffective—even the strongest barely prevented half of similar recommendations. This documents a concrete gap between user expectations and platform behavior, grounding platform accountability in empirical measurement. The findings suggest designers and policymakers need to rethink recommendation control architecture.

772.bp: Imagine a centralized platform (e.g., a hospital scheduler) making decisions for many users (departments) while keeping each user's identity hidden. The platform needs to assign resources fairly based on individual preferences, but it must not reveal who wanted what. Anonymity is essential when decisions are sensitive.
772.wh: Standard decision-making algorithms either break anonymity (they track which user prefers which arm) or give up on optimality (they treat everyone the same). Adding anonymity constraints makes the problem harder: the decision-maker must assign options without leaving traces of individual preferences.
772.ap: The algorithm uses successive elimination (a bandit technique that narrows down good arms by testing them repeatedly) to map which users prefer which options, building a multi-graph structure. Then it applies greedy matching (assigning arms to users like a bipartite matching problem) to allocate fairly. All of this happens without recording which specific user wanted which arm.
772.ww: Successive elimination works well for discovery because it doesn't need to track individuals—only which arms were tested and how often. Greedy matching separates the discovery phase (which arms are good) from the allocation phase (who gets what), allowing anonymity to be preserved at the allocation layer while still learning efficiently.
772.po: The framework achieves anonymity while solving the assignment problem optimally (up to a small factor in regret). Users get fair, personalized decisions; the platform learns which options are good; but no one—not even the decision-maker—learns which specific user prefers which arm.

773.bp: Text-to-speech and voice conversion technologies can now synthesize speech so realistic that humans struggle to tell real from fake. Synthetic voices pose security risks: someone could impersonate another person and trick contacts into sending money or revealing secrets. Detecting deepfake audio is urgent and difficult.
773.wh: Self-supervised models trained on large audio corpora learn useful representations at many layers: early layers catch low-level artifacts (digital glitches), later layers catch semantic patterns. But existing detectors treat each layer independently. They ignore that synthetic artifacts often *propagate* across layers—a glitch early on distorts patterns downstream. Temporal sequences within frames matter too.
773.ap: HierCon models the dependencies *between* layers: it learns which layers matter for detecting which types of fakes and how information flows across them. It also models temporal patterns: attention mechanisms that look at frame sequences, not frame-by-frame. The learning is grounded in margin-based contrast—training the detector to separate real and synthetic embeddings with a learned margin.
773.ww: Hierarchical modeling captures that artifacts in synthetic speech are not isolated layer-by-layer—they're systematic patterns that span the representation hierarchy. By learning to attend across layers and time, the detector picks up on these systematic distortions. Margin-based contrast makes the learned representations robust across different speech synthesis techniques and recording conditions.
773.po: Detection accuracy improves significantly: 36.6% and 22.5% error reduction on two benchmark datasets. The method generalizes to unseen synthesis techniques and real-world recordings. Attention visualizations show the framework learned to look at the right layer combinations for different types of deepfakes.

774.bp: AI agents now browse websites and make purchases, book flights, or transfer money on behalf of users. But a user granting an agent access to their bank account is dangerous: the agent might be tricked into authorizing the wrong transfer. How do you let agents do critical tasks while giving users fine-grained control over what the agent can do?
774.wh: Websites were designed for human interaction: you enter your password once, then do many actions. AI agents need to make many sequential decisions, but you can't ask the user to approve every action—that defeats the point of delegation. Standard authorization systems (OAuth, for example) give all-or-nothing access: either the agent can do everything or nothing.
774.ap: The paper proposes designing websites with built-in access control for agents: certain actions (like viewing balance) might not need approval, while others (like transfers over a threshold) do. The agent follows authorized steps without human intervention on low-risk actions, but the system blocks high-risk ones or asks for explicit approval. This requires modifying both website design and the authorization protocols.
774.ww: By distinguishing risk levels—some agent actions are safe by default (viewing public info), others need approval (spending money, deleting data)—you reduce approval burden while maintaining safety. Clear protocols mean the agent knows in advance what it can and cannot do, avoiding failures mid-task.
774.po: Agents can delegate tasks like bill payments to users without requiring approval for every keystroke, yet users retain control over critical actions. The framework demonstrates that access-controlled websites for agentic AI are technically feasible and usable.

775.bp: Imagine billions of AI agents (from different companies, with different goals) discovering each other, contracting with each other, and coordinating on tasks—all without a central authority. This is the agentic web. For it to work at scale, agents need to find each other (registry), trust each other (reputation), and agree on value (pricing). The internet's early foundations (DNS, HTTP) answered these for humans; what do we need for agents?
775.wh: Agents are not humans: they don't read natural language contracts or negotiate in real time. They need machine-readable standards, formal protocols, and incentive mechanisms built in. Decentralized identity, pricing, and reputation are hard unsolved problems when you can't trust a central authority.
775.ap: The tutorial outlines NANDA—three layers. *Foundations* (discovery, identity, protocols): agents need ways to find and authenticate each other, like DNS for agents. *Agentic Economy* (pricing, reputation, markets): agents trade services and build trust through transparent transaction histories. *Agentic Society* (governance, coordination): as populations of agents emerge, norms and incentives keep them aligned without central control.
775.ww: By treating the agentic web as having distinct layers (each solved separately but building on lower layers), you can design the infrastructure incrementally. Reputation systems naturally emerge from transaction history. Pricing and markets let agents converge on what services are worth. Identity and discovery are prerequisites for everything else.
775.po: The tutorial provides a conceptual framework for understanding what infrastructure the agentic web needs and why—grounded in lessons from the human web's evolution. It highlights open research challenges and positions next steps for building safe, scalable systems where autonomous agents coordinate at scale.

776.bp: Adversarial prompts can trick powerful language models into generating harmful content by carefully rewording requests or embedding hidden instructions. Defenses typically scan prompts for keywords or fine-tune the model, but these are slow and evasion-prone. You need a fast, lightweight defense that lives inside the model without slowing it down.
776.wh: Most defenses happen before the model generates (checking the prompt) or after (filtering outputs), both expensive. Modifying the model itself requires retraining. The hard part: finding internal signals that distinguish jailbreaks from legitimate requests quickly, without changing the model or incurring high latency.
776.ap: PADD prepends a harmless safety prefix to each prompt and measures how attention patterns shift between the original and prefixed versions. Jailbreaks typically use adversarial phrasing designed to manipulate attention in specific ways; harmless requests don't trigger these shifts. The detector compares attention distributions and plasticity (how responsive attention is), flagging high divergence as likely jailbreaks.
776.ww: Adversarial prompts and safe prompts affect the model's attention mechanisms differently—harmful instructions trigger attention patterns that bypass safety, while normal requests don't. By comparing against a prefixed version (a kind of control), the system isolates the effect of the adversarial content itself without needing to modify weights or fine-tune.
776.po: The defense blocks 96.7-99.6% of jailbreaks across multiple models while rejecting very few legitimate requests (0-5.2% false positive rate). Because it runs in a single forward pass, latency is low. No model modification or fine-tuning is needed—it works immediately on existing LLMs.

777.bp: Language models claim certainty even when they're guessing. They don't recognize knowledge gaps or conflicts in their training data. For reliable AI systems, you need the model to introspect—assessing its own uncertainty, spotting contradictions, and knowing when to slow down and think carefully instead of rushing to an answer.
777.wh: A single LLM can't reliably assess its own confidence. Multiple models (an ensemble) see different things, but they need to coordinate: which models are reliable for this question? When should the system take time to deliberate instead of answering fast? How do you measure and act on self-awareness?
777.ap: The system computes a Metacognitive State Vector (MSV)—a five-dimensional score capturing emotional response, correctness judgment, experience matching, conflicting signals, and problem importance. Each ensemble member gets an MSV score. The system then routes simple queries to fast System 1 processing (quick answers) and complex ones to System 2 (careful deliberation with specialized roles: Domain Expert, Critic, Evaluator, Synthesizer). Role assignment is based on MSV states.
777.ww: By modeling five dimensions from cognitive psychology, the system captures the kind of self-awareness that humans use to decide when to think carefully. Routing based on MSV automatically dedicates computation to hard problems while letting easy ones run fast. Specialized roles in System 2 (Critic questions answers, Evaluator judges quality) ensure deliberation is structured.
777.po: The proof-of-concept demonstrates that LLM ensembles can introspect meaningfully, routing queries appropriately and executing deliberation with different role assignments for different question types. Users can see how query complexity triggers System 1 vs. System 2 modes.

778.bp: Finding similar items in large databases powers recommendations, search, and personalization. The standard setup: you have a single reference (a query) and search for neighbors. But real applications need more: 'Find products similar to *all* of these favorites' or 'Find items similar to *any* of these interests.' Multi-reference search is more useful but unsupported by existing methods.
778.wh: Existing approximate nearest neighbor algorithms are built for single-reference queries. Extending them naively—searching separately for each reference and intersecting results—is slow. You need a unified approach that can score items based on their combined similarity to multiple references and execute efficiently on existing graph indexes.
778.ap: The paper defines new distance metrics: for all-k queries (similar to *all* references), score items by their minimum distance to any reference; for any-k queries (similar to *any* reference), score by minimum distance. Then it shows how to search these metrics on standard ANN graph indexes by adapting the traversal strategy. A two-stage search variant improves performance further.
778.ww: By defining clear distance metrics first, the problem becomes: how do you search for items matching these metrics on existing indexes? The key insight is that graph traversal can be adapted—starting from multiple entry points and following different rules—to find items matching the all/any-k criteria without rebuilding the index.
778.po: Applications can now query for multi-reference similarities efficiently: 'Show me products liked by all my family members' or 'recommendations matching any of these interests.' The method works on real-world datasets and outperforms baselines that solve the problem inefficiently.

779.bp: Misinformation thrives on social media because it's diverse, context-dependent, and exploits human psychology. A single detector can't catch all types. But multiple AI agents reasoning together, each spotting different red flags, can build a stronger case. The challenge: how do you coordinate multiple agents so they focus on what matters, not on the noise?
779.wh: When you feed agents all available information, they drown in truthful content and miss weak deceptive signals. Most multi-agent systems treat all information equally or let dominant patterns overwhelm subtle cues. Agents need to specialize and communicate without amplifying bias—easier said than done.
779.ap: PAMAS organizes agents into three levels. *Auditors* examine specific feature subsets (images, audio, text sentiment) and flag anomalies. *Coordinators* aggregate their findings while maintaining diversity—combining perspectives without letting one strong signal drown out others. *Decision-Maker* has full context and evolving memory, synthesizing all auditor insights into a verdict. The system also optimizes agent topology and routing dynamically.
779.ww: By giving agents specialized views and aggregating hierarchically (auditors spot anomalies in their domain, coordinators combine without bias, decision-maker synthesizes), the system avoids information drowning. Auditors working on feature subsets naturally surface weak deceptive cues that a full-context agent would miss. Memory helps the decision-maker learn patterns over time.
779.po: The multi-agent framework detects misinformation more robustly than single-agent approaches, explaining its reasoning through visible anomaly cues and specialized evidence. Dynamic routing and topology optimization reduce communication overhead, making multi-agent misinformation detection practical for real-time deployment.

780.bp: Websites need to predict changes in user traffic and behavior patterns before they happen. When usage drops or spikes unpredictably, services crash or waste resources. Time series forecasting (predicting future values in a sequence of numbers, like daily visits) sits at the heart of keeping web services running smoothly.
780.wh: The core problem: models trained on language understand words, not numbers. Fine-tuning them costs too much compute. But retraining from scratch also fails because the model's learned skills don't transfer to a totally different domain.
780.ap: They inject example numbers into the frozen language model using a learnable adapter—a small neural component that compresses several past examples into a single context vector, then feeds that vector into every layer of the language model during prediction. This vector acts like a translator, telling the frozen model 'here's what recent data looks like' without changing the model's weights.
780.ww: Language models excel at using patterns shown in-context (learning from examples you show them during inference, not retraining). By distilling example time series into a compact vector and injecting it throughout the model, the method hijacks this existing skill—the model learns to interpret the injected numbers as context and adapts its predictions accordingly, all without any retraining.
780.po: The approach keeps the language model frozen (no expensive fine-tuning) while improving forecast accuracy over naive application of the model. This cuts compute overhead drastically while delivering better predictions than a language model used straight out of the box.

781.bp: Creating convincing synthetic speech (voice cloning) is increasingly practical, but doing it via cloud services means your voice recordings—biometric data tied uniquely to you—get sent to a third party and stored somewhere. A person building a speech system needs the capability locally where data never leaves their device.
781.wh: Existing commercial voice cloning services work well but require uploading your voice to their servers, raising privacy and security risks. Building a local system that matches professional quality demands careful engineering: it needs to learn a voice from only a few seconds of audio, adapt to new writing styles with moderate data, and run on regular consumer laptops without special hardware.
781.ap: They package an existing open-source speech architecture (Coqui XTTS-v2) into a locally-run application that can clone a voice from a short 5-10 second sample instantly, or train a custom model from 10-30 minutes of personal audio using a parameter-efficient technique (LoRA—a trick to fine-tune only a tiny fraction of the model's weights). They add data cleaning, verification, and a web interface around it.
781.ww: Running inference locally avoids transmission entirely, eliminating the privacy risk. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (LoRA) lets the model adapt to a user's voice without retraining everything, keeping latency and memory low. Automating preprocessing and using cosine similarity scores (a mathematical measure of voice match) ensures quality stays high even on consumer hardware.
781.po: Users get professional-quality voice synthesis (similarity score >0.998 on tested hardware) running on their own laptop, never touching a cloud server. The system handles both instant cloning and rapid custom training, with a simple web interface—making privacy-preserving speech synthesis practical for real people.

782.bp: Fake news spreads quickly online and undermines trust in institutions and each other. To combat misinformation at scale, we need automated systems that can verify whether a claim is real or fabricated by finding evidence that corroborates or contradicts it.
782.wh: Simply retrieving documents using the original news headline usually fails because the phrasing of the news doesn't match the phrasing of evidence that would prove or disprove it. A headline might say 'Stock market up' but relevant evidence uses terms like 'equities surge'—lexical mismatch breaks naive search. Meanwhile, existing approaches either tweak the evidence retriever or tweak the fact-checker, leaving the query gap untouched.
782.ap: They train a small language model to act as a query rewriter, taking the original news text and rewriting it into better search queries that will retrieve the most relevant evidence. A frozen large language model then reads the news and the retrieved evidence and makes a verdict. The system iterates: the rewritten queries are refined again based on what was already retrieved, progressively improving the search results fed to the fact-checker.
782.ww: The gap between news phrasing and evidence phrasing is the real bottleneck—a well-formulated search query (written in the language of evidence databases) retrieves far more useful material than the raw headline. By focusing learning on query quality, the system attacks the true problem. Iteration refines queries further, catching evidence the first pass missed.
782.po: The approach consistently improves fake news detection on two real-world datasets. By rewriting and refining search queries, it retrieves more relevant evidence, which feeds a more accurate fact-checking decision—without retraining the frozen fact-checker itself.

783.bp: In networks (social, financial, transportation), some nodes matter more than others—centrality measures quantify importance. Security analysts and investigators rely on these metrics to spot key players and hidden structures. But what if the people you're studying know you're measuring them and want to hide?
783.wh: An adversary can create many fake accounts (Sybil attack) and carefully distribute connections among them to camouflage their true importance. For simple measures like node degree (how many connections), computing the optimal hiding strategy is tractable. But for more sophisticated measures like closeness or betweenness (how much you lie on shortest paths between others), the optimization problem becomes computationally intractable—there's no known efficient algorithm.
783.ap: For the hard cases (closeness, betweenness), they borrow ideas from community detection literature to design practical heuristics—algorithms that don't guarantee optimal answers but work well in practice. These heuristics group and redistribute connections in ways that minimize the attacker's detectability, running in reasonable time on real networks.
783.ww: Real networks have structure (they cluster, have bottlenecks, etc.) that limits how effectively you can hide by adding fake nodes. Community detection algorithms exploit this structure to design hiding strategies that are nearly optimal even though finding the true optimum is mathematically hard. In practice, the constraints of realistic networks make heuristics very effective.
783.po: Experiments on real covert networks show Sybil-based obfuscation substantially outperforms previous hiding techniques. The work highlights a critical vulnerability: security analysts who trust centrality-based identification without accounting for Sybil attacks can be seriously misled, especially on betweenness and closeness metrics.

784.bp: Web services generate massive logs of every transaction and error. When something breaks, engineers dig through logs to find the problem. Automating anomaly detection (finding unusual log entries) saves time and catches issues before they become critical failures.
784.wh: Existing deep learning approaches discard important exact text during preprocessing, making results uninterpretable to engineers ('where did this anomaly come from?'). Other systems use dense numerical representations that hide the original data. Meanwhile, real industrial systems need fast inference on commodity hardware and explainable outputs—you can't explain 'the embedding said so.'
784.ap: They use a language model purely to propose candidate patterns (sequences that look like anomalies), then feed those proposals to a deterministic verifier that confirms or rejects them using mathematical rules. Anomalous patterns are extracted into regular expressions for fast matching. The system refines by creating specialized child patterns and adding targeted exclusions to improve precision.
784.ww: Language models excel at spotting irregular patterns in text without being explicitly programmed. A deterministic verifier (a set of concrete rules) ensures explainability and correctness—engineers can read the regex and understand exactly what the system flagged. Two-stage refinement (increasing recall, then precision) extracts the maximum useful signal from both the model and the rules.
784.po: On three real Huawei Cloud datasets, the system achieves F1 score 0.9877 (very high accuracy), outperforming neural baselines. Logs stay human-readable throughout, regular expressions enable fast online matching on CPUs, and engineers can understand and audit every decision.

785.bp: Short video platforms (TikTok, Instagram Reels) evolve rapidly—new types of harmful content emerge daily (new slang, meme formats, trends). Moderation teams need to spot these emerging issues and update their policies before the content spreads to millions.
785.wh: Human review of emerging issues is slow and reactive. By the time one person flags 'this new trend is problematic,' the video has circulated widely. Traditional rule-based moderation policies miss what they weren't written to catch. Expanding manual review doesn't scale.
785.ap: They deploy a multimodal language model agent (one that understands both images and text) to automatically search for videos with potential unreported issues, cluster similar problematic videos together, and automatically generate updated annotation policies describing the new issue and how to spot it.
785.ww: Language models can reason about visual and textual content at scale, spotting patterns humans would miss. Clustering groups related cases, revealing what the issue actually is. Automatic policy generation turns these discovered issues into actionable rules. The speed—checking thousands of videos in minutes—outpaces any human review process.
785.po: Deployed in a real system, the agent improves emerging-issue discovery (F1 score improvement >20%) and governance (reducing problematic video views by ~15%). More importantly, it dramatically cuts the time needed to detect and respond to trends, allowing policies to stay current rather than perpetually behind.

786.bp: Web designers and 3D artists need to generate realistic materials (wood, metal, plastic surfaces) that look convincing and respond correctly to light in interactive environments. Hand-authoring these textures is slow; automation could accelerate creative workflows.
786.wh: Text descriptions of appearance are ambiguous and incomplete—'shiny silver' could mean many things. RGB texture images (the usual output) bake in shadows and highlights from a single lighting direction, so they look wrong when the light changes. Relying on only one type of guidance limits control.
786.ap: They build a system that takes three kinds of input simultaneously: a reference image (showing fine visual details words can't capture), a text description (conveying the overall intent), and geometric shape information (anchoring the texture to the object's form). The system outputs not RGB pixels but industry-standard material parameters: albedo (base color), metallic (how reflective), and roughness (how smooth or scratched)—separate numbers that work correctly under any lighting.
786.ww: Each input type captures something the others don't: images give high-frequency details, text gives intent, geometry grounds the result spatially. Decoupling into PBR parameters (physical-based rendering) means the material stays realistic under any illumination, essential for dynamic web environments where lighting changes. Multimodal guidance reduces ambiguity.
