825.po: The result is a fully automatic, interpretable score for dialogue engagement that works on both synthetic test conversations and real-world chats, requiring no human labels—freeing up researchers and product teams to benchmark and improve their chatbots without hiring scorers.

826.bp: Messaging apps like WhatsApp and SMS move billions of images daily, and a significant fraction contain malicious content: scams, abuse, illegal material. Large platforms need to catch these automatically and at scale, but existing image filters were built for other domains and miss the subtle abuse patterns specific to personal messaging.
826.wh: MMS (text-with-pictures messaging) spam is structurally different from web images or social media content—the context, disguises, and toxic styles are novel and vary widely. Standard datasets don't cover these categories, and off-the-shelf image classifiers fail to handle the domain shift, leaving platforms blind to harms.
826.ap: The researchers catalog all the common types of malicious images in MMS (eight categories total), build a clean training set from public image sources balanced across those types, then add two more evaluation datasets with real spam examples from actual messaging systems. They adapt CLIP—a model that understands both image content and text descriptions—to predict which category each image belongs to.
826.ww: A classifier built specifically for this domain, trained on the actual kinds of images that appear in spam reports, learns the right features and boundaries. By mapping the real-world spam taxonomy first, then training on authentic examples, the model avoids the mistake of applying a generic image detector and instead learns what makes an image problematic in *this* context.
826.po: The fine-tuned CLIP model catches inappropriate MMS images with accuracy matching GPT-4o but at a fraction of the computational cost, making it practical to filter billions of messages in real time and protecting users at the scale platforms need.

827.bp: Online gaming, video calls, and live streams all fail when the network hiccups. Jitter—sudden, erratic delays between packets—is the hidden villain: it's not about average latency but about *variability* that breaks the experience. Network operators need to spot which flows are jittery so they can fix them, but traditional tools miss the problem because they only look at big-picture delays.
827.wh: Most network diagnostics measure end-to-end or hop-by-hop delays but ignore fine-grained, packet-by-packet irregularity within a single data stream. A flow with smooth average latency can still be ruined by unpredictable micro-stutters. Additionally, networks carry millions of flows simultaneously, so any detection method must work without examining every packet in detail.
827.ap: JitterSketch uses a three-stage pipeline: first, it filters out stable flows by checking if inter-arrival times are consistent; second, it removes flows with few packets (likely not problematic); third, it uses specialized data structures to detect and report flows with high jitter. The entire process is designed to run in one pass through the network traffic with minimal memory.
827.ww: By focusing specifically on arrival-time irregularity *within* flows and using a sketch algorithm (a space-efficient counting technique), you can identify the small subset of flows that actually harm user experience without storing or processing everything. The three-stage filtering approach quickly eliminates the well-behaved flows, then concentrates analysis on the candidates that matter.
827.po: The algorithm boosts both recall (catching jittery flows that matter) and precision (avoiding false alarms) by up to 50 percentage points over simpler approaches, and when deployed in real QoS systems, it noticeably improves the quality of service users experience.

828.bp: As language models grow more fluent, they can now generate convincing fake news at scale—news that feels authentic but is entirely fabricated. Publishers, platforms, and fact-checkers need to identify which headlines were written by humans and which by AI, especially when speed of detection is critical and access to training data is limited.
828.wh: AI-generated text keeps improving and looks more human-like by the month. A detector trained on one month's model output may fail on next month's version. Additionally, the most powerful models (like GPT-5) are black boxes accessed only through an API, making it impossible to see the internal weights or run custom analysis. And acquiring lots of labeled fake news examples is hard and expensive.
828.ap: Researchers generated about 22,000 fake headlines using five different AI models, then systematically analyzed four linguistic dimensions: toxicity (how harsh the language is), sentiment (negative vs. positive tone), moral framing (which ethical values are invoked), and lexical similarity (word choice patterns). They tested whether advanced language models could use these dimensions to spot AI fakes when given a few examples or explicit linguistic hints.
828.ww: Even though AI and human writing look similar, they differ subtly in consistent ways: AI tends to be more extreme in sentiment, uses more emotionally charged words, relies on authority-framing language, and shows different moral emphasis. These textual fingerprints are measurable and can guide classification even when general model knowledge (zero-shot) fails. By grounding the detector in these empirical differences, you get a signal that doesn't change as fast as model architecture does.
828.po: While simple guessing (zero-shot) is only about 60–68% accurate, adding linguistic hints or a few examples lifts accuracy to around 70% for both GPT-4o-mini and GPT-5-mini, providing a practical baseline for headline verification without special training.

829.bp: Mixture-of-Experts models—where different specialized sub-networks handle different types of inputs—are efficient and powerful, but they're enormous. Running them on phones, tablets, or edge devices seems impossible because the full model doesn't fit in GPU memory. Yet that's exactly where users want fast, private inference to happen.
829.wh: Offloading unused expert weights to CPU main memory works but creates a new bottleneck: predicting *which* experts you'll need before you fetch them is error-prone, so you end up pulling data unpredictably and stalling the GPU waiting for slow CPU transfers. Simpler workarounds like quantization (shrinking number precision) slow down overall speed.
829.ap: Self-Speculative Decoding for MoE is an algorithm-system co-design: (1) a small "draft" model uses only a subset of the routed experts to produce candidate output tokens quickly; (2) the GPU's memory acts as a cache for experts, updated on-demand; (3) a confidence policy decides whether to accept the draft tokens or re-route through more experts for verification, adapting the computation to match task difficulty.
829.ww: A key insight is that many tasks are easy—they don't actually need all experts. If you can quickly generate a rough draft answer using only a few experts, you can then selectively verify which parts are risky. This two-step process (draft, then verify selectively) means you use fewer expert fetches while staying accurate. Confidence-based decisions then decide when to trust a draft versus re-computing with more experts.
829.po: The method achieves 3.72x faster decoding than prior edge approaches while maintaining accuracy, and even under strict verification modes, it outpaces 4-bit quantized models in both speed and quality.

830.bp: Libraries—especially in non-English-speaking regions—often have millions of books cataloged by title alone, with no subject tags, summaries, or metadata. A user asking for "books about managing teams" has to guess the exact title or keywords, and even then won't know if the results are any good. Traditional search engines don't work because the data is too sparse.
830.wh: Without rich metadata, retrieval becomes a guessing game. Users don't know what to search for, the system doesn't know what they mean, and even if both guess right, nobody verifies whether the result is actually what the user wanted. Simple keyword matching misses synonyms and domain-specific language. Users also often lack expertise (e.g., a business student doesn't know that "organizational behavior" is what they need).
830.ap: Smart Book Seeker runs three coordinated agents in a loop: (1) a User-Needs Agent converses with the searcher to extract what they're actually looking for; (2) a Librarian Agent formulates keyword queries and retrieves candidate books; (3) a User-Proxy Agent (equipped with domain knowledge) validates whether each result truly matches the need, using multi-turn dialogue with the Librarian to refine results.
830.ww: A multi-agent team where one agent asks clarifying questions (to understand what the user really wants), another searches the catalog (applying better keywords), and a third acts as a knowledgeable filter (verifying that the book matches) overcomes the triple problem at once. Each agent compensates for a different weakness: the first handles ambiguity, the second handles vocabulary, and the third handles expertise gaps.
830.po: On a real library of 20,000 Chinese books, the system achieves 87% hit rate and 57% precision in the top 5 results—improvements of 28% and 90% over traditional keyword retrieval—making sparse-metadata libraries searchable again.

831.bp: When you're classifying something by looking at multiple viewpoints (e.g., diagnosing disease from both imaging and lab work, or categorizing a movie by both dialogue and visual scenes), different sources have different strengths. The challenge is combining them without letting a weak source ruin the overall judgment.
831.wh: Existing methods treat all views the same way, applying identical quality constraints to a high-quality image feature and a noisy text feature. But images from one source might have confusable cases that inherently mix (like similar-looking fruits), while another source might simply be low-fidelity. One-size-fits-all penalties either over-penalize and hurt accuracy, or under-penalize and let noise through.
831.ap: The method quantifies feature ambiguity by measuring which classes are hardest to distinguish within each view, then relaxes penalties for those confusable cases. It also scores each view's quality by checking consistency in its outputs, then strengthens constraints on unreliable views. The combined adaptive regularization is then used during training to balance confidence across all views.
831.ww: If you measure and account for *source-specific* problems—ambiguity within a view (which classes naturally look similar?) and quality across views (which sources are reliable?)—you can apply lighter penalties to inherently ambiguous cases and stronger penalties to weak sources. This adaptive approach respects what each view can actually achieve and harnesses what it does well.
831.po: Experiments across multiple datasets show the adaptive approach consistently outperforms uniform-penalty methods, delivering more reliable predictions and better handling of real-world data quality variations.

832.bp: Graphs where each node has text associated with it—like academic papers linked by citations—are more expressive than plain graphs, but that richness is a new weakness. An attacker can subtly edit a few node descriptions or rewire a few edges, and if the model uses both text and structure, small perturbations can fool it completely. This threatens any system relying on text-attributed graphs.
832.wh: Text-attributed graphs are usually processed by two different kinds of models: graph neural networks (which reason about structure) and language models (which reason about text). These models have wildly different architectures and encodings, so an attack that fools one might not fool the other. Moreover, large language models are often only accessible via slow APIs in black-box mode, not as downloadable weights.
832.ap: BadGraph is an attack framework that uses an LLM to reason about graph structure, identify influential nodes, and generate coordinated perturbations to both node text and graph edges. A "target influencer retrieval" module leverages known graph properties to construct shortcuts that guide the LLM's perturbation generation, making the attack practical and universal across architectures.
832.ww: A large language model has rich general knowledge about graph structure, relationships, and semantics. By asking an LLM to reason about which nodes to attack and how, you can generate perturbations that target both the graph topology *and* the text semantics in a coordinated way—an attack that generalizes across both GNN and LLM backends because it's not tailored to either, but exploits universal patterns.
832.po: BadGraph causes performance drops of up to 76.3% on both GNN-based and LLM-based models with simple text edits and edge flips, demonstrating that text-attributed graphs have a common vulnerability that affects many architectures.

833.bp: Large language models power chatbots and search now, but each query burns energy proportional to how hard the model has to think. Pushing reasoning-intensive techniques like "chain-of-thought" (making the model explain its reasoning) to every query causes enormous carbon emissions and makes AI inaccessible in regions with less power infrastructure. We need models that think hard only when they need to.
833.wh: Current systems apply the same reasoning depth to all queries: a simple factual question ("What is the capital of France?") and a complex logic puzzle get the same amount of computation. This is wasteful—many questions need just quick retrieval, while others need careful reasoning. Predicting query difficulty on the fly without pre-computing everything is the hard part.
833.ap: EcoThink trains a small model (via distillation from a larger teacher) to classify queries as easy or complex. Easy queries skip reasoning and go straight to factual retrieval; complex queries run full chain-of-thought reasoning. The router learns which patterns predict complexity, then makes routing decisions on the fly for each new query.
833.ww: A tiny, efficient router can be trained to estimate query complexity using only shallow features, then route simple queries to a fast path and complex queries to the reasoning path. Since the router itself is cheap, the total energy savings far exceed the small cost of routing. This adaptive strategy mirrors how humans think: we don't deliberate equally on everything.
833.po: Across nine different benchmarks, EcoThink cuts inference energy by 40.4% on average (up to 81.9% for factual queries) without hurting accuracy, and simultaneously reduces the computational barrier to accessing AI in low-resource regions.

834.bp: False claims spread faster when they mix text and images—a headline about a politician with a doctored photo is more convincing and harder to debunk than either alone. Fact-checking systems need to reason across both modalities, gathering evidence and explaining the verdict to users, but current tools treat image and text as separate evidence streams rather than an integrated whole.
834.wh: Multi-modal large language models can now see both images and text, but they often treat visual evidence as window dressing rather than central to the proof. The models fine-tune on rigid templates, so explanations are scripted and miss context-specific nuances. Additionally, retrieval of supporting evidence (finding relevant images or text to compare against) is limited, so the model reasons with incomplete information.
834.ap: FactCompass integrates three components: (1) semantic and knowledge-enhanced retrieval to surface relevant comparison images and text; (2) reasoning-aware fine-tuning where GPT-4o's explanations teach the smaller model to reason about evidence; (3) self-refining reinforcement learning using rejection sampling and policy optimization to improve reasoning across broader datasets without gold-standard labels.
834.ww: By combining reasoned fine-tuning (teaching the model to explain its logic like a human fact-checker), retrieval augmentation (finding diverse evidence images and text to compare), and reinforcement-based refinement (learning from corrections), you create a system that reasons step-by-step over rich evidence, adapts to new claims, and explains itself convincingly.
834.po: The framework deepens reasoning over multimodal evidence and improves evidence utilization, enabling more reliable fact-checking of claims that mix text and images—the most dangerous and fastest-spreading form.

835.bp: Fake news detectors typically use either graph structure (how the story spreads through social networks) or language (analyzing the text for lies). Each approach catches different deception styles: structural analysis spots coordinated inauthentic behavior, while text analysis spots semantic trickery. Why not use both, but in a way that lets them check each other?
835.wh: Fake news is produced by adversaries who actively camouflage both the structure (by faking shares and likes) and the semantics (by imitating trusted writing styles). No single detector—whether graph-based or language-based—catches all tactics. Naive hybrid approaches that chain a GNN and LLM lose the independence between the two judges, and most methods need enormous labeled datasets of fake examples, which are expensive to produce.
835.ap: S2MOE-F uses a Mixture of Experts design: (1) a GNN expert and LLM expert each produce predictions; (2) one-class classification constrains true news tightly and marks outliers as fake, reducing dependence on fake labels; (3) high-confidence pseudo-labels are generated when both experts agree or diverge meaningfully, letting unlabeled data improve the model through multi-turn refinement.
835.ww: Two independent experts (a graph expert and a language expert) cross-validating each other's judgment catches more deception than either alone. When they agree, confidence is high; when they disagree, you know something is suspicious. By requiring fake news to be far from the normal distribution ("one-class" reasoning), you use abundant unlabeled true news as an implicit constraint, sidestepping the need for scarce fake examples.
835.po: The framework reduces reliance on scarce fake news labels while using complementary structural and semantic perspectives, achieving robust detection against diversified modern camouflage tactics.

836.bp: Databases power every business: sales records, customer histories, inventory. To predict something useful (Will this customer churn? What inventory do we need?), you need rich features that combine information across tables. But hand-crafting these features requires deep domain knowledge and manual SQL work, making prediction tasks slow and brittle.
836.wh: The feature space is combinatorially huge: hundreds of tables, thousands of columns, and infinite ways to combine them (sums, averages, ratios, joins). Nobody can enumerate all sensible options by hand. Machines struggle because they need supervision (examples of good features) that doesn't exist, and reasoning about schema structure is hard for most algorithms.
836.ap: ReFuGe deploys three coordinated LLM agents: (1) a schema selection agent reads the database structure and picks relevant tables and columns; (2) a feature generation agent proposes diverse candidate features (joins, aggregations, transformations); (3) a feature filtering agent validates each feature through both reasoning and empirical testing, and the loop iterates until performance plateaus.
836.ww: Large language models already understand natural language descriptions of database schemas and can reason about which tables relate to each other. By asking an LLM to act as a domain expert, you can generate candidate features intelligently, then filter them by predictive power rather than requiring gold-standard labels upfront. An agent framework makes the search structured and iterative.
836.po: The framework substantially improves prediction task performance on real relational databases without manual feature engineering, making database prediction tasks accessible to non-experts.

837.bp: Recommendation systems trained locally on each user's device (federated learning) protect privacy, but they struggle when users or items have very few interactions. A new user hasn't rated anything, so the model can't learn who they are. A niche product has almost no ratings, so the global model knows almost nothing about it. Both gaps hurt recommendation quality.
837.wh: Local training on sparse data is underconstrained: with few ratings, a user embedding could fit almost anything. Global aggregation (averaging across users and items) loses information when some dimensions have almost no signal. Standard techniques don't exploit the key insight that similar users might have complementary information, or that item knowledge can be transferred.
837.ap: KE-FedRS operates at two levels: (1) locally, each user gets an auxiliary embedding that captures knowledge from similar-embedding users, enriching sparse interaction data; (2) globally, clients are selected based on how divergent their item embeddings are, ensuring high-entropy learning and better coverage for items with few ratings.
837.ww: If you build an auxiliary embedding for sparse users and average it across similar users before merging with the main embedding, you enrich sparse local data with hints from neighbors. Similarly, by prioritizing which client devices contribute to the global model based on how different their item knowledge is from others, you ensure rare items get covered despite sparse training data.
837.po: The hybrid enhancement strategy tackles data sparsity at both user and item levels, improving recommendation quality in federated settings where privacy and local compute are constraints.

838.bp: Networks of genes, proteins, citations, or collaborations often contain clusters of high-influence nodes whose removal would fragment the network or halt information flow. Identifying these influential groups helps biologists find disease-critical genes, lets social scientists spot echo chambers, and helps companies identify key teams. But when nodes also have attributes (a gene's function, an author's field), the problem changes entirely.
838.wh: Most influence algorithms ignore node attributes, treating the graph as pure structure. But attributes carry critical information: a protein's known cellular role constrains which other proteins it likely influences; an author's publication history hints at their network impact. Methods that mix structure and attributes face a hard combinatorial problem (there are exponentially many node groups to evaluate) with no clear way to reason across both modalities together.
838.ap: GGUN (Global Graph UNderstanding) applies a GNN to the attributed graph, then uses perturbation analysis to measure each node's importance: nodes whose removal most disrupts the model's output are most influential. The combinatorial optimization (finding the best group of k nodes) is relaxed into a continuous problem with theoretical guarantees, making it computationally tractable.
838.ww: Graph neural networks learn to fuse structure and attributes layer-by-layer, propagating information through the graph in interpretable steps. By using perturbation-based explanation (removing nodes and watching predictions change), you can measure how important each node is for maintaining the GNN's confidence in the overall graph. This bridges the gap between deep learning and discrete graph reasoning.
838.po: The framework identifies influential node groups that account for both structure and attributes, outperforming purely structural methods on both real-world datasets and human-judged importance in networks like protein interactions and citation graphs.

839.bp: Recommendation systems amplify what users already like (because it's what they'll click on), trapping them in bubbles of similar recommendations. A movie fan gets only more movies, a music listener gets only similar genres, missing gems that would genuinely expand their taste if they tried them. The problem is baked into how LLMs learn from training data.
839.wh: Large language models naturally optimize for likelihood: they predict what a user is most likely to engage with next. But users have diverse interests and conflicting preferences—you like both action movies and quiet dramas depending on mood. A model that always picks the highest-probability item for each user confirms their biases rather than surfacing serendipitous matches or broader appeal.
839.ap: SCoTRec builds detailed user profiles from sentiment extracted from reviews, then applies chain-of-thought reasoning that simulates how people navigate conflicting preferences. Human-like judgment operations (backtracking through sentiment, discarding weak signals, retaining strong ones, aggregating across perspectives) replace simple preference aggregation. Social sentiment from friends informs reasoning to counteract individual confirmation bias.
839.ww: If you simulate how users navigate their own conflicting sentiments—thinking through different angles, checking perspectives from friends, backtracking when they change their mind—you break the bias toward the single most likely recommendation. By explicitly modeling social influence and emotional reasoning, you can recommend things users wouldn't naturally expect but might genuinely want.
839.po: On benchmark datasets, the framework reduces confirmation bias and improves recommendation quality by reasoning through users' diverse sentiments and social context, rather than mechanically picking the highest-probability items.

840.bp: Social networks store detailed information about us—who we know, what we like, what we believe. When a person asks for their data to be deleted, the network should erase not just their account, but the traces of them woven through the entire graph of connections. The goal is to make it as if they never existed on the platform, protecting privacy.
840.wh: When you delete a node from a graph to preserve privacy, the statistical patterns that remain can actually become *more* skewed about sensitive traits. Imagine a social network where women and men followed different posts. If you carefully erase a woman's profile, the remaining graph's gender correlations might become even more stereotypical, since you removed a data point that contradicted the bias.
840.ap: FairGU builds a two-part shield: first, it has a fairness detector that watches for sensitive attributes (like gender or race) getting amplified during deletion. Second, it uses a data protection module that removes not just the person's node, but also strategically prunes connections in ways that keep sensitive information from leaking. The system treats fairness and privacy as codependent problems, solving them together.
840.ww: The insight is that deletion impacts fairness because it changes the statistical balance of the graph. By proactively monitoring and adjusting which edges survive deletion, you can delete someone completely while keeping the demographic proportions and biases stable. It's like erasing a person from a photo while keeping the overall color balance.
840.po: FairGU lets platforms delete user data *and* guarantee that the leftover model won't become more discriminatory. On real social networks, it outperforms both standard privacy-deletion methods and fairness-enhancing models at the same time, earning back both utility (accuracy) and fairness metrics simultaneously.

841.bp: Network protocols—the rulebooks that let computers talk—are embedded in routers, servers, and infrastructure worldwide. A single misunderstanding of what the protocol *really* means can create a security hole. Testing protocol implementations is like proofreading a legal contract: you need to find not just crashes, but subtle ways the code misinterprets the rules.
841.wh: Existing tests watch for crashes or wrong bits, but they miss semantic bugs: cases where the code technically 'runs' but violates the spirit of the protocol spec. For example, a protocol might say 'ignore this field,' but if the implementation actually reads it and acts on it, that's a semantic flaw. The challenge is expressing 'what should never happen according to the spec' in a way that actually generates test cases to catch it.
841.ap: SemFuzz uses a large language model to read RFC specifications—the official English prose that defines a protocol—and extract the actual rules in a form the test tool can understand. Then it generates test messages that intentionally break those rules, feeds them to real implementations, and compares what comes back to what *should* come back according to the spec. If the behavior doesn't match, a vulnerability is uncovered.
841.ww: The reason this works is that RFCs are already written in careful, rule-heavy prose. An LLM can extract patterns like 'the server must not process X if Y condition holds' and convert that into concrete test constraints. By deliberately violating these rules, you're creating a stress test that finds implementations that misunderstood or ignored the spec.
841.po: In testing seven real protocol implementations, SemFuzz found sixteen potential vulnerabilities, ten confirmed, five new, and four given official CVE numbers—the kind of security flaw that warrants an emergency patch. This shows the practical power of reading the spec semantically rather than just fuzzing with random bytes.

842.bp: Real-world forecasting—predicting power demand, server load, or traffic—relies on many sensor measurements at once. But sensors break, privacy rules mask data, or systems get upgraded and replace old sensors. You're left trying to predict the future from an incomplete set of measurements, like forecasting the weather with half your thermometers offline.
842.wh: When training data has all measurements but test data is missing some, there's a mismatch the model never trained for. On top of that, sensor data shifts: some correlations between sensors change (users' TV habits differ by season), and the distribution of single sensors drifts too (today's power usage differs from yesterday's). The existing playbook—'just fill in the missing values, then forecast'—ignores these shifts and fails in the real world.
842.ap: SRDI splits the problem into stable patterns and unstable patterns. For the stable part (the core correlation between sensors that doesn't change), it learns once and reuses it. For the volatile part (the noisy, fluctuating differences between time windows), it rebuilds on the fly using a denoising process that adapts to the shift. Then it forecasts using both pieces, balancing what stays the same with what needs to adapt.
842.ww: The reason separating stability from volatility helps is that some structure in data is real and persistent—if two sensors correlate in training, they likely will later too—while other variation is just noise or temporary drift. By learning to impute the stable relationships and then adapting the volatile layer, you get a model that can handle missing measurements and shifting conditions simultaneously.
842.po: On real-world time-series datasets with missing variables and distribution shift, SRDI produces more accurate forecasts than methods that pretend the test distribution is the same as training. This matters for web-scale services where forecasting failures cascade—bad power prediction leads to outages, bad load prediction leads to slowdowns.

843.bp: Imagine a tool that predicts public opinion about a new political issue, a product, or a technology—but it was only trained on opinions about past topics. The challenge is *stance detection*: classifying whether someone favors, opposes, or is neutral toward a target they never saw during training. This is the zero-shot task—predicting on the unseen.
843.wh: Models trained on, say, stances about 'climate policy' often fail when asked about 'Arctic drilling' because the language is different, the framing is different, and the semantic structure doesn't fully transfer. Beyond that, stance embeddings—the numerical summaries of text—can be fragile or overly narrow, restricting which new targets the model can generalize to.
843.ap: DPSD combines three moves: first, it uses an LLM to generate diverse, stylistically varied training examples about new targets, enriching the pool of stances. Second, it fuses two kinds of features—deep learned features from a language model and simple, shallow lexical patterns—using a gating mechanism that learns when each is useful. Third, it uses contrastive learning (a technique that pulls similar texts closer and pushes dissimilar ones apart in the feature space) to sharpen the representation. Finally, it maintains a dynamic prototype pool—a set of example stances for each class—that updates over time while remembering history.
843.ww: Combining shallow and deep features works because shallow features (word counts) catch explicit signals ('I oppose this') while deep features catch subtle tone. Contrastive learning refines the space so the model learns which aspects of text matter for stance. The dynamic prototype pool solves the stability problem: it remembers what you learned from past targets while adapting to new ones, anchoring the model's reasoning.
843.po: On three benchmark stance datasets, DPSD achieves strong zero-shot accuracy—classifying stances on previously unseen topics—and remains interpretable because the prototypes are actual example texts rather than black-box weights. The dynamic memory means it doesn't forget old knowledge when learning new stances.

844.bp: Live shopping streams on TikTok and similar platforms are a booming business: a streamer shows products, viewers watch, and when viewers have questions ('Is this available in blue?'), the streamer needs to answer fast. Currently, streamers manually handle this, which is slow and errors happen. The goal is to automate the boring parts—product information retrieval and question answering—so the streamer can focus on engaging the audience.
844.wh: The data a streamer has is messy: product info lives in multiple places (catalogs, images, descriptions), and viewers' questions come in at random times, mixed with comments. You need to reliably extract what product someone is asking about, generate an accurate answer, and do it in near real-time. The challenge is bridging the gap between the product database (structured, static) and live chat (unstructured, flowing).
844.ap: Click-to-Ask has two halves: offline and online. Offline, it takes multimodal product information (images, descriptions, specs) and converts it into clean, structured data, then generates promotional copy that follows platform rules. Online, during the stream, when a streamer clicks a question, the system retrieves the relevant product info from the offline work and pairs it with a memory of recent interactions in the stream to answer the question in context.
844.ww: The reason this two-stage approach works is that products don't change minute-to-minute, so you can afford to spend time understanding the product once, offline. During the stream, you only need to match incoming questions to products and craft quick responses, which is much faster. The memory of recent events keeps answers from sounding robotic—they reflect what's been discussed today.
844.po: On TikTok live-stream data, Click-to-Ask achieves 91.3% accuracy at recognizing which question is being asked and 0.876 quality score on the generated responses. This translates to a real product: streamers spend less time preparing data and can answer viewer questions in seconds instead of minutes, directly increasing sales.

845.bp: Recommendations work better when you know not just that a user bought a book, but also that they browsed it, added it to a wishlist, and reviewed it. These multiple types of interaction—multi-behavior—paint a richer picture than purchase-only data. But weaving them together is tricky because each type of interaction has its own patterns, confounding effects, and biases.
845.wh: When users browse more than they buy, the raw signals are noisy. A user might browse a book out of curiosity but never buy it; another might buy without browsing because they know exactly what they want. This noise masks true preference. Also, a user's browsing *habits* (how often they browse at all) and item popularity (how many people view it) are confounding factors—they change the apparent relationship between an interaction and actual preference.
845.ap: MCLMR uses a causal graph—a formal diagram of 'what causes what'—to model the confounding. It then performs interventions: mathematically asking 'what would the preference be if we removed the effect of habit or popularity?' Once it has unbiased preferences, it uses a mixture-of-experts router that learns which behaviors are most informative for each user-item pair and blends them accordingly. Finally, it uses contrastive learning to align the representations of different behaviors so they're on the same footing.
845.ww: Causal reasoning helps because it separates signal from noise: if a user with a browsing habit tends to browse everything, the causal model can recognize that their browsing is *not* a strong signal of preference for this specific item. By correcting for that, the model sees preference more clearly. The mixture-of-experts then figures out which behavior type is actually trustworthy for each case.
845.po: On real recommendation datasets, MCLMR improves accuracy over standard multi-behavior methods and can be plugged into any recommendation architecture. This matters because platforms like Amazon or Netflix have huge amounts of multi-behavior data but struggle to use it correctly; MCLMR extracts more signal from it.

846.bp: Child mental health screening is critical but faces a bottleneck: not enough psychologists, and subjective scoring of drawings creates variance. The Draw-A-Person test (a child draws a person, and psychologists interpret it) is a nonverbal way to elicit psychological insights. Web-based screening with AI could scale access, but only if the AI correctly interprets drawings the way a trained expert would—measuring genuine psychological constructs, not just pattern-matching.
846.wh: Multimodal AI models like GPT-4V can analyze drawings, but do they actually measure what psychologists measure? A model might see 'this drawing is crude' and flag it as concerning when it's just age-appropriate development. Or worse, it might drift between drawings: give one score to one child's drawing and a different score to a very similar drawing. The tension is between automation (scalability) and validity (measuring what you claim to measure).
846.ap: DAPWeb defines a clinically grounded benchmark: real drawings analyzed by human experts, organized by six psychological constructs (like emotional maturity, body image), and each construct tested for three abilities—determination (identifying if a construct is present), detection (flagging concerning signs), and comparison (scoring relative to age norms). It then tests multimodal models on this benchmark and measures not just accuracy but construct validity and consistency across similar drawings.
846.ww: The reason grounding in constructs matters is that it prevents the AI from optimizing for a generic 'good prediction score' and instead forces it to optimize for what psychologists actually care about. By testing determination separately from detection, you reveal which part breaks: maybe the model sees concerning signs but can't prioritize them correctly.
846.po: DAPWeb reveals that current multimodal models fall short on most screening abilities but perform comparably to experts on the 'determination' task, suggesting that DAP-based screening could be feasible if paired with human oversight. This gives web-based child health platforms a roadmap: AI can help triage, but psychologists should review high-stakes cases.

847.bp: Large platforms—YouTube, Meta, Google Ads—run fairness audits to check if their algorithms discriminate. But audits disagree: different metrics, different sample sizes, different subgroup definitions yield different verdicts. When regulators ask 'is this fair?', the platform can pick the audit that says yes. The need is a principled way to combine conflicting audits into a single, defensible claim about fairness.
847.wh: Audits are like doctors: two equally competent doctors might disagree on a diagnosis because they ordered different tests or weighted symptoms differently. With fairness, the disagreement comes from metric choice (should we measure equal opportunity or equalized odds?), sampling variance (small audit samples are noisy), subgroup definitions (intersectional vs. coarse), and dataset drift (data changes over time). A single point estimate—'this platform is 84% fair'—hides all this uncertainty and gives false confidence.
847.ap: The audit-of-audits uses Bayesian statistics to pool multiple audits (even partial ones with incomplete data) into interval-valued claims: instead of 'fair or not,' it says 'fairness likely lies between 78% and 91%, with this risk profile for wrong decisions.' It enforces soft coherence constraints so that coarse-grained and intersectional group definitions stay consistent. It quantifies the value of information: should you run more audits to narrow the range, or is the current range tight enough for decision-making?
847.ww: Bayesian pooling works because it treats each audit as evidence with its own uncertainty and weight. By combining them formally, you get an interval that captures what you collectively know, plus explicit acknowledgment of what you don't. The value-of-information calculation tells you whether running another audit will actually change the decision—often it won't, saving effort.
847.po: On content moderation and ad-delivery case studies, the meta-evaluator achieves better interval coverage and fewer flip-floops in fair/unfair verdicts than existing approaches. For platforms under regulatory pressure, this translates to defensible fairness claims with clear confidence intervals—much harder to challenge than point estimates.

848.bp: Streaming recommendations recommend the next movie, video, or song based on your history. The challenge deepens when sequences are long: a user's viewing history over months can contain dozens of interests, and recent clicks aren't necessarily the best predictors—older patterns matter too. But longer sequences also introduce noise: irrelevant videos the user clicked by mistake, or just lost interest in.
848.wh: Long sequences don't just mean more data; they mean more noise and more interest drift. A user might love sci-fi for a month, then pivot to cooking videos, then return to sci-fi months later. This isn't random noise—it's the 'session hopping' pattern where interests are stable within short windows (sessions) but jump between windows. Standard sequential models either ignore this structure or weight everything by recency, missing the returning patterns.
848.ap: Mixture of Sequence (MoS) learns to partition a user's history into theme-based subsequences—groups of sessions that share a hidden interest theme. It does this with a routing mechanism that labels each session with a theme, then assembles only theme-aligned sessions into coherent subsequences for prediction. This automatically filters out off-topic sessions. To handle multiple time scales, it extracts subsequences at different granularities, letting the model pick which timescale matters for the next prediction.
848.ww: The reason thematic partitioning helps is that it treats interest drift not as noise but as structure to exploit. A user's interest graph naturally has clusters—sci-fi, cooking, sci-fi again—and by recovering those clusters, you can predict based on 'all previous sci-fi' instead of 'all previous regardless of topic.' The multi-scale extraction means you don't commit to a single timescale for what 'recent' means.
848.po: On real sequential recommendation benchmarks, MoS outperforms models that treat sequences as uniform streams, especially on long sequences where naive recency weighting fails. This matters for streaming platforms: better next-item prediction means more watch time and higher engagement.

849.bp: Large language models can reason step-by-step, but when the task requires strict logic—working through a math problem or formal proof—they stumble. A single misplaced parenthesis in their reasoning breaks the conclusion. The goal is to enhance LLMs' ability to do logical reasoning where every step must be verifiable and each misstep must be caught and corrected.
849.wh: Chain-of-thought prompting helps but doesn't enforce correctness. Neuro-symbolic methods use external formal solvers to check steps, but solvers are brittle: a tiny formatting mistake in the LLM's output breaks the parse. And when the parse fails, the system can't recover—it just crashes. So you're stuck: LLM-only reasoning is sloppy; LLM plus solver is fragile.
849.ap: MatrixCoT represents the entire reasoning plan as a matrix, where each row is a step and columns show dependencies and citations. The LLM generates this matrix, and the matrix becomes a verifiable artifact: you can check which claims depend on which premises. When verification fails, a replanning mechanism identifies the gap ('step 3 contradicts step 7'), rewrites the matrix to fix it, and produces a corrected version without restarting from scratch.
849.ww: Matrices are more robust than linear chains because they make global dependencies visible—you see at a glance that step 5 depends on steps 2 and 3 but not 4. When an error is caught, the matrix tells you exactly which steps to revise, and you can rewrite in context rather than starting over. The feedback-driven replanning means the system improves its reasoning iteratively.
849.po: MatrixCoT improves LLMs' performance on logical reasoning tasks by separating the 'generation' phase (LLM makes a plan) from the 'verification' phase (check it and replan if broken). This matters for applications like code generation or mathematical proof where a single error derails the result.

850.bp: Mobile super-apps like WeChat integrate dozens of services—messaging, payments, games, shopping—through miniapps (small programs). Security is supposed to be handled by the platform: apps are vetted before release, and users can report suspicious apps via a built-in interface. But what if a malicious app fakes the reporting interface itself, so user reports never reach the platform? The goal is to detect these deceptive apps that weaponize trust.
850.wh: The threat is subtle: an official reporting interface is a screen with a button labeled 'Report to Platform.' A fake one looks identical but sends reports to the attacker's server instead. The platform's vetting doesn't catch this because the fake interface is *inside* the app—the platform never sees it. Users think they're reporting the app, but they're actually helping the attacker cover their tracks. This is a classic adversarial scenario: the attacker exploits the very mechanism designed to stop them.
850.ap: The researchers built a dataset of 3,587 malicious miniapps with deceptive reporting interfaces among 135,274 official-alike interfaces. They then analyzed the malware's behavior patterns: some discard reports entirely, some redirect them to attacker servers, some obfuscate their code to evade vetting, and some batch-register multiple copies of the same app to distribute risk. This dataset and behavior taxonomy become the basis for detection.
850.ww: Detection works because the malicious patterns are behavioral, not just cosmetic: the fake interface actually *sends requests to wrong servers* or *logs events differently* than the real one. By analyzing network traffic or log patterns from miniapps, you can distinguish a fake reporting interface (which phones home) from a real one (which phones to the platform).
850.po: The research identifies a major security gap in super-app ecosystems: deceptive interfaces that subvert the reporting mechanism. The dataset of 3,587 confirmed malware examples and their behavioral patterns gives platforms and security researchers a foundation for building detection systems and tightening app review.

851.bp: Millions of people use ChatGPT and similar conversational AI daily. What are they doing with it, and how are those behaviors changing? Are they asking quick factual questions, or are they building ongoing relationships with the bot? The goal is understanding the real-world adoption patterns and risks that emerge as these systems become embedded in daily life.
851.wh: Large-scale studies usually rely on synthetic data, surveys, or anonymized logs. But logs don't capture *intent* (why did this person ask this question?), and surveys are limited in scale. Getting authentic, detailed data requires people to volunteer their real conversations—which is rare because of privacy concerns. The research opportunity is to use GDPR data rights: users can request their data back from platforms like OpenAI, and researchers can analyze it with consent.
851.ap: The researchers collected 825,000 ChatGPT conversations from 300 users who donated their data through GDPR requests. They analyzed three dimensions: purpose drift (what topics do conversations cover over time?), social framing (how much do users treat the bot as a social entity?), and steering dynamics (how often do users follow the bot's suggestions?). The dataset spans months of real usage.
851.ww: Analyzing real conversations reveals patterns invisible in controlled studies. For instance, the researchers found that users increasingly disclose personal information and ask about health and mental health topics—areas where a misunderstanding between human and bot could be harmful. They also found that conversational steering (the bot suggesting a direction, and users following it) quadrupled after GPT-4o's release, suggesting the model's improving quality changes how people interact with it.
851.po: The study shows a fundamental shift: conversational AI is no longer a tool for quick queries but a social partner for ongoing discussions, advice, and emotional support. This raises governance questions: when people treat an AI as a friend, do they disclose too much? Can the AI handle mental health conversations responsibly? The data foundation opens the door to answering these.

852.bp: Autonomous systems—AI agents, robots, recommenders—need to make decisions that align with human values. But values are abstract (fairness, honesty, compassion) and culturally diverse. The goal is finding a universal principle that can guide an AI system to make ethical decisions across cultures and contexts without needing exhaustive programming of specific rules.
852.wh: Most approaches to AI ethics hardcode specific rules: 'don't discriminate,' 'don't lie,' 'maximize welfare.' But these rules conflict (maximizing welfare might require a small lie), and they don't translate universally across cultures. A more principled foundation would derive ethical behavior from a simpler core, the way physics derives forces from symmetries. The challenge is finding that core principle.
852.ap: The paper proposes the Golden Rule—treat others as you'd wish to be treated—as the foundation. It formalizes this within game theory: each agent reasons about what others would want and reciprocates. Through mathematical analysis, the authors show that adherence to the Golden Rule leads to fairness (equal treatment), honesty (reciprocal trust), and cooperation. They demonstrate how the principle can accommodate cultural variation while remaining universal.
852.ww: The reason the Golden Rule works is that it creates a feedback loop: if I treat you well, I'm incentivizing you to treat me well in return, stabilizing cooperation. In game-theoretic equilibrium, mutual Golden Rule adherence outperforms selfish strategies. The principle is symmetric—it doesn't privilege any agent—so it naturally encodes fairness.
852.po: For AI agents and reinforcement learning systems, using the Golden Rule as a training objective means the system learns to cooperate, respect others' preferences, and build stable equilibria rather than exploiting weaknesses. This offers a path to alignment that is interpretable (the principle is simple), universal (it crosses cultures), and mathematically grounded.

853.bp: Social media platforms—Telegram, Reddit, Twitter—struggle to moderate billions of posts and comments. Ideally, they'd proactively flag harmful content before it goes live. But predicting which posts will attract toxic or hateful comments requires understanding what *will happen* after posting—an inherently uncertain task. The goal is to forecast audience reactions from post content alone, enabling smarter moderation and safer communities.
853.wh: Comment toxicity or sentiment depends on both the post content and the audience composition, neither of which the platform controls. A neutral post about a controversial topic might attract thoughtful debate in one community and vitriol in another. The challenge is extracting predictive signals from the post alone, without access to comments (which don't exist until users see the post). It's like forecasting audience laughter from a comedian's script before the show.
853.ap: EmoTg extracts features from the post using two methods: traditional NLP (word counts, syntax patterns) and LLM-based analysis (semantic meaning, style, emotion). It combines these into a feature vector representing linguistic, stylistic, semantic, and emotional traits. Then it trains an XGBoost classifier to predict comment-level reactions (is the comment cute? toxic? conflicted?) based solely on the post features. The model learns which post traits correlate with which audience reactions.
853.ww: Using both shallow NLP and deep LLM features works because shallow features capture explicit markers ('bad word present') while deep features capture subtle tone ('this comment seems joking'). XGBoost can then learn non-linear relationships: maybe posts with certain semantic structures attract humor, while others attract conflict. The combination gives the model enough signal to beat random guessing by a large margin.
853.po: On Telegram data, EmoTg achieves 85% accuracy on emotional attributes and 71% on toxic comment prediction. This means moderators can proactively flag high-risk posts before comments flood in, reducing harm and giving platforms time to intervene. The SHAP explainability shows which features drive predictions, enabling human oversight.

854.bp: Recommendation systems face a pervasive problem: most users interact with a small set of popular items, while the vast majority of items are rarely consumed (the 'long tail'). Recommenders trained on this skewed data excel at suggesting bestsellers but struggle with niche items. For users who love obscure music or unpopular books, the system fails. The goal is to improve recommendation for the long tail without sacrificing quality for mainstream users.
854.wh: Simply boosting tail items risks breaking the model: if you artificially increase weight on niche items, the model learns spurious patterns from scarce data, and recommendations for mainstream users degrade. Existing methods try to enrich tail items with knowledge from popular items or additional context, but they often sacrifice head performance or don't address the core problem—tail items have inherently fewer signal samples.
854.ap: TADA explicitly models tail data scarcity through augmentation: it learns the co-occurrence and correlation between unpopular items (using a linear model to capture what is stable), then creates synthetic interactions via two operators. T-Substitute replaces a popular item in a user's sequence with a correlated unpopular item, creating plausible alternative histories. T-Insert adds an unpopular item to existing sequences. These augmentations boost the tail's sample count without modifying head data.
854.ww: Augmentation helps because it respects the structure already in the data: if two unpopular items are correlated, synthetic sequences mixing them are realistic. By augmenting only the tail, you increase tail learning without introducing noise into the head. The head remains unchanged, so head performance doesn't degrade. The model learns from both real and synthetic tail interactions, improving its understanding of niche preferences.
854.po: On sequential recommendation datasets, TADA improves tail recommendation accuracy while maintaining head performance. For platforms like Netflix or Spotify, this means users interested in niche content get better suggestions, while mainstream users aren't harmed. This is especially valuable for long-tail businesses where engagement with obscure items drives retention.

855.bp: When a company files its annual 10-K report with regulators, it must disclose what has changed in its business—new risks, strategic shifts, financial performance. Investors who want to spot trouble early need to spot these real changes, but 10-K filings are bloated with repeated legal boilerplate that hides the signal in noise. The goal is to automatically extract what actually changed year to year, so a fund manager can see a red flag (or opportunity) hiding in thousands of pages.
855.wh: The core tension is that most of a 10-K is copy-pasted from last year unchanged. Analyzing the whole document treats that repetition as real signal. What actually matters is *what moved*—which sentences disappeared and which appear for the first time—because that's where genuine business changes hide.
855.ap: The paper takes a two-step approach. First, it uses neural sentence matching to align sentences from year t with year t+1, marking each as Kept (unchanged boilerplate), Deleted (removed), or Added (new). Then it computes a net sentiment shift: take the average sentiment of newly Added sentences minus the average sentiment of Deleted ones, using FinBERT (a financial-tuned sentiment model). The difference becomes a single 'Core Sentiment' score that captures whether disclosures genuinely got more or less optimistic.
855.ww: This works because it strips away the noise of repetition. By ignoring what stayed the same, you force the model to measure only real change. If a company newly discloses a legal risk (negative), that Deleted optimistic language elsewhere won't drown it out. The magnitude of the shift matters: a small positive disclosure added alongside large positive deletions signals a real pessimistic turn, which raw sentiment would hide.
855.po: The framework produces a cleaner risk signal: investors can now detect meaningful business pivots buried in annual filings, and the method outperforms standard bag-of-words sentiment on real 10-K data. This opens the door to semi-automated compliance analysis and early detection of strategic shifts before quarterly earnings calls.

856.bp: Large language models are now the main way people search and reason over web data, but they often hallucinate or contradict each other because they work from statistical pattern-matching alone. Knowledge graphs—structured databases of entities and their relationships—offer the opposite: explicitly curated facts with clear links. The goal is to combine both powers: let LLMs reason flexibly, but ground them in a structured graph so their answers stay true and explainable.
856.wh: LLMs alone are beautiful for natural conversation but unreliable for facts. Knowledge graphs are precise but rigid—they don't handle ambiguity or reasoning steps well. Putting them together is hard because LLMs generate freeform text while graphs demand structure. How do you make an LLM consult a graph mid-reasoning? How do you validate that what the LLM generated actually follows from the graph?
856.ap: GLOW (the workshop topic) focuses on architectures that weave graph structure into LLM reasoning: the LLM learns to query a knowledge graph as a retrieval step, verifies its answers against graph facts, and explains its logic by walking through explicit relationships. Instead of the LLM speaking freely, it treats the graph as a source of truth to check against, and the graph acts as a scaffold for the LLM's reasoning chain.
856.ww: Graphs provide semantic scaffolding that LLMs can lean on. When an LLM generates a claim, the graph can instantly check: 'Does this relationship exist in our curated data?' This creates a feedback loop—the LLM learns to make claims the graph will validate, and the graph fills in relational context the LLM can't derive from text alone. Transparency emerges because every reasoning step is now traceable through graph edges.
856.po: The payoff is web-scale systems that are both conversational and trustworthy. Users get natural language access to data without sacrificing accuracy or explainability. For enterprise applications (medical records, compliance, supply chains), this hybrid approach lets machines reason over messy real-world data while staying verifiable and auditable.

857.bp: Retrieval-augmented generation pairs an LLM with a search engine: the engine finds relevant documents, the LLM reads them and answers a question. This is how most chatbots avoid hallucinating on private data. The bottleneck is speed: searching through millions of documents and then feeding all their text to the LLM is slow and expensive. The dream is to compress documents down to their essential meaning so the LLM gets more signal per unit of compute.
857.wh: Naive compression (shrinking documents uniformly to save tokens) backfires. If you crush a long document equally everywhere—squeezing technical details, examples, and boilerplate at the same rate—you lose what mattered for *this specific query*. A query-agnostic compression treats a medical article the same whether someone asks about symptoms or drug interactions. The obvious math-efficient solution (autoencoders that compress everything) actually hurts the LLM's ability to answer because it discards query-relevant facts alongside noise.
857.ap: Instead of compressing every document the same way, the paper proposes SeleCom: train a small selector model to read a document *and the query together*, then output only the sentences that matter for that query. The selector learns to flag relevant passages and discard irrelevant ones, acting as a query-aware filter rather than a compression machine. Training uses synthetic Q&A pairs graded by difficulty, so the selector learns to recognize relevance at different complexity levels.
857.ww: This shifts the goal from 'make small' to 'pick what matters.' Because the selector sees both the query and document, it can spot that a medical paper's symptom section is relevant for one user but irrelevant for another asking about side effects. Smaller output happens as a side effect of this precision filtering, not at the expense of information density. The selector learns task-specific relevance rather than generic compression.
857.po: SeleCom matches or beats standard RAG (which uses full documents) while slashing context size and latency. This makes RAG practical for resource-constrained applications and enables faster, cheaper LLM reasoning at scale. The synthetic training dataset can be adapted to new domains, making the approach reusable.

858.bp: Current spam filters, fake news detectors, and grammar checkers work at the document level: they say 'this email is spam' or 'this review is fake' but don't show *where* in the text the problem is. For real-world applications, a user needs to know which sentence to rewrite, which phrase is suspicious, which part of a message triggered the alarm. The goal is fine-grained anomaly detection—pinpointing exactly which words or phrases are out of place.
858.wh: Document-level analysis is too coarse because a fake review might be 95% legitimate sentences with just a few planted promotional words. Global pattern-matching models trained on 'spam vs. not spam' miss local weirdness because they average over everything. And most anomaly datasets only label documents, not individual words, so training fine-grained detectors is impossible without manual annotation.
858.ap: The paper introduces token-level anomaly detection: instead of labeling a whole document, they annotated three datasets (spam, reviews, grammar errors) word-by-word to mark which tokens are anomalous. Then they built a unified framework that can operate at both document and token levels—predicting not just 'is this text wrong' but 'which parts are wrong and why' (spam keywords, fake review markers, grammatical errors).
858.ww: By training on token-level labels, the model learns to recognize that a few specific phrases like 'act now' or 'limited offer' are red flags in reviews, while the same phrase in a marketing email is normal. Word-level supervision teaches the model to spot inconsistency and deviation in context, not just global oddness. The dual-level approach lets it generalize: a spam detector trained this way can also flag suspicious passages in other domains.
858.po: Annotated benchmarks now exist for token-level anomaly detection, enabling precise, explainable content moderation. A spam filter can tell a user exactly which words got it flagged. A grammar checker can highlight the specific error. Suspicious reviews can be examined word-by-word, making moderation decisions auditable and helping users fix problems rather than just reject content.

859.bp: Federated learning lets thousands of organizations train an AI model together without sharing raw data—each site trains on its own data, sends only model updates to a central server. This is crucial for sensitive domains like healthcare and finance. But federated learning is vulnerable to poisoning: a bad actor can send malicious updates to sabotage the global model. Recent work moved to ranking-based federated learning (FRL), which only communicates discrete rankings instead of continuous numbers, making poisoning harder. The question is: can adversaries still attack ranking-based systems in new ways?
859.wh: Traditional federated learning poisoning is easy to spot—malicious updates look extreme and get filtered out. Ranking-based FRL was designed to be robust because rankings are discrete; you can't smoothly optimize an attack in the continuous space. But the researchers found a blind spot: an attacker can still manipulate which rankings win, creating a fine-grained control attack that looks normal on the surface while secretly degrading specific models—like silently crippling a competitor's accuracy while maintaining the appearance of normal convergence.
859.ap: The Edge Control Attack (ECA) works in two stages. First, the attacker maps the global model update process to understand which discrete ranking 'edges' (comparisons between model versions) drive convergence. Then they craft local poisoned data that inverts specific edges—making the global model prefer slightly worse directions that favor an attacker's target. Unlike blunt denial-of-service attacks that crash the model, ECA drifts the update direction incrementally, avoiding statistical red flags.
859.ww: ECA succeeds because discrete rankings hide continuous manipulation. By flipping small edge comparisons, the attacker exploits the ranking system's trust in majority vote. The global model thinks it's improving (it's following the consensus direction) but actually slides toward a poisoned target. Detection is hard because the convergence curve looks normal—the model improves, just not as well as it should, and that gap is easy to miss.
859.po: The paper reveals that ranking-based federated learning, while more robust than traditional FL, is not immune to sophisticated attacks. This motivates new defenses tailored to ranking-based systems (e.g., Byzantine-robust ranking aggregation). The work pushes federated learning security forward and shows that moving to discrete representations doesn't eliminate adversarial risk—it only changes the attack surface.

860.bp: Electronic health records (EHRs) contain millions of medical codes and concepts—diagnoses, procedures, medications. Each one currently gets a separate numerical representation (an embedding) stored in memory. As hospitals scale, this balloons into gigabytes of tables. The deeper problem: these embeddings ignore the natural hierarchy of medicine (pneumonia is a type of respiratory infection, which is a type of infection) so models miss the semantic structure that doctors use to reason. The goal is to compress medical concepts while preserving hierarchical meaning.
860.wh: Naive compression (squashing medical codes into smaller vectors) destroys hierarchy. You lose the fact that appendicitis and hepatitis are both inflammatory conditions. Recent work tried to encode concepts as discrete codes (like codebooks), which saves memory, but treats every concept independently—a flat assignment rather than a layered one. A model trained on this discrete flat representation can't leverage the medical ontology structure that would help it generalize to new procedures or unseen diseases.
860.ap: MedRQ (ontology-driven residual vector quantization) treats the medical hierarchy as a scaffold. Instead of assigning each concept a single discrete code, it assigns sequences of codes that align with multi-level medical ontologies. A code at level 1 might represent 'infection,' level 2 'respiratory infection,' level 3 'pneumonia.' During training, the model is supervised to generate codes consistent with this hierarchy. Residual quantization means each level adds detail to the previous level's representation.
860.ww: Hierarchical supervision teaches the model to cluster concepts meaningfully: if two diseases are siblings in the ontology, their code sequences should be similar. This forces the model to learn that appendicitis and gastroenteritis are both GI inflammation, which helps predict complications or drug interactions across similar conditions. The hierarchy acts as an inductive bias—the model doesn't have to discover these relationships from scratch; it's built into the training signal.
860.po: MedRQ shrinks memory overhead dramatically while improving prediction on clinical tasks (patient deterioration, readmission risk). Clinicians also gain interpretability: the multi-level codes reveal *why* the model makes a prediction. A model that groups a rare disease with known common cousins can generalize to unseen diagnoses, which is crucial in healthcare where true novel cases appear regularly.

861.bp: Recommender systems on shopping sites need to instantly suggest relevant items from millions of candidates. A two-stage approach is standard: first narrow down to 100s using fast math (e.g., inner product of user/item vectors), then re-rank the top candidates with a heavier model. The bottleneck in the narrow-down stage (retrieval) is that simple math doesn't capture why a user likes an item. The question is: how do you make retrieval smarter—capturing richer preference signals—without blowing up latency?
861.wh: Traditional item-to-item collaborative filtering recommends items similar to what the user liked. But 'similarity' is often measured by inner product, which only catches surface-level patterns. A user who bought a phone case and a laptop sleeve might not want a laptop bag, even though all three are accessories. The truncation step that pre-filters the item pool also bleeds quality: if you aggressively cut items to stay fast, you discard borderline candidates that might be perfect for some users but not others. One-size-fits-all filtering wastes personalization.
861.ap: PI2I uses two stages. First, an 'Indexer Building Stage' relaxes the truncation threshold—keep more candidate items initially, trading speed for recall. Second, a 'Personalized Retrieval Stage' deploys an interactive scoring model that replaces simple inner product with learned interactions. Instead of computing score = user_vector · item_vector, the model learns to reason: 'This user liked X; does Y play a similar role?' The model is trained on negative samples built from trigger-target relationships (items a user would engage with given their history), ensuring training and real-world behavior align.
861.ww: Keeping more candidates upfront ensures good items don't get filtered prematurely. The interactive scoring model then decides which matter for *this user*, using richer signals than raw similarity. By training on items the user would realistically consider next (trigger-target pairs), the model learns true preference structure—not just 'similar' but 'similar *and* aligned with their journey.' Deployed on Taobao, this beats rigid truncation strategies.
861.po: PI2I achieved a 1.05% online uplift in transaction rates at Taobao scale. For e-commerce, that translates to millions in incremental revenue. The framework is reusable: any domain with millions of items (streaming, social feeds, job boards) benefits from personalized retrieval that combines precision and speed.

862.bp: AI systems now ingest mixed media—text, images, audio, video, sensor streams. Making sense of what's happening requires both AI reasoning and visual explanation so humans trust the output. A healthcare AI that flags a scan as concerning is useless without showing the doctor *which part of the scan* it saw as anomalous. The goal is to build tools that combine multimodal AI reasoning (the compute) with interactive web visualization (the explanation) so humans and machines can collaborate.
862.wh: Multimodal AI models are blackboxes: they fuse images and text and produce a prediction, but don't explain their reasoning. Classical visualization tools are built for single modalities (text analytics, image annotation) and don't align across image, audio, and video streams. Web platforms today are siloed—speech systems live in isolation, image understanding lives elsewhere. Building an integrated system requires stitching together incompatible pieces.
862.ap: AAIMVT (the workshop) brings together four concrete applications: a privacy-preserving voice-cloning platform with unified web UI (users upload speech, customize tone, retrieve output); a cybersecurity ontology tool that bridges policies and operations via interactive web graphs; a harmful-meme detector that works even when modalities are missing (no image, only text); and infographic reconstruction that parses static graphics back into structured data. Each uses the web as the integration layer.
862.ww: Web interfaces are the connective tissue. Because they run in browsers, they're platform-agnostic: a voice-cloning system, a cybersecurity ontology, and a meme detector can all live in the same application. The browser also handles UI composition naturally—you can show audio waveforms, graph visualizations, image annotations, and text explanations side-by-side. This makes multimodal systems feel coherent to users.
862.po: The workshop surfaced working systems that combine applied AI with visualization, proving that web-native tooling accelerates deployment. Voice privacy, cybersecurity governance, content moderation, and data extraction all became tractable through integrated web platforms. The patterns established here—unified UIs for heterogeneous modalities, browser-as-platform—are now reusable templates for other multimodal AI applications.

863.bp: Federated learning is how hospitals, power plants, and manufacturing sites train AI without uploading sensitive data to the cloud. But the traditional approach—each site sends model parameter updates to a central server—is slow (lots of data) and leaky (adversaries can reverse-engineer raw data from gradients). Recent work uses retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to avoid sending parameters at all—sites send only semantic knowledge extracted from their data. The challenge is diagnosing rare equipment failures across sites that have sparse examples and strict privacy rules.
863.wh: Long-tail faults (rare but critical failures) are hard anywhere. In federated settings, they're doubly hard: one site might have zero examples of a failure, another site has three, scattered across time. Traditional federated learning struggles because gradients computed from scarce samples are noisy (gradient starvation). Gradient inversion attacks can also extract raw data from those updates. Multimodal data (vibration signals + thermal readings) adds complexity—aligning different sensor types across sites is non-trivial.
863.ap: Fed-S2 abandons parameter sharing entirely. Instead, each site builds local semantic embeddings of its sensor data (vibrations, temperature, sound), sanitizes them via 'Semantic Shielding' (a privacy technique), and uploads only those lightweight vectors to a central knowledge graph. The server constructs a global graph connecting these embeddings across sites. At inference time, when a new fault pattern arrives, the system performs retrieval-augmented generation: retrieve similar past faults from the graph, then use a frozen LLM to reason about what the new fault most likely is, even with zero prior examples.
863.ww: Embeddings are privacy-safer than gradients because they're task-specific, not raw data. The adversarial game (min-max optimization under information-bottleneck bounds) ensures that inversion attacks yield noise, not reconstructed signals. Frequency-domain alignment handles multimodal sensor fusion—different modalities are aligned in spectral space before embedding, so vibration and temperature data integrate naturally. The frozen LLM acts as a universal reasoner, generalizing across sites without retraining.
863.po: Fed-S2 improves long-tail fault identification from 38.5% to 84.2% and achieves 68.5% zero-shot accuracy on new fault types where traditional federated learning fails entirely (0%). It cuts communication by 93% compared to standard parameter-sharing FL. For critical infrastructure, this means faster fault detection, lower bandwidth, and provable privacy—enabling real-world deployment where lives and infrastructure depend on it.

864.bp: The Web evolves: pages change, links break, new content appears, trends rise and fall. Understanding these temporal dynamics—how information spreads, how topics evolve, how institutions adapt—requires studying the Web through time. But most tools treat the Web as a static snapshot. The goal is to build infrastructure for temporal web analytics: tools to archive the Web, query it across years, and spot patterns that only emerge over time—like suicide risk signals rising in online communities.
864.wh: Querying the temporal Web is hard because there's no unified standard for time-aware queries. Do you want pages as they appeared on January 1, 2020? All edits in 2021? The intersection of two events across different websites? Web archives (like the Internet Archive) exist but are queried via full-text search, not structured temporal queries. Scaling analysis to millions of pages across decades requires infrastructure that doesn't yet exist.
864.ap: TempWeb (the 16th workshop) covers the full spectrum: temporal information extraction (finding when events occurred in text), temporal information retrieval (retrieving documents from specific time periods), web archiving infrastructure (building queryable historical snapshots), and large-scale temporal data analysis.
