Contributions range from benchmarks for temporal reasoning to applications like early detection of suicide risk by monitoring linguistic shifts in online forums.
864.ww: Temporal structure reveals causality and emergent phenomena that snapshots miss. If you see suicide-risk language rising in a forum over weeks before an incident, you can intervene. If you track how a company's web presence evolved over years, you spot business pivots. The temporal dimension turns the Web from a static knowledge base into a living historical record where patterns unfold over time.
864.po: The workshop established temporal analytics as a first-class citizen in Web research. Contributors now have benchmarks for temporal IE/IR tasks, infrastructure recommendations for archiving and querying temporal data, and validated applications (health monitoring, platform safety, Web evolution studies). This enables research that was previously impossible—understanding long-term dynamics, detecting early warning signals, and learning how the Web transforms.

865.bp: Building predictive models on tabular data (spreadsheets of customer records, sensor readings, financial data) requires feature engineering—combining raw columns into new ones that the model can leverage. A machine learning engineer might spend weeks crafting features by hand: ratios, aggregations, domain-specific combinations. The dream is automatic feature engineering: let an AI system discover useful features without human guidance. But traditional automated approaches generate code blindly, making mistakes that are hard to debug.
865.wh: LLMs are amazing at code generation, but when they generate entire features from scratch, edits are coarse-grained. If an LLM writes 'new_feature = log(abs(X1) + 1)' and you ask it to tweak this, it might rewrite it entirely rather than adjusting just the log or the absolute value. Without a structured representation, it's hard to enforce constraints (feature must be positive, must fit in memory, must preserve causality). This makes the search space chaotic and features hard to interpret.
865.ap: AFE-Master uses a domain-specific language (DSL) to represent features as abstract syntax trees (ASTs)—structured recipes instead of free-form code. A feature like 'log(abs(X1) + 1)' becomes a tree node: log(abs(sum(X1, const=1))). The LLM now manipulates this tree, making targeted edits: swap the log for exp, replace sum with multiply, push the constant to a different branch. A guided local search explores nearby variants, keeping only edits that improve model performance. The structure also lets you enforce semantic constraints (no division by zero, features must decompose hierarchically).
865.ww: Trees make edits traceable and composable. Because features are hierarchical, you can reason about what each layer contributes. Swapping a logarithm for an exponential has a clear semantic effect (compression vs. amplification). Guided local search then finds efficient paths through the space—instead of randomly sampling features, it follows gradients through syntactic neighbors. Interpretability emerges because every feature is a readable tree, not a black-box mutation.
865.po: AFE-Master discovers information-dense, human-readable features faster than traditional evolutionary approaches. On Kaggle and OpenML benchmarks, it outperforms both automatic feature generators and human-designed baselines. Practitioners get features they can explain to stakeholders, and the DSL makes the search process auditable—you can see every transformation the LLM proposed and accepted.

866.bp: Dense retrieval (searching by semantic meaning rather than keywords) powers modern search engines and RAG systems. But these neural retrieval models—fine-tuned transformers that compare queries and documents—can be fooled by adversarial tricks: add a few planted sentences to a document and the model might rank it as relevant even when it's not. Worse, users have no idea *which part* of a document actually matched their query. The goal is robust retrieval that resists attacks and explains its decisions.
866.wh: Dense models rely on learned patterns and are vulnerable to data poisoning. If someone adds a phrase like 'Barack Obama was born in Kenya' to a document, a retrieval model might rank it highly for any query mentioning Obama, even though the sentence is false and unrelated. Adversarial attacks are easy to craft and hard to detect because the model treats all parts of a document equally. Models also lack explainability—they return a relevance score with no indication of *why*.
866.ap: The paper uses counterfactual analysis borrowed from causal reasoning. Train the retrieval model to be sensitive to key passages: if removing a passage drops the relevance score sharply, that passage is truly relevant; if removing filler has little effect, it's noise. They formalize this as a game where the model tries to produce high variance for key passages and low variance for filler, using unsupervised counterfactual passages (synthetically generated variants of documents with key phrases swapped out or removed).
866.ww: Sensitivity to key passages makes the model robust. An adversary who adds a planted sentence now faces a problem: if they sneak in 'Obama born in Kenya' to push relevance up, the model learns to be indifferent to it (low variance when removed). Over time, the model learns to weight genuine relevance signals and ignore planted text. Counterfactuals force this learning without labeled adversarial examples—the model discovers robustness by practicing on synthetically perturbed documents.
866.po: Counterfactual-trained retrievers resist adversarial attacks better than standard models, and their variance structure lets you extract which passages actually influenced the ranking—enabling explainability. Users can see 'your query matched these three sentences in the document,' making the model's decision auditable. On IR benchmarks, the approach maintains performance while improving robustness and transparency.

867.bp: Causal reasoning is how humans understand the world: why did sales drop? What caused the equipment failure? Which policy change drove unemployment? But reasoning over knowledge graphs (databases of interconnected facts) is hard because graphs are messy—data is incomplete, entities have multiple names, relationships are indirect. The goal is to do causal reasoning *directly over knowledge graphs* rather than extracting flat data first, enabling reasoning on incomplete, heterogeneous information.
867.wh: Standard causal frameworks assume flat, fully observed data. Real knowledge graphs violate every assumption: entities are heterogeneous (people, products, events), relationships are multi-relational (X owns Y, X employs Z, Y depends on Z), and data is incomplete (we don't know all facts). Causal discovery (learning which variables cause which) becomes impossible without ontological grounding—how do you know if a missing fact is truly absent or just unobserved? Causal inference also breaks because relational dependencies between entities violate independence assumptions.
867.ap: The thesis proposes CauseKG, SemMatch, HyKG-CF, and BaLu—an end-to-end pipeline. CauseKG integrates ontological semantics: represent causal relationships as typed edges aligned with domain ontologies (medical, financial). SemMatch handles entity disambiguation and resolution. HyKG-CF performs counterfactual prediction: given a graph, reason about what would change if we perturb an entity or relationship. BaLu aggregates results across graph fragments under the Open World Assumption (unobserved facts may exist). Together, they enable query-based causal reasoning.
867.ww: Ontological types ground causality. A relationship 'drug X causes symptom Y' means something different from 'gene X causes disease Y'—the semantics differ. By anchoring to ontologies, you encode domain knowledge into the causal structure. Counterfactual prediction over subgraphs then becomes tractable: to ask 'would lowering a patient's sodium cause a better outcome,' you simulate the graph perturbation using learned causal rules specific to medical ontology.
867.po: The pipeline enables causal intelligence over messy real-world data. Hospitals can reason about patient outcomes. Economists can model policy effects. Supply chain managers can trace failure cascades. Each domain gets domain-aware causal reasoning without rewriting the machinery. The framework unifies causal discovery (learning what causes what), causal inference (estimating effects), and counterfactual reasoning (simulating alternatives), making causal analysis accessible on knowledge graphs.

868.bp: Peer review is how science validates itself—experts read papers and decide what's worth publishing. But reviewers are human: they miss details, write careless comments, sometimes contradict each other. The goal is to build systems that audit peer reviews at scale: check whether reviews are thorough and factual, whether reviewers actually engaged with the paper, and whether conclusions are backed by evidence. This supports better journals and helps emerging researchers understand why their work was rejected.
868.wh: Assessing review quality is subjective. What makes a review 'good'? Is it specific (mentions particular equations, figures) or vague (generic feedback)? Is the tone constructive or dismissive? How do you verify that a reviewer's criticisms are actually supported by the paper? Expert humans can judge this reliably, but there are millions of reviews every year. Automating this requires understanding both the review text and the underlying paper—a hard task that tests LLM reasoning and grounding.
868.ap: The work builds two systems. First, a review-quality assessment module that evaluates reviews on dimensions like specificity and tone, comparing zero-shot LLM predictions against expert-annotated benchmarks. Second, a factual verification module that takes a reviewer's claim (e.g., 'the authors use dataset X') and checks whether the paper supports it by retrieving relevant sections and matching. They compare static metrics (text length, readability), machine learning baselines, zero-shot LLMs, and fine-tuned models.
868.ww: Combining natural language assessment with retrieval-based verification provides multiple signals. An LLM is good at understanding intent ('this review is dismissive'), while retrieval + matching is good at factual grounding ('this claim has textual support'). Hybrid approaches outperform LLMs alone because they anchor language understanding in evidence. The benchmarks ground evaluation in human expert judgment, so you can measure progress objectively.
868.po: Deployable systems for auditing reviews at scale enable new accountability in peer review. Journal editors can prioritize reviews for deeper inspection, authors understand whether criticisms are supported, and systems can flag potentially unfair or shallow reviews. This infrastructure supports research integrity—not replacing human reviewers, but augmenting them with systems that catch low-quality feedback and surface fairness issues.

869.bp: Granger causality is a statistical method for discovering cause-and-effect from time series: if variable X's past values help predict variable Y better than Y's history alone, then X probably causes Y. This is how economists detect policy effects on markets, how doctors diagnose patient deterioration, and how manufacturers spot equipment failures. But time series are messy—data has outliers, multiple scales, and context (a spike might be seasonal, not causal). The goal is to improve causal discovery by enriching time series with semantic context from language models.
869.wh: Raw time series are context-blind. A temperature spike looks the same whether caused by a broken sensor, a maintenance event, or external weather. Granger causality methods find statistical relationships but can't distinguish spurious correlation from true causality without domain knowledge. LLMs encode world knowledge—'temperature rises seasonally in summer'—but they work on text, not numbers. Bridging the gap requires converting time series to semantic space where an LLM can reason about context.
869.ap: LLM-GC encodes time series and text simultaneously. For each time series (e.g., stock price, patient vitals), generate semantic descriptions using an LLM ('stock price rose 5% amid economic optimism'). Then align temporal features (numerical trends) with semantic features (text descriptions) using cross-modal retrieval. A causality-aware self-attention mechanism (inverted from standard attention) highlights causal patterns that appear consistently in both modalities. The model learns that if numerical causality (X predicts Y in numbers) aligns with semantic causality (descriptions support the relationship), it's a robust causal link.
869.ww: Multimodal fusion disambiguates spurious patterns. A numerical correlation between two time series might be coincidence, but if semantic descriptions align ('both increased due to regulation'), it becomes credible causality. The inverted attention mechanism forces the model to attend to causal patterns explicitly, filtering out noise. LLMs as semantic priors inject domain knowledge—the model learns faster because it doesn't derive all context from scarce data.
869.po: LLM-GC outperforms existing Granger causality methods on synthetic and real benchmarks. Applications gain speed and accuracy: faster diagnosis of equipment faults, more reliable detection of policy effects on markets, better understanding of disease progression. The framework is the first bridge between LLMs and causal discovery, opening new hybrid methods that combine statistical rigor with semantic reasoning.

870.bp: When you shop online, the product information you see—photos, descriptions, prices, categories—comes from a catalog. That catalog is only useful if it's accurate and complete. For large retailers selling thousands of items, keeping all that data clean and consistent is exhausting work, and mistakes slip through. This paper asks: can an AI system fix those mistakes automatically, by comparing a retailer's messy catalog against a brand's clean reference data?
870.wh: The obvious approach would be to fix each product entry in isolation: find mistakes in one row, correct them, then move to the next. But real-world catalogs are tangled; a single product might have the wrong category *and* missing attributes *and* a typo in the name all at once. Fixing them one at a time means you might correct the category, then realize the typo actually implies the category was half-right. You need to see the whole picture.
870.ap: This work uses two things together: a large language model (a machine that reads and reasons about text) and a brand's knowledge base (a clean, structured list of product definitions). The LLM acts as an agent—a worker that can follow instructions, read messy data, consult the reference, and make decisions. The key move is that it does both repair *and* matching at the same time. Instead of fixing the entry, then searching for a match, it reasons about what the entry should be *while* finding which reference product it belongs to.
870.ww: When you try to match a messy product entry to a clean reference, both cleaning and matching inform each other. An LLM can hold both problems in mind: "This entry has a typo and a wrong category, so when I look for the matching reference product, I should ignore those noise signals and focus on what's actually being described." Doing them concurrently means the LLM can course-correct itself as it learns more.
870.po: The paper shows this approach actually works—it improves the quality of large product catalogs automatically. For e-commerce, this means customers see accurate, complete product pages, which boosts trust and click-through rates. For retailers, it means less manual data cleanup and fewer customer complaints about wrong shipping or mismatched descriptions.

871.bp: Recommendation systems are everywhere: Netflix suggests shows, Spotify suggests songs, Amazon suggests products. But most recommendation systems have a blind spot: they're obsessed with popular items because those get the most clicks and sales. Unpopular but really good items—indie movies, niche music, specialized tools—almost never surface. This paper tackles that unfairness: how do you make recommendations that surface hidden gems, not just blockbusters?
871.wh: The core tension is that popularity and quality are not the same thing. A recommendation system trained on who-clicks-what will learn that popular items get clicked a lot, so it learns to recommend them constantly. But many users would actually prefer something less mainstream if they knew it existed. The problem gets worse the more unpopular an item is: the system has less data about it, so it's less confident, and confidence is often how systems rank candidates. Result: long-tail items stay invisible.
871.ap: SAGERec builds a representation (a compressed summary) of each user based on two signals: the user's own data and the data from the most informative items they've actually clicked. The trick is identifying which items are "most informative." Instead of picking them with a hard rule, the paper trains a separate neural network to learn which items matter most—a learner learning what to pay attention to. Then they use two expert sub-models that each score items differently, and a gating mechanism (a learned decision-maker) that blends those scores based on whether an item is from the long tail or not.
871.ww: Why does this help? First, focusing on the most informative items means you're not drowned in noise from items the user clicked-but-didn't-really-care-about. Second, training separate experts for tail vs. popular items means each can be optimized for its regime. The gating mechanism then acts as a kind of traffic cop: for long-tail items, it trusts the tail-specialist expert more. This breaks the feedback loop where popular items get recommended more because they're popular.
871.po: Experiments on real datasets show SAGERec recommends long-tail items much better than older systems while staying competitive on popular items. The concrete payoff: users discover items that match their taste but aren't trending, which makes their experience richer and supports creators of niche content.

872.bp: Misinformation spreads fast online. Fact-checking is the counterforce: journalists and tools verify whether a claim is true. But fact-checking is hard because claims are often complex. A single sentence might assert three things at once: "This policy was passed in 2019 and raised unemployment in rural areas by 3%." You have to check each piece, and those pieces often depend on each other—you can't verify "rural unemployment rose" without first knowing whether the policy actually passed.
872.wh: Recent fact-checking systems use large language models and break complex claims into simpler sub-claims to check each one. That's smart: it's easier for a machine to verify "The policy passed" than to verify the whole sentence at once. But the gap is that these systems treat each sub-claim as independent. They never ask: "Does the answer to sub-claim #2 change what sub-claim #3 means?" For claims that need you to follow a chain of reasoning (multi-hop reasoning), that's catastrophic. You verify each link of the chain in isolation, and miss contradictions between links.
872.ap: This paper proposes DagFC (Dependency-Aware Fact-Checking). Instead of breaking the claim into sub-claims at random, it builds a knowledge graph—a map showing which sub-claims depend on which others. For instance, if checking "the policy passed" is needed before checking "unemployment rose," the graph captures that dependency. Then, the system verifies sub-claims in an order that respects those dependencies. When it finishes verifying one, it uses that result to guide the verification of the next, carrying intermediate findings forward. The term "dag" refers to the shape of that dependency map (a directed acyclic graph).
872.ww: The first-principles reason this works: humans do multi-hop reasoning by keeping intermediate conclusions in mind and using them to check the next step. "The policy passed *in 2019*, so I should check unemployment data *from 2019 onwards*." By encoding dependencies, the system mimics that practice. It also avoids verifying the same sub-claim twice; if "the policy passed" has already been verified, the next sub-claim can reuse that verdict instead of re-checking from scratch.
872.po: The concrete payoff: complex claims with multi-hop reasoning get verified more accurately because the system respects the logical structure. This means fact-checking tools can handle the trickiest claims—the ones bad actors craft precisely to confuse simple, step-by-step verification.

873.bp: Imagine a ride-sharing app that doesn't just get you from A to B, but that learns *why* you chose that route. Maybe you took the scenic route because you wanted fresh air, or you chose a neighborhood because you heard it had a cool vibe. The real goal is moving beyond "Where do people go?" to "Why do people feel drawn to places?" This paper builds a system to collect that sensory and emotional data at scale, so future recommendations can consider not just popularity, but how a place *feels*.
873.wh: Existing recommendation systems for places (maps, ride-sharing, tourism apps) rely on reviews and ratings, which are text-based signals. But whether a place appeals to you depends on subtler, multisensory things: Is it noisy? Does it smell fresh? Are the colors pleasing? Is it crowded? These nuances are almost impossible to capture in a review text. And different people react differently to the same sensory input depending on their personality—someone who seeks thrills might love a loud, chaotic market; someone who seeks calm might hate it. Standard systems don't model that.
873.ap: The paper presents FreePOST, a location-based app where users submit photos along with tags describing their sensory experience (noisy, crowded, calm, vibrant, etc.) tied to specific places. Over three months in Kyoto, 69 people contributed over 8,000 posts. The system also collected personality data using standard psychology questionnaires (Big Five Inventory, Sensation Seeking Scale) so that the sensory impressions could be paired with who reported them. The data is visualized on an interactive map in real time.
873.ww: The insight is straightforward: sensory experience of a place is real and varies by observer. By collecting both the sensory tags *and* the personality profile of who tagged it, the system can later learn patterns like "people high in openness love vibrant, crowded places" or "people low in extraversion avoid noisy locations." This is the data foundation for personalized recommendations that consider how a place fits a person's sensory and temperamental preferences, not just the average rating.
873.po: This data collection provides a foundation for future location recommendation and mobility services that feel more human. Instead of recommending the "best-reviewed" place, a system could recommend places that match a user's personality and preferred sensory experience. The concrete payoff is captured in the paper: a foundation for "personalized search and recommendation in MaaS contexts"—meaning ride-sharing and mobility apps can eventually recommend routes and destinations that suit the person, not just the destination's average popularity.

874.bp: When you ask a smart assistant a question in the middle of a conversation, the assistant needs to find the right answer in a massive database of interconnected concepts and facts. A knowledge graph is a structured database where information is represented as connected nodes: "Barack Obama" (a person) is connected to "2008" (a year) which is connected to "U.S. Presidential Election" (an event). The challenge is: how do you find the right node when the question is messy, contextual, and embedded in a multi-turn conversation?
874.wh: The obvious approach: translate the user's question into a search query, find matching nodes, rank them by some score. But that misses context. If the user previously asked about "U.S. elections," and now asks "Who won in 2008?", the context matters. Also, a single answer node ("Barack Obama") is surrounded by a neighborhood of related nodes ("Democratic Party," "Illinois," "Hope"), and different searches might care about different neighbors. A naive system that only looks at whether "Barack Obama" lexically matches the question might miss it entirely if the question uses synonyms.
874.ap: DRAGON (Diverse Relevance signal Aggregation via Graph cONvolution) takes a different approach. For each candidate answer node, it first builds a sub-graph—a small map of the candidate, its neighbors, and their connections. Then, it computes many fine-grained relevance signals: How well does the current turn of the conversation match the candidate node's name? How well does it match its neighbors? What about previous turns? All these signals are represented as sparse vectors (lists of numbers). DRAGON then uses graph convolution—a neural technique that propagates signals through the sub-graph—to blend and transform all these signals together, eventually producing a ranking score for that candidate.
874.ww: The reason this works: different parts of the sub-graph are relevant at different moments in the conversation. By propagating signals through the graph, the system can learn that "Obama" is relevant because the candidate node itself matches, but also because its neighbors (Democratic Party, 2008) match previous turns. Graph convolution naturally captures these multi-hop relationships. By explicitly representing many fine-grained signals (not just one score), the system also has more information to work with, reducing the chance it misses a good answer.
874.po: The payoff is better entity retrieval in conversational systems. When you ask a multi-turn question about a knowledge graph, the system finds the right node more often, leading to smarter, more contextual answers from voice assistants, chatbots, and other conversational systems.

875.bp: Misinformation spreads online because people believe it. Understanding why people believe false claims is the first step to stopping the spread. Unlike systems that only analyze the text of false claims (does it sound true?), this paper flips the lens: it asks what linguistic features actually *predict* whether people will find something believable, and it does so by analyzing real human judgments from social media discussions.
875.wh: Most misinformation detection systems work backwards. They assume a claim is true or false, then try to detect which is which using facts, sources, or the text's logical consistency. But that's not how humans judge credibility. Humans read a claim and feel an intuitive sense of whether to trust it, based on cues in the language itself. A sentence with clear verbs and specific dates feels more credible than a vague one. Proper nouns feel more credible than pronouns. This intuition can be wrong, but it's powerful. Systems that only look at factual accuracy miss what actually persuades people.
875.ap: The paper analyzed real social-media discussions where people posted claims and others voted on whether they believed them. It collected both the human believability judgments *and* linguistic features of the claims: which verbs were used, whether proper nouns appeared, the emotional tone, the sentence structure. It also collected user features: the commenter's personality proxies (inferred from their writing), their engagement level, their tone. Then it trained a graph neural network (a type of model good at learning from interconnected data) to predict believability from those signals, encoding both the linguistic features and user features as edge properties in a social graph.
875.ww: Why does this work? Because people's judgment of credibility depends on both the text and who's saying it. A claim about politics written by someone with a history of political engagement feels more credible than the same claim from someone who rarely engages. And certain linguistic patterns—mixing emotional and contradictory cues (what the paper calls "ambivalence")—are correlated with deception. By modeling both together in a graph, the system captures how credibility is a product of both message and messenger.
875.po: The concrete payoff: misinformation detection improves when you model human credibility judgments alongside linguistic signals. The paper shows that incorporating believability signals as features improves detection substantially over text-only systems. The deeper payoff is insight: the paper reveals domain-specific linguistic markers—politics uses emotion-cognition tension, entertainment uses sentiment mixing—suggesting that deception has recognizable patterns.

876.bp: When you click an ad on your phone or see a product recommendation, a system somewhere predicted whether you'd click on it. That's click-through rate (CTR) prediction. For advertisers and e-commerce sites, even a 1% improvement in accuracy translates to millions of dollars in revenue. CTR prediction relies on learning patterns in user behavior from past clicks. The challenge: as data grows, how do you build models that efficiently capture many different kinds of click patterns at once?
876.wh: Modern CTR systems use parallel architectures—imagine multiple parallel pipelines, each specialized for a different kind of pattern. One pipeline might capture gender-based patterns, another price-sensitive patterns, another seasonal patterns. But there are two problems. First, all pipelines typically start with the same base features (mathematical descriptions of user history, item features, etc.), so they're not truly specialized—they see the same input, so they can't learn truly different signals. Second, as you stack more layers (attempting to capture complex, multi-way patterns between features), each layer can introduce errors that propagate downstream, degrading the final prediction.
876.ap: DGNet (Decoupled Gated Network) solves this in two parts. First, a Decoupled Embedding Generator creates pipeline-specific versions of each input feature. Instead of all pipelines using the same representation of "user age," the generator creates a version optimized for the gender-pattern pipeline, another for the price-pattern pipeline, etc. Second, a Gated Fusion Module dynamically picks out the most useful signal from each layer of each pipeline before it propagates to the next layer. It's like a filter: "Layer 1 of the price-pipeline has learned a useful signal, but layer 1 of the gender-pipeline is just amplifying noise, so reduce its contribution going forward.
876.ww: Decoupling embeddings means each pipeline can learn the signal it's specialized for without interference from other pipelines' noise. The gating mechanism prevents error accumulation: instead of letting all signals propagate unchanged through layers, it learns to dampen weak or noisy signals and amplify clean ones. This is especially important for CTR prediction, where the majority of instances are non-clicks (you don't click 99% of ads), so noise can easily dominate the signal.
876.po: The result: DGNet consistently improves the performance of existing parallel CTR models, statistically significantly, with the same basic architecture. This is valuable because it's "model-agnostic"—you can add it to systems already deployed. The concrete payoff for advertising and e-commerce: better click prediction means better ad placement and more relevant recommendations, which improves user experience and platform revenue.

877.bp: Large language models like ChatGPT and PaLM are trained on huge amounts of text scraped from the internet. But the internet isn't neutral; it's written by humans with opinions, biases, and blind spots. This paper asks a straightforward question: Does the internet text reflect political bias, and if so, does that bias leak into the language models trained on it? Understanding this is crucial because biased models can mislead users or reinforce false beliefs at scale.
877.wh: Most studies of bias in language models look at the model's outputs directly ("Does it generate left-leaning or right-leaning text?"). But that's after-the-fact diagnosis. The harder, more fundamental question is whether the bias *originates* in the training data. Few studies have done large-scale analysis of political bias in web text itself. The C4 corpus is a 700 billion token dataset of web text used to train T5, PaLM, and LaMDA—flagship models. If the corpus is biased, those models probably are too. But proving that requires carefully annotating thousands of pages for political stance and running statistical tests to rule out random variation.
877.ap: The paper analyzed 15 politically sensitive topics (gender equality, LGBTQ rights, abortion, economic policy, etc.) in the C4 corpus. They used an LLM itself to annotate each page from multiple political perspectives ("How would a progressive person evaluate this?" "A libertarian?"), then validated those annotations with rigorous statistical tests (equivalence testing, multiple testing correction, so false positives are ruled out). They also ran experiments correlating corpus-level bias with the output of models trained on that corpus, and tested whether fine-tuning could reduce the model's bias.
877.ww: The mechanism is straightforward: if text A contains more left-leaning content than text B, a language model trained on A will statistically predict left-leaning next-tokens more often. The LLM doesn't have values; it's just learned from the data distribution. So corpus bias flows directly into model behavior. The paper provides evidence for this by showing correlations between corpus-level bias and model output bias.
877.po: The paper reveals clear patterns: the C4 corpus has left-leaning, supportive bias on social and cultural topics (gender equality, LGBTQ, abortion) while economic topics are more balanced. This bias propagates into models. The concrete payoff is twofold: (1) awareness that major language models carry these biases, and (2) empirical evidence that the root cause is the training data, not the model architecture, which opens the door to better data curation or filtering as a mitigation strategy.

878.bp: When you search for something, your initial query is often vague or incomplete. "Machine learning libraries" is better than "ML," but even better would be "Python machine learning libraries for computer vision that are easy to learn." Query expansion fixes this: instead of searching for your exact words, the system supplements your query with related concepts, so it retrieves documents you actually need, not just documents with your keywords. The challenge is making that expansion rich and diverse, not narrow and repetitive.
878.wh: Recent systems use large language models to do query expansion: you give an LLM your query and it generates pseudo-documents (made-up content that's relevant to the query). Those are added to the search. But LLMs tend to stay in a narrow lane. They generate content that's closely similar to the original query, missing the broader context or diverse angles that a human might consider. For example, expanding "climate change solutions" might generate many documents about carbon taxes, missing renewable energy, afforestation, and industrial processes. The expansion lacks breadth.
878.ap: AMD (Agent-Mediated Dialogic Framework) uses three specialized agents working together like a conversation. First, a Socratic Questioning Agent rephrases the initial query into three sub-questions, each inspired by a different angle (e.g., historical, technical, societal). For "climate solutions," it might ask "What are the historical approaches?", "What new technologies exist?", "What policy frameworks work?". Second, a Dialogic Answering Agent generates pseudo-answers to each sub-question, enriching the query with multiple perspectives. Third, a Reflective Feedback Agent evaluates which pseudo-answers are actually good and filters out the noisy ones. The three agents together refine the expansion iteratively.
878.ww: Why does this work? Multi-agent dialogue is inherently diverse. Each agent has a different role, so they push on the query from different angles. The Socratic dimension ensures breadth—it forces the system to think historically, technically, and societally, for instance. The feedback step acts as a quality gate, removing expansions that aren't coherent or relevant, keeping only the high-confidence additions. This is richer and more diverse than a single LLM making one pass.
878.po: Experiments on standard benchmarks (BEIR, TREC) show AMD expands queries better than prior LLM-based methods. The concrete payoff: when a user searches for something, the system retrieves more relevant documents because the query expansion is broader and more thoughtful, leading to better search results across the board.

879.bp: This is a vision statement rather than a research paper. The author is asking: what comes next after traditional recommendation and search systems? Foundation models (large, multimodal models that understand images, video, audio, and text) are now powerful enough to do more than spit out ranked lists. They can reason, understand context, and explain their reasoning. What if we combined that into a single personal assistant that discovers information, recommends, and helps you learn?
879.wh: The old systems (2000s-2010s) were specialized: a recommender system for products, a search engine for documents, a decision-support tool for analysis. Each solved one narrow problem. Now, foundation models can do many things at once. But the gap is in *personalization* and *alignment*: how do you make a single model that understands your preferences, your goals, your context, and your values? How do you ensure it reasons correctly and doesn't hallucinate? That's the unsolved problem.
879.ap: The paper sketches three trends to watch. First, moving from specialized systems to a single multimodal model that can see images, hear audio, watch video, and reason about all of it together. Second, fundamental research on *how to personalize* these models—how to make them genuinely adapt to individual users, not just serve generic recommendations. Third, combining "System 1" (fast, intuitive, pattern-based thinking) and "System 2" (slow, deliberate, reasoning-based thinking) into a single assistant that can both quickly recognize patterns and carefully reason through hard problems.
879.ww: The reasoning: current systems are fragmented (search vs. recommender vs. decision support), which creates friction. A truly universal assistant would integrate all three. By combining multimodal understanding with reasoning and personalization, you'd get a system that feels more like talking to a knowledgeable friend, not a machine serving ranked lists.
879.po: This is a research agenda, not a concrete product, but the payoff the author envisions is clear: a single AI assistant that can discover relevant information, recommend actions, explain reasoning, and adapt to the individual user, across all modalities (text, image, video, audio). This is aspirational and marks a shift in thinking from "build better recommenders" to "build better personal reasoning partners.

880.bp: Citation networks map how research papers reference each other, forming a web of knowledge. Scientists use these networks to trace ideas ("who cited who first?"), find related work, and assess influence. But citation networks are typically sparse in metadata—some papers have rich author affiliation data, some don't; some have keywords, some lack them. Richer metadata would make these networks more useful for discovery and clustering researchers. The question: can language models fill in the gaps?
880.wh: Citation metadata comes from publication metadata databases, but that metadata is incomplete or inconsistent across papers. One paper might list detailed author affiliations and keywords, while another is missing both. Using that incomplete data directly to analyze a citation network gives a distorted picture. You could try to fill gaps manually, but that's slow and expensive for millions of papers. Language models could do it automatically, but they can hallucinate—they might make up plausible-sounding but false information ("John Smith is from MIT" when he's actually from Stanford).
880.ap: The paper proposes using LLMs to generate factual descriptions for sparse metadata fields. For instance, if a paper has an incomplete author biography, the LLM writes a concise factual summary. These descriptions are then encoded into numbers using DeBERTa (another language model, used for compression). Those numerical representations become node features in a heterogeneous citation network—a graph where papers, authors, and venues are all nodes with rich features. To reduce hallucination, the authors used Chain-of-Thought prompting (asking the LLM to "think step-by-step" before generating answers) and evaluated the generated descriptions manually.
880.ww: Why does this help? Rich metadata allows citation networks to capture semantic meaning, not just citations. An author's description tells you what they work on, so you can find related researchers who've never cited each other (but should have). Better features lead to better author classification ("Is this author a machine learning researcher or a biologist?") and author clustering ("Which researchers are in the same field?"). The LLM does the annotation, so it scales to millions of papers.
880.po: Experiments show author classification improves by 2-4.5% and author clustering improves by 8.9-18.1% when using LLM-generated metadata, outperforming traditional hand-crafted features. The concrete payoff: researchers can discover collaborators and related work more effectively using richer, more complete citation networks.

881.bp: When you're asking a conversational AI a question in a multi-turn dialog, you're not just asking it to find a document—you're asking it to retrieve a *structured entity* from a knowledge graph (a database of connected concepts and facts) that's relevant to your context and your previous questions. For instance, if you ask "Which actor played Batman in the 2005 film?" the system needs to retrieve the entity "Christian Bale" from a knowledge graph that connects movies, actors, characters, and years. This is harder than it sounds in a conversational setting.
881.wh: Previous systems for entity retrieval weren't built for conversation. They assumed a single, context-free query. But in conversation, context matters: if you previously asked about "Christopher Nolan films," and now ask "Who directed that Batman movie?", the system should remember that you mean Nolan, not just any Batman movie. Also, knowledge graphs have structure—entities have types, properties, and neighbors. A naive system might only look at whether "Christian Bale" lexically matches your query, and miss the entity entirely if you phrase it differently.
881.ap: The paper introduces QBLink-KG, the first benchmark dataset for Conversational Entity Retrieval from Knowledge Graphs (CER-KG), adapted from conversational reading comprehension data. It then proposes two neural architectures. NACER aggregates lexical and semantic relevance signals from the local neighborhood of candidate entities (nearby entities in the graph). DRAGON (also described in this batch) improves on NACER by using graph convolution and self-attention to model fine-grained relationships across the sub-graph, explicitly accounting for dialog history.
881.ww: The reason structure-aware retrieval works: entities in knowledge graphs are not isolated; they're surrounded by related entities and properties that provide context. By modeling the local graph structure, the system can infer meaning. If "Batman" is connected to "Christian Bale" and "2005," and your dialog mentioned 2005, the system can make the connection. Graph convolution and self-attention let the model learn which neighbors and properties matter for a given query and dialog history.
881.po: The payoff is better conversational entity retrieval. In conversational AI systems—whether voice assistants or text-based chatbots—users can ask follow-up questions, and the system correctly retrieves the right entity from a knowledge graph, taking previous context into account. This feels more natural and less frustrating than systems that ignore context or miss entities.

882.bp: News recommendation systems suggest articles to readers. But text descriptions of news can be exaggerated or biased, which degrades recommendation quality. What if you also had the news image? A picture of a storm is more objective than a headline saying "Catastrophic flooding." This paper asks: can images help debias text, and can a language model learn to extract factual knowledge from text by being trained on text+image pairs, then later use just the text alone?
882.wh: Text-only news recommendation relies on extracting key facts from article text. But article text is often editorialized: "The devastating policy cut benefits" vs. the more neutral "Policy X reduced benefits by Y amount." A standard text processor can't easily separate fact from opinion. Images are harder to bias than words—a photograph of something happened, while words can spin it. But images aren't always available. The gap: can you use image+text pairs to teach a model to extract unbiased facts, then compress that knowledge into a text-only model so it works even when no image is available?
882.ap: IGKnow (Image-Guided Knowledge distillation framework) uses a large multimodal language model (one that reads both text and images) to extract factual triples (subject-relationship-object facts, like "Policy X reduced benefits by 5%") from articles that have both text and images. This multimodal model serves as a teacher. The factual triples are grounded in visual information, so they're less likely to be biased. Then, a text-only model is trained to reproduce those triples using only the article text. The paper also introduces TriSFT, a special training technique that makes the model robust to different orderings of facts (so it learns the facts, not their order).
882.ww: Why does this work? Multimodal learning acts as a debiasing signal. If text says "devastating" but the image shows moderate damage, the image ground truth wins. By extracting triples from this grounded source, you get cleaner facts. Then, compressing those facts into a text-only model is like asking: "Given only the text, how would you say these facts?" The model learns to focus on language that signals factuality, not emotional language. TriSFT prevents the model from memorizing the *order* of facts, forcing it to learn their meaning.
882.po: The payoff is better news recommendation. When the system uses these debiased, image-grounded facts for ranking articles, recommendations are more objective. Users see articles that match their interests based on actual content, not on emotionally charged language. Experiments in sequential news recommendation (where previous articles influence future suggestions) show that debiased triples improve recommendation quality.

883.bp: This is a workshop proposal, not a research paper. The organizers are hosting a forum to discuss how generative models (like ChatGPT) and large language models are changing recommendation and search systems. The underlying premise: these systems used to be built with traditional machine learning techniques (neural networks trained to predict clicks, ratings, etc.). Now, foundation models and generative systems have arrived, and the field needs to rethink everything.
883.wh: The old paradigm: build a model to predict the next item a user will click/buy. The new paradigm: generate personalized text, images, or recommendations on-the-fly using a foundation model. But there's a gap in the research community: academics are publishing in generative modeling, but only some of that research speaks directly to recommendation and search. Meanwhile, industry is rapidly deploying generative systems for recommendations. The workshop bridges that gap by bringing both communities together.
883.ap: The workshop focuses on the intersection of generative models and recommendation/search. Topics include how language models can be used for recommendation, how to personalize generative systems, how to combine traditional collaborative filtering (learning from user-item interactions) with generative understanding (understanding the meaning of items and users semantically). The event expects over 100 attendees from academia and industry.
883.ww: The reasoning: generative models can do things classical recommenders cannot—they can generate explanations, adapt on-the-fly to new users, understand semantic meaning. But they also have new risks (hallucination, bias, slower inference). The workshop exists to answer: what's the right way to combine classical and generative approaches for recommendation?
883.po: The payoff is a shared understanding across academia and industry about how generative AI is reshaping recommendation systems, and potentially new research directions and collaborations emerging from the cross-pollination of ideas.

884.bp: Many real-world prediction tasks involve regression on tabular data—predicting house prices, user engagement scores, revenue forecasts. These systems are deployed online, where they receive new data constantly. The problem: the distribution of incoming data can shift over time (a recession changes user behavior, a new competitor enters the market, a trend changes). A model trained on old data might perform terribly on new data. This paper asks: how do you adapt a regression model at inference time, without retraining, when the data distribution shifts?
884.wh: Existing approaches for handling distribution shift assume you know what the new distribution looks like, or that you can afford to retrain the model. But online systems don't have that luxury. You can't stop serving predictions while retraining. Also, in regression, a common challenge is data imbalance in the target: lots of easy predictions (predicting a price for a common item) and few hard predictions (predicting a price for a rare item). When distribution shifts *and* you have imbalance, the rare cases become even rarer in the new distribution, and the model falters.
884.ap: The paper proposes a two-part approach. First, a Region-Aware Mixture of Experts: use a Gaussian Mixture Model (a statistical technique) to identify distinct clusters or regions in the data. Train separate expert sub-models, each specialized to one region. Synthesize training data for rare regions so each expert gets enough examples. Second, Test-Time Self-Supervised Expert Aggregation: at inference time, don't use a fixed weighting of experts. Instead, look at each incoming test instance, figure out which region it belongs to, and dynamically upweight the expert trained for that region. This happens without retraining, just by adjusting how you combine expert predictions.
884.ww: Why does this work? By decomposing the problem into regions, each expert can optimize for its own regime. The Gaussian Mixture Model automatically finds where the data naturally clusters. At test time, adjusting expert weights on-the-fly means rare instances get the right specialist, not a model trained mostly on common cases. The self-supervised step uses only the features of the incoming test instance, not labels, so you can adapt without retraining.
884.po: The payoff is better regression performance when deployment distributions shift. For web applications—price prediction, engagement forecasting—this means the system stays accurate even as user behavior or the market changes. Real-world experiments on four datasets show this framework handles imbalanced regression under distribution shift significantly better than fixed models.

885.bp: When heavy rain falls on a city, water pools in low-lying areas and overwhelms drainage systems, flooding streets and damaging homes. To warn residents and dispatch emergency crews in time, we need to predict not just whether it will rain, but where water will actually collect on the ground—which depends on both rainfall and terrain shape, not just weather forecasts.
885.wh: The core tension: traditional physics-based models need perfect terrain and weather data that no city has; data-driven models ignore the geography entirely and just match historical noise.
885.ap: Waterlogformer runs two parallel neural pathways. One learns rainfall patterns over time (how rain grows and shrinks hour to hour). The other combines this with static terrain maps to compute where water naturally collects as it flows downhill. A separate fusion module then joins these two insights, using a learning technique that pushes the model to notice which neighborhoods have similar geography, so it generalizes better to new areas.
885.ww: By explicitly computing water accumulation based on terrain—not just hoping the model discovers it from data—the system builds in a hint about the true physics. This forces the model to align its internal patterns with real water flow, so it can transfer what it learns in one city to another city with similar slope and drainage. The geographic learning step teaches it to treat nearby neighborhoods as similar by construction.
885.po: On a real-world urban dataset, Waterlogformer reduces prediction error compared to methods that ignore terrain or treat water collection as a pure pattern-matching puzzle. This means emergency managers can issue more accurate warnings and position trucks before streets actually flood.

886.bp: When a 911 call comes in, a human operator must stay calm, ask the right questions in sequence, and make split-second decisions about whether an ambulance or police car is needed. Training new call-takers requires them to practice hundreds of scenarios, but live role-play is expensive and constrained by how many emergencies dispatchers can realistically simulate. The goal is to let trainees practice safely and often, learning from each attempt.
886.wh: The tension: we need AI to make the simulation responsive to each decision, but trainees need *real feedback on whether they made good choices*, not just smooth banter.
886.ap: SHIELD is a conversational AI system that generates realistic call scenarios with the AI playing the 911 caller. As a trainee responds, the system tracks exactly what they said, how long they took to respond, and what mistakes they made. After each simulated call, the AI analyzes the trainee's behavior and gives them feedback framed as a coach's insights—not just 'you were wrong,' but 'here's why that question mattered' or 'you spent 40 seconds on something that could have waited.' The feedback is designed to trigger reflection, a key principle in learning: when you think about *why* you did something, you remember the lesson.
886.ww: By logging every decision and response, the system can show trainees patterns they didn't notice themselves (e.g., they always forget to ask about allergies). By framing feedback as guidance, not judgment, trainees feel safe trying new strategies. The AI learns what good call-handling looks like from the training data, so it can spot when a trainee is heading toward a dead end and nudge them back on course.
886.po: Trainees can practice dozens of scenarios without scheduling instructors or actors, and they get personalized feedback on decision-making and timing—something a video-recorded scenario can never provide. Early testing with a real 911 center showed the system can run continuous training at a fraction of the cost of traditional methods.

887.bp: When predicting a number—like house price from its features, or crop yield from soil and weather—trees are simple and interpretable: 'if rain > 20mm, then predict high yield.' But trees rely on binary yes-or-no splits, which force them to ignore nuanced trade-offs. For example, a house might be worthwhile at a medium price *or* if it has a pool, but a binary tree struggles to capture this 'either/or' logic naturally, so it makes crude approximations and gets the prediction wrong.
887.wh: The core problem: multi-branch trees are more expressive, but the search space is too vast, and existing methods produce nonsensical rules that overfit to noise.
887.ap: GraphBeam-LLM replaces trees with directed acyclic graphs (DAGs)—a data structure where each decision point can branch into multiple paths, and paths can rejoin. Instead of searching randomly, the system uses beam search: at each step, it keeps only the most promising candidates and builds on those. Crucially, when generating new rules, it asks a large language model: 'what would be a sensible condition to split on here?' rather than trying random thresholds. The LLM generates conditions that sound meaningful (e.g., 'price per square foot > median for neighborhood').
887.ww: The LLM acts as a semantic filter—it steers the search toward human-understandable rules by design. Beam search ensures efficiency by focusing computational effort on promising branches rather than exploring dead ends. The graph structure itself is more powerful than trees because it allows data to flow along multiple paths and merge, capturing complex interactions between features more naturally.
887.po: On regression benchmarks (predicting abalone age, wine quality, cholesterol levels), GraphBeam-LLM reduces prediction error by 6.7% to 14.5% compared to standard tree methods. Crucially, the resulting rules are interpretable—a data scientist can explain why the model made a prediction—because the LLM ensures rules make business sense.

888.bp: Across Europe, thousands of community food-sharing projects (swap events, food banks, community gardens) operate quietly in neighborhoods, but city planners, social researchers, and community organizers have no systematic map of where they are or what they do. Building such a map would help cities understand their informal food systems and support grassroots efforts. The challenge is that these initiatives exist scattered across websites, social media, and local news—no central directory.
888.wh: The tension: we need to find these initiatives automatically across many languages and websites, but the web is a noisy, multilingual maze where genuine initiatives look similar to spam or irrelevant noise.
888.ap: The CULTIVATE system chains three automated steps. First, it translates a search query (e.g., 'community food garden') into multilingual variants using an LLM, then uses these to find candidate webpages. Second, it re-ranks and filters the results by asking the LLM to classify each page: 'Is this a genuine food-sharing initiative, or spam, or outdated?' Third, human experts manually verify the machine's classifications to catch false positives and fix errors. Then the system is scheduled to re-crawl these sites periodically to notice when projects close or new ones start. The frontend is an interactive map where users can explore these initiatives by location and type.
888.ww: By using an LLM to understand language and content semantics before classification, the system avoids brittle keyword matching. By building in human verification, it ensures quality without requiring experts to find all the initiatives manually. By re-crawling, it keeps the map current instead of becoming stale.
888.po: The SHARECITY 200 database now maps food-sharing initiatives across 200 European cities, making invisible grassroots work visible. Users can search by city and type (food bank, garden, share event, etc.), and researchers can now analyze patterns in urban food resilience. The architecture generalizes—the same pipeline works for any domain where initiatives are scattered across websites (tool libraries, repair cafes, maker spaces, etc.).

889.bp: Large language models power chatbots, code generators, and medical diagnosis assistants, but when they give an answer, how do we know if it's right? When a model predicts a medical diagnosis, we need to understand *why*—not just trust it. Explainability is the ability to tell a human what the model was thinking. Without it, we can't fix the model when it fails, and we can't trust it in high-stakes decisions.
889.wh: The core problem: models are so complex that any single explanation is almost certainly incomplete, and the easiest explanations to generate are often lies.
889.ap: This tutorial argues for a different approach: instead of trying to fully explain *how* the model works internally—which is theoretically impossible for very large models—we should focus on what a human *needs to know* to trust or use the model effectively. This means identifying high-level concepts the model responds to (e.g., 'sentiment,' 'factuality,' 'expertise'), showing how input changes affect those concepts, and allowing humans to edit the model's behavior by modifying concepts they care about, rather than tweaking weights they don't understand.
889.ww: This approach is practical because it stops chasing an impossible ideal (perfect transparency) and instead solves the real problem: humans need to understand if the model is safe and reliable enough for their decision. By focusing on interpretable concepts, we give humans something they can actually verify and act on. By allowing inference-time intervention (e.g., 'tone down speculation'), we let humans steer the model without retraining it.
889.po: This reframes explainability from 'show the reasoning' to 'enable human-AI collaboration.' For medical diagnosis, instead of asking 'why did the model predict pneumonia?', we ask 'what symptoms is the model weighting heavily, and are those reasonable?' This is something a doctor can actually use to decide whether to trust the diagnosis.

890.bp: When a model is trained on English text, it develops a strong understanding of English concepts and relationships. If we want it to work in Mandarin or Arabic, a naive approach is to just show it examples in those languages and hope it transfers. But language models map words to numerical points in a space, and each language's word cloud is shaped differently—English clusters certain concepts together in ways that don't align with how Mandarin clusters them. So knowledge learned in English often doesn't transfer smoothly, especially when the training data in the low-resource language is small and noisy.
890.wh: Tension: multilingual models need to align concepts across languages (so 'happy' in English connects to '高兴' in Mandarin), but they also need to preserve each language's unique semantic texture and robustness to noise.
890.ap: XLingLearn adjusts how the model builds its numerical representation space. First, it computes how clustered each language's concepts are and deliberately pushes overly similar ones apart—creating more breathing room in the representation space so each semantic distinction stays sharp. Second, it adds a constraint that forces the model to learn the *same directional relationships* across languages (e.g., if 'happy' and 'sad' are opposite directions in English, the same should hold in Mandarin). Third, it stabilizes this shared direction by making sure attention patterns stay consistent across languages. Finally, it includes a debiasing term that corrects for the fact that data augmentation (adding variations of text to train) can warp the representation space in unexpected ways.
890.ww: By actively pushing representations apart rather than letting them collapse, the model preserves semantic granularity. By enforcing directional consistency, it shares *structure* across languages while allowing local differences. The debiasing term prevents augmentation tricks from introducing artifacts that hurt robustness.
890.po: When tested on cross-lingual tasks (predicting if two sentences mean the same thing, or if one entails the other), XLingLearn transfers knowledge from high-resource English to 17 low-resource languages better than prior methods. Crucially, it remains robust even when the low-resource data is noisy or when the model encounters grammatical structures it hasn't seen before—a major practical win for real-world deployments.

891.bp: When a company deploys a large language model to answer customer questions, it faces two separate problems: the model must retrieve the right information from the company's databases and documents (so it doesn't hallucinate), and it must sound like a company representative, not a generic internet chatbot. Generic models are trained on public internet text and represent world knowledge, but they don't know company policies, brand voice, or legal compliance requirements. Companies need LLMs that are both grounded in internal facts and shaped by company culture.
891.wh: The gap: retrieval gives factual accuracy; fine-tuning gives style; but combining them robustly is hard, and the model may still make decisions that contradict company policy or brand values.
891.ap: This talk describes a hybrid approach: selective fine-tuning on high-quality examples of good company responses (so the model learns the style and judgment of experienced employees) combined with context orchestration—carefully structuring what information is retrieved and how it's presented to the model. Context orchestration means treating different types of company data differently: some facts are mandatory (legal compliance, brand values) while others are optional context (relevant documents). The system prioritizes mandatory information so the model always respects company policy, while optional context helps it sound natural.
891.ww: By fine-tuning on expert employee responses, the model learns not just facts but judgment—when to prioritize customer satisfaction versus compliance, for instance. By orchestrating context (deciding what to give the model and in what order), the system ensures critical information is never missed even if retrieval returns a weak set of documents. Together, they build an 'enterprise world model'—a system that acts like a trained employee, not a generic chatbot.
891.po: The result is an LLM that answers customer queries with accuracy (retrieval-grounded), tone (fine-tuned on internal examples), and judgment (orchestrated to prioritize policy). This talk shares the hybrid framework for building such systems at scale, treating fine-tuning and retrieval as complementary rather than competing approaches.

892.bp: Traffic forecasts are crucial for route planning, congestion warnings, and public transit scheduling. Models trained on historical traffic data can predict normal flows well, but real traffic is punctuated by accidents, weather, events, and system failures—anomalies that create sharp spikes or dips that historical patterns can't explain. A model that ignores anomalies will miss the very situations where accurate predictions matter most.
892.wh: Core tension: models trained on real data (including anomalies) learn to average them out; models trained on only 'clean' data won't see real-world anomalies when deployed.
892.ap: The framework runs in two stages. Stage one: an unsupervised anomaly detector learns what normal traffic looks like by training on historical data and learning to reconstruct typical traffic flows. When the reconstruction error is high (the model struggles to explain what it sees), that's flagged as anomalous. Stage two: once anomalies are marked, a second model trained on normal patterns only will now predict the normal component of traffic flow. But to prevent the normal-patterns model from underfitting (learning only crude averages), it uses a memory module—essentially a cache of stored 'typical' traffic scenarios for each location and time—plus a sparsity constraint that encourages it to use few stored patterns per prediction, keeping explanations interpretable. The two pieces of the model (one for spatiotemporal dependencies, one for memory) work together to predict clean traffic.
892.ww: By separating anomaly detection from forecasting, the model can learn each task well. The memory module allows the model to say 'this is traffic pattern #3 that we've seen before in similar conditions,' which is more robust than trying to synthesize a prediction from scratch. The sparsity constraint prevents the model from memorizing every edge case and instead forces it to generalize.
892.po: On real traffic datasets, the model outperforms standard deep learning approaches especially during anomalous conditions—accidents, storms, events. This means navigation apps and traffic centers can issue better warnings and route recommendations when it matters most: during disruptions, not just normal flow.

893.bp: When images contain personally identifiable information—like someone's face, home address visible in a photo, or a child's name written on a shirt—people have a legal right (GDPR, COPPA) to ask platforms to remove it. But simply deleting all images with that person is extreme; the photo might also contain important scenery or other people. The goal is to remove only the specific object (a face, a license plate, a sign) while keeping the rest of the image intact and coherent.
893.wh: The core problem: models don't store objects as discrete, removable units; they're woven throughout the model's representations, so partial removal risks destroying the image or leaving behind recognizable traces.
893.ap: The framework uses scene graphs—structured representations of images that list objects ('person', 'car', 'tree') and their relationships ('person' is 'to the left of' 'car'). When a user requests removal of a specific object (e.g., 'remove that face'), the scene graph is edited to drop that object while keeping its relationships to other objects. The model is then retrained (or fine-tuned) using three unlearning techniques—fine-tuning on modified data, model redaction (surgically removing weights), or combinations—to 'forget' that object. The system validates that the object is actually removed (or made unrecognizable) while the rest of the image stays intact.
893.ww: By using scene graphs, unlearning becomes structured: instead of blindly erasing parts of the model, you edit the semantic description of the scene and retrain on that edited description. This ensures the model learns to generate an image without the object, rather than just deleting it or memorizing an exception. The three unlearning techniques target different layers of the model (early layers, weights, etc.), making the removal robust.
893.po: Users can request removal of specific objects ('remove that person') rather than the whole image, and the result is a realistic image with that object gone—not a blurred hole or a clearly edited artifact. This balances privacy (the object is truly gone) with utility (the rest of the image is preserved), enabling GDPR compliance without destroying valuable data.

894.bp: Machine learning companies train neural networks on massive datasets and sell access to them as services (model-as-a-service platforms). These models are valuable intellectual property, the result of expensive data and computation. But once a model is sold or deployed, the company risks losing control: competitors might reverse-engineer it, or buyers might use it in prohibited ways. Watermarking—embedding a hidden signal that proves ownership—is a practical solution, but traditional approaches require a central authority to verify ownership, which doesn't work in federated learning where many clients collaboratively train a model.
894.wh: Core tension: federated learning avoids central control; watermarking seems to require it. Also, watermarks need to survive multiple attacks without being noticeable to users.
894.ap: FWDV (Federated Watermarking with Distributed Verification) lets each client independently embed a watermark into its local copy of the model. Each client has its own secret key, so it can verify ownership without a central server. The framework also designs the watermark to be robust against fine-tuning, pruning, and distillation by embedding it in patterns that are hard to remove without destroying model accuracy. The watermark is hidden (it only triggers on a specific input sequence that only the owner knows), so it doesn't degrade user-facing performance.
894.ww: By distributing verification to each client, the system avoids a central bottleneck. By designing the watermark to survive pruning and fine-tuning (it's embedded in multiplicative patterns across many weights rather than isolated regions), removal becomes more costly than retraining from scratch. The hidden nature of the watermark ensures no legitimate user notices it.
894.po: On federated learning benchmarks, FWDV successfully embeds and verifies watermarks with minimal impact on model accuracy, and the watermark survives fine-tuning, pruning, and distillation attacks—making it practical for protecting collaborative models where no single party controls the system.

895.bp: City planners need to decide where to build new roads, widen existing ones, or redesign intersections to reduce congestion and improve emergency response times. The stakes are high: building a road costs millions and disrupts neighborhoods, so planners want confidence the design will actually work. Traffic simulation lets them test layouts in software before construction, but finding the optimal layout among billions of possibilities is intractable—even testing 1,000 layouts requires thousands of CPU-hours.
895.wh: Tension: realistic simulation is accurate but slow; fast search methods are crude. We need a way to search intelligently without evaluating every candidate.
895.ap: The framework uses diffusion models, a neural architecture that learns to generate new candidates by gradually adding realistic-looking details to noise. First, the system collects a dataset of randomly generated layouts and simulates each one, recording which layouts perform well (low congestion) and which perform poorly. Then, a diffusion model is trained to recognize patterns in good layouts—it learns to generate realistic, performance-aware layouts by iterating a process that gradually improves a random layout. A second neural model (a performance predictor) learns to estimate how well a given layout will perform without running the full simulation. Together, they form a search loop: generate candidates with the diffusion model, quickly rank them with the predictor, and occasionally run full simulations on the most promising ones to refine predictions.
895.ww: Diffusion models are recent neural architectures designed to generate high-quality samples; they're strong at learning the structure of good layouts from examples. The performance predictor acts as a fast proxy for simulation, allowing the search to evaluate thousands of candidates cheaply and only invest simulation time on promising ones. This dramatically reduces total computation while keeping quality high.
895.po: The system finds traffic layouts that reduce congestion and improve emergency routing—measured in the simulator—with orders of magnitude fewer simulations than brute force or genetic algorithms would require. The layouts are also more interpretable than those from pure search: because the diffusion model learns from real data, it generates layouts that obey real-world constraints without being explicitly programmed.

896.bp: Short-form video platforms (TikTok, Instagram Reels, YouTube Shorts) are flooded with content every second, and algorithmic recommendation systems decide what billions of people watch. Creators sometimes manipulate the algorithm by hiding text or audio in videos to trigger specific recommendations, or by stealing others' viral videos and reposting them with minor edits, hoping to capture engagement metrics. Detecting these manipulations at scale is crucial to maintain trust in the platform and fairly reward genuine creators.
896.wh: Core problem: we need to detect fine-grained manipulation (hidden text, slight color shifts, cloned audio) at massive scale, but general-purpose multimodal models are slow, prone to hallucination, and vulnerable to adversarial tricks.
896.ap: The system decomposes video understanding into three specialized roles, each optimized for one task. A Perceiver Agent examines the video in detail and extracts raw signals (text it can read, audio transcripts, objects detected, pixel-level anomalies). A Retriever Agent uses the signals to search for similar videos in a database—if the current video is highly similar to an old viral video, that's a red flag for theft. A Reviewer Agent (a high-capability reasoning model) takes the evidence from the Perceiver and Retriever and makes a final call on whether the video is original or manipulative. The system further optimizes scale by caching semantic representations of old videos (so retrieval is fast), filtering out obvious negatives early, and measuring token usage to avoid expensive computations on videos that are clearly clean.
896.ww: By decomposing the task, each agent can be optimized independently and scaled differently: the Perceiver runs on all videos, the Retriever only on suspicious ones, and the Reviewer only on difficult cases. Caching and filtering dramatically reduce compute. The appeal to retrieval ("have we seen this video before?") is powerful because content theft leaves statistical fingerprints that are hard to dodge.
896.po: The system can detect modality misalignment (hidden overlays designed to manipulate recommendations) and content theft (reposted videos) across billions of short-form videos without the compute cost or hallucination risk of running large models on everything. Creators are protected from theft, the algorithm stays honest, and the platform can scale detection.

897.bp: When recommending apps to a new user who has never used the platform before, the system has very little information—maybe just their device model or app category preferences. This is the cold-start problem: without a history of installs and ratings, generic methods (popularity rankings, category-based rules) perform poorly. New users want personalized recommendations, not just 'most popular apps.' But personalization requires understanding the user, which history provides.
897.wh: Tension: attribute features (simple, available for new users) and behavioral sequences (rich, absent for cold-start users) have fundamentally different statistics and learning needs, so learning them together in a single model hurts cold-start performance.
897.ap: AFIM decouples learning of attributes and behavioral sequences by running them through separate pathways before combining them. Attributes flow through one lightweight module; behaviors flow through a specialized attention mechanism designed to extract user interest from sequential patterns. These separate representations are then combined in a fusion layer that decides how much to trust each source—for cold-start users, it learns to rely more on attributes because behavior data is sparse. The decoupling also includes a dynamic fusion mechanism that learns how to blend the two sources differently for different users.
897.ww: By separating the learning process, each feature type can be optimized for its own statistics and learning complexity.
