For cold-start users, the system naturally learns to emphasize attributes because behaviors are unavailable. The attention mechanism on behaviors ensures that rich sequential patterns (e.g., a user installing photo apps in sequence) are captured accurately, not diluted by simpler attribute signals.
897.po: On public and industrial datasets, AFIM significantly outperforms prior methods at recommending apps to cold-start users while remaining competitive for warm users. This means new users get better personalized recommendations faster, improving retention and engagement from day one.

898.bp: Large language models are exceptional at generating fluent text, but recommender systems have traditionally relied on ID-based collaborative signals—'users who liked this also liked that'—which the LLM has no access to. Recent work tries to blend the LLM's broad knowledge (understanding what a movie is about, who might enjoy it) with collaborative data (what actual users rated highly). But combining these requires being careful: merge them poorly, and the LLM's knowledge drowns out the collaborative signal, or the collaborative signal introduces noise that confuses the LLM.
898.wh: Core tension: we want both the LLM's nuanced understanding and the collaborative data's ground truth, but they have incommensurable statistics.
898.ap: HDRec uses two separate low-rank adaptation (LoRA) modules, each fine-tuning the shared LLM for one semantic source. Low-rank adaptation is a parameter-efficient method for customization: rather than retraining the entire LLM, you train a small set of parameters that reshape the LLM's behavior for your specific task. One LoRA adapts the LLM to handle collaborative ID signals; the other adapts it for text semantics. During inference (when making recommendations), the system uses text as the primary signal (it's robust) and adaptively blends in collaborative insights from the ID LoRA only if they strengthen the prediction. To prevent the two LoRAs from conflicting during training, the system alternates training between them, ensuring neither dominates.
898.ww: By using separate LoRAs, each can specialize in its own semantic source without interference. Using text as primary ensures robustness; selective blending ensures collaborative signals help when useful but don't introduce noise. Alternating training prevents the gradient conflicts that occur when two objectives pull the model in different directions.
898.po: On sequential recommendation benchmarks, HDRec outperforms both traditional collaborative filtering and pure LLM-based methods. It combines the LLM's ability to reason about item properties with the historical accuracy of collaborative signals, enabling better recommendations while remaining interpretable.

899.bp: Searching for information in one language is standard—you type a query in English and get English results. But the web is multilingual: a Spanish document about climate change may be exactly what an English speaker needs, but typical search engines return no results because the query and document are in different languages. Retrieval-augmented generation (augmenting LLM answers with retrieved documents) is becoming standard in AI systems, but if you only retrieve documents in the user's query language, you miss half the web's knowledge.
899.wh: Tension: traditional retrieval methods (word overlap) fail across languages; neural methods need multilingual training data that's limited.
899.ap: This WSDM Cup competition challenges participants to build systems that search a multilingual document collection using English queries. The task is straightforward but reveals real challenges: retrieve relevant documents in any language, given queries in English. Participants can use translation, multilingual embeddings, or hybrid approaches, and will be evaluated on how accurately they find relevant documents regardless of language.
899.ww: By making multilingual retrieval a competition goal, the workshop surfaces practical challenges in cross-lingual search. Because the application is LLM-augmented generation (the LLM can post-process documents into the user's language), the system doesn't need to return same-language documents—it needs to return relevant ones, which LLMs can then present to the user in a readable form. This shifts the incentive from same-language matching to relevance, simplifying the problem.
899.po: Winning systems will demonstrate effective multilingual retrieval strategies that can power better search and retrieval-augmented generation in a multilingual world. The challenge surfaces state-of-the-art techniques and datasets for bridging languages in information retrieval.

900.bp: When a new user shows up with almost no purchase history, a recommendation system has almost nothing to learn from. The real goal is to quickly suggest items they might like using only a handful of their first interactions, while the system keeps evolving as millions of new users arrive with their own preference patterns.
900.wh: The tension is between two opposing forces: you need a general model that works for anyone (trained on many past users), but you also need to adapt that model to each person's unique tastes. As preferences shift over time and new users continuously arrive, the old general model gets stale; but retraining from scratch wastes everything you learned before.
900.ap: The paper proposes a method that splits the learning into two paths working together. One path preserves the broad patterns of preference across all users (the general model). The other path learns to adjust those patterns for each new user as they arrive and show their preferences over time. When new users arrive in batches, the system replays examples from past batches to prevent the general model from forgetting, while a separate mechanism picks which old examples to replay so they stay relevant.
900.ww: This works because human preferences do have common threads (many people like popular items), but also idiosyncratic differences. By keeping both the shared knowledge and the personalized tweaks separate, the model can adapt quickly to a new person without destroying what works for everyone else. Replaying past examples prevents catastrophic forgetting—the problem where a neural network forgets old lessons when learning new ones.
900.po: The system can now recommend items to brand-new users faster and more accurately as preferences shift over time. The paper shows this approach outperforms methods that either stick rigidly to one general model or methods that learn each user entirely from scratch, by preserving the best of both strategies.

901.bp: Large language models are now being used as agents that can call external tools—search engines, calculators, APIs, databases—to solve real problems. The hard part is teaching the model which tool to use for which situation, especially when the toolset is messy, incomplete, or keeps changing.
901.wh: Real-world training data is a mess: some tools are used way more often than others (long-tail distribution), some specialized tools have almost no examples, some instructions directly contradict available tools, and some examples in the training set are just wrong or partially correct. Standard supervised learning treats all examples equally, but if you learn from bad examples, the model learns bad habits.
901.ap: The paper proposes TOOL-CURE, which uses reinforcement learning—a method where the model learns from rewards instead of direct labels. Instead of treating all training examples the same, they organize examples into easy ones first (foundational skills) then harder ones (edge cases), teaching the model gradually like you'd teach a person. They also add a filter to spot and skip low-quality training examples—ones that look wrong, partially right, or just noisy.
901.ww: Reinforcement learning works here because the model can learn 'what happens if I pick this tool' by seeing real outcomes, rather than blindly copying labeled examples. Curriculum learning (easy-to-hard progression) prevents the model from getting confused by hard cases before it masters the basics. Filtering noisy examples removes misleading signals that would push the model in the wrong direction.
901.po: The model learns to pick the right tool even for specialized, rare cases and adapts when the toolset changes. Testing shows the method handles imbalanced, noisy, and conflicting training data much better than standard supervised learning, and produces more stable training than vanilla reinforcement learning.

902.bp: When earthquakes, protests, or disease outbreaks happen, people post about them online with photos and text. Automatically detecting these real-world events from social media is crucial for emergency response and public safety, but you have to work with whatever messy, unstructured data appears in the wild.
902.wh: The old way required someone to hand-label thousands of posts as 'earthquake' or 'protest'—expensive and impossible to scale to all event types. Also, if you train a model on predefined event categories (say, 10 types), it fails when event type 11 happens in the real world. You can't predict how many event types exist before they occur.
902.ap: The paper proposes a label-free approach: instead of needing labeled examples, they use a large language model to look at raw image-text pairs and automatically enrich them with descriptions. For each post, they ask the model 'what's the event theme, event type, and image details' and construct enriched versions. They then use a two-stream network to learn which posts are related to each other (similar images and text go together) without any hand-crafted labels.
902.ww: This works because posts about the same real-world event naturally share visual and textual patterns even if you've never labeled them before. A language model can reason about events from general knowledge without needing specific training. By learning which things are similar (self-supervised learning), the model naturally groups posts by underlying event, discovering the event types organically instead of guessing them upfront.
902.po: The system can now detect new event types it has never seen before, and it works without requiring expensive hand-labeled datasets. The method handles the dynamic, open-ended nature of social media where new events constantly emerge.

903.bp: Online ads platforms need to predict whether a user will complete a purchase (conversion rate prediction) so they can price ads and rank them. But sales behavior changes wildly during big sales events like Black Friday or 618 Shopping Day—millions of extra buyers, changed habits, completely different patterns.
903.wh: Models trained on normal days fail catastrophically during sales events because the patterns are so different. Retraining from scratch each time wastes months of learning from normal days. The trick is knowing which parts of what you learned still apply (stable patterns everyone follows) versus which parts need to flip for the event (event-specific behavior).
903.ap: The paper proposes a split-brain approach: one part of the model learns stable, event-independent patterns from raw user data. Another part is an event-aware specialist that adjusts predictions for the current situation. They align the stable part across normal days and sale days so the features match up cleanly. They also build a 'gate' mechanism that decides how much to trust the specialist versus the stable part, adapting per user and per prediction.
903.ww: This works because some user behavior is truly universal (people who normally buy often still buy), while other behavior is purely event-dependent (new buyers show up during sales). By splitting the model, you get stable knowledge transfer (the stable part) combined with situational awareness (the specialist). Alignment ensures the model speaks the same language on normal and event days.
903.po: Deployed on a real short-video ad platform during a major sale event, the system improved conversion rate predictions by 7.5% and platform revenue by 4.3%, while barely increasing model size or latency. The approach handles the periodic swings in user behavior that break traditional models.

904.bp: Large e-commerce recommendation systems use multiple separate search models in parallel to get fast, diverse suggestions: one model finds popular items, one finds items similar to what you've bought, one finds trending items, etc. Combining them is efficient, but it risks showing redundant suggestions because some results appear in multiple models.
904.wh: If all the separate models return similar results, showing users every overlap wastes ranking slots. You want new, non-redundant results, but you can't just ask models to avoid previous results—they were designed independently. The naive fix of filtering duplicates is too blunt and loses useful information.
904.ap: The paper proposes focusing on results that only the new model found—samples that didn't appear in previous models. They call this 'incremental' samples. They then build a separate learning system trained to rank and emphasize these incremental samples. A second mechanism ensures these samples also have high real-world value (users will actually interact with them), not just technical uniqueness.
904.ww: This works because redundancy is real waste—if five models all return the same top item, showing it five times doesn't help. By explicitly optimizing for what's new rather than just relevant, you use ranking slots more efficiently. Measuring real exposure probability ensures the model doesn't just pick obscure samples; it picks samples that are both new and valuable.
904.po: Deployed on Taobao's homepage recommendations, the system increased transaction count by 1% just by better balancing novelty and value. It shows that treating multi-model retrieval as an incremental learning problem, rather than just aggregation, improves real business outcomes.

905.bp: A bookstore wants to recommend books: it has a book database but sparse reviews within each store's local inventory. By looking at the main store's reviews (books, ratings) plus a small store's inventory, it might transfer knowledge about which books sell well. But 'popular in the main store' might mean something completely different in a niche store.
905.wh: Naive transfer assumes knowledge from one domain applies to all others—'this book is good' should mean the same everywhere. But it doesn't. A business book might be niche and slow-selling in a used bookstore but hit hard in a corporate setting. Blind transfer can actually make recommendations worse because you're forcing concepts across incompatible contexts.
905.ap: The paper builds a graph where items connect to topics (extracted from book descriptions), and topics connect to words. They then classify each word as 'this word means something specific to one domain,' 'shared across all domains,' or 'universal meaning independent of domain.' Using this graph structure, the model learns item representations that separate out the domain-specific noise from universal signals.
905.ww: This works because language is ambiguous: the word 'novel' means different things in literary fiction versus tech conferences. By explicitly disentangling these meanings, the model can transfer the universal signal ('these topics matter') without importing domain-specific baggage. A word's frequency across domains reveals which bucket it belongs to.
905.po: The system predicts ratings and rankings better across different store types because it avoids negative transfer—learning bad patterns from one domain. It shows that simple transfer fails for recommendations, but careful disentanglement succeeds.

906.bp: In a social network, some people are more influential than others—they know more people, their opinions spread further. 'Katz centrality' is a math way to measure this influence. Computing it exactly requires huge matrix operations that take forever on billion-node networks.
906.wh: The exact formula involves matrix powers that grow exponentially with network size. For large graphs, exact computation is prohibitively expensive—cubic time complexity means trillions of operations. Existing approximation methods exist but don't parallelize well, so they can't harness modern multi-processor computers.
906.ap: The paper proposes two Monte Carlo algorithms—methods that use random sampling instead of exact calculation. The algorithms simulate random walks through the network (imagine dropping a ball on a node and watching it bounce to random neighbors). After many simulated walks, you count how often the ball lands on each node; that count approximates its influence.
906.ww: Random walks converge to the true centrality distribution through the law of large numbers—if you simulate enough walks, the frequency of landing on a node approaches its true importance. Monte Carlo is highly parallelizable because thousands of random walks can run independently on different processors. You trade a little accuracy for massive speed.
906.po: The algorithm runs 100 to 1000 times faster than exact methods while maintaining high accuracy in ranking the most influential nodes. The approach scales to billion-node networks on modern parallel hardware.

907.bp: When you search for shoes on Amazon, you no longer see a simple list—you see a grid of images, filter panels on the side, brand suggestions, price ranges. Ranking these elements matters because layout and visual design shape which items users notice and buy. But old ranking systems assume a vertical list, not this complex 2D layout.
907.wh: Position bias (click-through depends on where an item sits) isn't linear anymore—the top-left corner item and middle item have different effects. Also, companies want long-term happier customers, not just today's clicks. But measuring long-term satisfaction is hard because results take weeks (did this user come back? buy again?), and you can't easily trace which item caused which future behavior.
907.ap: The paper proposes a framework that models how item relevance, 2D position, and visual design all interact. They use causal inference to measure long-term satisfaction from observational data (quasi-experiments: 'when we showed item X in position Y, what happened to users over 14 days'). They then test the full layout-aware model with real A/B testing on live Amazon traffic.
907.ww: This works because the right item in the wrong spot on the page is nearly invisible, while the wrong item in the perfect spot gets clicked. By modeling layout explicitly, you can find the true ranking. Causal inference extracts long-term signals from observational data without waiting months for outcomes, letting you optimize faster.
907.po: The system improved brand relevance (a customer experience metric) by 1.86% and revenue by 0.05% on live e-commerce search. It shows that page layout matters as much as item ranking, and measuring long-term impact unlocks better optimization.

908.bp: Recommendation systems that generate text (like generating a playlist description or explaining why something was recommended) can produce better results with longer user history. But longer history means more computation—slower real-time response, higher server costs, less room for other features.
908.wh: A user's purchase history might have 500 items. Feeding all 500 items into a language model is expensive. You could truncate to the last 50, but then you lose signal about long-term interests. You want to compress without losing meaning.
908.ap: The paper proposes using item categories (which already exist in the database) to compress history. Instead of remembering 'bought phone, bought charger, bought screen protector, bought phone stand,' you remember 'bought 4 phone accessories.' By grouping items by category and summarizing counts, you retain the signal (this person likes phone accessories) in a fraction of the space.
908.ww: This works because the pattern 'bought many phone accessories' captures the user's interest better than each individual item. Item categories are already meaningful human-defined groups, so you're not throwing away information that matters. The model still sees the distribution across categories, which is what drives recommendation.
908.po: The method achieves 6 times faster inference and 39% higher recommendation accuracy at the same computational cost as a longer history baseline. It proves that smart compression using existing metadata (categories) outperforms longer, denser sequences.

909.bp: Imagine you run a network of hospitals and want to estimate: if we give this patient a new treatment, how much will it help? This is hard in a network because patients see each other (information spreads), and which patients get treatment might depend on hidden factors like social connections or unobserved wealth.
909.wh: Networks create two problems: (1) Confounding: unmeasured factors like wealth influence both whether someone gets treatment and their outcome, making it hard to separate treatment effect from those hidden factors. (2) Spillover: if your friend gets treatment, it might affect you (they share advice, reduce disease spread). You can't just look at treated versus untreated; the untreated group is contaminated by spillover.
909.ap: The paper proposes learning three separate latent factors for each person: one that influences treatment assignment (instrumental factor), one that's a confounding variable, and one that adjusts outcomes. They learn these by looking at network structure (friends reveal information patterns), applying reweighting (up-weight people who look like they shouldn't have received treatment but did), and adding regularization constraints that ensure the three factors are actually separate.
909.ww: This works because hidden factors often have distinct roles. Wealth influences both treatment and outcome (confounder), but a doctor's belief in a treatment influences who gets it without directly affecting outcome (instrument). By learning these roles separately with network structure guiding the learning, you can identify which variation is pure treatment effect versus confounding or spillover.
909.po: The method produces better estimates of individual treatment effects in networked settings. Theory guarantees the latent factors are identifiable, and experiments on synthetic and real data show the approach outperforms methods that ignore network structure or hide confounding.

910.bp: Manufacturing plants, power grids, and hospitals collect thousands of sensors continuously (temperature, pressure, voltage)—a multivariate time series. When something breaks, you see anomalies: a sudden temperature spike, an unusual pressure pattern. But detecting anomalies is hard because normal operation has natural variation.
910.wh: Most anomaly detectors are trained to predict all sensor streams simultaneously—if you're forecasting 100 sensors, the model spreads its effort across all 100. But some sensors are more important than others, and the model's error gets diluted across all streams. You want focused detection on the sensors that matter most.
910.ap: The paper proposes focusing anomaly detection on one important sensor at a time. For that target sensor, you use neighboring sensors with similar patterns as additional input features (since they provide context). The model learns to predict only the target sensor, concentrating all its predictive power on that one stream.
910.ww: This works because narrowing focus reduces dilution. When a model must predict 100 things and does each with 10% error, small errors in each multiply into big errors overall. But when predicting one thing carefully, all learning capacity targets that one stream. Neighbor sensors provide context (this machine usually heats up when temperature rises) without added complexity.
910.po: Evaluation on industrial sensor data shows 1.7 to 7.5 times higher anomaly detection accuracy than methods predicting multiple streams. The simple idea of 'one target plus its neighbors' dramatically improves practical anomaly detection.

911.bp: Extracting information from text—finding person names, organizations, event types—requires understanding both the language and how information maps to predefined categories. But every company uses different category definitions. Training a model on one company's categories makes it forget another company's.
911.wh: The 'schema alignment tax' is the cost of learning multiple schemas: if you train a model on both Company A's event types and Company B's different event types, the model often loses ability on both because the definitions conflict. For example, Company A's 'hiring' event differs from Company B's 'promotion' event.
911.ap: The paper proposes separating the task into three phases. Phase 1: The large language model learns to find entity and event spans (the raw information) across all companies' data at once, ignoring categories. Phase 2: The model assigns semantic concepts to each span ('this looks like a hiring event' as a concept, not a category). Phase 3: Small, lightweight models map these concepts to each company's unique schema.
911.ww: This works because finding spans is universal (everyone writes names and events the same way in text), but mapping to categories is company-specific. By separating general ability (span finding and conceptualization) from category mapping, the large model doesn't have to memorize conflicting definitions. Lightweight models easily handle company-specific mappings.
911.po: The method avoids the performance drop that normally happens when training on multiple schemas, and the first two phases are reusable for any new company. It shows that schema-agnostic information extraction outperforms direct schema-dependent approaches.

912.bp: Named entity recognition—identifying names of people, places, organizations in text—requires labeled training data, which is expensive to collect. Self-training is a method where you train on labeled data, then use the model to label more data, then retrain. But the model often makes mistakes on its own unlabeled data, and then learns from its mistakes.
912.wh: Confirmation bias is the core problem: if the model confidently labels something wrong, it reinforces that wrong belief in the next training round. You need a way to filter out high-confidence mistakes before they corrupt the learning process.
912.ap: The paper proposes using a large language model as a judge. After the main model generates predictions on unlabeled data, they prompt the LLM to evaluate whether each prediction looks correct, using prompts that encode task-specific rules (mined from the labeled data). They then blend the main model's confidence with the LLM's judgment, and apply probability smoothing to reduce overconfident predictions.
912.ww: This works because large language models have broad knowledge of entity types and can spot incoherent predictions (e.g., 'the date March 15 is a person name' is obviously wrong). Their judgment breaks confirmation bias. Blending multiple confidence signals and smoothing reduces the risk that any single signal dominates. The prompts built from labeled rules give the LLM task-specific guidance.
912.po: The method outperforms other self-training approaches on multiple named entity recognition benchmarks. It shows that leveraging an LLM's broad knowledge as a filter makes self-training practical and reliable.

913.bp: When you ask a large language model 'What is the capital of France?', a retrieval-augmented system first retrieves relevant documents (Wikipedia article on France), then asks the model to generate an answer using those documents. This is more reliable than pure generation because the model can cite sources.
913.wh: Real-world knowledge comes in many forms: tables (census data), graphs (social networks, knowledge bases), trees (documents with sections), unstructured text. Each form requires different handling—you can't treat a table the same as free text. Also, retrieving wrong information is dangerous in high-stakes settings (medical advice, financial decisions).
913.ap: The paper is a tutorial (not a research paper) that surveys retrieval-augmented systems from a structural perspective. It reviews how different knowledge structures (tables, graphs, text) require different retrieval and generation strategies, covers the full pipeline from indexing through generation, and addresses safety concerns like adversarial retrieval and misuse prevention.
913.ww: This works as a teaching resource because structure matters deeply. A table query needs different retrieval than a text query. A graph requires link traversal. By teaching the structural perspective, practitioners can design retrieval systems appropriate to their data type, rather than treating all external knowledge the same.
913.po: The tutorial provides a unified framework for understanding retrieval-augmented systems across their full lifecycle and different knowledge structures, plus guidance on safety. It helps practitioners choose the right approach for their data type.

914.bp: Matrix deflation is a mathematical technique where you decompose a matrix into layers (rank-1 pieces), subtracting each layer one by one until the matrix is empty. It's useful for image compression, dimensionality reduction, and data analysis. Traditionally, a human decides when to stop (usually when the remaining noise is small enough).
914.wh: Deciding when to stop is arbitrary—thresholds like 'stop when remaining norm is 10% of original' are human guesses. For noisy data, the norm might never reach 10%, or it might hit 10% before extracting the real signal. You need an adaptive decision, not a fixed threshold.
914.ap: The paper proposes an agent-based approach: a large language model generates proposed rank-1 layers (singular value decompositions), and a vision model looks at the intermediate result and decides 'does this layer look meaningful? should we continue?'. The vision model replaces the numeric threshold. They improve the language model's output by permuting rows/columns to expose cleaner visual structure.
914.ww: This works because visual judgment can detect signal without math. A human can look at a partially deflated image and say 'this looks like half of a digit, keep going' or 'this is just noise, stop.' By teaching a vision model to make this judgment, you replace threshold-hunting with learned pattern recognition. In-context learning lets the language model see good examples and refine accordingly.
914.po: On synthetic data where the true rank is known, the agent achieves deflation within 1.75 units of the target. On real image data, it matches traditional numerical results while adapting thresholds dynamically, showing that agentic, threshold-free deflation is viable.

915.bp: Social media memes often spread harmful narratives that inflame conflicts between groups. To counter this, we need systems that can understand what a meme actually means—not just its surface appearance, but the cultural context, satire, and messaging layers embedded in it—so platforms can identify which memes promote real harm versus which are ironic commentary or reclaimed speech.
915.wh: A meme is inherently multimodal: the image, the caption text, and the social context around it all shape meaning. When you try to search for or classify a meme using typical methods, irrelevant but superficially similar memes act as noise—they have matching imagery or keywords but point to the opposite conclusion (satire vs. sincere hateful intent, for example). The challenge is reasoning through that noise while staying grounded in actual evidence (like related articles that clarify what a meme references).
915.ap: The researchers built a system that combines images, captions, and linked documents into a retrieval-augmented approach: you feed the meme to the model, it pulls relevant documents as context, and then uses a special loss function that simultaneously rewards correct answers while penalizing answers that matched misleading distractors. They also built a dataset with intentionally hard confusions—similar but misleading images grouped by difficulty.
915.ww: By pairing the model's reasoning with real evidence documents and explicitly teaching it to ignore semantic red herrings, the system learns the difference between surface-level similarity and actual meaning. The key insight is that the loss function acts like a coach that says: 'Getting the right answer matters, but so does *not getting fooled* by plausible-looking wrong answers.' This mirrors how humans actually evaluate memes—we don't just look at pixels, we check references and context.
915.po: The system improved F1 scores by 7.7 points over baseline retrieval methods, and showed even larger gains (better accuracy) for memes requiring cultural knowledge like satire or mixed media. It degrades gracefully as noise increases, meaning it stays reliable even when faced with adversarial or chaotic data—a practical requirement for real platforms.

916.bp: Machine learning models can now predict the energy and forces inside chemical materials far faster than quantum mechanics simulations, allowing scientists to design new materials and simulate realistic systems that would otherwise be computationally impossible. But these models are trained on tiny systems and evaluated on benchmark datasets—we have no idea if they stay accurate when predicting behavior in large, realistic, complex systems over long time periods.
916.wh: A model trained on small clusters of atoms might work perfectly on the test set but then drift, accumulate errors, or fail when run through a long molecular dynamics simulation (which is like a video of atoms bouncing around). The model also might not generalize across different chemical compositions. Standard validation checks don't catch these failure modes because they only test on static snapshots, not actual dynamical trajectories.
916.ap: The researchers designed a validation protocol that runs the trained model forward in time, simulating a real molecular dynamics trajectory, and tracks prediction errors as the simulation evolves. They also systematically change the chemical composition and monitor whether the model's accuracy changes. This is like taking the model out for a real-world test drive instead of just checking it on a practice exam.
916.ww: By tracking error accumulation along actual dynamical paths, you see whether the model has learned underlying physics or just memorized patterns in static data. A model that drifts over time or breaks down under compositional changes is unreliable for real design work, even if it scores well on benchmarks. This validation exposes those failure modes early.
916.po: For the specific material tested, the model showed consistently low energy errors with no systematic drift and no accuracy loss as composition varied—meaning it's trustworthy for real simulations. This diagnostic complement can be applied to other materials and models, giving practitioners concrete confidence that their ML tool is ready for actual engineering use.

917.bp: When someone asks a complex question that requires piecing together facts from multiple documents—like 'Who won the award that was given to the researcher who developed this technique?'—we need systems that can break down the question, find relevant information step by step, and integrate it into a final answer. This is fundamental to intelligent search and information retrieval.
917.wh: The naive approach is: decompose the question, search for each subquestion independently, and read the answer. But this breaks down because decomposition and retrieval are interdependent. A poor initial retrieval might lead to a bad subquestion, which then retrieves irrelevant information, which leads to a worse subquestion, and so on—cascading failures. Yet if you decompose first without any context, you might decompose in the wrong direction entirely.
917.ap: The system works in rounds with four modules. A Planner generates a subquestion based on what evidence you've found so far. An Evaluator checks whether you have enough information to answer the main question or should keep reasoning. The Retriever fetches documents based on the current subquestion. The Reader extracts an answer from those documents. Then the loop runs again with new subquestions informed by what you've found, until the Evaluator says you're done.
917.ww: By treating decomposition and retrieval as a two-way street, the system corrects its own path: if early evidence is sparse or misleading, the next subquestion adjusts. This mimics how humans actually reason through complex questions—we don't plan the whole path upfront; we explore, learn, and refine. The feedback loop prevents cascading errors because each round has a chance to self-correct.
917.po: The system generalized strongly to unseen datasets without retraining, and performed well across diverse multi-hop question datasets. This suggests the reasoning pattern—iterate between decomposition and retrieval—is a fundamental principle that transfers, rather than a fragile set of memorized patterns.

918.bp: Knowledge graphs grow over time as new facts, entities, and relationships are discovered. A system that understands these graphs needs to remember old facts while learning new ones, and adapt to changing patterns in the data. Real-world knowledge graphs have these three complicating factors: entities connect differently (some are central hubs, others peripheral), new information arrives in bursts or trickles, and there's often imbalance between core knowledge and rare details.
918.wh: Existing lifelong learning methods assume the graph grows in a steady, predictable way. But real graphs don't: a sudden influx of entities (like news breaking) can overwhelm the model, or the model might forget old core facts while chasing novel details. Uneven connectivity means some nodes are natural anchors while others are outliers, and treating them identically leads to poor structural understanding. The model also drifts in how it represents entities across time.
918.ap: The DyGM framework has three layers. First, it uses topological metrics (measures of how nodes connect) to structure the ordering of new knowledge and guide learning from old to new. Second, it replays old examples and distills knowledge from earlier versions of the model to prevent forgetting. Third, it dynamically reweights the importance of old versus new information during training, so the core structure stays stable while peripheral details can flex.
918.ww: By grounding the ordering in graph topology, the system learns how entities naturally relate instead of randomly shuffling them. The replay and distillation prevent catastrophic forgetting—you keep reinforcing what matters. The dynamic weighting prevents the model from either obsessing over novelty or stubbornly clinging to outdated patterns. Together, these layers act like a human expert who remembers the canonical structure while staying open to new discoveries.
918.po: The method was tested on new non-stationary knowledge graph datasets and showed stronger embedding performance than prior lifelong learning methods, with more stable retention of core structural-semantic dependencies. This means the system can handle real, messy knowledge graphs that grow unpredictably.

919.bp: Knowledge graphs—databases of facts structured as entities and relationships—are incomplete by design; new relationships are constantly discovered. We need to predict which new facts will be added. Large language models are good at language reasoning but don't naturally 'see' the graph structure; structural models are good at patterns but don't understand semantics. The real challenge is combining both without one dominating the other.
919.wh: Most LLM-based methods lean heavily on text descriptions of the graph, so they miss structural patterns (like 'entities that frequently co-appear are likely to be related'). Methods that use structural information often can't dynamically adjust based on query context—they treat all entity candidates equally instead of ranking them based on what question you're asking.
919.ap: ST-KGLP does three things. It learns alignments between structural and textual representations, so each modality informs the other. Then it computes query-aware attention weights between the query and each candidate entity—not fixed weights, but weights that shift depending on what relationship you're predicting. This ranking then re-orders the candidate list for the final prediction.
919.ww: Structural patterns (like connection paths) and textual patterns (like semantic similarity in descriptions) are complementary signals—neither alone is enough. By aligning them, the model uses the strength of both. Query-aware weighting ensures that the same entity might be ranked high or low depending on what you're predicting; for example, a node might be a likely target for 'written_by' but unlikely for 'located_in', and the model learns these distinctions dynamically.
919.po: ST-KGLP achieved average improvements of 3.81% to 11.52% across four evaluation metrics over prior state-of-the-art methods. The gains were largest when both structure and text were needed to make accurate predictions, confirming that the combined approach is more powerful than either alone.

920.bp: AI systems that make consequential decisions—healthcare recommendations, hiring tools, customer support—must account for the fact that humans are the ones interpreting outcomes and making choices. If the system recommends something but the human misunderstands it, or if it ignores cultural context, or if it fails to reason about professional norms, it will fail in practice. Building AI that aligns with human values requires understanding how humans communicate and connect.
920.wh: Standard AI training focuses on predicting outcomes from data alone. But humans communicate through language, images, body language, and social connections—and meaning varies across cultures and professions. A system trained on one dataset might generalize to different demographics, languages, or professional contexts poorly. There's no existing benchmark for checking whether an AI 'understands' a human in the full, rich sense.
920.ap: This research develops methods to augment data representations across multiple modalities (text, images, behavior) to capture the full breadth of human expression. It also builds graph-based representations of how humans and information connect (social networks, semantic networks). Finally, it creates evaluation frameworks that explicitly test reasoning consistency across different cultural, linguistic, and professional groups.
920.ww: Human alignment happens when the AI can 'see' the full context: what someone said, how they said it, who they're connected to, what their professional role is. By augmenting representations to include all these layers and testing across diverse contexts, the system learns to adapt rather than assume one-size-fits-all responses. This mirrors how humans themselves achieve trust across cultural differences—by actually paying attention to communication style and context.
920.po: The work provides practical frameworks for evaluating whether AI systems can reason consistently across diverse human contexts, which is essential for deploying trustworthy systems in real organizations with varied user bases and high-stakes outcomes.

921.bp: E-commerce and advertising platforms want to predict whether a user will complete a purchase after clicking on a product (conversion rate). This is the final funnel step—it's the most valuable prediction because it predicts real revenue. The challenge is that you only have clear labels for people who clicked; for everyone else, you don't know if they would have converted or just never saw the ad.
921.wh: This creates a fundamental asymmetry: to predict conversions, you're trained only on people who clicked (clicked-then-converted or clicked-then-didn't-convert). But at serving time, you predict conversion rate for everyone who sees an ad, whether they clicked or not. The model is trained on a selected subset but applied to the full population—this is called sample selection bias. Additionally, among non-converters, some didn't click (unknown whether they would convert) and some clicked but didn't convert (definite non-converters). Treating these the same is a mistake.
921.ap: ChorusCVR introduces a Negative sample Discrimination Module that learns to assign different confidence scores to non-clickers versus click-but-non-converters. It also uses multiple learning objectives across the full exposed population (not just clickers), which shifts the training distribution toward what the model will actually see at serving time. The system treats factual negatives differently from ambiguous negatives, giving them different learning signals.
921.ww: By explicitly distinguishing between 'we know this person didn't convert' (clicked but didn't) and 'we don't know if this person would convert' (never clicked), the model learns more reliable conversion patterns. The click-but-non-convert group is informative; ignoring it is throwing away signal. Training on the full population (entire exposed space) also reduces the train-serve gap: the model learns patterns on the same distribution it will later encounter.
921.po: ChorusCVR achieved more robust conversion rate predictions with better sample-selection bias handling than prior methods that also aimed to use the full population. The discrimination between negative sample types made the model more reliable across different business contexts.

922.bp: When recommending financial investments (stocks, funds, bonds), a recommendation system faces a genuine conflict: users want returns, but returns without diversification lead to losses when markets shift. A personalized recommendation should balance what the user will actually adopt with what actually makes money. The system needs to respect user risk tolerance and diversification goals, not just push high-return assets.
922.wh: Standard recommender systems optimize for relevance (does the user like this item?) or for a single objective (maximize returns). But financial recommendations require multi-objective reasoning: a high-return stock might have high volatility, making it wrong for a conservative investor. Additionally, adoption likelihood varies—users are more likely to act on recommendations they find credible. Trying to optimize both adoption and outcome quality creates tradeoffs that simple ranking can't resolve.
922.ap: RURA is a re-ranking module that takes the top candidates from a recommender system and optimizes for a user-specific expected-utility function (a mathematical combination of expected return and risk tolerance). It includes adoption probability in the calculation—not just 'is this high-return?' but 'will this user adopt it and will it actually work for them?' A tunable hyperparameter controls how aggressively the system pursues diversification without destroying the upstream ranking order.
922.ww: Expected utility combines return with risk in a principled way that respects how different people value tradeoffs—a conservative investor shouldn't get the same recommendation as an aggressive one, even if both have the same wealth. By factoring in adoption probability, the system avoids recommending brilliant investments no one will follow. The re-ranking approach keeps the module lightweight; it plugs into existing systems without retraining.
922.po: RURA improved return-on-investment (ROI) over risk-aware baselines while maintaining ranking quality (nDCG) within acceptable ranges. It delivered higher expected utility across different risk groups, meaning users with different risk tolerances all received better-calibrated recommendations.

923.bp: Graph neural networks (deep learning on graph-structured data like social networks, knowledge bases, or molecular structures) achieve strong performance but are 'black boxes'—you can't tell why they made a decision. This matters for high-stakes domains like healthcare, finance, and hiring. We need explanations that help data scientists debug models and let non-technical stakeholders understand and challenge the system.
923.wh: Early explanation methods (GNNExplainer, etc.) show which nodes or edges matter for a single prediction, but they're limited: they only explain one layer of reasoning, they focus on narrow tasks (node classification), they can't be queried or refined dynamically, and a data scientist can't trace where exactly in the model an error crept in. Real debugging needs to know whether layer 2 or layer 5 is responsible for a mistake.
923.ap: GNN Explainers 2.0 extends beyond point explanations to provide multi-faceted, layer-wise provenance—tracing how a data point transforms through each layer of the network and where it diverges from correct behavior. It also makes explanations queryable and configurable: you can ask 'what if this node had different features?' or 'show me analogous patterns,' and the system provides answers structured as relational queries or counterfactuals. Non-technical stakeholders get explanations in familiar formats (comparisons, structured queries, narratives).
923.ww: Layer-wise provenance reveals where errors originate—essential for fixing bugs instead of just reporting accuracy. Queryable explanations let stakeholders ask follow-up questions rather than passively receiving one explanation. Multimodal explanation (relational, counterfactual, narrative) accommodates different expertise levels and question types. This mimics how real expert explanation works: you explain the reasoning step-by-step and answer questions as they arise.
923.po: GNN Explainers 2.0 addresses practical needs for both technical debugging and non-technical accountability, extending the utility of GNNs from accuracy-focused tasks into domains requiring explainability as a core requirement.

924.bp: A user who has interacted with items in one domain (e.g., books in a library) might want recommendations in a new domain (e.g., movies), but the system has no history of their movie preferences. This cold-start cross-domain problem is common and important: platforms often want to leverage past behavior to bootstrap new domains rather than starting from scratch.
924.wh: Naive transfer learning requires expensive computation—either learning a full model on the source domain then fine-tuning on the target, or running complex multi-step adaptation. These approaches don't scale well to platforms with many domains. Additionally, user preferences across domains aren't always similar; a book lover might not like a film adaptation of the same story, so blind transfer fails. We need a lightweight method that's both scalable and respects domain differences.
924.ap: SimTranGCN constructs a similarity matrix between source and target domains (how similar are items across domains) and uses this matrix to infer what the user would like in the target domain based on their source-domain preferences. It combines this with graph convolutional learning (understanding the item network structure in both domains) and KNN-style similarity measures. The approach is computationally light because the similarity matrix is pre-computed and reused.
924.ww: Item similarity across domains provides a bridge: if a user liked books in the sci-fi genre, they're likely to engage with sci-fi movies, even if the book and movie preferences diverge otherwise. Graph convolutions capture the structure (how items relate to each other), while similarity matrices transfer specific preferences. This is more efficient than learning full transfer models because you're not retraining anything; you're using pre-computed similarities as a lookup table.
924.po: SimTranGCN achieved state-of-the-art performance on two paired domain transfer tasks, outcompeting methods that required more computation. The lightweight approach made it practical for real recommender systems while handling the cold-start problem effectively.

925.bp: Recommender systems usually track what users have browsed and clicked on, but they miss a rich signal: what users actually search for. Search queries reveal intent directly—if someone searches for 'running shoes for flat feet,' they're signaling a specific need. By combining this search signal with browsing history, recommendations should get more precise and help users discover items they didn't know to search for.
925.wh: Sequential recommendation (predicting the next item a user will interact with) typically relies only on browsing history or clicks, which are passive signals. Search queries are explicit intent signals but are usually siloed in a separate search engine. Combining them is non-trivial because the two systems have different vocabularies and user interaction patterns (search is direct and specific; browsing is exploratory). Also, not all users search, so the approach must handle missing search data.
925.ap: The system builds a generative model that learns to predict what users will search for next, using both their browsing history and past search queries. This predicted search intent is then fed into a sequential recommendation system using a query expansion approach—similar to how search engines broaden queries to find related results. The combination of predicted intent and browsing history together makes the sequential recommendation more accurate.
925.ww: Search queries are a high-signal intent indicator that browsing history alone can't capture. By predicting what users might search for, the system fills in intent even when no search occurs. Query expansion bridges the vocabularies—it finds semantically similar items that match the predicted search intent, improving recall. This treats search and browsing as complementary signals rather than separate silos.
925.po: The integrated approach showed significant performance improvements over traditional sequential recommendation, particularly in scenarios where users have sparse or ambiguous browsing history. By leveraging search behavior, the system provided recommendations that better matched what users actually wanted.

926.bp: Recommendation systems need to quickly retrieve the most relevant items from millions of candidates. The challenge is that user preferences shift over time—what someone wanted to buy last month might be different today. A fast, scalable method that captures these dynamic patterns without expensive retraining is essential for real-time systems.
926.wh: Traditional methods track long-term user preferences or static item features. But the most predictive signal for 'what will this user engage with next' is often short-term co-occurrence patterns: if two items were frequently viewed together recently, they're likely to co-occur again. Capturing these patterns requires tracking recent interactions (expensive in memory) and updating quickly (expensive in computation). Most systems either ignore short-term dynamics entirely or use expensive neural methods.
926.ap: RPE4Rec is a lightweight plugin module using Relative Position Encoding (RPE)—a technique borrowed from sequence models—to capture the ordering and timing of recent co-occurrences. It uses a hashtable-based neighborhood memory that stores short-term interaction patterns without high memory cost. RPE encodes how recently and how frequently items co-occurred, making this information available to the main recommendation model with minimal overhead.
926.ww: Position encoding (learned representations of 'first', 'second', 'third') is an efficient way to capture ordering and recency without explicitly storing sequences. Short-term co-occurrence is predictive because user preferences cluster in time—if someone just viewed item A and then item B, they're likely interested in items similar to both. The hashtable avoids the quadratic memory cost of storing all pairwise interactions, keeping the method scalable.
926.po: RPE4Rec substantially improved item retrieval performance across multiple datasets with minimal computational cost. The lightweight, plugin nature meant it could augment existing recommendation models without retraining, making it practical for production systems.

927.bp: Hypergraph neural networks (models that reason about groups of items, not just pairs) can capture complex, high-order relationships in data—like 'this person, that book, and that reviewer form a trusted subgroup.' But these models are expensive to run. Distillation (training a smaller student model to mimic a larger teacher) can speed them up, but naive distillation loses information because the student is forced to replicate all behaviors equally.
927.wh: A teacher hypergraph model might be experts at reasoning about some nodes or hyperedges but worse at others. Telling the student to copy everything equally wastes the student's limited capacity on easy cases and poorly handles hard ones. Additionally, the student model (often a lightweight MLP) has different architecture from the teacher and might learn different internal features that could be useful if leveraged properly. Static distillation ignores these per-item differences and the student's own learning capacity.
927.ap: ARCHER (Adaptive and Reinforcement-Guided Contrastive Hypergraph Distillation) has three layers. First, it computes per-node and per-hyperedge confidence scores, so guidance from the teacher is weighted by how reliable the teacher is on each component. Second, it adds contrastive learning: the student learns not just to match the teacher but to learn distinct internal representations, using both teacher outputs and its own features. Third, it uses reinforcement learning (multi-armed bandits) to dynamically balance multiple training objectives so neither overfits.
927.ww: Adaptive weighting respects that some nodes are easier to model than others; the student learns faster on high-confidence regions. Contrastive learning lets the student grow beyond just mimicking—it learns to recognize different patterns in its own features, becoming more expressive. Reinforcement learning for balancing objectives prevents one loss term from dominating and causing premature convergence or instability. Together, these allow a lightweight MLP to outperform the heavy teacher.
927.po: ARCHER achieved better performance than existing hypergraph distillation methods across six benchmark datasets, with the student model actually outperforming the teacher model while remaining lightweight and efficient. This shows that smart distillation can transfer high-order reasoning to models that would otherwise be too simple.

928.bp: Machine learning models trained on real-world data often inherit biases from the data—hiring algorithms that discriminate against certain groups, medical models that work worse for underrepresented populations. Fixing fairness requires changing either the model or the data. Model-centric fixes (special loss functions, architecture changes) add complexity and overhead. A simpler alternative: fix the data instead.
928.wh: Most fairness work modifies the model, which adds training complexity and makes it harder to deploy in modular pipelines where the data comes from one system and the model from another. Also, model-specific fairness techniques don't transfer well across different downstream tasks—a fair model for hiring might not be fair for lending. But data is fundamental: if the training data itself is balanced and representative, any model trained on it is more likely to be fair.
928.ap: FairData synthesizes a new training dataset by optimizing a gradient-matching objective: the model trained on synthetic data should have the same training dynamics (how loss decreases over iterations) as one trained on the original data, but the synthetic data is explicitly optimized to reduce group disparities. The synthetic dataset stays in the original input space (images, text, numbers) rather than abstract feature space, making it directly usable.
928.ww: Matching training dynamics ensures the synthetic data teaches the same underlying patterns as the original, just without the bias. By working in input space (not abstract features), the dataset is model-agnostic—any architecture can learn from it. Since fairness is baked into the data itself, not the model, the approach is lightweight and works across downstream models without modification.
928.po: FairData reduced group disparities consistently across four benchmark datasets and multiple architectures while maintaining competitive predictive performance. By shifting fairness to a data-centric approach, it offers practitioners a lightweight, reusable tool that doesn't require model re-architecture or additional training overhead.

929.bp: Node classification in graphs (like determining the category of a product or the type of person in a social network) requires labeled examples, but in many real applications, you don't have any labeled data for the target class. Zero-shot learning aims to classify nodes using only the class name as guidance. For text-attributed graphs (where nodes have descriptions), this is challenging but powerful.
929.wh: With no labeled examples for a class, standard supervised learning fails completely. You could try using a pre-trained language model, but it doesn't see the graph structure—just text. A graph model sees structure but doesn't know what class names mean. Zero-shot learning requires bridging both modalities: using the graph structure and textual descriptions while leveraging what class names imply about expected node properties.
929.ap: The ZPT (Zero-shot Prompt Tuning) framework first pre-trains a graph-language model on unlabeled data to jointly understand both graph structure and text. Then it trains a conditional generative model that learns the joint distribution of nodes and text for each class. This generator creates synthetic node embeddings and text representations for each class based solely on the class name. Finally, these synthetic examples are used for continuous prompt tuning, adjusting the model's predictions toward the unseen classes.
929.ww: Pre-training on both modalities teaches the model what combinations of graph structure and text are typical. The generative model then imagines what nodes of each class would look like—their probable embeddings and text patterns—based on the class name and learned patterns. Synthetic examples act as pseudo-labeled data, allowing the model to learn without real labels. Prompt tuning fine-tunes the model specifically for the zero-shot classes.
929.po: The ZPT framework outperformed existing state-of-the-art methods for zero-shot node classification across benchmark datasets. Ablation studies confirmed that both the bimodal generator and the zero-shot prompt tuning components were necessary, validating the approach of learning from both graph and text to handle completely unseen classes.

930.bp: Online stores want to predict whether a shopper will buy something, so they can show better deals or personalized product pages to the right people at the right moment. The better the prediction, the more revenue the store makes.
930.wh: The hard part is that different customers behave in completely different ways. A typical prediction model uses the same mathematical rules for everyone, which misses how unique each customer's decision-making actually is. Traditional approaches also try to use the same features to both understand the customer and to adjust how the model works, which creates competing demands in the math—like trying to serve two masters with one rule.
930.ap: This paper proposes APPNet, which splits features into two buckets. One bucket feeds into the main prediction model (the part that decides buy or no-buy), and the other bucket tells the system how to personalize that prediction model for each customer. Instead of hand-picking which features do what (which requires human guessing), the system learns automatically during training which features should go in which bucket by watching where the math goes wrong.
930.ww: By separating the features, you avoid the tug-of-war—each bucket can do its job without fighting the other. Letting the system figure out the split automatically, rather than guessing ahead of time, means it discovers which features actually predict customer types and which predict whether they'll buy. This way, each customer gets rules tailored to them.
930.po: The paper shows this system predicts purchases better than models that treat all customers the same, and better than older personalization methods that guessed which features to use for grouping.

931.bp: Training machine learning models needs lots of labeled examples (like 'this email is spam' or 'this image is a cat'), but creating that data by hand is slow and expensive. Scientists use large language models to generate fake data to use for training instead.
931.wh: Most people have been doing this backwards without realizing it. The natural order is: first generate diverse examples of things (emails, articles, images), then label what they are. But most researchers put the label in the prompt first ('generate a spam email'), which forces the model to work backwards from the label to make matching data. This reversal might create data that's systematically different from real-world examples.
931.ap: This paper tests both directions. They use the same language model to create synthetic datasets two ways: the natural way (generate first, then label), and the popular way (label first, then generate). They then train two types of models on each synthetic dataset and test against real human-labeled data to see which approach gives better performance.
931.ww: When you generate first then label, the model creates natural diversity and the labels come later as honest descriptions, mimicking how real data arises. Backwards generation squeezes everything to fit the label, leaving artificial patterns. Real data doesn't come from labels; labels describe data that already exists.
931.po: Models trained on naturally-ordered synthetic data stayed much closer to real performance (accuracy drops of 4.9% to 13.7%), while backwards-ordered data caused massive drops (up to 59.1%), showing the direction of generation matters significantly for training quality.

932.bp: Fact-checkers need to verify claims by looking up evidence, and large language models can help do this automatically by searching for relevant information and deciding if a claim is true or false. This matters for fighting misinformation at scale.
932.wh: Language models have a deep problem: they have their own internal knowledge from training, and sometimes that knowledge is wrong. When you fetch external evidence that contradicts what the model 'knows,' the model may ignore the evidence and stick with its incorrect belief—especially if it's confident. Standard fact-checking systems don't handle this collision between internal and external knowledge.
932.ap: This paper introduces KnowFC, which recognizes that language models need to distinguish what they actually know from what they don't know. The system uses reinforcement learning to teach the model to be honest about its knowledge gaps (inspired by the Dunning-Kruger effect, where overconfident people don't know what they're missing). When checking facts, the system retrieves evidence more carefully based on where the model's knowledge boundaries are, then builds a reasoning graph from evidence and uses math from causal analysis to block the model's internal knowledge from interfering with the verification.
932.ww: By making the model aware of its own knowledge boundaries, it stops confidently asserting wrong things and becomes more willing to trust external evidence. The causal math removes the hidden influence of the model's pre-existing beliefs, so the model judges the evidence fairly rather than filtering it through what it already thought.
932.po: The framework navigates the conflict between internal knowledge and external evidence more reliably than prior fact-checking systems, improving correctness and reducing cases where the model confidently states false things based on outdated internal knowledge.

933.bp: Knowledge graphs—structured databases of facts like 'Albert Einstein discovered relativity'—help companies organize information for search, recommendation, and decision-making. To apply causal reasoning (figuring out if X causes Y) over these graphs, you need to know the true effect of each action.
933.wh: Knowledge graphs have two problems that break traditional causal methods. First, many attribute values are missing (the 'open-world' assumption: just because you don't see a fact doesn't mean it's false). Second, entities aren't independent—changing one person's age affects recommendations to their friends, creating spillover effects that simple causal math ignores. Existing methods assume you have complete data or pretend entities don't interact.
933.ap: BaLu reformulates the problem as two connected prediction tasks using graph neural networks. First, it fills in missing attributes by learning patterns from the rest of the graph (predicting which entities connect to which attributes). Second, it estimates causal effects by treating the entities and their relationships as a network where information flows through connections, capturing how one entity's treatment affects neighbors.
933.ww: Graph neural networks learn by passing information between connected nodes, so they naturally capture how entities influence each other—the spillover effect. By training both tasks together, the system learns attribute patterns and causal patterns in one go. This way, filling in missing data and estimating effects reinforce each other.
933.po: BaLu outperforms existing methods on benchmark datasets, even when those baselines use powerful separate attribute-filling techniques, showing that joint learning handles incomplete and interconnected knowledge graphs better.

934.bp: Phishing websites fool people into giving away passwords and personal information by impersonating legitimate sites. Detecting these fraudulent domains protects billions of users from theft and fraud.
934.wh: Phishing sites are designed to look and feel like real sites, so surface-level tricks don't work well. Traditional machine learning looks at features of the domain name and HTML structure, but clever attackers constantly evolve their tactics to bypass old detection rules.
934.ap: U-Proof tests two approaches side by side: large language models and traditional machine learning algorithms. The system ingests a mix of real phishing websites from September 2024, along with genuine banking and postal service URLs, and evaluates how well each model type spots phishing. The tool also generates explanations showing what red flags each model saw, to help users understand the attack.
934.ww: Large language models can understand semantic meaning and contextual clues (e.g., subtle wording that mimics but doesn't exactly match a real bank). Traditional ML picks up on structural patterns in domains and code. Testing both gives you more signals and helps pick the best approach for this particular problem.
934.po: The paper compares LLM and traditional model performance on a custom dataset of recent phishing sites, offering a tool that combines both approaches for detection plus human-readable explanations to raise user awareness.

935.bp: Online recommendation systems need to suggest what item a user will want to interact with next based on their past history. Getting this right means more engagement and user satisfaction across platforms like Netflix, Spotify, and Amazon.
935.wh: Sequential recommendations are tricky because you need to track the order of past clicks and purchases—not just which items matter, but when they mattered. Most modern diffusion approaches squeeze all the history into a single summary, losing the rich temporal details. Meanwhile, explicit signals like 'user clicked item A right after item B' exist but are underused.
935.ap: DCRec uses diffusion models (systems that gradually add and remove noise to generate new sequences) with two types of conditions. Implicit conditions capture the overall summary of user behavior, and explicit conditions feed in user-item relationships and sequential patterns directly. The system embeds both types of conditions into the forward and reverse diffusion process (the phases where noise is added and removed), so neither signal gets lost.
935.ww: By carrying both implicit and explicit signals through the entire diffusion process, the model preserves the rich sequential structure while also respecting hard facts about user interactions. Using explicit patterns directly grounds the generation in observed reality, preventing the model from inventing implausible sequences.
935.po: The model generates more accurate next-item predictions by keeping both the overall behavior patterns and the specific sequential relationships intact, as shown in experiments on Amazon datasets.

936.bp: Causal learning—understanding which variables cause which outcomes—is becoming essential in healthcare, business, and policy. But researchers building new causal methods have no standard way to compare performance fairly, making it hard to know which method to trust.
936.wh: The causal learning field is growing fast with many new algorithms, but there's no agreed-upon collection of benchmark datasets, evaluation metrics, or protocols. Different researchers test on different data and report different metrics, so you can't tell if algorithm A is actually better than algorithm B or just was tested differently.
936.ap: CausalBench is a workshop and framework aimed at surveying existing benchmarking efforts, categorizing them by technical type, and identifying gaps. The workshop solicits papers on benchmark datasets, algorithms, models, and metrics for causal learning tasks like causal discovery (finding which variables cause which) and causal inference (estimating the size of causal effects).
936.ww: A shared benchmarking effort creates a level playing field. When everyone tests on the same datasets and reports the same metrics, you can genuinely compare algorithms and make faster progress. It also encourages reproducibility and forces researchers to think about bias and fairness from the start.
936.po: The workshop pushes the field toward standardized benchmarks, making it easier for users to pick the right causal method and for researchers to validate new algorithms objectively.

937.bp: Researchers need to find relevant papers to read, cite, and recommend. Program committees need reviewers who understand submissions. Funding agencies need peer reviewers. Better search and recommendation makes academic science more efficient.
937.wh: Academic papers live across many sources (arXiv, journals, conferences), each with different indexing and metadata. A single search API doesn't exist. Also, papers aren't just isolated documents—they're connected by citations and authorship, and different ranking methods (some neural, some linear algebra) capture different patterns.
937.ap: Scholar API (SAPI) provides a unified interface that talks to multiple data sources behind the scenes. Users can pick from four different ways to rank papers: Specter (deep learning on abstracts), ProNE-s (linear algebra on the citation graph), SciNCL (fine-tuned neural embeddings), and a graph neural network approach. The system federates requests across sources, letting researchers mash up recommendations creatively.
937.ww: Offering multiple ranking methods lets you experiment with combinations—e.g., finding papers that neural methods agree are relevant but linear-algebra methods also support, which might be more robust. A unified API with flexible backends means you don't rebuild the data pipeline each time someone has a new idea.
937.po: SAPI simplifies building academic search and recommendation tools by offering convenient access to multiple data sources and ranking methods through one interface, demonstrated through baseline implementations.

938.bp: When a model is trained to recognize people's faces in photos and write captions about them, it learns to associate faces with identities. If someone later asks the model to forget them (a right granted by privacy law), we need proof the model actually forgot, not just stopped mentioning their name.
938.wh: Current approaches to machine unlearning (removing a person's influence from a model) are hard to evaluate fairly. The same caption—'a woman smiling'—might be correct after unlearning or might be incorrect because the model is now hiding information it still actually knows. There's no standard way to measure whether the model truly forgot or is just being evasive.
938.ap: CelebCaption is a dataset of 15,000 photos of 150 famous people with four captions per photo—some detailed, some brief, and some with or without the person's name. This variation lets researchers test three things: whether the model stops using the name (Identity Removal), whether it stops relying on person-specific patterns (Specificity Reduction), and whether the captions are still good quality (Performance Preservation). The paper benchmarks existing unlearning methods against these three criteria.
938.ww: The varied captions isolate different aspects of what 'forgetting' means. A model that truly forgot won't use the name or person-specific details, but will still generate reasonable captions. A model that's just hiding information will fail one of these tests.
938.po: The benchmark shows that current unlearning methods fail to truly erase identity information from models—they either degrade caption quality or still leave hidden person-specific patterns—revealing the gap between current practice and real privacy.

939.bp: The web is built on graphs—hyperlinks connect pages, social networks connect people, knowledge bases connect facts. Understanding these graphs helps with search, misinformation detection, and building trustworthy online systems.
939.wh: Traditional graph algorithms don't explain why they made a decision, making them hard to trust. Large graphs change over time, requiring algorithms that adapt. And building one giant model for the entire web is impractical—you need methods that work across decentralized systems.
939.ap: WEB&GRAPH 2026 is a workshop bringing together researchers to discuss better graph algorithms, particularly focusing on interpretability, adaptation, and human-AI collaboration. Topics include detecting false information, tracking how information spreads, handling evolving networks, and building systems that explain their reasoning.
939.ww: By uniting web search, data mining, AI, and social science perspectives, the workshop creates space for methods that are both mathematically sound and socially aware—algorithms that work at scale but also explain themselves and respect human values.
939.po: The workshop aims to advance the field toward graph systems that are explainable, trustworthy, and aligned with human values, particularly for critical applications like misinformation detection and recommendation.

940.bp: Online stores often sell bundles—like 'video game + controller + game pass' or 'shampoo + conditioner + brush'—as a unit. Recommending bundles is different from recommending individual items because people care about the whole package together.
