940.wh: Bundle recommendation has a tough problem: new bundles are created constantly and have no historical user interactions. Traditional methods can't recommend a bundle if nobody has ever rated it before. The old approaches also ignore that some items go well together—a controller matters more if you're buying a gaming console.
940.ap: EpicCBR uses graphs to connect items, bundles, and users, then applies contrastive learning (a method that pushes similar things close together and pulls different things apart). It identifies which items are central to user interests, builds profiles of users likely to want new bundles based on their past item preferences, and characterizes new bundles by looking at similar historical bundles and user preferences. A multi-view system handles both cold-start (new bundles) and warm-start (established bundles) scenarios.
940.ww: By thinking about item relationships and user preferences directly, rather than waiting for bundle interactions, the system can reason about new bundles. Using multiple views (user-item, bundle-item, historical patterns) means you have several signals to evaluate a new bundle, so you're not blindly guessing.
940.po: The method significantly outperforms prior bundle recommendation systems in cold-start scenarios (improvements up to 387%), allowing stores to recommend new packages immediately after they're created.

941.bp: Taxonomies organize concepts hierarchically—like 'Animal > Mammal > Dog'—and they're fundamental to search engines, e-commerce, and knowledge management. As the world changes, new entities (like 'cryptocurrency' or 'metaverse') need to be slotted into the right place.
941.wh: Picking the right parent-child relationship for a new entity requires understanding subtle semantic similarities. Existing approaches score each possible position with traditional contrastive learning, using negative examples that are randomly chosen. Random negatives are often too easy—the model solves the problem without learning anything useful. Cherry-picking hard negatives requires human judgment, which is impractical.
941.ap: TaxoDiff uses a diffusion model (a generative system) to create negative examples dynamically during training. At each training step, the system generates negative examples with varying difficulty—some easy to distinguish from the right answer, some harder. The diffusion process lets you control this hardness by sampling from different noise levels, automatically creating a curriculum of challenges.
941.ww: A curriculum of negative examples—starting easier, getting harder—helps a model learn robust features rather than overfitting to one particular type of wrong answer. The diffusion model's ability to generate examples on-the-fly means you adapt to what the model is struggling with, rather than guessing in advance what negatives to use.
941.po: The method achieves state-of-the-art taxonomy completion performance on three benchmarks by dynamically generating hard negatives throughout training, outperforming systems with fixed or random negative sampling.

942.bp: Recommendation systems predict what a user will want to watch or buy next based on their browsing and purchase history. Sequential context matters—someone who just searched for 'running shoes' is more likely to buy socks than someone browsing electronics.
942.wh: Diffusion models are good at generating diverse, realistic sequences, but existing diffusion recommendation methods have two problems: they lose stability when adding noise to the sequence (sample drift), and they don't handle real-world data well, which is often noisy and incomplete.
942.ap: GSDiffRec adds two specialized modules to diffusion-based recommendation. The Semantic-Targeted Guidance Module uses an enhanced transformer with special attention patterns and convolutional layers to understand user behavior more deeply. The Geodesic Diffusion Module adds geometric constraints during the noise-adding and noise-removal phases, keeping the generated sequence on a smooth manifold (a mathematical surface that respects the structure of real data).
942.ww: Geometric constraints during diffusion keep the generation process stable and grounded in realistic patterns, preventing the model from drifting into implausible sequences. The enhanced transformer captures semantic richness, so the guidance is actually meaningful rather than just steering randomly.
942.po: The method outperforms prior diffusion-based and traditional recommendation systems on Amazon datasets, with ablation studies showing both modules contribute meaningfully to performance.

943.bp: Social media shapes how people think, feel, and organize politically. Understanding the emotional dynamics—anger, joy, fear—helps explain why polarization spreads and how misinformation takes hold. Better understanding of emotion could inform better platform design.
943.wh: Research on social media has mostly focused on *what* people share (information flow) and *who* they connect to (network structure), but treated emotion as incidental. In reality, emotion is the driver—it determines what you pay attention to, who you trust, and how you respond.
943.ap: This talk uses natural language processing to measure emotions and moral sentiments in online text. It analyzes how emotions spread between people (emotional contagion), showing that exposure to others' emotions influences your own emotional expressions, beliefs, and sense of belonging. The research tracks emotional dynamics across political discourse, showing how in-group and out-group interactions differ emotionally.
943.ww: Emotions aren't just expressed; they're contagious and reshape entire populations' psychology. When you measure actual emotional patterns in posts (anger toward out-groups, joy in in-groups), you see the mechanism by which polarization becomes entrenched—it's not just disagreement, it's emotional organizing.
943.po: The evidence shows emotional dynamics underlie political polarization (characterized by in-group favoritism and out-group animosity) and collective social phenomena, revealing emotion as the hidden driver of social behavior that information-centric approaches miss.

944.bp: Doctors need to predict patient outcomes—readmission risk, length of stay, disease progression—to make better care decisions. Electronic health records (EHRs) contain rich patient histories, but they're messy and incomplete, making it hard to use them directly for prediction.
944.wh: EHR data is enormous (many lab tests, diagnoses, medications), heterogeneous (numbers, dates, text), and sparse (not every patient has every test). Language models can help by using medical knowledge to fill gaps, but most prior work treats this as a general compression problem—the model cleans up the EHR without knowing what prediction task it's being cleaned for. This wastes information.
944.ap: ReToP (Rewrite-To-Predict) trains an LLM-based system end-to-end for a specific prediction task. It generates synthetic training examples using a clinician-driven feature selection strategy to show the model different ways to rewrite patient records. Importantly, it uses a novel scoring method (Classifier Supervised Contribution) that measures how much each rewritten record helps the downstream prediction model, so the rewrite process focuses on clinically relevant changes.
944.ww: By tuning the rewrite directly to the prediction task, the system learns which parts of the EHR matter for *that particular prediction*—e.g., lab values matter for sepsis prediction but maybe not for appointment no-show prediction. This task-aware approach generates rewrites that actually help predict, rather than generic cleaning.
944.po: ReToP outperforms baseline models on three clinical prediction tasks using MIMIC-IV data, showing that aligning EHR rewriting with the prediction goal improves performance.

945.bp: When you read what people think about a product or movie, you face a sea of conflicting opinions. The goal is to create a summary that honestly shows *why* people disagree—what divides them—so someone can understand the landscape of sentiment, not just an averaged middle ground.
945.wh: Their method starts by identifying the mainstream opinion, then groups the remaining documents by how they differ from that center. For each divergent group, they extract specific evidence—facts or claims that explain the disagreement. They use mathematical optimization to pick evidence that best illustrates the splits without being redundant.
945.ww: This works because it treats disagreement as a structural problem, not noise. By first anchoring to consensus, then deliberately expanding outward to capture the edges, you preserve the core while making room for genuine alternatives. The optimization step ensures you pick maximally informative evidence, not just any disagreement.
945.po: On two benchmark datasets, their method beats baselines in both matching gold-standard summaries *and* in human evaluation, where humans confirm it identifies more comprehensive evidence of where opinions actually diverge. It keeps computational cost low while doing this.

946.bp: In a factory, your sensors stream readings constantly. Suddenly one spikes far out of normal—that's an anomaly, a sign something is breaking or behaving unexpectedly. Finding these weird moments across vast time series is how you catch problems before they cause damage.
946.wh: Time series anomaly detection sounds simple, but the landscape is fragmented: methods from the 1980s still work in some domains, new deep-learning approaches claim superiority, yet simple baselines often win. The bigger problem: no one agrees on how to measure success, and models trained on one dataset fail spectacularly on another.
946.ap: This is a tutorial survey covering the full arc—from classical algorithms to recent foundation model approaches. It also introduces new evaluation frameworks and a taxonomy to organize the confusion. Critically, it surfaces that modern automated model selection often fails to beat random choice, exposing a real blind spot in the field.
946.ww: By gathering methods across decades and confronting them with fair benchmarks, you uncover what actually works versus what merely sounds good. The finding that automation underperforms randomness is humbling but useful: it tells you the field needs better intuition about *why* a method works for a specific time series type.
946.po: Practitioners and researchers get an interactive system to explore trade-offs between methods and datasets, plus evidence-based guidance that simple approaches often suffice. The surprising conclusion—that foundation models haven't yet broken the curse of generalization—points researchers toward harder problems.

947.bp: When you ask an AI a factual question about the world—like 'Who founded this company?'—you want it to give you verifiable facts with proof, not a fluent-sounding guess. The dream is an AI that reasons through a structured knowledge base, like Wikipedia's links and facts, to *know* its answer is grounded.
947.wh: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) helps by looking up relevant facts before answering. But current systems use ad-hoc search heuristics and leave you blind: you don't know *what questions* the system asked the knowledge base or *why* it picked certain facts. This opacity makes it hard to trust or debug wrong answers.
947.ap: Their idea: treat retrieval as a *planning problem*, not search. Before querying the knowledge base, the AI analyzes the question, figures out what *types* of facts are needed—the logical relationships and constraints—and builds a retrieval plan. It then follows that plan, stopping early if constraints are met, and replans if it hits dead ends.
947.ww: Plans are explicit and auditable: you can see what the system thought it needed to look up and why. This structure prevents wild-goose chases and forces the AI to think through the problem before querying. Bounded exploration (early stopping) keeps cost down while completeness (replanning) ensures it doesn't give up too fast.
947.po: The framework enables 'controlled, auditable reasoning' that balances getting complete answers against computational cost. Tests on Wikidata-based question datasets will show whether this rigor improves both accuracy and transparency compared to heuristic RAG.

948.bp: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are how AI learns patterns in networks—social graphs, molecules, road systems. They work by having each node absorb information from its neighbors in waves. The goal is to make sure this message-passing captures the true structure and relationships, not a blurred average.
948.wh: When nodes send information to their neighbors and aggregate it, something breaks: if many neighbors send signals, the central node's own features get drowned out or homogenized. This 'aggregation collapse' is especially bad when nodes have very different numbers of neighbors—a popular node's signal gets diluted differently than an isolated one's.
948.ap: They identify two types of loss: feature collapse (values become indistinguishable after mixing) and structural collapse (node degree information vanishes). To fix it, they add two techniques: (1) before aggregating, reshape and re-scale feature distributions so they stay diverse, and (2) after aggregating, encode structural information (like node degree) separately.
948.ww: Diversity in feature space prevents bottlenecks where all nodes end up looking alike. Encoding structure *after* aggregation lets the network remember 'this node had many neighbors' even after merging signals. Together, they preserve both content and topology, so the network can learn finer patterns.
948.po: Tests show their fixes improve GNN performance and scalability without requiring architectural overhauls—the techniques slot into existing models. The fixes are theoretically grounded and simple to implement, making them practical for practitioners.

949.bp: When you chat with a recommendation system—'I like sci-fi movies'—it should suggest items *and explain why*. The explanation matters as much as the pick: you trust a system that says 'based on your love of space travel,' not one that just says 'here's your movie.' But explanations need real knowledge about products.
949.wh: Language models alone often don't know item details (does the phone have 5G? What's the battery life?). Retrieval fixes this by looking up facts, but it pulls back a mess of loosely-relevant information mixed with noise. The system then struggles to pick what actually matters from this cluttered context.
949.ap: MOCHA adds a multi-stage reasoning process. First, it uses Chain-of-Thought reasoning to pick the best item to recommend. Then, in a second stage, it reasons through features of that item to pick the ones that justify the recommendation to the user. Both stages use retrieved knowledge selectively.
949.ww: Breaking the problem into two stages forces clarity: first nail *which product*, then *which of its features* sell it to this user. This staged reasoning filters noise at each step rather than trying to parse everything at once. The retrieval becomes focused because the system knows what it's hunting for.
949.po: On two public conversational recommendation datasets, MOCHA beats baselines in recommendation accuracy and generates explanations that are both informative and factually correct—users get not just the right item but the right reasons.

950.bp: A similarity graph has millions of nodes and you want to spread labels through it—label a few movies as 'good' and predict labels for the rest. Graphs like this arise naturally from embeddings or recommendation systems. The challenge: classical algorithms need memory proportional to n-squared, infeasible for millions of nodes.
950.wh: Standard Label Propagation requires storing the full adjacency matrix (n x n). For n = 1 million, that's a trillion entries—impossible. Yet for low-rank graphs (where similarity comes from a product of embedding vectors, not arbitrary structure), you don't actually *need* that full matrix; the information is already compressed in the embeddings.
950.ap: VLP (Vector-Based Label Propagation) skips building the matrix entirely. Instead, it does all the math in the embedding space directly—labels propagate through matrix algebra on the dense vectors, not sparse graph operations. Mathematically, it's equivalent to classical Label Propagation.
950.ww: By working in the embedding space, you reduce memory from O(n²) to O(nd), where d is the embedding dimension (usually dozens). On GPUs, this dense math is fast. The method is exact, not an approximation, so you lose nothing in speed-up.
950.po: Label Propagation now works on graphs with millions of nodes, previously out of reach. The first convergence proof for LP in the low-rank case provides theoretical reassurance that this isn't a shortcut with hidden gotchas.

951.bp: For decades, 'personalization' meant: predict what user will click next and nudge them that way—reinforcing habits. A new frontier asks: can AI systems reason and plan *on your behalf*, surfacing insights you'd miss and guiding you toward growth, not just repeating what you already like?
951.wh: Doing this well is philosophically hard—if an AI 'reasons about' your future self, who decides the goals? It's technically hard too: systems need to understand you deeply, integrate multiple modalities (text, voice, images), and coordinate reasoning across planning and creativity, not just pattern-matching in past behavior.
951.ap: The talk traces evolution: AI as data augmenters for recommendation pipelines, then as recursive self-improving language models, and finally as personalized reasoning agents that can plan and create. Each stage relies on new capabilities from foundation models (multimodal, speech-aware, reasoning-capable).
951.ww: Each generation builds on better models: language models let you reason about preferences, multimodal models let you understand context across images and text, and reasoning agents let you plan steps toward a goal. Stacking these lets systems move from 'predict next action' to 'imagine your path forward.'
951.po: The talk identifies specific opportunities (reasoning agents) and blockers (how to align AI goals with user growth, not just engagement) for this shift, grounded in recent foundation model advances and findings from the WSDM community about what works and what doesn't.

952.bp: A good recommendation should use all available signals: images, text, video, audio. But in real systems, modalities are missing all the time—a product has no image, a user has no review text. Most recommenders break gracefully or assume you'll fill in the blanks, adding complexity for little gain.
952.wh: Late-fusion designs encode each modality separately, then align them. When a modality is missing, imputation adds layers of approximation and hyperparameter tuning. The system becomes fragile: the alignment learned on complete data doesn't transfer well to incomplete data.
952.ap: EFMRec does early fusion: take whichever modalities are present, project them into a shared semantic space using pretrained multimodal models, then aggregate the available signals directly without reconstruction. The architecture then propagates these unified representations through a graph and combines them with collaborative filtering.
952.ww: Projects them into shared semantic space ensures modalities can talk to each other even if some are missing—you're not trying to reconstruct what isn't there. Early aggregation means the system learns jointly how much weight each modality deserves, adapting to missingness naturally. No separate imputation machinery.
952.po: On three benchmarks, EFMRec beats strong baselines in *both* complete-data and incomplete-data settings, proving it's robust to missing modalities while matching performance when everything is present. This real-world resilience is the key win.

953.bp: Software contains bugs that hackers can exploit to steal data or crash systems. Code vulnerability detection automates finding these weak spots before deployment. Catching them early saves money and prevents breaches.
953.wh: Code structure matters: a vulnerability often hides in the *flow* of control and data dependencies, not surface patterns. Sequence-based models see word-by-word linearly and miss these flows. Graph-based methods capture flow (abstract syntax trees, control flow) but struggle to learn rich semantic meaning—what each operation truly does—from that graph structure.
953.ap: Vul-GRT combines graphs with multiple learning layers. It uses Graph Attention Networks to absorb structural dependencies, then Restricted Boltzmann Machines to mine latent patterns from the graph. Separately, it incorporates code language models to get semantic meaning. These signals fuse into comprehensive node representations. A hybrid loss function trains both vulnerability detection and path tracking.
953.ww: Graph Attention lets you learn which structural edges matter most (not all control flows are equally important for a bug). RBM extracts hidden patterns unsupervised (bugs often follow subtle archetypal flows). Language models provide semantic grounding (you need to know what a function *does* to spot misuse). Path tracking during loss ensures the model learns to point to *where* the vulnerability is.
953.po: The combined approach captures both structure and semantics, improving detection effectiveness. Path tracking makes the model more interpretable—when it flags a vulnerability, it can show the data/control flow path that led to the flaw.

954.bp: Recommender systems face a brutal trade-off: for users with history, precise algorithms work great. For brand-new users with no data, precision fails and you must guess. Most systems pick one strategy. The insight: different users need different approaches, and a smart coordinator can switch between them.
954.wh: A single algorithm either specializes in old users (high precision, fails on new ones) or new users (high novelty, mediocre precision on repeat customers). You can't have both—or can you? The real problem is assuming *all* users need the same machinery.
954.ap: MARS uses a central Manager Agent that routes each user request based on context. Warm-start users with rich history go to a Bayesian Personalized Ranking model (a proven, tight precision baseline). New cold-start users get routed to semantic search (using Sentence-BERT to find conceptually similar items). Different pathways for different needs.
954.ww: Algorithms that learn from history naturally excel at pattern-matching for frequent users. Semantic similarity doesn't need history—it works from item descriptions alone. By acknowledging these strengths and routing accordingly, you get precision *where it matters* and discovery *where it helps*. The orchestration adds minimal overhead.
954.po: Experiments on MovieLens 20M show MARS matches BPR precision for warm-start users while delivering 10x higher novelty for cold-start users (14.40 vs 1.24 novelty score), *and* is 20x faster for cold-start. A rigorous quantitative benchmark of precision-vs-discovery trade-offs emerges.

955.bp: False information spreads online now from both humans and AI systems. Humans and machines lie differently: LLM-generated falsehoods are fluent, persuasive, harder to spot than a human's rambling mistake. A veracity system that uses the same fact-checking strategy for both fails.
955.wh: Current Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems use one uniform strategy: 'retrieve N facts, check the claim.' But LLM falsehoods may need different evidence (more retrieval, different search angles) than human lies. Systems don't adapt to source or recognize they need a different strategy.
955.ap: MoARE (Mixture of Adaptive Retrieval Experts) uses a Mixture-of-Experts network trained with reinforcement learning. For each post, it dynamically decides: should we retrieve at all? If so, how much evidence? The network learns different retrieval strategies and picks them based on input characteristics, without needing to know the source directly.
955.ww: Different sources have different semantic patterns—this requires different retrieval queries and evidence thresholds. By learning a *mixture* of strategies and training it to balance accuracy against cost (retrieving facts takes time), the system adapts on the fly. Reinforcement learning optimizes the routing: which strategy gives best accuracy-per-dollar?
955.po: On mixed human-LLM datasets, MoARE beats state-of-the-art RAG baselines in accuracy while using less retrieval time. It's more efficient (lower time cost) and more effective (higher accuracy), showing that adaptive routing outperforms uniform strategies.

956.bp: A machine learning model can be a valuable business asset or security system. If someone can copy its behavior by only querying it (like a black box), they steal its value without ever seeing the code. Understanding this risk and defending against it matters.
956.wh: Hyperdimensional Computing is a bio-inspired, efficient learning scheme. Model stealing usually requires either training data or white-box access (knowing internal weights). The hard challenge: steal under 'data-free, black-box'—you can only feed inputs and see outputs, with zero knowledge of training data or internals.
956.ap: StealHD exploits characteristics of HDC itself: the algorithm's sensitivity to certain input patterns. The attacker generates a surrogate dataset using noise and data augmentations known to matter for HDC. They query the victim model with these inputs, observe output similarities, and train a new HDC model to mimic the victim's behavior.
956.ww: HDC has identifiable Achilles heels: particular noise patterns and augmentations affect it predictably. By understanding the algorithm, the attacker can craft inputs that expose these weaknesses without needing the original training data. The learned surrogate model then replicates the victim's decision boundary.
956.po: Tests on three datasets show StealHD successfully steals HDC models under the tightest constraints—data-free and black-box. This exposes a vulnerability in HDC deployment and highlights that even efficiency-focused models aren't immune to intellectual property theft.

957.bp: Search engines don't return the same results to everyone—they personalize based on location, past searches, and other signals. The risk: if search results differ by geography on controversial topics, people in different regions get different pictures of the world, reinforcing regional bubbles instead of shared understanding.
957.wh: Measuring this 'geo-personalization bias' is hard: you need to run searches from multiple locations, control for confounding factors, and *objectively judge* whether results are biased. Traditional metrics (click-through rates) don't tell you if results are biased toward a region's views. You need a perspective-aware evaluator.
957.ap: The study queries two major search engines on six controversial topics, varying location while controlling other factors. Instead of human judges (expensive, slow), they use LLM annotations that represent multiple distinct perspectives. This scales evaluation across geography and time.
957.ww: LLMs can label results from different viewpoints—what one ideology sees as fair, another sees as biased. By gathering multiple LLM perspectives and comparing what each region receives, you can quantify whether filter bubbles form. LLM annotations scale beyond what human reviewers could handle.
957.po: The study proves filter bubbles exist and evolve with regional events. It documents how search engines (and their personalization algorithms) contribute differently to this fragmentation, and shows that topic type matters—some topics form stronger regional bubbles than others. Public code enables reproducibility.

958.bp: Financial traders want to profit from market-moving information: news articles, SEC filings, tweets. But extracting signals from millions of documents and testing whether they're actually predictive is slow and subjective when done by hand. Automated hypothesis generation could accelerate discovery.
958.wh: Traditional finance relies on expert intuition: a fund manager reads the news and forms a hypothesis ('increased tariffs hurt retail stocks'). Testing one hypothesis takes time; exploring the space of possible hypotheses is impossibly slow. Automating this requires extracting facts, building causal links, and rigorously testing strategies, all at scale.
958.ap: AutoHypo-Fin chains several AI components: information extraction mines facts from web data and filings, a knowledge graph links them, retrieval-augmented generation forms hypotheses, and backtesting with optimization validates them. The loop is autonomous: generate a hypothesis, test it on historical data, refine based on results.
958.ww: Each component feeds the next: extracted facts become nodes in a graph, the graph enables retrieval-augmented reasoning (you can ask: 'what factors predict tech stock rallies?'), and backtesting grounds speculation in reality. Optimization tweaks strategies to maximize risk-adjusted returns. Automation lets you explore hundreds of hypotheses where humans explore one.
958.po: Backtests from 2019–2024 show AutoHypo-Fin outperforms traditional strategies in risk-adjusted returns, hit rate, and drawdown control. Ablation studies confirm each component contributes. The system offers 'scalable, fully automated' hypothesis generation—a tool for quantitative finance to move faster.

959.bp: When you're deciding something important, you want multiple viewpoints: Ask five friends, you get five answers, and you learn how differently people think. Yupp brings that to AI: show the same question to Claude, GPT-4, Llama, and compare their answers side-by-side.
959.wh: Each AI model has different strengths and weaknesses, different training, different biases. No single model is 'the best' for everyone—some excel at code, others at explanation, others at creativity. Individual comparison sites exist, but they're hard to use and don't aggregate user preference feedback at scale.
959.ap: Yupp is a consumer product where users see responses from multiple AI models in parallel. Users indicate which response they prefer, and this feedback is aggregated into leaderboards that rank models on different dimensions (accuracy, clarity, creativity, etc.). Different tasks get different leaderboards.
959.ww: Side-by-side comparison makes trade-offs visible: you see that Model A is faster but less accurate, Model B is thorough but verbose. Crowd-sourced preference feedback (vibes from many users) captures what matters in real-world use, which academic benchmarks often miss. Leaderboards motivate model creators to improve.
959.po: Yupp delivers immediate value (users get multiple perspectives on their question) and secondary value (the aggregated leaderboard becomes a crowd-sourced benchmark of model quality). The product also generates research insights: what preferences emerge across diverse populations, and how do models collaborate in multi-party dialogue?

960.bp: Weather and climate scientists need to understand patterns that repeat—seasonal cycles, lunar tides, annual temperature swings. The real goal is to build math that automatically finds these repeating rhythms in messy real-world sensor data (like temperature recordings) so forecasts can separate the predictable cycles from noise.
960.wh: The authors split the problem in two: they first strip out a straight linear trend from the data, then model what's left as a mix of cosines and sines—the building blocks of any periodic pattern. To nail the phase ambiguity, they explicitly let each frequency have its own starting position. For extra flexibility, they also build a deep version where a neural network learns nonlinear shapes layered on top of the sine-cosine basis.
960.ww: Cosines and sines are the most natural language for periodic phenomena—any repeating cycle can be built from them, like mixing primary colors to make any hue. By learning which sine and cosine components matter and with what amplitudes, the model automatically discovers which frequencies (daily, weekly, seasonal) are present. Letting each frequency have its own phase offset cuts through the ambiguity: no two time shifts are indistinguishable anymore.
960.po: On climate data from NOAA (the US weather service), the linear version (FG-Linear) beats trend-only models and deep learning baselines, getting the lowest error. The deep version (FG-Deep) doesn't help on this particular small, regular dataset, showing that the simpler approach wins when data is clean and orderly.

961.bp: Ad platforms sell 'cost-per-click' (OCPC) bidding: you pay when someone clicks your ad, but the real win is a later purchase. The platform tries to predict whether each click will turn into a sale, and charges you accordingly. The goal is a fair, accurate price per sale that keeps both buyers and the platform happy.
961.wh: Here's the catch: after a user clicks, the platform waits days or weeks for a purchase signal to come back. Predictions made on clicks that haven't converted yet are totally blind—you're guessing whether someone will eventually buy when you still haven't seen what they do. Ignore this delay and you'll think every click is worthless (predicting 'no purchase' too often), leading you to bid too low and losing money.
961.ap: The authors borrow survival analysis—a statistical tool from medicine that predicts 'how long until an event happens.' Here, the event is 'customer converts to a purchase.' They build a model that can predict conversion probability even for customers still waiting in the pipeline, using their immediate clicking patterns to estimate the future. They offer two versions: one using multitask survival modeling (learning across many related prediction jobs), and one using Cox survival regression (a simpler statistical standard).
961.ww: Survival analysis was built exactly to handle this: situations where you're waiting for an outcome and don't yet know who succeeds or fails. By modeling the time-to-conversion as a probability curve, you can estimate 'this person is 60% likely to convert in the next 2 weeks' even if they clicked just now and you haven't seen the outcome. This lets you charge fair prices for delayed sales.
961.po: Both versions improved platform revenue in live experiments on real ads. The fix lets bidders accurately price clicks that will convert later, avoiding the bias toward underbidding and ensuring the platform earns what sales are actually worth.

962.bp: Big e-commerce and streaming sites need to show the right product to millions of people. They do this in stages: first, scrape data and decide which items matter; then build a model to score items; finally, serve predictions at query time. Each stage usually ignores the others, even though decisions in stage one ripple through stage three.
962.wh: In real systems, products connect to each other (people who buy socks also buy shoes), relate to user history in subtle ways, and vary wildly by context (seasonal, regional, personal history). Building a data set without capturing these relationships means the model is blind to clues. Training a model without remembering that those relationships exist means it can't learn them. And at query time, you can't adapt to new users or new items instantly.
962.ap: RankGraph-Context is a framework that runs the relationships through all three stages. During data prep, it catches which items and users connect (building a graph of relationships). During training, it feeds those relationships as structured information so the model learns how to use them. At prediction time, it can update itself when a new user arrives or product appears, learning their patterns on the fly without retraining.
962.ww: Graphs naturally encode 'who relates to whom.' If the model knows that socks and shoes are related, it can make better guesses about what a new customer wants. By threading the graph through all stages instead of siloing each one, you build a system that learns from relationships at every step—the opposite of the old 'train in isolation' approach.
962.po: Across production systems, the framework improved results on hard scenarios: new users with no history (cold-start), rare products with few sales (long-tail), and showing variety (cross-surface). It also enabled safe online learning—the system can tweak itself based on live feedback without constant retraining.

963.bp: Facebook needs to suggest friends—people you might know. This is harder than recommending products because friendships are social: they rely on shared communities, proximity to mutual friends, and subtle social norms. The real goal is to help real people find real friends at scale across billions of connections.
963.wh: Facebook's graph of 3 billion users is so large that standard graph learning (like neural networks that walk the graph) is computationally infeasible—you'd need to touch too many machines and memories. Yet simple heuristics that ignore the rich structure of social ties miss many good friend suggestions. You need something that's fast enough for billions but smart enough to use social structure.
963.ap: The authors use a pre-trained language model (like GPT-style models) paired with a feature aggregation trick. For each person, they gather information from their friends-of-friends (second-degree connections), extracting both what the graph structure looks like around them and semantic patterns in profiles/activity. The transformer model then learns to score likely friendships by ingesting this richer context.
963.ww: Language models excel at learning from text and sequences; they're fast even on large scale. By converting graph structure into features the language model can consume (who your friends are, what they do), you get the benefits of social awareness without the computational nightmare of graph neural networks on billions of nodes. The aggregation is a bottleneck you can control, keeping memory in check.
963.po: Live on Facebook, the approach improved friend connections: more users found new friends every day. It scales to billions of users and catches relationships that simple similarity misses because it understands both the local social structure and what kinds of people actually become friends.

964.bp: Recommendation systems have a fairness problem: they show you what they think you want most, narrowing your view. If you like both classical music and pop, but your favorite is classical, the system might show only classical forever, cutting you off from pop entirely. The goal is 'calibration': recommendations should reflect your real distribution of interests, not just your top preference.
964.wh: Most systems optimize for accuracy—showing the item you'll like most. That works if your top interest is all that matters, but humans have a spectrum of interests. Calibration requires the system to spend some recommendations on your secondary interests, which means accepting lower average accuracy. Also, people's tastes change over time; static calibration (one set of interest proportions) breaks when a user's preferences shift.
964.ap: The authors extend calibration to dynamic systems where user preferences evolve. They define calibration that adapts to changing taste distributions and simulate long-term effects: if a system maintains calibration over weeks or months, do users actually benefit? They also run a user study to see what people think of calibrated recommendations in practice.
964.ww: If your interests shift but recommendations stay locked to your old proportions, you'll see stale content. By tracking how preferences change and adjusting the balance of recommendations over time, the system stays aligned with your actual interests. User studies reveal whether calibration actually feels good—not just in theory but in lived experience.
964.po: The research illuminates calibration's real value and limits in dynamic settings. Some users love the diversity; others find non-optimal recommendations annoying. The work pushes beyond static theory to show how calibration plays out as preferences evolve over weeks.

965.bp: Social networks and recommendation graphs grow every day: new users join, new relationships form, old ones fade. You want your learning system to stay sharp as the network changes—learning about the new shape without forgetting what you already knew. The goal is continuous learning that handles growth without collapse.
965.wh: Classic learning algorithms have a deadly flaw: when you feed them new data that looks different from the old data (like a graph with new communities), they catastrophically forget what they learned before—the old patterns evaporate. This is called catastrophic forgetting. Worse, evolving graphs have non-stationary distributions: the patterns that mattered yesterday might not apply today.
965.ap: Instead of tweaking weights and parameters (the standard approach), the authors maximize mutual information—a measure of overlap—between node representations (numerical profiles of each node) at consecutive time steps. If your representation at time T is similar to your representation at time T+1, you've preserved what you knew. By keeping representations stable while learning new relationships, you prevent forgetting.
965.ww: Representations (the learned numbers describing each node) capture what the model has learned. If representations stay similar, the model is preserving its understanding. By explicitly maximizing similarity between consecutive time steps while learning new structures, you balance old knowledge and new information. The mutual information trick is a direct signal: high overlap means retention.
965.po: On real evolving networks, the approach consistently beats standard continual learning algorithms. Nodes keep their learned features stable as the graph grows, meaning the system learns new community structure and relationships without amnesia.

966.bp: When customers shop online, they buy sets of items for their next purchase: grocery trips, clothing hauls, streamer setups. Predicting these 'next baskets' helps retailers stock shelves and recommend bulk discounts. The goal is to anticipate what items will appear together in someone's next shopping trip.
966.wh: Real shopping has quirks that simple models miss. People intentionally add low-value items to hit free-shipping thresholds ('I need two more dollars of stuff to qualify'). Meanwhile, shoppers both repeat past purchases (a predictable pattern) and explore new things (much harder to predict). Existing methods treat repetition and exploration as mixed-up signals they can't untangle.
966.ap: The authors use diffusion models—generative systems that learn by gradually denoising random noise into realistic outputs. They run two denoising processes in parallel, one for spatial patterns (which items go together across categories) and one for temporal patterns (how purchase patterns shift over time). They also use information bottleneck theory—a principle that limits information flow—to force the model to route repetitive signals one way and exploratory signals another, keeping them separate.
966.ww: Diffusion models excel at learning compositional structures (how pieces fit together) by learning to reverse noise corruption. Running two parallel denoising flows lets you model time and space independently. Information bottleneck is a mathematical way to say 'this channel can only carry information about exploration, not repetition,' providing a mechanical separation that lets the model learn cleaner patterns.
966.po: The framework captures threshold-meeting behavior (a real but previously unstudied phenomenon), disentangles repetition from exploration, and improves basket prediction accuracy. It's the first to apply diffusion to this task, unlocking new generative capability.

967.bp: Chatbots and virtual assistants need to stay in character: a helpful assistant should be consistent across all messages, a formal bot should stay formal. Inconsistency erodes trust. The real goal is to detect when a bot contradicts its personality and fix it before users see the mistake.
967.wh: Consistency is slippery to detect. A bot might say 'I'm Jane, tech support' in one message and 'I'm Bob, sales' in another—that's obvious. But what if the bot agrees with the user on Tuesday and disagrees on Wednesday about a topic that should reflect the persona? These indirect contradictions are hard to spot because they don't mention the persona directly.
967.ap: The authors build PersonaKG, a knowledge graph capturing commonsense assumptions about personas—if someone is conservative, they probably value tradition; if they're laid-back, they probably don't stress rules. They construct a dialogue dataset with both explicit contradictions (name changes) and subtle ones (conflicting values). Then they train a two-step model: first recognize inconsistent responses, then rewrite them to align with the persona.
967.ww: Common sense about personality is encoded in the knowledge graph: neighbors in the graph represent related traits and values. By checking if a response aligns with the graph's implications for that persona, you catch subtle contradictions. The rewrite step isn't just deletion—it preserves meaning while twisting it to fit the character.
967.po: On their benchmark dataset, the method improved consistency metrics by 12% automatically (and 10% by human judges). It's the first to address indirect contradictions, moving beyond simple disagreement detection to cultural and value-based consistency.

968.bp: Recommendation models are biased: they overweight popular items and neglect rare ones. Inverse propensity scoring (IPS) is a famous statistical trick to correct this bias by reweighting each training example. Many systems use IPS, but do people actually use it correctly?
968.wh: The research question is subtle: does IPS work because it fixes bias (making risk functions unbiased), or does it work for some other reason? If IPS is just a side effect, then using it for bias correction might miss the real mechanism—and might even hurt in some scenarios.
968.ap: The authors analyze what IPS actually does mathematically. They find that under typical assumptions, IPS's benefits come less from unbiased risk and more from accidentally enriching the learned representations (the features the model uses) by forcing multi-task learning. They show experimentally that reweighting can harm performance if not paired with multi-task structure, and that multi-task learning alone often does the job better.
968.ww: IPS reweights examples: rare items get high weight, popular items low weight. This forces the model to pay attention to rare items, implicitly learning richer features for them. But the mechanism isn't bias correction per se—it's feature enrichment through imbalanced training. Multi-task learning (training the model on multiple related prediction jobs) achieves the same enrichment more robustly.
968.po: The paper reveals that IPS can actually hurt if applied naively; it's best paired with multi-task approaches. This rewrites how practitioners should think about bias correction in recommendations: multi-task learning offers a more principled path than reweighting alone.

969.bp: E-commerce search is hard because shoppers type vague queries: 'wireless thing' could mean earbuds, chargers, or routers. Search engines try to expand queries—add related words—to catch more matching products. The goal is to automatically guess what a customer meant and broaden the search without adding noise.
969.wh: Users type short, ambiguous phrases against catalogs of millions of products. Semantic similarity (finding synonyms) misses domain context—'wireless' has different meanings in audio vs. power tools. Few-shot prompting (asking an LLM for synonyms) ignores the actual product catalog and can suggest irrelevant terms. You need to ground expansion in what's actually sellable.
969.ap: REFLEX uses reinforcement learning with a live search engine in the loop. An LLM generates expanded queries, but instead of trusting it, the system tests each expansion against the real product catalog and measures how many relevant items it retrieves. Rewards balance two goals: expanding to items relevant to the original query, and increasing breadth (retrieving diverse products). The LLM is trained on this real-world feedback without requiring labeled training examples.
969.ww: The catalog is the ground truth: if an expansion retrieves relevant products, it's good; if it retrieves junk, it's bad. By closing the loop—testing expansions against real search results—you avoid hallucinations and domain drift. The LLM learns what expansions work in practice, not what similarity scores suggest.
969.po: On a large production dataset, REFLEX beat strong baselines in semantic coverage and retrieval effectiveness. Live A/B testing on real users showed measurable gains in relevance, diversity, and engagement—the system learned what expansions work at scale.

970.bp: Smartphones and smart home devices can't send every prediction to a remote server: privacy rules forbid it, networks disconnect, and latency kills user experience. You need powerful recommendation models running on your device itself. The real goal is to give phone users personalized recommendations instantly, locally, without uploading behavior.
970.wh: Large language models are powerful but huge—often billions of parameters consuming gigabytes of memory. A phone has kilobytes to spare. Shrinking an LLM by 100× while keeping it accurate enough for recommendations is a hard engineering problem. Naive compression often breaks performance.
970.ap: OD-LLM uses two complementary techniques. First, Singular Value Decomposition (SVD)—a mathematical trick that removes redundant patterns from weight matrices, shrinking the model without erasing essential patterns. Second, a tokenization normalization technique that makes tokens (the input units) more compatible with low-rank compression. Third, progressive alignment: after compression, iteratively fine-tune layer by layer to recover lost capability.
970.ww: Weight matrices in neural nets often have redundancy: similar patterns repeat across many parameters. SVD exposes and removes this fat. The tokenization normalization ensures that the simpler representation can still capture the model's intended behavior. Progressive layer-wise refinement recovers capability incrementally, avoiding the cliff where compression suddenly breaks everything.
970.po: On sequential recommendation benchmarks, OD-LLM achieved full-model accuracy with 50-100× fewer parameters, small enough for phones. Users get instant, private, personalized recommendations on their device.

971.bp: Graph neural networks are workhorses for social networks, recommendation graphs, and knowledge bases. They excel when similar nodes connect to similar nodes ('homophily'). But in the real world, nodes often connect across groups—conservative and liberal voters in politics, different music genres in playlists. These 'heterophilic' networks stump traditional graph neural networks.
971.wh: The problem sits at bridge nodes—the few nodes connecting different groups. A bridge node's neighbors are dissimilar (by design), violating the homophily assumption. Existing heterophily-aware models still smooth information across the bridge (averaging neighbor features), blurring the boundaries between groups and confusing the classifier.
971.ap: Bridge Breaking Graph Neural Network (BBGNN) identifies bridges without needing labels: it computes a 'bridge ratio' metric measuring how disparate a node's neighbors are. For genuine bridges, it uses a special aggregation mechanism that avoids over-smoothing—instead of averaging all neighbors equally, it adapts to preserve the differences that bridges intentionally connect.
971.ww: Bridges are structural bottlenecks; their neighbors *should* be different. Standard aggregation treats this diversity as noise and averages it away. By identifying bridges (nodes with high neighbor diversity) and using context-aware aggregation around them, the model respects the graph's real structure instead of forcing false homophily.
971.po: Across benchmark datasets, BBGNN significantly improved classification accuracy on bridge nodes and overall graph performance. It's a targeted fix that restores graph neural network effectiveness on heterophilic networks.

972.bp: Recommending to new users (cold-start) and new products is a core problem. New items have no click history, new users have never interacted. Yet both have textual descriptions and structural connections (category, price range, similar products). The goal is to harness text and graph structure together to make smart guesses without interaction history.
972.wh: Graph neural networks learn from connections but stumble when there are no connections to learn from. Text similarity finds synonyms but ignores graph structure. Neither alone solves cold-start for items you've never seen and users with no past behavior.
972.ap: G-TRAC combines two information sources: text (item descriptions, user profiles) processed by transformers (the engine behind systems like GPT), and graph structure (categories, related products) processed by graph neural networks. By learning alignments between the textual and structural representations—forcing them to agree and complement each other—the model uses both sources of information to represent new items and users.
972.ww: Text and structure encode different knowledge: text captures meaning and nuance, graph structure captures similarity and relationships. By aligning them—making sure representations from both sources point to the same high-level understanding—you combine the strengths. A new product can be represented through both what its description says and where it sits in the product graph.
972.po: Experiments show G-TRAC enhances recommendation quality on cold-start scenarios and generalizes across diverse product types. The dual representation exploits both information sources to handle unseen users and items.

973.bp: Sequential recommendation predicts your next purchase by watching your purchase history. But for brand-new users with no history, the model is blind. Yet you know other things about them: demographics, device, context. The goal is to infer what a new user wants from their attributes, then feed that into a sequential model that normally requires past purchases.
973.wh: Cold-start users break sequential models because there's no sequence to model. Simple workarounds (using demographics or social info) ignore the sequential patterns that make sequential models powerful. You need a way to generate a synthetic sequence that captures new-user preferences, then hand that to a standard sequential recommender.
973.ap: CDMRec uses diffusion modeling (a generative technique that builds samples gradually from noise) to create synthetic preference sequences for new users. First, it constructs a Preference-Dominant Sequence from whatever data is available (demographics, context, user attributes), filtering to the most informative signals. Then causal inference identifies which attributes truly drive behavior. Finally, it runs a diffusion process conditioned on these causal features, generating a realistic behavioral preference sequence.
973.ww: Diffusion models learn to build complex structures from noise; conditioned diffusion lets you steer generation toward specific attributes (gender, age, device). Causal inference cuts through spurious correlations: some attributes correlate with purchases by accident, others drive them. By conditioning only on true drivers, you avoid conflating correlation with causation.
973.po: CDMRec integrates into existing sequential recommenders without modification—it supplies them with generated sequences that work as if they were real. Across three benchmarks, it improved cold-start sequential recommendation and seamlessly pairs with mainstream models.

974.bp: Streaming services (Netflix, Spotify, YouTube) have billions of users and millions of hours of content. They're now experimenting with generative AI—using large language models and image generators to personalize experiences, tag content, and create recommendations. The goal is a forum to share best practices and research findings.
974.wh: Generative AI in streaming is nascent and fragmented: researchers publish papers, companies build proprietary systems, and few exchange learnings. Academic research and production systems rarely talk. Problems at Netflix differ from YouTube, but both could learn from each other. No unified understanding exists of what works and what pitfalls lurk.
974.ap: GenAI4SM is a workshop—a gathering of academics and industry practitioners. Attendees share deployed systems, ongoing research, production insights, and technical challenges. The format encourages cross-pollination: researchers learn what industry actually needs, companies learn what's possible in labs.
974.ww: Workshops accelerate learning by compressing knowledge transfer: a deployed solution that took Netflix 10 people and 6 months might take Spotify only 2 months if the design is shared. Real streaming data and scale constraints differ hugely from benchmarks, and practitioners know these gaps. Researchers bring theoretical depth and generalization insights.
974.po: This is a venue, not a research result—the payoff is the conversations and connections fostered. It positions generative AI in streaming as a coherent research area and builds community around shared problems like personalization at scale, content generation, and responsible deployment.

975.bp: Spotify needs to show ads and promote podcasts to listeners, but new advertisers or new podcast promotions often have barely any data about what works—so the system starts cold and has to guess. The challenge: how do you recommend something promising when you've never seen it before, without annoying users or wasting money on bad bets?
975.wh: Existing separate pipelines waste knowledge: when one advertiser learns what kinds of users stream indie folk, that insight dies there. New advertisers can't borrow it. The system also has to pick between optimizing just clicks or just streams, not both—but real business needs juggle multiple goals at once.
975.ap: The team built one unified model that learns from the entire history of ads and promotions together, using a shared foundation of user features, content, and context. When a new advertiser arrives, the model isn't starting blind—it draws on patterns learned from hundreds of past campaigns, then fine-tunes itself to that specific advertiser's data. The model simultaneously optimizes for multiple outcomes (streams, clicks, follows) like a multi-purpose engine.
975.ww: When you learn from many related tasks together, you pick up general principles: which kinds of users care about podcasts, how context shifts behavior, what creative elements attract attention. A new advertiser inherits these deep patterns instantly, then just adapts them slightly to their own niche. Optimizing multiple goals simultaneously actually helps—one goal's signal steers the model away from cheating the others.
975.po: In real testing on Spotify, the unified model cut the cost to get a listener to stream a podcast by 22%, and increased stream rates by 18–24%. The gains were sharpest for small, lesser-known podcasts that would normally starve for attention. The system also became simpler to run and scale—one model to maintain instead of dozens.

976.bp: Networks are everywhere—social ties reshape opinions, brains rewire themselves as they learn, power grids shift as demand changes. The real world rarely gives us perfect knowledge of these systems. Epidemiologists don't know every contact that could spread disease, power engineers don't know next year's demand exactly. How do you predict what a network will do when you can't fully describe it?
976.wh: Standard dynamical network analysis assumes you know the network structure exactly. It ignores that contact patterns are uncertain, transmission rates fluctuate, or that the network itself changes over time. You can't just slot in guesses and hope—uncertainty itself changes how the system behaves.
976.ap: This tutorial brings together two usually separate fields: the science of networks in motion, and the art of tracking and quantifying uncertainty. It teaches techniques for asking not just 'what will happen?' but 'how wrong could I be, and how does that wrongness propagate through the network?'
976.ww: When you systematically track uncertainty, you spot which parts of the network matter most (maybe a few key hubs, or a fragile link). You can design robustness: if edge weight X is uncertain, what structure keeps the system stable anyway? You shift from false precision to honest prediction.
976.po: Practitioners learn practical methods for modeling epidemics, power grids, and neural adaptation with incomplete information, discovering which uncertainties sink predictions and which ones stay tolerable.

977.bp: Graph neural networks have proven powerful for tasks like social network recommendation, molecule classification, and fraud detection. But real-world graphs are gigantic—millions of nodes, billions of edges. Training models on graphs this large is slow and expensive. Can we compress a graph to one-tenth its size and still answer the same questions accurately?
977.wh: Existing graph compression methods copy features pixel-by-pixel but skip the relational skeleton. They also produce dense, redundant condensed graphs that don't save much memory or computation. The condensed graph becomes just another unhappy middle ground.
977.ap: The researchers designed a framework that represents many nodes by discrete codes (like having a alphabet of node types in the codebook), then uses low-rank matrix math to preserve the connection patterns from the original graph. Node features themselves get compressed losslessly by breaking them into compact discrete pieces.
977.ww: Discrete codes work like a vocabulary: instead of storing every node's float vector, you store which code it matches, massively shrinking memory. Low-rank approximation of graph connections means you capture the broad 'traffic patterns' of the network without storing every edge. Together, you get a graph that runs faster, uses less memory, but still sees the same structural patterns.
977.po: The compressed graph preserves accuracy on downstream tasks while slashing storage and computation time. It removes noise (redundancy in features) while locking in structure, making the condensed graph more efficient than the original for prediction.

978.bp: Graph neural networks now make decisions in high-stakes domains—fraud detection in financial networks, content moderation on social platforms, diagnostic systems for diseases. If someone can subtly poison the network (adding fake accounts, injecting false links), they can trick the model into wrong decisions. How do you attack these systems invisibly?
978.wh: Surrogate models leak information but also misalign with reality. Discrete graph structures make gradient-based attacks fail. Most attack papers ignore defending systems, making them look stronger than they'd be in practice.
978.ap: The team built a reinforcement learning system that learns to inject nodes (fake accounts) and edges (false links) by trial and error, without needing a copy of the real model. It softens the discrete choices to avoid dead ends, designs a smarter edge sampler that respects graph topology, and explicitly learns what defenses expect so it can evade them.
978.ww: Learning by trial and error on the real system (feedback-only) is slower but honest—you're actually measuring against what you'll face. Softening discrete choices helps you escape local dead ends (you can't improve by 0.1 edge, but the algorithm treats it as if you could, then rounds at the end). Understanding defense mechanisms means you stop building attacks for 'ideal' systems and actually threaten real ones.
978.po: The attack method successfully fools graph neural networks even when those networks have built-in defenses, and it does so stealthily—the injected nodes and fake links look plausible, making the attack hard to detect.

979.bp: When you search a knowledge base—finding co-authors, tracking treatment paths, tracing idea lineage—the answer often lies in a multi-step journey: paper to author to paper, or symptom to drug to outcome. These paths follow patterns, but those patterns are hidden in the data and never written down. How do you find them automatically?
979.wh: Manual rules don't scale. Rules that work for one knowledge base fail on another. Rules that work today become stale as the domain evolves. You need the system to discover patterns by watching downstream tasks succeed or fail.
979.ap: The system learns retrieval rules by watching real feedback. When it gets a hint that a paper-to-paper query should succeed (maybe users clicked on a result), it explores: did the rule 'go through co-authors' work better than 'go through venues'? A reinforcement learning layer picks promising rules, then a second layer refines the scoring function for those rules, iterating together.
979.ww: By coupling rule discovery with retrieval refinement, the system doesn't waste time on rules that sound logical but don't work in practice. The feedback loop means rules adapt as the task changes. Jointly optimizing rules and scores means a mediocre rule with great scoring beats a perfect rule with bad scoring.
979.po: The system discovers retrieval patterns automatically and matches retrieval quality achieved by hand-coded rules—sometimes surpassing them—without requiring human domain expertise upfront.

980.bp: Recommendation systems use graphs of user-item interactions (a person clicks a movie, a user follows an artist) to predict what someone will like next. Learning from these patterns works well for popular items, but lesser-known items get barely clicked, so the system never learns good representations for them. How do you recommend the obscure stuff?
980.wh: Random graph augmentation is crude. For long-tail items, random changes can wipe out the little signal there is. You need augmentation that preserves structure while adding diverse views.
980.ap: The researchers use a diffusion model (a process that adds noise, then carefully removes it) to create multiple views of the graph. First, they compress the graph to its structural essence using matrix math, which speeds up the diffusion. Then the diffusion model creates views that keep the graph structure but vary details. For rare items specifically, they guide the denoising by telling it: 'this should look like the broader graph,' using global structure as a helpful constraint.
980.ww: Diffusion processes can be precise about what to change and what to preserve—noise and signal separate cleanly. Compression captures the big-picture structure before creating views, so no view accidentally tosses the skeleton. For long-tail items, global constraints act as a lifeline: 'use what you learned from popular items to help predict this rare one.'
980.po: The system learns better representations for rare items by anchoring them to the overall graph structure, improving recommendation quality especially for the obscure content that platforms neglect.

981.bp: Recommendation systems at scale (YouTube, TikTok, Spotify) often generate textual identifiers for what to show next—not human-readable text, but a learned 'semantic ID' that compresses everything the system knows about a user or video into one token. The challenge: that ID needs to bring together different types of data (video features, creator info, transcripts) that speak different languages. How do you make one ID that understands them all?
981.wh: Different modalities compete. If you just concatenate features, text dominates, graph signals get lost. Different data types need alignment—translation into a shared meaning space.
981.ap: The team built a general framework (SEALNet) that aligns the semantics of each modality: it learns how to interpret the graph's signals in terms of the image's signals, how to translate the LLM's meaning into a common language. Once aligned, features merge into a single learned semantic ID. They demonstrate two flavors: one blends video understanding with creator collaboration networks, another weaves in LLM-based semantic understanding.
981.ww: Alignment lets you ask 'what does this collaboration graph statement mean in terms of video content?' and get a coherent answer. The shared semantic space is learned, not hand-coded, so it adapts to what actually matters for recommendation. Different modalities then contribute honestly to the same ID instead of fighting.
981.po: A single semantic ID now captures meaning across modalities, letting large-scale systems generate personalized recommendations using unified learned representations grounded in video, creator networks, and LLM understanding simultaneously.

982.bp: Fake news detectors are trained to spot false articles, but attackers can bypass them by adding comments (like 'I saw this firsthand' or 'peer-reviewed study confirms it') that shift a reader's belief in the article's truthfulness. How can attackers generate comments that fool the detector without human raters noticing the manipulation?
982.wh: Generic comments don't exploit what the detector actually uses to decide. You need surgical precision: identify the tokens (words/phrases) that the detector leans on most, then craft comments that use those very tokens but twist their meaning.
982.ap: The attack system uses an explainability tool (SHAP) to identify which words the detector considers most important for real vs. fake judgments. Then it prompts an LLM: 'Write a human-like comment using these strategic words,' and the LLM generates realistic-looking text. Those comments get added to the article and tested against several published detectors (TextCNN, RoBERTa, dEFEND).
982.ww: Explainability reveals what the detector actually relies on (not what designers hoped it relies on). An LLM's job is to make natural text, so prompting it for comments that include strategic words yields human-sounding but adversarial comments. The combination respects what the detector 'sees' while evading what detectors 'expect' to see in natural comments.
982.po: The attack successfully fools state-of-the-art fake news detectors by appending LLM-generated comments, and the generated comments read naturally—they'd pass human readers' scrutiny because they use realistic language while weaponizing words the detector over-relies on.

983.bp: LLMs can now edit text fluently. An attacker could subtly reword news to shift how credible it seems—removing a qualifying phrase, tweaking a causal claim—without making it obviously false. How much can such small edits sway human belief? And how hard is it for an LLM to find the right edits?
983.wh: Small edits hide from human scrutiny but can flip perception. Finding them requires understanding causal language, qualifying statements, and credibility markers. Brute-force search is impractical.
983.ap: The researchers had an LLM make targeted edits to news articles—removing hedging language ('said,' 'might'), shifting causal claims, introducing opposing evidence—while keeping the core story intact. They focused on four kinds of subtle, credibility-shifting changes that preserve readability. Then they measured: do human readers judge edited articles as more or less believable?
983.ww: Causal and hedging language are how writers signal certainty. An LLM trained on real text understands these nuances implicitly—it knows that removing 'reportedly' hardens a claim's perceived strength, or that adding counter-evidence seeds doubt. Small changes in these markers shift the article's tone from 'information' to 'accusation' or 'speculation.'
983.po: The work demonstrates that LLM-crafted minimal edits reliably shift human perception of news credibility—small, hard-to-spot changes move readers' judgment, proving that subtle adversarial manipulation of believability is both achievable and effective.

984.bp: Can a code generation model (ChatGPT, Codex, Claude) solve a competitive programming problem? Testing just the final code ('does it run?') misses half the story—you miss whether the model understood the problem, whether it picked the right algorithmic strategy, and whether it could explain its approach. How do you evaluate the actual thinking, not just the output?
984.wh: Pass@k metrics are binary: code works or doesn't. This hides whether failures come from bad problem understanding, weak algorithm selection, or sloppy coding. It doesn't measure what matters for real programming: reasoning and problem-solving.
984.ap: The researchers built a four-phase evaluation benchmark: first, does the model understand the problem's examples? Second, does it select a sensible algorithm? Third, can it describe a solution approach? Fourth, does the code work? Each phase has intermediate checkpoints, graded by an LLM with specialized instructions. They curated 197 hand-picked competitive programming problems from Codeforces.
984.ww: Decomposing code generation into phases lets you see where the model breaks down. If it fails phase two (algorithm selection), that's a different weakness than failing phase four (coding). Each phase depends on the last—if a model doesn't understand the problem, no algorithm will save it. This dependency structure reveals whether code failures are surface-level or deep.
984.po: The benchmark reveals consistent gaps in code generation models' understanding and algorithmic reasoning, showing that models pass@k scores don't capture real weaknesses, and that each reasoning phase's quality directly predicts the next one's performance.

985.bp: Large language models can now act as judges in information retrieval—deciding if a document is relevant to a query. But they're susceptible to bias: if they just judged three documents as relevant, they're more likely to judge the fourth one relevant too, regardless of its actual content. Psychologists call this 'priming'—and it skews judgments silently. Can we teach an LLM to resist this?
985.wh: Simple fixes like randomizing order or flushing memory work partially but not fully. The problem runs deep in how models process context.
985.ap: The team tested whether simulated personalities reduce priming. In psychology, personality traits (like openness or neuroticism) correlate with bias susceptibility. They prompted LLMs to adopt Big Five personality profiles (which psychologically correspond to various trait levels), then measured priming on relevance labeling tasks from TREC 2021 and 2022.
985.ww: Personality frameworks are psychologically grounded—they've been shown to predict bias in humans. When an LLM adopts a 'high openness, low neuroticism' profile, it may adopt the cognitive patterns those traits typically exhibit, including resistance to priming. Simulating personalities essentially borrows psychological knowledge about robust human judgment.
985.po: Certain personality profiles (notably high openness, low neuroticism) consistently reduce the LLM's susceptibility to priming, and this holds across multiple LLM models and task types, suggesting personality prompting as a practical technique to improve LLM-based relevance judging.

986.bp: YouTube recommends billions of videos daily, shaping what people watch and believe. Is the algorithm trapping users in filter bubbles, serving them only content that mirrors their existing views? Auditing this at scale is nearly impossible—you can't fake being millions of different users without getting caught. How can researchers reproducibly and ethically test what YouTube actually recommends?
986.wh: Scale, realism, reproducibility, and ethics all pull in different directions. A simple bot gets caught. A large-scale audit with real accounts is unethical and violates terms. Existing tools don't let you compare different personas' recommendation paths transparently.
986.ap: TRACE is an open framework that automates browsers like humans would, creating simulated personas with specific interests and demographic profiles (via LLM-based persona generation). It runs experiments on YouTube at scale, logs everything to a database for traceability, and uses LLMs to synthesize context-aware behaviors so personas act realistically rather than robotically.
986.ww: Containerized browser automation is practical and difficult to detect. LLM-driven personas generate natural sequences of searches and clicks—not hardcoded patterns—making the simulation realistic. Database-backed logging means every decision is recorded, so other researchers can audit your methodology and reproduce your findings. The modular design lets researchers swap in different personas or behavioral strategies.
986.po: TRACE enables large-scale, reproducible, transparent audits of YouTube's recommendation ecosystem, allowing researchers to empirically test whether personalization creates filter bubbles and to share findings in a verifiable, ethically grounded way.

987.bp: You have some money to invest. You're willing to take risk, but you want good returns. How much should you put in tech stocks vs. bonds vs. emerging markets? This is portfolio optimization—balancing diverse assets under your risk tolerance. Most optimization methods find one best answer. But different investors have different appetites for risk. How do you flexibly generate many good portfolios across risk levels?
987.wh: Flexible methods are complex. Direct methods are rigid. Neither handles risk preference smoothly.
987.ap: The researchers use a diffusion model—a process that starts with random noise and iteratively refines it into clean structure—to generate portfolios directly. The diffusion process has a built-in 'risk guidance' mechanism: you can adjust a dial that biases the refinement toward either high-risk or low-risk outcomes without retraining. The model learns the distribution of good portfolios from historical market data.
987.ww: Diffusion models are built to gradually transform noise into fine structure, and that process is reversible—you can steer it mid-way using guidance signals. Risk guidance means the same trained model adapts to any risk level instantly, like turning a knob. The model learns to sample from the distribution of actually good portfolios, not to forecast future prices (which is hard) or optimize a surrogate objective (which can diverge from the true goal).
987.po: The diffusion model generates diverse, high-quality portfolios at any risk level, outperforming baselines in returns, risk management, and overall reliability across real market datasets.

988.bp: Recommender systems decide what movies, music, and products get promoted to you. A malicious actor could inject fake user accounts that rate things artificially high or low, shifting the system's recommendations to favor certain items or creators. These 'shilling attacks' threaten system integrity. How can someone attack a recommender using LLM-generated fake users and reviews?
988.wh: Simple attacks are detectable. Ignoring reviews means the fake users are incomplete. Low-knowledge attacks (using only what an attacker can observe from outside) usually don't work well against defended systems.
