988.ap: The team built AgentSA, a framework that uses LLM-based agents to generate fake user profiles. The agents read target items, generate plausible reviews (using an LLM), select what to rate (guided by targeted mechanisms that maximize impact), and maintain a memory of what they've 'done' to stay consistent. All of this is coordinated to maximize manipulation while avoiding detection.
988.ww: LLMs are trained on real human text, so reviews they generate sound natural. Multiple agents coordinating means attack patterns aren't just one user doing obvious things—it looks like varied, independent behavior. Targeting mechanisms ensure fake interactions push the system in intended directions. Behavioral camouflage (staying consistent, not doing anything too obviously weird) makes the attack stealthy.
988.po: LLM agents can execute shilling attacks that consistently outperform existing methods in both effectiveness (manipulating recommendations) and stealth (avoiding detection), revealing a new class of threats to recommender systems enabled by sophisticated LLM-based impersonation.

989.bp: When an LLM recommends something, can it explain why? 'Because your taste resembles other users who liked it' is one kind of reason. But LLMs have their own knowledge base—they know that sci-fi fans often enjoy certain themes. Recommendations work better when the system uses both collaborative patterns (what similar users did) and LLM knowledge (semantic meaning). The hard part: explaining how those two sources align. Can an LLM generate coherent rationales bridging both?
989.wh: The semantic gap blocks explainability. LLM knowledge and collaborative signals speak different languages. Direct fusion doesn't produce coherent explanations.
989.ap: ARROW (Adaptive Reasoning for LLM-based Recommendation With explainability) uses chain-of-thought prompting—asking the LLM to 'think out loud' about why a recommendation fits. It then measures the uncertainty of that reasoning using statistical tests, and adaptively adjusts how much weight to give the reasoning vs. the collaborative signal. When the reasoning is confident and coherent, it dominates the decision; when uncertain, collaborative signals take over.
989.ww: Chain-of-thought reasoning lets an LLM articulate semantic connections between user preferences and item meaning. Uncertainty quantification prevents the model from confidently BS-ing—if the reasoning is shaky, the system knows to distrust it. Adaptive weighting means you get human-interpretable explanations when possible, but fall back to reliable collaborative signals when reasoning breaks down.
989.po: ARROW produces recommendations with human-interpretable explanations by bridging LLM semantic understanding and collaborative patterns, achieving strong accuracy while providing coherent rationales for why each item was recommended.

990.bp: When you ask a search engine or recommendation system to rank items, that system has learned from real-world data. But real-world data carries human biases—maybe certain groups are shown less often, or treated worse. We want ranking systems to work fairly for everyone, not amplify hidden societal patterns already baked into the data.
990.wh: Existing fairness solutions typically ask you to know which attributes matter (gender, race, age) and label them in your training data. This is hard in practice—sensitive data is often private, expensive to label, or legally risky to even collect. You need a way to detect and fix bias without needing these explicit labels.
990.ap: The method starts training on examples the model finds easiest (lowest loss). As it improves, it gradually adds harder examples into the training mix. Throughout, it watches whether the prediction errors differ between demographic groups, even though it never actually sees group labels. The size and pattern of those errors serve as a proxy for bias, letting the learning process self-correct.
990.ww: The core insight is that a model's loss (how wrong it is on each example) can tell you about bias. When the model makes confidently wrong predictions on items from one demographic group, that's often a sign of bias. By training in stages—first getting good at easy examples, then hard ones—the system learns to weigh examples fairly and doesn't overfit to biased patterns in the data.
990.po: On a real search benchmark (MS MARCO), their method reduced gender bias without needing demographic labels, and the ranking quality stayed the same or got better compared to other approaches. The fix was built into the learning process itself, not bolted on afterward.

991.bp: In real systems, measurements change over time and depend on each other—like network traffic, stock prices, or sensor readings in a factory. To make better decisions, we need to know which measurements actually cause changes in others, not just which ones tend to move together. This is especially hard when there are hidden factors influencing everything.
991.wh: Real-world time series have confounders—unobserved forces that affect multiple variables at once. For example, a holiday might boost both website traffic and product orders, but the holiday itself isn't measured in your data. Standard causal discovery methods assume you measure everything important, which breaks down when confounders hide.
991.ap: The method builds two kinds of causal graphs in parallel. Coarse-grained graphs capture relationships across entire sequences (does variable A always lead to variable B?), while fine-grained graphs zoom in to local time windows (does the relationship change here?). A separate neural network specifically designed to find proxies for unobserved confounders sits alongside, detecting which hidden factors are at play and adjusting the causal conclusions accordingly.
991.ww: By modeling confounders at multiple scales (some steady over time, some shifting moment-to-moment), the system can explain away the effects of hidden variables and reveal the true direct relationships between the things you do measure. This works because hidden influences have characteristic patterns—persistent ones show up the same way at every time step, while transient ones don't.
991.po: The framework handles real time series data with hidden confounders and captures how causal relationships shift over time, enabling better interpretation and decision-making in domains like finance, operations, and healthcare where the ground truth often changes.

992.bp: Recommendation systems often rely on knowledge bases—structured facts like movie genres, actor relationships, or product properties. These knowledge bases help systems recommend things intelligently. But real-world knowledge bases are messy: facts are missing (incomplete), some facts are wrong (noisy), and this mess directly damages the quality of recommendations.
992.wh: Most recommendation systems focus on building clever models to extract value from messy data as-is. But if the data itself is full of errors and gaps, even the cleverest model can't fix that. You need a way to clean up and fill in the knowledge base itself, not just tolerate its messiness.
992.ap: The method trains a special diffusion model that learns the actual distribution of knowledge graphs (which facts tend to go together, which entities relate to which). This model is shaped to care most about facts that matter for recommendations. Once trained, it can take the real, messy knowledge base and gradually refine it, removing noise and inferring missing facts until it produces a high-quality version suitable for downstream recommendations.
992.ww: Diffusion models are trained to gradually turn pure noise into realistic data by learning the true patterns in data. The insight here is that a knowledge base is just data—so a diffusion model can learn the true patterns of what correct, complete knowledge looks like, then convert a messy real knowledge base into a clean synthetic one that preserves the original structure but fixes quality issues.
992.po: The method treats knowledge base quality as a data problem, not a model problem. By generating high-quality facts to fill gaps and removing noisy ones, the system improves recommendation performance without requiring manual annotation or domain expertise, working on real knowledge graphs used in production systems.

993.bp: Information retrieval—search, ranking, answering questions—sits at the intersection of technology and power. These systems decide what information billions of people see, who gets found in searches, and whose voice reaches whom. Today, they're increasingly sites of conflict between helping people access truth and oppressing them through manipulation and surveillance.
993.wh: Current fairness and transparency approaches focus on algorithmic metrics—bias numbers, attention weights—but miss the bigger political question: whose interests does the system serve? In an era of democratic erosion and tech concentration, a well-calibrated bias number doesn't prevent a system from being weaponized for oppression or surveillance.
993.ap: Rather than proposing a technical solution, this positions information retrieval as a political practice that must engage with critical theory—asking not just 'is this ranking fair?' but 'fair to whom, and toward what end?' It challenges researchers to design systems explicitly with emancipatory goals and to resist surveillance and authoritarian capture of information infrastructure.
993.ww: The argument is that information access is not a neutral technical problem. Who controls search engines and what they choose to rank shapes society. Systems can be simultaneously 'fair' by metrics and deeply unjust in practice. Real emancipatory work requires understanding power structures and centering the experiences of marginalized communities in system design.
993.po: This is a call for the research community to take seriously the political and social dimensions of information retrieval, to build critical theories and practices into the field, and to recognize that the technical and the political are inseparable.

994.bp: People ask questions expecting useful, appropriate answers tailored to who they are and what they need. Over decades, researchers built systems that understood questions, found relevant information, and generated coherent responses. Now large language models can generate fluent text, but old questions remain: how do we know an answer fits the person asking it? How do we balance accuracy with understandability?
994.wh: The jump from document retrieval to generative AI feels like a clean break, but it leaves unsolved problems behind. Large language models are powerful but opaque, and user modeling—understanding what each individual actually needs—is harder than ever. How do you ensure an LLM-generated answer is right for a particular person, not just plausible-sounding?
994.ap: The talk surveys the history of how question-answering systems handled these two dimensions—understanding information needs through sophisticated dialogue, and tailoring answers to the audience (complexity, terminology, depth). It positions modern large language models as tools for these old problems, not replacements for thinking about them.
994.ww: The core insight is that generating any old answer isn't enough. Good answers depend on two things: the information need (what are they really asking for) and the user (who are they, what do they know, what can they understand). This was true fifty years ago with symbolic systems and remains true today with LLMs.
994.po: The paper bridges historical work in user modeling and natural language generation with modern large language models, showing that old insights about personalization, clarity, and coherence still matter even when the underlying technology has changed completely.

995.bp: For two decades, search meant finding and ranking documents. Today it's shifting: instead of returning documents, we want systems that can read evidence, think through a problem, and actually do things—book flights, analyze data, plan projects. This changes what retrieval means and creates new technical challenges.
995.wh: When you have a reasoning system connected to the internet, it's not obvious what should trigger retrieval (when to stop reasoning and look something up), what information matters most, or how to evaluate whether the system worked. These questions barely existed when search just meant ranking documents.
995.ap: Systems like FlashRAG provide modular platforms where the reasoning model and the retriever collaborate. The reasoning model decides when and what to search for, the retrieval system finds relevant information, and the model integrates it. The hardest new problems are tracking what's been retrieved (maintaining memory), checking whether retrieved information is accurate, and evaluating whether a multi-step reasoning-and-retrieval process actually solved the problem.
995.ww: The mechanism is that large reasoning models can explain their reasoning transparently (here's what I know, here's what I'm unsure about, here's what I should search for). By giving them access to retrieval, they can interrupt their reasoning to look things up, then resume. This is much more flexible than the old pipeline where retrieval came first and reasoning second.
995.po: Real systems like Search-o1 and DeepAgent demonstrate that modern language models can chain reasoning with active search—they know when their knowledge ends and go fetch what they need. This creates qualitatively new capabilities: deep research over many steps, tool use at scale, and systems that actually execute information-seeking goals.

996.bp: People search differently depending on who they are—age, language skill, cultural background, and the task at hand all shape how someone formulates queries and interacts with results. If a search engine is designed for one type of searcher, it won't work well for others. Understanding these differences helps build fairer, more robust systems.
996.wh: Most search systems are evaluated on average performance across all users, which can mask failures for specific groups. If a system works great for one demographic but poorly for another, traditional benchmarks won't catch it. You need to understand the underlying patterns in how different people search differently.
996.ap: Researchers had participants of different ages, genders, and language abilities perform search tasks and recorded their query formulation, click patterns, and session behavior. They extracted simple underlying 'dimensions' that capture the variation (like how structured vs. exploratory someone's search strategy is), and showed these dimensions explain observed behavior better than just saying 'age groups are different.'
996.ww: Instead of assuming everyone searches the same way, the insight is that people pick different strategies based on their experience and comfort level. Younger users might prefer shorter queries and quick scanning, while older users might structure queries more carefully. Neither is worse; they're just different. Understanding this helps systems adapt to each person rather than punishing anyone whose style differs from the norm.
996.po: Through controlled user studies, the work shows that age is the strongest predictor of search behavior—older users formulate queries differently and navigate results differently than younger users. Gender and language effects exist but are more selective. Most importantly, these differences reflect strategy choices, not inability—they're variations in how people approach the task.

997.bp: Recommendation systems work by learning what items are similar to each other. But similarity in the real world isn't just structural—it's emotional. You might want music that sounds happy even if it's orchestrated totally differently, or books with similar themes even if they're in different genres. Baking emotion into how systems measure similarity improves what they recommend.
997.wh: Graph-based recommendation systems treat items as nodes and similarity as edges. But two items can be structurally adjacent (nearby in the graph) while being emotionally different (one uplifting, one depressing). When the system propagates information along edges, it mixes signals from items that shouldn't influence each other, degrading recommendation quality.
997.ap: The method encodes emotional dimensions (extracted from language models) as a topological structure that represents the affective space. As the system learns to rank items, it adds a loss function that rewards embeddings aligned with this affective structure. This gently steers learned representations toward emotional consistency: items close in the learned space are not just structurally similar but also affectively similar.
997.ww: Human-centered preference isn't just facts—it's feelings. When you model items using only their structural relationships, you miss the affective dimension. By extracting emotional properties (valence: positive vs. negative; arousal: energetic vs. calm) and ensuring the learned representations respect these emotional boundaries, the system produces recommendations that feel right, not just structurally plausible.
997.po: The system improved top-K recommendation accuracy across multiple music, book, and media datasets while actually reducing computational cost compared to baseline methods. This shows that emotional alignment is not just nice-to-have but actively improves practical recommendation performance.

998.bp: Search engines are adding generative summaries (AI Overviews) directly at the top of results, before the traditional ranked links. This is a major interface change. We need to understand how this affects user behavior—do people still read the traditional results, or do they stop at the summary? Does this help or harm how people search?
998.wh: When you change the layout of a search result page dramatically, users might navigate differently than before. The question isn't just whether they like the new feature—it's whether it changes fundamental search behavior in ways that could be harmful (less exploration, higher dependency on summaries) or beneficial (faster answers, less reading required).
998.ap: Researchers placed eye-tracking cameras while users performed search tasks on an interface with AI Overviews placed above traditional results. They measured gaze patterns, recorded which results users clicked, and asked follow-up questions. The data showed increased engagement with AI content but persistent patterns from prior research—users still use traditional results substantially.
998.ww: Generative summaries are attractive and prominent, so people naturally look at them first. But they're not a complete replacement—users still value the original ranked links because they offer different information (you can click through and verify, explore multiple viewpoints, judge source credibility). The system works when both coexist and users can choose which to use.
998.po: Eye-tracking shows that users do engage more with generative summaries than before, but they still look at traditional ranked results and follow similar patterns documented in decades of prior research. The classic "golden triangle" of attention (top-left section gets most gaze) still holds. Users are making a choice to engage with new features while maintaining existing behaviors.

999.bp: Large language models can reason and make recommendations, but current systems rely on a single reasoning path—one train of thought that leads to a final recommendation. This is limiting because there might be multiple good ways to think about the problem, each leading to different (but valid) recommendations. Exploring multiple reasoning paths could find better and more diverse recommendations.
999.wh: When you only explore one reasoning path, you risk missing better alternatives. Imagine a recommendation system that thinks 'this user liked action movies so they'll like this thriller' but never considers 'this user also likes emotional depth, so they might prefer this drama.' Multiple different reasoning chains could reach different but valuable conclusions.
999.ap: The system generates a diverse set of reasoning paths by introducing variations in how the model processes information (dropout applied at inference, small perturbations to internal representations). It then evaluates the quality of each path and selects the highest-quality subset. Finally, it uses reinforcement learning to decide how to weight and combine them, producing a recommendation that aggregates the best insights from multiple independent reasoning chains.
999.ww: Human reasoning works this way—we consider different angles before deciding. The insight is that large language models already have this capability built in; it's just that standard training uses one greedy path. By deliberately introducing controlled randomness during inference (not training), you can make the model explore multiple valid reasoning chains and combine the best ones.
999.po: By exploring multiple reasoning paths and intelligently combining them, the system produces recommendations that are both more accurate (finding more recommendations users actually like) and more diverse (avoiding repetitive suggestions). The method doesn't require additional training on labeled data.

1000.bp: Generative recommendation systems work differently than traditional systems—instead of scoring and ranking items, they generate item identifiers directly, like a language model generates words. This requires solving two intertwined problems: encoding items into tokens (so the model can generate them) and training the model itself to generate good tokens. Current systems solve these separately, which causes misalignment.
1000.wh: Building a generative recommender requires first deciding how to encode items as tokens (words that the model will generate). This encoding step is usually trained only to make tokens easy to decode back into items, not with any consideration for whether those tokens will actually lead to good recommendations. So you get tokens that work okay at reconstruction but poorly for recommendation.
1000.ap: The system sets up two optimization levels: the lower level trains the recommender on tokenized sequences (producing recommendations), and the upper level optimizes the tokenizer based on both how well it reconstructs items and how well the recommendations perform. A meta-learning approach solves this bi-level problem efficiently, and 'gradient surgery' prevents conflicting signals from the two objectives from canceling each other out.
1000.ww: The key insight is that tokenization and recommendation are codependent—good tokens for recommendation aren't necessarily good for reconstruction. By optimizing both objectives together, considering how each change affects the other, the system ensures that tokens are informative (encode important item properties) and discriminative (different recommendations get meaningfully different tokens).
1000.po: The framework jointly optimizes tokenization and recommendation through a two-level approach, ensuring that item identifiers are both interpretable and aligned with the recommendation objective. Experiments show this improves recommendation quality on multiple real-world datasets by fixing the misalignment that hurts traditional approaches.

1001.bp: Educational systems need to diagnose what students understand and don't understand to provide personalized tutoring. Currently, they only track whether answers are right or wrong, missing crucial information about exactly what misconception led to a wrong answer. This limits how well the system can diagnose problems and offer targeted help.
1001.wh: Traditional cognitive diagnosis models treat each answer as simply correct or incorrect, ignoring that different wrong answers reveal different misconceptions. If a student answers 'B' instead of 'C' on a multiple-choice test, that's a richer signal than just 'wrong.' But analyzing what each wrong answer reveals requires understanding the problem deeply—something traditional machine learning models struggle with.
1001.ap: An LLM analyzes each quiz question and produces structured descriptions of what each answer choice reveals about student thinking. These descriptions are converted to embeddings (numerical representations of meaning). The diagnosis model then learns to fuse these semantic embeddings with the student's actual behavior (which answer they picked, how long it took), projecting both into a shared space where they can directly influence each other. Finally, an interpretable diagnosis layer produces both predictions and human-readable explanations.
1001.ww: Large language models understand language and can analyze problems deeply. The insight is to use them to interpret what each answer choice represents (what misconception would lead to choosing it), then feed this semantic understanding into the diagnosis model alongside behavioral data. This combines the strengths of language models (understanding meaning) and behavioral modeling (predicting from patterns).
1001.po: The system produces more accurate diagnoses of student knowledge and generates personalized learning plans that address specific misconceptions revealed by their choice of wrong answers, not just the fact that they answered incorrectly.

1002.bp: Ranking systems learn to score items with large numbers so they can order them correctly. But extremely large scores cause a separate problem: the scores become overconfident, poorly calibrated. When a ranking system gives a relevance score of 1000 vs. 1001, that's meaningless—they're just saying 'first is better than second.' Real applications need scores you can trust to express how much better one item is.
1002.wh: ListMLE is a modern listwise ranking loss that learns to order entire sequences correctly. It works well for ranking, but as a side effect, it creates a feedback loop that keeps pushing scores to larger and larger values. Even after the model learns the correct ordering, gradients keep pushing scores higher, making them poorly calibrated.
1002.ap: During training, the method applies temperature scaling—essentially dividing scores by a temperature parameter that constrains their magnitude. It also modifies the loss to reduce the gradient contributions from positions that aren't directly involved in ordering, preventing the asymmetric tail effects that drive inflation. The result is models that learn correct rankings but maintain reasonable, well-separated scores.
1002.ww: Score inflation happens because the loss function has a built-in asymmetry: certain pairs of positions always contribute gradients even after ordering is correct. By understanding this mechanism mathematically, you can design fixes that constrain how large scores can grow and balance the gradient contributions, preventing inflation without sacrificing ranking quality.
1002.po: By controlling score inflation during training using temperature scaling and adjusting the loss to reduce asymmetric gradient contributions, the method produces ranking models with properly calibrated scores while maintaining ranking accuracy. This matters for real systems where scores need to be interpretable and trustworthy.

1003.bp: Multi-vector retrieval systems like ColBERTv2 represent each document with multiple dense vectors (one per passage chunk) rather than a single vector. This gives much better accuracy but is computationally expensive—comparing a query to millions of documents means millions of comparisons. Making this fast enough for real systems is hard.
1003.wh: GPU systems are great at massive parallelism but process too many candidates. CPU systems are smarter about which candidates to check but can't take advantage of parallel computation. The ideal system would combine both: efficiently reducing candidates like CPUs do, while exploiting GPU parallelism like GPUs do. It's not obvious how.
1003.ap: The system implements a candidate generation kernel optimized for GPUs that preserves the effective filtering strategy of CPU systems. It then adds a score reordering mechanism that reduces the need for expensive synchronization between GPU threads, and a batching strategy that feeds queries and candidates through in batches that fit GPU memory and processing capability.
1003.ww: The key insight is that GPU parallelism and candidate filtering don't have to work against each other. By restructuring the candidate generation process to maintain the efficiency of filtering while exposing more parallelism, and by carefully orchestrating batches to minimize synchronization overhead, you get both benefits—fast filtering and fast computation.
1003.po: The method achieves 11x faster query throughput and 7.6x lower latency than the previous best GPU approach while using the same retrieval accuracy, and is 2.3x cheaper per query than CPU-based systems. This makes multi-vector retrieval practical for production systems with millions of queries per second.

1004.bp: Knowledge base question answering answers questions using structured facts (like Freebase or Wikipedia's knowledge graph). A question like 'Who directed movies with Tom Hanks?' requires understanding the structure of the knowledge graph and finding the right path through it. Modern large language models can help, but generating correct complex structures is hard.
1004.wh: The core insight is that errors propagate. Rather than trying to generate a perfect logical form in one shot, you can generate one hop at a time, check whether it makes sense against the knowledge graph, fix it if needed, then continue. This converts a hard global problem into many easier local problems.
1004.ap: The method decomposes the question into steps, generating one hop of the logical form at a time using a fine-tuned language model. After each step, it checks the intermediate result against the knowledge graph to make sure it's executable and makes sense. If it finds issues, it uses knowledge graph facts as hints to calibrate and correct the model's next generation. Finally, it assembles the corrected hop-wise forms into a complete query.
1004.po: By breaking down logical form generation into steps (hop by hop), using knowledge graph facts to correct errors as they accumulate, and then assembling the paths, the system generates executable queries that work on the knowledge base at scale, dramatically reducing non-executability (queries that crash).

1005.bp: When someone searches online, the system must decide which documents matter most from billions of options. Most search relies on slow, exact-match methods or huge neural networks that need expensive servers. This paper tackles the middle ground: making 'sparse retrieval' fast enough to run cheaply while still using neural-network-style understanding of what users really mean.
1005.wh: The naive approach—checking every document—is too slow. Smarter systems group documents into blocks and skip whole blocks at once, but figuring out which blocks to skip takes time itself. The real tension is that making skip-decisions faster tends to make your results worse, because you're discarding information about whether documents actually match the query.
1005.ap: The authors propose a simpler way to score whether a block of documents is worth visiting: instead of computing expensive scores for every grouping, they use a lightweight scoring scheme that doesn't waste computation on redundant block-level calculations. They pair this with a compact way to store the index and a configuration that works across different neural retrieval models without retuning.
1005.ww: The insight is that you don't need a perfect score for every block—you just need good enough. By mathematically showing that their simpler scoring preserves what matters for ranking, they prove that you can throw away computation without hurting the actual quality of results. It's like skipping every third decision in a checklist if you can show those decisions don't change the outcome.
1005.po: On real search benchmarks, their method runs fast enough for CPU servers while keeping relevance competitive with fancier approaches. The practical benefit is that dense, expensive models can now run on ordinary hardware at scale, making neural search cheaper to deploy.

1006.bp: To find images, videos, or mixed-media content across different websites, systems need to convert everything into one common form—a kind of universal language where similar things are close together. Most systems use large multimodal models trained to match photos to text, but they're built for generation (writing), not for this comparison task. The question is whether that's the best foundation.
1006.wh: Multimodal models trained to write the next word naturally scatter information across many parts of a neural network. That works for generation, but for retrieval you need everything about an image compressed into one small code. A model trained for writing doesn't learn to do this compression because it's never forced to—it can always write by reading from anywhere. So neural codes from generation-trained models stay diffuse and weak.
1006.ap: The authors restructure the model's internal attention flow and add a new training task: given only the final 'summary' code from the model, try to reconstruct the original image and text. This forces the model to pack all important information into that code. They call this process 'collaborative attention reconstruction.'
1006.ww: When a model has to squeeze everything into one code and then rebuild the input from it, that code must contain everything that matters. The same principle lets you compress a video into a short summary—you lose detail but keep the essence. By training with this reconstruction goal first, the codes become dense and useful, and then regular learning-from-pairs training works better on top.
1006.po: On multimodal benchmarks, images and text matched this way retrieve more accurate results. The practical win is that you can now take models built for writing and efficiently adapt them for the cross-modal search tasks that power image search, video recommendation, and mixed-media platforms.

1007.bp: Recommender systems must decide what to show a user next without experimenting (playing items and watching if they click), because experimenting hurts the current experience. Instead, they learn from logged past behavior. The challenge is that one user might like cooking videos and action movies—two completely different things—and the system must learn to recognize both interests, not average them into mediocrity.
1007.wh: Standard recommendation policies (which just pick the single 'best' item) fail here because they can't represent 'a user likes both X and Y'—they can only output one thing. If you train them with loss functions that reward single peaks, they collapse to averaging position between different interests, producing items nobody actually wants. Even newer diffusion models that generate complex patterns are too slow at serving time when you need an answer in milliseconds.
1007.ap: The system uses a mathematical structure (a 'flow model') that can represent all the things a user might like. First it trains this flow model to mimic the historical behavior patterns. Then it uses a 'value function' (a neural network that learns which actions are good) to identify which parts of that flow represent high-quality recommendations. Finally, it distills that into a single-step policy using an 'advantage condition'—a mathematical switch that tells the model 'pick from the good parts only.'
1007.ww: The flow model works like a map of user preferences, showing all the peaks and valleys. The value function marks which peaks are actually good (users spent time there). By conditioning on high-value regions, you train a fast model to sample only from neighborhoods you know are safe. It's like learning that a user likes both comedies and dramas, then building a fast filter that samples only from those two shelves, not the whole store.
1007.po: Tests on five real datasets plus a live recommendation platform show the method generates recommendations users actually choose, with faster response times than diffusion baselines. The payoff is a recommendation system that serves accurate, diverse suggestions in real time.

1008.bp: Social media spreads misinformation through chains of reposts and comments. Detecting fake news is critical for platform trust. Smart systems look at the structure of these chains (who reposted what) rather than just reading the words, because true news spreads differently than false news. But now LLMs can craft convincing fake posts, making this task much harder.
1008.wh: Graph-based detectors learn patterns from how information spreads: true stories tend to spread in certain shapes, while false stories spread in others. But when an attacker uses an LLM to inject posts that agree or disagree in ways that confuse the detector, they pollute both the text signals and the structural pattern. A detector trained on clean data gets fooled by these adversarial posts because they break the rules it learned.
1008.ap: The authors use a large language model as a teacher, not to detect fake news, but to explain each piece of information: 'This post says X, and it fits/doesn't fit with the overall narrative.' They compute these explanations offline (once, for all data) so no LLM runs at detection time. Then they train the detector to align with these explanations, ignoring posts that contradict the overall narrative and trusting ones that fit it.
1008.ww: An LLM can articulate whether a message contradicts the broader story—and that check is robust because it looks at global sense, not just surface patterns. By using an LLM-written narrative as a stable anchor, the detector learns structural invariances (things that don't change when adversaries tinker). Even if an attacker injects a post that looks structurally normal, if it contradicts the narrative, the detector learns to distrust it.
1008.po: On three real datasets including adversarial LLM attacks, the method catches more fake news than existing methods, and does so without needing to call an LLM during detection (keeping inference cost low). The benefit is a detector that stays robust as generation models improve.

1009.bp: When asking an AI system a question that requires outside knowledge (like 'Who won the World Cup in 2022?'), feeding in many relevant documents usually helps—but reading 10,000 words makes the response slow and sometimes the AI gets confused by contradictions. The tradeoff is real: you want enough context to be accurate but not so much that computation explodes or the model trips over itself.
1009.wh: Current systems trim context by ranking it (most likely to be useful comes first) and cutting off at a fixed threshold. But this assumes all documents are equally important for the task—they're not. One source might be crucial for answering 'when,' while another matters only for 'where.' A fixed cut loses information the model actually needs, and ranking doesn't know what the model will ultimately ask the retrieved facts to explain.
1009.ap: Instead of trimming context before giving it to the language model, the authors teach the model itself to pick what it needs as it's generating the answer. The model is trained with a mechanism that lets it flag which parts of the context window are relevant right now, so it can read selectively rather than scanning everything. This is like a reader skimming for one piece of info while ignoring the rest.
1009.ww: Only the model knows what detail it needs to answer this specific question correctly. By learning to select context as it writes, the model can adapt its reading to the question and the generation so far. When it needs dates, it pulls date-bearing passages; when it needs names, it focuses elsewhere. This dynamic selection is more efficient and more accurate than pre-ranking.
1009.po: Across multiple question-answering benchmarks, answers are more factually correct and latency improves because the model reads less. The practical payoff is question-answering systems that are both faster and more reliable, which unlocks real-time QA for time-sensitive queries.

1010.bp: Recommending products based on images and descriptions is harder than recommending based on past purchases alone, because visual and textual information don't always align—the same item looks different in photos and descriptions. The goal is to build user profiles from mixed signals (what they viewed, what they liked) and item profiles from mixed signals (image, text, past buyers) that actually work together.
1010.wh: When you initialize a user's preference from their viewing history, you get noise: someone who clicked once by accident drags the profile in the wrong direction. For items, you build a graph (item A connects to item B because similar users bought both), but the graph is full of weak links—items that happen to co-occur without being similar. Both noise sources degrade recommendation quality, and they compound when you try to learn from noisy signals.
1010.ap: For users: the system writes out what each user actually did in plain language, then asks an LLM to interpret it ('This user favors outdoor gear and cookbooks'), creating a cleaner profile than raw clicking patterns. For items: instead of relying on raw co-occurrence, the system removes weak graph edges using a statistical threshold, then adds back edges that represent 'if you like this item, you'll like that one' based on which audiences buy both.
1010.ww: LLMs excel at reading behavior and inferring intent—they're trained on human explanations. Using them to interpret history bypasses raw noise from accidents or stale preferences. For item graphs, removing weak edges and strengthening audience-based links creates a denser signal where remaining edges are more meaningful, much like pruning a garden to make it healthier.
1010.po: On multimodal recommendation benchmarks, this approach improves the ability to suggest items users click on. The payoff is that visual and textual features start working in concert, boosting recommendation accuracy for e-commerce and media platforms.

1011.bp: Training a recommender system requires feeding it negative examples—items the user definitely doesn't want—so it learns what not to recommend. Picking those negatives smartly is crucial: bad negatives waste compute and let the model learn wrong patterns. The question is how to automatically identify which items are truly disliked versus items the user just hasn't seen yet (and might like).
1011.wh: Simple strategies (random negatives, picking popular items) create false negatives: they pick items that seem disliked but actually match the user's interests—you just haven't proven it yet. The recommender then learns to avoid items it shouldn't. Hard-negative mining (picking close-but-wrong items) also tends to pick items in the same cluster as items the user did like, which means they might be similar to the target—again, false negatives. You need a way to say 'this item is truly different from what the user likes,' not just 'this item is hard to distinguish.'
1011.ap: The authors model items as points in clusters (unsupervised grouping by similarity). When a user likes an item, they sample negatives from three regions: the same cluster (but with decreasing probability over time to reduce false negatives), nearby clusters (hard negatives), and far-away clusters (easy negatives). They adjust these probabilities as training progresses, like an exploration-exploitation balance in a slot machine.
1011.ww: True negatives (items the user truly dislikes) are structurally different, so they tend to live in different regions. False negatives live near the positive item. By starting conservative and gradually shifting away from the positive cluster, the model learns which nearby items are actually false positives, and trains on true negatives instead. It's like progressively broadening your search circle as you learn more.
1011.po: Across three sequential recommenders and three datasets, this sampling strategy speeds up training and improves ranking quality. The payoff is that recommender systems train faster and learn better from the same compute budget.

1012.bp: Language models can now answer complex questions by using tools (searching the web, running code, checking databases), but orchestrating multiple tools is hard—the model must know when to search versus compute versus check, and in what order. Building agents that reliably use tools well requires large amounts of trajectory data, which is expensive to generate.
1012.wh: If you just prompt a model to use tools, it makes mistakes—calling the wrong tool, missing steps, or looping. Training data of tool-use trajectories is scarce and expensive. Synthetic data from the model itself is biased (it learns its own mistakes). You need data that covers both easy cases (building confidence) and hard cases (learning new strategies), but generating and labeling all of it is labor-intensive.
1012.ap: The system generates synthetic tool-use trajectories in two ways: one that greedily picks steps, and one that explores alternatives. This gives diverse examples. Then it filters out bad trajectories and organizes the remaining ones from simple to hard (curriculum). It trains the model in two stages: first with supervised learning to imitate good trajectories, then with reinforcement learning to refine decisions using rewards for tool coordination and accuracy.
1012.ww: By mixing greedy and exploratory generation, you capture both typical behavior and creative solutions. Organizing by difficulty (easy first) is how humans learn—you don't start with the hardest problem. Supervised learning establishes baseline tool-use patterns, and reinforcement learning refines the boundaries between when to use which tool. A model that starts with supervised imitation learns faster under reinforcement learning than one starting cold.
1012.po: On 13 benchmarks including web navigation, the model chooses tools more effectively and completes tasks more often. The payoff is LLM-based agents that can reason through complex, multi-step problems that require strategic tool use.

1013.bp: When you want to find similar images across two different databases (one from Getty Images, one from Flickr), the visual style differs enough to fool simple matching. A model trained on one dataset often performs worse on another because the appearance, lighting, and composition rules are different. The challenge is matching without any labeled pairs from both datasets to learn from.
1013.wh: Existing unsupervised methods learn from within each dataset (finding groups of similar images) and then try to match across. But internal structure doesn't guarantee cross-domain alignment—a 'group of photos' in one domain might not correspond to a 'group of photos' in the other if the way they're organized is different. Without labeled pairs, the model can easily misalign. You need stable, external guidance that works across domains.
1013.ap: The authors use a pre-trained vision model (one that's seen billions of images) to judge which images are conceptually similar without fine-tuning. They build two concept banks (one per domain) using this external judge, marking image pairs that are confidently similar across domains and confidently different. Then they train with a loss that pulls similar images close and pushes different ones apart, while also keeping images within each domain well-organized.
1013.ww: A pre-trained model has already learned what 'a dog' or 'a car' looks like across styles, so it can provide stable anchors across domains without retraining. By using it to build concept banks first, the model learns from reliable external signals rather than guessing from internal structure. The geometry-based organizing (pull-and-push forces around concepts) maintains structure within each domain while aligning across.
1013.po: On cross-domain image-retrieval benchmarks, this approach finds similar images more accurately than methods that only use internal patterns. The payoff is that search engines can match images across different sources and styles reliably, enabling federated image search.

1014.bp: When evaluating search results, human judges often score multiple dimensions: Is the answer exact? Does it cover all angles? Is it relevant to the question? Using an LLM as an automated judge is cheap but raises a question: can these multi-faceted grades help train the search system itself, not just evaluate it?
1014.wh: Search systems learn to rank by optimizing a loss based on binary judgments (good or bad). Multi-criteria LLM grades are richer but it's unclear how to use them—they look like evaluation signals, not training signals. You could average them, but that loses the information that 'contextual fit' might matter more than 'exactness' for this query. The tension is between the detail in multi-criteria judgments and the simplicity required for training.
1014.ap: The authors treat each criterion grade (exactness, coverage, topicality, contextual fit) as a separate feature in a learning-to-rank model. They train the ranker to optimize based on these features rather than raw retrieval scores alone, using existing evaluation data from human judgments to validate the approach.
1014.ww: Each criterion captures a different reason a result matters. By giving the ranker access to all of them, it can learn that sometimes 'contextual fit' outweighs 'topicality,' depending on the query. It's like telling a search engine 'I know you thought relevance was the main thing, but this question cares more about whether the result is timely.' LLMs grade these dimensions reasonably well, so their output becomes training signal.
1014.po: Results improve by 14-36% in ranking quality, with gains strongest for weaker search systems and complementary for strong ones. The practical payoff is that LLM-based evaluation becomes a training loop: evaluate queries, feed grades back to training, improve system, repeat.

1015.bp: Recommender systems use neural codes (short sequences of numbers) to represent items, then add new items and update these codes as user behavior changes. Updating codes carefully is crucial—change them too much and the model that uses these codes stops working; change them too little and you miss important signals.
1015.wh: New items are assigned codes based on what other users did with them (collaborative signals). But real-world streams add new items constantly and user behavior drifts—what 'similar to other electronics' meant last month might shift this month as new competitors enter. Blindly retraining both the tokenizer and recommender is expensive. Trying to fine-tune just the tokenizer risks flipping codes for old items, breaking the recommender's learned associations.
1015.ap: The system tracks which items are drifting (changing patterns) and which are stable. It fine-tunes the codes for drifting items while keeping stable items fixed. It uses a module that computes 'drift confidence' for each item based on how much its collaborative patterns have shifted. Then it reassigns codes in stages: first loose (allowing more change), then strict (locking in), so the recommender can adapt gradually.
1015.ww: By identifying which items actually changed, you don't waste adaptation budget on items that are stable. The recommender learned alignments between old codes and meanings—codes that didn't change don't break those alignments. Gradual reassignment (loose-to-strict) lets the recommender's weights adjust to the new codes incrementally, like adjusting glasses gradually rather than suddenly changing the prescription.
1015.po: On benchmarks with streaming item arrivals, this approach avoids forgetting old items while incorporating new information. The payoff is a recommender system that adapts to new items and behavior shifts without expensive full retraining or catastrophic breakdowns.

1016.bp: When a researcher or patent examiner reviews hundreds of documents to find relevant ones, they must decide when to stop looking. Look too early and you miss important documents; keep looking too long and you waste time. The question is how to set the stopping point based on the actual cost of missing a document versus the cost of reading more.
1016.wh: Existing approaches try to achieve a fixed recall target (find 95% of relevant documents) without considering why the user needs documents at all. But the value differs: a patent examiner might desperately need every relevant prior art reference, while a researcher doing a systematic review might accept some misses if they've found enough patterns. One person's 'done' is another's 'incomplete.'
1016.ap: The authors use decision theory to derive three stopping rules based on the value of perfect information—a mathematical concept that says: how much would it be worth to magically know if the next unseen document is relevant? If that value is less than the cost of reading it, stop. They weight the rules by the true cost of missing documents versus the cost of reading.
1016.ww: In decision theory, the optimal stopping point is where the expected cost of one more read (reading time plus potential cost of misses) equals the expected benefit (finding a relevant document). By computing this mathematically, the system adapts to different tasks: patent examining (high cost of missing references) stops later; systematic review (lower cost) stops sooner. It respects the actual reason for searching.
1016.po: On patent and medical review datasets, the method recommends stopping earlier (saving effort) when it's safe and continues longer when misses are costly. The payoff is a stopping rule that's tuned to the task, not a one-size-fits-all threshold.

1017.bp: In search engines, users click on results, but clicks don't always mean relevance—a user might click on a result just because it's at the top of the page, even if it's not ideal. Fixing this bias is important for learning accurate ranking. Two-tower models try to separate 'how relevant is this' from 'why did the user click,' but there's a fundamental problem: you can't always tell them apart from clicks alone.
1017.wh: Mathematically, identifiability is the question: given click data, can you uniquely determine what the model's parameters must be, or could many different parameter sets explain the same clicks? If the same documents appear in different positions across many queries, you can separate position bias from relevance. But in real data with sparse positional coverage, this separation breaks down and you can't trust the learned bias.
1017.ap: The authors test whether each parameter is truly identifiable by deliberately changing it, retraining the model on real data, and measuring whether the click-prediction loss increases significantly. If the loss doesn't change when you shift a parameter, that parameter isn't identified by the data—you can set it to anything. If loss increases sharply, it's identified.
1017.ww: Identifiable parameters are constrained by the data: the data is incompatible with wrong values. Unidentifiable parameters are invisible to the data—wrong values fit equally well. By testing this directly on the real dataset and model, you find which parameters the clicks actually inform. This diagnostic works because it doesn't assume infinite data or specific click-logging policies.
1017.po: On simulated and real search datasets, the diagnostic reveals which bias parameters can be learned and which are unidentifiable due to data sparsity or logging policy. The payoff is knowing when a two-tower model has actually learned position bias versus when it's just fitting noise, preventing false confidence in ranking fixes.

1018.bp: Modern neural networks (like ModernBERT) beat older BERT at almost everything—dense retrieval, classification—yet they mysteriously underperform on sparse retrieval, where you're matching keywords in queries to keywords in documents. The mystery deserves solving because sparse retrieval is practical: it works on CPU and is interpretable.
1018.wh: Older BERT uses a limited vocabulary of common words and morphological variations are grouped together. Modern BERT uses a raw, unreduced vocabulary that preserves every spelling variation. This was smart for generation (lossless reconstruction), but for retrieval it means the model wastes capacity distinguishing 'run,' 'runs,' and 'running' when they're the same concept for matching. It's like forcing a keyword searcher to distinguish them instead of treating them as the same.
1018.ap: The authors map modern BERT's vocabulary to a coarser, older-style vocabulary (grouping morphological variations). They preserve the model's learned geometry using a spatial topology method (keeping similar words near each other in the new vocabulary). They also add a calibration mechanism that realigns the model's learned patterns with the new structure without 'dying' neurons or collapsing to dense vectors.
1018.ww: Sparse retrieval benefits from a vocabulary where 'run' and 'runs' are the same token because it reduces the space of possible word patterns the model must learn. Modern neural theory shows this coarse-grained vocabulary reduces the complexity the model must learn, tightening generalization bounds. By preserving the geometry of learned similarity, you keep the model's linguistic knowledge while fixing its vocabulary mismatch.
1018.po: ModernBERT adapted this way reaches state-of-the-art performance on sparse retrieval benchmarks (+4.7 improvement), matching or beating older BERT. The payoff is that you can use modern, more powerful architectures for both dense and sparse retrieval, unifying the field.

1019.bp: In real e-commerce, users interact with items in multiple ways: they view products, favorite items, add them to carts, and purchase. Each interaction type tells you something different. Recommender systems that use multiple behaviors together are more accurate than those using purchase alone. But real-world data arrives as a stream—new views and purchases arrive constantly—and systems must adapt without forgetting.
1019.wh: Most multi-behavior recommendation models are trained offline on static datasets. When data arrives in a stream, retraining them from scratch is expensive. Fine-tuning on new data causes 'catastrophic forgetting': the model unlearns what it knew from old purchases and views. Yet you can't ignore new behaviors, because they carry current user interests. The tension is between efficiency (avoid retraining) and learning (adapt to new signals) while maintaining knowledge (don't forget old patterns).
1019.ap: The system builds a graph of users and items where edges are labeled by behavior type (view, favorite, purchase, cart). It uses incremental graph convolution (updating the graph structure as new edges arrive) and multi-task learning (optimizing for predicting each behavior type simultaneously). It tracks which parameters are changing due to new data and updates them carefully.
1019.ww: Incremental updates let you process new edges without rescan the whole graph. Multi-task learning maintains knowledge across behavior types by forcing the model to stay good at all of them (if it forgets views to focus on purchases, the view-prediction loss climbs). The key insight is that heterogeneous behaviors compete for model capacity—by jointly optimizing, you preserve the balance.
1019.po: On streaming benchmark datasets, this approach adapts to new items and behaviors while maintaining recommendation quality on old items. The payoff is a recommender that stays current as new data arrives without full retraining or catastrophic forgetting.

1020.bp: When you show someone a video or a stream of events, what grabs their attention? Usually the exciting moments at the start and end. But when a recommendation system watches your viewing history to guess what you'll like next, it needs to pay equal attention to the middle parts—the quiet but informative behaviors—not just fixate on your first and last clicks. The system's architecture is literally broken in a predictable way, and this paper fixes it.
1020.wh: Attention-based systems (the kind that look at a sequence of items and try to understand patterns) have an unexpected quirk: they tend to ignore the middle of the sequence, treating the beginning and end as more important. This happens even when you shuffle the data around, so it is not about where things sit in the sequence—it is baked into how the system is designed. The problem is deep, not superficial.
1020.ww: By directly counteracting the architectural quirk during training and then cleaning up the leftover bias at prediction time, the system learns to distribute its attention more fairly across all moments in a user's history. The middle behaviors—which often contain the most meaningful signals about preference—get proper weight again.
1020.po: The fix leads to measurably better ranking quality across multiple datasets. The improvements are consistent because both the training masking and the inference calibration work together: one prevents the model from learning bad habits, the other catches any slips that still occur.

1021.bp: Finding a specific person from a text description in a crowded photo—say, 'tall man with glasses'—is crucial for public safety and criminal investigations. Existing systems fine-tune enormous vision-language models like CLIP on this task, but doing so fully is expensive and the model tends to overfit to narrow examples and fails on new scenarios. There is a smarter way to adapt these massive pre-trained models without retraining the whole thing.
1021.wh: Fine-tuning giant models costs huge amounts of compute and memory. Partially adapting them (using lightweight parameter-efficient methods) keeps costs down, but these methods struggle with the fine details of identity clues and are easily thrown off by noisy training data with mismatched image-text pairs. The system is caught between efficiency and accuracy.
1021.ap: This paper builds a lightweight adapter that captures both broad patterns (the full person silhouette) and fine details (specific facial features) separately, using a multi-level relational approach. It also learns to downweight confusing or wrong training examples on the fly, and adds a cross-modal verification step that checks the image-to-text and text-to-image alignment to catch ambiguous cases where the same text might match multiple people.
1021.ww: By modeling features at multiple scales (coarse and fine), the system picks up both the obvious and subtle identity markers that full fine-tuning would capture, but using far fewer parameters. Downweighting noisy examples prevents the model from learning wrong associations, and the verification step removes ambiguities that would otherwise poison the final ranking.
1021.po: The result is a system that works well on new, unseen people and domains without full retraining. It keeps computational costs low while improving matching accuracy, making it practical for real-world deployment on criminal investigation databases.

1022.bp: A recommendation system that shows you what movies to watch, what songs to listen to, or what products to buy must juggle a tension: people actually enjoy both mainstream hits (the popular things everyone watches) and niche favorites (the obscure gems only they care about). Most systems squash this diversity by letting popular content dominate the signal, drowning out the personalized stuff. The goal is to recommend both fairly.
1022.wh: When a system builds a recommendation model using graph-based learning (a method that treats users and items as nodes in a network and spreads information through connections), it treats all interests the same way. Information from popular items overwhelms the signal, and niche interests get buried. The system has no way to say 'this user cares deeply about indie horror films, even though most people watch blockbusters.'
1022.ap: This paper separates the user-item network into two independent parts: one that models popular interests and one that models niche interests. It does this by decomposing the network signals using frequency-domain math (thinking of interests like sound waves—high frequency for niche, low frequency for popular). It also uses a four-quadrant graph structure that lets the system think about behaviors and popularity separately, then combines them through multiple supervised learning tasks at once.
1022.ww: By splitting the network into two pathways, each interest type is modeled with its own logic and weight. Popular interests do not drown out niche ones because they are on separate channels. The frequency decomposition is based on a real principle: similar frequencies should influence similar things, so popular and niche interests, which have different 'frequencies', naturally separate.
1022.po: Across four real production datasets, the system recommends items with both higher accuracy (people like more of what it suggests) and better diversity (it actually surfaces niche items alongside mainstream ones). Users get better personalization because the system respects both the hits they watch and the deep cuts they treasure.

1023.bp: When you ask a question like 'which countries have a population over 100 million?', the answer might live in a table buried in some Wikipedia article. Yet finding that table is hard because the structure of the table (rows and columns) does not immediately tell you what it contains semantically. Most systems need labeled examples to learn the connection between queries and tables, making them useless when no training data exists. This paper finds tables with zero labeled examples.
1023.wh: Existing table retrieval systems either mangle the table into text (losing structure) or require large labeled datasets showing which tables answer which questions. In a cold-start scenario—day one with a new table corpus and no queries yet—both approaches fail. The system must infer meaning from the table's own structure and content without any external guidance.
1023.ap: Instead of learning from query-table pairs, this system learns the structure of the entire table corpus first. It represents each table using both its internal structure (columns, data types) and links to external knowledge graphs (like Wikidata). At search time, it uses three retrieval signals in parallel: dense semantic matching (like traditional search), symbolic graph traversal (following connections in the knowledge graph), and sparse keyword matching (exact term matches). These three signals are combined dynamically based on the query.
1023.ww: By modeling the corpus itself rather than query-table pairs, the system grounds its understanding in what the tables actually contain. The external knowledge graph links provide semantic anchors (e.g., 'population' is a demographic attribute). The hybrid retrieval approach—combining dense, symbolic, and sparse methods—means no single weakness matters: if keywords work, great; if the structure is clear, that works too; if semantic similarity helps, it will be found.
1023.po: On public benchmarks, the system retrieves the right tables with high precision and recall, even for implicit queries where the connection between question and table is not obvious. It works on day one with no labeled training data, solving the cold-start problem that plagues existing methods.

1024.bp: A legal researcher trying to find relevant court cases from thousands of documents needs precision—every wrong result wastes time and can lead to bad arguments. The standard approach runs a fast, coarse search first, then a slower, detailed re-ranking step second. But when the fast search misses the target, the slow step cannot fix it, and when the fast and slow steps disagree, quality suffers. A unified system could do both jobs better.
1024.wh: Two-stage retrieval pipelines suffer from cascade errors: if the first stage filters out the right document, the second stage will never see it. Also, the fast and slow stages may have learned contradictory signals, so they pull in different directions. And both stages can assign high confidence to documents that are actually irrelevant—a 'phantom hit' that breaks the ranking.
1024.ap: This paper builds a single model that does both retrieval and re-ranking at once, with shared weights between them. To stop the phantom-hit problem, it trains the model to see pure-negative document groups (documents that are definitely wrong), teaches it to be uncertain about borderline cases, and uses entropy regularization to avoid overconfident wrong answers. The training objective pushes different margins of confidence for different difficulty levels.
1024.ww: By unifying the stages, errors do not cascade: the model reasons about the full document space at once. By explicitly training on pure-negatives and penalizing overconfidence, the model learns to say 'I do not know' rather than guess. The entropy regularization means the model spreads its confidence more fairly, so truly relevant documents stand out.
1024.po: On legal benchmarks, the system beats both independent two-stage pipelines and other unified approaches, achieving state-of-the-art precision and recall for legal document retrieval. The improvement is especially large on borderline cases where confidence calibration matters most.

1025.bp: Recommendation systems running on phones and smart watches need to use very little memory and power. Yet most systems store recommendation models with high-precision numbers that take up megabytes. Quantization shrinks the model by using low-precision numbers, but doing so naively (rounding all numbers the same way) loses accuracy. For recommendation systems with complex network structures, a smarter quantization strategy can keep accuracy high.
1025.wh: Graph-based recommendation models treat users and items as nodes in a network. The numbers attached to each node (called embeddings) vary wildly—some nodes are similar to many others, while some are unique. Quantizing all embeddings with the same precision scheme does not work because a uniform quantization breaks the delicate differences between nodes. The system needs to understand which nodes are easily confused and which need more precision.
1025.ap: Instead of quantizing all dimensions of an embedding uniformly, this paper groups the dimensions of each node's embedding into multiple chunks based on how their values spread. Then it quantizes each chunk separately. During training with the model still learning, the chunk boundaries are learned dynamically. After training, the system clusters similar nodes and applies chunk-wise quantization based on what it learned. Some nodes get fine-grained chunks (more precision), others get coarse chunks (faster, smaller).
1025.ww: By treating each chunk independently, the quantization respects the actual distribution of values in the network. Nodes that are similar get similar quantization, preserving the neighborhood structure that the recommendation algorithm relies on. The dynamic learning during training means the model learns what precision is actually needed for each part of each node.
1025.po: Across multiple real datasets, the quantized models match the accuracy of full-precision models while using far less memory and compute. This makes it practical to run recommendation systems directly on resource-limited devices without losing recommendation quality.

1026.bp: Given a single 2D photograph of a scene, find all the 3D models in a library that match it. This is hard because a 2D image and a 3D model are fundamentally different: they express the world in different dimensions and from different viewpoints. Most prior work needs labeled 3D-to-2D pairs to learn the bridge, but labeling is expensive. This paper learns the bridge with no such labels.
1026.wh: The 2D-to-3D gap is enormous: a 2D image loses depth, a 3D model has no single viewpoint, and categories have imbalanced representation (some objects are common, others rare). Previous unsupervised methods get confused by these gaps, and their decision boundaries for 'same object' versus 'different object' drift differently in the 2D and 3D spaces. Also, not all neighbors of a query image should be equally important; some are more structurally similar than others.
1026.ap: This paper attacks the problem in three coordinated ways. First, it carefully constructs mini-batches that balance category representation so rare objects are not ignored. Second, it uses an adversarial technique to align the decision boundaries between the 2D and 3D worlds—making the model prefer sharp separation between similar and dissimilar objects in both spaces equally. Third, it builds a cross-modal graph showing which 2D and 3D samples are neighbors, then spreads this relational structure through the model, ensuring that the neighborhood relationships discovered in one modality are preserved in the other.
1026.ww: The balanced batches prevent category bias. The aligned decision boundaries mean 'close' and 'far apart' have the same meaning in both modality spaces. The graph-based neighborhood consistency is a direct signal: if two images are neighbors in the 2D space, their matched 3D models should be neighbors too. This preserves the semantic structure that the model learns.
1026.po: On benchmark datasets for image-based 3D model retrieval, the system consistently outperforms prior unsupervised methods, finding the matching 3D models with higher accuracy. The improvements come entirely from smarter use of unlabeled data, no additional labels needed.

1027.bp: Depression is a silent disease—people often hide symptoms in public. But social media reveals spontaneous, unfiltered behavior: the videos someone posts, the tone of their voice, the visual style they choose. Mining these signals from real social media data could enable early screening at scale, far earlier than clinical detection. The challenge is combining visual (video) and acoustic (audio tone) information intelligently.
1027.wh: Combining multiple types of data (modalities) is hard because they speak different languages: a video frame shows what someone looks like, but audio tone shows how they feel, and these do not directly relate. Naive fusion methods just average or concatenate the signals, missing the fact that visual and audio should inform each other. Also, there is a gap in what each modality means—visual and acoustic features are fundamentally different and hard to align.
1027.ap: This paper builds a system where visual and audio information guide each other dynamically. It constructs a graph showing which visual samples are similar to which audio samples, finding complementary information (visual cues the audio misses, and vice versa). For each modality separately, it uses a graph-informed residual learning approach (adding small learned corrections to base features, guided by the graph structure). After refining each modality separately, it fuses them together and makes a final prediction.
1027.ww: By having modalities guide each other, the system learns which visual signals matter for depression and which audio signals matter, rather than treating them as separate problems. The graph explicitly captures cross-modal relationships, so the refining step for audio is informed by what visual cues mean. The residual approach adds only small, targeted corrections, preserving each modality's integrity while improving alignment.
1027.po: Tested on real social media depression datasets, the system detects depression more accurately than methods that ignore the cross-modal guidance. The improvements are consistent, suggesting the mutual guidance actually captures meaningful patterns in how depression manifests across visual and acoustic behavior.

1028.bp: When recommending a sequence of items (like a playlist or a binge-watch order), systems often think in frequency-domain terms, decomposing a user's preference patterns into high-frequency (recent, quick changes) and low-frequency (stable, long-term) signals. Yet most systems handle both simultaneously in one model, not recognizing that short-term mood shifts and long-term taste require different reasoning. A smarter system treats them separately.
1028.wh: Frequency-domain reasoning in recommendations is powerful but crude: amplifying high-frequency signals to capture recent trends also amplifies random noise. Also, short-term and long-term preferences have different temporal rhythms and should use different model paths. One model trying to do both ends up compromising on both. The system needs dedicated pathways for different timescales.
1028.ap: This paper separates the recommendation model into distinct pathways: one for long-term preference (stable, low-frequency patterns) and one for short-term preference (recent, high-frequency shifts). For noise handling, it intelligently suppresses low-energy noise in each frequency band while keeping the important signal components. The two pathways make their predictions independently, then a learned gate dynamically decides how much weight to give each pathway based on the current context.
1028.ww: By decomposing into separate pathways, each pathway can be tuned for its own temporal characteristics. The energy-aware denoising respects the fact that some frequency bands are inherently noisier than others—it adapts to each band's energy distribution rather than using a one-size-fits-all denoising. The dynamic gate means long-term taste dominates when the user is browsing calmly, but short-term mood matters when they are actively searching.
1028.po: On five real datasets, the system improves ranking metrics (how well predicted rankings match user clicks) by average of 6.67%, with particularly large gains in capturing recent preference shifts. The noise suppression also improves stability, reducing spiky incorrect predictions.

1029.bp: Large multimodal models (systems that see both images and text) can make mistakes—maybe they misidentify a person or get a fact wrong. Retraining the entire model is impractical. In-context editing offers a shortcut: can you fix a specific mistake just by adding context to the input, without changing the model weights? The challenge is controlling which part of the model actually makes the edit.
1029.wh: Naive in-context editing (just adding corrective context to the input) is unreliable because the model might ignore the context or misunderstand which mistake to fix. The system needs to know precisely which neurons or components inside the model are responsible for the error and which context matters. Without this targeting, editing feels like a lucky guess.
1029.ap: This paper identifies specific neurons inside the model that are involved in the mistake (called 'contextual neurons'). It then selectively updates only those neurons with context-aware changes. The identification process looks at which neurons respond to both the image and the text context. The editing step then injects new information into exactly those identified neurons, leaving the rest of the model untouched.
1029.ww: By targeting specific neurons, the edit affects only the relevant reasoning path inside the model. The system does not need to retrain anything; it just modulates internal signals at inference time.
