This is like knowing exactly which neuron in a brain cares about 'who is in this photo' and nudging just that one, rather than dosing the whole brain with a medicine.
1029.po: Tested on three popular large multimodal models with benchmark edits (correcting wrong associations between images and descriptions), the system successfully fixes mistakes without affecting unrelated knowledge. The neuron-level approach is more targeted and reliable than previous in-context editing methods that just add context blindly.

1030.bp: When you see the name 'Washington' in text, does it mean the US state, the capital city, or a person's surname? The answer depends on context and corroborating signals. Multimodal entity linking uses text, images, and structured knowledge together to disambiguate. The challenge is that different modalities offer contradictory clues, and one modality can dominate unfairly, drowning out the others. A fair system balances all signals.
1030.wh: Existing systems either couple all modalities tightly (so one error propagates to all) or use global aggregation (averaging modality signals, which loses nuance). Some entities have clear visual signatures (the Statue of Liberty is distinctive), while others are only identified by text or metadata. Forcing a uniform strategy ignores these differences. The system also needs to know not just if the modalities agree, but precisely how they should agree.
1030.ap: This paper uses expert networks that handle different aspects of the problem in parallel (a divide-and-conquer strategy). Each expert specializes in one type of correspondence—say, visual cues or textual mention patterns. The system learns which experts should matter using a routing mechanism guided by KL divergence (a measure of how different two probability distributions are). It also builds a hierarchical graph showing relationships at multiple levels of detail, and lets the modalities refine each other through this graph rather than just averaging.
1030.ww: By separating the problem into independent experts, one modality's error does not ruin the others. The KL-guided routing means experts learn to specialize: one might focus on visual cues, another on mention patterns, and the system adaptively weights their input. The hierarchical graph captures both coarse (this is a person, not a place) and fine (this is a historical figure, not a celebrity) distinctions.
1030.po: On benchmark datasets for multimodal entity linking, the system consistently ranks higher than prior methods, correctly disambiguating entity mentions even when modalities conflict. The improvements are largest on ambiguous cases where modalities gave contradictory signals.

1031.bp: Complex questions often need multi-step reasoning: 'Which Nobel Prize winners published papers at MIT in the last five years?' requires finding Nobel laureates, checking their MIT affiliations, and verifying recent publications. Typical retrieval-augmented generation systems treat this as one big retrieval problem, but the reasoning and retrieval needed for each step is different. Splitting the task into specialized subtasks could work better.
1031.wh: A single model trying to handle high-level planning (what are the sub-questions?) and detailed execution (find papers on this specific topic) ends up doing both poorly. It gets distracted by irrelevant details while trying to plan, or loses sight of the big picture while executing. Also, different parts of the question benefit from different tools—some need a fact-checking database, others need semantic search.
1031.ap: This paper separates the task into two layers. A high-level planner decomposes the complex question into subtasks and coordinates the overall strategy. For each subtask, a specialized agent equipped with specific tools (knowledge bases, search engines, reasoning modules) handles execution. The planner reasons about how to combine the results from different agents into a final answer. Each agent can focus on its own domain without distraction from the overall goal.
1031.ww: By separating planning from execution, the planner can think strategically without the noise of implementation details. Each specialized agent becomes expert in its domain because it sees only relevant subtasks. This mirrors how humans solve complex problems—we break them down, assign specialists to pieces, then synthesize results—rather than trying to do everything with one person.
1031.po: On complex cross-modal search benchmarks (questions that require combining information from text, tables, and images), this hierarchical approach significantly outperforms flat retrieval-augmented generation systems. The separation of concerns leads to both better reasoning and better execution.

1032.bp: When an AI agent needs to retrieve a table from a database to answer a user's instruction—'find a table with sales data by quarter, excluding 2024'—relevance depends on both topical similarity (sales, quarterly) and following specific constraints (exclude a year, include certain columns). Existing table retrieval systems focus on topical relevance alone and ignore constraints. A system needs to actually follow instructions.
1032.wh: Topical relevance and instruction-following are fundamentally different tasks. A table about 'quarterly sales for all years' is topically relevant but disobeys the 'exclude 2024' instruction. Existing systems have no way to model constraint satisfaction separately from semantic similarity. Also, schema awareness is weak: most systems do not reason carefully about column names and data representation choices.
1032.ap: This paper formalizes a new task: instruction-following table retrieval, where a system must find tables that satisfy both topical relevance and explicit constraints. It introduces a benchmark with tables annotated for inclusion/exclusion requirements and schema constraints. It also proposes a new metric that checks whether retrieval rankings actually adapt to the instruction (compared to ignoring the instruction). The benchmark is large-scale and created via a structured annotation pipeline.
1032.ww: By making constraint satisfaction a formal requirement and measuring it separately, systems can now be trained and evaluated on following instructions. The metric catches systems that do well on topical retrieval but ignore constraints. Schema awareness naturally improves because the benchmark explicitly rewards understanding column semantics and representation choices.
1032.po: The benchmark reveals that existing retrieval models struggle with fine-grained instruction constraints, exhibiting systematic biases toward surface-level semantic cues. By providing the first large-scale evaluation setting for instruction-following table retrieval, it enables future research in this underexplored area and reveals current systems' blind spots.

1033.bp: Generative recommendation systems create a personalized ranking by generating predictions directly, rather than computing similarity scores. Flow matching (a deep generative technique) has been applied here with promise. Yet the standard training objective does not push different users toward different preferences. Without explicit separation between users, the system generates bland, averaged preferences that do not distinguish one person from another.
1033.wh: Directly applying contrastive learning (a technique that pushes different entities apart) to the final output of a flow model causes false repulsion: if two users happen to like the same movie, pushing their scores apart makes the model learn something false. Flow matching is also sensitive to input perturbations, so standard contrastive learning view construction breaks the output—positive pairs become semantically mismatched.
1033.ap: Instead of contrasting the final predictions, this paper applies contrastive learning inside the model, at an intermediate layer (the encoder) before the final output. This avoids the false repulsion problem: even if two users have similar final preferences, their internal representations can still be pushed apart. The system decomposes the flow model into an encoder (shared across users) and a prediction head (per-user), applying contrastive regularization to the encoder representations.
1033.ww: Constraining users' internal representations to be distinct does not force their final preferences to be different. This solves the false repulsion problem: the model learns to represent users differently internally, which naturally leads to personalized outputs without breaking semantic meaning. The encoder-head decomposition provides a clean place to apply the constraint without disrupting the flow-matching process.
1033.po: On collaborative filtering benchmarks, the contrastive flow matching approach generates more diverse and personalized recommendations compared to flow matching with only regression loss. User separation leads to higher-quality rankings where individual preferences come through, not averaged preferences.

1034.bp: LLM-based agents can do complex tasks by calling external tools. But which tool to use? If the tool descriptions are vague ('format: string', 'does conversion'), the agent wastes time trying wrong tools or gives up. This is an acute problem for the Model Context Protocol ecosystem, where thousands of third-party tools exist and descriptions are often unclear. Automating the generation of clear, function-oriented documentation could solve this.
1034.wh: Tool creators write documentation in free-form text, emphasizing human readability over machine searchability. They often hide the actual function signatures inside code, leaving them out of docs entirely. When tools have overlapping names or ambiguous descriptions, an LLM agent retrieving tools sees only noise. The gap between implementation and documentation makes retrieval nearly impossible.
1034.ap: This paper builds an automated pipeline that extracts the actual tool implementation from source code (a white-box analysis), generates precise descriptions for each function based on what the code does, then aggregates these into a structured server-level overview. The pipeline operates in stages: extract tool inventory with metadata, refine each tool's description grounded in its implementation, synthesize a searchable server overview. It also constructs a benchmark of real-world tool discovery queries to measure retrieval quality.
1034.ww: By grounding descriptions in the actual code implementation, there is no gap between documentation and reality. The staged approach (tool-level then server-level) means detailed function information is preserved and then intelligently summarized. The benchmark enables evaluation of retrieval quality, showing whether descriptions are actually useful for finding tools.
1034.po: On a benchmark of 3000+ real open-source MCP servers, the system generates structured documentation that significantly improves tool discovery retrieval compared to raw, unstructured documentation. Agents can now find the right tools more reliably, making complex multi-step tool workflows more practical.

1035.bp: When you chat with a search assistant across multiple turns, asking follow-up questions and building on earlier responses, how do you actually know if it's doing a good job? This paper tackles the real-world problem of measuring whether conversational search systems work well—a task that's become critical as chatbots handle more complex information-seeking tasks.
1035.wh: The tricky part is that traditional evaluation methods, which compare outputs to reference answers, don't fit well here because conversations are dynamic; each turn depends on the previous one, and what counts as 'good' changes as the conversation unfolds. Meanwhile, using language models as judges is faster and cheaper than hiring humans, but these AI judges often get things wrong in biased ways and don't generalize well across different systems and datasets.
1035.ap: FACE works by breaking down each conversational turn into small, meaningful pieces—the core information units—and scoring each piece according to different criteria (like relevance or clarity). Instead of using a fixed prompt to score everything, it uses a search-then-optimize strategy called beam search and bandit optimization to find the best prompt instructions for each specific aspect of quality. These optimized prompts are then applied consistently to score the atomic pieces, which get rolled up into an overall dialogue score.
1035.ww: This works because it tackles two real problems at once: by scoring small chunks rather than whole conversations, you catch problems at the granular level where they actually occur, and by optimizing prompts for each quality aspect independently, you avoid the bias that comes from a single all-purpose prompt. The optimization approach learns which prompts are actually effective rather than guessing.
1035.po: The result is that FACE correlates far more reliably with human judgments than existing methods, and because the optimized prompts transfer across different language models and datasets, you can reuse the same approach on new systems. Most importantly, it doesn't just give a single number—it breaks down exactly which parts of the conversation failed and where, making it actionable for system builders.

1036.bp: When you ask a search system to write a long, detailed answer to a complex question, you need to pull in facts from many different documents. The real-world challenge here is ensuring your answer covers all the important angles—if you only find facts about symptom management but miss prevention and epidemiology, your answer is incomplete even if what you did find is correct.
1036.wh: Dense retrieval systems (which find documents by comparing meaning rather than keywords) are built to find relevant documents, but 'relevant' usually means one-to-one: does this document answer this query? They don't naturally optimize for bringing back diverse angles or comprehensive coverage. If you want multiple different perspectives on a question, you get back similar documents that cover the same ground, and the system never explores the edges of the topic.
1036.ap: CoveR trains a neural retrieval system using two learning objectives that work together: one based on picking documents that cover different aspects of the question (built from synthetic training data where each document is labeled for which sub-question it answers), and one based on copying learned knowledge from simpler systems. The training data itself comes from breaking down long questions into natural sub-questions and using language models to judge whether candidate documents would answer each sub-piece.
1036.ww: This works because by teaching the system to explicitly model which sub-questions each document addresses, you force it to learn what diversity actually means for this task. The twin learning objectives—one pushing for breadth across angles and one preserving the ability to find truly relevant items—create a natural tension that produces a system optimizing the trade-off rather than collapsing to either extreme.
1036.po: CoveR retrieves 10% more novel, non-redundant facts than baseline methods while maintaining the same ability to find relevant documents. This matters directly for long-form generation: an AI writing a comprehensive answer gets both the relevant pieces and the missing angles, producing answers that feel complete rather than lopsided.

1037.bp: A keyphrase is a concise phrase capturing what a document is really about—the words you'd use to index it in a library or tag it in a search engine. Extracting these automatically is important because it gives you a quick summary of each document's essence, which flows into recommendation, search, and content organization systems.
1037.wh: Modern language models are great at finding keyphrases that are semantically important across the whole document, but documents aren't uniform: they have multiple sections, and a phrase might be important only for understanding one subtopic buried on page three. A global importance score misses these local, subtopic-specific keyphrases that matter if someone is reading that particular section.
1037.ap: MUDY uses two different scoring channels in parallel: one that estimates how likely a language model would naturally generate each candidate phrase (a measure of semantic centrality), weighted by how unique that phrase is in its local context; and another that inspects the internal attention patterns of the language model at different scales—both across the whole document and within individual segments—to measure how much focus the model pays to each candidate.
1037.ww: By examining the model's internal attention at multiple scales, you're essentially asking: 'At what levels does this model consider this phrase important?' A phrase might be ignored globally but highlighted within its section, and that local signal matters. The dual approach captures both the semantic weight of a phrase and its contextual salience—different concepts measured in parallel.
1037.po: MUDY extracts more keyphrases correctly across multiple real datasets, especially at picking out the subtle, locally-important phrases that traditional methods miss. The method also reveals something deeper: by checking what keyphrases the model should have found but didn't, you learn what your extraction system actually does and doesn't understand about the document.

1038.bp: Dense retrieval systems like ColBERT compress whole documents down to dense numerical vectors that let you quickly find relevant results. The problem is they do this per-token—every single word gets its own vector stored in memory—so searching through millions of documents means storing billions of vectors, which is expensive and slow.
1038.wh: Existing attempts to throw away low-importance token vectors either pick them randomly or use heuristic scores like 'does this token appear often in the data?' These approaches don't have a principled justification—they work sometimes, but you don't really know when or why, and you often lose important tokens by accident.
1038.ap: This paper thinks about tokens geometrically: it treats each token's embedding as occupying a region in high-dimensional space (called a Voronoi cell in mathematics), and argues that a token is important if its region is large—meaning it covers a lot of ground that wouldn't be covered if you removed it. By computing these regions using heat-diffusion kernels, the authors derive a principled score for each token's actual contribution to the system's ability to distinguish documents.
1038.ww: The insight is that importance isn't a property of the token in isolation; it's about whether the token occupies unique territory in embedding space or whether other nearby tokens would capture the same information anyway. If you prune a token whose region is completely covered by its neighbors, nothing breaks. But if you prune a token that uniquely occupies a region, you lose discrimination power.
1038.po: This geometric framework lets you prune away 20-30% of tokens without hurting retrieval quality, shrinking your index substantially. More importantly, because the approach is grounded in geometric principles rather than heuristics, it's more predictable and interpretable—you can look at which tokens got pruned and understand why the system thought they were redundant.

1039.bp: Long conversations with a chatbot—where you ask a question, get an answer, ask a follow-up, refine, build on that, and keep going—naturally accumulate a lot of history. The challenge is: how do you remember everything useful without your context window exploding, while still being able to retrieve and weave together memories from earlier in the conversation when they're relevant to a new question?
1039.wh: Simply summarizing old conversations loses the thread—you squash rich details into a paragraph and lose the narrative structure that made each exchange meaningful. Cramming everything in memory works until your context limit, then you're stuck choosing what to forget. And when you do need to retrieve a memory to answer a new question, you have to search through a flat list of summaries rather than a structured mental map.
1039.ap: Dynamic Memory Forest (DMF) organizes conversation history like a forest of trees: each conversation session gets 'consolidated' into thematic units that preserve the logical flow of that session, then these units are arranged into tree structures and dynamically connected to existing trees through a voting mechanism that decides whether a new session 'attaches' to previous related sessions or stands alone. Retrieval uses entropy—measuring uncertainty—to decide which memory trees might hold relevant answers to the current question.
1039.ww: This mimics how human memory actually works: related memories cluster together, and you navigate by following associations rather than searching a database. By preserving the internal structure of each session (consolidation) while allowing sessions to link dynamically (growth), the system keeps both detail and navigability. The entropy-driven search means you explore uncertain regions where the answer might hide.
1039.po: A system using DMF can maintain coherent conversations over many sessions without forgetting important details or losing track of conversational threads. When you ask a new question, the system can find and recall relevant earlier moments even if they're separated by many turns, because they're organized by theme rather than chronology.

1040.bp: Evaluating search systems requires human judges to label whether retrieved results actually answer the search request. But this labeling is expensive and slow, and it's becoming common to use language models as judges instead. The question this paper asks is: does it actually work better if you give the LLM judge a detailed, structured description of what the user is looking for, rather than just the search query?
1040.wh: When judges (human or AI) only see a bare query like 'machine learning', they interpret it wildly differently—one person thinks you want algorithms, another thinks you want applications, another thinks you want theory. This high disagreement makes it hard to tell if retrieval systems are actually getting better or if you're just getting lucky with your judge.
1040.ap: The researchers take language models and use them to write out structured topic descriptions that include context, background, and specific boundaries—essentially formalizing what the user was really asking for. They compare LLM judges working from bare queries against LLM judges working from these richer descriptions, testing on real search benchmarks with hundreds of documents labeled by humans.
1040.ww: When the judge sees the full context of the information need, it can make more consistent, defensible decisions about relevance. Bare queries are ambiguous; a structured topic is less so. The result is that agreement improves—both between different LLM judges and between LLM judges and humans—because everyone is interpreting the same underlying request.
1040.po: LLM judges working from structured topics are substantially more reliable than those working from queries alone. This simple finding has a direct payoff: if you want to evaluate search systems cheaply using LLMs, you should invest the effort to formalize your information needs rather than just copying over the original query.

1041.bp: Cross-domain recommendation means: you've built a great recommendation system for movies, but now you want to use that knowledge to recommend books. You have rich data on what users liked in movies (the source domain) and you want to transfer that understanding to make better book recommendations (the target domain), especially when you have little book data.
1041.wh: The standard approach trains the system separately in each domain, learns a mathematical function to transform the movie-understanding into book-understanding, then applies that transformation. The problem is you're throwing away information: when you transform from one domain to another, you lose the specific details about what the user actually did in each domain. A user who loves action movies but rarely buys books is different from a user who loves action movies and buys books constantly—that source-and-target history together tells you something special.
1041.ap: SetCDR directly uses each user's full history—their movie ratings and their book ratings together—as a set of item-rating pairs. Instead of processing these sequentially (which would require defining an arbitrary order), it uses a neural architecture that doesn't care about order: the network produces the same result whether you feed in the history chronologically or shuffled. A lightweight label attaches to each history item, marking whether it came from movies or books.
1041.ww: Order-invariance is powerful here because user history is fundamentally unordered: it's a collection of things they did, not a sequence. Traditional neural networks are built for sequences and either force an arbitrary order or require special tricks to ignore it. By using an architecture that naturally handles sets, you remove noise and get cleaner signals. The domain label lets the model learn different patterns from different domains without one overwhelming the other.
1041.po: SetCDR makes better recommendations in the target domain, especially when target-domain data is scarce. Because it processes both histories directly without losing information to transformation, it captures the nuance of cross-domain transfer: how a user's source-domain preferences actually inform what they'll like in the target domain.

1042.bp: Recommendation systems are increasingly using language models to understand items and users, then generating an ID or index token representing the item to recommend. The problem is that the same user's history might be described differently depending on how you write the prompt, or which item attributes you choose to emphasize, and this variation creates inconsistency.
1042.wh: If you ask a language model to recommend the next book for a reader using a detailed prompt, you get one answer. Use a simpler prompt emphasizing different aspects, and you get a different answer. Neither is wrong, but they disagree. Averaging or picking one doesn't work well because the recommendations are often based on genuinely different understanding of what the user wants—they're not just noise, they're different valid perspectives.
1042.ap: MVIGER learns to treat prompt variations and different item-indexing schemes as different information sources, each with their own lens on the user's preferences. It models which source to trust or whether to blend multiple sources as a learnable decision: during training it learns what combination of perspectives tends to be right, and at test time it can either pick the single best source or adaptively blend them based on the situation.
1042.ww: Instead of fighting the variation, this approach embraces it: each prompt or indexing scheme does capture something real about the user's interests, just from different angles. By learning to weight or combine these perspectives intelligently, you get robustness—the system doesn't break if the prompt changes, because it learned that variation is normal and meaningful.
1042.po: MVIGER gives consistent, high-quality recommendations regardless of how you've written your prompts or chosen your indexing scheme. Users get better recommendations, and system builders can iterate on prompts without worrying about accuracy degradation.

1043.bp: Imagine searching for a specific scene in a massive library of untrimmed video—say, finding the moment in a cooking video where they add salt. You need to both find the right video and pinpoint the exact moment within it. This is video corpus moment retrieval, and it matters for video search, content moderation, and video summarization.
1043.wh: Standard retrieval systems compare shallow visual and textual features—like color histograms or keyword overlap—which can't capture semantic subtlety. A query about 'adding salt' is visually and texturally very different from salt-adding scenes in the video: you're looking for salt-related visual concepts and keywords, but the real signal is semantic understanding.
1043.ap: Video-GAR flips the problem: instead of trying to match query to video, it trains the system to reconstruct the query from video segments. This reconstruction ability becomes a signal that the system deeply understands what's in the video. It uses an efficient backbone (Bi-Mamba) that processes video efficiently, a fusion module with a decoder that helps the system calibrate its understanding without slowing down inference, and a localization strategy that explicitly models where moments begin and end.
1043.ww: Reconstructing the query from the video segment requires genuine semantic understanding, not just surface-level matching. If the system can reliably generate the original query from a video moment, it must have captured the semantic essence. The efficient backbone keeps computational costs down, while the training-only decoder provides supervision without runtime overhead.
1043.po: Video-GAR retrieves relevant moments more accurately and localizes them more precisely than discriminative baselines, across standard benchmarks. Because it's built on reconstruction and semantic understanding rather than pattern matching, it handles fine-grained queries better.

1044.bp: Recommending the next place to visit based on where someone has been is the core of location-based recommendation systems. But people's actual locations are complicated: sometimes you go to a café because you love it, sometimes because it's the only place near your office and you have to grab lunch somewhere.
1044.wh: Standard systems assume every check-in directly reveals what you truly like, but real human behavior is mixed: some visits are authentic choices, others are external constraints. Worse, people sometimes go to a place that's close to where they actually wanted to go but was too far or unavailable. If the system treats all these equally, it learns a distorted preference map that doesn't match what users genuinely want.
1044.ap: MPDC attacks this from two angles: it uses a behavior-aware component that looks at contextual patterns (like the difference between morning commute and evening browsing) to separate authentic preference signals from context-driven behavior, and a spatial-aware component that infers where users probably wanted to go based on their overall movement patterns and the distances they typically travel. The system uses diffusion-based contrasting learning, which learns by asking: which alternatives would a truly preferred location look like?
1044.ww: By modeling the gap between observed behavior and true preference, you correct for the bias in raw data. The spatial awareness captures the idea that small deviations from a location often indicate the true target wasn't available or wasn't obvious. Diffusion-based learning helps the system explore what valid alternatives look like, building a more accurate mental map.
1044.po: MPDC recommends locations more accurately, especially for users with complex mobility patterns. By filtering out context-driven noise and recovering intended destinations, it learns what users actually prefer rather than what their forced behavior suggests.

1045.bp: Recommendation systems often discover that users have multiple distinct interests: someone might like both action movies and documentaries, but not as an average of the two—they're genuinely different moods. Multi-interest recommendation tries to capture this by generating multiple user 'profiles' each representing a different facet.
1045.wh: The problem is that weighted averaging methods (the standard approach) end up blending all interests together into a smooth average, losing the distinctness that makes each interest useful. You wanted to distinguish 'action fan' and 'documentary fan' but instead get 'action-documentary blend', which doesn't reflect how the user actually behaves.
1045.ap: DMI uses diffusion models—probabilistic systems that add noise then learn to remove it—to extract interests. Rather than reconstructing a single next item (which tempts the model to collapse everything into a middle-ground prediction), it reconstructs the full multi-interest vectors themselves. A cross-transformer module looks at specific subsets of the user's history relevant to each interest, guiding the diffusion to extract interest-specific patterns rather than merging them.
1045.ww: By reconstructing the full interest space rather than downstream items, you preserve the independence of different interests. The model can't cheat by merging them into an average because there's no single item to optimize for—it must preserve the structure. The history-guided diffusion ensures that each extracted interest actually has support in what the user did.
1045.po: DMI produces more distinct, non-overlapping multi-interest representations, leading to better recommendations when the system actually has multiple interests. By preventing over-smoothing, it captures the real diversity in user behavior.

1046.bp: Session-based recommendation operates on limited data: a user arrives with no prior history and performs a few actions in one session (clicking items, maybe buying), then you must recommend next items. You can't build a rich user profile the way you do with years of history.
1046.wh: Language models are powerful at understanding behavior, but they're expensive and sometimes hallucinate—they confidently claim preferences that don't match the actual session data. In session-based settings where context is already scarce, hallucinations are especially damaging. Also, using an LLM for every user at inference time is computationally infeasible for large platforms.
1046.ap: SPRINT uses LLMs selectively: during training, only on sessions where the model is uncertain about intent, and it validates predicted intents by checking whether they actually improve recommendations. The LLM outputs are constrained to choose from a global pool of common intents, reducing hallucination. At inference, a lightweight neural intent predictor learned during training handles all sessions without calling an LLM.
1046.ww: By using LLMs only for difficult cases during training, you get their semantic reasoning power where you need it most without paying the inference cost. Validating against recommendation performance filters out hallucinations: if the LLM's intent doesn't improve recommendations, it's discarded. The lightweight predictor at inference captures what the LLM learned without the computational burden.
1046.po: SPRINT outperforms state-of-the-art methods and scales to real-world session-based systems because it captures LLM reasoning during training but runs efficiently at inference. Recommendations are also more interpretable because they're tied to discovered session intents rather than opaque user embeddings.

1047.bp: Recommendation systems store a dense numerical vector for every user and item, which lets them quickly compute similarity and make recommendations. At scale, storing billions of vectors consumes enormous memory. Hashing is a standard trick: map many vectors to the same bucket, saving space.
1047.wh: Hashing forces crude choices: if two vectors hash to the same bucket, they're treated as identical even if they're different. This hurts both accuracy (you lose meaningful distinctions) and personalization (users with different preferences get mapped to the same representation).
1047.ap: Graph Diffusion Gated Embeddings (GDE) uses a different approach: instead of hashing, it precomputes heat-diffusion patterns from a small set of 'seed' vectors, using mathematical kernels that diffuse influence from each seed across the graph. These diffusions become probabilistic gates that mix a small set of learnable embeddings. Each node (user or item) gets represented by a weighted combination of seed embeddings determined by its diffusion pattern.
1047.ww: Diffusion naturally explores the local structure around each seed, so similar nodes get similar diffusion patterns and thus similar mixing weights. By using probabilistic mixing instead of hard bucket assignments, you preserve nuance: two slightly different nodes still get meaningfully different representations even if they rely on overlapping seed embeddings.
1047.po: GDE achieves better accuracy on both retrieval and click-through rate prediction than hashing methods, using a much smaller embedding table. Because the mixing is soft and structure-aware, the system is both more accurate and more personalized.

1048.bp: Active learning on graphs means: you have a partially labeled network of nodes (like papers with some labeled topics, some not) and you want to intelligently choose which unlabeled nodes to label next to improve your classifier most efficiently. In practice, you'll encounter novel node types you didn't know existed when you started labeling.
1048.wh: Existing active learning algorithms assume all classes are known upfront and just find informative nodes for known classes. But real-world graphs are open-world: new categories emerge after you start. You need an algorithm that both improves classification on known classes and discovers entirely new ones, but existing methods don't handle both.
1048.ap: The approach uses hierarchical clustering: first cluster nodes in feature space to find promising regions of the graph (rather than looking at individual nodes), then within the selected cluster, use semi-supervised sub-clustering to find the single most informative example. It scores cluster informativeness not just by classification uncertainty but by measuring whether the cluster likely contains novel classes. A self-distillation loss helps the network learn to produce clustered embeddings.
1048.ww: By working at the cluster level first, you can efficiently explore large unlabeled regions and spot where novelty is likely hiding (clusters with mixed properties are prime candidates for novel classes). Once you've identified a promising region, fine-grained sub-clustering picks the best single example to label. The dual objective prevents the system from ignoring either known-class improvements or novel-class discovery.
1048.po: The algorithm discovers new classes while improving classification on known classes, more efficiently than methods that focus only on known-class uncertainty. By identifying informative regions rather than just informative points, it explores the graph's structure effectively.

1049.bp: Short video platforms need to recommend what to watch next by understanding user preferences from their behavior. But 'behavior' on short video platforms is nuanced: a like, a follow, a share, and a watch-till-end all mean different things about what the user wants.
1049.wh: Binary models (like/dislike) lose this nuance, treating all engagement the same. Temporal models that ignore action type miss that the sequence of action types is meaningful—first you watch, then you like, then you follow conveys something different from the reverse sequence.
1049.ap: A2Gen models the specific actions users took (like, follow, watch-till-end, etc.) as a sequence over time, using an attention module to enrich each action with contextual information from the video it was applied to. A hierarchical encoder learns temporal patterns in the action sequences. Finally, the system generates the next action sequence that it expects, and uses that prediction to recommend items.
1049.ww: By modeling actions as a sequence, you capture that user intent evolves over time and through interaction: watching suggests interest, then liking confirms satisfaction, then following commits to future recommendations. The generation approach learns not just what items to recommend but what engagement pattern will follow—which is a richer signal of preference.
1049.po: A2Gen makes recommendations for short video that account for user engagement sophistication, improving accuracy by capturing the patterns in how users interact (not just what items they engage with). The action-sequence model is also interpretable: you can see what engagement pattern the system predicted.

1050.bp: Companies constantly decide which products to discount and by how much to maximize profit. If you offer too much discount, you lose money per sale. Too little, and customers buy from competitors instead. The real goal is figuring out the exact price cut that turns each customer into a buyer without leaving profit on the table.
1050.wh: Knowing how many extra sales a discount creates (the treatment effect) sounds like it should solve this—but it doesn't automatically tell you the right discount amount. Two very different discounts might create the same number of new buyers; the math of optimization requires something sharper: predicting the exact threshold price where each customer switches from 'no sale' to 'sale', which is a different prediction problem altogether.
1050.ap: The method works in two stages. First, it makes a rough guess at where each customer's price threshold lies by using a clever trick: sorting past purchase decisions to detect patterns, and noting that expected threshold prices are mathematically independent from observed actual purchases. Second, it fine-tunes these guesses by using an unequal penalty—penalizing certain kinds of mistakes more heavily than others—to lock in better estimates. Finally, it ranks candidates by their 'bang for buck' (Sharpe ratio) to pick which ones actually get the discount under a budget cap.
1050.ww: The independence trick works because what someone would have bought at different prices is not the same as what they did buy; this hidden threshold is separable from the noise in what we actually observed. The asymmetric penalty works because real-world costs are lopsided—leaving profitable customers unsubsidized hurts more than slightly overspending on price-insensitive ones—so penalizing mistakes differently mirrors the real economic stakes.
1050.po: In three public datasets and a live A/B test on a real platform, this method beats existing approaches, delivering measurably higher profit from subsidy allocation. It correctly predicts which customers need a discount and which price points flip them into buyers.

1051.bp: Computers need to find objects in images using only weak labels—for example, knowing a photo contains a 'bicycle' but not where it is in the frame. This is cheaper than manually drawing boxes around every object, but it tricks the algorithm into focusing on easy-to-spot textures (like a wheel rim) rather than understanding the whole thing (the complete bike frame).
1051.wh: Weak supervision breaks two ways: the model zones in on one distinctive part (part domination—seeing only the wheel) or blurs the object's edges into the background (merged detection—seeing wheel plus tablecloth as one blob). Both stem from the same root: the model never learns that an object is made of parts that fit together in a specific way.
1051.ap: The method builds up from parts to wholes, mimicking how humans see. It creates a dictionary of 'semantic parts' (wheel, seat, handlebars, chain) using large language models as a guide. It then trains smaller detectors to recognize each part in isolation by finding consistent patterns across many training images. Finally, it assembles these detected parts into complete objects, enforcing that parts only stick together in sensible configurations.
1051.ww: Teaching the model about structure works because parts are simpler to learn than whole objects—a wheel is a wheel whether it's on a racing bike or a cargo bike. Once the model knows what parts exist and how they connect, it can build complete objects, and it no longer gets fooled by stray textures that happen to share color or edge patterns.
1051.po: On standard benchmarks, this approach outperforms existing weak-supervision methods. More remarkably, it can detect new types of objects it has never seen—because instead of memorizing category names, it knows parts and how they combine, so it can generalize to any object describable by its components.

1052.bp: E-commerce sites want to know which customers will actually buy, not just which ones are interested. Someone might click, add to cart, read reviews—all signs of interest—but then abandon the purchase because of price, stock, or choice paralysis. These hesitant customers are different from ones who aren't interested at all, and treating them differently could convert more sales.
1052.wh: Most recommendation systems bin every non-purchase into one bucket: 'negative' or 'not interested'. But that conflates two different groups: people who actively disliked the product (true negatives) and people who wanted it but didn't complete the buy (hesitation). Mixing them corrupts the model's learning because it hides a large group of high-value opportunities.
1052.ap: The method learns to separate hesitation from disinterest using a two-part inference system. It first identifies successful conversions and learns what 'intent to buy' looks like from those cases. Then it applies that learned intent-detector to the abandoned cases, asking: 'If this customer had followed through, what would their intent signal have been?' This surfaces high-intent hesitators. To separate genuine hesitation from cases where customers switched to a competitor's item instead, it adds a penalty for competitor alternatives, sharpening the distinction.
1052.ww: This works because intent and final purchase are connected but distinct: many intent signals lead to purchase, but some don't (that's hesitation). By learning intent first and then spotting where intent exists without purchase, the model correctly identifies who wanted the item but stumbled before checkout. The competitor penalty works because one specific alternative temptation is different from general loss of interest.
1052.po: The framework accurately flags high-intent hesitators who can be re-engaged with targeted interventions like discounts or stock notifications. This lets platforms focus retention effort on customers most likely to convert, rather than wasting effort on truly uninterested users.

1053.bp: Searching for 3D scenes (architectural spaces, room layouts, outdoor environments) using natural language queries is difficult because text and 3D structure live in completely different worlds—one is sequential words, the other is spatial geometry. Currently, doing this well requires collecting and labeling thousands of matching text-scene pairs, which is expensive and brittle when queries or scene types are unfamiliar.
1053.wh: Existing approaches treat retrieval like learning a single joint space from paired examples, which requires massive labeled datasets and fails on novel scene types or open-vocabulary queries the system never trained on. The real blocker is the mismatch: text describes scenes abstractly and globally, while 3D data encodes spatial and visual specifics that don't translate directly.
1053.ap: Instead of forcing text and 3D into a shared space, the method converts both into a common textual representation. It reads the 3D scene (extracting what's there, how things relate, spatial layout) and describes it in natural language using large language models. The query stays as text. Both now speak the same language: plain descriptions compatible with off-the-shelf text embedding models. To handle complex scenes without breaking the LLM's coherence, it breaks scenes into 'roles' (foreground objects, spatial relations, materials) and builds each piece separately. For matching, it uses a structured alignment strategy: instead of comparing whole descriptions, it homes in on the relevant part of the query and aligns it locally against matching pieces of the scene description.
1053.ww: Text-to-text comparison is far more stable and generalizable than text-to-3D gaps, because large language models have already learned rich structure from vast amounts of text. Converting 3D to text leverages this learned structure. The local alignment works because queries are often about specific spatial details or object relations; pinpointing those in the scene description before comparing reduces noise from irrelevant scene context.
1053.po: The method retrieves correct 3D scenes from queries without any paired training data. It beats both systems trained on large labeled datasets and other zero-shot baselines, and it generalizes robustly to unfamiliar scene distributions and open-vocabulary queries.

1054.bp: Movie or music recommendations rely on collaborative filtering: the insight that if Alice and Bob rated the same movies similarly before, Bob's unrated movies are probably good recommendations for Alice. The simplest versions (comparing users based on how similar their past ratings are) often work better in practice than complex deep-learning models, yet they're fundamentally limited to comparing immediate neighbors, missing bigger patterns.
1054.wh: A similarity-based recommender only looks one step away: 'users who are similar to me'. But it misses patterns like 'a group of friends who collectively love indie films' or 'users three degrees away who share niche tastes'. Computing similarity at group-level or across multi-step paths is combinatorially explosive—there are too many possible combinations to check them all.
1054.ap: The method extends similarity-based methods to groups and multi-hop connections while keeping computation feasible. It uses MinHash, a probabilistic technique for quickly estimating set overlaps: instead of actually checking all possible pairs in a group or path, MinHash gives a fast approximate answer. This lets the model capture how similar a user is to different groups of friends, or how their tastes align with friends-of-friends, without the exponential blowup in compute that exact calculation would require.
1054.ww: MinHash works by hashing items to signatures that preserve overlap information—if two sets share many items, their hashes are likely similar. This approximation is loose enough to be fast yet tight enough to be useful for ranking. Extending similarity this way captures combinatorial patterns: a user might not match one friend closely, but match a trio of friends together, and that group signal is what drives good recommendations.
1054.po: On three public datasets, this extended similarity-based approach matches or beats state-of-the-art deep models while remaining interpretable and efficient. It demonstrates that the simplicity and transparency of similarity-based methods, when enhanced to see beyond immediate neighbors, is a competitive and practical alternative.

1055.bp: Finding communities in graphs—tight clusters of nodes with lots of internal connections—is useful everywhere: from detecting fraud rings to finding topic-specific user groups in social networks. Recent neural methods learn to recognize communities, but they require training on a specific graph and won't work on a new graph without retraining from scratch, which is expensive and slow.
1055.wh: Most neural models overfit to the specific structure of their training graphs. If the graph changes (different network topology, different neighborhood patterns), the model's learned features no longer match reality. The core problem is that real-world graphs vary wildly in their local density, connectivity direction, and whether nodes with strong ties have similar attributes or opposite ones—neural models trained on one don't transfer.
1055.ap: The method trains once on diverse source graphs and deploys directly to unseen graphs without retraining. It uses two key techniques. First, it aligns feature dimensions and semantics across domains using spectral analysis (which captures global structure properties) in a community-aware way, so a feature learned on one graph's community structure can map sensibly to another graph's structure. Second, it tokenizes both local and global structural context into a sequence and feeds it to a Transformer, then applies diffusion-based smoothing to adapt predictions when encountering unexpected graph properties on new data.
1055.ww: Spectral alignment works because global connectivity patterns (degree distribution, clustering tendency) are somewhat stable across graph domains, providing an anchor. The diffusion-based refinement works because it's a gentle process that doesn't require full retraining; it gradually pushes predictions toward consistency with local neighborhoods on the new graph, correcting drift without catastrophic forgetting.
1055.po: The framework successfully finds communities in entirely new graphs that it never trained on, with performance matching or beating retraining-based methods. This cuts deployment time dramatically and enables one trained model to be deployed across hundreds of different graph problems.

1056.bp: Large language models answer questions well when users know exactly what they want, but real queries are messy: vague, evolving, shaped by mental habits and biases ('I know AI is taking over' as a premise). The model guesses what the user really means and sometimes reinforces bad premises instead of correcting them. The real gap is that models don't model the user's mental state—what they know, what they're biased toward, how that shifts—so they can't personalize deeply.
1056.wh: Existing fixes ask clarifying questions iteratively, which helps narrow down intent but then defaults to generic responses. The problem is that understanding intent isn't enough; you also need to understand mental state: what prior beliefs is the user carrying? What are they biased toward? Does the user's thinking evolve as they interact? These stable but evolving mental patterns are invisible in standard interaction models.
1056.ap: The method builds a neural network model of the user's mental state as a three-layer graph, inspired by how neuroscientists model mentalizing in the human brain. It stores long-term mental states (beliefs, preferences) and updates them with each interaction. When a new query arrives, it uses a spreading activation algorithm (letting signal propagate through the mental graph with older beliefs decaying faster) to surface the most relevant mental context for that query. This context then gets encoded and injected into the language model via a lightweight adapter (LoRA), steering the model toward responses aligned with the user's actual mental state rather than generic answers.
1056.ww: The spreading activation mechanism works because mental states form networks: one belief connects to others, and understanding which beliefs are currently active requires spreading activation through those connections. Temporal decay is important because recent thoughts matter more than old ones. Injecting this context via LoRA works because it guides the language model without fully retraining, making the adaptation lightweight yet effective.
1056.po: The system generates personalized responses that reflect the user's actual mental model, beliefs, and evolving context, rather than generic answers. It tracks how the user's thinking changes across interactions, delivering truly personalized intent understanding that outperforms standard iterative clarification approaches.

1057.bp: People choose between search engines and AI chatbots for different reasons, and those choices reveal deeper differences in how they think about finding information. Understanding these differences is critical for designing better search tools: should your system emphasize finding authoritative sources or providing quick, polished summaries? The answer depends on what users actually expect and how they behave in different situations.
1057.wh: We don't have clear empirical data on when and why people pick one tool over another, how they actually use them (versus what they say they prefer), and how that varies by information need. People often say they value different things than they actually do—for example, claiming to value verification while trusting chatbot summaries on health questions.
1057.ap: Researchers surveyed 84 people about their actual recent experiences with both search engines and chatbots, asking about the types of tasks, what triggered each tool choice, what they found, and which tool they'd pick again. They categorized the patterns that emerged from analyzing these reports.
1057.ww: Real behavior often contradicts stated preferences because people have multiple goals in tension: wanting reliable sources but valuing speed, wanting authority but accepting personalized shortcuts when stakes feel low. Asking about actual recent interactions (not hypotheticals) captures this friction, revealing the real tradeoffs people make.
1057.po: The study found that people use search engines with a 'Browse and Verify' mindset—they gather multiple sources and check them—whereas they use chatbots with a 'Delegate and Consume' mindset—they trust the AI to summarize. However, people paradoxically turn to chatbots even for high-stakes decisions (health, relationships), suggesting tool choice depends on urgency and perceived authority, not just stated information-seeking philosophy. This misalignment points to design opportunities for tools that support reliable assessment and transparent sources.

1058.bp: Large internet companies operate multiple separate apps (video, reading, shopping, gaming), but users move between them and their interests cross over—someone who watches cooking videos might enjoy recipe articles and shop for kitchen gear. Current recommendation systems ignore these cross-domain interests, treating each app in isolation and missing valuable signals about what users actually care about across their life.
1058.wh: When a user's behavior sequence flows across apps, it's usually pooled together into simple summaries for efficiency, losing the rich pattern information. Different domains emphasize different features (one is text-heavy, another has images), so features don't line up neatly across domains. And existing methods don't model how the same user's intent changes depending on which domain they're in right now—sports interest might sway video recommendations but not book recommendations.
1058.ap: The system (STAR-CDR) builds cross-domain interest by threading three components together. First, it extracts cross-domain interest signals by keeping detailed behavior sequences and marking which domain and scenario each action came from, preserving fine-grained context. Second, it routes the signal through domain-specific expert components adaptively—different experts for video vs. reading—and recalibrates which experts activate based on the current scenario and task, so the same user's interest is expressed differently depending on context. Third, it aligns multimodal features (images, text, ID numbers) by using the cross-domain interest as a guide for gating, ensuring features from different domains are weighted appropriately.
1058.ww: Keeping detailed domain-scenario-task context works because user interest is truly different across contexts: someone might want trending viral videos but niche books in the same session. The adaptive routing works because it lets the system dynamically weight different expertise paths instead of forcing a one-size-fits-all model. Feature alignment through interest-guided gating works because it lets the system decide which modality matters for which domain (video needs strong visual features; reading emphasizes text), rather than forcing all domains into the same feature space.
1058.po: The system delivers recommendations that account for user interests that span apps—if someone engages with a certain type of content across multiple domains, that signal boosts relevant recommendations in each domain. Industrial deployment shows this captures cross-product collaboration and recommendation quality improvements over domain-isolated baselines.

1059.bp: Social media platforms struggle to detect automated bot accounts (fake engagement, misinformation distribution) because bots don't necessarily act like other bots—they're created to mimic different types of users. A good bot detector needs to spot when an account's behavior pattern doesn't match its stated or apparent type, which means understanding both the account itself and its neighbors in the network.
1059.wh: Existing neural methods assume that a user's friends reveal who they are—your neighbors predict your nature. But this breaks on Twitter-like platforms where people follow politicians they disagree with, celebrity fans follow strangers, and bot networks deliberately connect to diverse accounts to appear organic. In sparse, directed, and heterophilic graphs (where friends often differ from each other), this assumption fails catastrophically.
1059.ap: The detector explicitly models discrepancy between self and neighbors. It learns what each account is like from its own attributes (tweets, profile text, follower count) without assuming the network neighborhood confirms it. Then, it sends messages through the network using a bidirectional aggregation: one path for incoming interactions ('who follows me') and one for outgoing ('who I follow'), capturing asymmetric behavior separately. Crucially, it preserves the mismatch between self-representation and network signals instead of smoothing over it. If an account looks like a bot but has typical human neighbors, or vice versa, that discrepancy is the signal, not noise to eliminate.
1059.ww: Self-neighborhood discrepancy is diagnostic because bots often mask themselves—mimicking user behavior in attributes while maintaining network ties to other bots, or conversely, acting like humans but connected to bot networks. Capturing incoming vs. outgoing separately matters because bot networks often have asymmetric follow patterns (bots follow each other in coordinated ways). Preserving discrepancy works because over-smoothing the network signal erases the very patterns that distinguish bots.
1059.po: On multiple benchmark datasets, the detector consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods. It is more effective at catching bots that hide in networks where a neighborhood assumption would fail, making it practically deployable on real social platforms with complex, sparse graphs.

1060.bp: AI systems answer complex multi-step questions by searching for documents, reading them, reasoning, then searching again (retrieval-augmented generation). The challenge is showing users *why* the answer is correct: what exact part of which document proved it? With text-only retrieval, this is vague—users get a document title and have to hunt through pages. With visual documents (slides, PDFs with charts), converting to plain text loses spatial reasoning and layout logic entirely.
1060.wh: Parsing documents into plain text creates two problems: users must manually locate evidence in lengthy documents, and visual reasoning is destroyed. Slides with diagrams, timelines, or spatial arrangements become meaningless text once converted. But most retrieval systems work with text only, so they can't leverage visual structure even when it's the key to understanding.
1060.ap: The system (Chain of Evidence) takes screenshots of retrieved documents and reasons over them directly using a vision-language model (Qwen-VL). Instead of parsing text, it keeps the visual layout intact. When the model identifies evidence for answering a query, it outputs a precise bounding box on the screenshot, showing exactly where the evidence is. This visual citation chains together: query → retrieved document → exact visual location → answer. It evaluates on both web pages (structured layouts) and presentation slides (complex diagrams).
1060.ww: Vision-language models trained on large multimodal datasets understand both text and spatial layout, so they can reason over documents as humans do—seeing a chart's title, axes, and data simultaneously. Bounding boxes are more precise than text citations because they pinpoint the exact visual region, and they preserve all context including diagrams, colors, and layout that make the evidence obvious to humans.
1060.po: The system retrieves evidence with precise pixel-level attribution, eliminating manual document hunting. On web pages and especially on complex slides with diagrams, fine-tuned Qwen-VL significantly outperforms text-based retrieval, capturing visual semantic content that text conversion discards. Users see exactly which part of a document proves the answer.

1061.bp: Video search systems retrieve clips matching natural language descriptions—'show me a dog running in the park'—but they typically assume the clip *exists* in the video. In reality, sometimes the queried moment isn't there, or the user's phrased query implies something incorrect ('the robot dancing' when it's actually a person). A robust retrieval system needs to refuse bad queries instead of hallucinating false matches.
1061.wh: Simply retrieving the best-matching moment assumes the query is answerable, which fails in two realistic ways. First, similar but irrelevant moments interfere—a cat running looks similar to a dog running, so the model gets confused. Second, once the model makes a wrong decision (retrieving an irrelevant moment), that mistake affects future reasoning in unrecoverable ways, because the system can't backtrack and reconsider.
1061.ap: The system (ARROW) learns to detect and resist interference using an adversarial approach. It has two parts: a Gradient-induced Semantic Adversary that actively probes the model by amplifying exactly the kind of semantic confusion that trips it up (similar-but-wrong moments), and an Adversarial Reliability Predictor that observes how the model behaves under this pressure and assigns confidence scores to its decisions. High confidence means the decision is stable under interference; low confidence flags unreliable predictions that should be rejected.
1061.ww: Testing under adversarial perturbation reveals fragility: if your model's decision flips when you slightly emphasize distractors, it's not trustworthy. By actively amplifying the hardest cases during training, the predictor learns to distinguish confident decisions from lucky ones. The gradient information helps because it shows exactly where the model is vulnerable. Stability under pressure is a better measure of reliability than raw accuracy on clean data.
1061.po: The system correctly retrieves relevant moments when they exist and rejects queries when no matching moment is present, handling cases with semantically similar but irrelevant interference. It significantly improves practical robustness compared to systems that always assume relevance exists.

1062.bp: Recommender systems predict what users will like by modeling user-item relationships as a graph (users and items as nodes, interactions as edges). Graph neural networks excel at this because they can capture how one user's taste connects to another through shared items. However, these models struggle with the actual patterns: they can't express complex nonlinear preferences, they miss big-picture structure across the entire graph, and noise in user interactions tricks them.
1062.wh: Standard graph neural networks model primarily pairwise relationships—'this user liked this item'—which is limited. They can't capture that three users collectively prefer certain item combos in ways that wouldn't be obvious from pairs. They also tend to wash out global patterns by over-smoothing local neighborhoods. And when users accidentally click on junk, that noise propagates through the graph without being filtered.
1062.ap: The method (FHCL) uses two complementary approaches together. First, it applies Fourier Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (a type of neural function decomposer) to disentangle complex user-item preference patterns into simpler pieces, then reconstructs the graph structure using a generative model (VGAE), capturing global information while discarding noise. Second, it creates a denoising view by selectively removing noisy edges and then checks how similar the denoised graph is to the original structure. These two views are compared using contrastive learning—the model learns to make them agree when they're both looking at the same good patterns, and disagree when one captures noise the other doesn't.
1062.ww: Decomposing interactions via Fourier KAN works because complex user preferences often hide simpler underlying components—factorization reveals them. Reconstructing through VGAE works because it forces the model to encode global structure, not just local edges. The contrastive framework works because comparing a clean view against a noisy view lets the model learn what robust patterns look like without explicit noise labels—agreement means the signal is strong enough to persist despite denoising.
1062.po: On recommendation benchmarks, this approach significantly outperforms prior graph neural network methods. It delivers more accurate predictions by simultaneously improving the model's nonlinear expressiveness, incorporating global structure, and building robustness against noisy interactions.

1063.bp: Educational videos (lectures, tutorials, demonstrations) contain diagrams, formulas, and visual explanations that are critical to answering questions correctly, yet large vision-language models often overlook these key visuals and instead focus on generic distractors (backgrounds, text labels). When a model answers 'what does this diagram show?' wrong, it's usually because it paid attention to the wrong region, not because it can't understand diagrams.
1063.wh: Vision-language models encode an image into features, and during generation, certain task-critical regions (a labeled diagram) end up with weaker feature signals than distractors (bright colors, prominent text). This isn't a training problem; it's a fundamental encoding-decoding mismatch. Simply training on more examples doesn't fix it because the model's attention during generation is already committed to ignoring weak signals.
1063.ap: The method (BAEI) intervenes during response generation without retraining the model. A lightweight neural network watches the model's internal attention patterns and predicts which candidate evidence regions (detected diagrams or key visuals) should be boosted, and by how much. It operates at two levels: in earlier layers, it cranks up the contribution of evidence signals; in later layers, it monitors prediction uncertainty and if confidence is shaky, it applies adaptive corrections. The policy network itself is trained via reinforcement learning (GRPO) to maximize final answer accuracy.
1063.ww: Intervening at decoding time works because the visual encoding is frozen but attention weights are plastic—boosting signals during generation rebalances where the model looks without full retraining. Operating at two levels works because early layers build representations and late layers make final decisions; tuning both provides coarse and fine control. GRPO training works because it optimizes directly for downstream performance without requiring manual annotation of which regions are evidence.
1063.po: On educational video QA benchmarks, the system significantly improves factual correctness by ensuring task-critical visual evidence receives appropriate attention. The model's backbone remains frozen, so the intervention is plug-and-play, and the approach generalizes across different educational datasets.

1064.bp: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems answer questions by finding documents and reading them to construct answers. They work well when factual questions have clear, objective answers. But they fail in realistic decision-making scenarios where people have biases—asking for advice while harboring false beliefs, seeking confirmation rather than truth. The system then retrieves documents that confirm the bias, and the hallucination becomes worse, not better.
1064.wh: Standard RAG ranks documents by semantic relevance: 'Does this document match my query?' But when a query contains a false premise ('AI is definitely stealing all jobs'), relevant documents about AI actually reinforce the error. The real problem is treating relevance as a proxy for usefulness—they're not the same in biased decision-making. We need to know whether a document has enough evidential strength to steer someone toward correctness *despite* their bias.
1064.ap: The system (CoRM-RAG) uses causal reasoning to handle bias. During training, it synthetically creates user biases by perturbing queries (adding false premises, confirming biases, introducing logical fallacies). It learns to identify documents that are strong enough to correct these biased framings—documents with conflicting but authoritative evidence. This knowledge is distilled into a lightweight Evidence Critic that scores whether a document can actually guide a biased reasoning process toward correctness. The critic is then used during deployment to select retrieved documents.
1064.ww: Creating synthetic biases during training works because you can learn what 'strong enough evidence' looks like by observing which documents reliably correct various biases. The Evidence Critic works because it learns to value documents not by relevance but by corrective power—a document might not perfectly match the query but if it contains authoritative counter-evidence, it's more valuable. This aligns retrieval with decision safety rather than similarity.
1064.po: On decision-making benchmarks with adversarially biased queries, the system retrieves documents that steer the model toward correct answers despite cognitive biases, significantly outperforming standard dense retrievers. It also enables 'robustness scoring'—the model can abstain from answering when it detects insufficient evidence to overcome a query's bias, improving reliability.

1065.bp: When you ask a recommendation system why it suggests something, the best systems think through your preferences step-by-step (like a person would), but explaining all that reasoning in real time makes the service impossibly slow and resource-hungry. We want lightweight systems that have somehow absorbed that thinking ability.
1065.wh: Large language models can reason deeply and explain their logic, but they're too big to run on real servers at scale, and even smaller models that know how to reason still talk through every step out loud, which means each recommendation takes several seconds. You face a brutal tradeoff: deploy the small model for speed but lose the reasoning, or keep the big model for its thinking but sacrifice latency and resources.
1065.ww: When a large model thinks through a problem and explains itself, it reveals which signals matter and in what order. A small model trained to mimic many such explanations learns the underlying pattern—like how reading many car reviews teaches you what features actually matter, so you stop needing to read the reviews. By forcing the small model to match the outputs of multiple large teachers, you ensure it picks up robust reasoning, not just lucky guesses.
1065.po: The small model now recommends items as accurately as the large reasoning models but responds in milliseconds instead of seconds, and uses a fraction of the memory. The authors show it beats existing shortcuts on multiple recommendation tasks and actually speeds up inference by orders of magnitude—making reasoning-powered recommendations practical for real services.

1066.bp: When hateful videos are posted online, you need to catch them quickly—but also to explain *why* a video is hateful so the platform can respond appropriately and users understand the decision. Simple yes/no systems fail because they don't show their work.
1066.wh: Videos contain sound, text overlays, and images all at once, and the hateful elements might be subtle or layered. Some words only become hateful in context (depends on tone, visuals, surrounding claims). A simple classifier will spot *some* hateful content but can't explain which visual moment or quote mattered, and different people legitimately disagree on borderline cases—so the system needs to show reasoning.
1066.ww: Forcing the model to write out its reasoning (linking specific video moments to the hateful judgment) prevents lazy shortcuts—like just pattern-matching offensive words without understanding context. When you explicitly teach the model which reasoning chains are legitimate and which are not, it learns to ground its decision in actual evidence from the video, not spurious patterns.
1066.po: The system now flags hateful videos *and* shows concrete evidence—"this image combined with that audio equals hate speech"—which makes moderation decisions defensible and helps content creators understand what got flagged. The authors release two new annotated datasets to benchmark this kind of reasoning-grounded detection.

1067.bp: In biomedical text, a named entity like 'depression' could refer to the psychiatric condition, a medical symptom, or a life event—you need to link mentions to the right concept in a medical knowledge base, which directly determines whether a doctor sees the right information or gets confused.
1067.wh: Medical knowledge bases are structured hierarchies where 'disorder' has subtypes like 'mood disorder' which has 'depression'; this hierarchy matters because `depression as a symptom' and `depression as a syndrome' are logically distinct. Most neural systems treat the knowledge base as a flat lookup table and just measure text similarity, so they miss logical inconsistencies—they might link 'depressed mood' to a condition called 'Major Depressive Disorder' when the hierarchy says a symptom can't equal a full disorder.
1067.ww: Logical rules encode real structure of medical knowledge (e.g., 'a symptom cannot be the same as a syndrome'). By enforcing these rules during training, the neural model learns representations that respect the hierarchy, not just surface similarity. It's like training a student to match textbook definitions rather than surface resemblance—over time, the student internalizes the structure.
1067.po: The system correctly disambiguates mentions that pure neural systems flub—fixing 71% of errors on ambiguous cases where logic actually matters. On standard biomedical datasets, it surpasses previous methods by up to 4.2%, and the combination of speed and logical soundness makes it practical for real medical text processing pipelines.

1068.bp: Edge computing (small local servers close to users) can run language models cheaper and faster than cloud servers, but each server has limited storage and compute. You want to serve local users better by keeping the most relevant knowledge on their server, without duplicating all knowledge everywhere.
1068.wh: A generic knowledge base is big and covers everything, so it either bloats every edge server (wasteful) or requires going to the cloud (defeats the point). If you're smart and keep only local knowledge on each server, you'll fail on queries that need information you don't have stored nearby—because you don't have a quick way to route to a better server.
1068.ww: Specialization works because most queries within a region or topic cluster benefit from localized knowledge—fewer irrelevant results to sift through. Routing via summaries is fast and cheap (summaries are tiny).
