Distributing knowledge based on relevance matches documents to servers that will retrieve them best, so overall retrieval quality stays high even though each server holds less.
1068.po: The system delivers faster answers (lower latency) with better relevance, uses less storage per server, and keeps the system up-to-date simply by refreshing local indexes—no retraining needed. It's a practical design for deploying language models across many small edge servers.

1069.bp: When an e-commerce site tracks whether users bought something after clicking an ad, these labels are messy—someone might click but not see the product fully, or abandon it for unrelated reasons. A ranking model trained on noisy labels will optimize for the noise, not real purchase behavior.
1069.wh: Clicks and conversions happen in sequence: a user clicks an ad, then might buy. If the click label is wrong (mislabeled), the downstream conversion label is contaminated too—the noise compounds. Typical denoising methods handle one source of noise, but here the hierarchy matters: cleaning clicks without considering their effect on conversions (or vice versa) leaves systematic errors.
1069.ww: Layered noise means you can't just flip signs blindly; you need to model the hierarchy. By deriving an unbiased loss—mathematically proving it removes noise without losing signal—you ensure the model learns true purchase behavior. The forward-correction version is a practical shortcut that avoids numerical breakdown when dealing with thousands of training examples.
1069.po: The ranking model now learns from real purchase preferences despite noisy labels, which directly improves recommendation quality and revenue in real e-commerce systems. The framework is general enough to handle other hierarchical noise patterns in recommender systems.

1070.bp: Millions of people search for podcasts on platforms like Spotify and Apple Podcasts, but we don't know which search systems work best or how robust they are. If you're building a podcast search engine, you need evidence that your ranking actually helps users find what they want.
1070.wh: Podcast search is hard because spoken words get transcribed by automatic speech recognition (which makes mistakes), different transcription attempts produce slightly different text, and people ask about the same podcast in different ways. Testing whether a search system works requires a ground truth: what should rank first for a given query? Getting humans to judge that is expensive and slow.
1070.ww: By using multiple query phrasings, systems, and transcriptions, they expose where search breaks: do all systems fail on speech-recognition errors, or only some? Do query reformulations help or hurt? LLM judges are fast and consistent (though not perfect), making large-scale evaluation feasible.
1070.po: The community now has the first large-scale empirical study of podcast search, revealing which approaches are robust to transcription noise and how much query wording matters. This benchmark enables future systems to be tested rigorously before deployment—reducing the risk of bad search quality at scale.

1071.bp: A generative search system learns to output document IDs as a sequence (like a language model), which is elegant, but breaks down when new documents are added—the model's weights are frozen with knowledge of old documents baked in, so it can't 'learn' new ones.
1071.wh: Fine-tuning a model to add new documents causes catastrophic forgetting: the model forgets how to retrieve old documents because it's optimized only on new ones. The model-as-index paradigm stores everything in weights; traditional databases update indexes incrementally, but neural models can't do that easily.
1071.ww: By keeping the core model frozen, old knowledge is safe. The memory module is large enough to encode new documents but small enough to avoid overlap with old knowledge—a clean separation. Memory lookups are fast and sparse, so they don't slow down inference.
1071.po: A generative search model can now be deployed on dynamic collections: add new documents by updating memory, keep serving old documents instantly, and avoid the stability-plasticity tradeoff that crippled prior methods. This is the first practical approach to continual learning for document-ID generation.

1072.bp: Conversational search (asking multi-turn questions to refine a search) is evaluated by hiring people to talk to a system, which is expensive, or by replaying fixed conversations, which misses real diversity. A faster alternative is simulating a user via a program, but how realistic does the simulation need to be?
1072.wh: Real users learn during conversation (remember earlier questions) but also forget. Simulated users from prior work tried to model both, but it's unclear whether that realism is necessary for fair system comparisons. You might be spending effort modeling memory that doesn't affect which system wins.
1072.ww: Long-term memory lets the simulator track what was already discussed (so it doesn't repeat), which stabilizes its behavior and better matches human conversational flow. Short-term memory (remembering intermediate states) adds noise—artificial short-term decisions don't map to real human patterns. The lesson: simulate what matters, skip the rest.
1072.po: Evaluators can now use simpler, faster user simulators without sacrificing reliability—skip the short-term memory and keep only long-term tracking. This makes evaluation of conversational search more reproducible and cheaper, while maintaining the ability to fairly rank systems.

1073.bp: When a recommendation system suggests something you don't want, it's helpful to know 'if you had interacted differently—say, liked different items—the system would have suggested better things.' But generating these minimal tweaks is hard: you need to respect that only certain changes are realistic.
1073.wh: Naive approaches try local perturbations (flip one interaction at a time) or masking, but these often require unrealistic changes to many items, or the results are fragile—tiny ranking shifts break the explanation. You want the *smallest* realistic change that alters the recommendation, but 'small' and 'realistic' are hard to define precisely.
1073.ww: Diffusion models are strong at sampling realistic data (in this case, realistic interaction histories). By guiding each step toward the counterfactual goal, the final output is both realistic and effective. No need for explicit budgets or heuristics—the guidance naturally produces small, natural changes.
1073.po: The system now generates counterfactuals that require minimal changes (fewer items modified) and are semantically coherent—changes feel like real alternative user behavior, not random flips. The authors also introduce a finer-grained evaluation protocol that reveals explanation quality beyond what coarse metrics show.

1074.bp: Recommendation systems that use large language models have an advantage: LLMs understand natural language meaning (if you say 'I like sci-fi', it knows what that means). But LLMs don't understand the raw numerical signals from user-item interaction graphs ("user 1234 clicked item 5678")—a gap that limits their power.
1074.wh: Traditional collaborative filtering (finding users with similar taste) uses ID numbers for users and items; LLMs can't interpret those numbers. You could translate each ID into text, but then you lose the graph structure—the fact that 'users who liked A also liked B'—which is collaborative filtering's core insight.
1074.ww: Language is a bridge: the LLM understands meaning (why items are similar) and can reason about text descriptions of graph structure. By encoding graph neighborhoods as text summaries, you preserve the collaborative signals while making them interpretable to the LLM. The LLM then leverages both semantic understanding and collaborative patterns in one unified model.
1074.po: The system recommends as accurately as traditional collaborative filtering *and* modern LLMs—beating zero-shot LLM baselines. Generated user and item profiles are human-readable, so you can inspect *why* a recommendation was made, which neither pure collaborative filtering nor black-box LLM scoring gives you.

1075.bp: LLMs are increasingly used as agents that search the web repeatedly to answer complex questions—'think before you act by searching again.' To understand these systems and improve them, we need to see real patterns in how agentic search unfolds: how many steps do people take, how do they reformulate questions, and what evidence do they act on?
1075.wh: Agentic search logs are unstructured (just queries and timestamps). You need to infer when a multi-turn session ended, what the goal was, and whether new query terms came from retrieved evidence or were independent. Without careful annotation, you're flying blind.
1075.ww: By clustering and labeling at scale, patterns emerge: fact-seeking sessions show different behavior than reasoning sessions (fact-seekers repeat more; reasoners explore broadly). Measuring evidence adoption quantifies whether the agent is genuinely *using* retrieved documents or just making new guesses.
1075.po: The study reveals that most agentic sessions are short (median ~ten steps), which is good for efficiency. Fact-seeking and reasoning sessions have distinct patterns, suggesting systems should adapt their strategy. The finding that 54% of new terms trace to retrieved evidence suggests agents do learn from search results—useful for designing better re-ranking.

1076.bp: When you start typing a search query, the search engine suggests your next query—'did you mean this?' This is powerful for refining searches, but the system must suggest the *right* next query, using the session context, in under 30 milliseconds or it feels slow.
1076.wh: Generative models (which produce suggestions word-by-word) capture session context beautifully but are slow—several hundred milliseconds to run. Caching old suggestions is fast but doesn't adapt to new trends or session context. You can't simply use faster inference; you need a fundamentally different approach.
1076.ww: Retrieval is fast because approximate nearest-neighbor search is parallelizable and highly optimized. An asymmetric design is natural here: the session and query have different roles, so encoding them separately lets the model learn each role better. Contrastive learning (comparing good vs. bad suggestions) sharpens the model's sense of relevance.
1076.po: The system suggests queries with quality matching generative models but responds in ~30 ms (30× faster). It scales to billions of historical queries, updates instantly by refreshing the index (no retraining), and handles low-coverage cases (novel queries) by mixing retrieval with generation. All tested on real search logs, not synthetic data.

1077.bp: When a vision-language model (that understands both images and text) answers a question, it often hallucinates—invents details that aren't in the image. Retrieving relevant text or images to ground the answer helps, but the model should choose *which* retriever to use based on what it's currently thinking.
1077.wh: Different queries need different retrieval strategies: a question about a person's age might need a biography (text), while 'what color is the shirt?' needs the actual image. Fixed retrieval pipelines use the same strategy for everything, missing the opportunity to match retrieval to the question's needs.
1077.ww: Dynamic routing works because different types of reasoning need different evidence. Intermediate rewards teach fine-grained coordination—step-by-step, pick the right expert—which works better than learning only from right/wrong final answers. Multiple experts with different strengths mean no single retriever is a bottleneck.
1077.po: The model answers questions 7% more accurately on open-domain QA benchmarks and adaptively combines evidence (sometimes text, sometimes images) based on reasoning state. It's a generic framework: swap out experts for new modalities or knowledge sources without retraining the core model.

1078.bp: False medical claims spread online and can cause real harm—people might skip vaccines or take dangerous supplements. An automated system that checks medical claims should be practical: small, fast, and work with imperfect web evidence.
1078.wh: Large language models can reason about medical evidence, but they're slow and expensive to run at scale. Smaller models lack the reasoning depth. Prior work assumes you have 'gold' evidence (curated facts), but in reality, web search returns messy, incomplete, and sometimes contradictory information.
1078.ww: Small models are fast, but they need to learn reasoning patterns from larger models. Filtering out bad reasoning traces prevents the small model from learning spurious shortcuts. Training with web evidence (which is noisy) but testing the same way ensures the model learns to handle real-world evidence, not an idealized version.
1078.po: A small, fast claim-checking model that outperforms proprietary LLMs (like Gemini 2.5 Flash) at a fraction of the compute cost. It's practical for deploying across platforms and handles real web evidence—making automated medical claim verification accessible to smaller platforms.

1079.bp: Fact-checking requires hunting through sources ("find info on whether this claim is true") and reasoning through noisy evidence ("this source says X, that source says Y; which is reliable?"). Real fact-checking is multi-hop: initial evidence points to sub-questions, which require more evidence.
1079.wh: Large language models struggle with iterative retrieval: they either get stuck in loops (asking the same question repeatedly) or miss relevant evidence because they didn't think to ask for it. Supervising this with detailed reasoning annotations is expensive. Training with only final labels (true/false) gives weak signal for the intermediate retrieval and reasoning steps.
1079.ww: Multi-stage curriculum learning avoids the cold-start problem: the model first learns reasoning, which is easier, then learns to retrieve evidence. Rule-based rewards (checking if the reasoning follows a valid format) give dense feedback without expensive annotations. Joint training lets retrieval and reasoning co-adapt—the model learns to retrieve what it can actually reason about.
1079.po: The system performs multi-hop fact-checking using only final veracity labels—no expensive reasoning annotations needed. It iteratively retrieves evidence, reasons over it, and decides when it has enough to verify or refute a claim. This is a practical path to deploying fact-checking at scale.

1080.bp: When you use chat bots or AI systems to recommend products, movies, or books, those systems learn from watching what you interact with—whether you click, like, or buy. The goal is to make recommendations so good that you actually want what they suggest. But unlike traditional recommenders that just score items, generative recommenders literally compose text descriptions of products, asking the system to *generate* what to show you next.
1080.wh: The hard part comes from the messy reality of user feedback. Some clicks mean 'I really want this,' others mean 'I was curious,' and some mean 'this was available when I had five seconds.' The same click from two people can mean opposite things. If you treat all feedback the same when tuning the recommender, you're asking it to learn from noise—contradictory signals that pull the system in different directions at once.
1080.ap: This team built a system that learns *confidence* for each piece of feedback, then adapts how hard it pushes the recommender based on that confidence. When the system is certain a user action means 'yes, recommend more like this,' it trains aggressively. When it's uncertain—say, a click that might just be accidental—it trains gently, accepting that the system won't learn cleanly from that signal. They also add a brake that prevents the recommender from forgetting to assign decent probabilities to the items you marked as preferred.
1080.ww: This works because it mirrors how a good teacher acts: hammering home the lessons you're sure about, and staying flexible on ambiguous cases. By letting the system express how confident it is in each feedback signal, and then using that confidence to control training intensity, you avoid the trap of overfitting to random clicks. The brake on probability collapse prevents the recommender from gaming the system by just lowering all scores indiscriminately.
1080.po: On real recommendation datasets, this approach beats older methods by improving how often users click on the top suggestions. The system learns which signals truly matter and trains more stable, personalized recommenders that don't chase every noisy click equally.

1081.bp: When you search Google or browse a shopping site, you see a ranked list of results. But that ranking is affected by two very different things: how relevant each result actually is *and* where it sits on the page. Results at the top get clicked more simply because they're there, even if something lower down would have been more helpful. Teasing apart these two effects is crucial for making search better.
1081.wh: Every method today assumes there's *one* true answer: item X is relevant or not relevant, position Y has a certain bias. But in reality, you never see the truth directly—you only see clicks, which mingle relevance and position together. And here's the real problem: you don't know how uncertain you should be in your answer. Maybe the click pattern you see today will look completely different next week, or on a different device. Traditional methods give you a single number—'this item is 80% relevant'—but they hide their doubt.
1081.ap: These researchers built a system that outputs not single numbers but *probability distributions*—essentially, a range of plausible answers with varying confidence. Instead of saying 'the item is relevant,' it says 'this distribution of relevance-values best describes what we know, given the data we've seen.' The system learns these distributions using a deep neural network that takes item and position features and outputs a beta distribution for each factor (relevance and bias).
1081.ww: This captures something profound: past data can't tell you everything. A click might mean high relevance, or it might mean good positioning, or both, or neither. By outputting distributions, the system admits this uncertainty explicitly. On unseen data (like next week's searches), this honest uncertainty becomes an asset—you know which predictions to trust and which ones are guesses.
1081.po: The method successfully estimates how much you should trust each prediction of relevance and position bias, whereas standard approaches pretend certainty even when the data is ambiguous. This matters for ranking systems because it flags when to ask for more information rather than confidently giving a wrong answer.

1082.bp: Modern recommendation systems can use images and text together—not just collaborative signals like 'people who liked this also liked that.' A movie recommender might show you a poster, synopsis, and reviews all at once. But fusing all these sources is tricky: text and images need to be represented in compatible ways, and user-item interactions (what you clicked) can conflict with what the images and text suggest.
1082.wh: The core tension: collaborative signals (your clicks) and semantic signals (the visual and textual content) live in different worlds. A user might click a horror movie after browsing thrillers, but if the images show a peaceful forest, those signals contradict. Additionally, the connections between users and items (from clicks) can be noisy or sparse—you've only clicked a tiny fraction of items. And when merging multiple graphs (one for user-item clicks, another for item-item connections via images), it's unclear how to weight them or even if they should be treated separately.
1082.ap: The system builds multiple graph layers and learns to clean them up automatically. It starts with a user-item interaction graph (clicks and ratings) and a separate item-item graph built from shared visual and textual features. Instead of treating these edges as fixed, it iteratively *reweights* them during training, turning noisy connections down and strong ones up. Simultaneously, it aligns the semantic space (from images and text) with the collaborative space (from clicks) by enforcing that aligned concepts should predict each other, and applies a lightweight cleanup to remove redundant dimensions across views.
1082.ww: Reweighting edges dynamically works because the system learns which connections actually matter—users do click together for semantic reasons sometimes, and those signals amplify. By forcing the two representation spaces to align, you prevent the image-based view from contradicting the click-based view. Removing redundancy stabilizes learning because you're not training the same pattern twice in different coordinate systems.
1082.po: On Amazon product datasets, this multi-graph fusion beats simpler baselines by 7-8%, improving both ranking accuracy and recall—more relevant recommendations, and more of them. The system successfully disentangles meaningful semantic relationships from noisy clicks.

1083.bp: Mathematicians publish thousands of papers a year, and finding related work is hard because a paper on permutation groups might be deeply connected to a paper on computational topology, even though they use completely different vocabulary and never cite each other. A mathematician writes 'prove that X implies Y using the sandwich lemma,' while another writes 'the homotopy-theoretic dual shows that Z is a generalization of W.' Same ideas, different words—or subtly different ideas in the same domain. Recommending relevant papers means understanding these conceptual links.
1083.wh: Text-based similarity fails: two papers about the same proof technique might share almost no sentences. Citation networks fail: papers in different eras or fields rarely cite each other even if they're cousins. And relevance isn't one-dimensional—a paper might be related through 'uses the same algebraic structure,' 'extends the main theorem,' or 'applies the technique to a new domain.' These aspects of relatedness can conflict: a paper might extend the theorem but use a completely different proof structure.
1083.ap: The team built a dataset of expert-rated recommendations (GoldRiM, hand-labeled) and a larger automatic version (SilverRiM). Then they created a graph neural network that ingests three types of information at once: the text of abstracts, the citation network, and the author lineage (who trained whom, who collaborates). The network learns to weight these channels differently depending on which aspects of relatedness matter for the current recommendation task—essentially, it conditions its decisions on 'what kind of relation are we looking for?'
1083.ww: This works because mathematics is built on lineage, networks, and shared techniques that transcend text. By explicitly modeling authorship (who co-authored with whom, academic genealogy), the system captures intellectual influence that citations miss. By conditioning on aspects, it acknowledges that a paper can be related through multiple distinct mechanisms, and learns to weight them appropriately.
1083.po: On hand-labeled mathematical data, the system beats prior aspect-based recommenders on all measured aspects, and significantly outperforms pure text-based methods. The key insight is that mathematical relatedness is structural and genealogical, not just textual.

1084.bp: Modern recommenders use large language models (LLMs) to understand what items are about and to reason about good recommendations. But LLMs need short, crisp identifiers for items—product IDs, user tags, etc. The way you label an item dramatically changes how well the LLM can work with it. A bad identifier is confusing; a good one helps the LLM reason correctly.
1084.wh: Traditional identifiers (product names, catalog numbers) are inconsistent in length and mix semantic meaning with database artifacts. An LLM might struggle with 'Product-2847-Blue-XL-Refresh-2024' because it's verbose and mixes multiple concepts. Existing methods that assign short learned codes (like 'item_512') ignore what items are actually about—the LLM has to guess from context. And when you add new items or move to a different catalog, these learned codes don't transfer; you have to start from scratch.
1084.ap: The team built a graph neural network that encodes both collaborative signals (how users interact with items) and semantic signals (item features like category, price, description). The network produces compact, meaningful identifiers. They then cluster these representations using a tree-based hierarchy, where the depth of the tree controls the length of the final code. This is faster than old spectral clustering methods and allows quick updates as new items arrive, without retraining the whole system.
1084.ww: Fusing attributes and collaborative signals means the identifier captures both 'what is this item?' (from features) and 'who wants it?' (from user behavior). A hierarchical tree naturally produces short codes at the top levels (fast, general) and longer codes for fine-grained distinctions. This structure lets an LLM use the code as a meaningful abbreviation: 'Electronics/Audio/Headphones/Wireless/Premium' might become a compact token that the model recognizes semantically.
1084.po: Across five benchmark datasets, the method achieves strong ranking accuracy and generalizes well to new datasets without retraining. The identifiers are interpretable and compact, and the system scales efficiently for real-world catalogs with millions of items.

1085.bp: You ask an AI system 'What is the capital of France in an alternate reality where Napoleon won?' and it should use your question to override its training—preferring the alternate scenario over real history. But LLMs are biased toward facts they've seen millions of times in training. They often ignore your contextual facts and confidently answer based on their parametric knowledge: 'Paris,' not 'London' or whatever your alternate scenario specifies.
1085.wh: The problem is that LLMs encode world knowledge deeply and broadly. When you provide a fact that contradicts training data—'In this scenario, the capital moved'—the model's learned associations are so strong that they leak through. The model sees 'capital' and 'France' and fires the 'Paris' pattern regardless of your setup. Even reasoning models with long thinking chains fail here because reasoning happens after the prior knowledge has already biased the answer space.
1085.ap: The approach is elegant: find entities mentioned in both the context and the question, then replace them with generic labels that strip away real-world associations. 'Paris' becomes 'City‖1⟩' and 'France' becomes 'Country‖1⟩.' This preprocessing stage is entirely offline—you don't retrain the model. At test time, the system substitutes these abstract names into the prompt. After the model generates an answer using these neutral labels, you map them back to the real entities.
1085.ww: This works because you're removing the spurious associations while keeping the relational structure intact. The model sees 'City‖1⟩ is in Country‖1⟩' and reasons about that relationship without the baggage of 'Paris → tourist destination → fame → override?' The abstraction lets the model focus on structure: if the context says 'City‖1⟩ moved to City‖2⟩,' the model can follow that logic without fighting ingrained world knowledge.
1085.po: On counterfactual and knowledge-conflict benchmarks, this lightweight preprocessing beats even state-of-the-art reasoning models by up to 25% for medium models (0.5B–18B). It's fast, requires no retraining, and works across open and closed-source models.

1086.bp: Imagine a movie recommender trained to generate recommendations using an LLM. It learns to say 'try Inception, it's sci-fi and visually stunning.' But when a new movie arrives tomorrow (cold-start), the system has no training data for it and recommends nearly random garbage. The system can't handle dynamic catalogs where new items appear constantly.
1086.wh: Retraining the full model with new item data is prohibitively expensive and slow. In real systems, new items arrive hourly or minute-by-minute. The traditional response—collect interactions on new items, then retrain—creates weeks of lag. But there's a deeper issue: sequential recommendation data (the sequence of movies you watched) doesn't have the clean structure of NLP sentences. In NLP, a sentence has subjects and objects, and you can inject facts: 'Paris (City‖1⟩) is in France.' In recommendation, there's just a sequence: 'Movie A, Movie B, Movie C.' Where do you inject the new item?
1086.ap: The team adapted model editing—a technique from NLP that surgically updates facts in LLMs without retraining—to recommendation. They model the sequence context as generating semantic identifiers (short codes representing each item). To inject a new item, they (1) explicitly model how the sequence context predicts the next item's identifier, giving a structure that mirrors NLP's subject-object binding; (2) edit the model's weights at token level iteratively, injecting bundles of related item codes; (3) use a rank-one update (a lightweight matrix modification) that minimizes disruption to existing recommendations.
1086.ww: Model editing works because you're making a surgical change: 'whenever we see context pattern X, output this new item code.' By doing this at the model's weight level rather than the data level, you avoid the lag of retraining. Iterative token-level edits allow handling multi-token item bundles because you're building up the update gradually rather than trying to inject a complex pattern at once.
1086.po: The system can inject new items into a trained generative recommender without retraining, addressing the cold-start problem. Experiments show it recovers recommendation quality for new items in minutes rather than days, making it practical for real platforms.

1087.bp: Large e-commerce and social platforms like Alibaba or TikTok have both search (users type keywords) and recommendation (personalized suggestions). These are treated as separate functions, but they're connected: if you search for 'running shoes,' later recommendations should adapt. The challenge is mixing these signals effectively—search history reveals explicit intent, but not every search is useful for predicting what you'll click next.
1087.wh: Search queries are noisy: you might search for 'best pasta recipes' out of curiosity, 'laptop repair' out of frustration, or 'birthday gifts for engineers' with real intent to buy. Naive methods either ignore search history or treat all searches as equally predictive. But search behaviors frequently contain outdated or irrelevant signals—you searched for winter coats in July, and that's probably not relevant now. The system needs to *select* which search signals matter for the current recommendation task.
1087.ap: The team built a system that (1) encodes both search and recommendation histories into a unified latent representation (a compact internal code capturing your overall interests), (2) then performs iterative reasoning within that latent space to identify which search signals are most relevant to the current recommendation. The reasoning mimics how humans think: 'What does the user actually want?' and then 'Which of their past searches illuminate that intent?' They use a contrastive learning objective to guide this reasoning—making sure the selected searches align with positive recommendations and away from negative ones.
1087.ww: Working in latent space (a compressed representation) rather than raw history lets the system generalize: it learns abstract patterns of when search is useful, not memorizing specific search terms. Iterative reasoning over this space mirrors human decision-making: identify intent first, then search backward through your memory for relevant signals. The contrastive objective ensures the system isn't just picking random searches; it's selecting ones that actually predict good recommendations.
1087.po: On large-scale search-and-recommendation logs, this method beats baselines that either ignore search or use all search equally. It improves recommendation click-through rates by filtering out noisy, outdated, or irrelevant search signals while amplifying the ones that predict what users will actually engage with.

1088.bp: In online advertising, platforms decide how much to bid for ad slots and how to budget across the day. If you bid too high, you hemorrhage money; too low, your ads disappear. And the feedback you get is delayed: you place bids every minute, but advertisers see spending totals only at the end of the day. This is a control problem: you're making rapid decisions but evaluating them slowly.
1088.wh: The core mismatch is temporal granularity: decisions happen at millisecond scale (each auction), but meaningful feedback (did I spend right and get good results?) comes at the day or hour scale. This creates sparse reward signals—you make a thousand decisions before knowing if any were good. Additionally, the feedback is noisy: an ad placement's success depends on user behavior, which is chaotic. Standard reinforcement learning assumes dense, immediate rewards; here you're flying blind.
1088.ap: The team built a generative model that mirrors how humans think about this: plan at multiple time scales at once. They use a multi-scale approach that first generates day-level budget trajectories, then hour-level pacing, then individual bids. They compress the diverse feature types (bid amounts, budgets, times, campaigns) using a hierarchical quantizer (a multi-scale VQVAE—a lossy encoder that treats different types of information at appropriate resolution). The final model integrates state and action directly to capture long-term dependencies without needing auxiliary prediction networks.
1088.ww: Planning coarse-to-fine works because coarser time scales have denser, more reliable feedback: 'did we spend the budget?' is easier to evaluate than 'was this specific bid good?' By generating at multiple scales, the model can learn stable patterns at the day level, then instantiate them into fine-grained decisions. Compressing features via a hierarchical quantizer lets different types of information (continuous amounts, categorical campaigns, temporal positions) be handled naturally rather than forced into one representation.
1088.po: In both offline simulations and real advertising systems, this multi-scale generative approach outperforms standard reinforcement learning baselines. It produces more stable bids, better budget adherence, and improved return-on-ad-spend by treating the fundamental granularity mismatch explicitly.

1089.bp: When a user profile has missing information—age, location, interests—recommendation systems must guess. One approach is to copy values from the user's graph neighbors or propagate features across connections: 'this user is friends with Alice, and Alice likes jazz, so let's guess they do too.' This works okay but can overfit to the graph structure: if the graph is accidentally sparse or biased, the propagation amplifies those biases.
1089.wh: The fundamental problem is structural overfitting: diffusion-based methods assume the graph captures all relevant information, but real graphs have artifacts. Users might be disconnected not because they're genuinely unrelated but because of platform design or privacy choices. The propagation smooths features across neighbors, but it also flattens diversity—everyone ends up similar. Worst of all, when you deploy to a new platform with a different graph structure (an inductive setting), the method fails catastrophically because it learned to exploit the specific graph you trained on.
1089.ap: The team addresses this in three steps. First, they augment the graph globally: connect disjoint components to allow diffusion to flow across islands. Second, they learn a semantic manifold (an internal structure representing natural feature patterns) via masked autoencoding—like BERT, they hide features and learn to reconstruct them, capturing what realistic features look like. Third, crucially, they add a test-time correction: when deploying to a new graph, they project biased features back onto the learned manifold, correcting for structural distortions before inference.
1089.ww: Global augmentation solves the connectivity problem by bridging isolated users. The masked autoencoding learns what features should *look* like naturally, independent of graph structure—it's a kind of semantic prior. Test-time correction is the key insight: even if the new graph is different, you can rectify the distorted features by pulling them back to the learned manifold, bridging the inductive distribution gap.
1089.po: On a new real-world dataset from voyage records (Sailing), this framework mitigates all three failure modes: it maintains performance on disconnected test graphs, preserves semantic diversity without over-smoothing, and generalizes to new graph structures. The test-time rectification is particularly powerful for practical deployment.

1090.bp: When you read a news article mentioning 'the meeting on Tuesday' and later 'the decision three days after the meeting,' you need to understand that 'the decision' happened on Friday. Understanding time relationships between events is essential for machines to comprehend narratives, timelines, and causal chains.
1090.wh: The task is deceptively hard. The full temporal relation set is rich: one event can be DURING another, BEFORE, AFTER, EQUAL, OVERLAPPING, and more. But datasets and benchmarks have been progressively simplified: early work attempted all relations, but researchers found it too difficult and switched to simpler subsets, like just event-to-event relations. By narrowing scope, progress stalled—real systems need the full expressivity.
1090.ap: Instead of directly predicting complex interval relations (e.g., 'Event A overlaps Event B'), the approach decomposes the problem. It first classifies simpler point relations: the start of Event A is BEFORE the start of Event B, the end of Event A is AFTER the end of Event B, etc. Once you know the relationships between all four endpoints, you can decode these point constraints into an interval relation—e.g., if both starts are ordered and both ends are ordered in matching ways, you have DURING or OVERLAPPING.
1090.ww: Decomposing intervals into points is powerful because point relations are much simpler and more reliable to predict. A model can confidently classify 'timepoint X comes before timepoint Y' more easily than 'Event A during Event B.' By solving the simpler problem first, you avoid the combinatorial explosion of interval relations. The decoding step is deterministic: given point relationships, the interval relation follows logically.
1090.po: On the TempEval-3 benchmark, this approach achieves 70.1% temporal awareness, a new state-of-the-art. By returning to the full set of interval relations instead of simplified subsets, it enables richer temporal understanding for downstream NLP applications.

1091.bp: Dense retrievers (neural networks that embed questions and documents into similar spaces) are great at understanding meaning but sometimes rank irrelevant documents highly just because they're topically similar. Traditional sparse retrieval (BM25, keyword matching) is more conservative and less prone to false positives, but misses paraphrases and semantic variations. The ideal system would combine their strengths.
1091.wh: The problem is that failure modes are orthogonal. Dense retrievers fail by promoting 'similar-looking but irrelevant' passages; sparse retrievers fail by missing relevant passages that use different vocabulary. If you just average their scores, you're averaging across failure modes—sometimes the dense retriever is confident and wrong, sometimes the sparse retriever is confident and wrong, and you can't tell which is which.
1091.ap: The insight is elegant: relevant passages cluster in the region where *both* retrievers score highly (consensus). The team builds a re-ranker that (1) identifies anchor documents where both sparse and dense agree, (2) expands the query using these verified anchors (words and concepts from highly-agreed-upon documents), and (3) applies geometric gating to suppress drift from the original intent. The gating ensures the expanded query stays close to the original, preventing the expansion from chasing irrelevant tangents.
1091.ww: Consensus is a reliable signal: if both a lexical matcher and a semantic matcher rank a document highly, it's probably actually relevant. Expanding the query through these anchors introduces new vocabulary that both methods considered important. Geometric gating prevents the expansion from wandering—you're saying 'use these new words, but stay true to the original intent.'
1091.po: On TREC Deep Learning benchmarks, this method improves over both dense-only and sparse-only approaches by 3-5%, with a compact 33M-parameter model. Notably, these gains require no additional parameters or training beyond using retrieval signals more effectively—pure algorithmic improvement from trusting consensus.

1092.bp: Large platforms like TikTok recommend content across multiple scenarios: the homepage (general discovery), a user's following feed (accounts they track), and live streams (real-time interactions). Each scenario has different user behavior patterns—people interact differently when browsing casually versus watching a specific creator's live stream. The challenge is building a single recommender that personalizes across all these contexts.
1092.wh: Naive approaches use a shared representation for all scenarios, but this causes representation entanglement: the system can't distinguish scenario-specific signals from global ones. A better approach adds scenario-specific networks, but these don't share knowledge effectively. The real problem is distribution mismatch: user interests are expressed differently in each scenario. On the homepage, engagement might signal 'I'm browsing,' while on a live stream, it signals 'I'm focused on this creator.' Training on mixed distributions confuses the model.
1092.ap: The team builds scenario-specific prototype spaces—abstract canonical representations for each scenario. They use a multi-gate mixture of experts (a routing network that assigns items to different processing paths) to extract shared features, and independent networks for scenario-specific features. Then, they project both into their respective prototype spaces. Crucially, they use unbalanced optimal transport (a mathematical technique for matching distributions) to align distributions: it finds the best correspondence between points in each scenario's distribution, accounting for imbalances.
1092.ww: Prototype spaces are useful because they capture 'what does a good engagement look like in this scenario?' without entanglement. The multi-gate MoE efficiently routes information to the right expert. Unbalanced optimal transport is powerful because it doesn't assume scenarios have equal weight—it flexibly aligns heterogeneous distributions, solving the core problem of scenario mismatch.
1092.po: On TikTok-like multi-scenario recommendation tasks, this method improves over parameter-sharing and scenario-specific baselines by better capturing scenario-specific distributions while enabling knowledge transfer. It improves recommendation quality across all scenarios simultaneously.

1093.bp: News readers have filter bubbles: if you read a lot of U.S. politics, the recommender keeps showing you U.S. politics, never world news. This narrows your perspective and can radicalize. Platforms want to gently nudge readers toward broader coverage. But how do you diversify reading habits without making people angry by showing irrelevant articles?
1093.wh: Simple exposure diversity doesn't work: you can show diverse articles, but readers won't click if they're irrelevant. The deeper problem is that people have genuine preferences—some readers truly care less about world news than others. You can't force diversity without annoying them. And generic nudges ('try something different!') rarely work; they need to be personalized to the reader's actual interests.
1093.ap: The team ran a real field experiment with 120 news readers for five weeks using the POPROX platform. They designed two algorithmic nudges: (1) a topic-locality dual calibration that gently pushes the recommendation ranking to include both domestic and world news in proportion to the user's interest, and (2) an LLM-based presentation nudge that personalizes how each article is displayed based on the reader's prior interests—e.g., highlighting how an article relates to topics they've previously read.
1093.ww: Dual calibration works because it doesn't force diversity; it adjusts recommendations proportionally based on measured interest. If you read some world news already, show more; if you've never clicked it, nudge gently. LLM personalization works because readers engage with content better when framed in terms they understand—connecting unfamiliar topics to familiar ones increases click-through without manipulation.
1093.po: The experiment found that algorithmic nudges successfully increased diversity exposure and consumption (readers clicked more diverse articles), and longitudinal exposure shifted reading habits toward valuing balanced news from both domestic and world sources. Presentation nudges had variable effects, with relevance-based framing outperforming generic personalization.

1094.bp: Current recommenders learn from thousands of interactions—clicks, ratings, purchases—specific to each user. But what if you had a model that could recommend from just a few examples, like a human expert who can infer preferences instantly? Such a system could work with new users without waiting for data, and generalize across different platforms and item catalogs.
1094.wh: Most recommenders are dataset-specific: train on Netflix, works on Netflix; train on Amazon, works on Amazon. They need weeks of interaction data per user. The reason is that they learn specific patterns for each domain. What's missing is a *general* ability to infer preferences from small numbers of examples—the kind of generalization humans have. Scaling up recommenders with more data helps marginally, but it doesn't solve the fundamental problem of domain transfer.
1094.ap: The team created a 'prior-fitted network' trained entirely on synthetic data—simulated clickstreams generated from a structural causal model (a generative model that mimics how user preferences and item features interact). The real innovation: pretraining on this synthetic diversity acts like a Bayesian prior, teaching the model to perform amortized inference. At test time, you give it a few real interactions, and a simple transformer conditions on them to make predictions—no weight updates, just a forward pass.
1094.ww: Training on synthetic data with diverse causal structure teaches the model invariant principles: 'how do preferences manifest across different user types and item catalogs?' Because the training distribution is broad and structured, the model learns to generalize. Amortized inference means the model has learned a kind of Bayesian reasoning: given a small support set of observations, compute the posterior distribution over preferences, then use it to predict.
1094.po: Across eight public benchmarks, RecPFN achieves state-of-the-art zero-shot performance (no fine-tuning on target domain) while remaining competitive with fully supervised methods in low-data regimes. It's deployment-efficient, robust to domain shift, and offers a practical path to data-efficient, generalizable recommenders.

1095.bp: When you search for information online, you and another person using the same search engine often behave very differently. One might carefully read through each result, another might skim and jump around. This paper asks: why? The big picture is that people think differently—some people like breaking problems into parts and analyzing details, others like seeing the whole picture first. If search engines understood these thinking styles, they could present information in ways that match how each person's brain naturally works.
1095.wh: Right now, search engines treat everyone the same. They show the same results page layout, the same number of results, assume everyone reads the same way. But if you think in pictures and patterns, a dense page of text will exhaust you quickly. If you like analyzing details, a cursory overview frustrates you. The hard part is that these thinking styles are invisible—the search engine has no way to measure them automatically, so it can't adjust.
1095.ap: This study brought 40 people into a lab and had them search for information while wearing a special headband (fNIRS) that measures blood flow in the front part of the brain where decision-making happens. The researchers measured three things simultaneously: what the person actually did (which links they clicked, how long they read), how tired they felt doing it, and the physical brain activity in two specific regions that handle working memory and planning. They focused on one moment in the search: after the person had found a few results and was deciding what to explore next.
1095.ww: The brain regions that light up (VLPFC and DLPFC) are like the 'workbench' of your mind—they handle the mental load of organizing information and making decisions. The study found that people with different thinking styles showed different patterns of brain activity doing the same search task. Analytically-minded people needed more brain activity to handle detail-heavy pages, while holistic thinkers showed different activation when they had to process lots of individual items. This proves that thinking style is a real, measurable thing reflected in how the brain works.
1095.po: The payoff is concrete: search engines could now measure or infer a user's thinking style (perhaps from how they interact in the first few clicks), then automatically adjust. For detail-oriented thinkers, show more information density, richer snippets, deeper navigation. For big-picture thinkers, show fewer items per page, highlights, summaries. The paper's evidence that brain activation differs across styles makes it plausible that such a system would actually reduce mental effort and improve satisfaction.

1096.bp: When you shop online, you often want different things: good jeans, yes, but also a shirt that goes with them. Or you want both thriller and romance novels, depending on your mood. Recommendation systems that know you like only one genre or one product type miss huge opportunities. This paper tackles a real business problem: how can a recommendation system understand that each user has multiple, separate tastes so it can suggest a good mix that actually fits your life?
1096.wh: The obvious approach is to just learn from what you buy or click on, but that's noisy and incomplete. Maybe you bought a cookbook once as a gift, but you hate cooking. Maybe you browse mystery novels but buy romance. Also, many items don't have lots of user behavior data (new products, rare interests), so the system can't learn what they're good for. Existing systems that mix large language models (which read text and understand meaning) with recommendation systems often do shallow work—they just align representations from two different systems without actually letting the meaningful knowledge flow through.
1096.ap: The idea is architectural. Instead of having two separate systems that try to match their outputs, the researchers built a tool that says: let the language model (which reads descriptions, reviews, and metadata) generate semantic understanding, then use that understanding to directly shape the inner parameters of the recommender system itself. Specifically, they use a hypernetwork—a neural network that generates parameters for another network—conditioned on what the language model learned. This way, the language model's understanding of items flows directly into how the recommender discovers and separates your multiple interests.
1096.ww: Why does this work? Because parameters in a neural network are like the 'settings' that control what the network learns. By having those settings generated from semantic knowledge, you're essentially saying: 'before we even look at user behavior, we already know what the important dimensions of difference are.' A language model reading that item A is 'sporty' and item B is 'elegant' can feed that knowledge into the parameters before training. When training then happens, the system already has scaffolding to separate 'sporty' interests from 'elegant' ones, even with sparse behavior data.
1096.po: Tests on real shopping data showed the method improved recommendation quality by 26% for inferring which products are substitutes (you'd buy one or the other) and 39% for complements (you'd buy both together). This is significant because it means the system can actually suggest diverse, multi-interest-aware product mixes that feel personal and relevant, especially for new products with little behavioral history.

1097.bp: Imagine you take a photo of your electricity bill or a tax form and want to find the answer to 'How much do I owe?' or 'What's the account number?' A computer needs to understand not just the text but where on the page it sits and what form it takes. This is about making AI systems that can read real documents the way humans do: by knowing that the thing you want is usually in the top right, or under a specific label, and that visual layout matters as much as the words themselves.
1097.wh: Current document-reading AI systems look at the entire page as one big image and try to find the relevant information by having the system 'pay attention' to the right spots internally. But this is inefficient and imprecise. If a document is crowded with different sections (a bill with charges, taxes, discounts all over the place), the system has to scan the whole thing and guess where the answer is. Also, it's slow: processing a full-page image uses a lot of computation, and if you're doing this at scale, it becomes expensive and slow.
1097.ap: The approach has two parts working together. First, there's a routing system that learns which regions of the document are relevant to a given question, doing this without drawing boxes—it just assigns relevance scores to different areas. Second, there's a pooling mechanism that takes dense features (detailed information) from those relevant regions and compresses them into a small number of region-tokens (simplified representations) that preserve what matters. The researchers also created a dataset of 105,000 real documents with 350,000 question-answer pairs, where they manually marked which region on the page contained the answer.
1097.ww: Why compress to region tokens? Because the original dense features from the whole page are computationally expensive, and you don't need all that detail—you need the parts that matter. By routing to relevant regions first, you avoid wasting compute on irrelevant cluttered parts of the form. The region tokens preserve the 'grounding' (where on the page the answer came from) while being small enough to process quickly. This is a middle ground between two extremes: you're neither ignoring spatial structure (like older systems) nor processing every pixel equally.
1097.po: Tests on 12 different document datasets showed that this region-aware approach significantly improved both accuracy and speed. The system can now answer questions on bills, forms, and complex documents better than systems that treat the whole page uniformly, and it does so faster because it's not processing irrelevant regions. For real-world deployment (e.g., processing thousands of bills), this matters both for correctness and cost.

1098.bp: Online stores face a practical challenge: when you view one product, what should they suggest next? Should they recommend a different brand of the same thing (if your first choice is sold out), or should they suggest items that go well together? These are fundamentally different problems—one is about substitution, the other about combination. The paper tackles how to learn what products truly substitute or complement each other from messy real-world data.
1098.wh: The naive approach is to just look at what people actually bought together or clicked on together. But that's very noisy. Co-browsing doesn't always mean the items are substitutes or complements—sometimes users are just exploring. Also, popular items get lots of signals but obscure items get almost none, so the system can't learn what a rare product goes well with. Finally, understanding the real relationship requires looking beyond behavior—you need to know what the product actually is. A language model can read that product A is 'a wireless headphone' while product B is 'a smartphone case'—they're likely to be complementary. But behavior alone won't reveal that if few people bought them together.
1098.ap: The method combines three ideas. First, use a multimodal foundation model (a system trained on images and text together) to encode what each item is—reading its descriptions, metadata, images. Second, add a self-supervised denoising module that learns from the noisy user behavior but actively tries to clean up that noise by learning to separate true relationship signals from random co-browsing. Third, unify everything through hierarchical aggregation—combining item features at different levels of detail. They also used a language model to help label some relationship examples, reducing noise in the training data.
1098.ww: Why does denoising from noisy behavior work? Because many noisy observations of the same underlying relationship still contain signal. If 100 people co-viewed item A and B by chance, but 5,000 did so intentionally because they're true substitutes, the noisy signal is still stronger than the noise. By explicitly modeling this noise and learning to separate signal from it, the system can extract accurate relationships even from imperfect data. The multimodal foundation model provides prior knowledge (products with certain features tend to substitute with others) that guides this denoising.
1098.po: On five real e-commerce datasets, this method predicted substitutable items 26.1% better and complementary items 39.2% better than existing systems. Importantly, it worked well even for items with sparse data (the cold-start problem), because the semantic understanding of what the product is doesn't require lots of user behavior. For a store, this means better recommendations, more relevant up-sell and cross-sell suggestions, and better handling of out-of-stock scenarios.

1099.bp: Imagine a search engine or recommendation system that doesn't just score items one by one, but generates an entire good list of recommendations in one go, like a DJ curating a whole playlist rather than playing songs individually. This is faster and better because the system can ensure variety and flow in the list. But how do you train such a system to improve in real time as users interact with it, when user preferences shift daily and the old training data becomes stale?
1099.wh: Training systems to generate lists is hard because of two interconnected problems. One, you can't use the standard tricks from training systems that score items one-by-one (surrogate losses that are indirect and approximate). Two, picking items is discrete—you either include an item in the list or you don't. Neural networks learn by calculating gradients (a signal of how to improve), and gradients don't work well with discrete choices. Existing systems fake it by using indirect loss functions that only approximately point toward the true goal, and this breaks down when real-world preferences shift rapidly, which happens constantly in e-commerce.
1099.ap: The researchers noticed something: if you build a system with a generator (that produces the list) and an evaluator (that scores the list), the evaluator is just a neural network. So you can calculate gradients through it. The idea is to make item selection continuous instead of discrete using two tricks: (1) NeuralSort, a differentiable sorting operation that acts like a soft approximation of actual sorting, and (2) Gumbel noise, a mathematical trick that makes discrete choices look continuous during training. This allows gradients to flow all the way through picking items to how well the final list performs.
1099.ww: Why does making discrete choices continuous help? Because gradients are the signals that neural networks use to improve. If item selection is discrete, you get no gradient signal (it's like trying to improve a light switch—it's either on or off). By softening it into a continuous approximation during training, the system can see gradients and improve directly toward the true goal: maximizing the quality of the entire generated list. Once trained, you can snap the soft choices back to discrete (pick the top items) for actual use.
1099.po: The paper shows that this approach, called Environment Policy Optimization (EPO), can be trained in real-time on streaming e-commerce data, adapting to daily shifts in user preferences without the instability and inefficiency of older methods. For a large online retailer updating recommendations constantly, this means better lists generated faster, with less computational waste from indirect loss functions, and the ability to adapt to trends quickly.

1100.bp: Recommending medication is not like recommending a movie. If the system suggests the wrong drug combination, someone gets hurt or dies. Doctors need to trust the recommendation enough to use it, which means they need to understand why the system suggested each drug, and they need confidence that the system has considered safety for their specific patient (an elderly person has different risks than a young athlete). This paper is about building a recommendation system that is interpretable (you can see why it said yes) and safe (it accounts for individual risk).
1100.wh: Existing drug recommendation systems are often black boxes—they might give good answers but the doctor has no idea why, which kills trust. Also, they often use generic safety rules ('never give drug X with condition Y'), which don't account for the fact that some patients can tolerate more risk than others. An elderly person with few years left might accept a risky drug combination for quality of life; a healthy young person shouldn't. The system has to reason about what the patient needs, what drugs address that need, and what risks are acceptable for this specific patient.
1100.ap: The approach has two stages. First, the system is trained to explain itself: using a language model, it generates step-by-step reasoning about the patient's condition, pulling in medical facts from a knowledge graph. This reasoning is distilled from examples, teaching the model to think out loud like a clinician. Second, the system then learns a policy (decision rule) that balances helping the patient against keeping them safe. It does this by constructing patient-specific prototypes—templates of what good drug features are and what dangerous features to avoid for that particular patient—then adjusting recommendations toward those safe prototypes using reward shaping (adjusting the score based on safety).
1100.ww: Why explain first, then optimize for safety? Because if a system can explain its reasoning, doctors can catch errors before they happen. And by building patient-specific safety prototypes instead of using one-size-fits-all rules, the system can adapt risk tolerance to reality: this 75-year-old should get a different recommendation than a 30-year-old with the same symptom. The two-stage approach also ensures that the safety reasoning isn't an afterthought tacked on at the end—it's built into the learning process.
1100.po: The method allows a drug recommendation system to offer transparent recommendations ('here's why I suggest these drugs based on your history and condition') while dynamically adjusting safety to the individual patient. For a doctor using such a system, the payoff is higher confidence in recommendations plus the ability to override safely (because they understand the reasoning) and to adjust risk tolerance ('this patient wants to try a riskier option').

1101.bp: Real-world networks of relationships—friendship graphs, citation networks, disease spread networks—often have a surprising property: people or nodes are often connected to others unlike themselves, not similar others. This breaks many graph-learning algorithms, which assume the opposite (homophily: 'birds of a feather flock together'). The challenge is to learn from these 'heterophilic' networks without the usual tricks that rely on similarity between neighbors.
1101.wh: Standard graph neural networks work by having each node look at its neighbors and aggregate their information, assuming neighbors are similar and useful for prediction. But in a heterophilic graph, neighbors are often different, so this aggregation actually hurts. For instance, in a web of people with opposing political views, knowing someone's neighbors tells you almost nothing about their view. The system starts learning wrong patterns (spurious correlations) that accidentally work on training data but fail on new data. Understanding why these failures happen is hard because the patterns are hidden inside the network structure.
1101.ap: The researchers took a different angle. They identified that within heterophilic graphs, there are recurring small subgraph patterns (small repeated structures) that look like they should be helpful for prediction, but they're actually 'shortcuts' that teach the model non-causal, spurious relationships. For example, a structure that often appears before misclassifications acts as a misleading signal. The method then uses causal inference (a formal way to distinguish real causes from coincidences) to build a causal graph that explicitly blocks the paths that create these shortcuts. The neural network is then trained to use only the genuine causal signals, ignoring the spurious ones.
1101.ww: Why does identifying and blocking spurious subgraphs work? Because machine learning models will use any pattern that helps predict the training data, even if it's spurious (like 'this node-pattern appears before misclassifications, so avoid it'). By formally modeling which paths are causal (likely to generalize) versus spurious (likely to fail on new data), the system can prune the confusing signals before they distort learning. On heterophilic graphs, this is essential because the obvious patterns (looking at neighbors) are often wrong, so you must identify the subtle, genuine signals.
1101.po: Tests on real-world datasets showed that this causal approach significantly improved classification accuracy on heterophilic graphs compared to standard methods. The system was also more robust—it maintained accuracy when the network changed slightly, which matters because real networks evolve. For applications like fraud detection or content moderation in networks where bad actors actively work to hide (making neighbors unlike themselves), this robustness is crucial.

1102.bp: When you search for information using an advanced search engine, the first pass often retrieves hundreds of candidates. The system then ranks them. A useful trick is to look at the top few results and ask, 'what phrases or concepts appear in these results that weren't in my original query?' Then rerun the search with those new phrases added. This is called pseudo-relevance feedback. The challenge is doing this efficiently when the search engine uses dense mathematical representations instead of keyword matching.
1102.wh: Modern search uses dense vectors—each query and document is turned into a long list of numbers that capture meaning. This is much better than keyword matching, but it makes traditional pseudo-relevance feedback expensive. The standard approach would require re-encoding many queries, which is slow. Also, figuring out which of the retrieved results are actually good examples to learn from (avoiding noise) is tricky with dense representations.
1102.ap: Instead of re-processing everything expensively, the method leverages something that already exists in the search index: centroid vectors. These are pre-calculated summaries of token vectors grouped into clusters for efficiency. The method treats these precomputed centroids almost like traditional words in feedback: identify which centroid vectors appear in high-ranked documents, select a small diverse set of high-value ones, and append them to the query. Then rerun the efficient search with the expanded query. This keeps computational cost low while still benefiting from looking at what the top results contain.
1102.ww: Why does reusing precomputed centroids instead of recalculating everything keep costs down? Because the expensive work (computing and storing vector representations) is already done during indexing. By treating centroids as surrogate 'expansion terms' like traditional feedback does, the method avoids redundant computation while still capturing what made the top results relevant. The diversity constraint ensures you don't just amplify noise—you pick a balanced set of concepts.
1102.po: Tests on benchmark datasets (MSMARCO and BEIR) showed that this method improved ranking quality by up to 4.3% on standard metrics while adding much less computation than standard dense-retrieval feedback methods. The payoff for a search engine is better ranking with acceptable cost, making it practical to deploy pseudo-relevance feedback even at scale.

1103.bp: Learning-to-rank is a fundamental problem in search: given a query and a set of documents, train a system to order them from most to least relevant. But ranking is tricky mathematically because it's about permutations (orderings), not individual scores. Newer approaches use differentiable sorting networks—they create soft, continuous approximations of sorting that neural networks can learn from. The challenge is making these approximations accurate and handling cases where there's no single correct ranking.
1103.wh: Sorting networks are clever, but they introduce two problems. One, the soft approximation might drift far from the actual hard permutation (the true ordering), so the model's learned rank might not correspond to any real ranking. Two, in real-world ranking, relevance judgments are often imprecise or tied—a set of three documents might all be equally relevant, so there's no unique correct ordering, just a set of valid orderings.
1103.ap: The method introduces two fixes. For the first problem, they add a relaxation operator combined with random hard swaps during training. This explicitly controls how far the learned soft permutation can drift from a valid hard permutation, keeping approximations faithful. For the second problem, they introduce a new loss function (Variational Order Uncertainty) that allows the system to optimize over sets of possible orderings rather than a single ground-truth order. It captures that multiple orderings might be correct.
1103.ww: Why does controlling approximation error with random hard swaps help? Because training on a poor approximation teaches the model incorrect behaviors. By ensuring the soft permutation stays close to at least one valid hard permutation, the model learns meaningful orderings that will translate correctly to actual ranking. For tied relevances, modeling order uncertainty formally (as a variational problem) is better than forcing a single answer, because it admits that multiple orderings are valid while still learning to differentiate truly better documents from worse ones.
1103.po: Experiments on both public benchmarks and real large-scale ranking systems showed that this approach outperforms existing sorting-network methods and extends to more realistic scenarios where relevance is ambiguous. For a search engine, this means better training of ranking systems and the ability to use ranking feedback even when human judgments aren't perfectly consistent.

1104.bp: When someone in a conversation expresses an emotion, that emotion comes from somewhere—something happened, they remembered something, they want something and didn't get it. Extracting emotion-cause pairs from conversation is useful for customer service, mental health chatbots, or media analysis. The challenge is that conversations are complex: people have personalities, they remember what happened earlier in the conversation, and emotions build up over time.
1104.wh: Existing systems treat emotion extraction as a pure text analysis problem: read the conversation, highlight sad-sounding words, find clauses that look causal. But this misses the human reality. The person's personality shapes how they react (some people are dramatic, others stoic). The context of the whole conversation matters (a joke is funny only if you remember what happened before). Understanding why someone is sad requires modeling their internal state and reasoning process, not just scanning for emotional words.
1104.ap: The method builds an agent around the speaker—modeling their personality, their understanding of the conversation scenario, and their emotional memory. It uses a multi-part reasoning process: first, it builds a model of the speaker's personality and situation awareness; second, it simulates emotion perception by tracking what the person notices and remembers (hybrid memory); third, it uses a hierarchical reasoning process that explores multiple paths from emotion to possible causes, weighing them. The output is interpretable: you can see the reasoning steps that led to each emotion-cause pair.
1104.ww: Why model the speaker's cognition and personality? Because emotions don't follow text alone—they follow the person's interpretation of events. Two people reading the same conversation might extract different cause-pairs because they prioritize different things. By making the system's reasoning explicit and anchored in the speaker's perspective, the results are more interpretable and more psychologically realistic. Hierarchical cause reasoning (multiple paths, not just one) also captures that emotions often have multiple interconnected causes.
1104.po: The paper reports that this framework outperforms text-only emotion extraction methods on benchmark datasets. For applications like customer service analysis or conversation therapy, the payoff is interpretable emotion understanding—you can see not just 'customer is frustrated' but 'frustrated because the delivery was late (cause A) and they felt ignored (cause B)', which is much more actionable.

1105.bp: Many organizations store trustworthy information internally—legal statutes, company policies, medical records. They want to use a powerful language model (LLM) as an interface to this information, but they also want the model to access current web information for things like today's weather. The tension: if the model reads something from the web that contradicts the trusted internal source, should it believe the web or the internal truth? In high-stakes domains, the internal source must always win.
1105.wh: The problem is that language models are credulous. If they read something confidently stated on a web page, they'll often adopt it and use it to answer questions, even if it contradicts an internal source marked as ground truth. This is especially dangerous in law (where a statute is the source of truth, not a web comment) or medicine (where official guidelines matter, not a random blog). There's no easy technical fix because you'd need the model to understand which source to trust in every possible situation, and that's context-dependent.
1105.ap: The system, called PurifAI, works at the cache level (before the model generates responses) and operates proactively. It automatically generates diagnostic questions from trusted internal documents ('what does statute X say about Y?'). It then searches the web for answers to these questions and compares them to the ground truth. If it finds conflicting content, it marks and neutralizes that content before the language model even sees it. The system is designed specifically to maintain alignment with a defined 'trusted knowledge core', not to be a general fact-checker.
1105.ww: Why intercept at cache level before model generation? Because once the model reads conflicting information and starts reasoning about it, it's hard to correct—the model has already incorporated it into its thinking. By filtering the web results before they reach the model, you prevent the confusion from ever happening. Generating probes from the trusted core ensures you catch conflicts specifically where they matter most, rather than fact-checking everything generically.
1105.po: Evaluations on news, encyclopedic, and legal domains showed that PurifAI effectively blocked conflicting web content and kept the model aligned with trusted internal sources. For an enterprise deploying an LLM interface to sensitive data (legal contracts, medical guidelines, financial regulations), this provides concrete assurance that the model won't accidentally contradict official sources by adopting web content.

1106.bp: Recommending the next item in a sequence (what song comes next in your playlist, what product you'll want next) is harder than just recognizing what you like now. The system has to model how preferences evolve over time. A diffusion-based recommender (one that starts with noise and gradually refines predictions) is promising, but most treat time as just an external label, not woven into the generation process itself.
1106.wh: Standard diffusion models treat time as conditioning information added from outside ('generate the next item, conditioned on the time'). But real temporal sequences have structure: the third item usually depends on how the second item changed your preferences compared to the first, not just on absolute time. Ignoring this temporal structure means the model misses the dynamics of how preferences actually evolve.
1106.ap: The method integrates temporal flow directly into the diffusion process. At each step of the refinement, instead of just adding noise, the model also mixes each position's representation with the representation from the preceding position—capturing how sequences unfold. The researchers derived a closed-form mathematical solution for this temporal mixing that allows efficient parallel training with no extra computational cost (O(1) complexity relative to sequence length). They also ensure that this temporal-aware process has a corresponding reverse process, maintaining mathematical soundness.
1106.ww: Why integrate temporal transitions into diffusion steps rather than adding time as conditioning? Because diffusion naturally models refinement over time, and if you make that refinement time-aware (each step mixes with the previous position), the model learns the real dynamics of sequence evolution. The closed-form solution for this mixing is key: it means you can compute it efficiently without extra steps, so you get better temporal modeling for free.
