But this ignores something obvious: some documents are useful for many queries (they're authoritative, cover broad topics), while others are niche. The design bakes in a computational bottleneck: all query-dependent scoring must happen when the user types.
1146.ap: The paper reframes relevance as a Bayesian posterior inference: combine a query-dependent component (how well does the query match?) with a query-independent prior (how generally useful is this document?). The prior can be computed once and cached offline. At query time, you only need to fuse precomputed scores, not rerank from scratch. It draws on classical probabilistic retrieval theory and applies it to modern neural systems.
1146.ww: By separating query-dependent and query-independent components, you can compute the expensive parts in advance. The mathematical decomposition exposes where you can shift work: ranking can happen offline for the priors, leaving only lightweight fusion for live queries. This preserves accuracy because the prior captures real document authority.
1146.po: Experiments show a learned prior improves first-stage retrieval (up to Δ nDCG@10 ≈ 3 or 4 points) with minimal query-time cost—just score fusion. In deployed systems, this means faster responses for users without accuracy loss.

1147.bp: Dementia affects over 50 million people globally. Current retrieval-augmented generation systems—which synthesize answers by reading documents—assume users can write coherent queries, interpret answers reliably, and remember context. None of these are safe assumptions for someone with dementia or cognitive impairment. The goal: redesign information systems for people whose cognitive state is unstable and variable.
1147.wh: Existing RAG systems are built for cognitively stable users. But with dementia, queries are inconsistent (the same question phrased differently each time), feedback is unreliable (a user might not accurately remember which answer was helpful), and cognitive load matters enormously (complex multi-clause answers overwhelm comprehension). Additionally, caregivers are often gatekeepers—they need to verify and oversee what information the person receives. Current systems are designed for a single autonomous user.
1147.ap: The paper proposes functional requirements for cognitively adaptive RAG: temporal user modelling that tracks how cognitive ability changes over time, caregiver-in-the-loop retrieval that lets a family member verify answers, consent-aware evidence access that respects fluctuating capacity to authorize information sharing, and cognitive-load-aware presentation that adjusts answer complexity to comprehension level. These aren't optional features—they're foundational redesigns.
1147.ww: By modelling users as cognitively dynamic (not stable), the system can adapt moment-to-moment. A caregiver's presence adds a verification layer, protecting against both misunderstanding and manipulation. Adaptive presentation keeps cognitive load manageable. Temporal tracking lets the system learn individual patterns rather than assuming all people with dementia need identical support.
1147.po: The outcome is a set of design principles grounded in participatory research with 41 members of dementia and MCI communities. These shift RAG from a consumer-grade model toward a healthcare-grade model that's actually usable by cognitively diverse populations.

1148.bp: Regulators increasingly mandate that certain information be forgotten: removed from search results, scrubbed from generated answers. The right to be forgotten in GDPR, takedown notices, and redaction orders all require systems to erase facts. The problem: retrieval-augmented systems (which read documents to generate answers) can delete a document but still regenerate the same fact from other sources or even infer it. How do you audit whether forgetting actually happened?
1148.wh: Current compliance checks are surface-level. They verify that a document was deleted from the retrieval database, but they don't verify that the system still generates the same forbidden fact in answers. A system might genuinely exclude the removed document but reconstruct the fact from context clues or other sources. Document-level compliance is insufficient if answers still leak the forbidden information.
1148.ap: Forgetting-by-Design (FBD) is an audit mechanism that runs before-and-after tests. It probes the system in two modes: one where the fact is revoked, one where it's allowed. It checks two channels independently: retrieval (does the system still cite the removed document?) and generation (does the answer still contain the forbidden fact?). It measures both compliance (did forgetting succeed?) and utility (did we lose access to lawful information that should still be available?).
1148.ww: By separating channels and measuring independently, the audit catches failures that single metrics miss. A system might suppress citation while still leaking facts in prose, or over-correct and hide lawful information. The before-after structure with matched controls mimics medical trials, giving clearer causal evidence.
1148.po: Applying FBD to real RAG systems reveals systematic compliance gaps: retrieval can be suppressed while answers still leak. The audit report card guides which interventions matter most and where over-corrections harm legitimate access.

1149.bp: Researchers measure information retrieval progress through metrics: does a new ranking method score higher on standard benchmarks than the old one? We interpret metric improvements as real progress—better systems. But metrics are abstractions: they measure small, simplified tasks, not the messy reality of what users actually need from search. The question: how do we know if our metrics are measuring what matters?
1149.wh: The validity gap is fundamental. A metric might improve because the system now ranks the most relevant document first, or because it learned to game the metric in ways users don't care about. As systems grow more powerful (especially with large language models as judges), the risk grows: optimizing toward an LLM's notion of relevance might not correlate with user satisfaction. We've abstracted so far from reality that improvements in metrics might mean nothing.
1149.ap: The paper proposes practical ways to discuss and improve evaluation validity. It asks: does the evaluation task resemble real information seeking? Are the measures aligned with what users actually want? Can we validate that metric improvements correspond to real improvements? These questions encourage researchers to design evaluations that reflect actual needs, not just convenience.
1149.ww: By connecting evaluation design explicitly to real-world outcomes, research stays grounded. If metrics improve but users don't prefer the result, the research was misdirected. Validity forces a reality check: are we optimizing the right thing?
1149.po: The outcome is methodological: researchers can make better choices about evaluation protocols, catch cases where metrics mislead, and optimize toward systems people actually want rather than systems that maximize numbers.

1150.bp: When researchers want to know whether a new ranking method beats an old one, they run a statistical test to see if the difference is 'significant' or just luck. The Wilcoxon signed-rank test is widely recommended as safer than the t-test for this task. It's the default choice in IR research for decades. But the paper argues this recommendation is dangerously wrong.
1150.wh: Wilcoxon was designed for small samples of paired measurements and assumes the data follows a specific structure. But IR benchmarks violate these assumptions dramatically. Metrics across topics are highly non-normal, correlated in complex ways, and collected from small pools of documents per topic. The test has a hidden failure mode: it loses control of false positives in exactly these conditions. Researchers might declare a system 'significantly better' when there's no real difference—and not notice because statistics textbooks don't fully explain the assumptions.
1150.ap: The paper reviews IR evaluation practices systematically, showing where Wilcoxon breaks down mathematically. It demonstrates through TREC data that the test frequently produces wrong conclusions. The fix isn't to pick a different test mechanically—it's to understand the actual structure of IR data and choose methods accordingly. For IR specifically, alternatives exist that don't assume normality but also don't break under realistic conditions.
1150.ww: By understanding the assumption violations, researchers can see why Wilcoxon fails. It's not a safe default; it's a trap. The cumulative effect across published papers is a field claiming statistical significance for improvements that don't reliably exist.
1150.po: The practical outcome: abandoning Wilcoxon in IR research improves methodological soundness. Researchers can choose tests that are actually appropriate for non-normal, correlated IR metrics and avoid false-positive discoveries that undermine field progress.

1151.bp: Information systems today are fragmented: search engines handle 'find me documents', recommenders handle 'suggest products I'd like', chatbots handle 'have a conversation'. Users constantly switch between them. The vision here is a unified system that can mix all three modes—search, recommendation, conversation—to help a person complete a task, whatever form that task takes. The goal: one system that adapts its interaction mode to what the person actually needs.
1151.wh: Separate systems miss the context that makes each mode effective. A person searching for a hotel might benefit from recommendations based on past bookings. A person browsing products might need a conversational explanation. Current systems don't share understanding of what the person is trying to do, so each starts from scratch. They also don't share user context, making interactions feel fragmented.
1151.ap: GIANT (General Intelligent Information Agent) is proposed as a unified framework. It models four things: the situation (what's happening right now), the content (what information is available), the task (what is the person trying to accomplish), and the user (their preferences and history). Using these models, the system decides whether to search, recommend, or converse—and what to show—to minimize the person's effort while staying resource-efficient. The core architecture uses a Markov Decision Process, which can optimize long-term outcomes rather than immediate answers.
1151.ww: By unifying the models, the system can learn when each mode helps most. A recommendation might be better than a search result if you're browsing. Conversation might save time if the person needs explanation. The MDP architecture plans ahead: this interaction might set up a better next move. Context flows between modes instead of each starting blind.
1151.po: The outcome is an architectural vision: how to formalize a unified agent and how to evaluate it using simulated users who behave realistically. This gives researchers a common framework instead of isolated optimization of search, recommendation, and conversation separately.

1152.bp: E-commerce platforms often bundle products: 'buy these three items together for a discount'. Bundle recommendations combine two steps: building good bundles from the catalog, then recommending which bundles to each customer. The question: do these steps actually work well together in practice, or is the whole pipeline weaker than the parts suggest?
1152.wh: Research has tackled bundle creation and bundle recommendation separately, with each showing progress. But in deployment, they're entangled: the bundles you offer shape what users see, and user feedback shapes which bundles you build. There's no comprehensive evaluation of the full pipeline, so it's unclear whether integration problems are hiding. Do item-level adjustments (swapping one product for another in a bundle) break recommendation models? Does cold-start (few user interactions) hit one stage harder?
1152.ap: The paper implements eight bundle-editing methods (ways to create bundles), nine item-level methods (ways to tweak bundles), and seven recommendation models across six real datasets. It runs them through a complete pipeline: edit → recommend → measure. This reproducibility study doesn't propose new methods but rather documents what works and what fails.
1152.ww: By measuring the full pipeline end-to-end, the paper exposes bottlenecks that single-stage research misses. A method might work well in isolation but break when integrated. The systematic evaluation across datasets and interaction densities reveals which failures are universal problems versus dataset-specific quirks.
1152.po: Key findings: bundle-level editing struggles to create high-quality bundles; item-level replacement is a universal bottleneck; recommendation models degrade when combined with editing; cold-start (sparse feedback) exacerbates all problems. This roadmap guides where future work should focus.

1153.bp: Modern retrieval-augmented generation systems use large language models to rephrase queries ('tennis player' becomes 'famous athlete in racket sports'). Different phrasings can retrieve different documents. Running the entire pipeline for every reformulation is expensive, so the question becomes: can you predict which variant will produce the best final answer before you incur the cost of retrieval and generation?
1153.wh: Traditional query performance prediction (QPP) estimates how 'hard' a query is—does it have clear answers? But here the problem is different: picking the best variant among many reformulations of the same question. Worse, the variants that maximize retrieval metrics (nDCG—getting relevant documents ranked high) often don't produce the best generated answers. There's a systematic divergence: what makes documents rank well doesn't always make answers good.
1153.ap: The paper evaluates pre- and post-retrieval prediction methods on variant selection across TREC-RAG benchmarks. Pre-retrieval predictors estimate variant quality before retrieving documents; post-retrieval ones estimate after seeing retrieval results. The key insight is measuring 'utility gap': how often do high-ranking variants (good for document ranking) fail to produce good answers?
1153.ww: By measuring the gap between retrieval and generation objectives, the work explains why simple ranking-based heuristics fail. A variant that retrieves authoritative-looking documents might still produce a worse answer if those documents don't align with the reasoning path the language model needs. The divergence is structural, not random.
1153.po: Practically, lightweight pre-retrieval predictors can often match or beat expensive post-retrieval methods at identifying variants that improve end-to-end quality. This enables fast filtering: discard clearly bad variants without full pipeline execution, run full pipeline only on promising candidates.

1154.bp: Large language models now rewrite queries to find better documents: 'tennis' becomes 'professional athletic competition in racket sports'. Many papers report query reformulation works great. But they test under different conditions: different LLMs, different datasets, different retriever types. The question: which results actually replicate, and which depend on one specific setup?
1154.wh: A method might work brilliantly with dense neural retrievers but fail with sparse keyword search. Larger language models don't always produce better reformulations. Results depend on implementation details: which prompts were used, which LLM, which retriever. Published papers don't standardize these choices, so you can't tell if an improvement is real or an artifact of favorable conditions.
1154.ap: The paper implements ten representative reformulation methods under strictly controlled conditions. It tests them with multiple LLMs at different scales, three retrieval paradigms (lexical keyword search, learned sparse search, dense neural search), and nine datasets. It publishes all prompts, configurations, and results via QueryGym, an open toolkit with a leaderboard.
1154.ww: By controlling variables systematically, the paper reveals which improvements are robust versus which are fragile. If a method only works with dense retrievers but not sparse ones, that's a finding. If larger LLMs don't help, that's worth knowing. Replication under uniform conditions grounds the field.
1154.po: Key finding: gains from reformulation are retriever-dependent—improvements on keyword search don't reliably transfer to neural retrievers. Larger LLMs don't uniformly help. QueryGym provides infrastructure for transparent comparison, so future work can build on verified successes rather than rediscovering failures.

1155.bp: Search engines need to know which documents really answer your question. One way to do that is to look at the *entities* mentioned—people, places, things—in both the query and the documents, and use them as signals to guess whether a document is relevant. This paper examines whether that actually works in practice.
1155.wh: A method called QDER claimed to do this really well, showing strong results on benchmark tests. But when researchers tried to rebuild it from the published code, they couldn't reproduce those results. The gap was huge—the results didn't match what the paper claimed at all.
1155.ap: The authors dug into the published code and found a subtle but fatal flaw: the training data was set up to leak information. Specifically, they oversampled entities that only appear in known relevant documents, then used this biased data to train a model that ranks documents. The model essentially memorized which entities signal relevance, rather than learning to infer relevance from the query and document text.
1155.ww: When a model trains on data where it sees entities tagged as relevant or irrelevant, it learns shortcuts. It stops trying to understand whether an entity is *actually* relevant to the information need, and instead just recognizes the entities it saw during training. This is why the method fails when deployed—it can't judge relevance of unseen entities in the real world.
1155.po: The paper confirms that knowing entity relevance would help search. But the specific methods published cannot figure out this relevance on their own. Any system built on this work would collapse in production because it relied on information that won't be available for new queries and documents.

1156.bp: Large language models can now rank search results by looking at a document and saying whether it answers your query. But generating text for every document is slow—milliseconds add up when you have thousands to rank. This paper looks for faster shortcuts by examining the hidden thinking inside the model.
1156.wh: Earlier methods generate probabilities by having the LLM produce text (slow) or by reading off the model's internal scoring numbers. But both approaches are bottlenecks: one requires full text generation, the other doesn't always rank reliably. The ideal would be to pull the ranking signal directly from the model's guts without text generation.
1156.ap: The authors look at the internal attention mechanisms—the parts of the transformer where information flows—and find a pattern: relevance signals are strongest in the middle layers of the model, weaker at the start and end. They use this discovery to propose Selective-ICR: instead of reading attention from all layers, look only at the middle layers where the signal is clearest.
1156.ww: Transformer models process information in stages. Early layers handle low-level details, middle layers bind concepts together (where relevance judgment happens), and final layers prepare output. By focusing attention-reading on the middle layers, you capture the ranking decision while skipping the computational overhead of layers that don't help rank.
1156.po: The method cuts inference time by 30–50% while maintaining the same ranking quality. On hard question-answering tasks, it produces faster results without sacrificing correctness—a direct win for speed without losing accuracy.

1157.bp: Recommender systems that work with graphs—where users, items, and their connections form a network—can separate true preferences from noise by filtering the graph by frequency (which parts matter, which are garbage). Several papers claim these approaches work very well. But do the published results really hold up when you try to rebuild them?
1157.wh: Different papers report results on different datasets using different evaluation setups. Some use flawed implementations—for example, computing Recall wrong by accident. Others don't disclose their hyperparameter choices, making it impossible to replicate. When you can't rebuild a result, you can't trust the ranking of which methods are best.
1157.ap: The authors implement three families of spectral graph methods from scratch, carefully track which papers can be reproduced and which can't, and then run all of them side-by-side on the same datasets with the same hyperparameters. They also test how sensitive each method is to data sparsity (when you have very few user ratings).
1157.ww: A unified comparison reveals the truth: some papers have real algorithmic breakthroughs, while others owe their results to implementation bugs or dataset-specific luck. Testing all methods fairly shows which ones generalize and which were oversold. Simple classical methods (kNN, regression) often stay competitive when tuned properly.
1157.po: The paper establishes that not all spectral graph methods are equally good, and that several published claims can't be trusted. But spectral methods do help with something beyond accuracy: they improve catalog exploration, helping users discover items they might not have rated yet. This capability wasn't obvious from the flawed benchmarks.

1158.bp: Searching a huge document database means encoding both the query and each document, then finding the most similar ones. Most systems use a simple dot-product formula to measure similarity. A method called Hypencoder tried to replace this formula with a custom, learned one that adapts per query, promising better search. This paper checks if that actually works.
1158.wh: Using a formula that adapts to each query is more powerful than a fixed formula. But it also means you can't use the standard speed tricks (like precomputed lookup tables) that make search fast. You need to prove that the gains in accuracy are worth the cost in latency.
1158.ap: Hypencoder uses a smaller model (a hypernetwork) that looks at the query and generates the weights for a custom scoring function. So instead of using the same dot-product for every query, each query gets its own, personalized formula. They also designed an efficient search algorithm to make this fast enough in practice.
1158.ww: A query-specific formula can distinguish subtle signals that a fixed formula misses. For example, for a query about biology, relevance might weight mentions of 'genes' highly, while for a chemistry query the same word matters less. A learned, adaptive formula can make these distinctions, while a fixed formula cannot.
1158.po: The paper confirms Hypencoder beats a standard approach on standard benchmarks and that the latency is acceptable. On some hard queries it wins decisively. But on others, the gains are fragile—they depend on how the model was trained and what you compare against. Standard dot-product search is still faster even if slightly less accurate.

1159.bp: Multi-vector search methods like ColBERT represent documents and queries using many vectors instead of one, giving more fine-grained information about what each part means. This should handle longer, more complex queries better. But when researchers tested these methods on real, wordy queries from TREC, the methods failed badly—performance dropped 86–97%. This paper investigates why.
1159.wh: ColBERT and ConstBERT were designed for queries of moderate length, with one core ranking mechanism (MaxSim: finding the best match for each query vector). But long, narrative queries have filler words mixed with signal. The MaxSim formula treats all tokens equally, so filler noise drowns out the relevant parts.
1159.ap: The authors test ColBERT-v2 and ConstBERT on long queries and show that performance plateaus—adding more query terms stops helping after about 20 words because the method can't distinguish which words matter. They also uncover hidden implementation parameters that, if set wrong, lose 8 points of accuracy. Training on more data actually hurt performance by up to 29%, showing the model can't adapt.
1159.ww: The MaxSim operator finds the best-matching vector for each query vector, then sums these matches. But if the query is half filler words (like 'the', 'and', 'what'), MaxSim wastes effort matching them to something, and these noisy matches pollute the final score. The architecture itself can't learn to ignore filler because the design assumes all query vectors are equally important.
1159.po: The paper proves that architectural choices (not just training choices) limit these methods. No amount of fine-tuning or more data can overcome the fundamental constraint. For real-world long queries from user studies, these multi-vector methods plateau in effectiveness and cannot be fixed by the usual levers.

1160.bp: Search engines can be organized two ways: document-at-a-time (check each document from most to least relevant) or score-at-a-time (process all documents that mention term A, then term B, etc.). Score-at-a-time is faster on paper but rarely implemented. This paper compares two implementations head-to-head to understand why one might be better.
1160.wh: The two implementations differ in many ways at once—how they compress data, which formulas they use, which CPU instructions they call. These differences pile up, making it impossible to say which one is genuinely faster or why. To compare fairly, you need to isolate each difference.
1160.ap: The authors build tools to make both systems identical in every way except the piece they want to test. Then they swap out compression codecs (SIMD BP-128 vs Elias Gamma VB), run timing tests, and measure the impact. They also test on different CPUs—server-grade and desktop—to see if the speedup depends on hardware.
1160.ww: A faster compression codec doesn't just reduce file size; it also reduces the CPU work needed to decode, which is the actual bottleneck at search time. Compression methods that decode to fast CPU instructions win even if they compress less. The right codec for server CPUs differs from the right one for desktop CPUs.
1160.po: The paper reveals that codec choice matters: SIMD BP-128 and QMX outperform Elias Gamma when deployed, contrary to prior claims. On servers, JASSv2 is faster on average latency; on desktops, both are even; IOQP has better tail latency everywhere. The choice of codec explains most of the speed differences between the two systems.

1161.bp: Question answering systems that fetch documents to read (retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG) struggle with questions that need multiple search steps. A recent method called MetaRAG tried to solve this by letting the language model think about when to stop searching. This paper attempts to reproduce MetaRAG and compare it to a simpler method.
1161.wh: MetaRAG relies on an LLM to decide when it has enough information to answer. But LLMs change over time—OpenAI updates their models, prompts get tweaked, implementation details are hidden. Without the exact version and prompt, reproducing results is nearly impossible. And if the method is sensitive to these details, it's fragile in practice.
1161.ap: The authors re-implement MetaRAG by reading the paper and running the same experimental setup, then compare it to a simpler baseline (SIM-RAG) that uses a lightweight second model to decide when to stop. They also test what happens when you add better document re-ranking in the middle of the process.
1161.ww: A system that uses an LLM to critique and decide gains from the LLM's reasoning ability. But if that reasoning is fragile—dependent on the exact model version or prompt wording—the method won't work reliably in production. A simpler method with an explicit learned decision rule might be more robust even if it scores lower on benchmarks.
1161.po: MetaRAG does work better than basic RAG, confirming the paper's claims. But the absolute scores are lower than originally reported, likely because the LLM has changed. MetaRAG improves more from re-ranking than from its critique mechanism alone, and it's more robust than the simpler SIM-RAG when you add extra features.

1162.bp: Recommender systems that chat with users, asking what they like to narrow down suggestions, are an active research area. But different papers use the same ReDial benchmark dataset in different ways—they preprocess it differently, use different language models as the backbone, and define 'ground truth' (the correct recommendation) differently. This makes it nearly impossible to tell which method is actually better.
1162.wh: Variations in dataset preprocessing and ground-truth definition are small and invisible, but they change the leaderboard rankings massively. Fine-grained metrics like Recall@1 (did we rank the right item first) are especially sensitive. Confounding factors like 'which LLM did you use' sometimes matter more than the method itself.
1162.ap: The authors test seven prominent conversational recommendation methods under identical conditions: same dataset preprocessing, same LLM versions, same evaluation metrics. They also measure a property no one had looked at before: how much of the method's success comes from 'repetition shortcuts'—just recommending the same items as often as possible—versus real conversation understanding.
1162.ww: A benchmark can hide poor methods if you don't measure the right thing. Traditional Recall@1 can be gamed by recommending the most popular items over and over (the 'repetition shortcut'). A method claiming 40% Recall might only have 25% real conversational understanding; the other 15% is just saying what's popular. Real user engagement depends on novelty and actual understanding.
1162.po: Nearly half of the reported gains in these conversational systems come from repetition shortcuts, not genuine improvements. The choice of LLM backbone matters more than the conversational method itself. When you measure user-centric utility (would a real person find this helpful?), traditional metrics overstate system effectiveness. This establishes a clearer baseline for future work.

1163.bp: Dense retrieval uses neural network embeddings (compact numerical summaries) stored in vectors to search huge document collections quickly. But embeddings are memory-hungry. Product Quantization shrinks them by replacing each with a cluster ID. Joint Product Quantization takes this further by retraining the clusters and the encoder together. This paper checks if this technique actually works across different models and tasks.
1163.wh: A technique designed for one model and dataset often doesn't generalize. Quantization is especially risky—it loses information that the original model relies on. The question is: does JPQ's retraining make it general enough to work on models it wasn't designed for?
1163.ap: The authors implement JPQ from scratch and test it on different models (STAR, TCT, TAS-B, and larger models like RepLLama), different datasets (standard document retrieval and retrieval-for-QA), and at different scales (from thousands to millions of documents). They measure whether accuracy survives the compression.
1163.ww: Retraining the model and clusters together after quantization lets the model learn to work with the quantized vectors. For smaller models, this adaptation works—they adjust their behavior to match the lossy quantization. For much larger models, the adaptation fails because the model's knowledge is spread across too many dimensions; quantization destroys essential information faster than retraining can recover it.
1163.po: JPQ works on modern mid-size models like TCT but fails on larger models like RepLLama. However, it scales to huge document collections, letting you use dense retrieval for question-answering on massive corpora while keeping 32x less data. The method's applicability is narrower than hoped, but within its scope it enables practical large-scale dense retrieval.

1164.bp: A recent paper claimed that adding irrelevant documents to a question-answering system (asking it to read garbage alongside real evidence) actually improves answers—the 'Power of Noise' effect. This seems counterintuitive. This paper checks whether this surprising effect is real or an artifact of how the experiment was set up.
1164.wh: The original experiment used specific language models, specific prompts, and specific limits on answer length. These choices interact in complex ways. Change the model or the prompt, and the effect might disappear. Without testing many variations, you can't know if the effect is fundamental or an accident of the setup.
1164.ap: The authors reproduce the original experiment and confirm the Power of Noise effect exists under those exact conditions. Then they flip each major choice: use newer LLMs, change the prompt style, allow longer answers, and combinations of these. After each change, they measure whether the noise benefit survives.
1164.ww: The effect depends entirely on fragile implementation details. Newer LLMs don't show it. Looser prompt wording makes it vanish. More answer-length freedom changes the outcome. The mechanism appears to be: when constrained by the original rules, the LLM gets confused by noise and generates malformed text; humans interpret this confusion charitably as the LLM 'recovering.' With better prompting, there's no confusion and no illusion.
1164.po: The Power of Noise effect cannot be confirmed as a general benefit of adding noise to retrieval-augmented generation. It's an artifact of constrained experimental conditions. This highlights a broader lesson: benchmark results depend heavily on experimental setup, and surprising findings should be stress-tested across variations before calling them breakthroughs.

1165.bp: In e-commerce, price is one of the biggest factors in whether someone buys. Recommender systems that ignore price leave money on the table. Several papers proposed methods to incorporate price as a first-class signal, reporting improvements. But they were never tested against each other fairly—each used different datasets and setups. This paper compares them.
1165.wh: Three different methods (CoHHN using hypergraph networks, PASBR using graph neural networks, PUP using graph convolutional networks) come from different communities and were never evaluated in the same place. Without head-to-head testing on the same data and metrics, you can't tell which one works best or why.
1165.ap: The authors implement all three methods and test them on six public datasets using standard ranking metrics (HR@20, MRR@20, NDCG@20—measures of whether the recommended item is ranked highly and how well recommendations are diversified). They measure which method wins most consistently across datasets.
1165.ww: Some methods use architectural features (like heterogeneous hypergraphs, which handle different types of nodes differently) that make them more expressive. Others are simpler but more rigid. In fair testing, architectural choices matter: the most flexible architecture should adapt to various datasets better than rigid ones.
1165.po: CoHHN's hypergraph architecture proves most robust, winning across metrics and datasets consistently. PASBR's graph neural network approach works in some domains but not others. PUP generalizes poorly. The hypergraph design (which lets different types of entities interact in structured ways) is genuinely superior for price-aware recommendation.

1166.bp: Generative retrieval treats search like language generation: the system outputs a document ID as text, token by token, ranked by probability. A method called PAG improved on this by planning ahead—using a second pass to estimate which identifier prefixes are most promising, then focusing the main search on those prefixes. This paper checks if this planning actually helps under real, messy queries.
1166.wh: Planning ahead assumes the plan stays valid as decoding proceeds. But queries aren't clean: people misspell, reword, use synonyms. If a small change in query wording shifts the plan dramatically, the planning signal becomes useless because it pointed toward a different set of document IDs.
1166.ap: The authors reproduce PAG and then systematically introduce variations: typos, word reordering, synonyms, paraphrases, and shifts in phrasing. For each variation, they check whether the planner's candidate pool stays the same or shifts. They measure at what point the plan becomes invalid and the method degrades to unguided search.
1166.ww: A plan is only useful if it's stable under small input changes. But language is messy—the intended meaning (find documents about 'machine learning' vs 'ML') is often captured by surface variations. If the planning step is sensitive to these surface changes rather than semantic meaning, the plan will collapse frequently in practice.
1166.po: PAG's planning signal is brittle. Intent-preserving typos can cause 'plan collapse,' where the planner produces a completely different candidate set, draining the planning signal of value. The method works in the controlled lab setup but would be unreliable on real user queries with natural variation.

1167.bp: Recommender systems can be hard to trust because it's unclear why they suggest what they do. Counterfactual explanations offer one approach: tell the user 'if you had rated these items differently, you would get different recommendations.' This reveals the logical path from your preferences to recommendations. But eleven different methods for generating these explanations exist, evaluated separately in different papers. No one knows which is best.
1167.wh: Different explanation methods were evaluated on different datasets, different recommender models, different metrics, and even different explanation formats (some show item lists, some show numbers). These variations make direct comparison impossible. It's like trying to declare which basketball player is best when some were measured in centimeters and others in inches.
1167.ap: The authors implement all eleven explanation methods from scratch, then build a unified benchmarking framework. They test every method on three real datasets and six recommender models, using the same metrics and evaluation protocol. They measure across three dimensions: explanation format (lists vs. numbers), evaluation level (one item vs. ranked lists), and scope (user ratings vs. whole graphs).
1167.ww: Fair benchmarking reveals which methods' advantages are real versus which are accidents of evaluation. Some methods that claimed superiority only looked good because they were measured on easy tasks or permissive metrics. Methods generalize differently—what works for one recommender model fails for another. This only becomes visible under unified testing.
1167.po: The paper establishes which counterfactual explanation methods are genuinely robust and which only work in narrow cases. It shows that explanation quality and computational cost vary dramatically, letting practitioners choose based on their priorities. The unified framework lets future methods be fairly compared.

1168.bp: Learned sparse retrieval methods like SPLADE assign learned weights to words, deciding which words from the vocabulary matter for each query and document. This is simpler and faster than neural ranking but claims to stay interpretable—you can see which words matter. However, some expansion terms added by SPLADE are semantically bizarre (not meaningful), raising questions about whether the method is actually interpretable.
1168.wh: If the model assigns high weight to words that have no relationship to the query (call them 'wacky' terms), interpreting the model becomes impossible. You can't trust that a high weight means 'this term is relevant'—it might just mean the model found a numerical trick during training. The prevalence and impact of these weird terms is unknown.
1168.ap: The authors systematically identify wacky weights by defining a formal measure of 'wackiness' based on whether an expanded term shares lexical meaning with the query. They count how many wacky terms each version of SPLADE produces, test how prevalent they are across different model configurations (vocabularies, regularization strengths), and measure how much they contribute to ranking.
1168.ww: Larger vocabularies and weaker regularization (the training pressure to avoid overfitting) lead to more wacky terms. This happens because the model is learning to predict which words appear in relevant documents, not which words are conceptually related to the query. Regularization pushes back against this shortcut, but only partially.
1168.po: Wacky weights are real and prevalent, limiting interpretability claims. Larger vocabularies make the problem worse. However, wacky terms still contribute positively to ranking—they're statistically predictive of relevance, even if semantically odd. This reveals that SPLADE's interpretability is limited; the model learned statistical patterns that humans can't easily explain.

1169.bp: ColBERT uses many vectors per query and document instead of one, giving richer search signals but using more computation. To speed it up, you can throw away some vectors. Several pruning strategies exist: keep the top-weighted vectors, remove common words (high IDF means less information), or prune to a fixed count. This paper tests which pruning method balances speed and accuracy best.
1169.wh: Pruning vectors faster requires some rule for which ones to drop. Different rules work differently depending on the query, corpus, and model. Without systematic testing, you're guessing whether a simple rule like 'discard common words' actually generalizes.
1169.ap: The authors compare pruning methods side-by-side: weighted token pruning (keep high-weight vectors), IDF-based pruning (drop common words), and fixed-count pruning (keep only K vectors). They measure the accuracy-efficiency tradeoff for each and see how sensitive the results are to the pruning threshold.
1169.ww: Weighted pruning exploits what the model learned about importance—if the model trained itself to downweight uninformative vectors, you can trust that weighting when pruning. IDF is a corpus-level statistic (word commonness), not query-specific, so it misses cases where a common word is crucial for this particular query.
1169.po: Weighted token pruning yields the best accuracy-efficiency tradeoff, better than IDF-based or fixed-count approaches. But very simple pruning methods work fine when the model itself is trained properly—the training setup matters as much as the pruning method. A well-trained model can sacrifice vectors without losing much accuracy.

1170.bp: When you ask a search engine a complex, multi-sentence question like 'What are the environmental impacts of hydroelectric dams in Southeast Asia and how do they compare to solar farming?', you want relevant papers—but the system needs a reliable, predictable way to rank them. This matters because reasoning-heavy questions are becoming normal as AI assistants help with complex research, yet most search tools were built for short keyword queries like 'hydroelectric dam impacts'.
1170.wh: The problem: if you simply feed a long, complex query into BM25 (a 50-year-old text-matching baseline), it treats each word equally and gets overwhelmed by length and detail. The naive version of BM25 doesn't know how to emphasize the important parts of your multi-part question versus the filler words, so it struggles to find truly relevant papers.
1170.ap: The researchers found that BM25Q—a variant that flips the weighting logic—works much better on long questions. Instead of just weighing the question itself as raw text, BM25Q applies BM25's statistical importance-scoring to the question terms first, essentially identifying which parts of your question are the distinctive keywords before matching against papers. They then tested this across five additional datasets to see if the trick was universal.
1170.ww: When you ask a long question, most of the words are ordinary (and, the, for), while a few words actually carry the meaning (hydroelectric, dam, environmental impact). BM25Q finds those meaningful words automatically and says 'these are the query words that actually matter', leading to better matches. The weighting mimics how humans instinctively identify the core ideas in a long sentence.
1170.po: On the BRIGHT benchmark (a dataset of complex reasoning-focused questions), BM25Q consistently beats standard BM25. However, the authors discovered that BM25Q's gains don't transfer reliably to other datasets, whereas blending BM25Q with standard BM25 gives steady improvements everywhere. This means the strongest baseline for long-query search is not a single trick but a mixture of approaches.

1171.bp: A conversational search agent—think of a chatbot that remembers what you asked earlier and adapts its answers to your preferences—is far more useful than a one-shot search engine. Building such systems requires rich real-world test data with actual conversations, user profiles, and the messy ground truth of what humans actually want.
1171.wh: The obstacle: most public datasets have only short, isolated conversations. Real users ask questions across multiple sessions over days or weeks, refining their needs and switching contexts. Also, measuring whether a personalized response is 'better' is subjective and expensive—you need human judges who understand the context deeply. Without datasets like this, researchers can only guess.
1171.ap: TREC iKAT 2025 collected complex information needs and long, multi-session conversations (many dialogues per user) with manually designed user profiles and dynamically evolving user models. The collection includes both human-written conversations and interactions between automated systems and realistic user simulators. Every response was judged by humans at scale to provide ground-truth labels.
1171.ww: To build personalization that actually works, you must see how users' preferences shift over time within a single interaction and across separate sessions days apart. Without that longitudinal pattern, any personalization system will fail to capture the real challenge: recognizing when a user's intent has genuinely shifted versus when they're just refining an earlier question. The multi-session, human-judged format exposes these patterns.
1171.po: The iKAT 2025 collection provides researchers with 1000+ conversations spanning multiple turns per user, real user profiles, simulated user models, and large-scale human assessments. This publicly available resource enables reproducible research on conversational personalization—the next frontier in search—rather than ad-hoc lab prototypes.

1172.bp: Scientists publish papers filled with jargon, statistical details, and specialist assumptions—which means ordinary people cannot access crucial health and safety information. If we could automatically simplify biomedical abstracts into plain language, patients, families, and informed citizens could make better decisions about treatments, vaccines, and health policy.
1172.wh: The hard part: simplification is not just about swapping hard words for easy ones. Scientific language uses complex grammar, nested ideas, and implicit assumptions about what the reader already knows. A good simplification must preserve the actual meaning and nuance while using simpler words and shorter sentences, and it must work at the document level—explaining how one finding connects to the next—not just tweaking individual sentences.
1172.ap: BioCLEAR is a benchmark combining Cochrane systematic reviews with plain-language summaries written by humans, aligned at both the document and sentence level. It includes abstracts, their plain-language versions, sentence-level simplifications from other datasets, and submissions from dozens of AI systems tried on the task. This lets researchers see what works and what doesn't.
1172.ww: By providing aligned pairs—original abstract next to a plain-language version—researchers can train and test systems to recognize what *good* simplification looks like. The document-level aspect is crucial: a reader needs to understand not just individual sentences but how findings flow together, which is why this benchmark captures discourse structure (the logical flow) that simpler, sentence-by-sentence datasets miss.
1172.po: BioCLEAR enables systematic measurement of simplification quality across AI models, revealing which approaches preserve meaning and which collapse nuance. It also surfaces what current models still struggle with—likely subtle concepts and domain-specific reasoning—guiding future research in making science accessible.

1173.bp: Lawyers, judges, and citizens need to find relevant court decisions to argue a case or understand precedent. In many countries (especially those with civil law systems like Korea), there are no centralized citation networks showing which cases reference which others. Building a reliable search tool for legal documents is crucial for justice and efficiency, yet the technical and legal challenges are formidable.
1173.wh: The barrier: law is jurisdiction-specific, and what makes two cases 'relevant' involves both factual similarity (did both involve a breach of contract?) and legal reasoning (did the judge cite the same legal principle?). In common-law countries, judges cite precedents explicitly, so search tools can follow citation chains. In statutory-law countries like Korea, cases do not cite each other as much, making relevance judgments purely based on semantic and conceptual matching—far harder to learn from.
1173.ap: KCC provides 2,942 query–case pairs from 38,372 real Korean court decisions, each pair hand-labeled by legal experts with a four-level relevance rating (e.g., 'highly relevant', 'marginally relevant'). The labeling process captures both factual similarity and legal reasoning. The authors also published their annotation guide so other countries can adapt it to their own legal systems.
1173.ww: Expert-validated labels are essential because laypeople cannot reliably judge whether two legal cases are truly analogous. The four-level scale reveals that relevance is not binary; some cases are partially relevant (worth reading but not directly applicable). Training systems on these nuanced labels teaches them to recognize the patterns in legal reasoning—what makes a case truly on point.
1173.po: Researchers can now benchmark legal search systems—traditional text matching, neural rankers, and LLM-based methods—on a Korean-language dataset with expert ground truth. This opens the door to improving legal access in civil-law jurisdictions and provides a reusable framework for building similar benchmarks in other countries with different legal traditions.

1174.bp: Open-source software is built by millions of people collaborating across organizations. Understanding how code flows between teams, which organizations lead innovation, and how security vulnerabilities spread through dependency networks is crucial for building faster, safer software. But most research looks at individual projects in isolation.
1174.wh: The challenge: individual GitHub repositories are separate islands. To understand large-scale patterns—how one organization's innovation spreads to others, or how a security flaw affects the whole ecosystem—you need to see the full graph of who uses whose code and how. This requires massive data collection and careful handling of the social and technical layers simultaneously.
1174.ap: GONets maps over 230,000 GitHub organizations, 2.5 million users, and 4.3 million repositories as a bipartite network (users on one side, repos on the other, with edges showing contributions). The dataset includes detailed organizational metadata—size, creation date, follower count—and the pipeline automatically collects this information via GitHub's public API, then aggregates contribution patterns.
1174.ww: A bipartite network reveals asymmetries: some organizations maintain many repositories with many contributors; others are single-person shops. By mapping contributions at the organizational level rather than project level, researchers can see patterns invisible in traditional studies—how innovation spreads between organizations, which teams act as gateways, and where security risks concentrate.
1174.po: Researchers can now study how code reuse patterns evolve, trace collaboration dynamics between teams, and map the security ecosystem of GitHub organizations. The released dataset and collection pipeline enable reproducible, large-scale studies on open-source governance and risk—questions that were previously unanswerable.

1175.bp: Millions of people speak African languages and dialects, yet machine learning systems almost never work well for them. Building search tools that work in Ehugbo (the Afikpo dialect of Igbo, spoken by 150,000 people in Nigeria) seems like a technical problem, but it exposes a deeper design flaw in multilingual AI.
1175.wh: The intuitive assumption: if you build a machine learning model on diverse African language data, it should perform well on any African language. But the paper reveals a shocking finding: African-focused models trained on Igbo actually fail at retrieving relevant documents in Ehugbo (under 5% accuracy), while global models trained on many unrelated languages succeed (85% accuracy). Why? Knowing the language is not the same as bridging it to other languages.
1175.ap: The researchers created an evaluation benchmark from Ehugbo Bible audio (1 hour) aligned with English translations, giving a clean parallel corpus for testing. They tested African-centric models (Serengeti, Afro-XLMR, AfriBERTA) against global models (LaBSE). Through visualization and error analysis, they traced the gap: African models deeply understand Igbo's linguistic structure but lack internal 'bridges' between Igbo and English representations.
1175.ww: Global models work because they were trained on explicit translation data—seeing the same idea expressed in many language pairs teaches the model to map all languages to a shared underlying space. African-focused models were trained on in-language text, which builds deep understanding but no cross-language bridges. This is a fundamental architectural issue: deep understanding and cross-lingual alignment are different capabilities.
1175.po: The paper reveals the 'Alignment Gap': regional models cannot handle cross-lingual retrieval despite superior language knowledge. This finding reshapes how we should design multilingual systems for low-resource languages: translate-supervised training is essential, not optional. Without this insight, builders might waste effort on more language data when they actually need bridge-building between languages.

1176.bp: When you ask an AI system 'write me a 500-word summary of this research paper', how do you know the answer is any good? You could hire human judges, but that's expensive and slow. Can an LLM itself reliably judge whether another LLM's answer is correct? This question matters because we increasingly rely on AI-generated answers in research and decision-making.
1176.wh: The trap: an LLM asked to judge another LLM's output might favor answers that sound confident or resemble its own style, even if they are factually wrong. It might also favor longer or more complex answers because they feel more thorough. And it might struggle with subtle errors—a citation that looks right but points to the wrong paper, for example. Without ground truth (human judges), you cannot know if the LLM judge is reliable.
1176.ap: Auto-Judge is a benchmark pairing AI-generated answers (from retrieval-augmented generation systems) with human judgments, plus a standardized protocol for testing LLM judges. Researchers submit their own LLM-based judging methods, which are run against the benchmark to see how well they correlate with human ratings. The benchmark includes diagnostic tests for known failure modes: self-preference (favoring its own outputs), circularity (using the answer to verify itself), and manipulation (responding to adversarial inputs).
1176.ww: To improve LLM judges, you must first measure them against ground truth (humans), then stress-test them against tricks and edge cases. This forces researchers to think deeply about how judges can be fooled. Over time, benchmark results accumulate, revealing which judging strategies are robust and which are fragile.
1176.po: The Auto-Judge resource and leaderboard let researchers compare LLM judging methods systematically. It exposes vulnerabilities and validates robust approaches, gradually building a repertoire of trustworthy methods for evaluating AI-generated research summaries and citations—critical infrastructure for AI-assisted science.

1177.bp: When you search for 'best restaurants in Brooklyn under $20', the search engine might suggest 'best restaurants in Brooklyn', 'cheap restaurants near me', or 'date night dining'. These suggestions help you refine your intent. Measuring whether suggestions are good is hard because it depends on what you actually want next—which only you know.
1177.wh: Most systems test suggestions against static lists: 'did the user pick one of our top-5 suggestions?' This ignores the real process: you scan suggestions, dismiss most, and maybe click one that sparks a new direction. Worse, online A/B testing (showing suggestions to real users) is costly, slow, and hard to reproduce for different systems.
1177.ap: SIQSE uses an LLM as a synthetic user that reads suggestions and picks the most contextually relevant one based on its stated search intent. Unlike naive protocols (assume users pick top suggestions), this model simulates actual selective behavior—scanning, filtering, and choosing. The researchers validate this by checking if the model's picks correlate with real human selections across datasets.
1177.ww: By modeling users as thoughtful selectors rather than passive acceptors, SIQSE captures an essential dynamic: good suggestions are not just relevant, they must surprise or clarify your intent. An LLM as synthetic user can express preference based on context, approximating human judgment. The final evaluation metric is not LLM-based—it's a traditional ranking measure—so the result is objective even though the simulation is AI-powered.
1177.po: SIQSE enables reproducible, fast offline evaluation of query suggestion systems that reflects real-world selection behavior. Researchers can now benchmark multiple systems cheaply and repeatedly, accelerating innovation in query suggestions—a crucial feature in modern search where users frequently refine and explore.

1178.bp: Large language models power everything from customer service to medical diagnosis, yet they almost never work in Traditional Mongolian. Without a standard evaluation framework, engineers have no way to know what's broken or whether their fixes actually helped. This problem affects millions of language communities worldwide.
1178.wh: Creating an evaluation benchmark is expensive and requires expertise. For high-resource languages like English, thousands of hours have gone into building benchmarks. For Traditional Mongolian, there's no systematic evaluation infrastructure, so every company or researcher builds ad-hoc tests and findings do not accumulate. Also, simply translating English benchmarks misses language-specific challenges.
1178.ap: TM-Bench combines three construction methods: human-verified translations from English benchmarks, expert-written original tests in Mongolian, and semi-automated synthesis. It covers five tasks (understanding and generation), with 18,357 test instances total. The authors evaluated representative LLMs, using both automatic metrics and double-blind human judging.
1178.ww: By mixing translated, original, and synthesized content, the benchmark covers both universal reasoning skills and language-specific phenomena. The dual evaluation (automatic + human) reveals when a model's scores mislead: low automatic scores might mean the model output is unreadable gibberish (a real problem they found), which human judges can spot.
1178.po: TM-Bench reveals that current models almost fail on Traditional Mongolian understanding tasks and collapse into gibberish on generation. This benchmarks creates shared ground truth, enabling researchers and builders to track progress, compare approaches, and diagnose specific failures—essential infrastructure for building Mongolian-language AI.

1179.bp: Wikipedia is humanity's knowledge platform, but it is editable—and sometimes editors subtly reshape history and cultural attribution. In the Russo-Ukrainian conflict, some editors might gradually shift credit for cultural achievements from Ukraine to Russia, or reframe agency and legitimacy in ways that appear factual but are cumulatively tendentious. Detecting these narratives is crucial for maintaining integrity in shared knowledge.
1179.wh: Misinformation is obvious: a false claim is wrong. Narrative manipulation is insidious: each edit might be defensible individually, yet the accumulation reframes cultural heritage. Detecting this requires comparing sequences of edits, understanding what implicit assumptions change, and distinguishing legitimate rewording from motivated reframing.
1179.ap: The dataset captures paired Wikipedia revisions (before and after edits) in the Russo-Ukrainian context, with editorial history and consistent human annotations showing how cultural attribution and agency shift. Editors labeled specific mechanisms: which cultural elements were credited to which group, how responsibility is framed, what legitimacy is granted.
1179.ww: By examining revision pairs and their context, researchers can train systems to recognize patterns of incremental reframing. A single edit (changing 'Byzantine' to 'Eastern European') seems minor, but patterns of such changes reveal coordination or bias. With labeled pairs, machine learning can generalize to new narratives.
1179.po: The dataset enables systematic study of narrative manipulation—a subtle form of information control that poses new challenges for information retrieval and content moderation. Researchers can develop methods to detect and flag incremental reframing campaigns, protecting shared knowledge platforms from this form of distortion.

1180.bp: Running a shared task (an online competition where researchers submit systems to a common benchmark) is a powerful way to advance research. But conversational search is tricky: systems must interact with simulated users in real-time, and every interaction must be recorded in a standard format. The infrastructure challenges are substantial.
1180.wh: The technical bind: in a typical shared task, you submit a file of results ('run files'). For conversational search, you need live interaction—your system chats with a user simulator, the simulator responds, and the conversation evolves. This means both systems must be online simultaneously, which breaks the file-submission model. Without a clean infrastructure, organizing such shared tasks is a nightmare.
1180.ap: Sim.API is a middleware layer that exposes user simulators as simple web API endpoints and handles recording conversations in a standard format. Researchers' systems call these endpoints (like calling any web API), and the middleware logs every exchange automatically. There's no need for special run files or complex orchestration.
1180.ww: By abstracting the simulator as an API, Sim.API lets each system interact naturally without worrying about the plumbing. The middleware invisibly records everything, so organizers collect uniform, reproducible logs. This turns an infrastructural headache into a straightforward programming task.
1180.po: Sim.API makes it practical for shared-task organizers to include user simulation, and for researchers to develop conversational search systems without custom integration. This accelerates research in conversational AI by lowering the barrier to participation and standardizing how systems are evaluated.

1181.bp: Finding your next apartment requires balancing price, location, and amenities. A good search tool must rank apartments by relevance to *you*—your budget, your commute, your priorities. But real-estate markets are spatially complex (neighborhoods matter enormously) and temporally dynamic (prices shift weekly). Building such ranking systems requires data with rich spatial and temporal signals.
1181.wh: Most ranking datasets are static snapshots. Real-estate is different: a location's value changes over time (a new transit line opens, a neighborhood gentrifies), and comparability depends on geography (a $2M apartment in Manhattan is a different asset class than a $2M apartment in rural Montana). You need a dataset capturing how neighborhoods evolve and how transport accessibility drives price.
1181.ap: RRE-GTC aggregates 456,182 geo-temporal clusters derived from Russian apartment listings, preserving privacy by grouping listings rather than releasing individual addresses. Each cluster contains price dynamics over time (percentile distributions), building stock details, and transport-accessibility signals (proximity to transit, density of transport options). Crucially, the authors derived a 'transport-isolated' price signal via attribution modeling—the price variation explained purely by location versus intrinsic quality.
1181.ww: By clustering and aggregating, RRE-GTC protects privacy while preserving the richness needed for research. The transport-attribution model is clever: it separates two sources of price variation. This lets researchers study whether their ranking system is responding to 'location value' (being near transit) versus 'intrinsic quality' (building condition, amenities)—which would reveal why it's making recommendations.
1181.po: RRE-GTC enables research into geo-temporal ranking (improving apartment search across cities) and market-aware recommendations (systems that understand why prices change). It also supports explainable search—a recommendation can be justified by pointing to specific factors (good transit, recent neighborhood improvement), making the system transparent to users.

1182.bp: Detecting fraud—a criminal using stolen credit cards, a scammer fabricating transactions—is a massive problem for banks. But training fraud-detection systems requires realistic transaction data, which banks guard fiercely due to privacy and competitive concerns. This creates a catch-22: researchers cannot access data to build better detection systems.
1182.wh: Public datasets are too simple or unrealistic: they might show only aggregate fraud rates without capturing real patterns, or they might lack the temporal, relational, and contextual richness of actual banking networks. Oversimplified data leads to systems that work on the benchmark but fail in production.
1182.ap: F2-Gen is an interactive web platform that generates synthetic transaction data and transaction graphs based on parameterized fraud scenarios. Users can configure fraud patterns (e.g., 'small high-frequency purchases from multiple merchants'), visualize the data, and export it. The platform includes automated screening to remove fields that accidentally leak labels, tutorials, baseline scripts, and sanity checks.
1182.ww: By letting researchers configure scenario parameters, F2-Gen bridges the realism gap: simulations can approximate real fraud patterns without revealing actual bank data. The visual exploration and sanity checks ensure the synthetic data is plausible (not obviously broken), and automated screening ensures experiments are not accidentally cheating (using a column that always predicts fraud).
1182.po: Researchers can now generate realistic synthetic transaction data for benchmarking anomaly-detection, graph-learning, and teaching. Because the data is configurable, they can test how systems perform under different fraud regimes—a capability impossible with fixed real datasets. This accelerates research and makes results reproducible and shareable.

1183.bp: You read a book in English, then weeks later you recall a scene but can't remember the exact phrasing: 'What's the word for when someone's on the tip of your tongue?' This 'tip-of-the-tongue' query is hard—you remember context and meaning but not exact wording. Building search systems that handle such fuzzy queries is valuable for retrieval beyond English, where speakers of Chinese, Japanese, or Korean face the same challenge.
1183.wh: Most retrieval benchmarks focus on English and assume clear, well-formed queries. Tip-of-the-tongue queries are vague and describe concepts indirectly, making them much harder. Extending benchmarks to other languages is not trivial: you cannot simply translate English tip-of-the-tongue queries, because what feels fuzzy or context-dependent varies by language and culture.
1183.ap: The researchers built multilingual tip-of-the-tongue benchmarks for Chinese, Japanese, Korean, and English using LLM-based simulation. They systematically tested how the prompt language and the source document language affect the realism of simulated queries, then validated simulated queries by checking if system rankings match rankings from real human tip-of-the-tongue queries.
1183.ww: Simulating tip-of-the-tongue queries requires language-aware prompting. The researchers discovered that using non-English source documents matters—English Wikipedia alone is insufficient because some concepts are better understood in their native cultural context. By validating against real queries, they ensured the simulated queries are realistic, not just plausible-looking.
1183.po: Four new multilingual tip-of-the-tongue benchmarks with 5,000 queries each enable researchers to build and test retrieval systems that handle fuzzy, context-dependent queries in multiple languages. The paper also provides practical guidance on how to construct realistic synthetic queries for under-resourced languages—a recipe applicable far beyond tip-of-the-tongue retrieval.

1184.bp: Building a complete conversational search system requires multiple specialist components: understanding what the user means, ranking candidate results, generating a natural response. Researchers develop new ranking algorithms or response generation techniques, but integrating them into a working end-to-end system is tedious. A modular platform could let each researcher contribute one piece without rebuilding everything.
1184.wh: Conversational search systems are complex: they combine query reformulation, retrieval, ranking, and response generation in a pipeline where outputs of one stage feed into the next. Most researchers code custom systems, making it hard to reuse components and nearly impossible to compare fairly. Existing platforms are either too rigid (no customization) or too bare-bones (everything is a pain).
1184.ap: Orcheo is a modular open-source platform where each component (query reformulation module, ranking module, response generator) is a single-file node. Components expose a standard interface and can be swapped or combined. The platform includes 45+ off-the-shelf modules for common tasks. It supports both prototyping (Python for development) and production deployment (with credentials, telemetry, logging).
1184.ww: Modularity via single-file components lowers the integration cost: a researcher implements a new ranking algorithm in one file, plugging into the standard interface, and it works with any other module. The dual execution mode (prototype vs. production) means researchers can test ideas quickly locally and then deploy to real users with confidence. Built-in AI coding support lowers onboarding friction.
1184.po: Orcheo accelerates conversational search research by cutting implementation time dramatically. Researchers can now focus on their innovation (a better ranking model, a smarter response generator) rather than reinventing infrastructure. The platform also enables fair comparative studies—different research groups use the same base system, differing only in the component under investigation.

1185.bp: Children with autism often struggle to regulate their emotions and sensory experiences, and music can be a powerful therapeutic tool. Healthcare providers need to match music to each child's emotional needs—calming a child who's overwhelmed, or lifting one who's withdrawn—but there's no organized way to test whether retrieval systems can find the right music for these therapeutic goals.
1185.wh: Music emotion recognition is fuzzy by nature: the same song affects different children differently, and even experts disagree on what makes music therapeutic. Existing music search systems treat emotion as a binary (happy/sad) rather than capturing the nuanced therapeutic intent—does this song help settle anxiety or redirect attention? Without a real dataset of music annotated by therapists and tested with actual users, researchers can't build or compare systems reliably.
1185.ap: The authors created a dataset of 432 music tracks by layering seven distinct musical elements (tempo, harmony, instrumentation) across four base compositions, giving precise control over what influences emotion. A machine learning model proposed candidate emotion labels, a language model wrote natural descriptions, and human raters ranked the top three emotional intents each song conveyed. Final labels were aggregated using a voting procedure that averages across raters' rankings.
1185.ww: By building music modularly from components, the researchers can isolate which musical features matter for therapy—a slower tempo with minor chords might consistently calm, while arpeggios might distract. The human-in-the-loop pipeline harnesses machine speed for suggestions while keeping human judgment central to therapeutic validity.
1185.po: The dataset reveals that existing classifiers recognize emotion at only moderate accuracy (best F1 score 0.60) and almost never guess all three therapeutic intents exactly right (0.10 match rate), but do better when ranked by top-3 similarity (0.48), suggesting future systems should predict graded relevance rather than binary yes-no.

1186.bp: Search engines shape what information billions of people see daily. When they systematically rank higher-ranked results for some genders or marginalize others, they reinforce societal prejudice and deny equal access to information. Query reformulation—rewriting a search to find better results—is a proven retrieval technique, but it's typically blind to whether the rewritten query perpetuates gender bias.
1186.wh: The tension is stark: a better search result (by standard metrics) may still amplify bias. If the original query is biased and rewriting it yields higher accuracy but reinforces the same bias, you've optimized the wrong thing. Balancing two competing goals—finding correct, useful results while eliminating hidden prejudice—requires data explicitly labeled for both effectiveness and fairness, which hasn't existed at scale.
1186.ap: The authors created a dataset of over 600,000 query pairs (original and reformulated versions) categorized into three subsets: Optimal pairs achieve top search rank and zero gender bias; Effective pairs improve both relevance and fairness simultaneously; Fair pairs reduce bias regardless of whether results improve. They tested dense and sparse retrievers, measuring gains in retrieval ranking and gender bias reduction.
1186.ww: By providing data where reformulation explicitly targets both goals—better results and lower bias—systems can learn to treat fairness as a first-class criterion, not an afterthought. Showing that some rewrites achieve both improvements (Effective subset) proves the goals aren't fundamentally opposed.
1186.po: Retrievers fine-tuned on this data showed consistent gains of up to 76% in ranking accuracy, demonstrating that fairness-aware reformulation doesn't sacrifice search quality. The three subsets let researchers choose their priority: pure performance, pure fairness, or practical balance.

1187.bp: Most data in the real world—in spreadsheets, databases, financial records, scientific tables—lives in rows and columns, not natural language. Yet large language models were trained on text, making them struggle with structured data. We need to know: can these models actually reason over tables the way humans do, reading across columns, computing summaries, or joining information?
1187.wh: Tables hide their meaning in structure: a human sees a column labeled 'Revenue' and instantly understands scale and context, but a model sees text tokens without semantic grounding. Beyond simple lookup, table reasoning requires understanding hidden relationships—which columns to combine, how to weight rows, when a value is an outlier. Existing benchmarks don't systematically measure this range of abilities.
1187.ap: The authors built a taxonomy of 26 table-reasoning tasks from shallow (finding a specific cell) to deep (inferring patterns or making predictions from table structure). They created a high-quality dataset using automated synthesis with careful curation and designed an evaluation framework testing three different ways models can access tables: full visibility, filtered rows, or reformatted text. They measured model performance across all three modes.
1187.ww: By distinguishing shallow tasks (does the model understand table structure?) from deep reasoning (can it infer relationships and predict trends?), the benchmark isolates where models fail. Testing multiple access modes reveals whether poor performance stems from understanding tables themselves or how the interface presents them.
1187.po: Results show major gaps: existing large language models still struggle significantly, suggesting table reasoning is a critical bottleneck for real-world data processing. The publicly available dataset and framework enable systematic progress tracking and fair comparison across models.

1188.bp: Voice search is becoming primary for millions—smart speakers, phones, cars—yet acoustic noise ruins these systems. Wind, traffic, speech overlap, and background chatter distort audio, breaking recognition and retrieval. We need to measure how robust retrieval really is under real-world noise before deploying systems that fail when users need them most.
1188.wh: Noise isn't incidental; it fundamentally distorts the acoustic signal in ways that are hard to reverse. Existing retrieval benchmarks test clean speech, creating a false sense of robustness. When real noise hits—especially extreme noise—systems degrade unpredictably. Different retrieval pipelines (speech-to-text then search, versus end-to-end) fail in different ways, but no dataset systematically tests this spectrum.
1188.ap: The authors gathered 37,317 real queries from existing English and Chinese retrieval datasets, synthesized speech from 200 real speakers, and mixed in 17 categories of authentic environmental noise (traffic, rain, crowd, machinery) at varying volume levels.
