They tested both cascaded systems (convert speech to text, then retrieve) and end-to-end systems that bypass text conversion, measuring retrieval ranking accuracy across noise conditions.
1188.ww: By using authentic speaker voices and real-world noise samples at controlled loudness ratios, the benchmark reflects actual deployment scenarios rather than artificial test conditions. Testing multiple system architectures reveals which approaches degrade gracefully under noise.
1188.po: All systems, including large-scale models, show sharp performance drops as noise increases, with inconsistent degradation across different system types. This reveals that robustness to noise remains an unsolved problem and provides a reproducible testbed for diagnosing where each system breaks.

1189.bp: Software libraries contain thousands of functions and classes; external users want to use them to build applications by invoking functions in the right order, not by modifying the library code itself. Yet guiding an AI agent to explore an unfamiliar codebase, find the right functions, and chain them correctly is a different and harder task than traditional code generation focused on bug fixes.
1189.wh: When using a library, the challenge isn't writing new code—it's navigating someone else's design. A function's exact signature, what it returns, how it interacts with sibling functions—all must be discovered and reasoned about. Large models see millions of code examples but not the interactive exploration workflow an expert developer uses: peek at docs, try a call, inspect the output, then adapt.
1189.ap: The authors built a benchmark of real Python libraries paired with natural-language instructions (e.g., 'download and process a CSV file') and ground-truth scripts showing which APIs to call and in what sequence. They then created a multi-agent system: a Retriever explores the codebase hierarchically to find candidate functions, a Verifier re-ranks them and checks correctness, and a Coder generates the working script, iterating on errors.
1189.ww: By decomposing the task into retrieval, verification, and generation, the system mirrors how humans actually use unfamiliar code: find candidates, validate them, then compose. The feedback loop (Coder tries, fails, gets error message, tries again) mimics the interactive exploration that's crucial for unfamiliar code.
1189.po: The multi-agent framework consistently outperforms simple retrieval and generation baselines, and the benchmark enables fair comparison across models, driving progress on the practical problem of helping developers leverage existing code rather than rewriting it.

1190.bp: When companies need to form teams to solve a problem—a startup hiring to build a product, a research lab assembling collaborators, or a consulting firm matching experts to a client—success depends on picking people with complementary skills and proven ability to work together. Automated team formation could save enormous time and tap into talent pools that humans miss.
1190.wh: Teams aren't just collections of individuals; they're webs of relationships and dependencies. A person strong in skill A might thrive paired with someone strong in B, or clash with another expert in A. Gender and popularity biases also distort team selection—underrepresented groups get overlooked even if equally skilled. Standard ranking ignores both the network structure of collaboration and fairness concerns.
1190.ap: The authors extended an earlier system by adding four dimensions: (1) fairness modules that reduce bias based on demographic traits and popularity, (2) graph neural networks that model teams as connected expertise networks to capture who works well together, (3) sequence models that treat team formation as prediction over time, and (4) temporal training to account for how skills and collaborations evolve. All components integrate into a single framework.
1190.ww: By modeling teams as graphs rather than individuals, the system captures skill dependencies and collaboration patterns. Fairness-aware reranking explicitly corrects for historical biases. Temporal modeling ensures the system adapts as teams form and skills evolve.
1190.po: The framework achieves both strong effectiveness (recommending successful teams) and improved fairness (reducing gender and popularity disparities), all within a unified, reproducible system that researchers can extend and compare against.

1191.bp: Email archives contain valuable business intelligence and research material, but they also harbor private information: health details, family secrets, financial records. Users want to search their archives without exposing sensitive content, and organizations need tools to manage this risk. The problem is: how do we build and test systems that deliver useful search results while keeping private information invisible?
1191.wh: Sensitivity is context-dependent and subjective: a health mention might be sensitive in one organization but routine in another. Screening out all potentially sensitive content yields empty results; allowing some through leaks privacy. You need both relevance and privacy working in tension, and to measure both fairly, you need data explicitly labeled for sensitivity alongside search relevance.
1191.ap: The authors annotated the famous Enron email corpus (real business emails) for sensitivity, crowdsourced 150 distinct search queries across 50 topics, and collected 11,471 human relevance judgments paired with sensitivity labels. They then used a language model to extend the collection with additional judgments and sensitivity annotations, following best practices for AI in evaluation.
1191.ww: By anchoring the dataset in real email content with dual labeling for both usefulness and sensitivity, systems can learn the tradeoff between search accuracy and privacy. Testing on real data with real queries and human judgments builds trust in results.
1191.po: The collection provides baseline performance metrics for relevance retrieval, sensitivity detection, and sensitivity-aware search together, revealing the gap between generic retrieval and privacy-respecting retrieval. It enables researchers to measure how much privacy protection costs in search quality.

1192.bp: When you search on Google or Bing, the results page isn't just a list of links anymore—it includes featured snippets, knowledge panels, local business listings, ads, maps, and more. These elements drastically shape how users interact with search. But researchers studying search interfaces use inconsistent terminology, making it impossible to compare findings across studies or build reproducible science.
1192.wh: Search Engine Results Pages have evolved into complex mosaics of different element types, each with its own purpose and design. Without a standard taxonomy, one researcher calls something a 'feature' while another says 'knowledge display,' creating confusion. Cataloging all elements across multiple search engines is tedious and error-prone, yet necessary for rigorous study.
1192.ap: The authors systematically examined leading search engines (Google, Bing, Yandex, Yahoo, Baidu, DuckDuckGo) and identified all distinct elements displayed. They assigned consistent names to each element type and organized them into three categories: organic results (traditional blue links), sponsored results (ads), and features (specialized elements like maps or snippets). The catalog encompasses 143 unique elements.
1192.ww: Standardizing terminology makes it possible to replicate studies and compare designs across engines. A consistent catalog reveals patterns: which features are universal, which are engine-specific, which have emerged recently.
1192.po: The published catalog and website provide a reference point for future research on search interfaces, enabling researchers to discuss results without ambiguity and to track how interfaces evolve over time.

1193.bp: Hundreds of millions of people speak languages with little digital resources—tribal languages in India, minority languages worldwide. These communities face a digital divide: tools like search, spelling correction, and named entity recognition (identifying names and places in text) barely work for their languages. Building these tools requires data, and for low-resource languages, that data is scarce.
1193.wh: Most language models and tools were trained on major languages like English and Mandarin. Applying them to tribal or minority languages often fails because the languages have unique grammar (many are agglutinative—they stick morphemes together to build meaning), rare words, and different entity types tied to local culture. Training new models requires annotated datasets of real text, which are expensive and time-consuming to create.
1193.ap: The authors created a gold-standard dataset for entity recognition in seven Central Indian languages (Baigani, Chhattisgarhi, Surgujia, Sadri, Kudukh, Halbi, Gondi), spanning Indo-Aryan and Dravidian families. They annotated 166,444 words across 8,391 sentences with 22 entity types reflecting local culture (flora, fauna, geographic features). They then tested three multilingual pre-trained models using parameter-efficient fine-tuning and a novel pivot-based adaptation strategy.
1193.ww: By creating a culturally grounded dataset with local entity types and testing multiple adaptation strategies, the work reveals which approaches work for morphologically complex languages. The pivot strategy leverages script similarity to transfer knowledge across related languages.
1193.po: Results show that pivot-based adaptation helps distant languages through script alignment but can hurt morphologically complex languages, a surprising finding that challenges assumptions about transfer learning. The dataset enables future work on inclusive information retrieval for tribal communities.

1194.bp: Large language models are increasingly deployed as autonomous web agents that can search products, compare prices, and complete transactions. Yet testing these agents on live websites is expensive and unreliable (results change daily, sites may block access). An offline simulated benchmark would let researchers rapidly prototype and compare agents without infrastructure headaches.
1194.wh: Existing offline benchmarks (WebShop, WebArena) simulate single online stores with simple shopping tasks. Real e-commerce ecosystems have multiple shops with different product catalogs, pricing strategies, and layouts. Agents must search across shops, compare offerings, handle missing products, and navigate unfamiliar interfaces—tasks that single-shop simulations don't capture.
1194.ap: The authors built WebMall, an offline simulation with four synthetic shops populated with real product data from the Common Crawl. Tasks range from finding a specific product to comparing prices across shops, or identifying complementary or substitute goods, and finally completing a checkout. They evaluated eight different agents varying in how they observe the web page and how they interpret results.
1194.ww: By populating multiple shops with heterogeneous, realistic product data and designing tasks that require cross-shop reasoning, the benchmark forces agents to handle complexity they'd face on real e-commerce sites. Testing multiple agent architectures reveals which approaches generalize best.
1194.po: WebMall provides a reproducible, scalable testbed for evaluating web agents on complex shopping tasks, enabling systematic research without the overhead and variability of live-web testing. The benchmark identifies which agent designs handle multi-shop search and comparison effectively.

1195.bp: Live streaming is exploding—millions watching streamers in real time, gifting, commenting, building communities. Recommendation systems must capture constantly evolving content (streams start and end), dynamic user tastes (someone might watch only today's streamer), and real-time interactions (comments and gifts reveal intent). Traditional recommendation datasets assume static collections and batch preferences, so they miss what makes live streaming unique.
1195.wh: A film recommendation dataset assumes Netflix's catalog is stable. Live streaming flips this: rooms disappear when streamers go offline, new rooms pop up constantly, and users might engage with entirely different content than yesterday. Real-time interactions—a viewer gifts during one stream but not another—signal context-dependent preference. Existing datasets don't capture this temporal flux and interaction richness.
1195.ap: The authors released KuaiLive, data from a major Chinese streaming platform spanning 21 days with 23,772 users and 452,621 streamers. The dataset includes precise timestamps for when streams begin and end, multiple interaction types (clicks, comments, likes, gifts), and rich features for users and streamers. They analyzed patterns and tested several recommendation methods on the data.
1195.ww: By recording exact stream start-end times and multiple interaction types, the dataset lets systems model how user preferences shift as fresh content appears and disappear as streamers log off. Real-time interactions reveal fine-grained preference signals beyond binary view-or-not.
1195.po: Analysis reveals patterns unique to live streaming (e.g., audience behavior changes as a stream progresses), and baseline recommendation methods can be evaluated on this realistic, dynamic setting. The dataset fills a gap for researchers studying real-time personalization in streaming contexts.

1196.bp: Clinical trials recruit patients who match specific medical inclusion criteria (age, disease severity, comorbidities). Matching patients to trials manually is slow and error-prone; automated systems could surface relevant trials to patients and help recruiters. Yet most research happens in English, despite the desperate need for trial recruitment in non-English-speaking regions.
1196.wh: Patient-to-trial matching requires understanding medical language—symptoms, conditions, test results—often expressed colloquially in patient notes. Translated text loses clinical nuance. Cross-language matching is even harder: a patient description in one language must find trials designed in another, requiring bilingual medical knowledge. No cross-lingual benchmark existed.
1196.ap: The authors created CTCL, a cross-lingual benchmark by machine-translating existing English trial data, then having medical experts validate translations and match patient cases to trials across seven languages. They benchmarked 14 large language models and embedding models on the cross-lingual retrieval task, measuring how well models handle languages with varying amounts of training data.
1196.ww: By combining machine translation with expert annotation, the authors scale up to seven languages while maintaining medical accuracy. Testing multiple multilingual models reveals which ones transfer knowledge across languages effectively.
1196.po: Results show how cross-lingual capability varies with language and data availability, identifying gaps in current models' ability to match patients across language barriers. The dataset enables development of multilingual trial matching systems serving global populations.

1197.bp: Peer review shapes science: reviewers evaluate research quality, suggest improvements, and decide which papers advance knowledge. Large language models now assist reviewers, drafting and polishing text. But how much of a review came from the human expert's judgment versus the AI model's suggestions? Detecting AI-assisted reviews is crucial for understanding research integrity, yet current binary detectors (human vs. AI) can't capture the mixed reality.
1197.wh: Real review workflows are hybrid: a human might conceive the key criticisms (intellectual content) but let an AI model rewrite for clarity (surface text). Binary detectors—checking if text looks AI-generated—conflate two separate things: where ideas came from and who wrote them. A human idea in polished AI text might fool a detector into marking it 'AI-generated,' falsely crediting the model with intellectual contribution.
1197.ap: The authors created PeerPrism, a benchmark of 20,690 peer reviews with controlled generation regimes spanning fully human, fully synthetic, and multiple hybrid versions. They systematically created reviews where the intellectual ideas came from humans but text was AI-polished, or vice versa. They tested state-of-the-art detection methods on each regime.
1197.ww: By systematically varying what's human (ideas vs. text) and what's AI, the benchmark exposes the conflation problem. If detectors disagree on who-wrote-what when ideas are human but text is AI, it proves they can't actually separate intellectual contribution from stylistic choices.
1197.po: Detection methods show high accuracy on binary tasks but diverge sharply on hybrid regimes, proving that authorship must be multidimensional. The benchmark demonstrates that surface text detection isn't enough—future systems must track idea provenance separately from stylistic realization.

1198.bp: Billions of datasets exist across research repositories, open-data platforms, and archives. Researchers need to find the right dataset for a project, but searching is frustrating: dataset metadata (title, description) is often vague or missing, and you can't tell from text alone whether a dataset suits your needs. Understanding what's actually *in* the data—its semantic structure—would help search engines match researchers to datasets.
1198.wh: Metadata search is brittle: a dataset titled 'Survey Data' gives no clue about its contents. Manually sifting through files is tedious. Existing dataset search systems rely on sparse, human-written descriptions that don't capture the relationships and semantics hiding inside the data itself—what columns correlate, what patterns emerge, how entities link together.
1198.ap: The authors introduced CoDaKG, a content-enriched knowledge graph that extracts relationships not just from metadata but from the actual data files themselves (examining column names, data types, linked entities). They built an open-source toolkit to construct these graphs for any dataset collection and tested the approach against an established benchmark.
1198.ww: By analyzing data content, not just metadata, the system understands semantic connections that metadata alone misses. Graph-based re-ranking leverages these enriched relationships to surface more relevant datasets.
1198.po: Experiments show that content-enriched signals improve both baseline search and graph-based re-ranking, proving that looking inside the data itself yields better dataset search than metadata alone.

1199.bp: Scientific literature explodes exponentially—millions of papers published yearly across fields. Summarizing a field's progress by reading thousands of papers is impossible. Automated survey generation could synthesize literature at scale, helping researchers get up to speed and identify gaps. Yet building and testing this capability at scale requires tools that don't exist.
1199.wh: Survey generation is intricate: models must retrieve relevant papers, extract key ideas, identify their relationships and contradictions, and synthesize them into a coherent narrative with accurate citations. Existing evaluation methods rely on small human evaluations or custom metrics tied to specific pipelines, making fair comparison and scalability impossible.
1199.ap: The authors created SurGE, a benchmark with over one million papers and expert-validated ground-truth surveys. They designed a multi-dimensional evaluation framework combining automated metrics (e.g., citation accuracy) and language model judgments, and verified that these correlate with human expert assessments. They tested both retrieval-augmented generation (retrieving papers then summarizing) and agentic pipelines (agents actively searching and organizing).
1199.ww: By providing ground-truth surveys and a framework validated against human experts, the benchmark enables fair comparison across approaches. Testing both RAG and agentic methods reveals their different strengths and weaknesses.
1199.po: Results show agentic approaches generate better-structured surveys but struggle with citation accuracy, while RAG systems are more factual but less organized. The benchmark identifies key gaps (e.g., linking cited papers correctly) and scales evaluation beyond small manual studies.

1200.bp: Japanese companies and researchers need to search through financial documents written in Japanese—earnings reports, economic surveys, news—but the tools that measure how well these searches work have been built almost entirely around English. A good benchmark is what lets you know if a search tool is actually working.
1200.wh: The authors built the first benchmark designed from the ground up for Japanese financial text, including both retrieval tasks (finding the right documents) and classification tasks (labeling documents by sentiment or category). They tested many different models—Japanese-only models, multilingual models, and commercial services—to see how they actually perform.
1200.ww: A benchmark that reflects real financial scenarios forces models to handle both the general language challenges and the domain-specific terminology and context. By testing against multiple model types at once, you can see which approaches work best and where the gaps are.
1200.po: The benchmark is now public and gives the Japanese financial community a shared standard for measuring progress. This lets researchers compare their tools fairly and know exactly where improvements are needed.

1201.bp: When you search online today, you might want to find a research paper, the dataset it used, a survey variable it measured, or a tool that others mention—all from one search box. Modern search engines need to handle this mixed-category world, but existing evaluation benchmarks haven't caught up.
1201.wh: Most evaluation benchmarks assume you're searching one category at a time. Real users, though, want to find different kinds of things together: if I'm researching poverty, I might want papers, actual survey data, the specific variables researchers measured, and data-gathering tools all in one search.
1201.ap: The authors took queries from a real social science search platform and built a benchmark with four categories of results: Publications, Research Data, Variables, and Instruments & Tools. They used an LLM to write descriptions of the topics and to judge whether a result was actually relevant, which saved human labor.
1201.ww: When you evaluate a search system across multiple categories at once, you force it to rank items fairly across different types—not just finding the best paper, but also surfacing the dataset and tools alongside it. A shared benchmark makes everyone's systems comparable.
1201.po: The benchmark gives the research community a realistic testbed for building search systems that can handle the messiness of real scholarly information needs, where the answer is rarely just one type of thing.

1202.bp: News stories are full of events—a company's merger, a natural disaster, a political conflict—and extracting who did what to whom, in what order, across multiple articles is how we build timelines, understand causes, and prepare for similar situations. But large language models haven't been tested thoroughly on this kind of analysis.
1202.wh: Event analysis isn't just one task; it lives on a spectrum from the simplest (is this a merger event?) to the hardest (what's the causal chain of events across ten articles? what happens next?). Existing benchmarks test only pieces of this, and the data quality is often questionable because hand-labeling events is expensive and subjective.
1202.ap: The authors built a benchmark with four core tasks at increasing difficulty: detecting that an event happened, reasoning about how events relate to each other, inferring the full structure of a narrative, and predicting what comes next. They used an LLM-driven system to help generate labels automatically, then verified the quality, to make the process scalable.
1202.ww: By testing across all four levels, you expose which parts of event reasoning models actually understand and where they break. A good model might spot a merger event but fail to connect it causally to a competitor's response or predict the industry fallout.
1202.po: The benchmark shows exactly where today's best models fall short on real event analysis—whether in extracting details, cross-document reasoning, or forward prediction. This tells researchers what to build next.

1203.bp: Sometimes the answer to a question lives buried across multiple sources—you need to find the first source, then use information from it to know what to search for next, and repeat until you have the full story. Training agents to do this multi-step reasoning well requires examples of the right reasoning path.
1203.wh: Most training datasets show either the question and final answer (not the reasoning) or show multi-step reasoning but without the actual documents being searched. You need datasets that show what a good agent should actually *do*—which searches to run, in which order, and why.
1203.ap: The authors created a dataset of 9,000 multi-step questions (easy, medium, and hard) and had a state-of-the-art reasoning agent execute them, recording every search action and reasoning step. They then verified the final answers are correct. They also released open-source training code that lets you train agents using reinforcement learning with different reward signals.
1203.ww: When an agent learns from traces that show both the actions taken and the reasoning, it can imitate the patterns that work. Different reward signals—rule-based (did you find the right answer?) versus LLM feedback (does this reasoning step make sense?)—teach different things.
1203.po: Agents trained on this dataset and framework achieve state-of-the-art performance on challenging multi-hop reasoning benchmarks. The public release means anyone can build on it and try new training approaches.

1204.bp: As AI assistants become long-term companions in your life, they should remember your preferences, habits, and goals—not just answer the current question in isolation. But building and evaluating systems that actually do this well is hard because personalization happens across many subtle interactions.
1204.wh: Personalization has two hard parts: first, extracting what a user actually wants (some preferences are explicit, some hidden in how they respond); second, remembering and using that information correctly over weeks or months as conversations drift and preferences evolve. Most benchmarks either ignore this memory aspect or use fake, synthetic conversations that don't match real patterns.
1204.ap: The authors curated 2,500 long conversation sequences from WildChat (a real dataset of human-AI chats) and had humans mark down the explicit and implicit signals about each user's preferences. They then defined four tasks: can the model extract what it learns about a user, update that memory over time, retrieve the relevant memory when needed, and use it to give better responses?
1204.ww: Testing all four tasks in sequence reveals breakage at each step. A model might extract preferences well but fail to keep memories consistent as new conversations add information. Even if memory is perfect, using it to generate emotionally resonant responses is a different problem entirely.
1204.po: The benchmark shows that frontier models struggle most at memory updating and retrieval in large memory pools. Explicit memory structures help with recall but don't automatically make responses feel more personalized—pointing to new research directions.

1205.bp: Online marketplaces like Taobao face an endless stream of product listings that violate their policies—banned items, fake reviews, misleading claims. Using AI to catch these is critical, but vendors keep finding new ways to hide policy violations through word tricks, cropped images, or coded language.
1205.wh: Evasive content is deliberately designed to slip past filters while still communicating the forbidden claim. A model needs two rarely-combined skills: understanding complex policy rules and inferring intent from deliberately obfuscated text and images. Most benchmarks test one or the other, not both together.
1205.ap: The authors built a dataset of 2,833 Chinese text samples and 13,961 images from e-commerce, each labeled by experts with violation category and evidence of evasion. They tested 26 major LLMs and vision-language models to see which could both understand policy rules and catch intent-hiding tricks.
1205.ww: Obfuscation defeats simple pattern matching; the model must infer what the original forbidden product or claim was despite deliberate disguise. Evasive content forces reasoning about both rules and hidden intent simultaneously, which is where models typically fail.
1205.po: Even state-of-the-art models show significant gaps, especially on image-based evasion. The benchmark gives platforms concrete proof of what needs improving and gives researchers the data to build better defenses.

1206.bp: Climate scientists want to understand how communities experienced and survived past extreme weather—not just temperatures and rainfall, but how people responded, what broke, what held. Historical news archives hold these stories, but they're buried in millions of pages of old newspapers with poor image quality and archaic language.
1206.wh: Retrieving relevant historical news from a huge noisy archive is hard because old text recognition is poor and language changes over centuries. Then, even if you find the right documents, an LLM must pick out the human story—vulnerability, adaptation, resilience—from incomplete and sometimes contradictory 19th-century accounts.
1206.ap: The authors built a benchmark with over one million historical news segments. They designed two tasks: retrieval (find the relevant weather-related news) and assessment (can an LLM extract societal vulnerability and resilience indicators and answer questions about them?). They tested different retrieval strategies and different LLMs end-to-end.
1206.ww: Dense retrieval systems trained on modern text fail on old terminology and language patterns. LLMs often misread fragments of old narratives, filling in reasonable-sounding details that weren't actually there. Testing the full pipeline shows where each part breaks.
1206.po: The benchmark identifies specific failure modes—which retrieval methods struggle with archaic language and which LLMs hallucinate when historical text is vague—pointing researchers toward better historical understanding in AI.

1207.bp: Training trustworthy AI agents that can do complex reasoning requires them to show their work—not just the final answer but the step-by-step reasoning. Existing training data has a problem: it either shows only answers or shows reasoning that isn't grounded in actual documents.
1207.wh: To build an agent that searches documents and synthesizes answers, you need training data that shows real reasoning traces—which documents were examined, in what order, what each revealed. Without this grounding, an agent might learn to sound reasonable while making things up.
1207.ap: The authors built a platform called AgentSim that simulates what an agent searching through documents should do: it systematically explores a document collection, generates reasoning steps for each decision, and tracks what each step actually found. They used multiple LLMs to generate traces, had them debate when they disagreed, and used humans to verify hard cases. They released 103,000 reasoning steps grounded in real documents across three benchmarks.
1207.ww: When you train on traces where reasoning is actually tied to what the documents say, the agent learns the difference between sound reasoning and plausible-sounding nonsense. Disagreement between models reveals where reasoning is ambiguous, so human effort concentrates on the genuinely hard cases.
1207.po: The public corpus lets researchers compare how different models approach the same information-seeking task. It's concrete evidence that frontier models search differently and suggests new avenues for designing better agents.

1208.bp: User simulation is a way to evaluate search engines cheaply and automatically—you run a simulated user through a search system and see if it behaves like real users would. But today, building simulations requires coding expertise, which keeps most researchers from trying it.
1208.wh: Existing simulation tools are code libraries. They're powerful but require researchers to write custom code to design an experiment, run it, and share results reproducibly. This friction blocks adoption and makes it hard to share or repeat work.
1208.ap: The authors built a web-based workbench that lets researchers visually design simulation experiments without code, run them, and publish the results with full experiment details stored. The system tracks versions of components, makes it clear what was changed between runs, and supports sharing experiments through Git.
1208.ww: A visual interface lowers the barrier for novices to learn simulation concepts while still letting experts run large experiments efficiently. Version control and provenance tracking mean that anyone can verify whether results can be reproduced.
1208.po: The workbench is available as both a hosted service and a containerized version researchers can run locally. It demonstrates a real shared-task workflow, making user simulation more accessible to the IR community.

1209.bp: User simulators help evaluate search systems without recruiting real people, but simulators come in different flavors—some mimic human behavior closely, others produce reliable rankings of systems. These are actually different goals that can conflict.
1209.wh: A simulator that produces realistic user behavior might not produce valid system rankings, and vice versa. If you measure only 'realism' (does this simulator act like humans?), you might miss that it's useless for ranking systems. There's no standard toolkit for measuring both.
1209.ap: The authors released SimEval-IR, which measures simulator quality on two distinct dimensions with actual metrics. Behavioral realism uses metrics like click-depth distance and Fréchet distance of session patterns. Tester reliability measures whether a simulator correctly ranks one search system as better than another.
1209.ww: By separating measurement, you can see which simulators are realistic but don't rank systems properly, and which rank correctly but don't match human behavior. Different research questions need different trade-offs, so making the choice explicit matters.
1209.po: The toolkit and benchmarks show that the standard 'human-likeness' test used in prior work has almost no correlation with ranking validity. This finding redirects researchers away from a dead-end metric and toward metrics that actually predict system-ranking validity.

1210.bp: English-speaking researchers have many ways to build evaluation benchmarks for search systems using LLMs, but researchers working on Arabic face a problem: is this technique even reliable in Arabic? Do the same methods that work in English work for a different language?
1210.wh: LLMs were trained primarily on English text. When you ask them to judge relevance in another language, you don't know if they're applying the same logic or if language-specific quirks break their judgment. Existing studies all focus on English.
1210.ap: The authors took an Arabic test collection (ArTest), had three LLMs generate relevance labels for 10,000 queries and document pairs, and then checked: did the LLMs agree with each other, did they rank systems the same way as human-labeled data, and where did they differ?
1210.ww: If LLMs agreed with each other and with human labels, the method is likely reliable. If they disagreed, it points to language-specific problems—maybe cultural context, linguistic ambiguity, or LLM training gaps.
1210.po: LLMs generally work for Arabic relevance labeling, with agreement levels similar to English results. The finding is encouraging for researchers in languages with few labeled resources, though with some caveats around manually-verified high-performing systems.

1211.bp: A new retrieval method called the Hypencoder encodes search queries as tiny neural networks that predict which documents are relevant. The challenge is making this practical—spending less computation while keeping quality high.
1211.wh: Using a neural network as a query can be overkill for simple searches. You might be able to use a smaller, faster network without losing much accuracy. But adapting a system to use multiple sizes is non-trivial.
1211.ap: The authors extended the Hypencoder to support multiple query-network sizes, inspired by Matryoshka representation learning, which trains embeddings to work at multiple scales. The system can now choose a smaller network when quality loss is acceptable and a larger one when accuracy is critical.
1211.ww: Smaller networks have fewer parameters to compute during scoring, so they're faster. By training together, the smaller versions reuse insights from the larger ones, so they stay effective even with fewer parameters.
1211.po: In tests, the multi-size version achieves the same search quality with 7 times fewer active parameters in familiar data and half as many in new data, translating to 1.6-3.4 times faster throughput. This makes the Hypencoder practical to deploy.

1212.bp: When you search for an expert at a university or research institution, you might search by the person's name (looking for someone specific) or by topic (exploring who knows about a subject). Over a session, users often switch between these search modes as they learn more.
1212.wh: Most expert search systems treat name search and topic search as entirely separate problems. But real users mix them—maybe a name search yields a person who sparks interest in a topic, leading to topic searches, which lead back to looking for names. Understanding these transitions could improve recommendations.
1212.ap: The authors analyzed 500,000 queries submitted to an institutional expert search system, classifying each as name-based, topic-based, or unclear. They looked at whether queries in the same session stayed in one mode or switched, and whether clicks (signs of success) made mode-switching more likely.
1212.ww: Mode-switching happens, but more when a user finds something—a click prompts them to search differently. This suggests the system is working well enough that users feel confident exploring from a different angle.
1212.po: The finding that mode-switching is success-driven suggests expert search systems should explicitly support transitions—if someone finds an interesting person, offer topic searches about their work; if someone finds a topic area, offer names of leading researchers.

1213.bp: Online advertising relies on automatic bidding systems that allocate budgets across ad placements and adjust bids in real time. But these systems face a modern challenge: feedback is slow and noisy (it takes days to know if an ad led to a sale), making traditional control algorithms unreliable.
1213.wh: Sparse and delayed conversion signals (someone sees an ad today, buys three weeks later) break the feedback loops that control systems depend on. Traditional cost-per-acquisition targets become meaningless if you don't know which purchases came from which ads. Meanwhile, long-term patterns and advertiser intent are hard to encode into a control system.
1213.ap: The authors proposed a two-level system: an LLM analyzes ad content and historical trends to plan daily spending with explicit cost tolerance (high-level strategy), while a Model Predictive Controller tracks those plans via minute-by-minute bid adjustments (low-level execution). The LLM runs infrequently; the controller runs constantly.
1213.ww: Using an LLM to reason about high-level strategy lets you incorporate intent and patterns that a pure feedback loop misses. A controller then translates that plan into actions while staying robust to noise and delays.
1213.po: In production deployment, this system increased conversions by 1.8% and significantly improved stability when conversions are sparse. It shows how hybrid human-LLM-controller systems can handle real advertising complexity.

1214.bp: A recent retrieval approach encodes items as discrete IDs and treats search as generating the right ID sequence. To keep up with new items and changing popularity, these IDs need to be refreshed periodically, but rebuilding and retraining the whole system is slow.
1214.wh: If you create new IDs based on recent user interactions, the retriever—which was trained on old IDs—no longer works. Retraining from scratch wastes computation. The challenge is updating IDs without invalidating the existing trained model.
1214.ap: The authors proposed a lightweight update: given fresh IDs derived from recent logs, they align them to the old ID vocabulary so the trained retriever is still compatible. Standard fine-tuning then adapts the model to the new interactions without requiring a full rebuild.
1214.ww: By mapping new IDs to semantically similar old IDs, the model's learned patterns stay valid. Fine-tuning can then adjust for shifts in user behavior without starting from scratch.
1214.po: Across three benchmarks, this alignment update improves retrieval quality and reduces training compute by 8-9 times compared to full retraining. It makes it practical to keep generative retrieval systems fresh as items and user preferences change.

1215.bp: Depression is a crushing public health crisis—it crushes individuals and overloads the few mental health professionals available. Most people never talk to a doctor about it; instead they confess online in forums, Reddit, subreddits, social media. If we could read these raw confessions and automatically spot the telltale signs of depression, we could flag people who need help and lift some load off scarce clinicians.
1215.wh: The problem is that depression doesn't announce itself the same way each person expresses it. The clinical definition of depression has 21 distinct symptoms—sadness, loss of appetite, sleep problems, guilt, concentration trouble, and so on. A single sentence "I haven't eaten in days" is crystal-clear evidence of appetite loss. But "I've been staying in bed" could mean appetite loss, fatigue, loss of interest, or something else entirely. Most LLM systems either try to answer with zero examples, learn from a few in-context examples, or are fine-tuned, but they all struggle because the imbalance is extreme—guilt and shame come up constantly; suicidal ideation almost never—and the criteria for what counts as evidence drift across different doctors' training data.
1215.ap: The researchers created a dataset called BDI-Sen, where humans labeled sentences from online text with which of the 21 symptoms they show evidence of. Then they built Symptom Induction: instead of asking the LLM to classify directly, they feed it a small set of labeled examples and ask it to write out a short, plain-English summary of "what counts as evidence of this symptom." Those summaries become reusable guidelines that condition every classification decision afterward.
1215.ww: This works because LLMs are extraordinarily good at squeezing complex patterns into brief, interpretable rules. The guidelines act as a shared contract: "fatigue is when someone reports extreme tiredness, inability to move, or constant sleepiness," full stop. By making the criteria explicit and consistent, the LLM doesn't have to reinvent its decision threshold for every new example. The guidelines also generalize—a rule for "guilt" in depression often captures similar guilt in bipolar disorder or eating disorders, so the same approach works across different diseases.
1215.po: Across eight different LLM models, this approach consistently beats zero-shot, in-context learning, and standard fine-tuning. The biggest wins come on rare symptoms where the dataset has almost no examples—the guidelines help the model generalize from scarce evidence. On an external test set covering bipolar and eating disorders, the induced guidelines still perform well, showing that the approach doesn't overfit to depression.

1216.bp: Real-world networks are alive—they change by the hour. Social networks pulse with new users joining and old accounts dormant; cryptocurrencies flow between wallets; message graphs expand with every conversation. Within these churning networks, fraud and abuse happens silently: a bot army suddenly coordinates, money laundering accelerates, suspicious accounts wake up and disappear. Detecting these anomalies without labeled training data is the goal—you can't afford to label every node as normal or malicious when the network shifts faster than your annotations.
1216.wh: The dilemma is that anomalies are rare and weird—they don't repeat in the same way. A local detector might spot an isolated node that suddenly explodes with activity, but miss a coordinated ring of actors far away who look normal individually. A global detector remembers that "globally similar behavior is usually normal," but applying that requires labeled data to know what normal is. And there's a causality trap: if you're trying to detect fraud at time T, you can't peek at messages that haven't arrived yet—you can only use the past.
1216.ap: The method, DGRA-CL, works in layers. First, it treats the dynamic network as a sequence of time steps and learns what "normal behavior" looks like using an unsupervised technique called self-learning—pairs of similar nodes are pushed close together, dissimilar ones pushed apart, all without labels. Second, it retrieves from memory: for any node at time T, it digs through the pool of historical normal nodes and finds the closest matches, but crucially, only using data from times before T (strict causality). Third, it blends: it constructs a "baseline normal pattern" by averaging the retrieved neighbors, weighted by how similar they are. Finally, it scores: any node that deviates sharply from its baseline is flagged as anomalous.
1216.ww: This cascade works because normal behavior tends to cluster—most users just chat normally, most transactions are routine. By learning to recognize normal patterns globally while respecting causality, the detector can spot both isolated weirdness and coordinated rings. The retrieval step ensures you're comparing each node to truly similar peers, not to the entire network, which dramatically sharpens the detection.
1216.po: On real networks (message graphs, Bitcoin transactions, social platforms), the method gains 1-2 percentage points in detection accuracy (AUC) over the best prior methods on most benchmarks. Those small-sounding gains matter hugely at scale—even 1% more anomalies caught in a billion-node network is massive fraud prevented.

1217.bp: Personalized learning is the dream: adapt the lesson difficulty, pacing, and content to what each student actually knows. To do that, a system needs to constantly infer each student's knowledge state—which algebra concepts they've mastered, which they're foggy on, which they haven't seen yet. This inference only works if you have data on what each student did; but many students generate very little data—a few quiz attempts, skipping most lessons. How do you reliably guess a student's knowledge when you have almost no signal?
1217.wh: The bottleneck is sparsity. Traditional knowledge-tracing systems (systems that track what students know) fine-tune themselves on individual students' history. If a student has only 20 interactions, that's too little signal to distinguish "they forgot this skill" from "they never learned it." Prior work tried self-supervised learning: take one student's sequence, artificially shuffle or crop parts of it, and train the model to match the two versions. The problem is that synthetic augmentations are noise—shuffling events doesn't capture real learning, and the model only sees this one student's trajectory.
1217.ap: This paper (RACL) flips the strategy: instead of comparing a student to fake versions of themselves, compare real students to each other. The key insight is that students with similar skill profiles—one student who's strong in arithmetic but weak in fractions, another who matches that profile—often exhibit comparable learning trajectories. So you construct positive examples by finding naturally similar students and using their real sequences as signals. Negative examples are naturally dissimilar students. The system learns to represent each student's trajectory in a space where similar learners cluster.
1217.ww: This is powerful because genuine pedagogical similarity is far richer than synthetic augmentation. Two real students who both struggled with variables and then conquered it are a stronger signal than one student's artificially shuffled sequence. The system essentially borrows strength from similar peers—if a sparse student's trajectory looks like a well-tracked peer who's similar, the model can infer knowledge more confidently.
1217.po: On four benchmarks, the method improves accuracy by 1.2% on average over prior methods. More crucially, when trained on only 20% of the data (simulating very sparse students), it retains 97% of its normal accuracy, whereas competitors degrade sharply. This means the method enables effective personalization for students who otherwise wouldn't generate enough data.

1218.bp: Recommender systems rank items for users—which movie, article, product to show first. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly good at ranking because they can reason about nuanced preferences from free text. But LLMs process sequences one token at a time, left to right. If you present items in one order, the model might rate them differently than if you shuffle them—even though logically, the set of items hasn't changed. This inconsistency is a nightmare: your top-ranked movie might only rank high because it happened to come second in the prompt, not because it's actually best.
1218.wh: The problem is architectural. LLMs have something called positional encoding—they track where each word is in the sequence so they know context. When you list items [Item A, Item B, Item C], the model uses position information plus the item descriptions to score each one. Permute to [Item B, Item A, Item C] and the positions change, the model's reasoning changes slightly, and the scores shift. This is order sensitivity, and it's not a small bug—it violates the core principle that recommendations should depend on preferences, not on how you happened to arrange the prompt.
1218.ap: InvariRank addresses this at the architectural level. It uses two tricks. First, it modifies the attention mechanism—the part of the LLM that lets each item "see" other items—to block cross-item attention. This prevents the score of one item from being influenced by another item's position. Second, it uses a special positional encoding called Rotary Positional Embeddings that has a mathematical property: when combined with the structured attention mask, it effectively makes position irrelevant to scoring. All items are scored in a single forward pass, not in multiple permutations.
1218.ww: Blocking cross-item attention means each item's score depends only on the item itself and the query, not on what other items surround it. Combined with rotation-invariant positional encoding, this ensures that shuffling items doesn't change their scores. It's pure mathematics: the rotation properties of RoPE interact with the blocked attention to cancel out position dependence.
1218.po: On recommendation benchmarks, InvariRank maintains competitive ranking accuracy—it doesn't sacrifice quality. More importantly, it produces stable rankings: shuffle the candidate set ten different ways and the relative rankings stay identical. Crucially, it does this in one forward pass, no permutation tricks, so it's also faster and more practical than methods that require re-ranking the same set multiple times.

1219.bp: Search engines need to answer queries instantly—you type and expect results in milliseconds. Modern search uses dense embeddings, which are compact learned representations of text—think of each document as a point in a high-dimensional space. When you search, your query becomes a point too, and the system finds nearby points (similar documents). This is fast and accurate, but computing and storing millions of high-dimensional points is expensive. Under heavy load—when thousands of queries hit simultaneously—the system might bottleneck: does it serve queries slowly, or drop some entirely?
1219.wh: The tension is load-dependent: when traffic is light, you want maximum accuracy, so full-resolution embeddings shine. When traffic is heavy, you need to cut costs and avoid timeouts. But most systems use fixed-resolution embeddings year-round. You either overtune for peak load (wasting compute under normal load) or undersize for peak (and drop queries during surges). The naive fix—always use smaller embeddings—hurts accuracy. The catch is timing: you can't predict when the next surge hits or how long it lasts.
1219.ap: This paper proposes a load-sensitive approach: monitor the query queue in real time. If queries are piling up (high queue depth) or if a query has a deadline approaching, adaptively shrink the embedding dimensionality on the fly. For example, use 768-dimensional embeddings when queues are empty, but drop to 128 dimensions when the queue fills. They test two dimensionality-reduction strategies: PCA (classical linear compression) and Matryoshka embeddings (a learned multi-scale representation). Both can be applied dynamically at inference time without retraining.
1219.ww: This works because embedding quality degrades gracefully with dimension. A 256-dimensional embedding is much smaller than 768 but still captures most of the information—you lose some nuance but keep the broad strokes. By tracking queue depth and query deadlines, you're making a real-time speed vs. accuracy trade-off that matches actual system pressure. When the system is quiet, you're not penalizing users with worse results.
1219.po: Empirically, the load-aware approach beats static dimensionality reduction across varying loads. Interestingly, the paper also shows that PCA-based compression outperforms Matryoshka embeddings when used with this adaptive strategy, suggesting that simpler compression is sufficient when you're already adapting to load. The practical payoff is consistent effectiveness-to-efficiency trade-offs—no need to manually tune for average, worst-case, or typical load.

1220.bp: Search systems sometimes use clustering to organize documents into groups, which makes large-scale retrieval faster—instead of searching 8 million documents, you search a few cluster centers first, then drill into the top clusters. The question is how to partition 8 million documents into, say, 100,000 clusters efficiently. K-means, the classical clustering method, works well conceptually but becomes glacially slow when you have hundreds of thousands of clusters. This paper revisits an old-school partitioning method and tweaks it to handle massive document sets.
1220.wh: K-means is simple: you pick K cluster centers, assign each point to the nearest center, then move the centers and repeat. But when K is large (say, 100K), each iteration touches every point and every center, so you're doing massive matrix multiplications over and over. On 8 million documents, this is prohibitively slow. Bipartite graph partitioning (BP) is a classical alternative that recursively splits documents in half, which scales logarithmically—you do log(K) splits, each roughly linear in the number of documents. But BP doesn't use K-means, so it might cluster differently.
1220.ap: The paper proposes a hybrid: K-means-guided bisection. Instead of running full K-means with K clusters, you recursively bisect (split in two) while using K-means principles to guide each split. At each step, you find the split that best mirrors what K-means would prefer, but you only do one bisection at a time. After log(K) splits, you've partitioned documents into K groups with K-means-like quality but logarithmic time complexity instead of linear-per-iteration.
1220.ww: Bisection is mathematically efficient: every partition doubles the number of clusters, so you need only log₂(K) steps. By guiding each bisection with K-means logic, you keep the clustering quality high without paying K-means' full cost. The recursive structure also means earlier bisections can be parallelized independent of later ones.
1220.po: On real document sets (8.8 million passages from MS MARCO), the method is 29–414× faster than K-means variants and reduces final retrieval latency by up to 32% compared to basic bipartite partitioning. So you get both speed and better clustering quality than prior alternatives.

1221.bp: Neural retrieval systems learn to rank documents by searching through massive collections and returning the most relevant ones. The quality of results depends heavily on preprocessing: how you clean up text, tokenize it, chunk it into passages, augment it with synonyms—dozens of small choices. Most teams hand-craft a preprocessing pipeline once and use it for all datasets. But different datasets (scientific papers vs. news articles vs. short tweets) need different preprocessing. Ideally, you'd customize preprocessing per dataset, but trying 700 different pipelines by hand is infeasible.
1221.wh: The trap is that preprocessing and neural retrieval are usually treated as separate: first you preprocess, then you train the retriever. This means preprocessing choices are fixed before you even know how the neural model will respond to them. It's like tuning the engine and transmission in separate buildings—you lose the opportunity to optimize them together. Additionally, there are 700 possible preprocessing configurations (choices about cleaning, tokenization, chunking, augmentation), and trying them all by brute force would take forever.
1221.ap: PrepRet reformulates preprocessing selection as a differentiable optimization problem. Instead of trying configurations one at a time, the system represents each choice (e.g., "should we apply lowercase? yes or no?") as a soft, learnable parameter. These parameters are adjusted using gradient descent—the same mechanism that trains neural models. A hierarchical mechanism captures dependencies between preprocessing stages, so the system can learn that if you lowercase, you shouldn't apply a stemmer (they conflict). The gradient-based search explores the space of 700 configurations efficiently, taking only 1.1 GPU-hours.
1221.ww: Gradient-based optimization is exponentially faster than brute force because it follows the signal—it learns which preprocessing choices help or hurt the final ranking quality. The hierarchy captures that preprocessing isn't a bag of independent choices; operations in sequence build on each other, and the system learns those dependencies.
1221.po: On MS MARCO, the learned pipeline achieves 0.533 nDCG@10 (a ranking quality metric), beating hand-crafted baselines by 7.7% and a strong pretrained retriever (Contriever) by 11.7%. When tested zero-shot on eight other domains (scientific papers, medical text, entity-rich queries), it generalizes well, with especially strong gains on specialized domains. This means one learned preprocessing pipeline adapts across datasets.

1222.bp: Recommendation systems learn from implicit feedback: clicks, purchases, watches. But not every click means "I liked this"—sometimes you misclick, sometimes you buy something that disappoints, sometimes you accidentally view an item. These false positives are noise that corrupts the training signal. If you naively treat all clicks as positive preferences, the model learns misleading patterns. Most denoising methods try to filter out suspicious (high-loss) samples, but this creates a trade-off: by penalizing high-loss samples, you also weaken the signal on hard-to-learn true positives.
1222.wh: The core tension is ambiguity. When a sample has high loss during training, it could mean two things: the model is struggling to learn a genuinely hard true positive, or it's encountering a noisy false positive. Standard denoising methods can't distinguish—they just downweight high-loss samples indiscriminately. This breaks learning on hard but real preferences. The implicit feedback problem is fundamentally a labeling uncertainty problem: for each click, the true label might be "user liked it" or "user didn't like it," and you don't know which.
1222.ap: PLLD reformulates the denoising problem through the lens of partial label learning (PLL). In PLL, for each sample, you know the true label is somewhere in a candidate set (maybe it's positive OR negative, but you don't know which). Treated this way, denoising becomes label disambiguation: for each high-loss sample, the system learns to decide which label in the candidate set is most likely correct. Instead of heuristically filtering samples, it directly resolves the ambiguity using PLL techniques.
1222.ww: PLL is designed exactly for this setting: when you have multiple possible labels per sample and need to find the true one. By treating implicit feedback as a PLL problem, the system can learn to distinguish true positives (clicks that reflect genuine preference) from false positives (misclicks) without throwing away hard examples. The PLL machinery ensures you keep learning from hard true positives while filtering noisy ones.
1222.po: On recommendation benchmarks, PLLD outperforms existing denoising methods by more robustly recovering clean signals from noisy implicit feedback. The method is especially effective when feedback is sparse or when the noise rate is high—situations where naive filtering methods historically fail.

1223.bp: Large language models are increasingly used to rerank search results—you get a rough set of candidates from a fast retriever, then use an LLM to score them more carefully. LLMs are good at this because they understand nuance and context. But adapting an LLM to a specialized domain (e.g., medical literature, legal documents) requires collecting and annotating domain-specific training data, which is expensive and time-consuming. Task vectors offer a shortcut: they capture domain-specific knowledge learned during training and can be transplanted into a model.
1223.wh: Task vectors are derived from continuous pretraining—they encode the knowledge an LLM picked up while learning domain-specific text. But applying task vectors to a model is tricky: you can't just add them (too aggressive), and scaling them is sensitive to tuning the scale factor. Use too small a scale, and you get weak domain adaptation. Use too large a scale, and you degrade the LLM's core ranking ability or even confuse its behavior across domains. There's no one-size-fits-all scaling factor.
1223.ap: The method learns parameter-wise scaling: instead of a single scale factor, the system learns a separate scale for each parameter in the task vector. These scales are optimized using a language modeling loss—the system just needs to continue predicting text, not to label retrieval examples. All model parameters are frozen, so only the scales are learned, which is fast and computationally cheap.
1223.ww: Parameter-wise scaling is more expressive than a global scale. Some parts of the task vector might transfer cleanly to reranking (e.g., domain terminology), while others might not (e.g., generation style from pretraining). By learning per-parameter scales, the system automatically learns which parts to integrate fully, which to dampen, and which to ignore. The language modeling loss is a stable training signal that doesn't require domain-specific labeled data.
1223.po: On a general-domain benchmark and five specialized domains, the method provides stable improvements across most domains without the performance degradation seen with fixed scaling. On larger and smaller model scales, the method consistently helps, showing that it generalizes across model sizes. The approach is practical: you need only unlabeled domain text and a small amount of compute to adapt an LLM reranker to a new domain.

1224.bp: Recommendation systems use embeddings—learned vectors that represent users and items in a shared space, where similar users and items are close together. Recently, systems have started refining pre-trained embeddings after initial training to improve recommendation quality. But current methods only refine item embeddings, leaving user embeddings alone. This asymmetry breaks the alignment between the two types of embeddings, like tuning one speaker of a stereo but leaving the other as is.
1224.wh: User and item embeddings are jointly trained under a low-rank assumption—roughly, their interactions can be modeled by multiplying user and item vectors. Refining only items disrupts this alignment: the refined items are optimized for the original user vectors, which were trained differently. The embedding space becomes distorted, and the system ends up recommending a narrower range of items (bad for diversity) or misses good matches (bad for accuracy).
1224.ap: REFORM reformulates post-training refinement as a matrix factorization problem. The system constructs a target matrix that incorporates two objectives: preserving the angular structure of pre-trained embeddings (which reliably encodes which users prefer which items, regardless of popularity) and incorporating frequency signals (recent items and popular items carry more confidence). It then jointly refactorizes the user and item embeddings to match this target, keeping both aligned.
1224.ww: By treating refinement as factorization, the system naturally keeps user and item embeddings in sync—they're jointly learning to match the target matrix. The angular structure preservation ensures that the refined embeddings don't throw away hard-earned preference knowledge from pretraining. Frequency signals let the system incorporate recent data without overweighting rare items.
1224.po: On three benchmark datasets, REFORM gains up to 26.9% in recall and 29.2% in NDCG (ranking quality metrics) over post-training baselines. Crucially, it maintains higher effective rank—the embeddings continue to represent a wider diversity of items—and better item coverage, so users see more varied recommendations. This solves a long-standing trade-off between accuracy and diversity.

1225.bp: Sequential recommenders predict what a user will interact with next by looking at their history—if you watched action movies, then comedies, then action again, the system infers you're in an action mood. But in real systems, there's a lag: interactions are logged asynchronously, so when the model makes a prediction, it hasn't seen the user's most recent actions yet. If someone clicked three items in the last hour but those clicks take 30 minutes to appear in the log, the model's decision is based on a stale, incomplete history.
1225.wh: The problem is temporal misalignment. Traditional sequential models assume they see the true, immediately observed sequence of actions. But with delayed logging, the visible sequence is censored—some recent real actions are missing. The model thinks the user's trajectory ended an hour ago, when actually they've continued interacting. This causes the model to make outdated predictions or miss trends in progress. Different delays (5 minutes vs. 1 hour) affect different parts of the user's history differently, compounding the confusion.
1225.ap: DVGD models user-item interactions as a dynamic graph and learns to route information across multiple time lags. The key insight is decoupling: separate out which features matter (feature-wise dependencies) from how those features change over time (temporal dependencies). The system learns a time-lag adjacency tensor—essentially, for each possible delay, it learns how to weight historical connections. When making a prediction, it accounts for the fact that some recent data might be missing.
1225.ww: By explicitly modeling lag, the system learns that recent censored data (missing actions) follows predictable patterns from the history it does see. If you saw someone click home goods, then nothing, then the model knows recent clicks probably clustered around that interest. The variate-temporal decomposition lets the system learn feature-specific and time-specific patterns independently, making the lag-modeling more flexible.
1225.po: On benchmarks with controlled, simulated delays, the method consistently beats baselines, with larger gains when delays are longer or vary wildly. While validation on real delayed logs is pending, the method shows promise for deploying sequential recommenders in real-world systems with latency.

1226.bp: Entity linking is the task of tying mentions of things to their definitions—when you read "Paris" in an article, is it the French city or Paris Hilton? With images, the problem is richer: an image of a person or object might show their Wikipedia article, if you could recognize them. Multimodal entity linking combines text and image signals to identify entities. In practice (product catalogs, news archives, social media), these systems need to work at scale: millions of entities, millions of lookups per day, which means both speed and storage matter.
1226.wh: Current state-of-the-art methods encode text and images separately into high-dimensional vectors, then search for the closest match in the knowledge base. This is accurate but slow and memory-hungry: encoding each entity takes time, storing millions of high-dimensional vectors consumes gigabytes. There's a speed-memory-accuracy triangle: current methods pick two (e.g., fast and accurate but storage-heavy, or compact but slow).
1226.ap: FAST-MEL uses a lightweight encoder that produces a compact fixed-size representation for each entity and mention, combining both text and visual information into a single vector. The key is making the representation small enough to store efficiently but rich enough to preserve matching accuracy. The system then uses these compact representations to match mentions to entities.
1226.ww: Compact representations save storage (one order of magnitude less than competitors) and reduce computational cost. By merging text and image information early into a unified vector, the system avoids redundant encoding and can perform lookups rapidly. The careful design of the representation ensures that similarity is preserved despite the compression.
1226.po: The method matches the accuracy of the best existing systems while being three orders of magnitude faster (faster by 1000×) and consuming one order of magnitude less storage. This is a rare win-win: you get speed, accuracy, and storage efficiency simultaneously, making the system practical for large-scale deployment.

1227.bp: Large language models are increasingly used to evaluate search results and question-answering systems, especially in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipelines where the system finds documents and generates answers from them. Automated LLM evaluation works by checking whether an answer covers all the key facts (nuggets) that should be present. The challenge is constructing a good nugget bank: the set of facts that the answer should address. A bank that's too small might miss important details; too large and evaluation becomes prohibitively expensive (hundreds of LLM calls per answer).
1227.wh: This works because contrastive signals are high-signal. If system A beat system B on a particular query, the differentiating factor is often something specific—more relevant sources, more detail, better evidence. By grounding nuggets in these real differences, the system generates nuggets that are both discriminative (they separate good from mediocre) and concise. You get fewer nuggets but with higher utility.
1227.ap: The paper proposes deriving nuggets from contrastive pairs: when comparing two systems' outputs, which one is better? The nuggets should capture the differences between top-performing systems. The system looks at winner-loser pairs and extracts nuggets that capture differences in topicality, detail level, and evidence quality. These nuggets are naturally specific (since they reflect real system differences) yet sparse (since they only capture what actually differs between systems).
1227.po: The resulting nugget banks are both compact and discriminative, enabling reliable evaluation of RAG systems while keeping the cost reasonable. Because nuggets are derived from actual system behaviors, they naturally scale with system quality—improving systems generate new meaningful differentiators for future evaluation.

1228.bp: Conversational search lets people refine information needs through dialogue—instead of crafting a single query, you chat with the system, ask follow-ups, and correct misunderstandings. But incorporating personal preferences into ranking remains hard. Some preferences are explicit ("show me cheaper options"), others implicit (you hate clickbait). Traditional reranking looks at topical relevance but not user constraints, so good documents get hidden if they don't match formatting preferences or run counter to stated dislikes.
1228.wh: The difficulty is that instructions for personalized search are buried in the conversation and user profile—they're implicit, not written out. Plus, different queries need different levels of personalization. A simple query like "hotels in Paris" just needs straightforward ranking, but a complex query with multiple constraints ("under 100 euros, no shared bath, near metro, good reviews") needs careful instruction-following. Standard approaches apply the same reranking method to all queries, which adds latency and noise on simple queries.
1228.ap: APR (Adaptive Personalised Reranking) routes queries based on complexity. For simple queries, it uses fast, basic reranking. For complex or constraint-heavy queries, it generates tailored instructions by reading the user's history and profile ("this user prefers boutique hotels", "this user has a tight budget"), then uses an instruction-following reranker to score documents against those instructions. The routing decision is learned, so the system automatically learns which queries benefit from instruction-following.
1228.ww: Routing is efficient: you only pay the cost of instruction-following for queries that need it. For simple queries, you skip the overhead. The generated instructions are grounded in user data, making them personal rather than generic. An instruction-following model can enforce complex, multi-faceted constraints (price, format, style, sentiment) in ways that topic-only ranking can't.
1228.po: On TREC conversational search benchmarks, APR shows that instruction-following acts as a "rescue" mechanism for hard queries—it prevents failures on complex requests. When trained with synthetic data (no hand-annotated conversational preferences), APR competes with strong baselines like MonoT5 while opening new research directions. The method is practical and runs at conversational speeds.

1229.bp: Online travel platforms (booking sites) face a multistage buying process: first, you scan a list of hotels and click on one that catches your eye. Then, inside that hotel's page, you see rooms of different types and prices and choose one to book. Pricing decisions are tightly coupled: if you reduce the price of the deluxe room, some customers will upgrade from standard; lower the suite price and some will downgrade. Accurately predicting demand and setting prices requires understanding this substitution effect—how changes in one product's price ripple through a set.
1229.wh: Most current methods collapse this into a single stage (just predict booking or not) and ignore substitution effects entirely. This creates biased demand estimates because they don't account for the fact that lowering one room's price doesn't just increase its demand—it steals demand from other rooms in the same hotel. Without modeling intra-hotel substitution, pricing optimization fails: you might lower a room's price expecting it to sell more, but the incremental revenue is eaten by losing sales of higher-margin rooms.
1229.ap: BFSNet models the two-stage booking funnel explicitly: first, predicting whether a user will click a hotel; second, predicting whether they'll convert within that hotel. To capture substitution effects, it uses a mixing network that incorporates economic theory—specifically, monotonic substitution relationships. The idea is that if price of room A goes up, demand for similar room B goes up (people substitute toward B), but with a well-behaved mathematical relationship, not chaotic jumps.
1229.ww: Separating the funnel stages lets the model learn hotel-click and within-hotel conversion patterns independently, which is more interpretable. The mixing network, grounded in economic theory, ensures that learned substitution relationships are realistic (price changes produce smooth, monotonic demand shifts, not paradoxes).
1229.po: On benchmarks, BFSNet delivers more accurate demand predictions than collapsed single-stage models, especially when substitution effects are strong. This translates to better revenue management: pricing recommendations account for real consumer choices, avoiding the costly errors of ignoring substitution effects.

1230.bp: When you have a new dataset full of strange values or outliers, you want to know which of dozens of possible detection algorithms will work best for it. Right now, people have to run each algorithm from scratch to see which one wins, which is impossibly slow on huge datasets.
1230.wh: The core problem is that you have no history with this particular dataset, so you're starting from scratch. And even if you could recommend something, most systems just say "try this" without explaining why—which doesn't help you understand the recommendation.
1230.ap: They build a two-step system: first, they train a machine-learning model on past outlier-detection experiments, learning how certain meta-features (basic properties describing a dataset) predict which algorithms perform well. The system borrows an idea from psychology testing called item response theory to capture three interpretable dimensions: how hard a dataset is to process, how well each algorithm can discriminate between normal and outlier points, and how challenging the dataset itself is. Second, when you bring a new dataset, they compute its meta-features and feed them through the trained model to predict how each candidate algorithm would perform—without actually running any of them.
1230.ww: This works because meta-features (like the shape and spread of your data) do encode real signal about which algorithms will succeed. By using the psychology-inspired framework, they make the predictions human-readable—you can see that algorithm A handles hard datasets well but struggles with datasets where abnormalities are subtle. That transparency is what makes people trust the recommendation.
1230.po: The system recommends which outlier-detection algorithm to use for a new dataset without running a single one, achieving better recommendations than simpler baselines while explaining its reasoning in terms of dataset hardness and algorithm strengths.
