By combining both results—direct visual matches and images attached to semantically related text—they recover images that caption-only search would miss. The final answer shows both text and the retrieved images side-by-side.
1380.ww: This works because images are rarely searched for in isolation; they live in a web of textual context. A screenshot might not have words describing its content, but the surrounding documentation text does. By finding text first, you locate the *context* where visual artifacts matter, then pull those artifacts forward. Direct visual search catches things captions describe well; text-based expansion catches things that live nearby but weren't captioned. Together, they cover both paths to finding an image.
1380.po: On real enterprise systems, this approach improves the ability to find the right images by 22% (measured as Hit@10—whether the correct image appears in the top 10 results) and improves recall by 20%. The payoff is concrete: when an employee asks how to do something, the system now surfaces actual screenshots and video clips that show the steps, not just a text explanation of them.

1381.bp: When a product team changes their ranking system and wants to know if the change is good, they run an A/B test: show the old system to some users, the new system to others, measure who makes more money. The problem is that revenue is lumpy—a handful of big spenders create almost all the money, while most users spend nothing. This lumpiness makes it hard to tell whether a small change actually helped, because luck and randomness drown out the signal.
1381.wh: Revenue metrics are dominated by outliers. Imagine 99 users spend a dollar, but 1 user spends a thousand; the mean revenue is $10.99, but it's entirely determined by one person. If that one person happens to see the new system, the test will look amazing even if the new system is worse. If they see the old system, it will look terrible. With such high variance, you need huge numbers of users to be confident in a result—which means running tests longer and slower.
1381.ap: They split users into groups based on their pre-experiment spending levels before the test even starts (a technique called post-stratification). They might group users into 'light spenders,' 'medium spenders,' and 'heavy spenders' based on historical data. Then within each group, they measure the effect separately and combine the results. This way, if a random whale lands in the new system, they account for it because they know what that whale's spending level usually is. They combine this grouping with another variance-reduction trick (CUPED), which uses historical spending patterns to smooth out noisy estimates.
1381.ww: The intuition is simple: variance comes from not knowing whether a big revenue difference is real or just unlucky user assignment. If you pre-split users by spending level, you control for that—you're comparing apples to apples within each tier. Heavy spenders will exist in both the test and control groups in predictable amounts, so their randomness washes out instead of creating false signals.
1381.po: The payoff is that the company can reach the same statistical confidence level using 45% fewer users. Instead of running a test for two weeks on a billion users, they might reach the same conclusion in one week on 500 million users. This is a direct business win: faster decisions, cheaper tests, ability to run more experiments.

1382.bp: On a platform like Pinterest, when you're looking at something you haven't seen before (a new pin, a fresh artist's work), the recommendation system struggles because it has no history of whether you like that creator's style. This is the cold-start problem: how do you recommend something *new* when you have no data points yet? The platform's business depends on helping creators get discovered and keeping users engaged, so getting cold-start right is crucial to long-term growth.
1382.wh: Normal recommendation systems learn from patterns: if you liked this 100 times, the system learns you like this kind of thing. But with a brand-new pin, there are no likes yet, no engagement signals. You can't learn from history that doesn't exist. You could use the content itself (the image, metadata) but that's noisy—many good pins get buried just because they haven't had time to rack up signals. You also have very little data about whether the creator's *previous* pins (if any) appeal to you, so you're flying blind on both fronts.
1382.ap: They use hierarchical item IDs learned from the dataset—think of this as a semantic taxonomy. Instead of just storing 'pin #4837291,' they store 'pin #4837291' as part of a tree: it's a 'fashion photo' → 'streetwear' → 'men's sneakers' → 'vintage-inspired.' This rich structure lets them make educated guesses about new pins by looking at semantic similarity before engagement data exists. They also add engagement information (how people interact with items) into the ID system itself, and use multiple view learning (comparing queries to items, items to each other) to align these representations with real engagement. On Pinterest's full system, they test this across multiple surfaces (Home Feed, Search, Closeup) and content types (organic pins, e-commerce products).
1382.ww: The core insight is that semantically similar things tend to get liked together. If the system understands that a new pin is 'mid-century modern furniture' (via the hierarchical ID), it can look at how users engaged with other mid-century pins and make a reasonable guess. The hierarchical structure also naturally helps with cold-start because fresh content shares semantic prefixes with established content, so the model generalizes knowledge. By encoding engagement patterns into the ID space itself, rather than treating IDs as opaque numbers, the system can predict engagement for truly new items.
1382.po: On Pinterest's production system serving billions of requests daily, this approach drives a 3.67% increase in fresh engagements (repins) and a 0.05% increase in daily active users retained, which at Pinterest's scale is enormous. The system has been deployed and is actively making recommendations at production scale.

1383.bp: Short-form video platforms like TikTok and Douyin live on two tensions: users want interesting content (so show what they'll watch), but creators need opportunities to grow their audience (so give emerging creators visibility). Right now, systems almost always choose: maximize watch time, even if it starves new creators. But if all creators give up, the platform dies. This paper asks: can we optimize *both* at once—make users happy *and* give creators a fair shot?
1383.wh: These two goals fight. The videos with the highest watch time tend to come from established creators with large audiences. If you always show those, users are happy but new creators get zero exposure. If you force exposure for new creators, users watch less and the platform's engagement tanks. Previous work either tackles one goal (maximize creator fairness) or ignores the creator side (just maximize views). The real challenge is that these aren't separate decisions you can optimize one by one—the system recommends videos to millions of users simultaneously, and those decisions ripple across the entire platform's creator economy.
1383.ap: They frame the problem as a constrained optimization: maximize total user satisfaction while ensuring creator exposure meets certain thresholds. The trick is that enforcing global constraints across all users in real time seems computationally impossible (checking millions of recommendations against a constraint is too slow). They use a primal-dual algorithm, which is a technique from optimization theory that decouples the global constraint into local decision rules. Each individual recommendation decision follows a simple rule derived from the global constraint, so you don't need to check all recommendations against each other—each one locally respects the global goal.
1383.ww: The insight is that global fairness doesn't require global coordination. By using primal-dual methods, they convert the problem from 'enforce a global constraint on millions of decisions' into 'apply a local rule to each individual decision.' The local rule is derived from the constraint mathematically, so following it automatically satisfies the global property. It's like saying instead of 'make sure exactly 5% of exposure goes to emerging creators,' you say 'each recommendation has a 5% chance of promoting an emerging creator,' and when you multiply that across millions of decisions, you hit the global target without any coordination.
1383.po: On a large-scale short-video platform, this approach achieves measurable improvements in joint user-creator value compared to baselines that optimize only one objective. The framework is practical enough to deploy in real systems where decisions must be made in milliseconds, suggesting the method unifies creator interests and user satisfaction without sacrificing platform speed.

1384.bp: In fashion and interior design, some combinations of items look great together and some clash—a sofa pairs well with certain tables but not others, a sweater matches some pants but not those. Recommending visually compatible items is a big part of e-commerce, from outfits to home decor. But 'compatible' is deeply contextual: mid-century modern furniture follows different rules than minimalist design; a navy sweater and a red scarf work together in ways a neon sweater and a bright red scarf might not. The goal is to teach machines to *see* these subtle visual rules.
1384.wh: Compatibility is not a property of individual items—it's a relationship between items in context. A generic image recognition system can tell you 'this is a brown sofa,' but it can't judge if that brown sofa matches a green chair without understanding style, material, period, and countless other nuances. Existing methods treat compatibility as a fixed property in some abstract space (like 'sofas go in this neighborhood, tables go in that one'), but that ignores the fact that a sofa's compatibility *depends* on which item you're pairing it with. A leather sofa pairs differently with a glass coffee table than with a rustic wood table.
1384.ap: They build a model that uses both images and text descriptions. The key idea is that compatibility is conditional—you're asking 'is this item compatible *with that item*?' They use an attention mechanism that looks at textual descriptions (like 'mid-century modern' or 'oak finish') to selectively focus on relevant visual features. Instead of learning one generic 'sofa representation,' the model learns to *highlight different parts* of the sofa image depending on what it's being paired with. When pairing a sofa with a table, emphasize wood tone and edge style; when pairing with a curtain, emphasize color and texture. They train this using triplets (compatible pairs and incompatible pairs) to learn these conditional compatibility rules.
1384.ww: The core insight is that vision and language collaborate on style. A visual model alone can't distinguish mid-century modern from minimalist without explicit guidance, but text ('mid-century modern') can. By conditioning visual attention on textual context, the model learns to weight visual features appropriately for each style. A text like 'oak finish' tells the model to pay attention to wood grain and color in the image, automatically making compatibility judgments that account for material. This is more flexible than rigid category-specific rules because new styles can be described in text without retraining.
1384.po: The model shows improvements on established fashion and interior design benchmarks. By leveraging text descriptions to guide visual understanding, the approach captures style nuances that image-only methods miss, enabling more accurate recommendations of visually compatible items—tangibly useful for e-commerce platforms trying to help customers find items that work together.

1385.bp: E-commerce marketplaces like Amazon and local classified platforms operate under countless rules: no counterfeit items, no misleading photos, no prohibited substances. When someone lists a product, that listing must be checked against every rule to ensure it's allowed. With millions of daily submissions and thousands of rules, checking every listing against every policy is computationally prohibitive. The goal is to quickly filter safe items and flag suspicious ones for human review, without checking everything exhaustively.
1385.wh: The naive approach—test each new listing against each of the thousand policies—is too slow. It would create a bottleneck that slows down the marketplace's ability to accept new listings. You need a fast filter that catches problematic items before they reach the expensive verification step. But the filter must have high recall: missing a policy violation is worse than being a bit overzealous and flagging something for further review. So you need speed *and* accuracy, which don't usually go together.
1385.ap: They use language models to convert policy documents (which are often complex legal text) into concise, searchable descriptions. These descriptions are stored in a vector index (a searchable space where similar items live nearby). When a new product is listed, they quickly search this index to find which policies are most likely relevant to that item. This acts as a high-speed router: most items get a quick 'looks fine' result and skip the expensive verification step, while suspicious items are routed to specific policy classes for deeper checking. To improve accuracy, they use hard negative samples—when training, they deliberately feed the model examples of items that *almost* violate a policy but don't quite, forcing it to learn the boundaries more precisely.
1385.ww: The efficiency comes from search instead of exhaustive testing. Instead of running a complex rule engine on every item for every policy, you ask: which policies are *relevant* to this item? Then you only check the relevant ones. Using language models to compress policies into searchable vectors makes this possible. Hard negatives improve accuracy because they teach the model that being 'close to' a violation is still different from violating—an item that almost looks counterfeit but isn't is valuable training data for understanding where the line is.
1385.po: On an internal e-commerce dataset, this retrieval-based approach achieves 3.8% better recall at a fixed rate of false positives compared to standard dense retrieval. Adding hard negative examples to the index improves recall by 26.3% on average. The practical payoff is that the system can filter listings much faster without needing to manually check every listing against every rule.

1386.bp: Large language models like GPT can answer questions about business data—'what revenue did we get from sales in July?'—by reading a CSV or database table and synthesizing an answer. But hallucination is a killer risk: if the model makes up a number or misinterprets the data, a business decision based on that answer could be wrong. This work tackles the specific problem of making table question answering reliable enough for production analytics, where a wrong answer costs money or credibility.
1386.wh: Direct preference optimization (a popular technique for making language models better at following instructions) works by showing the model pairs of answers: 'this is a good answer, this is a bad answer.' But it doesn't capture *why* one is better. Maybe one answer is more accurate, another more helpful. By mixing these signals, the model learns a blurry notion of 'good.' For table question answering, you need the model to deeply understand *factual correctness*, not just general helpfulness. The existing approach throws away the reason behind each preference, losing information.
1386.ap: They introduce a reason-aware version of preference optimization. Instead of just showing 'answer A is better than answer B,' they show 'answer A is better than answer B *because* [reason: it correctly joins the tables / interprets the date filter / aggregates the right column].' The model learns these explicit reasons alongside the preference, so it learns to internalize what makes a factually accurate answer. The reasons act as a bridge that helps the model understand *why* a table query is right or wrong, not just that one answer is preferred.
1386.ww: Reasons act as an explanation layer that makes learning more precise. When a model learns from a reason ('the answer is wrong because it summed the wrong column'), it can't just learn a superficial preference—it must reason about the structure of the problem. Over time, it internalizes these reasoning patterns, making it better at handling new queries. The reason essentially decomposes a complex preference signal into interpretable steps, which helps the model generalize to cases it hasn't seen.
1386.po: Evaluated on real-world advertising datasets, RAPO shows substantial improvements over standard preference optimization in factual accuracy. The payoff is that language models become more trustworthy for answering business-critical questions over structured data, reducing hallucination risk in production analytics.

1387.bp: Customer service AI systems often recommend actions to customers: 'Click here to reset your password,' 'Follow these steps to change your shipping address.' The system's job is to guess what the user actually needs right now. It currently looks at the customer's past interactions ('they reset their password last month, so they probably need account help') but ignores a key insight: what a customer *needs now* is connected to what they're *about to do next*. If they're about to leave a product review, they might need formatting help; if they're about to make a purchase, they might need payment options. The goal is to make these intent recommendations more accurate by predicting the next action.
1387.wh: Historical behavior alone is a lagging indicator. By the time a customer clicks 'reset password,' they've already decided they need to reset. The system's recommendation comes too late or is already obvious. More subtly, what the customer needs depends on their trajectory—where they're going next—not just where they've been. A customer who looked at product pages and then went to checkout needs different help than a customer who looked at product pages and then left. Current methods ignore this forward-looking signal.
1387.ap: They build a model that first predicts what the customer will do next (next action/behavior). This prediction happens in two ways: (1) forward deduction—looking at past actions and inferring likely continuations, and (2) reverse tracing—working backward from known action sequences to fill in gaps. They supervise this with 'closed-loop' feedback: comparing predicted next actions to what actually happened later. Then they use this predicted-next-action to guide the main intent recommendation model, progressively activating latent representations in the model that correspond to the anticipated next action.
1387.ww: The insight is that next actions and current intent are coupled. If you accurately predict what someone will do next, you can align your current recommendation to match. When you predict 'this customer is about to review a product,' you can recommend 'here's how to write a review' rather than generic help. The closed-loop training ensures the next-action predictor is calibrated to real behavior, not just theoretically plausible—so it's actually useful for guiding the main model.
1387.po: On offline experiments, the model shows effectiveness in capturing intent. In online A/B testing on a real customer service platform, NBA-Net achieves a 5.6% relative improvement in click-through rate, meaning more customers use the recommended actions. This is a concrete gain in system usefulness.

1388.bp: In emerging-market e-commerce, platforms often have basic product categories ('clothing,' 'electronics') but lack detailed attributes ('material: cotton,' 'brand: Nike,' 'size: M'). Without these fine-grained attributes, search is weak—customers can't filter 'show me blue cotton shirts' because the system doesn't know material or color. Rebuilding this from scratch by hand is expensive and slow. This work automates bootstrapping of product attribute taxonomies using language models and human feedback, starting from absolutely nothing.
1388.wh: Creating an attribute taxonomy is hard because you need to: (1) figure out what attributes even matter (different product categories need different attributes), (2) define the valid values for each attribute (colors, sizes, materials), (3) validate that the taxonomy actually works for the product catalog. A language model might generate plausible attributes, but they could be wrong, redundant, or miss domain nuances. You need human validation, but that's expensive. Existing solutions either require hand-labeling (slow, expensive) or use generic attribute ontologies that don't fit emerging markets.
1388.ap: They use a human-in-the-loop pipeline. A language model generates candidate attributes for a product category. Then two stages of human review: (1) developers spot-check for nonsense and filter out bad suggestions before they go to the second stage, and (2) local domain-expert staff validate and refine the attributes. This feedback is fed back into the generation pipeline—each round, the prompts are tweaked based on what went wrong before. The loop repeats until the taxonomy stabilizes. Once the taxonomy is solid, language models tag individual products with their attributes, enriching the catalog.
1388.ww: Human-in-the-loop works here because the loop is tight and local. Each iteration, humans see concrete outputs ('the model suggested 'color' is an attribute, is that right?') and can give targeted feedback. Developer review catches obvious errors quickly, so domain experts aren't wasting time on garbage; expert validation catches domain-specific nuances that models miss. By cycling feedback directly back into prompts, the language model learns to align with local expectations.
1388.po: Once the attribute taxonomy is built, the platform gains multiple benefits: customers can now do faceted filtering ('show me blue cotton shirts only'), ranking models get structured features to learn from, and dense retrieval (semantic search) gets richer representations to work with. The real payoff is that platforms in emerging markets can now bootstrap sophisticated search without enormous upfront tagging effort.

1389.bp: Fashion e-commerce platforms use vision-language models (AI systems that understand both images and text) to extract structured information from product photos: 'what brand is this?' 'what color?' 'what material?' But these models are general-purpose (trained on internet images) and haven't been tuned for fashion. Before betting on a model for production, teams need to know: which model actually works best for our specific tasks? How sensitive is each model to how you ask it questions? This work creates a benchmark to answer these questions in real e-commerce settings.
1389.wh: Off-the-shelf vision-language models weren't designed for fashion extraction. A model trained to caption generic internet images might struggle with fashion-specific attributes or the structured extraction tasks that e-commerce workflows demand. Testing every model on every task is expensive and slow. Moreover, different models behave differently depending on the prompt (how you phrase the question), and some models update over time, sometimes improving and sometimes degrading. You need a benchmark that captures these production realities.
1389.ap: They define five specific extraction tasks across two types of images (outfit photos and individual product photos) and test six commercial and two open-source models with multiple prompt variants. They try a standard prompt and model-specific prompts (prompts the model's creators suggested as optimal). For each model-prompt-task combination, they measure success and analyze error patterns. The benchmark is grounded in real fashion e-commerce needs, not generic vision tasks.
1389.ww: Benchmarking reveals task-specific patterns. The finding that best-performing models vary by task means no single model is universally best—you must evaluate on *your* tasks. Error patterns being model-dependent rather than prompt-dependent means you can't fix a bad model just by asking better; the model itself matters. Updates sometimes helping and sometimes hurting specific tasks shows that model versions aren't uniformly better, so you need continuous monitoring.
1389.po: The benchmark provides concrete guidance for teams deploying vision-language models in fashion: evaluate on your specific tasks, don't trust generic benchmarks, and monitor continuously as models update. This is a practical contribution—it doesn't build a better model, but it shows teams how to rigorously evaluate candidates before production deployment.

1390.bp: Search and recommendation systems rank results by relevance, but e-commerce platforms also want to make money. They can rerank the top results to promote 'sponsored' (paid) listings, or products with higher profit margins, increasing platform revenue. But reranking too aggressively kills relevance—if users don't find what they searched for, they'll shop elsewhere. The problem is balancing revenue against relevance and fraud constraints: maximize money without tanking user satisfaction or promoting scams.
1390.wh: The naive approach—just promote sponsored items to the top—destroys relevance and user trust. A principled approach would solve a mathematical optimization problem: 'maximize revenue subject to keeping relevance above a threshold and fraud risk below a threshold.' But solving this perfectly for every single search query is computationally expensive; you need an answer in milliseconds for a live search. Exact optimization is too slow for production.
1390.ap: They formulate the problem as an integer linear program (a mathematical optimization problem) and then build a lightweight approximation algorithm called PermR (permutation reranking). PermR works by repeatedly looking at adjacent pairs of results in the ranking and deciding whether to swap them. Each swap either improves revenue or fixes a violated constraint (brings fraud risk under control, or pushes relevance back above the threshold). The algorithm terminates when no swaps improve things further. This greedy approach is fast enough to run per-query at production latency.
1390.ww: The approximation works because you don't need the mathematically perfect answer—you need a good-enough answer fast. Swapping adjacent items is a simple local operation: if reranking item 5 and 6 helps, do it; repeat. This greedy strategy doesn't find the global optimum, but it finds a reasonable solution quickly. The constraints (keep relevance above X, keep fraud below Y) are maintained throughout, so you never accidentally create a bad ranking just to squeeze out one more dollar.
1390.po: In offline testing across multiple e-commerce categories, PermR achieves about 63% of the ideal revenue improvement that perfect optimization would provide, while staying within production latency limits and respecting all constraints. In a 14-day online A/B test on 56 million search queries, PermR increased platform revenue by 2%, demonstrating the approach works at scale.

1391.bp: Short-form video platforms like TikTok serve recommendations based on watching history. A user might have watched hundreds or thousands of videos, and the system needs to learn their patterns from all of that. The longer the history you use, the better you might understand them—but processing thousands of items is computationally expensive. Modern deep learning systems (Transformers) get slower as sequences get longer because they compare every item to every other item. The goal is to handle ultra-long watch histories at billion-user scale while staying within computational budgets.
1391.wh: There are two bottlenecks. First, video IDs are typically just numbers ('video #482916') which don't carry meaning—the system has to learn what that ID means by looking it up in a table. As the catalog grows to billions of videos, the lookup table gets huge, and cold-start (recommending new videos) is hard because the ID has no semantic signal. Second, Transformers scale poorly: comparing every item to every other item takes quadratic time, so increasing watch history from 100 to 1000 items doesn't just take 10x longer, it takes 100x longer. For a billion-user platform, this becomes prohibitive.
1391.ap: They replace raw video IDs with semantic IDs—a hierarchical structure where each ID encodes content type, genre, and specifics. Instead of just 'video #482916,' it's 'short-form video → comedy → sketch comedy → group jokes.' This hierarchical structure is much smaller than listing every possible video individually. For the computational problem, they build a new Transformer layer that compresses long sequences using temporal folding (grouping nearby items) and global query integration (summarizing key information globally). These techniques reduce the quadratic complexity of standard attention to something more manageable.
1391.ww: Semantic IDs reduce the problem's size. By using hierarchy, you shrink embedding tables from billions of entries to thousands of semantic nodes, and new videos automatically share the semantic prefixes of similar content (solving cold-start). Temporal folding works because watch patterns often have local structure—consecutive videos watched in a session probably reflect immediate interests—so you can combine nearby items without losing much information. Global queries ensure rare but important information isn't lost in the compression.
1391.po: On production infrastructure, this framework reduces peak memory usage by an order of magnitude and dramatically reduces computation time, allowing the system to model ultra-long sequences at billion-scale. The semantic IDs also help with cold-start, since new videos inherit meaning from their semantic ancestors. This enables the platform to personalize recommendations based on vastly longer watch histories than previously possible.

1392.bp: Large-scale recommendation systems at companies like Alibaba use a two-tower architecture for speed: one tower learns user representations, another learns item representations. They compare them quickly at recommendation time. This architecture is fast, but the downside is that the two towers are independent, so the system can't easily use fine-grained information about how this specific user might interact with this specific item (what fashion researchers call 'interaction effects'). The goal is to inject more semantic understanding into pre-ranking—the fast first stage of ranking—without sacrificing the speed advantage.
1392.wh: Two-tower models are decoupled for efficiency—each tower can be computed independently and in parallel. But this decoupling is also their weakness: they can't see the target item during user representation, so they can't capture subtle user-item interactions. A user might like minimalist fashion in general, but hate minimalist shoes; standard two-tower models would struggle with these fine-grained preferences because they learn a single 'user representation' that doesn't know which item it's being matched against.
1392.ap: PGSF is a plug-in that works during training but preserves the two-tower efficiency at serving time. During training, they (1) use the target item to guide user representation learning, creating item-aware user profiles, (2) build a discrete semantic space of user interests (using RQ-VAE, a compression technique), and (3) hierarchically select interests from that space relevant to the target item. At serving time, the two towers remain decoupled and fast—the system only uses the pre-computed user and item representations. The training procedure learns to bake item-awareness into the representations without requiring item information at serving time.
1392.ww: The trick is that information baked into a representation at training time is still there at serving time, even if you stop providing the information. By training the user tower with knowledge of the target item, the learned user representation implicitly captures patterns about which items matter for which users. When you serve only the representation (not the items), that knowledge is latent but present. This lets you get some of the accuracy benefits of joint user-item modeling while keeping the speed of decoupled inference.
1392.po: On Tmall App (Alibaba's shopping platform), PGSF shows +2.66% improvement in clicked-through items and +3.13% improvement in page views. The system integrates smoothly into existing two-tower setups, meaning it can be deployed without overhauling existing infrastructure. Code is published, suggesting it's a practical technique other platforms can adopt.

1393.bp: Novelty is the enemy of boredom. If a recommendation system only shows users what they already like, they'll watch the same content forever and eventually get bored. But novelty must be *relevant*—showing completely random content isn't novelty, it's annoyance. This work tackles the hard problem: how do you compose recommendation lists that are both personally relevant *and* meaningfully different from what the user has recently consumed, on a platform with millions of users and hundreds of thousands of items?
1393.wh: Maximizing relevance and maximizing novelty are in tension. The most relevant item is probably similar to things the user watched yesterday. The most novel item is probably something they'd hate. Prior work either optimizes relevance alone (boring lists), or adds a diversity penalty without really understanding how to balance the two. Language models offer a new angle—they can reason through both objectives, but they need supervision to do it well. However, supervision is scarce: you can't ask humans to label 'is this list the right balance of relevant and diverse?'
1393.ap: BALANCE decomposes novelty recommendation into three stages that an LLM reasons through step-by-step. First, generate a 'Novelty Tag' that specifies an exploration direction ('I've watched a lot of cooking content, explore food from other cultures'). Second, refine an 'Interest Topic' that specifies the user's intent in concrete terms ('recipe discovery for international cuisines'). Third, construct the actual recommendation list ensuring facet coverage (diverse types of international recipes). To handle data scarcity, they synthesize training data by mixing real behavior logs with structured explanations of novelty transitions. To fix a reward mismatch (standard reinforcement learning gives one reward per list, but item-level errors matter), they use a new optimization method (SIPO) that balances both list-level and item-level rewards.
1393.ww: Breaking the problem into three stages makes it learnable. Each stage has clear semantics (novelty direction, interest topic, facet coverage), so the model can reason through them. Synthesized supervision gets around the scarcity problem by using real behavior to ground the reasoning—if someone switched from cooking to food travel content, that's a real novelty transition; the model learns from that. Joint sequence-and-item rewards matter because one item-level error (recommending something totally irrelevant) ruins the whole list; by optimizing both granularities, the model learns to construct cohesive, diverse lists.
1393.po: On a large e-commerce platform, this hierarchical reasoning framework improves novelty recommendation over baselines that optimize either relevance alone or relevance with a simple diversity penalty. The approach enables the platform to surface content that keeps users engaged over the long term by introducing meaningful variety, not just optimizing one-day relevance.

1394.bp: On e-commerce platforms, when you buy something, you might use a discount code or it might be on sale. The platform wants to predict whether you'll complete the purchase (conversion rate). They use this prediction to rank products in search results or recommend them. But most models ignore a key signal: the discount rate. If an item is 50% off, you're much more likely to buy. If the price is marked up 200%, you'll walk away. The goal is to build a model that understands how discounts drive purchasing decisions.
1394.wh: Discount rates are important for conversion but tricky to model. Discount patterns are complex: some users respond strongly to discounts (discount hunters), others ignore them (brand loyalists); seasonal promotions have periodic patterns (higher discounts during holidays); and discounts correlate with user spending habits (big spenders might not care about a 10% off sale). Models that ignore discounts miss this signal. Models that naively add discount as a feature often learn spurious patterns because discounts are non-uniformly distributed—heavy discounts on clearance items, zero discounts on premium items—creating confounding.
1394.ap: They build DANet (Discount-Aware Network) with three specialized components: (1) a time-frequency module that transforms discount history using Fourier analysis to capture long-term trends and periodic patterns (seasonal effects), (2) a distribution de-bias module that removes confounding from user-specific and promotion-specific discount patterns, and (3) a supervised auxiliary task that predicts the item's discount level, forcing the model to learn explicit discount representations. The auxiliary task acts as a regularizer: by making the model predict discount amount directly, it ensures discount information is properly learned rather than ignored.
1394.ww: Frequency analysis (Fourier transform) captures patterns across time. A discount pattern that repeats every month will show up as a peak in the frequency spectrum, letting the model distinguish periodic promotions from random discounts. De-biasing works because it separates real signals from confounding: a user might buy more when there's a discount, but that's partly because deep-discount items are already more likely to be bought. By separating the discount effect from the item-effect, the model learns the true conversion lift from discounts. The auxiliary task works because predicting discount level is an easier subgoal that forces the model to encode discount information before predicting conversion.
1394.po: On real e-commerce datasets, DANet improves offline AUC (a standard ranking metric) by 1.61%, and online A/B testing shows 3.63% improvement in conversion rate (pCVR) and 2.23% improvement in gross merchandise value (GMV). The approach has been deployed successfully on e-commerce platforms, meaning it's production-ready and delivers measurable business value.

1395.bp: When you search on Amazon or eBay for 'shoes,' the engine needs to know you mean shoes-the-product, not shoe-repair or shoe-reviews, so it can show you the right category of items and organize the page sensibly. This is called query classification: taking what a person typed and deciding which bucket it belongs in.
1395.wh: Real e-commerce systems have thousands of categories, and shoppers almost always ask about popular ones (running shoes, boots, heels) rather than obscure ones (orthopedic shoe inserts for diabetics). Traditional classifiers are like a student who memorizes the popular answers and flails on anything rare. Also, new categories emerge all the time—once the system ships, you cannot just retrain it on thousands of new labels. You need a way to handle a brand new category label the moment someone creates it.
1395.ap: Instead of memorizing which queries historically went with which categories, the paper treats categories like people: each has a profile—a rich description of what it means. A query like 'waterproof hiking boots' and a category like 'waterproof hiking footwear for outdoor expeditions' are now scored by their semantic similarity—how much they mean the same thing—rather than by looking up whether that exact phrase has appeared before. This lets a rare query find the right category even if nobody has ever asked it before.
1395.ww: This works because meaning and co-occurrence are different things. A query and a category might have never appeared together in historical data, but if their descriptions are semantically aligned—if they literally talk about the same thing—then they belong together. For a brand new category, the system just reads its description and immediately understands which queries it should serve.
1395.po: The paper shows their system beats existing methods and, crucially, handles rare queries better than the traditional approach. It also solves the 'zero-shot' problem: add a new category description to the system, and it starts working immediately, without retraining on thousands of examples.

1396.bp: When you search Spotify for '70s funk,' the system shows you songs and playlists. Someone (a human or an automated judge) must decide whether those results are actually good—whether they match what you were looking for. At massive scale and in many languages, paying humans to rate millions of searches is impossible, so companies are starting to use large language models as automated judges.
1396.wh: Language models are powerful but they can hallucinate: they reason based on world knowledge and semantic similarity, but they may not know how *real users actually behaved* on this exact search. If a search is ambiguous—say, 'Paris' could mean the city or the person—the model might confidently rate an irrelevant result as good just because it's written well. Worse, in different languages and cultural contexts, user intent drifts.
1396.ap: The paper teaches the language model to be a judge that cites its reasoning. For each search result shown, it creates a small 'evidence card' that says: 'Here's how users actually clicked on similar searches and results in the past.' When the model sees these cards, it can now say 'I think this result is good because (1) semantic reasoning says X, and (2) real users clicked similar results in the past.' The model learns to use both signals together.
1396.ww: Ambiguity needs ground truth, not just logic. If I ask about 'Paris' and you can say 'real people who searched for "Paris fashion" clicked this fashion link 500 times,' that's evidence worth citing. The model, which is trained to explain itself, naturally learns to trust evidence over pure reasoning when they conflict, and that makes its judgments stick closer to what real people actually wanted.
1396.po: On Spotify searches, this approach improved alignment with user preferences by 5% overall, and by 91% on tricky, disagreement-heavy cases. On multi-language datasets, it boosted accuracy by another 15%, showing that historical user behavior transcends language and helps clarify intent.

1397.bp: AI systems now answer questions by finding relevant text on the web and citing where they got the information—like how a lawyer cites case law. But AI answer engines only cite a handful of sources. If your website is mentioned but not cited, users never see it. The question is: what makes a source get cited first?
1397.wh: This is a new kind of competition. In traditional search, websites competed on ranking (position in results). Now they must compete on being cited—and the rules are different. Being ranked number one does not guarantee you get cited; the AI might pick a different source. Understanding what makes a source 'citable' is opaque because it depends on how the language model reasons, not just on keyword matches.
1397.ap: The paper builds a clean experiment: show the language model exactly two sources that differ in only one way—say, one has 'buy for $19.99' and the other does not—and count which one gets cited first. They repeated this 252,000 times, trying different factors like relevance, price, date, trust signals, and formatting. They also shuffled source order to make sure the AI was not just picking whichever came first.
1397.ww: By isolating one factor at a time, you can see which ones actually matter in the model's reasoning. Topical relevance and position came out as the strongest drivers; price and recency also help. But pure formatting (bolding, layout) barely moves the needle. This tells you what the language model actually 'cares' about when deciding to cite something, rather than guessing.
1397.po: The paper gives practitioners a ranked checklist: optimize for these factors in this order. They tested it at Sprinklr (a marketing platform) and teams found it actionable. This work opens a new field—Generative Engine Optimization—which is now as real as traditional search optimization, but with different rules.

1398.bp: E-commerce search uses a multi-stage funnel: first, retrieve the most likely products; then pre-rank them to narrow the list; then rank them by relevance; finally, apply business rules. Pre-ranking is the speed bottleneck. It must be fast enough to handle millions of users without making the page slow, but smart enough to cut out irrelevant results before expensive ranking kicks in.
1398.wh: The challenge is that user behavior is sparse and diverse. Most users only browse a handful of items, so the system has little data to learn from. Also, a single user might search for completely different things (tennis rackets one day, kitchen sinks the next), so their behavior does not paint a coherent picture. Finally, pre-ranking is so latency-critical that even small computations add up across millions of simultaneous searches.
1398.ap: The paper splits user behavior into two streams: one capturing strong signals (items they clicked recently) and one capturing weak signals (items they browsed but did not engage). They compress each stream into fine-grained chunks, then use an attention mechanism that does not compute pairwise comparisons between all chunks—instead, it computes a single score per query. This reduces computational complexity from O(N) to O(1), meaning the cost does not grow with the number of items. They also add a mechanism to move knowledge from high-volume categories (lots of data) to sparse categories (little data).
1398.ww: By separating strong and weak signals, the system can weight them differently: strong signals are crisp and recent, weak signals are noisy but reveal broader interest. By compressing these into chunks and using query-centric scoring, the system avoids the quadratic blowup that would kill latency. And by transferring learned patterns from popular categories to rare ones, it bootstraps intelligence in sparse regions.
1398.po: The paper shows a 36% latency reduction and significant accuracy gains. More importantly, they deployed it in a live large-scale e-commerce system, proving it works under real load. Users see faster search results without losing quality.

1399.bp: E-commerce sellers need search to return their products when customers search. But simple keyword matching fails on complex searches like 'waterproof jacket that breathes for winter hiking.' Modern language models can reason through these queries brilliantly, but they are slow—each answer takes 100+ milliseconds because the model generates text token by token. In real-time search, that is unacceptable.
1399.wh: Knowledge distillation (teaching a small model from a large one) is the usual answer, but it forces a brutal trade-off: either you keep the large model's reasoning ability and lose interpretability, or you make a small fast model but destroy the reasoning. And if you try to preserve reasoning by forcing a human to write out the reasoning steps for every training example, the cost becomes astronomical.
1399.ap: The paper proposes a three-step pipeline. First, they fine-tune a large language model teacher using only binary labels (relevant or not) and a reward signal that pushes the model to improve its reasoning—specifically, the reasoning should help predict relevance. The model learns to generate step-by-step reasoning without requiring human annotations. Second, they train the model to score items with a single token output (no lengthy reasoning), keeping the internal reasoning alive for interpretability. Third, they transfer both the reasoning and the scoring ability to a 0.6B parameter student model through a specialized form of knowledge distillation.
1399.ww: By using only binary labels and task-aligned rewards, the system avoids the annotation cost. By decoupling reasoning from ranking (reasoning inside, single-score output), it becomes fast and deployable. By distilling both aspects together, the small model retains the 'why' of its decisions, not just the 'what.'
1399.po: A tiny 0.6B student model achieves comparable accuracy to much larger models, generates step-by-step reasoning users can see, and runs fast enough for production search. This bridges the gap between interpretability and speed that previously seemed impossible.

1400.bp: Search engines rank items, but the language model behind the ranking has a weird bias: it pays too much attention to the first document, almost regardless of relevance. This is called 'attention sink drift'—the model's internal mechanism gets stuck on early items. In production search serving billions of queries, this bias kills accuracy and forces teams to run expensive calibration after ranking, which halves throughput.
1400.wh: The bias is structural: in standard transformer models, the first token naturally accumulates weight during the computation. Engineers assumed this was baked into the model architecture and could only be fixed by recalibrating results after ranking. Recalibration works but is painfully slow because you must rank all candidates first, then reprocess them.
1400.ap: The paper proposes training the model differently so it fixes its own bias without needing post-processing. During training, they use a special attention head designed to suppress background noise and highlight retrieval heads (the parts that actually care about relevance). They also introduce a new training objective that aligns attention weights with semantic importance—if a document is relevant, the model learns to attend to it; if it is not, the model learns to ignore it.
1400.ww: By moving the calibration into training, the model learns to overcome its positional bias during inference, without any extra computation. The attention heads learn to differentiate between 'document at position 1' and 'actually relevant document,' so position does not trick the model.
1400.po: Deployed at WeChat (over 1 billion users), the method achieved a 3.3x latency speedup (down to 26.56ms), improved engagement metrics like click-through rate by 0.4%, and boosted user satisfaction by 1.25%—all while running much faster than the old recalibration approach.

1401.bp: Advertising platforms need to generate lots of different headlines for ads so they do not bore or annoy users by showing the same message over and over. But language models have a tendency to converge on a few popular patterns (they call this 'mode collapse')—they generate the same handful of headlines repeatedly, defeating the purpose of using machine generation.
1401.wh: A large language model trained on diverse ad data still learns that certain words and structures appear most often in successful ads, so it gravitate toward repeating those patterns. Diversity techniques like random sampling can produce varied output but often make the headlines incoherent or irrelevant. You are trapped: chase diversity and lose quality; chase quality and lose diversity.
1401.ap: The paper builds an end-to-end training system that explicitly optimizes for multiple goals at once. First, they create high-quality training pairs synthetically—different variations of ad descriptions and desired outcomes. Second, they use reinforcement learning to train the model to balance three objectives: diversity (generate different headlines), faithfulness (headlines match the product), and business metrics (predict clicks). The model learns to optimize all three simultaneously, not one at a time.
1401.ww: By explicitly optimizing for diversity as a learned objective—not as a sampling trick—the model internalizes diversity as part of what it means to be a good ad headline generator. The reinforcement learning signal tells it: 'If you generate the same headline twice, that is bad; if you generate varied coherent headlines, that is good.' Unlike sampling-based tricks, this shapes the model's learned behavior.
1401.po: On Xiaohongshu (a major platform), the deployed system increased advertiser value by 4% and click-through rate by 1.4% compared to previous approaches. Users saw more varied ads, advertisers got better results—a win on both sides.

1402.bp: E-commerce products have two faces: a title and an image. A query like 'blue waterproof jacket' might match the image perfectly but the title might just say 'All-Weather Jacket' (vague marketing speak). Real relevance ranking must understand both modalities and figure out which parts of the query are answered by the image versus the text. But language models that can reason through this are too slow for production ranking.
1402.wh: Existing methods either ignore one modality or treat title and image as separate signals without fine-grained reasoning. A language model can reason through which query terms are answered by the image and which by the title, but it takes 100+ milliseconds per item. A small fast model cannot do this reasoning. The gap between capability and speed is the problem.
1402.ap: The paper trains a large language model to reason step-by-step about which query terms each modality satisfies, using chain-of-thought reasoning guided by rewards based on term coverage. This reasoning happens once during training, offline. Then they distill this reasoning into a small, fast model using a specialized distillation strategy that forces the small model to inherit the term-level reasoning logic, not just memorize outputs.
1402.ww: By using chain-of-thought rewards, the language model learns to generate fine-grained reasoning that mirrors the actual reasoning needed for ranking. By distilling at the term level, the small model learns to replicate that reasoning pattern, so it can apply the same logic to new queries and products at serving time.
1402.po: A small model inherits the large model's ability to reason about multi-modal relevance term-by-term and can execute this reasoning at production speed. Offline experiments show significant improvements; online deployment would confirm the real-world lift.

1403.bp: Apps like TikTok, YouTube, and Reddit increasingly have built-in chatbots that suggest topics to users ('Want to talk about?'). The chatbot needs to suggest topics the user will actually engage with. But the vast majority of user data is about videos or content they consumed, not conversations they had. How do you recommend conversation topics when you have little conversation data?
1403.wh: There is a domain gap: preferences revealed by content consumption (what videos you watched) are not the same as preferences revealed by conversation (what you talk about). Watching a makeup tutorial does not mean you want to chat about makeup tips. If you try to directly apply the content preferences to topic recommendation, you get poor suggestions. But if you only use the scarce conversation data, you do not have enough signal to learn anything reliable.
1403.ap: The paper proposes a two-stage framework. First, they learn how to adapt user content preferences to the conversation domain—they identify what aspects of content preference transfer and what aspects differ. Second, they align these adapted preferences to the user's real-time context—what they are doing *right now*. For example, if someone just finished a cooking video, the system might suggest cooking-related topics, but only if the user is in a conversational mood right now.
1403.ww: By explicitly modeling the domain gap and learning how to bridge it, the system leverages the abundant content data (lots of video watches) to bootstrap understanding in the sparse domain (few conversation starts). The real-time alignment layer ensures suggestions feel contextual, not random.
1403.po: Deployed on a large-scale application, the system significantly improved chatbot engagement—more users clicked the suggested topics and started conversations. This shows the domain-transfer approach actually works at scale.

1404.bp: E-commerce search ranking depends on knowing whether a product is truly relevant to a query. Language models are phenomenal at reasoning about this, but they need context (product description, reviews, specifications) to make good decisions. If that context is noisy or wrong, the model becomes confused. Also, production systems have strict latency budgets—there is no time for multiple passes or refinement.
1404.wh: External knowledge (product descriptions, reviews, specs) is often noisy, stale, or contradictory. A product description might claim a item is 'waterproof' but customer reviews say it leaks. A language model cannot easily tell which source to trust, especially when it has a strict time limit and no room for follow-up reasoning. It must make a simultaneous decision about both relevance and context trustworthiness in a single forward pass.
1404.ap: The paper uses reinforcement learning to teach the model to learn which context to trust and which to ignore. During training, they show the model two versions: one with external context, one without. By comparing how much better the model's decision becomes with context, they teach it a 'trust signal'—a number that says 'this context is worth using' or 'this context is misleading, ignore it.' This happens within a single inference pass using structured chain-of-thought reasoning.
1404.ww: By training on both contexts and comparing them during learning, the model learns empirically which context matters and which does not, without needing a human to label 'this context is trustworthy.' The structured reasoning format keeps the decision transparent and fast.
1404.po: Deployed in Taobao (hundreds of millions of users), the system improved ranking accuracy on query slices with noisy context, particularly for long-tail queries where external knowledge is sparse or contradictory. A single-pass inference architecture delivers these gains without added latency.

1405.bp: Job search starts with vague queries: most people search with three words or fewer ('senior software engineer'). The system needs to infer intent (What industry? What company size? Remote or on-site?) and suggest refinements interactively. At scale, these suggestions must be fast, personalized, and accurate.
1405.wh: A three-word query is massively ambiguous. 'Senior software engineer' could mean embedded systems, web development, machine learning, or finance. The system could ask the user to filter by category, but building a rigid taxonomy of all possible filters is tedious and breaks when new job types emerge. Also, suggestions must arrive in milliseconds during live search.
1405.ap: The paper proposes a ranking pipeline for real-time facet (attribute) suggestions. First, they curate a taxonomy of job attributes offline (company size, industry, remote status, seniority, etc.). Then at query time, they use embedding-based retrieval to find candidate facets (say, top 20 candidates for what the user might care about), and rank them with a small language model. The model is distilled to run with minimal latency—single-token scoring and batch prefixing to enable fast serving.
1405.ww: By separating taxonomy curation (offline, strategic) from retrieval (candidate generation) and scoring (fast, learned ranking), the system avoids the rigidity of hand-crafted rules while staying fast. Embedding retrieval quickly filters candidates, and the small language model does precision ranking.
1405.po: Online A/B testing showed significant lifts in suggestion engagement and downstream job search outcomes. The system helps job seekers refine vague queries into concrete searches and find better matches faster.

1406.bp: LinkedIn has millions of job postings, each messy and unstructured—some are one paragraph, some ramble, some use marketing jargon instead of standard job terminology. The system must convert these into standardized fields (required skills, seniority level, job category, etc.) to power search, recommendations, and recruiter tools. This is called 'job understanding,' and it must work at massive scale.
1406.wh: Job postings are written by humans with no template, so they use different words for the same concept. One posting lists 'Python' and another says 'coding in Python.' A small language model struggles with this variability. A large one could handle it but is too slow to run on millions of postings. Also, new job types and attributes emerge constantly, so the system needs to generalize beyond its training data.
1406.ap: The paper trains a small language model (not a giant one) using two strategies. First, they create synthetic training tasks that combine two modes: taxonomy-guided classification (if the posting mentions 'C++,' label it as 'programming language') and taxonomy-agnostic entity extraction (find any mention of required skills, even if they are not in the taxonomy). Second, they add reasoning traces—step-by-step explanations—to the synthetic data, so the model learns not just to memorize but to explain its decisions. Finally, they use multi-adapter architecture, so different downstream tasks (extracting skills vs. extracting company size) have specialized parameters but share the main model.
1406.ww: By combining classification and extraction, the model learns structured understanding in both directions: 'fit into known buckets' and 'surface new information.' Reasoning traces teach the model to generalize beyond exact matches. Multi-adapters let each task specialize without fragmenting the model into separate systems.
1406.po: Offline and online A/B tests show significant improvements in accuracy and operational simplicity. LinkedIn's teams report easier model management and better generalization to new job types.

1407.bp: E-commerce search ranking depends on product descriptions, but many descriptions are long and verbose, padded with marketing speak. For ranking in real-time with a cross-encoder architecture (a model that looks at query + product together), passing the full description is computationally expensive. The system needs concise, query-relevant summaries to rank fast without sacrificing accuracy.
1407.wh: A summary is only useful if it highlights the parts relevant to the query. Generic summaries miss crucial details. But generating query-specific summaries during ranking is slow. If you pre-compute summaries without knowing the query, they are not optimized for ranking. There is no way to know what summary will help ranking most without running ranking itself.
1407.ap: The paper proposes using reinforcement learning to generate summaries offline that are optimized for downstream ranking. The process: generate a summary of the product (using only product information, not the query), then use that summary in ranking and measure how well it ranks relevant items. The ranking quality becomes the reward signal during summary generation. This trains the model to generate summaries that, even without seeing the query, highlight ranking-critical information.
1407.ww: By using ranking accuracy as the reward, the summary generation process learns what matters for ranking. The generated summaries might never mention the query directly, but they unconsciously emphasize the attributes that most queries care about (e.g., size, color, durability, warranty).
1407.po: Summaries can be generated and cached before any query arrives, so there is zero latency overhead at serving time. In online A/B tests, ReLSum improved user engagement metrics like orders per visitor by meaningful margins, proving that smarter summaries actually help people find products better.

1408.bp: Companies operate in their own industries with specialized language and domain knowledge. A telecom company needs to understand customer opinions about specific services (5G quality, customer support, competitor strengths) from messy forum posts and reviews. Large language models are powerful but they are trained on general internet text, not telecom jargon. How do you adapt them to vertical domains cheaply?
1408.wh: Adapting a language model to a new domain usually means pretraining it on domain data (continuous pretraining), then fine-tuning on specific tasks. But continuous pretraining is expensive in compute and often does not help much when the base model is already strong. For low-resource languages like Traditional Chinese, it is even harder. The usual approach wastes time and money.
1408.ap: The paper tests this empirically with Chunghwa Telecom. They adapt three open-source models (LLaMA-3, Qwen, Mistral) for the specific task of extracting structured opinions from unstructured forum discussions. Their main finding: continuous pretraining on domain data provides little benefit when you already have a strong instruction-tuned model. Instead, they focus on high-quality instruction fine-tuning (training on specific tasks with human-written examples) and strategic data curation.
1408.ww: Strong instruction-tuned models already know how to follow directions and reason, so they rapidly adapt to a new domain when given clear task examples. Continuous pretraining tries to teach them new words and concepts, but that is redundant if they can already generalize from a few task examples.
1408.po: The paper provides practitioners actionable guidance: skip the expensive continuous pretraining step and invest in quality instruction examples instead. This significantly reduces the cost and time to deploy domain-adapted models in low-resource settings.

1409.bp: E-commerce search relies on embedding-based retrieval: the system converts queries and products into numerical vectors (embeddings) and finds the nearest neighbors. This is fast and scalable to billions of items. But as systems grow, the quality of these embeddings matters more—a query embedding that does not match product embeddings well means wrong results.
1409.wh: There are two gaps. First, the model is trained on narrow datasets (say, 100,000 products) but must retrieve from 100 million. The training optimized the model against a small set of competitors per query, not against the full corpus. Second, as companies upgrade to better models (say, from DistilBERT to GTE), they cannot just swap the old embeddings for new ones without disrupting the retrieval logic—the new embeddings might rank items in completely different orders.
1409.ap: The paper proposes two solutions deployed at Walmart. First, they improve training signals: instead of mining hard negatives (difficult false matches) only offline, they add online cross-batch sampling during training, which finds hard negatives in real-time from millions of products. They combine this with offline mining using a cross-encoder (a more sophisticated ranker) and metadata heuristics. Second, they transition to a better model using 'warm-start distillation': the new model learns from the old model's embeddings and decisions, ensuring the new model inherits domain-specific expertise from its predecessor.
1409.ww: By increasing the diversity and difficulty of negatives seen during training, the model learns a richer embedding space. By distilling from the old model during transition, the new model does not start from scratch—it bootstraps on the old model's knowledge and gradually improves.
1409.po: The unified pipeline scales embedding quality without disrupting retrieval. Extensive offline and online experiments validate the approach, showing improvements in retrieval precision and seamless model transitions.

1410.bp: When you watch short videos on your phone, the app needs to decide which video to show you next. It tracks many signals: how long you watched, whether you liked it, whether you shared it, and so on. The goal is to learn from all these different signals at once to predict what you'll click on next, which makes the whole system more engaging and profitable.
1410.wh: The hard part is that these signals are tangled together. If you show the system just the 'watch time' signal and the 'like' signal separately, they interfere with each other—each one learned specialized knowledge that doesn't quite work well when combined. Also, as you add more and more signals, the system gets exponentially slower to train and run because it's doing redundant work for overlapping signals.
1410.ap: SCOPE splits the problem into specialized mini-experts, where each expert handles a particular kind of signal. The system then learns which experts to use for which decision, using a Transformer (a mechanism for weighing multiple pieces of information) to figure out how the different signals relate to each other. To keep experts from stepping on each other's toes, the system adds constraints that push experts to be different from one another and to stay focused on their assigned task.
1410.ww: This works because you're now training separate, focused learners that can each specialize without interference. The Transformer piece lets the system discover that, say, watch-time predictions should feed into the final ranking decision in a specific order. By explicitly penalizing redundancy, you're forcing the system to divide labor cleanly instead of all experts learning the same thing.
1410.po: On Alipay's real video platform, this approach increased user engagement by 2.47% more video views, while cutting computational cost by 43%—the system is now faster and more efficient because it's doing less wasted duplication.

1411.bp: Click prediction—guessing whether someone will click an ad or link—is one of the most important problems in online advertising and content feeds. The traditional way to solve it is to build one big model and optimize it toward a single goal. The real challenge is that after the model gets reasonably good, it plateaus and can't improve further.
1411.wh: A single model trained toward a single goal tends to get stuck in a local optimum—imagine a ball rolling downhill and getting caught in a shallow valley, never reaching the deeper valley far away. Without something pushing the model to explore different strategies, it can't escape this trap and find better solutions.
1411.ap: DPEO creates two learners instead of one, each learning slightly different strategies. They compete with each other: one becomes the 'reference' (the current best) and the other is pushed to beat it. The system keeps swapping which one is the reference and which one is trying to improve, creating an ongoing evolutionary race. The losing learner gets feedback designed to make it better than the current winner.
1411.ww: This works because competition creates pressure to explore. If you only have one model, it optimizes greedily toward immediate improvement. With two models competing, one is always being told 'you're close but not quite beating the other'—which forces it to try different approaches, escaping local traps. The role-swapping ensures neither model gets comfortable in a dead-end strategy.
1411.po: The model escapes saturation and keeps improving, with real experiments showing the system can break through performance plateaus that single-model approaches get stuck on.

1412.bp: In recent years, recommender systems have started using generative models—systems that learn to create suggestions word-by-word, like a language model. This is powerful because it can reason about complex preferences end-to-end. But there's a catch: the feedback signal from real users (clicks, purchases) is noisy and sparse, which makes the system unstable and prone to weird failure modes.
1412.wh: When you train a generative recommendation system with reinforcement learning (learning from user feedback), the sparse and noisy reward signal causes two problems. First, the system 'hacks' the reward—it learns to game metrics rather than make good recommendations, like a student memorizing test answers without understanding. Second, it drifts away from being a good language model, producing garbled or nonsensical suggestions.
1412.ap: AIPO uses two anchoring strategies. First, it cleans up the training data by identifying high-confidence user purchase signals and weighting those examples more heavily, filtering out the noisy signals that lead the system astray. Second, it adds a 'prior anchor'—a constraint that pulls the model back toward the original untrained language model, but only as strongly as needed depending on how much drift the model is experiencing.
1412.ww: Cleaning the data removes noise that causes poor learning. The prior anchor works like a penalty: it says 'stay close to the original' but doesn't enforce this uniformly—when the model is stable, the constraint is loose, but when it starts drifting badly, the constraint tightens. This balance prevents reward hacking while letting the model still improve.
1412.po: On real e-commerce datasets, AIPO produces stable training and better recommendation quality, avoiding the collapse into nonsensical or gamed suggestions that simpler approaches suffer from.

1413.bp: Converting raw text into useful question-answer pairs is valuable for building question-answering systems, search tools, and knowledge bases. Most of the world's text is unstructured (just paragraphs), so being able to automatically extract QA pairs would save enormous human effort. The challenge is doing this well at scale, especially in languages like Chinese.
1413.wh: Traditional methods either generate questions and answers separately (losing context) or do it end-to-end but are slow and can't handle ambiguity well. Building datasets for training is expensive, and systems trained on one language or domain often fail on others. There's also the hallucination problem: models invent plausible-sounding questions that don't actually match the source text.
1413.ap: The team built a large Chinese QA dataset from 143,846 documents and tested multiple language models on it. They discovered that Code Llama (a model trained on programming code and English text) actually performed better than Chinese-specialized models on Chinese text. They then created Code Llama-M by adding Chinese words to Code Llama's vocabulary, making it even better.
1413.ww: This works because Code Llama was trained on precise, structured code where accuracy matters—a misplaced semicolon breaks everything. This forces the model to be meticulous about accuracy, which transfers well to QA extraction. The extra Chinese vocabulary removes a bottleneck: Code Llama had to translate Chinese internally, wasting capacity.
1413.po: Code Llama-M produces fewer hallucinations and higher-quality QA pairs than language models built specifically for Chinese. When deployed in a real assistant system called Luo Ying, users reported meaningful satisfaction gains.

1414.bp: When an e-commerce platform sells display ad space, advertisers buy contracts guaranteeing a certain number of impressions (views) for their ads. The platform must decide which ads to show in each available slot on a webpage to satisfy all advertiser contracts while maximizing revenue. This sounds simple but becomes complex when a page has multiple ad slots.
1414.wh: Most systems treat each ad slot independently, which causes problems. Advertisers end up competing for the same slots, some contracts get fulfilled while others starve, and revenue gets concentrated in a few high-demand positions. There's no global view of what's best across all slots at once.
1414.ap: This paper formulates the problem as matching viewers and advertisers optimally across an entire page view, not slot-by-slot. The system uses a bipartite matching algorithm (pairing viewers with advertiser campaigns) and adds constraints that prevent too much exposure concentration—ensuring popular ads don't dominate all slots and less popular ads still get fair access.
1414.ww: Optimizing globally instead of locally is more efficient because you see that slot 1 and slot 2 are competing for the same valuable audience. By solving the whole matching problem at once, you can give slot 1 to the best fit and slot 2 to the second-best, rather than both going to the best (which wastes one slot). Contract roulette prevents monopolies.
1414.po: On Meituan's platform, this approach increased revenue per user by 28.99%, stabilized contract fulfillment across all advertisers (not just the biggest), and achieved better balance overall.

1415.bp: On live-streaming platforms like TikTok, the goal is to show viewers the live streams that match their interests. The system ranks streamers by predicted relevance. But there's a tension: the most popular streamers get shown to everyone, their servers get overwhelmed, and the experience suffers. Meanwhile, less-popular streamers get almost no viewers.
1415.wh: If you only optimize for relevance (matching viewers to their interests), you naturally concentrate viewers on the most popular streamers, causing server bottlenecks. The capacity constraint—that streamers can only serve so many concurrent viewers—gets ignored. Some viewers end up waiting in queues or experiencing poor video quality, and less-popular streamers never get a chance.
1415.ap: LiBRA treats the problem as a graph: viewers on one side, streamers on the other, with edges representing potential matches. The system first learns each streamer's capacity (how many viewers they can handle smoothly) using reinforcement learning. Then, a graph algorithm solves for the best matching that respects these capacity limits while still being as relevant as possible, maximizing overall viewer satisfaction globally.
1415.ww: This works because you're explicitly modeling reality: streamers have limits. Once you know those limits, you can solve for the assignment that maximizes total viewer happiness while respecting capacity, rather than greedily overfilling popular streamers. The global graph view reveals that spreading viewers more evenly actually increases total satisfaction.
1415.po: On TikTok Live, the system reduced queue times, improved stream quality for viewers who would have been on overloaded streamers, and gave less-popular streamers a fair shot at viewers who might enjoy their content.

1416.bp: On mobile e-commerce apps like Taobao, users search for products and then decide what to search for next. Predicting the next search helps the app show relevant products proactively and keep users engaged. The real-time nature (user interests change fast) and mobile constraints (phones have limited battery, memory, and network) make this tricky.
1416.wh: Sending all inference to a cloud server is slow and expensive: every user action triggers a network round-trip, adding latency and draining battery. Users' interests shift minute-by-minute as they scroll, so delayed predictions miss the window. Cloud solutions also cost a lot at scale.
1416.ap: RecGPT-Mobile runs a small language model directly on the phone.
