Instead of sending raw data to the cloud, the phone uses this local model to understand what the user is interested in, then sends only a compact semantic summary to the backend. The backend combines this with other signals to rank recommendations.
1416.ww: Running on-device eliminates latency: predictions happen instantly without network delay, and you get real-time adaptation as users browse. The model is small enough to fit on a phone but powerful enough to reason about semantic meaning (understanding that 'winter coat' is different from 'summer dress' without the server explaining it). This reduces data sent, lowering costs.
1416.po: Offline tests and online experiments show recommendation accuracy improved significantly. The approach is now practical for mobile devices at scale and reduces the cost of running LLM-powered systems in production.

1417.bp: E-commerce recommendation systems have traditionally used separate models for different stages (retrieval, ranking, final scoring), each optimized toward different immediate goals. This causes misalignment—earlier stages might retrieve products that later stages filter out, wasting computation. Using a single generative model end-to-end solves the misalignment but is too slow and expensive to run online.
1417.wh: Traditional multistage systems are efficient but optimize locally: each stage doesn't know what the downstream stage cares about. Generative models (like language models) can reason holistically but are too slow for real-time serving. You also need to handle very different shopping scenarios (someone browsing casually vs. searching for a gift), which generative models struggle with without separate retraining.
1417.ap: OxygenREC uses a two-speed strategy. Offline, a large language model thinks deeply (using methods like MCTS tree search) to create instructions for reasoning—summarized constraints and hints about the right kind of reasoning. Online, a smaller, fast encoder-decoder model follows these instructions to generate recommendations in milliseconds. It also learns to retrieve relevant product descriptions using a retrieval mechanism guided by these instructions.
1417.ww: This works because you offload heavy thinking to offline time. The fast online model doesn't have to rediscover reasoning from scratch; it follows the precomputed instructions, so it runs instantly. You also handle multiple scenarios with a shared backbone and scenario-specific instruction adjustments, avoiding retraining.
1417.po: On Alibaba's platform, this achieves both end-to-end semantic reasoning and practical speed, delivering measurable gains in Gross Merchandise Value and order volume across multiple shopping scenarios.

1418.bp: Understanding what users actually want to buy is the heart of e-commerce recommendation. Users have complex, evolving interests—they might want a 'blue winter coat' one day and 'blue bike accessories' the next. Capturing this complexity requires reasoning through multiple levels of abstraction: broad categories first, then specific items.
1418.wh: Earlier generative recommendation approaches do single-step prediction: they jump directly from user history to the next item. This misses the intermediate reasoning—which brands matter, which size, which color. Some use chain-of-thought (explicit reasoning steps) but lose information when translating between reasoning steps. Others do implicit reasoning but it becomes unpredictable and hard to control.
1418.ap: M2GR uses a multi-level chain-of-thought, all working in the item/product space (not abstract reasoning space). First, it predicts coarse-grained attributes in parallel: 'this user likes this brand' and 'this user likes this category' together. Then it refines these into fine-grained predictions: the exact next click item. Building on that, it predicts even more complex behavior like what the user will buy next.
1418.ww: Working entirely in item space preserves all the behavioral information—you don't lose details when translating. Coarse-first reasoning is intuitive and mirrors how humans browse: first you narrow by category, then by price, then pick the item. Parallel coarse predictions also diversify reasoning paths, creating more variety in what the system suggests.
1418.po: Online A/B tests show M2GR outperforms single-step and naive chain-of-thought approaches. The system scales to Alibaba's production infrastructure and can be added to existing recommendation pipelines without retraining.

1419.bp: Large ad platforms like Facebook retrieve candidate ads from millions, then rank them in two stages: a fast early stage and a slower, more careful final stage. This pipeline is efficient but wasteful: early stages often send ads that final ranking immediately filters out, wasting computation and latency.
1419.wh: The pipeline stages don't communicate: early ranking doesn't know what final ranking will reject, so it wastes effort sending low-value ads. Also, final ranking might see the same bad ad repeatedly from different users and reject it each time, rather than learning 'this ad is always bad' once and avoiding it upfront.
1419.ap: Cross-Stage Signal Propagation adds two-way communication. Forward: final ranking detects stable decisions (ads that consistently score low) and caches the outcome, so future low-value ads skip final ranking entirely. Backward: early ranking feeds low-value decisions back to retrieval, which then suppresses those ads at the source before they enter ranking.
1419.ww: Forward propagation eliminates redundant computation—if an ad scored terribly for 100 similar users, why compute its score again for user 101? Caching avoids recomputation. Backward propagation prevents low-value ads from wasting retrieval's time in the first place. Both work because they recognize that 'consistently bad' patterns repeat.
1419.po: On Facebook Feed, the system reduced CPU in final ranking by 10.68%, CPU in early ranking by 11.20%, and GPU by 13.01%, while keeping user and advertiser metrics stable—you're just skipping ads that weren't going to work anyway.

1420.bp: Product images, videos, and text are rich but hard to understand at scale. A recommendation system could do much better if it really understood what's in those videos and images—the style, mood, colors, objects. Multimodal language models (systems that understand both images and text) are powerful but too slow for real-time ranking at scale.
1420.wh: Traditional systems summarize multimedia as generic numerical features that miss nuance. Multimodal language models understand the content deeply but take seconds per item to run; if you have millions of items, that's infeasible. You need to extract the richness offline but make it available for fast online ranking.
1420.ap: This system uses a multimodal language model (LLaMA2 extended to handle images and video) to generate detailed captions for each product offline—describing the look, style, and context. These captions are then converted into categorical features that the recommendation model learns to use online. This separates the expensive understanding step from the fast ranking step.
1420.ww: Captions extract semantic meaning that numerical features miss (e.g., 'sleek minimalist design' vs. just pixel patterns). By running the language model once offline per item, you get rich information without real-time latency. The categorical features are fast to compute with online, so the system stays responsive.
1420.po: On real recommendation data, this approach increased offline ranking quality (AUC) by 0.35% and online user satisfaction metrics by 0.02%, showing that understanding multimedia content depth does translate to better recommendations.

1421.bp: E-commerce search is hard because product similarity depends heavily on context: a 'blue item' might be similar to another 'blue item' in clothing, but completely irrelevant in electronics. Text-based similarity often misses these category-specific nuances. The goal is to search for products that are truly similar in the way that matters for the current context.
1421.wh: Traditional embedding-based search (converting items to vectors and finding nearby vectors) treats all products the same. An algorithm might think a 'blue phone' is similar to a 'blue shirt' because both are blue, missing that the similarity metric should be different in each category. Ranking based on raw text requires processing the full product description for every candidate.
1421.ap: This approach extracts structured product attributes offline using an LLM (size, color, material, brand, etc.) organized by product category. It builds a reusable attribute graph with schemas that vary per category. At search time, instead of computing similarity over full text, the system ranks using this structured graph, reasoning about which structured attributes matter for similarity.
1421.ww: Structured attributes are efficient: instead of processing raw text for every candidate (expensive), you use precomputed attributes (fast). Category-aware schemas mean similarity metrics adapt to context: a 'size' attribute is crucial for clothing but irrelevant for electronics. The graph structure makes relationships explicit.
1421.po: Ranking precision improved by over 5% in zero-shot scenarios (no training data needed), token usage per product dropped 57%, and the approach generalizes across diverse product categories without retraining.

1422.bp: Ad platforms like eBay serve ads in two ways: keyword-targeted (advertiser picks search terms like 'blue sweater') and item-targeted (ads shown based on semantic similarity to what the user searched). Each method works but has gaps—keyword targeting needs manual setup, item-targeting fails on broad or new queries.
1422.wh: Keyword targeting requires advertisers to manually specify relevant search terms, which is labor-intensive and misses unexpected queries. Item-targeting is automatic but relies on semantic similarity, which doesn't capture all the ways an item might be relevant—a user searching 'gifts for dad' might click a power drill ad even though 'power drill' isn't semantically similar.
1422.ap: The system extracts successful query-item pairs from keyword-targeted campaigns (these clearly worked). It then uses semantic similarity to identify other similar queries that weren't in the manual list. It transfers these new query-item associations into item-targeted ads, expanding the coverage. To avoid showing irrelevant ads, it uses adaptive thresholding based on similarity confidence.
1422.ww: This works because keyword campaigns have proved the relevance: users clicked. By finding similar queries, you expand coverage without manually creating new keyword lists. Adaptive thresholding ensures you only use high-confidence associations, avoiding noisy similarity matches.
1422.po: On eBay, the approach achieved over 5% incremental impression coverage for broad and new-item queries, while maintaining click-through rate and conversion rates—expanding reach without sacrificing quality.

1423.bp: Travel recommendation systems optimize for user satisfaction and engagement, but ignore environmental impact. Popular recommendations reinforce overcrowded destinations and carbon-intensive travel. The goal is to help users make travel choices that they'll enjoy but that are also more environmentally sustainable.
1423.wh: Simply recommending 'greener alternatives' often feels preachy or restrictive to users, and they ignore it. Users also aren't always aware of the environmental impact of their choices. Traditional systems can't adapt recommendations dynamically based on a user's revealed sustainability preferences because those preferences are hidden.
1423.ap: TRACE uses a multi-agent system coordinated by an orchestrator. Different agents specialize in different tasks: one elicits sustainability preferences through conversation, one builds a detailed user persona, one generates recommendations. A key innovation is using 'counterfactual explanations'—when recommending a destination, the system also shows 'here's a similar destination that's less crowded and has lower carbon impact,' letting users see greener alternatives without being lectured.
1423.ww: Counterfactual explanations work because they invite comparison and reflection without prescription. The system surfaces the option to the user, but doesn't force it. Building a detailed persona means the system understands the user's real constraints and preferences, so recommendations stay relevant while being greener. The multi-agent design lets each component focus on its specialty.
1423.po: User studies show the system effectively supports more sustainable travel decisions while maintaining recommendation quality and conversation responsiveness. Users appreciate seeing alternatives without feeling judged.

1424.bp: Transformer-based ranking models like MonoBERT power modern search systems, deciding which documents are most relevant to a query. They work well but are black boxes: we don't understand which parts of the model drive the ranking decision. This limits our ability to debug, improve, or trust these systems.
1424.wh: Neural ranking models have millions of parameters and complex interactions. Traditional interpretability methods (like attention visualization) don't reveal the full picture because attention isn't always where the real decisions happen. To understand what's happening, you need methods that can trace how information flows through all the internal components.
1424.ap: IR Lens uses two interpretability techniques. Neuron Integrated Gradients measures how much each internal component (neurons, attention heads, layers) contributes to the final ranking decision, revealing which parts matter. Targeted ablations delete specific components and observe how predictions change, testing whether a suspected mechanism actually influences ranking.
1424.ww: Integrated Gradients work by measuring the path of gradients from output back through every component, showing which components 'light up' for different inputs. Ablations are direct: if you remove component X and ranking quality drops, X clearly matters. Together, they map the system from multiple angles.
1424.po: IR Lens provides interactive visualization of ranking decisions, enabling IR practitioners to debug models, test hypotheses about how they work, and use this understanding to improve ranking quality.

1425.bp: Over 932,000 people speak Tetun in Timor-Leste, yet AI-powered conversational tools—the kind that let you ask questions and get helpful answers—were built almost entirely for English and other languages spoken by billions. This matters because speakers of smaller languages get cut off from useful AI services that others take for granted, keeping them at a disadvantage in the digital economy.
1425.wh: AI conversational assistants are trained on vast amounts of text from the internet, which means they've absorbed millions of examples of English and Mandarin but only scraps of Tetun. When these systems try to answer questions in Tetun, they often produce nonsense or ignore what speakers actually need, because the system hasn't learned the patterns of how Tetun questions should be answered. The obvious approach of just scaling up the LLM doesn't fix this—you still need the assistant to know what Tetun-speaking communities actually care about.
1425.ap: The researchers took existing AI conversational systems and adapted them specifically for Tetun by crafting instruction prompts that teach the model how Tetun speakers pose questions and what kinds of answers matter to them. This is essentially giving the model a cultural primer in how to be useful to Tetun speakers, rather than forcing Tetun into English-shaped communication patterns.
1425.ww: When you show an AI system examples of how real Tetun speakers communicate and what they find helpful, the system learns to anticipate their needs and generate answers that fit their context, not just generic responses in the right language. This targeted approach works because the system is now being steered by the actual patterns of what Tetun-speaking users care about.
1425.po: User studies found that 91% of tasks completed successfully and users rated satisfaction at 4.30 out of 5, demonstrating that language-specific customization actually delivers. The paper shows a practical playbook that any community speaking a small language can follow to unlock AI-powered services that aren't yet mainstream for them.

1426.bp: In today's job market, being visible on professional networks like LinkedIn can make or break your career—employers and collaborators find you through what you post. But most professionals lack the marketing skill to produce high-quality posts regularly, and when they turn to AI to help, they run into a frustrating wall: the AI produces generic, forgettable content that sounds like everyone else's.
1426.wh: Standard AI systems work by predicting the most statistically likely next word, which naturally pushes outputs toward the average and the common. When thousands of people are using the same AI assistant to write LinkedIn posts, everyone ends up with similar wording, similar examples, and similar tone. The result is 'lexical homogenization'—the feed becomes a sea of nearly identical AI-generated posts, and none of them stand out. An individual's unique expertise and personality get buried under statistical mediocrity.
1426.ap: SOMIN takes a different approach by building an 'agentic' system—one that plans multiple steps of content generation rather than just writing one post at a time. It uses dynamic retrieval, meaning it actively goes searching for fresh ideas and examples unique to your expertise and context, then uses those findings to generate a post that's grounded in real specifics about you, not generic patterns. The system works through planning (what angles to take), retrieval (finding relevant facts about you), and generation (writing a post that uses those specifics).
1426.ww: Because the system retrieves specific facts about your work and background before writing, the post ends up rooted in concrete details that are unique to you. This blocks the AI from sliding into generic phrasing—you can't sound like everyone else if your post is built on particular examples and achievements that only you have. The multi-step planning also means the system can explore different angles and pick the most interesting one.
1426.po: The paper demonstrates that agentic systems produce more distinctive, higher-performing content than single-prompt AI assistance. By bridging the gap between raw AI ability and the domain expertise that makes someone hireable, professionals can maintain a high-quality public presence without becoming a marketing specialist themselves.

1427.bp: Deep research—the work of finding answers by reading across dozens or hundreds of sources, cross-checking facts, and synthesizing a coherent report—is becoming increasingly important for AI systems and organizations. But doing deep research at scale, where you need to process thousands of similar research jobs in parallel, reveals a hard constraint: current AI assistants are designed to chat one-on-one, not to crunch batch jobs like a factory.
1427.wh: Today's AI assistants were built for interactive conversation where you talk to one agent at a time. That design makes sense for chat, but it doesn't map onto the needs of production workflows where you might need to analyze a thousand research questions at once. You can't efficiently run a thousand separate chat sessions in parallel; you need a system designed from the ground up for concurrent processing, the way data-processing systems are designed to handle millions of records at once.
1427.ap: C3Flow treats each AI agent as a scheduled, isolated worker in a factory line (following the SIMD—Single Instruction, Multiple Data—pattern from computer architecture). Each agent handles the same multi-step research task independently: retrieve evidence, read it, extract facts, check them, synthesize a report. The system logs every step of each agent's work and can route different tasks to different models if needed. Multiple agents run in parallel, so you can process batches of research jobs rather than one at a time.
1427.ww: By isolating each task as an independent unit and running them in parallel, the system bypasses the bottleneck of sequential chat. The logging means you can inspect what each agent did, debug failures, and understand which steps are slow. The system also gets to benefit from routing more complex tasks to stronger (or more expensive) models while using cheaper models for simpler parts—you can be strategic about where to spend compute.
1427.po: On one benchmark, C3Flow improved accuracy from 48.44% to 61.59% (a substantial jump) and handled a fact-checking task 5.9× faster than human annotators while maintaining 87.5% accuracy. This shows that the batch-processing approach unlocks both better results and dramatic speedup for large-scale research.

1428.bp: When AI systems answer questions, they need to ground their answers in real information from the internet or a database—otherwise they just guess. The gold standard approach (called retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG) is to search for relevant documents first, then have the AI read those documents and answer based on what it found. The infrastructure for this already exists in academic research tools, but there's been a gap: those tools weren't designed to plug directly into AI assistants.
1428.wh: Researchers have built powerful toolkits like Pyserini (for searching) and RankLLM (for ranking search results by relevance) that academic labs use for information retrieval research. But AI assistants have their own world of tools and APIs. The two communities speak different languages, so researchers experimenting with how to make AI better at using search have to build bridges manually. There's no standard way to wire a research toolkit directly into an AI agent.
1428.ap: The paper presents MCP servers—adapters that follow an emerging industry standard called the Model Context Protocol. These adapters take the capabilities of Pyserini and RankLLM (sparse search, dense search, reranking, multimodal search) and expose them as callable tools that any AI assistant can invoke. An AI agent can now say 'search for this query' or 'rerank these results' and get back structured answers, the same way it might ask for the weather or a calculator result.
1428.ww: By following a standard protocol (MCP), the system becomes pluggable—any AI assistant that supports MCP can now use these research tools without custom integration code. This matters because it connects the academic IR research infrastructure (which has decades of refinement in search quality) to the emerging world of AI agents. Researchers can now quickly experiment with different retrieval and reranking approaches without rebuilding infrastructure.
1428.po: The paper demonstrates end-to-end workflows combining search, reranking, and reasoning across different AI models (open-source and proprietary). This is the bridge that lets researchers experiment with how AI and search should work together, accelerating progress on making AI-powered assistants more factual and grounded.

1429.bp: In peer review, scientists evaluate each other's work, and the fairness and quality of that review directly affects which ideas get published. But reviewers often make claims in their reviews that are opinions stated as facts, or criticisms that don't actually match what the paper says. There's no systematic way to audit whether a reviewer's claims are accurate, so unfair or careless reviews can influence publication decisions unchecked.
1429.wh: Peer reviews are long, dense documents, and checking every claim manually would require re-reading the original paper alongside each review and making judgment calls on dozens of statements. At a conference with hundreds of submissions, doing this manually is impossible. The obvious approach—having another human check—creates even more work and still requires expertise to judge edge cases.
1429.ap: Peerispect is a system that automatically extracts statements from peer reviews that are 'check-worthy' (claims about what the paper did, what results it achieved, whether a technique is sound). For each extracted claim, the system retrieves relevant passages from the manuscript and runs a natural language inference check—essentially asking 'does the paper actually support this claim?'. The results are shown in a visual interface where you can see the claim and the evidence highlighted in the original paper side by side.
1429.ww: By automating the extraction and retrieval steps, the system makes verification tractable at scale. A reviewer or program committee member can scan the claims and their supporting evidence in minutes instead of hours. The system doesn't make the final judgment (that's still human), but it does the laborious work of finding the relevant parts of the paper that address each claim, dramatically reducing cognitive load.
1429.po: The paper shows that Peerispect can help reviewers, authors, and program committees verify whether review statements are actually grounded in the submission. This creates a practical auditing tool for peer review fairness and allows conference organizers to catch problematic reviews before they influence decisions.

1430.bp: Marketing and advertising often rely on beautiful, persuasive videos to make people want to visit a place or buy a product. Generating these videos at scale is expensive when you need to hire videographers and editors, but automated video generation still struggles with reliability—the generated videos often contain errors or nonsensical visuals that undermine the advertiser's message.
1430.wh: Naive approaches to automated video generation take a description like 'a beach at sunset' and try to generate an entire video at once. This often produces inconsistent results—the sky might change color between frames, or objects might vanish. The system doesn't plan the overall composition or check whether what it generated actually matches what was requested. Video generation is inherently a multi-step problem (choosing themes, generating scenes, checking quality), but most systems try to do it in one shot.
1430.ap: ATVG breaks video generation into a planned sequence of steps: first, it decides what themes or scenes should appear (e.g., landmarks, culture, food for a travel ad); then, for each scene, it retrieves a real image from the internet to use as an anchor point, which constrains the generation to something grounded in reality; it expands that image into a detailed description of the video scene; and finally, it checks the generated video for visual artifacts and errors before assembling the final result. The system works through planning, retrieval, expansion, and verification.
1430.ww: By using real images as anchors, the system grounds its generation in reality—the generated video is constrained to show things that actually exist. By planning before generating, the system ensures thematic consistency across scenes. And by verifying the output, it catches errors before the video reaches customers. Each step reduces the ways the system can go wrong.
1430.po: Testing on real cities shows that ATVG produces more coherent multi-scene videos with better factual accuracy than a simpler baseline. The system can generate travel ads from just a city name, demonstrating that careful agentic planning can overcome the reliability problems that plague naive video generation.

1431.bp: Graphs—data structures showing how things connect to each other (like social networks or knowledge graphs)—are everywhere in real-world applications. Companies and researchers often want to ask questions about groups or communities within these graphs, like 'find all clusters of highly connected users' or 'find groups of products frequently bought together'. Current database systems have no natural way to express these kinds of questions efficiently.
1431.wh: Traditional database query languages work well for finding individual rows or simple patterns, but they struggle with questions about group structure or set-level constraints. If you want to ask 'find all maximal cliques'—groups where everyone is connected to everyone—that's hard to express and slow to compute in standard databases. You end up writing custom code to iterate through the graph manually, which is error-prone and inefficient.
1431.ap: MonacGraph extends a graph query language (Gremlin) with new syntax for reasoning about sets of nodes and their relationships. It introduces monadic second-order logic (MSOL)—a mathematical formalism that lets you write questions like 'find all subsets of nodes where certain properties hold'. The system executes these queries by first evaluating simpler first-order checks efficiently, then combining results to answer the full question. It stores graph structure in a way that precomputes which nodes form communities, so community queries can be answered fast.
1431.ww: By building the query language and storage around the mathematical framework of set-level reasoning, the system makes community queries expressible and efficient. Precomputing community structure means the database doesn't have to re-compute it every time. The web interface lets non-experts write and visualize these queries, making complex graph analysis accessible.
1431.po: MonacGraph demonstrates a working graph database where you can express and execute complex set-level queries on real graph data. This opens up analyses that were previously impractical to express, allowing organizations and researchers to extract insights about community structure and group patterns at scale.

1432.bp: Museums worldwide have digitized their collections—millions of objects described in records, alongside images and historical information. But this data lives in isolated silos: catalog databases, image repositories, and text descriptions don't connect to each other. Visitors and researchers can't easily explore how artifacts relate to each other, who created them, or what cultural connections link different pieces together.
1432.wh: Museum data is heterogeneous—some information is structured (item ID, acquisition date), some is images, and some is free-form text descriptions. Connecting these requires someone to manually build bridges between the different systems, and even then, the data isn't organized in a way that invites exploration. If you find one artifact and wonder 'what else is connected to this?', there's no obvious way to follow those threads.
1432.ap: MuseKG builds a unified graph (a knowledge graph) that brings all these sources together into one queryable structure. Objects, artists, organizations, images, and extracted concepts all become nodes in the graph, and relationships between them become edges. When you ask a natural language question like 'show me works by this artist', the system maps your question to relevant graph entities and returns the connected neighborhood of evidence—the artwork, related objects, biographical context, all linked together.
1432.ww: By unifying heterogeneous data into a typed graph, the system makes relationships explicit and traversable. A visitor can see not just isolated artifacts but how they connect—who created it, what period it's from, what other pieces relate to it. The natural language interface means visitors don't need to learn database query syntax; they just ask.
1432.po: MuseKG supports exploration tasks like attribute lookup ('who made this?'), relation exploration ('what else did this artist create?'), and relation-aware retrieval ('show me pieces from this collection that relate to this theme'). The system makes museum collections legible as a connected whole rather than isolated records.

1433.bp: Recommending food or recipes to people can help nudge them toward healthier eating, but food recommender systems have a problem: unhealthy foods are often more popular and easier to predict, so the system recommends them more often. Even when a system identifies a healthier option, it's hard to explain why that trade-off makes sense in a way that actually convinces people to try it.
1433.wh: Most recommendation systems are trained to predict what users will click or rate highly, which means they learn that people gravitate toward popular foods even if those foods aren't nutritious. Adding explanations helps, but explaining why a salad is better than a burger requires translating dry nutritional data into language that resonates with a user's actual goals and concerns. Testing whether explanations actually change eating behavior requires running studies with real users, which is expensive and technically complex to set up.
1433.ap: XFoodRec is a mobile app that combines recipe recommendations with automatic explanations. The system recommends dishes personalized to your preferences, but when it suggests a healthier option, it uses an AI language model to turn nutritional information into natural-language explanations tailored to the user's health goals. The app also includes built-in A/B testing infrastructure, so researchers can assign users to different explanation styles and measure whether the explanations actually change what people eat.
1433.ww: By personalizing the explanation to the user's stated health goals (e.g., reducing sodium, increasing protein), the system makes the case for healthier food in language the user cares about. By baking A/B testing into the app itself, researchers can measure real behavioral impact without running separate studies—the app automatically logs what recommendations people accept and reject across different explanation styles.
1433.po: XFoodRec bridges the gap between algorithmic recommendation and real-world dietary behavior change. The paper demonstrates that the platform enables researchers to study how different explanation strategies actually influence food choices in practice, not just in simulation.

1434.bp: Researchers reading academic papers often hit moments where a concept is unclear or they want to explore related work, but switching to a search engine breaks their focus and interrupts their reading flow. Ideally, the system could proactively suggest relevant related papers or clarify concepts as they read, without making them leave the document.
1434.wh: Suggesting relevant papers while someone reads sounds simple, but the hard part is knowing what's relevant to them personally. The same paper on neural networks might mean something different to an NLP researcher than to a computer vision researcher—they have different backgrounds, different questions, and different knowledge gaps. A one-size-fits-all suggestion system will generate irrelevant noise. The system needs to understand the reader's background and intent, which isn't visible on the screen.
1434.ap: H-MAPS maintains three layers of memory about the user: a long-term profile (what field are they in?), a reading-session memory (what paper are they reading now?), and a real-time memory (where in the paper are they, and what did they just look at?). When the system detects that you've paused on a concept or section, it uses these three levels of context to infer what you're trying to understand, generates a natural language question that captures your likely information need, and retrieves papers relevant to that specific need. The retrieval happens locally on your device for privacy.
1434.ww: By maintaining hierarchical context, the system can disambiguate what a concept means to this particular reader. The same word triggers different searches for an NLP researcher and an HCI researcher because their profiles are different. By inferring intent from reading behavior (pauses, mouse movements, where you're looking) rather than asking you to type, the system feels proactive rather than intrusive.
1434.po: The paper demonstrates that H-MAPS can generate profile-specific questions and retrieve distinct papers tailored to different users' backgrounds, all triggered by implicit reading behavior. This shows that proactive information retrieval can enhance reading without interrupting the flow.

1435.bp: Large organizations—governments, corporations, law firms—work with regulatory documents and contracts that evolve over time. Each revision produces a new version, but comparing versions manually is incredibly tedious because documents are often hundreds of pages long. Lawyers and auditors need to spot inconsistencies and contradictions introduced by changes, but character-by-character diffs miss the real semantic issues.
1435.wh: Simple diff tools (character-level comparisons) fail when text has been reworded. If a phrase 'this must be reviewed' gets rewritten as 'review is mandatory', a character diff sees them as entirely different, but they mean the same thing. A semantic diff needs to understand that these paraphrases are equivalent. But running semantic comparison on legal text is risky—you need high confidence that your analysis is correct, and you need the system to explain its reasoning.
1435.ap: SLeDoC uses a combination of information-retrieval techniques and large language models to compare legal paragraphs at the semantic level. It identifies corresponding sections between two document versions, then uses language models to judge whether the meaning has changed or merely been reworded. The system goes beyond simple 'same or different' judgments and captures nuances like whether a clause has been strengthened, weakened, or clarified.
1435.ww: By using state-of-the-art language models (which are trained to understand meaning across paraphrases), the system can recognize semantic equivalence even when wording changes. By grounding the comparison in information-retrieval matching, it can handle long documents efficiently. The combination lets the system be both semantically accurate and computationally tractable.
1435.po: SLeDoC was evaluated on a benchmark of legally annotated document pairs, showing that it can accurately detect semantic shifts beyond what character-level tools can achieve. The system makes document auditing practical for legal and compliance professionals, reducing the manual labor required to track changes in complex regulatory texts.

1436.bp: Wikidata is a massive knowledge graph—structured facts about millions of people, places, and concepts. But like all knowledge graphs, it's incomplete. There are billions of true relationships that haven't been added yet because no one has bothered to include them. Identifying missing facts and adding them would make Wikidata more useful, but humans can't manually check every possibility.
1436.wh: Automatically predicting missing relationships in knowledge graphs is possible—there are algorithms (embedding-based models) that can suggest likely connections. But an automated suggestion is only useful if it's grounded in evidence. If the system suggests a fact that's wrong, it pollutes the knowledge graph. And if the suggestion has no evidence, how can a human editor verify it or know whether to trust it?
1436.ap: WikiRAG combines three steps: first, it uses knowledge graph embeddings (a mathematical technique for representing entities as vectors) to suggest candidate relationships; second, it retrieves relevant Wikipedia passages as evidence for each candidate; third, it uses an LLM to assess each candidate by reasoning over the retrieved passages. The system presents candidates alongside their evidence, allowing humans to inspect the reasoning and validate or reject each suggestion before adding it to Wikidata.
1436.ww: By retrieving evidence before asking the LLM to make a judgment, the system ensures that every candidate suggestion comes with grounding in real information. The human-in-the-loop design means the system can be confident (it can suggest high-risk additions) while still letting humans make the final call. This balance reduces both false negatives (missed facts) and false positives (wrong facts added).
1436.po: WikiRAG demonstrates an end-to-end workflow for evidence-based link prediction on Wikidata. The system enables batch validation and export of confirmed triples, making it practical to systematically complete knowledge graphs with human oversight.

1437.bp: When large language models generate long-form text—essays, articles, reports—they sometimes invent facts that sound plausible but are false, a problem called hallucination. Detecting these hallucinations is crucial if you want to use AI for high-stakes applications like writing news articles or research summaries. But existing fact-checking tools are slow, require expensive API calls to external services, and rely on outdated knowledge bases.
1437.wh: Fact-checking long-form text is inherently difficult because you need to verify multiple claims across potentially hundreds of sentences. The obvious approach—checking each claim against a search engine or knowledge base—is slow and expensive if you rely on paid APIs. And if your knowledge base is outdated, you'll miss facts that are actually true. You also need to handle ambiguity (the same name might refer to multiple people) and decide when a paraphrase counts as verification.
1437.ap: FactOWL is a fact-checking tool that decomposes long-form text into individual factual statements, then retrieves evidence from Wikipedia and Wikidata for each statement. It handles ambiguity by checking a statement against multiple Wikipedia pages and aggregating evidence from multiple sources. The system uses open-source language models (not paid APIs) and real-time Wikipedia access (not stale knowledge bases), making it fast and affordable.
1437.ww: By checking each claim against multiple sources and aggregating the results, the system reduces false negatives—it's less likely to call something wrong when it's actually right. Using open-source models and real-time Wikipedia means the system is fast (because it avoids API latency) and stays current. The multi-source approach also helps resolve entity ambiguity by seeing which page actually supports the claim.
1437.po: FactOWL is at least 10× faster than the prior state-of-the-art fact-checking tool (FActScore) and is freely available. The paper demonstrates that efficient, open-source fact-checking is now practical, enabling researchers and practitioners to verify LLM outputs without expensive infrastructure.

1438.bp: Trademark protection requires examining whether a new trademark might be confused with existing ones—the 'likelihood of confusion' test. This is a complex judgment involving visual similarity, pronunciation, conceptual meaning, and the types of goods being sold. Lawyers currently search for conflicting trademarks manually and make these judgments themselves, which is slow and subjective. Could AI help systematize this reasoning?
1438.wh: A simple ranked list of similar existing trademarks isn't enough for trademark clearance because the judgment isn't just 'which marks are most similar?' but 'for these specific candidate marks, is there a real risk of consumer confusion across all these dimensions?'. This requires weighing multiple factors (appearance, sound, concept, goods), resolving edge cases (is a generic symbol confusable?), and producing a clear risk score. A retrieval system gives you candidates, but the real work is comparative judgment across multiple dimensions under the examination rules.
1438.ap: T-RADAR uses agentic simulation to handle this multi-dimensional judgment. First, it retrieves potentially conflicting trademarks using multimodal search (visual and semantic similarity). Then, instead of just ranking, it simulates an adversarial examination between a mock Examiner and an Applicant, where they debate the visual, phonetic, conceptual, and goods-related aspects of similarity. The simulation produces a Conflict Risk score and Registrability score based on this debate.
1438.ww: By simulating the actual examination process (rather than trying to predict the score directly), the system can capture the nuanced reasoning that trademark examiners use. The adversarial format means the system has to consider counterarguments—both why marks might be confused and why they might not be. When multiple candidates are tested, comparing their simulated outcomes reveals high-risk pairs.
1438.po: T-RADAR demonstrates that agentic simulation can be used as an interface for complex, multi-criteria judgment. The system produces interpretable risk scores that serve as review prioritization signals, helping lawyers focus their effort on the genuinely risky cases.

1439.bp: Researchers and students often read mathematical papers and articles filled with formulas and equations, but standard PDF readers treat math as just pixels on a page—you can't search for formulas, click on an equation to find related work, or ask the system to explain a derivation. This isolation of mathematical notation from the rest of the text creates a barrier to exploration and learning.
1439.wh: Mathematical content is hard to index and search because formulas are visual structures—a Laplace transform looks like a series of symbols on the page, but there's no underlying text to search for. Standard full-text search is useless for math. Meanwhile, specialized math search tools exist but they're separate from PDF readers, forcing readers to switch windows and lose context. The tools and document viewers exist in silos.
1439.ap: MathMex-PDF integrates mathematical extraction and multimodal retrieval into a single PDF reader. It processes PDF pages to detect where formulas are, recognizes the mathematical notation (converting pixel images into structured representations like LaTeX), and grounds those formulas in the document layout. You can then search using natural language ('find the convolution operator'), LaTeX (' find \\ast'), or mixed queries, and click on any rendered formula to trigger a reverse search that finds related papers containing similar formulas.
1439.ww: By recognizing and indexing formulas alongside text, the system makes mathematical content discoverable in the same workflow as text. By supporting multiple query types (natural language, LaTeX, hybrid, query-by-example), it meets users where they are. By applying reciprocal rank fusion to combine formula and text rankings, it weights both modalities appropriately.
1439.po: MathMex-PDF demonstrates unified math-text retrieval in an interactive PDF reader, making it practical to explore mathematical content without leaving the document. The system also provides accessibility features like spoken-math annotations, helping readers with visual impairments engage with mathematical papers.

1440.bp: Comics are everywhere—in print, online, streaming—but finding the one you're looking for is oddly hard. You can search by title or character name, sure, but what if you remember only the art style, the pacing of the story, or that the main character was a tough woman? Traditional search treats comics like simple text documents, missing everything that makes them special.
1440.wh: Comics pack three languages at once: pictures (backgrounds, character expressions, panel layout), words (dialogue and captions), and rhythm (how fast the story unfolds through panel size and composition). When you ask an AI to find what you like, it either retreats to text metadata or throws all the complexity into a neural network, leaving you wondering why it picked what it picked. Fans trust systems more when they can see the reasoning.
1440.ap: ESCOMIC watches what you actually click and hover over, learning which visual traits and story qualities matter most to you personally. It breaks down each comic into factual bits (genre, character gender, pacing speed) and visual patterns, then ranks results by combining all these signals. When you hover—a signal users give without thinking—the system quietly adjusts which factors to weight more heavily. Every result comes with a clear explanation: 'This one ranked high because it has the fast pacing you seemed to like, plus a confident female lead.'
1440.ww: Humans care about explanations because they want to know if a recommendation makes sense for them specifically. Fans who see why something ranked high can immediately judge whether to trust the system next time. The adaptive part works because people's tastes shift as they browse; a system that locks in one interpretation misses that drift. Showing the logic—not hiding it—builds confidence.
1440.po: In user tests with eye-tracking, people using ESCOMIC found better comics faster, felt more satisfied with results, and trusted the system more than standard search or opaque AI ranking. The effect is concrete: explicit explanation + personal adaptation = users actually using the tool instead of giving up.

1441.bp: Visual media—films, archives, security footage, medical imaging—lives everywhere, but searching it is fragmented and frustrating. You might use one tool for face recognition, another to find objects in a scene, a third for audio, and a fourth for metadata like dates. WISE asks: what if you could search all of these at once, in one place, without being a machine-learning engineer?
1441.wh: Each modality (images, video, audio, faces, text transcripts) has different technical requirements and specialized models. Tying them together into a single system that actually works fast enough and scales to millions of items is a massive engineering puzzle. Most people who need this are archivists, researchers, or security teams without the budget or expertise to wire up seven different systems.
1441.ap: WISE bundled together a collection of open retrieval models—one for object detection (finding 'horse' in any scene), one for face matching (finding that specific person), one for audio events (finding the 'wood creak' sound), one for scenes (finding 'empty street'). Each model lives in its own module. You can search by natural language ('show me trains in Germany'), by images you upload, or by audio samples. The results come back as a single ranked list, even though the search happened across totally different data types.
1441.ww: Vector search—converting images, audio, and text into points in a mathematical space where similar things cluster together—makes this practical at scale. Since each modality gets its own module, adding a new model later is straightforward: plug it in, and it works with everything else. The system is small enough to run locally, protecting private footage or sensitive archives from cloud exposure.
1441.po: Users can now ask questions they couldn't ask before: 'Find this face anywhere in our archive,' or 'Show me all scenes with German trains,' or 'Retrieve everything with that specific audio artifact.' The same system handles real-world collections from historical archives to security footage. No machine-learning background required.

1442.bp: Patents matter enormously to companies and researchers—they signal innovation, reveal technological directions, and help you spot threats and opportunities. But existing patent databases are shallow, listing basic facts like dates and inventors. For serious decisions about whether a patent is truly valuable or where a technology is headed, you need depth—understanding the real innovation, how it connects to other discoveries, and whether it's transformative or incremental.
1442.wh: A patent's real value isn't obvious from its title or abstract. You need to understand what the claimed invention actually does, how it differs from prior work, and how it sits within a web of related patents. Most R&D teams lack the time or expertise to assemble this picture manually. Large language models can help, but they generate summaries that still don't show you the connections or trends.
1442.ap: PatentMerit uses large language models to read and analyze patent text deeply, mapping where each patent sits in the landscape of technology clusters. It builds a visual network showing how patents cite each other—revealing genealogies and evolutionary paths. It tags patents with fine-grained classifications and identifies 'disruptive' ones (patents that break from the usual trajectory). It extracts key technical topics and generates written reports summarizing all this analysis.
1442.ww: Network visualization works because innovation doesn't happen in isolation—each patent builds on prior work and sparks later inventions. Seeing this web immediately reveals whether a technology is mature (many related patents over years) or emerging (sudden spike in citations). Identifying disruption mathematically—anomalies in the citation and classification networks—flags patents that genuinely change things, not just incremental tweaks.
1442.po: An R&D team can now ask: 'Is this a disruptive technology we should watch?' or 'How has this field evolved over five years?' or 'What technologies do we compete with or complement?' with concrete, justified answers. The system automates the cognitively heavy work of assembling a complete picture.

1443.bp: Searching documents using images and layout—not just text—is starting to matter. Imagine you're hunting through a thousand PDFs and you remember something about a table in the middle of page 5, or a specific diagram style. Traditional text search misses it entirely. 'Visual retrieval' systems that understand layout and design can find what you're after, but they generate thousands of vectors per document, making search prohibitively slow at scale.
1443.wh: Modern retrieval systems break each document page into visual patches and represent each patch as a vector. This captures layout and design details text-based search misses. The problem: a single page might produce 5,000 vectors, so searching a million-page collection means comparing billions of vectors, which is expensive and slow—sometimes impractical.
1443.ap: The Visual RAG Toolkit uses pooling—mathematically combining nearby vectors into single, denser summaries, the way you might take an average of neighboring pixels in an image. It creates two layers: a coarse layer with just a few dozen vectors per page for fast filtering, and a fine layer with full detail for a second pass of exact ranking. When you search, the system first uses the coarse vectors to quickly narrow to the most promising documents, then does precise matching only on those finalists.
1443.ww: This two-stage design mirrors how humans actually search: you skim quickly to eliminate obviously irrelevant pages, then read closely only what might be relevant. The pooling doesn't lose the information you need—it just compresses redundancy. Because this happens before any model training, you don't need to retrain the system for different documents, making it immediately practical.
1443.po: Document search runs about four times faster, using far fewer vectors in storage, while keeping the same accuracy. A person searching a large collection of technical PDFs or contracts now gets near-instant results without sacrificing the ability to find a diagram or table by its visual pattern.

1444.bp: Retrieval-augmented generation—augmenting large language models with relevant documents pulled from databases—is powerful but intimidating. Most people think you either need to be a machine-learning expert or pay cloud companies for managed services. EasyRAG asks: what if beginners could learn this hands-on, starting from the basics and building up intuition?
1444.wh: RAG involves many moving parts: finding the right documents, feeding them to the language model, deciding how to rank results, tuning speed versus quality. Tutorials jump straight to code without building intuition. Newcomers hit dead ends—unclear why retrieval failed, unsure whether their setup is reasonable, unable to debug problems without deep expertise.
1444.ap: EasyRAG layers learning in three stages. Level one uses APIs (Google Search, for example) as the retriever, so you see the core idea—fetch external knowledge, feed it to the language model—without infrastructure overhead. Level two implements three concrete, related methods side-by-side: Fusion-in-Decoder and its lighter variant, then Stochastic RAG, each extending the previous so you see where complexity buys you gains. Level three opens the door to full customization.
1444.ww: Teaching through concrete examples and progression is faster than abstract theory. Comparing methods side-by-side—all in the same codebase with the same data—makes the trade-offs visceral: using lighter retrieval is faster but slightly less accurate; end-to-end optimization is powerful but expensive. Starting with APIs lets people separate 'how does RAG work?' from 'how do I build an efficient retriever?'
1444.po: A beginner can now understand RAG deeply enough to deploy it and tune it for their own problem, without hiring a specialist. The progression means you build real intuition, not just copy a tutorial.

1445.bp: Nepali is spoken by 26 million people, yet there is no standardized test collection to systematically evaluate how well search systems work for Nepali speakers. This means researchers can't compare approaches, and companies can't benchmark improvements. Search quality for underserved languages stagnates because there's no common yardstick.
1445.wh: Building a rigorous test collection requires thousands of genuine search queries, relevant documents, and human judgments of what counts as a good match. For major languages like English, this work is funded and public (TREC collections, etc.). For Nepali—a low-resource language—funding and expertise are scarcer, and the quirks of Nepali grammar and script make the work harder to outsource.
1445.ap: This paper proposes a methodology for creating a Nepali IR benchmark that includes three scenarios: Nepali speakers searching in Nepali (monolingual), English speakers searching for Nepali results (cross-lingual), and speakers mixing Nepali and English in queries (code-mixed). The work identifies existing Nepali documents and would use native speakers to judge relevance.
1445.ww: A standardized benchmark works because everyone tests on the same data, making results comparable. Nepali's rich morphology—one word can take many forms—is actually valuable for research: methods that handle Nepali's complexity transfer well to other morphologically rich languages. Code-mixed queries reflect reality: many bilingual users switch between languages mid-query.
1445.po: With a public benchmark, researchers can rigorously develop and compare retrieval methods for Nepali. Companies can measure their progress. The infrastructure becomes reusable for related languages.

1446.bp: Hausa and Fongbe are spoken by millions in West Africa, yet information retrieval research for these languages is nearly nonexistent. When people search in these languages using systems designed for English, results are often irrelevant or wrong. Understanding what techniques (reranking, query expansion) actually help—or hurt—is foundational before building better systems.
1446.wh: Large language models work much better for some languages than others. Hausa, spoken by tens of millions, has more training data in LLMs than Fongbe, spoken by fewer. Query expansion—using an LLM to rephrase a search query—might help by clarifying intent, or it might confuse the system by injecting errors. You need rigorous experiments to know. And the data gap is huge: when you translate something into Fongbe, an LLM often produces gibberish.
1446.ap: This study directly compared several retrieval approaches: keyword-based search (BM25), multilingual dense retrieval (learned representations of meaning across languages), LLM-based reranking (using an LLM to score results), and LLM-based query expansion (asking the LLM to rephrase the query). They tested these on Hausa and Fongbe, using commercial LLMs, and measured both quality and the data characteristics.
1446.ww: The data reveals the mechanism: LLMs trained on English and high-resource languages transfer poorly to low-resource languages. Query expansion helps some problems (clarifying a confusing query) but hurts others (introducing errors when the LLM doesn't understand the target language well). Reranking—scoring existing results—is more robust than expansion because it doesn't inject new errors.
1446.po: The concrete finding: for Fongbe especially, straightforward multilingual dense retrieval often outperforms LLM-based expansion. This guides teams building real systems for these languages: invest in translation quality first; don't blindly assume LLM expansion helps. The benchmark and methodology open the door to iterative improvement.

1447.bp: People search in the languages they speak. When users query in Hindi, Bengali, or a mix of languages, search systems almost always interpret the query in English, often failing to find relevant results. Small language models are starting to serve as the 'smart router' layer in search pipelines, but they're almost always prompted in English, leaving linguistic diversity on the table.
1447.wh: Prompting an AI model in English when the user thought in their native language is a mismatch. The model might understand 'what is your name' better in English than in Hindi because it saw more English training data. But that doesn't mean English-only prompting is optimal—the model still understands Hindi, and asking in multiple languages might give it more angles to solve the problem.
1447.ap: This team prompts the same frozen language model in three languages—English, Hindi, and Bengali—on the exact same query classification task, then averages the results (weighting by the model's confidence in each language). No retraining, no translation, no extra data needed. They test nine models, from 1 billion to 9 billion parameters, on four benchmark datasets.
1447.ww: Different languages emphasize different aspects of meaning. A Hindi prompt might make certain query intents clearer; a Bengali prompt might catch nuances English misses. Averaging predictions across languages combines these perspectives without requiring the model to be fluent in all of them. The modest computational overhead (1.2–1.4 times slower) is worth it because classification accuracy jumps 3–5 percentage points.
1447.po: Query classification—routing a search to the right handler—now works measurably better for multilingual speakers without retraining or translation services. This matters in regions with widespread code-mixing (mixing languages in one sentence) and shows the technique scales to larger models.

1448.bp: Chichewa is spoken by 12 million people, but when someone wants to ask a database a question in Chichewa, there's a chasm: no systems exist. Text-to-SQL—converting natural language questions into database queries—works well in high-resource languages but has barely been explored for African languages. Bridging this gap unlocks database access for millions of people excluded from the digital economy.
1448.wh: Text-to-SQL is hard because a language model must understand both the natural language intent and the database schema. It's especially hard in Chichewa because there's almost no training data, and Chichewa's grammar is different from English (where most Text-to-SQL systems were trained). A model that works in English might stumble on Chichewa's structure.
1448.ap: This work first built a Chichewa Text-to-SQL dataset: 400 genuine questions paired with correct SQL queries, grounded in realistic data (agriculture, commodity prices, population). They then tested open-source language models with zero-shot (just asking), few-shot (showing examples), and retrieval-augmented (pulling relevant examples from the dataset) prompting, in both English and Chichewa. Finally, they fine-tuned selected models with QLoRA, a parameter-efficient method, and combined it with retrieval.
1448.ww: Retrieval-augmented prompting works because it retrieves similar examples from the limited Chichewa dataset; this acts like a teacher showing the model similar problems. QLoRA fine-tuning is crucial for low-resource settings because it's cheap (trains only a small set of parameters, not the whole model). The combination—retrieval showing patterns + fine-tuning adapting the model—narrows the accuracy gap from 56.7 percentage points (English-only) to 23.4.
1448.po: A Chichewa speaker can now ask database questions and get results, with 53.3% accuracy—a world of difference from zero. More concretely, farmers asking about commodity prices or weather conditions can get answers through a natural-language system trained with realistic low-resource techniques.

1449.bp: Rayalaseema, in southern India, is drought-stricken, and most farmers there are small landholders who need reliable agricultural advice—about water management, crop choice, drought coping. But this advice exists in English and Hindi, not Telugu, the language they speak. There are no question-answering datasets in Telugu for agriculture, so systems can't be built or evaluated.
1449.wh: Agricultural information retrieval for underserved regions requires more than translating English systems. Drought-specific advice (e.g., 'which crops survive with 300mm rain?') is locally critical but rarely in English. Farmer literacy is 60%, so systems must handle varied input (misspellings, short questions, rural dialect). Building a benchmark requires access to local experts and relevant materials.
1449.ap: This paper documents the gap: agricultural QA datasets exist in Hindi, Tamil, and Bengali, but not Telugu. It identifies available information sources (government extension materials, Kisan Call Center records—thousands of farmer calls recorded and transcribed). It proposes a methodology: extract questions from call center logs, pair them with authoritative answers from extension materials, validate with Telugu-speaking agriculturalists, and build a public benchmark.
1449.ww: Call center logs are gold because farmers ask real questions they actually need answered, not hypothetical ones. Local extension materials are authoritative and context-aware. A dataset built this way is immediately relevant to the deployment context—systems trained on it will handle the actual needs and language variations farmers use.
1449.po: Once built, this benchmark enables targeted development of Telugu agricultural QA systems. It serves 74 million Telugu speakers and creates a model for similar low-resource language + domain combinations (e.g., Marathi health information, Assamese fisheries).

1450.bp: Marathi speakers in India want timely information—news, local events, job postings—but large language models with built-in web search often fail to find relevant results in Marathi. The dream of 'talk to the web in your language' is undermined by gaps in search, retrieval quality, and how well LLMs handle low-resource languages.
1450.wh: Web-augmented LLMs are powerful in English but struggle in Marathi. The LLM might invoke a search tool multiple times, but if the web returns results in mixed language or the LLM misunderstands the results, the final answer is wrong. Testing this requires carefully designed queries that capture real user needs (not just translated global queries) and metrics that isolate what's failing: search retrieval, result integration, or language understanding.
1450.ap: MarathiWeb is a benchmark with two types of queries: global needs translated into Marathi (e.g., 'weather in London') and natively authored local needs (e.g., 'where can I buy fresh turmeric in Pune?'). Each query has golden-standard answers. They tested two frontier LLMs with web search against a Google-based retrieval baseline, and analyzed failure patterns and cost (how many web calls).
1450.ww: Local information retrieval is harder than global because fewer sources cover local topics in Marathi, and LLMs have even less training data. Separating translated queries from native ones matters because failure patterns differ: global queries fail due to language degradation; local queries often fail because sources don't exist. Shallow retrieval (one web call) beats deep multi-step search in Marathi, likely because each additional step introduces more opportunities for language understanding to fail.
1450.po: The benchmark exposes that LLM web search breaks down in Marathi, especially for local information. It provides both a diagnostic tool and a concrete challenge for improving low-resource language information access. The finding that shallow retrieval outperforms deep search is counterintuitive and actionable for system design.

1451.bp: Summarizing multiple documents in languages like Vietnamese, Thai, or Indonesian is useful for news aggregation, research synthesis, and decision-making. But large language models that generate summaries are too expensive to run on a single GPU in countries with limited compute infrastructure. Extractive summarization—picking the best existing sentences rather than generating new ones—is cheaper but needs to work across typologically diverse low-resource languages.
1451.wh: Abstractive summarization (generating new text) requires massive models. Extractive summarization (choosing existing sentences) avoids hallucination but is harder in low-resource languages because learning which sentences matter depends on language-specific understanding. Standard transformer models are expensive; you need a lightweight approach.
1451.ap: This team combined two technical ideas: mixture-of-experts embeddings (which adapt to different languages without retraining) and graph neural networks that model how sentences relate to each other (discourse structure). The full model has only 3.2 million trainable parameters—30 times smaller than typical transformer approaches—making it trainable on a single GPU in hours, not days.
1451.ww: Discourse structure matters: good summaries preserve the flow and connections between ideas, not just high-scoring sentences in isolation. Graph neural networks capture these relationships. Mixture-of-experts avoids training a separate model per language; a single model adapts to the linguistic properties of Vietnamese, Thai, etc. The small parameter count means the approach is truly accessible to resource-limited teams.
1451.po: Teams in Vietnam, Thailand, or Indonesia can now run the system locally on modest hardware, summarizing multi-document collections in their language without cloud cost or privacy concerns. The approach scales across unrelated language families (Austroasiatic, Kra-Dai, Austronesian), showing the technique generalizes.

1452.bp: When large language models generate answers to agricultural questions in Swahili, are they any good? How can you tell if an answer is reasonable versus nonsense? In low-resource settings, there's often no gold standard to compare against. Understanding whether LLM-generated answers are detectably different from human expert answers is a first step toward quality control.
1452.wh: LLMs sometimes hallucinate—they output plausible-sounding but false information. In Swahili agricultural IR, there's limited prior work to guide what 'quality' should look like. You can't always run human evaluations at scale. If LLM-generated answers have consistent, detectable patterns (e.g., always longer, always less diverse in word choice), you could use that as a signal for quality assessment.
1452.ap: This team collected 127 Swahili questions about maize and got answers from three sources: human agricultural experts, ChatGPT, and Gemini. They measured textual properties: answer length, lexical diversity (do they use varied vocabulary or repeat words?), and semantic similarity (how much do they overlap in meaning with human answers?). They then trained a classifier to predict whether an answer came from an expert, ChatGPT, or Gemini.
1452.ww: LLMs tend to output more uniform text than humans. A person answers a question directly; an LLM often elaborates, hedges, and rambles. These patterns—longer length, lower diversity, moderate semantic overlap—are mathematical signatures. A classifier learns these signatures because LLMs are trained on vast text that differs from how a specific expert in Swahili agriculture speaks.
1452.po: You can now automatically flag likely LLM-generated answers as needing human review, without building an expert panel for every query. The 98% classification accuracy suggests this approach could be practical for quality assurance in low-resource agricultural IR systems.

1453.bp: Machine translation from English into Tetun (Timor-Leste) or Bislama (Vanuatu) is often mediocre because training data is sparse and highly skewed toward general text, not medical or disaster relief terminology. But local health workers and disaster response teams need accurate translation of urgent information. They don't have time to fix machine errors; they need systems that 'just work' in their domain.
1453.wh: Generic machine translation uses data mostly about politics and social topics, making medical terminology a weak point. A small team in Timor-Leste can't afford to collect thousands of domain-specific sentence pairs to retrain a full model. They need a system that leverages limited in-domain resources without massive retraining.
1453.ap: Tulun combines standard neural machine translation with retrieval and large language model post-editing. When you translate a medical sentence, the system retrieves similar examples from a small, curated in-domain memory (translation glossaries and examples specific to medicine), shows these to the LLM, and asks the LLM to review and improve the translation. Users can add their own domain-specific terms and examples, which are immediately used in subsequent translations.
1453.ww: This design is practical because in-context learning—showing an LLM examples from your specific domain—works without retraining. Retrieval means you only show the LLM relevant examples, keeping the prompt focused. User-configurable glossaries mean the system adapts to local terminology. The transparency (showing users which examples guided the translation) builds trust.
1453.po: Medical translation accuracy improved 16–22 points over baseline MT without needing expensive retraining. Disaster relief teams in Vanuatu and health workers in Timor-Leste now have a tool that adapts to their needs in real time and they can see why translations were chosen, allowing them to correct and improve the system.

1454.bp: Shona is spoken by 12 million people in Zimbabwe and Southern Africa, yet retrieval research almost never addresses it. Shona has rich morphology—one root word takes many prefixes and suffixes that change meaning—which makes retrieval harder than for languages like English. Building a retrieval system for Shona requires understanding these morphological patterns and having a benchmark to test against.
1454.wh: Standard retrieval methods treat each word form as separate. In Shona, 'to go', 'going', 'went', 'will go', and 'should have gone' are all variations of one root; treating them as different words means the system misses relevant documents. Solving this requires morphology-aware processing, but development is blocked without a benchmark—no public test set for Shona retrieval exists.
1454.ap: This work ran initial experiments using standard sparse retrieval (BM25) and dense retrieval on Shona text, demonstrating significant performance gaps compared to English. Based on these findings, it proposes a plan to build a large-scale Shona IR benchmark and develop methods aware of Shona's morphological structure.
1454.ww: Morphology-aware retrieval works because it groups related word forms, connecting 'going' and 'went' as variations of the same concept. A benchmark is essential because it lets you measure whether morphological processing actually helps and provides a standard for comparing approaches. Building this foundation for Shona is a step toward equitable IR across language families.
1454.po: Once a Shona IR benchmark and morphology-aware methods are in place, the system can handle the full range of how people naturally speak Shona. This work charts a path for similar effort on other morphologically rich low-resource languages, advancing digital inclusion and equitable access to information technology.

1455.bp: In rural Namibian schools, students cannot access learning materials because the internet is unreliable and expensive. When education relies on finding resources online, kids with poor connectivity are shut out entirely. This paper flips the problem: instead of pulling information from the cloud, what if the school itself became a library, with search tools built right into the local network?
1455.wh: Most search systems assume you have bandwidth, fast machines, and power to spare. They rank results by relevance scores that need heavy computation, and they gather logs of user behavior to improve over time. But in a school with spotty electricity, a single shared tablet, and maybe a 2G connection, these luxuries vanish. Teachers need practical answers: how do you rank documents when you have gigabytes, not terabytes? How do you know if your system actually works without lab A/B testing?
1455.ap: The team built a search system that lives on a local server inside the school—not in the cloud. It stores a curated collection of STEM materials (textbooks, videos, exercises) relevant to the Namibian curriculum. When a student searches, the system uses BM25, a proven ranking method that works fast and offline, and offers faceted search so learners can filter by topic or grade level without needing advanced hardware.
1455.ww: By keeping everything local, search latency drops to milliseconds even on slow networks. The system designers explicitly shaped the ranking and facets around what teachers recognize from the curriculum, so results feel relevant without needing user behavior data. The team also planned their evaluation differently: instead of A/B testing millions of users, they'll watch real classroom interactions, collect teacher judgments, and listen to students directly.
1455.po: Teachers and learners get instant access to structured STEM content without waiting for cloud round-trips or data plans. The paper demonstrates a design approach for offline search in resource-constrained settings and proposes new evaluation methods that work when logging and large-scale experiments are not realistic.

1456.bp: When a lawyer needs to know if a case applies to a particular law, they must manually search through hundreds of statutes—a slow, error-prone bottleneck in legal work. For Vietnamese judges and lawyers, no automated system exists yet because building one requires both a large corpus of rulings and annotated laws, which is expensive to create. This paper builds that missing foundation and a search system to use it.
1456.wh: Finding the right statute for a case is harder than finding a relevant document, because it requires understanding deep legal reasoning: whether specific facts in the case actually trigger the statute's conditions. General search methods that rely on keyword overlap or simple similarity fail here. Additionally, Vietnamese legal text is a low-resource setting—few annotated datasets exist, and the writing style and structure differ sharply from English legal language.
1456.ap: The team created ViCSR, a benchmark of 10,000 actual criminal judgments paired with citations to the 1,122 statutes they invoke.
