They then built a two-stage retriever: first, a fast neural model (fine-tuned for Vietnamese) narrows down from all statutes to a shortlist using semantic similarity. Second, a compact graph neural network reranks by exploiting the legal structure—statutes cite and reference each other, forming a dependency graph that the model learns to navigate.
1456.ww: By splitting into two stages, the system avoids slow computation on all statutes while still leveraging legal structure. Training the first stage on Vietnamese legal text teaches it to recognize domain-specific language patterns. The graph reranker exploits a fact that a lawyer knows intuitively: if statute A applies to this case and statute B always appears alongside A, then B is likely relevant too.
1456.po: The system outperforms both keyword-based and standard neural retrieval on the new benchmark. By releasing the annotated corpus and trained models, the paper creates an infrastructure for legal information retrieval in Vietnamese, directly enabling judicial efficiency in a language that previously lacked such tools.

1457.bp: A Tanzanian child who speaks Hehe at home is invisible to Google, Siri, and most online knowledge systems—they only work in English or Kiswahili. Across Tanzania's 120 languages, nearly all native speakers of ethnic minority languages are cut off from digital information access. This gap is not a technology problem but a data problem: without training examples in these languages, no search or voice system can exist.
1457.wh: Building a search system for a language requires first having text and speech data in that language, labeled and aligned to known languages so models can learn. For a language like Hehe with fewer than 50,000 speakers, there is no Wikipedia, no corpus of digitized books, and no large dataset of transcribed speech. Creating this from scratch is labor-intensive and requires linguistic expertise and community trust.
1457.ap: The Ethnic Voices project works directly in Tanzanian villages, collecting text and audio in Hehe and Luguru (two low-resource ECLs). They gather over 800 pairs of sentences where each Hehe sentence is linked to its Kiswahili translation, plus over 95 hours of native speech recordings. They also survey speakers about what information they want to access, learning that multilingual and voice-based search are high priorities.
1457.ww: Parallel sentence data (Hehe-Kiswahili pairs) allows models trained on Kiswahili to adapt to Hehe without retraining from scratch. Speech recordings teach systems to recognize the unique sounds and patterns of Hehe. By grounding data collection in real community needs, the project ensures the resulting resources will actually address barriers that speakers face.
1457.po: The project produces foundational IR infrastructure: data, insights on what speakers need, and evidence of demand for multilingual and voice search. This creates the raw material for researchers to build search and speech systems for Tanzanian languages, taking the first steps toward including previously invisible communities in digital information access.

1458.bp: When you see a search result page today, there is usually a text box, a list of links, and increasingly, an AI-generated summary at the top. But we barely understand what users actually look at, what they trust, or how they adjust their search strategy when that AI answer sits above the traditional results. This matters because small design choices—where the answer appears, how certain it looks—influence whether users find information and make good decisions.
1458.wh: Eye-tracking studies of search behavior date back decades, but almost all assume a traditional interface: text box, keyword results, nothing else. Generative AI summarizers break those assumptions. We do not know if users read the AI answer first or skip to results below. We do not know whether they assume the AI answer is fact-checked (it is not always). We do not know how the presence of AI changes the kinds of queries people formulate.
1458.ap: The researchers designed two eye-tracking experiments. In the first, they watch how users form a search need and type a query—does AI-enhanced search change how people think through their information problem? In the second, they show participants a real SERP with an AI summary above the ten blue links and track which elements they look at, in what order, and for how long. They then compare these patterns to historical data from human-only search interfaces.
1458.ww: Eye-tracking reveals where cognitive attention goes, which self-reported surveys cannot capture. By documenting differences between traditional and GenAI SERPs, the research isolates the effect of AI placement and framing. This grounds interface design in observable behavior rather than speculation.
1458.po: The study will produce empirical evidence on how users actually interact with AI-augmented search, identifying which interface designs reduce cognitive load and increase trust. The findings can guide search engine designers toward interfaces that better match how humans naturally seek information in the era of AI summaries.

1459.bp: A public health official reads a claim: 'A new study shows masks reduce COVID transmission by 95%.' They need to quickly verify this claim against the actual research literature—did the study really show 95%? Do other papers support or contradict it? This is scientific fact-checking, and it is critical because bad data shapes medical policy, research funding, and public trust. Automating this is urgent because the volume of scientific papers is growing faster than human experts can verify.
1459.wh: Automated fact-checking has two parts: find evidence (retrieval) and decide if evidence supports the claim (verification). Most progress has been on verification—building models that read text and make judgments. But retrieval is treated naively, as generic search: 'find papers similar to the claim.' This fails because a claim like 'masks reduce transmission by 95%' should retrieve papers about mask efficacy, but also papers questioning the 95% number, explaining methodological limitations, or reporting different findings. A verification system needs precisely the evidence that contradicts a false claim, not just surface-level similar papers.
1459.ap: The paper argues that retrieval for scientific fact-checking must be redesigned. Instead of treating verification as a black-box downstream task and retrieving generic similar documents, retrieval should be aware of what verification actually needs: both supporting papers (to validate a claim) and papers that highlight limitations, alternative interpretations, or conflicting data. This reframes retrieval as a question-specific task that adapts to the verification goal.
1459.ww: When retrieval understands the verification task, it can prioritize papers differently. A paper that methodologically critiques a high-profile study becomes more valuable to retrieve, even if it is less similar by keyword overlap. By aligning retrieval strategy with downstream verification needs, the system improves the chances that fact-checkers (human or automated) will encounter the evidence most relevant to the claim.
1459.po: The paper outlines a new direction: rethinking scientific fact-checking as a tightly coupled retrieval-verification pipeline rather than two separate stages. Early evidence suggests this produces more reliable automated verification and supports human fact-checkers in high-stakes domains like medicine and public policy.

1460.bp: Imagine searching for 'best laptop for video editing under 2000 dollars.' You start with a query, get results, then refine: maybe you ask about battery life, or whether gaming performance matters, or which brands are reliable. Good search systems help you explore and refine. But most systems are passive—they wait for your next question. A proactive system would notice you are exploring video editing and suggest relevant questions you have not asked yet: 'most editors care about GPU; would you like to see benchmarks?'
1460.wh: Users often do not know what to ask next. They may not realize that disk speed matters for video import, or that external GPU support is cheaper than a powerful built-in card. A reactive system, even one that understands context, cannot help here because the user has not articulated the need. Anticipating what users should explore requires inferring their latent, unstated goals from the conversation flow itself.
1460.ap: Proactive conversational search systems observe the flow of a multi-turn dialogue—what the user asked, how they refined, what they seemed satisfied or frustrated by—and use these signals to predict what they should explore next. The system then surfaces relevant recommendations before the user asks, reducing the effort required to complete the search task. This is fundamentally different from just clarifying ambiguous queries or maintaining context; it is about predicting unmet information needs.
1460.ww: The conversation history encodes valuable signals about the user's evolving goals. When a user shifts from battery life to processing power, that pivot suggests they are weighing portability against performance. A model trained to recognize such patterns can infer the next useful exploration direction. By proactively surfacing options, the system reduces the cognitive load of deciding what to research next.
1460.po: Proactive systems can reduce the number of turns needed to satisfy complex information needs, making search less frustrating and faster. The paper contributes an evaluation framework for measuring how well proactive systems anticipate user goals, establishing a new direction for conversational search beyond reactivity.

1461.bp: When you search for something like 'recommend a running shoe for pronation correction,' the best result might be very different depending on whether you are an avid runner or a casual jogger, whether you have knee issues, or whether you have specific brand loyalty. Personalized search accounts for this—it tailors results to your unique background. But building truly personalized search systems is hard because real user context is buried in messy, months-long logs of past behavior, and it is unclear whether personalization actually helps or hurts for every query.
1461.wh: Current personalized search systems have two problems. First, they apply the same personalization strategy to every query, but personalization does not always help—sometimes a generic result is actually better. Second, real-world user profiles are noisy and incomplete: a log of past searches tells you something about a user, but the signal is buried in thousands of clicks and queries. Approaches that rely on clean, hand-written user profiles work in papers but not in practice.
1461.ap: The team proposes a modular framework where specialized agents handle different parts of search: one agent reformulates the query, another retrieves candidates, another ranks them. A central orchestrator decides dynamically whether personalization should be applied and how aggressively. For query reformulation, they first gathered human annotations asking 'does this query benefit from knowing about this user?'—some queries do, others do not. A classifier then learns to predict this for new queries. For user profiles, they extract signals directly from noisy interaction logs instead of assuming clean oracle profiles.
1461.ww: By making personalization optional rather than always-on, the system avoids degrading precision on queries that should be answered generically. Extracting profiles from real logs acknowledges that user context is messy but learnable. A modular agent architecture allows different personalization strategies to be tested and combined based on the query.
1461.po: The framework enables adaptive search that knows when to personalize and when not to, improving retrieval quality on personalized queries without hurting generic ones. The paper demonstrates that effective personalization does not require perfect oracle profiles but rather a dynamic, query-aware strategy grounded in real interaction data.

1462.bp: A researcher writing a grant proposal needs to answer: 'What is the current consensus on CRISPR safety?' They ask an AI assistant, which generates an answer citing 15 papers. But when they check the citations, three papers do not support the claims attributed to them—one actually says the opposite. This is the hallucination problem: LLM-based question answering is fluent and confident, but it lies. For decision-making, this is dangerous. This paper tackles how to build LLM QA systems that are faithful—meaning their answers and citations actually match the evidence.
1462.wh: LLMs are trained to generate fluent text, not to verify claims against evidence. When an LLM writes 'according to Smith et al., CRISPR off-targets are rare,' it may sound authoritative but Smith et al. may never have said that. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is the current fix: retrieve evidence first, then generate an answer grounded in that evidence. But this fails when the retrieved evidence is sparse, conflicting (different papers disagree), or rapidly evolving (new findings emerge weekly). A system that cites a study from 2020 in a field where 2025 data contradicts it is still wrong.
1462.ap: The paper studies faithful LLM QA by examining how to handle imperfect evidence: when sources disagree, which should the system cite? When evidence is sparse, should the system admit it knows less and return less confident answers? When knowledge evolves (as in technical fields), how can systems identify and surface recent contradicting findings? The approach likely combines filtering noisy retrieved documents, ranking evidence by reliability, training the LLM to abstain when evidence is weak, and maintaining uncertainty about facts that are disputed.
1462.ww: By making evidence quality central to generation, the system improves over naive RAG. A faithful answer might be 'most studies show X, but recent work suggests Y—the evidence is mixed.' This is less confident than hallucinated answers but far more trustworthy. Abstention (saying 'I do not know') is actually valuable in high-stakes settings, not a failure.
1462.po: The research produces systems and evaluation frameworks for detecting and reducing hallucinations in LLM QA. The result is question answering that is safer for technical and academic decision-making because answers are grounded, citations are verifiable, and uncertainty is transparent.

1463.bp: Two people with different levels of expertise search for 'machine learning for healthcare' in a system that combines a traditional search engine (with ranked links) and an AI chat interface. One person skims links carefully; the other focuses on the AI summary and asks follow-up questions. Are they using these tools differently because of how much they know? Yes—prior knowledge shapes what information people need and how they seek it. Understanding these differences helps build search interfaces that adapt to the user's knowledge level.
1463.wh: Search interfaces are usually designed as one-size-fits-all: same ranking, same layout, same defaults for everyone. But someone new to a topic needs different help than an expert. A beginner benefits from summaries and context-setting; an expert wants precise technical details and may skip introductions. Current hybrid search systems (combining links and chat) do not adapt to user knowledge, so they may frustrate both novices (who get overwhelmed by technical jargon) and experts (who must scroll past basic explanations).
1463.ap: The study uses Bloom's Taxonomy, a framework that ranks thinking from basic recall ('what is machine learning?') through comprehension, application, analysis, synthesis, to evaluation. Researchers measure user knowledge, track where they look (via eye-tracking), how they click, how they formulate queries, and which interface elements (links or chat) they engage with. By correlating knowledge level with observable behavior, the study builds a map of how expertise shapes interaction patterns in hybrid search.
1463.ww: Eye-tracking and behavioral data reveal cognitive load: if an expert is spending time reading introductory text, that is wasted cognitive effort. If a novice is struggling to parse technical results, the interface is failing them. By observing these patterns, the research identifies which interface adaptations—maybe auto-hiding introductions for experts, or providing guided glossaries for novices—would reduce friction.
1463.po: The paper enables personalized search interfaces that adapt to user knowledge. For a novice, the system might promote the AI summary; for an expert, it surfaces technical papers and citations. This reduces cognitive load and helps both groups find information faster.

1464.bp: A search engine's knowledge becomes stale: new papers are published, facts evolve, and yesterday's results become outdated. Current generative retrieval systems (which generate document IDs or answers from learned model parameters) must be retrained from scratch to incorporate new information, a process that takes days or weeks. This creates a tension: real information needs are constantly changing, but systems that learn this information through retraining are stuck in the past.
1464.wh: Traditional retrieval systems can add new documents without retraining—just index them and search. But generative retrieval encodes knowledge inside model parameters, so new information is invisible until retraining occurs. Retraining is expensive (compute-intensive) and risks catastrophic forgetting: the model might optimize for new documents while losing what it knew before. Additionally, facts have temporal dimensions: a query for 'COVID mortality rates' depends on the date, and a system that retrieves 2020 statistics in 2026 is wrong regardless of its model quality.
1464.ap: The paper investigates continual learning for generative retrieval under realistic conditions: text corpora grow over time, facts evolve temporally, and sometimes corpora are multimodal (text plus images plus video). Rather than full retraining on all data, the system uses efficient adaptation techniques—perhaps updating only the newest parameters, or learning a lightweight adapter that maps new documents into the existing model's representation space. For temporal facts, the system learns to associate queries with appropriate time windows and retrieves documents that match both the query and the relevant time period.
1464.ww: Continual learning allows incremental updates instead of full retraining, cutting costs dramatically. By learning temporal associations, the system can distinguish between facts that are timeless and facts that are date-specific. Multimodal generative retrieval extends this to images and video, which are increasingly important sources of information.
1464.po: The result is generative retrieval that stays current without retraining, handling continuously growing and evolving corpora. This makes deployed systems more practical and responsive to changing world knowledge, crucial for applications like news retrieval and scientific search.

1465.bp: Netflix recommends shows to you based on your watch history; its algorithm does this by pooling data from millions of users to find patterns. But what if sharing your watch history with Netflix is a privacy risk you do not want to take? Federated recommendation systems solve this by training the recommendation model without collecting user data in one place—each device trains locally and only sends model updates (not raw data) to a central server. But federated learning is harder than regular learning, and recommendations in particular require collaboration between users. How can you build good personalized recommendations when users' data never leaves their devices?
1465.wh: Federated recommendation training is fragile. Each device has only its own user's history (sparse—maybe 10 movie ratings), and collaborative patterns require seeing across users. Standard federated averaging (averaging model updates from all devices) assumes all users contribute equally, but in reality some users are active and some are inactive, some have niche tastes and some have mainstream preferences. Averaging dilutes the useful patterns. Additionally, in cross-device settings, participation is uneven: not all devices join every training round, so the model trains on incomplete and biased data.
1465.ap: The paper proposes redesigning federated recommendation around four interconnected ideas. First, use similarity-aware aggregation: instead of averaging all device updates equally, weight them by how similar the devices' users are. A user similar to you contributes more to your model update. Second, refine how personal user representations are learned so they are not washed out by averaging. Third, explicitly handle the sparse signal problem by learning from incomplete data. Fourth, design transfer mechanisms so that learning from one domain (e.g., movies) can help in another (e.g., music), even when devices never share raw data.
1465.ww: Similarity-aware aggregation preserves collaborative patterns by upweighting devices with users who have tastes like yours. Personalized representations ensure the model captures individual preference nuances. Multi-domain transfer means limited data from one domain can be enriched by learning patterns from related domains, all without ever exposing user data.
1465.po: Federated recommendation systems can match or exceed centralized systems' accuracy while keeping user data private. This is particularly valuable for sensitive use cases (dating apps, health apps, financial tools) where privacy is a dealbreaker.

1466.bp: Imagine a scientist reading a dense research paper: it has a paragraph describing methodology, a table of numerical results, a figure showing trends, and a discussion interpreting what it all means. A question answering system must pull information from all of these modalities, not just text. But how should the system divide the paper into searchable chunks? Should it break at sentences, paragraphs, entire sections, or individual figures? For text, decades of research show that finer chunks (passages) work better than full documents, but multimodal papers have not been studied this way.
1466.wh: When a QA system retrieves only full documents or entire sections, it has to search through dense information to find the relevant part. A document about three experiments might be retrieved just because one experiment answers the query, forcing the reader to filter out irrelevant material. But when documents are chunked into smaller pieces (passages), retrieval becomes more precise: the exact relevant passage is returned. However, multimodal documents complicate this—a table is one chunk, a paragraph is another, but should a figure and its caption be one chunk or two? Should a table and the text that explains it be grouped together or kept separate? Current systems usually inherit text-centric chunking decisions rather than redesigning for multimodal evidence.
1466.ap: The paper investigates granularity of chunking for multimodal QA. A researcher likely develops datasets where they ask complex questions about scientific papers that require reasoning over text, tables, and figures, then systematically test how different chunking strategies affect retrieval precision and QA accuracy. For example, if a figure and its explanatory paragraph are separated, can the QA system still reason over both? If they are joined, does that make unrelated figures harder to retrieve?
1466.ww: Finer-grained chunking improves precision in text retrieval because it narrows the search space. For multimodal retrieval, the same principle should hold: if a query asks about 'Figure 3's results compared to Table 2,' the system should retrieve that specific pair, not the entire paper. But chunking too finely might lose context—a figure without its caption is meaningless. The optimal granularity reflects how humans naturally parse multimodal documents.
1466.po: The work establishes evidence-based chunking strategies for multimodal QA, improving both retrieval precision and downstream reasoning accuracy. This is particularly valuable for scientific and technical QA where evidence is inherently multimodal.

1467.bp: Search engines are built for humans, but now they also serve LLMs: when ChatGPT or Claude needs information, they query Google or other engines programmatically. This creates a strange dual role: LLMs are both components inside search engines (generating summaries, reranking results) and external users (querying engines thousands of times as part of multi-step reasoning). Search infrastructure that worked fine for humans may fail or become inefficient when LLMs are the primary user.
1467.wh: Human search queries are diverse, conversational, and relatively infrequent—maybe a few queries per day per person. LLM queries are voluminous, often generated in rapid bursts (while reasoning through a problem), and highly structured (e.g., always formatted as 'entity + property'). Search systems optimize for human patterns: spell-checkers smooth out typos, query normalizers standardize language, caches store popular human queries. But these optimizations may be pointless or even harmful for LLM traffic. If an LLM generates 10,000 unique queries per second (never repeating), caching wastes storage and memory. If a spell-checker 'corrects' an LLM's semantically meaningful query reformulation, it degrades results.
1467.ap: The paper identifies the dual transformation: LLMs integrated into search pipelines (as retrieval and reranking components) and LLMs as external users (querying the system). It then outlines necessary infrastructure changes: rethinking query normalizing, caching, spell-checking, and other stages of query processing to handle LLM patterns. For downstream components, reducing computational cost is urgent because LLM-based retrieval and reranking are expensive.
1467.ww: Infrastructure must be rearchitected to handle dual roles. LLM-based retrieval components are dense and compute-intensive; distributing this across millions of queries is challenging. LLM users generate predictable but unique queries; infrastructure designed around caching popular queries will fail. By identifying these mismatches, the paper points toward systems optimized for both humans and LLMs.
1467.po: The work outlines a research agenda for search infrastructure that scales under dual transformation: supporting both LLM components and LLM users efficiently, reducing compute costs, and maintaining effectiveness across very different query distributions.

1468.bp: You are reading comments on a news article and see a thoughtful response from a human followed by a similar comment from an AI bot. If everyone else finds the human comment convincing, do you shift your own view toward that position? This is social conformity—a well-known psychology effect where people align with the majority. But when both humans and AI agents are present in the same discussion space, new dynamics emerge: people may trust AI differently, or weight its presence differently when deciding what to believe. Understanding this is urgent as AI agents populate social media and discussion threads.
1468.wh: Most research on conformity examines human-only groups or AI-only groups separately. The dynamics in mixed groups are likely different: humans may be more or less influenced by AI depending on whether they trust the AI, whether they realize it is AI, or whether the AI is positioned as an expert or a peer. Additionally, AI-specific factors (how many AI agents are present, where they appear, what persona they adopt) can shift conformity patterns in ways not predicted by human-only research.
1468.ap: The paper studies trustworthiness judgments and conformity in mixed human-AI information environments. Researchers likely set up discussions where humans and AI agents post responses to information or claims, then measure whether and how human participants shift their beliefs based on majority opinion. They vary factors like the number of AI agents, their positioning (expert vs. peer), and their apparent confidence, observing how each factor influences conformity.
1468.ww: Social conformity is a fundamental mechanism of human judgment; when AI is present, that mechanism does not disappear but is modulated by trust and AI-specific cues. By mapping these dynamics, the research reveals what interface designs and agent behaviors lead users astray (amplifying false beliefs through conformity) versus supporting sound judgment.
1468.po: The findings reveal how to design mixed human-AI spaces that reduce conformity bias and support critical thinking, rather than encouraging users to follow AI-generated consensus uncritically. This matters for social platforms, news sites, and educational forums where AI agents increasingly participate.

1469.bp: A researcher searching for papers on 'quantum computing applications' finds 10,000 results—too many to evaluate manually. A weak supervision approach tries to automate relevance judgment by pooling multiple imperfect heuristics: one heuristic is 'does the abstract mention quantum algorithms?' another is 'does the paper appear in a top venue?' and so on. But the quality of a heuristic varies with context: 'top venue' is reliable for computer science papers published recently, but less reliable for older papers from niche communities. Most weak supervision systems assume each heuristic has uniform reliability across the entire corpus, an assumption that often fails.
1469.wh: Citation networks have structure—papers cluster around foundational works, creating communities where papers are more similar to near neighbors than to distant ones. A heuristic's reliability often depends on this position in the network: if a heuristic 'paper cites Smith 2020' works well for assessing papers close to Smith's work (because Smith's context is shared), it may fail for distant papers that cite Smith only tangentially. Current weak supervision methods ignore this structure, treating all papers uniformly, which introduces systematic bias.
1469.ap: The paper proposes Topological Homophily of Heuristic Reliability: the hypothesis that a heuristic's accuracy depends on a document's position in the citation graph. The method then learns per-location reliability: for papers in Smith's neighborhood, one weighting of heuristics; for distant papers, a different weighting. This requires embedding heuristic reliability as a function of topology and learning which heuristics matter where.
1469.ww: By acknowledging that heuristic quality varies spatially in the citation graph, the system becomes more robust. Homophily—the tendency for similar nodes to cluster—means nearby papers share similar retrieval challenges; a heuristic that works for one should work for similar neighbors. Encoding topology into reliability estimation is a form of structure-aware learning.
1469.po: The method improves weak supervision for scientific IR by incorporating citation topology, producing more accurate relevance judgments without requiring large labeled datasets. This is particularly valuable for scientific search where manual annotation is expensive but rich structural data (citations) are freely available.

1470.bp: Climate science relies on sifting through thousands of studies scattered across different disciplines—geophysics, biology, economics—to synthesize what we know about how human activity is changing the planet. The problem is that no two climate papers use the same terms or look at the same regions, and the truth often lives in numbers and maps embedded in the text, not in tidy summaries. A researcher hunting for what is known about Amazon rainfall shifts or Arctic methane release faces a needle-in-a-haystack search problem at planetary scale.
1470.wh: Standard search and ranking tools break down here because they assume you can match keywords or find similar documents. Climate research crosses disciplines with wildly different vocabularies—a physicist talks about 'albedo feedback', an economist talks about 'climate damage costs', and a hydrologist talks about 'snowpack loss'. There are no agreed-upon labels. Time-series and geographic maps hide the real facts inside images and data tables. And because climate studies often disagree or qualify their findings carefully, a naive automated system can't tell the difference between a strong result and a tentative one.
1470.ap: The tutorial frames this as a 'stress test': it walks researchers through building automated systems that try to pull together studies across fields, extract key findings from mixed text and maps, and then trace back exactly which studies they drew from. It looks at a real test case called the AMOC experiment (Atlantic circulation patterns) to show where purely automated systems fail—like when they miss studies from regions outside the typical search territory, or when they miss knowledge that experts hold but never write down explicitly.
1470.ww: By forcing researchers to name the specific failure modes—geographic bias, tacit knowledge that can't be search-retrieved—the tutorial clarifies where humans and machines have different roles. A machine can quickly read thousands of abstracts, but it cannot judge whether a study's methods are sound enough to count. A human expert can't read everything, but knows which regions and quirks matter. The insight is that evidence synthesis is not a pure retrieval problem; it's a human-in-the-loop pipeline where the machine's job is to surface candidate studies and flag what it couldn't find, not to replace expert judgment.
1470.po: Participants learn to diagnose specific failure modes in climate-retrieval systems, understand where to add human checkpoints, and design pipelines that track their sources so you can always explain why a claim is in the report. The concrete payoff is systems that can speed up evidence synthesis without hiding the gaps or mistakes—critical for science that will drive billion-dollar policy decisions.

1471.bp: Search and recommendation systems now learn your tastes and habits to give you personalized results—your music, news, or shopping suggestions. But the more powerful these systems become, the more they can inadvertently reinforce stereotypes, hide entire categories of people from visibility, or harvest private data. As AI systems talk directly to users in plain language, you see recommendations but rarely know why you got them or whether they reflect your actual needs or the algorithm's biases.
1471.wh: The core tension is that personalization and trustworthiness pull in opposite directions. A system that adapts to your behavior in real time can inadvertently amplify a user's worst instincts or isolate them in a bubble of content that matches their current preference but narrows their horizons. When the pipeline is end-to-end—meaning each component learns from the output of the previous one—small biases can compound silently. A reranking step that slightly favors one group, combined with a ranking step that learns from clicks, combined with a logging choice that over-represents engaged users, creates a feedback loop where unfairness snowballs and becomes nearly invisible until someone runs an audit.
1471.ap: The tutorial maps the entire pipeline: how to measure unfairness in ranking (does the system surface the same diversity of viewpoints to all users?), how to design interfaces that show users why they got a recommendation (so they can push back), how to let people retrieve their own private data (like old emails) without the system learning and reselling patterns about them, and how to handle multimodal data (images, text, video) where bias can hide in subtle ways. It gives concrete evaluation tools and red flags to watch for.
1471.ww: The first-principles insight is that you cannot bolt fairness onto a system after the fact. If the data you trained on was already skewed toward certain groups, or if your logging only records clicks from engaged users, then auditing the final system will always be playing catch-up. Instead, fairness constraints must be baked into every step: how you collect data, how you define the ranking objective, how you surface alternatives, how you communicate uncertainty. Multimodal systems are especially risky because a model can learn to associate faces with stereotypes in ways that numerical audits might miss.
1471.po: Practitioners walk away with concrete protocols to evaluate personalized systems for bias before deploying them, lists of common failure modes to watch for (e.g., minority groups getting worse recommendations), and a blueprint for auditing end-to-end pipelines. The payoff is systems that can personalize without quietly disadvantaging whole groups of people.

1472.bp: Search systems have traditionally ranked documents by semantic similarity—if your query is 'solar panel efficiency', they find documents that use those words or similar ones. But the real world demands more. A researcher asking 'what are the most efficient materials for solar panels?' doesn't just need related documents; they need the system to connect ideas across papers—to know that silicon leads to such-and-such efficiency, and that perovskite leads to different trade-offs, and to reason about which is 'most efficient' given multiple competing measures. This is a problem of reasoning, not just matching.
1472.wh: Naive ranking treats all documents as isolated items competing for position. It has no way to enforce logical constraints (like, the same material can't be both cheap and highly efficient at the same time), no machinery for multi-step inference (if A implies B and B implies C, then A implies C), and no way to gather evidence from multiple sources and decide which is most credible. Modern large language models can do some of this, but they tend to hallucinate or make confident-sounding mistakes. And each research community—AI, statistics, symbolic logic, physics—has invented its own approaches to reasoning, making it hard for IR researchers to know which tools to borrow.
1472.ap: The tutorial maps reasoning approaches across all these communities: techniques that let language models 'think step-by-step', systems that explicitly encode logical rules, probabilistic methods that represent uncertainty, and geometric approaches that reason about relationships in space. It then frames reasoning in IR as a two-way street: IR helps reasoning systems by surfacing the right documents to reason over, and reasoning helps IR by letting it enforce consistency and verify claims across sources.
1472.ww: The core insight is that reasoning is structured inference: you start with facts (from retrieved documents), apply rules or logical chains (like 'material X has property Y, property Y enables Z, therefore X could enable Z'), and produce justified conclusions. Pattern-matching alone can't do this—you have to track what you know, what you infer, and what still has uncertainty. When you build this structure into retrieval, you go from 'find documents similar to the query' to 'find documents that, taken together, answer the question with justified reasoning paths visible to humans.'
1472.po: Researchers gain a framework to reason about reasoning: which approaches are fast, which are verifiable, which work for sparse information, which need dense background knowledge. The payoff is retrieval systems that can handle questions requiring logical chains, multiple sources, and enforcement of constraints—moving search beyond document ranking into genuine assistance with complex reasoning tasks.

1473.bp: Personalization in AI has reached a crossroads. Language models like ChatGPT are powerful but generic—they treat every user the same. Yet every user has their own context: their prior knowledge, their goals, their preferences. A medical student asking about heart disease wants a different explanation than a practicing cardiologist. A job seeker asking about resume writing wants advice tailored to their industry and experience. The gap between generic and truly personalized is where user satisfaction lives.
1473.wh: Building personalization is hard because there are so many places it could fail. You could personalize at retrieval time (find documents relevant to this person's context), at generation time (rewrite the answer for their level), or at the training level (fine-tune the model on their past interactions). Each choice has trade-offs. If you personalize too late in the pipeline, you miss opportunities for the model to use context early. If you do it at the training stage, you have privacy concerns and the system can't adapt to new users quickly. And if you try to do it everywhere, the costs explode and the system becomes a black box of interactions.
1473.ap: The tutorial lays out three stages of a personalized system and shows how each works. Pre-retrieval: understand what the user actually wants (not just their words, but their background and intent). Retrieval: fetch sources that are not just relevant to the topic but relevant to the user's level and context. Generation: compose an answer that assumes the right background knowledge and speaks to their goals. It then extends this to agentic systems: the system doesn't just answer once, but can plan multiple steps, use tools (like looking up data or running code), and adapt based on feedback.
1473.ww: The first-principles insight is that personalization works best when it's systemic: every stage of the system sees the user's context and makes decisions based on it. If only the final generation stage knows who the user is, it has to overcome all the earlier stages being generic. But if retrieval systems know the user's background and pull sources at the right complexity level, and if the planning stage understands their goals, then generation has much less to fix. The payoff isn't just better answers—it's that the system can explain its reasoning in language the user understands.
1473.po: Practitioners learn how to weave user context through a complete RAG system, handle updates when user preferences change, and test whether personalization actually helps (vs. just adding noise). The concrete deliverable is a working architecture blueprint: how to store user models, where to inject context, which datasets exist for benchmarking, and how to measure success without violating privacy.

1474.bp: When you evaluate a search engine or recommender system, you need to test it on simulated users making realistic choices. But creating realistic test users is hard. You could hire humans to use the system, but that's slow and expensive. Or you could prompt a language model to act like a user—it's fast and cheap. But how do you know the simulated user is actually making the choices a real person would make? And if the language model harbors stereotypes, does that mean your system is being tested unfairly against minority groups?
1474.wh: The central problem is that language-model user simulators are black boxes. When a simulator chooses not to click on a recommendation, you don't know if it's because the recommendation was bad or because the simulator has absorbed some bias about what kinds of people should see what kinds of items. Traditional statistical testing tells you whether differences are real, but it can't diagnose why a simulator behaves the way it does. And if your simulator is biased, you might build a system that looks fair in tests but discriminates in the real world.
1474.ap: The tutorial proposes a design framework with seven auditable pieces: a Persona (description of who this simulated user is), a Contract (what tasks they're supposed to try), documented Execution (exactly what the simulator did step-by-step), an auditable Trace (a log of all choices), Verification (checking whether choices match the persona), structured Feedback (what the simulator learned), and a Refinement loop (updating the persona if needed). It walks through two hands-on labs: evaluating a recommendation list and formulating search queries, so participants can inspect exactly how their simulators behave.
1474.ww: The insight is that reproducibility and fairness both require transparency. If you can see why the simulator made a choice, you can check whether it's reasonable. If you can run the same simulator against different personas (a user from Japan, a user from Nigeria, a user with a high-school education), you can spot whether it treats demographic groups differently. The key is moving from 'we have a simulator' to 'we have a simulator we can debug and defend.'
1474.po: Teams get a checklist for auditing their own user simulators before deploying evaluation campaigns, concrete tools for spotting demographic bias in simulated behavior, and a shared vocabulary for discussing simulator fidelity. The payoff is that evaluations become more credible because the test environment itself is transparent and defensible.

1475.bp: Information retrieval has exploded in scope over the past decade. You used to build a system by combining a few standard components—a tokenizer, a ranking function, maybe a neural re-ranker. Now you have hundreds of choices: lexical search, dense neural retrieval, large language models that can answer directly, different ways to combine them. A researcher trying to compare approaches or test a new idea faces a combinatorial problem: which components to use, how to glue them together, whether they actually work better.
1475.wh: The friction is that each retrieval method lives in its own corner. One library handles neural embeddings, another handles lexical search, another handles large language models. Combining them requires writing glue code, managing dependencies, and accepting that you might be mixing incompatible assumptions. Building an experiment means wrestling with five different APIs instead of focusing on your research question. Most researchers end up building ad-hoc scripts that are hard to reproduce and hard for others to reuse.
1475.ap: PyTerrier solves this by providing a unified Python interface: you describe your retrieval pipeline as a series of transformations (retrieve, rerank, generate), and PyTerrier handles the machinery of combining them and measuring results. It comes with built-in access to major methods—dense retrievers, lexical search, large language models, re-rankers—and a growing ecosystem of plugins for other approaches. The tutorial interleaves lecture with live code: you learn about a method, then immediately write and run a PyTerrier pipeline that uses it.
1475.ww: The first-principles insight is that composability accelerates research. When you can write a three-line pipeline instead of 300 lines of plumbing, you can test more ideas faster. And when other researchers can easily understand and modify your pipeline (because it's not buried in custom code), your work becomes a building block for future research. PyTerrier lowers the activation energy for experimentation.
1475.po: Participants leave with hands-on experience building IR systems from components, understanding the trade-offs between methods (lexical vs. neural, fast vs. accurate), and confidence that they can prototype and compare approaches without writing dozens of integration scripts. The concrete payoff is faster iteration on research ideas and more reproducible results because the pipeline is explicit and shareable.

1476.bp: Information changes over time. A piece of news is relevant today but dated next week. A scientific claim is true until better evidence contradicts it. A person's medical condition evolves, and what treatment was right last year might be wrong today. Yet most information retrieval systems treat time as invisible—they rank documents as if they're all equally current or equally out-of-date. The real world demands systems that know when information is valid, track how knowledge shifts, and reason about temporal relationships.
1476.wh: Temporal reasoning in retrieval is hard because time appears in text in wildly different ways. 'March 2020' is explicit. 'Last quarter' is relative—it means different things depending on when you're reading. 'When the pandemic hit' is implicit—you have to know when that was. And in sources like scientific papers or medical records, events are often described in prose, not in clean timestamps. A system has to parse time expressions, figure out which ones refer to the same moment, and reason about sequences: if Event A happened, then Event B happened, what can we infer about what's true now?
1476.ap: The tutorial covers the complete pipeline. Temporal Information Extraction: identifying time expressions in text and normalizing them to absolute times. Temporal Information Retrieval: ranking documents by not just relevance but temporal applicability (is this still true?). Temporal Question Answering: answering questions that depend on time, like 'what changed between 2020 and 2024?' or 'when will this policy take effect?' It traces how these methods evolved from hand-written rules to modern transformer-based systems that can reason about time implicitly.
1476.ww: The key insight is that time is a structural dimension, not an afterthought. When you know that Document A is about 2020 and Document B is about 2024, you can rank them differently depending on the query. When you extract the time an event occurred, you can answer 'has this changed?' by comparing documents from different periods. When you reason about temporal relations—'X happened before Y, and Y happened before now'—you can infer implications that aren't explicitly stated. Temporal reasoning is powerful because it adds a natural ordering to knowledge.
1476.po: Researchers gain methods for extracting and reasoning about time at scale, learn how to build retrieval systems that know which information is still valid, and understand the pipeline for temporal question answering. The concrete payoff is IR systems that can answer questions like 'how have employment trends changed?' or 'is this medical treatment still recommended?' by comparing temporal snapshots of knowledge.

1477.bp: E-commerce recommendation is not a problem of finding the best product for a user in isolation—it's a problem of orchestrating multiple concerns at once. Should the system maximize the chance they buy now, or build long-term trust? Should it surface the highest-margin item, or the item that best solves their stated problem? Should it encourage exploration of new categories, or play it safe with items similar to past purchases? A large language model can reason about all these trade-offs and explain its choice. But coordinating multiple LLM-based agents and making decisions that balance speed, cost, and accuracy at scale is an engineering challenge.
1477.wh: Traditional recommender systems optimize a single objective—usually 'predict the rating' or 'maximize clicks.' Large language models can multi-task: they can retrieve, rank, explain, negotiate trade-offs, and even use external tools (like checking inventory or pricing). But this power comes with costs: LLM inference is slow and expensive, so you can't call it for every decision. And when you have multiple agents running in parallel (one optimizing for conversion, one for satisfaction, one for margin), they need to coordinate without creating loops where each agent undoes the other's work.
1477.ap: The tutorial walks through real deployments at scale: how to set up an orchestration framework where multiple agents run on the same data and need to agree on a recommendation, how to fall back to faster methods (traditional ranking) when LLMs are too slow, how to monitor multi-agent systems so you can spot when one agent is making poor choices, and how to log and analyze decisions so you can debug and improve. It includes a full project walkthrough: data definition, model training, deployment infrastructure, monitoring for drift.
1477.ww: The first-principles insight is that agents are tools for reasoning over structured data, not replacements for traditional ranking. A fast lexical search can pre-filter 1 million products to 100. An LLM-based agent can then reason over those 100, weigh trade-offs, explain why it chose one, and even invoke tools like 'check if this is in stock.' The payoff comes from using each method where it's cost-effective. Traditional systems handle speed; LLMs handle reasoning and personalization.
1477.po: Teams learn the engineering patterns for multi-agent recommenders in production: how to trace decisions through multiple agents, how to optimize costs without sacrificing quality, how to validate that the system is making good choices, and how to iterate when something goes wrong. The concrete payoff is a reusable blueprint for deploying LLM-based reasoning in high-volume recommendation scenarios.

1478.bp: A large language model is trained on billions of tokens from the internet. It absorbs statistical patterns that let it predict the next word with uncanny accuracy. But it doesn't know you. When you ask it for advice, it gives the same generic answer to every user. Personalization means changing that: instead of a one-size-fits-all model, you want a model that remembers what you've told it, adapts to your communication style, learns your goals, and evolves as your life changes. The challenge is doing this without violating your privacy or breaking the model's efficiency.
1478.wh: Standard language models have no memory beyond the current conversation—they can't learn from your past interactions. Fine-tuning a model on your personal data is one option, but it's slow, expensive, and raises privacy concerns (your data could leak or be resold). You could prompt the model with your context every time (tell it who you are, your preferences, your goals), but that eats up tokens and forces the model to compress a lifetime of context into a prompt window. And as your preferences evolve—your job changes, you learn new skills—the system needs to track that change without catastrophic forgetting (losing old knowledge while learning new patterns).
1478.ap: The tutorial maps five core components of LLM personalization. User memory: how to store and retrieve a compact representation of what the model knows about you. Personalization architecture: where to inject context (in the prompt, in the model's parameters, in the retrieval system). Alignment and post-training: techniques to fine-tune the model toward your goals without breaking its general knowledge. Inference-time adaptation: changing the model's behavior on-the-fly based on your context. Deployment: how to do all this at scale without exposing your data.
1478.ww: The first-principles insight is that personalization works best when it's multi-faceted. Storing a user memory (embeddings or summaries of their past interactions) lets the model recall context without re-reading your entire history. Injecting context at retrieval time (finding the most relevant past interactions) reduces the computational cost of personalization. And using post-training to align the model toward your preferences means the model's weights themselves encode your goals, not just the prompt.
1478.po: Practitioners learn frameworks for building personalized LLM systems, methods for updating user models as preferences shift, privacy-aware techniques for storing and using personal data, and ways to evaluate whether personalization actually helps without leaking data. The concrete payoff is personalized AI assistants that remember context, adapt to user needs, and improve over time without compromising privacy.

1479.bp: E-commerce search is not the same as web search. When you search for 'laptop' on Google, you want information. When you search for 'laptop' on Amazon, you want to buy one. The success metric is not engagement or time-on-page; it's whether you add something to your cart and check out. The data available is different—you know not just what users clicked, but what they viewed, what they compared, what they bought, and what they returned. And the system has to handle multimodal data: product images, descriptions, specifications, reviews, videos.
1479.wh: E-commerce platforms face unique challenges that traditional IR doesn't handle well. Users sometimes type vague queries like 'that blue thing' when they mean a specific product. Ranking algorithms can't rely on traditional relevance signals (like link authority) because products don't have links. The platform has to balance organic search results with sponsored results, and users need to understand which is which. And the goal shifts: early in the user's journey, the system should surface diverse options so they can explore; later, it should surface exactly what they want because they're ready to buy.
1479.ap: The workshop focuses on emerging trends: how users interact with e-commerce systems in 2026 (conversational search, agentic recommendations, multimodal browsing), how to evaluate large language models in e-commerce (they can write product descriptions and answer customer questions, but are they accurate?), and how to balance organic and sponsored results so users trust the feed. It emphasizes discussion and peer learning rather than lectures, so researchers and practitioners can compare notes on what's working in their systems.
1479.ww: The insight is that e-commerce search is a complete ecosystem, not a single ranking problem. Users engage with text, images, and prices. They research on the site, check competitors elsewhere, and make decisions over hours or days. The system has to support all these stages: discovery (browsing categories), comparison (showing alternatives), and conversion (making the final step easy). When large language models enter the picture, they can help with semantic understanding ('what is the user really asking?'), but they can hallucinate or make confident mistakes about product details.
1479.po: Participants engage in structured discussions about emerging interaction patterns (voice search, visual search, agent-assisted browsing), leaving with insights into what other e-commerce teams are trying and what's working. The concrete outcomes are shared understanding of evaluation challenges for LLM-based e-commerce features and a community roadmap for next-generation e-commerce search systems.

1480.bp: Search and recommendation systems make millions of decisions that shape what information reaches users. When a system decides to show you one job listing instead of another, or recommends one doctor instead of another, that decision has real consequences for your opportunity and well-being. Yet most IR systems give you results with no explanation: no rationale for why you got this ranking, no transparency about how the algorithm works, no way to challenge the decision. As regulations demand accountability, explainability has become essential.
1480.wh: Making IR systems explainable is hard because the systems themselves are complex. A neural ranking model is a high-dimensional mathematical function—it's not designed to produce human-readable explanations. Traditional methods like bag-of-words ranking have simpler logic (this document has your keywords), but they miss nuance. Modern deep learning systems capture nuance but hide their reasoning. And even when you can explain a system's decision in hindsight ('you got this job posting because it matches your skills'), you might not capture why it ranked this job #1 and another equally good job #5.
1480.ap: The workshop brings together diverse perspectives on explainability: methods that highlight important features in documents, techniques that generate natural-language explanations, approaches that trace decisions through model layers, and design patterns for communicating uncertainty to users. It focuses on moving beyond one-off explanations toward a cohesive research agenda: shared definitions of explainability, common evaluation datasets, and practical guidelines for IR system designers.
1480.ww: The first-principles insight is that explainability is not just about transparency—it's about legitimacy. If a search system decides 'you don't see this result,' the only way a user can accept that decision is if they understand why. And if the explanation is technical jargon they don't understand, it feels like a black box. Good explanations work at the user's level of understanding: why did you choose this; what alternatives exist; how would my profile need to change to see different results?
1480.po: The workshop produces a shared roadmap for explainability research in IR, identifying key challenges and proposing concrete next steps. It also proposes a journal special issue to consolidate recent work, building a foundation for researchers to design IR systems that users can trust because they understand how the decisions are made.

1481.bp: Conversational search is when users interact with a search system through natural back-and-forth dialogue instead of typing a single query and getting a ranked list. 'What movies won Oscars in 2024?' 'Show me the comedies.' 'Any sci-fi among those?' In a conversation, context from earlier turns shapes later results. This is closer to how humans actually ask questions—we refine and clarify—but it breaks the assumption that each query is independent.
1481.wh: Building conversational search systems is hard because context compounds. When a user says 'Show me the comedies,' the system has to remember that they were asking about Oscar-winning movies, not just any comedies. If the system forgets context or misinterprets the user's intent, the conversation derails. Users expect the system to correct misunderstandings mid-conversation (if they ask 'show me action films' but the system knows they usually like drama, should it ask 'do you want to switch genres or are you looking for something different?'). And evaluating conversational systems is much harder than evaluating single-query search because success depends on the entire dialogue, not just individual turns.
1481.ap: The workshop celebrates SCAI's 10-year journey in conversational AI and focuses on emerging opportunities: personalization in conversational search (tailoring responses to this user's patterns), the reintroduced TREC iKAT shared task (a benchmark for interactive knowledge assistance), and hands-on evaluation of state-of-the-art conversational systems. It includes a break-out session where participants try real systems and critique what works and what fails.
1481.ww: The insight is that conversation is a problem of maintaining and exploiting context. Each system component—understanding what the user means, finding relevant documents, deciding what to say next—needs to be aware of what came before. And the user needs to feel in control: they should understand why the system is making recommendations, and be able easily steer the conversation in a different direction if it's going wrong.
1481.po: Researchers and practitioners exchange ideas on the hardest conversational AI problems (maintaining context accurately, handling misunderstandings gracefully, evaluating multi-turn interactions), see working systems in action, and contribute to the TREC iKAT shared task if they're interested. The concrete outcome is a richer understanding of the research frontiers in conversational search.

1482.bp: Neural retrieval models (systems based on deep learning) can find nuanced matches between queries and documents that traditional keyword search misses. But they're slow and expensive to run at the scale of a real search engine: if you have a billion documents and millions of queries per second, a neural model might take 10 times longer per query than a traditional keyword index, which is unacceptable. The challenge is keeping the power of neural retrieval while making it fast enough to deploy.
1482.wh: The tension is fundamental. Neural models learn distributed representations of meaning, which makes them powerful—they can match a query to a document even when they use completely different words. But that power comes from matrix multiplications and neural layers, which are inherently slow. A keyword index can be binary-searched for a match in microseconds; a neural model needs to score every document, which takes milliseconds. At scale, milliseconds become prohibitive. You could simplify the model to run faster, but then you lose the semantic understanding that makes it better.
1482.ap: The workshop focuses on the measurement and benchmarking problem: how to fairly compare the speed and accuracy of different neural retrieval methods on standard hardware setups, so you can make reproducible trade-off decisions. It advocates for efficiency to be a first-class research goal (not an afterthought), standardized evaluation procedures, and shared benchmarks that researchers can use to compare approaches. It organizes a shared task where teams compete on both effectiveness (how good are the results?) and efficiency (how fast?), incentivizing faster methods as a legitimate research contribution.
1482.ww: The first-principles insight is that efficiency is an engineering problem, not an optional feature. When you set efficiency targets (e.g., 'retrieve 100 documents in 50 milliseconds'), you force trade-off decisions that lead to innovation: using smaller models, approximating distances instead of computing them exactly, caching results, batching queries. And when efficiency is a shared benchmark, the community can compare notes on which tricks work.
1482.po: The workshop establishes standards for measuring neural retrieval efficiency, provides a shared benchmark for comparing methods, and includes a shared task where participants compete on both speed and accuracy. The concrete outcome is a community push toward efficient neural retrieval, making it more viable to deploy neural methods at scale without sacrificing effectiveness.

1483.bp: The internet is increasingly filled with AI-generated content. Language models write product reviews, news articles, social media posts. Image generators create stock photos and illustrations. These can be useful—they fill gaps and reduce costs—but they also pose risks. A review of a product might be fake. A news article might be generated from unreliable sources. And as more content is generated, search engines and recommender systems have to operate in a mixed environment where some content is human-authored (and presumably more reliable) and some is synthetic.
1483.wh: Evaluating search and recommendation systems becomes harder in this mixed environment. Traditional evaluation assumes you're ranking human-authored documents and that relevance judgments are about whether a document answers the query. But if half the documents are generated, then 'relevance' becomes ambiguous: is a well-written generated summary as relevant as a human-authored one? And if the evaluation data itself contains generated content, then metrics trained on it might inadvertently favor algorithms that work well on generated content but poorly on human content.
1483.ap: The workshop frames this as a system-level challenge, not just a model-level one. It examines how retrieval and recommendation systems behave differently when they operate in mixed information environments, looks at evaluation metrics that might not be valid when the corpus changes, and explores how to maintain user trust when content provenance is unclear. It emphasizes human-centered design: how do you help users distinguish generated from human content, and what should systems do differently in each case?
1483.ww: The insight is that the introduction of synthetic content shifts the fundamental assumptions of information retrieval. When all content was human-authored, you could assume a certain baseline of quality and intentionality. Now you have to reason about provenance. And the metrics you use to evaluate systems might not transfer: a metric that assumes human content might be unfair to systems trained on mixed data.
1483.po: The workshop produces concrete outcomes: reflection on how evaluation methods need to change for mixed information environments, discussion of human-centered design principles for disclosing provenance, and potentially proposals for new shared tasks or evaluation tracks (TREC, CLEF, FIRE, NTCIR) that explicitly test systems on mixed corpora. The payoff is a research community more prepared for information systems that operate in a world where synthetic and human content coexist.

1484.bp: Information systems are never neutral. When Google decides to show certain search results to certain users, or when a hiring platform uses algorithmic ranking to surface candidates, these decisions shape opportunity and access. Historically, information retrieval as a research field has treated these systems as technical problems—optimize the ranking, improve the model—and avoided questions about power, justice, and democracy. But search and recommendation systems are places where society's inequalities are encoded, reproduced, or resisted.
1484.wh: The central tension is that IR researchers and practitioners have been taught to abstract away from politics. We talk about optimizing 'relevance' or 'user satisfaction' as if there's a neutral technical answer. But relevance to whom? Satisfaction for whom? If a search system buries certain viewpoints, it's not just a technical failure—it's a decision about which voices reach users. And if the system is designed by corporations optimizing for profit, the goals might directly conflict with democratic or emancipatory values.
1484.ap: The workshop proposes a different frame: treating information access as fundamentally political and asking what it means to design systems that resist corporate and state capture. It's a dialogical workshop using collaborative methods to workshop a community manifesto. Participants explore questions like: What role should search systems play in democracy? How should platforms handle censorship or surveillance? What does an emancipatory IR system look like?
1484.ww: The first-principles insight is that neutrality is impossible—every design choice reflects values. When you decide to rank popular content highly, you're choosing to amplify existing voices. When you personalize, you're choosing whether to reinforce preferences or expand horizons. When you log user behavior, you're choosing whether that data can be used to profile and target people. Instead of pretending these are neutral technical problems, the workshop asks: what values do we want our systems to embody?
1484.po: The workshop produces a tangible outcome: a collaboratively written manifesto articulating the role IR research should play in supporting democratic access to information, resisting authoritarian control, and serving emancipation rather than oppression. The concrete payoff is a shared vocabulary and set of principles for IR researchers who want their work to explicitly serve social justice.

1485.bp: When you ask a AI system to find information or answer a question, you trust it to give you true, safe, fair answers. But these systems are now making real decisions in real workflows—hiring, medical diagnosis, loan approval. If something goes wrong, the consequences cascade: a biased system rejects qualified people, a system gamed by attackers returns false information, or it learns to manipulate users into bad choices.
1485.wh: Generative systems are black boxes that produce outputs people can't easily predict or audit. They can be tricked with carefully crafted inputs, they absorb biases baked into their training data, and they can be tuned to subtly nudge user behavior. Unlike a traditional database, you can't just patch the vulnerability—the system learns across millions of examples and touches every user differently.
1485.ap: This is a workshop—a day-long gathering where participants present attacks they've discovered, defenses they've built, and open questions. The workshop structure lets people share concrete examples of what breaks, discuss why, and debate solutions in real time.
1485.ww: By gathering researchers from information retrieval, cybersecurity, and related fields to study these failures together, the community can map the real risks and share defenses. A cybersecurity expert knows how systems get hacked; an IR researcher knows how search results shape behavior. Together they see vulnerabilities an isolated team would miss.
1485.po: The outcome is a synthesized map of known vulnerabilities and a shared research agenda. Teams working on IR systems get a checklist of risks to test for; security researchers learn what makes IR systems unique targets; the community has a public record of what's broken and what defenses to invest in.

1486.bp: Your computer now runs dozens of specialized AI agents—one drafts emails, one finds flights, one answers math questions, one schedules your calendar. But you don't have a menu or search engine for agents themselves. If you need a tool, you either guess, ask a friend, or accept whatever your current app offers. The real challenge is: how do we let people, teams, and systems find and pick the right agent for the job?
1486.wh: Agents aren't like web pages or documents. An agent is an executable program with behavior that changes based on inputs, context, and time. A flight-finding agent might be great for round trips but fail on one-ways; one agent might be fast but less accurate than a slow one. How do you describe an agent's true capability in a way a search system understands? How do you rank agents when their quality depends on the specific task and constraints?
1486.ap: The workshop brings together IR researchers and practitioners to define how agents should be represented (what metadata captures capability?), how to rank them (what makes one agent better than another for this task?), and how to evaluate rankings (does the person actually choose the right agent after seeing the results?). It also explores practical issues: Is it safe to let users pick any agent? How do you explain why one was ranked higher?
1486.ww: Information retrieval is already good at finding things people need from a huge pile. If you can describe agents' capabilities in a structured way, and define what 'relevant' and 'good' mean for agents, then IR methods—indexing, ranking, explaining results—suddenly become tools for agent discovery. The key is that agents, like documents, have structure and tradeoffs you can model.
1486.po: The output is a framework for agent indexing and search—structured representations of agent capability, ranking algorithms that consider multi-dimensional performance, and evaluation methods that test whether the system actually helps people find usable agents. This unlocks a marketplace where agents can be discovered and evaluated systematically.

1487.bp: Today, personalized search and recommendation systems build a model of who you are—your interests, what you're shopping for, whether you like action movies—and use it to show you relevant results. Traditionally, this model was handcrafted features or implicit patterns in your clicks. But now large language models can reason about people in natural language. Instead of 'likes action movies,' an LLM can parse 'I loved Blade Runner because it blends noir with philosophy.' This unlocks richer personalization, but it raises hard questions: Is this actually more accurate? Does it respect privacy? How do you know if it's working?
1487.wh: Old profiling systems were brittle: you had to decide ahead of time which features matter (age, location, past purchases), and handcode rules or train classifiers on them. An LLM can reason about context, nuance, and intent in a single step—but that flexibility cuts both ways. You can't easily audit whether the LLM is capturing what users actually mean, and the model changes every time you retrain it. Also, to profile someone with an LLM, you might need to feed it sensitive personal data (chat history, search history), which raises privacy and trust concerns.
1487.ap: The workshop convenes researchers and practitioners to share approaches: How do you extract profile information from user text? Should you summarize user behavior or reason about underlying intent? How do you update profiles over time? How do you evaluate whether a profile is actually useful (does it improve search or recommendation)? How do you build this without violating privacy? They also organize lightning talks, panels, and paper presentations to synthesize emerging progress.
1487.ww: LLMs are naturally fluent in language, the way people actually express themselves. Asking an LLM to summarize someone's interests from their own words is more direct than training a classifier on click patterns. And LLMs can reason across multiple sources and contexts—'I'm a parent looking for budget laptops for online school'—in a way handcrafted features struggle with. The upside is richer, more context-aware profiles.
1487.po: The result is a toolkit and best practices for LLM-powered profiling in search and recommendation systems. Teams get clear guidance on when LLM profiling helps vs. hurts, privacy-preserving approaches, evaluation methods that test real impact, and a shared understanding of the open challenges (temporal dynamics, fidelity, responsible deployment).

1488.bp: When you search for 'tropical sunset,' you get back images, text descriptions, sometimes videos. When you ask a system to generate a new image of a tropical sunset, it creates pixels from scratch. Modern systems can do both—and they do it by reasoning about images and text together in a single model. The challenge is: How do you know if a generated image is good? Unlike a retrieved image (which exists and you can check), generated images are new and can be subtly wrong—bad lighting, wrong composition, misleading details. The IR community needs tools to evaluate whether these systems are working.
1488.wh: Evaluating retrieved results is hard but established: does the image match the query? Is it high quality? For generated results, evaluation explodes in complexity. Did the system generate an image of a sunset or a sunrise? Is the composition balanced? Does the image convey mood or just pixels? If the system mixes information from multiple sources (retrieval-augmented generation), did it blend them coherently? There's no ground truth to compare against (the image didn't exist before generation), so you can't use simple matching metrics.
1488.ap: The workshop brings researchers together to tackle: What makes a generated image or text actually good for the user's task? How do you measure relevance when the output didn't exist before? Should you evaluate generation, or retrieval, or both? How do you scale evaluation to thousands of generated samples? What does an evaluation framework look like for multimodal retrieval-augmented generation systems?
1488.ww: If you break generation quality into components—relevance to the query, visual coherence, semantic accuracy, stylistic consistency—you can evaluate each. The IR community has decades of experience in relevance assessment and ranking; the key insight is that multimodal generation is still a search and ranking problem at its core, just with an extra step of synthesis. Bringing together experts in IR, natural language processing, computer vision, and multimodal AI means each discipline brings its evaluation strengths to bear.
