1488.po: The output is a set of evaluation methods and metrics for multimodal generation and retrieval. Teams working on these systems get concrete ways to measure whether they work—relevance rubrics for generated content, scalable evaluation protocols, principled ways to combine metrics, and a shared benchmark. This allows the IR community to advance multimodal systems with the same rigor they've applied to traditional search.

2000.bp: Real-world search engines and information systems face constant data drift—news, products, user interests all shift daily. A retrieval system that looked perfect on June data can fail in July if it cannot automatically adapt. This matters for every product that serves living, changing data: news search, recommendation feeds, customer support systems.
2000.wh: Training a retriever requires labeled query-document pairs (expensive to maintain) and assumes tomorrow's data looks like today's. Stream retrieval breaks this assumption: new topics arrive with zero ground-truth labels. Retraining from scratch is too slow; static models ignore drift entirely.
2000.ap: CREAM watches incoming queries and documents, clustering them into semantic groups and storing prototypical representations in flexible memory. When a new topic arrives, it measures how different that topic is from what it has seen, then updates its stored prototypes and refinement models—all without needing anyone to annotate ground truth. Three techniques work together: fine-grained similarity matching, regularized cluster centers that don't collapse, and smart sampling to keep memory compact.
2000.ww: Self-supervised learning lets the system learn from raw queries and documents by finding structure (similar documents cluster together; similar queries emerge). The stratified memory acts as a sketch of the topic landscape; when adjusting prototypes, regularization keeps them stable so new topics add signal rather than noise. Adaptive clustering means if the trend shifts, the system recognizes and adjusts.
2000.po: In practice: 27.79% higher success rate and 44.5% better recall on unseen topics vs. unsupervised baselines, matching or beating supervised methods that did have labels. Real retrieval systems can now deploy updates without waiting for manual annotation cycles.

2001.bp: Tropical cyclones kill thousands and cost billions yearly. Early, accurate forecasts—deployed on satellites and coastal warning systems in resource-scarce regions—save lives. Today that requires powerful data centers; distributing that intelligence to the edge means forecasting without waiting for cloud connectivity.
2001.wh: Physics tells us that maximum sustained wind depends on complex nonlinear interactions: sea surface temperature, pressure, latent heat release all interact polynomially, not linearly. Standard neural networks need thousands of parameters to approximate that. Satellites and edge processors have severe memory and compute budgets—a 19MB model cannot fit.
2001.ap: KAN-FIF uses spline-based Kolmogorov-Arnold networks (which express functions as sums of univariate splines composed together) instead of dense matrix multiplications. Splines are efficient: one univariate spline approximates one variable's contribution, reducing redundancy. The framework layers MLPs, CNNs, and KAN modules, letting each learn its role—CNNs extract spatial features from satellite images, KAN layers capture the polynomial nonlinearities among meteorological variables.
2001.ww: Splines are computationally cheaper than dense layers and exactly suited to physics: many physical laws are piecewise polynomial. KAN's compositional structure (univariate functions composed) matches how weather variables interact—wind depends on temperature and pressure, not on arbitrary learned mixtures. This alignment reduces the "search space" the network must explore.
2001.po: Concrete: cyclone models shrink from 19MB to 0.99MB and run in 2.3ms per forecast on edge hardware (vs 7.35ms). Prediction error drops 32.5%. A satellite processor can now forecast cyclone intensity in real time, sending alerts before traditional systems compute anything—critical for fast-moving storms.

2002.bp: Oceans regulate climate, weather, and food security. Accurate sea temperature and current forecasts inform hurricane tracking, fisheries management, and climate modeling. Today's forecasts update slowly; a faster, continuous method opens real-time coastal warnings and climate feedback loops.
2002.wh: Ocean dynamics are nonlinear and continuous in time (eddies, shear, stratification evolve smoothly). Data comes at discrete time steps. Diffusion models generate predictions step-by-step, accumulating noise; each step costs compute. Meanwhile, pure data-driven models ignore physics—they learn statistics but may violate conservation laws (energy, mass).
2002.ap: KFTD uses a two-stage pipeline: first, it projects the ocean state into Koopman space, where nonlinear dynamics become linear (a deep learning insight: many systems linearize under the right coordinate change). Then, Fourier analysis interpolates continuously between time steps using those linear dynamics—no diffusion noise, just harmonic reconstruction. A lightweight residual network refines the result. A physics-informed loss (D-PP) enforces PDE constraints: energy and mass conservation.
2002.ww: Koopman linearization means a few matrix multiplications and exponentials replace iterative sampling. Fourier interpolation is exact for band-limited signals and extremely efficient. Enforcing physics constraints (PDEs) prevents the model from predicting impossible states—no negative temperatures, no spontaneous energy creation—which cuts hallucination and boosts generalization.
2002.po: Empirical: MSE drops 5.6% on average (up to 12.7% for sea surface temperature), and it runs 76% faster than MCVD, a diffusion baseline. Forecasts maintain physical plausibility. A coastal forecast center can now run ensemble models in real time instead of hours later.

2003.bp: Open-source ML models are valuable intellectual property: Llama, Mistral, Qwen. Model theft via replication or misuse erodes incentives to share. Watermarks embed a secret trigger—unique query patterns that only the owner recognizes—proving ownership. If watermarks fail, so does model IP protection.
2003.wh: Current watermarks rely on crafted queries that produce specific outputs. The problem: a watermark is a black-box function, and attackers can query it, measure its behavior, then train a substitute network that mimics it without replicating the original model. Once mimicked, the watermark is removed.
2003.ap: SEW measures specificity: how precisely the watermark responds to its true keys vs. approximate/fake keys. High specificity means an attacker's reverse-engineered key produces wrong outputs, even though it's "close." SEW uses adversarial training: the system tries to find approximate keys (like an attacker would), then updates the watermark to reject those approximations—a cat-and-mouse loop.
2003.ww: Specificity blocks the key extraction path: if an attacker must find *exactly* the right key, not approximately right, the search space explodes exponentially. Adversarial training with multiple candidate keys forces robustness at the boundary of the key space, making approximation fundamentally harder.
2003.po: In practice: SEW defends against all six tested removal attacks—fine-tuning, model pruning, distillation, quantization, etc. Watermark stays embedded and verifiable; the model still works normally on real tasks. Open-source maintainers can now distribute models with confidence in IP protection.

2004.bp: Manufacturing plants lose millions when machines fail unexpectedly. Predictive maintenance—forecasting failure arrival time—transforms costly downtime into scheduled service. Sensors track temperature, vibration, pressure in real time; the challenge is that as machines age, failure patterns change.
2004.wh: A machine that shows subtle vibration for weeks might suddenly accelerate (bearing wear), or it might plateau (adjusted imbalance). Static models trained on historical data miss these shifts. Different lifecycle stages (early wear, accelerating damage, imminent failure) need different predictive rules. Online learning must keep pace without retraining the entire history.
2004.ap: TimeCast segments the sensor stream into stages: early (stable), mid (gradual change), late (acceleration). Within each stage, the interdependencies between sensors differ—early wear shows low correlation, critical wear shows high correlation. The system detects stage transitions from these dependencies, trains or updates a separate LSTM for each stage, and switches models as conditions change.
2004.ww: Stage-specific models capture the right temporal dynamics for each regime—what works for stable machines fails for failing machines and vice versa. Detecting stages via sensor correlation is unsupervised and fast. Online updates (only processing new data) scale linearly.
2004.po: In practice: higher accuracy than end-to-end methods, discovered real stage transitions in industrial data, and runs online with linear complexity. Plants can now forecast failure time within a tighter window, scheduling maintenance more efficiently.

2005.bp: Electronic health records contain decades of patient history—vital signs, labs, medications, notes. Predicting the next diagnosis saves lives: catching infection early, identifying hidden complications. LLMs excel at reasoning over text but can hallucinate common diagnoses. Deep learning excels at patterns but struggles to explain its picks.
2005.wh: LLMs trained on thousands of cases overfit to the most frequent diagnoses (diabetes, hypertension, infection). Rare conditions (endocarditis, sarcoidosis) appear rarely in training but are time-critical in practice. LLMs also cannot easily extract structure (abnormal labs vs. normal, temporal order) from raw notes. Deep models learn the structure but black-box their decisions.
2005.ap: EviCare runs three pipelines in sequence. First, a deep model (trained on structured EHR) ranks candidate diagnoses, filtering noise. Second, it extracts evidence from structured data (labs, vitals, meds, procedures)—abnormal sodium, elevated WBC, new antibiotic—and prioritizes this evidence by its correlation with each candidate diagnosis. Third, for novel diagnoses (absent from history), it constructs relational evidence: "similar patient with these findings received diagnosis X." All this structured evidence is composed into a prompt that tells the LLM *which* facts matter and *why*.
2005.ww: Hybrid reasoning divides labor: deep models handle the structure-extraction burden (parsing dense timelines), LLMs handle semantic reasoning (interpreting evidence). Evidence prioritization narrows the LLM's focus, reducing hallucination. Novel diagnosis reasoning by analogy (relational evidence) teaches the LLM to recognize unseen patterns it has learned from similar cases.
2005.po: Empirical: 20.65% average gain in precision/accuracy vs. baselines. On novel diagnoses—the hardest, most clinically valuable task—30.97% improvement. A clinician using EviCare sees ranked diagnoses with supporting evidence, making diagnosis faster and catching rare conditions.

2006.bp: Recommender systems run A/B tests to compare algorithms: does algorithm A increase engagement vs. algorithm B? Live testing is gold standard but costs money (real users see worse recommendations), time (weeks to significant results), and carries risk (negative impact). Simulation replaces testing with synthetic data.
2006.wh: Simulating users is hard: recommendations are visual (thumbnail, title, rating); users click based on visual appeal and memory (I liked that actor, or I'm tired of cooking shows). Real users have fatigue, context, preferences that evolve during a session. LLMs understand language but not visual perception; they don't fatigue or remember sequences.
2006.ap: A/B Agent constructs a recommendation sandbox (multi-page, multimodal—text descriptions, visual features). The agent receives screenshots (page state) and decides what to click, based on its profile (preferences learned from initial context), fatigue (it stops clicking after many items), and memory (recall of liked items). It also integrates macroeconomic or user-context signals to adjust its behavior.
2006.ww: Multimodal perception lets the agent see what users see (recommendations, layouts) and reason about appeal. Fatigue and memory models make behavior realistic—users do slow down and repeat likes. Profile and action memory let the system model individual heterogeneity. Simulated interactions can then train the next recommender generation without live risk.
2006.po: In practice: synthetic user interactions correlate with real A/B test results. Data generated by A/B Agent can train new recommenders effectively. Companies can iterate on recommendation algorithms 10x faster, testing changes in simulation before live deployment.

2007.bp: Wildfires are interconnected with climate: jet streams steer weather patterns that carry moisture; surface temperatures set fuel dryness; atmospheric dynamics drive wind. Predicting global fire activity means understanding this coupled system. Early forecasts enable resource pre-positioning and evacuation planning.
2007.wh: Fires span multiple scales: local weather (kilometers, days), regional atmospheric circulation (continental, weeks), global climate modes (planetary, seasons). Standard deep learning captures one scale poorly or requires massive networks to fuse them. Graph networks handle connectivity but not continuous time; sequence models struggle with long-range dependencies and irregular spatiotemporal grids.
2007.ap: HiGO builds a hierarchical graph: low level = weather grid (local dynamics), mid-level = atmospheric blocks (regional patterns), high-level = global modes (climate oscillations like El Niño). Neural ODE modules at each level learn continuous dynamics: how weather evolves, how blocks flow, how climate oscillates. Adaptive message passing between levels fuses information upward (local weather feeds regional patterns) and downward (global trends constrain local weather).
2007.ww: Hierarchy respects physics: small-scale turbulence averages to regional flows, which cluster into planetary patterns. Learning continuous ODEs avoids discretization artifacts—the model predicts smooth trajectories, not jumpy time steps. Message passing between scales is differentiable, so gradients flow from forecasting error all the way through the hierarchy, improving each level's representations.
2007.po: Empirical: beats all baselines on long-term wildfire forecasts (8+ weeks ahead). Predictions are observationally consistent—they don't violate known climate patterns. Fire forecasting systems can now anticipate seasonal and regional fire seasons with enough lead time to mobilize resources.

2008.bp: Enzymes are biological catalysts that convert substrates to products. Knowing which enzyme acts on which substrate enables metabolic engineering: designing cells to produce medicines, biofuels, food ingredients. Databases of enzyme-substrate pairs are incomplete; building them experimentally is slow and expensive.
2008.wh: A chemical reaction is (educt, enzyme, product) or more complex: multiple substrates → multiple products via one enzyme. Traditional pairwise knowledge graphs (head-relation-tail) miss this many-to-many structure. A hypergraph captures it: one hyperedge connects all participants. But hypergraph embeddings are rare and hard to train; linking them to knowledge graph completion (predicting missing edges) is novel.
2008.ap: Hyper-Enz represents reactions as hypergraph nodes (compounds) and hyperedges (which compounds participate in which reaction). A hypergraph transformer learns compound embeddings by attending to other compounds in the same reactions, capturing global context. Simultaneously, it treats the hypergraph as a knowledge graph (compound-reaction triples) and trains a KGE model to predict missing triples, inferring new enzyme-substrate pairs.
2008.ww: Hypergraph attention captures higher-order interactions: if compounds A, B, C all appear in reaction R, their learned embeddings reflect their co-occurrence. KGE models then extrapolate: if enzyme E catalyzes compounds in reactions with similar fingerprints to a new reaction, infer E acts on the new substrate. Combining both signals (transformer embeddings + KGE reasoning) over-constrains the model to learn compact, generalizable representations.
2008.po: In practice: Hyper-Enz predicts enzyme-substrate pairs unseen in training by reasoning over reaction structure. Metabolic engineers can screen predicted interactions experimentally, prioritizing high-confidence candidates and reducing wet-lab costs.

2009.bp: Manufacturing equipment (pumps, compressors, turbines) degrades in stages: micro-scratches, cavitation erosion, bearing wear, catastrophic failure. Detecting the *severity* of damage (diagnosis) is critical: early-stage faults need gentle maintenance; advanced faults need replacement. Misclassifying early as normal or vice versa costs money.
2009.wh: Classes are hierarchical: "cavitation" is a fault; within it, "mild," "moderate," "severe" differ in intensity. Standard classification treats each class independently. If the model misclassifies mild cavitation as severe, it's a near-miss (both are cavitation) but penalties are equal to confusing cavitation with bearing wear. Also, subtle intensity differences demand fine-grained feature learning that standard losses don't enforce.
2009.ap: DHK loss has two parts. Tree loss creates a hierarchy: same-attribute faults (all cavitation subtypes) cluster together; different subtypes spread proportionally to their tree distance. Focal weighting emphasizes hard examples (borderline mild/moderate calls). Triplet loss with hierarchical dynamic margin picks triplets (anchor, positive, negative) such that margin scales with hierarchical distance: mild-moderate (close in tree) need smaller margin than cavitation-bearing (far apart).
2009.ww: Tree-structured penalties guide the model to learn: faults of the same type share core features, and intensity affects *magnitudes* of those features, not their existence. Triplet loss with dynamic margins prevents the model from over-separating nearby classes (collapsing information) while properly distinguishing far classes. Hard-example emphasis (focal weighting) forces the model to learn the subtle boundaries where misclassification is likely.
2009.po: Empirically: superior results on four real industrial datasets (cavitation sensors from SAMSON AG and public benchmarks). The model reliably ranks fault severity, enabling predictive maintenance to order interventions by urgency and cost.

2010.bp: Algorithmic trading automates buying/selling decisions to maximize returns. Models trained on 2021-2022 data (low rates, growth stocks) fail in 2023 (rate hikes, value flip). Robust trading requires adaptation to macro shocks: Fed policy changes, geopolitical events, sentiment shifts. Without robustness, backtest performance evaporates.
2010.wh: Market data has temporal correlations (prices trend), cross-instrument correlations (related assets move together), and macro-driven correlations (rate hikes hit finance, help energy). GANs generate synthetic data but often miss these dependencies. Even if data is good, training a policy on one regime creates overfitting: the agent exploits quirks of 2021 that don't exist in 2023.
2010.ap: The framework has two components. Generator: a macro-conditioned GAN uses macroeconomic indicators (rates, inflation, sentiment) as control variables, generating synthetic price paths with realistic temporal, cross-asset, and macro correlations. Policy: a trading agent competes in a Bayesian game against an adversary. The adversary perturbs macro indicators to shift regimes (simulating surprise policy changes or shocks). The trading agent learns a robust policy: one that maintains profitability even when the adversary shifts the game.
2010.ww: Macro-conditioning ensures generated data respects real dependencies—if rates rise, certain sectors react predictably. Adversarial training is a min-max optimization: the agent minimizes loss while an adversary maximizes it. This forces the agent to learn strategies that work across regime boundaries, not just within one regime. Bayesian reasoning (quantile belief networks) captures uncertainty about macro conditions, guiding hedging decisions.
2010.po: In practice: the trained agent maintains profitability across historically different markets. Synthetic data generated from the macro-conditioned GAN is realistic and diverse enough to bootstrap learning. Traders can backtest on diverse simulated regimes before risking capital.

2011.bp: Research fields accumulate knowledge in papers. A biologist must read hundreds to understand the state of enzymatic pathway research; a machine learning researcher must track 10,000+ papers yearly. LLMs trained on all text perform poorly at "find papers relevant to this question" or "summarize the consensus on X in this domain" because they lack structured domain knowledge.
2011.wh: General LLMs see papers as raw text, not as nodes in a knowledge network. They miss relationships: "paper A cites B, B contradicts C, C builds on D." They misuse terminology: "network" means neural network in ML but biological network in biology. Benchmarking domain LLMs is hard: no standard suite of literature-specific tasks exists, and curating domain graphs is labor-intensive.
2011.ap: LitBench automates graph curation: given a domain (e.g., enzyme engineering, quantum computing), it fetches papers, extracts metadata (citations, keywords, authors), and builds a literature graph (nodes = papers/concepts, edges = citations/co-authorship/keyword overlap). It then generates tasks at multiple levels: node-level (classify this paper by venue/year), edge-level (predict missing citation), application-level (generate a related-work section for a new paper). Training/eval splits are generated automatically from graph structure.
2011.ww: Graph-based curation is scalable: one workflow handles any domain. Automatic task generation ensures benchmarks are rigorous and diverse. By embedding papers as graph nodes, LLMs can learn domain-specific relationships during training (e.g., "if A cites B and B cites C, then A should probably know C") and leverage that for downstream reasoning.
2011.po: LitBench enables researchers to develop and evaluate domain-specific LLMs across any field: materials science, climate, neuroscience. An LLM fine-tuned on physics papers with LitBench tasks becomes a physics research assistant, accurately citing sources and explaining connections. The tool democratizes domain-LLM development.

2012.bp: Last-mile delivery relies on tracking what delivery drivers do: walking, standing still, climbing stairs, picking up packages. Sensor data (accelerometer, gyroscope from phones/watches) captures these. If the system recognizes activities accurately, logistics can optimize routes, detect unsafe behavior, and improve efficiency. But sensors vary: phone brand, placement (pocket vs. hand), carrier type.
2012.wh: Activity patterns shift across sensor types, placements, and people. An accelerometer on a wrist captures different signals than one in a pocket—same activity, different data. Standard models trained on data from wrist sensors fail on pocket sensors (domain shift). Retraining for each sensor type is infeasible for a logistics company operating in dozens of cities.
2012.ap: GenHAR tokenizes the raw sensor stream (frames of 3D acceleration and rotation) into tokens, each representing a time window. A transformer learns relationships between tokens, discovering which patterns matter (e.g., high-frequency vibration suggests running; smooth curves suggest walking). Selective masking masks out 50-90% of tokens during training, forcing the model to infer missing sensor data—a self-supervised trick that generalizes to new sensor types. Efficient attention (linear or quadratic, not cubic) reduces compute.
2012.ww: Tokenization abstracts away sensor minutiae: a token represents "strong vibration in Z-axis for 100ms", generalizing across sensor types and placements. Masking forces the model to learn robust features that survive missing data—if it can predict a masked token from neighbors, it understands the pattern. The transformer learns these patterns in a domain-agnostic way.
2012.po: Empirical: 9.97% accuracy gain vs. state-of-the-art, 6.4x fewer FLOPs (critical for edge devices on delivery worker phones). Deployed in 4 cities, recognized 2.15 billion activities reliably. Logistics company can now use sensor data to optimize delivery routes and driver safety without retraining per city.

2013.bp: Live streaming platforms host millions of rooms with minimal human moderation. Coordinated bad actors (scam groups, harassment mobs) hide inside normal-looking chats but cause real harms. The goal is catching these campaigns before they escalate, without manually reviewing millions of hours of footage.
2013.wh: The core tension: you see only room-level signals ("this room is risky") but the bad actors disperse their actions across users and time windows, camouflaging themselves within normal chatter. You can't label individual user actions cheaply, only say whether a whole room was problematic, making this a weak-supervision nightmare.
2013.ap: The paper treats each live room as a bag of instances, where instances are time-windowed behavioral capsules (what one user did in minutes 5-10, etc.). Instead of assuming bad actions all come from one spot, they build a neural encoder that watches both individual user arcs and cross-user coordination patterns. Multi-scale temporal and graph signals feed into a single room-risk score.
2013.ww: Multiple Instance Learning sidesteps the labeling bottleneck by learning from room labels alone. Capsule sequences let the model discover that *sequences* of actions matter more than isolated events. Modeling both serial (one user over time) and parallel (many users at once) paths lets it spot when disparate actions synchronize—the hallmark of coordination.
2013.po: On Douyin's industrial data, AC-MIL catches malicious rooms with less false alarms than prior MIL/sequential methods. It also points to *why* a room is risky (which user-timeslot sequences triggered the flag), giving moderation teams actionable leads rather than opaque predictions.

2014.bp: Digital tutoring is exploding, and LLMs can draft unlimited problem sets on-demand. But most generated questions just ask "which formula applies?" when deep learning means figuring out *why* that formula works in a new context. Schools need a way to push LLMs to ask the hard questions automatically.
2014.wh: LLMs trained on massive text default to pattern-matching, which tends toward fact retrieval. The prompting strategy must actively steer toward synthesis, evaluation, and creation (top levels of Bloom's). Without explicit guidance, the model prints easier, repetitive questions—they're statistically likelier and require less reasoning.
2014.ap: They analyze 20,700 questions from six LLMs (Qwen, InternLM, Claude, etc.) across CS, K-12 math, social science using Bloom's six levels. A human-AI protocol tags each question's cognitive level. Then they test new prompts that explicitly request multi-level questions and measure *cognitive shift intensity*—how much the model jumps from recall to analysis to creation.
2014.ww: Targeted prompts work because they make the cognitive demand *explicit* in the input, removing the model's freedom to default to easier reasoning. By measuring shift intensity (how much the model moves *between* cognitive levels), they capture whether it's genuinely stretching or just adding complexity. Chain-of-Thought refinement lets the model self-correct during generation.
2014.po: InternLM3-8B's higher-order output jumps from ~60% to 71%, and questions repeat 24% less on Qwen. The paper gives educators/LLM teams reproducible prompts and metrics to audit their generation systems, enabling personalized learning at scale without a tutor.

2015.bp: Four-cycles (two-hop friendships that return) are a motif of trust, collaboration, or fraud in networks—they signal tight communities. Platforms process graph edges in one shot (stream), can't store the full graph, yet need fast cycle counts for clustering coefficients, anomaly signals, or recommendation scoring.
2015.wh: Counting cycles exactly is Γ(m^{3/2}) or worse; you can't afford that at streaming scale. Existing approximations treat all edges equally, ignoring that real networks are sparse (bounded degeneracy). Also, cycles can cluster on a few nodes (unfair distribution) or spread evenly—a one-size-fits-all algorithm fails both cases.
2015.ap: Algorithm 1 (two-pass): sample induced subgraphs proportional to degeneracy κ and triangle-wedge abundance. Store enough samples to estimate the full count with error bounds ε. Algorithm 2 (one-pass): same idea but keep only one stream buffer; works when cycles don't concentrate on single nodes/edges. Both use classic reservoir sampling to stay in O(κm/√T) space.
2015.ww: Degeneracy κ (max min-degree in any subgraph) is usually much smaller than m for real networks, cutting space by orders of magnitude. Sampling induced subgraphs preserves local structure; counting cycles within them recovers global counts. Cycle distribution awareness lets Algorithm 2 handle the common case (social networks) with one pass, not two.
2015.po: On real social and collaboration graphs, both algorithms beat prior streaming methods on space/accuracy tradeoff. Algorithm 1 matches the known lower bound Ω(m/√T) up to log factors for constant-degeneracy graphs, proving optimality. Practitioners get practical code that works on billion-node networks.

2016.bp: Users interact with platforms in many ways: clicking, sharing, liking, purchasing. Each signal means something different. A click says "I noticed this," a purchase says "I committed money." Mixing them naively loses the nuance. The real win is predicting *which item to recommend next* by synthesizing all signals into a unified preference profile.
2016.wh: Prior models treat behaviors as rigid channels or map them all to the target (purchase) deterministically. But user preferences are latent and fuzzy—the same user preference could lead to a click (low-barrier) or a purchase (commitment). Deterministic scoring can't capture this ambiguity; sparse, skewed behaviors (many clicks, few purchases) make dense discrimination impossible.
2016.ap: They train a Multi-Behavior AutoEncoder (MBAE) that compresses all behaviors into a joint latent preference space. Then a diffusion model generates new preferences in that space, starting from noisy random vectors and refining toward target-behavior specific outputs. Behavior-aware RoPE (rotary positional embeddings) fuses information across behavior channels during this generation process.
2016.ww: Diffusion models excel at capturing uncertainty and diversity because they learn *distributions*, not point estimates. Starting from noise and iteratively refining is gentler than direct scoring, especially on low-entropy behaviors. The MBAE bottleneck forces the model to find a true shared representation, and RoPE fusion ensures behavior-specific signals (e.g., purchase bias) guide the final refinement.
2016.po: FatsMB generates diverse candidate recommendations with proper uncertainty estimates, outperforming prior behavior-fixed and behavior-specific methods. Users get fresh, accurate suggestions tailored to their latent preferences across all interaction types, not just the dominant behavior.

2017.bp: Vector search powers search engines, recommendation feeds, LLM retrieval, and ranking. The bottleneck: millions of simultaneous queries (users asking "find similar documents") against billion-sized vector databases. GPUs can parallelize, but current designs waste their potential, leaving queries waiting or forcing expensive data moves.
2017.wh: Query-centric kernels process each query independently, loading data into GPU shared memory just for that query, then discarding it. The next query reloads the same data. Batch reordering optimizes throughput but breaks query-arrival order, so slow queries stall fast ones—killing user-facing latency guarantees.
2017.ap: Hitcher reverses the thinking: group queries by *cluster* (which database vectors they search). One GPU block handles many queries against the same data chunk, reusing that chunk in shared memory. Within a batch, hitch-ride ordering runs queries in arrival order but *batches computation* on shared data. CPU and multi-GPU paths offload cold data, reducing PCIe traffic.
2017.ww: Cluster-centric kernels maximize data locality and shared-memory reuse—GPUs excel here. Hitch-ride ordering is the key insight: you don't need queries to *wait* for batch formation if you batch only the *compute* on already-loaded data. Arrival order is preserved for the user; efficiency is preserved for the hardware.
2017.po: Real-world benchmarks show P99 latency drops from 500ms to 20ms (22×) and throughput grows 9×, crucial for LLM systems serving human chat and interactive search. Hitcher is a drop-in optimization for existing vector-search systems.

2018.bp: Knowledge graphs, document networks, and paper citation graphs naturally embody hierarchies: broad topics branch into subtopics, then specific techniques. A flat node embedding loses this structure, treating "deep learning" and "backpropagation" as unrelated nodes. Preserving hierarchy lets systems discover coarse clusters (research areas) and fine-grain distinctions (methods) together.
2018.wh: Hierarchical structure isn't usually explicit in graph data; it's latent in node text and edge semantics. Existing TRN models either ignore text (pure GNNs) or treat it as a flat feature (no hierarchy). Building a hierarchy automatically is hard: you need to cluster docs at multiple levels without ground truth, then enforce that hierarchy doesn't contradict the learned embeddings.
2018.ap: TIER first runs contrastive learning on node texts to create a clustering-friendly embedding space. Then hierarchical K-Means discovers level-by-level clusters, and an LLM refines those clusters (checking coherence, merging/splitting as needed). Finally, cophenetic correlation (a measure of hierarchy-embedding alignment) is added as a regularization loss during embedding training, pulling similar vectors to appropriate hierarchy levels.
2018.ww: Contrastive learning surfaces natural clusters in text because the model learns to push semantically similar nodes together. Hierarchical K-Means respects that structure while discovering levels. LLM refinement catches mistakes that geometric clustering alone would miss. Cophenetic loss is elegant: it penalizes embeddings that contradict the hierarchy, guiding the model to learn representations faithful to both semantics and structure.
2018.po: Learned embeddings now encode hierarchical information, enabling coarse topic grouping and fine-grain distinctions. Downstream tasks (link prediction, node classification) improve, and interpretability jumps because you can ask "why are these nodes related?" at multiple levels.

2019.bp: Traffic departments manage thousands of sensors across city grids, predicting flows 15 minutes ahead to route traffic, signal timing, and ramp metering. Historical patterns work until an accident shuts lanes or a thunderstorm hits—then predictions fail catastrophically because incidents are rare and hard to predict in advance.
2019.wh: Most forecasting models (GNNs, RNNs, Transformers) learn patterns from historical sequences. Incidents are outliers that break patterns. Including them as inputs is tempting but naive: incidents are rare (you can't learn to predict them), and their impact varies wildly (small fender-bender vs. multi-car pileup on a highway vs. minor fender-bender on a surface street).
2019.ap: IGSTGNN splits incident handling into two modules. Incident-Context Spatial Fusion (ICSF) captures *where* an incident hits and its heterogeneous ripple (a highway accident affects distant intersections more than a side-street fender-bender). Temporal Incident Impact Decay (TIID) models *when* the incident fades—congestion doesn't disappear instantly but dissipates over minutes as vehicles clear.
2019.ww: By separating spatial (where) and temporal (when) components, IGSTGNN avoids treating all incidents alike. ICSF learns context-aware diffusion; a major highway accident spreads impact further than a minor surface-street one. TIID learns decay curves; rush hour takes longer to recover than mid-day. The paper also releases a curated incident-timestamped dataset, enabling the model to learn these patterns.
2019.po: On the new benchmark, IGSTGNN predicts flow during incidents far better than prior methods (including ones fed incident labels). Cities get actionable 15-minute predictions even during crises, improving response times and detour routing.

2020.bp: Recommendation systems thrive when they know *why* users care about items. A user interested in machine learning papers, data visualization tools, and research conferences has a coherent profile. Knowledge graphs encode *structural* links ("this paper cites that") but not *semantic* richness ("this paper's core insight is regularization"). LLMs can extract that richness.
2020.wh: Prior KG-based recommenders treat entities as isolated nodes, missing semantic nuance. Profile-based recommenders assume hand-crafted profiles (expensive). LLMs can generate text-based profiles, but profiles alone don't propagate influence through the graph. A single rich profile on one entity stays local; you need the graph to amplify.
2020.ap: SPiKE has three stages. First, LLMs generate semantic profiles for all KG entities ("who is this person, what are they known for"). Second, these profiles are embedded and integrated into the KG, enriching the graph structure. Third, during training, user-item preference matching aligns LLM-based semantic representations with learned KG-based embeddings via contrastive loss.
2020.ww: LLMs excel at reasoning over diverse knowledge sources and compressing into rationale-like profiles. KGs propagate those profiles to neighbors via graph walks, letting entity richness inform far-away users. Contrastive learning during training ensures both modalities (semantic + structural) pull toward the same preference signal, avoiding conflicts.
2020.po: SPiKE beats KG-only and LLM-only recommenders on real datasets. Users get recommendations grounded in both structural similarity ("others like you liked this") and semantic coherence ("this aligns with your inferred interests"). Profiles are also interpretable—you can read why an item was suggested.

2021.bp: Hospitals, banks, and research labs hold sensitive graph data they can't share. Federated learning trains a shared model by keeping data local and sending only parameter updates. But GNNs need the full neighborhood structure to compute gradients; sharing parameters across dozens of rounds with dozens of clients drains bandwidth and battery on edge devices.
2021.wh: Naive federated GNNs send model parameters every round (linear in clients). Non-IID data (one hospital's patient graph differs from another's) causes model drift—each client trains on biased local data. Traditional averaging doesn't account for local graph structure variance.
2021.ap: CeFGC inverts the flow: clients *generate* not *transmit*. Each client trains a local generative diffusion model that captures its graph distribution. This generative model (smaller than the GNN) goes to the server, which redistributes it to all clients. Clients use it to generate synthetic graphs matching the server's aggregate distribution, mix with their local graphs, train local GNNs, and send only the trained weights back—three total rounds.
2021.ww: Generative diffusion models are compact (fewer parameters than a GNN) and statistical (capture distribution, not data). Synthetic-graph augmentation addresses non-IID by giving each client exposure to the aggregate distribution. A single diffusion model round is cheaper than many parameter-exchange rounds. Theoretically, three rounds is provably optimal for this setup.
2021.po: On graph datasets (molecular, citation), CeFGC matches centralized GNN performance with 3-10× communication reduction. Edge devices and privacy-sensitive organizations can train better GNNs without leaking data, enabling federated knowledge discovery.

2022.bp: Online tutoring platforms know student responses (right/wrong) on knowledge concepts and infer what they've mastered. Accurate diagnosis enables adaptive learning—give harder problems to fast learners, review basics with strugglers. But real student data is noisy (guessing, off-day performance) and tutoring systems need models that ignore noise and generalize to new students.
2022.wh: Standard cognitive diagnosis models (CDMs) assume clean labels. Real tutoring data is corrupted: students guess, misclick, or rush. Also, CDM architectures are hand-designed by researchers (rules like "use RNN for temporal, graph for prerequisite structure"), missing better designs that aren't obvious. Manual design limits generalization.
2022.ap: OSCD applies evolutionary NAS to cognitive diagnosis. It constructs a search space of architectural options (temporal modules, graph modules, fusion strategies, attention blocks) and trains a weight-sharing supernet via a complete binary tree topology—each node is a choice point. Then an evolutionary multi-objective optimizer searches for architectures that balance accuracy *and* noise robustness.
2022.ww: Weight-sharing supernets (one model representing many architectures) are efficient; each architectural path reuses weights. Multi-objective search ensures you don't just optimize accuracy (which can overfit to noise) but also robustness (which reduces sensitivity to label errors). Tree topology is elegant for binary branching decisions.
2022.po: OSCD finds architectures that diagnose student mastery accurately even with noisy response labels. On real ITS data, discovered models outperform hand-tuned baselines, and robustness metrics confirm reduced noise sensitivity. Tutoring platforms get adaptive systems that work with messy real data.

2023.bp: A patient with a tumor gets MRI, CT, and SPECT scans—each modality reveals different tissue properties. Fusing them improves diagnosis (tumor boundary, type, staging) beyond any single modality. Clinics need fast, reliable systems that work across disease types and imaging hardware, not bespoke models per modality or disease.
2023.wh: Naive fusion (concatenate features) misses modality-specific structure and wastes computation. Modality-specific models don't share complementary signals—one modality might excel at boundary detection while another excels at tissue density. Existing methods are compute-heavy, locking out resource-limited clinics. Adversarial noise (imperceptible perturbations) can flip diagnosis, a reliability nightmare in medicine.
2023.ap: MAIL combines two components. Efficient residual attention blocks capture modality-specific multi-scale patterns without heavy computation. A cross-attention module learns complementary shared representations (the fusion) by attending across modality channels. Robust-MAIL adds random projection filters and modulated attention noise during training, teaching the model to ignore subtle adversarial perturbations.
2023.ww: Attention mechanisms let the model learn *where* to focus within each modality (boundary vs. density) and *which* modalities to trust for each task. Residual learning keeps computation lean. Random projections + noise augmentation simulate adversarial attacks during training, forcing robustness without expensive adversarial optimization.
2023.po: MAIL matches or beats heavy models on 20 public datasets while using 42× fewer parameters—clinics can deploy on GPUs or even CPUs. Robust-MAIL additionally resists adversarial attacks, critical for safety-critical medical AI. Generalization improves: same model works across multiple diseases and imaging protocols.

2024.bp: Different databases describe the same real-world entities (people, companies, locations) using different schemas and modalities (text, images, structured fields). Aligning equivalent entities across sources enables merged knowledge bases, better NLP pipelines, and LLM-grounded retrieval. Seed pairs (known alignments) normally enable alignment, but collecting them is expensive.
2024.wh: Unsupervised alignment uses pseudo-seeds (guessed equivalences) from multimodal similarity. But modalities have different coverage: text may be rich for products, images for people. Pseudo-seeds accumulate in high-density regions (popular entities), leaving sparse-graph regions (niche entities) underrepresented. Contrastive learning then overfits to dense regions, ignoring sparse ones.
2024.ap: PSQE starts with coarse pseudo-seeds from multimodal similarity matching. Clustering groups entities by similarity, revealing sparse vs. dense regions. Resampling upweights pseudo-seeds in sparse regions, balancing coverage. The module sits as a preprocessing layer before any contrastive MMEA model.
2024.ww: Theoretical analysis shows pseudo-seeds affect both attraction (pulling matched pairs closer) and repulsion (pushing non-matches apart) terms in contrastive loss. Imbalanced coverage causes models to optimize only for dense-region repulsion (cheap, high gradient), neglecting sparse-region attraction. Resampling fixes gradient flow, letting the model learn uniformly.
2024.po: PSQE is a drop-in module for existing contrastive MMEA methods, improving baseline precision and enabling models to align sparse entities that were previously invisible. Knowledge-base merges become more complete, benefiting downstream NLP, retrieval-augmented generation, and LLM applications.

2025.bp: AI-generated and manipulated videos are proliferating—deepfakes of politicians, revenge deepfakes, synthetic media. Detection is a cat-and-mouse game: the generator improves, detection must follow. Systems need fast, lightweight models deployable on phones and edges, and must generalize to new manipulation types unseen during training.
2025.wh: Separate spatial (inconsistent face geometry), temporal (unnatural eye blinks), and spectral (compression artifacts) detectors miss *interactions*. A video might pass all three individually but combine artifacts that only surface when analyzed jointly. Heavy CNNs work on known manipulations but fail on new ones. Edge deployment needs tiny models.
2025.ap: SSTGNN represents each video as a graph: nodes are spatial regions or frames, edges encode consistency (spatial adjacency, temporal continuity, or spectral correlation). A GNN with learnable spectral filters reasons over this graph, jointly weighing spatial inconsistencies, temporal artifacts, and spectral distortions. The graph structure forces joint reasoning.
2025.ww: Graph representations are sparse and lightweight compared to dense CNN feature maps. Spectral filters (learned Fourier bases) capture subtle frequency-domain manipulations (compression, generation artifacts). Spatial-temporal differential modeling (edge weights reflecting frame-to-frame changes) highlights unnatural transitions. Joint reasoning via message-passing catches correlations invisible to separate detectors.
2025.po: SSTGNN detects deepfakes with superior in-domain and cross-domain accuracy, using 42× fewer parameters than prior methods—deployable on mobile devices. Generalization improves: models trained on one manipulation type detect others better, addressing the cat-and-mouse arms race.

2026.bp: Real users like and dislike items—recommendations ignore dislikes at their peril. Today most systems only learn from positive signals, missing half the story. SPGNN realizes that dislikes are data too.
2026.wh: Standard GNNs aggregate all neighbor signals equally, treating dislikes as noise. Transformer approaches see the full graph but waste computation and struggle with sign patterns. Neither path captures the local geometry of positive and negative ties.
2026.ap: SPGNN brings two ideas: first, it measures proximity locally (among nearby nodes) and globally (through long paths) while respecting plus and minus signs. Second, it initializes node features thoughtfully, grounded in balance theory—a principle saying users avoid contradiction (liking A who dislikes B).
2026.ww: Proximity that respects sign structure naturally reflects how real preferences propagate. A user who dislikes a category will skew away from items that category approves of. By encoding this locally and globally, the model learns richer representations faster.
2026.po: Experiments show SPGNN beats prior signed-graph work on recommendation tasks. It lifts top-K accuracy by modeling the structural role of negative feedback—what dislikes really mean in the context of a user's web of preferences.

2027.bp: Understanding one person's decision-making—not average behavior, but *this person's* next move—opens doors to better social science and customer insights. LLMs are trained on the aggregate; what if we taught them to think like individuals?
2027.wh: Standard LLMs see billions of words but no continuity of a single life. They learn statistical patterns across humanity but lose the narrative arc—yesterday's decision shapes today's mood shapes tomorrow's choice. That continuity is invisible in web text.
2027.ap: HumanLLM curates real user timelines from platforms: Reddit posts, tweets, reviews, comments over weeks or months. It cleans and synthesizes these into profiles of beliefs, preferences, and reasoning patterns. Then it fine-tunes a base LLM on tasks like 'given this person's history, what will they do next?'
2027.ww: A person's past is the best predictor of their future. By seeing coherent trajectories (not just snapshots), the model learns that context matters. When you know someone thinks X about politics, Y about food, and has a pattern of Z reasoning, you can extrapolate accurately.
2027.po: Benchmarks show HumanLLM predicts individual behaviors far better than baseline LLMs. The payoff: social researchers can simulate synthetic populations; companies can tailor experiences to *you*, not to the median user.

2028.bp: E-commerce lives on ad auctions: every millisecond, a bid decision. Bidding too high wastes money; too low loses sales. Advertisers want automation that learns from their past bids yet finds better strategies than what history shows.
2028.wh: Past bids reflect budget limits, mistakes, and outdated beliefs—not wisdom. An RL agent trained purely to mimic history gets stuck in local optima. But ignoring history entirely risks catastrophe (overspending). The tension: trust but transcend.
2028.ap: QGA learns a Q-value function (how good each bid is) alongside a Decision Transformer (how likely each bid was historically). It trains both jointly: the Q-value pulls toward better actions; the transformer ensures those actions stay plausible. To explore safely, it conditions on different 'return targets' and perturbations, always checking each candidate against Q-values before trying it.
2028.ww: Q-values ground speculation. An unexplored bid might help, but only if the model thinks it could pay off. By fusing imitation (we tried this before) with valuation (here's why it's good), the agent escapes local optima without wild swings.
2028.po: On both public benchmarks and real auction simulations, QGA bids more efficiently than imitation-only or vanilla RL. The result: better ROI for advertisers, fewer wasted impressions.

2029.bp: Fraud and cyberattacks hide in network patterns: unusual connections, atypical timing. Real networks evolve—new users, new links—but trained fraud detectors often fail on tomorrow's data. And anomalies are *rare*, so a model trained naively learns to say 'normal' always.
2029.wh: Transductive models assume a static graph; real networks shift daily. Imbalanced training (99.9% normal, 0.1% fraud) teaches models to ignore the rare class. Augmenting the rare class artificially is tempting but risky: fake anomalies might not match real structure.
2029.ap: The framework uses diffusion (the same process that generates images from noise) to learn the local topology of real anomalies. Given a real anomaly, it generates synthetic ego-graphs—neighborhoods around nodes—that preserve structural patterns. During training, it uses a curriculum: early on, focus on abundant anomaly types; later, shift weight toward rare, hard-to-spot variants.
2029.ww: Diffusion captures distributional structure, not just a few examples. A curriculum teaches the model progressively harder cases, like practicing scales before concertos. Together, they produce balanced training data that generalizes to unseen network shifts.
2029.po: On five datasets, the framework detects anomalies better than prior work, especially on new graph structures and rare anomaly patterns. The payoff: fraud systems that adapt as networks evolve.

2030.bp: A product has a photo (visual), description (text), video (temporal). Blending all three should give richer recommendations. But images carry camera noise, text has language quirks, video has frame artifacts. Today's fusion systems treat all signals equally, amplifying trash.
2030.wh: Each modality lives in its own statistical space. Text embeddings might cluster at scale 0.9, images at 1.2. When you average them, noise from the lower-variance modality screams louder. Also, phases (orientations) can mismatch—two embeddings pointing in opposite directions still average, canceling each other.
2030.ap: DAMPS applies Fourier analysis: decompose each modality's embeddings into amplitude (strength) and phase (direction). For phase, compute the optimal offset between modalities and rotate them into alignment. For amplitude, apply a filter that suppresses low-signal modalities and preserves strong, modality-specific components.
2030.ww: Fourier decomposition separates 'how much' (amplitude) from 'which direction' (phase). Misaligned phases cause destructive interference; fixing them ensures signals add constructively. Amplitude filtering is like tuning a radio: boost clear stations, quiet noisy ones.
2030.po: Benchmarks show DAMPS recommendations improve accuracy over naive fusion. The payoff: recommendation systems that extract signal from multimodal clutter without manual tuning per modality.

2031.bp: A network's robustness is how well it stays connected if parts fail. Biharmonic distance measures this: sum all pairwise distances and you get a global connectivity score. Improving it by adding k edges matters for infrastructure, supply chains, and resilience.
2031.wh: Computing which k edges help most requires evaluating every subset. That's exponential. Greedy approximation is tractable but still O(n³)—infeasible for networks with millions of nodes. Theoretical results don't guarantee a good solution, just a bounded error.
2031.ap: The paper proposes greedy algorithms with three acceleration techniques. First, projection: prune edge candidates early. Second, Laplacian solver: use matrix algebra tricks to compute distance changes faster. Third, convex hull: find which edges matter most geometrically, not exhaustively.
2031.ww: Projection eliminates obviously bad candidates early. Laplacian solvers exploit the structure of the distance metric—it's tied to the graph's Laplacian matrix, which has fast algorithms. Convex hulls restrict the search space to candidates on the boundary of feasibility.
2031.po: Scaling from cubic to nearly linear enables biharmonic optimization on real graphs: thousands of nodes, millions of edges. Infrastructure planners can now compute which connections to add for maximum resilience.

2032.bp: Training across hospitals, phones, or edge devices keeps data private. But each site's data differs—patient demographics vary, user behavior differs. A model trained on everyone's data should work everywhere, but heterogeneity breaks optimization.
2032.wh: Knowledge distillation (forcing all local models to match a global teacher) ensures consistency but bakes in the teacher's biases. Local models can't explore far from it, even if better solutions exist. Without distillation, models diverge and forget shared knowledge.
2032.ap: FedKDMR uses dynamic KD: the global model teaches local models, but the strength of that teaching varies. Alongside distillation, it encourages model recombination—systematically perturbing merged parameters to explore the solution space. Local models stay somewhat aligned yet probe new regions.
2032.ww: Perturbation forces exploration; KD prevents divergence. Together, they escape sharp minima. Strong convexity ensures convergence despite perturbations; the averaged updates still march toward a good solution, just more robustly.
2032.po: Benchmarks on federated datasets show FedKDMR beats baseline KD and model averaging. Models converge faster and perform better on held-out heterogeneous data, crucial for privacy-critical deployments.

2033.bp: A model trained on cats and dogs should reject a photo of a giraffe. Vision-language models (which understand both images and text) can compare a photo to words like 'cat' and 'dog'. If neither match well, it's OOD. But picking good 'negative' labels (things the giraffe isn't) is surprisingly hard.
2033.wh: You can't label all OOD examples—there are infinitely many. So you pick heuristic negatives: random words, semantic opposites. But heuristics bias toward easy negatives, missing harder ones. A 'horse' is closer to 'dog' than 'cloud' is. The sampling of negatives is skewed, making OOD detection unreliable.
2033.ap: The paper develops a theory: assume negatives follow an unknown distribution. Correct for sampling bias indirectly by relating the biased sample to the true distribution. Then, convert this into Monte Carlo sampling—simple, efficient. Use labeled in-distribution data and unlabeled wild data to estimate which words are true negatives.
2033.ww: Correcting bias algebraically ensures the negative set reflects the true OOD space, not just the heuristic's blind spots. Monte Carlo provides a practical algorithm: resample from a corrected distribution, not a heuristic list.
2033.po: Experiments across OOD benchmarks show the debiased approach catches more true out-of-distribution cases, raising detection rates while lowering false alarms. The payoff: VLM-based OOD detection suitable for production deployments.

2034.bp: Agentic AI talks to tools: 'call function X with params Y.' Today's pipeline loads a huge LLM, feeds it a fat prompt listing all functions, and waits for it to generate tokens one by one. For real-time apps, this stalls.
2034.wh: The large model processes the entire function library for every query, even though only a few functions are relevant. It generates full token sequences, much of which is repetitive boilerplate (brackets, commas, colons). All three costs are incurred per call.
2034.ap: HyFunc distills a large model into a small 'soft token' (a learned embedding) representing the user's intent. This token goes to a retriever (picking relevant functions) and a smaller prefix-tuned model (generating the final call). Separately, dynamic templating fills in syntactic boilerplate within the vLLM engine, not via token generation.
2034.ww: A soft token captures essence without token overhead. The retriever focuses the context window. A smaller model, given narrowed choices, generates only the semantic content; syntax is injected post-hoc. Each step cuts latency; combined, the speedup is dramatic.
2034.po: On the BFCL benchmark, HyFunc achieves 0.828 second latency with minimal accuracy loss. The payoff: agentic systems that respond instantly to user intents, enabling interactive experiences.

2035.bp: Warehouses pack boxes into trucks using robots. Today, boxes arrive in batches: morning's toys differ from afternoon's electronics. A neural network trained on mixed batches fails when batch characteristics change. Yet lookahead is available—warehouses know tomorrow's shipment types.
2035.wh: Pure DRL learns statistics of all goods but brittle to batch shifts. When morning goods are suddenly heavier or bulkier, the policy collapses. Using lookahead naively (generating fixed plans) ignores the present state. The tension: adapt to now while planning for what's coming.
2035.ap: MCTS, the same algorithm that powers game-playing AI, builds a search tree: 'if I place box A here, then B, then C...' Each node is scored by both the learned RL policy (what's likely good) and a random policy (robust baseline). An auxiliary reward penalizes spatial waste. Lookahead parcels tune the exploration balance—when batches are volatile, trust the random policy more.
2035.ww: MCTS combines foresight (lookahead) with learning (RL policy). The random policy prevents overfitting to training batch statistics. Penalizing waste explicitly prevents short-sighted placements. Adaptive exploration balance lets the algorithm respond to changing conditions.
2035.po: Real-world experiments show 10% gains under distribution shifts and sustained 4-8% improvement in online deployment. The payoff: logistics systems that handle variable conditions robustly, cutting labor and transportation costs.

2036.bp: Online shopping sessions are short: 'user viewed X, Y, Z; what's next?' Two users with similar interests might browse in different orders. Current systems retrieve similar sessions to improve context. But what if the best similar session was never observed?
2036.wh: Real session data is sparse—most session sequences are unique. Neighbors are rare. Retrieving only *observed* neighbors misses the interest space: two sessions might be kindred spirits yet look different superficially (one browsed via search, one via categories).
2036.ap: DiffSBR uses diffusion to imagine latent neighbor sessions. First, a retrieval-augmented module: take observed neighbors as guiding signals, then diffuse (add noise iteratively to a random session, then reverse it) to generate synthetic sessions aligned with real neighbors. Second, self-augmented module: directly diffuse using the current session's signals (text, images) as guidance via contrastive learning.
2036.ww: Diffusion models are known to generate images and text realistically by learning distributions. Here, they learn the distribution of sessions. Conditioning on retrieval guidance ensures variety; conditioning on the current session's multimodal signals ensures relevance. The result: plausible latent neighbors.
2036.po: Experiments show DiffSBR recommends better items than retrieval-only or simple augmentation. The payoff: session-based systems that infer from sparse, noisy histories by synthesizing rich contextual neighbors.

2037.bp: A user browses movies on Netflix, music on Spotify, books on Amazon. Each platform learns preferences separately. Ideally, movie taste informs music taste (sci-fi fans might like synth-pop), yet platforms can't share raw data for privacy.
2037.wh: Prior work assumes overlapping users or items, or needs to share data directly. But privacy regulations forbid sharing user histories. Domain-specific models are isolated; merging them naively loses signal because the models have learned incompatible representations.
2037.ap: MergeRec initializes a merged model using training-free merging (parameter averaging with domain-aware weights). Then, it synthesizes pseudo-user data: treat each item as a virtual user's sequence (if movie A led to movie B in data, a pseudo-user 'liked' A then B). This gives training signal without real users. Finally, optimize merging weights jointly via recommendation loss (merged model ranks correct items) and distillation loss (preserved knowledge from source models).
2037.ww: Pseudo-user data circumvents privacy: you're not synthesizing user identities, just plausible sequences. Training-free initialization starts intelligently. Collaborative weight optimization respects both domains' learned signals while blending them.
2037.po: Experiments show MergeRec transfers knowledge across domains better than baselines, especially in sparse scenarios. The payoff: platforms can improve recommendations via model sharing, not data sharing.

2038.bp: Cities need to forecast traffic or power demand a week ahead across thousands of locations. Spatial-temporal models capture how patterns spread (traffic on Main Street affects Side Street tomorrow). But long horizons multiply computation: each step processes the whole graph.
2038.wh: Standard graph convolution and self-attention scale quadratically or worse with graph size. A week ahead is 672 steps at 15-minute intervals; multiplying by thousands of nodes yields infeasible memory and compute. Models designed for short-term (24-hour) forecasts collapse under this load.
2038.ap: FaST introduces two ideas. First, adaptive graph agent attention: instead of processing all nodes, assign each node an 'agent' that selectively attends to relevant neighbors. This reduces attention cost. Second, parallel Mixture-of-Experts: replace dense feed-forward layers with sparse expert routers and Gated Linear Units (GLUs). Each token routes to a few experts, not all, cutting memory.
2038.ww: Adaptive attention exploits locality: traffic patterns are regional, not global. Sparse routing via MoE works because forecasting doesn't need all parameters per step; different regions use different expertise. GLUs add nonlinearity efficiently.
2038.po: Benchmarks show FaST forecasts accurately week-ahead on real graphs with thousands of nodes, achieving 10× speedup over dense baselines. The payoff: infrastructure operators can forecast long horizons in practice, enabling proactive resource planning.

2039.bp: Social platforms need to catch deepfakes and manipulated news as they emerge, not just recognize patterns from yesterday. Speed matters because false narratives spread fast, and retraining every day is impractical.
2039.wh: The classic approach trains once, then applies the model forever. But news topics shift (elections, pandemics, celebrity scandals). A model trained only on past topics watches new events slip through undetected. Retraining requires labeled data you don't have yet.
2039.ap: RADAR flips the script: at test time, when a new video arrives, it searches for similar videos already labeled in the source domain. Videos that are 'stable' (high-confidence, low-entropy) become anchors. Unstable new videos align their learned features to these anchors, essentially saying 'you're like this other video, so you should behave similarly.' Pseudo-labels are then refined using the stable neighbors' information.
2039.ww: Stable references act as landmarks. An unstable video drifting toward a fake reference will be pulled toward a real reference instead. The distribution-level matching grounds the adaptation in shared structure, not just surface similarity. Self-training then scales this to the full target batch.
2039.po: In live tests, RADAR catches fake videos on unseen topics with strong margins over baselines. The system adapts on the fly, generating reliable pseudo-labels even when label distribution shifts (imbalanced, rare classes).

2040.bp: Ride-hailing platforms live or die on prediction accuracy. Get ETAs wrong by 5 minutes and riders cancel; supply-demand balance collapses. But cities have millions of road segments and shifting traffic patterns hour to hour.
2040.wh: Route-level models see the big picture (A to B) but miss that a single clogged intersection cascades across a district. Link-level models capture local dynamics but explode in complexity on a million-road network. Inference must stay under 100ms. Existing methods also assume traffic is stationary; it's not—rush hour, weather, accidents rewire the graph constantly.
2040.ap: MixTTE runs two models in parallel. Link-level uses spatio-temporal external attention (a learnable mechanism that attends to relevant roads globally) to capture traffic wave propagation. Routes then combine these link predictions. A mixture-of-experts layer routes each traffic scenario to the expert best suited to it, avoiding one-size-fits-all bottlenecks. An asynchronous incremental learning thread silently retrains on fresh data without interrupting serving.
2040.ww: External attention scales linearly, not quadratically, so millions of roads stay tractable. Mixture-of-experts exploits the insight that rush-hour congestion needs different logic than late-night flow. Incremental learning keeps the model current as distribution shifts.
2040.po: DiDi's real platform reports substantial accuracy gains and stability. The system now reliably handles long-tail cases (rare intersections, unusual weather) and adapts to seasonal shifts without offline retraining cycles.

2041.bp: Manufacturing—stamping metal, forging, drawing—depends on predicting how material deforms under extreme stress. Simulations must be accurate to avoid costly trial-and-error, but high-fidelity simulations (fine meshes, plasticity) take hours per case.
2041.wh: You can generate cheap low-fidelity data (coarse mesh, linear assumptions) quickly but it misses reality. High-fidelity is accurate but you can only afford a few hundred cases. Standard deep learning wants thousands of high-quality examples. You're stuck between speed and accuracy.
2041.ap: FilDeep trains a neural network on a mix: thousands of fast, approximate simulations plus hundreds of slow, accurate ones. An attention module learns which low-fidelity patterns are trustworthy and which need correction using high-fidelity examples. The network learns to 'read between the lines' of cheap data and trust it where it's proven reliable.
2041.ww: Attention enables fine-grained weighting: 'this geometry pattern looks similar in low-fidelity data I've seen corrected, so I'll adjust.' The network discovers which features of deformation are robust across fidelities (e.g., final shape) vs. brittle (e.g., stress distribution).
2041.po: FilDeep achieves high-fidelity-level accuracy while training on a mixed dataset that's much cheaper to produce than pure high-fidelity. Manufacturers can now use learned models for quick-turn design iteration without per-case simulation.

2042.bp: Mental health is stigmatized and data-scarce. Social media posts revealing depression or anxiety are rare and sensitive. Yet early detection saves lives. Models trained on real data are brittle—they miss novel expressions because the training set was small and uniform.
2042.wh: Expert psychiatrists annotate posts with symptom labels (anhedonia, insomnia, suicidality). It's slow, expensive, and requires ethics clearance. You end up with hundreds of labeled examples, all in English, all from Reddit or Twitter. The model sees 'I can't sleep' as anhedonia but fails on 'everything feels grey' from a poet's account.
2042.ap: SynSym prompts an LLM (instructed with psychiatric knowledge) to expand each symptom into sub-concepts (e.g., 'depression' → 'low motivation', 'negative self-talk', 'sleep disruption'). For each sub-concept, the LLM generates expressions in diverse linguistic styles (formal, colloquial, poetic). It also composes multi-symptom posts respecting clinical co-occurrence (if depression co-occurs with insomnia in real data, synthetic posts mix them similarly).
2042.ww: LLMs implicitly encode linguistic diversity and clinical relationships from their pretraining. Sub-concepts anchor generation to real symptoms (not hallucination). Clinical co-occurrence constraints ground synthetic data in empirical patterns.
2042.po: Trained on pure synthetic data, models match real-data baselines. Real-data fine-tuning then pushes accuracy higher. SynSym democratizes mental-health NLP—research labs without large labeled datasets can now build generalizable detectors.

2043.bp: Training an LLM costs millions of dollars and months of compute. Every percentage improvement in data efficiency translates to huge savings. But mixing diverse sources (books, code, web, scientific papers) is an art—nobody knows the optimal recipe.
2043.wh: Static data mixing (always 50% books, 30% code, 20% web) ignores how the model changes. Early in training, raw diversity helps; mid-training, you need harder examples; late, polishing trumps breadth. A single reward objective (e.g., 'minimize loss') ignores that low-quality data can poison multi-lingual or code performance even if average loss looks good.
2043.ap: HDS models data scheduling as a reinforcement learning agent controlling source weights at each step. The Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) algorithm balances exploration (try weird mixtures) and exploitation (stick with what works). The reward function combines three signals: (1) a quality score from a data-classifier, (2) a loss-driven signal measuring inter-domain influence (does adding code help or hurt text performance?), and (3) a model-driven signal from weight norms (is the model becoming unbalanced?).
2043.ww: Multi-objective rewards prevent gaming—optimizing purely for loss might sacrifice generalization. SAC's entropy regularization ensures stable exploration without wild swings in mixing ratios. The continuous control space (any mixture is valid, not discrete buckets) lets fine-grained adaptation.
2043.po: On The Pile, HDS reaches the final perplexity of the next-best method using 44% fewer tokens—a dramatic efficiency gain. The agent discovers adaptive schedules (e.g., ramping code in middle training) that humans wouldn't intuit.

2044.bp: Smartphones and robots have inertial sensors. Understanding motion from IMU (is the phone being shaken? is the robot falling?) in natural language lets models reason about physical states without cameras. But IMU is abstract numbers; language is concrete.
2044.wh: You can label videos with text ('person walking upstairs'). You can record IMU during those videos. But the alignment is loose: a 'walking' label spans 3 seconds while IMU oscillates 100 times. It's unclear which frequencies or patterns in the IMU correspond to 'walking' vs. 'ascending.' Humans find this tedious and inconsistent.
2044.ap: Vistar treats vision as a bridge. Offline: encode video frames (with a pretrained vision model) and text ('person walking') jointly; separately, encode the paired IMU signal. A contrastive loss (e.g., SimCLR-style) pulls IMU encoders closer to matching video-text pairs. Hierarchical matching ensures both global events and fine-grained motions align. At test time, given a new IMU signal and a candidate text, Vistar retrieves similar (IMU, text) pairs from a database, re-ranking them structurally (do their IMU patterns match?) and using them to refine the generated description.
2044.ww: Vision models are pretrained on billions of images—they 'understand' motion semantics. By anchoring IMU to pretrained vision, the framework leverages that knowledge without manual labels. Retrieval-augmented generation handles residual misalignment by seeing analogous examples.
2044.po: Models fine-tuned on Vistar embeddings accurately retrieve text descriptions for unseen IMU sequences. The 57.45% improvement shows the framework closes the semantic gap, enabling LLMs to reason about sensor data from smartphones, wearables, and robots.

2045.bp: ISPs and CDNs monitor quality metrics for millions of user sessions. When something breaks, engineers ask 'what if we had applied algorithm X to the data from last week?' Replaying historical data through new anomaly detectors or alerting logic is common, but existing tools are slow or imprecise.
2045.wh: Traditional warehouses store raw sessions (10B+ rows, TB+ data). Replaying new logic means scanning all history, which is expensive. Sampling misses rare anomalies. Sketches (e.g., HyperLogLog) are fast but aren't designed for this use case. You can't efficiently answer 'what alerts would algorithm X have fired, grouped by user location?'
2045.ap: AHA redesigns the storage and aggregation layer around alternative-history workloads. Key insights: (1) aggregations decompose—e.g., 'sum(revenue by location)' can be broken into independent sub-sums, (2) only a few attribute-value combinations are active (e.g., most locations see few sessions), and (3) modern columnar DBs (like Clickhouse) are very efficient at filtering by attribute. AHA pre-computes and caches decomposed statistics, marks sparsity (which sub-populations matter), and routes queries to specialized fast-path logic when possible.
2045.ww: Decomposability eliminates redundant computation. Sparsity means you only reprocess sessions from the active sub-populations (e.g., 5 countries, not 200). Columnar storage makes filtering-heavy queries (where device='iPhone' AND location='NYC') very fast because it only reads relevant columns.
2045.po: AHA serves complex alternative-history queries in seconds with full fidelity, not approximations. Engineers can experiment with multiple alert-logic variants retroactively, reducing bugs and improving confidence in deployments.

2046.bp: Real-world QA (customer support, search, knowledge bases) demands sub-second latency and high accuracy. Not all questions are equal: 'what is 2+2' needs instant reply; 'how do I troubleshoot a rare printer error?' needs careful reasoning with multiple document checks.
2046.wh: Using a single approach fails: pure LLM (fast but hallucinates) and full retrieval+reasoning (accurate but slow). Retrieved documents are often noisy or contradictory. If a document says 'printer model X has 64MB RAM' in one place and '128MB' elsewhere, the model gets confused. Consistency degrades over time.
2046.ap: R2R deploys a Query Critic Agent (QCA) that rates query difficulty by analyzing it without full reasoning. Simple queries bypass retrieval; the LLM answers directly (fast). Complex queries trigger a Memory Augmented Agent (MAA) that iterates: (1) formulate a question based on long-term memory (stable facts) and short-term memory (current knowledge gaps), (2) retrieve documents, (3) a Supervised Retrospection module re-scores retrieved documents against the long-term facts, filtering contradictions, (4) update both memories and repeat until confident.
2046.ww: Long-term memory anchors reasoning in facts established early—if the printer has 64MB, trust that unless overwhelming evidence contradicts. Short-term memory tracks 'what do we still need to know' without noise. The critic agent's routing avoids unnecessary compute on simple queries. Document validation prevents contradictions from poisoning reasoning chains.
2046.po: R2R cuts latency for 70% of queries (simple cases) while maintaining 95%+ accuracy on complex queries via grounded iteration. Live chat systems report better user satisfaction due to faster simple answers and more confident complex answers.

2047.bp: Social networks, recommendation graphs, and knowledge bases have billions of nodes and edges. Fitting them in GPU memory is impossible; distributed training is complex. Storage-based training (loading subgraphs from NVMe SSD) is a practical middle ground, but many small I/O requests kill throughput.
